title: ANALYSIS-Brazil may be spending its way towards a downgrade
text:
SAO PAULO, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's finances are set to deteriorate substantially next year, leaving the government with few options to revive a sputtering economy and raising the threat of a credit downgrade.

The government is likely to miss its key 2014 budget target, the primary surplus, by as much as 50 billion reais ($22 billion), delivering only about half its goal, estimates by Reuters and private economists show.

Unlike most other countries, Brazil's most-watched budget goal strips out interest payments on its debt, meaning its overall deficit would widen if the primary surplus dwindles.

Such an event could deal a major setback to Latin America's biggest economy, which won its investment-grade credit rating in 2008 through a commitment to fiscal responsibility and strong economic growth.

Growth, however, has slowed sharply since 2011, and President Dilma Rousseff has unleashed costly tax breaks and credit subsidies in response.

The strategy has not only failed to support the economy, but also has exacerbated Brazil's fiscal woes. Meanwhile, with Rousseff expected to enter a hotly contested run for a second term next year, she is unlikely to make major spending cuts because they could anger her fragile political coalition.

A credit downgrade, already priced in by credit default swap markets for mid-next year, would put Brazil's rating just one notch above junk status, making government and corporate borrowing more expensive and further eroding economic growth.

A downgrade could also complicate efforts to curb inflation by triggering further weakness in Brazil's currency, which has lost 10 percent of its value against the dollar this year.

Reuters spoke to analysts at two ratings agencies who highlighted the risks imposed by Brazil's slow economic growth at a time when there is little room for additional stimulus.

"We recognize that even though there is some room for countercyclical fiscal policy in Brazil, that room is actually very limited," said Sebastian Briozzo, a director with Standard & Poor's, which placed a negative outlook on Brazil's BBB credit rating in June.

"Between this year and next, this is what we will be evaluating for the rating outlook to see how it is resolved," he said.

The government still says it will meet its target for a primary surplus of 2.1 percent of gross domestic product, but it is relying on projections that most economists think are wildly optimistic.

The primary surplus is the government's excess revenue before interest payments on its debt.

While most analysts expect Brazil's economy to grow about 2.3 percent in 2014, in what would be a fourth consecutive year of mediocre expansion, Rousseff's government projected growth of 4 percent when preparing next year's budget.

The government's growth forecast resulted in an overly optimistic estimate for tax collection, which in turn allowed authorities to justify a more than 10 percent expansion in public expenditures next year.

The picture looks different when the forecast economic growth rate is changed.

By projecting the increase in revenues for next year given the GDP growth rate expected by private economists, including provisions for inflation, Reuters found that the government's projected primary surplus would fall short of what authorities are expecting.

Private economists including Felipe Salto, professor at Fundacao Getulio Vargas, and Catarina Braga, analyst at MCM Consultores, had similar conclusions.

Asked about the gap between official and private forecasts, Brazil's Finance Ministry reiterated its estimates. Last month, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said that current government forecasts for the primary surplus would be revised early next year, which could lead to budget freezes.

UNREALISTIC GOAL

Rising public spending was part of Rousseff's big policy bet for 2013: that Brazil, which required a bailout by the International Monetary Fund bailout in 1998, had matured enough for investors to accept single-digit interest rates and less austerity.

Her government has changed tack since S&P issued its warning, but economists say none of the improvements so far - such as a 10 billion reais budget freeze announced in July - has been a game-changer.

Even if the economy does not slow as expected next year, the budget goal will likely remain unrealistic. Brazil's government has overestimated one-off revenues from toll road and airport concessions, economists said, while underestimating the spending likely to be made by states and cities in an election year.

The government already lowered its closely watched goal for the primary surplus, from 2.3 percent of GDP, to the current 2.1 percent projection, though some economists said it was mostly a half-hearted attempt by policymakers to be more transparent after years of relying on accounting tricks to meet the target.

Private forecasts suggest Brazil's government won't even come close to its goal next year, with Barclays projecting a primary surplus of only 1.1 percent of GDP.

Analysts are also monitoring Brazil's recent intervention in currency markets as it tries to support the real after it reached nearly five-year lows. Brazil's central bank has so far kept the door closed on its vault of $370 billion in foreign reserves, but may need to open it in the next few months if investors continue to lose faith in the country's slow-growing economy.

"A severe loss of international reserves and/or deterioration in government debt composition could also put pressure on the rating," Shelly Shetty, head of Latin America Sovereigns at Fitch Ratings, wrote in an email.

Moody's Brazil analyst Mauro Leos, who rates Brazil as Baa2 with a positive outlook, was not available to comment.

However, a potential change in outlook by Moody's in the second half of the year will be "a key event to focus on," David Beker, chief Brazil economist for Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch, wrote in a recent investor note.

In a July speech, Rousseff said her government remained committed to fiscal responsibility, telling ministers and business leaders: "The principle is that we can only spend what we have, so we don't compromise our fiscal balance."

But many analysts and investors may need more convincing.

"This government is never going to make a strong fiscal adjustment," said Waldemir Quadros, an economics professor at Pontificia Universidade Catolica in Sao Paulo who specializes in public finances. "Forget it."

title: POLL-Emerging nations to fight alone against further  FX  falls
text:
SAO PAULO/BANGALORE, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Emerging nations are unlikely to join forces to intervene in foreign exchange markets in the next few weeks to prop up their ailing currencies, even though there is more pain ahead, a Reuters poll predicted.

The U.S. Federal Reserve's move toward trimming its stimulus has triggered a sell-off in emerging market currencies and a flight to the dollar, resulting in a round of interventions and monetary policy moves from Istanbul to Mumbai to prop them up.

The survey of over 50 leading foreign exchange strategists showed deep skepticism about India's plans to seek support for coordinated offshore intervention, with analysts saying each developing country will fight their own battle against further falls.

Indeed, the probability of joint intervention by emerging-nation central banks within the next few weeks is just 15 percent, according to the poll consensus. Only three institutions said the likelihood is greater than 50 percent.

"I see India is suffering a lot, but this affects other nations in very different ways, and each one of them has different needs. I'm very skeptical about joint action," said Newton Rosa, chief economist at SulAmérica Investimentos, a Brazilian asset management firm owned by Dutch bank ING Group.

The Reuters poll results come as leaders and policymakers from the Group of 20 developed and emerging nations meet this week in St. Petersburg, Russia, with the effects on the global economy from the Fed's pull-back high on the agenda.

Reuters reported exclusively last month that India was seeking support from fellow emerging market countries for coordinated intervention but had received little public backing from other nations.

The Indian rupee has lost nearly 20 percent to the dollar this year, hitting record lows almost daily since end of May, when Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke hinted at a stimulus rollback.

However, the need for urgent action seems to be lower in Brazil than in India.

After a near 20-percent plunge in its currency from May to mid-August, Brazil has announced a huge intervention program with up to $60 billion in derivatives and repurchase agreements by year-end, and has been successful so far in stabilizing the real.

"Each country has it own currency intervention strategy. For example, India and Argentina adopted capital controls, while Brazil offered currency swaps," said Adriano Beuren, an economist with Banco Sicredi, in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

"The need for foreign money is different in each country. That creates difficulties for a deal."

Economists in Brazil were particularly skeptical of such a move following comments by Finance Minister Guido Mantega that the largest Latin American country, one of the most affected by the emerging currency rout, was not involved in any plans to intervene in offshore foreign exchange markets.

What has kept leading emerging countries busy, Mantega said, are plans to create a bank and a reserve fund by the BRICS group - including Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

China's deputy central bank governor, Yi Gang, also called on Wednesday for China and other Asian countries to broaden the use of regional currencies in bilateral trade and investment settlements and close more currency swap deals to facilitate capital flows.

The Fed is expected to start reducing its $85 billion per month bond-buying programme when it meets on September 17-18, according to all nine of the Reuters polls of economists conducted on the subject.

If the Fed goes ahead with its plan then emerging market currencies are expected to trade lower, according to 30 of 53 analysts polled. Another 13 said significantly lower, three said unchanged while the remaining seven said somewhat higher.

"There is probably still more downside for the emerging markets but they've been hit pretty hard already so there may not be that much more downside," said Benjamin Reitzes, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

The global Reuters foreign exchange poll this week found the U.S. dollar is the only currency that stands to benefit in the near-term from that. (Additional polling by Shaloo Shrivastava in Bangalore; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Brazil's Real Ends Stronger on Local Rate View
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real gained ground against the dollar to end stronger Thursday after the country's central bank reinforced hints that it would continue to raise local interest rates through the end of the year.

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.3202 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.3542 to the dollar Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders noted the currency reversed early weakening to make a sharp move stronger midway through the session. The real's move stronger came as the country's central bank pledged to hold firm against the inflationary effects of recent depreciation in the minutes of its August rate meeting.

"Following today's minutes, we revise our Selic forecasts and now expect interest rates to be adjusted by 50bps and 25bps in October and November, respectively," said Enestor dos Santos, analyst at BBVA. "This is broadly driven by the recent depreciation of the exchange rate."

In the minutes, the bank raised its reference rate for the local currency to BRL2.40 to the dollar from BRL2.25 previously, and acknowledged a negative impact for inflation.

Meanwhile, the influence of the minutes seemed to overshadow the effect of upbeat economic news in the U.S., where improvements in jobs data and service-sector activity reinforced the possibility of monetary-policy tightening there as well.

The prospect of rising rates in Brazil also dovetailed with the growing impact of exchange market intervention by the central bank.

Brazil's central bank sold $497.3 million in foreign exchange swaps early in the session Thursday as part of its ongoing effort to provide liquidity and foreign exchange hedge to the market.

The central bank has scheduled some $100 billion in swap and dollar repurchase auctions for the end of the year. The currency swaps allow investors to exchange bonds indexed to domestic interest rates for paper tied directly to the U.S. dollar and frequently lead to a strengthening of the Brazilian real.

Traders noted that with the interventions, investors were backing away from recent projections of a stronger long term weakening of the real.

"The sudden strengthening of the real was a clear sign that investors are unwinding some long dollar positions," said Reginaldo Galhardo, Forex Manager at the Treviso brokerage.

The trend was reinforced earlier in the week when the Central Bank over a two day period sold some $2.5 billion in swaps above the amount of its scheduled daily auctions.

text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Wednesday as strong Chinese service sector data supported investors' appetite for risk, although sentiment remained fragile with a possible strike in Syria and prospects for less U.S. stimulus. The Mexican peso gained 0.5 percent after data showed China's services sector hit a five-month high in August, the latest evidence that the largest consumer of Latin American commodities may have avoided a sharp slowdown. The swap sale was part of a $60 billion forex intervention program announced by Brazil's central bank last month. The plan is expected to stabilize the real at around 2.35 per dollar over the next few months, according to a Reuters survey of 33 banks and research firms.

 Risks to the performance of emerging-market currencies remained high, however, as President Barack Obama continued to push for congressional approval to launch a limited military strike on Syria. Fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve may this month announce a pullback in its bond-buying program also kept investors on edge. The Fed's program has provided a steady source of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets over the past few years. "The market remains more fearful than cheerful. Everybody is trying to limit losses," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a manager at the foreign exchange desk of Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo.

title: DJ  Emerging Markets Hope to Get Some Attention at G-20, Too
text:
Leaders from the Group of 20 economies have been preoccupied by Syria ahead of their summit this week, but some are still hoping to find a way to steady the suddenly shaky fortunes of emerging markets.

In recent years, most of the economic threats tackled by the G-20 have stemmed from large flows of capital from developed countries to developing ones in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. But now that flow has begun to reverse, posing new challenges to the global recovery.

The turnaround has accelerated in recent weeks as investors anticipate an end to the U.S. Federal Reserve's period of extraordinary monetary stimulus this year. The result has been sharp falls in developing-country currencies.

The central banks of three G-20 members-Brazil, Indonesia and Turkey-have raised interest rates, intervened in currency markets or both in recent weeks to try to stem the declines.

In India, where the rupee has suffered the most-precipitous decline among large Asian economies, the central bank has also taken the step of selling dollars to state-run oil refiners via a commercial bank to shift demand for dollars away from the open market.

The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development on Tuesday warned that an already subdued recovery in global economic growth could be weakened further if the outflow of capital from developing economies intensifies.

Some leaders are hoping that the issue can still be addressed, even if the meetings in St. Petersburg on Thursday and Friday are dominated by the crisis surrounding the alleged use of chemical weapons in Syria's civil war.

For instance, a person familiar with Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff's thinking said she hopes the summit will produce agreement on ways to ease the impact of the anticipated change in Fed policy.

"The tone of her speech [at the summit] will show how upset she may be with U.S. policies," said a Brazilian government official.

Brazilian officials say they have the backing of other developing countries in seeking moves to address recent currency volatility, although they are unclear about which among the G-20 members will be offering support. In particular, they want the Fed to improve the way it communicates its intentions to reduce market swings.

With the U.S. government focusing on efforts to boost support for its approach to Syria, those developing economies may be left frustrated. But even without Syria, the U.S. would have been unlikely to make major concessions, economists say.

"Other than a vague commitment to take into account the effects of its monetary policy on other countries, the Fed is in practice likely to make no concessions to developments elsewhere," said Capital Economics, a London-based research firm.

title: Leaders Seek Balm for Emerging Markets at G-20 Summit
text:
Leaders from the Group of 20 economies have been preoccupied by Syria ahead of their summit this week, but some are still hoping to find a way to steady the suddenly shaky fortunes of emerging markets.

In recent years, most of the economic threats tackled by the G-20 have stemmed from large flows of capital from developed countries to developing ones in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. But now that flow has begun to reverse, posing new challenges to the global recovery.

The turnaround has accelerated in recent weeks as investors anticipate an end to the U.S. Federal Reserve's period of extraordinary monetary stimulus this year. The result has been sharp falls in developing-country currencies.

The central banks of three G-20 members--Brazil, Indonesia and Turkey--have raised interest rates, intervened in currency markets or both in recent weeks to try to stem the declines.

In India, where the rupee has suffered the most-precipitous decline among large Asian economies, the central bank has also taken the step of selling dollars to state-run oil refiners via a commercial bank to shift demand for dollars away from the open market.

The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development on Tuesday warned that an already subdued recovery in global economic growth could be weakened further if the outflow of capital from developing economies intensifies.

Some leaders are hoping that the issue can still be addressed, even if the meetings in St. Petersburg on Thursday and Friday are dominated by the crisis surrounding the alleged use of chemical weapons in Syria's civil war.

For instance, a person familiar with Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff's thinking said she hopes the summit will produce agreement on ways to ease the impact of the anticipated change in Fed policy.

"The tone of her speech [at the summit] will show how upset she may be with U.S. policies," said a Brazilian government official.

Brazilian officials say they have the backing of other developing countries in seeking moves to address recent currency volatility, although they are unclear about which among the G-20 members will be offering support. In particular, they want the Fed to improve the way it communicates its intentions to reduce market swings.

With the U.S. government focusing on efforts to boost support for its approach to Syria, those developing economies may be left frustrated. But even without Syria, the U.S. would have been unlikely to make major concessions, economists say.

"Other than a vague commitment to take into account the effects of its monetary policy on other countries, the Fed is in practice likely to make no concessions to developments elsewhere," said Capital Economics, a London-based research firm.

In an effort to exercise more control over their currencies, the governments of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa have been working on a joint proposal to set up a $100 billion Contingency Reserve Arrangement by pooling central-bank reserves.

Leaders may make some progress in St. Petersburg, since that doesn't require input from the U.S. or other developed countries, although the new fund is unlikely to be launched until next year.

In March, finance ministers of the five "Brics" countries signed an agreement to kick-start the arrangement during their annual meeting in South Africa. China will contribute $41 billion, followed by Brazil, Russia and India with $18 billion each, and South Africa with $5 billion.

The focus on Syria will also probably mean that developed-country members of the G-20 pay less attention to a long-running dispute over whether to set binding deadlines for stabilizing their budget deficits and beginning to cut their debts.

In recent months, German officials have pushed the G-20 nations to agree to hard targets for reducing debt after the current deficit-cutting agreement expires in 2016. But the effort ran into strong U.S. opposition when finance ministers met in Moscow in July, with Treasury Department officials insisting that the priority had to be boosting jobs and growth as opposed to reducing debt.

Rather than a hard target, the G-20 countries are expected to lay out "medium-term fiscal strategies" to show how they will achieve "sustainable growth" after 2016, a German official told reporters in Berlin on Monday.

"This is better than no strategy, but these aren't binding targets," the official said.

G-20 leaders are also set to produce a plan for supporting growth and creating jobs.

A U.S. administration official said an overriding U.S. goal at the summit is persuading other nations that they need to help boost demand world-wide. Global demand is "improving," but "remains weak," the official said.

"We need to rededicate ourselves to promoting a lasting rebalancing of global demand," the official said. "We welcome signs that Europe's long recession is ending and their critical steps to restore financial stability. But important challenges remain, including boosting demand and addressing record-high unemployment levels."

Beyond that, the U.S. wants to make progress toward another goal: cracking down on tax evasion.

That issue was front-and-center at a separate meeting of the Group of Eight nations in Northern Ireland in June.

"We will also be working in St. Petersburg to get support globally for the kinds of measures that we have laid out for countries to close tax loopholes and avoid a race to the bottom where tax competition leads countries to lose revenue and companies to make inefficient decisions when they locate where they pay the lowest tax, rather than where it's most productive for them to produce," an Obama administration official said.

--Peter Nicholas and Anton Troianovski contributed to this article. [ 09-03-13 1333ET ]

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Stronger on  Intervention , Overseas Data
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Monday as central bank intervention and positive economic data from overseas lifted the currency.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.3696 per U.S. dollar, stronger from Friday's closing price fix of BRL2.3824, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Brazil's currency was boosted at the session's start by better-than-expected manufacturing data from China, Brazil's largest trade partner and an important consumer of commodities such as iron ore and soy. Global tensions surrounding Syria also eased, as U.S. President Barack Obama said that he would seek congressional approval before punishing Syria for alleged chemical weapons attacks.

The real strengthened further after the Brazilian Central Bank carried out two successful sales of foreign-exchange swaps. The bank sold all of the 30,000 contracts on offer equivalent to $1.49 billion. The bank held its regularly scheduled auction of $500 million in swaps as part of the $60 billion intervention program through the end of 2013. A second auction of $1 billion in swaps was announced Friday to calm volatile currency markets.

Late Monday, the bank said that it would sell 10,000 swaps valued at $500 million in a regularly scheduled auction.

The swap auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar. The auctions typically help the real strengthen against the greenback by giving investors more options for hedging in the dollar.

"The central bank has calmed down the market," said Marcos Trabbold, chief of trading operations at Sao Paulo's B&T Associados. The central bank's program of planned currency market intervention has made the bank's strategy "perfectly clear" to the market, rinsing some of the pressure on the real from speculators out of the market, Mr. Trabbold added.

While Brazil's predictability will help companies and investors in need of hedging or liquidity, the local currency market will still likely see some volatility until the U.S. Federal Reserve gives a clearer picture of U.S. monetary policy, Mr. Trabbold said. Uncertainty about when the Fed will start to taper its bond purchases has caused many investors to bail out of emerging-market investments such as Brazil.

Despite market uncertainty, dollars continue to flow into Brazil and will keep the Brazilian Central Bank from using the $375 billion in foreign currency reserves to back up the real, Mr. Trabbold added.

"Only if the [central bank] starts to feel some distortion in the market, such as net outflows, it could sell dollars into the market," the trader said.

Mr. Trabbold still sees some space for the real to gain more ground on the greenback, perhaps strengthening to about BRL2.30 per dollar in the medium term.

UPDATE 3-Brazil hikes interest rates again to regain market confidence
text:
* Central bank hikes Selic rate by 50 bps as expected

* Weaker currency adds to inflationary pressures

* Bank leaves door open for more rate hikes   (Adds analyst comment and context)

By Anthony Boadle and Alonso Soto

BRASILIA, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Brazil raised its benchmark interest rate to a 16-month high of 9 percent on Wednesday, maintaining the pace of monetary tightening to fight inflation and rebuild investors' confidence in Latin America's largest economy.

The central bank's monetary policy committee, known as Copom, voted unanimously for a third straight half-percentage-point rate hike to ease inflationary fears that have risen on the back of a plunge in the value of the local currency.

Forty-four of 46 economists polled by Reuters expected the bank to raise its Selic rate to 9 percent from 8.5 percent as part of a tightening cycle that started in April.

The central bank left the door open for more rate hikes by reiterating that the latest increase is part of a rate-adjustment process.

"Continuing the adjustment of the benchmark interest rate, Copom decided unanimously to raise the Selic rate to 9 percent," said the bank in its post-decision statement that repeated exactly the language  of the last communique in July.

Monetary authorities from India to Indonesia are scrambling to offset the massive outflow of capital triggered by expectations of a withdrawal of stimulus in the United States and a stronger dollar. The exodus of investors have dragged down the value of currencies in most emerging-market nations, pushing inflation higher via pricier imports.

The stakes are even higher for Brazil where a mix of erratic policy that includes government intervention in sectors of the economy plus supply-side bottlenecks have severely hit investor confidence in the once-booming emerging-market nation.

Higher interest rates would help Brazil not only tame price increases, but also bolster investors' confidence, the International Monetary Fund said in a report about the South American nation published earlier on Wednesday.

The double-digit slump of the real had even prompted some market bets for a larger rate hike on Wednesday.

However, central bank President Alexandre Tombini threw cold water on those expectations by saying on Aug. 19 that the steep rise in the yield of interest rate future contracts was excessive. The bank also launched a $60 billion intervention program to halt the plunge of the real, which has been one of the worst performing currencies in the world this year.

The scope of future rate hikes will likely hinge on the pace of depreciation of the real as well as the strength of the economic recovery in Brazil, analysts said.

"I think... (the central bank) will follow the data and decide accordingly. There will be at least another 50 basis points that will come in mid-October and we could see things heading on their way to 10 (percent) afterwards," said Jose Francisco de Lima Goncalves, chief economist with Banco Fator.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

TEXT-Brazil central bank decision statement

INSTANT VIEW on central bank rate hike

INSIGHT-Brazil's Tombini: An inflation hawk

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The central bank has argued that high inflation ultimately hurts the economy by discouraging investment in the country and domestic spending by local businesses and consumers.

The Brazilian economy likely rebounded in the second quarter, but recent data show that the recovery will again disappoint with growth of just 2 percent this year. Brazil's statistics institute will release second-quarter gross domestic product figures at 9 a.m. (1200 GMT) on Friday.

ERRATIC POLICY

The bank started to raise the Selic in April after a spike in consumer prices, surprising investors with the aggressive pace of tightening that brought rates from record lows of 7.25 percent to 8.50 percent in July.

Annual inflation has eased since then, but at 6.27 percent remains well above the mid-point of the official year-end target of 4.5 percent, plus or minus two percentage points. Inflation expectations also remain high for next year.

A possible hike in gasoline prices in Brazil expected later this year could also fuel inflation by raising transport costs.

The inflation problem partly stems from a flurry of consumption-stimulus packages implemented by President Dilma Rousseff's government, which also raised tensions between her administration and the central bank, analysts have said.

The government's aggressive spending is seen as one of the main reasons why the central bank started to boost rates this year, even as the economy struggles to find its footing.

The likely normalization of monetary policy in the United States has added to inflationary concerns in Brazil, a country ravaged by bouts of hyperinflation in the 1980s and 1990s. Although analysts do not expect inflation to get out of control, authorities are under pressure to contain any surge in prices.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega has blamed the Fed for fueling a "mini-crisis" with mixed messages - about winding down or not, its liquidity expansion program (quantitative easing).

Adding to the uncertainty in markets is a likely military strike by the United States and allies on the Syrian government, which is accused of using chemical weapons against civilians. title: UPDATE 1-Brazil has 'ammunition' to combat global turmoil, Rousseff says
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Brazilian economy has enough firepower to stem the impact of global market turmoil, President Dilma Rousseff said on Wednesday, in an attempt to reinforce confidence in the nation's currency.

Rousseff blamed the recent slump in the real, Brazil's currency, on expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve is on its way to tightening monetary policy. She said Brazil has "large international reserves," which she suggested were "ammunition" that could help ease market volatility.

"Do you know that old story about keeping your money beneath your mattress? Well, Brazil doesn't but it does have between $378 billion and $372 billion in international reserves," she told radio stations in the city of Belo Horizonte in an interview. "We have what is called 'ammunition' to deal with those global situations."

Investors are questioning Rousseff's economic policy, saying it has made the country more vulnerable to rising debt and inflation, state interference in some sectors and a weaker real. The government has defended its stance by saying policies - such as ample tax breaks and loan disbursements from state-run banks to aid the industry - are cushioning Brazil from global turmoil.

WHIPLASH

The real, along with India's rupee, has weakened more than any other major currency since May. Its tumble of over 15 percent is forcing businesses, policymakers and consumers to prepare for consequences, including inflation and a costlier fundraising.

The decline has become another symbol of Brazil's fall from grace among investors and produced a severe case of whiplash among producers, who complain that the basic pillars of Latin America's largest economy have constantly shifted under Rousseff's left-leaning government.

Rousseff reiterated that the government is neither targeting any level nor a direction for the currency. "Our policy is one of a flexible currency," she said in the interview.

The currency strengthened 0.6 percent to 2.358 to the dollar in late morning trading, running counter to global markets.

In an effort to shore up the real and stem volatility, Brazil's central bank last Thursday said it would intervene in foreign exchange markets with daily cash and currency swaps valued at $60 billion by the end of the year.

The central bank's monetary policy committee, known as Copom, is widely expected to deliver another half a percentage point hike in interest rates on Wednesday.

Brazil's low growth in her 2 1/2-year tenure as president has been the result of a slow global expansion, Rousseff said, adding that Brazil's public finances remain "very good."

The real was trading at BRL2.3667 to the dollar, after closing at BRL2.3652 to the dollar Tuesday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Brazil's real has weakened by about 20% so far this year as investors shift their portfolios to position for the possibility of improving returns abroad.

The central bank's continued market interventions also are helping stanch the big losses that the Brazilian currency had seen in previous sessions. The bank has been rolling over expiring foreign-exchange currency swaps in order to meet demand for dollars, and as a result slow the real's decline against the greenback.

The contracts are part of some $60 billion in central bank intervention scheduled for offer by Dec. 31.

The currency swap contracts allow investors to exchange bonds indexed to domestic interest rates for paper tied directly to the U.S. dollar. The swap auctions typically lead to a weakening of the U.S. dollar and a strengthening of the Brazilian real.

title: Mexican Peso, Emerging-Market  Currencies  Slip on Fed Worries
text:
The Mexican peso and most other emerging-market currencies slumped Monday, resuming the selloff that has plagued them in recent weeks.

Investors returned their focus to the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting, where the Fed could start to trim its bond-buying stimulus program that had sent investors on a hunt for yield in past years. The threat of less Fed stimulus has rapidly tamped investors' enthusiasm for higher-yielding emerging-market assets, and has caused many to reinvest in U.S. assets.

Several emerging-market currencies recovered slightly on Friday in the wake of larger intervention efforts on the part of Brazil's and Turkey's central banks over the course of the week. However, these currencies once again took on a bearish tone Monday, with little sign of such interventions having an effect as Brazil's and Turkey's currencies weakened.

"September's getting closer and closer," said Win Thin, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. "It's pretty much a full-scale emerging-market selloff continued."

Mexico's currency led the way, diving 1.8% against the dollar, which bought MXN13.1827, according to CQG. The peso often acts as a proxy for emerging-market currencies, since it is one of the more heavily traded and accessible currencies in the asset class.

Brazil's currency also weakened sharply, despite the Brazilian central bank's heightened efforts to stop the real's seeming one-way decline last week. Brazil's central bank on Thursday said it would provide at least $60 billion more in dollar liquidity through the end of the year. Under the plan, the bank will offer $3 billion of dollar loans and swaps per week in regular auctions starting Friday. Still, the real fell 1.4% against the dollar, which bought BRL2.3813 late Monday.

In Asia, the rupee weakened, though India's central bank was suspected of intervening in the foreign-exchange market toward the close of local trading Monday. The rupee slid 1% against the greenback, which traded at INR64.32, according to CQG.

The rupee and Brazilian real have been severely punished by traders this month as their countries have large current account deficits. These current account gaps force them to rely on foreign portfolio inflows to meet financing needs, but these flows could lessen if the Fed pulls back stimulus, analysts say.

The Indonesian rupiah, however, saw some recovery in response to a group of measures the government announced last week aimed at narrowing the country's current account gap. Indonesia's central bank announced additional measures Friday aimed at stabilizing local markets and the economy as well.

The rupiah fell 1.7% to IDR10,845 against the dollar.

"The measures from both the government and central bank are certainly well-intentioned and a step in the right direction,' said HSBC ASEAN economist Su Sian LIM in a note Monday.

In Europe, the Turkish lira underperformed, despite continued intervention by Turkey's central bank, which sold $350 million in foreign exchange to support the lira Monday. After hovering near record lows earlier in the session, the lira slipped 0.5% against the dollar, which bought TRY1.9982, according to CQG.

The cost to insure Argentine sovereign debt against default ticked higher as investors continue to digest the latest development in the country's legal battle with holdout creditors. A US appeals court ruled against Argentina Friday, saying the country must pay bondholders who held out on a restructuring offer years ago if it continues to pay those who accepted the deal. Now, investors are waiting to see if the Supreme Court will weigh in on Argentina's case. If the Supreme Court refuses to hear the case, that significantly raises the risks of default, analysts say. title: *DJ Brazil's Government Will Not Allow Excessive  Currency  Volatility -Mantega
text:
26 Aug 2013 14:14 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank Could Intervene on Spot Market, If Needed -Mantega

26 Aug 2013 14:15 EDT *DJ  Turbulence in Brazil's Currency Market Coming Mainly From Overseas -Mantega

26 Aug 2013 14:29 EDT DJ  Brazil's Government Will Not Allow Excessive Currency Volatility - Mantega

SAO PAULO--Brazil's government will not allow excessive volatility in its currency market and reserves the right to intervene whenever necessary to curb abrupt shifts in the value of the Brazilian real, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Monday.

Speaking at a news conference, the minister said, "The central bank will not allow excessive fluctuations in foreign exchange values."

He noted that the Brazilian Central Bank has intervened frequently in the foreign exchange market in recent weeks, mainly via the sale of foreign exchange currency swap contracts on the futures market and through auctions of short-term U.S. dollar credit lines.

However, he added, "The central bank could also intervene in spot trading, if necessary."

So far, the central bank has avoided the direct sale of U.S. dollars from its foreign reserves. Reserves stand at over $370 billion.

The Brazilian real has seen a 14% depreciation against the U.S. dollar so far this year.

Mr. Mantega said, "Most of the pressure has come from the futures market, not the spot market." Consequently, the government has preferred to intervene in futures trading, through the swap contract auctions, rather than the spot market.

Mr. Mantega added, "Most of the volatility is coming from overseas, not from us." He said volatility struck the Brazilian market when the U.S. Federal Reserve Board began hinting that it would gradually reduce U.S. dollar liquidity in world markets. The expected policy shift has led to higher U.S. interest rates, which tend to siphon investment money away from emerging-market countries such as Brazil and back to the U.S.

title: Brazil gets whiplash as  currency  heads the other way: down
text:
By Paulo Prada and Guillermo Parra-Bernal RIO DE JANEIRO/SAO PAULO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Two short years ago, Brazil had a terrible problem with its currency - it was far too strong. Local factories, unable to compete with Chinese imports made cheaper by the real's appreciation, were closing their doors. Fernando Pimentel, the trade minister and a close adviser to President Dilma Rousseff, declared that "Brazil has joined the team of countries with strong currencies" and urged industries to adapt to the new reality. Now, as global investors shed assets in emerging markets worldwide, Brazil's problem has abruptly turned upside-down. The real, along with India's rupee, has weakened more than any other major currency since May. Its tumble of 16 percent is forcing businesses, policymakers and consumers to prepare for consequences including inflation and costlier foreign financing.

 The decline has become another symbol of Brazil's fall from grace among investors and produced a severe case of whiplash among producers who complain that the basic pillars of Latin America's largest economy have constantly shifted under Rousseff's left-leaning government. Consequences will be felt everywhere from fuel pumps in Sao Paulo to retail outlets in Miami and New York City, where Brazilians were such prolific shoppers during the strong-currency years that the U.S. Travel Association referred to them as "walking stimulus packages" in 2012. The depreciation, Finance Minister Guido Mantega told a São Paulo newspaper over the weekend, "isn't good for anybody."


    
    
     
    "It changes the calculation for just about everyone," says
Neil Shearing, chief emerging markets economist at Capital
Economics in London. "What makes sense when you have a strong
currency no longer does at a weaker level."
    Until this year, the real was on a tear.
    A decade-long period of steady growth appeared to put Brazil
on the fast track toward first-world status, attracting record
amounts of foreign investment and making the real one of the
most coveted currencies in the world.
    Since May, when investors turned back toward developed


markets amid bets of a U.S. recovery, the real has tumbled, trading Monday at 2.39 per dollar. Last week, it approached a five-year low which,compared with a peak of 1.54 per dollar in mid-2011, represents a fall of 37 percent.


    
    HIGHER COSTS AND HIGHER UNCERTAINTY
    The biggest threat of a weaker real is that of inflation,
especially in a country with a long history of dramatic price
increases. Annual inflation at the end of July was at 6.27
percent, just below the ceiling of the government's target band.
    With a weaker real, the cost of imported food, industrial
supplies, consumer goods and other goods rises. Over the past
year the price of wheat flour, a staple that is Brazil's biggest
food import, spiked 29 percent according to central bank data.
    The higher costs pose operational challenges for companies
with big dollar expenses and those who need affordable access to
foreign capital. Airlines, who import jet fuel, are so worried
that last week they asked Brazil's government for tax breaks.
    The government was surprised by the sudden fall, which could


further complicate an expected re-election bid by Rousseff next year. Her approval ratings, until recently among the highest of any leader worldwide, fell sharply after mass protests in June against everything from poor public services to rising prices. Yet economists say there is nothing behind a weaker real that should have caught anyone off-guard. Demand for Brazil's commodity exports, one of the drivers of the boom, slowed as growth in China and other big customers cooled. A nascent recovery in the United States clearly meant that the dollar, suppressed in recent years by loose monetary policy now ending, would appreciate. "Any economic model would tell you that this was going to happen," says Marcio Garcia, an economist at the Catholic University in Rio de Janeiro and a visiting scholar at the MIT Sloan School of Management. "The question was when."


    
    SCRAMBLING
    That, of course, is what has Brazil scrambling.
    In an effort to shore up the real and stem volatility,
Brazil's central bank last Thursday said it would intervene in
foreign exchange markets with daily cash and currency swaps
valued at $60 billion by the end of the year. 
    "I'm glad they decided to go for this, but one thing I can
tell you: it's too late," said Lawrence Pih, chief executive of
Grupo Pacifico SA, which owns Latin America's largest wheat mill
and is considering price hikes to handle the higher costs.
    Many other companies have taken measures to cope, too.
    Travel agencies are shrinking already small margins in order
to limit the hike in air fares.
    Others, including state-run energy company Petroleo
Brasileiro SA, or Petrobras, have adjusted accounting methods to
smooth currency fluctuations on their balance sheets. 
    The changes during the second quarter enabled Petrobras,


most of whose debt is denominated in dollars, to avoid 8 billion reais of currency related charges. The company is also in the difficult position of having to import many fuels and sell them, because of government price controls, at a loss. Companies are also adopting new hedges against further volatility. According to data provided by Cetip SA Mercados Organizados, Latin America's largest securities clearinghouse, Brazilian companies increased their use of so-called non-deliverable forward contracts, which are settled in dollars, by 30 percent since the end of last year. The short-term pain of a weaker real could pose an opportunity in the long run. With slower growth, rising prices and stagnant investment, Brazil could finally have to tackle long-pending tax, labor and other reforms that business leaders argue are necessary to make the country more competitive. "The current scenario is unsustainable," says Marcos Mendes, an economist who advises Brazil's senate. "The way out of this is reform."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Real soars on cenbank plan, U.S. data buoys Latam  FX
text:
By Walter Brandimarte SAO PAULO, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real rallied more than 3 percent on Friday after the central bank unveiled a currency intervention program that will provide $60 billion worth of cash and currency hedges to the foreign exchange market by the year-end. Weak U.S. housing data also supported the real and Latin American currencies in general because it dented expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will slow its monetary stimulus program next month. For years, bond buying by the Fed has provided a steady source of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets. Fears the bank would soon start cutting back on bond purchases have roiled most emerging market currencies, but the Brazilian real was sold off more sharply than its peers because investors were also worried about the country's economic outlook.

Brazil's currency intervention plan, announced after markets closed on Thursday, was seen by analysts as a bold move by the central bank to give credibility to its currency intervention policy. The bank failed to stop the real from slumping to near five-year lows over the past few days. The measure is likely to curb the recent extreme volatility of Brazil's foreign exchange market, allowing the real to trade more in line with peer currencies. Still, analysts say it is unlikely to reverse the currency's depreciation, which is related to a global portfolio reallocation caused by the expected withdrawal of U.S. stimulus measures. "The measure should help contain excessive bearishness around the real and even bring it back to the 2.35-2.40 range," Barclays strategists Marcelo Salomon and Guilherme Loureiro wrote in a research note. The real closed at 2.3527 per dollar, 3.3 percent stronger for the day, while the Mexican peso gained 1 percent and the Chilean peso rose 0.4 percent. Brazilian interest rate futures <0#2DIJ:> also dropped sharply, with the contract maturing in January 2017 falling 43 basis points to 11.44 percent, as the outlook for a more stable real over the next few months eased concerns about inflation stemming from more expensive imported goods. Under its new intervention program, the central bank will sell, on Mondays through Thursdays, $500 million a day of currency swaps - derivative contracts designed to provide investors with hedge against a weaker real. On Fridays, the central bank will offer $1 billion on the spot market through repurchase agreements. The program "represents one of the boldest attempts yet by an emerging market central bank to shore up its currency following the rout of recent weeks," Neil Shearing, chief emerging markets economist with Capital Economics in London, wrote in a note to clients. "It's worth noting that history suggests FX intervention tends to smooth currency adjustment, rather than prevent the adjustment from happening altogether," he added.

title: Brazil 's Real Gains Sharply After  Central Bank  Steps Up  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real gained sharply against the dollar on Friday morning, as a $60 billion intervention program unveiled by the central bank provided some much-needed relief to the Brazilian currency.

The central bank's program is aimed at providing companies and investors with the certainty they will be able to buy dollars if needed. It continues the intervention steps taken by the central bank in recent days and weeks to try to prop up the currency, but adds more visibility and predictability.

"The measure should help contain excessive bearishness around the real and even bring it back to the 2.35-2.40 range," Barclays Capital said in a note. "But the measure should not reverse the weakening trend of the currency, which has been driven by changes in U.S. monetary policy stance and uncertainty around local fiscal policy."

On Friday morning, the Brazilian currency gained to BRL2.3811 per dollar, from BRL2.4406 late Thursday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Late Thursday, the central bank said it would provide at least $60 billion more in dollar liquidity through the end of the year. Under the plan, the bank will offer $3 billion of dollar loans and swaps per week in daily auctions starting Friday through Dec. 31.

The central bank's move was welcomed for providing more visibility to its interventions, replacing what have so far been unpredictable daily auctions. The central bank has already sold some $45 billion in dollar swap contracts so far this year. It is seen as continuing the central bank's policy of trying to restrain wild swings in the currency, rather than halting it in its tracks.

"Crucially, [it] doesn't look like the government are trying to impact the currency too hard," said a London-based trader in a research note.

Unlike other central banks around the world, the Brazilian intervention doesn't have a direct impact on the country's $375 billion of foreign-currency reserves.

Yet the plan underscores how much the financial world has changed since the U.S. Federal Reserve said it was contemplating an end to the easy-money policies adopted to cope with the financial and economic crisis that began in 2008.

Brazilian officials in recent years have struggled with an overvalued currency, not a falling one. Finance Minister Guido Mantega became known for complaining he was the victim of a "currency war" as Brazil's real gained against the dollar.

That has now turned sharply. The Brazilian currency has weakened around 16% against the dollar so far this year, and about 2% so far this week. The currency had touched BRL1.55 per dollar in mid-2011.

While much of the turn in market sentiment has been blamed on the Fed, the problems have been compounded by sluggish growth and high inflation in Brazil. Critics blame missteps in economic policy, including too much public spending, and say the currency will continue to weaken unless that changes.

"We reckon that the absence of any hint of a structural change in the economic policy mix is likely to limit the efficiency of such [central bank] measures in the medium term," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist at BES Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

title: Brazil 's  Intervention  Plan Brings Relief To Emerging Market  Currencies
text:
Measures announced by Brazil's central bank to support the real provided relief to a range of other emerging market currencies Friday, at the end of a turbulent week of losses unleashed by the prospect of tighter U.S. monetary policy.

Brazil's central bank said Thursday it would provide at least $60 billion more in dollar liquidity through the end of the year, in an effort to limit the depreciation of its currency, one of the weakest links within the emerging markets space.

The news helped lift the real from a four-year low of BRL2.4560 to settle around BRL2.4350 in European hours before the local Brazilian market opens at 1200 GMT. Analysts said the move by Brazil was also helping other bruised emerging market currencies, such as the Turkish lira, to gain a more solid footing.

"Intervention in Brazil has been a positive sign for all emerging markets. It signalled investors that central banks are there and becoming more reactive and aggressive. They are ready to accelerate their intervention to stabilize markets," said Luis Costa, an emerging market strategist at Citigroup.

Sebastian Brown, an analyst at Barclays, said the intervention could signal that "the tolerance for weaker exchange rates across emerging markets is close to running out, given some evidence of increasing inflationary pressures."

Countries with significant current account deficits have so far paid the highest price, reflecting investors' concerns that they will struggle to pull in the cash they need when the Federal Reserve starts winding down the easy-money era. The U.S. central bank is expected to taper it monthly $85 billion bond-buying program as early as September.

First in the firing line, and under significant strain earlier this week, are Indonesia, Turkey and India.

Since the end of May, both the rupee and the rupiah have lost about 15% against the U.S. dollar. The lira swooned to record lows Thursday. But after large declines this week, all have steadied Friday.

Also helping: Indonesian authorities on Friday announced a package of measures to stabilize the rupiah and to reduce the current account deficit, which will include the introduction of a higher import tax on luxury goods and the reduction of a quota on mineral exports.

Meanwhile, the Turkish lira has recovered somewhat. The central bank there launched an auction of $350 million for the second straight day.

Brazil's action will resonate with peers in Turkey's central bank, said Tim Ash, an analyst at Standard Bank in London. But like many other observers, Mr. Ash said the effect may prove fleeting. "The intervention program should provide a bit of short-term relief, but I'm not sure if it really will avoid the need in Turkey itself for a more substantive rise in policy rates. It could though buy them a bit more time," he said.

Some investors and analysts cautioned that beefed-up efforts to support hobbled currencies are unlikely to end the pain.

"Measures provided some relief but the process of adjustment started at the end of May [when the Fed first hinted at a change in its monetary policy] has not finished yet. The dollar will continue to be firm. Treasury yields are not at equilibrium level and we expect more weakness of the emerging market side," said Clive Dennis, portfolio manager at Schroders, which had $388 billion under management at the end of June.

Mr. Costa at Citigroup said the new measures in Brazil and Indonesia and persistent efforts by Turkey to ease the pressure on the lira are somewhat late. "The market has already deteriorated significantly since May. Will they be enough? Not yet. Central banks are under significant pressure to trigger growth in their economies," Mr. Costa added.

The dollar was at Y98.938 against the yen, compared with Y98.72, while the euro was at Y32.20 compared with Y131.85.

The pound was trading at $1.5619 against the dollar, compared with $1.5586 late Thursday in New York. The Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, which tracks the dollar against a basket of currencies, was trading at 73.964, compared with 73.92 late Thursday in New York.

title: Brazil  Stocks Climb on  Central Bank Currency Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazilian blue-chip stocks climbed Friday, led by homebuilder and retail stocks, as the central bank set out its longer-term strategy for reining in the Brazilian currency's weakness.

The Ibovespa index of most-traded stocks rose 1.6% to 52197 points, for a weekly advance of 1.3%.

The Brazilian Central Bank said late Thursday that it would intervene daily in currency markets to ensure investors and companies had access to U.S. dollars. The move, which will give more clarity and predictability to the central bank's intervention plans, caused the Brazilian real to strengthen sharply against the dollar.

Because the real's weakness against the dollar boosts the cost of imports and a result increases inflationary pressures, some traders saw the move as helping keep down interest rates in the medium term. Last week's central bank survey, the most recent one published, shows that the market expects the benchmark Selic interest rate to climb from 8.5% currently to 9.25% by year end, and then to 9.5% by the end of 2014.

On Friday, the long end of the rate curve dipped somewhat, reflecting a changing outlook for inflation. With some expectations that rates may climb less than previously forecast, stocks of companies more dependent on consumer credit jumped.

Real estate developer Rossi Residencial surged 9.5% to three reais ($1.27), leading gains on the index. Rival Gafisa SA added 8.4% to BRL3.10, while homebuilder PDG Realty SA gained 8% to BRL2.43, and Brookfield Incorporacoes rose 6.2% to BRL1.88.

Leading online retailer B2W jumped 7.2% to BRL13.51, while clothing company Cia. Hering SA climbed 5.3% to BRL 31.90, and retailer Lojas Renner SA advanced 4.1% to BRL60.62.

The stronger real also lifted shares of state-run oil company Petroleo Brasileiro SA, which rose 1.6% to BRL18.55. The real's recent weakness against the dollar had increased the cost of gasoline and diesel the company imports to meet domestic fuel demand.

Shares of Eike Batista's EBX Group of companies also were gainers during the session. Oil company OGX advanced 5.2% to BRL0.81, while mining company MMX added 4.9% to BRL2.35.

But just as the stronger real favors importing companies, it didn't favor exporters such as mining company Vale SA, one of Brazil's largest exporters. Vale shares slipped 0.4% to BRL32.28.

Aircraft manufacturer Embraer fell 1.8% to BRL19.81, while Suzano Papel e Celulose sank 2% to BRL8.87.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  Recover as U.S. Data Disappoint
text:
The Indian rupee gained against the dollar as weaker-than-expected U.S. housing data and a spate of central bank interventions boosted emerging-market currencies around the globe.

The dollar fell 0.8% against the rupee, trading recently at INR63.96, according to CQG data, ending a string of consecutive record lows for India's currency.

Disappointing housing data out of the U.S. bolstered emerging-market currencies, as the weaker-than-expected figures increased traders' uncertainty about when the Federal Reserve will start to wind down its bond-buying program. The stimulus has injected cheap money into the economy and driven investors toward high-yielding emerging-market assets.

Sales of newly built homes in the U.S. hit a nine-month low, falling 13.4% in July and increasing concerns that higher mortgage rates will hurt the housing recovery.

The Brazilian real gained the most among emerging-market currencies, additionally bolstered by central bank intervention. Late Thursday, Brazil's central bank unveiled a $60 billion intervention program designed to stem the rapid decline of the real, which has lost about 15% to the greenback this year. The bank will offer $3 billion of dollar loans and swaps per week through Dec. 31, adding to the some $45 billion it has sold in dollar swap contracts so far this year.

The dollar fell 2.8% against the real, trading recently at BRL2.3667.

"This better-than-expected plan, selling dollars via an automatic system, helps to restore [market] confidence [because] it's consistent and predictable," said Maya Hernandez, senior currency strategist at HSBC in New York. The planned daily auctions mark a change from the central bank's more erratic previous interventions, so they have the potential to be more meaningful in boosting the real over time, Ms. Hernandez said.

"Regulation has not been a forte of Brazil's government, and asset prices have shown that," she said. "This mechanism is much more market friendly than what we've had so far. It speaks very well for the government--this is a shift in the right direction."

The real gained on the back of the central bank's announcement, despite news Friday that Brazil's current-account deficit widened in July to $9.02 billion from $3.95 billion in June, due to increasing imports.

The dollar also declined against other Latin American currencies, falling 0.7% to buy the Mexican peso at MXN12.9979 and 0.6% against the Chilean peso to trade at CLP509.50.

The dollar fell 0.6% against the South African rand to buy ZAR10.2167. The Indonesian rupiah climbed 1.3% to the greenback, which recently bought IDR10891.

Meanwhile, the Turkish lira slid against the dollar, which bought a record TRY2.0 as Turkey's currency continued to suffer from the recent foreign investment exodus, despite continued central bank intervention measures.

--Matthew Cowley contributed to this article

That's not the way economists want to see housing supply increase. Based on July figures, it'd take 5.2 months to buy up the supply of newly built homes on the market -- the most in at least a year. title: DJ  Brazil 's Real Closes Sharply Stronger on  Central Bank Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed sharply stronger against the U.S. dollar Friday as a $60 billion intervention program unveiled by the central bank provided some necessary relief to the Brazilian currency.

The central bank's program is aimed at providing companies and investors with the certainty they will be able to buy dollars if needed. It continues the intervention steps taken by the central bank in recent days and weeks to try to prop up the currency, but adds more visibility and predictability.

"The central bank is providing much-needed clarity to Brazilian markets, which we didn't have for a long time," said Ilan Solot, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman in London. "As far as stopping the bleeding, it does a really good job."

The Brazilian currency gained 3.3% to exit active trading at BRL2.3534 per U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger than Thursday's closing price at BRL2.4406, before the central bank announced its new intervention program.

Late Thursday, the central bank said it would provide at least $60 billion more in dollar liquidity through the end of the year. Under the plan, the bank will offer $3 billion of dollar loans and swaps per week in daily auctions starting Friday through Dec. 31.

The program, however, could be extended beyond the end of 2013, if needed, according to Tulio Maciel, head of the central bank's economics department. Mr. Maciel said the central bank planned to do what was needed to "supply liquidity and assure hedge" for the normal functioning of the foreign exchange market.

In the first of the regularly scheduled auctions of dollar-credit lines held Friday, the central bank agreed to buy an undisclosed volume of the U.S. currency on Jan. 2 at an exchange rate of BRL2.4651 per dollar. The bank had offered to sell up to $1 billion at the auction. Similar dollar-credit line sales will be held every Friday through the end of the year. The central bank also will hold its first swap auction under the new strategy on Monday, when swaps worth the equivalent of $500 million will be offered.

The central bank's move was welcomed for providing more visibility to its interventions, replacing what have so far been unpredictable daily auctions. The central bank has already sold some $45 billion in dollar swap contracts so far this year. Unlike other central banks around the world, the Brazilian intervention doesn't have a direct impact on the country's $375 billion of foreign-currency reserves.

The strategy is seen as continuing the central bank's policy of trying to restrain wild swings in the currency, rather than halting it in its tracks. Yet the plan underscores how much the financial world has changed since the U.S. Federal Reserve said it was contemplating an end to the easy-money policies adopted to cope with the financial and economic crisis that began in 2008.

Brazilian officials in recent years have struggled with an overvalued currency, not a falling one. Finance Minister Guido Mantega became known for complaining he was the victim of a "currency war" as Brazil's real gained against the dollar.

That has now turned sharply. The Brazilian currency has weakened around 16% against the dollar so far this year, and about 2% so far this week. The currency had touched BRL1.55 per dollar in mid-2011.

"Ultimately, markets always end up taking a currency where they want it to go," said Chris Gaffney, senior market strategist at EverBank Financial Corp. (EVER). EverBank trades about $100 million across about 20 different currencies per day, while also holding about $1 billion in foreign-exchange deposits.

Most of the current market movements, especially where emerging markets are concerned, are being driven by bets that the Fed will start reducing its bond purchases by $15 billion as early as September, Mr. Gaffney said. While he thinks a Fed move in September is unlikely, the announcement will have an immediate, negative impact for emerging-market currencies, Mr. Gaffney added.

"I think the beginning of the taper will be the shock," with markets then likely to take a step back to evaluate how long before the cheap cash runs out, Mr. Gaffney said. EverBank is holding its currency positions steady until after the Fed's September meeting, with a plan to adjust positions afterward.

While much of the turn in market sentiment has been blamed on the Fed, the problems have been compounded by sluggish growth and high inflation in Brazil. Critics blame missteps in economic policy, including too much public spending, and say the currency will continue to weaken unless that changes.

But Mr. Gaffney said that he still owns the real, adding that expectations for higher interest rates to fight inflation and upcoming events such as next year's soccer World Cup and 2016 Summer Olympics could eventually boost the currency. "If [the Brazilian Central Bank] can get in front of inflation, some of the hot money may move back into Brazil," Mr. Gaffney said.

--Gerald Jeffis in Brasilia contributed to this article.

The firm also notes new-home sales are based on signed contracts, "and we would expect any weakening in the housing market to show up here first, as opposed to in existing home sales which are recorded at the time of closing and, therefore, tend to lag changes in sentiment and activity by several months." July pending home sales Wednesday will also add more color. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

Moody's Analytics says Canada's housing market is likely headed for a multi-year period of below-trend growth, but not a crash that some forecast. It says home sales have begun to slip and price growth is slowing, "in part because of government efforts to discourage debt-fueled property speculation." Moody's says those tighter mortgage financing rules have cut demand at the high end, with notable effect in expensive markets such as Vancouver. "At the same time, elevated price-to-rent ratios have tempered much of the enthusiasm that drove home buyers in recent years," Moody's adds. (don.curren@wsj.com)

A big drop in new home sales forcing anti-Treasurys bets to unwind. The short covering sent the 10-year yield to a session low of 2.802%. But some traders caution that new home sales has been a volatile gauge of the housing market. The bond market needs persistently weak data to reverse the rout since May. Andrew Brenner of National Alliance Capital Markets still sees the 10-year yield hitting 3% "sooner rather than later," the key datapoint being the September 6 jobs report. Larry Dyer, head of US interest rate strategy at HSBC Securities USA, questions the strength of 2H growth and bets the yield will end the year down around 2.6%. Ten-year notes up 20/32, yielding 2.818%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

Brazilian Central Bank's move to hold daily currency market interventions through the end of 2013 will help end the "feeding frenzy" surrounding the real, says Gradual Investimentos. The central bank "wants to give companies that are being punished by the US dollar's appreciation a way out," firm says. Gradual notes dollar-denominated obligations held by companies are at $180B, up from $100B during the 2008 financial crisis. The goal is not to strengthen the real specifically to BRL2.20 per dollar, but to end speculation that it could weaken to BRL2.75, Gradual adds. BRL holding gains, with the dollar down 2.3% to BRL2.379. (jeff.fick@dowjones.com)

Argentine bonds are mostly higher Friday despite a major ruling against the country in favor of holdout creditors. A US federal appeals court ruled that Argentina can't pay bonds it issued under a swap deal unless it pays the holdouts full value at the same time, but left a suspension of enforcement in place while the Supreme Court considers an appeal. The NY law, dollar-denominated 2017 bond is up 0.1% at ARS725. The NY law dollar-GDP warrants rose 0.1% to ARS71.00. (shane.romig@dowjones.com)

10:52 EDT - Plunge in July new-home sales, "combined with downward revision to earlier data, stand in stark contrast to the recent strong gains in the homebuilder survey," writes Joshua Shapiro, chief US economist at MFR Inc. Maybe July's an outlier, he says, but it's "certainly a warning signal" that conditions "are nowhere near as rosy as homebuilders, real estate agents, and their enablers in the media are so keen to represent." Not to mention, MBA data show weaker mortgage applications for purchases in recent months, suggesting that higher interest rates are having an impact on demand, "and also highlighting the fact that speculative demand continues to be the main driver of the existing home market." (john.shipman@wsj.com)

10:48 EDT - Gold prices are sharply higher as the annual rate of US new-home sales posted its steepest drop in 3 years last month. While the FOMC minutes on Wednesday offered no new clues as to the Fed's likely action on stimulus in September, traders remember his mantra about looking at economic data for guidance. With new-home sales plunging, some gold bugs are clearly hoping the Fed will stay the course at next month's meeting and keep supportive measures in place a while longer. Comex December gold is up 1.7% at $1,394.10/troy ounce. (tatyana.shumsky@wsj.com @MissShumsky)

Even in today's rebounding housing market, there's not a ton of new homes being sold each month, so it would stand to reason it's not that hard to get good reads--even initially--on activity. That's what makes the size of June's revision, cutting the annualized sales rate for the month 8.5% from initial data a month ago, so shocking. On an unadjusted basis, the Commerce Department said in July that 48K new homes were sold in June. Today, that number has been cut to 43K, with the biggest change coming in the South's numbers. And May's total has been dropped yet again, from 45K initially to 43K last month to 41K in today's report. July's initial number is 35K; what's the chance that doesn't get revised notably? (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

title: DJ MARKET TALK: Brazil  Currency  Move to Calm Market Short Term
text:
8:25 EDT - Brazilian Central Bank's $60B intervention scheme unveiled late yesterday should calm the local currency market short term, but its efficacy could be limited further out barring deeper changes in economic policy, Espirito Santo Investment Bank says. Namely, a reining-in of domestic demand, without which the current-account balance could further deteriorate. "But the recent currency moves were not being driven just by economic fundamentals, and it was bound to provoke an economic disruption if the government did not act," bank says. Real opens sharply stronger, recently trading at BRL2.3897 to the dollar. (paul.kiernan@wsj.com)

8:19 EDT - Down 13% the past 2 1/2 weeks, much of it following this week's downbeat F2Q report, Dick's (DKS) is liable to stay in the doghouse "until earnings growth re-accelerates and again tops expectations," says Oppenheimer as it downgrades the retailer to perform and cuts its price target to $44 from $56. A rebound could take a while as the investment bank anticipates "a potentially waning product cycle in categories such as golf, increasing competition and merchandising challenges in fitness to constrain topline growth." As such, "we remain concerned that slower trends lately in the sporting-goods sector could lead to more-aggressive promotions in coming months as retailers attempt to drive stronger traffic." DKS closed Thursday at $46.49. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

8:14 EDT - Raymond James cuts Pandora (P) to market perform from outperform, citing mainly valuation after shares have run up more than 135% YTD. P's 2Q results were strong, RJ says, "driven by increasing mobile monetization (mobile revs up 92% y/y) and lower content costs," though 3Q EPS guidance is below the firm's and Street's views due to increased investments. RJ also says listener metrics slowed in 2Q, "and the launch of Apple's iRadio (expected in September), could create some headline risk for shares." P down 6.6% premarket at $20.28. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

7:54 EDT - As constrained overhead costs helps ANN post a strong F2Q EPS beat, same-store-sales growth was underwhelming versus consensus views. But merchandise margins rose from a year ago, showing the Ann Taylor and Loft operator hasn't resorted to major discount in efforts to stoke demand. Whether ANN will be able to continue that is at question as Loft inventories jumped 18% while they rose 11% at the chains' outlets. With such locales posting SSS declines last quarter and Loft's regular stores logging 3.7% growth, supplies built up during the summer and will need to move. And while posting a muted 3Q sales view and again trimming the year's target, investors are liable to overlook the EPS beat today. ANN, inactive premarket, is up 2.9% this week. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

Crucially, it "doesn't look like government [is] trying to impact the currency too hard." (matthew.cowley@wsj.com)

The entity long ago stopped being a core business of QCOM, but today's announcement is still a guidepost in a tech company's ability to transition and essentially come to lead in a new market, as QCOM has with cellphone chips. But inventories appear in check, meaning markdown risks should be limited for the time being. FL, down 5.9% this month, is inactive premarket. Shares have gone nowhere the past year. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

Chances that Brazil will raise gasoline, diesel prices are rising, despite persistent inflationary pressures that have made the government reluctant to approve increases, says Banco Itau Chief Economist Ilan Goldfajn. Goldfajn notes the big differential between domestic and international fuel prices, which is hurting state-run oil company Petrobras (PBR, PETR4.BR). BRL's recent losses against USD of about 8% this week is also causing fuel-price spread to widen. But with inflation at 6.15% through mid-August, the government in a "difficult" spot, Goldfajn says. "We're not seeing major outflows of dollars," says Goldfajn. "What we're seeing is a lot of action on the futures market. Everybody wants to be hedged." The pressure on the futures market has led Brazil's central bank to intervene there, rather than in the spot market, using foreign-exchange swap contracts to help contain the real's decline.
