title: UPDATE 2- Brazil central bank  launches $60 bln  currency intervention
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank announced a currency-intervention program on Thursday that will provide $60 billion worth of cash and insurance to the foreign-exchange market by year-end, a move aimed at bolstering the country's currency, the real, as it slips to near five-year lows against the dollar.

The bank said in a statement it will sell, on Mondays through Thursdays, $500 million worth of currency swaps, derivative contracts designed to provide investors with insurance against a weaker real. On Fridays, it will offer $1 billion on the spot market through repurchase agreements.

Both are designed to prevent companies and individuals with dollar obligations from scrambling to the market at the same time, afraid that waiting will force them to pay more to buy dollars. When that happens, the real tends to weaken further and faster.

"This shows the firm determination of monetary authorities to keep the exchange rate from slipping further," said Andre Perfeito, chief economist with Gradual Investments in São Paulo.

The program starts on Friday and runs until December, the central bank said, adding it may announce additional auctions if it sees fit.

The move comes as the government seeks ways to control inflation and keep the real from sliding while at the same time trying to kick-start an economy that has stagnated despite a rapid expansion of credit. While a weaker real can help Brazil's export of commodities and manufactured goods, it makes raw materials and other imports more expensive, helping drive inflation higher.

Brazil cut its outlook for gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 2.5 percent from 3 percent in 2013 and to 4 percent from 4.5 percent for 2014, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said in an interview with Brazil's Globo Television Network late on Thursday.

For Perfeito, the move signals the central bank's intention to limit interest rate hikes. In addition to controlling inflation, higher rates would attract investment to Brazil, helping the real firm against the dollar. At the same time higher rates could also slow growth by making borrowing more expensive.

"I think that this is an effort to adjust expectations a bit because $60 billion is a lot," Perfeito said. "This kind of attitude just before a Copom meeting shows that exchange rate controls won't be carried out only through monetary policy."

The bank's Copom monetary policy committee, which sets Brazil's benchmark rate, meets on Aug. 28.

Interest-rate futures contracts suggest that there is a 76 percent chance that the central bank will raise the benchmark Selic target rate half a percentage point to 9 percent and a 24 percent chance of raising it 1.25 percentage points to 9.25 percent, according to Thomson Reuters data.

The real's weakening and the Copom meeting come as the United States' central banking authority, the Federal Reserve, is moving closer to ending a bond-buying program that has injected billions into the U.S. economy driving down interest rates.

As a result investors have been searching for higher-yielding, emerging market securities.

With the end of the Fed's "quantitative easing" program expected soon, capital flows have flowed out of emerging markets such as Brazil and back to the United States and other developed countries, helping to weaken the real.

"Today, the big problem is there is a structural change (in the world economy)," said Eduardo Velho, chief economist with Miami-based investment bank INVX Global Partners LLC, in São Paulo. "The central bank's move is an important measure to reduce volatility and slow the pressure on the exchange rate. I see this as positive."

On Thursday Brazil's real firmed 0.1 percent to 2.4305 reais to the dollar.

title: Brazil  Central Bank  to Hold Regular  Forex  Auctions to Offer Hedge
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's central bank will hold regularly scheduled auctions of foreign exchange swaps and credit line repurchases in order to offer hedge and liquidity to the local market, the central bank announced Thursday.

The bank said it will hold regular auctions beginning Friday and extending through Dec. 31.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real sinks to near 5-year low after Fed minutes
text:
(Recasts, updates throughout) MEXICO CITY, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's real plunged to a near five-year low on Wednesday, leading losses across Latin American currencies as investors looked at the minutes of the U.S. Federal Reserve's latest policy meeting for clues as to the timing of a stimulus wind-down. The Mexican peso and the Brazilian real have tumbled for at least six of the past seven sessions on fears that the Fed is about to cut back on its bond-buying program, which for years has provided a steady source of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets. Minutes from the Fed's July meeting, released on Wednesday, showed members of the Federal Open Market Committee had different opinions as to when the Fed should start winding down its bond purchases. The overall view, however, was that the statement did not materially change the market's expectation of a September tapering.

 The Brazilian currency plummeted 2.3 percent to close at 2.4501 per greenback, its weakest level since December 2008. The real's tumble prompted the central bank to announce it would offer to sell up to $4 billion on the spot market through repurchase agreements on Thursday, the second time this week that the bank has resorted to this form of intervention. Brazil's central bank has been selling swaps in the futures market to provide investors with a hedge against a further depreciation of the real, which has already lost more than 18 percent of its value since the beginning of May. Mexico's peso slid 2.23 percent to 13.27 per dollar, its lowest level and biggest drop since late June. Also weighing on the Mexican peso was local data showing retail sales were stagnant in June, one day after the government lowered its 2013 growth estimate to 1.8 percent from 3.1 percent on disappointing growth data. The Fed's program currently injects $85 billion a month into the market, and investors and economists forecast it could be reduced by something between $10 billion and $20 billion as of next month.

title: DJ  Brazil  Central Bank  to Buy Back Dollars at BRL2.5179, BRL2.4674
text:
"Brazil Central Bank to Buy Back Dollars at BRL2.5179, BRL2.4674," at 11:11 a.m. EDT, misstated in the fourth paragraph that the central bank bought dollars for 2.399 reais. The central bank sold dollars for 2.399 reais.

SAO PAULO--Brazil's central bankintervened for a second and third time in the country's foreign-currency market on Tuesday to rollover expiring swap contracts and to sell dollar credit lines.

The bank sold all of the 20,000 swap contracts that it will use to replace existing contracts that expire at the start of next month. The bank sold $986.3 million in the swap auction.

Earlier in the day, the central bank held a swap auction at which it sold $993.4 million in new swap contracts, placing all 20,000 contracts it offered. The swap contracts allow investors with bonds linked to local interest rates to exchange them for paper indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auctions typically help the real appreciate against the U.S. dollar by offering investors increased options for hedging the greenback.

The central bank also offered dollar credit lines at a Tuesday auction. The bank sold dollars to the market, with the promise to buy back the dollars in January and April of next year. The bank bought dollars for 2.399 reais and committed to repurchasing those dollars on Jan. 2 for a price of BRL2.4674 per dollar, the central bank said Tuesday. On April 1, it will buy back dollars at BRL2.5179.

The central bank has been picking up the pace of intervention in recent days as it tries to slow the slide in the country's currency.

Despite the central bank's intervention, the real remains close to its weakest level since March 2009. The real was trading at BRL2.4007 per dollar after the credit line auction, after opening the day at BRL2.3862 to the dollar.

The expected unwinding of easy-money policies in the U.S., together with sluggish growth at home and deteriorating government accounts, have caused the real to plunge against the dollar, making it one of the worst-performing currencies so far this year.

title: DJ Brazil's Real Ends Six-Session Losing Streak
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's besieged currency ended a string of six straight losing sessions against the dollar Tuesday as the central bank intervened--and speculative investors paused to mull a series of sharp warnings from local authorities.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.3964 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with its previous close of BRL2.4136. Monday saw the real settle at its weakest level in more than four years.

Brazil's currency, which until recently was considered overvalued by local exporters and industries, has seen far heavier losses than its counterparts in recent months, which threatens to fuel already-high inflation. The dollar has gained nearly 18% against the real in the past three months while advancing only 4.1% against the euro and 5.6% against the regional neighbor Mexican peso.

The real's decline had begun to steepen in the past few sessions, with the currency weakening to current levels from BRL2.2703 on Aug. 11. But a round of intervention by local authorities, combined with a growing view among market participants that the real had gone too far, helped to stop the bleeding Tuesday.

Brazil's central bankintervened to prop up the real three times Tuesday, holding two auctions of dollar-swap contracts and another auction of up to $4 billion in dollar credit lines. The former instrument helps investors hedge against currency fluctuations via the futures market, while the latter offers cash dollars that must be returned to the central bank at a later date.

In addition to intervening directly, Finance Minister Guido Mantega and Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini have both hinted this week that more forceful measures could be taken.

In a special statement posted on the central bank's website Monday, Mr. Tombini "reminded" market participants that "the concentration of positions in a single direction can bring losses to those that bet on one-directional movements of the currency."

Mr. Mantega, for his part, said in an interview Tuesday with the local Estado news agency that he's not worried about the currency, adding that authorities have sufficient tools at their disposal to deal with volatility.

"It's good to heed the warnings that, instead of making money, one can lose," Mr. Mantega said. "Just like the dollar goes up, it can go down. Whoever thinks they're just going to win can lose money in this game."

Brazil's central bank has yet to draw from its nearly $374 billion in international reserves to defend the currency, a move that has market participants divided as to its potential for success. Some say it could be perceived as a sign of vulnerability and launch an even greater speculative attack on the real.

Luiz Carlos Baldan, director of Sao Paulo's Fourtrade brokerage, disputed the strength of local authorities' verbal warning to the market as well as Mr. Mantega's claim that the situation is "under control."

"At this rate, a lot of people's forecast of BRL2.70 will come true very soon, and if the central bank finally decides to auction dollars at that point, it will be too late," Mr. Baldan said.

title: Real halts 6-day slide as  Brazil  steps up  currency intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's real gained for the first time in seven sessions on Tuesday after policymakers raised their rhetoric against currency speculators and the central bank stepped up intervention on the foreign exchange market.

The real opened higher following overnight comments by Finance Minister Guido Mantega and central bank chief Alexandre Tombini, both of whom advised investors to avoid strong bets against the real.

Their comments, which came on Monday after the real closed at its weakest level since March 2009, suggested they believed the currency had overshot as it plummeted nearly 6 percent during six straight sessions of losses.

Most emerging-market currencies have sold off over the past few days as investors prepare for an expected withdrawal of U.S. stimulus measures. The Brazilian currency has been specially hard-hit, however, as the country's slow-growing economy has fallen out of favor with investors.

After gaining more than 1 percent in the first hour of trading, the real shed some of its gains to rise a more modest 0.5 percent, at 2.4029 per dollar.

Also supporting the currency were two auctions of traditional currency swaps, derivatives that emulate an injection of dollars in the futures market, and a third auction of spot dollars through repurchase agreements.

"The real is gaining because the central bank is providing liquidity to both the spot and the futures market," said Sidnei Nehme, director at NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo. "By intervening in both markets, the central bank is breaking the leg of speculators."

In the first swap auction, the central bank sold 20,000 new contracts maturing on Jan 2. The second auction is designed to simply roll-over expiring maturities.

The central bank has been selling swaps in the futures market to provide investors with protection against a further depreciation of the real. They are part of a government strategy to ease demand for dollars without burning the country's $370 billion in foreign reserves.

Still, many analysts say that strategy has run its course as companies are unwilling to hedge again currency risk at current exchange rate levels. Instead, they say, demand is growing for dollars on the spot market.

In an attempt to satisfy that demand without depleting its reserves, the central bank is also selling up to $4 billion in spot dollars on Tuesday with repurchase dates set to Jan. 2 and April 1. It is the first time in two months that policymakers resort to this type of intervention.

Major regional currencies, such as the Mexican peso and the Brazilian real , posted gains for the first time in at least seven sessions as U.S. benchmark 10-year Treasury note yields dropped to 2.82 percent from Monday's close of 2.88 percent.

Investors had been dumping emerging market currencies in the past few days as expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will cut back on its bond-buying program have sent Treasury yields soaring to two-year highs, reducing the allure of higher-yielding assets globally.

Analysts said, however, that Tuesday's recovery could prove to be temporary as investor jitters are not going away anytime soon.

Crucial for investors' expectations about the future of U.S. stimulus measures will be the release on Wednesday of minutes of the Fed's latest monetary policy meeting.

* The Brazilian real ended 0.9 percent stronger after slumping some 6 percent over six consecutive sessions of losses. The currency was also supported by the central bank's active intervention amid policymakers' heightened rhetoric against speculators.

* In a strategy to shore up the currency, Brazil's central bankintervened in both the futures and spot markets, selling traditional currency swaps and spot dollars through repurchase agreements.

Rupee Hits Record Low as Tapering Expectations Prompt Selloff
text:
The Indian rupee sank to a record low Monday, leading a broad-based selloff of emerging-market currencies on expectations that the Federal Reserve will begin to wind down its fiscal stimulus as soon as September.

The Brazilian real hit a four-year low against the dollar, while the Turkish lira and Hungarian forint hit multiweek lows. Despite the absence of economic data from the U.S. on Monday, investors continued to gear up for the possibility of less Fed stimulus, which pushed U.S. Treasury yields higher and drove down emerging-market currencies and bonds.

Stronger U.S. economic data in recent weeks has reinforced expectations that the Fed will start to taper its $85 billion-a-month bond-buying program in September. This asset-purchasing program has kept rates low in the U.S. and increased liquidity across global markets, making emerging-market currencies more attractive to foreign investors.

"The market is yet again trying to gauge when Fed tapering will be happening," said Guillaume Salomon, emerging-market strategist at Societe Generale. "All of this is happening on the background of [Group of Seven countries'] yields going higher and becoming a competitor for emerging-market yields, especially when central banks have been cutting rates over the past couple of years. This is all quite a challenging environment for [emerging markets]."

Countries such as India that have large current account deficits have been particularly affected by the emerging-market selloff, as their currencies are seen as less resilient because these countries rely on foreign capital flows to fund their current-account gaps.

The dollar gained more than 2% against the rupee, to trade as high as INR63.58. It traded recently at INR63.33, according to CQG data.

Emerging-market assets took an additional hit after the Bundesbank said Monday that its forward guidance isn't set in stone, which the markets read as a hint that rates could rise earlier than expected.

The Indonesian rupiah slid to a four-year low Monday, falling 1.6% against the U.S. dollar, which bought IDR10,551.0. On Friday, data showed that the country's current account deficit widened to $9.8 billion in the second quarter from $5.8 billion previously, due to rising imports and declining exports.

Elsewhere in Asia, the Thai baht fell to THB31.410 against the dollar after Thailand's economic activity contracted by a seasonally adjusted 0.3% in the second quarter, meaning the country is technically in a recession. Exports fell 1.4% on the previous quarter on the back of waning demand from China, Thailand's largest market. The country's current account balance also swung into the red, printing a $5.1 billion deficit compared with a $1.3 billion surplus in the first quarter.

Commodity-linked Latin American countries, which rely heavily on exports, also suffered as Fed tapering concerns dragged down commodity prices. The Brazilian real weakened to a four-year low as the dollar climbed above BRL2.40 for the first time since March 2009. Despite repeated central-bank intervention, the real has continued to fall amid Brazil's waning growth potential, doggedly high inflation and a large current account deficit. Brazil's central bank stepped into the currency market three times Monday to sell foreign-exchange swap contracts aimed at stabilizing the real. The dollar bought BRL2.4145 late Monday, from BRL2.3927 the previous session, according to CQG.

The dollar gained some 1% against the Mexican peso, recently buying MXN13.0664. The greenback also climbed against the Chilean peso, changing hands at CLP518.80 compared with CLP512.70 late Friday.

The South African rand, which often acts as a proxy for other emerging-market currencies because it tends to move in line with broader market sentiment, fell almost 1% to the dollar, which bought ZAR10.1891.

In emerging Europe, the Hungarian forint fell to an eight-week low against the euro, which recently bought HUF300.40. The Turkish lira sank to one month-low against the dollar, which changed hands at TRL1.9535.

title: DJ Brazil's  Currency  Slides To New Low
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 8/20/13) 
   By Erin McCarthy 

Brazil's currency hit a new low against the dollar amid increasing concerns that the country's policy makers are failing to reinvigorate the South American economy.

The real weakened to 2.4098 to the dollar on Monday, trading above 2.4 for the first time since March 2009. The decline came on the same day the central bank held a series of auctions that injected $3.6 billion into the foreign-exchange futures market, in an attempt to bolster the real.

Latin America's largest economy is grappling with sluggish growth and high inflation, a combination that has left policy makers in a bind and Brazilian assets, including its currency, under pressure. The pace of the real's slide accelerated in late May, when U.S. Federal Reserve officials began to signal that the central bank was prepared to wind down its bond-buying program later in the year.

Investors anticipating higher interest rates in the U.S. began pulling money out of emerging markets, with already struggling economies such as Brazil hit hardest. Funds that buy Brazilian bonds have seen $918 million in outflows since late May, according to data provider EPFR Global.

Brazil's central bank has tried to fight the outflows by raising interest rates three times this year, raising the yields on the country's debt. It also has stepped up market interventions, pumping $7.6 billion into the currency-futures market in the past week and $45.8 billion since May 31. The real is down more than 10% over that period.

"They're intervening like crazy, and it's still not working," said Sara Zervos, portfolio manager of the $11.7 billion Oppenheimer International Bond fund. "It's gotten to the point where investors and even domestic citizens have lost confidence in the ability of the government to navigate the country into growth."

Her firm has been steadily cutting its holdings of the Brazilian real and real-denominated Brazilian government bonds.

The central bank will continue to offer liquidity to the market as needed, Alexandre Tombini, the bank's president, said Monday. Mr. Tombini also warned against betting too much on currency moves in one direction.

Analysts say the real's slide is unlikely to reverse until the economic outlook improves. Forecasters expect economic growth of 2.2% in 2013, according to a central-bank survey. That is up from last year but a far cry from the 7.5% growth in 2010. Meanwhile, inflation ran at 6.3% in July, near the top end of the government's target range. Brazil also swung to a $5 billion trade deficit through July, after a $9.9 billion surplus a year ago.

Barclays on Friday predicted the currency would hit 2.45 to the dollar in 12 months, from an earlier forecast of 2.20.

To be sure, the central bank says its interventions prevent dangerous levels of volatility, and a number of investors agree that there might otherwise have been even steeper falls in the real.

"Central-bank intervention is absolutely essential for controlling volatility," said Joao Paulo de Gracia Correa, foreign-exchange manager at brokerage Correparti. He said the currency could have fallen as low as 2.7 per dollar in the past two weeks without the central-bank auctions.

And since its interventions are in the futures market, Brazil isn't drawing on foreign-exchange reserves. Other emerging markets, including Turkey, have seen their influence weakened in the market as they spent reserves.

Some investors also are willing to put up with a sliding currency to take advantage of Brazil's 8.5% benchmark interest rate, one of the world's highest.

Peter Wilson, co-manager of Wells Fargo Advantage International Bond Fund, holds real-denominated debt, and recently exited from currency bets aimed at protecting against a drop in the real. He said he expects Brazil's economic problems to prove short-lived. "Over the longer term, we quite like" Brazil's bonds and currency, he said.

Still, others worry that the interventions are a half-step -- too small to support the real, but large enough to drive off investors by introducing uncertainty about policy makers' next move.

"When you do this enough in small sizes, it becomes counterproductive," said James Barrineau, a portfolio manager on the Schroder Emerging Markets Multi-Sector Bond Fund at Schroders PLC, which has $357.5 billion under management. He said the real could weaken beyond 2.5 per dollar "if policy makers sit on their hands."

Mr. Barrineau owns Brazilian government bonds, but last week started buying contracts that protect those holdings should the real decline further.

title: Brazil  Real Strengthens on  Central Bank 's  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real strengthened Thursday after an unexpected central bank auction of foreign exchange swap contracts.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.2830 to the dollar, stronger against the Wednesday close of BRL2.3086, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real strengthened slightly against the dollar in early trading as global investor sentiment improved. Investors were cheered by Chinese trade data showing a rise in imports by the Asian giant. Increased China demand brought a rise in global commodities prices. Brazil, in particular, benefits from greater Chinese demand since the Latin American country is a major exporter of farm commodities and mineral ores.

Early in the session, most traders had downplayed chances for central bank intervention Thursday, noting that the bank rarely intervenes when the Brazilian currency is strengthening.

Nevertheless, at noon local time, the central bank offered up to $1 billion in foreign exchange swap contracts at auction. The market bought $631 million in the contracts.

The auctions offers investors the opportunity to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar. The auctions typically strengthen the real by giving investors greater opportunities to hedge in the American currency.

"It [the auction] was a bit unexpected," said Mauricio Gaioti, a trader at Sao Paulo's Ouro Minas brokerage. "It shows that the government is very, very interested in pulling down inflation."

The Brazilian real has depreciated about 11% against the U.S. dollar so far this year, contributing to Brazilian inflation. The weak real makes imports more expensive, including key products such as fuels, wheat and components for everything from mobile phones to motor vehicles.

Inflation is currently running at 6.3%.

"Bringing down inflation is still the government's top priority," said Mr. Gaioti. However, he noted, such factors as increased risk perception by foreign investors could mean more U.S. dollar outflows from Brazil. "There is still a market trend toward weakening of the real," he said, predicting more central bank intervention in the coming weeks as the government fights down inflation.

title: WSJ Blog:Brazil's Former Central Banker Says Economic Woes Are Home-Grown
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's MoneyBeat blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/moneybeat/)

By Luciana Magalhaes

RIO DE JANEIRO -- The sluggish economic growth and high inflation fueling pessimism about Brazil are more self-inflicted than the result of outside influences, as the government has failed to restrain spending and curtail interventionist economic policies, according to Arminio Fraga, Brazil's former central bank president.

Sentiment over Brazil has swung from euphoria to pessimism in the space of two years, reflecting the ups and downs of the economy. After a surge back from the global crisis with 7.5% growth in 2010, two poor years have culminated in last year's growth of 0.9%. The outlook for 2013 isn't much better.

"Our main problems are internal, as always," said Mr. Fraga, also a former fund manager for billionaire George Soros, in an interview at his offices in Rio de Janeiro. "I would intuitively say that the order of magnitude is of four or five to one," he added, comparing the impact of domestic and international problems on the Brazilian economy.

The criticism of the administration of President Dilma Rousseff comes from an economist who ran Brazil's central bank from 1999 to 2002 under former President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. Mr. Fraga, 56 years old, won much credibility for re-establishing stability after the floating exchange-rate regime was adopted, and for introducing inflation targeting. Before that, he had worked for Mr. Soros and his Quantum Fund.

Mr. Fraga now runs Gavea Investimentos, a Brazilian asset-management firm he helped found in 2003, which has around $7 billion in assets under management. In 2010, J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. bought a majority stake in the firm.

External events seen affecting Brazil--slower growth in China, which consumes a lot of Brazilian raw materials, and a possible end to U.S. monetary stimulus--have been less of a problem for the South American country than its own failure to rein in inflation and curtail public spending, according to Mr. Fraga.

A reduction in Fed asset-buying, which could be seen as a positive sign of a healthier U.S. economy, could cause difficulties for bond markets that have benefited from abundant flows, he said. Brazil's dependence on China, meanwhile, is less than many think given its closed economy, he added.

Mr Fraga said he believes that since 2006, economic policy under former President Luis Inacio Lula da Silva and then under his hand-picked successor, Dilma Rousseff, has been much more statist, boosting the role of public-sector banks while showing less concern for the efficiency of business and leaving Brazil with inadequate infrastructure.

"This model hasn't been able to deliver the expected rate of growth," he said.

A spokesman for Mr. Silva said the former president declined to comment for this article. A spokesman for President Rousseff also didn't comment.

Mr. Fraga is most concerned about what he sees as a weakening of two of the three main pillars of the economy that were a key part of the legacy of the Cardoso administration: public spending restraints and inflation targeting. He is less concerned about the third pillar, the floating exchange rate.

The government needs to bring inflation down to the 4.5% target and then slowly begin reducing that target. "The government has been trying to secure inflation by managing prices, a recipe that's well known as doomed to failure," he said. Inflation is currently 6.4%.

Mr. Fraga thinks the central bank will likely have to raise interest rates further in the short term to quell inflationary pressures, but that over the long term, with a little more fiscal discipline, the trend should be for rates to fall.

Brazil's currency, the real, has weakened about 30% against the U.S. dollar over the last two years as the local economy has stalled and the U.S. economy has showed signs of recovery. The central bank's regular interventions in the currency market to iron out volatility have led some to suggest Brazil has abandoned the floating exchange rate, but Mr. Fraga disagrees.

"The central bank has said it doesn't have a goal, but the market understands that it has a goal," Mr Fraga said. "In practice, it's clear that it [the central bank] hasn't made a huge effort to meet a particular value for the currency. I can only speculate that it's concerned with volatility [when it intervenes], it's not a sign of desperation."

Recent protests saw hundreds of thousands of Brazilians pour onto the streets of cities and towns across the country to demonstrate against rising living costs and to demand better public services.

Mr. Fraga said the demonstrators were right to be angry: Taxes are very high, and people "have every right to complain about education, health and transportation."

On the positive side, he said the government has made some changes recently, such as resuming the sale of concessions for private-sector firms to explore for oil and to manage some of the country's largest airports, while also passing a law to encourage new investment in ports. Yet other harmful policies remain in place, such as a gasoline subsidy, which he said is "asphyxiating" the government-run oil company, Petroleo Brasileiro SA.

"It's too early to throw in the towel and say Brazil has problems that can't be solved," he said.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes at Four-Year Low Despite  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's currency swung sharply Wednesday, ending the session at its weakest level against the dollar in more than four years, amid aggressive intervention by the Central Bank of Brazil, although in a late-afternoon twist, it was U.S. monetary policy that ultimately set the tone.

In an unusually lively day of action, Brazil's central bank sold $2.25 billion in dollar-futures contracts, a move investors have said is designed to arrest some of the currency's depreciation. Brazil is once again caught in the global spotlight, struggling to avoid stagflation while the U.S. economy shows signs of a faster recovery than had once been expected.

"We think Brazil needs a weaker currency," says Marc Chandler, global head of currency strategy at New York-based Brown Brothers Harriman, adding that he sees the real headed for BRL2.40. "We suspect the intervention is really meant to smooth it out rather than reverse it."

With the U.S. Federal Reserve expected to begin removing some of its easy-money policies in coming months, Mr. Chandler said, emerging markets are losing their allure.

The monetary stimulus, which began during the 2008 financial crisis, left world financial markets flush with liquidity that often headed for emerging markets such as Brazil. Yet signs of stronger growth in the U.S. have fed expectations that the Federal Reserve may begin to cut back on its $85 billion in monthly asset purchases.

The outlook for the U.S. economy contrasts sharply with Brazil, where forecasts for growth this year have been slashed to around 2.3%, from around 4% at the beginning of the year. The once-dynamic South American economy, which expanded 7.5% in 2010, could be headed for a fourth straight year of growth below 4% if current expectations for this year and next play out.

The Brazilian central bank has expressed concern that currency weakness may hamper its efforts to curtail inflation, which is running at around 6.7% per year, well above authorities' 4.5% target.

On Wednesday, the central bank held three auctions to sell swap contracts, which give buyers an opportunity to protect themselves against abrupt foreign-exchange fluctuations and tend to prop up the real against the dollar. It sold $2.25 billion in total in the first two auctions, but decided not to accept any bids in the third auction. The central bank says it intervenes in the market to try to prevent too much volatility.

The move, however, was seen as particularly surprising given that the market was engaged in month-end jostling to set the exchange rate for settling futures contracts that expire Thursday. The central bank has in the past avoided intervention on these settlement days, preferring to let the market set the tone.

"I think we're going to continue seeing quite a lot of pressure on the Brazilian currency, which will also feed inflation," says Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora de Cambio Ltda. in Sao Paulo.

The central bank's auctions had some temporary effect on the real, sending it stronger against the dollar, although ultimately the currency continued to weaken, pushing up close to BRL2.2300.

Yet, in a final twist, the Federal Reserve on Wednesday confounded some of the expectations about U.S. economic growth. The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, in its statement, suggest growth was "modest" rather than "moderate." Investors immediately pushed back their expectations for when the stimulus would come to an end, and plowed money back into emerging markets. The real recovered most of the day's losses, ending at BRL2.2765 a dollar, compared with BRL2.2727 at Tuesday's close.

By Matthew Cowley

SAO PAULO--Brazil's currency recovered some of its early-morning losses against the dollar after unusually aggressive intervention by the Central Bank of Brazil, in a highly volatile session.

The monetary authority held three lightning dollar swap auctions Wednesday, as it sought to arrest the rapid depreciation of the real against the U.S. dollar. The exchange rate had slumped sharply ahead of data releases in the U.S., approaching BRL2.2300 per dollar.

At that point, the central bank stepped, and sold $1.491 billion in dollar swap contracts due Jan. 2 in the first auction and $757.5 million due Feb. 3 in the second auction. The central bank didn't accept any bids for the third auction.

These steps were separate from the auctions held in recent days, in which the central bank rolled over $5.7 billion in contracts that are due to expire on Aug. 1.

The swap contracts offer investors the opportunity to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar. They effectively offer investors a hedge against abrupt foreign exchange fluctuations and typically help support the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar.

The interventions were unusual given that monthly futures contracts expire Thursday. They will close out based on Wednesday's average foreign-exchange rate, known as the Ptax rate. The futures expiry often brings volatile trading as banks and investment funds jockey to influence the Ptax rate.

The central bank has in the past avoided stepping into the market on such days, although it did so at the end of June.

The real recovered some of its losses against the dollar, although it lost ground again after the result of the third auction was announced. by 11:09 ET, the real was trading at BRL2.2846 to-the-dollar, having earlier touched BRL2.2992, the weakest level since March 2009. text:
* Brazil central bankintervenes 3 times to support real

* Fed offers no hint of imminent stimulus tapering

* Real falls to lowest in over 4 years but then erases losses

By Walter Brandimarte and Bruno Federowski

RIO DE JANEIRO, July 31 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency ended little changed on Wednesday after heavy central bank intervention and a U.S. Federal Reserve decision to continue its bond-buying program propped up the real after it fell to the lowest in more than 4 years.

The Brazilian central bankintervened three times in the market during the morning as it fought to stop the real from weakening past the psychologically relevant mark of 2.3 per dollar - avoiding an additional currency depreciation that could add to inflation.

The interventions came right after the real slumped to as much as 2.3022 per dollar, its weakest level since April 1, 2009. The slide was magnified by investors trying to influence an official month-end exchange rate known as PTAX, which is reference for a broad range of contracts including foreign loans.

At the end of the day, the real closed 0.08 percent weaker at 2.2809 per greenback.

"The central bank wants to keep the exchange rate between 2.2 and 2.3 per dollar in order to avoid a very undesirable inflation pressure in the next few months," said Eduardo Velho, chief economist at INVX Global brokerage in Sao Paulo. "It looks like the central bank will fight hard to keep the currency at that level. The question is whether it will succeed. I believe it can win in the short term."

In two separate auctions, the central bank sold a total of 45,300 traditional currency swaps, derivative contracts that emulate an injection of dollars in the futures market.

However, it found no demand for the swaps offered at a third auction, leading some analysts to conclude that the operations served to provide enough liquidity to the foreign exchange market for now.

The central bank has been forced to provide dollar liquidity as investors anticipate a slowdown in the pace of U.S. bond purchases by the Fed. Part of the dollars the Fed has injected in the U.S. economy has been flowing to emerging markets during the past few years.

Speculation that the Fed would hint at reducing its stimulus program increased after data showed the U.S. economy unexpectedly accelerated in the second quarter.

The data showed U.S. gross domestic product expanded at a 1.7 percent annual rate in the second quarter, above the 1 percent rate forecast by economists and up from the first quarter's downwardly revised 1.1 percent expansion pace.

The U.S. economic picture was also brightened by a report showing the U.S. private sector added 20,000 jobs in July.

But at the end of its two-day meeting, the Fed said the economy is still in need of support and that it will keep buying $85 billion in mortgage and Treasury securities per month.

The government also cut its own growth estimates, now seeing the economy expanding 3% this year, down from the 3.5% previously. The government, seeing lower growth, said it would cut spending this year to ensure that it meets its primary surplus target. On Monday Finance Minister Guido Mantega said he would freeze BRL10 billion in planned spending this year, bringing the total amount of spending the government is freezing this year to BRL38 billion.

Further jolting markets was a third day of central bank intervention in currency markets. Since Thursday, the central bank has been holding foreign exchange-swap contract auctions to replace expiring contracts. Some $5.7 billion in such contracts are due to expire on Aug. 1, with another $5 billion expiring Sept. 2, and the bank has been acting daily to roll over those contracts and keep the market flush with dollars.

The swap contracts offer investors the opportunity to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar, and they effectively support the real against the dollar.

But what finally drove the real up against the dollar was disappointing data from the U.S., which showed existing-home sales fell 1.2% in June. Economists had predicted that sales would rise 1.9%, and the weak data drove down the dollar against most currencies. A weak U.S. economy means that the Federal Reserve is less likely to end its easy-money policies. "We're all in the same boat," he told reporters at an impromptu news conference. "Other currencies have also depreciated against the dollar. The stronger dollar is an international trend."

Finance Minister Mantega said "Investors have exaggerated somewhat. They are trying to get ahead of the Fed's decisions."

Mr. Mantega declined to comment on government intervention in the foreign exchange market. Brazil's central bank has intervened frequently in recent weeks in efforts to stem the often steep depreciation of the real against the dollar. title: WSJ Blog:Brazil's 'Cinderella Story' Gets Sidetracked
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's MoneyBeat blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/moneybeat/)

By Melvin Backman

Few emerging markets have taken it on the chin quite like Brazil.

A combination of internal turmoil and Fed-driven worries have punished one of the world's largest emerging markets more than its peers.

Its benchmark stock index, the Ibovespa, is scraping four-year lows and its currency, the real, is at an equally low point against the dollar since that time.

But have the travails created a buying opportunity? Or should investors wait for the dust to settle before deciding to get back into Latin America's biggest economy?

Since Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke first caused investors to fret about the end of QE on May 22, the Ibovespa has fallen 17.1%. By comparison, India and Peru, two emerging markets with high current account deficits and credit ratings hovering above junk status, have each seen their benchmark stock indices fall 7.1% and 8.3%, respectively.

But Brazil's problems extend beyond the past month. In the past year and a half, U.S.-based emerging market equities funds have averaged $3.5 billion in monthly inflows, according to Thomson Reuters data. U.S.-based Brazilian equities funds, on the other hand, coughed up $179 million on average every month during that period. While the MSCI Emerging Markets index eeked out half a percentage point in gains since Christmas 2011, the Ibovespa has tumbled by 19%.

This fall has put even the biggest emerging markets fans on edge. Win Thin, global head of emerging markets at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. and a self-described EM bull, said he's cautioning clients to stay away from Brazil for at least three to six months.

"Loose U.S. monetary policy (and elsewhere in G10, for that matter) was a big factor behind the EM rally," he wrote in an email. "Now that the easy money is getting less easy, we see outflows from most EM assets over the next couple of quarters."

The Brazilian IPO market got off to a record start this year, and looked to be on track to bounce back from a slow 2012. But the slide in Brazilian stocks has cooled the IPO market. In recent weeks, Votorantim Cimentos pulled its IPO, citing poor market conditions, and MoneyBeat reported that Azul has shelved plans for share sales.

Michael Fitzgerald, an IPO specialist and the chair of Latin American practice at law firm Paul Hastings, doesn't see things bottoming out for a while.

"In Latin America, I've given up looking into the crystal ball," he said. Offering his most educated guess: "I'm talking at least a two-year period."

While Brazil is getting caught up in the capital flight from emerging markets, its fundamentals are also contributing heavily to its market declines, evidenced by the looming possibility of an S&P downgrade.

"They're caught in a perfect storm of probably five bad winds," Fitzgerald said.

Rafael Dix-Carneiro, an assistant economics professor the University of Maryland, said the country has issues that run deeper than the much-publicized protests over corruption and bus-fare hikes. High inflation, depressed commodity prices and missteps from an interventionist government are weighing down growth, he said.

"Brazil still has serious structural problems, which casts doubt on how it will perform economically in the short to medium run," he said.

While the market perception of higher interest rates in the U.S. has aggravated the situation, Brazil's underlying economic problems are also reason for concern.

"The combination of inflation remaining above the central bank's comfort zone and economic growth projections that were recently revised down has seen dark clouds creeping over Brazilian markets," wrote Wisdom Tree analyst Rick Harper in a note to investors.

Brazil was once one of the poster childs for the emerging markets, but market activity has changed that view.

"There gets to be a growing sense that the Brazil Cinderella story has gotten sidetracked," Thin said.

text:
* Real tumbles to over 4-year low on Fed, China concerns

* Interest rate futures soar as weaker real seen fueling inflation

* Central bank intervenes with FX swaps, dollar sales on spot market

* Treasury repurchases local government debt to stabilize market

By Walter Brandimarte and Natalia Cacioli

RIO DE JANEIRO, June 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency fell sharply on Thursday and interest-rate futures soared for a second day, defying government efforts to stabilize both markets, as investors fret about a likely withdrawal of U.S. stimulus and an economic slowdown in China.

The real closed 1.6 percent lower at 2.2568 per dollar, its weakest level in more than four years, complicating government efforts to rein in inflation. Since the beginning of May, the real has lost more than 11 percent.

The currency rout deepened a day after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the U.S. central bank will probably reduce its stimulus program this year and finish it by mid-2014. The Fed's stimulus has kept U.S. interest rates low for years, supporting investor appetite for emerging-market assets.

Chinese factory activity slowed in June to a nine-month low, adding to worries about slower demand from the main market for some of Brazil's principal exports such as iron ore and soybeans.

"Markets are going through a panic moment. The central bank, within its possibilities, is doing its job (to calm down investors) but the sentiment is pretty bad," said Glauber Romano, a trader at the Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Earlier on Thursday, Brazil's central bank sold 30,000 traditional currency swap contracts due on Sept. 2 and another 30,000 contracts maturing on Oct. 1, a strategy that emulates the sale of dollars in the futures market.

The contracts provide investors with a hedge, a kind of insurance, against further declines in the dollar. The intervention only briefly supported the real, however.

In early afternoon, the central bank returned to the market with an auction of as much as $3 billion directly on the spot market, in an attempt to provide temporary dollar liquidity to the system.

The bank said it intended to sell the greenbacks with repurchase agreement dates set for September 3 and October 1.

INTEREST-RATE FUTURES SOAR

The rout in the currency market contributed to pushing interest-rate futures sharply higher on the BM&FBovespa exchange.

Investors fear that the sharp depreciation of the real will further stoke inflation by increasing the price of imported goods, forcing the central bank to increase its benchmark Selic interest rate more aggressively.

The spike in interest-rate futures came in spite of news that Brazil's two biggest cities agreed to revoke an increase in public transportation fares following nationwide protests against poor public services.

Lower bus fares should reduce the benchmark IPCA inflation index by 0.1 percentage point, calculated Daniel Cunha, an economist with XP Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

The move seemed insufficient to ease concerns about the long-term inflation trends. Reports of heavy selling of domestic government bonds by foreigners also contributed to the increase in local interest rates, traders said.

In an attempt to stabilize the secondary market for domestic debt, the Brazilian Treasury conducted extraordinary auctions to repurchase government bonds for the second time this week, resorting to a strategy it had not used since 2008.

"After the Fed statement, we understand the market needs price parameters," said a Treasury official who asked not to be named. "That is the reason for those extraordinary auctions."

On Thursday, the Treasury bought back a little over 1 million LTN and NTN-F notes, fixed-rate debt instruments regularly sold by the government. It had initially offered to repurchase as much 4 million of such notes.

It also bought back 240 million inflation-protected NTN-B notes, out of an initial repurchase offer of up to 2 million of those instruments.

Additional repurchase auctions of LTN, NTN-F and NTN-B will be held on Friday, the Finance Ministry said in a statement.

text:
* Fed likely to reduce stimulus this year, end it by mid-2014

* Brazil real slumps to weakest level since April 2009

* Central bank refrains from intervening to curb FX slide

By Bruno Federowski

RIO DE JANEIRO, June 19 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency slumped nearly 2 percent on Wednesday to close at a more than four-year low after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke suggested the bank's stimulus program, which has supported investors' appetite for emerging market assets, could end within the next 12 months.

The real closed at 2.2198 per dollar, its weakest since the end of April 2009 and down 1.9 percent for the day, as investors feared a reduction in U.S. stimulus measures would ease the flow of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets.

The currency had firmed slightly earlier in the session as exporters decided to take advantage of the real's recent slide to sell some dollars. But gains vanished in the afternoon after the Federal Reserve said in a statement that downside risks to the U.S. economic outlook had diminished since the fall.

The selloff gained traction after Bernanke said that, if economic forecasts are correct, policymakers will likely reduce the pace of bond purchases this year, before ending the program by the middle of next year.

"First, the Fed brought more positive (economic) forecasts and then Bernanke said the bank is nearing the moment to cut down on stimulus," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

"I expected Bernanke to calm down investors who were worried about a reduction in the purchases (of bonds), but he indicated that those investors are on the right track."

After Wednesday's slump, the real has weakened about 9 percent since the beginning of May, when it was trading around 2 per dollar.

Despite the sell-off, Brazil's central bank did not intervene in the market, a sign that policymakers considered the real's depreciation in line with that of other currencies. In Mexico, the peso also slid more than 2 percent after Bernanke's comments.

title: Brazil's Tombini: Global Liquidity Won't Disappear Suddenly
text:
BRASILIA--The world will have high levels of liquidity for quite some time, but the Brazilian central bank will be ready to intervene in currency markets if volatility gets too intense, said Brazil's central-bank president Alexandre Tombini on Tuesday.

In a regular testimony to senators, Mr. Tombini said that inflation "is and will remain under control."

The IPCA price index, closely monitored by the monetary authority, has been around 6.5%, the top of the bank's targeted range. As a result, interest rates were upped to 8% in May, from 7.5%. New increases are expected.

Mr. Tombini said the central bank "is vigilant and will do what is needed in a timely fashion" to bring inflation down.

The bank has also been very active in currency markets for the past two weeks, as investors sold off Brazilian reais and other emerging-market currencies. The trend was sparked by a perception that the U.S. Federal Reserve will reduce monetary stimulus in place since the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.

Mr. Tombini said the bank's interventions are meant to "remove volatility when we think it is excessive," but that the policy is to let the real float. "We have a floating [currency] policy...to absorb positive shocks as well as negative ones," he said.

title: Brazil  central bank  sees 'no limits' for interest rate hikes -paper
text:
* Tombini hints Selic could go back to double-digit levels

* C.bank to keep intervening in currency markets

SAO PAULO, June 17 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank will not shy away from hiking interest rates back to double-digit levels if inflation fails to slow, president Alexandre Tombini said in an interview published on Monday by a local newspaper.

"Monetary policy will do what needs to be done," Tombini told Valor. When asked if it could raise the Selic rate back to double-digit levels, he replied: "We don't have a limit, nor a budget (for the rate hike cycle)."

The central bank raised its benchmark Selic rate to 8.00 percent last month, the second increase in a row, after slashing it to 7.25 percent last year to boost the economy. Economists expect the bank to raise them to 9 percent in coming months, according to a weekly central bank survey.

Benchmark interest rates in Brazil have stayed above 10 percent for most years since the country's real currency was adopted in 1994.

Creating the conditions for keeping rates below that level was championed as one of President Dilma Rousseff's main achievements until high inflation started to eat into her record-high popularity rates and erode businesses' confidence.

Tombini also reiterated that the central bank will intervene in currency markets to reduce volatility, selling dollars in the spot market, offering swap contracts or auctioning off credit lines in dollars. The exchange rate will remain flexible, though, according to the interview.

"You never know if the exchange rate will go to 2.15 (per dollar), if it will improve, or if it will head towards 2.20."

Tombini also played down concerns about the impact of any measures by the U.S. Federal Reserve to scale back the massive stimulus offered in recent years to prop up its economy.

Fears of an imminent reversal of those policies have sent the real and other emerging market currencies lower in the past few weeks as investors anticipated capital outflows from developing countries.

"We know how to manage cashflows and we know how to manage money markets in times of stress. We were born in such environment," Tombini said.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Sharply Weaker as  Central Bank  Stays on Sidelines
text:
--Brazil's central bankintervenes after active trading closes

--Local currency market "anxious" ahead of U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, trader says

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.1734 to the U.S. dollar


 
  By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real ended sharply weaker against the U.S. dollar Monday as the nation's central bank opted to intervene in the local currency market after the session had ended.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.1734 to the U.S. dollar, weaker from Friday's closing price fix of BRL2.1439, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was the real's weakest level since May 2009.

However, Brazil's currency recovered slightly in after-hours trading after the central bank sold the equivalent of $1.96 billion in currency swap contracts. The real was at BRL2.1629 per dollar as of 2020 GMT. The swap contracts offer investors the opportunity to exchange bonds indexed to domestic interest rates for paper tied directly to the U.S. dollar. In essence, the swaps increase the market availability of financial instruments hedged in U.S. dollars. Typically, the swap auctions lead to a weakening of the U.S. dollar and a strengthening of the Brazilian real.

Central bankers had remained on the sidelines during Monday's session as the real weakened past the key BRL2.15 level. The decision to stand pat was criticized by traders, who noted that the bank had intervened last week when the real reached similar levels.

"This is really strange," said Marcos Trabbold, chief of operations at Sao Paulo trading house BT Associados. "The central bank shouldn't let the currency reach these levels because it doesn't benefit anybody."

The weaker real only adds to Brazil's inflationary pressures, with consumer prices in May rising at the 6.5% ceiling of the central bank's target range for inflation, Mr. Trabbold added.

When the real breached BRL2.16 and quickly followed that move up with a jump past BRL2.17, the market showed that it was "demanding liquidity" that only the central bank could provide, Mr. Trabbold said. But only after the session ended did the central bank step in.

Traders were expected to test the central bank during Monday's session amid expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve, which is meeting this week, will give global markets a signal that the monetary authority will start to taper its asset-buying program known as quantitative easing. The Fed will release its policy statement Wednesday, followed by comments from Chairman Ben Bernanke.

The expected end to easy global monetary policy, which has allowed foreign investors flush with cheap cash to seek out higher rates of return in emerging markets such as Brazil, has caused the real in recent sessions to slide to its weakest level against the dollar in four years.

"The market is very anxious about the results of the meeting," said Reginaldo Siaca, foreign-exchange manager at Sao Paulo's Advanced brokerage. While trading fundamentals weren't behind the real's sharp move Monday, Mr. Siaca warned that the real could lose its "reference point" and decline to BRL2.20 per dollar if the central bank fails to stem volatility.

Also overhanging the real was another downbeat outlook for the economy in the central bank's weekly market survey, released before trading started Monday. Economists and market analysts once again cut their forecast for economic growth this year to 2.49%--well off the 3.5% expected at the start of 2013. Estimates for year-end inflation rose to 5.83%, causing the outlook for interest rates to climb to 9%. Brazil's benchmark Selic base interest rate currently stands at 8% after the central bank implemented interest rate increases at its past two meetings.

In an interview with local newspaper Valor Economico, central bank President Alexandre Tombini indicated that interest rates would rise as much as necessary to force inflation to converge on the bank's 4.5% target. "Monetary policy will do whatever needs to be done," Mr. Tombini said. In May, inflation was running at the 6.5% ceiling of the government's tolerance range.

Typically, indications that local interest rates were trending higher would be enough to support the real against the dollar, but that is not the case right now, market watchers said.

"If the central bank doesn't intervene, the real is going to continue to weaken until the market is balanced," Mr. Trabbold said. The head trader estimated that the real could trade between BRL2.18 and BRL2.20 later this week without central bank action.

title: DJ  FX  HORIZONS: This Ain't No Emerging Market Crisis
text:
By Michael J. Casey

Don't confuse the recent rout in developing countries' currencies with an "emerging market crisis."

In a period of slowing global growth in which the Federal Reserve is seen reining in its monetary stimulus, most developing world governments are more than happy to see their currencies weaken. In fact, it's part of a natural and necessary rebalancing in the world.

As U.S. bond yields rise and American growth prospects appear to outshine those of other places, money is being reallocated back to dollar assets. Meanwhile, with the Japanese yen still down 20% from its lows of September, emerging market producers are worried about lost competitiveness for their exporters. It's why many central banks are holding off on intervention and letting their currencies fall. Softer exchange rates are just what the doctor ordered.

That is, unless you belong to a group I'll call the TIBS.

With apologies to Jim O'Neill of BRICS coinage fame and to whomever came up with that jarring PIGS acronym, TIBS stands for Turkey, India, Brazil and South Africa. The currencies of these countries have borne the brunt of the emerging market selloff this month. That's because domestic political and economic problems make them more vulnerable to outflows of money--to the point that the currency sell-off risks igniting national crises. The TIBS are the exceptions that prove the rule.

Turkey, India and Brazil have all aggressively intervened in foreign exchange markets to bolster their flagging currencies. They simply can't afford to take the sanguine view of depreciation that, say, Chile or Malaysia are taking.

In Brazil's case, it's an inflation problem. Brazil's failure to tackle rigidities in its labor market has left its inflation rate at the very top of its central bank's acceptable range, which is why it hiked rates by an unexpectedly large half-percentage point two weeks ago even as economic growth was showing signs of grinding to a halt. The last thing the central bank needs is a plunging Brazilian real, which would generate inflation via higher import prices.

Turkey and India, the other prominent interveners, have successfully beaten back the inflation bogey that nagged them two years ago, but the legacy of that fight and the problem of large current-account deficits mean investors continue to fear a loss of market confidence in the Indian rupee or Turkish lira. (Complicating matters for Turkey is the political uncertainty sown by the violent protests against Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan.)

The TIBS member that's really in trouble, however, is South Africa. As with Brazil, South African inflation is stubbornly high -- just a hair below 6%, the top of the central bank's target range. But unlike the other three countries, it doesn't have a deep pool of dollars with which to prop up the South African rand. Following a 4.3% plunge last month, the country's foreign exchange reserves stood at a modest $48 billion at the end of May. It means that South Africa's authorities can only pray that the rout in the rand doesn't go so far as to fuel imported inflation. That would simply add to the country's long list of problems, which include industrial strife in its all-important mining sector and international declines in prices of the minerals its sells.

Yet one of the principal causes of South Africa's pain--a slowdown in China--provides a kind of mixed blessing to other emerging markets. Few are happy about weaker Chinese demand, of course, but at least it means they don't have to worry about inflation. Over the weekend, China reported that producer prices were down 2.9% on the year. For a country that manufactures so much of what we all buy, that's a powerful disinflationary force to unleash on the world. It means that for almost all countries outside the TIBS group, emerging market currencies will be free to keep falling if they have to.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Stronger as Markets Recover, Measures Awaited
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened for a second day on Wednesday as investors await new measures by the Brazilian government to encourage inflows and as global markets recovered from the previous day's volatility.

The real opened at 2.1244 per dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, stronger than the previous day's close at BRL2.1355 to the dollar.

Many investors were expecting the government to announce Tuesday that they would ease taxes and other restrictions on currency inflows. Finance Minister Guido Mantega met with President Dilma Rousseff during the day, but didn't introduce any changes in policy. The last time the two met, Mr. Mantega said the government was reducing the so-called IOF tax on fixed-income investments held by foreigners -- a measure put in place originally to keep the real from strengthening too quickly.

According to analysts, the market is still expecting some easing of rules to encourage the entrance of foreign investors, especially as the Federal Reserve gives signals it will reverse stimulus measures. Those stimulus measures encouraged investment in emerging markets, and their possible end is expected to bring a massive slowdown in the flow of money to those markets.

After the massive sell-off of emerging markets on Tuesday, Brazil rebounded Wednesday along with a number of other currencies. The Indian rupee, the South African rand, the Turkish lira and the Mexican peso also partially reversed losses on Wednesday.

The repeated interventions in the currency market by Brazil's central bank in recent days is also keeping the real relatively in line. After the currency weakened to the lowest level against the dollar in four years earlier this week, the central bank carried out a number of auctions of foreign-exchange currency swap contracts. The swap contracts have the effect of adding dollars to the market and strengthening the real.

After two months without such auctions, the central bank piled on in the last two days, holding two auctions a day to contain weakness and signaling to the market that it wouldn't allow too much weakness in the real.

title: DJ Emerging Markets See Money Exit
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 6/12/13) 
   By Alex Frangos and Daniel Inman in Hong Kong and Patrick McGroarty in Johannesburg 

Money streamed out of emerging markets Tuesday, destabilizing currencies, sinking stocks and creating headaches for policy makers already worried about faltering growth.

In the latest signs of turmoil, highflying stock markets fell sharply in Asia, while currencies in South Africa, India and Turkey reeled in the face of a surging U.S. dollar. Mexico's peso, which just a month ago was trading at its strongest level in almost two years, moved to its weakest level since late November.

Emerging-market currencies rebounded somewhat in New York trading hours but remained broadly weaker on the day. The volatile trading reflected the difficulties investors face in trying to predict when developed-world banks might start to withdraw stimulus and how such moves will ripple across global markets.

Yields on U.S. Treasury bonds have risen as investors gird for the possibility that the Federal Reserve could ratchet back the monthly bond purchases it has been making in a bid to stimulate growth. That, along with a sense that the U.S. economy is outperforming the rest of the world, is making U.S. assets and the greenback look more attractive than relatively risky emerging-market stocks and currencies.

An exodus from emerging markets threatens to hurt the financing and growth prospects of developing economies that have come to rely on large inflows of foreign capital in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Investors' nervousness was exacerbated Tuesday by a continuation of weak economic data from emerging economies. The Philippines said exports dropped 7% in April compared with the year before, reinforcing a global slowdown in trade. Unrest in Turkey, investor disappointment over a Bank of Japan decision to leave its bond-buying program unchanged and renewed concerns over Europe's efforts to repair its fragile financial system added to the mix.

Asian stock markets were among the first hit. Thailand's benchmark index fell 5%, while the Philippines' sank 4.6%, the worst day for both markets since late 2011. Indonesia's lost 3.5%.

"It feels like the party is ending," said Howard Wong, managing director at Doric Capital Corp. in Hong Kong.

Facing the loss of foreign capital, central banks in these emerging markets have scrambled to prop up their home currencies.

India's central bank dove into foreign-exchange markets Tuesday to stop the rupee's slide at a record low of 58.98 to the dollar before it recovered. Pressured to attract capital to the country, a top Indian economic official promised a new round of measures to allow foreign investment in currently restricted parts of the economy.

Turkey's central bank on Tuesday announced new measures to attract capital after spending much of the past four years trying to stop too much money from flooding into its economy. That helped to stem the lira's fall to near a multiyear low against the dollar as police moved in on protests in Istanbul. Turkey's capital measures echoed Brazil's move earlier this month to eliminate a 6% tax on foreigners' bond investments.

Meanwhile, Poland's central bank said last week that it sold foreign currency to prop up the tumbling zloty.

But the capital exodus has continued apace, especially for economies heavily dependent on commodities, whose prices have been falling. Foreigners have been selling local mining stocks and countries' prospects for generating foreign exchange through commodity exports appear weaker than before.

In platinum- and gold-rich South Africa, the rand fell nearly 2% to 10.38 to the dollar, marking a 23% plunge from the beginning of this year, before recovering some of that ground. Australia, seen as a proxy for emerging markets in Asia because of its liquid currency and exposure to Chinese and Indian demand for its raw materials, also saw its currency plummet to its weakest point against the U.S. dollar since 2010. The Brazilian real faced fresh losses Tuesday as foreign investors continued to pull up stakes from Latin America's biggest economy.

Brazil's central bank stepped up intervention in the face of the rapid currency depreciation that began on May 28, with a series of five foreign-exchange swap auctions in two weeks. The auctions allow investors to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar. The auctions tend to stall depreciation, but not for long.

Just two months ago, a wave of money was coursing around the globe, searching for yield. The massive quantitative-easing program the Bank of Japan announced on April 4 coincided with a rate cut from the European Central Bank and expectations that the Federal Reserve would continue its $85 billion in monthly bond purchases for the foreseeable future.

Several things have changed. Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke telegraphed last month that bond buying could slow later this year. The Bank of Japan's liquidity boost has heightened turmoil in financial markets, with a spike in Japanese bond yields and a 20% selloff of Japanese stocks.

And there is mounting evidence that these economies just aren't growing as fast as people expected, while growth prospects in the U.S. are holding up, causing investors to favor U.S. assets over emerging markets.

Chinese data in recent days showed exports grew only 1% in May from the year earlier, the slowest pace in 10 months, weighed down by poor demand from ailing customers in Europe. Brazil and India are both suffering from slowdowns that have confounded policy makers and taken the shine off what had been among the most promising big economies in the world.

South Africa's central bank warned last week that growth this year will likely fall short of its already tepid forecast for gross domestic product to expand 2.4%. Thailand's central bank governor said on Monday that the bank would soon lower its forecast for 5.1% growth this year.

Dimming growth expectations have also prompted a number of interest-rate cuts to prop up economies in South Korea, India and Thailand, Turkey and Israel.

India's economy is among the hardest hit by the recent reversal in capital flows. The country's slow growth-- less than 5% annually in the past two quarters compared with nearly 10% a few years ago-- and the weak rupee have made a fragile economy more vulnerable.

A weaker rupee makes it more expensive to pay for critical imports such as oil and coal. It also widens the government's already-large deficit, much of which goes to pay for fuel subsidies. More expensive imports also exacerbate inflation, limiting the central bank's ability to cut interest rates to spur growth.

South Africa is battling the same contradictory forces. As growth slows, the South African central bank has been reluctant to cut interest rates because annual inflation is threatening to breach its target ceiling of 6%.

The outflows had been mostly orderly and some currency weakening was welcomed because over the long term it can make a country's exports more competitive globally. But the orderly pace changed Tuesday, when investors rushed for the exits.

"Until very recently the conversation was all about capital inflows causing asset-price bubbles," said Gareth Leather, an economist with Capital Economics in London. "It's switched very quickly."

title: Brazil  Finance Minister Mantega Sees Less  Intervention  in  Forex  Market - Report
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's government will intervene less in the foreign-exchange market, the country's finance minister said, even though the Brazilian real is facing pressure to depreciate amid a rising deficit in its overseas accounts.

"Despite the volatility, we now have a foreign exchange that's more flexible, more floating than at other times, with less intervention," Guido Mantega said in an interview published Thursday in the financial newspaper Valor Economico.

On Tuesday, the government stripped away a 6% tax called IOF on foreign purchases of local debt. The tax was originally put in place in 2010 to stabilize the nation's currency, the Brazilian real. Heavy financial inflows at that time were causing an unwanted currency appreciation and harming exports of the world's second-largest developing economy after China.

"We are gradually retiring the IOF tax. We had retired it in the past from investments in equities and now we retired it for investments in fixed income," said the minister, who highlighted that country's forex policy don't changed. "This is the same policy, adapted to the moment."

According to analysts, the move came as the deficit in the country's overseas transactions account is growing, and the government needs to attract dollars inflow.

Brazil's current account deficit, the sum of most non-investment capital inflows and outflows, widened to $70 billion in April, hitting the equivalent of 3% of gross domestic product for the first time since 2002. Last year, the deficit was $54 billion.

In past years, the current account deficit was offset by foreign direct investment, the kind of nuts-and-bolts factory expansion undertaken by foreign companies, as Brazil emerged as a source of growth while developed economies stagnated. But foreign direct investment, at $65 billion over the past 12 months, is no longer enough to close the gap.

Mr. Mantega said that in general the government is prompting less intervention on the forex market. "The central bank is not acquiring dollars [on the forex market]."

The Brazilian Central Bank had largely remained on the sidelines in recent weeks, despite the currency approaching the BRL2.15 mark. But a sharp sell-off in recent sessions forced the central bank to sell foreign-exchange-swap contracts, which typically cause the real to strengthen against the dollar.

Still, the central bank hasn't been accumulating foreign-exchange reserves. Total reserves so far this year fell around $4 billion to the current level of $374.9 billion.

Mr. Mantega said the measure isn't supposed to help with inflation, as that's the central bank's task, to be managed through the use of the key lending rate, the Selic.

"The central bank acted to contain accelerating inflation expectations and also to avoid a spread of inflation. It will not impact investments. This [Selic rate decisions] is a task of the central bank rate committee, not a task of President Dilma Rousseff nor mine," said Mr. Mantega.

Last week, the central bank surprised analysts increasing the Selic rate more than expected by 50 basis points to 8%.
