title: Brazil Takes Steps to Lure Back Foreign Capital
text:
After spending years discouraging return-seeking investors and their "hot money," Brazil is taking steps to lure foreign investment funds back.

But so far many investors aren't biting, underscoring the challenges facing the sixth-largest economy and policymakers struggling to rein in inflation in spite of subpar economic growth.

A day after Brazil's government abruptly scrapped a tax on bonds purchased with money coming in from outside the country, Brazil's currency neared a fresh four-year low. The tax was first implemented in October 2010 to fight off the billions of dollars of cash that was flooding Brazil's financial system and causing the real to strengthen, a situation that eroded the competitiveness of the country's exporters.

Abolishing the tax initially lifted the real when trading opened Wednesday morning. But the currency soon fell so far that Brazil's central bankintervened to support it. The real ended at 2.1325 per dollar, slightly stronger on the day.

The real's volatile performance on Wednesday was the latest sign that government and central-bank officials are finding their usual tools are proving ineffective at stabilizing financial markets. The currency has dropped 4% since the start of last week, even as Brazil's central bank hiked interest rates and intervened twice in the foreign-exchange market.

On Wednesday, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega called lifting the tax a "long-term measure" that wasn't aimed at boosting the real.

Brazil's government has slapped taxes on a growing list of financial transactions since October 2010, ranging from overseas credit card purchases to foreign loans. In each case, the intention was to avoid an unwanted appreciation of the real by slowing the inflow of foreign capital.

Lately, Brazil's had the opposite problem. Investors have pulled $916 million this year through May 29 from funds that mainly buy Brazilian bonds, compared with nearly $20 million in outflows during the same period last year. Those outflows could accelerate if the Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy later this year, analysts say.

Some investors say the removal of the tax may actually encourage further selling of Brazilian bonds in the short term. Worries have been growing that Brazil's high yields wouldn't be enough to compensate for a swiftly declining currency, worsening trade flows and stubbornly high inflation. Yet until now, some investors were reluctant to sell, as they would have had to pay a 6% surcharge to get back in should conditions improve.

Lifting the tax "is not going to be that big a game changer going forward," said Naveen Kunam, senior portfolio manager at ING Investment Management, which manages $179 billion in assets.. Mr. Kunam's firm owns Brazilian bonds denominated in reais, but has started to reduce its exposure.

Brazil's economy expanded by only 0.9% in 2012, and economists forecast growth of 2.5% this year. At the same time, Brazil is also suffering a renewed bout of inflation. The country's inflation rate is currently 6.5%, the top end of the range the central bank has said it will tolerate.

For much of the last year, Brazilian policymakers have been torn over whether to make boosting growth or lowering inflation a priority. Last week, the central bank hiked its Selic base interest rate a half percentage point to 8.0%, saying in a statement it will pursue its strategy of tightening monetary policy to keep a lid on rising prices. However, higher interest rates may make it even more difficult for the economy to grow.

Reflecting Brazil's dim prospects, Brazil's benchmark Ibovespa stocks index is down 13% this year, compared with a 16% increase in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

The government is betting that investors "will risk Brazil for better returns," setting aside worries about the country's sluggish economy to take advantage of higher yields than similar investments in emerging markets like Chile, Mexico and Turkey, said Durval Correa, a trader at Sao Paulo's MultiMoney brokerage.

The elimination of the tax could help lure investors back to Brazil if it makes progress on its other problems, said Michael Lee, a portfolio manager with Wells Fargo Advantage International Bond Fund, which manages $1.68 billion.

"Brazil still needs to do certain things to get their economy right, but compared to where yields are around the world, Brazil still looks attractive," Mr. Lee said. He's buying more real-denominated bonds now that the tax is lifted.

-Tom Murphy, Erin McCarthy, Prabha Natarajan and Rogerio Jelmayer contributed to this article.

title: Barron's Blog:Brazil Ends Tax on Foreign Investors, Stocks Fall
text:
(This story has been posted on Barron's Online's Emerging Markets Daily at http://blogs.barrons.com/emergingmarketsdaily/)

By Ben Levisohn

Foreigners can invest freely in Brazil again. The question now is if they'll want to.

Late yesterday, Brazil removed a tax on foreign investors that had been put in place to prevent a rush of short-term cash into that nation's financial markets. The Wall Street Journal has the details:

With Brazil's currency weakening, Finance Minister Guido Mantega Tuesday lifted a years-old tax on foreign bond buyers and other overseas investors...The tax was cut to zero from 6% because of changes in the global financial landscape, he said.

Talking to reporters after a meeting with President Dilma Rousseff, Mr. Mantega said the conditions that made his ministry levy the tax a couple of years ago are no longer in place. "We had a flood of capital," he said, referring to inflows of dollars in emerging markets from investors seeking better returns.

Marketfield's Micheal Shaoul ponders the timing:

Barclays' Guilherme Loureiro and Marcelo Salomon think the move could be counterproductive:

We welcome the move as it reduces the distortions created by penalizing flows into Brazil and believe that in the short run the currency will test again the 2.05 level against the USD. Moreover, the very attractive carry that Brazil offers could favor bull flattening of the curve. However, we are also of the view that zeroing the IOF tax eliminates an important barrier that prevented foreign investors from liquidating local rates positions (as they would have had to pay tax again to push money into Brazil). And the elimination of this barrier should, in fact, increase the volatility of USD/BRL, especially in moments of stress in global capital markets. While the decision to cut the IOF tax helps attract foreign flows, it also will demand more FX intervention from the BCB to dampen excessive volatility.

title: Brazil Real Falls After Official Says Weakening 'Inevitable'
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.1348/dollar

--Central bank director says weaker currency "inevitable"

--Central bank intervention seen less frequent in future


 
 By Paulo Winterstein 
 

SAO PAULO--Brazil's real weakened Tuesday after the director of monetary policy for the central bank said the currency's decline against the U.S. dollar was "inevitable," leading many traders to see room for a further drop in value.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.1348 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, after closing on Monday at BRL2.1253 per dollar.

The real opened stronger after statistics institute IBGE said output at Brazil's mines and factories rose considerably more than economists had expected in April. Industrial production rose 1.8% in April from March, more than the 1% month-on-month increase expected by economists polled by Brazil's Agencia Estado news service.

But the real weakened rapidly after Aldo Mendes, monetary policy director at the central bank, said global currencies are all weakening against the dollar, and so the real's weakness is inevitable. "There's nothing I can do," he said about the real's weakness.

"The market was fine until these comments from Aldo Mendes," said Jose Carlos Amado, a fixed-income trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo. "He basically said that they're going to leave the currency alone since it's a general tendency."

Whereas in the past the central bank intervened in markets to contain sudden losses to the real, Tuesday's comments signaled that the central bank could stay on the sidelines in the near future.

"We only react when we aren't together with the others," Mr. Mendes said. "If we're moving in step with the other currencies of the world, there's no reason to enter the market."

Still, the real shied away from the mark of BRL2.15 per dollar, a level it last breached in 2009.

Last week, the real approached BRL2.15, but traders were surprised by a central bank intervention meant to strengthen the real.

Brazil last Wednesday reported weaker-than-expected growth in the first quarter, and that was quickly followed by a bigger-than-expected increase in the country's benchmark Selic interest rate. Concerned about faltering growth, investors on Friday sold off the real in droves. After the real traded as weak as BRL2.1443 per dollar, the central bank sold $877 million of foreign-exchange swap contracts--normally used to strengthen the real--and temporarily halted the decline.

Traders said that such auctions are uncommon on the last day of the month, when exchange rates for futures contracts are settled. As such, the auction signaled that policy makers are still reluctant to let the real weaken too quickly against the dollar, even though such weakness could help a recovery in Brazilian exports of manufactured goods. For the past six months, the government has tended to step in whenever the currency strayed too far from a range of BRL1.95 to BRL2.05 per dollar, but in recent weeks the government has let the real slide a bit more.

BRASILIA, June 2 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank chief on Sunday said  the recent weakening of the local real currency   should have "limited" impact on inflation, but that the bank is ready to step in if needed to stem currency volatility.

The real ended at 2.1412 per dollar on Friday, its weakest level since May 2009, because of increased global risk aversion on concerns of a possible withdrawal of U.S. stimulus measures and speculation by local investors about policymakers' tolerance to a weaker currency.

"This is a global movement of the U.S. dollar not something peculiar to Brazil," Alexandre Tombini said in comments provided by the bank's press office during a media briefing in Istanbul, Turkey. "Provided that the exchange rate regime is flexible as it is the case in Brazil the pass through should be limited."

Tombini was participating in a seminar organized by the central bank of Turkey in Istanbul.

The sharp weakening of the real could push up the value of imported goods, stoking already high inflation in the South American nation that only two decades ago was suffering with  hyperinflation.

To fight inflation the central bank on Wednesday surprised investors by speeding up the pace of its monetary tightening cycle with a 50-basis-points rate hike.

In theory, that rate hike should ease the pressure on the real as it increases the appeal of Brazilian fixed-income assets that lures more U.S. dollars into the local market.

However, neither the rate increase nor a central bankintervention in the market on Friday was able to prop up the real.

Tombini reiterated that the bank could intervene again to stem "excessive volatility" in the real via the sale of currency in the spot and future market as well as by providing dollar trade lines to exporters.

The central bank offered trade lines to Brazilian exporters in 2008 when external financing dried up during the global financial crisis.

31 May 2013 16:02 EDT DJ  Brazil Real Weakens to Lowest Level in Four Years

--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.1480/dollar

--Real at four-year low despite central bank action

--Investors worry about widening current account deficit

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real ended active trading Friday at a four-year low, with more losses possible next week as investors re-evaluate the country's economic and investment prospects.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.1480 to the dollar, considerably weaker than the Wednesday close of BRL2.1084. Thursday was a religious holiday with Brazilian financial markets closed.

The Friday value for the real was the lowest since May 2009, a period when Brazil was still suffering direct effects of the global financial crisis.

The real piled up losses Friday despite Brazilian Central Bankintervention. In early afternoon trading, the central bank held a spot auction of foreign exchange swap contracts, selling $876.7 million worth of the contracts.

Typically, the sale of swap contracts helps strengthen the real against the dollar by making more dollar-hedged bonds available to investors. In fact, the auction initially helped strengthen the real slightly against the dollar. However, in later trading, investors once again pushed up the value of the greenback against the Brazilian currency.

"This morning, there were those who said the real could depreciate to BRL2.20 against the dollar by the end of the year," said Mauriciano Cavalcanti, a trader at Sao Paulo's Ouro Minas brokerage. "Now, I would say we're going to reach BRL2.20 a lot sooner than that."

There are many reasons for the real's weakness.

"One reason is the fact that the U.S. dollar has been gaining against currencies world-wide," said Joao Paulo Correa, foreign exchange manager at the southern Brazilian brokerage of Correparti. "The Brazilian real is no exception to that trend."

Although economists differ on the timing, few disagree with the idea that the U.S. Federal Reserve will have to reverse its long-standing policy of monetary loosening. Once that happens, investors may end up flocking to U.S. investments, all but abandoning emerging markets.

That process may have already begun, according to Mr. Cavalcanti. "Next week, we may get a better idea of how that is affecting the Brazilian market," he said.

Because of the intense focus on the Fed, investors in Brazil effectively shrugged off Brazil's own interest rate hike, which was ordered on Wednesday night. The Brazilian Central Bank raised its base rate by a half point to 8.0% as part of a strategy against inflation.

The Brazilian rate hike had no effect on Brazilian foreign exchange trading Friday. However, it did hit hard at Brazilian stocks. In late afternoon trading, the benchmark Ibovespa index was down more than 2.5%, given that higher domestic interest rates will likely cause investors to shift from stocks to fixed-income investments.

Inflation is another of the factors making investors take another, and more skeptical, look at Brazil.

Brazil's inflation rate is currently running at a worrisome 6.5%. But economic growth in the first quarter was unexpectedly low, with the economy expanding only 0.6% against the fourth quarter of 2012, not the more robust 0.9% analysts had expected.

"This is the new strategy," said Paulo Faria-Tavares, managing partner of Sao Paulo's PTX Lending consultants. "Low growth and high interest rates."

Other problems include Brazil's fast-growing current account deficit. The deficit widened in April to a 12-month level of $70 billion, significantly greater than the year-end 2012 level of $54 billion. Simply put, that means more dollars going out than coming in. And the pace of the net outflow is increasing fast.

title: UPDATE 3-Brazil real hits 4-year low, interest-rate futures rally
text:
* Brazil real slumps on risk aversion, cenbank intervenes

* Selic increase by 50 bps sends rate futures rallying

* Markets see turning point in fight against inflation

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, May 31 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real closed at a four-year low on Friday despite central bank efforts to support the currency, while interest-rate futures rallied after policymakers raised the benchmark Selic rate by more than investors expected.

The real ended at 2.1412 per dollar, its weakest level since May 2009, even after the central bank stepped up its campaign against inflation, a move that potentially increases the appeal of Brazilian fixed-income assets.

Currency losses were triggered by a combination of global risk aversion related to a possible withdrawal of U.S. stimulus measures and speculation by local investors about policymakers' tolerance to a weaker currency.

Not even a central bank intervention earlier on Friday was able to prop up the currency. The bank sold currency swaps, derivative contracts designed to strengthen the real, but the auction only temporarily cushioned the real's decline.

A weaker currency is a headache for the central bank as it could add to inflation by making imported goods more expensive. A sharp depreciation of the real could also increase currency risks to companies exposed to exchange rate fluctuations.

For now, however, government officials might just be giving some time for investors to digest a series of market developments domestically and abroad.

In an interview with Reuters, a government source said policymakers "have to wait and see what is going to happen" to the U.S. bond-buying program, which for years has provided a steady source of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets.

A higher-than-expected increase in Brazil's Selic rate also "tends to mitigate" the depreciation of the real, the source said.

"It's still early to say at which level the central bank wants the real to trade, especially after (finance minister Guido) Mantega said a weaker currency is good for exporters, which caused all that speculation," said Glauber Romano, a trader with Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"But the central bank is already signaling it won't allow the real to weaken much further," Romano added.

INTEREST-RATE FUTURES RALLY

Brazilian interest-rate futures rallied, however, after the central bank's decision to speed up the pace of monetary tightening was seen as a turning point in the bank's fight against inflation.

Brazil's central bank on Wednesday evening lifted the Selic by 50 basis points to 8.0 percent in a unanimous decision announced hours before the start of a national holiday on Thursday, which shut financial markets.

Ahead of the announcement of the decision, many economists and investors had bet policymakers would keep raising borrowing costs at a more modest pace as economic activity falters.

"The acceleration in the rate hike pace and a unanimous decision shows a surprising resolve of the central bank to renew focus on inflation," Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies and Co, wrote in a research note.

While yields paid on short-dated interest rate contracts are surely going to rally, the real question is whether investors will continue to ask for more inflation premium in the longer-dated contracts, Morden said.

So far on Friday, the shape of Brazil's domestic yield curve remained little changed, with the most liquid contracts rising in block.

Interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2014, one of the most traded, jumped 36 basis points to 8.42. Longer-dated contracts expiring in January 2017 also rose 36 basis points, to 9.74 percent.

Brazil's yield curve now prices in at least another Selic hike of 50 basis points in July, according to Reuters' calculations. Some analysts said an additional and final rate hike of 25 or 50 basis points could also be on tap.

That is a sign that investors expect policymakers to aggressively fight inflation even after key GDP data on Wednesday showed Brazil's economy expanded 0.6 percent in the first quarter, less than the 0.9 percent forecast by economists.

Responding to concerns rate hikes could hurt growth, central bank chief Alexandre Tombini on Thursday said in a TV interview the central bank's move will increase investors' "confidence in the pillars of the Brazilian economy," helping in the economic recovery.

--Brazil's first-quarter GDP grew 1.9% from a year earlier, below expectations

By Luciana Magalhaes

SAO PAULO--Brazil's currency and stocks finished lower Wednesday on disappointing first-quarter economic data, which lead economists to cut estimates for the full year.

The Brazilian real, now trading at its lowest levels since December 2012, exited active trading at BRL2.1084 to the dollar, after closing Tuesday at BRL2.0718 to the dollar.

Most stocks in the Ibovespa index also finished lower. The index closed down 2.5% at 54634 points.

Brazil's gross domestic product grew 1.9% in the first quarter from a year earlier, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, or IBGE, said. The figure was below economists' estimates for 2.38% expansion.

The data signal that the Brazilian economy will be stuck in a range below 3% for longer-than-expected period, according to Tony Volpon at Nomura Securities, who cut his estimates for 2013 growth to 2.5% from 3.4%.

Banco Fibra also revised down its growth projections for the year, to 2.4% from 2.8%. "In terms of demand, GDP's growth in the first quarter of 2013 has slowed in all its components compared to the previous quarter, with the exception of investments, which went up from 1.3% in the fourth quarter of 2012 to 4.6% in the first quarter of 2013," the bank said in a note to the market.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega admitted in a press conference Wednesday that the latest official growth estimate of 3.5% in 2013 would now need to be revised. He also said the recent weakening of the Brazilian real reflects investors' expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will soon reverse some of its monetary easing. However, the minister added, the weaker currency isn't a concern for the government at the moment as it will help Brazil's trade balance.

"Whenever Mr. Mantega talks, he brings volatility to the markets," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a forex manager at brokerage Treviso, adding the ministers estimates constantly have proven wrong.

The real is "having a bad hair day" trading thru BRL2.10 after the Finance Minister talked down the currency, Nomura Securities' Aloisio Teles said in a note to the market mid-afternoon. "Corporates are starting to get uneasy and if authorities do not do anything in line with past actions we can easily see an uncontrolled move," he added.

Traders have been on a currency watch, expecting Brazil's central bank might act at any time to shore up the real. Some said it didn't happen Wednesday because the central bank decided to postpone an intervention for a calmer day.

Brazil's central bank will decide later Wednesday if the key interest rate should be raised as part of its efforts to control inflation. Economists expect a rate hike but are divided over whether the central bank will raise rates by 0.25% percentage point or 0.50 percentage points. The base Selic rate currently stands at 7.50% per year.

"I believe the central bank will wait till Friday, following a holiday this Thursday, to intervene to drive down the dollar," said Luiz Carlos Baldan, a director at local brokerage Fourtrade.

In the Brazilian stock exchange, most shares finished in the red. The Ibovespa fall was led by oil firm OGX Petroleo e Gas Participacoes, controlled by billionaire Eike Batista. The company's shares fell 8.43% to BRL1.52.

Brazilian blue ships also finished lower. Mining behemoth Vale shares fell 0.74% to BRL29.55. Shares of government-run energy firm Petrobras fell 0.85% to BRL19.90.

Meanwhile, shares of Brazilian real-estate developer Gafisa had the biggest gains in the index on reports the company could be close to selling its Alphaville Urbanismo unit. Shares finished 3.02% up at BRL4.10.

Gafisa has received offers from bidders including Equity International, controlled by magnate Sam Zell, and U.S. investment advisory firm Blackstone and Patria Investments, a Brazilian firm, according to a source. Offers have ranged from around BRL1.5 billion to around BRL2 billion, and Blackstone and Patria, which are bidding together, seem to be ahead, the person added.

Gafisa, Equity International and Blackstone declined to comment. Spokespeople at Patria weren't immediately available for comments.

By Matthew Cowley

SAO PAULO--Known for his eternal optimism, Brazil's Finance Minister struck a more sober tone on Wednesday, acknowledging that economic growth would likely fall short of the government's latest forecast following weaker-than-expected first-quarter growth.

The latest official forecast for growth this year is 3.5%, and Guido Mantega said that would have to be revised following the first-quarter result.

Brazil's gross domestic product grew 0.6% in the first quarter compared with the fourth quarter of 2012, below the 0.9% that had been expected. The disappointing number has already led some private-sector economists to lower their forecast for this year: Banco Fibra cut its forecast to 2.4% for the year, from 2.8% previously.

"Our preliminary estimates for GDP growth in the next few quarters aren't at all cheering," says Banco Fibra chief economist Cristiano Oliveira in a note. "There are constraints on the supply side that will impact Brazilian growth in this period. The rate for potential GDP growth has shown a significant and worrying deceleration in the last quarters."

Weaker growth may feed into the Brazilian central bank's decision on interest rates due later Wednesday. The central bank began raising its key interest rate, the Selic, at its last meeting, amid worryingly high inflation.

After the data was released, investors pared back some of their bets on Wednesday's decision, and now expect an increase of 0.25 percentage point, which would lift the rate to 7.75% per year, from the previous expectation of 0.50 percentage point.

Mr. Mantega said he believes the first quarter was evidence of "strong" economic growth, despite adverse international scenario, and one in which investment in particular showed signs of recovery. The economy started the year in better shape than it started 2012, and "satisfactory" growth can be achieved this year, he said.

"Finally investment is reacting to the stimulus that the government has been providing in recent years," Mr. Mantega said.

Nonetheless, there was a change in tone, as the minister said that consumption would no longer be the main driver of economic growth. As such, the government won't offer any new stimulus measures, he said.

Meanwhile, the minister said that the government will ensure that electric power rates don't rise. Congress may block a decree signed earlier this year by Brazil's President Dilma Rousseff earlier this year that lowered electric power rates.

The recent weakening of the Brazilian currency is due to the fact that investors are starting to bet the U.S. Federal Reserve will withdraw some of its monetary easing, Mr. Mantega said. The weaker Brazilian real isn't a concern, as it will help the country's trade balance, the minister said.

The minister said the government isn't intervening to weaken the currency, and market forces are driving the move.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Weaker for Fourth Straight Week
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed weaker against the dollar Friday to cap off a fourth straight week of gradual losses, as investors continued to question the currency's ability to hold up amid deteriorating trade flows and the prospect of tighter monetary policies abroad.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0482 per dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL2.0430 at the end of Thursday's session.

The currency has lost 2.4% of its value since April 26 and occasionally broke above the psychological threshold of BRL2.05 to the dollar in intraday trading. Brazil's central bank, which has intervened at such levels in the past, remained on the sidelines.

Concerns weighing on the real are twofold. Recent talk of the U.S. Federal Reserve ending its bond-buying program known as quantitative easing, implemented during the 2008-09 crisis, could limit the amount of cash available to foreign investors attracted to Brazil's comparatively high interest rates.

Meanwhile, a persistent trade deficit so far this year has left some wondering if one of Brazil's key economic motors--exports of commodities such as iron ore and soybeans--is losing steam next to a growing appetite for imported goods.

Imports this year, through the third week of May, rose 7.3% from the same period in 2012 to $89.27 billion. Exports fell 5.9% to $84.18 billion.

Behind the rising imports and declining exports is an overvalued currency: many goods and services cost much more in Brazil than abroad. A McDonald's quarter-pounder hamburger costs $5.37 in Rio de Janeiro, compared with $3.89 in Lower Manhattan.

Joao Querino de Santos, a currency trader at Sao Paulo's J. Alves brokerage, said that if the real continues its slide, Brazilian importers with debts abroad could start to get nervous, potentially creating a scramble for dollars that could throw the market off balance.

"I think the importers are getting a little out of control," Mr. Santos said. "If the currency gets to BRL2.06 or BRL2.07, they'll definitely be buying dollars."

Mr. Santos said he thinks the real could weaken to BRL2.11 in June. But with a holiday-shortened week in Brazil coming up, things should be quiet, he added.

Next week nevertheless promises to be heavy on news and data, with the government due to report Brazil's first-quarter gross domestic product and the central bank's monetary-policy committee scheduled to make a decision on interest rates Wednesday.

A majority of 12 economists and analysts surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires this week expect the central bank to increase its benchmark Selic rate by 0.50 percentage point, to 8%. A minority expect a quarter-point hike.

title: Brazil Real Strengthens vs Dollar on Fed Continuity, Tombini Speech
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened slightly Tuesday after some members of the U.S. Federal Reserve signaled their support for continuing an asset-purchase program, while Brazil central bank President Alexandre Tombini reiterated his mission to combat inflation ahead of next week's monetary policy meeting.

The real reversed weakness from earlier in the day and exited active trading at 2.0354 per dollar, slightly stronger than the previous day's close at BRL2.0365 per dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

In a Tuesday speech, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President James Bullard voiced his support for continuing the so-called quantitative-easing program, which injects more dollars into markets. The Fed's William Dudley, meanwhile, said that while bond-buying could slow, it remains possible the Fed may in fact have to increase its purchases if the economy needs support.

That alleviated concern the Fed would stop its bond-buying program, which has helped keep global markets flush with dollars and the greenback relatively weak against global currencies. Those concerns earlier in the day had led the dollar to strengthen against the real.

"Here and across the world we've seen currencies be very volatile on the question of liquidity," said Anderson Rodrigues, a fixed-income manager at Daycoval Asset Management. "While we have one group at the Fed defending the elimination of the stimulus, others are saying that unemployment is too high and inflation too low."

That, of course, contrasts with the situation in Brazil, where unemployment is at record lows, further pressuring inflation that has remained stubbornly close to the upper limit of the central bank's inflation target.

In a speech Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Tombini repeated that the central bank will act in a "timely manner" to control inflation, stoking debate about whether the next interest-rate increase will be a half-percentage point or a quarter point.

The central bank raised rates for the first time in almost two years last month as consumer prices climbed faster than the 6.5% upper limit of the bank's inflation target. With inflation expectations remaining high--a weekly central bank survey of economists published Monday showed estimates for inflation at 5.8% for this year and next--the central bank is widely expected to raise the rate to 8.25% by year-end.

"If we had a more efficient market, that increase in rates would have a stronger effect on the currency, but since the market here is inefficient that doesn't pass through," Mr. Rodrigues said.

Higher rates at home than abroad often attract overseas investors to borrow abroad and buy Brazilian securities. However, the Brazilian government has put in place some barriers to keep its currency from strengthening too quickly, discouraging some investors from coming to Brazil. Frequent interventions by the central bank also helped corral the currency into an informal trading band for the past several weeks.

On Tuesday, the real almost weakened to BRL2.05, a level which usually has prompted some reaction from the central bank. According to Mr. Rodrigues, the market will continue testing the central bank's willingness to keep the currency range-bound.

* Data raises concern about US economic recovery

* Data also suggests Fed will keep monetary stimulus

* Mexico peso drops 0.2 percent, Brazil real flat

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, May 16 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso dropped on Thursday after surprisingly weak U.S. housing and jobs data weighed on prospects for the Mexican economy.

Other Latin American currencies had a slightly better performance, however, as the same data fueled hopes that U.S. monetary stimulus will remain in place.

The peso was 0.2 percent weaker at 12.23 per dollar, after hitting a three-week intraday low of 12.277. The currency was hurt by data that raised concerns about the economic recovery of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

The reports showed the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits climbed last week at the fastest pace in six months, while ground-breaking at home construction sites tumbled and consumer prices fell the most in over four years.

However, the same data eased fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve would scale back its bond-buying program, a decision that would remove a key source of global liquidity that has sustained investors' appetite for high-yielding emerging-market currencies.

"The dollar had been gaining in the past few days on a possible reduction in U.S. monetary stimulus. But the price data released today hinders any monetary tightening as there are no inflation pressures at the moment," said Martin Ferrer, a currency desk manager at Capital FX in Santiago.

The Brazilian real was practically unchanged at 2.0235 per dollar. Its losses were also capped by bets that the central bank would prevent any currency depreciation that could add to inflation, which is running just a tad below the ceiling of a government target.

Brazil's central bank last intervened in the foreign exchange market at the end of March, when the real neared the level of 2.03 per dollar. Analysts believe that, despite a poor performance in the country's trade balance, policymakers will not allow the real to weaken much further than that.

"While a weaker real could be a natural buffer for the widening current account deficit, the fiscal thrust and the tight labor market suggest that currency depreciation could add more pressure to the IPCA," JPMmorgan's analysts wrote in a research note, referring to the country's key consumer inflation index, which is running at 6.49 percent in the 12-month period through April.

"The chatter from the policy circles points toward the need for a weaker real, but in real terms. A nominal depreciation accompanied by higher inflation would backfire just as it did in 2012," JPMorgan added, revising its forecast for the currency to 2.05 from 1.95 per dollar.

SAO PAULO, May 3 (Reuters) - Most Latin American currencies strengthened on Friday after a stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report eased concerns about a sharp slowdown in the world's largest economy, encouraging investors to take on risk in emerging markets.

The currencies of Mexico and Chile gained 0.7 percent and 0.5 percent, respectively, after the report showed U.S. employers added 165,000 new jobs last month, more than the 145,000 expected by economists. The U.S. jobless rate fell to a four-year low of 7.5 percent as a result.

The U.S. data was especially relevant for Mexico, which sends most of its exports to its northern neighbor.

The Brazilian real softened slightly in thin trading, however, as investors had little incentive to bet on a stronger currency due to a weak domestic data and possible central bank interventions in the market.

Among the latest data underscoring Brazil's economic challenges, industrial production for March rose about half as much as investors expected. On Thursday, another report showed Brazil recorded in April its third traded deficit in four months as local industry struggled.

"The market is much quieter and investors are cautious due to domestic and external uncertainties," said Reginaldo Siaca, a manager at Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo.

He noted the government seems to be comfortable with an exchange rate around 2 reais per dollar, which limits investors' willingness to make strong bets on different currency levels.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Weaker After Interest-Rate Hike
text:
--Small Selic Increase Driving Bets Against the BRL

--Traders Believe Central Bank Will Have to Help the Real

--Brazil's Market Intervention Driving Investors Away, Says Analyst


 
   By Paulo Trevisani 
 

BRASILIA--The Brazilian real weakened against the dollar Thursday, in the first trading day after Brazil's central bank announced its first interest-rate increase in almost two years.

The BRL exited active trading at BRL2.0150 per dollar, roughly 0.8% down from Wednesday's closing of BRL1.9976, according to FactSet.

Late Wednesday, the central bank had changed to 7.5% the target for its benchmark rate, known as Selic. It was up from the 7.25% level the Selic had been since October.

The move also marked the reversal of a monetary easing cycle that began in August 2011, when the Selic was cut to 12% from 12.5%, and was subsequently trimmed every two months or so.

But inflation started to pick up in the past few months and government officials recently said inflation would not be tolerated. That drove many traders to bet the Selic would go to 7.75%.

"Future markets were [already] pricing in a tightening cycle," said Robert Wood, a Latin America specialist at the Economist Intelligence Unit in New York, but it came at "only 25" basic points, he said.

An interest-rate increase usually drives up the currency value, but the relatively small rise seemed to have caused the opposite effect, with some players apparently believing inflation will remain strong and thus weaken the real.

"They will have to intervene to avoid further depreciation" of the currency, said Claudio Irigoyen, head of Latin America foreign exchange strategy at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch in New York. He thinks the BCB will act before the currency touches BRL2.05 per dollar. "Players understand that, so they go short on the dollar, long on BRL/dollar. They know the central bank will be on their side."

The lower-than-expected increase also means the real will have less of a carry than previously thought. That could make the BRL less attractive to yield-seeking investors.

But there could be other factors at play, as well, including a perception that Brazil has become less friendly to investors' hot money.

For instance, some observers had expected the real to get stronger after the Bank of Japan's April 5 announcement of a massive bond-buying program, which would lower yields in Japan, thus driving investors to other markets, Brazil included. But Brazil hasn't seen much of that money so far, and some believe it is so because of capital controls in the South American nation.

"The Brazilian currency is closely managed," said Nick Cowley, of Henderson Global Investors, in London. He said the real will remain within the BRL1.95-to-BRL2.05 band it has traded in the past couple of months. However, the measures Brazilian government uses to keep that band could drive investors away.

"A lot of Japanese investors went to the Mexican peso" instead of the real because they see less government intervention in the Mexican market, Mr. Cowley said.

title: POLL-Scant room for more rate cuts in Latin America this year
text:
* For Latin America poll data click on

* GDP forecasts broadly unchanged from Jan poll

* Economists see growth divide between Pacific and Atlantic

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, April 11 (Reuters) - Latin American central banks will probably leave interest rates unchanged for now after relatively low inflation allowed them to give their economies an extra boost earlier this year, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.

The clear exception is Brazil, where inflation has pierced the official target ceiling and will probably force the central bank to raise interest rates soon.

The poll of 95 economists and analysts worldwide also underscored that economic growth is not at peril in most of Latin America, with forecasts broadly unchanged for most of the countries from a similar poll conducted three months ago.

In the latest regional Reuters poll in January, economists presaged correctly that there would be a window of opportunity to trim interest rates after a surprise slowdown in inflation. While prices have not become a threat in most of the region, economists now see scant room for further rate cuts.

Mexico's central bank trimmed its benchmark lending rate to a record low of 4 percent last month. It will probably leave it at that level through end-2014, according to the median of 18 forecasts in the poll.

Colombian policymakers took more aggressive action and chopped interest rates to 3.25 percent, the lowest in the region, as inflation hovered below the bottom end of the inflation target band. Now they will probably leave rates unchanged for the rest of the year, hiking them back to 4.25 percent only in 2014, the poll showed.

The possibility of further easing should not be ruled out, though, as a tool to fight massive capital inflows triggered by easy monetary policies in countries like Japan.

"If the Mexican peso continues to appreciate fast, the central bank might consider further rate cuts," wrote HSBC's economists led by Sergio Martin in a research note.

In Chile, authorities have considered raising rates to prevent the economy from overheating.

Economists say no action will be taken until the fourth quarter of this year as forecasts for inflation remain comfortably within the government's target.

Concerns about excessive currency gains should also affect monetary policy in Peru, where borrowing costs should be unchanged at 4.25 percent through the end of 2014, at least.

GROWTH DIVIDE

Despite an overall healthy outlook for economic growth in Latin America, economists notice a gap between fast-growing Pacific countries like Peru and Chile, and slower Atlantic economies such as Brazil and Argentina - where heavy government intervention has scared off foreign investors.

"Mexico is likely to outperform Brazil over the next few years. And while near-term growth in Peru and Chile should hold up fairly well, we expect Venezuela and Argentina to flirt with recession for the foreseeable future," wrote economists at Capital Economics in a note.

Mexico and Colombia, where interest rates dropped recently, will both grow between 3.5 and 4.5 percent in 2013 and 2014, and Peru will continue to expand by more than 6 percent annually - one of the best performances in the world.

Among the Latin American countries with inflation-targeting regimes, Brazil is the clear exception.

The central bank, which shocked markets by slashing interest rates 10 straight times in the past two years, is expected to raise borrowing costs from May on to push inflation back to the target bank.

The poll also showed that the political uncertainty in Venezuela after the death of President Hugo Chavez has taken a toll on forecasts for economic growth. The oil exporter will probably grow just 1.0 percent this year, down from a previous estimate of 2.0 percent, the median of 11 forecasts showed.

title: FACTBOX-Actions by Mexico's  foreign exchange  commission
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's foreign exchange commission said on Monday it will suspend a process of offering dollars to the market on days of sharp moves in the peso currency.

Mexico has a much more hands-off approach toward its currency than many of its peers, largely eschewing the direct market intervention practiced by countries such as Brazil and Colombia.

Policy on the peso is set by the foreign exchange commission, a joint effort of the Finance Ministry, the central bank and other state agencies.

The following is a list of some of board's key decisions in past years:

October 2008 - Mexico's central bank says it will auction $2.5 billion to stop the peso's most dramatic slide since the so-called Tequila Crisis in the mid-1990s.

The central bank, which ends up selling $998 million in the market, also announces it will offer $400 million whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent during a single session.

The amount of the daily dollar auction was trimmed to $300 million in March 2009 and to $250 million in May 2009. The auction mechanism was suspended in April 2010.

March 2009 - The foreign exchange board says it will sell $100 million daily, irrespective of peso levels, in a new mechanism to stop the peso's decline.

April 2009 - The central bank gets a swap line from the U.S. Federal Reserve to sell dollars among local financial institutions.

May 2009 - Daily dollar auction cut to $50 million.

October 2009 - Daily dollar auctions suspended.

February 2010 - The board resumes monthly dollar "put" option auctions to add to the country's federal reserves as a measure to cushion the economy from external turmoil. By using this mechanism, the central bank purchased $600 million between 1996 and 2001.

November 2011 - Mexico says it will halt monthly put option auctions and reinstate daily offers of $400 million whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent against the dollar during a single session.

March 2013 - The foreign exchange commission suspends the daily offers triggered by 2 percent falls in the peso, saying volatility in currency markets has decreased.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso rallies to 19-month high, Brazil real flat
text:
* Optimism about upcoming U.S. jobs data encourages risk taking

* Investors alert for possible Brazil cenbank intervention

* Mexico peso jumps 0.8 pct; Brazil real unchanged

By Michael O'Boyle and Bruno Federowski

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, April 2 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso hit a 19-month high on Tuesday as a rally on Wall Street encouraged investors to take on riskier emerging market assets, but the Brazilian real ended nearly unchanged for the second consecutive session on fears of a central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso jumped 0.8 percent to 12.2720 per dollar, its strongest level since early September 2011, as major U.S. stock indexes rose to record levels.

Investors were growing optimistic that key U.S. jobs data on Friday will show the U.S. economy is on solid footing, increasing prospects for Mexican exports. The United States is Mexico's main trading partner.

"The peso could reach 12.15 per dollar with a good U.S. jobs data on Friday, but people should start buying dollars then," said Mario Copca, an analyst with CI brokerage in Mexico City.

The peso has rallied more than 6 percent from a December low, helped by bets the new government will push through major economic reforms.

But the surge may be petering out. Technical momentum indicators show the peso in "overbought" territory, and the currency's moving-average convergence divergence (MACD) indicator was on the verge of flashing a "sell" sign.

In Brazil, the real ended practically unchanged at 2.0201 per dollar, with investors wary of a possible central bank intervention.

Many analysts believe the Brazilian central bank wants the real to remain within a tight range of 1.95 reais to around 2 reais per dollar - slightly stronger than it was at the end of 2012 - to avoid inflation passthrough.

"There is no reason for bigger changes in the exchange rate. If you are going to test the currency band, you want to do it carefully or as the central bank can suddenly dump dollars on the market," said Mario Battistel, a manager at Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazilian policymakers last intervened in the market last Wednesday, when the real neared the level of 2.03 per dollar. On Tuesday, central bank president Alexandre Tombini reiterated that the bank is always ready to intervene to make sure the foreign exchange market is working properly.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Little Changed Ahead of Trade Figures
text:
By Jeffrey T. Lewis

SAO PAULO--Brazil's real opened little changed against the dollar Monday ahead of monthly trade figures for March.

The real was trading at about BRL2.0199 Monday morning, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, from BRL2.02020 Friday.

Brazil's trade ministry will report figures on the trade balance for March on Monday afternoon. In February, the country had a deficit of $1.28 billion, and markets expect a surplus of $150 million for last month, according to Darwin Dib, an economist at CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

Traders are keeping an eye on Brazil's central bank this week, after the bank intervened in the market on March 27, via a currency-swap auction, when the real weakened in morning trading to nearly BRL2.03 versus the dollar.

As long as the real stays away from the level, the central bank should remain out of the market, said Luiz Carlos Baldan, director of the Fourtrade brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"If the real stays around current levels, we don't expect them to get in," he said of the central bank.

Meanwhile, Brazilian economists and analysts increased their forecasts for the country's inflation rate for the next year, for the third consecutive week, while they kept unchanged their outlook for this year, according to a weekly Brazilian Central Bank survey released Monday.

Analysts said they now expect inflation for the end of 2014 to be 5.68%, up from last week's 5.60%. For the end of 2013, economists maintained their view for inflation at 5.71%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real up on  central bank , rates fall on Rousseff
text:
* Brazil central bankintervenes to stem currency losses

* Brazil rate futures drop on Rousseff's inflation comments

* Brazil real gains 0.3 pct, Mexico peso up 0.1 pct

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 27 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real rose on Wednesday after the central bank intervened in the market to stem currency losses, while interest-rate futures dropped following comments by President Dilma Rousseff on inflation.

Other Latin American currencies started the day with losses as investors remained worried that the solution to Cyprus' banking crisis, which included heavy losses for large depositors, could be used as a template to resolve banking problems in other troubled euro-zone economies.

Later in the day, however, the currencies of Mexico and Colombia rebounded in thin trading as many traders took off for the Easter holidays. The Mexican peso rose 0.1 percent to 12.3450 per dollar while the Colombian peso gained 0.3 percent to 1,825.00 per greenback.

The Brazilian real ended 0.35 percent stronger at 2.0090 per dollar after the central bank sold all of the 20,000 contracts of traditional currency swaps, which are derivatives contracts designed to strengthen the real.

Investors had been on the lookout for a possible central bank intervention since last Thursday, when the real weakened past the level of 2 per dollar - considered a boundary of an informal trading range imposed by the central bank.

On Tuesday, the real had closed at two-month low of 2.0160 per dollar.

Many analysts believe Brazilian policymakers want the currency to remain within a range of 1.95-2.0 reais per dollar, slightly stronger than it was at the end of 2012, to avoid inflation pass-through.

"On one hand, the government is trying to curb inflation, but at the same time, it is worried about local industry," said Flavio Serrano, an economist with BES Investimento in Sao Paulo, referring to the impact of the exchange rate on exports.

"Maybe they found a comfortable level between 1.95 and 2.0 reais," he added.

BRAZIL RATES

Brazilian interest-rate futures fell sharply on the BM&FBovespa exchange after President Dilma Rousseff said she will not support policies that attempt to curb inflation by slowing down the economy.

Investors interpreted her remarks as a sign that policymakers were in no rush to hike the benchmark Selic rate, currently at an all-time low of 7.25 percent.

After interest rates fell, Rousseff said her comments were misinterpreted, and that fighting inflation is a "value in itself" in her government.

Despite that, interest-rate futures closed lower. Contracts maturing in January 2014 dropped 5 basis points to 7.74 percent.

"The most important thing was the president's remark. It was the same as saying that interest rates will not go up," said Waldir Kiel, an economist with H.Commcor brokerage in Sao Paulo.

title: Brazil  Real Strengthens on  Central Bank Intervention
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0066 to the dollar, versus BRL2.0137 the previous day

--Real strengthens after central bank sells swap contracts

--Trading range likely to remain at BRL2.00-BRL2.03 versus the dollar


 
   By Tom Murphy 
 

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real ended active trading Wednesday stronger against the U.S. dollar following a central bank auction of currency swap contracts.

The real ended active trading at BRL2.0066 to the dollar, stronger against the Tuesday close of BRL2.0137, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The central bank intervened in the market, via the currency-swap auction, after the real weakened in morning trading to nearly BRL2.03 versus the dollar.

The swap auction allows investors to exchange contracts linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auction tends to weaken the dollar, and strengthen the real, by putting more dollar-hedged contracts in investors' hands. Wednesday's auction resulted in the sale of nearly $1 billion in swaps.

"The auction was in line with the idea that the central bank doesn't like a lot of volatility in daily trading," said Mauricio Gaioti, a trader at Sao Paulo's Ouro Minas brokerage. Mr. Gaioti said it was likely the real will trade in a fairly narrow range during the next few days between BRL2.00 and BRL2.03 to the dollar.

Longer term, however, the real could see some slippage against the dollar because of poor investment inflows. "We could soon see a range of BRL2.01 to BRL2.05 to the dollar," Mr. Gaioti said.

Global investors have become highly risk-averse in light of new debt and political problems in Europe.

"The news from Europe is all bad and that is weighing on currency markets, stocks and commodities," said Marcos Morais, a trader at Sao Paulo brokerage Intercam.

Tiny Cyprus faces continued problems as its government wrestles with a complex banking and debt crisis, while Italian political parties have come to an impasse on the formation of a new government. Both countries are weighed down heavily by debts.

More broadly, signs from Europe on Wednesday were negative regarding economic recovery. The region's economic sentiment index fell in March to 90.0 points from 91.1 points in February, the first decline since October. It was an apparent indication that consumer and business confidence are feeling the pressure from continued debt problems.

The European worries led to a decline in the euro against the U.S. dollar and undermined prices of stocks and commodities world-wide. Lower commodities prices hurt Brazil, in particular, since Brazil is a major commodities exporter.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Little Changed Versus Dollar
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real opened little changed against the dollar Tuesday as investors remained cautious about possible intervention by the local central bank despite headwinds in global markets.

Around 8:50 EDT, the currency was quoted trading at BRL2.0118 to the dollar, slightly stronger against Monday's close of BRL2.0120.

Notwithstanding the gain, Brazil's real remains around its weakest levels versus the dollar since late January, when the exchange rate broke below BRL2.0 after several months of trading above that mark.

The Brazilian central bank was the catalyst back then, through a series of interventions aimed at strengthening the real to control rising inflation, analysts said. After trading mostly between BRL1.95 and BRL2.0, the currency weakened beyond that range last week amid financial troubles in Cyprus.

Though Cyprus appears to have avoided becoming the first country to exit the euro zone, the terms of its 10-billion-euro bailout package worried investors and precluded a global relief rally. The country implemented capital controls to avoid a run on its banks and imposed losses on large depositors, setting a worrisome precedent in the euro-zone debt fiasco.

Given the tumult in global currency markets, Brazil's central bank has so far declined to intervene to bring the real back down. RBC Capital Markets said steeper losses related specifically to the real could trigger action from the bank, however.

Brazil's SulAmerica Investimentos said it sees a gradual return to normalcy following the Cyprus bailout.

"The environment of greater risk aversion from the Cypriot crisis has kept the real pressured, causing the dollar to break the BRL2.0 barrier," the firm said in a weekly outlook. "The dollar should return to trade below that level, distancing the need for intervention by the central bank."

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.0105 to the dollar on Friday, compared to BRL2.0056 the day before, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. Thursday, the real reached its lowest level since late January amid concerns with the international economy and a deteriorating outlook for foreign currency inflows.

"All investors were betting the central bank would intervene the moment the currency hit BRL2.00 to the dollar, said Luiz Carlos Baldan, director at Brazilian brokerage Fourtrade. "Brazil's central bank didn't act because it knows this is not a speculative move."

According to Reginaldo Galhardo, a forex manager at Brazilian brokerage Treviso Corretora, Brazil's central bank believes that an intervention at this point would likely not produce results as moves reflect concerns with the situation in Cyprus.

Brazil's central bank is trying to keep the real in a range of BRL1.95-to-BRL2.00 to the dollar, Mr. Galhardo said.

Central bank president Alexandre Tombini said Friday that the international outlook remains "complex," with growth likely to stay low for some time still. In Europe, he said, the consequences of the current debt crisis will take a while to dissipate.

Mr. Tombini also said the central bank is ready to act in the currency markets at any time to make ensure stability. Though the bank doesn't have a target range for the currency, it is ready to act to reduce volatility, as well as to continue building up its foreign-currency reserves as the market allows.

Mr. Tombini also said Brazil's economy shows signs of improvement, and likely grew at an annualized rate of 4% in the first quarter of this year.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weak and Investor Wonder If  Central Bank  Will Act
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real opened flat against the U.S. dollar on Friday after reaching its lowest level since late January Thursday. Investors now wonder if Brazil's central bank will act to prevent further weakening of the currency.

The real was trading at BRL2.0070 to the dollar Friday morning after exiting regular trading Thursday at BRL2.0056, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

"The central bank hasn't acted yet because the trend reflects what is happening internationally," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a forex manager at Brazilian brokerage Treviso Corretora. "Probably they think an intervention now wouldn't change things much," he added.

Brazil's central bank is trying to keep the real in a range of BRL1.95 to BRL2.00 to the dollar, Mr. Galhardo said, adding that difficulties faced by Cyprus showed the debt crisis can still create "other victims."

Cyprus is in negotiations with a delegation of international inspectors, known as the troika, trying to set a plan for the troubled economy.

During the last three days, the Cypriot government has been trying to set another plan to raise 5.8 billion euros ($7.5 billion), in order to receive a EUR10 billion bailout package.

Meanwhile, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Thursday in a Senate hearing that the country's currency was at an improved to support the local industry.

Brazil's central bank president, Alexandre Tombini, will speak Friday at the Brazil-France Chamber of Commerce in Sao Paulo. He is expected to discuss the outlook for Brazil's growth and inflation.

Brazil's midmonth consumer price index, or IPCA-15, rose 0.49% through mid-March compared with a 0.68% in the period through mid-February, the Brazilian Geographic and Statistics Institute, or IBGE, said Friday.

* Mexico says any FX intervention would be rules-based

* Brazil real drops 0.6 pct, Mexico peso 0.5 pct lower

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 21 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real and the Mexican peso slid on Thursday as fears of a financial meltdown in Cyprus, combined with signs of economic weakness in Europe, drove investors to the safety of the dollar.

The Brazilian real dropped 0.6 percent, crossing the 2-per-dollar mark that many analysts considered a boundary of an informal trading band imposed by policymakers.

It was the first time since Jan. 30 that the real traded weaker than 2 per dollar, leaving investors on guard for a possible central bank intervention in the currency market.

"We have to see if the central bank will act now that the real has weakened past 2 per dollar," said Jaime Ferreira, a currency trader with Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"I believe it is too early for an intervention but, if this lasts till Friday, the central bank may very well do something."

Analysts believe the Brazilian central bank wants the real to remain within 1.95-2.0 per dollar, slightly stronger than it was at the end of 2012, to help lower the price of imported goods and anchor inflation expectations.

The Mexican peso lost 0.5 percent as investors feared an escalation of the euro zone crisis if Cyprus' banking system is allowed to collapse in the next few days.

On Friday, the European Union gave the island an ultimatum to raise the billions of euros it needs to secure an international bailout before the European Central Bank cuts off liquidity to Cypriot banks.

"People are worried about Cyprus. Either it accepts the EU conditions or it goes bankrupt," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a currency manager with Treviso brokerage.

Investor concerns were also fueled by purchasing managers' data showing French businesses had their worst performance in four years in March, likely pushing the euro zone's second-largest economy into recession, while Germany also seemed to be running out of steam.

The Mexican currency had hit its strongest level in more than 1-1/2 years on Wednesday, leaving some investors wondering whether the government was growing uncomfortable with the strength of the peso.

But on Thursday Finance Minister Luis Videgaray said Mexico will continue with its flexible exchange rate and that any intervention in the currency market would be based on rules.

title: Brazil Real Slips 1% To BRL2 To The Dollar; Weakest Since January
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real slid further on its recent path lower Thursday to end at its weakest level since late January as investors mulled an uncertain international environment and a deteriorating outlook for foreign currency inflows.

The real exited regular trading at BRLBRL2.0056 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.9871 to the dollar Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the currency began the session moving weaker in reaction to soft activity data in Europe and lingering doubts over whether European authorities could find an exit for a fiscal crisis in the Mediterranean nation of Cyprus. That country's parliament this week rejected a planned bailout that would be backed by taxes on bank deposit holders.

The extension of a nagging fiscal crisis in Europe and slow recovery of growth in other economies has left doubts for some analysts about whether Brazil will continue to attract investment and trade inflows.

Brazil's central bank Wednesday reported that the country saw net dollar outflows of $990 million in the first 15 days of March and $3.5 billion in the year to date.

Local authorities, meanwhile, are giving few hints of whether they may prepare to intervene in the currency market to curb a weakening of the real and its potential adverse impact on inflation.

Brazil's 12-month IPCA consumer price index has run at higher than 6% in recent months, pushing the top end of the country's inflation targeting band.

Speaking at a Brazilian Senate hearing Thursday, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the country's currency was at an improved level to support local industry and that the government's policy was to continue to allow the real to "float" against the dollar.

Meanwhile, in the absence of more intervention to hold the real at a stronger position, Brazil's central bank is seen possibly moving to raise the country's base Selic interest rate as early as its May monetary policy meeting to help discourage rising prices and attract more incoming foreign investment.

title: Brazil  Real Opens Stronger, Despite Cyprus Vote, On  Intervention  Concern
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened Wednesday as investors shook off worries about Cyprus and grew wary of local central bank action to curb losses in the currency as a way to rein in inflation.

The real opened at BRL1.9794 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, stronger than Tuesday's close at BRL1.9845 to the dollar.

The parliament of Cyprus voted against a bailout deal with the euro zone on Tuesday, due in large part to a controversial tax on individual bank deposits. A government delegation has headed to Moscow to try to get money from the Russian government in exchange for stakes in the island's assets.

Still, investors were expecting the news, said Paulo Petrassi, a fund manager at Leme Investimentos said.

"If news from Cyprus gets worse, we could see the real weaken," he said. "The market is buying dollars, but it's scared that the central bank could enter the market again."

The real has been trading between BRL1.95 to BRL2 per dollar for the past two months, with the central bank holding auctions to contain gains or losses whenever the currency threatens to break past those bounds. After weakening to almost BRL2 per dollar in recent days, the real strengthened again Wednesday.

Part of that investor concern resulted from central bank comments in the minutes of its latest monetary policy meeting. The central bank cut the benchmark Selic rate to a record low of 7.25% last year, and despite climbing inflation had said that keeping rates low for a "sufficiently prolonged period," inflation would return to the central bank's target. During its March 6 decision, however, the bank removed that language from its statement, opening the door for rate increases.

In minutes of the March 6 meeting, however, the central bank stated the need for "continued caution" in setting monetary policy.

"That talk of 'caution' led investors to think they won't raise rates in the short term," Mr Petrassi said. "Since they won't raise rates, they will continue using the real to contain inflation."

Although the central bank has said that it has no ideal rate for the real, and that it intervenes only to reduce market volatility, investors recognize that allowing the real to weaken too much raises the costs of imports, stoking inflation.

title: Brazil  Real Weakens On  Central Bank Intervention
text:
--Brazilian real ends an active trading day at BRL1.9556 Vs. BRL1.9477

--Central bank sells reverse-swap contracts, weakening real

--Some traders see range of BRL1.95-2.00 to the dollar

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened Monday against the U.S. dollar, after the central bank intervened with an auction of reverse swap contracts.

The real ended the trading day at BRL1.9556 to the dollar, weaker than Friday's finish at BRL1.9477, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real strengthened slightly in early trading, but that brought a swift response from the central bank. In a mid-morning auction, the bank sold so-called reverse-swap contracts. The contracts amount to central bank purchases of U.S. dollar futures, thus reducing the availability of dollar-hedged contracts for investors and strengthening the dollar. The central bank sold the equivalent of $1.35 billion in reverse swaps. "The central bank is showing it doesn't want the dollar to weaken beyond BRL1.95," said Durval Correa, a trader at the Multi Money brokerage.

Traders speculated that the central bank may be trying to enforce a trading range of BRL1.95 to BRL2.00 to the dollar, with BRL1.95 designed as a limit to protect exporters.

In a research note Monday, economists at Banco Itau forecast a year-end value for the dollar at BRL2.00. Economists at RBC Emerging Markets Research, also in a research note, put the current fair value of the Brazilian currency at BRL1.9580, or very close to Monday's close.

The reverse-swap auction also reinforced the widely held view that the central bank will not attempt to use currency appreciation to fight inflation. "The central bank will fight inflation with interest rates," said Mr. Correa.

Most economists expect the central bank to raise interest rates over the next few months to push down Brazil's worrisome 6.3% inflation rate. The next rate hike could come as early as April, with most economists predicting a quarter-point increase, and some a half-point. The Selic base rate is currently at a historic low of 7.25%. RBC economists predict three quarter-point hikes in a row for Selic from April through July, leaving the rate at 8.0%.

In principle, higher interest rates could strengthen the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar by attracting more foreign investment inflows. But traders said any such effect could be easily counteracted by central bank interventions such as Monday's reverse swaps.

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real was slightly stronger against the U.S. dollar in early trading Monday ahead of possible interest rate hikes that could come as early as April.

Early in the session, the real was trading at BRL1.9443 to-the-dollar, stronger against the Friday close of BRL1.9477, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Brazilian inflation is currently running at 6.3%, up from 5.84% at the end of 2012. The 12-month inflation rate has been climbing all year and is now perilously close to the 6.5% ceiling of Brazil's inflation-targeting range.

Rising inflation has caused economists to revise their forecasts for interest rates.

This week's central bank survey, released earlier Monday, showed economists predicting a rise in the Selic base interest rate to 8.0% by the end of the year. The previous forecast by economists was for maintenance of the Selic rate at the current 7.25% throughout 2013.

According to many economists, rate hikes could begin as early as the next central bank monetary policy meeting in April.

Higher interest rates would tend to strengthen the real against the dollar by attracting more foreign investment inflows.

Some foreign exchange traders are now forecasting a new range for the real against the greenback. Since early this year, market forecasts had focused on a range of about BRL1.95 to BRL2.00 to the dollar. But that view is now changing.

"I'm beginning to think we'll see a range more like BRL1.90 to BRL1.95," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. He said Brazilian central bankintervention in the market was unlikely at current levels.

Once again, inflation may be orienting central bank policy. A stronger Brazilian real can help the government combat inflation. At BRL1.90 to-the-dollar, a range of imports from oil products and wheat to mobile phone components become cheaper for Brazilian consumers and businesses than at BRL1.95 or BRL2.00 to-the-dollar.

Traders noted that the Brazilian market was largely ignoring international factors Monday, including a decline in most commodities prices and a slightly weaker euro. Investors are focusing on domestic factors, they said.

"While risks of intervention have increased with the outperformance and the build up of speculative positions, the appreciation trend, if measured, should not raise eyebrows in the government at the current juncture," Cassiana Fernandez, an analyst at JPMorgan in Brazil, wrote in a research note.

text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real appreciated Friday to its strongest level against the U.S. dollar since early May, while the central bank remained on the sidelines, lending support to views that local authorities plan to use the currency to help combat inflation.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.9477 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.9602 at the end of Thursday's session.

The break past BRL1.95 to the dollar marked a major psychological milestone, as many market participants had previously assumed that level to be an unofficial floor the central bank would enforce through intervention in the currency market. Brazil's real last raised eyebrows in late January when it was allowed to appreciate beyond BRL2.0 against the dollar for the first time in several months.

"I think they're going to use the dollar to anchor inflation," said Durval Correa, head trader at Sao Paulo's Multi-Money brokerage. "The market tested, and it looks like the dollar no longer has a floor at BRL1.95."

Brazilian authorities, led by Finance Minister Guido Mantega, have often expressed a preference for a weaker currency in recent years to offset some of the competitive disadvantages the country's manufacturers and exporters face. But rising inflation in recent months may have forced policy makers to rearrange their priorities, some analysts say.

The official IPCA consumer price index rose to 6.31% in the 12 months through February, precariously close to the 6.5% upper limit of the Brazilian central bank's target range.

As a result, economists increasingly expect the central bank to raise its baseline Selic interest rate this year from the current, record-low 7.25% in order to rein in the inflationary pressures. Higher interest rates tend to cause the real to strengthen by making yields on Brazilian fixed-income securities more attractive to foreign investors.

In its latest monetary-policy statement, on Wednesday, the central bank discarded language suggesting interest-rate stability, for the time, being in favor of a more vigilant tone. The bank said it will "follow the evolution of the macroeconomic environment until the next meeting, to then define the next step in monetary-policy strategy."

But a higher Selic could threaten Brazil's nascent economic recovery following two years of subpar growth. An alternative to rate increases, some analysts say, would be for authorities to allow some currency appreciation to bring down the relative cost of imported goods.

Carlos Hamilton Araujo, the central bank's economic-policy director, said last month that a 10% appreciation in the currency, over the course of a year, would be estimated to shave 0.70 percentage point off annual inflation.
