title: INSIGHT-Brazil's leftist president fights to win back business
text:
(For PDF version of this story: http://link.reuters.com/hyg46t("http://link.reuters.com/hyg46t"))

BRASILIA, March 4 (Reuters) - The conversations with Brazil's top business leaders often last two hours, and up to four. President Dilma Rousseff asks detailed questions but otherwise listens intently, staring back with an inscrutable frown that occasionally unnerves her guests.

There is talk of investments, and the need for shared prosperity - a favorite topic of Rousseff's. But in these meetings, the conversation inevitably comes back to the severe bottlenecks that have brought the economy back to earth after a historic boom last decade.

"Brazil needs to focus now on issues like productivity and reducing costs, because that's the only way we can grow in a sustainable fashion," said Marcelo Odebrecht, who runs a global conglomerate that bears his family's name.

"I think we've realized that, and the president is moving in that direction," he said in an interview. "That's her focus - looking at these obstacles, and getting Brazil growing again."

The meetings, which have intensified in recent weeks, are a critical part of Rousseff's efforts to convince Brazilian executives to start investing again and help lift the economy following two straight years of disappointing growth.

The chats with well-known figures such as Odebrecht and mining and energy tycoon Eike Batista come as Rousseff, a Marxist guerrilla in the 1970s who evolved into a pragmatic leftist, struggles with a perception that she is unfriendly or even hostile toward the private sector.

Just past the halfway point of her four-year term, the 65-year-old daughter of a Bulgarian aristocrat has indisputably made many enemies in the business world. She has condemned banks for charging high interest rates, intervened heavily in Brazil's exchange rate, and undertaken contentious reforms such as a cut in electricity rates that wiped billions of dollars from the market value of foreign and locally owned companies.

Rousseff has said all her decisions respected existing contracts and laws, and were necessary to try to return Brazil's economy to its glory days of fast growth in the late 2000s.

Her ability to convince business leaders that's true will be key to the rest of her presidency.

Without a rebound in investment, which has steadily fallen since Rousseff has been in office, Brazil will not have the resources to address supply-side bottlenecks in infrastructure and labor that caused the economy to grow just 0.9 percent in 2012.

A persistent economic slump could, in turn, endanger Rousseff's expected bid for re-election next year.

Reuters spoke with several ministers, presidential aides and business leaders who have participated in the meetings, trying to determine why executives have generally not yet heeded Rousseff's call to take risks and let their "animal spirits" flourish - a reference to a term used by the British economist John Maynard Keynes, one of her favorite historical figures.

Business leaders say that Rousseff seems receptive to their feedback and focused on the right problems. But she is also not shy about defending her strong belief that the state must try to shape the economy so that all Brazilians can prosper.

That philosophy has guided Brazil for the past 10 years under Workers' Party rule, and helped make it one of the few countries where inequality fell as the economy grew. Yet it may also explain why some of her decisions have backfired, some say.

"She always challenges these guys - You have to think as a business, but you have to think about Brazil too," said Trade and Industry Minister Fernando Pimentel, one of Rousseff's closest aides, who sits in on some of the meetings.

"You want to earn money, that's natural. But how is everybody going to earn money? How will everybody get better? It can't get better just for one group, only for you," Pimentel said in an interview.

A VERY POPULAR LEADER

Since taking office on New Year's Day in 2011, Brazil's first woman president has earned mostly high marks from voters. Her personal approval rating has hovered in the high-70s, thanks largely to record-low unemployment levels that have been sustained despite the lackluster economic growth.

By cracking down on corruption and embracing some free-market policies such as the privatization of airports and highways, Rousseff has moved beyond the shadow of her popular predecessor, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who plucked the career civil servant from relative obscurity and helped her win her first-ever campaign - for the presidency - in 2010.

In a region characterized by charismatic leaders such as Lula and Venezuela's Hugo Chavez, Rousseff stands out for being gray - or intimidating, depending on the beholder.

Aides say she detests ceremonial aspects of the presidency, eschewing dinners and the schmoozing with congressmen and foreign visitors that Lula excelled at.

She rarely gives news conferences, and she abandoned Twitter almost immediately after she won the election. "Let's chat more often in 2011," her most recent tweet says.

Yet, for the most part, Brazilians see these as the signs of a serious, hard-working leader. Especially among the poor, whose lives have improved dramatically in the past decade, Rousseff is seen as a kind of stern benefactor - the "mother of Brazil," as Lula baptized her in 2010.

In the corporate suites of Sao Paulo, the country's business and financial capital, executives tend to take a dimmer view.

While virtually no one accuses Rousseff of being a hard leftist in the vein of Chavez or Bolivia's Evo Morales, many say she has taken too heavy-handed a role in managing Brazil's $2.2 trillion economy - and scared off some investors who never quite know what she'll do next.

"I think most investors understand she's not reintroducing old-style socialist ideas. That's not what this is about," said Paulo Vieira da Cunha, a former deputy governor at Brazil's central bank who is now a partner at Tandem Global Partners, a hedge fund in New York.

"What it is about is her belief in central planning, in an active industrial policy, where the government makes critical decisions," he said. "That's not unique to Brazil, by the way 


... But it has bothered some people."
     


A HEAVY HAND

Indeed, there is no big economic sector that Rousseff hasn't touched in a meaningful way in the past two years.

Brazil's banking industry was turned upside down by the central bank's surprise decision, starting in Rousseff's eighth month in office, to slash its benchmark interest rate, which has since fallen from 12.5 percent to an all-time low of 7.25 percent.

Rousseff publicly shamed private-sector banks for not cutting their lending rates fast enough to match the benchmark's declines, calling their actions "inadmissible." Meanwhile, monthly inflation hit its highest level in almost eight years in January, leading some investors to say the cuts went too far.

Rousseff has also been personally involved in the management of the exchange rate, which has oscillated between 1.52 and 2.13 per dollar during her term. The government has tried to alternately strengthen or weaken the currency in unpredictable ways, playing havoc with companies' business plans.

Even the business world's favorite policy tactic - cutting taxes - has generated uncertainty under Rousseff.

Instead of announcing an across-the-board cut, Rousseff has moved sector-by-sector, implementing targete [20130304 110009 GMT]

d tax reductions of sometimes uncertain duration for industries like autos or home appliances. Her government has made more than two dozen separate announcements of stimulus packages.

Finally, Rousseff has made some decisions that openly work against the interests of private capital. They include forcing state-run oil giant Petrobras to import gasoline and sell it at a loss, a policy that has jeopardized the company's investment plans and contributed to a 30 percent decline in its publicly traded shares since she took office.

All told, Brazil's main stock index has tumbled 20 percent during Rousseff's presidency - compared to an 18 percent gain in Mexican shares and a 20 percent rise in the Dow Jones Industrial Average in the United States during the same period.

The Eurasia Group, a think-tank, said in a note in February that the government's policies and poor communication have led to "a credibility problem with the private sector."

The result: Investment fell 4 percent in 2012, and now stands at just 18.1 percent of gross domestic product.

That gives Brazil the lowest such ratio among big Latin American economies, well behind the rates of 28 percent or so in Peru, Colombia and Chile. As a result, some among Rousseff's economic team fear Brazil's potential economic growth rate may be capped at a mediocre 3 percent or so for years to come.

TRYING HER BEST?

Inside the Palacio do Planalto, Rousseff's modernist palace on the high plains of central Brazil, one word best describes the reaction to the way some investors are behaving: bewilderment.

To hear her ministers and aides tell it, Rousseff has spent much of her presidency explicitly catering to Brazil's business community. In fact, many of the policies for which she has been most criticized were the results of feedback she received from executives, they say.

There is truth to that. In a keynote speech in 2010 prior to the presidential campaign, Armando Monteiro Neto, then the head of Brazil's main industrial lobby group CNI, cited taxes, interest rates, an overvalued real, and high input costs such as electricity as the economy's main problems.

Rousseff has made faster progress on all those issues than any economist or political analyst predicted, although some initiatives - including her recent plan to force electricity costs down - have caused heavy losses for certain companies.

"I think she's done what business people have asked for, and with a certain speed," said Luiza Helena Trajano Rodrigues, the chief executive of retailer Magazine Luiza and another executive who has met frequently with Rousseff.

"Some of the criticism seems a little strange," Rodrigues said in an interview. "She's done a lot of difficult things."

Despite being elected primarily as a figure of continuity, Rousseff has made some pro-business moves that were unthinkable under Lula, who rose in politics as a labor union leader.

She stood up to criticism from the left wing of her Workers' Party to privatize airports in Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and elsewhere. She also moved to cut pension benefits for incoming government workers - a decision that will help shore up Brazil's finances, which she has maintained in orderly shape.

One interpretation of Brazil's struggles is that after the last decade's boom lifted some 30 million people from poverty, the policies that worked under Lula had run their course.

Namely, there was no more room to grow the economy by expanding consumer credit - the main engine of growth from 2007 to 2010. So it has fallen to Rousseff to make tough structural reforms that could eventually open up a new era of economic growth - but have generated uncertainty in the short term.

The minister, Pimentel, who has known Rousseff for four decades, said the dire global economy also caused her to become more reformist around the one-year mark of her presidency.

"She clearly saw the bottlenecks that the Brazilian economy had, and has," he said. "She knew we couldn't put off facing these bottlenecks because in a world totally convulsed by the European crisis, we could risk totally losing our competitiveness."

SHARING THE WEALTH

Racing to prevent such a scenario, Rousseff has thrown open her doors to a variety of business leaders from finance, steel, aviation and elsewhere - and has won over some executives who were skeptical of her.

She is mostly listening for new policy ideas and trying to gauge the economy's health. But she is also not shy about asking her guests to part with their money.

For example, in a Jan. 10 meeting with Odebrecht, she asked him to consider investing in upcoming airport concessions, an aide said. In a Jan. 16 sit-down with Batista, whose holdings include oil company OGX, Rousseff urged him to participate in a major round of oil auctions later this year.

Rousseff has also gathered two dozen or so top executives at a time for regular "CEO forums" inside the palace, with the next pow-wow scheduled for March 19.

Still, giving executives face time has been no guarantee of convincing them to invest.

Rousseff's closest contact in the business world is arguably Jorge Gerdau Johannpeter, a 76-year-old steel magnate whom she appointed to lead the Chamber of Management and Competitiveness, another nexus between government and the private sector. Gerdau is often in Brasilia, and sat down with Rousseff for four hours in one meeting in January.

Yet on Feb. 21, the company which he chairs - Gerdau SA , the world's No. 2 maker of steel for builders - said it was cutting its five-year investment plan by 17 percent.

It said it slashed capital spending by 24 percent in the fourth quarter alone, and attributed its decisions to "uncertainties hurting the global economy." A spokeswoman for Gerdau did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

The malaise in Brazil's private sector explains why Rousseff may be vulnerable to a more market-friendly candidate, such as PSDB party Senator Aecio Neves or Pernambuco state Governor Eduardo Campos, in next year's election.

Yet polls indicate that, for now, Rousseff is popular enough to win easily. Meanwhile, an unexpected 0.5 percent rise in Brazil's overall investment in the fourth quarter of 2012 suggests that some business leaders, too, may be coming around.

Odebrecht, who after meeting Rousseff said his company would invest $8.5 billion this year, up a third from 2012, said executives may learn to live over time with some discomfort.

"People may argue - 'Oh, I would have done this a different way,'" he said. "But the concepts and intentions, I think it's tough to criticize her. What she's doing is right for Brazil."

title: Brazil's Real Opens Stronger as Governments Tries to Reduce Inflation Worries
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real opened stronger against the U.S. dollar Thursday following Brazil's government efforts to reduce inflation worries.

The real was trading at BRL1.9667 to the U.S. dollar, stronger than Wednesday's closing price at BRL1.9722, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Brazil's high inflation rate scared away private investors in the past, but the current macro-economic stability in the country favors an increase in private investments, President Dilma Rousseff said Wednesday.

The government last year announced a series of plans to attract private financing for the construction or improvement of roads, railways, ports and airports.

This year's economic conditions should favor growth, Ms. Rousseff said Wednesday. The situation in Europe is much better, and China appears to have achieved a soft landing for its economic growth, she said.

Brazilian officials have been saying in the last few weeks that the country is prioritizing the control of inflation. In the 12-month period through mid-February, the IPCA-15 rose 6.18% versus a 6.02% advance in the same period through mid-January. That remained above the government's official inflation target of 4.5%, but within a tolerance band of plus or minus two percentage points.

Rousseff's economic team commitment to controlling prices has created expectations that the central bank could raise interest rates, currently at a record-low 7.25%, despite economic weakness.

Earlier in the week, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the country's exchange rate has stabilized to a "favorable" level, lessening the need for interventions.

Brazil's central bank last stepped into the foreign-exchange market on Feb. 15, when it held a sale of reverse-swap contracts to keep the real trading weaker than the BRL1.95 level per dollar.

The minister also said Brazil's central bank can adjust monetary police if it believes it's necessary. "The central bank has the independence to raise interest rates if it thinks necessary," he added.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Stronger as Italy Tensions Ease
text:
--Italy completes bond sale, but yields jump to highest level since October

--Real stabilized, lesser need for currency intervention, Brazil's finance minister says

--Brazilian real opens at BRL1.9766, stronger from Tuesday's close at BRL1.9829

By Jeff Fick

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real opened slightly stronger against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as market tensions surrounding Italy's inconclusive election results eased and the U.S. Federal Reserve pledged to maintain its stimulus efforts.

The local currency tracked a stable euro, seen as a barometer for the local currency, after Italy carried out a successful bond auction. The real opened trading at BRL1.9766 to the U.S. dollar, stronger from Tuesday's closing price fix at BRL1.9829, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Global markets were attempting to bounce back from a sharp selloff to start the week, when election results in Italy raised concerns about political stability in the debt-troubled country. Without a firm ruling coalition, the prospect that the country could abandon austerity measures aimed at curtailing Italy's debt load created a fresh wave of uncertainties surrounding the euro zone's financial crisis.

Moody's Investors Service said Wednesday that the election results has negative implications for Italy's sovereign credit rating and other weaker members of the single-currency bloc--and also raises the risk of a renewed flare-up of the debt crisis. Tensions eased slightly after demand for Italian bonds was strong at an auction, but the country was forced to pay the highest interest rates since October to attract investors.

Currency market players in Brazil also received some direction late Tuesday from Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal that the real has stabilized at a "favorable" level, lessening the need for intervention. Brazil's real has traded in a narrow range between BRL1.95 and BRL2.00 since the start of this year.

The exchange rate is now less volatile and at "a level that we can live with," Mr. Mantega said.

Mr. Mantega and Brazilian Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini have both attributed a surge in inflation partly to the real's sharp depreciation against the U.S. dollar in 2012, when the currency tumbled about 10% versus the greenback. Mr. Tombini has said that the central bank would move to raise interest rates, currently at a record-low 7.25%, should inflationary pressures not retreat from an upswing to start the year. Through mid-February, inflation was running at 6.2%.

In the U.S., meanwhile, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke indicated that the central bank will continue recent bond-buying programs also known as "quantitative easing" until the U.S. economic recovery gains traction. Mr. Bernanke, who will continue congressional testimony Wednesday, acknowledged that the increased liquidity in global markets could encourage risk-taking and someday destabilize markets or the economy.

"Keeping long-term interest rates low has helped spark a recovery in the housing market and has led to increased sales and production of automobiles and other durable goods," Mr. Bernanke said.

title: Brazil Makes Inflation Control A Priority
text:
NEW YORK--Brazil's exchange rate has stabilized to a "favorable" level, lessening the need for interventions, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Tuesday.

Brazil's currency, the real, has fluctuated in a wide range over the past 12 months, largely driven by central-bank interventions in the market as well as capital controls introduced by the government.

This month, however, the real has traded in a relatively narrow range, between BRL1.95 to BRL2 per dollar. It traded at BRL1.9855 Tuesday afternoon in New York.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Mr. Mantega said that the exchange rate is now less volatile and at "a level that we can live with."

His comments reflect a shift for Mr. Mantega, who was one of the first to use the phrase "currency war" in 2010 to refer to a widespread effort among global policy makers to weaken their currencies to make exports more competitive. Brazil has been one of the more frequent interveners in its currency.

Mr. Mantega said Tuesday that Brazil was sitting out the latest round of the currency war.

"Since we've been able to bring the exchange rate to a favorable level for the country, at this time we're not suffering what would've been characterized as a currency war," he said, adding that the real is close to a "balanced situation."

That's part of the reason Brazilian authorities have been intervening less and less, and Mr. Mantega said that new measures are "not necessary."

Brazil's central bank last stepped into the foreign-exchange market on Feb. 15, when it held a sale of reverse-swap contracts to keep the real trading weaker than the BRL1.95 level per dollar.

Now the currency is at a level where Brazil can still be competitive but doesn't add to inflationary pressures, Mr. Mantega said, adding that it has stabilized "roughly" to the area of BRL1.90-BRL2.10 per dollar. Both he and Brazil Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini have attributed the recent rise in inflation partly to the real's sharp depreciation in 2012, when it fell about 10% against the dollar. Consumer prices have accelerated recently, with annualized inflation reaching 6.2% in mid-February.

Some analysts have said that the central bank may have been too aggressive in its decision to cut its benchmark interest rate to a historical low of 7.25% in 2012, given persistent inflation in Brazil.

Mr. Mantega, however, defended the central bank, calling its series of rate cuts to 7.25% the "correct" move.

Now, with inflationary pressures still clouding Brazil's recovery outlook, a number of analysts expect the central bank to start raising interest rates this year. There has been some speculation that the government would try to pressure the central bank not to raise rates, as the record low level is seen as a major achievement for President Dilma Rousseff.

But Mr. Mantega said the central bank can adjust monetary policy as it sees fit.

"The central bank has the independence to raise interest rates if it thinks necessary," he added.

He, however, believes that inflation is still on a downward trend this year, in part because the currency has stabilized after last year's sharp depreciation.

"Inflation will be better this year than last year," he added.

--Brian Baskin and Paulo Trevisani contributed to this article.

title: Brazil  Central Bank  President: Growth is Not A Goal For The  Central Bank
text:
The Brazilian central bank's priority is fighting inflation, and not spurring growth, its president said in an interview before policy makers meet to set interest rates, even as Latin American's biggest economy struggles to escape a long stretch of slow growth.

Brazil's economy expanded around 1% in 2012, down from 7.5% as recently as 2010. At the same time, annualized inflation hit 6.2% in mid-February, close to the maximum the government has said it would tolerate.

Analysts say the perception of dueling policies aimed at stimulating the economy and tamping down inflation have created confusion in the market, causing the Brazilian real to gyrate from multi-month lows to highs in the space of a few months.

"Our goal is inflation, so we have to adjust and calibrate our policies to meet our goals," Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini told The Wall Street Journal. "Growth is not a goal for the central bank."

While few economists expect the central bank to raise rates from their record low 7.25% when Mr. Tombini and other policy makers meet March 5 and 6, some say the bank could signal in its monthly policy statement that it is considering rate increases in the future if inflation remains a problem.

"Inflation in the last few months has shown more resilience than we'd like it to show," Mr. Tombini said Saturday. "We're keeping a very close eye on these developments."

The markets are likely to welcome any signs the central bank is addressing inflation, analysts say.

The government has "realized that the perception about policy credibility was very low and they started making a big effort to try to solve that," said David Beker, Brazil economist at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch in Sao Paulo.

These concerns have led some foreign investors to prefer other emerging markets, including regional rival Mexico, complicating Brazil's efforts to raise investment ahead of the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympic Games. Brazilian stocks are down about 3% so far this month, and have dived 20.5% over the past 12 months, according to the MSCI Brazil index.

"This is why Brazil's underperforming," said Kathryn Rooney Vera, senior macroeconomic strategist at Bulltick Capital Markets. "Policy risk is a big deal [because of] the issue of potentially spiraling out of control inflation and the crippling effects it can have on the Brazilian story."

Mr. Tombini, who took over the top post at Brazil's central bank in January 2011, said inflation remained stubbornly high because of a rise in food prices last year and a sharp decline in the value of the real, which tumbled 10% against the dollar in 2012.

He said he didn't expect a repeat performance from the currency this year.

"I don't see the market driving the real that way," he said.

Brazil has been at the forefront of the so-called currency war, where central banks across the globe are trying to weaken their currencies to keep their exports competitive. Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega, in 2010, was one of the first to use the term, and the government has applied targeted controls to stem capital inflows.

But Mr. Tombini said Brazil has more pressing problems than fighting off large capital inflows resulting from easy monetary policies elsewhere.

"I don't think this is a war for Brazil to fight at this moment," he said.

Brazil's central bank used market interventions to keep the real trading between 2 and 2.10 to the dollar for much of the second half of 2012. The currency has traded anywhere from around 2.14 to 1.95 per dollar since December, however, causing some investors to speculate that the central bank was using the currency as a monetary policy tool to help the economy recover and combat inflation. Mr. Tombini called such speculation misguided.

"None of that is the reality," he said. "[The] exchange rate is not an instrument either to combat inflation or to sustain economic growth."

The central bank can step into the foreign exchange market to "shave off" excessive currency volatility, he added.

Ultralow interest rates in the developed world and asset purchase programs by some major central banks, including the Federal Reserve, have resulted in a flood of liquidity in global financial markets--driving large capital flows into higher-yielding markets like Brazil's.

Despite such efforts, "slow [global] growth will remain with us for a while," Mr. Tombini said, adding however that he sees a lower risk of a shock to the world economy.

Policy makers across the globe, however, will have to ensure that unwinding such easy monetary policies and withdrawing excess liquidity is a smooth process.

"Going forward the concern will be how the world will exit this...new normal," he said.

--Matthew Cowley contributed to this article. [ 02-24-13 1804ET ]

title: DJ Brazil's Economic Policy Becomes Guesswork For Traders
text:
--Brazil's economic policy becomes guesswork for traders

--Investors struggle to play Brazil as policymakers seem to diverge

--Markets long for a steady hand on Brazilian policy making 


 
   By Paulo Trevisani 
 

Investors may take courage from Brazil's projected economic pickup this year but they are still spooked by divergent remarks coming from policy makers and their effects on the country's currency, the real, as authorities juggle the need to fuel the economy with that of keeping inflation at bay.

For the time being, anyway, investors are hanging on to the idea that authorities will keep the real in a relatively tight range between BRL1.95 and BRL2.00 to the U.S. dollar.

The seesawing of the exchange rate in recent months has highlighted the difficulties of trying to manage a currency that is still considered to be free-floating despite the introduction of targeted capital controls over the last year or so.

"Investors still like Brazil," said Tony Volpon, head of Emerging Markets Research Americas at Nomura Securities in New York. But the country now has "adverse movements while other countries are doing well," partly because of mixed signals sent by the Brazilian government, he said.

Earlier this month, after a period of appreciation of the local currency against the U.S. dollar, a comment from Finance Minister Guido Mantega briefly led market participants to believe the exchange rate could be headed toward BRL1.85. The minister then clarified that the government has no target and won't let the real appreciate much.

Since then, some traders have adopted BRL1.95 to BRL2.00 as the closest thing to an unofficial target range.

On Friday, Mr. Mantega again shook up trading desks when he said interest rates--and not the exchange rate--remain Brazil's main weapon against inflation. This drew some applause as it suggested the government wouldn't prevent the central bank from raising interest rates to combat inflation, which accelerated to 6.15% in January. The benchmark Selic rate target is at a record low 7.25%.

"The more-hawkish stance is very welcome," said Barclays Capital analyst Marcelo Salomon.

But for some, a hawkish stance is far from enough.

"You don't know what they want," said Nomura's Mr. Volpon, referring to Brazilian policy makers. "They don't care so much about predictability."

It doesn't help that the Brazilian central bank is part of the Finance Ministry, which makes Mr. Mantega the boss of central bank President Alexandre Tombini. In addition, Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff, an economist by training, is more hands-on regarding economic policy than her predecessor, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

While Brazil has always had a reputation for strong government intervention in the economy, its policy-making hasn't always been such a mystery for investors who now think its hand has become more unsteady.

Since controlling hyperinflation in the mid-1990s, Brazilian authorities have gained investors' confidence by keeping a clear anti-inflation stance, even when it meant raising interest rates to 45% in 1999.

Now, prices are creeping up amid strong income growth, with unemployment just above 4%. The central bank--which just a few years ago would have been certain to raise interest rates to contain inflation--has the markets trying to guess what it will do.

"The goodwill [towards Brazil] has vanished," said Goldman Sachs chief Latin America economist Alberto Ramos, "and it has migrated to Mexico, which is more orderly."

Smaller Latin American economies such as Peru, Colombia and Chile have shown more consistency in their policies. While investors tend to like that, they haven't flown en masse to those markets because they are still small. But Mexico, Latin America's second-largest economy after Brazil, seems to be benefiting, at least in its stock market, given investor concerns regarding Brazil, Mr. Ramos added.

Most economists are now forecasting modest economic growth above 3% in Brazil this year, with inflation near 6.5%, the top of the central bank's target range. An increase in interest rates is predicted for late this year or early 2014.

Fernando Sotelino, an adjunct professor at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, said Brazil needs to "come back to reality" after years of growth fueled mainly by global demand for its commodities and promote reforms to reduce the cost of doing business in the country.

"There is an obsession with the short term," he said, but Brazil needs to start building long-term credibility.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil yields rise on rate hike bets, real slips
text:
* Mantega says rates, not FX, are right tool to fight inflation

* Mexico yields flat after investors tame rate cut bets

* Brazil real weakens 0.38 pct as central bank intervenes

(Adds comments, updates prices)

MEXICO CITY, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazil's interest-rate futures soared on Friday after the country's finance minister suggested policymakers could raise interest rates to fight rising inflation.

Brazil's real currency, meanwhile, weakened after the central bank intervened to stop it from strengthening past 1.95 per dollar.

In Moscow for a meeting of the G20 group, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said that a rise in inflation above the government's target raises a yellow flag and that monetary policy, not the exchange rate, is the right tool to control prices.

Nomura analyst Tony Volpon said the central bank was likely to tweak its language in its March decision and remove a pledge to keep its benchmark interest rate at a record low of 7.50 percent for a "prolonged period."

"The Brazilian central bank has put its finger on the trigger," Volpon wrote in a note to clients.

Yields on interest-rate contracts jumped to price in a strong chance that the central bank will lift the base Selic rate as soon as in May.

Interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2014, among the most traded, jumped about 21 basis points to bid at 7.62 percent, closing at their highest level in four months.

Concerns about inflation have driven the real to strengthen 4 percent so far this year as investors bet policymakers would favor a stronger currency to cheapen the price of imported goods, but would still be forced to raise the Selic later.

Brazilian policymakers have intervened heavily in the currency market in recent years, acting to weaken the real against the dollar when they are concerned the exchange rate is hurting local manufacturers, but also moving to strengthen the currency when inflation becomes a worry.

The real briefly strengthened past the level of 1.95 per dollar for the first time in nine months early in the session. The central bank intervened with an auction of reverse currency swaps - derivative contracts that are designed to weaken the real against the dollar.

The real last bid down 0.38 percent at 1.9645 per dollar.

On Thursday, a source on President Dilma Rousseff's economic team said policymakers are more worried about curbing volatility in the foreign exchange market, indicating the real could strengthen past the level of 1.95 per dollar as long as the appreciation is gradual.

Meanwhile, Mexican interest rate swaps and bonds posted little change after a volatile week as the market gauges when the central bank of Latin America's second biggest economy could cut its 4.50 percent benchmark rate.

The interest rate swap market trimmed bets on the chance of a 25 basis point rate cut in March this week after Mexico's central bank chief Agustin Carstens on Wednesday warned that lower interest rates are not a "done deal."

Investors have priced in a 25 bps cut by April and some economists are eyeing the chance for a 50 bps or 75 bps point cut this year.

Mexico's peso traded little changed, edging 0.04 percent stronger to 12.6845 per dollar. Mexico's peso has pulled back from a 10-month high hit in January after the central bank signaled it could cut interest rates if inflation keeps cooling.

Lower interest rates could curb the attraction of the peso to global investors.

title: Brazilian Real Notches Strongest Close Since May 10
text:
--Brazil's real exits active trading at BRL1.9577 to the dollar

--Strongest close for local currency since May 10

--Market is "testing" central bank's tolerance for real strength amid inflation worries


 
   By Paul Kiernan 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real posted its strongest close against the greenback since May 10 on Thursday, as investors tested local authorities' willingness to accept a stronger currency in light of rising local inflation.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.9577 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.9642 at Wednesday's close.

Brazil's central bank, which intervened with a reverse-swap auction to stem a rally by the real Friday, remained on the sidelines.

"The market is testing the central bank again, but it was a slower, calmer move," B&T Associados trading chief Marcos Trabbold said.

The real's appreciation Thursday ran contrary to the predominant trend in international markets, as stocks and other currencies such as the euro and Mexican peso lost value amid weak economic data from the troubled euro zone.

Analysts increasingly believe Brazilian authorities--who last year actively promoted a weaker real amid a recession in local industry--are prepared to allow some currency appreciation in order to help rein in inflation.

"In Brazil, which led the charge in the global currency wars just two years ago, priorities are shifting," the Eurasia Group said in a report, noting the government's presumed desire to preserve record-low interest rates. The central bank "is silently pushing for a stronger currency."

Sidnei Nehme, director of Sao Paulo's NGO trading house, said Brazilian banks are "extremely short" dollars, heeding the central bank's perceived desire for a stronger currency rather than market fundamentals.

"We've got negative currency flows persisting in Brazil since December," Mr. Nehme said. Banks are betting on a stronger real on the expectation that Brazil's foreign-trade deficit so far this year will reverse itself and that reduced capital controls will start attracting more foreign money to the country, he said.

But participants in the local currency market soon will have to repay the central bank for several billion dollars in credit lines that expire in coming weeks, unless the central bank rolls them over.

"We're going to have some pressure in the market at some point because the banks will have to deliver dollars to the central bank," Mr. Nehme said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil  real weaker on cenbank  intervention , euro-worries weigh
text:
* Brazilian real closes down 0.05 pct, after cenbank move

* Brazilian Cenbank gives nod to stronger real

* Mexico peso down 0.05 pct, investors eye global woes

By Alexandra Alper and Walter Brandimarte

MEXICO CITY, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency cooled on Friday after the central bank intervened to slow the real's rally, while other Latin American currencies were mostly flat on renewed concerns about the Euro-zone crisis.

The real eased 0.05 percent to close at 1.9715 after the central bank moved to halt the rapid rise of the currency -- which has gained about 8 percent since November.

The intervention came despite comments by a number of policymakers, including Finance Minister Guido Mantega, suggesting the government was ready to accept a stronger currency to cheapen the price of imported goods and put a lid on inflation.

In an interview with Reuters on Thursday night, Mantega said the real, which last week gained past the level of 2 per dollar for the first time in seven months, "has found a reasonable floating band."

The central bank's move followed a week of intense volatility in the currency market as investors scrambled to figure out how policymakers were adjusting Brazil's foreign exchange policy.

"While investors may be skeptical about Brazil's intentions near-term, a solid and ongoing commitment to a stable real, instead of a weaker real, may end up marking its return to being a favored emerging market trade," Brown Brothers Harriman's analysts said in a research note.

The real is now likely to enter the traditional Carnival lull that will halt Brazilian markets for most of next week.

The Mexican peso cooled 0.05 percent to 12.727 per dollar, as renewed euro-zone concerns and upcoming U.S. spending cuts weighed on the currency of Latin America's no. 2 economy.

The peso has gained more than 1 percent since the close of 2012, but has been slowly pulling off a ten-month high reached on Jan. 17.

Investors "are waiting for any pretext to get some air," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico city, who said European central bank governor Mario Draghi's comments on Thursday were still weighing on the peso.

On Thursday, Draghi said the exchange rate is important for growth and price stability, which investors perceived as a sign the bank is concerned with the common currency's recent advance and potentially could act to stem its strength.

Gordillo predicted that the peso would fall to around 12.90 to 13 pesos per dollar, as the deadline for automatic spending cuts in the United States - March 1 -- draws near.

"A lot of us analysts are saying that the peso is at its last phase of strength," he said.

title: CORRECTED-WRAPUP 2-Brazil's  central bank  points to new  FX  trading band
text:
(Corrects 16th paragraph to say reverse swap auction mimics central bank purchase of dollars, not sale of dollars)

* Real initially rallies as government seen favoring strong FX

* Central bank intervenes to halt currency gains

* Mantega suggests government willing to accept stronger real

* Analysts see new trading band of 1.95-2.05 per dollar

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bankintervened to halt a currency rally on Friday, setting the boundaries of a new informal trading band that government officials hope will help curb inflation without hurting exporters.

The intervention followed a week of intense volatility in the currency market as investors scrambled to figure out how policymakers were adjusting Brazil's foreign exchange policy. The real, which stabilized and closed the week at 1.9715 per dollar, is now likely to enter the traditional Carnival lull that will halt Brazilian markets for most of next week.

The real was rallying for a second day early on Friday after comments by a number of policymakers, including Finance Minister Guido Mantega, suggested the government was ready to accept a stronger currency to cheapen the price of imported goods and put a lid on inflation.

In an interview with Reuters on Thursday night, Mantega said the real, which last week gained past the level of 2 per dollar for the first time in seven months, "has found a reasonable floating band."

The minister, who has always defended a weaker real to support exporters, sounded more amenable to a stronger currency as he cited the 1.85-per-dollar threshold as an example of a level that would not be allowed.

His remark came shortly after central bank chief Alexandre Tombini told a Brazilian newspaper that he was worried about rising consumer prices in the short term, comments that many interpreted as a sign the central bank was favoring a stronger real to curb inflation.

In the interview, Mantega sounded less concerned about inflation than Tombini, but the two appeared to be converging on currency policy. Economists say the central bank favors a slightly stronger real to help slow inflation, whereas finance ministry officials have argued that a firmer currency could spur investment by making it cheaper for companies to import capital goods and machinery.

Just last week, Mantega and Tombini appeared to be on a collision course when the central bank intervened in the opposite direction to halt a currency sell-off, also triggered by Mantega.

Taken together, Mantega's and Tombini's now converging comments were interpreted as a green light for a stronger real, driving the currency more than 1 percent higher in early trading on Friday.

The real had already gained about 0.8 percent on Thursday on growing speculation that the government would use the exchange rate to curb inflation, which is dangerously close to the ceiling of a government target.

Brazil's currency had lost nearly 30 percent against the dollar between July 2011 and last November, but gained about 8 percent since then.

TOO FAST?

Signs that the government was not happy about the speed of appreciation of the real in the past couple of days were already evident early on Friday, when a source on President Dilma Rousseff's economic team told Reuters gains had been "somewhat exaggerated."

After piercing the level of 2 per dollar last week, market analysts estimated the real's informal trading range, which for months was set at 2.0 to 2.1 per dollar, was shifting to around 1.95 to 2.05.

Investors, eager to test that theory, pushed the real to a nine-month high of 1.9510 per dollar on Friday morning.

That was when the central bank intervened, offering to sell as much as 30,000 reverse currency swaps - derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market and are often used by policymakers to weaken the real.

"They seem to be doing two things: one is to try to slow down the appreciation of the real, but they also seem to be putting a boundary for the real at 1.95 per dollar, at least for now," said Enrique Alvarez, chief of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York.

Further adding to the notion of a new trading band around the level of 2 per dollar, Development Minister Fernando Pimentel told Valor Economico newspaper that a real between 1.96 and 2.05 per dollar would be acceptable to industry.

Some analysts wondered whether the government was clumsily trying to stem currency volatility, a factor that some economists say muddies Brazil's investment climate.

"While investors may be skeptical about Brazil's intentions near term, a solid and ongoing commitment to a stable real, instead of a weaker real, may end up marking its return to being a favored emerging market trade," Brown Brothers Harriman's analysts said in a research note.

"We're not there yet, not with all these policy flip-flops," they added.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam stocks up despite Brazilian  currency  worries
text:
* Brazil's Linx, Mexico's Sanborns make market debuts

* Brazil markets to close from Monday to 1 p.m. Wednesday

* Brazil Bovespa rises 0.21 pct, Mexico IPC up 0.16 pct

By Danielle Assalve

SAO PAULO, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Latin American stocks ended slightly up on Friday but Brazilian gains were limited because of concerns that a strengthening real will hurt exports.

Despite the modest gains, Brazil's Bovespa index fell 3.1 percent for the week, its worst weekly performance since November last year.

Analysts said the poor Bovespa showing reflected larger concerns about the Brazilian economy. Earlier this week Brazil announced that consumer prices jumped in January by the most in almost eight years, pushing annual inflation up to 6.15 percent, and scaring off risk-averse investors.

On Friday, Brazil's central bankintervened to halt a currency rally, setting the boundaries of a new informal trading band that government officials hope will help curb inflation without hurting exporters.

"There is a perception that Brazil is in macroeconomic disarray and this affects the outlook for companies," said Silvio Campos Neto, an economist at Tendencias Consultoria in Sao Paulo. "Investors want a more stable environment for investing."

The Bovespa ended the day up 0.21 percent at 58,497.83 points after data showed Chinese exports grew more than expected in January. China is Brazil's biggest trade partner.

Nonetheless, market participants said optimism over the Chinese data was limited because Brazil's currency, the real , strengthened sharply in recent sessions, hitting its strongest level in nine months on Thursday.

A stronger currency can help curb inflation because it makes

imports cheaper for local consumers. It hurts exporting firms, though, especially in a commodities powerhouse like Brazil, because it makes their goods more expensive abroad.

In Brazil, state oil giant Petrobras drove gains, adding 1.37 percent, while shares of Linx SA, Brazil's largest maker of management software for retailers, rose 18.52 percent in their first day of trading on the Bovespa.

The firm's initial public offering priced at the top of the suggested range, according to a filing on Wednesday. A fund manager who participated in the IPO attributed strong demand to Linx's established name in Brazil.

Brazilian markets will be closed on Monday through Wednesday for carnival.

Mexico's IPC index was up 0.16 percent, but down 1.48 for the week.

Shares in the off-IPC Grupo Sanborns, the Mexican retailer and coffee chain owned by Carlos Slim, saw a rocky market debut, starting the day up before falling off to end at 28.46 pesos/share, slightly up on the 28 peso/share list price.

Chile's bourse was nearly unchanged. The IPSA ended the week up 0.5 percent.

title: POLL-Latam  FX  to keep governments under pressure
text:
* For poll data see

* Colombia, Peru, Mexico currencies to extend gains

* Chile peso seen weakening, but intervention not ruled out

* Brazil to keep currency in tight range

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Latin American governments will probably have a tough time trying to curb currency gains this year as improving market conditions boost dollar inflows, a Reuters poll showed.

After failing to foresee a surge in many Latin American currencies in the past few months, economists and strategists revised their forecasts to predict another leg of currency appreciation in Mexico, Peru and Colombia.

Such an outlook means that investors should remain wary for further government intervention - not only in those countries but also in Brazil, the birthplace of the latest "currency wars", and in Chile, where prospects of a weaker peso did not eliminate chances of increased dollar purchases.

"There's a good chance that in the current 'risk on' environment the Chilean peso will continue to appreciate towards 460 per dollar," said Michael Henderson, an economist with Capital Economics. "We think if it approaches 460 that might provoke the central bank into announcing measures such as foreign exchange purchases to weaken the peso."

The Chilean peso should remain at the current 472 per dollar this month, weakening to 480.00 in six months and to 486.59 in 12 months on prospects of feeble copper prices, according to the median of 13 forecasts.

Dollar purchases - the classic government tool - have already been used in Colombia, with little success so far. After increasing the daily amount of dollars purchased to $30 million from $20 million, Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said the government is planning to take on less external debt.

Six out of seven analysts who replied to an extra question on the Reuters poll said they expect additional government measures to curb the Colombian peso's gains in the next six months. The most cited was the extension of the dollar purchase program from May to the end of the year.

Even so, the Colombian peso is seen gaining ground to 1,780 per dollar in one month, 1,772.50 in six months and 1,770 in 12 months, according to the median of 14 forecasts. It last traded at 1,790.10 per dollar on Wednesday.

Peru has been more aggressive than Chile and Colombia in protecting its currency. Not only has it bought dollars, the government also announced it would prepay up to $1.5 billion in debt this year and flirted with capital controls by tightening reserve requirements on bank accounts denominated in dollars.

Analysts still expect Peru's currency, the nuevo sol , to strengthen this year, though.

It should trade at 2.560 per dollar in one month, 2.530 per dollar in six months and 2.520 per dollar in twelve months. It was at 2.5775 on Wednesday.

All the five top Latin American currencies gained between about 1.5 and 7 percent since mid-November. In the latest Reuters poll, in October, analysts said that currencies had little room to strengthen as government intervention was expected to yield better results.

The strongest intervention so far has been seen in Brazil, where the central bank has been keeping its currency, the real, trading within a narrow band between 1.98 and 2.05 per dollar through dollar purchases and currency swap auctions.

Mexico is the country less likely to intervene in currency markets. However, a rate cut could help stem further gains in its currency, analysts said.

title: Brazil's Industrial Outlook Still Unclear After Slow 2012--Trade Group
text:
BRASILIA--The outlook for a strong recovery of Brazilian industry in coming months remains unclear following signs of deceleration of activity late in 2012, officials at the National Confederation of Industries, or CNI, said Wednesday.

CNI economists said that they still expect a "gradual recovery" of Brazilian activity ahead following a "lost year" in 2012, but this will depend on a resumption of investment, which remains uncertain.

"Although there were some signs of improvement during 2012, they weren't with the intensity needed to characterize a recovery of industrial activity," said CNI Chief Economist Flavio Castelo Branco.

The CNI's latest industrial data released Wednesday showed that use of installed capacity declined by 0.6 percentage points over 2012 to end the year at 80.9%, while hours worked declined 1.5 percentage points.

On the upside, industrial sales rose 2.4 percentage points during the year. However, this likely reflected adjusted inventories as companies sold previously produced goods.

"There's no pattern of clarity in the latest data," Mr. Castelo Branco said. "We need to see some more months of continued improvement to determine whether we're in a recovery."

Brazilian industry, he said, is holding out hope for reduced costs and growing productivity brought by recent government initiatives to cut payroll taxes and lower electricity prices. But the full impact from these moves may only be determined late in the first quarter, he said.

However, local companies remain concerned about factors that continue to weigh against a resumption of activity, including still-sluggish and competitive conditions in global markets, and recent unexpected currency strengthening.

"The prospect that we had was that the exchange rate would show more stability in 2013 at around BRL2.10 to the dollar," said Mr. Castelo Branco. "But recent actions by the central bank brought appreciation, so this represents some uncertainty for the year ahead."

Amid concerns over accelerated inflation, Brazil's central bankintervened periodically in the foreign-exchange market over recent weeks in an effort to boost the strength of the real. As a result, the currency moved from levels near BRL2.05 to the dollar to stronger than the BRL2.00 per dollar mark.

A further hurdle for increasing local productivity, the CNI said, is a low supply of qualified labor for new projects as Brazil's unemployment rate tests historic lows.

"If this was a problem during a slowdown, imagine if there's any growth," said CNI economist Marcelo D'Avila. "We need to watch this because it could affect costs."

In the face of these factors and a still uncertain recovery of demand, CNI officials said there was little guarantee local industries would seek to swiftly expand their operations this year.

"If there's idle capacity that can still be used, then industries will be less inclined to invest for new production," Mr. Castelo Branco said.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Moderately Weaker amid Global Selloff
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed moderately weaker against the dollar Monday amid broad losses in global stocks and foreign currencies, though investors found little relevant news for the local market.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.9918 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.9862 shortly after the open and BRL1.9865 at Friday's close.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which Brazilian assets sometimes track, was recently down 0.9%; the euro weakened against the dollar and Brazil's Ibovespa stock index hovered 1.5% lower with less than an hour of trading left in the session.

Reginaldo Galhardo, foreign-exchange manager at Sao Paulo's Treviso brokerage, said the currency was mainly following international markets Monday.

With high inflation fueling speculation that Brazilian authorities--who wield heavy influence upon the real--might allow the local currency to strengthen beyond current levels, "the market is cautious," Mr. Galhardo said.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega last week suggested investors shouldn't expect the real to strengthen suddenly against the dollar, saying the local currency isn't a tool for controlling inflation. The Brazilian Central Bank, for its part, carried out a number of operations in the market that effectively induced the real to strengthen beyond the BRL2.0 threshold for the first time since July.

"We've got our friend Mantega saying one thing and the central bank saying another," Mr. Galhardo said. "There aren't clear signals about whether the real will be an instrument to control inflation or if capital inflows will pick up."

Prices for some of Brazil's key commodity exports such as iron ore, sugar and coffee stood lower in 2012 than in previous years. At the same time, financial investments slipped amid a sharp slowdown in the local economy and occasional, heavy-handed intervention by Brazilian authorities.

Brazil received a net inflow of $16.75 billion in 2012, down from $65.28 billion the previous year.

In the first four weeks of January, a net $2.69 billion left the country, according to central bank data.

title: Investors wonder who's in charge of Brazil's  FX  policy
text:
* Investors see tension between Mantega, Tombini over FX

* Central bank seen winning case for stronger real

* Real could gain to 1.95/dlr without cenbank resistance

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Feb 1 (Reuters) - When Brazil's central bankintervened on Wednesday to halt a currency sell-off triggered by comments from Finance Minister Guido Mantega, many investors wondered who is really in charge of Brazil's foreign exchange policy.

It was the second time in about two months that Mantega and central bank chief Alexandre Tombini appeared to clash publicly over the appropriate level for the real - a debate that has been growing as Brazil's economic recovery has faltered and inflation has stayed above target.

Both episodes, if not evidence of conflict among Brazilian policymakers, are seen at the least as being an example of the sort of seemingly contradictory policy action that has worried investors and put a chill on Brazil's business climate.

On Wednesday, just one day after the real had gained past 2 per dollar for the first time in seven months, Mantega warned the government was ready to correct any "excess" in the exchange rate and that a "speculative appreciation" of the real would not be tolerated.

His comments brought the currency back to the 2-per-dollar mark, but the change was erased minutes later when the central bank announced it was rolling over $1.2 billion in dollar repurchase agreements that would expire two days later.

When the real traded at around 2.10 per dollar on Nov. 23, Mantega told a crowd of business leaders in Sao Paulo that the exchange rate was at a "reasonable though not totally satisfactory level" to support industry. He added that a real weaker than 2 per dollar "was here to stay".

In moves similar to this week's action, the currency fell on Mantega's comments only to be rescued minutes later by the central bank, whose recent interventions are seen by analysts as a sign of growing inflation concerns.

"Uncertainty rules now," Ilan Solot, a London-based emerging markets currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman, said of Brazil's foreign exchange policy.

Like many analysts, Solot said it is tough to say whether the central bank was deliberately offsetting Mantega's comments or if the timing of its interventions was a mere coincidence.

Solot said, though, that it appears that Tombini is taking the reins of Brazil's foreign exchange policy with the blessing of President Dilma Rousseff, herself a trained economist who likes to have a say in key economic decisions.

"My interpretation is that there are two different lines of economic thinking (in the government). And the central bank's thinking is gaining precedence over the finance ministry's thinking," he said.

In Brasilia, a finance ministry source said there was no conflict between Mantega's Wednesday speech and the central bank's action. "There was no contradiction. The central bank just did a (dollar line) rollover."

Citi strategists Kenneth Lam and Douglas Comin disagree.

"The central bank and the ministry of finance do not necessarily see eye to eye on the issue of FX," they wrote in a research note. "The central bank has won the battle of the day in convincing the government to let the real appreciate to ease inflation."

The central bank declined to comment.

IMPROVING COORDINATION?

Brazil's central bank and finance ministry had a long history of disagreement over economic themes such as the right level for interest rates and the currency during the eight years of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's government.

While Mantega was a voice in the chorus of discontent with Brazil's double-digit interest rates, the central bank, led by its former president Henrique Meirelles, carried out an orthodox policy of high interest rates and a relatively free-floating exchange rate to keep inflation at bay.

Under Rousseff and Tombini, however, the bank lowered the base Selic rate to a record low of 7.25 percent while allowing the real to devalue by nearly 30 percent in the period between July 2011 and last November. Both actions were part of a coordinated government action to boost economic activity.

But a persistent rise in inflation, combined with a still anemic economic recovery, seems to have magnified lingering tensions between the two institutions, with the central bank now pushing for a stronger real.

To be sure, the finance ministry has also been unwinding some of the measures taken early last year to curb dollar inflows, helping the real gain about 7 percent in value since the end of November.

On Wednesday, Mantega stressed that recent currency gains do not mean the government is changing its foreign exchange policy nor was it trying to use the exchange rate to curb inflation.

Instead, according to another source at the finance ministry, a stronger real is part of a strategy to cheapen imported capital goods and boost much-needed investment in industry - an explanation that can certainly be more easily digested by the exporters Mantega had pledged to protect with a weaker currency.

Market analysts, however, are not totally convinced.

"The central bank wants the currency to help as a cushion against inflation," said Bruno Eiras Martins, a trader at Banco Daycoval in Sao Paulo.

"Some are saying that a stronger real is an instrument to boost imports of capital goods and investment, but I'm not sure about that. I believe that, given rising inflation concerns, the central bank has adjusted its strategy."

While economists agree that a moderate currency appreciation would not make a substantial dent on inflation, the fact that the real pierced the mark of 2 per dollar earlier this week should at least help anchor inflation expectations.

For now, most analysts agree, the central bank should offer no resistance to a real as strong as 1.95 per dollar, as long as the appreciation is gradual.

title: South Korea's Won Weakens on Finance Ministry Comments
text:
South Korea's won resumed its two-week march lower Wednesday after a finance-ministry official outlined measures the government may take to weaken the currency.

On Wednesday in Seoul, Deputy Finance Minister Choi Jong-ku said taxes on currency trading and bonds should be considered to help limit speculative capital inflows. Among a series of other measures, he also said state firms should refrain from overseas borrowing.

The proposal highlights concern among Asian authorities over the continued low interest rates in the U.S., Europe and Japan that are driving capital flows to emerging markets and tipping off a renewed currency war from government officials. For emerging-market officials, this means adjusting to the relative strength of their currencies and a decline in export competitiveness.

"This is a protracted effort by the government to talk down the won," said Ilan Solot, an emerging-markets strategist based in London at investment bank Brown Brothers Harriman.

"We don't know exactly what measures they're going to take, but they definitely have the credibility," Mr. Solot said.

The dollar rose to KRW1086.2, from KRW1083.2 late Tuesday, according to CQG data.

The Brazilian real traded slightly lower as markets digested an announcement of new dollar credit lines along with comments from Finance Minister Guido Mantega.

The new credit lines, where Brazil's central bank will offer up to $1.273 billion, come as weaker-than-expected dollar inflows boosted demand for the U.S. currency.

"It's a liquidity measure that's very much within the realm of the [central bank]. It's not one of the tools they use to impact the [foreign-exchange] rate," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Stamford, Conn.

Comments from Mr. Mantega overshadowed the central bank measures as he suggested the government wouldn't use the foreign-exchange rate to control inflation and that a weaker real should help Brazil's competitiveness. Last year, authorities intervened to help the real weaken nearly 10% versus the dollar, and this has allowed local industry to become more competitive, he said. His comments caused some confusion amongst traders, particularly since just on Monday the real broke through the psychologically important level of BRL2.00 to the dollar.

Amidst the confusion, the real weakened 0.1% versus the dollar, to BRL1.9884, from BRL1.9862 late Tuesday.

"The reaction in the market...reflects the fact that the market is tired from so much noise and communication from a government that has too many objectives running at the same time with very few effective policy tools," Ms. Cattan-Naslausky added.

Meanwhile, the Mexican peso weakened following the first quarterly decline in U.S. economic growth since 2009.

U.S. gross domestic product declined at an annual rate of 0.1% between October and December, the Commerce Department said Wednesday. Mexico's main trade partner is the U.S., which leaves the country vulnerable to any weakness in the economic outlook of its neighbor to the north.

Against the dollar, the peso fell 0.25%, to MXN12.7485, from MXN12.7180 late Tuesday.

Investors' attention has now turned to the Federal Open Market Committee's January policy statement due later in the day. The last time Federal Reserve policy meeting minutes were released, emerging-market currencies broadly declined on signs that some Fed officials had wanted to bring the central bank's stimulus program to a close.

--Gerald Jeffris contributed to this article.

title: Inflation Worries Keep Market Guessing on  Brazil  Real Level
text:
--Central bank intervention Monday may signal growing inflation concerns

--Real trades stronger than BRL2.00 to-the-dollar for first time in months

--Markets pondering whether stronger level for currency may be permanent


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
 

BRASILIA--Brazil's central bank allowed the Brazilian real to strengthen past the BRL2.00 to-the-dollar level this week for the first time since July of 2012, signaling growing concern over inflation and leaving market participants guessing as to what range the bank now wants for the currency.

The central bank spent months defending an unofficial range of BRL2.00-to-BRL2.10 per dollar, but on Monday it sold $1.9 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts even as the real was strengthening against the dollar.

Sale of the swaps, which increase dollar availability in the futures market, tended to accelerate the real's strengthening trend Monday, with the real closing at exactly BRL2.00 per greenback, gaining from the Friday close of BRL2.0285. As of mid-afternoon Tuesday, the currency had gained even more, trading at BRL1.9873 to-the-dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Market participants see Monday's sale of swap contracts as confirmation that the central bank is now more concerned about price pressures than economic growth.

"The government made a cost-benefit decision between raising interest rates and letting the real appreciate, and they chose the latter," explained Ilan Solot, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman in London. "That's an admission that inflation is pressuring and could get worse."

A stronger real could help to bring down prices. Brazilian inflation is now running at a worrisome annual rate of 6.02%, well above the government target for this year of 4.5%.

"A stronger real will help the government combat inflation by bringing down prices of imports," said Lorenzo Rodrigo, a partner in Sao Paulo's Torre brokerage. Official inflation statistics are especially sensitive to essential imports such as wheat and fuel.

The central bank spent the last months of 2011 and most of 2012 cutting its benchmark interest rate by more than five percentage points, leaving it at a record low of 7.25%, in an effort to help spur flagging economic growth.

During the same period, the government implemented a series of measures to encourage a weaker real and boost exports. The pace of the country's economic growth had slowed from 7.5% in 2010 to 2.7% in 2011 and about 1% last year.

But the government is predicting faster economic growth this year, in a range of 3.5% to 4.0%. That puts the focus back on controlling price increases in a country with a long history of hyperinflation.

After Monday's auction of swap contracts and the so-far unopposed move of the real past the BRL2.00 to-the-dollar level Tuesday, investors and traders are now pondering what the new unofficial range will be for the currency.

"I'm thinking it will be BRL1.95-to-BRL2.00, but it's really early to be guessing at this point," said Reginaldo Siaca, a manager at the Pioneer brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The market is readjusting."

Mr. Solot at BBH agrees with Mr. Siaca's guess on the range, though Flavia Cattan-Naslausky at RBS said she sees a range of BRL1.98 to BRL2.02 and Alessio de Longhis of Oppenheimer Funds expects a wider range of BRL1.95 to BRL2.05.

--Prabha Natarajan in New York contributed to this report.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso weakens on rate cut fears, real jumps
text:
* Brazil real up 1.5 pct on Central Bank currency swap rollover

* Investors bet Brazil's move reflects inflation concerns

* Mexico's peso loses 0.45 pct as Carstens bolsters rate cut bets

(Updates prices, adds details)

By Jean Arce and Alexandra Alper

RIO DE JANEIRO, Jan 28 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso lost ground for the second trading session in a row on Monday after comments by the country's central bank governor bolstered bets that Latin America's No. 2 economy is eyeing a rate cut.

But Brazil's real gained 1.5 percent, bucking losses in other Latin American foreign exchange markets, after the central bank signaled it would favor a stronger currency to fight inflation.

The Mexican peso lost 0.45 percent to 12.7652 per dollar after Mexico's central bank head Agustin Carstens said the peso is trading at "a relatively competitive level."

His comments backed the bank's statement earlier this month that it could move to cut rates if inflation continues to cool and economic growth flags, dropping its threat to tighten policy.

The central bank's communique "takes support away from the (Mexican peso), which is faced with the expectation of a possible benchmark rate cut in the near future and much more dovish minutes than in the last communique," Banorte-IXE analysts said in a note to clients on Monday.

The peso has slipped about 1.33 percent from a 10 month high notched on Jan. 17, the day before the communique's release, and is still weaker than it was before the global financial crisis.

"It's going to be a cautious week for financial markets because of (U.S.) economic data that is coming out," said Rafael Camarena, an economist at Banco Santander, in reference to the U.S. preliminary fourth quarter GDP results, a Federal Reserve statement, and an employment report slated for later this week.

Camarena added that the peso would likely strengthen if the data is positive.

In Brazil, speculation that the government now wants a real around 2 per dollar - the latest in a series of changes of heart by policymakers - grew after the central bank announced on Monday that it was rolling over all of the 37,000 traditional currency swaps that expire on Feb. 1.

Those contracts, which mimic the sale of dollars in the futures market, were originally sold by the bank to boost liquidity in the foreign exchange market at the end of the year, a period when greenbacks traditionally are scarcer.

The swap rollover "is a good indication that the central bank is really becoming more tolerant to a stronger real, at least in the short term," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist with RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut. "I believe that is related to a deterioration in inflation."

The real closed at 2.0006 per dollar, 1.5 percent stronger from Friday's close. Investors could soon try to take the currency past 2 per dollar -- a mark it has not crossed since early July, when the government intervened to weaken the currency in order to boost exports.

Brazil's benchmark consumer inflation rate closed 2012 at 5.84 percent, well above the center of a government target of 4.5 percent, but still within a tolerance range of 2 percentage points. Prices continued to climb in the beginning of 2013 as items such as food and personal expenses rose.
