title: As Rhetoric Heats Up,  Currency  War Risks Rise
text:
Guido Mantega is finally getting some company.

In September 2010, the Brazilian finance minister caused a mini commotion when he declared that the world was gripped by a "currency war." Mr. Mantega complained that the hyper-loose monetary policies pursued by advanced countries, coupled with the exporter-backed exchange-rate manipulations of China, were deflecting unwanted "hot money" into emerging market countries and forcing them to take retaliatory currency-weakening measures of their own. Those remarks, which evoked the specter of the vicious cycle of beggar-thy-neighbor policies that exacerbated the Great Depression, triggered much debate and even provided the title for a bestselling book by investment banker James G. Rickards. But at the time economic pundits mostly dismissed it as an alarmist reading of what was really just a post-crisis policy realignment.

Two and a half years later, Mr. Mantega's bandwagon is getting some fellow riders. With the yen having lost 13% of its value against the dollar in four months as the Bank of Japan has caved into demands from new Prime Minister Shinzo Abe for looser monetary policy and with the U.S. Federal Reserve well into a new round of open-ended "quantitative easing," currency-war warnings are coming thick and fast. And they're coming from figures that might be expected to take a more sober view of the world.

In separate speeches Tuesday, outgoing Bank of England Gov. Mervyn King expressed fear that the global financial system was facing a wave of competitive currency depreciations and Deutsche Bundesbank President Jens Weidmann chastised the Bank of Japan for policies that "could lead to an increasingly politicized exchange rate." That followed similar warnings this month about the fallout from Japan's actions by St. Louis Fed President James Bullard and European Central Bank board member Benoit Coeure, and a complaint from Jean-Claude Juncker, Luxembourg's prime minister who heads the Eurogroup of finance ministers, that the euro was "dangerously high."

Emerging market governments are also piping up. Among others, Russian and South Korean central bankers have warned that other countries may follow Japan's lead and weaken their currencies.

By the reckoning of the Royal Bank of Scotland's foreign-exchange strategy team, 2013 could see this current round of "currency fracas morph into something more internationally combustible." So, in preparation for a global currency war, they came up with a matrix showing which central banks have the most "intent" and/or "capacity" to intervene. The top scorers on both counts: the banks of Chile, Thailand, Malaysia and, somewhat surprisingly, Sweden.

It might be tempting to dismiss all this as mere hyperbole. The situation is far less severe than the brutal currency wars of the 1930s, which were intrinsically linked to trade restrictions that governments used to protect their national industries and which drained world trade to a trickle. For now at least, governments are too respectful of the World Trade Organization to go down that route.

But a strongly held view exists that extreme monetary easing and proactive currency strategies, which lie outside the purview of WTO regulations, represent protectionism by another name. Either way, we are at risk of a series of tit-for-tat measures doing great harm to the global economy. The end result could be an all-out trade war or a wholesale loss of confidence in paper money, along with surging inflation.

By speaking about this threat, policymakers often justify their own bad behavior. Mr. Mantega might have taken a holier-than-thou stance when he attacked the Fed and the People's Bank of China but it gave him an excuse to launch Brazil's own intervention strategy, including a tax on capital inflows, to weaken its currency, the real.

In a similar vein, the BOE's Mr. King accompanied his cautionary remarks Tuesday with statements that the pound needed a 25% depreciation to rebalance the struggling UK economy and that his central bank would resort to more quantitative easing if needed.

Such statements do little to breed mutual trust among trading nations. Countries need to acknowledge the negative international impact of their policies and, where possible, foreswear actions that undermine global trade. (The Fed, for one, could simply acknowledge the self-evident truth that quantitative easing weakens the dollar and creates imbalances in the global economy-even if its intent is to boost domestic rather than external demand.) Only then can countries come together in the mutual interest of a free-floating currency system that enhances world commerce and promotes shared prosperity.

(Michael Casey is managing editor for the Americas at DJ FX Trader, a foreign-exchange news service from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal. His new book on the global financial system, "The Unfair Trade," was published in May. Write to Michael Casey at michael.j.casey@dowjones.com.)

title: Currency  Rally Hems In Latin America
text:
The recent rally in Latin American currencies has exporters in the region renewing calls for central-bank and government action to slow the appreciation they fear will blunt their competitive edge at a time of slowing demand for their exports.

In Chile, Colombia and Peru, the dollars are pouring back in as global economic jitters have subsided and U.S. investors again seek the higher returns on investments that emerging markets offer.

A strong local currency and high labor and energy costs are creating "a perfect storm" for exporters, said Wilfred Leigh, chief executive at Chilean vintner Bethwines.

"One solution would be to increase our wine prices but, as Europe is our largest market, if we raise prices nobody there would buy our wines," Mr. Leigh said. "Europeans are undergoing their own crisis."

Brazilian exporters blamed their strong currency, the real, for last year's drop in the country's trade surplus as exports declined 5% and imports fell only 1%.

"We're facing price competition not only in export markets but also in the domestic market," said Flavio Castelo Branco, chief economist of the Brazilian Confederation of Industries.

Calls by exporters for intervention in Chile picked up in recent weeks when the peso reached a three-month high against the U.S. dollar, twice closing around 470 Chilean pesos to the dollar, a psychological level at which investors estimate the central bank could intervene. That is where the peso was when the bank launched a yearlong intervention program in January 2011.

Others see renewed intervention as unlikely. They say the cause of the current appreciation is dollar weakness partly tied to the Federal Reserve's largess.

"At 470, investors buy dollars and the peso depreciates," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile.

Chilean central-bank governor Rodrigo Vergara gave no clues in an interview as to whether the bank would take action to curb peso strength. "Some sectors have benefited from significant price increases abroad," he said. "Others have a more complicated outlook. So naturally, some manufacturing or agricultural sectors have been much more affected than others and they speak out against this."

Currency intervention across Latin America has varied, with Brazil the most active in managing swings and Mexico among the most hands-off.

Nomura Latin America strategist Benito Berber said currency appreciation is bound to be an issue in the region in 2013, noting recent statements by Colombian officials about weakening the Colombian peso.

Moves to weaken local currencies could lead investors to shop around when choosing where in the region to park funds, since depreciation of the currencies reduces the gains on local-currency bonds. "It's something they take into account," Mr. Berber said.

Mexico's peso is one of the most-traded emerging-market currencies, and as a result it is among the most vulnerable to swings in investor mood.

The Mexican peso last week reached its strongest level since September 2011, moving below 12.60 pesos to the dollar. Finance Minister Luis Videgaray said the government and central bank will maintain the policy of accumulating foreign reserves as a "prudential measure" against bouts of international market volatility.

Colombia's Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas shrugged off cries for greater action to curtail Colombian peso strength, saying the recent appreciation is "transitory" and that the exchange rate would soon return to 1,800 Colombian pesos to the dollar.

The Colombian central bank currently buys at least $20 million a day, and the Finance Ministry makes discretionary dollar purchases.

"The problem goes beyond simply buying dollars...it requires more aggressive and more audacious measures," including possibly capital controls, said Augusto Solano, who heads a Colombian flower exporters association.

Costa Rica is planning just that. The government this week proposed to Congress temporary measures including stiff taxes on financial gains by foreign investors that are transferred out of the country. President Laura Chinchilla last week described short-term capital inflows as "genuine weapons of mass destruction" for receiving economies.

--Tom Murphy in Sao Paulo, Darcy Crowe in Bogota and Carolina Pica in Santiago contributed to this article [ 01-22-13 1941ET ]

title: DJ  Currency  Wars Are Back. Best Be Prepared Says RBS
text:
Talk is building of an all-out currency war as policy makers line up to complain that some countries are gaining an unfair trade advantage by depressing their currencies to improve their competitiveness.

But which countries are most likely to get involved if a currency war breaks out?

In a research note Wednesday, Royal Bank of Scotland says it has some of the answers based on a country's willingness to intervene in FX markets and its capacity to do so, given the structure of its economy.

Among emerging markets, the U.K. bank singles out Malaysia, Thailand, and Chile as three candidates likely to lean against currency appreciation, along with the Czech Republic, a relative "newcomer to currency manipulation."

RBS strategists David Petitcolin and David Simmonds say Sweden, which has traditionally not intervened in markets, could also join the melee.

In contrast, China's willingness to intervene is tempered by the resilience of its exports, while in Brazil exports account for only a small proportion of the overall economy, they say.

That sits oddly with Brazil's relatively aggressive intervention last year. Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega first coined the phrase "currency wars" in 2010 to describe the global fallout from the monetary policy easing in developed countries.

He accused the U.S. Federal Reserve and other major central banks of flooding financial markets with cash to depress their currencies as investors plowed this cash into emerging markets in search of higher returns.

Brazil and other emerging markets subsequently took steps to stem these pressures.

And more than two years on, the urge to keep currencies in check appears to be returning.

A new government in Japan looks determined to turn the tide on two decades of deflation and the yen has weakened to levels not seen since June 2010. At the same time, the Federal Reserve continues to pump money into the debt-laden U.S. economy.

"For the quantitative easing-leading Japan and U.S., currency competitiveness is not the lead policy obsession," said RBS. "Rather, it's a welcome consequence of the need to loosen financial conditions to reflate domestically."

But what's welcome for some countries is not so welcome for others.

On Wednesday, the Russian central bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev warned that these policies were leading to global imbalances. Meanwhile, Eurogroup head Jean-Claude Juncker spoke late Tuesday of a "dangerously high" euro exchange rate.

Even the Bank Of England, which has a history of not intervening, has railed in recent months against the strength of the pound.

As RBS puts it: "This year could see [the] currency fracas morph into something more internationally combustible: a global currency war."

title: Brazil's Real Closes Slightly Stronger in Slow Trading
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real strengthened slightly against the dollar in slow trading Monday, as little news came out of the local market and investors abroad digested mixed signals for the global economy.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0309 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL2.0331 at Friday's close.

U.S. equities, which Brazilian assets often track, were roughly flat as President Barack Obama and congressional Republicans reiterated their positions for upcoming debt negotiations, highlighting one of the key threats to stability in financial markets. Political impasse could force the U.S. to default on its obligations in mid- to late February unless Congress authorizes an increase in the country's $16.4 trillion borrowing limit.

On the other hand, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development released a report painting an improved picture for the U.S. and other major economies, while a top official at the U.S. Federal Reserve predicted monetary stimulus will continue into the second half of 2013.

The real traded steadily through it all. Market participants see little chance of the currency appreciating beyond BRL2.02 to the dollar or weakening beyond BRL2.05, as Brazil's government and central bank have intervened to limit large fluctuations in the local currency during recent months.

Brazil's real experienced some volatility during the final weeks of 2012 as companies bought dollars to import goods for the holiday shopping season, repatriate profits and pay dividends overseas, among other year-end transactions. The currency traded as weak as BRL2.14 to the dollar before central-bank interventions brought it gradually back toward current levels.

Joao Querino de Santos, a trader at J. Alves brokerage in Sao Paulo, said business has been slow so far this year.

"It's very calm, kind of weird," Mr. Santos said, adding he and his colleagues have been arriving in the office later and going home earlier than they were a few weeks ago. "They say the year starts and Brazil only gets up to speed after Carnival [holidays in February], so maybe things will heat up afterward."

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil  real, Chile peso drop on verbal  intervention
text:
* Chile finance ministry, central bank to discuss peso strength

* Brazil won't roll over dollar auctions with repo agreement -Estado

* Brazil real drops 0.5 percent; Mexican peso drops 0.3 percent

By Danielle Fonseca and Moises Avila

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 8 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real dropped on Tuesday on signs that the country's central bank does not want the currency to gain much further, while the Chilean peso weakened after that country's finance minister expressed concern about the impact of a strong exchange rate on exports.

Most Latin American currencies also fell as investors took a weak Wall Street session as a cue to pocket part of a recent rally, driving the Mexican peso 0.25 percent lower.

Brazil's real led losses in the region, falling 0.4 percent to 2.0373 per dollar, after local news agency Estado quoted an anonymous central bank source as saying that, at current exchange rates, the bank would not roll over the dollars it had sold with repurchase agreements late last year.

"That could be an indication that the central bank doesn't want the real too close to two per dollar," said a trader at a large Brazilian bank.

A central bank spokesman said the bank would not comment on a story based on an anonymous source.

Those dollar auctions were part of Brazil's strategy to provide liquidity to the foreign exchange market at the end of the year, when greenbacks are usually more scarce as Brazilians vacation abroad and foreign companies remit profits to their headquarters.

Although the central bank's most recent intervention was designed to strengthen the real and avoid additional inflation pressures, analysts believe policymakers also do not want the real to gain past two per dollar, which could hurt exporters.

In Chile, the peso erased early gains to close 0.21 percent weaker at 472.20 per dollar after Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said the government and the central bank may come up with "coordinated action" to prevent the currency from gaining further.

The Chilean peso has rallied more than 1 percent in the first few days of 2013, on top of gains of nearly 8.5 percent in 2012.

"The peso started the day stronger as foreign banks sold dollars," said Eugenio Cortes, head of forward contracts at EuroAmerica. The currency pierced the level of 470 per dollar when investors started buying dollars again and the finance minister came with his "verbal intervention," he added.

Local analysts say the central bank would be compelled to intervene if the peso strengthens past 467 to the dollar.

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Stronger, Market Expects Less  Intervention
text:
--Real trading at BRL2.0214 from BRL2.0289 at Monday's close

--Market sees change in government policy to permit stronger real

--Investors ready to test central bank on intervention level

By Jeffrey T. Lewis

BRASILIA--Brazil's real opened stronger against the dollar Tuesday as the market adjusts to a perceived change in government policy, signalled by the country's finance minister, that will mean less support for a weak currency.

The real was trading at BRL2.0214 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, from BRL2.0289 at the close Monday.

The government spent most of last year working to weaken the real versus the dollar to try to make Brazilian exports more competitive in world markets.

Brazil's government plans to ease back on policies to weaken the currency and lower interest rates in 2013 as economic growth starts to recover after two years in the doldrums, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said in an interview with Dow Jones published Friday.

The government is now looking to use the exchange rate as a tool to help control inflation, said Reginaldo Galhardo, forex manager at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"The market is reading between the lines and sees a moment for the real to strengthen, at least to the point the central bank decides it's at a good level," Mr. Galhardo said.

It remains to be seen what level the central bank will choose to defend. During much of the second half of 2012 the market assumed the central bank didn't want the real to strengthen past BRL2.0 to the dollar, and the bank stepped in and intervened on more than one occasion when the real moved close to that level.

The bank will probably continue to defend that level, though it might eventually permit a slightly stronger real to help keep inflation under control, Mr. Galhardo said.

Investors are probably going to test the central bank in coming days to try to establish where it will step in, he added.

title: *DJ Brazil Dollar Outflows Rise To $7.07 Billion For Dec. 1-21
text:
27 Dec 2012 09:37 EDT *DJ  Brazil Dec. 1-21 Dollar Outflows Reverse Hefty Nov. Inflows

27 Dec 2012 09:38 EDT *DJ  Brazil Dollar Outflows Have Meant Central Bank Intervention

27 Dec 2012 09:40 EDT *DJ  December Could Mark Biggest Brazil Dollar Outflows Of 2012

27 Dec 2012 10:09 EDT DJ  Brazil Dollar Outflows Rise to $7.07 Billion in Dec 1-21 Period

SAO PAULO--Pressured by heavy imports and profit and dividend remittances by multinational companies, Brazil showed net U.S. dollar outflows of $7.07 billion during the period Dec. 1 through 21, the Central Bank of Brazil said Thursday.

The figure marked a reversal following net November inflows of $4.88 billion. If the trend continues through the end of the month, December will mark the biggest month of net outflows of the American currency in 2012.

Brazilian foreign-currency flows flipped from net positive to net negative in just one month in large part because of heavy imports. Imports typically rise during the Christmas shopping season as Brazilians snap up imported consumer goods and even some perishables. For the three-week period ended Dec. 21, net trade outflows were $4.87 billion.

But Brazil also saw net outflows on the investment side for the period totaling $2.2 billion. Foreign-investor interest in Brazil has waned for a number of reasons. One is increased volatility in the foreign-exchange rate in recent months. Another is a rise in government intervention in the foreign-exchange market. A third reason is lower Brazilian interest rates, making fixed-income investments in Brazil less attractive. Brazil's benchmark interest rate now stands at 7.25%, down from its 2012 peak of 12.5%.

December's net dollar outflows have brought a consistent pattern of central-bank intervention in the foreign-exchange market in efforts to avoid an abrupt depreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar. Last week, the central bank intervened six times in the market, using various auction mechanisms to increase the availability of dollars or dollar-hedging opportunities for investors.

December also typically sees an increase in demand for dollars from the Brazilian subsidiaries of multinational companies as they remit profits and dividends to overseas parents before the end of the calendar year.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazilian real gains after  central bank  acts
text:
* Brazil's real up 1.39 pct after auction, swap offers

 * Mexico's peso edges lower, on fiscal cliff concerns 

(Updates prices, adds context)

 By Asher Levine and Alexandra Alper

 SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 26 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real strengthened on Wednesday following heavy central bankintervention in the currency market, while Mexico's peso was little changed as worries over U.S. budget talks weighed.

Brazil's central bankintervened three times in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday in an effort to limit recent weakness in the real, which has dropped nearly 9.0 percent against the U.S. dollar this year. 

 Early on Wednesday, the bank conducted an auction to sell up to $2 billion on the spot market with repurchase agreements, which aims to provide liquidity to the foreign exchange market at year-end.

 The move was followed by two currency swap auctions, both offering 40,000 contracts with a maturity of Feb. 1, 2013. The bank sold a combined total of 37,000 contracts, which are derivatives that emulate the selling of dollars in the futures markets.

 "The central bank wants the dollar around 2.05 reais, considering the market was very calm and there was no reason for it to step in," said Reginaldo Siaca, head of foreign exchange at Advanced Corretora in Sao Paulo. "With the auctions, it is signaling the band it is comfortable with for the end of the year."

 The real strengthened sharply after the interventions, gaining 1.39 percent to close at 2.05 per U.S. dollar.

Brazil's central bank had last carried out a swap auction on Dec. 3, when the real closed at 2.119 per dollar. 

 "The central bank saw that a dollar close to 2.10 reais would be harmful for inflation," said João Medeiros, head of currencies at Pioneer Corretora in Sao Paulo.

 The Mexican peso edged down 0.21 percent to 13.0120 per dollar as anxieties remained over unresolved austerity issues facing the United States, Mexico's biggest trading partner. 

 "Mexico is really the barometer for the reality of the market over the holidays, which is thin (trading) and growing concerns over the fiscal cliff," said RBS economist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky. 

 She pointed to U.S. President Barack Obama's decision to return early to Washington from vacation to tackle the looming package of tax hikes and spending cuts, along with an upcoming debt ceiling debate, as fueling investor concern. 

 The U.S. Treasury on Wednesday announced the first of a series of measures that should push back the day when the government will exceed its legal borrowing authority as imposed by Congress by around two months. 

 Without any action, Treasury said the government is set to reach its $16.4 trillion debt ceiling on Dec. 31. 

 Still, the Mexican peso has performed well this year, firming more than 7.0 percent since 2011, and Cattan-Naslausky warned against reading too much into market moves during periods of light trading.

 Chile's peso edged up 0.08 percent to 479.10 per U.S. dollar. 

Standard & Poor's raised Chile's sovereign credit rating a notch on Wednesday to AA-minus from A-plus, citing the export-dependent economy's resilience to fallout from the global slowdown.

* Mexico's peso slips 1.43 pct, Chile's peso off 0.67 pct

(Adds comment, updates prices, changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso tumbled by the most in five months on Friday after U.S. budget negotiations stalled and Brazil's real weakened despite efforts by the country's central bank to lift the currency.

Brazil's real shed 0.52 percent to 2.0732 per dollar, while Mexico's peso tumbled 1.43 percent to 12.9444 per dollar. The peso hit its weakest level since early December and headed for its worst one-day loss since late July.

Markets fell on Thursday after a budget plan proposed by a Republican leader failed to win support from his own party, raising the chances that austerity measures kick in next year.

U.S. lawmakers are struggling to come up with a deal to avert $600 billion worth of tax increases and spending cuts, a combination that could push the world's largest economy back into recession next year.

"The risk is rising that (talks) are going to drag into next year," said Delia Paredes, an analyst at Mexico's Banorte-IXE.

A U.S. economic downturn could hit Mexico the hardest among Latin American countries, since it sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

Bets on a deal by U.S. lawmakers before the end of the year had spurred gains in riskier assets, such as Latin American currencies. Mexico's peso hit a two-month high last week.

Brazil's central bankintervened twice earlier in the day, selling up to $4 billion in two auctions with repurchase agreements. The auctions were designed to increase the supply of foreign exchange before year-end, but traders and analysts said they aim at curbing excessive losses in the Brazilian real.

The central bank said after the market close that it will sell up to $2 billion on the spot market on Dec. 26 with a repurchase agreement.

"After all the central bank has done, I think it wants the foreign exchange rate below 2.1 per U.S. dollar. It can even strengthen past 2.05 per dollar," said Reginaldo Siaca, manager at Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Chile's peso shed 0.67 percent to 478 per dollar to close at its weakest in two weeks.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger as  Currency Intervention  Continues
text:
--Brazilian Central Bank sells dollar credit lines, plans Friday auction

--Pressure on real should ease as multinational companies close books

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0597 to the U.S. dollar


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Thursday as the central bank continued its recent string of currency market interventions, but selling pressure is expected to ease as multinational companies close out year-end business.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0597 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullet Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Wednesday's close at BRL2.0683. Brazil's currency broke the BRL2.06 level late in the session, after the Brazilian Central Bank announced that it would cap the week with another auction of U.S. dollar credit lines.

The dollar credit line sales have become the favored tool for currency market intervention over the past week, when the real weakened sharply amid heavy dollar outflows linked to seasonal remittances by multinational companies operating in Brazil. The real has come under pressure as the companies send profit and dividend payments back home, pushing the currency toward the BRL2.10 level seen as the ceiling of the real's recent trading range.

"It's practically the last week of the year, and businesses are clearing out the books," said Joao Querino de Santos, a trader at Sao Paulo's J. Alves brokerage. "Next week should be very calm."

The local currency market is also starting to feel the effect of recent moves to ease currency restrictions put in place earlier this year, when the real was at its BRL1.70 peak against the dollar, Mr. Santos said. The IOF financial transactions tax on overseas loans of greater than one year was lowered, while the central bank also boosted the exemption level on reserve requirements for short-dollar positions held by banks to $3 billion from $1 billion.

"When the real hit BRL2.10, the central bank flashed the yellow light and let the market know that was the currency's ceiling," Mr. Santos said. The government is keen to keep the real trading between BRL2.00 and BRL2.10 to the dollar, a level seen as beneficial for local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation.

Late Thursday, the central bank said it would sell up to $2 billion in U.S. dollars via the credit-line auction. The bank said it would sell the dollars at BRL2.0625 per dollar, Thursday's average daily foreign exchange rate known as the Ptax. The auction will then establish the exchange rate the bank will use to buy the dollars back on March 1, 2013, although the bank said that it will pay a maximum of BRL2.08445 per dollar.

The central bank kicked off the session with a similar auction, selling an undisclosed volume of dollars at BRL2.0791 and offering to buy them back on March 1 at BRL2.1017.

In its latest quarterly inflation report also released Thursday, the central bank struck a neutral tone and indicated that current record-low interest rates would be maintained for a "sufficiently prolonged" period. The central bank expects inflation to end 2012 at 5.7%, before easing back to 4.8% in 2013 and 4.9% in 2014. Economists, however, noted that the outlook remained above the government's 4.5% target, although within the tolerance band of plus or minus two percentage points.

11 Dec 2012 10:29 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Tombini: Investment To Grow In Coming Year

11 Dec 2012 10:50 EDT DJ  Brazil's Tombini: Stable Rates to Support Recovery, Low Inflation

BRASILIA--The maintenance of Brazil's interest rates for a prolonged period of time will be sufficient to support a gradual recovery of the economy and keep inflation on target, Brazil's central bank president Alexandre Tombini said Tuesday.

Speaking at an appearance before the Brazilian Senate Economic Affairs Committee, Mr. Tombini said that despite a continued adverse outlook abroad, local economic policies currently in place would assure a rebound of investment and growth following a slowdown seen this year.

"A gradual recovery of activity in Brazil is in course that should continue in 2013," the bank president said.

Mr. Tombini noted that measures to restore confidence and growth had been taken by authorities in key economies abroad, but that these may not be sufficient to bring a strong international recovery.

"In recent months important measures were announced that reduce the chance of extreme events, but these aren't ready to bring growth," he said, adding, "The international outlook continues to be for low growth for a prolonged period."

In particular, he said that debt negotiations in Europe and the U.S. continued to bring risks to a global recovery.

He said China was preparing to reestablish a trend of expansion, but said its outlook "is for growth somewhat below recent years."

In the meantime, the official said Brazil's central bank remains "vigilant" on inflation and would continue its efforts to bring inflation toward the country's 4.5% inflation target with stable interest rates.

Brazil's central bank in recent months has held the country's benchmark Selic interest rate record low of 7.25%.

Mr. Tombini acknowledged that low growth of around 0.9% in the third quarter brought frustration, but said that it was in line with the performance of other economies around the globe.

"In relation to countries in the G-20, the performance of the Brazilian economy was very reasonable," he said.

He further noted that foreign direct investment remained robust and that the government in the meantime was taking measures to improve investment rates in the country.

"The diagnosis is clear, measures are being taken, and investments will take off in the coming semesters," he said.

Brazilian credit Mr. Tombini said, remained in moderate expansion, and local banks continued to be "healthy and well-provisioned" despite difficulties faced by a small group of institutions following the international credit crisis in 2008.

As part of its policy to maintain local economic stability, Mr. Tombini said the central bank would seek to minimize volatility in the foreign exchange markets.

"Our floating exchange regime shouldn't be seen as a reason for bets on volatility," he said.

Brazil's central bank has recently intervened in the currency market and introduced measures to hold the currency stable at a level between BRL2.05 and BRL2.10 to the dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil's real at 'realistic' level - Treasury
text:
* Brazil's stimulus measures part of "permanent" policy

* Treasury secretary indicates exchange rate at good level for economy

(Adds quotes from Treasury secretary, background, byline)

By Danielle Fonseca

SAO PAULO, Dec 11 (Reuters) - Brazil will keep stimulating its economy next year but the government believes the exchange rate has already achieved a more "realistic" level to support domestic industry, Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said on Tuesday.

Augustin did not specify which stimulus measures he was referring to but said the government intends to take steps to boost growth on a "permanent" basis.

President Dilma Rousseff's government has offered several tax breaks and credit incentives to spur investments and revive economic growth after a near-recession in the past year. Some of the measures, such as a tax reduction on automobiles, are due to expire at the end of this year.

"Stimulus measures will continue this and next year, this is something permanent," Augustin said at an event organized by Bloomberg in Sao Paulo.

The Brazilian government has also acted in the past few months to weaken the currency, in an attempt to stimulate exports. But the real is at a more "realistic" level now after being excessively strong in the past, Augustin added.

The real has slipped about 10 percent since the beginning of the year after several market interventions by the central bank and a sharp cut in Brazil's base interest rate, the Selic. It traded at 2.0755 reais per U.S. dollar on Tuesday.

Augustin reiterated that the government doesn't have a target for the exchange rate. He said the central bank's recent interventions were aimed at curbing undesired volatility.

"There's no change to the currency strategy," he said. "The government aims to curb volatility in the exchange rate, and the central bank has been doing great work on that."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil rates rise sharply on inflation surprise
text:
* Brazil IPCA inflation rise 0.6 pct in Nov, above forecasts

* Mexican peso gains after stronger-than-expected US payrolls

* Brazil real sheds 0.6 pct, Mexico peso up 0.12 pct

(Updates prices, adds detail on Mexican peso position)

By Danielle Fonseca and Natalia Cacioli

SAO PAULO, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazil's interest-rate futures rose sharply on Friday after higher-than-forecast inflation data reduced the scope for additional monetary easing next year, while the Mexican peso gained after encouraging U.S. payrolls data.

Bets that Brazil would cut its base Selic rate next year to boost a faltering economy have knocked down domestic interest rates to all-time lows this week.

Yields on interest rate futures had fallen since last Friday, after data showed the country's economy grew at only half the pace expected by economists in the third quarter.

But interest-rate contracts jolted higher on Friday after Brazil's statistics bureau said November inflation accelerated to 0.6 percent, above economists' expectations for a 0.5 percent reading.

Interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2014, one of the most traded, jumped 13 basis points to 7.0 percent. That contract traded above 7.3 percent last week, before the disappointing GDP figure, and slid to 6.87 percent on Thursday.

"What's boosting those contracts is mostly the higher-than-expected IPCA, which poured cold water on those who expected interest rates to fall," said Decio Pereira Filho, a trader with Socopa brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"The latest comments by Tombini also reinforced the view that the Selic will remain stable," he added.

Brazil's central bank president Alexandre Tombini repeated late on Thursday that the Selic rate should remain at an all-time low of 7.25 percent for a "prolonged" period.

His comments echoed the content of minutes of the bank's latest monetary policy meeting, released earlier on Thursday, but the mere repetition of the "prolonged period" expression led some traders to interpret that bets on additional rate cuts were premature.

CURRENCIES STEADY

Meanwhile, the Brazilian real shed 0.6 percent to bid at 2.0904 per dollar, weakening after intervention by the central bank spurred four sessions of gains.

Brazil's central bank said on Friday it was conducting a survey to gauge demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market, suggesting that policymakers could intervene again early next week to support the currency and setting the real up to strengthen next week.

A series of measures by the government helped the real rally nearly 2 percent this week back from its weakest in 3-1/2 years.

The measures, which included strong central bank intervention and tax changes to facilitate dollar inflows, signaled an apparent reversal in a recent government strategy that favored a weaker currency to boost exports.

"The weekend is upon us so folks get more cautious. Investors' trust is shaken, they're asking themselves, 'what are the government's intentions?'," said Jaime Ferreira, a manager at the currency desk at Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Other Latin American currencies posted gains after data showed the U.S. economy created 146,000 new jobs in November, more than the 93,000 positions expected by economists.

The data supported appetite for risk globally, although the outlook for the U.S. labor market still seemed tepid as the country's jobless rate fell because people gave up searching for work.

The Mexican peso gained 0.12 percent, ending the week with an advance of 0.64 percent during the week.

Data showed speculators raised their bets in favor of the peso for the second straight week indicating increasing confidence in a rebound after a recent slump.

title: UPDATE 1- Brazil currency  set to gain as cenbank warns of  intervention
text:
* Cenbank conducting survey go gauge demand for dollars

* Real gains in futures market after announcement

(Adds market impact, background, byline)

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 7 (Reuters) - The Brazilian currency was set to strengthen early next week after the central bank warned late on Friday it was conducting a survey to gauge demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market.

The real ended 0.6 percent weaker at 2.0904 per dollar on Friday, interrupting a string of four winning sessions that had been spurred by a series of government measures designed to support the currency.

Right after the market closed, however, a central bank spokesman said the bank was in touch with currency desks at key banks in Brazil to gauge demand for traditional currency swaps -- derivatives that emulate the sale of dollars in the future market -- and for dollar sales with repurchase agreement.

Those were exactly the tools the central bank used on Monday when it acted to halt a slide that had taken the real to its weakest level in more than 3-1/2 years.

Although Brazil's spot currency market was closed when the central bank started its survey, dollar futures contracts moved sharply at the BM&FBovespa.

The contract for January 2013, the most liquid at the exchange, showed the real strengthening to 2.082 per dollar from 2.098 reais per dollar minutes before the announcement.

The central bank will announce its swap or dollar auctions through its regular messaging system if it finds demand for them, the bank's spokesman said.

title: DJ Brazil's  Central Bank  Thinks Real Weakening Too Fast - Source
text:
--Brazil central bank believes market has made an incorrect assessment of government policy, a person familiar with the policy says

--That impression in the market led to an "artificial depreciation" of the real, according to the person

--Brazil central bank believes the real doesn't reflect economic fundamentals, the person says

By Luciana Magalhaes

SAO PAULO--Brazil's central bank believes there has been "an artificial depreciation" of the Brazilian real as the market is working on an erroneous view of government policy, according to a person familiar with the central bank's thinking.

"The market is working based on conjectures, on a belief that the government wants a weaker real," said the person, who asked not to be identified. "But there's no band. There's no roof and no floor. The market determines the exchange rate."

Current exchange rate levels versus the dollar don't reflect the fundamentals of the Brazilian economy, which, in spite of the weak performance, is "growing more" than other economies, said the person.

While debate persists about the real's fair value--it's lost around 10% against the dollar so far this year, but many economists still see it as overvalued --there is also a general perception that it has shed weight too fast against the dollar in recent sessions.

There have been a series of press reports citing people close to the central bank that have helped strengthen the Brazilian real over the last two days. The real traded at BRL2.0782 on Thursday afternoon, stronger than Wednesday's close of BRL2.0978, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

The signals appear to have arrested a concerted effort by some in the market to test weaker levels for the Brazilian real. The real weakened to 2.1359 in intraday trading on Nov. 30.

Last week, as the currency touched BRL2.0978 per dollar during intraday trading, the central bank stepped in several times to strengthen the currency.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the central bank also relaxed some restrictions on capital inflows that had been introduced earlier this year to prevent an overappreciation of the currency. Although officially these were more aimed at specific issues in lending markets, market players saw the move as clearly directed at the currency market.

"We had a problem of dollar liquidity and the government acted to solve that", said Sidnei Nehme, executive director at Brazilian brokerage NGO. Next year could be challenging for the real, as the government intervention, combined with historic low interest rates, has made Brazil less attractive to overseas investors, Mr. Nehme said.

The efforts to avoid currency weakness come just as some in the rates market raised questions about monetary policy next year. There's a growing perception that the central won't raise rates in 2013 and may even start cutting them again to speed up the pace of recovery.

After timid 2.7% growth in 2011, the Brazilian economy is expected to grow just 1% or even less in 2012, despite a series of measures taken in an effort to spur growth. The government has often expressed concern that a strong currency hinders the competitiveness of Brazilian exporters.

But the central bank is also constrained from cutting interest rates by above-target inflation, which is running around 5.6%. That's more than a full point higher than its 4.5% target, though still within the 6.5% upper limit of its tolerance band.

Earlier Thursday, the central bank reaffirmed its commitment to the interest rate stability for a "sufficiently prolonged period," in the minutes of the central bank's monetary policy meeting from Nov. 27 and 28.

Meanwhile, the comments from the person familiar with the bank's consideration could once again raise tensions in Brasilia.

"The bigger question is whether this new 'strong BRL' policy signals, as some investors now believe, a change in the relative power between the Brazilian Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance over management of the currency," wrote Tony Volpon, a strategist at Nomura Securities in New York, suggesting the central bank may have recovered stewardship of the currency.

Still, there's no real contradiction between taking the real lower to help industry and the central bank's verbal intervention to moderate the recent sudden depreciation, Mr. Volpon said. The process has to be managed to minimize damage to companies from a stronger currency or inflation from a weaker real.

"But there is no doubt, given the dismal growth in Brazil, that a weaker real is what the government desires," he said. "We still believe that it will settle at a 2.08-2.12 level once the high levels of noise and uncertainty around the currency hopefully fade."

title: INTERVIEW-Brazil's Neves would end  currency  swap program, adviser says
text:
BRASILIA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Brazilian presidential candidate Aecio Neves will end a central bank currency swap program that has cushioned losses in the country's currency, the real, if he is elected later this month, Neves's choice for finance minister, Arminio Fraga, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Neves, a centrist who has promised to rescue the economy from recession, is running neck-and-neck with left-leaning President Dilma Rousseff in Brazil's tightest presidential election in at least two decades.

Fraga, a former central bank chief whom Neves has said will be his finance minister, said the program would end immediately and that the central bank's stock of currency swaps would be wound down as contracts expire.

"We would certainly not have that program," Fraga said in a telephone interview. "The government is intervening to prevent the depreciation of the currency and that should not happen except in times of great uncertainty. The best policy for Brazil is to have a free-floating exchange rate."

Since last August, Brazil's central bank has intervened daily in the foreign exchange market by selling currency swaps, derivatives designed to support the real.

Fraga, a Princeton-educated economist, said that Neves would likely include academics and market economists in the next central bank board if he is elected. (Reporting by Alonso Soto; Editing by Peter Galloway)

title: UPDATE 2- Brazil  to keep stronger  FX intervention  next month-source
text:
(Adds background on rollover rate of currency swaps)

By Patricia Duarte

SAO PAULO, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Brazilian policymakers are likely to roll over 100 percent of the currency swaps that expire in November in a bid to curb a sharp depreciation of the real, a source on President Dilma Rousseff's economic team said on Thursday.

"There is a very reasonable possibility," the source told Reuters when asked whether the bank would keep next month its increased rollover pace of currency swaps, derivatives designed to support the real.

The central bank on Tuesday announced it would intensify its currency intervention after the real closed weaker than 2.4 per dollar for the first time in seven months, hit by uncertainty about the outcome of the October presidential elections.

It increased to 100 percent from about 75 percent the rollover rate of currency swaps that expire in October. In previous months, the central bank had systematically allowed some swaps to expire.

Despite the bank's efforts, the Brazilian currency slid further on Thursday, closing at a seven-month low of 2.4294 per dollar, as investors feared higher interest rates in the United States as well as electoral polls in Brazil.

At these levels, "it begins to get dangerous" for those investors who are shorting the real, the source warned, explaining that any scenario reversal could cause a sharp currency adjustment that could impose large losses to investors.

Brazilian financial markets have been selling off whenever President Dilma Rousseff gains support in opinion polls. Investors accuse her of failing to curb inflation and driving the economy into a recession.

The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said policymakers do not plan to increase the daily supply of 4,000 currency swaps under a program that is set to continue at least until the end of the year.

Instead, the central bank is likely to offer dollars through repurchase agreements at the end of the year, when the spot currency market usually needs a liquidity boost.

There are no plans to offer dollar lines before that as the spot dollar market remains "liquid" despite its increased volatility, the source said. (Reporting by Patricia Duarte, writing by Walter Brandimarte; Editing by Diane Craft and David Gregorio)

The monetary authority will offer investors the rollover of up to 15,000 swap contracts at daily auction, compared with 6,000 contacts offered in previous sessions. The increase represents $750 million, compared with $300 million previously.

The swap auction is the equivalent of the sale of dollars in the futures markets. The futures market in Brazil for currencies is about eight times bigger than the spot market. Only 14 major banks are allowed to operate in the spot currency market, severely restricting access to the market and pushing a majority of players into the futures market.

In the most recent session, the Brazilian real closed at 2.408 reais to the dollar, the lowest level since Feb. 12, when the real closed at 2.42 per dollar.

The Brazilian currency lost ground in recent sessions as certain polls showed incumbent president Dilma Rousseff gaining ground versus her main contender Marina Silva, ahead of October's election.

Two polls released Tuesday showed Ms. Rousseff ahead of Ms. Silva for the first time since mid-August, though the two are still in a technical tie.

Investors say Ms. Rousseff's policies are too interventionist, and financial markets in Brazil have usually reacted negatively to good polling news for the incumbent. Shares in state-controlled companies have been especially sensitive to poll results.

title: Brazil's  Central Bank  Becomes an Unlikely Star in Presidential Campaign
text:
BRASÍLIA--Central bank governance isn't an issue most politicians waste much breath on, but Brazilian voters are getting an earful in the midst of a tight presidential race.

With the Central Bank of Brazil under fire for failing to stem inflation, the main candidates have come out swinging on who should control the institution.

Brazil's central bank is part of the Finance Ministry, though it has a special status and is largely autonomous. The bank's chief, Alexandre Tombini, has the title of minister and reports directly to President Dilma Rousseff. Brazil's central bank governors currently serve at the will of the president and have no fixed terms.

Ms. Rousseff defends this relationship as necessary to keep the bank focused on policies beneficial to all Brazilians, not just investors and the financial industry.

But with inflation hovering at around 6.5% and eating into Brazilians' pocketbooks, Ms. Rousseff's main rival, Marina Silva of the Brazilian Socialist party, is stumping for an independent central bank similar to those in the U.S. and Europe.

The front-runner in recent polls, Ms. Silva wants to establish set terms for the bank's eight governors and restrict the president's power to fire them. The aim, her advisors say, is to give central bankers the ability to raise the benchmark Selic rate as much as needed to fight inflation, without government pressure.

The topic, eye-glazing to most, has made for a surprisingly lively debate, with both candidates accusing the other of kowtowing to special interests.

The Silva camp says the central bank hasn't confronted inflation aggressively enough because it is concerned that additional rate increases would hurt growth and employment in an election year. After the central bank lifted the Selic by 3.75 percentage points between April 2013 and April 2014, it has kept the rate at 11%.

Ms. Silva's team has also lambasted the central bank for intervening regularly in the currency markets to prop up the real against the dollar. They view this activity as a risky back-door move to fight inflation that could lead to a large and swift devaluation of Brazil's currency when the intervention ultimately ends.

"Monetary policy can't be based on political whims and moods," Maurico Rands, one of Ms. Silva's top advisors said at a public forum on Monday.

Ms. Rousseff's government denies it intervenes in central bank decisions. She and her supporters have fought back with a television ad warning that an independent central bank could become a tool of the financial industry.

The spot shows food vanishing from the dinner table of average Brazilians as bankers sitting in a dark room plot to raise interest rates. An ominous voiceover says central-bank autonomy, as proposed by Ms. Silva, "would mean giving bankers great decision power over you and your family's life; the interest you pay, your job and even your salary."

The debate has struck a chord with some voters in a country where economic turmoil often vaults otherwise arcane issues into the headlines.

Ricardo Fernandes, a 25-year-old parking valet works just a couple of blocks from the central bank's imposing headquarters in Brasília. While unable to explain exactly how an independent central bank would affect his life, Mr. Fernandes said TV coverage has convinced him it's a good idea.

"I support central-bank autonomy," Mr. Fernandes said. "I think Marina is more likely to give autonomy to the central bank."

Meanwhile, Brasília resident André de Almeida said he, too, has seen headlines and TV spots and come to the opposite conclusion. The 28-year old business student said he opposes central-bank autonomy because "private banks will have too much influence over it, and banks tend to prefer higher interest rates."

Mr. Almeida wouldn't disclose who he'll vote for, but said the central bank issue wouldn't influence his decision.

Ms. Silva and other proponents of a fully independent central bank say Brazil's current system makes the bank vulnerable to political influence.

Former central bank governor Gustavo Franco said as much to The Wall Street Journal a few years ago. In an interview in New York, he said he was ousted from his post by then-President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in 1999 under political pressure.

At the time, Brazil's currency was being targeted by speculators, and Mr. Cardoso wanted to adopt a free-floating exchange rate to thwart them. Mr. Franco said he opposed the move since pegging the real to the dollar had been a key pillar of the government's plan to staunch hyperinflation earlier in the decade. A Cardoso spokesman declined to comment.

Ms. Rousseff maintains that her administration doesn't interfere with the bank's rate decisions and that the de facto autonomy she grants to the bank is sufficient.

Talking to reporters Sunday, Ms. Rousseff said that independence is equal to making the central-bank a "fourth power." She said that the bank doesn't prioritize job creation, thus independence "does indeed take food out" from workers' table, she said.

Jeffrey T. Lewis contributed to this article.

title: Exclusive:  Brazil 's Silva would cut spending, end  forex intervention  program
text:
BRASILIA (Reuters) - Marina Silva would push for large budget cuts and end a central bank foreign exchange program aimed at supporting the currency if she is elected Brazil’s next president in October, a senior economic adviser told Reuters on Thursday.

Alexandre Rands, an economist who helped draft Silva's economic plan, said she could cut up to 100 billion reais ($43 billion) - or about 2 percent of gross domestic product - in budget spending next year to send a strong signal to investors worried about the deterioration of public finances.

"Our priority is not to cut spending for the sake of it. Our priority is to control inflation in order to create an environment that will allow Brazil to grow more," he said in an interview that provided some of the most specific guidance yet about Silva's financial policies.

Silva, an environmentalist whom polls show is running neck-to-neck with President Dilma Rousseff in a likely runoff next month, has encouraged many investors with her market-friendly economic platform, which includes giving the central bank full independence.

A sluggish economy and growing fiscal deficits during Rousseff's four years in office has cost Brazil a downgrade of its debt rating and scared off some investors who say the leftist leader is too interventionist.

Rands said Silva would eliminate many of the economic distortions that have dragged the once-booming Brazilian economy into recession.

He mentioned the central bank's currency intervention scheme, which has kept the real stronger since last year, as one of those distortions that will be corrected under Silva.

"That does not mean that you cannot carry out small, temporary actions to eliminate volatility," Rands said.

The real weakened slightly in late trading due to Rands' comments, traders said.

Since last August, Brazil's central bank has intervened daily in the foreign exchange market by selling currency swaps, derivatives designed to support the real.

LESS PORK

Rands, who runs an economic consultancy in the northeastern state of Pernambuco, is part of Silva's team of economic advisers, which also includes well-known economist Eduardo Giannetti da Fonseca.

He said the budget cuts would spare initiatives such as the Bolsa Familia welfare program for poor families, focusing instead on pork-barrel spending for projects in lawmakers' districts.

"There is a lot of fat that can be cut and the Marina (Silva) camp is sending positive signals on that fiscal front," said Alex Agostini, chief economist with Austin Rating. "It could generate a confidence shock that will allow the economy to grow more in the future."

Rands said a Silva administration would also aim to lower the center of Brazil's official inflation target below the current 4.5 percent.

Economists complain that such a wide target range has allowed politicians to keep inflation high, hurting retailers and dragging down investments in Latin America's largest economy.

He said the campaign's economic team is debating whether to keep the current leadership at the central bank or opt for a new team during the transition toward full independence if she is elected.

Rands was a macroeconomics classmate of current central bank chief Alexandre Tombini at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.

"Brazil has a credibility problem. Once Rousseff is out of power part of that problem will be resolved," Rands said. "But we will need to win back credibility with the correct monetary and fiscal policies."

(Reporting by Alonso Soto; Editing by Diane Craft and Lisa Shumaker)

title: Beset by problems at home, Brazilian steel looks out at a hard world
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Whichever way Brazil's steel industry looks it sees pain.

At home, the economy is on the brink of recession and demand for the world's most used metal is on the wane. Abroad, Brazilian exports are hampered by a strong currency and global production overcapacity.

What is needed, steel executives say, is widespread reform, including higher infrastructure spending, lower taxes, and a weaker Brazilian real .

But although steel companies talk urgently of a state of crisis, and many analysts and economists agree, little change can be expected soon with a presidential election just two months away.

Last week, Companhia Siderurgica Nacional SA, known as CSN, the country's largest diversified steelmaker, posted a 96 percent drop in quarterly net income. "Only a crazy person would invest in Brazil right now," CSN Chief Executive Benjamin Steinbruch told a conference in Sao Paulo this week.

Strong words for a leader of an industry that remains fiercely nationalistic. The conference began with the national anthem and executives repeatedly stressed their patriotic credentials before sticking the knife in.

The problem for Brazil is that the suffering of its steel industry is both the result of a weakening economy, as demand from the construction and auto sectors drops, and a cause of economic weakness as the high price of steel stops companies investing.

HOME PAIN

In the past three years economic growth in Brazil has slowed to a crawl with a number of economists suggesting the country may have already fallen into recession. An economic activity index that measures the farming, industrial and services sectors fell in June for a fifth straight month.

The country's auto industry is on track for its biggest drop in sales in more than a decade, and inflation is leaning heavily against the upper limit of the central bank's target range.

Industry group Instituto Aço Brasil expects steel production to fall 2.5 percent this year, with domestic sales down nearly 5 percent.

Benjamin Baptista, CEO of the Brazilan unit of global steelmaker ArcelorMittal, tried to find a silver lining when asked for his forecasts. "It's hard to be worse than it is now," he said.

With the situation at home severe, exporting seems the answer. Steelmakers loathe to reduce production levels because it results in higher costs, politically sensitive job losses and puts companies at a disadvantage if markets pick up.

But international markets are flooded with steel from China, where a rampant increase in production over past decades has dramatically outstripped demand as Chinese growth slows.

Both Usiminas, formally known as Usinas Siderurgicas de Minas Gerais SA and one of the largest steelmakers in the Americas, and CSN say they are looking to export more steel products but acknowledge margins could suffer.

The biggest problem is the strong real. Some economists estimate that given Brazil's current account deficit, the real should be at a level of between 2.7 and 3.0 to the dollar.

On Friday it was trading at 2.27 to the dollar. Brazil's central bankintervenes regularly in the market to prop up the currency to keep inflation under control.

Steelmakers expect the real to weaken through to the end of the year, offering some respite. But the exchange rate is not the only problem.

HAVE YOUR CAKE AND EAT IT

According to Sergio Leite, vice-president for sales at Usiminas, the high tax burden in Brazil makes the industry uncompetitive.

He cited a study from Aço Brazil in 2012 that showed Brazilian steel had lower production costs than any of the world's five main producers: the United States, Germany, China, Russia and Turkey.

But "when this steel arrives in the hands of the consumer, with taxes added, it arrives as the most expensive," Leite said.

High taxes, however, are in essence the flip side of the protection from imports the industry enjoys through strict anti-dumping legislation. The steel industry, by asking for lower taxes but a continuing barrier to imports, wants its cake and eat it too.

But the sense that reforms are needed, and will be delivered by whoever wins the election, is gaining traction.

"There is now a consensus from various industrial sectors that reform is needed to improve the tax system, to simplify and reduce bureaucracy," said Luciano Coutinho, president of Brazil's powerful development bank, BNDES. title: Small Companies Taking More Time With Hires -- Market Talk
text:
12:55 EDT - Small US employers are taking nearly twice as long to fill job openings versus five years ago, a new report shows. Between January and May, businesses with fewer than nine employees took a mean 23.6 days to hire new workers, up from 12.8 days in 2009, according to an analysis of labor statistics by Dice Holdings. U.S. power plants used about 7 million tons of imported coal last year, up from about 5 million in 2012, when imports hit a 10-year low. They had peaked in 2007 at more than 30 million tons, but power plants that import coal have been some of the hardest hit by the move away from coal power. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam rallies on Ukraine; Brazil real supported by cenbank
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Latin American stocks and
currencies gained on Monday as geopolitical tensions related to
Ukraine eased, while the Brazilian real was further bolstered by
a central bank decision to speed up the rollover of currency
swaps, strengthening its intervention in the currency market.
    Appetite for risk in emerging markets increased globally
after Russia said it had finished military exercises near its
southern border. The action had raised fears of a direct
intervention by Moscow in Ukraine. 
    Benchmark stock indexes in Brazil and Mexico 
rallied over 1 percent, while MSCI's index for Latin American
equities jumped more than 2 percent.
    Shares of Brazil's Petróleo Brasileiro SA, or Petrobras
, gained 1.4 percent even after the state-run oil
company posted a larger-than-expected 20 percent slump in 
second-quarter profit late Friday. 
    Some analysts said, despite the profit miss, an increase in
Petrobras' oil production was a good development. The company on
Monday reaffirmed its forecast for a 7.5 percent increase in
output in Brazil in 2014. 
    Other analysts said Petrobras' shares were being driven by
bets a new government elected in October would change a policy
that forces the company to sell fuels in the domestic market at
a loss.
    In currency markets, the Brazilian real  gained
0.6 percent, also supported by the central bank's decision to
offer as many as 10,000 currency swaps per day to roll over
contracts maturing on Sept. 1, up from the 8,000 swaps it had
been offering since the beginning of the month.
    The move suggested the central bank was not comfortable with
a recent currency weakening that drove the real near the level
of 2.3 per dollar.
    "The market is a little less worried about Russia and,
around here, the central bank showed its face. That made room
for a correction in the real," said Reginaldo Siaca, head of
currency trading for Sao Paulo's Advanced Corretora.
    Siaca believes the central bank now wants the real to trade
within a range of 2.25-2.30 per dollar, weaker than the previous
range of 2.20-2.25 that was observed during most of the past
four months.

title: Brazil Ex-Insider Returns to Help Oust President
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO--With slow growth and high inflation hurting Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff's chances of winning a second term, a financial heavyweight has joined the opposition to persuade voters that Brazil needs a new economic steward.

Arminio Fraga, a former central banker, has been advising Aecio Neves of the Brazilian Social Democracy Party for several months. He's now talking openly of returning to government, perhaps as finance minister, if Mr. Neves can pull of an upset in October's presidential elections.

"I wouldn't make myself available if I didn't feel deeply bothered, and I am," Mr. Fraga, 57, said last week in an interview in his office in Rio de Janeiro.

Ms. Rousseff still holds a comfortable lead heading into the first round of voting October 5. But recent polls show Mr. Neves closing the gap in the event of a runoff, which is looking increasingly likely.

The president's Achilles' heel is the economy. GDP growth likely won't crack 1% this year; some analysts are even predicting a recession. But it is Brazil's stubbornly high inflation, which is hovering at around 6.5%, that is most worrisome to many voters. As recently as the 1990s, Brazil was bedeviled with hyperinflation; automatic cost-of-living increases are still built into salaries, rents and pensions.

Mr. Fraga appears to be positioning himself as something of an inflation whisperer. As president of Brazil's central bank from 1999 to 2002 under the administration of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, he helped stabilize the currency and rein in consumer prices. Mr. Fraga supports restrained public spending, tough inflation targeting and a floating exchange rate, policies that became known in Brazil as the "economic tripod."

He is highly critical of the Rousseff administration's decision slow inflation by capping gasoline prices and electricity rates, moves he dismissed as "gimmicks." He's also alarmed that Brazil's central bank has been intervening regularly in the currency markets to prop up Brazil's real against the dollar, a strategy he ridicules a "populist move."

Mr. Fraga said these are stopgap measures that already are proving unworkable and that Brazil needs to focus on long-term fundamentals like increasing private investment and balancing its books. Credit agency Standard & Poor's earlier this year cut the credit rating on Brazil's long term bonds to one notch above junk, citing deteriorating government accounts and rising debt.

"We have to give up on these gimmicks that have a lot of side effects and focus on bringing inflation down," Mr. Fraga said.

After leaving the central bank, Mr. Fraga helped found Gávea Investimentos, an asset management firm with around $7 billion in assets under management. He also served as chairman of Brazil's BM&F Bovespa SA, Latin America's largest stock exchange. Earlier in his career he worked at Soros Fund Management LLC in New York for 6 years.

But whether those prestigious credentials help boost Mr. Neves chances at the presidency remains to be seen.

A spokesman for Ms. Rousseff declined to comment. But on the campaign trail, the president and her political mentor, former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, constantly remind voters that millions of Brazilians have been lifted from poverty since their Workers' Party ascended to power with Mr. da Silva's election in 2002.

Economist Luiz Gonzaga Belluzzo, who has advised both Ms. Rousseff and Mr. da Silva, noted Mr. Fraga's ideas didn't translate into robust growth for Brazil.

"They speak about the 'economic tripod' as if it were holy trinity, but the fact is that during the eight years of Cardoso government the economy grew very little, an average of only 2.3%," said Mr. Belluzo, who is also an academic and writer.

Mr. Fraga contends that many Brazilians sense the country is on the wrong path and that current pessimism about the economy is well-founded.

"I believe our history proves that high inflation, high budget deficit and weak balance of payments have never been good for growth, on the contrary," he said.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: EXCLUSIVE-Brazil's Neves to allow  currency  to float freely if elected
text:
(Adds political context, adviser's comments on impact of float)

By Jeferson Ribeiro

BRASILIA, Aug 7 (Reuters) - If Aecio Neves wins the presidency this October, he would allow Brazil's currency to float freely, leaving the market to set the exchange rate in a move that would likely help local industries struggling with a strong real.

Mansueto Almeida, a top economic adviser to the Neves campaign, told Reuters on Thursday that a free floating real will help restore balance to Brazil's external accounts and make Brazilian manufacturers more competitive.

"If elected, a Neves government will aim to end the currency populism imposed by President Dilma Rousseff's government and return to a free floating exchange rate," Almeida said in a written statement in response to questions from Reuters.

Almeida is a member of the team of advisers led by former central bank governor Arminio Fraga that are coordinating the economic policy platform for Neves, who is Rousseff's main challenger in the Oct. 5 presidential election.

Since last August, Brazil's central bank has intervened daily in the foreign exchange market by selling currency swaps, derivatives designed to support the real. Many analysts say the central bank wants to avoid a sharp currency depreciation that would stoke already high inflation.

In June, the bank said it would extend the swap program until at least the end of this year.

The intervention program has turned the real into the best-performing major Latin America currency this year, even with some recent losses. Some of those losses came after Neves told an audience of industry leaders on July 30 that Brazil needs a weaker currency to make its economy more competitive in the global marketplace.

Industry and agribusiness leaders have called for a weaker currency to make Brazilian exports more competitive and boost investment in a flagging economy. Critics have accused the Rousseff administration of using the exchange rate as a monetary policy tool to contain inflation.

The left-leaning Rousseff remains the favorite to win a second term, though recent opinion polls point to a close race that looks almost certain to go to a second-round runoff against Neves, a centrist from the Brazilian Social Democracy Party.

Brazil's economy has underperformed since Rousseff took office in 2011 despite repeated attempts to jump-start growth through tax cuts and other costly subsidies. Industrial output is set to shrink this year and remains below pre-2009 levels, hit by stubborn inflation and high labor costs.

Neves, a former state governor who has vowed to restore economic growth and investor confidence, hinted last week at what his exchange rate policy would look like.

"Brazil, unfortunately, is being held hostage to what we can call currency populism, because the government seeks to control inflation through permanent intervention in the foreign exchange market," Neves told an industrial lobby in Brasilia.

Almeida, an economist with the government think tank IPEA, said a free floating real would improve Brazil's trade balance and help reduce the current account deficit.

"The country's external accounts would enter a virtuous circle, attracting more investment and improving the trade balance," he said.

Brazil's current account deficit is running at close to 4 percent of gross domestic product and will hit $80 billion by year end, he added.

"That's a reflection of the imbalance caused by a real that has been artificially strengthened to contain inflation." (Writing by Anthony Boadle; Editing by Todd Benson and Meredith Mazzilli)

title: Brazil's finmin disputes IMF report that economy is vulnerable
text:
BRASILIA, July 29 (Reuters) - Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Tuesday that an International Monetary Fund report that warns of the  vulnerability of the Brazilian economy makes no sense.               

In a report about risks to the global economy, the lender included Brazil in a list of emerging market countries with higher vulnerabilities. The IMF said that sluggish expansion in the developing world was increasingly likely due to structural, not cyclical, factors.               

"The report's conclusions that Brazil is fragile makes no sense," Mantega told reporters, adding that the lender is only repeating mistaken predictions made by market economists in recent months.               

In a separate report also published on Tuesday, the IMF said Brazil's external position is "moderately weaker" than fundamentals. The lender also said that the Brazilian real  was overvalued by between 5 percent and 15 percent in 2013 and that forex intervention should not be used to resist currency pressures.               

"Brazil has the confidence of international markets and it's a solid country from the point of view of its currency exchange" Mantega said.               

Mantega said that the country's current account deficit - country's widest measurement of foreign exchange flows - should improve next year.               

Brazil's external deficit hit a record $81 billion last year due to a drop in global prices of key exports such as soy and iron ore and robust demand for imports.               

Fewer dollars in the local market has put downward pressure on the real.               

The Brazilian central bank has intervened daily in foreign exchange markets since last year to keep the real from weakening too much and further stoking already high inflation.               

Mantega said that inflation in Brazil continues at "comfortable" levels and that government policies to control prices have been successful.
