LONDON STOCK EXCHANGE ANNOUNCEMENT

JPMORGAN BRAZIL INVESTMENT TRUST PLC

FINAL RESULTS FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30TH APRIL 2014

Chairman's Statement

Introduction and Performance

The year to 30th April 2014 was a difficult period for emerging markets as a whole, with the broad MSCI Emerging Markets index falling 11.5% in the year, underperforming developed markets, which rose 6.25%. The Brazilian market was hit hard by this negative investor sentiment towards emerging markets, falling further than the broader emerging markets index as local concerns about earnings growth and perceived government intervention in the economy saw valuations fall. The fall in the equity market was exacerbated by the weakness of the currency, with the Brazilian Real weakening against sterling by some 21% over the year. The Company recorded a total return on net assets for the year of -24.4%, underperforming the benchmark, the MSCI Brazil 10/40 Index which returned -17.1% for the same period. The share price return to Ordinary shareholders of -26.0%, reflected the widening of the share price discount from 7.2% to 9.1% over the year. At the time of writing this report, it stood at 5.2%.

The Trust's disappointing results for the year resulted from the poor selection of the individual stocks in which to invest the Trust's capital. The value lost through this poor selection of stocks was, to a degree, mitigated by the value created in the selection of the board industrial sectors in which to invest. The investment managers provide a detailed commentary on the markets and portfolio activity in their report

Revenue and Dividends

Gross revenue for the year amounted to GBP1,412,000 (2013: GBP1,605,000) and net revenue after taxation amounted to GBP487,000 (2013: GBP599,000).

The Company's dividend policy has been to distribute all, or substantially all, of the available income each year. The Board recommends a dividend of 0.85p per Ordinary share. Subject to shareholders' approval at the forthcoming Annual General Meeting on 12th September 2014, the dividend will be payable on 19th September 2014 to shareholders on the register at 22nd August 2014. Whilst this is a reduction on the 1.00p per Ordinary share paid last year, shareholders are reminded that the Company's investment objective, and thus the basis of the investment managers' decisions, is to provide shareholders over the longer term with returns predominantly in the form of capital.

Asset Allocation

In accordance with the Company's investment policy, the investment managers have continued to be substantially invested in equities. As at 30th April 2014, the Company's portfolio had 0.8% in cash.

Share Repurchases and Issuance

At last year's Annual General Meeting ('AGM'), shareholders granted Directors authority to repurchase the Company's shares. During the financial year, the Company repurchased a total of 5,154,624 Ordinary shares into Treasury at a discount, thereby marginally enhancing NAV per share. The Board's objective remains to use the share repurchase authority to manage imbalances between the supply of and demand for the Company's shares, thereby reducing the volatility of the discount. The Board believes this mechanism has been helpful and therefore proposes and recommends that powers to repurchase up to 14.99% of the Company's issued share capital be renewed for a further period.

Challenging market conditions have made it impossible to continue the share issuance at a premium, which the Company achieved in the period following flotation, and which benefited shareholders because it enhances NAV per share and improves liquidity in the market for the Company's shares. The Board intends to resume such issuance when market conditions permit, and therefore resolutions renewing the authorities to issue shares from Treasury and to issue new shares at a premium to NAV, and to disapply pre-emption rights over such issues, will be submitted for approval at the forthcoming AGM.

During the financial year, 3,000 Ordinary shares were issued upon conversion of Subscription shares. The Subscription share rights lapsed after the final subscription date of 30th June 2013 and in accordance with the shareholder resolutions passed on 13th and 16th September 2013, all outstanding Subscription shares were converted into deferred shares, repurchased by the Company and cancelled. The listing of the Subscription shares was cancelled on 30th September 2013.

Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive

The Company was required to comply with the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive ('AIFMD') in advance of its final implementation date of 22nd July 2014. As a result of this new European legislation and its incorporation into the local law and regulations in place in the UK, the Company has made a number of changes to its service providers to bring it into compliance with the AIFMD from 1st July 2014. The Company has appointed JPMorgan Funds Limited ('JPMF'), an affiliate of JPMorgan Asset Management (UK) Limited ('JPMAM') as its Alternative Investment Fund Manager ('AIFM') subject to the terms and conditions of a new investment management agreement. This new agreement leaves the Managers' remuneration and other commercial terms unchanged from the preceding agreement with JPMAM. From a portfolio management perspective, there will be no change in the resources or team working on behalf of the Trust as JPMF has delegated portfolio management to JPMAM. JPMF also acts as the new Company Secretary from 1st July 2014, replacing JPMAM in the role.

In complying with the AIFMD, the Company has also appointed Bank of New York Mellon to act as its Depositary from 1st July 2014. The Company's Custodian, JPMorgan Chase Bank will remain as the Custodian as a delegate of the Depositary.

Annual General Meeting

The AGM will be held at 60 Victoria Embankment, London EC4Y 0JP on Friday, 12th September 2014 at 2.00 p.m. The meeting will include a presentation from the investment managers on investment policy and performance. There will also be an opportunity for shareholders to meet the Board and representatives of JPMorgan after the meeting.

If you wish to raise any detailed or technical questions at the Meeting, it would be helpful if you could mention them in advance by writing to the Company Secretary at 60 Victoria Embankment, London EC4Y 0JP. Shareholders who are unable to attend the Meeting in person are encouraged to use their proxy votes.

Outlook

Near term prospects for Brazil's market are likely to be influenced by political developments, rather than fundamentals and an economic recovery which appears likely with companies continuing to meet earnings growth expectations. That said, the low ratings of Brazil stocks should provide better prospects for positive returns from the current levels. Additionally, and despite short term protests over the events, Brazil will benefit from longer term positive implications of hosting the World Cup this year and the Olympic games in 2016.

Regardless of who wins the forthcoming election later this year, the winner will face substantial economic challenges and a need to regain the confidence of investors. As a result the Board expects the new administration to introduce more market-friendly policies and reduce political interference in many aspects of the economy. The Board's concerns centre around the potential impact on the Company's investments of cyclical challenges in Brazil's economy and the resilience of the global economy in the face of rising interest rates.

Notwithstanding these short-term factors, the Board remains confident in the Investment Manager's approach of identifying companies with strong financial characteristics and niche growth opportunities, together with high quality management, for the Company's portfolio to achieve good long-term returns.

Investment Managers' Report

Market Review and Outlook

2013 was a difficult year for the Brazilian stock market with a combination of currency weakness, disappointing earnings, weak commodity prices and government interference all contributing to poor returns. Towards the end of the period under review, the Brazilian market picked up as opinion polls showed a decline in the voting intentions in favour of President Dilma Rouseff ahead of the October election. During 2013, the Real (BRL) declined steeply against Sterling and the US dollar (USD) as capital fled from Emerging Markets in response to concerns over current account deficits and as a result of worries over the impact of reduced quantitative easing in the US. In response to these flows domestic interest rates rose from 7.25% to 11%, dampening domestic growth. Following the decline in the market over the last 12 months, the market now appears good value. Earnings revisions have stabilised and we believe there should be nominal earnings growth of around 14% over the next 12 months. However we remain concerned about the currency. Our estimation of fair value is approximately 2.5 BRL/USD, so that even after falling significantly over the last 18 months, we believe the Brazilian Real is approximately 15% overvalued. Selic, the benchmark interest rate, rose 0.25% in April, but the Brazilian Central Bank signalled that this is likely to end the current monetary tightening cycle. As a result we do not see a threat that interest rates will have to rise significantly. It is also worth remembering that government finances are more robust than many comparable Emerging Markets with debt to GDP at a relatively modest 57%. [ 25-07-14 1546GMT ]

Brazil is likely to remain volatile in the face of political uncertainty ahead of the elections later in the year. Dilma Rousseff's approval ratings have fallen in response to higher inflation and much future government policy (e.g. towards energy subsidies) remains unclear. However, markets could react positively if there is a mandate for reform.

It is interesting to note that within Brazil, some 70% of installed energy generation capacity comes from hydro-electric power. With lower than expected rainfall in February and record low reservoir levels, the risk of electricity rationing continues to increase, representing a significant threat to the economy and hence to the government. With increasing usage of thermoelectric sources, the most likely scenario is one with much higher energy costs, which will have an impact on inflation and fiscal accounts as the government is likely to mitigate the impact on tariffs. Considering the impact on public opinion, we believe that the authorities will wait until the situation becomes extreme before announcing any measures.

Portfolio Review

Investing in this challenging environment requires fund managers to be selective and more demanding on valuations, particularly in markets that are facing currency and capital flow pressures. The clear tilt of our strategy towards quality companies with strong cash flows certainly helps mitigate the risks.

We continue to be overweight in consumer and industrial businesses. Consumer related stocks will benefit from long term trends like rising incomes, demographics and the increased penetration of organised services, e.g. credit cards, mortgages, insurance, modern retailing. Clear examples of this are Lojas Renner (a clothing retailer), Arezzo (a shoe retailer) and Linx (an IT retail service provider). Industrial stocks benefit from domestic and external demand across the region which we believe to be at cyclical lows and set to improve over the coming year. In addition, we are able to find a number of world class exporters that deliver consistent profitability after years of productivity enhancing investment. Brazilian exporters should benefit from weakness in the BRL as the currency trends towards fair value. We also have a large exposure to financials. The privately-owned banks are benefiting from lower competition from the state banks, higher margins, and lower costs.

In the out-of-favour commodity space, we continue to struggle to find compelling investments, given the uncertainty around product prices and, in a market such as Brazil, the risk of government intervention. We believe that the changing mix of economic growth in China and a global over-investment in capacity means the commodity super-cycle will continue to unwind. This is not a good environment for commodity businesses, many of which do not create value through the delivery of financial returns above their cost of capital through the cycle. Despite this view, we are pragmatic and will own high quality assets at the right valuation regardless of our longer term fundamentally negative views on the sector. In line with our views on political risk, we have moved to maintain a neutral position in Petrobras and Vale relative to the benchmark index as we think the stock will be driven by politics, not fundamentals, through the rest of the year.

Performance Commentary and Attribution

The trust underperformed its benchmark on a NAV basis over the twelve months to end April 2014, returning -24.4% versus the benchmark decline of 17.1%. During a very challenging and volatile period, sector allocation detracted from performance while stock selection contributed, albeit to a lesser degree.

The economic slowdown experienced by Brazil in the past year led to earnings downgrades for many Brazilian companies. These downgrades were particularly marked in the Industrial and Consumer sectors where we have been overweight, with the effects of a slowing economy and rising domestic interest rates yet to be balanced by any benefit arising from a weakened currency.

Given the prevalence of reduced confidence, and short term pessimism among investors in the market, it is not surprising that many investors were prepared to pay a premium for the larger, more liquid stocks in the market. As a result the small cap names in the portfolio detracted most significantly from performance, with domestic focused businesses suffering in the face of currency depreciation.

The top contributor was Itau, the leading Brazilian bank, and our largest position in absolute terms. We have been becoming more positive on financials after concerns earlier this year of rising non-performing loans as the central bank tightened policy. Despite the weakness in the domestic economy, the company announced strong results for 2013, which exceeded the market's expectations. It also announced an acquisition which will see it expanding and diversifying its business in Latin America, reducing its reliance on Brazil.

Consumer discretionary names detracted from performance in aggregate, whilst a more limited, underweight exposure to defensive stocks, particularly consumer staples contributed as investors started to move away from the more expensively priced, growth stocks. In consumer discretionary, the best performing sub-sector was Education. The government sponsored student loan program has stimulated demand and lead to over 30% growth in earnings for the sector. We did not hold enough in the sector and the position was built late in the year. In consumer staples, we trimmed our positions in Ambev and Souza Cruz during the year because of valuation. This contributed postiviely to performance.

Underweight positions, the size of which varied during the period, in both Petrobras and Vale, the bluechips of the Brazilian market, detracted from performance as the sought-after liquidity these names provided in challenging market conditions helped their resilience. As set out above, we have sought to build an index neutral position in these holdings towards the year end.

title: Brazil Central Bank FX Interventions  Could Lose Effect -- Market Talk
text:
09:55 EDT - The Brazilian central bank's actions to keep the real from losing value against the dollar, making the real a de facto managed currency, could be unsustainable, according to Sidnei Nehme, director of the NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo. The bank's policy of auctioning swap contracts, instead of using its large dollar reserves, exposes it to the risk of an abrupt change in the exchange rate, and keeping the real artificially strong hurts the Brazil's industrial sector, Nehme says. USD/BRL down 0.3% at 2.2155. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

9:52 EDT - McDonald's (MCD) big June SSS miss could have been due in part to the World Cup, some analysts speculate. "Anything that keeps folks at home watching TV keeps them away from their local McDonald's," says Janney. SSS skidded 3.5% in the US and 3.4% in Europe. But soccer doesn't explain why MCD expects soft July sales as well. A complex menu and slow service likely are bigger factors. We'll learn more when MCD's conference call starts at 11. Shares are down 2.1% at $95.50. (julie.jargon@wsj.com)

9:49 EDT - Centene (CNC) is working to "manage the utilization" of new hepatitis C drugs. The health insurer estimates the drugs' costs in 2Q were consistent with its estimates at $13.7M, versus $4.2M a year ago and $7.3M in 1Q. The segment's drug prices gotten plenty of scrutiny of late, but CNC notes the growth also reflects membership gains. It is talking to states about reimbursing the expenses, the impact from which is now "plateauing" as the number of new people starting treatment is down and some people are winding up their stay on the drugs. States recognize the issue and "are being very constructive," says CEO Michael F. Neidorff. (anna.mathews@wsj.com)

9:45 EDT - DuPont (DD) has identified further operations it can trim away as part of the agricultural and chemical giant's "redesign," a multiyear effort it's pursuing alongside DD's planned separation of its performance-chemicals business, which makes house paints. CEO Ellen Kullman says during the 2Q conference call that DD is "questioning and understanding" all aspects of its operating model, which "hasn't been recast in a while." The company plans to spin off performance chemicals, a major contributor to revenue but prone to booms and busts, to focus on agriculture and other businesses where DD can command higher profit margins and more-reliable sales. Shares are down 0.6% at $65.15 as results were in line with last month's warning. (jacob.bunge@wsj.com; @jacobbunge)

9:42 EDT - With Microsoft (MSFT) Chief Executive Satya Nadella about six months into the job, some investors are growing antsy for him to commit MSFT to buying back more of its own stock or boosting other cash returns. MSFT repurchased about $6.1B of its shares in the nine months ended March 31, or a little more than one-quarter of the cash generated by its operations over that stretch. Wall Street believes Nadella can easily increase that percentage. MSFT reports results after the close of New York trading; analysts estimate revenue up 16% from a year earlier to $23B, with net income up 2% to 60 cents a share. MSFT gains 0.4% to $45. (shira.ovide@wsj.com; @shiraovide)

9:42 EDT - Centene (CNC) says that as of June 30, it had some 75,700 ACA-marketplace enrollees who had also paid premiums, more than the approximately 70K the health insurer had projected. That as demographics are "in line" with the projections embedded in CNC's pricing. It adds enrollees are mostly relatively low-income, with about 90% eligible for federal subsidies. Overall, CNC expects "minimal" financial impact from the exchanges this year; it's selling marketplace plans in 9 states. The company says it's too soon to provide details about its planned 2015 exchange pricing. Shares jump 5% to $79.40, hitting a fresh record, on its latest beat-and-raise. (anna.mathews@wsj.com)

9:38 EDT - United Technologies (UTX) has a message for investors about a pair of engine failures which have marred the testing of its flagship military and commercial jet engines: nothing to see here. "These things do happen" in engine development, says CFO Greg Hayes, referring to the engine failure on a version of UTX's commercial geared turbofan engine and an engine fire which temporarily grounded the F-35 fighter jet. UTX's Pratt & Whitney makes both engines, and fixing the problems will be "relatively minor," says Hayes, adding engine development remains on schedule. UTX expects its first geared turbofan engines to enter service at the end of 2015. (ted.mann@wsj.com)

09:36 EDT - What comes after the biggest job cuts in Microsoft's (MSFT) history? When Microsoft reports earnings after the close of trading in New York today, the company for the first time will include a new segment with results from Nokia (NOK). The job cuts were about clearing the decks and creating a better cost structure, but Wall Street isn't sure new CEO Satya Nadella can both whack costs out of the Nokia business and at the same time lift the company's smartphone market share out of the sub-5% basement. (shira.ovide@wsj.com; @shiraovide)

09:32 EDT - New York-Presbyterian Hospital is renting "innovation space" at accelerator Blueprint Health, where the hospital will work with startups to more quickly develop new technologies that improve patient care as federal regulators have demanded, says NYP CIO Aurelia Boyer. She says the relationship with New York City-based Blueprint and the 50 health-care startups it currently hosts could lead to better health care technologies, some of which will benefit the hospital. "Having more dialogues as they're developing with us will get them a better product and...they'll develop around where we think we have needs," Boyer says. (clint.boulton@wsj.com)

9:29 EDT - Hedge-fund luminaries like John Paulson and George Soros are liable to be handsomely rewarded from CIT announcing this morning its planned $3.4B acquisition of retail bank OneWest. For those who don't recall, OneWest was IndyMac, which collapsed in July 2008 ahead of the financial crisis' peak thanks to hisk-risk mortgages cut amid the housing bubble. At the time, it was one of the biggest US-bank failures and cost the FDIC's insurance fund some $13B. Afterward, the likes of Paulson, Soros and Michael Dell invested as some billionaires saw the opportunity--through IndyMac and other bank failures--to buy distressed assets which might be successfully turned around. IndyMac's assets were sold for $1.5B, and it bought a failed California lender a year, making OneWest the largest SoCal-based bank. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

09:22 EDT - JPMorgan (JPM) says it's launching a new $30M, 5-year initiative to support small business "clusters," or accelerators, that help growing small businesses in certain fields across 10 US cities. The new program, Small Business Forward, will connect entrepreneurs with resources and help certain accelerators provide participating small businesses with workforce and management training, partnerships with colleges and universities, and supplier networks, among others. The program, which includes small businesses in Detroit, Newark and New Orleans, could also help the largest US bank by assets gain customers, whether it's individuals or businesses. (emily.glazer@wsj.com)

9:22 EDT - Brazilian inflation remains high, sticky and generalized following the end of the World Cup while economic growth remains slow, says Goldman Sachs' Alberto Ramos. Mid-month inflation cooled from June and was less than expected, but the annual rate rose and is still above the central bank's 6.5% target ceiling. Ramos adds price increases are expected to accelerate further in August. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

The investment bank had been operating on the assumption that a lack of imminent sanctions against Russia would allow investors to look at the fundamentals in Russia "where inflation has topped, domestic demand is weak and tight monetary policy was not justified." That has all changed in the wake of MH17, "and the probability of sanctions has significantly increased in our view." Nomura closes out its strategic trade in the local bond market and tactical trade in Russian credit. (matthew.cowley@wsj.com)

1323 GMT [Dow Jones]--Citigroup sees a pick-up in G10 currency trading volumes, but the breakdown of the numbers only gives USD buyers a slight edge despite the greenback's general strength Tuesday. The bank flows favored USD buyers vs AUD, EUR, JPY and CHF, but USD sellers against NZD, GBP and CAD. (gary.stride@wsj.com)

09:20 EDT - Home sales have disappointed analysts this spring but home prices still rose at a steady clip. An index maintained by the Federal Housing Finance Agency rose 0.4% in May, following a 0.1% increase in April, which was initially reported as no gain. For the year ended May, prices are up 5.5%, leaving them just 6.5% below their April 2007 peak. Still, the pace of increases has slowed in most of the US, with seven of nine Census regions reporting an annual gain that was lower than the one reported last May. (nick.timiraos@wsj.com; @NickTimiraos)

9:14 EDT - The National Association of Realtors will release data on June existing-home sales at 10, and watchers are waiting to see if May's results are repeated. The annual sales pace rose 4.9% from April, the initial print last month reported, generating a sigh of relief from many in the real-estate industry. The traditional spring selling season for homes got off to its worst start in years in March and April, so the question is whether May was just a one-month wonder. (joe.light@wsj.com)

1313 GMT [Dow Jones]--The ECB's balance sheet grew EUR5.4 billion to EUR2.06 trillion last week, according to the ECB's weekly report, somewhat bucking the recent trend of steady declines in its asset holdings. Still, the balance sheet is well below the EUR3 trillion-plus level from two years ago. The balance sheet should shrink again this week as banks repay a whopping EUR21.5 billion in three-year loans to the ECB. (brian.blackstone@wsj.com)

09:09 EDT - Treasurys hit session highs as buyers continue to pile in. The core CPI dips back below 2% on an annual basis. Core inflation is expected to remain at or below the 2% mark for the remainder of the year, says Millan Mulraine, rate strategist at TD Securities. Tame inflation "will continue to provide cover for [the Fed] to keep the policy rate on hold until Q4 2015, when we expect them to start tightening policy." Ten-year notes now 3/32 higher, yielding 2.462%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

9:06 EDT - Treasurys which guard investors from rising inflation are lagging their regular counterparts after the June CPI report showed little inflationary pressures outside of gasoline. Bond investors are paring their inflation expectations, which perked up after the May reading suggested pricing pressure was mounting. Three-year TIPS imply expectations for 1.77% average annual inflation the next 3 years, versus 1.82% before the report, while 10s reflect 2.21% expected inflation, from 2.23% beforehand. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

8:48 EDT - The tame core CPI reduces fears of an earlier Fed rate hike, encouraging investors to return to shorter-dated Treasurys. They have been under pressure lately as they're sensitive to changes in official rate-policy outlooks. Tame inflation also helps the long end recoup today's decline there, with the 10-year note now flat, yielding 2.476%. The 2-year is 1/32 higher, yielding 0.484%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

8:44 EDT - The dollar has added to its gains against the euro after June's CPI data were roughly in line with expectations, pushing the common currency to its lowest level against the greenback since Nov. 21. It got down to $1.3459, versus a pre-data $1.3482, before rebounding somewhat, and is down 0.4% so far in the Americas session at $1.3472. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

1239 GMT The low level of government bond issuance in August in the euro zone is an argument for government bond yields to go lower next month, says DZ Bank analyst Christoph Kutt. August is traditionally a month of very low aggregate new issuance and redemption, which follows the "great spate" of maturities in July, so repaid cash will be looking for a new home, he says. These pressures were already perceptible last week. "A high demand, low supply situation is now emerging, with almost two thirds of the scheduled supply being sub-five-year maturities," he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

title: Brazil 's  Currency Intervention  Hurting Its Factories -- Market Talk
text:
10:18 EDT - Brazil's efforts to prop up its currency to fight inflation are undercutting its factory sector, which is in a serious slump. Industrial production declines for the third straight month, according to figures out Wednesday. Part of the trouble is an overvalued real that hurts exports, says Alberto Ramos, chief Latin American economist at Goldman Sachs. "They're using an improper set of instruments to deal with inflation," Ramos says. "The industrial sector is also being hurt by a significantly overvalued currency." Brazil's central bank recently extended daily currency swap auctions to keep the real within a band of 2.20 to 2.25 per dollar to help tame inflation, which has been running near 6.5%. USD/BRL up 0.5% at 2.2133. (marla.dickerson@wsj.com)

10:13 EDT - New York's top financial regulator Benjamin Lawsky says U.S. authorities are closer to finding the right way to deter wrongdoing at financial firms, citing BNP Paribas' settlement over sanctions violations earlier this week. "The focus has to be on are we adequately deterring future bad conduct," Mr. Lawsky says on a radio show, noting there's been both criticism and praise of the BNP settlement. Aside from the record $8.9B fine that authorities handed to BNP, the bank also was forced to remove more than a dozen executives and faces restrictions on some business lines. The latter punishments represent Mr. Lawsky's push to impose penalties that have business consequences for financial firms that break the law. (andrewr.johnson@wsj.com)

10:06 EDT - In an unusual Q&A interview to an internal newsletter published last evening, Brazil's central-bank President Alexandre Tombini painted a benign scenario for inflation, but ended with a mixed message. Tombini said that, as "12-month inflation still shows resilience, monetary policy should stay vigilant to minimize risks," which seems to leave the door open for a new hike. But then he sort of pointed to the contrary, saying that "if current monetary conditions remain unchanged, inflation is trending towards a path that will converge" to the official 4.5% target. Inflation is now at 6.4%, while interest rates are at 11% after a year-long tightening cycle. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

10:05 EDT - The Canadian dollar could appreciate a bit more after its recent bout of strengthening, though investors are starting to find these levels attractive to short the currency again, says Charles St. Arnaud, executive director of foreign exchange research and economics at Nomura Securities. He says CAD's rise in recent weeks was mainly because investors who had been short were closing these positions as they come around to the view that the likelihood of a rate cut "is very close to 0" following stronger-than-expected inflation numbers. USD/CAD up 0.3% at 1.0661. (nirmala.menon@wsj.com; @NirmalaMenon)

1359 GMT [Dow Jones] European credit spreads might be set for a continued move tighter over the summer as bond supply dries up and new investor cash keeps pouring in. But Citigroup credit analyst Joseph M. Faith reckons the outlook is growing more complicated. Not only are investors running their highest exposure to credit in more than four years, according to a Citi survey, a pickup in U.S. growth could have wider implications on corporate funding costs as interest-rate expectations change. "While our central scenario remains bullish, we'd be looking to reduce our current tactical long should U.S. data continue to strengthen," he says. (ben.edwards@wsj.com @debtnerd)

1358 GMT [Dow Jones]--Hungary's plan to phase out foreign-currency loans by end-2014 with banks paying hefty compensations to borrowers will be "pretty negative" for GDP, says BNP Paribas. The refunds, especially if in cash, will boost consumption in 2H 2014 and early 2015 and CPI even beyond that. "A greater risk is that foreign banks will leave Hungary, and the sector will reduce its already limited willingness and/or ability to provide credit and fund a more sustainable investment recovery." As a result, Hungarian growth is likely to become even more dependent on external demand and fresh foreign direct investment inflows into its manufacturing industry. Exports will become even more crucial given Hungary's budgetary constraints. "With the country's public debt-to-GDP ratio still very high, at around 80% of GDP at end-1Q, the scope for countercyclical fiscal policy will be very limited in the years to come," BNPP says. mining company Vale SA helped keep Brazil's benchmark Bovespa
index in the black on Thursday, while the Brazilian real closed
stronger than 2.2 per dollar for the first time in more than two

the 0.15 percent gain recorded by Brazil's benchmark Bovespa

sessions on concern about the future of state-run oil company
Petroleo Brasileiro SA.

currency.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil  real up on  intervention , U.S. data boosts risk appetite
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, June 25 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real
rallied on Wednesday after the central bank announced its
currency intervention program will remain intact through the end
of the year, while disappointing U.S. economic data boosted
appetite for emerging market assets in general.
    The real  gained 0.8 percent to 2.2066 per
dollar after the central bank announced it will stick with its
daily auctions of much as $200 million worth of currency swaps -
the same amount of derivatives it currently offers to investors
who seek protection against currency losses. 
    The bank introduced regular auctions of currency swaps last
August in one of its most successful initiatives to stabilize
Brazil's volatile exchange rate. After strengthening in 2011 to
levels that threatened local industry, the real weakened
sharply in 2012-13, fueling inflation that has dragged on
President Dilma Rousseff's popularity.
    The steady supply of swaps has helped the real gain about 6
percent so far this year. During the past few months, the
exchange rate has remained largely within a range of 2.2 to 2.5
reais per dollar.
    "The rationale behind that program is to keep the dollar
within that range, helping curb inflation and reducing
volatility in the currency market," said Luiz Fernando Gênova, a
trader with the Daycoval bank in Sao Paulo.
    Gênova, as well as some other market players, were a bit
surprised by the central bank announcement. Many believed
policymakers would take advantage of a period of relatively calm
in global markets to wind down the intervention program, saving
firepower for moments of stress.
    Still, Gênova said, the announcement "brings certainty that
the daily offer (of swaps) will remain abundant."
    Meanwhile, other Latin American currencies posted more
modest gains as investors bet the Federal Reserve will take time
to raise interest rates after the U.S. economy contracted much
more than expected in the first quarter. 
    Low interest rates in the world's largest economy usually
boost investors' appetite for higher-yielding emerging market
bonds.
    The currencies of Mexico and Chile each gained
around 0.3 percent after the disappointing U.S. data.
    Latin American stock markets suffered with the
weaker-than-expected U.S. data, however, with MSCI's benchmark
stock index for the region 0.1 percent lower.
    Shares of Brazil's state-run oil company Petroleo Brasileiro
SA, or Petrobras, continued to slide on concern that a

transfer future Petrobras profit to government coffers.

title: Brazil likely to wind down  FX  program as real steadies
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, June 16 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank will likely scale back its foreign exchange intervention program within the next couple of weeks, hoping that a period of relative calm in global markets will help it unwind the plan without causing too much instability for the currency.

Brazil has tried a number of measures to stabilize its volatile exchange rate, which strengthened in 2011 to levels that threatened local industry but then weakened too fast in 2012-13, fueling inflation. Rising prices have hurt Brazilians' spending power, dragging down economic activity as well as President Dilma Rousseff's popularity.

In one of its most successful initiatives, the central bank last August started daily auctions of currency swaps.

The derivatives allow the bank to support the real without selling a single dollar from its $380 billion in foreign reserves. As a result, the real has been largely stable at between 2.2 and 2.3 per dollar in recent months.

But for the program to work, holders have to be able - at least in theory - to trade the swaps for cash in moments of crisis, which means the value of swaps in circulation cannot exceed the size of Brazil's foreign reserves.

Some analysts warn that the prudent threshold is much lower than that, and recommend policymakers curtail the intervention program even further. The central bank has already reduced the pace of sales in December, but the stock of swaps has since swollen to nearly $90 billion.

"The central bank can't sell swaps forever. It ought to use this instrument in specific situations," said Márcio Garcia, a visiting professor at Stanford University who has studied Brazil's intervention program.

"The forex market has been calm. It's not a moment for the bank to spend its dollar reserves or to sell derivatives that are backed by the reserves," added Garcia.

So far this year, the real has gained more than 5 percent against the dollar. The gains are partly a result of the steady supply of swaps but also due to prospects that U.S. interest rates will not go up before mid-2015.

Unwinding the program has proved to be more difficult than it seems, however.

When the central bank tried to slow the rollover pace of expiring swaps earlier this month, the real slumped 1.5 percent in one day, forcing policymakers to backtrack.

The bank not only returned to its previous rollover pace, but it promised to keep offering swaps past June 30, an action aimed at killing speculation that the intervention program's days are numbered.

Details of the length and the magnitude of the extended program are still to be announced and a central bank spokesman declined to provide any new information.

Currently, the bank offers as many as 4,000 swaps worth $200 million in daily auctions, on top of 10,000 contracts to roll over expiring maturities.

If the central bank keeps its intervention program unchanged, rolling over 100 percent of expiring contracts, its stock of swaps would grow to more than $115 billion by the end of the year, Credit Suisse analysts estimated.

By continuously intervening in the market, the central bank risks excessive distortions in the forex rate that could deepen Brazil's economic problems, including a low investment rate and a current account deficit of nearly 4 percent of gross domestic product.

The central bank could slow its intervention if the real is testing the 2.20-per-dollar area, said Win Thin, head of emerging markets currency strategy with Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. On Monday, it traded around 2.23 per dollar.

Jennifer Vail, head of fixed income at U.S. Bank Wealth Management, estimates the central bank could still increase the amount of outstanding currency swaps by 30 percent before investors get worried about the stock of these derivatives.

"There are always risks if they increase their exposure (to swaps) but I don't think it reached levels that are concerning the officials at this point," she said. (Reporting by Walter Brandimarte; Editing by Steve Orlofsky)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil Bovespa hits 7-month high, real adds to gains
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, June 10 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks and
currency climbed on Tuesday, with the benchmark Bovespa index
reaching its highest level in over seven months, on speculation
President Dilma Rousseff will lose more ground in upcoming
election polls.
    Other Latin American markets were slightly down as investors
started pricing in prospects of higher U.S. rates, which cut the
appeal of higher-yielding emerging market assets.
 
    Brazil's Bovespa index rose for a third consecutive
session, climbing as much as 0.5 percent to 54,549.50, its
highest intraday level since Oct. 30, 2013.
    Traders said investors were betting that upcoming opinion
polls would show growing chances of a second round in Brazil's
October presidential elections. Rousseff, whose interventionist
policies have been highly criticized by investors, remains a
favorite to win the vote but her lead has fallen in recent
polls.
    Contributing the most to gains on the Brazilian bourse were
shares of state-run companies such as Banco do Brasil 
and Petroleo Brasileiro SA, or Petrobras, which are
expected to benefit from less government meddling in their
businesses.
    Shares in Banco do Brasil, the nation's largest bank by
assets, jumped 2.7 percent while Petrobras' stock rose 0.7
percent.
    Other Latin American bourses were in the red as U.S. 10-year
yields hit a one-month peak, sapping investor appetite in
emerging market assets in general. Mexico's IPC stock index
 dropping 0.2 percent, while MSCI's index for Latin
America was practically unchanged.
    In currency markets, the Brazilian real  edged
0.15 percent higher to 2.2261 per dollar, keeping gains that had
been fueled by a central bank announcement that it would extend
its currency intervention program past June 30.
    Mexico's peso, on the other hand, weakened 0.1
percent to 13.0475 per dollar. The Mexican currency has been

title: POLL- Brazil  to extend  FX intervention , Mexico peso to gain
text:
* For poll details see

By Silvio Cascione and Jean Arce

BRASILIA, June 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank will likely extend beyond June its intervention in the currency market to avoid any abrupt losses in the exchange rate, though it could reduce the size of its currency swap sales, a Reuters poll showed.

Forecasts for the Brazilian real in Reuters' monthly survey of 31 strategists remained nearly unchanged. It points to a gradual weakening of the currency against the U.S. dollar from the current 2.27 per dollar to 2.47 in 12 months.

The poll also showed prospects of slight gains for the Mexican peso over the next 12 months, while the Russian rouble and the Turkish lira are expected to weaken against the dollar.

Emerging market currencies have benefitted recently from months of low volatility as the U.S. Federal Reserve tapers its monthly economic stimulus at a slow and predictable pace.

In Brazil, central bank intervention has also played a key role in stabilizing local markets, as a deteriorating trade balance and concerns over the outcome of the October election would probably weaken the currency.

Nine of the 11 who answered an extra question said they expect the Brazilian central bank to continue offering a daily ration of currency swaps after the end of this month, when the current intervention program is scheduled to end.

Currency stability is crucial for Brazil as authorities struggle to keep inflation under control. Rising prices have dented President Dilma Rousseff's wide lead in the run-up for the October re-election campaign.

"The intervention programme is likely to be left intact," said Michael Henderson, Latin America economist at Maplecroft.

"With the prospect of further monetary tightening seemingly ruled out by weakening GDP growth and October's impending election, currency management could play a critical role in the central bank's ability to prevent a near-term acceleration of inflation."

Of the nine economists who said the central bank would extend its intervention program, five expect the bank to reduce the number of contracts offered per day. The central bank offers an equivalent of $200 million per day currently.

Traders say the program has been successful in lowering volatility, keeping the real within an informal band of 2.20 to 2.25 for most of the past two months.

Elsewhere in Latin America, the Mexican peso is expected to gain slightly to 12.80 per dollar in 12 months from 12.95 currently, in a small improvement from the prior month's poll.

However, it remains far from the heights expected in early 2013, when President Enrique Pena Nieto started to work on an ambitious agenda of market-friendly reforms, especially in the oil sector.

"(The economy) has been too weak and it's all based on expectations. Macroeconomic data has not been strong enough yet to prop up the peso by year-end," said Carlos Ugalde, analyst at Signum Research, in Mexico City.

The survey also predicted that Turkey's lira, which stabilised after a free fall that triggered an aggressive central bank rate rise earlier in the year, will weaken slightly to 2.22 per dollar in a year, from 2.11 currently.

The rand is seen at 10.63 per dollar in 12 months, just slightly firmer from 10.73, where it is trading currently. (Additional reporting by Seda Sezer and Vuyani Ndaba; Polling by Ishaan Gera and Diptarka Roy; Editing by Ross Finley and Chizu Nomiyama)

SAO PAULO, May 22 (Reuters) - Foreign investors' demand for currency swaps under Brazil's central bankintervention program has decreased slightly, central bank president Alexandre Tombini said on Thursday.

"We have seen demand cooling down recently. Swaps continue to be channeled through non-financial companies, but foreign investors have pared back slightly (their demand)," Tombini said at an event in Sao Paulo.

The currency swaps provide hedges against currency losses. The central bank started its daily intervention program in the foreign exchange market in August to stem a sharp drop in the Brazilian real, but slowed its pace this year.

Tombini noted that the intervention program has helped reduce volatility in Brazil's markets, and reiterated that the central bank has about $380 billion in currency reserves that help reduce Brazil's vulnerability to foreign shocks.

Volatility has also decreased recently possibly because of expectations for another round of monetary easing in Europe, Tombini added. (Reporting by Aluisio Alves; Writing by Silvio Cascione)

title: Can Brazlian Real Continue To Gain? -- Barron's Blog
text:
Investors who bought the iShares MSCI Brazil Capped ETF (EWZ) in early February would have collected over 20% returns by now, in part because of the 10+% rally from the Bovespa equity index, but also thanks to a stronger Brazilian real.

To be sure, emerging markets currencies broadly rallied since early February. Indonesian rupiah gained 5.5%. South African rand advanced 6.2%. Turkish lira was up 6.7%.

But Brazilian real has done particularly well, advancing 7.8% since. Why is it?

Brazil's central bank has continued to intervene in the swap markets to support the real and it is still raising interest rates to combat inflation. But just like the stocks, the real may well have received a boost from President Dilma Rousseff's falling approval rating. Capital Economics analyst Neil Shearing explains:

The currency may have received a boost from the latest opinion polls, which suggest that support for President Rouseff is weakening and have led to speculation that a more market-friendly and less interventionist government might emerge from October's elections.

Can the real rise further? Capital Economics is skeptical:

Brazil is especially vulnerable if Chinese demand for industrial commodities weakens further, as we expect.

Any expectation that October's elections will herald a change in government and a shift in policy seems premature -- Ms. Rousseff is still the overwhelming favourite. Meanwhile, the economic outlook remains weak and we fear that new risks are likely to emerge over the next 6-12 months. In particular, the continued rapid expansion of credit in recent years seems to be storing up problems for the future.

More fundamentally, while the real does not appear as expensive as it once did, it still looks overvalued on several measures. The current account deficit remains large -- the 12 month rolling sum is still more than $80bn, just shy of 4% of GDP.

title: Central Banker Tombini Says Brazil Well-Prepared for QE Pullback -- WSJ Blog
text:
Brazil has built up enough domestic buffers against rapid shifts in capital flows to allow it to withstand a pullback from unconventional interest rate policy in the world's largest economies, Central Bank Governor Alexandre Tombini said.

Mr. Tombini agreed in part with Indian central bank chief Raguram Rajan, who argued during a Brookings Institution speech that aggressive monetary easing in advanced economies had made life harder for developing countries.

But he was less optimistic than Mr. Rajan about the likelihood of cooperation between monetary authorities of different countries.

"I'm skeptical that you can have too [much] international coordination" on monetary policy, Mr. Tombini said.

He was also much less concerned than Mr. Rajan about the possibility that a pullback in Federal Reserve bond buying and an eventual increase in interest rates would be strongly damaging to emerging market growth.

"We've been able to ride these global financial cycles in different ways. During the expansionary phase we take our measures and try to build up our [foreign reserve] buffers or recourse to multilateral liquidity facilities," Mr. Tombini said. "This buffer is now being handy during the exiting or normalization phase."

In particular, Mr. Tombini said that by intervening in foreign exchange markets Brazil was able to "implement a relatively independent policy from the rest of the world."

The Brazilian economy expanded only by 2.3% last year and is forecast to grow even less in 2014. Despite this weakness, high inflation has forced the central bank to repeatedly raise interest rates, which this month were lifted to 11%.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Stronger After  Central Bank Intervention
text:
BRASILIA--The Brazilian real strengthened against the dollar Friday amid signs that the government may not be willing to weaken the currency as some traders expected.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.2435 per dollar, stronger than BRL2.2826 at closing the day before, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The last time the real traded at the BRL2.24 level was in early November.

The appreciation comes one day after Moody's Investors Services said it will likely keep Brazil's stable rating outlook throughout the year. Moody's has an investment-grade rating on Brazil.

Last month, Standard & Poor's rating agency downgraded Brazil to the lowest investment grade.

High interest rates in Brazil may also be attracting foreign investors who are lured by returns that are higher than in developed markets, analysts say.

But the main force behind Friday's performance may have been the fact that Brazil's central bank didn't support the dollar as some had expected.

For months now the bank has been following a schedule of daily auctions of contracts meant to provide investors with an alternative to reduce their exposure to the Brazilian real. In these contracts, the central bank bets on the real strengthening in the future, while allowing investors to do the opposite.

As the contracts expire, the bank has the option to roll them over, thus strengthening the local currency.

But the real has accumulated gains against the dollars in the last few weeks, after bottoming out at BRL2.44 in January. That performance made investors believe that the central bank would roll over just a small amount of the derivative contracts, effectively weakening the real--something that could help Brazilian companies to better compete with foreign rivals. But the rollover came higher than many expected.

"The large rollover was the main factor behind the real today," said Paulo Petrassi, a partner at investment firm Leme Investimentos, in Sao Paulo. He said he thinks it a sign that the government likes the real strong because it can potentially curb inflation, even though Brazil's fundamentals may not support the appreciation.

"There is a lot of speculative capital flowing in," Mr. Petrassi said, "but economic fundamentals are very bad."

The analyst said low growth and high inflation expectations for 2014 are among the factors why the real should be weaker.

"I think the real's current level is its ceiling," he said.

Mr. Petrassi said he had expected the currency to end the year at BRL2.50, but is now thinking of changing that to BRL2.45.

title: Brazilian Bonds Make a Comeback
text:
U.S. fund managers are snapping up Brazilian debt, reviving a market that last year was among the biggest casualties of emerging-markets turmoil.

Brazilian government bonds denominated in the real, the local currency, have returned 3% to investors this year, the third-best performance, behind Indonesia and Thailand, among the 15 countries tracked on a J.P. Morgan index of emerging-markets local-currency debt. The share of Brazil's local-currency bonds held by foreigners jumped to a four-year high of 16.5% in January, according to J.P. Morgan data.

Investors say they are attracted to real-denominated government and corporate bonds because of their high yields and relatively low risk when compared with debt issued by other developing nations. Brazil's benchmark interest rate, the rate underlying trading in all other debt in the market, is 10.75%, compared with 3.5% in Mexico and 12% in Nigeria, according to data from J.P. Morgan.

"Brazil is the clearest case of mispricing in emerging markets," said Bryan Carter, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management, whose firm oversees $400 million in fixed-income assets. Mr. Carter said he recently boosted his Brazilian bondholdings to 13% of his portfolio, the biggest bullish position he has.

The rally highlights how investors' desire for income-generating investments is driving demand for riskier bonds at a time when safe assets offer meager returns. Brazil's 10% bonds due in 2021 are yielding 12.12%, compared with 2.3% on similar U.S. Treasury bonds.

Appetite for new bonds from yield-hungry investors is allowing troubled borrowers to raise new debt. That contrasts with previous emerging-markets crises, when bond markets shut their doors to companies and countries in the developing world.

In recent weeks, Brazilian oil company Petrobras received $22 billion of orders for an $8.5 billion bond sale.

Brazilian yields are high in part because the Brazilian real's 15% depreciation against the dollar last year and the country's 6% annual inflation pushed down bond prices. Yields rise when prices fall.

But some investors say the high yields overstate the threat to bond prices posed by inflation and rising interest rates.

Brazil's central bank last year started a currency-intervention program to stabilize the real, which has appreciated 2.2% this year against the dollar and outperformed most of its emerging-market peers. The central bank has raised interest rates at eight consecutive meetings and is widely expected to raise them again at its next meeting on April 2.

"The notion of this crisis in Brazil has abated," said Gorky Urquieta, co-head of emerging-market debt at Neuberger Berman, which manages $242 billion and has added to its Brazilian bondholdings this year. "It's a healthier environment."

Some bargain hunters also are snapping up bonds of Brazilian corporations that were hit by a flurry of high-profile bankruptcy filings, such as oil company OGX and sugar and ethanol producer Aralco SA Açúcar & Álcool. The filings prompted investors holding bonds of other Brazilian companies to sell, pushing prices down and yields up. That created bargains in the bonds of competitors such as Tonon Bionergia SA, says Robert Abad, who manages a $53 billion emerging-markets bond fund for Legg Mason's Western Asset Management Co.

To be sure, much uncertainty remains. Parts of Brazil are experiencing their worst drought in decades, which could lead to water shortages and subsequent price increases that will keep inflation high in the short run. Also, economic growth is expected to stay slow, as Brazil's economy nearly slipped into recession last year. Other challenges include Brazil's plans to host the FIFA World Cup in June and hold national elections in October, a sequence that some observers say could discourage needed government-spending cuts.

Two funds run by Pacific Investment Management Co., one of the world's biggest money managers, sold about $2.9 billion of Brazilian government bonds in the last three months of 2013, according to calculations based on Pimco data. Pimco, a unit of Allianz SE of Germany, didn't respond to requests for comment.

On Monday, Standard & Poor's Ratings Services cut its credit rating on Brazil to BBB-, the first sovereign downgrade for Brazil since 2002. S&P cited Brazil's slowing growth and large fiscal deficit, putting the country one notch away from junk territory.

While the move was largely anticipated by the markets, analysts at Credit Suisse say the downgrade could make it more difficult for Brazilian companies to raise money. S&P, along with Moody's Investors Service and Fitch Ratings, all have Brazil on a stable outlook, meaning another downgrade isn't imminent.

Other bulls on Brazil are buying stocks, not bonds. Mark Mobius, executive chairman of Templeton Emerging Markets Group, said in an interview Monday that he is especially bullish on Brazilian consumer stocks as rising wages in Brazil will lead to more domestic consumption--a trend that could hit bondholders, whose investments tend to do better in slow-growth environments.

Even so, some investors say they are happy to stay in Brazil for now since they feel they are adequately compensated for all the risks.

"Is Brazil an economy that can really go off a cliff tomorrow? No. And yet, it's paying you yields that are very compelling," said Javier Murcio, a portfolio manager at Standish Mellon Asset Management Co., which manages about $160 billion and has added to its Brazilian bondholdings this year.

title: *Brazil's Real Closes Sharply Weaker on 'Perfect Storm'
text:
27 Jan 2014 13:19 EDT *Brazil's Real Exits Active Trading at BRL2.4214 Per US Dollar

27 Jan 2014 13:20 EDT *Brazil's Real Closes at Weakest Level Since Aug. 22, 2013

Corrections & Amplifications

27 Jan 2014 13:51 EDT  CORRECT: Brazil's Real Closes at Weakest Level Since Aug. 22, 2013

27 Jan 2014 14:01 EDT  Brazil's Real Closes Sharply Weaker on Emerging-Market Worries

By Jeff Fick

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's currency closed sharply weaker against the U.S. dollar Monday as political and economic turmoil in developing economies around the world sent investors scurrying for safety.

The Brazilian real exited active trading at BRL2.4214 to the dollar, 0.9% weaker from Friday's closing price fix of BRL2.3993, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. Monday's close was the currency's weakest since BRL2.4334 on Aug. 22, the day before the Central Bank of Brazil announced a currency intervention program that has continued.

Concerns about growth in emerging-market powerhouse China and rising expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will further reduce stimulus measures are at the heart of the current sell-off, traders said. But images of protests in Ukraine and Thailand, as well as political and economic turmoil in Argentina and Turkey, have touched a nerve with investors and darkened the already gloomy outlook for the developing world.

"Markets are very nervous," said Win Thin, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman, calling the confluence of recent events a "perfect storm" for emerging markets. But the recent unease has its roots in late May 2013, when the first mention of an end to the Fed's easy-money policies first emerged, Mr. Thin said. "Ever since the chatter with tapering started, emerging markets haven't been able to gain any traction," Mr. Thin said.

The Fed is expected to announce another $10 billion reduction in its bond-buying program that would put it at $65 billion per month, following a similar move in December. The reduced stimulus has caused interest rates in the U.S. to rise ever so slightly, especially for 10-year Treasurys, making the paper more attractive than such emerging markets as Brazil.

Despite recent declines, Brazil's real has actually held up relatively well compared with Argentina and Turkey. Argentina's peso tumbled nearly 20% on Thursday before the government eased restrictions on dollar purchases, while Turkey's lira also tumbled to its weakest level ever against the greenback ahead of an emergency meeting of the country's central bank set for Tuesday.

"If emerging markets are selling off, Brazil will sell off as well," Mr. Thin said. "But the central bank's intervention plan is keeping Brazil from being a big underperformer."

The Central Bank of Brazil has so far avoided abrupt swings by supplying the market with dollars via foreign-exchange swap contracts sold in daily auctions that were first introduced last August. The bank sold about $1.43 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts during Monday's session, including the roll over of some contracts coming due in February.

The sale of foreign-exchange swaps typically supports the real against the U.S. dollar by allowing investors to exchange bonds indexed to domestic interest rates for paper tied directly to the dollar.

The real will likely continue to weaken in the near term as the issues in other developing countries exacerbate Brazil's homegrown problems with weak growth, high inflation and a widening fiscal deficit, traders said.

"All of this negative information is forcing multinational companies to buy dollars as a hedge against a speculative attack on the currency," said Marcos Trabbold, chief of trading operations at Sao Paulo's B&T Associados. Mr. Trabbold said that the real could reach BRL2.50 to the dollar unless the central bank increases the amount of swaps sold or reintroduces the sale of dollar credit lines that ended in late December.

title: Brazil 's Real Little Changed as  FX Intervention  Offsets Growth Concern
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real was little changed on Monday as continued central bank intervention helped contain weakness after economists whittled down their outlook for Latin America's biggest economy and the release of data showing slower-than-expected global economic activity.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.3761 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL2.3779 at Friday's close.

Brazilian economists surveyed by the central bank said economic growth last year likely reached 2.28%, down from a previous forecast of 2.3% growth. This year, growth is expected to slow even more, with the economy expanding 1.95% in 2014, down from a previous estimate of 2%, according to the weekly survey.

Meanwhile, Brazil's biggest trading partner, China, also posted disappointing economic data on Monday. The HSBC China services Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 50.9 in December from 52.5 in November, with growth in new orders the lowest in six months, HSBC Holdings PLC reported.

Europe and the U.S. also released PMI data. In Europe, the figure showed a slight drop to 51.0 in December, in line with estimates, while in the U.S. the number slipped to 55.7.

Despite the soft data, the real didn't repeat losses seen last week, when the currency touched 2.4 against the dollar. According to the latest central bank survey, the real is expected to weaken to 2.45 to the dollar by year end.

Further declines were prevented by continued central bank intervention. The central bank said it would continue holding regular auctions to supply dollar credit lines and foreign-currency swap contracts that help investors increase currency predictability. By allowing investors to hedge against future swings in the currency, there is less immediate demand for investors to buy dollars and thereby less weakness in the real.

On Monday, the central bank sold about $200 million in currency swap contracts.

Some have criticized the central bank's decision to reduce the scale of its intervention in markets. However, for analysts such as Banco Santander economist Adriana Dupita, the less intensive intervention could allow for longer-lasting intervention.

"Had the [central bank] opted for a more aggressive swap program instead, simple math would lead markets and rating agencies to question, at some point, the country's ability to preserve this status in the event there is a longer-than-announced swap program," the economist wrote.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 19 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slid about half a percentage point early on Thursday after the central bank announced it will slow down the pace of currency intervention as of next year, taking advantage of an initial upbeat market reaction to U.S. policymakers decision to cut down on stimulus.

title: Brazil Prepared to Deal With Easing of Stimulus, Says Rousseff
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil has reacted correctly during times of global crisis and is ready to deal with potential turbulence coming from the expected easing of stimulus measures in developed economies during 2014, the country's president said Wednesday.

President Dilma Rousseff added that her administration aims to improve her country's business environment and maintained her staunch defense of much-criticized Finance Minister Guido Mantega.

Ms. Rousseff said during an unusually long talk with reporters at the presidential palace that she hopes for an economic recovery in the U.S. and Europe and sustained growth in China, Brazil's three biggest trading partners.

The president spoke for almost two hours at a breakfast with reporters. The event marked the end of a year that saw criticism of her administration's handling of the economy, but also saw the president launch an ambitious program to overhaul key parts of the country's infrastructure with private-sector capital.

In the past few years, a number of changes, often temporary, in the tax code, combined with regulatory shifts have sparked criticism that uncertainty could be reducing Brazil's attractiveness for investment.

"You can't create a new tax one year, take it out in the next; make safety rules and step back just before they kick in," said Ilan Goldfajn, chief economist at São Paulo-based Itau Unibanco bank, in an interview. "All this creates uncertainties that cause investments to be postponed."

Ms. Rousseff defended her administration's actions, saying they were designed to counter the economic downturn that has seen three consecutive years of growth below initial government forecasts.

"All governments interfere with the economy during crises," Ms. Rousseff said, adding intervention efforts are "costly and the sooner they are removed, the better."

Brazil's gross domestic product expanded 7.5%, a historic high, in 2010, the year Ms. Rousseff was elected. GDP growth then slowed to 2.7% in 2011 and bottomed out at 1% in 2012. The economy is expected to grow less than 2.5% this year and at about the same pace in 2014.

Ms. Rousseff cited the bond-buying program by the U.S. Federal Reserve as an example of other governments' intervention.

The Fed's policy strengthened Brazil's and other emerging-markets' currencies, making their exports less competitive and causing some of them, including Brazil, to implement capital controls.

The outlook for the Brazilian economy going into 2014 is uncertain. There could be trouble in currency markets as developed economies are expected to resume growth and unwind stimulus measures. That could weaken the Brazilian real and other emerging-market currencies.

Even with relatively slow growth, inflation in Brazil is expected to remain near the top of the central-bank's target range of 2.5% to 6.5%. The 12-month reading now stands at 5.8%.

The central bank recently raised its benchmark interest rate to 10% to try to slow the pace of price increases.

Brazil's central bank "knows how to make the transition" to less stimulus spending in developed economies, Ms. Rousseff said.

Some observers agree Brazil is ready for tapering.

"Brazil is better positioned than many other emerging markets...to withstand the change in global liquidity that tapering would imply," said Marcela Meirelles, a Latin America analyst with fund-managing firm TCW.

"Brazil suffers from a weak growth outlook...and some fiscal metrics have deteriorated," she said. "But if you look at the long-risk indications, it is far from being vulnerable to balance of payment crises caused by a change in global liquidity."

The president, who is expected to run for re-election next year, is also preparing to reshuffle her cabinet as some ministers will have to step down to be able to run for public office.

Ms. Rousseff didn't provide any details of the possible plans but did say that Finance Minister Guido Mantega isn't expected to leave his post.

Mr. Mantega has played an important role in Brazil's economic policy for the last decade and is set to become the country's longest-serving finance minister. Yet he has also faced harsh criticism for the slow growth.

Mr. Mantega "is perfectly [fine] where he is," Ms. Rousseff said.

title: UPDATE 2- Brazil central bank  to slow pace of  forex intervention
text:
* Central bank to offer $200 mln worth of currency swaps per day

* Dollar sales through repos will hinge on market liquidity

* Additional dollar sales may happen if needed (Adds background, comment from finance minister)

By Walter Brandimarte

SAO PAULO, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank announced on Wednesday a likely slowdown in the pace of currency intervention next year, a move that appears aimed at taking advantage of an upbeat market reaction to U.S. policymakers' decision to cut back on monetary stimulus.

The central bank said in a statement that it will extend its currency intervention program with some adjustments through at least the end of the first half of 2014.

The program extension will provide investors with some $20 billion worth of currency swaps, derivatives that offer protection against a possible depreciation of the real. That compares to about $60 billion in swaps offered in the first leg of the program, which went into effect at the end of August.

The adjustment in the pace of intervention was announced after markets reacted positively to the Fed's decision to cut its $85 billion-a-month bond-buying program by an initial $10 billion as of next year.

Even as the decision could reduce the supply of dollars seeking higher returns in emerging markets, investors were encouraged by the Fed's suggestion that U.S. interest rates may remain near zero for longer than expected.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who earlier on Friday had called on U.S. policymakers to start cutting the stimulus sooner rather than later, said the first indications were that Brazilian markets were reacting well to the Fed's decision.

"That means we'll have less turbulence in the forex market. It means the dollar will strengthen less (against the real) than some maybe expected," he said in an interview with Globo TV.

$200 MILLION A DAY

Including previous interventions in the forex market this year, the stock of currency swaps offered by Brazil's central bank is expected to reach $100 billion at the end of 2013 and $120 billion by the end of June 2014, or about one-third of the country's international reserves of $375 billion.

As of next year, the bank will offer $200 million a day worth of traditional currency swaps, or $1 billion per week through its regular intervention program. That is half the $2 billion it currently offers every week in auctions held from Mondays through Thursdays.

Dollar sales on the spot market through repurchase agreements will "depend on liquidity conditions in the foreign exchange market," the central bank added in the statement.

Currently, policymakers offer as much as $1 billion worth of dollar repos on Fridays, but government sources have told Reuters that demand for such dollar lines has not been very strong.

The central bank said, however, that it may still sell dollars through "all instruments available" whenever it deems it necessary, leaving the door open for more aggressive currency intervention.

Brazil's intervention program was announced when the country's currency traded around 2.45 per dollar in late August, adding to inflation pressures. It has greatly contributed to stabilizing the real around the current level of 2.3 per dollar. (Additional reporting by Brad Haynes; Editing by Todd Benson, Andrew Hay and Ken Wills)

Brazil's central bank has been selling a daily "ration" of about $500 million in forex swaps since August as a measure to curb excess volatility and local currency weakening ahead of expected changes in Fed policy.

Because a weak real could pressure inflation, the central bank has been intervening to ensure stability in the currency.

For Monday, the bank rolled over $1 billion in expiring contracts and sold about $500 million in new contracts.

The central bank last week also released minutes of its most recent interest-rate decision meeting, when it raised the Selic rate by half a point, as expected. title: Brazil  Real Gains As  Central Bank  Promises More  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened against the dollar Thursday for the first time in five days after the central bank said it will continue offering currency hedge options next year.

After opening somewhat weaker, the real reversed direction and exited active trading at BRL2.3593 to the dollar, stronger than Wednesday's close of BRL2.3796 according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Speaking at a banking sector event in Sao Paulo on Thursday, Central Bank Governor Alexandre Tombini said that a currency-hedging program that was promised through the end of this year will be extended into next year. In August, the bank introduced a program of daily auctions of currency-swap contracts meant to reduce volatility as the Brazilian real lost value against the dollar.

The hedges have the practical effect of strengthening the real. By purchasing currency-hedge contracts, investors can lock in future dollar prices, eliminating the need to stock up on the currency to safeguard against future swings in prices.

"In 2014 the central bank won't exit this market," Mr. Tombini said, according to a transcript of his speech posted on the central bank's website. "With some adjustments, the central bank will extend the program offering currency hedges."

Mr. Tombini's speech came after the bank published minutes of its most recent interest-rate decision. Last week, the bank raised rates by half a point to 10%, as expected. On Thursday, minutes showed a central bank concerned with increasing currency volatility. Such volatility puts inflation control at risk, the bank has noted several times.

The minutes also hinted that Brazil could slow its pace of rate increases as the central bank gives time for past rate hikes to take effect.

The possible slowdown in rates comes at a difficult time, as the country is still seeing inflation close to the upper limits of the central bank's target, which ranges from 2.5% to 6.5%. Inflation currently stands at around 5.8%, and investors expect it to remain steady through the end of next year. title: Brazil 's Real Opens Stronger on  Central Bank Intervention

SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened against the dollar in early Wednesday trading as the central bank intensified intervention in currency markets after the real touched a two-week low against the greenback.

The real was trading at 2.3224 per dollar at 7:00 EST, after closing at BRL2.3314 to the dollar on Tuesday.

After markets closed on Tuesday, the central bank announced plans to hold an auction of new foreign-currency swap contracts as well as contracts to replace those expiring at the start of next month. The bank plans to sell up to $1.5 billion in new contracts, whereas a week ago the bank was selling just $500 million a day in regular auctions.

Whereas the bank waited until the end of October to roll over contracts expiring Nov. 1, this time the bank has been rolling over contracts maturing Dec. 2 since the start of the month. Traders say that the earlier rollover has assuaged investor fears that not all the contracts would be rolled over. Last month, the bank only rolled over about two-thirds of the almost $9 billion in maturing contracts. In December, about $10 billion in contracts mature.

The stepped up intervention has helped staunch sudden weakness in the real. Last week the Brazilian currency slid against the dollar after strong jobs data revived speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve could start tapering its bond-buying program this year. The bond-buying program made borrowing in dollars cheaper, and as a result pushed up the prices of global assets and currencies.

The possible reversal of stimulus policies in the U.S. comes at a time when Brazilian government accounts are deteriorating and doubts are rising about the willingness and ability of the federal government to slow spending. With presidential elections coming up next year in Brazil, many analysts are concerned spending will pick up, further unbalancing the country's accounts and possibly leading to a cut in the country's credit rating.
