title: Brazilian Real Slides as Holiday Amplifies Fed Speculation
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real weakened against the dollar Monday as the prospect of reduced U.S. stimulus measures following last week's strong jobs data continued to weigh on the currency at the same time that a holiday curbed trading volume and exaggerated losses.

The real exited active trading at 2.3335 per dollar, after closing at BRL2.3111 to the dollar Friday.

Job creation in the U.S. surprised on the upside last week, with the Labor Department saying that U.S. payrolls expanded by 204,000 jobs in October, almost double the 120,000 new openings expected. The data led to increased bets that the Federal Reserve could start tapering its bond-buying program as soon as December. The bond-buying program, by making it cheaper to borrow dollars, has helped lift emerging-markets assets and currencies, and a reversal of such a program is expected to rapidly weaken those assets.

After the currency slumped against the dollar Friday, it did so once more Monday, a move exacerbated by the fact that a U.S. holiday drastically reduced trading volume.

"Today orders are lighter than when you have inflows from foreigners, so you're going to have more volatility," said Italo Abucater, head of currency trading at ICAP Plc in Sao Paulo. "Add to that the fact that you have more dollar-buying because of really awful flows into the country in recent months."

From the start of the year through Nov. 1, a net of almost $5.4 billion had left the country, compared with net inflows of $18 billion at a comparable time last year. With international companies operating in Brazil traditionally sending home profits and dividends at the end of the year, that outflow will likely increase in coming months, as happened at the end of last year.

Brazil's central bank has been intervening in the market as part of its stated effort to reduce volatility. The bank sold about $500 million in foreign-currency swap contracts Monday and promised to start rolling over part of the $10 billion in contracts that expire next month.

The bank rolled over about two-thirds of contracts that expired Nov. 1 but waited until the end of the month to start rolling them over.

On Friday the bank announced it would start rolling over some contracts already, and that created some relief for investors, according to Mr. Abucater. The bank likely wanted to make clear it would roll over more contracts--which have the practical effect of strengthening the real against the dollar--after the currency slipped 6% over the past month, Mr. Abucater said.

title: Brazilian Real Falls on Deficit, U.S. Fed Worries
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real was one of the biggest losers against the dollar on Tuesday as global concerns that the U.S. Federal Reserve will start to withdraw its easy-money policies were compounded by concerns that the Latin American government isn't making serious efforts to curtail spending.

A number of emerging-market currencies have slipped against the dollar as investors are once again betting the Fed could start tapering its bond-buying program--which made borrowing in dollars less expensive and as a result has boosted the prices of overseas assets, including currencies in emerging markets. Some investors expect the Fed to slow its bond-buying program as soon as next month, and consensus is growing that the Fed will start unwinding the program early next year.

The main losers so far have been currencies such as the South African rand, the Turkish lira and the Hungarian forint, according to Dirk Willer, managing director for emerging-market strategy at Citibank. "But Brazil also is showing up," Mr. Willer said, in part because of a "further deterioration of the fiscal story."

Last week, the central government reported a surprisingly large deficit for September, at 10.47 billion Brazilian reais ($4.66 billion), nearly three times the figure economists had been expecting, which the government attributed to an unusual surge in social-security payments. The government is widely expected to miss its savings target for this year, while the amount of government debt as a ratio of gross domestic product may start to rise.

"Nobody in the government is talking seriously about more austere fiscal policy," said Paulo Nepomuceno, fixed-income strategist at Coinvalores brokerage in Sao Paulo.

At 4:44 p.m. GMT, the real was trading at BRL2.2831, about 1.8% weaker than the close on Monday. The currency has weakened nearly 6% since Oct. 17.

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega has in recent days addressed the issue, saying he wants to keep spending under control.

"The government is concerned about containing the rise in spending; that is a permanent preoccupation," Mr. Mantega told reporters on Monday.

Yet in a report in the Folha de S. Paulo newspaper on Tuesday, Gleisi Hoffman, President Dilma Rousseff's chief of staff, was quoted as saying she wants more flexibility on targets for government spending, which heightened the fears. Concern about public spending is especially crucial ahead of next year's election for president and state governors, when investors widely expect the government to loosen its purse strings even more.

The worries have already led one of the three major credit ratings firms to express a negative outlook for the Brazil's rating, raising the possibility of a downgrade. Earlier this year, Standard & Poor's lowered its outlook on Brazil's triple-B investment grade debt to negative, citing slow economic growth and "continued expansionary fiscal policy." A lower credit rating makes it more expensive to borrow money.

Still, Mr. Nepomuceno said he doesn't expect a "meltdown" in the Brazilian real because central-bank intervention in currency markets should be able to sustain the real at levels stronger than 2.35 reais per dollar.

Indeed, the Central Bank of Brazil is already committed to daily intervention in the currency-futures market. That daily mechanism was introduced in August, when the real touched 2.45 per dollar amid a previous round of fears about the withdrawal of Fed policy.

Mr. Willer said that some of the real's weakness is also due to the fact that investors were caught out by the suddenness of the real's move against the dollar, as they had been expecting the real to remain in a narrow range for some time, subdued by the central bank's intervention.

title: The New Latin America -- Barron's
text:
(FROM BARRON'S 11/4/13) 
   By Reshma Kapadia 

Blame it on Brazil. Or China. Heck, you can even blame it on the Fed. Emerging markets are doing terribly this year, with Latin America leading the way down. But the changing landscape has opened up some new opportunities for intrepid investors.

After growing at an average pace of 6.4% a year over the past decade, emerging markets are expected to expand by 4.5% this year, with Brazil's economy slowing even further, according to the International Monetary Fund. That's a bitter pill for investors who flocked to these countries for growth, and their dissatisfaction is evident in the market. Following a decade of returning 15% a year, the MSCI Emerging Markets index is down 2% so far this year, with Latin America down 9%. Compare that with the S&P 500's 23% return, and it's clear something is afoot.

For starters, there is China. The powerhouse nation has been a massive catalyst for growth in Latin America, gobbling up the region's commodities, from Brazil's iron ore and soybeans to Peru's copper. Between 2006 and 2012, Brazil's exports to China quintupled. But as China's economy slowed and its appetite for commodities waned, Brazil's exports to China fell for the first time since 2000, down 7% last year.

Brazil's economy is now expected to grow just 2.4% this year -- a far cry from 7.5% three years ago. The nation is now importing more than it exports, creating a current-account deficit that has made investors wary and contributed to a 50% decline in the Brazilian real over the past two years. With credit cheap around the world, thanks to the tone set by the U.S. Federal Reserve, Brazilian consumers went on a credit-fueled shopping spree and are now dealing with the aftereffects, as debt payments rise alongside interest rates. President Dilma Rousseff has tried reforming the nation's infrastructure and reducing the high cost of doing business in Brazil by pressing electric companies to cut prices and banks to lower rates. But these measures spooked rather than comforted investors because of their interventionist tones.

With Brazil making up 58% of the MSCI Latin America index, its misfortunes weigh on the entire region. More than $8 billion has left Latin America mutual funds this year, according to EPFR Global. But Latin America still has plenty to offer, such as an abundance of farmland and the fact that the middle class' consumer purchasing power of LatAm's five major countries is larger than China's, according to HSBC.

The opportunity, however, is fragmented. We asked four money managers to assess the current situation and tell us where they're putting their money. (For even more investment ideas, see "Latin America: Four Ways to Play" -- Barron's Nov. 4, 2013)

Adam Kutas has covered Latin America for nearly a decade and currently manages the $1.4 billion Fidelity Latin America fund (FLATX). After growing wary about Brazil a couple of years ago, Kutas is finding better opportunities now.

Mexico-born Luis Carrillo, manager of the $141 million JPMorgan Latin America fund (JLTAX), veers toward smaller companies with long-term growth prospects.

Jim Carlen, a former international economist at the U.S. Treasury Department, manages the $796 million Columbia Emerging Markets Bond fund (REBAX), which has one of the larger helpings of Latin American exposure among peers at 30% of assets. One attraction is the relative strength of many of the countries' balance sheets and favorable reforms in countries like Colombia.

Lewis Kaufman, who manages the $1.3 billion Thornburg Developing World fund (THDAX), shies away from debt-laden companies and countries, and leans toward consumer-oriented stocks. While he can invest anywhere in the emerging world, four of his top-10 holdings are in Latin America.

Barron's: It has been a rough year for Latin America. What's going on?

Carlen: Over the past 12 to 18 months, the problems are twofold: The Fed's continued injection of massive amounts of liquidity played a big role in running up asset prices in emerging markets, and made investors much less risk averse.

Barron's: In other words, money was pouring into Latin America in part because people didn't know where else to put it. What's the other issue?

Carlen: Demand for commodities isn't stimulating the economic growth it once did, and consumer spending is down. As a result, some of these economies are slowing down. That's been a challenge for some of these governments, too.

Kaufman: We are on an inexorable march toward higher interest rates. Countries with current-account deficits that have to be financed with stock and bond flows are going to suffer. Countries that don't require foreign investment to balance their budget are more structurally sound.

Barron's: What does that mean from an investment standpoint?

Kaufman: For the first group, we'd like to be tactical. If Brazil falls sharply, that would be a good buying opportunity, to lean against the grain in a country and currency we find to be less structurally sound. Structurally sound countries, primarily Mexico and the Andean region -- specifically Peru and Colombia -- have healthier external accounts. We'd look to buy when correlations are high and the market is treating Mexico or Central America like Brazil.

Barron's: What happens to the "structurally unsound" countries when investors pull out?

Kaufman: When countries need to finance deficits with stock and bond flows, it pressures the local currency, which can cause inflation. The surprise to investors in the next 12 to 18 months will be the effects of this on growth. As Brazil fights these pressures with higher interest rates, it could slow growth further.

Barron's: Latin Americans have been on a credit-fueled consumption spree over the past couple years. What's the state of the middle-class consumer there?

Kaufman: Consumption goes up when there's job growth, real wage growth, increased access to credit, and a falling savings rate. [Many Latin American countries have very high savings rates. As consumers feel more confident, they reduce their saving and increase consumption.] Each of those factors is very resilient in emerging markets. In places with lower credit penetration, like the Andean nations, the outlook is much better. Even in a country like Brazil, we are seeing consumption hold up.

Kutas: We see strains in the consumer in Brazil. And its central bank is facing stagflation, with slowing growth and rising costs. You don't understand how many [company] meetings I have in which flat margins is the new up. If you can maintain margins, you are pretty excited.

Barron's: That's pretty depressing from a stock perspective, isn't it?

Carrillo: When Brazil's stock market fell in 2011 and 2012, everyone thought the glass was half-full and it was a big opportunity to jump in. But the question should have been, "Is the glass the right size?" Brazil needs a smaller glass because of slower growth prospects. Now that expectations have corrected, with the market and currency falling, we feel more comfortable coming back in.

Barron's: Given the problems you've raised, is there a good reason to invest in Latin America at all?

Kaufman: It's still a very undeveloped place. For example, in Peru, 20% of retailers are chain stores; the rest are mom-and-pop stores. Compare that with the 40% of chain-store retailers in Brazil. Brazil may not be a high-growth area, but LatAm as a whole is. Look at Peru. Even with a commodity slowdown, it is looking at 4.5% to 5% gross-domestic-product growth. Chile is probably around there; Colombia is still growing on the back of oil production.

Barron's: And Brazil?

Kaufman: I don't necessarily need to be bullish on Brazil's economic development to buy Brazilian stocks. Brazil is easily the deepest capital market in Latin America.

Barron's: By deepest, you mean . . .

Kaufman: Breadth and liquidity. It's possible to find opportunities because the market is so much more developed. My biggest holding is a for-profit postsecondary education company, Kroton Educacional (KROT3.Brazil). It has the best earnings momentum, not just in Brazil but in my entire portfolio.

Barron's: What about fixed income?

Carlen: Latin America had a great period of growth because of a big commodity tail wind, bringing up the level of consumption in these economies. People forgot how much of that was commodity driven and not sustainable in the long term, but that doesn't mean a lot of good things haven't happened.

Barron's: Like what?

Carlen: Net debt to GDP has come down from 50% to the mid-30s. Fiscal deficits are consistently much lower, certainly compared with developed economies. And the amount countries can grow until running up against inflation constraints is higher than a decade ago. Many of these countries, like Brazil, became impatient with the level of growth and pushed the accelerator too hard and have run up against constraints. Inflation is higher. Central banks have to address those issues, but that doesn't detract from the long-term potential, which is why we still see good upside.

Carrillo: There are issues, but it's not 2000. Now 73% of the Latin American bonds in the JPMorgan EMBI Global Diversified bond index are investment grade. A decade ago it was just Mexico and El Salvador.

Barron's: Investors have often treated emerging markets all the same. How should they look at Latin America now?

Carrillo: During the first decade of this century, China helped all emerging markets. In the second decade, engines of growth are likely to be different everywhere. For us, this means stockpickers have a better time than in the previous 10 years because there are structural problems in the index.

Barron's: Because the MSCI Latin American index is commodities-heavy?

2 Nov 2013 00:03 EDT  The New Latin America -- Barron's -2-

Carrillo: Yes, along with other companies that don't represent the real economy. In 1994, oil, energy, and mining companies were privatized in Brazil. Those are the biggest companies with the longest track records, and have a big impact on the index. Brazil's weighting went as high as 71% in 2009 and is currently 58%.

Barron's: How is the market changing?

Carrillo: There were very few listings in the 1990s through 2005. We've seen probably 300 initial public offerings in the past three years.

Kutas: Look at recent transactions. Colombian companies are buying assets in Central America. They have maxed out market share in their own markets and need capital to go international. That means more investment options.

Carrillo: S.A.C.I. Falabella (FALAB.Chile) started in Chile and dominates that market. It has moved to Peru, Colombia, and now Brazil. Lima, Peru, has about half the GDP/capita of Santiago, Chile, so the prospect for growth in Peru is a lot longer-lasting.

Barron's: There are 74 Latin American companies that trade on U.S. exchanges as American depository receipts. Is that a good way for individuals to get into Latin America?

Kutas: ADRs tend to be Brazilian, cyclical, and more resource-oriented. In the past, an ADR was a sign that you had arrived. Now, there are $2 trillion of assets managed in Latin America, growing at 10% to 15%. As a local Brazilian company, your cost of capital is much cheaper if you can sell to the locals versus coming to the U.S. as an ADR.

Barron's: What about exchange-traded funds?

Carrillo: ETFs are easy competition for us. They have to look at the index. The Peru ETF doesn't include any consumer stocks, but Peru's economy is 60% consumer-driven.

Barron's: Emerging-market bond funds have taken in an unprecedented $111 billion since the beginning of 2008. Is there still an opportunity in bonds?

Carlen: Absolutely. More of these countries developed their local debt markets, supported in part by past pension reform. Such reform is one of the key steps an emerging market needs to undertake to develop a deeper, local capital market that can finance private and public debt placements. This is important because it gives government entities and local companies more financing options and makes them less exposed to swings in the exchange rate.

Barron's: It gives you a wider playing field?

Carlen: Yes. More issuers have come to the market, including quasi-sovereigns -- which are majority-owned by national or regional government that are often in strategic sectors like energy -- and emerging-market corporate bonds, both in dollar and local currency. Picking countries is important but so is finding the best way to express a view on a particular country. Having a greater variety of bonds to invest in helps that.

Barron's: Lets talk about Brazil. What's on tap for the economy and currency?

Kaufman: Brazil is the country with the greatest degree of imbalances. There's been too much easy credit for too long. The government has created jobs to produce things people don't want to buy, so unemployment is pretty low. Brazilian companies are lacking inputs for production and have to import them. It all makes the current-account deficit negative. Because the investment outlook is not good, the foreign direct investment to finance it is not there. So there's Brazil and the not-Brazil markets of Mexico, the Andean markets, and Central America.

Barron's: But you still own Brazilian stocks?

Kaufman: Let's say the credit cycle in Brazil has run its course, and things are going to look up in 18 months. You could play that through a bank, but ultimately the Brazilian consumer is relatively more indebted versus consumers in the rest of the region. So we prefer Brazilian health-care broker Qualicorp (QUAL3.Brazil), which benefits from a rising middle-class spending more on health care but isn't tied directly to the consumer. Regulation prevents insurance companies from raising prices if they sell directly to individuals, so they sell through affinity plans, like professional groups such as doctors. It's a faster-growth business that's less capital-intensive than banks and ultimately a better business.

Carrillo: Since we think long-term, we try to stay away from companies or sectors the government influences. We find companies that don't have to raise prices to make money, like Localiza Rent A Car [RENT3.Brazil], which has increased prices just 8% in 10 years. Competitors die amid the pricing pressure, and Localiza gets a bigger portion of the market just by controlling cost and being efficient.

Kutas: Brazilian companies have to pay 8% to 10% wage hikes, denting profitability. That's also the opportunity. We find companies focusing not just on revenue growth but also on profits through cost reductions. How can they do that? Become more automated.

Barron's: Who benefits from more automation?

Kutas: Industrias Romi [ROMI3. Brazil] is a $400 million Brazilian capital equipment company hurt in the last few years by the weaker economy, stronger exchange rate, and nonperforming loan issues. But they have cut head count by 40% and hiked prices by 15% and are buying back stock.

Carrillo: Weg [WEGE3.Brazil] is a Brazilian industrial that makes electric motors with gas and water pumps and turbine generators. About 85% of the engines in Brazil are theirs; I don't think that even Siemens has that market share in Germany. Weg has had a 20-year record of not losing money. No one gets paid bonuses if return on equity is not 20%.

Barron's: What about banks?

Kaufman: Brazilian banks are probably underpriced if you have a longtime horizon. There are two things I like better about the Peruvian banking market: It is very consolidated, with the top five controlling 85% of the market. And I prefer the Peruvian currency, the new sol, over the Brazilian real. One Peruvian bank I like is Credicorp [BAP]; it grows fast but with stable margins.

Barron's: So the Andean markets offer good growth, but these are small markets. How do you deal with illiquidity?

Carrillo: If you are willing to put money there for a very long time, it's a good opportunity. Peru's financial system and regulation is the strongest. They have the best credit bureau in LatAm, so the banks have not only the potential for growth, but also a better view into the cash flow of their borrowers.

Barron's: Jim, are some of the smaller countries also attractive from a bond perspective?

Carlen: Uruguay has some great things to recommend it from a macro standpoint. Its Treasury has 1 1/2 years of financing needs sitting in the bank, and it runs small fiscal deficits. They restructured their debt 12 years ago after Argentina's default, so debt to GDP has fallen from 60% to 40%. The mix has changed from all dollar-denominated to half local currency. And they have been able to attract significant foreign direct investment to a variety of industries. Agriculture and beef are big drivers.

Barron's: What about liquidity?

Carlen: The consumer price index-linked bonds we favor do have some liquidity issues and can cause volatility. But for a long-term investor with a three- to four-year horizon, it's a good opportunity.

Barron's: We haven't yet touched on Mexico. The market rose 29% last year while Brazil's market fell 5%. What's going on?

Kutas: Mexico underperformed for nearly 10 years, until mid-2011, while Brazil stole the show. In 2012, President Rousseff did a lot to scare away foreign investors and hurt sentiment and prospects.

Barron's: Contrast that to Mexico?

Kutas: At the same time, Mexico elected Enrique Pena Nieto president. He promised a lot of reforms people have waited a very long time for, including energy reform. He promised too much too soon, and the economy entered recession in the second and third quarters this year. From what I can see, the pact he had among the key political parties has fallen apart, so now he's scrambling. All I can see is higher taxes on the rich and a watered-down energy policy.

Carlen: I don't agree with that. All of us fall into the trap of expecting the political process to be smoother and more rational than it ever is. In Mexico, we fell into the trap that they were going to do education, energy, and fiscal reforms -- boom, boom, boom -- and it would be nirvana tomorrow. Of course, that's not how it happens -- a lot of sacred cows need to be slaughtered. We saw education reform, and that was a great step.

Barron's: What was the education reform?

Carlen: A change in funding and how they measure performance, which upset teachers. Politicians realized the steps were going to cause domestic volatility, and slowed things down. But they are still moving forward with energy and political reform and fiscal reform.

Barron's: What's the fiscal reform?

Carlen: Raising [sales, property, and top income] taxes to make up for lost revenue as a result of energy reform, which will reduce the amount of tax revenue that state-run oil firm Pemex sends to the government. It's also an incentive for skeptical congressmen to vote for the energy measures.

Barron's: But the market doesn't like that?

Carlen: Unfortunately, the actual proposed reform had more spending to stimulate growth and perhaps to attract votes, and wasn't strong enough on keeping the deficit in check by just raising alternative revenues. As a result, the market does not see this as fiscal reform but rather as an expansion of government expenditures. But the energy and fiscal reforms are somewhat linked; if you don't get one, you may not get the other. Mexico also has a lot of residual credibility from years of strong fiscal performance. I think they'll have reform progress by the end of the year.

Carrillo: The expectation is that the reforms are going to take off like a spaceship. It's not. It's just a plane.

2 Nov 2013 00:03 EDT  The New Latin America -- Barron's -3-

Kaufman: It's worse than that. Consumer-oriented businesses in Mexico have missed earnings estimates quite substantially, because the government has struggled to disburse money. That hurt consumption at exactly the moment investors expected it to pick up. Also, the Mexican stock market, especially compared with Brazil, is shallow.

Barron's: How is the Mexican stock market shallow?

Kaufman: There simply are not a lot of good consumer-oriented opportunities. Big banks like Grupo Financiero Santander Mexico [BSMX] or Grupo Financiero Banorte [GFNORTEO.Mexico] are two multiple-points more expensive than Credicorp with a similar penetration story, so they don't make sense. Big stocks like Walmex [Wal-Mart de Mexico, WALMEXV.Mexico] and Mexican bottler and retailer FEMSA [Fomento Economico Mexicano, FMX], both of which I own, lack earnings momentum for economic and company-specific reasons. The main point: Be creative. You can think about Mexico as "not-Brazil" and extend that to include companies in Central America or based elsewhere -- like U.S.-listed pawnbroker First Cash Financial Services (FCFS).

Kutas: First Cash is a $1.6 billion [market value] company that gets 60% of its earnings from Mexico. Most collateral historically has been jewelry, so many investors view it as a play on gold. But more customers on the margin are bringing in smartphones as collateral.

Carlen: And they want them back.

Kutas: Phones have become indispensable, especially in emerging markets where people can't afford laptops or PCs and don't have cable or land-line connections. So like grandmother's jewelry, they are reluctant to lose it and, therefore, pay off the loan. Growth comes from new stores in Mexico and maturation of existing ones. In the U.S., they are acquiring smaller pawnshops and benefit from the difficulty in accessing credit. Revenue growth is 15%. They generate 16% return on assets. If an average bank can do 2%, that's pretty amazing. It has no leverage and buys back stock.

Barron's: Mexico is also benefiting from the U.S. recovery and a rise in labor costs in China. How do you play that?

Carrillo: All the industrials, like petrochemical company Mexichem [MEXCHEM.Mexico] and conglomerate Alfa [ALFAA.Mexico].

Barron's: After running up 42% in 10 months, the Mexican stock market is down 17% since its April high. Is it a good time to get in?

Carrillo: No, it hasn't fallen enough. Expectations were too high.

Barron's: But in the long term, the outlook for Mexico's economic growth is healthy?

Kutas: This is a far better backdrop than 10 to 20 years ago. If the biggest issue is that reforms are not happening fast enough, that's way better than not happening at all.

Barron's: Should investors in Latin America have lower expectations going foward?

Carlen: The days of saying, "I'm going to throw my lure out to stream, and I'll catch fish" are over, at least for now. In bonds, it's a country-picker's market. Countries that have a current-account surplus or a deficit completely funded by foreign direct investment, and decent growth and macro policies, are the sleep-well-at-night bunch.

Barron's: Which countries does that describe?

Carlen: Peru and Colombia. We see a lot of potential in Colombia's sovereign debt, and more so, agency debt. We own an electrical company and a state-owned oil company, in both dollars and local currency. It's done a better job of structural reforms in the midst of its commodities windfall, such that they can continue to attract a lot of foreign direct investment. That creates a virtuous cycle and lifts its growth prospects, which in turn draws more foreign and domestic investment.

Barron's: What were some of the reforms?

Carlen: They opened up the oil sector to foreign investment. Peace talks with FARC [rebel group Revolutionary Army Forces of Colombia] helped, and they made fiscal policy more sustainable by creating a rainy-day fund and a sovereign wealth fund. All in all, it puts Colombia on track to follow in the footsteps of higher creditworthy countries like Chile. Guatemalan dollar-based bonds are also sleep-well-at night-[bonds], with very good policies and valuations that haven't caught up with how positive that story is. Mexico will be in that category next year when it gets out of the basement in terms of growth.

Barron's: Who is in the middle camp?

Carlen: Countries with issues but that we have confidence in their governments' ability to react. That's where policy becomes important; that's where you make your money. Whether Brazil is in this group is the big question. They will ultimately do the right thing -- after they have exhausted all the options. The good news is the political interference with the central bank has decreased. They raised rates in the midst of slowing growth. That has credibility.

Barron's: So what's the takeaway?

Carrillo: LatAm will still grow faster than the developed market, just not as much as 10 years ago. Really, it's Brazil dragging everything else down. Chile, Peru, Colombia are all having nice growth.

Kutas: Mexico and Brazil have moved down the development path. That's positive over the long term for less volatility and currency risk. In the shorter term though, Brazil is facing structural problems. They just have to work through them. But it's a region of more than half a billion people, so it's funny to hear people say it's over. There are still a lot of growth opportunities, but it's more about stock-picking than country calls now.

Barron's: Thanks, everyone.

title: Brazil Real Ends Weaker as Market Monitors Fed's Path
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real lost ground against the dollar to end weaker Friday as factors abroad, including recent signals from the U.S. Federal Reserve on policy, weighed against the local currency.

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.2548 to the dollar, after ending at BRL2.2287 to the dollar Thursday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the real began the session slipping against the greenback as local data and year-end demand for dollars influenced the market.

Brazil's IBGE statistics institute reported local industrial production came in below forecasts. Industrial output rose 0.7% during the month, a figure below projections of around 1.2%.

The soft output data is seen as possibly limiting any tightening of the local interest rate by Brazil's central bank, and thus continuing to help bring investment dollars into the economy.

But concerns abroad brought still more pressure against the real throughout the session as investors fretted over possible interest-rate tightening in China and the U.S.

Worries over the Fed were causing particular waves after authorities there hinted this week that the institution could act soon to curb its stimulus policies.

"The market knows that this stimulus can't continue indefinitely," said Reginaldo Galhardo, forex manager at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "At some point there will have to be an adjustment.

Locally, meanwhile, Brazil's own central bank is seen maintaining its market intervention with forex swaps and weekly dollar lending to help provide liquidity and hedge.

The bank Friday held its weekly auction of $1 billion in dollar credit. The bank sold dollars at BRL2.2522 under agreement to repurchase them at BRL2.3165.

The bank in August agreed to extend approximately $100 billion in foreign exchange swaps and dollar credit lines to the market through the end of this year, in order to curb excess depreciation of the real due to possible policy changes at the Fed and shifting flows of global investment capital.

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Weaker on Fed Bets, Easing  FX Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real slipped against the dollar in early Thursday trading as speculation mounts that the U.S. may reverse stimulus policies soon, while in Brazil more investors see the central bank easing back its currency intervention.

The real was at 2.1965 in morning trading, after closing at BRL2.1906 on Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The currency weakened to BRL2.2 per dollar in intraday trading as investors see signs that the Federal Reserve could start tapering its bond-buying program as soon as December.

The monetary policy panel of the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank sent mixed signals on Wednesday when it said that the country's housing recovery has "slowed somewhat," while eliminating references to rising mortgage rates dragging down the economy.

In Brazil, meanwhile, the central bank has signaled that it may slow the pace of forex intervention. In addition to carrying out daily foreign-currency swap auctions, where it offers investors a hedge against swings in the real, the central bank has also been rolling over part of the almost $9 billion in existing swap contracts that expire Friday.

"There's been a lot of speculation on whether the central bank will roll over all the swaps," said Anderson Rodrigues, a fixed-income manager at Daycoval Asset Management in Sao Paulo. "The central bank has been testing the market a lot, saying that it wouldn't carry out an auction, then gauging market appetite for future auctions. It looks like they're trying to keep the real at current levels" of about BRL2.2 per dollar, he said.

As of Thursday, the central bank had rolled over about $6 billion of the roughly $9 billion in contracts coming due. For Thursday, there were no rollover auctions announced.

The sharply widening deficit reported Thursday morning also helped weaken the real, Mr. Rodrigues said. Brazil's treasury reported a central government deficit of BRL10.47 billion, wider than the BRL432 million deficit posted in August.

title: Should  Brazil 's  Central Bank  Continue  Currency Intervention ? -- WSJ Blog
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Real Time Economics blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/economics)

By Paulo Trevisani and Jeffrey T. Lewis

Brazil's central bank finds itself caught in a quandary: After launching a new program to prevent the national currency from depreciating too abruptly during a volatile summer, officials must decide whether to abandon or alter the program now that the currency is gaining value.

The central bank, like many of its counterparts in emerging markets, has struggled for months to cope with the global market turmoil caused by the twists and turns of U.S. monetary and fiscal policy.

Its task is complicated because Brazil's inflation, at just under 6%, is running close to the top end of the central bank's target range. A weaker currency can add to inflationary pressures, but too strong a currency can harm the nations' exports.

Brazil's currency--the real--plunged during the summer after the U.S. Federal Reserve signaled it would start winding down some of its easy money policies as the U.S. economy strengthens. The Fed policies had held U.S. interest rates very low for several years, sending global capital flowing to Brazil and other fast-growing developing economies: Those flows started reversing at the prospect of the Fed changing course.

Investors in Brazil also feared a shortage of U.S. dollars if the Fed reversed gears too soon and began stocking up on greenbacks--causing the shortage to materialize and the real to fall to a four-year low of 2.45 reais to the dollar by Aug. 22.

The next day, Brazil's central bank responded by introducing daily preannounced currency interventions. Until that point, the central bank had not announced its intentions in advance. The bank said it was just seeking to tame volatility, but many investors saw the moves as an effort to prevent the real from falling any further.

Brazil's interventions differ from most other countries in the world, where central banks beef up local currencies by using dollars from cash reserves. Instead, the Brazilian central bank offers hedging contracts in the futures market-- either of currency swaps or of dollar credit lines--by which the central bank bets on the real and investors can bet on the dollar, easing their fears of getting stuck with a weakening currency.

By late August, the new program was working: the real steadied versus the dollar.

But suddenly, emerging market currencies--including Brazil's--started rising after the Fed surprised markets in September by not pulling back on its stimulus policies, and U.S. budget battles resulted in a 16-day partial shutdown of the U.S. government earlier this month. The Fed left its policies unchanged again at its policy meeting Wednesday.

The real now trades closer to 2.15 reais to the dollar, versus 2.45 reais when the program began.

That appreciation has generated speculation that at some point the real's rise could become a problem, prompting the central bank to stop its regular currency interventions.

"I don't think they're in panic mode, but [with the exchange rate] at 2.15 they're starting to get concerned," said Win Thin, an analyst at Brown Brother Harriman in New York.

Brazil Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini signaled earlier this month--during the U.S. government shutdown--that he would press forward with the daily currency interventions. "The program has proved successful in curbing volatility and could be extended beyond year- end if necessary," he said in Washington, DC, on October 12 in his speech during an event sponsored by the International Monetary Fund.

The bank has several options short of cancelling the auctions. When it holds the auctions, for instance, it can simply refuse to accept bids.

Tony Volpon, head of emerging-markets research at Nomura Securities in New York, said it would be good for the bank to stick to a predictable course.

"Taking away uncertainty is good," he said. "To change now would once again add uncertainty."

title: Brazil Real Weaker As Importers, Companies Buy Cheap Dollars
text:
SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened Wednesday as importers and companies with dollar-linked debts bought "cheap" U.S. dollars.

The real ended active trading at BRL2.1841 against the U.S. dollar, weaker against Tuesday's close of BRL2.1697, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders said a range of BRL2.15 to BRL2.17 against the dollar makes the American currency look "cheap" to those needing dollars. Dollars were selling for BRL2.22 at the beginning of October. Importers and companies facing U.S. dollar payments in the coming days snapped up greenbacks Wednesday.

The market was also betting that Brazil's central bank won't rollover all of the $8.9 billion in foreign exchange swap contracts expiring on Nov. 1. The swap contracts tend to support the real against the dollar by giving investors an added hedge in the American currency. Rolling over only a portion of the swaps, while allowing the rest to close out, will diminish hedging capability in the market and could strengthen the dollar in the next few days, traders said.

On Tuesday, the central bank rolled over $1 billion in swaps, then another $1 billion Wednesday. Later Wednesday, the central bank will announce details of a third, and last, scheduled auction of rollover swaps set for Thursday. Investors are anxious to see how close the central bank will come to rolling over the $8.9 billion in swaps expiring next week.

"It's unlikely the central bank will offer the equivalent of $7 billion in new swaps on Thursday," said Joao Paulo de Gracia Correa, foreign exchange manager of the Correparti brokerage in southern Brazil. "That would be too much intervention at one time."

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil  central bank 's delay in announcing swap auction weighs on real
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Brazil's real trimmed its gains to close only modestly stronger on Wednesday as a delay in the announcement of an expected swap auction by the central bank triggered speculation that policymakers were reviewing their program of daily currency interventions.

Brazil has been auctioning as many as 10,000 currency swaps on Mondays through Thursdays as part of a $60 billion intervention program designed to provide investors with protection against a possible depreciation of the real.

Doubts about the swap offering increased, however, when the central bank failed to announce, before markets closed on Wednesday, the details of the contracts that would be sold on the following day.

The bank usually issues a statement with such details around 2:30 p.m. local time (1730 GMT) on the day prior to the sale. This time, however, that statement was only released after 8 p.m., when the bank announced it would sell on Thursday 10,000 traditional swap contracts maturing on March 5, 2014.

That came too late to ease the pressure on the Brazilian currency, however. After rallying over 1 percent to a four-month high of 2.1551 per dollar during the session, the real closed only 0.2 percent stronger at 2.1735, lagging other Latin American currencies.

Although many investors believe the government is not completely comfortable with the recent strength of the currency, central bank chief Alexandre Tombini has repeatedly said that the current intervention program is working as expected and will last until the end of the year at least.

title: Brazil  Real Weaker as Market Questions  Central-Bank Interventions
text:
SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened Tuesday as investors increasingly questioned the need for central-bank action to support the currency.

The real ended active trading at BRL2.1812 against the U.S. dollar, weaker against the Monday close of BRL2.1743, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders said investors bought dollars late in the session on continued worries about the U.S. fiscal crisis. Traders noted that market volume Tuesday was low.

Brazil's central bank has been intervening in the market on a daily basis since August 22 by selling foreign-exchange swaps and U.S. dollar credit lines. The interventions have the effect of replenishing dollar supplies to the market and supporting the real against the U.S. currency.

However, many investors and analysts question the need for continued intervention.

The Brazilian real has lost about 9% against the U.S. dollar so far this year. According to most economists, the depreciation of the currency is contributing to Brazil's worrisome 6% inflation rate. However, on the other hand, an even weaker currency would help make Brazilian exports more competitive.

For the moment, the central bank seems focused more on the inflation problem than on foreign trade, according to economists. For that reason, the bank has adopted a policy of intervening to support the real. Daily interventions are due to continue through the end of the year.

In a research note, economists at Sao Paulo's LCA consulting group said that, without daily intervention, the real would likely weaken to about BRL2.25 against the dollar, giving a boost to exports.

Other economists suggest that winding down intervention would be a desirable policy move.

In their own research note, economists at private bank Itau said a gradual reduction in the volume of daily swaps and credit lines would help promote a modest currency depreciation that would make Brazilian exports more competitive. They suggested there was a possibility of such a policy change.

Meanwhile, the mere idea that the central bank could scale back on intervention has now become a market factor in itself, according to Vanderlei Muniz, a partner in southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. "At BRL2.17 or BRL2.18, buyers think the dollar is cheap," he said.

title: Brazil's Tombini: Decline in Inflation to Continue in 2014
text:
Washington, D.C.--Brazil Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini on Friday reinforced his view that Brazil's inflation will decline this year and next, just two days after the bank raised interest rates for a fifth time this year, and said that U.S. talks on its debt ceiling are causing "great concern" among policy makers.

"The central bank is committed to bringing inflation down," he told reporters in Washington, D.C., following a meeting with fellow central bankers. "We will have lower inflation this year than last year and continue experiencing lower inflation in Brazil next year."

As was widely expected, Brazil raised rates to 9.5% on Wednesday. In a statement accompanying the decision, the central bank maintained the same wording it used during previous decisions, keeping the door open for additional rate hikes. Many analysts had expected the central bank to give some sign that the cycle of increases were coming to a close as Brazilian growth sputters and inflation shows some sign of retreat.

Mr. Tombini declined to comment on what the statement means for future rate decisions, saying only that minutes of the meeting that will be released Oct. 17 could provide more clarity.

Mr. Tombini said the central bank will also monitor closely decisions by the Federal Reserve and by the U.S. government that could affect future monetary policy. The Fed has signaled it will continue through the end of this year with its current bond-buying program--a program that helped drive investment to emerging economies and strengthen their currencies. Meanwhile, Congress is deadlocked on talks to end a government shutdown, which could have ramifications in concurrent talks to raise the country's debt ceiling.

"The debt ceiling talks are important," Mr. Tombini said. "During our meeting they were asked about this and it's a subject that has caused great concern."

"It's an exorbitant risk for the world economy," he said.

Concern about the Fed program and the debt ceiling have caused some upheavals in currency markets, but Mr. Tombini praised intervention by Brazil's central bank for helping reduce wild swings. The government announced in August that it would inject about $60 billion into the market via foreign-exchange swaps and credit lines. That helped strengthen the real after it touched a four year-low against the dollar.

Asked about Janet Yellen's nomination to head the Fed, Mr. Tombini said that he knows her well from having worked with her for several years during his time at Brazil's central bank, but declined to comment further.

title: INTERVIEW-Brazil's Mantega urges Fed to communicate tapering 'clearly'
text:
(Adds comments on exchange rate, interest rates)

SAO PAULO, Oct 10 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve should communicate clearly how it will phase out economic stimulus over the coming months to minimize market instability and prevent problems for emerging economies, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said in an interview on Thursday.

The stimulus reduction should also be carried out "very gradually," Mantega said, noting that the nomination of Janet Yellen to replace Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke appears to be a step in that direction.

Mantega, who skipped this week's International Monetary Fund and G20 meetings in Washington to focus on domestic issues, said he believes that higher interest rates in Brazil will not be a drag on economic growth. With over $370 billion in international reserves, Brazil is also very well prepared to weather any market instability, Mantega said.

He added that leading emerging economies should have time to set up a joint reserve fund next year before the prospect of higher interest rates in the United States rekindles volatility.

"More clarity and more precision as the stimulus is reduced. This is what we've been recommending," Mantega said in the interview in his Sao Paulo office.

"If they announce: 'we are going to cut it by $10 billion a month; instead of $85 billion it will be $75 billion,' such a decision would clearly have no effect" on markets, he said.

Signs that the Fed could start tapering its $85-billion-a-month asset purchases in September sent shockwaves through world financial markets earlier this year, causing steep losses in emerging market currencies such as the Brazilian real .

Yellen, who next year will become the first woman ever to lead the U.S. central bank, is a strong advocate of the Fed's aggressive actions to support economic growth through low interest rates and asset purchases.

She and fellow policymakers may need to keep the stimulus at full gear for an even longer period as the current political deadlock in Washington hurts economic growth, Mantega said.

The United States looks poised to avert a default, Mantega added, which would likely leave the next round of heightened market volatility for when a Yellen-led Fed starts raising interest rates in a few years.

"I believe Janet Yellen will continue Ben Bernanke's policies," Mantega said. "There is an excess of monetary stimulus and at some point this will need to be reduced. The right way to do it is in a very gradual way."

EXCHANGE RATE HELPING EXPORTERS

If Mantega's prediction pans out, leading emerging economies should have time to create a joint reserve fund to streamline intervention by their central banks in currency markets.

The reserve fund of the BRICS group - including Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa - should be created by March with $100 billion in reserves, Mantega said.

He noted that the fund will need to be ratified by local parliaments then.

Mantega, Latin America's longest serving finance minister, has been a fierce critic of ultra-loose monetary policies in developed economies. He coined the term "currency wars" in 2010 to describe what he saw as an attempt by countries like the United States to devalue their currencies through very low interest rates.

Brazil reacted with several capital controls, but began unwinding some of them this year as market concerns over the U.S. stimulus tapering sent the real to a near five-year low in August. Now at 2.2 per dollar and kept in a tight trading range by daily central bank interventions, Brazil's exchange rate is helping local industries, Mantega said.

He stressed, however, that the government does not seek to keep the currency at any particular level.

"What I can say is that the exchange rate, at this level, is supporting exports, because I can see an improvement in exports of manufactured goods," he said.

HIGHER INTEREST RATES ARE NO TABOO

Mantega also said there is no "political taboo" preventing the central bank from raising interest rates back to double-digit levels if needed to fight inflation.

On Wednesday, Brazil's central bank gave no sign it would stop raising its base policy rate in coming months after lifting it for a fifth straight time to 9.50 percent, the highest among the world's largest economies.

The increase should have little impact on economic growth as real interest rates remain historically low, Mantega said.

One measure of real interest rates is the base lending rate adjusted for inflation. In Brazil, it is currently around 3-4 percent.

"What is important is that we are not returning to what we had in the past. Brazil used to have nominal interest rates as high as 40 percent," Mantega said.

"It doesn't seem necessary for us to have 40-percent interest rates again, or 8-percent real interest rates." (Additional reporting by Cesar Bianconi; Editing by Richard Chang and Andrew Hay)

title: Brazil Real Weakens Slightly; U.S. Debt Row, Rates in Focus
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real slipped against the dollar to end slightly weaker Tuesday, while investors maintained a conservative strategy amid doubts surrounding a lingering impasse over debt in the U.S. and the outlook for interest rates locally.

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.2044 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.2042 to the dollar Monday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the currency began the session moving stronger against the dollar, but held within a narrow range as investors struggled to identify longer-term market trends.

Still at the forefront of concerns were the implications of stalled talks in the U.S. on a government shutdown and the possible increase of the debt ceiling. Analysts noted that while the political dispute continues, the U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to prolong its loose monetary policy that has helped irrigate emerging markets like Brazil with dollars.

Locally, meanwhile, investors are considering the impact of likely continued interest rate hikes and their capacity to attract more incoming investment.

Brazil's central bank is expected to raise the country's benchmark Selic interest rate again this week, hiking it by as much as half a percentage point from its current 9% to curb inflation.

However, market observers note that so far Brazil's currency has been buoyed by central bank market intervention of some $500 million per day and still ample foreign reserves of more than $370 billion.

"Thanks to this cushion and the swap program, the real was the currency that most appreciated in emerging markets since the peak of depreciation in August," noted strategist Paulo Gala at Banco Fator.

Questions remain, however, about whether Brazil's currency will maintain its recent strength ahead given the country's still widening current account deficit and the possibility that the Fed could back away from its ongoing loose-money policies once a political impasse over the U.S. budget is resolved.

But until clearer signs appear on that front, traders said they expect Brazil's currency to hold within a range of BRL2.20 to BRL2.25 to the dollar.

Most currencies strengthened against the greenback as a resolution to the U.S. government shutdown still seems remote. On Sunday, U.S. House Speaker John Boehner said the government wouldn't return to normal until Democrats agree to broader talks aimed at reducing the country's deficit.

Brazil's central bank has been intervening in currency markets daily in order to ensure that investor demand for dollars is met.

"The market has been working at this level of BRL2.20 to BRL2.22, with investors selling [dollars] when the real weakens beyond that and buying when it strengthens," Mr. Amado said. "The central bank has been continuing its program and that leaves traders more comfortable."

title: Brazil Real Gains Against Dollar on U.S. Budget, Debt Debates
text:
SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real strengthened against the dollar in Monday trading as concern grew that the U.S. Congress would fail to avoid a partial government shutdown ahead of a debate over raising the country's debt ceiling.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.2145 to the dollar, stronger than the Friday close of BRL2.2555, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

U.S. lawmakers on Monday raced to settle on a budget deal with the government seemingly headed for a partial shutdown for the first time since 1996. That comes ahead of another battle the Congress will face in coming weeks, when it debates raising the debt ceiling before a mid-October deadline.

The uncertainty led the dollar lower against most currencies, with the real being no exception. Adding to the Brazilian currency's strength on Monday was the approaching expiration of futures contracts. Monthly foreign exchange futures contracts expire Tuesday. They will close out based on Monday's average foreign exchange rate, or Ptax rate. Expiry of foreign exchange futures contracts typically brings high volume to Brazil's spot market as holders of short-dollar positions battle with holders of long positions to influence the Ptax rate.

"It's all about the futures expiry," said Vanderlei Muniz, partner in southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. "Holders of long positions are fighting it out with holders of short positions."

Meanwhile, Brazil's central bank is continuing its policy of daily interventions in an effort to maintain orderly trading. The central bank has been auctioning the equivalent of about $500 million in daily foreign-exchange swap contracts, which allow investors to exchange bonds linked to domestic interest rates for paper indexed directly to the U.S. dollar.

text:

18 Jul 2012 14:58 EDT *DJ  Brazil Should Cut Interest Rates to International Levels -Arida

18 Jul 2012 15:24 EDT DJ  Brazil's Economic Stabilization Yet to Be Completed -BTG's Arida

--Brazil's stabilization yet to be completed, says BTG's Arida

--Brazil needs to reduce interest rates to international levels

--Brazilian real is under a "dirty float" regime -Arida 


 
  By Luciana Magalhaes 
 

SAO PAULO--Brazil's economic stabilization remains incomplete, according to one of the architects of the 1994 Real Stabilization Plan, as evidenced by persistently high interest rates and a foreign exchange regime adding up to a "dirty float" that's not yet free from government intervention.

"Brazil's economy suffers from a distortion, which is high interest rates," said Persio Arida in an interview. "Nominal and real interest rates have to converge toward international levels, which also implies the convergence of inflation to international levels."

While markets are not yet pricing a long-term convergence of Brazil's real interest rates toward international levels, Mr. Arida said he believes the gap will likely become considerably smaller over the years. "In this case, the market is wrong, in my opinion."

Now founding partner of BTG Pactual, Brazil's largest independent investment bank, and chairman of its asset management arm, Mr. Arida was president of the state-run National Development Bank, or BNDES, and then during the mid-1990s he was president of the Brazilian Central Bank during implementation of the Real Plan, which ended a long period of high inflation in Latin America's biggest country.

Although down from its 2011 peak of 12.5%, Brazil's base interest rate of 8.0% is one of the highest in the world. Inflation is running at 4.9%, down from 6.5% in 2011, but still high by international standards. According to Mr. Arida, even Brazil's official 2012 inflation target of 4.5% "is higher than other countries."

High interest rates, in turn, bring distortions to the Brazilian currency market since they serve as a magnet for often unwanted short-term foreign investment inflows.

Although technically a free-floating currency, the Brazilian real really operates under a "dirty float" regime subject to frequent government intervention. Interventions are usually aimed at keeping the currency comparatively weak as a way to encourage exports.

"The ideal, once interest rates normalize, would be for Brazil to move from a dirty float to a pure float," Mr. Arida said.

More broadly, he said Brazil should not seek to be competitive through currency controls but rather by adopting much-needed structural reforms. What needs to be done, Mr. Arida said, is to advance reforms, privatization and changes in the social security system, to eliminate distortions in the credit market, to reduce the tax burden and tariffs and barriers to the international trade.

"Even though the cycle of hyperflation ended 18 years ago, the consequences can still be felt today," Mr. Arida said. "At the time the Real Plan was launched, financial markets were atrophied and interest rates were extraordinarily high. Throughout the years, there has been a process of gradual normalization of the financial market, technically called 'financial deepening.'" But that process, he said, hasn't yet been completed.

Mr. Arida praised the current central bank administration, led by Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini. He took exception to those who say Mr. Tombini is more tolerant of inflation than his immediate predecessor, Henrique Meirelles.

"I don't agree with the characterization that Brazil's central bank is more tolerant than before," said Mr. Arida. "My evaluation is that what the central bank has done was positive, looking at the results and at the starting point, which was an overheated economy in 2010."

After robust growth of 7.5% in 2010, Brazil's economy has been slowing down, growing just 2.7% in 2011 and is likely to expand less than 2% this year, according to economists. Besides lowering the base interest rate, Brazil has announced a series of tax cuts and spending programs to accelerate the weakening economy.

"The best way to stimulate the economy, in the case of Brazil where the tax burden is extraordinarily high for an emerging country, is via tax cuts and not higher spending," Mr. Arida said.

Brazil's tax burden, at the time of the Real Plan, was 24% of gross domestic product. Now, it stands at 37% of GDP. "But interest rates have fallen immensely since then," said Mr. Arida. "Therefore, there should be lots of room to reduce taxes. But taxes have been used to finance higher government spending and not public investment. Clearly, there are inefficiencies associated with the way the state functions in Brazil and this weighs on economic growth."

In a year when economists have been proven wrong in their initial forecasts for Brazilian growth, Mr. Arida said Brazil is not alone. "The whole world has disappointed in terms of growth expectations. The only exception is Europe, because everybody already expected it.

"Brazil's economy is in its worst phase, but it will recover," he said, mentioning the lagging effects of the interest cuts and the fact that the country is already adopting a more expansionist fiscal policy.

title: Brazil's Real Unchanged as Government Measures Limit Volatility
text:
--Brazil real steady ahead of Bernanke testimony

--Government interventions limit exchange volatility

--Real exits active trading at BRL2.0351 to the dollar


 
   By Brian Asher 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real was unchanged Monday as investors awaited a Tuesday congressional hearing where U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke is expected to give signals regarding the direction of U.S. monetary policy.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0351 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, equal to Friday's close.

If Mr. Bernanke gives signals Tuesday that he is preparing a fresh round of quantitative easing, the real would likely gain against the dollar, reflecting both increased optimism over the world economy and a depreciating dollar.

The gains, though, would likely be modest, as in recent weeks the Brazilian government has suggested it will closely manage the currency.

With industrial production contracting 4.3% in the 12 months to May, the Brazilian government is committed to preventing any appreciation of its currency, a move meant to boost the competitiveness of Brazilian exports.

Comments by the Brazilian finance minister and the director of monetary policy at the central bank in recent weeks hinted that the central bank would sell reais or increase taxes on capital inflows in order to prevent the currency from appreciating past BRL2.00 to the dollar.

Meanwhile, a ceiling seems to be established at BRL2.10 to the dollar, with the central bank selling dollar-swap contracts in recent weeks at times when the real was weakening sharply against the dollar.

A weaker real raises the prices of imports for Brazilian consumers.

The result of these government measures has been a stable exchange rate.

"Today, we have an unofficial floor of BRL2.00 to the dollar and a ceiling of BRL2.10 to the dollar," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer brokerage in Sao Paulo. "Internationally, we're just seeing more of the same, and the market is unmoved."

Most traders agree the real will stay in the narrow band established recently.

"The central bank made it clear it doesn't want the real stronger than BRL2.00 to the dollar," said Marcos Trabbold, chief of operations at BT Associates brokerage in Sao Paulo. "For it to strengthen past BRL2.00 to the dollar, the government would have to alter the tax regime on capital inflows."

The Brazilian government maintains a slew of taxes on capital inflows and transactions, intensified earlier this year when the real was trading at BRL1.70 to the dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  gains on China; Brazil gains limited
text:
* Mexican, Chilean peso hit 2-months highs

* Brazil's real gains, but limited by intervention worries

* Brazil's real up 0.1 pct; Mexico's peso gains 1 pct

By Rachel Uranga

MEXICO CITY, July 13 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies strengthened on Friday after China's quarterly economic data allayed concern of a steep slowdown in the world's second largest economy.

Economic growth in China, the world's biggest consumer of raw materials, was in line with expectations, spurring optimism among investors who had feared signs the country was heading toward a hard landing. Gains in the real, however, were limited by fears about further intervention from Brazil.

"The market has been looking for some news that is not completely negative, and today we had this idea that the Chinese GDP could have been worse," said Sidnei Nehme, a director at NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The sentiment buoyed the Mexican peso, on track to close at a two-month high, up 1.05 percent to 13.3050 against the greenback. The Chilean peso also hit a two-month high, firming 0.65 percent.

Chile's currency was further bolstered by a more than 2 percent jump in the price of copper, the country's main export product.

Both currencies clocked weekly gains with Mexico's peso strengthening about 1 percent and the Chilean currency firming around 1.5 percent. But investors have held back, concerned about the fragile state of the global economy.

Investors "are still waiting for further economic data," said Marco Oviedo, an economist at Barclays in Mexico City, adding that next week's performance will "depend on how investors perceive the global economy."

Eyes will be fixed on Europe and U.S. industrial production data, he said, forecasting that the peso would likely trade between 13.20 per dollar and 13.40.

In Brazil, the real edged up 0.11 percent to 2.0367 per dollar, but concern about possible government intervention weighed.

Earlier this week, Brazil cut its key interest rate to a record low in a move to kickstart its sluggish economy. At the same time, the central bank has recently been buying and selling dollars in the local spot market to control volatility in the currency.

"There's very little incentive for a hedge fund or a real money guy to bet on appreciation if there is a clear risk of intervention to cap the move," said Diego Donadio, Latin America currency and debt strategist for BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

The currency has been trading within a very narrow range between 2.00 and 2.05 reais per dollar in the past eight sessions.

Investors have been holding back bets in Brazil and placing their money in Latin America's second largest economy, Mexico, where the central bank has a hands-off approach to its currency.

text:

11 Jul 2012 14:17 EDT *DJ  Brazil Will Need To Recover Soon After 2012--Goldman's O'Neill

11 Jul 2012 14:30 EDT DJ  'B' in BRIC Questionable if Brazil Doesn't Pick Up -O'Neill

--Creator of term "BRIC" says Brazil needs to grow faster in coming years

--What Brazil has done to the real is to be welcomed, says Jim O'Neill

--Expectations were too high and it was easy for Brazil to disappoint

By Luciana Magalhaes

SAO PAULO--The "B" in "BRIC" might be called into question if Brazil's economic growth doesn't pick up in the next few years, the economist who coined the famous acronym told Dow Jones Newswires on Wednesday.

Jim O'Neill, the chairman of Goldman Sachs Asset Management, who in 2001 identified Brazil, Russia, India and China as the economic powerhouses of the future, told Dow Jones that to maintain its coveted status, Brazil ought to improve from its average growth rate of the past decade.

"What happens in 2012 in terms of GDP growth isn't so crucial," O'Neill said in a written interview. "But for the decade, Brazil will need to recover to a stronger growth rate reasonably soon after.

"If it doesn't, then the power of the 'B' in 'BRIC' would start to look a bit questionable," he added.

But despite an ongoing slowdown, Mr. O'Neill said he still expects Brazil's gross domestic product to increase by 4.5% to 5% per year on average this decade.

After a Chinese-like 7.5% growth rate in 2010, Brazil reported a timid expansion of 2.7% last year. The economy has only slowed since then, with most economists now forecasting GDP growth of around 2% in 2012 in spite of broad government efforts to spur the economy and historically low interest rates set by the central bank.

But Mr. O'Neill said expectations for Brazil's economy may have become somewhat unrealistic, making it easy for the country to disappoint.

"People seem to forget that for much of the past 10 years, Brazil only grew by around 3.5% on average," Mr. O'Neill said. "The really strong years ... may have given people a false belief."

Outsized expectations were among the factors that attracted droves of foreign investors to Brazil in recent years. It contributed to a currency appreciation that left the Brazilian real "far too strong," Mr. O'Neill said. While acknowledging that it would be dangerous to assume all of Brazil's problems were caused by a strong real, he defended the local government's currency-intervention measures.

"I think what they have done with the real is to be welcomed," Mr. O'Neill said. "The currency can still move. It is just that the authorities have made it less attractive for people to buy."

Over the last two years, Brazil's government has instituted a series of taxes on some short-term investment inflows, among other measures.

Looking ahead, O'Neill believes Brazil should tackle tough issues related to domestic competitiveness and productivity, "which require supply-side reforms and, probably, less government intervention."

Brazil registers a 5.4 out of 10 on Goldman Sachs's Growth Environment Score, a measure of 180 countries' productivity and sustainable growth. Brazil's score puts it on par with China and above both India and Russia.

"It had become the favorite of the BRIC countries," Mr. O'Neill said. "The fact that this is fading, in turn, makes it a bit easier for Brazil."

title: Brazil Real Slightly Weaker Ahead of  Central Bank  Decision
text:
--Brazil real trades in narrow band as market settles

--Central bank expected to cut base rate Wednesday

--Real exits active trading at BRL2.0374 to the dollar


 
  By Brian Asher 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real was slightly weaker in Tuesday trading, as investors awaited a rate cut expected Wednesday and digested a mixed bag of international and domestic economic data.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0374 to the dollar according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, weaker than Monday's close at BRL2.0313 to the dollar.

Volatility was low, with the real staying close to BRL2.03 to the dollar throughout the day.

Many traders now expect the real to remain in a narrow band, as the Brazilian government appears to be targeting an exchange rate between BRL2.00 and BRL2.10 to the dollar.

In recent weeks, when the real has weakened sharply against the dollar, Brazil's central bank has intervened to prevent further depreciation of the real, selling dollar-swap contracts.

In addition, both the finance minister and a central bank official made comments last week suggesting the government will prevent the currency from appreciating past BRL2.00 to the dollar.

Brazilian industry declined 4.3% in the 12 months to May, and President Dilma Rousseff's government seems determined to boost the competitiveness of Brazilian exports through a weak currency.

Market watchers expect the Brazilian central bank's monetary policy committee to announce a half-point cut to the country's Selic base rate on Wednesday.

Such a cut would bring the Selic base rate to a historic low of 8.0%, putting pressure on the real to depreciate, but the cut has been expected for some time, meaning only a surprise decision to make a deeper cut or hold rates steady would strongly affect the real.

Also pressuring the real has been the dwindling growth prospects for Brazil's economy, where economists now expect growth of only 2% this year.

Business confidence in Brazil has been hurt by the euro-zone crisis, and European leaders Tuesday extended the deadline for Spain's budget cuts, but moved no closer to a European banking union.

"The euro weakened slightly, which could have helped the real weaken against the dollar here as well," said Luiz Carlos Arenelle, a trader a Dascam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

However, to Brazil's economy, Europe is of less concern than China, Brazil's largest trading partner.

Data released in China Tuesday was ambiguous, as exports were strong but imports disappointed.

The mixed data and expectations of exchange-rate targeting combined to produce a trading session with very little volatility.

"The market was very calm," said Luiz Carlos Baldan, director of Fourtrade brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The real weakened slightly on the expectation of the Selic base rate cut, but nothing unexpected happened and nothing expected didn't happen, so we didn't see any big movements."

Tomorrow, all eyes will be on Brazil's central bank as it announces its much-anticipated monetary policy decision.

title: Brazil Real Closes Little Changed, Gains Seen in Medium Term
text:
--The real exited active trading at BRL2.0248 to the dollar compared with Wednesday's close at BRL2.0260

--Movements are due to external events

--Real expected to gain against the dollar in coming weeks if outlook in Europe improves


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
 

BRASILIA--The Brazilian real closed little changed against the dollar Thursday, after multiple ups and downs, with traders and analysts expecting it to gain against the greenback in the coming weeks as Europe takes more measures to resolve its sovereign debt and bank crises.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0248 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with Wednesday's close at BRL2.0260.

The Brazilian currency strengthened in early trading after the European Central Bank cut its benchmark interest rate. The real reversed course and weakened at midday, then regained some of its earlier advance in late trading before closing the day nearly unchanged.

The ECB's move was welcome, as it should boost Europe's sluggish economy, and the improving outlook for the region's problems should help the real strengthen in coming weeks, said Clodoir Vieira, an economist at the Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"The real should strengthen a bit against the dollar, because if Europe comes to an agreement, then other currencies should be more stable," Vieira said. "The movement we're seeing here with the real is mostly because of external factors. Positive events in Europe will cause the dollar to weaken."

The ECB cut its benchmark rate Thursday to a record low of 0.75%, from 1.0%. The bank also cut its overnight deposit and lending rates by 0.25 percentage point each, to 0% and 1.50% respectively. Cutting the deposit rate is expected to encourage banks to lend out excess funds overnight instead of depositing them at the ECB.

The real is generally trending stronger against the dollar, and only interventions and comments from the Brazilian central bank and Brazilian politicians are helping to keep the currency around the level of two or more to the dollar, said Riberto Frederico, a trader at the OM brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"I think the real should return to BRL1.95 more or less, around there, but the central bank and the government have made it clear they don't want that," Frederico said.

Brazil's central bank has intervened repeatedly in recent months, at times to weaken the real, though at other times to strengthen it. Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff and Finance Minister Guido Mantega have also acted on multiple occasions to weaken the real in order to make the country's exports more competitive.

Earlier in the day, two more of the world's most important central banks moved to ease policy, with the Bank of England increasing its asset purchase program by 50 billion pounds to GBP325 billion, and the People's Bank of China cutting its benchmark interest rates.

"We have adopted the right foreign exchange policy to keep our exports competitive," Mantega said at a news conference. "We have intervened whenever necessary and this is now producing good results. Mantega's comments came just one day after similar remarks by Brazilian Central Bank Monetary Affairs Director Aldo Mendes. On Tuesday, Mendes said Brazil's government was worried about a Brazilian real stronger than BRL2.00 to the dollar.

Following Mendes' comments Tuesday, the real weakened from about BRL1.98 to the dollar to BRL2.00 to the dollar. The real closed at about BRL2.01 to the dollar on Tuesday.

At Wednesday's news conference, Mantega said, "The foreign exchange war I warned about long ago is not over yet. Many other countries have adopted intervention in their foreign exchange markets. We cannot be the ones excluded from this."

Mantega noted that the Brazilian real has shed about 20% of its value over the past 12 months, "leaving the currency, and Brazilian products, that much more competitive." He reiterated the government's forecast for a $20 billion foreign trade surplus this year. Brazil's foreign trade surplus in the first half of the year was just a little over $7 billion.
