title: Brazil  Central Bank : Would Resume Dollar Buys Via Futures - Report
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's central bank would resume dollar buying if necessary in the futures market before considering a return to spot market purchases, Monetary Policy Director Aldo Mendes said Tuesday, according to the Estado news agency.

"The dynamics (of the exchange market) have been concentrated in the futures segment," he said. "If we had to resume intervention, it would be in futures."

Brazil's currency, the real, has strengthened against the dollar in recent sessions after weakening sharply in the first months of this year in response to global market turbulence and investor risk aversion.

Because of the weakening, the bank earlier this year suspended long-running spot market purchases aimed at curbing volatility and building the country's foreign reserves.

To prevent excess weakening in recent weeks, the bank sold swap contracts that allowed investors to exchange paper indexed to domestic interest rates for bonds linked to the U.S. dollar.

While he didn't rule out further central bank intervention on either the buying or selling end, Mr. Mendes noted that the tendency of the local currency had reversed toward strengthening with improving sentiment brought by Europe's recent decision to support banks in that region.

"There's a better perception in relation to external risk," he said. "In a general manner, the announcement following the meeting (of EU leaders) brought some relief for risk appetite."

The central bank director said the institution didn't have a specific target level for Brazil's currency, the real, and intervened only according to market liquidity needs. However, he said he believed that a real stronger than BRL2.00 to the dollar would have negative effects on local industry.

"Industry has been weak," he said. "In a certain manner, this increases the possibility that the government might want to see the dollar at a stronger level than it is today."

Brazil's IBGE institute Tuesday reported that the country's industrial production fell 0.9% in May from April. The result represented a third consecutive monthly decline.

title: DJ Brazil Real Strengthens Past BRL2 Against Dollar
text:
SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real gained Monday to the strongest level in more than a month on continued optimism following last week's European summit, and as the prospect of continued intervention by Brazil's central bank to strengthen the real offset concerns about sluggish growth at home and abroad.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.9874 to the dollar, stronger than its previous close at BRL2.0104, and the first time it closed stronger than BRL2 versus the dollar since May, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

European markets were broadly higher Monday as the optimism generated by last week's summit of European Union leaders carried over to the start of the second half of the year. The hopeful outlook helped investors to look past some weak economic data, which showed activity at euro-zone factories continue to fall sharply in June, while the currency area's unemployment rate rose to a fresh record high in May.

"Everyone was saying that Spain and Italy were next to fall, but Germany and France decided to help inject liquidity so that what happened to Greece wouldn't happen to them," said Celso Siqueira, fixed-income manager at Sao Paulo brokerage Advanced Corretora.

In Brazil, meanwhile, economists once again reduced their estimates for Brazil growth this year, according to a weekly central bank survey published Monday. Economists expect gross domestic product to expand 2.05% this year, down from 2.18% estimated in the previous survey. Inflation expectations also fell, to 4.93% from 4.95%, reaffirming the view that Brazil's central bank has room to cut rates and stimulate growth as inflation heads toward its target of 4.5%.

The central bank began cutting rates in August, when the benchmark Selic stood at 12.5%, and it is widely expected to cut the rate by half a point next week to 8%. Economists surveyed by the central bank expect the Selic to end this year at 7.5%.

Falling rates reduce the appeal of Brazil, which in the past attracted heavy inflows as investors borrowed at near-zero rates abroad to snap up higher-yielding Brazilian assets.

To counter the weakening of its currency, Brazil's central bank has been stepping up intervention in the market, holding auctions to put more dollars in the market. Last week, the bank held three swap auctions, selling the equivalent of $9 billion in contracts.

Although $3 billion of those were to replace expiring contracts, the rest was new money, serving as "a clear signal" to some analysts that the government will prevent any weakening of the real beyond the level of BRL2.10 to the dollar, which it touched last week.

"The previous time we hit BRL2.10 per dollar, the central bank carried out $16 billion in auctions, and the real climbed back to less than BRL2 per dollar," Mr. Siqueira said in a phone interview. "Last week, they carried out several auctions, injecting almost $10 billion in the swap markets, and that was reflected in the market."

text:
* Brazil real gains on expectation of more cenbank action

* US data, fading Pena Nieto optimism weigh on Mexican peso

By Natalia Cacioli and Rachel Uranga

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY, July 2 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real on Monday dropped below 2 per dollar for the first time in over a month on rising expectations of additional central bank intervention, while the peso edged up after presidential elections.

The real gained 1.13 percent to 1.9865 per dollar as investors took Brazil's strong currency interventions last week as a sign policymakers will not allow the exchange rate to depreciate much further.

"The central bank's actions last week made it clear it doesn't like the real above 2 per dollar," said Darwin Dib, chief economist at CM Capital Markets.

Brazil's central bank last week eased rules on export prepayment and sold 180,000 currency swaps worth $9 billion in three auctions. While the first measure allows more dollars to flow into the country, the swap auction boosts the supply of greenbacks in the futures market.

In Mexico, the peso edged up 0.15 percent after presidential front runner Enrique Pena Nieto claimed a narrower victory than expected in Sunday's elections. Analysts said the lower level of support meant optimism about reforms he has promised could soon vanish.

Still, Pena Nieto vowed on Monday to focus his energies on energy, labor and tax reforms and said he was willing to strike deals with opponents to get his efforts passed before taking office in December.

"There was an expectation that not only would Pena Nieto win but in his ability to pass a very aggressive reform package," said Maya Hernandez, a Latin American strategist at HSBC in New York.

The president-elect's victory margin was smaller than expected and federal election results suggested his Institutional Revolutionary Party and its allies would struggle to win a majority in congress, complicating reform efforts.

"The first take impression is that he's not going to come in with an overwhelming majority in congress necessary to pass these reforms," Hernandez said.

Earlier in the session the peso slipped after data showed the U.S. manufacturing sector unexpectedly contracted in June, weighing on prospects for the Mexican economy. The United States accounts for most of Mexico's exports.

By Luciana Magalhaes

SAO PAULO--Brazil needs ambitious reforms to lift its long-term growth potential given the upheavals in the global economy, and not just measures that will likely have a temporary impact on the economy, said Paulo Leme, who in March was named chairman of Goldman Sachs operations in Brazil.

"What we are seeing in the world isn't cyclical. It's long term, therefore, you have to think about long-term measures," Mr. Leme said in an interview in Sao Paulo.

According to the executive, Brazil can't rely on the global economy, which will probably take very long to recover from the crisis. It must therefore look to its own internal market, and that will require considerable effort.

"The key to the safe is in the basement," Mr. Leme said.

The Brazilian government has taken a series of measures to spur growth, without much success so far. The central bank on Thursday said it expects 2.5% growth this year, while private-sector economists are increasingly looking at around 2% growth.

"I think that seeking higher growth is laudable...but, in relation to the measures taken by the government, I think they have some temporary effects. The results will depend on forces coming in the other direction," the chairman said.

Higher productivity, investments in education, lower taxes and more efficient public spending are all more concrete steps that the government should take, according to Mr. Leme. But those are all extremely difficult, both practically and politically.

"I think that they (the government) are conscious of the extent of the problem and, perhaps, they also know the political challenges that being more ambitious would bring," Mr. Leme said.

The government, Mr. Leme and many other economists have all been proven wrong this year in their expectations for economic activity, both in terms of growth and inflation. But for the executive, this isn't a surprise, given the huge problems in the global economy and the confusion that it has created.

"When you have structural fractures, the models don't respond adequately...we are not in a state of equilibrium, we are in a very dynamic situation of a financial global crisis that generates huge expectations and uncertainties," he said.

It would be no surprise if the Brazilian and the global economy again take unexpected turns, for better or for worse, in the coming months.

In December 2011, Mr. Leme forecasted Brazil's gross domestic product in 2012 would expand 3.5%. Now, the executive--who's views aren't necessarily the same as Goldman's economists -- sees the economy growing at between 1.5% to 2.0%.

The executive didn't want to make any forecasts for Brazil's exchange rate, but said it's clear that the currency is far from being the only factor that makes Brazilian companies more competitive internationally.

Brazil's government fought what it called a "currency war," seeking to weaken the Brazilian real. The currency reached BRL1.53 to the dollar last July and now is traded at around BRL2.02 to the dollar--following a sharp rally Friday after some positive news in Europe. The impact of the Brazilian government measures seeking to reduce the inflow of speculative capital was intensified by the risk aversion caused by the international crisis.

Despite doubts created by the continuous government intervention, Brazil is still considered an attractive country to international investors, specially the ones seeking to invest in the country for the long term, Mr. Leme said.

"The country has a lot of room to grow... but it needs to resolve its own inefficiencies," he said.

title: Brazil's Real Strengthens on  Central Bank  Swap Announcement
text:
--Real strengthens after central bank announces swap auction for Friday

--Auction will be third this week, $6 billion in swaps already sold

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0823 to the dollar


 
   By Brian Asher 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real strengthened in late trading Thursday after the central bank announced its third intervention of the week, a $3 billion dollar-swap auction set to be held Friday morning.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0823 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, slightly stronger than Wednesday's close at BRL2.0844 to the dollar.

The real had traded as weak as BRL2.0950 to the dollar Thursday, as persistent weakening pressures have dragged the currency down.

Thursday morning, the central bank sold $3 billion worth of dollar-swap contracts, its second such auction this week.

But the auction had little effect, as many banks used it only to roll over expiring swap contracts, traders said.

European officials Thursday hinted they may not be ready to sign any accord by the end of their summit on Friday, reinforcing fears of prolonged global economic distress and strengthening the dollar against most currencies.

Also weakening the real was a series of discouraging data releases in Brazil this week, where domestic growth is now forecast at just 2.18% for the year.

But the announcement of Friday's auction immediately strengthened the real in the spot market.

"Apparently, today's announcement was far more effective than Wednesday's announcement," said Reginaldo Galhardo, forex manager at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The real has been weakened by bad news in the U.S. and Europe, but also by the new economic reality here in Brazil. We'll see if this intervention can have a lasting effect or if the real goes back to its previous course."

Other traders predicted that central bank interventions will continue as long as demand for dollars remains high.

"The real is going to continue to weaken until there is less demand for dollars," said Marcos Trabbold, chief of operations at BT Associates brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The central bank sold 100% of the swap contracts it offered today and Wednesday. With that much demand for dollars, the real keeps depreciating, so I expect the central bank to offer swap contracts until it finds it can't sell them all, and then you'll see the real stabilize."

Also unique this week has been the central bank's decision to announce auctions with one day's notice.

Previously, auctions were announced and held the same day, but most traders find that the new tactic has little effect on the market.

title: Brazil  Real Weakens Despite  Central Bank Intervention
text:
-European debt crisis weighs on emerging market currencies

-Brazil central bank to hold dollar-swap auction Wednesday

-Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0701 to the dollar

By Brian Asher

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real weakened against the dollar Tuesday, as investors bought up greenbacks on expectations of prolonged turmoil in the euro zone and weak economic growth in Brazil.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0701 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, weaker than Monday's close at BRL2.0654 to the dollar.

Tuesday's depreciation of the real came in spite of a morning announcement that the central bank would auction 60,000 dollar-swap contracts Wednesday. The swaps on offer are worth a total of $3 billion.

The move was unusual in that past interventions have seen the central bank announce auctions to be held the same day.

"The intervention was strange. I can't remember the central bank intervening like this. Normally, if it announces a swap auction for the following day, it's at the end of the afternoon," said Ovidio Soares, a trader at the Interbolsa brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Dollar-swap auctions allow investors to exchange paper linked to domestic interest rates for contracts indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auctions are a tool to smooth volatility in the exchange market at times when the Brazilian real is weakening sharply against the dollar.

Wednesday's auction will be the central bank's first dollar swap contract auction since June 11.

The real strengthened slightly in afternoon trading after the central bank's statement, but not enough to gain back morning losses.

The perception that the euro-zone crisis is nowhere near its conclusion has battered emerging market currencies this week, as investors assume the European summit on Thursday and Friday will produce little in the way of concrete results.

A report Tuesday that German Chancellor Angela Merkel had already ruled out the possibility of shared European debt reinforced the low expectations ahead of the summit.

In Brazil, too, investors found causes for concern.

Sluggish economic growth shows no signs of picking up, and economists are now predicting an expansion of just 2.18% in Brazil's gross domestic product this year.

Tuesday, the Brazilian central bank released data that showed non-performing loans had increased yet again in May, stoking fears of a bursting consumer credit bubble in Latin America's largest economy.

"The announcement of the swap auction for tomorrow calmed the market a little bit, but overall current economic conditions are going to continue to pressure the real to weaken," said Reginaldo Siaca, manager of the Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The downgrade of Spain's banks, stagnation in the U.S., and lower than expected growth in China and Brazil have made investors want to protect themselves with dollars."

Mr. Siaca added that he expects the real to stay between BRL2.05 and BRL2.10 to the dollar in the near term.

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger Despite Euro-Zone Pessimism
text:
--Brazil currency strengthens, decoupling from euro

--Investors expecting continued uncertainty in Europe

--Real trading at BRL2.0636 to the dollar at 1215 GMT

By Brian Asher

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real opened stronger Tuesday morning despite a widely held view that the European summit on Thursday and Friday will bring none of the measures needed to restore confidence in the single currency.

The real was trading at BRL2.0636 to the dollar as of 1215 GMT, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, slightly stronger than Monday's close at BRL2.0654 to the dollar.

The Brazilian currency decoupled from the weakening euro, a rare occurrence since investors have generally fled emerging market currencies at times when the European crisis has intensified.

Traders noted that exporters typically sell dollars to the market when the real edges toward the BRL2.07 mark. But the European crisis could bring the real down again later in the week.

Spain and Italy each saw sharply rising borrowing costs in debt auctions early Tuesday, bringing new doubts over the survival of the euro at a time when pessimism regarding the ability of European leaders to resolve the crisis is at an all-time high.

Adding to the gloom was the downgrade of 28 Spanish banks by Moody's Investor Services late Monday.

Most analysts and investors are predicting that this week's summit will produce no concrete results, as Germany will continue to demand greater political union in exchange for any banking or fiscal union.

"The expectation for the European summit is for nothing new," said Sidnei Nehme, director and owner of the NGO Brokerage in Sao Paulo. "Maybe it will be a step forward, but I don't see a short-term resolution to the European crisis."

U.S. economic data due to be released Tuesday afternoon may distract markets briefly, but Europe is expected to remain the focus of the financial world for the rest of the week.

The real recently has traded in a narrow band between BRL2.03 and BRL2.07 to the dollar.

Previously, the real had swung wildly at times, prompting Brazil's central bank to intervene with dollar-swap contracts to stem the depreciation of the real.

After trading as high as BRL1.70 to the dollar in February, the real has depreciated to its current level as the euro-zone crisis intensifies and worries over slowing growth in Brazil itself persist.

But Nehme said he believes a comparatively narrow range will persist. "I see the real trading between BRL2.00 and BRL2.10 to the dollar for the rest of the year," he said. "In addition to the European crisis, the perceptions of growth here are worse all the time. We're going to have low growth this year."

On Monday, the central bank's survey of economists revealed that the average forecast for 2012 economic growth had fallen for the seventh consecutive week, now down to 2.18%.

Later Monday, investors will watch closely as the central bank publishes May credit data.

A key concern in Brazil has been rising consumer loan defaults, and fresh signs of a bursting consumer credit bubble that could negatively affect markets.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  fall on euro zone uncertainty
text:
(Updates prices, adds details)

* Investors worry EU summit will fail to solve debt crisis

* Expectations of cenbank intervention support Brazil real

* Real closes flat, Mexican peso falls 0.5 pct

By Natalia Cacioli

SAO PAULO, June 25 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Monday on fear that a summit of European leaders later this week would do little to stop the euro-zone debt crisis from spreading further and weighing on world economic prospects.

The Mexican peso lost 0.5 percent while the Chilean peso slumped 1.2 percent as investors pulled money from emerging-market assets and rushed to the perceived safety of the dollar, which gained around 0.4 percent against the euro.

In a sign of investors' growing aversion to risk, yield spreads between emerging market government bonds and U.S. Treasuries widened 7 basis points to 378 basis points, according to JP Morgan's EMBI+ index. The index is on track for its largest one-day spike since the beginning of the month.

The Brazilian real was an exception, however. It traded lower during most of the session but closed practically flat as investors feared the central bank could intervene to support the currency.

"World stocks are falling and the euro is weakening sharply, but the real is not reflecting those moves because investors believe the central bank will intervene," said Italo dos Santos, a manager at the currency desk of Icap brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The Brazilian central bank hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market with the sale of currency swaps since June 11, but the mere possibility of central bank action has helped curb the real's depreciation.

The real has weakened 2.2 percent so far in June, and remains about 9.4 percent down since the beginning of the year.

RISING EURO UNCERTAINTY

Uncertainty related to the euro zone is poised to rise this week, before European leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday and Friday, in a bid to put an end to the crisis which on Monday forced Spain to request a package worth up to 100 billion euros to rescue its banks.

But hopes of faster fiscal integration in the euro zone, the solution many investors would like to see, are fading as German Chancellor Angela Merkel repeats her opposition to shared liability for the region's debts.

"Markets remain very pessimistic and uncomfortable," said Silvio Campos Neto, an economist with Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo. "Investors are speculating that nothing will be decided at the EU summit this week."

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weaker on U.S. Growth Concerns
text:
--Investors continue to search for dollars amid global uncertainty

--U.S. data disappoints, adds to fears out of euro zone, China

--Real trading at BRL2.0566 to the dollar as of 1215 GMT

By Brian Asher

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real traded weaker Friday morning as investors continued to move cautiously after disappointing data Thursday revealed weakness in the U.S. economy.

The real was trading at BRL2.0566 to the dollar at 1215 GMT, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, weaker than Thursday's close at BRL2.0530 to the dollar.

Emerging market currencies have mostly tracked news out of the euro zone recently, with investors rushing to dollars on bad news out of Europe and buying back emerging market currencies when fears recede.

But this week, the focus has been squarely on the U.S.

Disappointing data released in the U.S. Thursday caused equity markets and emerging market currencies everywhere to tumble as housing data and jobless claims suggested the U.S. economy is slowing. This data came on the heels of a U.S. Federal Reserve announcement Wednesday that it had revised down its projections for 2012 economic growth.

But despite the gloomy economic outlook, the U.S. Federal Reserve did not choose to aggressively expand its monetary stimulus programs Wednesday, leading some investors to believe the Fed is running out of ammunition in the face of a deteriorating global economic situation.

Meanwhile China, Brazil's largest trading partner and a driver of world commodity prices, continues to see slower economic growth. The HSBC China manufacturing purchasing managers' index, or PMI, released Thursday showed that in June China's manufacturing sector had contracted for an eighth consecutive month.

With no major data releases expected Friday, traders will be watching equity markets and bracing for any news out of the euro zone.

Some traders expect Brazil's central bank to intervene in the foreign exchange markets if the real weakens past BRL2.08 to the dollar.

In recent weeks, the central bank has sold currency swap contracts in order to control volatility in the foreign exchange market and stem the depreciation of the real. Dollar-swap auctions allow investors to exchange paper linked to domestic interest rates for contracts indexed to the U.S. dollar.

The real has depreciated this year from BRL1.70 to the dollar in February to its current level close to BRL2.05 to the dollar.

Contributing to the real's depreciation has been a campaign by the central bank to aggressively cut the country's Selic base interest rate, now at a historic low of 8.5%. Data released Thursday in Brazil showed inflation decelerating, reinforcing expectations of further rate cuts this year and adding pressure on the real to weaken.

   By Brian Asher 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real strengthened against the dollar Tuesday as tensions in Europe's periphery economies eased slightly and investors expected U.S. officials to announce another round of monetary stimulus on Wednesday.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0300 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, stronger than Monday's close at BRL2.0608 to the dollar.

Brazil belatedly joined an emerging-market currency rally that began Monday after Greek voters elected a pro-euro government in parliamentary elections Sunday.

In other news out of Europe, Spain's bond auction was slightly less painful than expected, with yields on 12-month government bonds weighing in at 5.07%.

Midday rumors of a move by the European Central Bank to buy bonds from Europe's periphery economies proved to be unsubstantiated, and the woes in Europe's less competitive economies are certainly not over. European leaders at the Group of 20 summit in Mexico did, however, express support for a European banking union with the power to regulate banks and secure deposits.

Also boosting the real was the expectation that the U.S. Federal Reserve will unveil further monetary stimulus measures Wednesday to bolster a sluggish economic recovery in the U.S.

U.S. May housing data released Tuesday were mixed, with new housing starts falling short of expectations while new housing licenses reached their highest level since 2008.

Tuesday's gains bucked a recent weakening trend for the real, as investors have fled to dollars amid uncertainty over the European sovereign debt crisis.

Before recent losses, Brazilian exporters had struggled with an overvalued currency, with the real this year trading as high as BRL1.7 to the greenback in February before falling to its current band between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 to the dollar.

After complaining of an overvalued currency earlier this year, Brazilian policymakers now seem uncomfortable with the real's rapid depreciation.

Brazil's central bank has intervened in recent weeks, selling swaps to inject dollars into the market and stem the weakening of the real. But the central bank has not entered the foreign-exchange market since last week, and some analysts now say the central bank's main goal is not to peg the currency to the dollar but to prevent exchange-rate volatility.

"With regards to the currency, the central bank has in general shown that it doesn't have a target for the currency," Arminio Fraga, a former president of the central bank, said at an event. title: Brazil's Finance Minister: Growth Model Is Far From Exhausted
text:
--Brazil's growth model is far from exhausted, says finance minister in an interview

--Consumers, credit can continue to drive growth for years, says Guido Mantega

--Government not planning more measures to help economy, unless euro crisis worsens

By Luciana Magalhaes

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega made a stern defense of the government's growth model, saying that the domestic market and credit can continue to grow for many years to come.

"I think it is a mistake to say that the model has been exhausted," Mr. Mantega said in an wide-ranging interview, in which he indicated that the government isn't planning more steps to boost growth, and will only intervene in currency markets to tame volatility.

Brazil, the minister said, "is one of the few countries where the consumer market manages to grow."

There are still millions of Brazilians that can be lifted into the middle class and billions of dollars in investments to be made in areas such as infrastructure and logistics, Mr. Mantega said.

Consumers have become more cautious due to the global crisis, "although they do react to stimulus such as for example a reduction in prices and taxes," Mr. Mantega said. Much of the consumer debt is very short term and is paid off quickly, and Brazilians will be able to take on more debt as interest rates come down, he said.

"Credit is growing in Brazil, which shows that the theories about a depletion of credit don't hold up," he said.

There's growing criticism of the government's emphasis on domestic demand, and credit in particular, to drive the economy out of the current slump, largely a result of declining investment and industrial output--as well as the sharp drag from the global crisis. Some economists have suggested consumers are running out of steam, and that investment is in decline because the government has done little to tackle obstacles to growth in other parts of the economy.

Short-term relief has been plentiful. Tax breaks and other incentives--including new credit lines for state governments unveiled Friday--have been used to counteract the global problems, and the minister said more would only come if there is a real turn for the worse in Europe or elsewhere.

"We cannot ignore the gravity of the international crisis. The crisis has intensified," the minister said. "It hasn't improved and of course that ends up having an impact on the whole world and some effects here in Brazil."

But for now, the government seems ready to allow all the incentives to take effect.

"There's no shortage of measures which have already been taken," Mr. Mantega said. "I believe that there are now sufficient measures to provide a stimulus for the Brazilian economy."

The minister indicated he doesn't envisage any more changes to the currency controls, and said the depreciation of the real in recent months was welcome, as it helps Brazilian companies, both in terms of competing overseas or at home. The Brazilian real is trading at BRL2.04 per dollar on Friday, compared with BRL1.70 at the end of February.

"An exchange rate at today's levels is much more comfortable than it was a year ago," Mr. Mantega said. The currency continues to operate under a floating exchange rate, "so there's no ideal point," Mr. Mantega said.

"We don't have any new actions with regards to the currency. We are only moderating fluctuations," he said.

Mr. Mantega said that growth will pick up in the second half of the year, in response to the steps taken already, as well as the central bank's hefty interest rate cuts. The overnight rate has fallen to a record low 8.5%, and is widely expected to be cut again in early July.

Many economists now foresee growth below 3% this year, which would be in line with last year's disappointing 2.7%.

"We think it's viable for us to have growth this year which is greater than last year," Mr. Mantega said. The minister has previously said he expects growth to be greater than 3%. "If you take the months of May and June, you already detect a recovery in various segments," he said.

On Thursday, the government eased some restrictions on overseas borrowing by Brazilian companies, which Mr. Mantega said had been imposed to prevent excessive borrowing rather than to interfere with the exchange rate. The government has introduced a series of other measures over the last year designed to halt or reverse the strong appreciation of the Brazilian real, which it argued was harming Brazilian companies.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Stronger vs. Dollar After Volatile Session

title: Brazil  Real Closes Sharply Weaker Despite  Central Bank Intervention
text:
--Brazil's real weakens despite central-bank auction of dollar swaps

--Trade deficit, downward pressure on real offset Spain bank bailout

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0468 to the dollar


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

Brazil's real currency closed sharply weaker against the U.S. dollar Monday, despite a Brazilian central bank dollar-swap auction and early-session euphoria over a deal to bail out Spain's troubled banking sector.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0468 to the dollar, well off Friday's closing quote of BRL2.0248, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. The currency, however, failed to break the BRL2.05 barrier that the market believes is the Brazilian central bank's de facto ceiling for the real, with the currency hitting a session weakest at BRL2.0495 to the dollar.

"The market opened with the real a bit stronger, but from there we saw strong pressure for the weakening of the real," said Pedro Zotovici, a trader at Sao Paulo's Multi Money brokerage.

The currency had opened the session stronger, as investors cheered the weekend deal to recapitalize Spain's banking sector, which has been weighed down by bad loans doled out during the country's real-estate boom. The European Union will loan Spain up to $125 billion, with the final tally set to be disclosed by independent auditors later this month.

Despite the deal to rescue Spain's banks, investors still question whether the move will be enough to resolve the sector's troubles. In addition, the market is still nervous ahead of Sunday's elections in Greece. While the chances of a sudden Greek pullout from the euro zone have diminished, Greeks have reacted negatively to harsh austerity measures imposed as part of the country's rescue package and could opt to vote in politicians less willing to support the fiscal cuts.

The real weakened past the BRL2.03 mark in a swift reversal during mid-morning trade, luring the central bank from the sidelines with a dollar-swap auction. But the auction was far from a success, with the central bank selling $400 million worth of the $1 billion dollar-swap contracts it was prepared to sell. The real initially gained some ground against the dollar before falling back once again and weakening past the BRL2.04 mark.

The market did not like the terms set by the Brazilian central bank in the auction, Mr. Zotovici said. "The bank is going to need to lower the price of the dollar in its swaps if it wants to continue intervening," he said.

Dollar-swap auctions allow investors to exchange paper linked to domestic interest rates for contracts indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auctions are a tool to smooth volatility in the exchange market at times when the Brazilian real is weakening sharply against the dollar. Last week, the central bank sold a total of $2.02 billion in dollar swaps in two separate auctions.

The real also was undermined by Brazil's surprise trade deficit to kick off June, with the country registering a deficit of $325 million in the first 10 days of the month. The latest data made traders "nervous" and set off a search for dollars, Mr. Zotovici said.

But some traders said there weren't any fundamental reasons for the real to weaken so sharply.

"You're not seeing the stock market falling drastically. No one is desperately seeking dollars," said Olvidio Soares, a trader at Interbolsa. "What we see in the market right now is pure speculation that is causing this pronounced volatility."

Mr. Soares called the real's downturn "unjustified" and said the low volume of dollar swaps offered by the Brazilian central bank showed "there is no real rush for dollars."

-Brian Asher in Rio de Janeiro contributed to this article.

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger After Spain Requests Bank Bailout
text:
--Brazil's real opens stronger as Spanish bank bailout eases tensions in global markets

--Currency players expected to remain cautious ahead of Greek elections Sunday

--Brazilian real opens trading at BRL2.0197, stronger from Friday's close at BRL2.0248


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

The Brazilian real traded stronger at the open Monday as a European Union deal to bail out Spain's troubled banking sector boosted morale, although gains may be short-lived ahead of next weekend's elections in debt-saddled Greece.

Brazil's real joined other global currencies, especially the euro, in gaining ground against the U.S. dollar as the deal with Spain boosted investor sentiment. The Brazilian real opened at BRL2.0197 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Friday's close at BRL2.0248.

Global markets cheered the weekend deal to recapitalize Spain's banking sector, which has been weighed down by bad loans doled out during the country's real-estate boom. The European Union will loan Spain up to $125 billion, with the final tally set to be disclosed by independent auditors later this month. The deal eliminates, for the moment, a key pressure point in the ongoing European financial crisis.

The recapitalization plan should help reduce "market anxiety about how [Spain] will return to building its path out of the crisis," said Miriam Tavares, foreign-exchange director at Sao Paulo-based trading house AGK Corretora.

Looming on the horizon, however, are elections in Greece. While the chances of a sudden Greek pullout of the euro zone have diminished, the Greek people have reacted negatively to harsh austerity measures imposed as part of the country's rescue package and could opt to vote in politicians less willing to support the fiscal cuts.

Market watchers also reacted positively to economic indicators released over the weekend in China, a key market for Brazilian exporters. The country's trade surplus advanced and inflation decelerated in May, while industrial production topped April numbers despite coming in lower than expected. The figures showed that while China's economy should pick up in coming months, officials still have room to adopt additional stimulus measures after the country's central bank last week made its first interest-rate cut in three years.

In Brazil, the market is watching carefully for further central bank intervention after two dollar-swap auctions last week. The bank sold about $2.02 billion in dollar swaps last week at two separate auctions after the real weakened to near the BRL2.05 mark.

Dollar-swap auctions allow investors to exchange paper linked to domestic interest rates for contracts indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auctions are a tool to smooth volatility in the exchange market at times when the Brazilian real is weakening sharply against the dollar.

"The central bank moves suggest that levels above BRL2.05 will draw intervention with swaps, signaling that the [foreign-exchange rate] between BRL2.0 and BRL2.05 is likeliest at this time," Ms. Tavares of AGK Corretora said in her morning note to clients.

Economists and market analysts also continue to cut their outlook for growth in Latin America's largest economy, according to the latest weekly market survey released by the central bank Monday. The survey estimate for Brazil's 2012 gross-domestic-product growth is now 2.53%, down from 2.72% last week. That was the fifth-consecutive reduction to the forecast. The outlook for 2013 also was cut, to 4.30% from 4.50%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso up on cenbank statement; real trims loss
text:
(Adds Brazil intervention in FX market, Mexico peso gaining after cenbank statement)

* Mexico peso gains as cenbank dashes rate cut speculation

* Brazil cenbank says global downturn sapping inflation

* Chile's peso falls with copper prices, muted inflation

* Brazil real 0.1 pct lower, Mexico peso up 0.7 pct

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, June 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso strengthened on Friday as policymakers dashed speculation of imminent rate cuts in the country, while the Brazilian real trimmed early losses after the central bankintervened in the foreign exchange market.

Other Latin American currencies remained weaker, however, as investors worried about the global economic impact of an escalating European debt crisis.

The Mexican peso traded lower early in the session but bounced after the central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged at 4.5 percent. The bank made clear its next move could go either way, dropping a flirtation with a rate cut that had weighed on the currency.

The bank also acknowledged a "moderate" risk to inflation from a weaker peso, which has lost about 10 percent since mid March.

The Mexican peso was 0.7 percent stronger in the afternoon, at 13.9699 per dollar.

The Brazilian real also opened lower but trimmed losses after the central bankintervened in the foreign exchange market with a sale of currency swaps, which essentially increase the supply of dollars in the market.

That was the second time the central bank offered to sell currency swaps this week. The auction was announced when the real traded slightly above 2.04 per dollar, reinforcing a market perception that, at least for now, policymakers are drawing an informal line around 2.05 per greenback.

"When the real reaches a certain level, of 2.05 per dollar, we know the central bank will intervene," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist with BES Investimento in Sao Paulo.

The real was 0.13 percent weaker in the afternoon, at 2.0292 per greenback.

Other Latin American currencies weakened, however, as investors cautiously watched political and economic developments in the euro zone.

Spain is expected to request European aid for its struggling banks over the weekend, becoming the fourth and biggest European country to seek assistance since the euro zone's debt crisis began.

Chile's peso lost 0.12 percent as prices of copper , the country's main export product, fell to a six-month low in London.

"Markets are all in the red, with stocks falling, copper prices tumbling and the dollar strengthening against the euro - all those factors are negative for the peso," said a trader in Santiago.

Chile's lower-than-expected inflation reading for May also contributed to a weaker peso as it eliminated any speculation of an immediate rate hike by the central bank.

Chile's consumer price index was unchanged in May from the previous month, the government statistics agency INE said. Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast a median 0.2 percent increase for the index.

MORE RATE CUTS IN BRAZIL

Brazil's interest-rate futures slid on Friday after the central bank suggested it is poised to keep cutting the country's base interest rate.

Interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2013 <0#2DIJ:> dropped 7 basis points to 7.820 percent after policymakers said in minutes of their latest monetary policy meeting that a global economic downturn is helping to bring inflation back to target.

The bank's committee, known as the Copom, repeated its guidance that more rate cuts should be conducted "sparingly." Policymakers unanimously cut the benchmark Selic rate for a seventh consecutive time to a record low of 8.5 percent on May 30.

"This leaves the door open for additional rate cuts," said Alberto Ramos, a senior economist with Goldman Sachs, adding that the next cuts should be "moderate," or smaller than 75 basis points, and "somewhat data dependent."

Goldman Sachs expects Brazil will cut the Selic again to 8.0 percent in July.

"An extension of the easing cycle beyond the July meeting is certainly possible particularly if the external backdrop continues to deteriorate and the domestic real business cycle dynamics remain sluggish," Ramos said.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger On  Central Bank Intervention
text:
--Brazil's real strengthens after central bank sells $1.01 billion in dollar swaps

--European crisis, slowing global economy still key factor in trading

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0248 to the dollar


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

Brazil's real currency shrugged off a gloomy global scenario and low post-holiday volume Friday to end stronger against the U.S. dollar, gaining ground on the greenback after the country's central bank surprised the market with a dollar-swap auction.

Investors returned from the mid-week Corpus Christi holiday that closed Brazilian financial markets Thursday in a sour mood, with the real trending weaker at the start of trading amid concerns about Europe's ongoing debt crisis and a slowing global economy. "The market today suffered from a lack of liquidity throughout the session," said Luiz Carlos Baldan, a director at Sao Paulo trading house Fourtrade. "With the external situation still difficult and no resolution in the European crisis, we expected the [stock market] to fall and the dollar to strengthen."

The market's mood was defensive on growing expectations for disappointing news about the global scenario, traders said. China's decision to lower interest rates Thursday raised alarm bells that the rate cut was a pre-emptive move ahead of disappointing economic indicators. Wholesale and consumer price inflation figures are among a slew of data expected to be released in China over the weekend.

Worries about Spain's banks also dragged down the euro after Fitch Ratings downgraded Spain's sovereign debt three notches to just above junk territory. Press reports raised the prospect that Spain could be ready to ask for international aid to prop up its struggling banking sector, perhaps as early as this weekend.

The dour outlook pushed the real to a session-weakest BRL2.0411 to the dollar in late morning trade, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That drew the attention of the Brazilian Central Bank, which jumped into the market with a surprise dollar-swap auction--the second such move this week.

The central bank sold $1.01 billion in dollar-swap contracts, two-thirds of the $1.5 billion the bank was prepared to sell as it moved to inject some dollar liquidity. The bank sold 20,400 contracts at two maturities, July 2 and Aug. 1. Dollar-swap auctions allow investors to exchange paper linked to domestic interest rates for contracts indexed to the U.S. dollar. The auctions are a tool to smooth volatility in the exchange market at times when the Brazilian real is weakening sharply against the dollar.

The real immediately strengthened after the swap sale was announced, bouncing off session lows. The momentum held through the rest of the session, with the real exiting active trading at BRL2.0248 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Wednesday's close at BRL2.0298.

The central bank's latest moves have been designed to keep the foreign-exchange market on its toes, said Reginaldo Galhardo, foreign-exchange manager at Treviso.

"The central bank has intervened at varying levels in the market for dollars," Mr. Galhardo said, noting recent dollar-swap auctions held at BRL2.08, BRL2.05 and BRL2.03. "The central bank doesn't want the market to know at what level it will intervene."

The real has stabilized at slightly above the BRL2-to-the-dollar mark in recent weeks because that's what the market believes the government is targeting, Mr. Galhardo said. "The government wants the market to find an equilibrium that is good for everyone, not just one sector or the other," he added.

title: Brazil Real Slightly Stronger on Euro, Commodities
text:
--Real opens at BRL2.0145/dlr Vs BRL2.0195/dlr Tuesday

--Stronger euro, higher commodities prices support real

--Central bank seen "vigilant" against any volatility

SAO PAULO --The Brazilian real strengthened slightly against the U.S. dollar in early trading Wednesday, as the euro gained against the greenback and global commodities prices advanced.

The real was trading at BRL2.0145 to the dollar early in the session, stronger against the Tuesday close of BRL2.0195, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The euro strengthened against the dollar Wednesday after the European Central Bank held its base interest rate steady at 1.0%. Lower yields for Spanish and Italian debt also helped buoy the euro.

A stronger euro typically supports the real. Higher global prices for commodities also helped support the Brazilian currency against the dollar. Higher commodities prices bring more export revenue to Brazil.

Traders said market volume was thin Wednesday, ahead of a religious holiday Thursday that will keep Brazilian markets shuttered. Traders noted that many Brazilian businesses will remain closed Friday, with market volume likely to remain slim.

Analysts said the real's strength could prove temporary, however.

Brazilian inflation figures, released earlier Wednesday, showed an unexpected decline in the 12-month inflation rate to 4.99% as of May from 5.10% as of April. The decline in inflation should encourage the Brazilian central bank to speed up the tempo of interest rate cuts.

Brazil's Selic base interest rate is currently 8.5%. At its May meeting, the central bank cut the rate by a half percentage point. More rate cuts are likely in the coming months. With inflation in decline, the central bank could cut the base rate to 7.5% or even lower, according to some economists.

But lower interest rates will tend to make Brazil a less attractive venue for foreign investors, leading to a long-term weakening of the Brazilian real against the dollar.

Traders, however, noted that Brazil's central bank has also been vigilant against any abrupt alteration in foreign exchange values.

"The central bank has shown in recent days that even the slightest intervention can reverse the trend in trading," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage.

The central bank in recent weeks has limited its interventions to sale of foreign exchange swap contracts, rather than direct sale or purchase of dollars. Swap contracts allow investors to exchange paper indexed to interest rates for contracts linked to the U.S. dollar. The swaps offer investors a way to bolster their U.S. dollar hedging positions and typically strengthen the real against the greenback.

Muniz added, "The central bank seems comfortable with the real trading close to BRL2.00 to the dollar. Unless there is an abrupt departure from that baseline, central bank intervention is unlikely."

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, June 5 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real jumped more than 1 percent on Tuesday as the central bank resumed its market interventions after a week hiatus, but the Mexican peso weakened after an emergency G7 conference call failed to allay euro zone concerns.

Brazil's central bank offered to sell currency swap contracts early in the session when the real was practically unchanged from Monday's close of 2.0513 per dollar, reinforcing a market perception that policymakers were drawing a line around that level.

"The intervention is reinforcing that ceiling," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, Latin American currency strategist with RBS Securities. "The last time they intervened was on May 25, when the real was trading around 2.03."

Brazilian government sources have told Reuters, however, that the central bank would not draw any hard lines in the currency market that it cannot defend in the event of a strong market shock.

The real jumped more than 1 percent right after the swap auction announcement. It added to gains later to trade around 2.0295 per dollar as data showed the U.S. services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in May.

The U.S. data came in above economists' expectations, offering a gleam of hope to markets that have been battered in the past few days by a series of disappointing economic data in the United States, China and Brazil.

Data showing Chile's economy was slowing down in line with market expectations also supported the Chilean peso, which rose about half a percentage point to 512.40 per dollar.

"What is driving the peso is the domestic growth data," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile. "It shows the economy is solid, slowly decelerating as the rest of the world, but still attractive to foreign investors."

On the other hand, the Mexican peso lost 0.3 percent to 14.250 per U.S. dollar on concerns about an escalating European debt crisis.

Finance ministers of the Group of Seven industrialized countries held a conference call on Tuesday to discuss the euro zone but issued no statement after the talks, disappointing investors who expected a plan to deal with the crisis.

 * Brazil real dips 0.22 pct, Mexico peso firms 0.8 pct 

 By Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, June 4 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso firmed on Monday, helped by a poll showing the pro-market frontrunner in the presidential race still had a healthy lead, while Brazil's real slipped back to a level that could trigger intervention from the country's central bank.

 The peso received some support from a poll that showed Mexican opposition candidate Enrique Pena Nieto is still the frontrunner ahead of the July 1 presidential election, with a lead of nearly 14 percentage points. 

 The poll eased some investor nerves after a poll last week had shown leftist Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador had narrowed the gap to only four percentage points, stoking concerns that the race could be much closer than investors had been expecting.

 "Investors had become concerned that (Lopez Obrador) could rise from the ashes to take the election," said Clyde Wardle, a currency strategist at HSBC in New York. "The more recent polls have taken away a little of those concerns that the market had."

 Fund managers have been betting that a victory by Pena Nieto, from the opposition Institutional Revolutionary Party that ruled Mexico for most of the previous century, could unlock 15 years of stalled reforms and jump-start growth.

 The Mexico peso  firmed 0.8 percent to 14.2080 per U.S. dollar.

 The peso may also have gotten some support from rising expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve could deliver more stimulus to support the economy of the United States, which buys nearly 80 percent of Mexican exports. 

 U.S. data on Monday showed orders for manufactured goods dropped 0.6 percent in April, its third decline in four months. That report followed Friday's jobs report that was much weaker than expected. 

 "There is some optimism because the bad data seen in the United States could be the incentive for additional stimulus from the Fed," said Mario Copca, an analyst at the CI brokerage.

 Latin American currencies were also backed by gains in the euro on hopes Europe will use the euro zone's permanent bailout fund to rescue stricken banks. 

 Riskier assets, such as Latin American currencies, often track the euro. Chile's peso firmed 0.6 percent to 515.20 per dollar. 

 Fears that Europe's debt troubles could trigger another global financial crisis have driven Mexico's peso and Brazil real to three-year lows. Slumping growth in Brazil has also hurt the currency there.

 The Brazilian real , however, gave up early gains to bid down 0.22 percent at 2.0513 per dollar.

 Analysts have said the level of 2.05 reais per dollar became an informal floor for the currency after Brazil's central bank stepped up its market intervention when the real weakened past that level.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso hit by vote jitters, Brazil yields fall
text:
* Rise in support for leftist candidate hits Mexican peso

* No outflows seen yet, but foreign positions eyed

* Brazil yields fall on bets of further interest rate cuts

* Brazil real dips 0.1 pct, Mexico peso slumps 1.42 pct

(Rewrites throughout)

By Michael O'Boyle and Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, May 31 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso slumped to a three-year low on Thursday after a poll showed a surprising surge in support for the leftist presidential candidate, while yields in Brazil fell on bets of more interest rate cuts.

Mexican bond prices also dropped, pushing up yields, after a newspaper poll showed Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador has cut the gap on the front-runner Enrique Pena Nieto to just four percentage points.

Mexico's peso has been battered this month by fears that Europe's debt troubles are deepening. But investors had been confident of a clear victory by Pena Nieto, from the centrist party that ruled Mexico for most of the 20th century.

"If other polls confirm that the gap between Lopez Obrador and Pena Nieto has closed significantly, we should expect more pressure on the exchange rate," said Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura in New York, who was skeptical of the poll results.

"I don't think it is a correct assessment. I think it is strange that only one poll is saying this," he said.

The peso currency shed as much as 1.5 percent to 14.3850 per dollar, its weakest level since April 2009, before pulling back to 14.37, a 1.42 percent drop.

Mexico's central bank on Wednesday sold $107 million of $400 million on offer in only its second dollar auction since late 2009. The first auction was triggered last week.

The Mexican peso was set to clock its worst month since last September with a more than 9 percent tumble.

The sharp losses are putting pressure on the central bank's commitment to a free-floating peso. Mexico, perhaps the most orthodox of emerging economies, has held back from ad hoc market interventions seen in Brazil, India and Indonesia.

Investors in Mexican bonds have been betting that a victory by Pena Nieto could help push through stalled economic reforms and jump-start growth.

Fund managers said the poll raised concerns but added that no big foreign investors had dumped Mexican bonds yet. Traders attributed losses to local trading desks that were worried by the chance of outflows by foreigners.

Foreign investors have quadrupled holdings of Mexican peso debt since 2008 to around $85 billion.

The yield on the government's 10-year peso bond bid up 6 basis points to 6.14 percent. The weakness may be a buying opportunity if concerns of a Lopez Obrador victory prove unfounded.

PIMCO's Bill Gross, manager of the world's largest bond fund, said in a letter that markets might be signaling a "potential breaking point" in the world economy and that investors should buy bonds in the United States, Mexico, and Brazil.

SAMURAI BOND

Contrasting with the jitters hitting the Mexican peso and bond market, during Asian trading Mexico cracked the conservative Japanese market to sell the first unsecured Latin American debt issued in yen in more than a decade.

Mexico issued $80 billion yen ($1 billion) after painstakingly courting Japanese investors since last year.

"The Mexican samurai bonds drew a lot of demand because they were yen-denominated bonds," said Genzo Kimura, bond fund manager at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. "Japanese investors don't want to take risks when the situation in Europe looks very vulnerable."

Brazil's real was little changed at 2.0164 per dollar, while Chile's peso firmed 0.19 percent to 516.40 per dollar. Both currencies shed around 6 percent during the month on concerns about the global impact of Europe's mounting credit problems.

Brazil's real slumped to a three-year low last week. Heavy intervention curbed losses, and traders are eyeing the potential for more aggressive action from the central bank if the real weakens past 2.05 per dollar.

Yields on Brazil's interest-rate futures fell sharply after the central bank cut its base Selic interest rate by half a percentage point to an all-time low of 8.5 percent late on Wednesday. 7

The decision to cut rates was unanimous, and policymakers said they still believe inflation risks remain limited, leading investors to believe another cut of half a percentage point is in the works.

The yield on interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2013 bid down 4 basis points from its adjusted close on Wednesday to 7.93 percent.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Weaker On European Debt Concerns
text:
--Brazil's real ended active trading Wednesday at BRL2.014

--Weakening of real, ahead of central bank's decision, reflected European concerns

--Brazil's central bank didn't intervene in the currency market on Wednesday

By Luciana Magalhaes

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real ended weaker Tuesday as concerns about the euro-zone debt crisis once again came to the forefront. The currency was volatile, trading around the BRL2.00 level for most of the session.

The real exited from active trading at BRL2.014 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

"A month ago, we were mainly worried about Greece. Now, we observe worsening conditions in Greece and in Spain," said Alfredo Barbutti, economist at Brazilian brokerage Liquidez.

Spain's government Wednesday denied media reports that it had submitted a plan to the European Central Bank to recapitalize local lender Bankia SA through the central bank's lending facilities.

Earlier this week, the Spanish government said one option to recapitalize Bankia was to issue debt securities to the bank, which it would then use as collateral to raise cash from ECB lending facilities. Government officials have said this was just one of many possibilities. ECB officials have signaled they would oppose any attempt to fund the recapitalization via the central bank's lending facilities.

On Wednesday, Brazil's central bank, which was active in the market last week, didn't hold a dollar swap auction. Barbutti said the authority probably didn't intervene because the real's weaking wasn't an isolated move, as other major emerging market currencies also fell against the dollar.

Later on Wednesday, Brazil's central bank will announce a decision on interest rates. The market expects Brazil's benchmark interest rate will be cut from 9% to 8.5%, the lowest level on record in Brazil.

"Even though most people are expecting a 50 basis point cut, I wouldn't be surprised if the central bank decided to reduce the Selic by 25 basis points," said Mario Battistel, forex manager at Fair Brokerage. He said that given the uncertainties in overseas markets and the weakening of the real, Brazil's central bank could decide for smaller cut.

Not all share Battistel's view. In a note to the market, a trader said on Wednesday that "with this risk background and this important move in rates globally, I think the chances of, now, an out-of-consensus cut of 75 basis points grows by the second."

A larger rate cut could affect the forex market more directly, as it's likely to put off those investors that had been happy to park money and reap Brazil's juicy yields. A 0.75-percentage-point cut could lead some of them to exit positions, which could see the real weaken on Thursday.

"At this point, cuts in the Selic rate especially if beyond market expectations, will have a bigger impact on [foreign exchange]," RBS said in a note.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real dips as market tests  central bank
text:
* Brazil's central bank eschews intervention for second day

* Mexico peso boosted by bond flows, further gains seen limited

* Brazilian real slips 0.16 pct, Mexican peso up 0.52 pct

(Rewrites throughout, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle and Danielle Fonseca

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, May 29 (Reuters) - The Brazilian currency fell on Tuesday as the market tested the central bank's resolve to defend the real, while gains in other Latin American markets looked vulnerable to worries about Europe's debt troubles.

Brazil's real eased to briefly touch 2 per dollar, losing ground for the first session in five after aggressive central bank intervention last week drove the currency back from a three-year low.

Global investors are eyeing the risk that Greece could leave the euro zone following elections next month, while rising borrowing costs in Spain are adding to global jitters.

Analysts said Latin American currencies remained stuck in a downtrend and that Tuesday's gains in the Mexican peso likely would not last in the short term.

"There is still a lot of uncertainty," said Mauro Roca, a strategist at Deutsche Bank in New York. "If volatility does not reduce, it is going to be difficult to see the currencies trending stronger against the dollar."

Fears that Europe's debt troubles could detonate another global financial crisis hammered Latin American currencies during the last two months.

CENTRAL BANK TESTED

The real bid 0.16 percent weaker to 1.9859 per U.S. dollar at the close. T he currency shed as much as 1 percent earlier in the session as investors wondered whether the central bank would resume intervention, but policymakers stayed out of the market for a second straight session.

"The central bank is not going to act at any cost. The weakness today was not enough to drive the central bank into the market and the volume was not sufficient," said the head of a bank's trading desk in Brazil, who requested anonymity.

Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a Latin America forex strategist with RBS Securities said the market thinks the central bank could step up intervention efforts again at the 2.05 level.

Brazil's central bank started auctioning swaps to support the currency on May 18, when the real traded slightly above the 2 per dollar level. Po licymakers stepped up their defense as the real headed to 2.10 per greenback, sending the currency back to the level of 2 per dollar on Friday.

PESO BONDS

Hopes the Chinese government may unveil new stimulus measures that would benefit Latin American exporters provided some support to the region's currencies on Tuesday,

The Mexican peso firmed 0.52 percent to 13.8775 per dollar, b oosted by inflows into the country's bond market, traders said.

The yield on the country's benchmark 10-year peso bond

bid down 5 basis points to 6.08 percent as its price rose.

Foreign investors have more than quadrupled holdings of Mexican bonds during the last three years as debt troubles in more developed economies put the shine on Mexico's healthier public finances.

Foreign buyers, who held 1.185 trillion pesos ($85 billion) in local currency debt as of the latest central bank data on May 18, have taken advantage of the peso's recent weakness to add to their positions, traders and analysts said.

Deutsche Bank's Roca said the Mexican peso could outperform the region's currencies if Europe succeeds in calming fears about a break up of the euro zone.

"Mexico is closer to the United States, and the recovery in the United States should be an important driver for Latin America, barring any bad new from Europe," he said.

Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States.

On Monday, Mexican central bank governor Agustin Carstens said the peso will likely rebound once European debt fears dissipate.

Analysts noted Mexican bond yields were unlikely to drive much lower in the coming weeks since they are already trading near record lows and yields could be sent higher by more global risk aversion.

Chile's peso was also little changed at 512.30 per dollar after closing at a 4-1/2-month low of 512.70 in the previous session.

title: Reuters Summit-Former Brazil cenbankers urge economic reforms
text:
(For other news from Reuters Latin America Investment Summit, click on http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment12("http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment12"))

* Former cenbank chiefs Meirelles, Franco speak at summit

* See need for productivity gains, lower interest rates

* Both say Brazil is still a "buy," despite slowdown

By Asher Levine

SAO PAULO, May 28 (Reuters) - The outlook for Brazil's economy is still bright despite a recent slowdown, though structural reforms are needed if the country is to attain higher growth rates, according to two of the country's former central bankers.

Speaking on a panel to kick off the Reuters Latin America Investment Summit in Sao Paulo, Henrique Meirelles and Gustavo Franco argued that Brazil's consumption-driven growth model, supported over the past decade by newfound macroeconomic stability, high commodities prices and a large pool of available labor, is facing new challenges.

Both agreed that in order for Latin America's largest economy to expand more quickly, Brazil's government will have to address older challenges such as fiscal reform to keep a lid on public spending while also directing more funds to investment. That would help lower interest rates, boost investment rates, and eventually lead to higher productivity and healthier growth.

"Four percent (economic) growth is achievable," said Meirelles, who served as Brazil's central bank president under former President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and is currently chairman of J&F Participações, the holding company that controls Brazilian meatpacker JBS.

"Now the name of the challenge is productivity. We are talking about infrastructure, the tax structure, education and training," he added.

Meirelles, the longest-serving central bank president in Brazilian history, helped steer Brazil through its biggest economic boom in almost three decades. In 2010, the last year of his term, Brazil's economy grew 7.5 percent, as millions of Brazilians moved out of poverty and into the middle class.

That rapid growth slowed, however, to a mediocre 2.7 percent in 2011, and many analysts estimate Brazil's economy will barely surpass that figure in 2012.

In some ways, Brazil may be a victim of its own success, as record low unemployment, combined with historically scarce levels of long-term credit, make it difficult for businesses to hire workers or carry out expansion plans, said Franco, who briefly led Brazil's central bank under Lula's predecessor, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

"There is a feeling that perhaps the model of growth is not exhausted, but tired, at least in the sense of a growth model based on low investment rates and leveraged consumption," said Franco, who currently serves as president and chief strategist of Rio Bravo Investimentos, an asset management firm.

Franco pointed to Brazil's notoriously high interest rates as a key factor limiting higher investment rates and preventing the current growth model from progressing much further.

"Interest rates are the central problem," he said.

"Its a question of creating the fundamental conditions for interest rates to be normal. Perhaps this would be the one silver bullet that could put us into 'Asian-type' investment rates," Franco said, adding that fiscal reform and a larger primary budget surplus would be key elements that could lead to those conditions.

Brazil is currently running a primary budget surplus, which excludes debt servicing costs, that is just above 3.2 percent of gross domestic product.

IS BRAZIL STILL A BUY?

As the B in the BRICS group of big emerging economies, Brazil over the past decade attracted the attention of growth-seeking foreign investors. Between 2005 and 2007, more than 100 Brazilian companies went public, with foreign investors accounting for around two-thirds of the fresh funding.

This year, foreign investors flush with liquidity drove Brazilian stocks to a near 14 percent gain in the first quarter.

That trend has since reversed, as concerns over Brazil's economic growth trajectory and a drop in risk appetite among global investors dragged the country's benchmark Bovespa index down over 4 percent so far in 2012.

Another factor contributing to that decline, analysts say, is the increasing unpredictability of how or when Brazil's central bank will intervene in the currency market. Investors have also been unsettled by the central bank's focus on economic growth, which in the eyes of some economists casts doubt on its commitment to inflation targeting.

Franco denied, however, that recent policy actions by the central bank such as the aggressive lowering of interest rates and efforts to prevent swings in the exchange rate represent a significant shift from prior policies.

"Is it true that foreign exchange in Brazil is a full clean float? Probably not," Franco said. "Is it true that we do inflation targeting without concern for growth? No. But it has always been the case. I don't think we have really changed anything fundamentally."

Despite the recent turnaround in investment flows, both Franco and Meirelles, who both spoke on Friday to Reuters, reiterated their bullishness on the Brazilian economy.

"Brazil definitely is a buy," Meirelles said, emphasizing factors such as Brazil's large domestic market, growing middle class, and stable institutional framework.

"It is a more selective buy than it was before," Meirelles said, adding that the current concerns over Brazil's economic path are both "healthy and normal" for an emerging economy.

title: Brazil Real Strengthens On Greek Outlook, Exporter Dollars
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL1.9778 Vs BRL1.9972 Friday

--Real gains on rising hopes that Greece will remain in euro zone

--Exporters sell dollars as traders point to early-month "overshooting"


 
   By Tom Murphy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended active trading stronger against the U.S. dollar Monday as exporters sold dollars to the market following a period of what traders called "exaggerated" losses for Brazil's currency.

The real ended regular trading at BRL1.9778 to the dollar, stronger against Friday's close of BRL1.9972, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

As recently as last week, the real was trading as low as BRL2.09 against the dollar, causing exporters to hold back on sales of dollars to the market in hopes of even more lucrative rates later in the month. However, persistent central-bank intervention in the market last week brought an appreciation of the real, convincing exporters that BRL2.00 to-the-dollar is the likely limit for any near-term depreciation.

"Rates like BRL2.04 and BRL2.05 to-the-dollar that we were seeing just a few days ago were not realistic," said Durval Correa, a trader at Sao Paulo's Multi Money brokerage. "There was a speculative element at work. That led to an exaggerated depreciation of the currency."

Mauro Araujo, a trader at Sao Paulo's Vision brokerage, agreed. He called last week's level a case of "overshooting." He added, "The market is beginning to sense that the central bank is not comfortable with the real weaker than BRL2.00 to-the-dollar."

Brazil's central bank systematically intervened in the market last week to pull the real away from the BRL2.00 to-the-dollar level. The bank used auctions of swap contracts, sometimes at a pace of two auctions per day, to do the job. The auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange contracts indexed to domestic interest rates for paper linked to U.S. dollars. The auctions tend to support the real against the greenback by offering investors increased opportunities to hedge in dollars.

With the market convinced that BRL2.00 is the floor for the Brazilian currency, exporters are now in a mood to sell their pent-up dollar holdings, traders said.

Correa said, "The market is much more likely to head in the direction of BRL1.90 to the dollar than BRL2.00." Araujo predicted a short-term "band" for the currency in a range of BRL1.97 to BRL2.00 against the American currency.

The real was also boosted Monday by public opinion polls showing renewed support for Greece's conservative New Democracy Party, which backs the austerity policies required for that country to access a European bailout fund. The polls make it seem more likely Greece's political parties will be able to form a coalition after mid-June parliamentary elections and remain within the euro zone, thus avoiding a messy default and currency restructuring.

A stronger euro Monday helped boost global commodities prices, also a positive element for Brazil, a major commodities exporter.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real rallies past 2/dlr, Mexico peso falls
text:
(Adds Brazil gov't sources on intervention strategy, updates prices)

* Brazil cenbank offers FX swaps when real traded flat

* Real trades below 2/dlr for first time since May 15

* Peru cenbank sells dollars for 1st time since Oct. 2011

* Real ends 1.7 pct higher, Mexican peso weakens 0.16 pct

By Natalia Cacioli

SAO PAULO, May 25 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real on Friday rallied through the level of 2 per dollar for the first time in 10 days as the central bank stepped up its market intervention, but other Latin American currencies fell on European debt fears.

In a more aggressive intervention stance, Brazil's central bank on Friday offered to sell currency swaps early in the session, when the real was practically flat from Thursday's close.

The strategy left many investors wondering whether policymakers were uncomfortable with the level of the currency, but two government sources told Reuters the interventions were only aimed at limiting volatility after the real depreciated with "excessive" speed.

The real rose 1.7 percent to 1.9937 per dollar in its third consecutive session of gains. It was the first time it closed below the level of 2 per dollar since May 14, although it remains nearly 15 percent weaker from a late-February high.

Since it resumed the sale of currency swaps a week ago, this was the first time the central bank offered swaps when the real was trading stable against the dollar.

"The central bank is willing to make regular interventions to avoid that the real returns to the level of 2.1 per dollar," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

Some analysts also said it was too early to say the central bank was trying to draw a line at any specific exchange rate.

"We can't say the central bank is defending any specific currency level yet, as this was the first time it acted like that (when the real was stable)," said Mario Battistel, currency desk manager at Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"Maybe the central bank was worried about Europe's impact on our market, so it acted early to avoid putting out a fire later."

Fears about the impact of a possible Greek exit from the euro zone continued to weigh on global markets, keeping most Latin American currencies weaker.

Mexico's peso fell 0.24 percent to 14.0340 per greenback in its fourth consecutive session of losses. A sharp drop of the peso on Wednesday caused the Mexican central bank to call a dollar auction for the first time since 2009.

The Chilean peso declined 0.12 percent to finish at a fresh 4-1/2-month low of 509.40 per dollar.

Peru's sol ended practically stable at 2.695 per dollar after the central bank sold $2 million in the spot market for the first time since October 2011.

The Peruvian central bank has also been auctioning deposit certificates and repos in recent weeks to satisfy demand for dollars and curb the depreciation of the sol, which has been trading around its weakest levels for 2012.
