title: UPDATE 2- Brazil  has no target for  currency  -sources
text:
* Interventions aimed at limiting FX volatility

* Gov't won't draw lines it cannot defend in FX market

* Cenbank early Friday action to show "we're in charge"

(Adds comments from second government source, byline)

By Brian Winter and Patricia Duarte

SAO PAULO, May 25 (Reuters) - Brazil's recent interventions in the foreign exchange market were aimed at limiting volatility after the real depreciated with "excessive" speed, but do not signal a government target range for the currency, two senior officials told Reuters on Friday.

"The strategy is to prevent movements that are too fast and could distort the economy," one official said on condition of anonymity.

"On the other hand, we're also not going to draw any hard lines or do anything that over time we cannot defend" in the event of a strong market shock, such as a deterioration of the euro zone crisis, the official said.

Brazil's central bank began attempting to limit the real's losses on May 18 by selling currency swaps - which essentially increase the supply of dollars in the market. At the time, the real was rapidly depreciating, mostly because of concerns over the euro zone crisis.

The real touched a three-year low of around 2.10 per dollar on Wednesday, but swap sales since then have helped push the real back through the 2 per dollar threshold on Friday.

In a more aggressive intervention strategy on Friday, the central bank offered to sell swaps at the beginning of the session, when the real traded practically flat against the dollar.

"That was to show we are in charge," a second official said, also on condition of anonymity.

That source, who is a member of President Dilma Rousseff's economic team, said the recent volatility in the real had started to hamper Brazil's foreign exchange market.

"When the market starts to become dysfunctional, exporters and importers walk away," the official said. "We can't allow the forex market to be without a price reference."

Despite the central bank interventions, the real remains about 15 percent weaker than it was on March 1, making it one of the world's worst-performing major currencies over that period.

That sell-off was mainly a result of heightened concerns over the external scenario rather than lack of liquidity in the foreign exchange market, the second source said.

The first official also denied market speculation that Rousseff's government was trying to establish a new floor that would prevent the real from depreciating beyond 2.05 or 2.10 per dollar.

The official said the intervention was, instead, designed to keep the real from sliding too far, too fast, adding that flexibility in the exchange rate may prove necessary if the euro zone crisis deteriorates in coming weeks.

"Nobody really knows what's going to happen with Greece, with Europe," the official said. "We're in wait-and-see mode."

Brazil's currency regime is technically free-floating, although Rousseff's government has repeatedly taken steps over the past year to manage its trading level.

title: Brazilian Real Closes Volatile Session Little Changed
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended a volatile session not far from where it started but traded in a broad range Thursday, as an early selloff on dour economic sentiment prompted the central bank to intervene for a third consecutive session.

The real exited active trading in Sao Paulo at BRL2.0402 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, slightly stronger than Wednesday's close of BRL2.0419.

Following the release of negative data on China's manufacturing base, and an uninspiring effort by European leaders to stimulate economic growth and contain the debt crisis, the real skidded to as weak as BRL2.05 to the dollar in late-morning trading.

But an announcement by the Brazilian Central Bank of an auction to sell dollar swap contracts abruptly sent the currency stronger, and the real briefly approached BRL2.0280 before depreciating gradually over the afternoon.

Market participants say the Brazilian currency is unlikely to gain much ground against the dollar before Greece holds elections on June 17, when voters may effectively choose whether the debt-saddled and austerity-battered nation will stay in the euro zone.

In the meantime, Brazil's central bank has signaled a willingness to intervene in the currency market during sharp sell-offs. The bank has auctioned the equivalent of more than $4 billion in swap contracts since Tuesday, and the real has responded promptly by recovering from intraday lows versus the dollar.

This month's intervention pattern contrasts with that of April, when the central bank bought billions of dollars in the spot market to push the real weaker against the dollar. Brazilian authorities for the past couple of years have expressed a preference for a weaker currency, which they say is key to the industrial sector's competitiveness.

Barclays Emerging Markets Research said the local government's intervention--not only in the currency market, but also in the form of price controls on gasoline and pressure on banks to reduce loan spreads--has "pushed investors to the sidelines."

"Markets love to hate Brazil today," Barclays said.

But the firm added that investors' pessimism about a recent slowdown in the Brazilian economy is "overblown," as growth should pick up in the second half of the year.

"We would expect--global context permitting--some market optimism to re-emerge, though with less intensity than in the past," Barclays said.

title: Fund Manager Balances Brazil Yields With  Currency , Policy Risks
text:
--ING's Michael Mata feels compelled to hold Brazilian paper for its high yields

--But Global Bond Fund co-manager has been cutting exposure to and hedging real since March


 
   By Erin McCarthy and Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--ING fund manager Michael Mata finds himself in a curious paradox when it comes to Brazil: He dislikes the government's constantly changing policies, but feels compelled to hold Brazilian paper for its uniquely high yields.

The Brazilian real, however, is another story. The currency offers him a chance to express his view. Mata, who co-manages the ING Global Bond Fund with $734 million in assets under management, has been cutting his exposure to and hedging the Brazilian real since March, when the real started retreating from some of the strongest levels seen this year.

Mata's approach to Brazil represents the fence many longer-term investors have to straddle: local bonds' attractive yields in a low-rate world and a currency burdened by a government and central bank determined to weaken it. Since March, the Brazilian real has dived 19% against the dollar to three-year lows after the Brazilian government began a series of measures to weaken the currency. During this time, Brazil's central bank also has intervened directly in foreign-exchange markets to weaken the real.

Investors have begun to question the central bank's role in the easing, Mata said.

"Certainly, investors' perception of Brazil is that the central bank has become completely politicized," he said, adding that it no longer is focused only on controlling inflation but also has taken on the government's pro-growth push.

Rolling 12-month inflation in Brazil is at 5.05% as of mid-May, above the government's official central target of 4.5%. But analysts warn that the easing measures could push it to around 5.2% by year end and as much as 5.60% by 2013.

The central bank has "certainly lost some credibility with markets, and that's reflected in the value of the currency," Mata said.

Since Friday, the Brazilian real has been on a weakening spiral triggered by poor liquidity in its markets, and the central bank has had to step in and sell dollars to slow the real's excessive losses.

Despite the confusing moves and lack of clarity in direction, Mata has maintained the fund's "decent-sized position" in short-dated, Brazilian local-currency government bonds. He expects Brazil to continue to cut rates, by another 25 to 50 basis points. In recent months, the central bank has slashed the key Selic rate to a historic low of 9%, from 11% at the start of the year.

"We're close to the end of the easing cycle," he said.

The fund, for instance, currently has exposure to local-currency bonds maturing in 2014, which were recently yielding more than 8%.

Mata typically doesn't hedge the currency exposure on such debt. But, recently, he has hedged out most of the currency risk through non-deliverable forwards, and nearly all of the rate risk, using interest-rate swaps, he said.

Mata is unsure of his next move in the currency of Latin America's most dominant economy. He would like to buy the real, but speculation that central-bank policy could become more aggressive than expected is giving him caution, he said.

"There is some policy risk there that rates go even lower, which would weaken the real," he added.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com and Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com @djfxtrader [ 05-23-12 1010ET ]

text:
(Adds Brazil's 2nd FX swap auction, updates prices)

RIO DE JANEIRO, May 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's real trimmed losses o n T uesday after the central bank intervened twice to support the currency, which has slumped about 17 percent since the beginning of March.

Other Latin American currencies traded flat to weaker as investors remained skeptical that an informal meeting of European leaders this week would yield much progress in tackling Europe's debt crisis.

The real , weighed by economic concerns at home and abroad, fell nearly 1 percent to more than 2.06 per dollar when the central bank offered to sell about $2.5 billion in currency swaps. Not all contracts were sold right away, and the central bank announced a second auction when the real was sliding again.

The two consecutive operations, which have a market impact similar to the sale of dollars in the futures market, led some traders to believe the central bank was setting an informal ceiling around 2.05 reais per dollar for the currency.

"We can say that the central bank is not comfortable with the real at 2.06 per dollar," said Alfredo Barbutti, chief economist at BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo. He noted that the bank also intervened on Friday when the real neared the same level.

"I don't believe the central bank is worried about the impact of the currency on inflation at this moment. This is just to put the house in order," he added.

The real immediately erased losses after the announcement and seesawed near the unchanged mark afterward as the central bank sold a combined $2.2 billion worth of swaps in the two auctions. The currency last traded at 2.0474 per dollar, little changed from Monday's close.

The central bank on Friday sold currency swaps to support the real for the first time in nearly seven months, but did not change the currency's depreciation trend.

Investors have been revising down their estimates for the real as a recent string of disappointing economic data in Brazil suggested the government may resort to lower interest rates and a weaker currency to prop up the economy.

Putting additional pressure on the currency, Finance Minister Guido Mantega o n T uesday repeated that the currency currently stands at "a more favorable place for Brazil's competitiveness."

The Mexican peso lost 0.44 percent to 13.7575 per dollar and the Chilean peso was flat at 505.60.

title: UPDATE: Brazil Real Weakens To Three-Year Low On Europe Worries
text:
-- Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0589 Vs BRL2.0444 Monday

-- Real posts further losses in after-market trading at BRL2.0780

-- Real weakens despite government intervention via swap auctions

-- Worries over future of euro zone, Greek bailout weigh on market

(Updates with after-market trading in third graph, showing further losses for the real)


 
   By Tom Murphy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended active trading weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, hitting a new three-year low on continued worries about the vexing European debt crisis.

The real ended regular trading at BRL2.0589 to the dollar, weaker against Monday's close of BRL2.0444, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

In after-market trading, the real posted additional losses, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, at BRL2.0780 against the dollar, setting the stage for possible volatility again Wednesday.

The currency weakened despite determined government attempts to damp volatility by means of swap contract auctions.

The government ordered two separate auctions of swap contracts Tuesday, selling the equivalent of nearly $2.2 billion in the contracts.

The auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange paper linked to interest rates for contracts tied to the U.S. dollar, thus expanding the supply of available hedging mechanisms in the American currency.

"Increasingly, the market is seeing the level of BRL2.05 or BRL2.06 to the dollar as the trigger for government intervention," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. "Both interventions today [Tuesday] came as the real slipped beyond the BRL2.05 barrier."

The government also intervened in the market Friday, calling a swap auction when the real sank to BRL2.05 against the greenback.

Traders said much of the volatility in the Brazilian market in recent days has been speculative.

"More than anything, investors are testing the government," said Olvidio Soares, a trader at Sao Paulo's Interbolsa brokerage. "They're wondering what level the government will tolerate."

Muniz noted that there was little spot trading Tuesday. "Both importers and exporters held back," he said. "They're waiting to see the outcome of the dance between speculators and the government."

But the volatility also comes against the background of continued tensions in Europe, where the ever-present possibility of a messy Greek exit from the euro zone brought losses for the euro currency against the U.S. dollar Tuesday. European leaders are due to meet later this week in efforts to find a solution not only to the Greek debt dilemma but also to wider regional problems of growth and debt-management.

The European crisis has left the Brazilian market in a delicate situation, according to Ilan Goldfajn, chief economist at Brazil's huge Itau (ITUB, ITUB4.BR) bank. Goldfajn said the real could weaken to BRL2.20 or even BRL2.30 against the dollar in the event of a Greek pullout from the euro zone. "But that level would be short-lived," he said.

Muniz agreed, saying, "The central bank can stop the depreciation of the real against the dollar any time it wants by selling dollars directly to the market." The Brazilian Central Bank holds foreign reserves of more than $370 billion, much higher than the $205 billion it held at the time of the Lehman Brothers crisis of 2008.

title: Intervention  Dominates Emerging Market  Currency  Trading; Debt Steady
text:
--Currency intervention seen or suspected in Brazil and South Korea

--Broader global risks keep investors cautious

--Emerging market debt little changed


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies see-sawed Friday, driven primarily by external sources and triggering central-bank intervention in some markets.

Brazil's currency was in the spotlight as Brazil's central bank surprised markets by intervening late Friday afternoon to curb the Brazilian real's losses. Up until this point, Brazilian authorities had been taking a variety of measures to weaken the real.

Investors ultimately took on an overall cautious tone ahead of this weekend's Group of Eight meeting, as concerns about the euro-zone sovereign-debt crisis still loomed over markets.

"We're not in deep contagion mode; we've moved away from deep risk," said Sebastien Galy, senior currency strategist at Societe Generale. But investors would "rather stick to mostly risk-off positions ahead of the weekend," he added.

Heavy demand for dollars onshore in Brazil drove the real down more than 2% intraday Friday to its weakest levels since May 2009, taking out stop-losses for local players that had bullish bets on Brazil's currency, traders said. The rapid, uncontrolled move downward in the real spurred Brazil's central bank to sell the equivalent of $654.3 million in dollar swap contracts, much to the surprise of markets. Previously, Brazilian officials indicated they were comfortable with the dollar trading around BRL2. The dollar shot up to BRL2.0539, but later traded at BRL2.0223, after the central bank stepped in.

In South Korea, suspected intervention by local foreign-exchange authorities prevented a further slide for the won, which hit a five-month low against the dollar. The dollar bought KRW1,169 late Friday, easing back from KRW1,175.4 seen earlier in the session, according to CQG.

The Indian rupee was also in focus, falling to a record low against the U.S. dollar for a third straight session Friday before a recovery in local stocks and the euro pulled it into positive territory. The dollar traded as high as INR54.91 Friday, but later traded at INR54.40. India's central bank has been seen intervening heavily in the market in recent weeks to arrest the rupee's relentless slide against the dollar.

The Russian ruble was another underperformer Friday, hit by falling oil prices. Since Russia is the world's second-largest producer of crude oil, the ruble often mimics moves in oil prices. The dollar changed hands at RUB31.305 from RUB31.073 late Thursday, according to CQG.

Emerging market sovereign debt, however, was little changed on the day, in line with benchmark U.S. Treasurys, which also were largely steady. The spread on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened by two basis points. In price terms, the index slipped 0.3%.

title: Brazil 's  Central Bank  Surprises With  Intervention  To Steady Real
text:
--Brazil's central bank intervenes to prevent further currency weakness

--Investors snap up dollar swap contracts, equivalent to $654 million

--Traders not clear whether this was to prevent a panic, or to indicate a ceiling

By Matthew Cowley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank surprised the currency market with a move to try to stem some of the Brazilian real's losses, as the euro zone's sovereign debt crisis continues to roil global markets.

Although there'd been speculation that the central bank might step into the market at some point, given the recent weakness, some investors had let down their guard after the government signaled that it was quite content with the real's losses, as it helps industry and exporters.

On Friday afternoon, however, some traders reported heavy selling of the real by local investors in Brazil, which was starting to spiral out of control. The shrinking flow of dollars into the country created a liquidity gap, which led to a rapid depreciation by the real, market participants said.

The currency had plunged more than 2% against the dollar when the central bank intervened in the market offering to sell dollar swap contracts at auction. It's the first time it had intervened in three weeks; previously, however, it had been trying to deter real strength.

Traders weren't clear whether the central bank was signaling a ceiling for the real, at BRL2.05 per dollar, or whether it was simply stepping in to provide support in a market which was starting to become--in the jargon of the market--"disorderly."

According to Jankiel Santos, of BES Investimentos, the move on Friday to weaken the real was speculative, with traders testing the Central Bank's patience and trying to gauge at which level it feels it needs to step in. "There may be further interventions," Santos said. "With the global scene continuing to weigh, there's going to be more of the same in coming days. They could even sell dollars on the spot market."

The impact of the auction was immediate, with the real retracing to BRL2.03 per dollar, and then taking another leg down to BRL2.0155, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset. The currency was still nearly 1% weaker on the day, from BRL1.9974 in late trading on Thursday.

The central bank sold all 13,000 of the dollar-swap contracts on offer, equivalent to $654.3 million, according to a central bank statement.

The dollar-swap auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange contracts indexed to domestic interest rates for paper linked to the U.S. dollar. The central bank typically holds foreign-exchange swap auctions at a time when the Brazilian real is weakening against the U.S. dollar. The auctions often help to stem the depreciation of the real by offering investors the chance to obtain contracts linked to the U.S. dollar at a time of dollar scarcity.

Friday's dollar swap is the first since Oct. 28.

The intervention marks a turnaround for the central bank. Until recently, it had been buying up dollars, encouraging weakness in the Brazilian real, which the government has claimed is overvalued against the dollar. The last time the central bank intervened in the market to buy dollars was April 27.

As the euro-zone crisis intensified, however, the Brazilian real has been among the hardest hit in emerging markets. Although the government has welcomed the weakness as a boost for Brazilian industry and exporters, there had been speculation that any signs of a sudden collapse in the real could prompt central bank intervention.

Analysts say further flight into long-dated Treasurys could flatten the curve more, a blow to those betting on steepening. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  fall on Greece, real hits 2/dlr
text:
* Traders in Brazil speculate c. bank will intervene

* Brazil's real off 0.55 pct, Mexico's peso down 0.68 pct

By Danielle Fonseca and Rachel Uranga

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, May 14 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Tuesday w ith Brazil's real closing at a near three-year low, fueling speculation the country's bank could soon intervene.

Worries that new elections in Greece would harden domestic opposition to an international bailout and open the possibility that the country could exit the euro weighed on global markets and pushed Brazil's currency to its weakest level since July 2009.

"The market is seeing the possibility of Greece leave the euro zone as very likely," said Alfredo Barbutti, chief economist at BCG Liquidez.

The Brazilian real weakened 0.55 percent to 2 p er dollar.

Some investors have been pushing the real above the level of 2 per dollar to test the central bank's tolerance of a weaker currency that could spur inflation by raising import prices.

"We have some speculation in the foreign exchange market right now," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a manager at Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The market is wondering whether the central bank will intervene, so it is pushing the currency to 2 per dollar."

The Brazilian central bank bought dollars in the spot market from February to April, helping weaken the exchange rate from around 1.7 per dollar, which was considered harmful to exporters.

Some traders bet the central bank will intervene again if the real weakens beyond 2 per dollar. Government officials have indicated they still do not anticipate meaningful inflationary pressures from the currency at that level.

"At between 2 and 2.10, the possibility of intervention is really, really high," said Diego Donadio, Latin America currency and debt strategist for BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

The Mexican and Chilean pesos hit four month lows as a ttempts to form a new government in Greece collapsed spooking investors and raising the prospect anti-bailout candidates could sweep elections, sparking a fresh round of the euro-zone crisis.

The news from Greece weighed on riskier Latin American assets that tend to sell off when investors seek safety in currencies like the U.S. dollar.

Mexico's peso weakened 0.68 percent to 13.8350 per dollar. C hile's peso fell to four month lows, nearing 500 per dollar. The currency closed 1.42 percent weaker to bid at 499.30 per dollar.

"The 500 level is really difficult to break," said Francisco Schneider, director of trading at Celfin Capital in Santiago. "If it happens the next level could be 504 but if markets calm down, don't rule out the peso's recovery to new ranges between 490 and 500."

(Additional reporting by Moises Avila and Froilan Romero in Santiago; Danielle Ramos in Sao Paulo; Editing by Diane Craft)

SAO PAULO, May 14 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real weakened sharply in spot trading o n M onday and briefly crossed the 2 per U.S. dollar threshold for the first time since July 2009 as uncertainty over the impact of a potential Greek exit from the euro drove investors away from riskier assets.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Stronger Amid Inflation,  Intervention  Concerns
text:
--Real closes sharply stronger against dollar

--Real exited active trading at BRL1.9456 to the dollar versus BRL1.9695 Wednesday

--Signs of faster inflation sparked concerns central bank might sell dollars


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)-The Brazilian real closed stronger against the dollar Thursday amid concern the dollar's recent appreciation might fuel inflationary pressure and push the central bank to intervene by selling greenbacks.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.9456 to the dollar, stronger than BRL1.9695 Wednesday, a change of 1.2%, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. Wednesday's close was the weakest for the real in nearly three years.

After strengthening almost 10% against the dollar in the first two months of the year, the real has since given up those gains and more, amid concerns about Europe's sovereign debt crisis and sluggish economic growth in developed countries.

Government and central bank interventions intended to weaken the real and protect Brazilian exporters have also played their part. With the recent appreciation of the dollar, the real might have reached a balance point, past which the central bank might feel forced to step in and sell the U.S. currency, analysts said.

"It's not in our interest for the dollar to strengthen much more, because it can start to cause problems for inflation," said Paulo Fujisaki, an analyst at the Socopa brokerage in Sao Paulo. "If the real weakens much more than it has, the central bank could step in and start selling dollars."

On Wednesday the IBGE statistical agency showed a mild slowing in annual inflation as of April, to 5.10% from 5.24% the previous month. However, the monthly gain was a sharp 0.64%--compared with 0.21% in March--higher than forecast and a warning sign to analysts.

Central bank President Alexandre Tombini said the April inflation figures don't indicate a reversal in the trend of slowing inflation.

Speaking on the sidelines of the central bank's inflation-targeting seminar Thursday, Tombini said that inflation readings in the next three months are expected to come in below April's 0.64%.

"We are still in the process of converging on the target," Tombini told reporters. Brazil targets an annual inflation rate of 4.5%, with a tolerance of plus or minus two percentage points.

Brazil's central bank is keeping an eye on weakness in the country's currency, which could affect inflation, Tombini said.

"The dollar is in the process of a global appreciation at the moment," especially in relation to merging-market currencies, Tombini noted.

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The difference between interest rates charged by Brazilian banks and the country's Selic benchmark rate remain too high, an anomaly that needs to be corrected, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Friday.

Speaking at an event in Sao Paulo, Mantega said that state-owned banks have already reduced interest rates. "To reduce spreads, the Selic should continue to fall as long as conditions permit," Mantega said.

Increased lending by state-owned banks such as Banco do Brasil (BBAS3.BR) and Caixa Economica Federal should also help cut banking spreads "because this generates competition," Mantega said. "Competition is the best solution for reducing bank spreads."

Brazil announced Thursday measures to remove a key technical barrier to further interest rate cuts by the Brazilian Central Bank. The government reduced the fixed interest rate paid out by passbook savings accounts, which is linked to the Selic, so that the Selic could be cut below its historical low of 8.75%.

The Selic currently stands at 9%, and the central bank has indicated a willingness to further cut interest rates.

"Real interest rates at 2% are a dream every Brazilian should have because everyone will have credit available for buying," Mantega said. "When this moment arrives, it will mean that inflation is under control."

Mantega addressed concerns that the central bank may have turned its back on the fight against inflation, saying that inflation is "always a priority."

"The Selic will only fall if inflation is totally under control," Mantega said. Inflation is currently on a downward trend headed for a rate of 4.5% to 5% in 2012, the finance minister added.

Despite the changes to interest rates paid out by savings accounts, Mantega said the passbooks remain the best alternative for small savers. "The 100 million small savers should continue [with passbooks] because they have a good return," Mantega said.

Brazilians will also benefit by the move because lower interest rates will mean greater access to home loans at much cheaper rates, Mantega added.

title: REFILE-Brazil losing sparkle in eyes of investors
text:
(Refiles for technical reasons, no change to copy)

By Natalie Feary

NEW YORK, May 4 (IFR) - Long the darling of Latin America, Brazil is seeing investors start to turn their attention elsewhere in the region amid a slowdown in growth and a rise in government interventionism.

After boasting a 4.5% average growth rate in the five years up to 2010, the world's fifth-largest country saw growth tumble to 2.7% last year -- worse than many had expected.

And government moves to check the appreciation of Brazil's currency, the Real, by stemming capital inflows have stoked the ire of increasingly skeptical investors.

As analysts from Nomura bluntly put it in a new report: "We believe that the era of relative outperformance by Brazil in Latin America is over."

Of course, sovereign wealth funds and other investors clearly continue to allocate substantial sums to Brazil, and Brazilian debt still accounts for more than half of corporate dollar-denominated debt out of Latin America.

But one fund manager who asked not to be named told IFR he saw anecdotal evidence that some investors were starting to withdraw money from the country.

"This makes sense," the manager said. "There is a sense of frustration among those trading in the local currency space."

In April there were net outflows from Brazil-dedicated fixed-income funds of USD262m, while the previous month showed a decline in inflows. Fund flows were USD3.046bn in February, down from USD4.064bn in January, according to Lipper data.

A REAL PROBLEM

The government decided earlier this year to extend the 6 percent tax on short-term foreign loans or bonds known as the IOF, in a move intended to rein in the appreciating Real.

But that move has drawn heavy fire from critics, who say different measures could and should have been taken to tighten capital inflows.

"There is a lot of frustration regarding local currency in Brazil, as well as the recent [foreign exchange] intervention," said one New York-based investor.

"The upside of investments is capped on the currency."

This is of particular concern because Brazil, still a developing country, has real need for more infrastructure spending.

"The infrastructure is totally inadequate and needs private-sector investment," said the fund manager.

"It used to be a case where what the central bank did, and economists thought they should do, were the same thing. But it is no longer so. We have big concerns about the fiscal regime."

As those concerns grow, investors are taking a harder look at Brazilian debt -- and are starting to look at other countries in the region more favourably.

"Brazil has been the growth story over the last decade and still offers some opportunities, but investors are still not paying enough attention to other countries in the region," said one London-based fund manager who views Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico as offering more value.

In the banking sector, for instance, Jonathan Mann, head of emerging market debt at F&C Management, said Brazilian banks were looking expensive relative to their regional counterparts.

"When you consider where they are in the credit cycle, the slowing growth and rising delinquencies, they look expensive," he said.

Banco do Brasil's 2020 senior bonds offer a spread of 230bp. Bancolombia's 2020 bonds offer 353bp, while Mexico's BBVA Bancomer 2016 bonds pay a spread of 358bp.

Financial institutions outside of Brazil are popular with investors, owing to high reserve requirements as well as generally growing middle classes.

"Although spreads have widened in line with global banks, these should tighten in because [Latin American] banks are not highly leveraged like some from other regions," said Mann.

MEXICO & CO

Other sectors in Brazil look relatively even more expensive.

In the steel sector, Brazilian names are tight to where they have been trading historically and versus the comparables. The Gerdau 2021 bonds and the CSN 2020 bonds are trading with an average spread of 330bp.

ArcelorMittal 2021 bonds are trading at 400bp, BHP Billiton 2021s are trading at 102bp, and Rio Tinto's 2021 bonds are trading at 125bp.

Brasil Telecom is another name seen as fairly tight versus the comparables elsewhere. The 2022 bonds offer a yield of 5.3% and a spread of 350bp, while Deutsche Telecom's 2019 bonds offer a spread of 205bp. The spread differential has tightened 12bp on a one-year rolling average, according to one credit analyst.

"In countries like Chile, Colombia and Peru, we see value in the utility sector, particularly relative to Brazil, where we have seen some bankruptcy cases," said a New York-based investor.

"Ex-Brazil, we see value as electrical penetration is sub-optimal and not very developed. So, we would look to an active play in this sector."

Many accounts are putting their bet on Mexico -- which, unlike Brazil, is seen as having a stable and predictable fiscal and monetary regime.

Domestic consumption is expanding at 25% annually, while labour costs remain stable as productivity growth in the manufacturing sector has been averaging 2%-3%.

"Stronger growth in the US means Mexican companies should benefit and, most interestingly, the country is regaining market share from China," said a UK-based investor.

title: POLL-Gains in Latam  FX  to fade on dovish c.banks
text:
* For poll data see

* Modest gains seen after strong start to 2012

* Mexico peso, Brazil real to outperform, mainly in H2 2012

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, May 3 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies will rise modestly against the dollar in coming months as local central banks seem more dovish and prone to intervene in foreign exchange markets to stimulate their local economies, a Reuters poll found.

After sharp gains in some pairs so far this year, though, traders will probably have to wait until at least the second half of the year for a fresh round of appreciation.

The Mexican peso and the Brazilian real are likely to perform best, particularly the real with rising inflation in Brazil leaving limited room for currency interventions.

The shift in Latin American central banks' tones was notable, said Citigroup analysts in a note.

"The Mexican central bank sounds much more dovish, as does the central bank of Colombia, and Chile should soon follow suit," they added, noting that policymakers in the region also "have a preference for weaker exchange rates" through direct intervention.

But analysts remain wary of any major change to the global economic backdrop, which remains fragile.

Europe's lingering debt crisis, China's slowing economy and dwindling prospects for another round of U.S. monetary stimulus are the main risks, according to the poll of 37 economists and strategists across the region.

Chile's peso is seen at 490 per dollar in a month and at 485 in a year, slightly weaker than its current level of 484 units, while the Colombian peso is forecast nearly unchanged at 1768 per dollar within one year, the poll showed.

Both currencies strenghtened 7 percent and 9 percent this year so far, respectively, as strong capital inflows - fueled by more than 1 trillion euros in fresh money printed by the European Central Bank to fight the crisis - sought fatter returns in emerging economies.

The Colombian central bank stopped short of hiking rates and held borrowing costs for a second straight month on Monday, noting easing inflation and expressing concern about the effects of the strenghtening peso over the country's exports.

It also voted to extend for another three months its dollar purchase program. The bank will buy at least $20 million a day on the spot market until Nov. 2.

Chile's central bank, which also has a record of market intervention, cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 5 percent in January on fears that demand in Europe and China would turn sluggish and hit the export-dependent country.

The Mexican peso is expected to have better fortunes than its neighbours, according to the poll, gaining through April 2013 though at a slower pace. The peso has already surged over 7 percent so far this year.

The median forecast of 16 analysts see the Mexican currency at 12.73 per dollar within one year, around 2 percent stronger than Wednesday's 12.93 close.

Investors are expected to stay cautious ahead of July's presidential elections, waiting for the second half of this year to resume the currency's strengthening path.

"We know its going to be a continuation of the economic model, however we don't know what are going to be the main economic policies," said Alfredo Coutino, Moody's Analytics director for Latin America.

REAL TO RESUME GAINS

The Brazilian central bank's aggressive push to cut interest rates to near record-lows, allied with more than $18 billion in dollar official purchases since January, has already made the country's currency underperform its peers.

The real is now 3 percent weaker this year -- even after jumping nearly 8 percent in the first two months of 2012.

But Brazilian policymakers may need to temper their current stance as inflation picks up in the second half of 2012, according to a Reuters poll.

Brazil's currency is expected to remain nearly stable at 1.88 real per dollar by end-May, according to the median forecast of 24 estimates in the Reuters survey.

It should reverse losses from then on, trading at 1.85 real by end-July and at 1.82 per dollar by April 2013, according to median forecasts from the poll.

The Peruvian sol is expected to trade at 2.65 per dollar by end-May and at 2.61 within one year, the poll added, nearly flat from the current 2.64 rate.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso weakens on U.S. data, labor report eyed
text:
(Recasts, adds quotes from Mexico, Peru)

* Mexico's peso off 0.5 pct, Brazil's real gains 0.6 pct

* U.S. services report creates pessimism ahead of Friday's labor report

* Peru raises bank reserve requirements

By Caroline Stauffer

LIMA, May 3 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso weakened on Thursday on disappointing service sector data from the United States, though the real strengthened late in the session after Brazil took a break from market intervention.

Peru's sol weakened slightly as traders digested new bank deposit requirements and Chile's peso closed at its strongest level in more than a month a f ter the country's central bank said it had considered a rate hike at its last board meeting.

The U.S. Institute for Supply Management said on Thursday its services index fell to 53.5 in April from 56.0 in March, missing economists' forecasts for a modest decline to 55.5.

Analysts said the report's employment component pointed to lingering weakness in the recovery of the world's largest economy, leading to investor caution ahead of a highly anticipated April labor data scheduled for release on Friday.

In response, the Mexican peso weakened 0.5 percent to 12.9991 per dollar. The currency is particularly sensitive to U.S. data because Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States, tying its economy to that of its northern neighbor.

"Given the dependency we have with the U.S. economic cycle, in particular with consumption, these signals of weakness are normally related to a weaker currency," said Delia Paredes, director of Analysis at Mexico City brokerage Banorte-IXE in Mexico City.

"I'm concerned we'll see a contraction of employment in manufacturing in Friday's report," she said.

Peru's sol also weakened, closing down 0.08 percent to bid 2.64 per dollar.

The country's central bank earlier this week moved to curb appreciation of the currency by raising some deposit requirements on banks. The sol has traded around its strongest level in 15 years recently, helped by Peru's swift economic growth.

"The market continues to feel the impacts of the central bank's new measures and one of those is that now dollars are worth more than soles in the bank treasuries," said one trader in Lima who asked not to be named.

Chile's peso meanwhile strengthened 0.48 percent to close bidding 481.8 per dollar.

The Chilean central bank's latest minutes showed that although the bank's governing council voted unanimously to hold the benchmark interest rate at 5.0 percent last month, it considered raising it by 25 basis points.

REAL CHANGES COURSE

After weakening for much of the session, the real closed 0.64 percent stronger to bid 1.9117 per U.S. dollar as traders cheered less central bank intervention in the spot market.

"Two weeks ago we had nearly daily interventions from the central bank, but in the past three days the bank has stayed out of the market, decreasing pressure on the exchange rate," said one trader.

The government and central bank have tried to weaken the currency with taxes on financial transactions and dollar buys in the spot market in a bid to prop up Brazil's manufacturing sector.

The real closed at its weakest level since July 2009 on Wednesday.

Lower interest rates have also made the real, which has weakened nearly 3 percent this year, less attractive for investors.

In the latest sign more rate cuts lie ahead, a draft presidential decree seen by Reuters on Thursday showed President Dilma Rousseff will link returns on some national savings accounts to the central bank's lending rate.

The proposal carries enormous political and economic risks and amounts to a reengineering of one of the basic pillars of Brazil's financial system.

title: Why Wells Fargo's Norris, Emerging-Market Peers Are On The Sidelines
text:
--Fund manager is waiting for clearer picture on the global economy to emerge

--Norris still prefers emerging-market assets in longer term

--Fund remains overweight emerging-market debt but has hedged currency exposure in some countries


 
   By Erin McCarthy and Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--In the struggle that goes on in Tony Norris's mind, his cautionary bent has won out again.

The co-manager of the Wells Fargo Advantage International Bond Fund has decided he will wait for more positive signs from global economies in the coming weeks and months before adding emerging-market assets to his portfolio.

Norris isn't alone in this position. He belongs to a significant camp of investors who missed out on emerging markets' strong early-2012 rally but remain hesitant to wade back in even after those assets have fallen to cheaper values, despite that they describe themselves as long-term emerging-market bulls.

They are waiting for the dust to settle and a clearer picture to emerge on China's slowdown, on Europe's sovereign issues and on the course of the U.S. economy. Emerging currencies have been in a lull in recent weeks and continue to move in correlation with investor confidence.

With Asian powerhouses India and China facing decelerating rates of growth, with Brazil's government weakening its currency to boost its exports growth, and with many advanced countries painfully working down their budget deficits, investors' outlook toward emerging markets has dimmed.

However, Norris believes by mid-year, emerging-market assets including currencies can bounce back. He has a bearish dollar view that supports that outlook.

"The long-term negative for the U.S. is the twin deficits," he said, referring to fiscal and current-account deficits. "The short-term story is better relative growth."

That was the outlook of his fund at the start of the year, and it was positioned for a rough ride, especially in the first quarter, on expectations of a default from Greece on its debt payments. But emerging-market currencies rallied sharply in the first few months of the year.

Of late, most of the verve of that run has fizzled out. That is why Norris and his team are watching all the signs--economic-data releases, oil prices and market sentiment--in the coming weeks to guide the course of his portfolio of $1.73 billion.

A more-positive backdrop could lead to additional exposure to emerging-market foreign exchange and nonsovereign-emerging-market debt like corporate and high-yield bonds, Norris said.

However, he added one "major move" this year has been a shift in emphasis in the euro zone from the core to peripheral economies, after the region's improvement in sentiment following the European Central Bank's liquidity measures. In 2011, the fund had zero exposure to Italy and Spain, but this year it moved to a neutral position, Norris said. Despite the recent escalation of concerns on Spain, his team has decided to hold steady.

The fund remains broadly overweight emerging-market debt but it has hedged currency exposure in various markets to guard against foreign-exchange volatility. That view extends to Brazil, where a series of interventionist measures from the government and central bank have curbed the Brazilian real's appreciation.

The fund is still overweight Brazilian debt but it began hedging the currency in early March when the central bank accelerated its easing program with a rate cut of 75 basis points to 9.75%, Norris said. Since then, the central bank has eased by another 75 basis points and left the option open for more cuts. Norris prefers Brazilian global bonds that can be settled through foreign clearing-settlement system Euroclear.

"Our view on Brazil is it's a long-term value play," he said, adding with the "real yield available on Brazilian bonds, it's still one of the best value areas in the world."

Elsewhere in emerging markets, the fund is overweight Mexico, Czech Republic, Poland, South Korea and Malaysia, Norris said.

"If one looks at currencies year to date, small economies that have a better growth outlook have been the best performing," he said. "Over the longer term those currencies will continue to outperform."

-By Erin McCarthy and Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com; @djfxtrader [ 02-05-12 1952GMT ]

title: Brazil Real Weakens To BRL1.90 To US Dollar On Global Backdrop,  Intervention  Fear
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones) -- Brazil's real weakened past the psychological barrier of BRL1.90 to the U.S. dollar Monday as risk aversion grew worldwide and investors shied away from the Brazilian currency in particular amid fears of possible further government intervention in the market.

The real exited usual trading at BRL1.9047 to the dollar, weaker than its Friday close of BRL1.8837, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Spain's entry into recession and the downgrading of both Spain and a number of Spanish banks by Standard & Poor's renewed fears over the European economy, dampening risk appetite and leading the dollar to strengthen on international markets.

Spain officially entered recession after first-quarter data released Monday confirmed that its economy contracted for the second consecutive quarter. The government announced it will raise spending cuts to EUR20 billion, from the previously announced EUR10 billion. Expectations of anti-austerity protests grew amid fears that Spain's already towering 24.4% unemployment rate could rise even more.

However, sentiment among investors in the real was also hit by expectations that the Brazilian Central Bank will continue to take measures to "correct" the real's value, stemming any possible appreciation, following no fewer than 16 interventions during April via spot dollar purchase auctions. This fear explains why the real fell more than other Latin American currencies Monday, said Bruno Lavieri of Tendencias consultancy.

"Other Latin American currencies are more diversified," Lavieri said. "Brazil's central bank is acting very close to the market and the government's talk shows it could continue to pay an intensive role."

The recent easing of inflationary pressures in Brazil has given Brazil's central bank more freedom to take measures in the currency market, noted Lavieri. "However, a devalued real tends to pressurize inflation, so if inflation starts accelerating again, then the central bank's intervention framework may change," he said.

Inflationary pressures are also linked to commodities prices, which for the time being look set to remain depressed, according to the Tendencias economist.

For Flavio Serrano, economist with Espirito Santo Investment Bank, investors in the real "are prisoners to the will of the central bank," which spells more uncertainties for the coming days.

The central bank has "made it quite clear they don't want the exchange rate at BRL1.70, the rate of earlier this year," Serrano said. "Investors are afraid. The direction of the dollar has been only upwards and there's doubts where this will stop: they may only stop when inflation starts taking off."

Monday's trading may have been particularly volatile as this was the last day of the month, when the central bank sets its official exchange rate for the month, which usually leads to speculative trades, the economists said. In addition, thin training on the eve of the Labor Day holiday Tuesday, when Brazil's markets will be closed, may have added to the volatility, they said.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger, Gains Muted By  Intervention  Risk
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's settled barely stronger against the dollar after range-bound trading Friday, as the threat of intervention by local authorities limited the carryover of positive investor sentiment from other currency markets.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.8837 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.8845 at Thursday's close.

A below-forecast 2.2% expansion in U.S. gross domestic product during the first quarter raised expectations among some investors that the Federal Reserve might implement more monetary easing to shore up the economy. Friday's GDP report followed comments by Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke earlier this week indicating the U.S. central bank stands ready to use monetary stimulus to support job growth if necessary.

Such measures, known as quantitative easing, increase the money supply and tend to pressure the greenback weaker against other currencies. Dollar rivals such as the euro, Japanese yen and British pound all gained Friday, as did the Mexican peso, which got a boost when the Bank of Mexico held off on cutting interest rates in a monetary policy decision.

Win Thin, a currency strategist at New York's Brown Brothers Harriman, said such behavior in international markets would normally be reflected in gains by the Brazilian real.

But Brazil's Finance Ministry and central bank have become more successful at limiting the currency's appreciation this year than in the past, as a range of new taxes targeting foreign-exchange transactions have been aided by lower interest rates. The Brazilian Central Bank in recent weeks has intervened almost daily, buying dollars off the market in unannounced spot auctions and sending the real weaker.

Late in Friday's session, the bank bought an undisclosed amount of dollars for BRL1.8850 in a spot auction.

"It's too early to say people are throwing in the towel on the real," Thin said, adding that the macro factors such as the European debt crisis may be weighing on Brazil's currency more than some market participants realize. title: Japanese Retail Investors Find Replacements For Brazilian Real
text:
--Brazil's intervention to weaken the real has spurred Japanese investors to look for alternative currencies

--Japanese retail investors increase investments in Turkish lira and South African rand

--These investors are rotating out of Brazilian real


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Japanese retail investors may have finally found Brazil's replacement.

Japan's retail investor base, a powerful source of investment flows to emerging markets, has long been known for its large, bullish bets on the Brazilian real. These investments are often completed through currency-selective toshins, which are foreign-currency-denominated investment trusts that invest in high-yielding assets like stocks and bonds.

But with Brazil's government and central bank working aggressively to weaken the real, Japanese investors have pulled money out of the country. Those funds have found new homes in other emerging markets, with the Turkish lira, South African rand and Indonesian rupiah receiving more inflows, said Nomura analyst Peter Attard Montalto.

"We've seen a very large rotation by Japanese investors away from Brazil," Montalto said, adding Brazil's efforts to weaken the real are "making people look more closely at other alternatives."

Nomura data show Japanese investors purchased Y31 billion ($383 million) of toshins denominated in the Turkish lira in March, with those toshins holding JPY178 billion. They bought Y13 billion of toshins denominated in the South African rand in March, with those toshins holding Y74 billion last month.

These investors sold Y38.5 billion of toshins denominated in the Brazilian real in the same period. Outstanding Brazilian real toshin investments are still high, however, at Y4.716 trillion in March, according to Nomura.

Brazil's government has introduced various financial-operation taxes to curb the real's strength, and the central bank aggressively has cut interest rates and bought dollars in the foreign-exchange market to drag down the currency in recent months.

Firms aren't offering Brazilian-real products to Japanese investors as aggressively as they have in the past, said Koon Chow, emerging-markets strategist at Barclays in London.

While the Brazilian real still makes up the biggest chunk of assets under management in Japanese toshins, the Turkish lira is gaining in popularity, Nomura analysts said.

The lira's high yields and Turkey's strong growth story are driving the movement among Japanese investors to the currency, analysts said. Turkey's central bank maintains an interest-rate corridor of 5.75% to 11.5%, which the bank often uses for impromptu tightening to support the lira. However, Turkey's massive current-account deficit, around 10% of gross domestic product, still poses a risk for the currency, analysts have said.

Brazil's benchmark Selic rate stands at 9% after the central bank cut it 75 basis points in April as part of an aggressive easing cycle expected to continue.

South Africa also boasts a relatively strong growth story, with its wealth of commodity exports serving as a main draw for investors.

While these investments don't have much of an impact on the spot-foreign-exchange market since much of the exposures are hedged elsewhere, they do provide these countries with a steady source of investment flow governments are glad to see.

"The Japanese investors remain a force in emerging markets," said Nomura's Montalto. "Policymakers in emerging markets know that, whether it's in Turkey or South Africa."

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com; @djfxtrader [ 26-04-12 2010GMT ]

title: Brazil wants  currency  around 1.90/dlr -source
text:
* Brazil gov't wants currency around 1.90/dlr - source

* Pushing real closer to 2/dlr seen too costly

* Real is one of world's weakest currencies this year

By Patricia Duarte

SAO PAULO, April 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's government sees a "window of opportunity" to continue intervening in the currency market and maintain the real around the 1.90 per U.S. dollar level, although it will likely not seek to weaken the currency much further than that, a senior economic official told Reuters.

The real has weakened about 9 percent against the dollar since March. It has been one of the weakest performers among major world currencies this year, due to a combination of government action, Brazil's falling interest rates, and continued concern about the economic crisis in Europe.

The real closed official trading on Tuesday at about 1.88 per dollar following a session in which the central bank purchased dollars in the spot market. Such measures, plus new government taxes on financial transactions passed earlier this year, have had the net effect of weakening what was one of the world's most overvalued currencies throughout 2011.

President Dilma Rousseff has accused the United States and European nations of waging a "currency war" by deploying very accommodative monetary policy. She has said Brazil will defend itself to prevent the resulting wave of foreign capital from damaging its economy.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity to frankly discuss the rationale behind government policy, said that Brazil is trying to weaken the currency now because it believes inflationary risks are low and it anticipates foreign capital flows will pick up again later in 2012.

"What we see is a window of opportunity for the currency to achieve, without great risks or stress," an exchange rate of about 1.90 versus the dollar, the official said.

The official said that pushing the real closer to the 2 per dollar level was not part of the government's plans for now.

"It would require stronger action," the official said.

The official added that no new kinds of measures to weaken the currency are planned at this time.

The real has not been weaker than 1.90 per dollar since briefly puncturing that threshold in November.

Traders say the currency's short-term direction could depend more on global risk aversion related to the euro zone crisis than government intervention in Brazil.

Brazil's economy has experienced little to no growth since the second half of last year, a slowdown that Rousseff and other officials have blamed partly on the strong currency.

However, remaining inflationary pressures in Brazil's economy may also be deterring officials from trying to push the real to the 2 per dollar level.

(Writing by Brian Winter; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger As Overseas Bond Sales Cheer Market
text:
--Brazil's real currency opens trading stronger on successful EU bond sales

--Currency market players cautious, await minutes from Brazilian Central Bank meeting

--Brazilian real opens trading at BRL1.8770, stronger from Monday's close at BRL1.8810


 
   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency opened stronger Tuesday as successful bond sales in several troubled European Union countries boosted investor sentiment ahead of the release of several economic indicators.

Brazil's real tracked gains in overseas market, including the euro's rise against the U.S. dollar, traders said. The real opened at BRL1.8770 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Monday's close at BRL1.8810. The currency later strengthened further to trade at BRL1.8757 to the greenback as of 1224 GMT.

"Overall, the mood is still risk averse, still dominated by Europe's unchanging woes," said Societe Generale in a morning note to clients.

As has often been the case during the ongoing European sovereign debt crisis, Tuesday's session once again kicked off with positive signs. Italy, the Netherlands and Spain all held bond successful bond sales although there were still some signs of weakness, traders said.

The Dutch issue, which came a day after the country's government fell, saw interest rates fall on two-year notes but rise on 25-year bonds. Italy and Spain, meanwhile, paid a higher price to attract investors to a debt rollover auction as yields climbed.

In Brazil, the latest inflation reading is unlikely to derail the Brazilian Central Bank's recent rate-cutting cycle, traders said. The midmonth IPCA-15 consumer price index rose 0.43% through mid-April compared with a 0.25% advance in the same period through mid-March.

Key categories showed signs of accelerating in April, including food prices and housing costs, according to the data.

The latest inflation figure will heighten already intense interest in the meetings from the latest central bank meeting last week, when the bank reduced the benchmark Selic base interest rate to 9.0%. The bank left the door open for future cuts, saying in its accompanying policy statement that "the risks to inflation are still limited" while noting the "fragility of the global economy."

Lower local interest rates are expected to reduce Brazil's lure for investors seeking higher rates of return, thereby reducing pressure on the real to strengthen.

Currency market players are anxious to glean any indication about the future direction of interest rates from the minutes of the meeting, which will be released Thursday.

The real currency will likely take direction from the release of several economic indicators both here and abroad, including Brazil's March current account figures. In the U.S., data on home sales prices will be released and the Federal Reserve begins its latest policy meeting.

In Brazil, market players will be on the lookout for intervention by the Brazilian Central Bank. The bank has been especially active in recent weeks, snapping up dollars in spot-market purchases and restarting sales of foreign-exchange reverse swap contracts. Government officials have also continued the saber-rattling over possible measures aimed at containing the real's recent strength.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt Lag On Signs Of Weaker Global Growth

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and debt weakened Monday on escalating concerns about Europe and outcome of the Federal Reserve's meeting this week.

It didn't help that in the first round of French elections, President Nicolas Sarkozy trailed opposition candidate Francois Hollande; an upset could threaten existing ties in Europe.

Most emerging-market currencies trailed the euro's movement, as it fell more than 0.53% per dollar on the day.

The dollar gained the most against emerging-European currencies. The Hungarian forint, the Czech koruna and the Polish zloty all weakened, with the dollar gaining more than one percentage point against each of these currencies.

Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orban is on a visit to Brussels to meet with European Union officials and to make a case for his country to get the backstop support it seeks from the International Monetary Fund and European Union.

The euro once again edged close to HUF300, but backed off at HUF299.94. Tuesday, Orban has a critical meeting with Jose Manuel Barroso, president of the European Commission, to discuss a potential loan agreement.

Meanwhile, the collapse of budget talks in Holland and poor manufacturing data from Europe that pointed to a recession were enough to push for dollar strength.

Investors are keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve's open-market committee meeting, which could provide markets with clarity on whether the central bank would provide additional liquidity. Until then, emerging-market currencies are likely to trade in this limited range.

Latin American currencies weren't spared. The dollar slipped more than 0.5% against the Mexican peso, Brazilian real and Chilean peso during the day.

Investor interest in emerging-market currencies has dropped to subdued levels, HSBC's currency strategists said in a note. title: Mobius: Govt  Interventions  In  Brazil  Might Harm Economy
text:
Templeton Emerging Markets Group Executive Chairman Mark Mobius said that Brazil's government interventions in the markets might end up hurting Latin America's largest economy.

"We dislike the government's intervention in the natural functioning of the markets, and it creates another variable of uncertainty that in the end goes back and affects the country's economy due to the higher risk," he said in emailed answers to questions by Dow Jones Newswires.

Templeton Emerging Markets Group has approximately $5 billion invested in Brazil.

Brazil's government has been actively trying to weaken the country's currency with measures such as higher taxes and purchases of dollars on the market, which have become even more frequent in the last few days. Deploying an "arsenal" of measures, as described by Finance Minister Guido Mantega, Brazil has been able to lead the real to a lower level than at the end of 2011, after an almost 10% gain in the first months of 2012.

Over the past two years, some emerging market currencies have become overvalued on price-parity basis, creating a dilemma for policymakers as a strong currency can make the country's exports less competitive on the global market, Mobius said.

"It's a delicate balance," he wrote. In the case of Brazil, "it would be wise if the government would make reforms to promote efficiency and innovation, rather than just fight the exchange rate."

Mobius said that the Brazilian central bank is focusing not just on defending price stability, but also, and probably first, in promoting economic activity in the country.

"As the central bank is not independent in Brazil, this has created the view that it is working 'four hands' with the government and tolerating higher inflation."

While not formally independent, Brazil's central bank operates autonomously from the government.

Brazil's central bank cut the benchmark interest rate to 9%, from 9.75%, on Wednesday, the sixth consecutive cut by the bank's monetary-policy committee, or Copom, in the current easing cycle. Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff has been trying to spur growth, not only by weakening the real, but also by making credit cheaper and more available after a modest economic expansion of 2.7% in 2012.

Mobius said that, in the short-term, it is critical that Brazil's government addresses its spending, in size and quality terms. Over the long term, he said, Brazil should focus on increasing its productivity, especially in light of the strong currency.

"There should be structural reforms in areas such as education, tax, pension, the political system, privatizations and efforts to attract infrastructure investments," he wrote.

Mobius said he still finds attractive valuations in places such as Brazil, Russia, China and Southeast Asia, among others. When looking into investing in Brazil, he says he tends to give more emphasis to commodities and consumer companies.

"On the consumer side, we recently visited a beer and soft-drink producer in Brazil. Brazil has the potential to benefit from the increase of the minimum wage this year, and greater purchasing power is expected to increase beer consumption over cachaca (a popular Brazilian distilled alcoholic beverage)," he wrote, referring to Brazil's sugarcane liquor.

Meanwhile, Mobius said he dislikes stocks or sectors which have strong government interference. Even though critical of interventions in Brazil, Mobius said, he doesn't believe "the government wants to scare investors away as that would work against themselves, especially as the country is in the final lap to hosting major international events like the World Cup and generally seems to be behind schedule in delivering proper infrastructure."

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger As  Central Bank  Renews  Intervention
text:
--Brighter outlook abroad helps Brazil real gain against U.S. dollar

--Brazilian Central Bank enters market to buy dollars after one-day respite

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL1.8703 to the dollar

By Jeff Fick

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real recovered from a sharp sell-off the previous session to end stronger Friday, despite the return of Brazilian Central Bank intervention and renewed rhetoric from government officials

The real tracked gains in other currencies against the U.S. dollar, which gave up ground as economic data from Europe painted an improving picture of the single-currency bloc's economy. The real exited active trading at BRL1.8703 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Thursday's closing quote at BRL1.8859 to the greenback.

Solid economic data from Europe helped kick off the session, boosting investor sentiment, traders said. German business confidence advanced in April, according to the Ifo Institute's latest index. The survey rose to 109.9 in April from 109.8 in March, while the current assessment index surprisingly increased to 117.5 from 117.4. U.K. retail sales also surged last month, rising 1.8% from February, well above expectations of a 0.8% increase.

The recent success of bond sales in Spain and Italy also helped ease recent concerns that troubles in the two countries could be a repeat of last year's Greek drama, said Reginaldo Galhardo, foreign-exchange manager at Sao Paulo trading house Treviso.

"People are returning to Europe to recoup losses or lock in profits," Galhardo said.

Investors are also hopeful that the International Monetary Fund will complete a deal to expand its financial resources to stem the threat of contagion from the euro-zone debt crisis. Better-than-expected earnings from U.S. heavyweights Microsoft (MSFT) and General Electric (GE) also led to a brighter outlook.

Europe's troubles, however, remain squarely in focus. French elections on Sunday are overhanging the market as the cost of insuring the country's bonds against default climbed higher. Socialist candidate Francois Hollande, who has questioned the country's austerity measures, appears to be leading incumbent Nicolas Sarkozy in the race to be France's president.

But the biggest shadow overhanging Brazil's currency market remains the country's central bank and its recent string of heavy intervention, Galhardo said. The central bank sat out Thursday's session, when the real approached the BRL1.90-to-the-dollar mark. The currency weakened after Wednesday's expected interest rate cut, which reduced the Selic benchmark rate to 9.0%.

"The real has been under pressure from the central bank and also because of the new taxes the bank has imposed in recent months," Galhardo said.

Thursday's respite broke a string of five-consecutive sessions in which the central bank had held not one but two daily spot-market auctions. With the central bank's absence, traders picked up the game of cat-and-mouse with the central bank by driving the real to a session high near BRL1.86 during Friday's session. That was the central bank's trigger, with the bank jumping into the spot market to buy an undisclosed volume of dollars for BRL1.8710 to the greenback.

"The market is trying to discover at what rate the central bank will intervene," Galhardo said. "It's a question of balance to find the foreign-exchange rate at which the central bank wants the market to stabilize."

Finance Minister Guido Mantega, taking part in the International Monetary Fund and World Bank spring meetings in Washington this weekend, also renewed the government's rhetoric. Mantega repeated his oft-heard complaints about the use of easy monetary policies in the developed world. Brazil blames low interest rates abroad for the flood of liquidity that has often arrived on the shores of Latin America's biggest economy, where towering interest rates have proved an especially seductive lure.

The real's recent weakness, however, was largely attributed to a change in the central bank's most recent policy statement that accompanied Wednesday's interest rate cut. The statement showed that the bank was leaving the door open to further rate cuts with language suggesting that inflation risks in Latin America's largest economy remained low.

"The committee notes that until now, given the fragility of the global economy, the contribution of external environment has been disinflationary," the bank said. The statement represented a change in stance from previous minutes, when the bank indicated that it would likely hold rates at a level above the historic low of 8.75%.

Given the recent heavy central bank intervention and expectations for lower local interest rates, the real appears to have moved to a new level after trading between BRL1.80 and BRL1.83 for several weeks, Galhardo said. Galhardo expects the real to settle in a range between BRL1.85 and BRL1.90 in the near term.

-By Jeff Fick, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-21-2586-6085, Jeff.Fick@dowjones.com [ 20-04-12 2004GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil: No need to change savings accounts rules
text:
(Adds quotes from Brazil's finance minister, background)

WASHINGTON, April 19 (Reuters) - Brazil still doesn't need to change rules on savings accounts, one of the country's most popular investments, after the central bank cut its base interest rate to a near all-time low of 9 percent, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Thursday.

As falling interest rates drive down returns in most of Brazil's bond funds, investors are encouraged to move their money into savings accounts known as "poupanca," which are tax free and pay out a fixed interest of 0.5 percent per month plus a variable rate.

Brazil's central bank on Wednesday cut its base Selic rate by 75 basis points and surprised markets with hints that more cuts may follow to boost Latin America's largest economy.

If rates keep falling, the government would most likely be forced to change the rules of savings accounts - a complicated task that would require Congress' approval.

"With the base interest rate at 9 percent, we don't need to change the rules for savings accounts," Mantega told reporters in Washington after attending a meeting of the BRICS countries - Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

Mantega argued fixed-income funds can still remain attractive by lowering their administration fees.

"Those fees usually fall when interest rates fall," he said.

Asked about Brazil's interventions on the foreign exchange market, Mantega defended the move as necessary to protect the national industry against competitors that are benefiting from weaker currencies.

"We have proved that our currency interventions are efficient and can be used to mitigate the disadvantages that our industries have been facing."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real leads Latam  currencies  lower
text:
* Brazil's real weakens 1 pct; central bank intervenes

* Mexican peso loses 0.5 pct; Chile peso 0.9 pct weaker

* Commodity prices down ahead of Spain's bond sale

By Alonso Soto

SAO PAULO, April 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped to its weakest level this year on Wednesday and became the worst-performing major world currency so far this month, hit by falling commodity prices and relentless central bank interventions.

The real fell 1 percent to 1.8747 per dollar on Wednesday, after touching its weakest level since Dec. 29. The currency has lost nearly 2.7 percent since the start of April, the biggest slide among the world's 36 most traded currencies, according to Reuters data.

Brazil's central bank intensified its foreign exchange interventions this week with two dollar-buying auctions per day, its quickest pace this year, piling onto the weakening currency.

The auctions are part of the bank's efforts to build up reserves and coincide with the government's battle against the strong local currency, which has cut into exports and hurt local industries with a flood of cheap imports.

"A fall in commodity prices abroad, mostly oil, and forex intervention by the central bank has led to a sharp fall of the real versus the dollar," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for Brazil at WestLB.

The Thomson Reuters-Jefferies CRB Index, a global commodities benchmark, dropped 1 percent on Wednesday as investor risk appetite retreated, hurting the currencies of Latin America's major raw material exporters.

Renewed focus on the euro zone debt crisis also weighed on Latin American currencies a day ahead of a government bond sale in Spain, as the strains on the euro zone drove investors to the perceived safety of the dollar.

Mexico's peso weakened 0.5 percent to 13.1616 per dollar, and the Chilean peso shed 0.9 percent to 488.6 per dollar, while remaining in a narrow band that has penned in trading since early March.

"There was a lot of caution in the market, with the peso moving between 13.10 and 13.16 per dollar, which is the 100-day moving average, as everyone waits for Spain's auction tomorrow," said Cesar Elizalde, a trader at Banorte-IXE in Mexico City.

"If it goes badly, we could see the peso at 13.30 per dollar without a problem," he said.

The peso has lost about 2.4 percent this month after a sharp rally in the first two months of the year, pressured by concerns about the euro zone debt crisis, patchy economic growth in the United States, and the potential for a sharp slowdown in China.
