title: Brazilian Real, Emerging Market  Currencies  Fall; Debt Little Changed
text:
--Emerging-market currencies weaken broadly

--Brazilian real erases 2012 gains on ongoing central-bank intervention

--Emerging-market debt is little changed but Argentina underperforms


 
    By Erin McCarthy 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real led emerging-market currencies' fall Wednesday, while debt held steady, as concerns about the euro-zone debt crisis dominated markets and investors focused on ongoing intervention in Brazil.

Markets were anxiously gearing up for a Spanish bond auction Thursday, after Spain's borrowing costs rose in an auction earlier this week. Rising Spanish government bond yields have made the country the latest focal point of the euro-zone debt saga, especially as it struggles to rein in its fiscal deficit through tough austerity measures.

"I do get a sense that there's a little bit of nervousness as there's a Spanish auction tomorrow," said Win Thin, Brown Brothers Harriman's global head of emerging-market currency strategy.

Broader market concerns modestly weighed down emerging-market currencies like the Mexican peso and South African rand, which often takes cues from market sentiment. Emerging-market central-bank rate decisions were also in focus, with a string of policy-setting meetings this week.

The Brazilian real, however, stood out, as it erased all of its 2012 gains Wednesday on ongoing central-bank intervention. The dollar climbed to BRL1.8827, marking the real's weakest level since Dec. 29, 2011. Brazil's central bank stepped into the foreign-exchange market twice Wednesday to buy dollars. Brazil's Treasury also issued a sovereign bond denominated in reais in the international market this week, in part to help in the fight against the real appreciation.

This "more aggressive intervention" and is "not good for the currency," Thin said.

Investors also were waiting for Brazil's rate decision Wednesday night. The central bank is widely expected to cut the Selic benchmark rate by 75 basis points to nine basis points.

Elsewhere in the region, the Mexican peso slipped in line with U.S. stocks. It fell 0.4%, with the dollar buying MXN13.1616 late Wednesday, according to CQG.

The South African rand slipped 0.3% against the dollar, which traded at ZAR7.8356. Earlier Wednesday, data showed inflation in South Africa slowed to 6.0% on the year in March from 6.1% in February.

The Turkish lira, meanwhile, held up relatively well compared with other currencies' broad decline. The dollar traded flat on the day against the lira, at TRY1.7890. A more hawkish tone from Turkey's central bank provided support for the lira, analysts said.

Turkey's central bank Wednesday held all its key policy rates steady, in line with expectations, but warned it may have to tighten market interest rates more regularly to curb rising inflation spurred by higher oil prices.

title: UPDATE: Brazil's Real Gives Back Gains of 2012
text:
(Adds currency level in midafternoon trading and comments by Nathan Blanche, partner at consulting firm Tendencias Consultoria.)

By Luciana Magalhaes and Rogerio Jelmayer

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--After a strong start in 2012, the real lost ground against the dollar in March and April and gave back all gains saw this year, as the government's intervention has played a key role in curbing the local currency's appreciation.

To contain the real's almost 10% gains against the dollar in the beginning of the year, Brazilian authorities have stepped up interventions in the currency market. Brazil's Treasury has also issued a sovereign bond denominated in reais in the international market this week, in part to help in the fight against the real appreciation.

The Brazilian real traded earlier today at the BRL 1.866 level, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. The currency closed at BRL1.8664 at the end of 2011. In mid-afternoon session Wednesday, the Brazilian real was trading at BRL1.877 per dollar in Sao Paulo.

Foreign direct investment and financial flows to Brazil's high-yielding capital markets have drawn dollars to the emerging economy. Brazil's president, Dilma Rousseff, has been a vocal defender of lower interest rates, to reduce the costs of financing in Brazil and to make Brazilian assets less attractive to foreigners.

Even though in an easing cycle, Brazilian interest rates currently stand at 9.75% a year, while rates in the U.S. and Europe are near zero. Brazil's central bank is expected to cut the so-called Selic benchmark rate to 9% later Wednesday.

"The market is on the hands of the government", said Joao Medeiros, currency director at Sao Paulo brokerage Pioneer Corretora. He said that the market was previously expecting the real to end 2012 at the BRL1.75 level against the greenback. "Now, I think it's possible it will be at around BRL1.90 per dollar, but nobody knows. We have to ask Mantega," he said, referring to Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega.

"If you make projections based on fundamentals, it's very hard now to know where the currency is heading too. It depends on how much the Finance Ministry wants to spend to keep the real from appreciating", said Nathan Blanche, a partner at Sao Paulo-based consulting firm Tendencias Consultoria.

"Even with the current level of the currency, Brazil's central bank did auctions today. They are taking advantage of the lower inflation pressure to keep the real down", Blanche added. Brazil's central bank on Wednesday bought U.S. dollars at a spot-market in two auctions. The last one at BRL1.880 to the dollar. The central bank didn't reveal the volume of dollars purchased.

title: *DJ S&P Sees Brazil Risks 'Balanced' At Current Ratings Level
text:
17 Apr 2012 12:46 EDT *DJ  S&P: Progress In Brazil Is 'Very Slow and Gradual'

17 Apr 2012 12:46 EDT *DJ  S&P: Brazil Response To Global Crisis Hard To Assess Amid Turmoil

17 Apr 2012 12:46 EDT *DJ  S&P: Brazil Central Bank Proven Right On Decision To Cut Rates

17 Apr 2012 12:46 EDT *DJ  S&P: Hard To Assess Whether Brazil FX Intervention Is Appropriate

17 Apr 2012 12:46 EDT *DJ  S&P: Brazil Willing To Test, Not Cross, Limits On FX Intervention

17 Apr 2012 12:47 EDT DJ  Brazil Progress On Growth Obstacles Is 'Slow And Gradual' -S&P


 
  By Matthew Cowley 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones) -- Brazil's taxes are high, its investment is too low, and progress in tackling the deep-rooted issues underlying those obstacles to growth is "very slow and gradual," according to analysts at ratings agency Standard and Poor's.

"We see some progress in some areas, but we see the progress is very slow and gradual," said Sebastian Briozzo, S&P's director of Latin America credit. Such gradualism has been the case in Brazil over the last 15 years. For now, "the positive and the negatives on the credit are balanced at the current rating level," he told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview.

S&P upgraded Brazil to triple-B in November, with a stable outlook, a further reflection of the country's ability to cope with international crises. Brazil's economic stability over the last decade or so has provided the government with the means to respond to global crises, helping shore up the domestic economy. But the results have been uneven, which is no surprise given the extent of the international turmoil.

"There's a world out there that's very difficult to predict," Briozzo said.

Brazil's economy surged sharply in 2010, sparking fears of overheating, but then dropped back quickly in 2011, as those government efforts on spending and credit were withdrawn. Economists are expecting another surge in the second half of the year as the government once again moves into action. The tools are still in the early stages of development, and it's a tricky time to be putting them to the test.

The central bank's controversial decision last August to start sharply cutting interest rates has been proven right, even though it was widely criticized by many market participants at the time, Briozzo said.

As Brazil's growth ground to a halt late last year, amid a surging European sovereign-debt crisis, the central bank responded by cutting rates at a time when inflation was above the upper limit of its target and heading higher. Inflation ended the year at 6.5%; it has since dropped back to 5.2%.

Brazil's government also took steps to prevent what it sees as an over-appreciation of the Brazilian currency versus major currencies such as the dollar, arguing that the strength undermines the competitiveness of the nation's exporters and makes imports cheaper. The central bank has bought dollars to absorb inflows and build its foreign currency reserves, while the government has applied a financial transaction tax, known as IOF, to certain types of capital flows.

"How appropriate or not this is, is difficult to assess within this environment," Briozzo said. Although the IOF taxes do introduce distortions, letting the currency appreciate also has costs, Briozzo noted.

The government is walking a fine line between trying to deter short-term flows but attract longer-term foreign savings, which are much needed to lift investments, he said. The Brazilian government appears to be "willing to test the limits, but not to cross the limits," he said.

In particular, an inability to increase investment is one of the major sticking points for steadier, faster economic growth, Briozzo said. Brazil's economy grew at a sluggish 2.7% last year, the slowest rate in Latin America, and its performance in recent years compares unfavorably with other emerging-market juggernauts such as India and China.

"There's a long list of reasons ... but at the end of the day we come back to fiscal issues, and there's a government that invests too little. This is the main restriction for growing at more reasonable or higher growth rates over the medium term," Briozzo said.

"Despite all the strengths and the improvements, it's pretty difficult to get investment levels above 20%" of gross domestic product in Brazil, Briozzo said.

Brazil spends about 11.5% of government revenues on interest payments, versus 7% for most triple-B-rated countries, he pointed out. "This is one of the indicators where Brazil is completely an outlier," Briozzo said.

With interest rates coming down, it may be an opportunity to move away from debt linked to the central bank's Selic interest rate, he said. Changes in market sentiment, and therefore on interest rates, can have a much more immediate impact in terms of driving up the government's borrowing costs when debt is linked to the Selic, he said.

At the end of February, just under 28% of federal debt was linked to the Selic, the lowest level since 1997. In a recent interview, Paulo Valle, Brazil's Treasury deputy secretary, said the government is aiming to reduce that to between 10% and 20% of total federal debt, although he didn't specify a timetable for meeting that goal.

On the positive side, much of Brazil's debt is now denominated in local currency, and there's a deep pool of capital. However, "the terms of that debt is expensive, and shorter-term," Briozzo said.

The government's fiscal deficit last year was about 2.6% of GDP, but could fall to around 1.8% of GDP this year, as the country will be paying much less on interest, he said. Reducing interest payments is one way for the government to free up money for investments, he said.

Meanwhile, the analysts said the strong growth of credit in Brazil in recent years isn't a problem at the moment, but does require attention.

"Is it something about to blow up? No. We're looking at it. It's an issue that requires attention and that we're following very closely because it has the potential to become a problem. So far it's not," said Roberto Sifon-Arevalo, S&P's lead analytical manager for Latin America sovereign ratings.

-By Matthew Cowley, Dow Jones Newswires; +55 11 3544 7082; matthew.cowley@dowjones.com

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt Improve On Rising Confidence
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and debt posted sharp gains Tuesday on investors' increased confidence after a strong auction of Spanish bonds and rise in German investor confidence.

The South African rand and the Mexican peso led the rally in emerging-market currencies. The South African rand rallied after Citigroup indicated it plans to add South Africa to its world government-bond index Oct. 1.

The USD/ZAR is trading at 7.8060, down 1.66% on the day. The index inclusion is expected to lead to a surge in demand for South African bonds in the range of $5 billion to $7.5 billion from portfolio managers. Citi, however, cautioned South Africa would have to keep the size of its outstanding debt above $88 billion. The move by Citi puts South Africa in the same rank as other emerging-market nations in the index including Malaysia, Poland and Mexico.

The Mexican peso also had a similar strong run, with the USD/MXN pair trading at 13.0964, down 0.9% on the day.

"Latin American currencies, in general, recovered ground lost in previous session," said Alejandro Cuadrado, head of Latin American foreign exchange strategy at BBVA.

"However, Brazilian real continued to be the outlier on more central bank action, recurrent over the past few sessions," he said.

The dollar gained 0.30% on the real to BRL1.8529, pushing the cross much closer to nearly wiping out all the gains it has made so far this year. The central bank's continued intervention also has led to speculation Brazil may be pushing for a dollar level higher than BRL1.80. But BBVA's Cuadrado expects the USD/BRL pair to hover around the 1.83 to 1.84 level, with the central bank weakening the currency further during bearish sessions.

The market also awaits an expected cut of 75 basis points Wednesday on the selic rate, which would help the country prod domestic growth. On a similar theme, India's central bank cut its interest rates unexpectedly by 50 basis points as a way to spur production and consumption, in a country expected to have its growth rate slacken below 7%.

Argentina's announced move to take over the management of energy producer YPF SA (YPF, YPFD.BA) continued to reverberate through the markets with risk premiums on the country's bonds weakening by another 16 basis points to 882 basis points over comparable Treasury yields.

Other emerging-market debt traded tighter with risk premiums narrowing by seven basis points to 356 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Global.

Two sovereigns tapped the bond markets Tuesday.

Brazil's National Treasury launched BRL3 billion ($1.6 billion) in sovereign overseas bonds denominated in reais and due 2024, a part of its effort to improve its sovereign-debt profile and the liquidity of sovereign outstanding bonds, a person familiar with the deal said.

The bonds were priced with a yield of 8.6%, with proceeds to go toward buying back bonds with shorter maturities. Also, Brazil is offering to pay BRL1,205 for outstanding bonds due 2016 with a face value of BRL1,000, and BRL1,300 for bonds due 2022 with a face value of BRL1,000. The government is seeking to build a real-denominated yield curve similar to the curve of the country's domestically issued debt.

The Republic of Indonesia launched a $2 billion, 10-year bond and a $500 million reopening of its 2042 bond, according to investors familiar with the deal. The 10-year bond is set at a yield of 3.85% while the 2042 is at 4.95%, the investors said. Investors are eager for such dollar-denominated debt issued by emerging-market countries, especially those rated at investment grade like Indonesia.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Weaker On  Interventions , Chinese Growth
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real closed sharply weaker Friday, as concerns about China's economic slowdown and Spain's financial crisis cast a pall over global markets while the Brazilian Central Bank continued intervening to reduce the supply of dollars on the local market.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.8370 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.8308 after the open and Thursday's close of BRL1.8260.

Dampening investor sentiment from the start of local trading was a report from China, the world's No. 2 economy and the biggest buyer of Brazilian exports, showing that gross domestic product expanded in the first quarter by its slowest pace in three years.

Other data showed a surge in borrowing by Spanish financial institutions from the European Central Bank, reflecting weak demand from private investors and drawing attention to Spain's ongoing debt troubles. Stock markets fell broadly, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% at the close.

In Brazil, the central bank bought an undisclosed amount of U.S. dollars off the local spot market in two separate auctions, after it also held two auctions Thursday.

Currency analysts at Citi, who on Thursday identified a "sizable inflow" of as much as $2 billion expected from a mining company, said Friday that the capital was likely to enter Brazil gradually.

"Either the supposedly hefty inflow from the mining company was offset by another substantial outflow, or its inflow will be scattered between today and April 30," Citi analyst Conrado Lima said in a note. "With higher odds of the latter option, I personally believe that the Brazilian Central Bank will be able to net the inflow smoothly."

For the upcoming week, traders have their eyes on a monetary-policy decision by Brazil's Central Bank on Wednesday and data on February economic growth due out Monday.

Brazil's monetary-policy committee is widely expected to reduce its baseline Selic interest rate by 0.75 percentage point next week to 9%. With that, the current easing cycle is likely to close, analysts say.

"As we have said, the international scenario should continue weakening, causing worries among monetary authorities regarding more intense contagion on the domestic economy," Santander bank said in a weekly outlook.

In other local economic news, Brazil's Planning Ministry said Friday in a budget-guideline proposal that growth should accelerate next year while inflation will remain in line with government targets. The document said the economy should grow by 5.5% in 2013 and 4.5% this year.

Planning Minister Miriam Belchior also reiterated the government's commitment to keeping the currency from strengthening too much.

"We don't look at a defined parameter for the exchange rate," Belchior said. "We're going to work to avoid that it hurts the national economy, and we'll be working, as we have since 2010, to keep the rate from falling too low."

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Weakened By Global Concerns
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies and debt were weaker again as investors' worry about Europe and China escalated. The unexpected decline in U.S. consumer sentiment also weighed on markets.

A softer growth in China held emerging markets in check. The country's first quarter growth rate was at an 8.1% annualized rate, lower than expectations of 8.3%. At the same time, investors were too uncertain about Spain and closed positions ahead of the weekend leading to a weakening of yields on the sovereign's debt again.

The escalation of global concerns has led investors to scale back their exposure to assets with higher risk and higher returns such as emerging market assets. Many investors are taking profits and closing their positions earlier than expected. In sync with this trend is the outflow of $99 million out of emerging market focused funds in the week ended Wednesday, according to flows from EPFR Global.

Much of the outflows were driven by investors exiting local-currency and blended funds. This is the second time so far this year that emerging market funds have seen outflows; the previous time was during the week ended Jan. 18.

"In light of the global rout and price declines, it is somewhat reassuring that investor flows were not more severe," said David Spegel, global head of emerging markets strategy at ING Financial Markets.

"People are starting to kick the tires on their assumptions much earlier in the year," said Cameron Brandt, EPFR's director of research. "Peoples' tendency to sell and go away in May has now just advanced to late March and early April."

Currencies like the South African rand and the Mexican peso were weaker on the day, with the dollar gaining nearly a 1% on each. The dollar-peso was trading at MXN13.1638, up 1.04% on the day. While the dollar-rand pair was at ZAR7.9397, up 0.85% on the day.

Investors, while confident that emerging market economies would fare better than developed markets, expect these currencies to underperform in the next few months. In the short term, the Brazilian real is expected to keep weakening on central bank intervention measures, and the ruble strengthen on technical support and steady oil prices.

Emerging market sovereign bonds were weaker and risk premiums on these bonds widened by five basis points to 360 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Global. Risk premiums on Argentina's bonds widened by 13 basis points after reports of the government taking a majority stake on the country's largest energy producer surfaced. Market participants have been asking how the country plans to finance the acquisition.

Meanwhile, in other parts of Latin America, central banks of Brazil and Peru intervened in the currency market to moderate the pace of their currency appreciation.

Peru's central bank is likely to keep its key rates unchanged, and use its foreign exchange as a tool to tighten monetary policy, said Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura. The bank held rates at 4.25% Thursday. Since May 2011, the Peruvian sol's real effective exchange rate or inflation-adjusted value against a basket of peers has appreciated by 5%, mostly engineered by the central bank, he said. Peru's inflation pressures have eased, and there's little need to change rates.

That policy, however, could change if the U.S. Fed embarks on another round of economic stimulus measures termed "quantitative easing," or QE3, Berber said.

The dollar-sol pair remains almost unchanged at PEN2.660 on the day after another round of central bank intervention.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Closes Weaker On Concern About Growth,  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened Wednesday on lingering concern about Chinese and European demand, and as investors remain wary of possible intervention by Brazil's government to weaken its currency.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.8329 to the dollar, weaker than its previous close at BRL1.8299, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

"Markets have been suffering in recent days as a result of news from Europe and China," said Eduardo Galasini, a fixed-income manager at Banco Banif in Sao Paulo.

The real started to slump Tuesday after China reported weaker-than-expected import and export data, raising concern that Brazil's biggest trading partner could reduce its purchases of the Latin American country's commodities. In Europe, Italian and Spanish bond yields rose, reviving concern about the ability of the region to deal with high debt levels.

On Wednesday, yields improved somewhat, but that was countered by data from Spain showing that industrial production fell at a faster pace. That helped push up the costs of protection against a Spanish debt default.

Comments by Brazil Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Tuesday, meanwhile, affirmed the government's stance that a strong currency hurts exports so the government will act to stop any gains in the real. Mantega said that the government will continue with its exchange-rate policy to avoid an appreciation of the real and to boost competitiveness.

In the past, the central bank has stepped into currency markets to buy up excess dollars in an effort to boost the dollar against the real, while the Finance Ministry has on occasion imposed higher taxes, such as the so-called IOF tax on speculative inflows.

"You have declarations from the government that they won't let the real gain [against the dollar]," Banif's Galasini said in a phone interview. "With the reduction in interest rates and the IOF there's been a reduction in spreads and so speculative investors think twice" before pouring more money into the country, he said.

Data released Wednesday showed a slight uptick in Brazil's general price index, known as the IGP-M, but still within expectations. The data did little to dissuade traders from the view that the central bank will cut rates by 75 basis points, to 9%, when it meets next week to set the benchmark Selic rate.

Brazil has one of the highest rates in the world, which has attracted heavy inflows and worked against efforts to contain the real's strength, but each rate cut removes a bit of the appeal for traders, who borrow at near-zero rates from developed economies to buy fixed-income assets in Brazil.

At the margins there has also been an uptick in Brazilians sending money abroad as the central bank eases restrictions. Sao Paulo-based TOV Corretora said that since the central bank doubled in January the value of permitted transactions--raising to $100,000 from $50,000 the limit for how much Brazilian investors can freely send abroad in a single transaction--the brokerage has seen the volume of transactions go up by 40%.

TOV said in the statement that it expects the central bank to double that limit again soon, but the central bank declined to comment.

5 Apr 2012 11:11 EDT DJ  Brazil Real Seen Ending 2012 At BRL1.75, Despite Interventions--Bradesco's Barros

--Brazilian real likely to end 2012 at BRL1.75 to the U.S. dollar, Bradesco chief economist says

--Without intervention by central bank, government, real would trade at BRL1.64-BRL1.65

--Elevated commodities prices will keep appreciation pressure on real, Octavio de Barros says 


 
   By Rogerio Jelmayer and Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency will likely end 2012 at BRL1.75 to the dollar, despite continued intervention in local foreign-exchange markets by the government and Brazilian Central Bank, Banco Bradesco (BBD, BBDC4.BR) Chief Economist Octavio de Barros said Thursday.

Speaking on the sidelines of an event in Sao Paolo, Barros said, "looking only at the fundamentals, the real should be trading today at a rate of BRL1.64 or BRL1.65 [to the U.S. dollar]. This is based on the fact that the real is one of the so-called commodities currencies, such as the Australian or Canadian dollars.

"The only reason that the real is not trading at this level is because of government intervention," Barros added.

Brazil has been aggressive with interventions in local currency markets as well as implementing measures to stave off speculative inflows in recent months. The measures have included higher taxes on foreign-exchange derivatives positions, overseas loans and bond issues. The Brazilian Central Bank has stepped up spot-market dollar purchases and auctions of reverse-swap contracts, while also cutting interest rates to diminish investor interest in local fixed-income assets.

"The forces of foreign-exchange appreciation continue," Barros said, noting that the bias toward currency appreciation is largely based on commodities prices remaining at current high levels.

The central bank started the rate-cutting cycle in August, bringing the benchmark Selic base interest rate to 9.75% from a 2011 high of 12.5%. Brazil's interest rates, however, still remain among the highest of any major economy.

Bradesco expects the rate reductions to continue during the central bank's meeting later this month, with the Selic falling to 9%, Barros said. The central bank could also leave the door open for additional cuts, the economist added.

"My outlook is still that the Selic is going to fall to 9% and be maintained at this level for a long time, but yes, there is a possibility that it could fall below this level," Barros said.

The economist noted Brazil's surprisingly low inflation imprint in March, with the official IPCA consumer price index advancing 0.21% compared with February's 0.45% increase. Barros lauded the central bank's performance under bank President Alexandre Tombini, who deftly guided monetary policy during last year's persistent inflation fight.

"The IPCA surprised the whole market and proved that Tombini is enlightened," Barros said. "The scenario that the central bank outlined is becoming reality."

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weaker On Fear Of New Government Measures

   By Rogerio Jelmayer and Matthew Cowley

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's government claims success in preventing the currency from appreciating, but the negative collateral effects may now be spreading to the government's funding efforts.

"The government's intervention in the foreign-exchange market and its intention to issue bonds denominated in Brazilian reais are conflicting," said Rodrigo Fittipaldi, director of debt capital markets at BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo. "With these signals it is difficult to create an environment of confidence for international investors [to buy real-denominated bonds]," he added.

Brazil's government has fought to contain the strong appreciation of the Brazilian real, which it blames on easy-money policies adopted in places such as the U.S. and Europe to help resolve financial and economic crises. Brazilian officials say this makes Brazil's exports more expensive and imports cheaper, harming the local manufacturing base.

To prevent appreciation, the central bank has bought up dollars while the government has surgically applied a financial-transactions tax, or IOF, to target specific investments deemed to be "speculative." Finance Minister Guido Mantega this week reiterated the government's willingness to intervene as necessary.

The central bank has also cut interest rates aggressively, with its key rate falling to 9.75% per year, from 12.50% last July, and more cuts are expected. One of the effects of lowering rates is to reduce some of the yield over other countries, which has proved so alluring to investors.

After a strong start to the year, the real lost ground against the dollar in March, but is still about 2% stronger from year-end, after weakening 11% against the dollar in 2011. Investors blame a conflation of various events, including renewed fears about Europe's debt problems, but also because of the Brazilian government's constant meddling, making it hard for investors to discern a broader goal or stable market outlook.

"There's an impression that the government has run out of ideas," said Tony Volpon, of Nomura Securities. "There is no clear signal of what the policy is anymore."

That could now be weighing on the efforts to borrow overseas. Last week, Federal Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said the government continues to study opportunities to launch a sovereign bond abroad denominated in the local currency.

The government has argued that selling real-denominated bonds overseas helps counter the appreciation trend; investors still get a juicier yield than is available on a dollar-denominated bond, but they don't have to put their money directly into Brazil. That means less pressure on the currency--unless the government opts to repatriate the proceeds--and it can also attract investors that wouldn't traditionally invest in Brazilian assets.

"We continue to insist that the risk/reward is not attractive with constant foreign exchange intervention headlines from Finance Minister Mantega, which perversely threatens foreign exchange losses at a moment when public credit officials are reportedly seeking interest on [Brazilian real] global issuance," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies & Co, in a research report.

The most recent sale of bonds denominated in Brazilian reais took place in October 2010, when the Treasury raised BRL1.1 billion by reopening a Global bond maturing in 2028, at a yield of 8.85%. One month before that, it sold a U.S. dollar bond due 2041, paying 5.2%. For some investors, that difference will continue to make denominated bonds attractive.

"The political and economic situation in Brazil is very stable and, even with more risks, there is a demand by international investors for [real-denominated] bonds," said Paulo Petrassi, a fund manager at Leme Investimentos in Florianopolis, Brazil.

title: Brazil  Real Weakens On  Intervention  Fears, Europe Concerns
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's government has been able to keep currency traders at bay with threats to step into exchange markets to prevent a rapid strengthening of the real, but some investors say it may have to back up those promises and take real action soon.

Brazil's real was little changed Wednesday, weakening slightly against the greenback to BRL1.8269 per dollar, from its previous close of 1.8243. The real has been trading weaker than 1.80 since mid-March on concern the government will levy new taxes on currency trading--expanding existing taxes or imposing new ones--to curb gains in the currency.

"I have to take my hat off to the government," said Ovidio Plinio Soares, a currency trader at Interbolsa do Brasil, in Sao Paulo. "With numerous threats they've managed to leave the market very anxious, and that's prevented the dollar's decline, although it hasn't been able to strengthen it."

Last month the government extended the so-called IOF tax to overseas loans of up to five years, after previously extending it to cover loans of up to three years. In the following days, the central bank stepped in to buy up excess dollars in spot or forward auctions.

The government has reiterated its commitment to keeping the real at "reasonable" levels in order to help the competitiveness of its industry, but it hasn't announced new measures. More recently, the central bank, which used to carry out two auctions a day, has backed off and carried out one auction Tuesday while remaining quiet Wednesday.

Yet the nervousness remains, reflected in less-volatile trading sessions and a general weakening trend: since the end of February, the real has continually weakened from 1.70. That led a New York-based trader to say that "with the heightened governmental scrutiny, this very novel behavior can have legs," referring to the real's weakening trend.

Banco Santander noted the "escalating intervention" promise could push the real to 1.90 per dollar.

But for some, that trend won't depend on government bluster alone, but on government action as well.

Threatening intervention whenever the real strengthens "has an expiration date," Interbolsa's Soares said. "The time will come when the market will want to challenge the government," at which point policy makers will need a decisive response.

So far, Brazil's leaders have yet to test out a response, with bad news from Europe Wednesday quelling appreciation pressures on the real.

European markets were in decline after the Spanish government managed to sell just 2.56 billion euros ($3.36 billion) worth of bonds, at the bottom of its planned range, and at yields that were well above previous auctions. Following the auction, yields on 10-year Spanish government debt rose to the highest levels since Jan. 9 on doubts over whether the country will be able to meet a difficult budget deficit target.

The rise in Spanish yields, investors worry, could boost yields in other bond markets, testing the euro zone's ability to deal with the higher costs of debt.

In the U.S., meanwhile, private-sector payrolls increased 209,000 in March, down from a revised increase of 230,000 in February. The March number was a bit above estimates of 200,000 but didn't do much to alter the real's decline.

title: Goldman's O'Neill: Brazil Can Grow 4% Or More In Next 5 Years
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--One of the world's top bankers painted an optimistic picture Tuesday for big emerging markets, saying Brazil and China should continue growing their economies at a healthy pace in coming years.

"Brazil can grow 4%, if not more, in the next five years," said Jim O'Neill, president of Goldman Sachs Asset Management, at an event in Sao Paulo.

O'Neill also said he sees a possible slowdown in China, the world's second-largest economy, as the result of deliberate policies by the government. But growth should continue.

"China isn't landing anytime soon," the banker said.

Burgeoning Chinese appetite for commodities such as soybeans and iron ore, of which Brazil is among the world's top producers, has provided a key pillar to Brazil's economic boom in recent years.

But economists worry about the future trajectory of Brazil's economy amid stubborn inflation and a strong local currency that hurts the industrial sector's competitiveness.

Brazilian officials have become increasingly vocal in recent months about the role of excessive liquidity--a by-product of loose monetary policies in stagnating developed economies--in its currency's appreciation trend. Brazil has also launched wave after wave of measures and interventions to weaken its real.

"Policymakers are generally right to make [the currency] less attractive," O'Neill said. "But I don't think they should blame everybody else in the world."

O'Neill also said Brazil's government should encourage the central bank to act independently. The Brazilian Central Bank, which operates autonomously from the government, has been suspected by some analysts of coming under pressure from the government to spur growth in recent months.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico, Chile pesos gain on China, US data
text:
* Mexico peso gains 0.7 percent; Brazil real off 0.31 percent

* Real underperformed in 1st quarter, intervention fears weigh

* Chile peso gains 1.06 percent, copper up 1 percent

By Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO, April 2 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean pesos strengthened on Monday after manufacturing data from the world's two largest economies beat forecasts, though Brazil's real weakened on "the specter of intervention."

Data showed new factory orders in China rose to an 11-month high in March while growth in U.S. manufacturing surpassed economists' expectations in February.

China and the United States are Latin America's top trade partners. The price of metals such as copper, exported by many Latin American countries, rose after the manufacturing data pointed to sustained demand from the world's economic giants.

"The data showed growth is generally holding up reasonably well, commodities prices are making significant gains," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research at RBC Securities in Toronto.

Chile's peso gained the most out of the region's currencies, ending 1.06 percent stronger to bid 483.1 per U.S. dollar. That was its strongest close in two weeks.

Copper for delivery in three months rose 1 percent.

Chile gets more than half of its export earnings from the red metal, a key component in electrical and electronic equipment.

"This was a completely favorable scenario for the peso," said one trader in Santiago.

Mexico's currency, which had weakened for the five previous sessions, gained 0.7 percent to 12.7281 per dollar.

The Mexican peso is particularly sensitive to U.S. manufacturing data as many Mexicans work in U.S. factories and the United States buys nearly 80 percent of Mexico's exports by value.

REAL BUCKS TREND

Brazil's real, however, weakened 0.31 percent to close bidding 1.8277 per dollar. Government measures to weaken the currency and data showing the pace of manufacturing in Brazil had slowed for a third straight month weighed.

"The ongoing specter of intervention on the part of the government is the key reason," said RBC's Chamie.

"We also had a weaker-than-expected PMI," he said, referring to Markit's Brazil Manufacturing Purchasing Manager's Index.

The index edged down to 51.1 last month from 51.4 in February.

Brazil's central bank often purchases dollars in the spot market on days the currency is strengthening as policymakers aim to weaken the real in an effort to make Brazil's manufacturing exports more competitive.

The government has also raised its financial transactions or "IOF" tax and on March 12 extended its scope to foreign debt maturing in up to five years. Some traders have sold the real fearing the government could take additional measures like extending the tax to all financial transactions.

Investors are also down on the real because Brazil's central bank is expected to lower interest rates in coming months. That would curb potential returns in Brazil as economic growth slows.

"Even if they aren't introducing new currency measures, these are all factors that will restrain the real," said Nicholas Bennenbroek, head of currency strategy at Wells Fargo in New York.

"Chile has had one of the stronger currencies because inflation is favorable and the central bank is not likely to cut rates," he added.

The real strengthened 2.17 percent in the first quarter of 2012, reaching just a third of the Chilean peso's gains.

(Additional reporting by Froilan Romero in Santiago)

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weaker As Global Economic Outlook Sours
text:
--Economic data from abroad fail to excite global financial markets

--Concerns about sluggish growth weigh, especially prospects for Chinese slowdown

--Brazilian real opens trading at BRL1.8256, weaker from Friday's close at BRL1.8227


 
   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency weakened at the start of second-quarter trading Monday, undermined by economic data from abroad that continue to cast a pall over prospects for global economic growth.

Weak economic data from Europe and China kept global currencies from making any strong moves, with the euro trading in a tight range. The real opened at BRL1.8256 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was weaker from Friday's close at BRL1.8227. The currency later weakened further to trade at BRL1.8270.

Local players have shifted attention toward prospects for global economic growth while at the same time casting a wary eye toward Brazil's recent heavy intervention in the currency market. A slowing global economy would diminish demand for commodities and reduce prices, a key barometer for the real currency.

In China, conflicting figures on economic activity continued to raise concerns about a slowdown in the Asian giant, which is Brazil's leading trade partner and a key consumer of the country's commodities exports such as iron ore and soy. Japan's Tankan survey also showed diminished business confidence.

Europe, meanwhile, continued to struggle under the weight of austerity measures with indicators from France, Germany and Italy showing their respective economies contracting, while the number of unemployed in the single-currency bloc reached a record high.

The overseas troubles are also reaching Brazil, with the country's overvalued currency leading to a steep drop-off in Brazil's industrial sector. The government is expected to unveil Tuesday a new package of measures aimed at stimulating key segments of the country's industrial sector.

"Slowing global economic momentum is pitted against awesomely accommodative monetary policy. This was a one-sided fight in [the first quarter] as investors shunned the horrifically negative real rates of return on offer from safe and sensible assets and made rude gestures in the direction of bearish pundits," said Societe Generale in a note to clients. "[The second quarter] is likely to follow a similar pattern."

Harsher discourse by Brazil's government about the strength of the real also continues to weigh on the currency, according to Miriam Tavares, director of foreign exchange at Sao Paulo trading house AGK Corretora. In her week-ahead look at markets, Tavares said that "the foreign-exchange rate has been practically parked at a level a little above BRL1.80 to the dollar, with the tougher talk and intervention by authorities."

Last week, the Brazilian Central Bank rolled over reverse-swap contracts maturing April 2. The bank sold more than $2 billion worth of new swaps that will mature in June and July. Reverse-swap auctions are among the measures that the central bank uses to support the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real in local currency markets. The reverse swaps remove real exposure from the market by exchanging currency positions for paper linked to local interest rates, which is considered safer and less volatile.

Despite increasing expectations for inflation in Brazil, the central bank is also expected to continue its recent interest rate cutting cycle. Lower interest rates should diminish Brazil's allure for foreign investors seeking higher rates of return, traders said. The benchmark Selic base interest rate currently stands at 9.75%.

Currency trading will likely take further direction Monday from the U.S., where the Institute for Supply Management will release manufacturing data for March and the government will report construction spending for February.

title: UPDATE: Mexico Watches For Effects On Peso From  Brazil 's  FX Intervention
text:
--Bank of Mexico watching exchange rate for effects of Brazilian actions

--Official says sovereign upgrade warranted, but unlikely before elections

--Central bank considers diversifying currencies of reserves, a slow process

(Adds comments from Bank of Mexico official, details and background beginning in fourth paragraph)

By Juan Montes and Amy Guthrie

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--A Bank of Mexico official said Thursday that the central bank is keeping an eye out for possible peso appreciation as a result of investors shifting money into Mexico as Brazilian authorities take measures to damp down the appreciation of the real.

A number of analysts have said the exchange-rate policies of the Bank of Mexico and Mexican Finance Ministry make the peso an attractive option for taking advantage of higher-yielding securities with less risk of exchange intervention.

Jaime Cortina, director of operations at the Bank of Mexico, said at an event organized by financial information company Profit & Loss that the exchange commission, which is made up of central bank and Finance Ministry officials, is keeping an eye on that and will take it into account.

"Certainly, this is something we're monitoring and we're concerned about it," he said.

The peso has appreciated around 8.8% so far this year against the U.S. dollar, after a sharp depreciation at the end of 2011 on risk aversion caused by the European sovereign debt problems. The currency recently traded in Mexico City at MXN12.8410 to the dollar.

Late last year, at the height of peso volatility, the central bank stopped buying dollars through monthly dollar put options and activated instead a mechanism where it will sell up to $400 million a day on days when the peso depreciates 2% against the dollar from the previous session. So far no sales have been triggered under the mechanism.

Mexico's foreign reserves are currently at $148 billion, and Cortina said that reserves will continue to reach new highs as long as oil prices remain high and state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos changes dollars at the central bank rather than in the open market.

The bank is analyzing investing reserves in other emerging market currencies to secure greater yield, Cortina said, but such a decision would take a long time and central banks must be very cautious to not put reserves at risk.

The global trend, and the trend for Mexico, will continue to be diversification away from the U.S. dollar and into other currencies and assets, such as gold, Cortina said.

"The problem is that many of those other markets don't have the size that many central banks require," he added.

The Mexican central bank holds some reserves in gold, and has also diversified into currencies other than the U.S. dollar, according to Cortina.

Mexico deserves a better credit rating given the country's healthy public finances, with low budget deficit and debt, and record-high international reserves, Cortina also said.

"Clearly, there's margin for an upward revision. But I don't see the international credit agencies doing anything before July's presidential election."

Mexico has a lower medium-grade credit rating, despite having a budget deficit of 2.5% of gross domestic product in 2011 and a net debt of 32.4% of the GDP, relatively low compared with U.S., Europe and other developed countries.

Standard and Poor's sovereign rating for Mexican debt is BBB, similar to that of Fitch, while Moody's has Mexico one equivalent notch higher at a Baa1. All three agencies maintain a stable outlook.

-By Juan Montes and Amy Guthrie, Dow Jones Newswires; (5255) 5980 5178, mexico@dowjones.com [ 29-03-12 1925GMT ]

title: Brazil  Real Weaker On US Data,  Intervention  Worries
text:
--Real opens at 1.8193/dollar versus BRL1.8107/dollar Tuesday

--Disappointing U.S. durable goods data hurt confidence

--Investors fret over possible Brazil government intervention

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened in early trading Wednesday on disappointing U.S. economic data and continued worries about possible market intervention by the Brazilian government.

The real was trading at BRL1.8193 to the dollar early in the session, weaker against the Tuesday close of BRL1.8107, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

In the U.S., durable goods orders in February were up 2.2%, but that figure weighed in below market expectations of about 3.0%. The figures called into question the strength of the U.S. economic recovery at a time when investors are also worried about a possible recession in Europe and a slowdown in growth in China.

Worries about the pace of China's economic expansion hurt global commodities prices Wednesday, another factor counting against the Brazilian currency. Lower commodities prices spell declining export revenues for Brazil.

"Meanwhile, Brazil's government is always keeping an eye on the market," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. "Intervention is possible on any given day as the government keeps the currency in a box."

According to most traders and analysts, that "box" is currently between BRL1.80 to the dollar and BRL1.90.

The Brazilian market becomes nervous whenever the real strengthens, especially when it gets close to the BRL1.80 mark.

"Brazilian exports are not competitive when the real is too strong," said former finance minister Antonio Delfim Netto. "Government intervention in the market to prevent a strengthening of the real is part of a legitimate defense of Brazilian interests."

In recent days, intervention has come in the form of direct central bank purchases of dollars from the market. In recent months, the government has also slapped higher taxes on certain forms of investment inflows. Higher taxes are especially worrisome for investors, because they create uncertainty and make long-term planning more difficult, according to analysts.

But Muniz said worries about Europe and China were also likely to be market factors for Brazil on Wednesday.

"It's obvious that the European troubles are not over yet," he said. Continued worries about Europe's debt crisis tend to reduce investment flows both to Europe and to emerging market countries.

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 28 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened o n W ednesday after data showed lower-than-expected U.S. durable goods orders, while investors sold the Brazilian real in the face of central bank intervention to weaken the currency.

Brazil's real slid to its weakest close since Jan. 9 to bid 1.8627 per dollar, with a central bank auction to buy dollars contributing to its 0.56 percent depreciation.

Traders dumped the currency on Tuesday on fears the government was preparing to expand the scope of a tax on financial transactions.

Analysts said on Wednesday the fears were not yet substantiated but were still a concern.

Even though the currency had already been weakening on Wednesday, the Brazil central bank called an auction to buy U.S. dollars, setting the cutoff rate at 1.82 reais.

"They were trying to defend at 1.7 (reais per dollar) and they were successful in doing it, so now they have realized they can defend at 1.8 ... if they eventually move to 1.9 they will say: 'OK, let's defend at 1.9.' That's the approach of this government," said Diego Donadio, a BNP Paribas strategist in Sao Paulo.

Policymakers are trying to weaken a currency they say is too strong and hurts domestic manufacturers, made less competitive by cheap imports.

Brazil's government has raised its financial transactions, or "IOF," tax and extended its scope to foreign debt maturing in up to five years.

The central bank purchased dollars in the spot market in early February for the first time since September and the real has weakened around 6 percent since then.

The bank said on Wednesday it had purchased $1.896 billion so far this month.

"I'm very distressed about Brazil right now," said John Welch, emerging markets strategist and executive director at CIBC World Markets. "They are trying to get the dollar higher at a very high cost to the government and the country."

Meanwhile, Mexico's peso weakened 0.3 percent to 12.509 per dollar.

Latin America's only fully convertible currency had weakened as much as 0.77 percent after data showed new orders for U.S. manufactured goods slightly disappointed in February.

U.S. durable goods orders rose 2.2 percent last month, only partially reversing January's revised 3.6 percent decline in Mexico's top trade partner.

Analysts said riskier assets like emerging market currencies were looking for an excuse to back off gains that followed comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's commitment to accommodative monetary policy on Monday and Tuesday.

Economic growth in China and the debt crisis in Europe are still in the background, despite the United State's commitment to keeping borrowing costs low to spur growth.

"The market has had a bit of a run and investors don't trust it so they are trying to find anything to get out," said CIBC's Welch.

Chile's peso ended 0.61 percent weaker, bidding 489 per dollar. The country's central bank released a poll on Wednesday saying Chile's key interest rate will likely be on hold through October.

title: Brazil Currency  Shrugs Off  Intervention , Closes Stronger
text:
--Brazil real closes stronger despite central bank reverse-swap auction

--Real currency seen stabilizing in range between BRL1.80 and BRL1.82

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL1.8107 to the dollar


 
   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency closed stronger Tuesday despite intervention by the country's central bank as the real tracked overseas gains against the U.S. dollar by other currencies on expectations for greater liquidity in global capital markets.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.8107 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Monday's close at BRL1.8134 to the greenback and represented a sharp reversal from the weaker opening quote of BRL1.8193.

The currency market buckled early under the weight of expectations for intervention by the Brazilian Central Bank, which had announced a reverse-swap auction late Monday to roll over contracts coming due April 2. Players have paid closer attention recently to the increased rhetoric coming from government officials that has indicated Brazil is comfortable with the real trading at the level of BRL1.80 to the dollar. That likely means a continuing firm stance against short-term investment inflows and the possibility of capital outflows in the future, traders said.

"The currency was basically stable. That's the trend now for the foreseeable future," said Wilson Menezes, a trader at Sao Paulo-based brokerage Novo Mundo. The real will likely remain trading rangebound between BRL1.80 and BRL1.82 before ending the year at BRL1.85 to the greenback, Menezes said.

The real's early session weakness faded after the central bank carried out its reverse-swap auction, selling 41,200 contracts worth $2.1 billion at two maturities, on June 1 and July 2. The auctions, which allow investors to swap foreign-exchange positions for government paper linked to interest rates, typically support the dollar by removing Brazilian real exposure from the market. The auctions were used extensively in late 2005 and early 2006 before market interest in the swaps waned. The reverse swaps have been used infrequently since then.

The market also took direction Tuesday from weak economic data in the U.S., where the troubled housing sector continued to show declines in home prices in January. U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, meanwhile, also continued to indicate that the monetary authority's easy money policies will continue into the future. There also continues to be speculation about a third asset-purchase program, or QE3.

While Brazil's towering interest rates have made the country a favored destination for investors seeking higher rates of return, the government's recent measures to tamp down speculative inflows are working--perhaps too well, said one trader.

"We're going to have lower inflows," said Sidnei Nehme, director at the NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo. Foreign direct investment and exports are falling behind last year's tally, while the implementation of a financial transactions tax on overseas loans of less than six years was also affecting the flow of dollars into Brazil, Nehme noted.

"The great risk is if we end up with net dollar outflows, which will affect the ability to finance the current account deficit," Nehme said. Brazil expects to post a current account deficit of about $68 billion in 2012. "We may not have enough dollars [entering the country] to finance this $70 billion. The government would then need to use part of its reserves," Nehme said.

The real is likely headed for a long and subtle weakening to about BRL2.00 to the dollar by the third quarter, according to Nehme. Previously, the trader expected the real to reach that mark by the end of the year. "This is going to happen gradually because flows are going to turn negative," Nehme said. "The government will have to let the real weaken or mess with the measures it's implemented."

-By Jeff Fick, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-21-2586-6085, Jeff.Fick@dowjones.com [ 27-03-12 1932GMT ]

title: WRAPUP 1-Brazil growth to gain momentum, Tombini says
text:
* Brazil's economy to accelerate in 2012 and 2013 - Tombini

* Tombini confident inflation rate will slow to mid-target

* Strong retail sales beat forecasts in January

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, March 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's economic activity will gather momentum in 2012 and 2013, central bank President Alexandre Tombini said on Friday, shortly after stronger-than-expected retail sales figures for January highlighted the country's robust domestic demand.

Inflation in Brazil will likely slow to the 4.5 percent midpoint of the government's target "at some point around the end of this year," Tombini added in an event in São Paulo, letting interest rates stay near record lows in coming months.

The largest Latin American economy nearly dipped into recession in the second half of last year, lagging behind other fast-growing emerging nations after a series of interest-rate hikes to curb inflation, which had hit a seven-year high.

Yet retail sales beat forecasts in January, rising 2.6 percent in January from December, the government statistics agency IBGE said on Friday.

"The prospects for the recovery to gain momentum in 2012 and extend into 2013 are good," Tombini said. "The conditions - a low unemployment rate, a solid credit market, a slowdown in consumer price increases - are favorable for a resumption of growth this year and in 2013."

Brazil's government targets inflation at 4.5 percent, with a leeway of plus or minus 2 percentage points. Consumer prices rose 5.61 percent in the 12-months through mid-March , the government statistics agency IBGE said on Thursday.

President Dilma Rousseff's government has aggressively reacted to stimulate the economy by cutting taxes and interest rates. Brazil's government has also ramped up intervention in the foreign-exchange market to prevent its overvalued currency, the real, from hurting local manufacturers.

Brazil's central bank cut rates to 9.75 percent earlier this month and said it is very likely to slash rates again in coming months to "slightly above" the all-time low of 8.75 percent.

Brighter prospects for this year's economic expansion have led the central bank to revise upward its forecast for 2012's current account deficit to $68 billion from the previous estimate of $65 billion. In February, the country posted a current account gap of $1.77 billion.

title: UPDATE 1- Brazil  to keep  intervening  in  currency -Mantega
text:
* Finance Minister Mantega says steps to protect industry

* Vows to keep fighting excess inflows, strong currency

* Says renewal of power licenses offers chance to cut rates

(Add details on potential measures, comments, background throughout)

SAO PAULO, March 22 (Reuters) - The Brazilian government will continue to intervene in the local currency market in order to limit a rally in the real that risks derailing an incipient economic recovery and hampering manufacturers, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Thursday.

A series of measures including tax hikes and interest-rate reductions have helped pare gains in the currency, which is now at a "more favorable" level than a year ago, Mantega told reporters after a meeting with business leaders in Brasilia.

"The real can't gain further ground or else our exports will turn even less competitive," Mantega said "We will keep with our intervention policy in the currency market - that is a government pledge."

Mantega's remarks signal that the government remains convinced that a recent decline in manufacturing activity in Latin America's economy is more a function of unfair trade practices by the world's richest countries -- whose economies are struggling.

"There is a weak currency policy being implemented by some countries, and that is what puts Brazilian manufacturers in a disadvantageous position," Mantega said.

Yet, local business leaders say that high taxes and labor costs, outdated legislation and an aging infrastructure are more to blame for Brazil's flagging industry than external factors.

The real weakened for a fourth day on Thursday, shedding 0.3 percent to a bid price of 1.8242 to the dollar. The currency has gained 2.2 percent this year.

ELECTRICITY RATES

The government is considering additional measures to lower financing costs for companies, which, along with the central bank's rate cuts, will ease the burden on exporters and local manufacturers whose goods compete with imports locally, Mantega said. He did not elaborate on what measures were being considered.

He said logistics costs are too high in Brazil and that the government was analyzing ways to bring them down. At the meeting, according to Mantega, entrepreneurs complained about the high cost of power rates and transport bottlenecks as issues that increase their costs.

Mantega said the government was expected to decide whether or not to renew more than 60 percent of existing licenses for electricity generation, transmission and distribution -- and should take advantage of the process to push rates lower.

He added that the process should also allow the government to end a longstanding link between power rates and inflation indexes.

($1 = 1.824 reais)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm  currencies  fall as China manufacturing slows
text:
* Brazil real falls to lowest since Jan. 9; intervention seen

* Chile peso sheds 0.74 pct; top export copper at two-week low

* Mexico peso off 0.69 pct, real ends down 0.18 pct

By Caroline Stauffer

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 22 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Thursday as faltering factory activity in China cast doubt on the Asian giant's appetite for the region's commodities and surprisingly weak European data added to global growth fears.

China's industrial activity fell for the fifth straight month in March, a purchasing managers index showed.

In Europe, German and French manufacturing suffered sharp declines in March that even the most pessimistic economists had failed to predict, according to PMI data..

"When there's negative news out of China, Europe or the United States you have this risk-off trade," said Kathryn Rooney Vera, an emerging markets analyst at Bulltick Capital Markets.

"Bad news out of China pushes Latin American currencies weaker because China is a huge commodity consumer - that's the main driver here," she said.

Chile's peso shed 0.74 percent to bid 487.2 per dollar. It was the peso's weakest close in two weeks and its biggest single-day drop since March 6.

Copper prices fell to a two-week low on expectations of lower demand from China, the world's biggest metals consumer, and Europe. Chile is the world's top copper exporter, and its mines produce 30 percent of the world's copper supply.

Brazil's real weakened for a fourth day, losing 0.18 percent to bid 1.8207 per dollar. Declining industry performance in China, Brazil's top trading partner, led to the real's weakest close since Jan. 9.

Still, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Thursday the central bank would continue intervening to keep the real from gaining ground as it tries to maintain the competitiveness of Brazil's already expensive exports and spur economic growth. .

The central bank bought dollars on Feb. 6 for the first time since September of last year. The real has weakened 5.5 percent since it waded back into the market.

"They are intervening at 1.8 to stop the real's momentum, but I have a hard time, barring a significant global situation that would impact all of Latin America, seeing it going above 1.9," said Eduardo Suarez, currency strategist at Scotia Capital.

Though analysts doubt the interventions will drastically weaken the real, the efforts have led some to recommend the region's other currencies.

"Mantega and (President Dilma) Rousseff have made no bones about their intention to intervene, and for that reason we aren't extremely bullish on the real. ... The Finance Ministry should not be dictating monetary policy, but that's what you see going on here," said Bulltick's Rooney Vera, who favors the Mexican peso.

PESO RESPECTS MOVING AVERAGE

Latin American currencies mostly weakened despite signs of recovery in the United States, the world's largest economy. New U.S. claims for unemployment benefits dropped to a four-year low last week, a government report said.

Mexico, which sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States, saw its currency weaken 0.69 percent, to 12.7948 on risk aversion from the Chinese and European data.

But traders said the peso isn't likely to change its appreciation tendency because the Latin America's only fully convertible currency stayed below an important technical signal.

"I think the key resistance is the 200-day moving average, which is 12.935," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at Vector brokerage in Monterrey. "There's been resistance at 12.85, and I think there will be at 12.90 as well."

Colombia's peso strengthened 0.08 percent to 1,759.7 after the country posted 6.1 percent growth in the last quarter of 2011 versus the year-earlier period. Foreign investment and expanding consumer credit helped shield Colombia from global economic troubles.

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso slips on U.S. data, Brazil's real flat
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* U.S. data disappoints, hurts export-dependent Mexican peso

* Investors see Brazil cenbank defending real at 1.8

* Mexico peso off 0.39 pct, Brazil real ends near flat

By Luciana Lopez and Caroline Stauffer

NEW YORK/RIO DE JANEIRO, March 21 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean pesos weakened after disappointing U.S. housing data on Wednesday, while expectations of more intervention curbed enthusiasm for Brazil's real.

U.S. home resales unexpectedly fell in February and the supply of properties on the market rose, causing investors to opt for low-risk assets like U.S. Treasuries rather than higher-yielding emerging market currencies.

While U.S. employment figures have shown improvement and pointed to recovery in the world's largest economy, analysts point to persistent patches of weakness, such as the ongoing fallout from the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis.

"The data gives little indication that we have hit the bottom of this mortgage problem," said Enrique Alvarez, head of analysis at IDEAGlobal in New York.

Mexico's economy is particularly tied to its northern neighbor, as it sends around 80 percent of its exports across the border. The Mexican peso dipped 0.39 percent to 12.7041 per dollar.

Chile's peso ended 0.19 percent weaker, bidding at 485.10 per dollar, its weakest close in a week.

Although Latin American currencies weakened on Wednesday, discouraging U.S. data can in the longer term help emerging market assets by supporting bets that the U.S. Federal Reserve may yet move to inject a third round of liquidity into the market.

So-called quantitative easing has brought a flood of cash into Latin America's high-yielding assets in recent years.

The European Central bank has also injected more than 1 trillion euros into the market through two three-year lending operations in recent months.

"I expect a good portion of that money to end up in Latin America," said Alberto Bernal, head of fixed income research for Bulltick Capital Markets.

"Those resources will continue to generate some important appreciation for the currencies," Bernal said.

REAL SEEN UNDERPERFORMING

Brazil's real ended just 0.09 percent weaker than its Tuesday close, bidding 1.819 per dollar, but the currency's appeal has declined since the government started intervening in the spot market last month to contain its advance.

A stronger currency makes the country's exports more expensive and therefore less competitive, spurring the government and central bank to act. The real has lost more than 5 percent this month since authorities hardened their stance.

"The real is massively underperforming its peers," said strategist Diego Donadio of BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

He recommends selling Brazil's currency in favor of the Colombian or Mexican pesos as the central bank is no longer likely to tolerate a real stronger than 1.8 per dollar.

Brazil's central bank said on Wednesday it had purchased $1.214 billion on the spot foreign exchange market between March 1 and March 16.

title: Brazil Currency  Opens Weaker Amid  Intervention  Concerns
text:
--Overseas markets buoyed by Greek parliament vote on EUR130 billion rescue package

--Expectations for currency intervention in Brazil likely to weigh on real trading

--Brazilian real opens trading at BRL1.8217, weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL1.8190


 
    By Jeff Fick 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Concerns about further government intervention in Brazil's currency markets offset positive momentum in Europe's ongoing debt crisis to kick off Wednesday's session, sending the real to a weaker open against the U.S. dollar.

The real failed to join other global currencies in advancing against the dollar, including a stronger euro on the news from Greece. The euro's gains boosted global commodities prices, typically a key barometer for the real. The real opened at BRL1.8217 to the greenback, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL1.8190

After global markets were waylaid the previous session by concerns about economic prospects in China, Greece's parliament yielded a dose of good news as lawmakers in the debt-troubled country approved a deal with the International Monetary Fund, European Union and European Central Bank on a EUR130 billion aid package. Now, Greek lawmakers face the unenviable task of implementing harsh austerity measures to rein in government spending.

Concerns about China's outlook for growth, however, could continue to hang over local markets. China is Brazil's leading trade partner and a key consumer of the country's iron ore and other commodities. China previously reduced its target for growth to 7.5% in 2012, down from previous year's target of 8%. In addition, mining companies BHP Billiton Ltd. (BHP, BHP.AU) and Rio Tinto PLC (RIO, RIO.LN) raised concerns about the pace of a slowdown in China, citing the country's apparently declining appetite for iron ore.

In Brazil, meanwhile, the central bank remained active in the market by purchasing dollars in a spot-market auction. That is likely to limit any move by the real to strengthen in coming days, said Banco Santander. "Increasingly less benign prospects for commodities--given more abundant evidence of a China slowdown--and aggressive [foreign-exchange] intervention are likely to continue exerting a weakening bias on the [real], in our view," Santander said.

Currency market players will likely keep a close eye on foreign-exchange flows and data on the level of central bank intervention that should shed light on the size of net inflows over the past week, Santander added.

Markets will also be on the lookout for U.S. existing home sales data and a U.K budget proposal, analysts said.

title: Brazil 's Real Volatile On China Growth, Government  Intervention
text:
--Brazil's real falls with more concerns about China

--Brazil's Treasury could be more active on currency markets

--Brazilian traders expect the real to remain volatile Tuesday

By Luciana Magalhaes and Matthew Cowley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency weakened sharply Tuesday morning, amid considerable volatility, as traders played catch up with more concerns about China economic growth, and fretted about Brazilian government intervention.

Negative comments on China from BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto once again raised concerns about the pace of slowdown there, which could have an impact on demand for Brazil's raw materials, including iron ore.

"The day will remain volatile, with the currency vulnerable to the international news, specially coming from Asia", said Mauro Araujo, FX director at Sao Paulo's brokerage Vision Corretora.

Alfredo Barbutti, economist at brokerage BGC Liquidez Corretora agreed. "Today, the real is being affected by the trend in the Australian dollar," he added.

China's iron-ore demand is "flattening," according to Ian Ashby, BHP's head of iron ore, while David Joyce, Rio Tinto's managing director of iron-ore output, said China's economy was "slowing." Their comments came at a news conference at the Australian Journal of Mining global iron-ore conference in Perth.

The real was trading at BRL1.8292, weaker than the BRL1.8055 late Monday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Meanwhile, investors were also digesting a newspaper report in Brazil, which suggested the Brazilian National Treasury will take a more active role in the government's efforts to contain the appreciation of the Brazilian real versus the dollar.

The Treasury may buy back up to $15 billion in overseas debts ahead of schedule to ease pressure on the currency, according to a report in Tuesday's edition of the O Estado de S. Paulo newspaper.

In an interview with Estado, Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said the government is already in talks to pay back ahead of schedule a $2.9 billion loan from the Inter-American Development Bank, or IDB.

Estado said the comments indicated that the government isn't satisfied with the current level of BRL1.80 per dollar, and that it wants the currency to weaken further.

Augustin said that the Treasury's efforts are part of a broad government strategy in the foreign exchange market, and that the government will continue to "surprise" market players with the currency measures.

Treasury officials weren't immediately available for comment Tuesday morning.

Earlier this month, the official said the Treasury may buy back foreign-currency debt to help prevent Brazil's currency from appreciating too sharply.

The Brazilian real appreciated by about 10% against the dollar earlier this year before the central bank and the government took a series of measures that have so far managed to push the real back to 1.80 to the dollar in the most recent session.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies  Mixed; Debt Steady
text:
-- Emerging market currencies mixed ahead of weekend

-- Emerging market debt little changed


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies were mixed Friday, while sovereign debt was little changed, as broader markets lacked conviction.

Emerging market currencies' direction in recent days have largely been in response to the dollar's moves, as rising Treasury yields lifted the U.S. currency. But softer U.S. data and directionless U.S. equities Friday appeared to give traders less enthusiasm for emerging markets ahead of the weekend.

Investors are also reevaluating how much farther this year's rally for emerging market currencies can go, analysts say. However, calmer market dynamics should allow for investors to differentiate more among emerging market currencies, according to analysts.

"We're moving into a world where maybe idiosyncratic elements are increasingly more important," said Nomura economist Benito Berber.

The South African rand was the day's outperformer, but other currencies seen as risk proxies, like the Mexican peso and Turkish lira, were flat on the day as investors squared positions ahead of the weekend.

Emerging market sovereign debt was little changed, firming up slightly against U.S. Treasurys. The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, tightened three basis points to 320 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index slipped 0.2%.

Among currencies, the Brazilian real weakened slightly against the dollar, as the threat of further foreign exchange intervention looms over the currency. Brazil's government and central bank recently have undertaken a series of measures to curb the currency's strength, including financial-operations taxes on certain kinds of investments and dollar purchases in the foreign-exchange market, respectively. The dollar edged up to BRL1.8009 from BRL1.7983 late Thursday, according to CQG.

"The real continues to be a story of they're going to do more measures to contain appreciation," said Nomura's Berber.

The Mexican peso was nearly flat on the day, as U.S. stocks remained rangebound and Mexico's central bank stuck to the status quo, holding its key policy rate at 4.5% for the 25th meeting in a row. The dollar bought MXN12.6596 late Friday.

The South African rand bucked the trend Friday, gaining 0.6% against the dollar, which traded at ZAR7.5837. The rand has been "the strongest-performing currency" among African foreign exchange over the last month, though it started from a much lower base, analysts at Standard Bank said in a note.

Within emerging Europe, the Turkish lira was little changed on the day against the dollar, while the Russian ruble advanced modestly against the U.S. currency as it tracked rising oil prices. The dollar traded at RUB29.238 from RUB29.389 late Thursday.
