title: JP Morgan Brazil  CEO Sees Real Weaker On Rate Cuts,  Intervention
text:
--J.P. MorganBrazil chief executive sees currency weaker on lower rates, government measures

--Berquo: Over medium term, pressures on currency to appreciate will remain

--Berquo: Brazil capital-market activity is better than expected in early 2012


 
   By Rogerio Jelmayer and Matthew Cowley 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real will weaken in the short term, given falling interest rates and government intervention, said Claudio Berquo, the Brazil chief executive of J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. (JPM).

"The central bank is much more vigilant and it's clear that when the currency gets close to BRL1.70 the red lights come on," Berquo said during an interview at his office in Sao Paulo. He sees the real staying in a range of around BRL1.80 to BRL1.90 to the dollar.

Last week, Brazil's central bank cut its key rate, the Selic, to 9.75%, and Wednesday it indicated it will continue to cut rates, although it said they won't get as far as the historical low of 8.75%. The government also has unleashed a series of measures, from buying dollars to imposing taxes on some capital flows, to arrest the real's momentum.

Having touched BRL1.69 at the end of February, the Brazilian real has given back some of its gains; Friday, it traded at BRL1.80 per dollar.

As interest rates come down, Brazil's local banks will have to adjust, moving away from their reliance on government bonds and developing new products, Berquo said, adding J.P. Morgan sees this as an opportunity to offer its products.

The government, meanwhile, also must tread carefully, as Brazil will have to adjust to lower levels of interest rates, Berquo said.

"We are very enthusiastic about this but at the same time you have to be careful otherwise there could be a surprise," Berquo said. "You never know if there are going to be collateral effects."

Those investors who traditionally have parked their cash in high-yielding government bonds will start looking for other options, such as shares. But Berquo said even if a small part of that was to be diverted to equities, "there's not enough paper."

There is the ever-present threat of inflation, which is "the main enemy of all of us," Berquo said, adding the government could help with that by containing spending.

The currency, however, is likely to remain under pressure to appreciate over the medium- to long-term. Even if short-term investors withdraw, there will be more long-term foreign-direct investment, Berquo said.

Two years ago, J.P. Morgan added a foreign-exchange team to handle flow transactions--low-margin, high-volume currency contracts that are a booming business and allow J.P. Morgan to get a feeling for what is going on in the currency market, he said.

The Brazilian government's steps to contain the currency have had relatively little impact on companies or long-term investors, Berquo said. Most established Brazilian corporations that borrow overseas now take out 10-year loans; if companies aren't in that category, they have the option of a private placement, he said.

The steps may help develop the local corporate-bond market, which is practically nonexistent today. With interest rates coming down and companies locked out of the medium-term overseas market, local-bond sales "could start to fly," Berquo said.

Brazil's capital market has had a better start in 2012 than had been expected back in September and October, when the view appeared to be bleak, he said. "This year is the year of debt," Berquo said, adding he also expects to see a number of important share offerings. Much of the work will have to be done in the first part of the year, as the market will dry up as the U.S. election cycle gets under way later in the year, he said.

Overseas bonds issued by Brazilian companies soared in the first two months of 2012, as global markets leapt back to life after six months of worrying about European debts, according to the Brazilian Association of Capital Market Institutions, or Anbima.

Nonetheless, J.P. Morgan is slowing down its pace of growth in Brazil this year, preferring to absorb its recent rapid expansion and see how the market develops this year. After the bank tripled its staff in three years, it has 900 employees in Brazil, and plans to add around 50 more this year, Berquo said.

Brazil is "overbanked," with every major global player already present in a market of well-capitalized and extremely competitive local players, the executive said. J.P. Morgan is careful not to go up against local banking giants such as Itau Unibanco Holdings SA (ITUB, ITUB4.BR) and Banco Bradesco SA (BBD, BBDC4.BR, BBDO) in the areas in which they are strongest, he said.

"We want to be more local than the foreigners and more foreign than the locals," Berquo said.

J.P. Morgan doesn't have immediate plans for acquisitions in Brazil, Berquo said, either because there aren't players or they are too expensive.

title: Brazil  Real Weakens On  Intervention  Worries, Interest Rates
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL1.7820 Vs BRL1.7693 Thursday

--Market worries persist on possible government steps to stem inflows

--Inflation data underscores long-term trend toward lower base rate


 
   By Tom Murphy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended active trading weaker against the U.S. dollar Friday as investors continued to fret over possible government action to stem investment inflows.

The real ended regular trading at BRL1.7820 to the dollar, weaker than Thursday's BRL1.7693, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

It was the sixth straight session for the real to depreciate against the greenback.

"Government officials have come out with almost daily statements saying they could intervene in the market in order to force a depreciation of the real," said Olvidio Soares, a trader at Sao Paulo's Interbolsa brokerage. "Additional taxes on inflows are likely to be the government's weapon of choice."

Finance Minister Guido Mantega himself has led the chorus of officials proclaiming the need to protect Brazilian exporters and manufacturers from what he has called a global "currency war." In recent comments, Mantega has said Brazil's government reserves the right to adopt measures restraining short-term investment inflows as a way to reduce the appreciation of the currency.

"All of this has led to a somewhat speculative market," said Soares. "All it takes is a market rumor on possible intervention and investors start buying dollars."

In fact, Friday's session did not even see the more traditional form of intervention by means of central bank dollar purchases via snap auctions.

"Current levels for the real against the dollar seem agreeable to the government," said Hencorp Commcor Brokerage trader Luiz Henrique. "In recent days, with the real at this level, the government has held off from any market intervention."

Prospects for lower interest rates are also helping depreciate the real. High Brazilian interest rates have served as a consistent lure for foreign investment inflows, a major reason the government has targeted them in the past for higher taxes.

But earlier this week, Brazil's central bank signaled a more aggressive policy of interest rate reductions by cutting its Selic base rate three-quarters-of-a-point to 9.75%.

Most analysts expect more rate cuts to come, undermining the attractiveness of Brazilian fixed-income investments.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil  real hits 8-week low as  intervention  eyed
text:
* Speculation of sovereign wealth fund dollar spurs selling

* Real likely to keep lagging region-wide rally

* Brazil real slumps 1.29 pct, Mexico peso up 0.34 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slumped to an eight-week low on Friday on expectations of more big interest rate cuts and new intervention measures by authorities worried that a strong currency is crimping growth.

The real slumped by the most this week since the beginning of November when it was hit by panic about European banks, shedding 3.3 percent against the dollar and leading losses in March for the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Speculation that Brazil's sovereign wealth fund could soon start to buy dollars in the market spurred selling. Authorities have deployed a growing tool chest of measures designed to sap the real's strength, which is hurting local industry.

Still, analysts said global demand for higher-yielding assets would likely cap losses ahead in the real, which could soon begin appreciating again.

A recent liquidity boost of more than half a trillion euros from the European Central Bank is expected to keep driving financial flows into emerging markets offering higher yields, such as Latin America, in the coming weeks.

Europe's cheap financing adds to the global pool of money available at low-interest rates that can be invested in emerging markets.

"All this liquidity is the global force that authorities in Brazil are fighting," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York.

"The global forces suggest the real could still rally a lot. But all these measures by authorities could make it underperform the rally we are likely to see if money keeps pouring into emerging markets," Melzi said.

On Friday, the real sank 1.29 percent to 1.7835 to the dollar, paring losses that had taken it to its weakest level since mid-January.

Data on Friday showed inflation in Brazil eased in February to its slowest pace for that month in five years, reinforcing the central bank's argument for increasingly aggressive interest rate cuts. Lower rates could make investing in Brazilian bonds less attractive.

Late Wednesday, Brazil's central bank surprised analysts by cutting its benchmark interest rate three-quarters of a percentage point to 9.75 percent. After the cut, the median of a Reuters poll showed analysts see the rate falling to 8.5 percent this year, versus a previous floor of 9.5 percent.

That would still leave Brazilian interest rates among the highest in the world. Even if the return on fixed-income assets is falling, lower borrowing costs could boost growth and tempt more foreign investors to dive into the country's stock market.

Enrique Alvarez, an analyst at IDEAglobal in New York, expects the real to finish the year at about 1.70 to 1.75 to the dollar.

Other major Latin American currencies rose after the U.S. government reported that U.S. employers added more than 200,000 jobs for a third straight month, a sign the world's largest economy was strengthening.

Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States. Mexico's peso gained 0.34 percent to 12.6625 to the dollar for a third day. Earlier it reached 12.6010, its strongest in six months, before pulling back.

Rafael Camarena, an economist at Santander in Mexico City, expects the peso to trade laterally between 12.70 and 12.60 per dollar over the next week as investors look for further confirmation that the U.S. economy is improving.

Analysts said profit taking could be seen next week after Greece pushed through a bond swap needed to clinch bailout funds.

In March the peso's performance has been nearly the opposite that of the real, strengthening nearly 2 percent.

Alvarez thinks the peso could gain as much as 7 percent yet this year to reach 11.80 to the dollar, helped by investors shifting investment from Brazil to Mexico.

Brazil's intervention tactics are pushing more investors to eye the peso, since Mexico is not acting to deter speculators in its market, Alvarez said.

Mexico's central bank is seen holding its benchmark rate steady at 4.50 percent next week after inflation in February fell back into the central bank's comfort zone, below 4 percent.

Chile's peso firmed about 0.25 percent to 483.00 to the dollar from 484.40.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Up-And-Down Session Nearly Unchanged
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real, after being pushed and pulled between international optimism and domestic concerns, settled Thursday virtually unchanged from the previous session.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7693 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with Wednesday's close of BRL1.7680.

Traders said volume was relatively light, and the currency fluctuated in a fairly wide range. After opening stronger at BRL1.7595, the real weakened around midday to BRL1.78 before recovering in later trading.

The volatility came as the market eyed a variety of relevant headlines.

Hopes for a solid participation rate by private creditors in Greece's bond swap buoyed overseas markets from Shanghai to Wall Street.

But in Brazil, investors are concerned that local authorities have become less tolerant of a strong real than they were last year, when the currency rallied to BRL1.54 before a deterioation in Europe's debt crisis sent the currency into a tailspin.

Though the Finance Ministry and Central Bank unleashed a variety of measures last year to curb the real's appreciation, including taxes and near-daily interventions in the exchange market, Brazil's economy was coming off one of its best years in decades, having grown 7.5% in 2010.

By comparison, gross domestic product expanded by a paltry 2.7% in 2011, with the industrial sector's particularly sluggish growth attributed by Brazilian authorities to a strong currency that hurt exports and encouraged imports. Data released this week then showed a sharp downturn in January's industrial production, suggesting this year could also be difficult for factories.

"There's all kinds of news that the government is preparing more measures," said Joao Medeiros, foreign-exchange director at Sao Paulo's Pioneer brokerage. "[Finance Minister Guido] Mantega supposedly can't sleep at night because of all the capital that's entering the country."

Brazil received heavy financial flows at the start of the year as local companies took advantage of happy times in global markets to cheaply place debt abroad. By late February, the real pushed below the BRL1.70 level for the first time in four months, after closing 2011 at BRL1.8642.

Some analysts said the Brazilian central bank's 0.75 percentage point reduction of the benchmark Selic interest rate Wednesday could make the real less appealing to currency speculators attracted by the large differential with rates in other countries.

But even if the bank hacks Selic all the way to 8.5%--as a growing number of economists project after Wednesday's bigger-than-expected cut--Brazil will still have among the highest interest rates in the world.

"Brazil remains attractive for foreign investors, even with this cut," said Joao Querino de Santos, a trader at Sao Paulo's J. Alves brokerage.

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil industry slumps again, eyes on c.bank
text:
* Industrial production falls more than expected

* Weak manufacturing weighing heavily on economic growth

* Numbers bolster argument for bigger interest rate cut

(Recasts, adds details, quotes)

By Asher Levine

SAO PAULO, March 7 (Reuters) - A slump in Brazil's industrial production in January was nearly three times worse than analysts had expected, putting pressure on policymakers to take action as manufacturers struggle against the tide of a strong currency and a heavy tax load.

The data may bolster expectations of a sharper central bank interest rate cut later on Wednesday, a day after disappointing data showed Latin America's largest economy expanded just 2.7 percent in 2011, prompting pledges of aggressive stimulus measures from the government.

Interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> fell across the board following the data release.

Industrial production in Brazil fell 2.1 percent in January from December, government statistics agency IBGE said on Wednesday. It was the worst performance since a similar fall in April 2011.

Production had been expected to fall 0.8 percent, according to the median estimate of 20 analysts in a Reuters survey. The forecasts ranged from a 1.3 percent drop to a 0.3 percent decline.

January's industrial production contracted 3.4 percent from a year earlier, more than double the 1.5 percent drop forecast in the Reuters survey. Estimates for output ranged from a 2.1 percent drop to a 0.3 percent decline.

"The industrial sector has been a drag on overall real GDP," Goldman Sachs analyst Alberto Ramos wrote in a note to investors on Wednesday. Ramos expects the performance of the industrial sector to improve slightly throughout 2012 but to continue to lag overall real GDP growth.

Manufacturers have blamed most of their problems on Brazil's currency, the real, which has strengthened about 40 percent since the depths of the financial crisis in 2009 and 6 percent this year.

In response, Brazil's central bank has stepped up its intervention in currency markets in recent weeks, while Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Tuesday promised to support Brazil's flagging industrial sector with tax incentives and other unspecified stimulus measures.

"All the research shows exactly what we've been saying for quite some time about the deindustrialization process the country is experiencing," said Paulo Skaf, president of Sao Paulo state industry federation Fiesp, one of the country's most powerful industrial lobbies. "Now all that's missing is for the government to take the correct measures to face it."

Of the 27 industrial sectors surveyed, 14 shrank in January from December, including cars, mining and medical equipment.

In broader industrial categories, output of capital goods fell 16 percent for the month, the IBGE said. Production of consumer goods fell 0.1 percent month on month, and durable consumer goods dropped 1.9 percent.

Fourth-quarter earnings were a miss for most listed manufacturing companies in Brazil, signaling the shrinking role of industry as services take center stage. Many of those companies, especially miners, pulp and food processors and capital goods makers, are revising down their future investment plans to cope with a tougher economic outlook.

title: Brazil Currency  Opens Weaker On  Intervention , Rate Outlook
text:
--Heavy intervention in currency markets by Brazil's government weakening real

--Expectations for lower interest rates also undermining currency

--Brazilian real opens trading at BRL1.7325, weaker from Friday's close at BRL1.7278


   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market continued to respond Monday to government measures to contain the real's recent strength, with an eye toward an expected interest-rate cut later this week that should further diminish the currency's attractiveness to foreign investors.

The real opened at BRL1.7325 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was weaker from Friday's close at BRL1.7278.

Brazil's government has increased both the rhetoric and actions against the real's nearly 10% gain against the U.S. dollar so far in 2012, boosting the number of dollar purchases and reverse-swap auctions to sop up excess liquidity as well as implementing measures to cool inflows over the past week. That's sent the real tumbling back from the BRL1.70-to-the-dollar level that appears to be the "line in the sand."

The strong real is hurting exporters and manufacturers, and Brazil is prepared to use "a large arsenal of weapons" to fight the real's appreciation, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said recently.

Mantega has recently reiterated concerns about a "currency war" as low interest rates and sluggish economic growth abroad cause foreign investors to seek higher rates of return in Brazil. The key lure are Brazil's towering interest rates, with the Selic base interest rate currently at 10.5%.

The Brazilian Central Bank meets Tuesday, when its expected to reduce the benchmark Selic rate by at least a half-percentage point. But there is growing evidence that the bank could opt for a more aggressive rate cut that would further decrease investor interest in Brazil.

Yields on overnight futures contracts point to expectations by some that policy makers could slash rates by 75 basis points. That would accelerate the series of half-point cuts that initially started in August, when central bankers were concerned that fallout from the ongoing European debt crisis could affect activity in Latin America's largest economy.

Brazil's interest rates have made it a favored destination for the carry trade, with investors borrowing cheap cash in the U.S. and Japan, where interest rates are near zero, and then investing the proceeds in emerging-market countries such as Brazil, where returns are high.

Lower interest rates typically cause demand for assets to wane, which could give the real room to weaken, said J.P. Morgan in a recent research note. "This hectic behavior increases the chances of breaking the topside of the BRL1.70-BRL1.75 range," J.P. Morgan strategists said. "A Selic cut greater than 0.50 percentage point could push [the real] to BRL1.80."

But central bankers also face the real danger that the recent surge in inflows could just as quickly disappear should the scenario in Europe worsen. Capital Economics, for example, predicts the rapid inflows into Brazil won't continue unabated throughout 2012.

"Given that we expect the euro-zone debt crisis to deepen this year, the severe financial dislocation associated with any breakup (or even simply renewed fears of its demise) could cause capital flows to reverse," Capital Economists said in a research note. "Nonetheless, pinning down the timing of such events is clearly very difficult and, in the meantime, rapid capital inflows threaten to destabilize the region."

(Updates with comments from economist, trader in paragraphs 10-12)

    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended active trading weaker against the U.S. dollar Friday in the wake of persistent government intervention over the past two sessions.

The real ended regular trading at BRL1.7278 to the dollar, weaker than late Thursday's BRL1.7112, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Early Thursday, Brazil's government announced a 6.0% IOF financial operations tax on foreign loans carrying three-year terms or more. Later Thursday, the government slapped a 6.0% IOF tax on trade finance lines, offered by Brazilian banks, with terms of one year or longer.

Brazilian officials have been explicit in expressing their concern over the appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar this year. The real has gained about 10% against the dollar since the beginning of 2012.

According to Finance Minister Guido Mantega in recent interviews and statements, the strong real is hurting Brazilian exporters and manufacturers. In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires last week, Mantega said the Brazilian government was prepared to use "a large arsenal of weapons" to fight what he called an "ongoing global currency war."

In recent months, higher IOF taxes on various forms of investment inflows have shown themselves to be one of the main weapons in the government's arsenal.

Another weapon, frequent purchases of dollars from the spot market, was used aggressively Friday. The central bank bought unspecified volumes of U.S. dollars at two separate snap auctions Friday, further weakening the real.

The deeper problem for policy makers, however, is continued high Brazilian interest rates. Brazil's Selic base interest rate is a towering 10.5%.

While most economists expect central bank cuts to the base rate in the next few months, the rate reductions are unlikely to have much impact on the currency market.

"Even at 8.0%, Brazil's base rate would still encourage the carry trade," said University of Sao Paulo economist Manuel Enriquez Garcia. The so-called carry trade refers to investors who borrow in markets like Japan and the U.S., where interest rates are near zero, and then invest in emerging market countries, such as Brazil, where returns are high.

"This means we are going to have to live with a strong Brazilian currency for the next couple of years," said Garcia.

A currency trader, who wished not to be named, said, "The carry trade has been the predominant factor in the market in recent weeks. That's not going to end."

Given such underlying factors, tax increases and central bank intervention in the market are relatively innocuous measures, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs. "The authorities seem determined to escalate the level of direct FX market intervention," they said in a research note. "But the effects of these types of measures tends to erode over time as financial/capital flows migrate to areas that are less regulated/taxed or restricted."

title: DJ Brazil's Real Erases Losses As Minister Threatens More  FX  Steps
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency reversed course Thursday midmorning and gained against the dollar, even as Finance Minister Guido Mantega promised more steps to prevent the currency from appreciating too fast.

Earlier Thursday, the government extended a 6.0% tax on short-term foreign loans to loans of up to three years, it said through a decree by President Dilma Rousseff. Previously, the financial operations tax, or IOF, was charged only on loans of two years or less.

Mantega said there was cheap credit and excess liquidity in global markets, which is working its way into Brazil. The government will continue to take measures to stem the currency's gains, Mantega told reporters.

Most analysts, however, shrugged off this particular measure, although they expressed concern about the threat of more action down the line.

"We don't believe this will have a very significant impact in the market but, most importantly, this is a strong signal that the government is not comfortable with the current currency levels and aware and not comfortable with the inflows that are not aimed for investment, and this means that we cannot rule out the possibility of new changes soon," said one trader, in a note.

The measure is part of an explicit government effort to arrest the appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar, and followed two significant interventions by the Central Bank of Brazil on Wednesday. So far this year, the currency has gained about 10% against the U.S. dollar.

In this first assault on the key barrier of BRL1.70 per dollar, the government has been successful. After dipping below that level early Wednesday, at BRL1.6902, the Brazilian currency lost ground sharply against the dollar, and that continued Thursday morning.

The real weakened to BRL1.7239 per dollar early Thursday, versus a late Wednesday fix of BRL1.7141, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. But the currency erased those losses midmorning, and ended up pushing stronger, to BRL1.7133 at 1417 GMT.

Still, many analysts are skeptical that Brazil will be able to stem the tide. This week's move by the European Central Bank to provide banks with unlimited funding at rock-bottom rates through its Long Term Refinancing Operation is the latest in a series of measures taken in developed countries to inject vast amounts of capital into their stricken financial systems.

Some of that money is finding its way into countries such as Brazil, which has a relatively free-floating currency and stronger growth prospects. Barring a major crisis, many believe the Brazilian currency is set to gain against the dollar.

There was some relief that the government did not increase the IOF tax on foreign exchange derivatives introduced last July, which currently stands at 1%, but can be raised as high as 25%, said RBS Securities, in a note. Nor did the government reintroduce the IOF tax on foreign inflows into equities that was removed in December 2011, it said.

"But for sure, the government is showing its hand and considering the LTRO results and potential inflows to come out of improvement in global liquidity and risk appetite, no doubt more adjustments are ready to go if necessary," RBS said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real gains despite capital controls
text:
* Brazil widens scope of foreign-loans tax to stem inflows

 * Mexico peso strengthens 1.1 pct; Chile peso slips 0.4 pct 

(Updates prices, adds comments)

 By Guillermo Parra-Bernal and Rachel Uranga

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, March 1 (Reuters) - Brazil's real climbed on Thursday despite the country's latest capital controls. It was the opposite of the desired effect, coming on the same day that Brazil's president lashed out at U.S. and European monetary policies she blames for inflating the real's value.

 Brazilian authorities widened the scope of a tax on corporate foreign borrowing, and the move fanned speculation that Latin America's largest economy will fight capital inflows more vigorously.

 Analysts, however, doubt new measures will be enough to halt the real's advance.

 The Brazilian real gained 0.47 percent to 1.7120 per dollar, hovering near the 1.70-per-dollar mark the central bank has been seen defending.

 "You introduce these measures, and people just back away for a little bit. But in the end, everyone knows there are a lot of flows, and it's inevitable that the currency will break that" level of 1.70, said Italo Lombardi, a Latin American economist from Standard Chartered Bank in New York.      

 Brazil's so-called IOF tax was extended to foreign loans with maturities of up to three years from two years previously.

 BACKLASH AGAINST 'CHEAP MONEY'

 The move comes on the seventh consecutive day of the central bank purchasing dollars in the spot market and on top of  Wednesday's reverse currency swaps. 

 "We cannot discount the possibility of additional measures being announced to slow foreign-exchange inflows if the currency continues to threaten breaking below (the 1.70-real threshold)  on a sustained basis," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research at Royal Bank of Canada Securities in Toronto.

 Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff has even stepped in with a high-profile speech that slammed rich nations for unleashing a "tsunami" of cheap money that was "cannibalizing" poorer countries. 

 The European Central Bank and other countries' efforts to spur their economies with low interest rates and cheap loans have fueled gains in the real, which has appreciated more than 8 percent this year. 

 Foreign investors seeking returns higher than those found in developed countries are pouring more money into Brazil and in the opinion of government officials,  hurting local manufacturers by making the country's exports more expensive overseas. 

 Brazil's effort highlights concerns that short-term dollar flows are coming through disguised as intercompany loans, said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland Securities. She said the move may do little to arrest the real's rally, since many companies borrow abroad for longer than three years.

 A report by local newspaper Valor Econômico, citing sources familiar with the situation, said government officials are mulling a potential tax on foreign direct investment inflows while they remain in cash. The report said that the tax could be refunded once the funds are applied.

 According to Valor, the government is worried that a meaningful portion of direct investment, the type of capital spending used for productive purposes, is parked in Brazil to earn returns on government debt - which pays one of the world's highest borrowing costs. 

 Finance Minister Guido Mantega, speaking at a news conference in Brasilia, denied there were plans to tax foreign direct investment. The levy "will continue as it is," he said.

 "Taxing FDI inflows will be a very risky move, given FDI is seen as helping to improve Brazil's competitiveness, productivity and capital stock, so they will have to tread lightly here," Chamie said.

  In the year through Feb. 24, U.S. dollar inflows

into Brazil totaled $12.533 billion. Much of that money has flowed into the nation's stock market, helping boost the nation's benchmark Bovespa stock index by 16 percent in the same period.

 But Brazil's increasing use of interventions and capital controls has spooked some investors.

 "If I am bullish on emerging market currencies and I am bullish on Latin American currencies, I would much rather play Mexico than Brazil because there is no fear of intervention," Lombardi said. 

 The Mexican peso gained 1.05 percent to 12.7270 per dollar, while the Chilean peso weakened 0.35 percent to bid at 481.50.  

(Reporting by Guillermo Parra-Bernal in Sao Paulo and Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Jan Paschal)

--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their exchange rates.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking that has given credence to some emerging market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who authored the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and the currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that foreswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

-By Ian Talley, Dow Jones Newswires, 202-862-9285; ian.talley@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE:IMF Paper Advocates Temporary Emerging-Market  FX Intervention
text:
--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

(Adds IMF economists' comments, background and details throughout, starting in the third paragraph)

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their currencies.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

Far from being reluctant to use exchange rate intervention, "central banks should embrace its use as being fully consistent" with inflation-targeting, the economists said.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking, giving credence to some emerging-market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who wrote the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and their currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that forswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

The authors argued against sustained exchange rate intervention, saying it would prove too costly to an economy. Rather, under permanent market pressures, policy makers should allow the currency to adjust. Unlike Brazil or South Korea, which are largely recognized as floating economies despite some currency intervention, China's yuan has long been seen as persistently undervalued as the central bank buys foreign currency and sells yuan to give it a competitive advantage.

"You should not be intervening to sustain a misaligned exchange rate, you should be intervening to mitigate misalignment," Ostry said.

Emerging markets are particularly exposed to large international capital flows because government balance sheets don't have the depth to offset such investments and their economies aren't as flexible as industrialized countries. Like reeds in the wind, emerging markets have had to weather massive capital movements in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and euro debt woes.

The Institute of International Finance, an industry group representing more than 400 of the world's largest financial firms, expects capital flows to emerging markets to fall this year by an estimated $164 billion, contributing to a near-30% plummet in cash flows to those regions since 2010. That's likely to mean continuing pressure on their exchange rates. Earlier this month, Brazil's finance minister revived fears of an international currency war.

But the IMF staff said that as long as countries are simply seeking to return their currencies back into equilibrium with underlying economic fundamentals, intervention can play a stabilizing role in regional and global economies. By combining forex intervention with policy-rate decisions, central banks can afford to weaken their rate actions to achieve the same objective. That prevents a competition of too-low interest rates across emerging markets and avoid the resulting competitive interventions, the authors say.

The shift in perspective also highlights the growing say of emerging markets within the fund and the academic fallout from the financial crisis that eroded many long-held economist assumptions. The condoning of currency intervention--on a limited basis--addresses complaints from many developing countries that advanced nations should take into account the international impacts of monetary and economic policy. Brazil, for example, repeatedly cited the U.S. Federal Reserve's easing as helping to drive capital flows damaging to its economy. Brazil has intervened to prevent the real from further harm, drawing criticism from abroad.

-By Ian Talley, Dow Jones Newswires, 202-862-9285; ian.talley@dowjones.com

title: Brazil Central Bank Intervention  Drags Real To Weaker Close
text:
--Brazil real closes weaker as central bank intervenes twice during session

--Government "always evaluating" measures to contain sharp swings in currency

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL1.7141 to the dollar

By Jeff Fick and Luciana Magalhaes

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency closed weaker Wednesday as the central bank intervened in the market twice, reinforcing the government's desire to protect exporters and manufacturers by curtailing the real's nearly 10% gain against the U.S. dollar so far in 2012.

"The market is testing the central bank practically every day," said Clodoir Vieira, an economist at Sao Paulo brokerage house Souza Barros. "But the central bank is giving a clear signal that the floor for the real is about BRL1.70 to BRL1.71 to the dollar."

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7141 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL1.6992 to the greenback, and well off the opening quote of BRL1.6902 that triggered action from the Brazilian Central Bank.

An improving outlook for global economic growth and continued ample liquidity in financial markets have once again opened the door for a flood of investment inflows into Latin America's largest economy. Brazil's towering interest rates also continue to make the country a popular destination for investors seeking higher rates of return, traders said.

The latest fuel came after the European Central Bank granted EUR530 billion in inexpensive three-year loans to 800 banks as the single-currency bloc continues to struggle with its ongoing debt crisis. The latest wave of loans followed December's EUR489 billion in lending. The ECB aims to avoid an escalating crisis as banks struggle to pay off maturing debts and also to mitigate a sharp pullback in bank lending to customers across ailing European economies.

The real has also strengthened as local companies tap overseas debt markets with a series of bond issues.

Brazil's government is "always evaluating" measures to curb the real's appreciation against the U.S. dollar and there will be a greater chance of action following any sharp gain by the currency, a person familiar with the government's strategy said Wednesday.

The Brazilian Central Bank continued its recent string of aggressive actions to contain the real's nearly 10% gain against the U.S. dollar. The bank intervened twice early in the session after the real opened at BRL1.6902 to the dollar, below the psychologically important BRL1.70 mark that many traders consider the government's "line in the sand."

In the first move, the bank sold $1.52 billion worth of so-called reverse swap contracts at two maturities. The actions, which allow investors to swap foreign-exchange positions for government paper linked to interest rates, typically support the dollar by removing Brazilian real exposure from the market. The auctions were used extensively in late 2005 and early 2006 before market interest in the swaps waned. The reverse swaps have been used infrequently since then.

The central bank also purchased an undisclosed volume of dollars from the spot market at a snap auction Wednesday, paying BRL1.7032 to the dollar. The real weakened sharply after the two moves, climbing back above the key BRL1.70 mark to trade midafternoon at BRL1.7166 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

"Today's interventions were more aggressive than we would normally expect by the Brazilian Central Bank," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging market research at Nomura Securities International in New York.

Volpon added that Brazil's government, from now on, may promote a stronger correlation between exchange rates and interest rates. In congressional testimony Tuesday, Brazilian Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini once again strongly hinted at more interest-rate cuts to come.

Brazil's Selic base rate is currently 10.5%. Volpon said the rate could fall as low as 8.5%. Lower interest rates could help arrest the appreciation of the real by making Brazil less attractive as an investment venue.

Wednesday's government interventions also once again ignited market worries regarding sterner currency measures, such as the taxes Brazil's government slapped on some incoming investments in 2010 and 2011.

Last week, in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the government has "a large arsenal of instruments" that it will use "to prevent an excessive appreciation of the Brazilian currency."

text:
* Brazil cenbank intervention beats back real's surge

* Brazil real weakens 1.2 pct, Chile peso declines 0.6 pct

* Mexican peso trades flat

By Rachel Uranga and Asher Levine

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Feb 29 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real slipped sharply on Wednesday after the country's central bank stepped into currency markets to beat back the real's surge beyond the 1.70-per-dollar mark.

The real, which has appreciated more than eight percent since the beginning of the year, weakened 1.2 percent to bid at 1.7190 per dollar. Other Latin American currencies traded mixed.

"With foreign capital entering the local market, it will continue to get more difficult to hold the real at this level," said Maurico Nakahodo, an economist at Brazil's CM Capital Markets.

A flood of foreign investors seeking returns higher than those found in developed countries has helped strengthen the real, hurting local manufactures by increasing the cost of the country's exports.

Brazil's central bank said on Wednesday that U.S. dollar inflows to the country totaled $5.251 billion in the calendar month through February 24.

"Both the intervention as well as expectations that the government could employ other tools to hold back the real's gains helped weaken the real," he said.

The central bank used reverse currency swaps and spot dollar buys to cool the real.

The central bank sold 30,500, or 76 percent, of the 40,000 reverse currency swaps on offer in the auction for a financial value of about $1.5 billion. The contracts mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets.

In Peru, intervention efforts have failed to slow gains for the sol. The currency hit its strongest level in 15 years, advancing 0.11 percent to 2.673 per dollar despite the central bank's purchase of $118 million in the spot market, its third consecutive intervention this week.

Mexico's peso traded flat at 12.8321 per dollar. The currency trimmed early gains after banks gobbled up more than half a trillion euros of cheap three-year funds offered by the European Central Bank in an effort to stabilize the euro-zone financial system.

Stronger-than-expected U.S. fourth-quarter growth data bolstered an early firming of the currency. But comments by Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke, warning that the U.S. job market is far from normal, limited advances.

Bernanke told the U.S. Congress that unless growth accelerated, the unacceptably high U.S. unemployment rate would not keep dropping. But he stopped short of signaling further Fed bond purchases, tempering traders' hopes for monetary stimulus.

"Some see Bernanke's comments as an indication there will be no monetary stimulus in the short term," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with Forex Chile, a brokerage in Santiago.

Chile's peso weakened 0.65 percent to bid at 479.80 per dollar. Declining copper prices - Chile's main export - also contributed to the weakening of the peso.

title: UPDATE 1- Brazil  real slips beyond 1.70 after  intervention
text:
* Central bank ratchets up attack on stronger real

* Brazil sells 76 percent of reverse swaps at auction

* Real bucks regional FX firming after ECB cash injection

(Recasts, adds background)

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Feb 29 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank offered reverse currency swaps and bought dollars in the spot market on Wednesday, keeping Brazil's currency from appreciating beyond the 1.70 per dollar mark.

The real, which had firmed to 1.6860 in early trading, its strongest in four months, weakened after the intervention to 1.7138.

The intervention allowed Brazil's real to avoid the surge seen in other Latin American currencies following the European Central Bank's (ECB) offer of 530 billion euros of cheap finance to Europe's troubled banks.

The real has gained more than 9 percent since the beginning of the year on the back of massive inflows from investors seeking higher returns than they can get in more developed markets. Brazil's benchmark interest rate is 10.5 percent. In the United States the equivalent rate is zero to 0.25 percent.

The ECB's capital injection pumped even more low cost capital into world markets. Much of it is expected to move to higher-risk and higher-return assets in places such as Latin America.

A stronger Brazilian real has made the country's exports more expensive and hurt the competitiveness of local manufactuers prompting the Brazilian government to act.

The central bank sold 30,500, or 76 percent, of the 40,000 reverse currency swaps on offer in the auction for a financial value of about $1.5 billion. The contracts mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets.

The bank sold 20,000, 32-day reverse swaps maturing April 2,

99.9661 percent of face value for a nominal yield of 0.3941 percent and financial value of $999.7 million.

It also sold 10,500, 123-day reverse swaps maturing July 2, at 99.6850 percent of face value for a nominal yield of 0.9408 percent and financial value of $523.3 million.

On Wednesday, Brazil's real underperformed the Mexican and the Colombian pesos , which rose 0.5 and 0.15 percent to the U.S. dollar.

Earlier this month, the central bank sold only 3,500 contracts in a similar operation. It also bought U.S. dollar forwards and intervened in the local spot market.

Central bank chief Alexandre Tombini said on Tuesday that those auctions helped prevent the real from strengthening too much. National Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin also said that the country's sovereign wealth fund could buy dollars.

Brazil's speeding economic growth has been attracting foreign investments in infrastructure, bonds and equities. Its 10.5-percent benchmark interest rates also lures investors.,

The govenrnment is pursuing a tighter fiscal policy to pave the way for single-digit rates.

European Central Bank's push to shield its financial system by lending more than 1 trillion euros to banks made cheap money even more available in global markets.

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Price increases in Brazil will continue to slow over the course of 2012, getting closer to the central bank's goal of 4.5%, Alexandre Tombini, president of Brazil's central bank, said Tuesday.

The slowdown in inflation will come despite accelerating economic growth over the course of the year, with gross domestic product growing more in the second half than in the first, Tombini told a Senate committee.

The neutral interest rate in Brazil has declined in recent years, as the government has maintained a policy of fiscal responsibility and inflation goals have been met, Tombini said. The rate is expected to continue to decline in coming years, he added.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real firms despite cenbank, rates eyed
text:
(Updates with closing prices, Colombia raising rates)

* Real gains despite central bank auctions to buy dlrs

* Colombia extends dollar purchases through August, peso flat

* Brazil neutral interest rates seen higher than expected

* Mexican peso weakens on euro zone concerns

By José de Castro

Feb 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's real gained on Friday as persistent central bank intervention failed to fully absorb dollar inflows, while the country's interest-rate futures rose sharply after a survey suggested the economy needed tighter monetary policy to grow without higher inflation.

Most Latin American currencies were supported by commodity gains, although worries about the euro zone crisis weighed on the Mexican peso. Colombia's decision to extend dollar purchases through August could also curb a rally in its currency.

The Brazilian real trimmed some of its earlier gains, but still closed 0.23 percent higher at 1.710 per dollar after two dollar-buying auctions launched by the central bank less than one hour apart.

The bank's action came one day after it offered to sell reverse currency swaps for the first time since August and also bought dollars in the spot market, in an attempt to halt a rally that has been hurting the country's exporters.

The real has gained more than 9 percent so far this year and the central bank's interventions in the foreign exchange market added to the perception that the government is drawing a line at 1.7 reais per dollar.

"The psychological level has inevitably shaped around the 1.7000-handle in spot, though clearly the central bank is struggling to absorb the large debt inflows related primarily to external corporate debt issuance and overall strong capital account inflows," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, currency strategist at RBS Securities.

At Friday's auctions, Brazil's central bank initially bought dollars at a cutoff price 1.7059 reais, and then at 1.7057 reais.

INTEREST RATES JUMP

Concerns about the pace of monetary policy easing in Brazil were stoked after the central bank released a survey showing economists estimate the economy can grow without inflationary pressures if real interest rates are about 5.5 percent, higher than the 4.5-5.0 percent expected by many traders.

Brazil's benchmark interest rate currently stands at 10.5 percent after four half-percentage-point rate cuts since August. Inflation for the 12 months ended Jan. 31 was 6.22 percent, giving Brazil a real interest rate of about 4.3 percent - more than a percentage point below the neutral rate survey estimate.

"There is this feeling that the central bank might be exaggerating and, just to be sure, markets raised the rates," said a trader in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's interest-rate contract for January 2013 rose to 9.270 percent from 9.220 percent in Thursday's adjusted close. The contract for January 2014 jumped to 9.750 percent from 9.670 percent.

The Chilean peso rose as much as 0.7 percent during the session before ending broadly flat against the dollar, at 480.30, as local dollar purchases offset a jump in prices of copper, the country's main export.

In Mexico, however, concerns about the euro zone crisis drove the peso 0.65 percent lower to a one-week low of 12.9055 per dollar, according to the central bank's closing prices.

After trading within a narrow range in the past few days, the peso pierced a key Fibonacci resistance level around 12.86 per greenback, but analysts said light trading made it unclear whether those losses will be sustained.

COLOMBIA TO BUY MORE DOLLARS

Strong dollar inflows have provided a powerful tailwind to Latin American currencies this year, and analysts expect that trend to intensify as commodity prices rise and the European Central Bank floods the markets again with cheap money next week.

The Colombian peso gained as much as 0.4 percent during the day, but closed little changed at 1,776.00 per dollar, before the central bank announced its widely-expected decision to raise benchmark interest rates by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.

The bank also said it will extend its dollar-buying program, which includes daily purchases of a minimum of $20 million in the spot market, for at least three additional months until Aug. 4.

"We would expect this to help prevent further appreciation of the peso, but do not expect a reversion of the trend from recent months," Barclays Capital said in a research note.

title: Brazil  Real Gains,Limited By Government- Intervention  Speculation
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real strengthened against the U.S. dollar Friday on progress in the euro-zone crisis and on the outlook for continued investment inflows to the Latin American country, but gains were limited on speculation that the government will be more aggressive in containing the currency's rise.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7040 to the dollar, stronger than the previous close at BRL1.7094, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

The Greek Cabinet on Friday approved a EUR100 billion debt write-down for the country as part of a new multibillion-euro rescue plan Greece is seeking from its international creditors. European Union leaders will meet in less than a week to give final approval for the deal.

The bailout "doesn't solve the problem, but it does provide some relief," said Bruno Lavieri, an economist at the Tendencias consulting firm. "Today our markets accompanied the international scenario, while here the government made it clear that the dollar won't go below 1.70 without the government stepping in with heavy measures."

The central bank carried out two purchases on the spot market toward the end of the trading day Friday as the currency threatened to strengthen past 1.70 for a second consecutive day.

In Brazil, expectations are for continued inflows as investors in developed economies take advantage of low rates at home to borrow and invest abroad. Domestic companies are also seeking financing as markets open up again after last year's cautious tone due to European woes.

On Friday, the Getulio Vargas Foundation helped undergird that optimism, reporting that consumer confidence rose in February, rebounding from a January decline.

Brazil's high interest rates and relatively stable growth make it an attractive destination, especially after the lifting of some measures by the government to limit investment that were put in place last year.

But the government could put some of those same measures back in place as the currency strengthens past 1.70 to the dollar, analysts say.

"The central bank is trying to convey the message that it doesn't feel comfortable with sub-1.70 levels for the BRL, at least not with such a rapid move this year," Banco Santander economists wrote in a Friday note. "Going forward, the central bank will very likely have to be much more assertive in the spot market, buying large amounts to sterilize the FX inflows and give the market the signal that it is willing to tackle rapid appreciation of the BRL."

The central bank on Thursday also intervened in currency markets after the real strengthened past BRL1.69 to the dollar, with a sale of reverse currency swaps and a spot auction to purchase dollars.

title: Brazil Stocks Close Lower On Pessimistic Outlook For Europe
text:
--The Ibovespa index fell 0.4% to 65,819, from Wednesday's close of 66,092 points

--Pessimistic growth forecasts from Europe outweighed good news from U.S., Brazil

--European Commission forecast euro-zone GDP will contract in 2012

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazilian stocks closed lower Thursday after bad news from Europe outweighed positive indicators in the U.S.

The benchmark Ibovespa index fell 0.4% to 65,819 points, from Wednesday's close of 66,092 points.

The euro-zone economy is expected to contract in 2012, after falling into a recession at the start of the year, the European Commission warned Thursday. On an annual basis, the 17-country euro zone is forecast to contract by 0.3%, while gross domestic product in the larger European Union is seen flat on the year. The commission said it expects the euro-zone economy to contract in the first quarter by 0.3%, after dropping by the same amount in the last quarter of 2011.

Meanwhile, European Central Bank President Mario Draghi added to the pessimism about growth, by insisting that the region's worsening economic situation not be used as an excuse to relax deficit targets.

"There is no feasible trade-off" between economic overhauls and fiscal belt-tightening, Draghi said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal, his first since Greece sealed its second bailout deal.

Brazil's Labor Ministry announced shortly after the market opened that 118,895 jobs with formal documentation were created in January, even though this was 21.83% below the figure for the same month in 2011. The mining, services, construction and agricultural industries were the biggest job creators in the month, while the number of new jobs in the government administrative sector fell, as well as in the retail sector for seasonal reasons, the Ministry said.

In the U.S., the number of new claims for unemployment benefits remained stable in the week ending Feb. 18, a more favorable result than had been expected by analysts.

The good jobs news from the U.S. wasn't enough to buoy markets in Brazil, said Pedro Paulo Silveira, an economist at the TOV brokerage house in Sao Paulo.

"The market started falling because of the outlook in Europe," he said. "The U.S. data today don't change the pessimistic trend that the European information started."

Brazil's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market Thursday, holding a reverse currency swap auction at which $174.7 million in contracts were sold. The intervention also failed to cheer equities investors.

Earlier Thursday, Brazil's real strengthened to BRL1.6978 to the U.S. dollar, from its Wednesday close of BRL1.7051.

Blue-chips showed mixed performance.

Steelmaker Usinas Siderurgicas de Minas Gerais (USIM5.BR) slipped 1% to BRL11.87.

Utility Companhia Energetica de Sao Paulo (CESP6.BR) fell 2.6% to BRL36.93.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies  Mixed On Weakening Investor Confidence
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies were mixed and lacked direction Thursday as global concerns continued to weigh on investor confidence.

"There are three major global risks to watch and it is likely that global markets will await further clarification about those three before [they] can switch gear away from neutral," said Benoit Anne, head of emerging market strategy at Societe Generale. The events include implementation of Greece's agreement, the second long-term refinancing operation and its impact on global markets, and the recent surge in oil prices on escalation of concerns about Iran.

The blazing rally that led to between 5% and 10% gains across emerging market currencies in the first few weeks of this year has fizzled out, at least for now.

"Investors have switched to a wait-and-see mode, with the result that the momentum has been lost for now," Anne said. Asian currencies were listless through their trading session.

Germany's strong Ifo survey, which indicateded rising confidence in a resilient economy, buoyed investor sentiment some, as did U.S. data that showed no additional workers filed for jobless benefits last week. Currently, the South African rand and emerging European currencies such as the Czech koruna are up, the dollar having lost nearly a 1% against these currencies.

Risk premiums on emerging market debt weakened two basis points to 367 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index-Global. Despite the lackluster investor sentiment, some issuers went ahead with new issuance including India's Reliance Industries Ltd. (500325.BY) and Brazil's third-largest bank, Banco Bradesco SA (BBD, BBDC4.BR).

Reliance sold a $500 million tap of its 2022 dollar bond, after a $1 billion bond earlier in the month. The offering by the energy and materials giant--India's largest company by market value--priced at 101.018 to yield 5.267%, and was more than six times oversubscribed.

Bradesco, meanwhile, has a $1 billion bond that is expected to price at a yield of 5.75%, according to sources familiar with the deal.

In currencies, the euro returned to HUF289.90 against the Hungarian forint after hitting a high of HUF290.87 following a surprising poor show at a government bond auction where buyers demanded higher yield for these notes, though they bought more than the planned sale amount. However, continued inaction on the part of Hungary to fix controversial laws and escalating tensions with the European Commission have upset investors.

On the other hand, both the Polish zloty and Czech koruna gained trading at PLN4.1783 and CZK25.064 against the euro, respectively, according to CQG data. The South African rand continued to have a positive run, as its budget showed a deficit of 4.6% vs. 5.5% expected by the market. The dollar weakened to ZAR7.6536 against the rand.

In Latin America, Brazil and Peru saw their central banks intervene again. Market participants suggest that the dollar at BRL1.70 is a critical level for the central bank.

title: Brazil  Real Weaker After  Central Bank Intervenes ;More Action Seen
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened in late trading Thursday, after the central bank intervened twice to stem a trend that has led the real to appreciate 9% against the U.S. dollar so far this year. Economists expect further intervention in coming days.

The real exited normal trading at BRL1.7094 to the U.S. dollar, weaker than Wednesday's close of BRL1.7051, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Earlier in the day however, the real had strengthened to BRL 1.6978, tracking the euro and markets world-wide in a positive response to a measure of German business confidence that rose more than expected. Germany's IFO business climate index rose to 109.60 in February, from 108.30 in January, and above market expectations of 108.80.

The early strengthening of the real put the currency above the BRL1.70 barrier that economists view as an unofficial trigger point above which the central bank needs to take action to prevent excessive appreciation, which puts Brazilian exporters at a disadvantage on international markets.

Shortly afterward, the bank intervened with a sale of reverse currency swaps and a spot auction to purchase dollars, managing to push the real back to BRL1.7093, the other side of the barrier.

"They won't admit it, but BRL1.70 may be a barrier for the Central Bank," said Jankiel Santos of Espirito Santo Investment Bank. "Their actions stemmed the appreciation and had the desired effect."

For Raphael Martello of Tendencias Consultancy, the government showed itself to be "a bit bothered" by the real's crossing the BRL1.70 mark. "The real is one of the currencies that's appreciated the most so far this year," the economist said.

While the central bank sold only a fraction of the reverse currency swap contracts it offered at the first auction, this nonetheless helped stabilize the market, setting the level back at around BRL1.70, which was consolidated by the later dollar purchase auction, according to Martello.

Both economists said they expect further interventions in coming days, as foreign currency inflows continue strongly as Brazil is considered an attractive investment destination due to its continuing high interest rates and strong economic fundamentals.

The measures are likely to include more dollar purchase auctions and currency swap auctions, but are less likely to include new taxes on foreign investment, they said.

"Brazil needs foreign investments to finance its growth as local savings levels are low," Martello said.

MEXICO CITY, Feb 22 (Reuters) - The Brazilian currency strengthened on Wednesday to its strongest level against the dollar in almost four months, triggering the central bank to intervene.

Other Latin American currencies mostly weakened due to mounting fears that the euro zone may be heading toward recession and to persistent concern over debt-laden Greece despite a fresh bailout.

The Brazilian real gained 0.41 percent to 1.7070 per dollar, as the market digested positive news from earlier in the week after a two-day carnival holiday.

"The Greek rescue deal is adding momentum to the real as the market just reopened today," said Caio Duarte, chief economist with Lopes Filho in Sao Paulo.

The real has appreciated more than 9 percent so far this year.

The real's sharp gains could put the country's exporters at a competitive disadvantage and Brazil's central bank sought to curb its rise by buying dollars in the spot market on Wednesday.

Surveys of purchasing managers published on

Wednesday tempered appetite for riskier assets after they showed unexpectedly weak activity in Germany - the euro zone's most powerful economy - and in France.

The survey also showed continued weakness in Greece, which secured a 130-billion-euro rescue package on Tuesday to avoid a messy default after agreeing to a series of austerity measures.

The markets see Greece struggling to meet the demands of its new bailout deal.

"We will see some profit taking in the next month or two as we get closer to the general elections (in Greece). I think the real risk is what will the new leadership in Greece do," said Michael Woolfolk, an FX strategist with BNY Mellon in New York.

"That type of uncertainty is going to be a cloud over the market. It's going to be a good excuse to take profit on emerging markets, emerging market currencies, commodities and equities."

Mexico's peso lost 0.42 percent to 12.8450

The Markit Eurozone Composite Flash PMI fell to 49.7 in February from 50.4 last month, below expectations for a rise to 50.6 and under the 50 line that divides growth from contraction.

Preliminary data that showed China's manufacturing sector contracting also added to investors' worries that hurt the prices of key commodities such as copper.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latin America  FX  gains on Greece bailout hopes
text:
* Real spot market closed Mon and Tues for Carnaval holiday

* Mexican peso gains 0.4 pct, Brazil's real firms 0.11 pct

By Jean Luis Arce and Alonso Soto

MEXICO CITY/BRASILIA, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Friday as investors cautiously bet a Greek bailout deal would be struck on Monday, helping the country avert a messy default.

Against the U.S. dollar, Brazil's real appreciated 0.11 percent to 1.7140 while Mexico's peso gained 0.44 to bid at 12.7560.

Euro zone finance ministers are expected to finalize the details of a Greek rescue package on Monday but Eurogroup head Jean-Claude Juncker said there was still much work to be done to draw down the country's soaring debt.

After months of diplomatic hurdles and alternating market optimism and fear over whether Greece would avoid a chaotic default, investors remain wary ahead of the meeting.

"There is a moderate optimism that they are going to approve a second bailout package for Greece," said Erick Urtuzuastegui, an analyst at consultancy Prognosis in Mexico City. "There is every indication that in the short term there won't be a disorderly Greek default and that lowers risk aversion."

The real and the Mexican peso both gained about 0.4 percent this week. The Mexican peso traded between 12.6688 and 12.9943 per dollar this week while the real ran between 1.7090 and 1.7375.

"We are in a very narrow range and I don't think that is going to change until after a decision is made in Greece," said Enrique Alvarez, Latin America bond and currency analyst with IDEAGlobal in New York.

Latin American currencies have soared this year, largely on hopes the euro zone debt crisis could be easing and on signs of a recovering economy in the United States.

"The confirmation of that deal next week will probably get investors to seek higher-yield assets," said Reginaldo Galhardo, exchange trade manager for Treviso Corretora in Sao Paulo. "All that liquidity in more conservative positions will return to emerging markets with force."

Galhardo said currency traders are likely to push the real closer to the 1.70 per dollar mark to test the tolerance level of the central bank and the government.

In February, Brazil's central bank resumed currency interventions after the real gained more than 8 percent on a surge in risk appetite that has boosted other Latin American currencies.

"The market is testing the resolve of the central bank and the government," Galhardo said.

The Brazilian real spot market will be closed on Monday and Tuesday due to the Carnaval holiday.

Chile's peso ended flat, firming 0.06 to bid at 484.50 per dollar after prices for its main export fell.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  slips on US data, downgrades
text:
* U.S. retail data worse than expected

* Brazil's real weakens 0.3 pct, Mexico's peso loses 0.5 pct

By Rachel Uranga and Jean Luis Arce

MEXICO CITY, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Tuesday after poorer than expected U.S. retail sales and Monday's credit downgrade of six European nations knocked riskier assets worldwide.

Brazil's real pulled back after firming to a 3-1/2-month high on Monday. The real lost 0.37 percent to bid at 1.7210 per dollar.

Citing risks of Europe's credit crisis, rating agency Moody's cut the credit ratings of six countries including Spain and Portugal while for the first time it placed Britain's prized top credit rating in jeopardy.

"It was bad news," said Eduardo Suarez, an analyst with Scotia Bank in Toronto. "Mexico was the one that reacted strongest to it."

Hanging over markets is whether Greece will secure a second bailout needed to save it from a chaotic default that could throw international financial markets in disarray.

Mexico's peso is the most freely traded currency in Latin America, allowing speculators to easily pile on bearish bets when global markets sour.

Mexico's peso slipped 0.51 percent to 12.7650 per dollar.

Further pressuring the peso, U.S. retail sales rose less than expected in January as consumers cut back on car purchases and shopped less online.

The United States is Mexico's top trading partner and a slump in the economy harms Mexican exports.

Latin American currencies saw a huge rally at the start of the year, stoked by improving economic data from the United States and bets Europe's debt crisis could ease. Before its string of losses since last week, the Mexican peso had gained about 10 percent in 2012.

"The trader is looking for whatever pretext to take profits," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico City.

Chile's peso bid 0.9 percent weaker at 484.50 per dollar, pulling back from a five-month high last week as the price for copper, the country's top export, slipped.

Euro zone finance ministers dropped plans on Tuesday for an in-person meeting on Greece's new international bailout, as the cabinet in Athens argued over an austerity plan needed to secure the rescue package.

"When things become clearer (in Greece) in a few weeks, the enthusiasm is going to return," Gordillo said.

Of the 152 currencies tracked by Thomson Reuters, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico are in the top six gainers this year, advancing more than 8 percent.

The strong gains are hurting Latin American exporters, since costlier local currencies make manufacturers less competitive against cheaper imports.

Brazil intervened in its spot market last week for the first time since September. Traders said they were expecting the central bank to take further measures to curb the recent appreciation of the real.

Investors are wary that further gains toward 1.70 per dollar could trigger more intervention, with some fearing a new round of capital controls.

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega denied a report the government is considering raising taxes on floating-rate debt investments, saying that no tax increases of any kind are planned at this time.

(Updates prices)

By Rachel Uranga and Daniel Bases

MEXICO CITY/NEW YORK, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed to a 3-1/2 month high on Monday, raising concerns of interevention, while Venezuelan bonds gained after the opposition rallied behind a candidate to battle socialist president Hugo Chavez.

Greece's parliament approved tough austerity measures needed for a new bailout, which lifted appetite for riskier assets around the world and helped Brazil's real and Mexico's peso

last week.
