title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  weakens as Greek bailout falters
text:
* Worries about Greek debt hit risk appetite

 * Brazil currency slips 0.34 pct, Mexico's peso down 1.12 pct 

(Recasts, adds comments)

 By Lorena Segura and Rachel Uranga

 MEXICO CITY, Feb 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's real and Mexico's peso suffered their worst week in two months, as renewed worries that Greece could fail to meet debt payments hit global markets, while revived intervention tactics weighed in Brazil. 

 Latin American currencies weakened sharply on Friday after the leader of a party in Greece's ruling coalition refused to back a 130-billion-euro bailout agreement.

 The shock, after days of building expectations that Greece was nearing a deal to pass painful austerity measures, played into concerns that a rally in risk assets this year has gone too far, too fast. 

 There could be more profit taking next week given signs Europe is struggling to agree on terms for a second bailout deal for Greece, analysts said. 

 Still, many expect further gains in the coming months as a boost in liquidity from central banks eases fears that Greece's troubles could spark another financial crisis. 

 "I do not think we have seen the end of the rally in currencies or rates, if the real motivator is external liquidity conditions," said Joel Virgin, an analyst at Citigroup-unit Banamex in Mexico City. 

 In December, the European Central Bank provided emergency three-year funding for banks and last month the U.S. Federal Reserve said it envisions exceptionally low interest rates through late 2014. Low interest rates in major economies drive investors to seek higher yields in emerging markets. 

 The real  dipped 0.34 percent to bid at 1.7266 per U.S. dollar, pulling further away from the key 1.70-level that many think the central bank and government may try to defend with more intervention or capital controls.

Brazil's central bank threw its weight into the spot market on Monday for the first time since September in a bid to limit gains in the real, which has surged so far this year and is threatening the competitiveness of local exporters. 

 Flows to Brazil are being driven by a spate of corporate dollar bond sales, including Brazil's biggest ever by oil giant Petrobras, strong foreign investment in infrastructure projects, and a renewal of global interest in the country's stock market.  

 The Mexican peso lost 1.12 percent to 12.82 per dollar. Mexico's peso is the most liquid currency in the region, allowing investors to easily bet on losses when global risk appetite sours.  

 "It's not surprising that we are seeing this weakness, it's expected," said Mauro Roca, an emerging markets strategist at Deutsche Bank in New York. "The question going forward is going to be how long is it going to take for a solution. Then we will have more solid ground for a sustained rally."  

 Both the real and the peso have gained around 8 percent this year. They clocked their first weekly losses after surging in the first five weeks of the year and posting their strongest period since the rebound from the global credit crisis in early 2009. The real lost 0.6 percent this week while the Mexican peso shed about 1.1 percent. 

 Emerging markets rallied this year on improved economic data in China and the United States, key Latin American trading partners, and renewed hope that the euro zone debt crisis could be stabilizing.

 Euro zone officials say a bailout package must be agreed with Greece and approved by the European Union, the International Monetary Fund and European Central Bank by Feb. 15 to avoid a chaotic default that may threaten the global economic recovery. 

 Chile's peso bid 0.77 percent weaker to end at 478.70 per dollar, after hitting a five-month high during the last session. 

(Writing By Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weaker On Lack Of Accord In Greece: More Volatility Seen
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones) -- Brazil's real weakened in early trading Thursday, tracking the euro, after Greece's political parties failed to reach an accord on austerity measures seen as essential for the country to qualify for a bailout package to ease its debt problems.

The real traded at BRL1.7236 to the dollar at 1218 GMT, compared with BRL1.7178 Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders said further volatility could occur in the run up to a euro-zone meeting of ministers later Thursday to discuss the possibility of the European Central Bank getting involved in Greece's debt restructuring. This follows a protracted meeting between the Greek government and political party leaders, who wouldn't accept a cut of EUR300 million in benefits cuts, including retirement pensions. According to local sources, Sunday will be the deadline for the cuts to be agreed, allowing Greece to proceed with talks on a debt restructuring accord with creditors.

Market players also expressed concern that rising inflation in China could make expected cuts in interest rates less likely in the near future. Chinese consumer inflation rose 4.5% in January from a year earlier, from 4.1% in December.

Nervousness continues in the market in Brazil amid talk that new interventions by the Central Bank may occur to avoid appreciation of the real after several days of heavy foreign currency inflows, partly from a succession of company bond issues overseas.

The Central Bank on Wednesday intervened in the local currency market for the third time in four sessions, purchasing dollars via forward-delivery contracts.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed; Brazil real wilts on cenbank threat
text:
* Traders bet on further Brazil intervention measures

 * Chile's peso ends at 5-month high on Greece deal

 * Brazil's real slips 0.2 pct, Mexico's peso up 0.32 pct 

(Recasts throughout; adds closing prices)

 By Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Feb 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Thursday as traders poised for another round of central bankintervention, while Chile's peso firmed to a five-month high, driven by optimism that Greece will get its next bailout deal.

 Brazil's central bank threw its weight into the spot market on Monday for the first time since September in a bid to limit gains in the real, which has surged so far this year and is again threatening the competitiveness of local exporters.

 The real  dipped 0.2 percent to 1.7207 per U.S. dollar, pulling away from the key 1.70-level that many think the central bank and government may try to defend with more interevention or capital controls.

 While the central bank has not bought dollars since Monday, Joao Medeiros, head of trading at Brazilian brokerage Pioneer, said traders moved to the sidelines on expectations that policy makers could enter the market around the 1.7120 level.

 "That's it for free trading," Medeiros said.

 Still, analysts think Brazil will be unable to do much more than slow the real's advance due to a tide of dollar flows washing into Latin America's top economy. Intervention efforts have been repeatedly deployed in recent years around the region.

 Flows are being driven by a spate of corporate dollar bond sales, including Brazil's biggest ever by Petrobras, strong foreign investment in infrastructure projects, and a renewal of global interest in Brazil's stock market.

 "There is a lot of flow from corporates, which will come anyway. In a way there's too many dollars in the market right now," said Pedro Tuesta, Latin America analyst with 4Cast Inc in Washington.

 The real could get a bigger shock if the government revives a tax on foreign investment in the stock market, which was removed last year after global markets swooned.

 But improving economic data from the United States and China, Latin America's top trading partners, as well as expectations that central banks in Europe and the United States will keep interest rates low for years to come, has renewed appetite for riskier assets across the board.

 Latin American currencies were among the top emerging market assets during the first five weeks of 2012, when they posted their biggest gains since a rebound from the credit crisis in early 2009. 

 Worries about Greece and intervention efforts cooled the advance this week, but demand for riskier assets was lifted on Thursday after Greek leaders clinched an austerity deal on reforms needed to secure a second international bailout and avoid a disorderly default. 

 Chile's peso bid 0.55 percent stronger to end at 475.00 per dollar, a five-month high.

 Following the peso's recent sharp gains, traders say if the currency strengthens beyond 470 per dollar, Chile's central bank could start voicing concern about the exchange rate. But dollar purchases are seen as unlikely unless the peso breaches at least the 460 barrier and possibly even lower.

 Mexico's peso firmed 0.32 percent to 12.6750 per dollar. Central bank authorities are likely welcoming recent currency gains that could help cool inflation pressures.

 Mexico's annual inflation rate pierced the central bank's 4 percent ceiling for the first time in over a year in January.

 Investors sought protection in case consumer prices keep rising by piling into Mexican inflation-linked bonds, or Udibonos, pushing prices upward and yields lower.

 The yield on the December 2014 Udibono bid down almost 9 basis points to 1.28 percent. Strategists at Banorte project its yield could fall to a key support level at 1.20 percent and may break even lower to 1.07 percent. 

(Additional reporting by Helio Barboza in Sao Paulo and Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Gary Crosse)

title: Brazil Real Weaker Early As Market Watches  Central Bank  Moves
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)-- The Brazilian real was slightly weaker in early trading Tuesday as investors evaluated the likelihood the country's central bank would maintain a strong presence in the market to curb the strength of the local currency.

As of 1130 GMT, the real traded at BRL1.7250 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.7212 Monday according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

A sudden jump into the markets by the central bank in recent sessions has had market participants putting the central bank's target level for dollar purchase intervention at around BRL1.70 to the dollar.

"Just as we had expected, the [real] is likely to find it very difficult to break out from the 1.7-1.9 range as an ambitious policy strategy aims to prevent further deindustrialization along with containing inflation expectations," said analysts at Santander Economia in a note Tuesday.

They added, however, that the currency should face difficulties strengthening beyond the BRL1.7 to the dollar mark as investors show concerns over the ongoing impact of adverse fallout from the Greek and European debt crises.

Brazil's central bank intervened twice over the last two sessions, buying dollars in spot and forward auctions for the first time in five months.

Brazil's real has gained about 8% against the dollar since the beginning of the year under the influence of heavy overseas financing activity by companies operating locally and continued flows of portfolio investment into the country.

Among events recently influencing the market was Brazil's $14 billion privatization of major local airports this week and large-scale overseas debt sales by state-run oil company Petrobras (PBR) and top local telecom Oi (TNLP4.BR).

Meanwhile, market participants say they believe the central bank will remain on guard for sudden strengthening of the local currency as investors seek emerging market alternatives for their money as a haven from turbulence in Europe.

"We would expect Brazil's central bank (BCB) to continue efforts to prevent the [real] from strengthening unchecked, especially given strong M&A flows presently being seen," said HSBC Global Research analysts Clyde Wardle and Marjorie Hernandez in a note Monday.

Questions remain, meanwhile, on how strong either fixed or variable income returns will be locally this year as the country struggles to maintain growth amid an uncertain global scenario.

Top officials from Brazil's central bank have hinted the monetary authority will maintain a rate easing cycle in the first half of this year despite elevated inflation as it fights to prop up weakening activity in the local economy.

The bank has cut its reference Selic rate by two percentage points since August to 10.5% despite 12-month inflation near the 6.5% upper limit of the country's inflation targeting band.

--By Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; (5561) 9162-7863, gerald.jeffris@dowjones.com [ 07-02-12 1150GMT ]

title: Emerging Market Central Banks Back To Square One: Fighting  FX  Gains
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Five months later, and Brazil's central bank is back to where it was last September: buying dollars to tame the real's appreciation.

The hectic pace of the January rally in emerging markets has startled many central banks and forced some of them to take immediate measures to intervene to protect their currencies from further rapid appreciation and keep their exports competitive.

Investors who are already retooling their strategies to incorporate higher projected year-end levels now also have to factor in interventions and the effort by central banks to slow the pace of appreciation. Colombia's has already indicated that it will follow Brazil's lead and take measures to slow the Colombian peso's ascent.

Central banks, meanwhile, may feel compelled to shift from their focus on spurring growth to resuming their battle against currency gains. The announcements from Brazil's and Colombia's central banks were seen as signs of the times, with emerging market currencies now having recouped much of the losses that arose during last year's global risk fears, which saw many erase between 10% and 22% of their value against the greenback in the second half.

"In the short term, investors have to be concerned about intervention especially because of the magnitude of the recent rally," said Andres Garcia-Amaya, strategist at J.P. Morgan Funds. "It makes governments jittery as it makes exports less competitive."

The huge flow of capital into emerging markets this month--$11.3 billion into equity funds and $1.65 billion into bond funds, according to EPFR Global--was primarily stoked by liquidity measures from both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.

Still, as Guillermo Osses, head of emerging markets debt portfolio management at HSBC Global Asset Management, points out, "Investors won't indiscriminately purchase currencies," this time, unlike 2010, when a flood of buying forced many central banks to prevent further appreciation of their currencies.

Brazil, certainly, with its high interest rates, has seen a surge of foreign buyers of its local bonds, and now of its equities too as investors seek other ways to gain currency exposure. Latin America's largest economy, in a bid to keep its exports competitive and its manufacturing activity buoyant, last week purchased dollars and did so again Monday.

Colombia, the resource-rich commodities exporter, is trying to make sure that the flux of foreign capital flowing into the country consists of investments into the economy and not speculative trading. Its central bank said Friday it would start to buy a minimum of $20 million daily for at least three months in the foreign-exchange market.

But, for a while, the duo are likely to be the only countries intervening with their currency. Asian and European economies have a way to go before they start worrying about intervention, analysts and investors said.

Some investors, however, already are betting that the measures won't halt the overall appreciation trend, and are happy to hold onto currencies like the Brazilian real.

"It does not necessarily make me run to the exit," said Alexander Kozhemiakin, portfolio manager at Standish in Boston, adding that Brazil's intervention came a bit sooner than he expected, but his firm is currently long the Brazilian real against the Colombian peso. His read: central banks "are not protecting their currencies at a certain level; they're smoothing volatility."

Others are waiting for intervention to present an opportunity to go long the Colombia peso, placing bets that it will appreciate.

Alex Pigatto of Nomura Securities expects that Colombia's $400 million a month in dollar purchases would fall far short of its expected foreign inflows of $1.2 billion monthly.

"We are flat FX here, but watching for another opportunity to re-enter in long Colombia Peso [trade]," he said.

-By Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com @djfxtrader [ 02-06-12 1634ET ]

title: Brazil's Economy To Show Slow Recovery In 2012-Industry Group
text:
--CNI projects Brazil's economy to grow by about 3% this year

--Tax incentives for industry, and credit and interest rate easing measures may help improve industrial sales locally, economist says

--Industry prospects may be hurt by slow demand abroad and a strengthening of the real

BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's economy will show a slow recovery this year from a slowdown in the second half of 2011 amid lingering local structural challenges and continued difficulties abroad, officials from the National Confederation of Industries said Monday.

The group said the country's industrial sector ended 2011 in a situation of "near paralysis" as local manufacturing struggled to overcome stiff competition and diminished demand from developed economies.

"Industry is showing more or less the same level of production as three years ago, before the emergence of the global financial crisis," said CNI chief economist Flavio Castelo Branco.

The CNI reported Brazil's use of installed industrial capacity ended December at 81.3%, down on a seasonally adjusted basis from 82.5% in December 2010 and also well below a record high of 83.9% seen in early 2008.

Industrial employment, meanwhile, ended the year 1% lower than December 2010, though real industrial sales showed an advance of 3.4% over the same period.

Castelo Branco said he expects Brazil's economy to perform slightly better in 2012 than 2011, but "not substantially."

The CNI projects Brazil's economy should grow by about 3% this year. According to the group, Brazil's industrial sector accounts for about a quarter of the country's economic growth.

A recent slowdown in demand, Castelo Branco said, could help curb recent heavy imports. Tax incentives for industry, and credit and interest rate easing measures promoted by the government could help improve industrial sales locally, he said.

Industry's prospects may be hurt however, by still-slow demand abroad and more particularly by a strengthening of the country's currency, the real.

"The appreciation of the exchange rate is a problem for the Brazilian economy that brings increased foreign competition, and in the absence of other instruments to improve competitiveness, it tends to remain a problem," the CNI economist said.

Brazil's real has strengthened by about 8% against the dollar since the beginning of the year.

Brazil's central bank this week began purchasing dollars in the spot and forward markets for the first time in five months as the government sought ways to weaken the real.

The market interventions came after Brazil's trade ministry reported the country posted a $1.29 billion foreign trade deficit in January, its first monthly deficit in two years.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Weaker On Concerns About Greece
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies and debt were a tad weaker as markets took a pause Monday from last week's rally.

Greece, or the lack of an outcome from its debt negotiations, weighed on investors. The euphoria of Friday's strong U.S. employment numbers faded fast as Greek failed to meet deadlines on the finalization of a deal. Some investors saw this as an opportunity for profit-talking after many currencies posted 5% to 8% gains against the dollar so far this year.

"The overriding concern in the market right now just seems to be the stalling problems with the Greek negotiations," said Carl Forcheski, director of foreign exchange at Societe Generale, adding that the market "is starting to get a little anxious."

Emerging market sovereign debt was nearly unchanged on the day, as the spread on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened by two basis points to 390 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index edged down just 0.1%. Venezuela's debt firmed slightly; its spread tightened by six basis points to 1084 basis points over Treasurys. In price, however, its index fell 0.3%.

Issuance by Latin American issuers continued with Brasil Telecom SA (BTMC, BRTO4.BR), a subsidiary of Oi, launching a $1.5 billion offering of 10-year notes in U.S. credit markets Monday, according to a person familiar with the deal. The bonds will offer investors a yield of around 5.75%, compared to original pricing guidance of 6% and revised guidance of 5.85%.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Weaker As  Central Bank Intervenes  Again
text:
--Brazilian real backs off after second intervention by central bank in as many sessions

--Real closes weaker at BRL1.7212

--Central bank buys dollars in first spot auction since September


 
  By Paul Kiernan 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real finished slightly weaker against the dollar following choppy trading Monday after the central bank intervened in the market for a second consecutive session, further crediting the view that authorities are drawing a so-called "line in the sand" at current levels.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7212 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.7158 at Friday's close.

Brazil's central bank on Monday offered to buy dollars in the first spot-market auction in nearly five months shortly after the real touched an intraday high. The move followed an unexpected purchase Friday of dollars for forward delivery, in what many saw as local authorities' return to the policy of intervening against currency appreciation.

Brazil's real has gained around 8% since the end of 2011 as world financial markets started the new year strong on the back of improving economic data from the U.S. and China. A lull in the European debt crisis also contributed, resulting in favorable financing conditions abroad that several Brazilian companies have taken advantage of to sell bonds at cheaper rates than they can find at home.

The fact that companies have sold billions of dollars in overseas bonds since the beginning of the year had led some analysts to hold off on interpreting the central bank's intervention Friday as the start of a trend. Monday's snap auction likely swayed a few more opinions.

"This should be the answer to the market participants that were wondering if the last intervention was a one-off or a signal that (authorities) will intervene when they find necessary," one analyst wrote in a note.

Brazil's real tends to strengthen when global investor sentiment -- about issues such as the U.S. economy or the European debt crisis -- is optimistic. Perceived low likelihood of a shock in world markets emboldens investors to seek higher returns in traditionally volatile assets like stocks and emerging-market currencies.

"Most investors we talk to are looking to put more cash to work," HSBC Global Research said in a note.

However, a strong real leaves Brazilian industry at a disadvantage to imported goods and cuts into exporters' profit margins.

Brazil's finance ministry and central bank in recent years have been sensitive to such concerns. The central bank bought $47.91 billion on the spot market and $2.2 billion on the forward market last year, when heavy investment flows pushed the real to its strongest level against the dollar since Brazil adopted a floating currency regime in 1999.

As the real became more expensive in recent weeks, market participants wondered aloud at what level the authorities would step in to slow its gains. Finance Minister Guido Mantega said in late January that the government, which unleashed a cocktail of exchange-oriented taxes amid the real's rally last year, planned to stop the real from appreciating.

"We thought that the closer it got to BRL1.70, the more likely Mantega or the central bank would intervene," said Reginaldo Galhardo, foreign-exchange director at Sao Paulo's Treviso brokerage. "Apparently that level might be closer to BRL1.72."

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil  real strengthens despite  intervention
text:
* Brazil's real briefly reverses gains after intervention

* Real ends stronger on positive U.S. jobs data

* Central bank buys forwards first time this year

* Mexico, Chile pesos gain amid better global views

(Adds fresh analyst quote, closing prices)

By Silvio Cascione and José de Castro

SAO PAULO, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real closed firmer on Friday, extending its winning streak to four straight days after shrugging off central bank intervention aimed at stemming a rise in the currency that could potentially hurt profits of exporters and manufacturers.

The real closed 0.3 0 percent stronger at

1.7 166 to the dollar , marking the fifth straight week of gains. The currency briefly reversed similar gains earlier in the day after the central bank called an auction to buy U.S. dollar forwards -- its first currency intervention this year .

By buying forwards, the central bank soaks up excess dollars in the currency market by capping future supply of the greenback.

However, a jump in U.S. job creation bolstered the real.

"More encouraging data out of the United States helped strengthen the real," said Jose Carlos Amado, a trader with Renascenca Corretora in Sao Paulo. "But from now on the market will likely remain very attentive of further intervention."

The bank's first attempt to arrest the real's 8.3 percent jump this year indicates worries among government policymakers over the size and impact of the rally on exports and economic growth. A stronger currency usually makes Brazilian-made goods less competitive in global markets, hampering export revenue.

The last time Brazil's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market was on Dec. 15, when it tried to sell dollars on the spot market after the currency weakened sharply on fears the global economy was slipping back into recession.

Some of the gains in the real stem from massive capital inflows from investors seeking high-yielding, riskier assets such as Latin American stocks, bonds and currencies. A record $7.1 billion flowed into the Brazilian stock market last month, according to data by BM&FBovespa, the exchange operator.

Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff is seeking to help local carmakers by hiking taxes on some foreign-made cars last year. She also wants to rework a long-standing deal with Mexico for tariff-free bilateral trade in automobiles and parts.

Other major Latin American currencies kept strengthening on Friday on positive job data in the United States added to market optimism that the global economy is improving.

Chile's peso ended the day

at a fresh 4-1/2 month high, boosted by rising prices for top export copper.[ ID:nL2E8D32FC]

The Mexican peso

was trading 0. 84 percent firmer.

"As world volatility comes down investors are getting more constructive and you see a resumption of carry trade and a search for higher yields," said Igor Arsenin, an emerging market strategist with Credit Suisse. "Authorities in Brazil are very sensitive to the level of the currency. We are likely to see more interventions."

(Writing by Alonso Soto and Guillermo Parra-Bernal; Editing by Andrew Hay and Diane Craft)

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Rally After Strong US Jobs Data
text:
-- Emerging market currencies, debt rally

-- Mexican peso, South African rand hit multi-month highs

-- Brazil's central bank intervenes in foreign exchange market


 
    By Erin McCarthy 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--An overwhelmingly strong U.S. job reports triggered a rally for emerging market currencies and debt Friday.

Data Friday showed U.S. non-farm payrolls rose by 243,000 in January, nearly double the 125,000 increase expected. The positive surprise gives a boost to expectations for the U.S. economic recovery, which has cheered markets and also provided some support for currencies linked to growth.

The news sent emerging market currencies on a tear, with several hitting fresh multi-month highs, including the Mexican peso, Turkish lira and South African. The Brazilian real also managed to strengthen, despite measures from Brazil's central bank earlier Friday to weaken the real.

"Generally speaking if the U.S. is doing well, almost all emerging markets do well," said Sara Zervos, head of the global debt team and portfolio manager at OppenheimerFunds. "The bulk of emerging markets have a link to the U.S. economy whether it's through exports, commodity demand, [or] U.S. consumer demand."

Emerging market debt also firmed up, as the risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, shrank by 16 basis points to 385 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index rose 0.1%. Latin American sovereign debt outperformed, with Venezuela leading the way. Venezuela, whose debt often outpaces wider market swings, saw its spread tighten 45 basis points to 1084 basis points over Treasurys, and its index shot up 1.4%.

Latin American currencies also were top gainers, particularly the Mexican peso. The peso strengthened to its strongest levels since Sept. 9 against the dollar, which slid about 1% on the day to MXN12.6778, according to CQG. The peso typically reacts positively to solid U.S. economic data, given Mexico's close economic ties to its northern neighbor. Mexico sends about 70% of its exports to the U.S.

The Brazilian real edged up 0.2% against the dollar late Friday, even though Brazil's central bank stepped into foreign exchange markets early Friday to curb the real's gains for the first time in five months. The central bank held an auction to buy dollars in forward contracts, for delivery March 20, at a rate of BRL1.7383 Brazilian reais. On the Embig, Brazil's spread narrowed by 14 basis points to 205 basis points over Treasurys.

Other growth-sensitive currencies also outperformed. The South African rand strengthened 1.5% against the dollar to its strongest since September 2011, while the Turkish lira also hit a five-month high against the U.S. currency.

Earlier Friday, Russia's central bank left its key policy rates unchanged, as expected, saying that current levels will strike the right balance between risks to growth and rising consumer prices for the next few months.

The Russian ruble only gained modestly against the dollar, which slipped to RUB30.137 from RUB30.197 late Thursday.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger, Good US News Outweighs  Intervention
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real closed stronger against the dollar Friday after good economic news from the U.S. outweighed dollar buying by the central bank.

The real exited normal trading at BRL1.7158 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.7205 to the dollar Thursday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real traded weaker against the dollar at the start of the day amid suspicion the central bank might step in to stop the Brazilian currency from strengthening even further.

The central bank then validated those suspicions by holding an auction to buy dollars in forward contracts, for delivery March 20, at a rate of BRL1.7383 Brazilian reais. It was the first time in five months the bank moved to weaken the real.

By the end of the day, though, good U.S. jobs news overcame the effects of the intervention and pushed the real stronger against the dollar.

"The market is watching the whole world, not just Brazil," said Reginaldo Galhardo, foreign exchange manager at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "There's more enthusiasm about the U.S. economy after the jobs report, and that's helping."

The U.S. Labor Department's January data showed nonfarm payrolls rose 243,000 last month, marking the biggest gain since last April. The jobless rate fell by two-tenths of a point to 8.3%, the lowest it has been since February 2009. Both numbers beat expectations. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires expected a slowing to 125,000 jobs from December's 200,000. The unemployment rate had been expected to hold steady at 8.5%.

Those figures were good enough to trump the move by the Brazilian central bank, which followed days of statements by Brazilian authorities that they would work to curb the appreciation of the real, which is beginning to hurt Brazilian industry and exporters. In forward auctions, the central bank offers to buy contracts for delivery of U.S. dollars at future dates.

The real, which closed 2011 at around BRL1.86, has steadily strengthened against the dollar so far this year as concerns about the European debt crisis have subsided and the global economic outlook has improved.

A wave of bond issuances by Brazilian companies abroad, and growing world appetite for emerging-market assets, have fueled strong investment flows to Brazil, pushing the real up against the greenback.

title: 2nd UPDATE:  Brazil Central Bank  Steps In As  Currency  Gains
text:
--Central bank intervenes in market for first time in five months

--Bank buys unspecified volume of U.S. dollars for Mar 20 delivery

--Interventions, using various tools, became common in past years

(Updates with additional comment, background throughout.)


 
   By Paulo Winterstein and Paul Kiernan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian Central Bank on Friday showed its growing discomfort with the local currency's recent strength against the U.S. dollar, stepping into the market to ease demand for the Brazilian real for the first time in five months.

Following a five-week rally that saw Brazil's currency gain some 8% against the greenback, the central bank held an auction Friday, buying dollars for March 20 delivery. Such measures, tending to weaken the real, haven't been employed since September, when the local currency was in the midst of a selloff that saw it end 2011 at BRL1.8625 to the dollar.

Friday, the central bank bought an unspecified volume of dollars for March 20 delivery at BRL1.7383 each.

The intervention reflects renewed concerns about the currency's strength--a byproduct of stabilizing world financial markets--in a country whose manufacturers and exporters often struggle to compete with cheaper imported products.

In past years, central bank interventions became quite common, with the bank often buying or selling dollars on a daily basis. However, in recent months, the government appeared content to allow a steady depreciation of the currency as a way to boost exports and protect manufacturers.

The real has gained steadily against the dollar so far this year. A wave of bond issues by Brazilian companies abroad--including a $7 billion deal by state oil giant Petroleo Brasileiro (PETR4.BR, PBR), or Petrobras--and growing appetite for high-yielding, emerging-market assets have fueled strong investment flows to Brazil, pushing the real up against the greenback.

Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a currency strategist at RBS Securities in the U.S., noted that the bulk of capital inflows to Brazil so far this year have gone into the "real economy" in the form of corporate debt issuance abroad rather than short-term fixed-income investments. Dollar futures on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange don't point to expectations for significant appreciation by the real in coming months, she added.

"Taking that into consideration, I would not read the decision as being a broader or more important intervention signal," Cattan-Naslausky said. "In the past, when there was a change in currency policy, it was usually triggered by concerns that the money coming in was driven by speculative flows."

The real exited active trading Friday slightly stronger on the day at BRL1.7158, as investors cheered better-than-expected employment data from the U.S.

Friday's intervention came days after the most recent warning from Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who said in late January that the government planned to "continue with our policy of preventing the appreciation of the currency." Authorities last year unleashed wave after wave of measures aimed at slowing the entry of speculative cash that had pushed the real to renewed strength against the dollar.

Though market participants in recent weeks have increasingly eyed the possibility of renewed intervention, some were hesitant to declare a return of the so-called "currency wars"--a term used to describe the periodic rollout of capital controls and near-daily dollar purchases by the central bank.

Luiz Carlos Baldan, a director at Sao Paulo's Fourtrade brokerage, characterized Friday's auction as a "thermometer."

"The central bank decided to hold this auction to see how demand would look," Baldan said, adding that he sees the government aiming to keep the real between BRL1.75 and BRL1.85 this year. "It's premature to say that this is the first step in a new series of measures."

-By Paulo Winterstein and Paul Kiernan, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3544-7073; paulo.winterstein@dowjones.com

--Rogerio Jelmayer in Sao Paulo contributed to this article. [ 03-02-12 1902GMT ]

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Weaker As Investors See  Intervention  Risk
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real opened weaker against the dollar Friday ahead of key U.S. employment data and as recent gains have left investors increasingly wary of possible government intervention in the currency market.

Around 7 a.m. EST, the real was quoted in Sao Paulo trading at BRL1.7409 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.7205 at Thursday's close.

Brazilian financial markets, which often are heavily influenced by economic news abroad, will likely have a close eye on the U.S. Labor Department's monthly nonfarm payrolls report, due out at 8:30 a.m. EST. Economists tend to study the data for signs of improvement in the U.S. labor market, which remains feeble some two years after the global economic recession.

Signals from the U.S. Federal Reserve that it intends to keep interest rates at near zero until 2014 to shore up the economy "has strengthened the argument" for investing in emerging-market assets, Credit Suisse said in a research note.

Traders say investment flows to Brazil have been strong since the beginning of the year, supporting a nearly uninterrupted rally in the real, which ended 2011 around BRL1.86 to the dollar.

Reginaldo Siaca, a manager at Sao Paulo's Advanced brokerage, said heavy inflows mean the real should continue trending stronger.

"Interest rates in the U.S. aren't going up any time soon, so the market looks quite attractive for foreign clients," Siaca said.

But he said that BRL1.70 is considered a key level, beyond which concerns about competitiveness would likely spur the government to intervene in currency markets to slow the real's gains.

Reports Thursday that the Brazilian government is considering charging import taxes on cars produced in Mexico reinforce opinions that the real's gains this year are already causing worries about lost competitiveness, Santander bank said. That, in turn, "suggests that the risks of [foreign exchange] intervention may be rising in the short term."

"We would expect the central bank to first start buying [dollars] in the spot [market], but rhetoric can escalate and other new and creative mechanisms may be in the works if the real remains on a strengthening trend," Santander said.

Such measures were a fact of life for investors in Brazil last year, when the real surged to around BRL1.55 to the dollar before the European debt crisis sent it reeling along with other emerging-market assets.

But at least one key factor for the exchange market has changed since then. Local interest rates, which guarantee returns on fixed-income investments, are widely considered to be on a downward path.

Brazilian Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini said Thursday that authorities "have room" to cut the key Selic rate, which currently stands at 10.5%, without jeopardizing inflation goals. The rate in mid-2011 peaked at 12.5%.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies  Strengthen After US Jobs Report
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies soared Friday after a key U.S. jobs report showed robust signs of the U.S. economy's recovery.

The South African rand and Turkish lira surged to fresh session highs against the dollar, while the Polish zloty rose to its strongest levels of the session against the euro. U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose by 243,000 in January, nearly double the 125,000 increased expected.

The overwhelmingly positive surprise gives a boost to expectations for the U.S. economic recovery, which has cheered markets and also provided some support for currencies linked to growth.

The dollar slid to TRY1.7464 from TRY1.7560 shortly before the jobs data, while the U.S. currency fell to ZAR7.5446 against the South African rand from ZAR7.6146 just before the report, according to CQG.

Against the euro, the Polish zloty also shot to session highs.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com @djfxtrader [ 02-03-12 0850ET ]

-- Emerging market currencies rally after U.S. jobs data

-- Several currencies hit fresh multi-month highs

-- Brazil's real weakens on central bank intervention

(Updates with additional currencies, most recent levels and investor comments.)


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies strengthened Friday after a key U.S. jobs report showed robust signs of the U.S. economy's recovery.

The South African rand strengthened more than 1% against the dollar to its strongest since September 2011, while the Turkish lira also surged to a five-month high against the U.S. currency. Data Friday showed U.S. non-farm payrolls rose by 243,000 in January, nearly double the 125,000 increase expected.

The overwhelmingly positive surprise gives a boost to expectations for the U.S. economic recovery, which has cheered markets and also provided some support for currencies linked to growth.

"Generally speaking if the U.S. is doing well, almost all emerging markets do well," said Sara Zervos, a senior portfolio manager at Oppenheimer Funds, referring to most emerging markets' trade links to the U.S.

The dollar weakened against the Turkish lira to buy as little as TRY1.7464, from TRY1.7574 late Thursday, according to CQG. The lira later pared some of those gains, however. The Czech koruna also advanced, to its strongest since Nov. 7 against the euro. The common currency fell below the key CZK25 level Friday, most recently trading at CZK24.983.

The Polish zloty strengthened to fresh five-month highs against the euro, which was down 0.3% at PLN4.1768 most recently.

Other currencies that serve as more prominent proxies for risk also gained on the day. The South African rand climbed more than 1% against the dollar, which changed hands at ZAR1.7554. The Mexican peso, which is seen as the emerging market currency that is most tied to the U.S. economy, strengthened 0.6% against the dollar to trade at its strongest levels since last September.

The Brazilian real, however, wasn't able to join in the U.S.-inspired rally, since Brazil's central bank stepped into foreign exchange markets early Friday to curb the real's gains for the first time in five months. The central bank held an auction to buy dollars in forward contracts, for delivery March 20, at a rate of BRL1.7383 Brazilian reais. The dollar rose to BRL1.7244 against the real Friday, according to CQG.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com @djfxtrader

--Paulo Winterstein and Paul Kiernan contributed to this article. [ 02-03-12 1154ET ]

title: UPDATE 1-EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso rallies on China premier comments
text:
* Chilean Peso at its strongest in more than 4 months

* Brazil Real firms 0.58 pct, raises intervention fears

* Possible Chinese help to Europe improves global outlook

(Updates with new prices for Chile, Mexico, Brazil currencies)

By Anthony Esposito and Alonso Soto

SANTIAGO/BRASILIA, Feb 2 (Reuters) - The Chilean peso

ended at its strongest level in four and a half months on Thursday, leading a broad strengthening of Latin American currencies after a top official said China may take a bigger role in helping debt-stricken Europe.

World markets gained ground after Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said China is "considering increasing its participation in the solution of the European debt crisis" through the region's bailout fund.

Rising expectations that Europe will solve its debt crisis as well as Wednesday's upbeat global manufacturing data also helped boost sentiment.

Latin American currencies were among the best performing in emerging markets in January, after the European Central Bank calmed fears of a full-blown euro crisis by pumping 489 billion euros of cheap three-year loans into the banking system. [ID: nL2E8D1EI3]

"It's partly generation of expectations," said Hernan Jimenez, analyst with Forex Chile in Santiago. "(China's) signal that it could increase (its participation in) the European rescue fund generates... bigger expectations for investors to look for new investment alternatives, perhaps seeking more risk, like in the Chilean currency."

Investors tend to dump emerging market assets and buy safe-haven assets like the U.S. dollar to protect themselves against the risk of a deeper economic slowdown.

"Those comments from China have helped ease market worries ... It adds to this broader optimism that the world economy is improving," said Reginaldo Galhardo, exchange trade manager for Treviso Corretora in Sao Paulo. "This optimism is bringing investors back to emerging markets."

A drop in new claims for unemployment benefits in the United States also added strength to the Latin American currencies.

The Chilean peso, which was also boosted by stop-loss orders after mining companies, pension funds and banks sold dollars, led the way, closing 1.4 percent firmer to bid 479.90 per dollar.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.46 percent to 12.83 per dollar, pulling back slightly after hitting its strongest level since mid-September at 12.7850 during the session.

Brazil's real traded firmer, gaining 0.58 percent to bid 1.7233 per dollar.

A stronger real in Brazil has raised expectations of government intervention to tame a currency that has strengthened 8 percent so far this year.

A stronger real lifts the costs for Brazilian producers struggling with a flood a cheaper imports from China.

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said last week the appreciation was due to dollar weakness abroad, not speculation. However, government officials have said authorities are ready to take actions if the real continues strengthening.

Treviso's Galhardo said the market is testing the 1.70 barrier.

(Reporting By Anthony Esposito in Santiago and Alonso Soto in Brasilia; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: Brazil  Real Ekes Out Small Gain Despite  Intervention  Worries
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL1.7471 vs BRL1.7483 Monday

--Stronger real so far in 2012 could bring government intervention

--Foreign investors putting money into both stocks and fixed income


 
   By Tom Murphy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real eked out a tiny gain against the U.S. dollar Tuesday despite renewed worries about possible government intervention in the market.

The real ended regular trading at BRL1.7471 to the dollar, slightly stronger than the Monday close of BRL1.7483, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The Brazilian real has gained 7% against the U.S. dollar so far in 2012, once again raising the specter of possible government intervention.

In comments earlier this year, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the government was determined to avoid an "excessive appreciation" of the real against the dollar. He specifically said the government wouldn't allow the real to strengthen to BRL1.60 to the dollar. The strong real hurts exporters and manufacturers.

"As the real approaches BRL1.70 to the dollar, expectations for government intervention begin to rise and the real backs away a little," said Mauriciano Cavalcanti, a trader at Sao Paulo's Ouro Minas brokerage. The real strengthened to BRL1.7350 early Tuesday, before giving up most of its gains.

In a research note to clients Tuesday, Swiss bank UBS said government intervention, in the form of dollar purchases from the market or new taxes on investment inflows, could be imminent. "We see the potential for new official measures to curb BRL strength on the horizon," wrote UBS economist Andre Carvalho.

The real's strength so far in 2012 has been due, in part, to continued inflows of foreign investment dollars seeking high returns from Brazilian fixed-income investments and stocks. Brazil's Selic base interest rate is high, at 10.5%. Brazil's benchmark Ibovespa stocks index has gained 10% so far this year, making it an attractive investment as well.

"The central bank could target stocks this time if there are new taxes," said Cavalcanti.

Last year, Brazil's government raised taxes on fixed-income inflows from abroad as well as short-term loans and some foreign-exchange derivatives investments. Many foreign investors this year have preferred Brazilian stocks to fixed-income investments on expectations that the Brazilian central bank will cut interest rates in the months ahead.

Analysts noted that trading was a bit more volatile Tuesday than normal ahead of monthly expiry Wednesday of foreign-exchange futures contracts. The contracts will close out based on the average foreign-exchange rate, or Ptax rate, in Tuesday's trading.

title: Brazil Needs Legal Change To Make Real Convertible -Official
text:
--Regulatory changes to make real fully convertible have reached their limit

--Laws governing foreign exchange need changes to permit more flexibility

--Changes to the foreign exchange law "not on the agenda" at the moment


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency trades as freely as possible right now, given the relevant legal framework, and can only be made fully convertible with legislative action, a member of the government's economic team told Dow Jones Newswires on Friday.

"I think that, in practice, we've already advanced all we can from the point of view of regulation," said the person, who asked not to be identified. "To take more steps to make the market more flexible, we start to run up against the question of the law. From the point of view of regulation, what could be done has been done."

The current law is restrictive when it comes to foreign exchange operations because of the country's history, which includes periods of capital flight. Brazilians traditionally sought to buy dollars to protect the value of their savings, especially during periods of high inflation, and the government wanted to deter this to prevent dollar scarcity.

In recent years, the regulations covering currency exchange operations have been relaxed somewhat. For example, a plane ticket and a valid U.S. visa are no longer required for individual Brazilians to buy U.S. dollars. Such changes have helped eradicate the black market in dollars, but have reached a limit and the rules can only be further relaxed if the law is changed.

There needs to be a political debate, to decide what, if any, changes need to be made, although at the moment such a debate "isn't on the agenda," the person said.

The changes necessary to make the real fully convertible would reduce restrictions on who is permitted to trade the currency, remove limits on how much can be changed, and reduce the number of transactions that need to be registered with the central bank, according to the person.

There would be several advantages to permitting the real to trade more freely, chiefly a reduction in the cost of transactions for businesses and tourists alike, while the major drawback would be less government control over the exchange rate.

"Exchange policy would become more challenging for the government," the person said.

Brazil's weight in global trade isn't at the moment big enough for a fully convertible currency to be necessary, though in the long term it would be worth it for the country to advance in that direction, the person said.

Brazil was responsible for about 1.4% of world trade in 2011.

A regionally convertible currency might be a good first step, given that the real is already much more freely traded with Brazil's neighbors than it is in other parts of the world, the person said.

Brazil's government has intervened in the currency market in recent years to slow the appreciation of the real against the U.S. dollar. The central bank on occasion buys dollars to keep the real from strengthening past a certain level, and last July the government imposed a 1% tax on futures contracts for those holding short-dollar positions.

The tax has been in effect since late last year, although it still hasn't been collected because of the difficulties involved in calculating the amounts owed. The tax will eventually be collected, once the complexities have been ironed out, the person said.

-By Jeffrey T. Lewis of Dow Jones Newswires; +55 61 9278 5267; jeffrey.lewis@dowjones.com [ 27-01-12 1920GMT ]

title: Brazil  Real Weakens On Rate Outlook, Possible  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened slightly on Friday, slipping against the dollar on the outlook that aggressive interest rate cuts by the central bank will reduce demand for the Latin American currency and on concern the government will once again be active in halting the real's gain.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7400 to the dollar, somewhat weaker than its previous close at BRL1.7395, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real surged Thursday after the central bank said there was an "elevated probability" that the Selic rate will move "toward single-digit levels" from its current level of 10.5%.

The real jumped more than 1% Thursday on the outlook the rate cuts would spur growth in an economy that has already seen vibrant interest for stocks and bonds; more than $4.8 billion in bonds were issued during the first three weeks of January alone.

But the lower rates curb demand for fixed-income investments, a favorite vehicle for overseas investors who borrow developed market currencies at extremely low rates to buy assets linked to interest rates.

The real weakened on Friday after the U.S. reported economic growth of 2.8% during the fourth quarter. Though that represents a faster pace than seen in previous quarters, it still managed to miss market expectations of 3% growth.

"Our sense is that a more vocally dovish central bank and a potentially more fragile external environment may take a toll on the BRL," Banco Santander economists wrote in a Friday note.

Traders on Friday also were pocketing some of the previous day's gains in the real on the possibility that the government will step up activity to curb the real's strength.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega earlier this week said that the government will "continue with our policy of preventing the appreciation of the currency and the policy of trade defense."

The real opened the year at close to BRL1.87 to the dollar and has been strengthening since.

"People have been a bit cautious as they await moves by the government or the central bank in the market," said a trader.

title: Brazil's Real Posts Strongest Close In Two Months
text:
--Brazil's real closes at strongest level in more than two months

--Currency settles at BRL1.7605 to the dollar

--Appreciation has prompted speculation about possible government intervention


 
   By Paul Kiernan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real gained steam in Friday's session to settle at its strongest level against the dollar in more than two months, prompting speculation about the possibility of renewed government intervention in the local currency market.

The real exited active trading at BRL1.7605 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with Thursday's close of BRL1.7650. Friday's close was the local currency's best mark against the dollar since early November.

Emboldening investors was favorable news from Greece, the country at the heart of the euro zone's debt crisis. A week after talks between the debt-strapped Mediterranean country and its creditors broke down, the two sides on Friday approached a deal to write down 50% of the face value of Greece's debt by exchanging existing bonds for new ones bearing longer maturities and lower interest rates.

U.S. stocks posted modest gains while the euro weakened after a week of steadily rising in value against the dollar. Both assets are key barometers of global market sentiment, which frequently sways emerging-market currencies such as the real.

The real has appreciated steadily since ending 2011 at BRL1.8642, spurring talk among market participants about whether local authorities may soon intervene. A strong local currency puts Brazil's exporters and industry at a disadvantage.

"I think that, when it breaks BRL1.70, they'll have an obligation to enter the market," said Durval Correa, a currency trader at Sao Paulo's Multi Money brokerage.

Until shockwaves from the European debt crisis sent the real's value spiraling downward against the dollar around September, Brazil's Finance Ministry and central bank spent much of last year devising ways to keep the local currency from strengthening too quickly.

The measures included taxes on things such as foreign investment in fixed-income securities and higher reserve requirements on banks' short-dollar positions. In addition, the central bank bought billions of dollars in spot auctions on the local market, and also auctioned reverse-swap contracts to effectively remove bets against the dollar.

"The tendency, if the central bank doesn't quickly get in with auctions and exchange swaps, is for the exchange rate to fall," Correa said. "There's a lot of investment. With people investing in bonds and stocks, money is quickly coming in and the supply naturally knocks down the dollar's value."

Local media have reported in recent days that authorities are growing uncomfortable with the real's path.

But Banco Itau, Brazil's largest private bank, said it is "too early to think seriously about concrete actions" by the government.

"Tough talking is always the first line of defense," the bank said.

-By Paul Kiernan, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3544-7074; paul.kiernan@dowjones.com [ 20-01-12 1915GMT ]

title: Brazil Real Opens Little Changed As Attention Turns To Greece
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real was little changed in early trading Friday as the dollar held up against other major currencies and investors kept an eye on negotiations between Greece and its private creditors.

Around 7:20 a.m. EST, the real stood at BRL1.7654 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, very slightly weaker than its Thursday close of BRL1.7650.

The real, which frequently reacts to developments in international markets, has remained steady in recent sessions amid generally positive news about the U.S. economy. A wave of sovereign ratings downgrades last week in Europe, the main source of concern for investors in volatile foreign-exchange markets, did little to derail the Brazilian currency.

Reports that the Greek government and its private-sector creditors were nearing a debt-restructuring deal encouraged investors ahead of the opening bell in U.S. financial markets. Talks between the two sides resumed this week after breaking down last Friday on the basis of interest rates that Greece would pay its bondholders.

In a 2012 outlook released Friday, HSBC's Pablo Goldberg, head of the bank's global emerging-markets research team, said he favors the Brazilian real and Colombian peso among Latin American currencies.

"We see the (real) range-bound between BRL1.75 and BRL1.90 for most of this year," Goldberg said in the report. "High growth and interest-rate differentials should continue to attract strong FX inflows, but a more dovish central bank and an unstable FX regulatory environment are real-negative."

Though growth has slowed from 2010's red-hot pace of 7.5%, Brazil's gross domestic product is still expected to outpace the rest of the world's largest economies this year, as the U.S. struggles with high unemployment and Europe battles its debt crisis. Brazil remains home to some of the highest real interest rates in the world, even after the central bank cut its overnight Selic rate by 50 basis points this week, to 10.50%.

HSBC said the likelihood of intervention by Brazil's central bank in the exchange market "supports our rangebound view," and added that commodity prices will also be a key factor for the currency. Brazil's shipments of raw goods such as sugar, coffee, soybeans, orange juice, meat and metals place it among the world's top commodities exporters.

The real spent much of last year at levels that exporters and industry found uncomfortably strong against the dollar. Though the real's value remains well below mid-2011 levels of near BRL1.55, the currency has rallied since closing 2011 at BRL1.8642.

The gains have prompted speculation about whether local authorities might start intervening in exchange market to stem the real's rise if they see it threatening the country's competitiveness.

title: Brazilian Companies Look Overseas To Escape Volatile Real
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--A strong real spurred Kepler Weber (KEPL3.BR) to manufacture grain storage products outside of Brazil last year. They're not expecting another spike in 2012, but have no plans to reverse their decision.

In 2011, when the real traded against the dollar at its peak of BRL1.53 in July, the company hired a company in Egypt to manufacture the structures for steel silos, grain dryers and grain cleaning machines for a client there.

The move makes the company less vulnerable to swings in the real, because more of its costs and revenue come from outside Brazil. Kepler Weber plans to conduct more manufacturing overseas, even as the real has weakened in recent months, Collas said.

Kepler Weber isn't alone. While Brazil's exports rose 27% in 2011, the share from manufactured goods fell to 36.1%, from 39.4% a year earlier. Manufacturers have been gradually moving out of Brazil for years as the cost of doing business in the country has risen, with the strengthening real a major factor.

The pressure to leave Brazil is only likely to get worse for the country's exporters. Analysts don't expect the real to immediately return to last year's heights, but see a stronger currency in the long run. A strong real raises production costs within Brazil, and makes exports more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

"For manufacturing companies, it's hard to export from Brazil," says Oscar Becker , CFO at Iochpe-Maxion S.A . (IOCJY), a Brazilian manufacturer of auto parts and railroad cars. Iochpe-Maxion increasingly relies on its factories overseas to supply foreign buyers, while its Brazilian production meets local demand.

Becker expects the real to trade mainly in the range of BRL1.75 to BRL1.80 in 2012. The real traded Thursday at BRL1.8389 to the dollar, 20% below its July peak.

Like many emerging markets, Brazil's central bank has intervened recently to slow its currency's slide. That marked a sharp reversal from earlier in 2011, when the government enacted a tax on some foreign exchange trading to curb a surging real. The Brazilian government has also announced it is studying new incentives for local industries to halt the slide in manufacturing export.

"Brazil has been losing competitiveness for the last 10 to 12 years. This is a structural problem," said Paulo Vieira da Cunha, a former director at Brazil's Central Bank and a partner in the investment company Tandem Global Partners. The currency valuation adds an extra layer to the problem, he said.

But even a weaker real won't necessarily reverse some companies' move out of Brazil. They think that even if the real stays far below its 2011 peak this year, it's only a matter of time before the currency surges again. Relocating factories and personnel also takes large amounts of time and money, making the decision to head overseas difficult to reverse.

It's not just manufacturing that's leaving Brazil. JBS S/A (JBSAY), the world's largest meat-packing company, in 2011 began taking out loans in U.S. dollars and paying off debt priced in reais. As with exports, a stronger real raises the cost of financing loans compared with other currencies.

The current program, also motivated by tax savings, involves the transfer of around $2 billion, and could be expanded, said Jeremiah O'Callaghan, JBS's investor relations officer.

"We want to have our debt in areas where it is cheaper," he said, adding that he expects the real to trade between BRL1.80 and BRL1.90 this year.

Brazilian companies not expanding international operations are still seeking protection from the fluctuating real. A study by research firm Instituto Assaf found an average growth of 21% in the number of future contracts opened at Brazil's BM&FBovespa between 2009 and 2011.

Most of that growth reflects a need for protection from currency moves, rather than speculation, said Fabiano Guasti Lima, a researcher at Instituto Assaf.

"Brazilian companies are increasingly setting up mechanisms to reduce risk," Lima said.

-By Luciana Magalhaes, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2856; luciana.magalhaes@dowjones.com;

title: CORRECT: Latin American Stocks,  Currencies  Slide In 2011 On Euro Zone
text:
("Latin American Stocks, Currencies Slide In 2011 On Euro Zone," published at 1702 EST, misstated the 2011 percentage decline of Mexico's IPC stock index in the second paragraph. The correct version follows.)

--Stock indexes end 2011 in red, but select consumer plays flourish

--Currencies tumble against the dollar amid heightened risk aversion

--Latin American GDP growth seen at 4.3% this year

--Europe's debt troubles to continue pressuring assets in 2012


 
   By Amy Guthrie 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Major Latin American stock indexes and currencies declined in 2011 as investors shunned conventionally risky assets and exporters amid the euro-zone debt crisis and signs of a slowing global economy.

Yet the region's major economies continued to grow, and with that growth came greater domestic demand, inspiring double-digit gains in shares of select consumer-driven companies, such as Brazilian phone carrier TIM Participacoes and Mexican beverage and retail group Femsa, both of which rose close to 40%. Brazil's broader Ibovespa stock index fell 18.1% on the year, while Mexico's IPC index retreated 3.8%.

The Brazilian economy, Latin America's biggest, is expected to have grown by 3.5% in 2011 while Mexico's is seen having expanded by 3.9%. The U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean predicts the region as a whole will grow 4.3% this year and 3.7% in 2012, well above the 2.6% forecast for the world next year.

Still, Latin America is not immune if Europe's troubles spread. European bank problems and fears of a global credit crunch took a high toll on Latin American currencies during 2011, with the highly liquid Mexican peso ending down 11.5% at MXN13.9725 to the U.S. dollar, its weakest ever year-end close, and the Brazilian real depreciated 11% against the dollar, to BRL1.8625.

"Throughout the year we were rudderless, as money managers, economists and the [local] government weren't really able to determine what the outlook would be," said Reinaldo Zakalski, director of BI Asset Management in Sao Paulo.

Among other Latin American currencies, the Chilean peso lost more than 10% this year, to CLP519.20/dollar, after having flirted with a three-year high earlier in 2011. The Chilean central bank's $12 billion currency intervention program fattened the nation's foreign currency reserves while also helping tame the peso. A strong peso can cut into the competitiveness of Chilean products abroad, with exports representing roughly 60% of the country's gross domestic product.

The Argentine peso finished at ARS4.3040/dollar, bringing its year-to-date loss to 7.6%, while the Colombian peso closed the year at COP1,938.38/dollar for a slighter loss of 0.9%. The Peruvian sol, meanwhile, appreciated 3.92% against the U.S. dollar to end 2011 at PEN2.697.

Market watchers expect major Latin American currencies to remain weak in early 2012 as European governments continue to grapple with heavy debt burdens. That currency weakness has also generated concerns of inflationary pressures in the near future.

Inflation in Brazil, for instance, is at a worrisome 6.6%, with the government there pledging to pull it down to 4.5% by early 2013. Brazil's government intervened in September, selling dollars in order to avoid what officials called "a disorderly market."

Mexican officials have also instituted a policy to halt the peso's depreciation on days in which the currency slides 2% against the dollar, although they have not had to use the dollar-sale mechanism since announcing the plan in late November. Several economists believe the Mexican peso's weakness has begun to pass through to consumer prices, although a devastating drought in northern Mexico has also led to sharply higher prices for a number of agricultural goods. Inflation in Mexico is at 3.85%, near the 4% top of the government's target range.

Throughout Latin America, caution led equity investors this year to bulk up on shares of defensive plays--such as phone companies, utilities, makers of paper goods and beverage firms--while reducing their exposure to capital-intensive industries such as construction or export-oriented firms such as steelmakers. Shares of Brazilian steelmaker Usinas Siderurgicas de Minas Gerais, for instance, slid 40%.

In Colombia, a boom in the mining and oil sectors, combined with robust consumer spending, especially in the housing and automobile sectors, is driving expectations for a 6% expansion in GDP this year. Yet the country's Colcap stock index ended 14% lower, albeit after a 33% year-on-year surge in 2010.

The Chilean economy will likely have expanded by 6.2% this year, yet that country's blue-chip Ipsa stock index lost over 15%. Peru's General Index shed 16.8% despite an expected 6.8% expansion in GDP, and Argentina's benchmark Merval stock index plunged 30% after having surged 52% in 2010.

title: Brazil Real Slightly Stronger Friday, But Still Weaker For 2011
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL1.8625 Friday, versus BRL1.8664 Thursday

--Brazilian currency posts 11% depreciation against dollar in 2011

--Real could rebound in 2012 on rising multinational investments


 
    By Tom Murphy 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real strengthened slightly against the U.S. dollar Friday in thin trading, but still accumulated significant 2011 losses because of international uncertainties.

The real ended regular trading at BRL1.8625 to the dollar, slightly stronger than the Thursday close of BRL1.8664, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Brazil's financial exchanges were closed Friday as part of year-end holiday celebrations. Foreign exchange trading was limited to the interbank market, with small and midcap banks buying the U.S. currency to build up year-end dollar reserves.

The real suffered significant losses in the second half of 2011 as worries over a global slowdown and a spreading European debt crisis brought a surge of interest in safe-haven U.S. dollar investments.

At midyear, the real traded at its 2011 peak of BRL1.53 to the dollar, but the global worries brought a swift depreciation of the Brazilian currency against the U.S. dollar. The 2011 trough for the real was reached in September at BRL1.90 to the dollar.

For 2011 as a whole, the real posted a depreciation of 11% against the U.S. currency.

For 2012, analysts are looking at continued volatility early in the year but with improving prospects for the Brazilian currency later.

The currency market will open 2012 in a jittery mood, said Paulo Faria-Tavares, managing partner at Sao Paulo's PTX Lending consultants. "There are no foreseeable solutions for Europe," he said.

Guilherme Monaco, a trader at the Hencorp Commcor brokerage in Sao Paulo, said, "The real could reach BRL1.90 to the dollar again on European worries, but that would bring Brazilian government intervention, as in the past."

Brazil's government intervened in September, selling dollars in order to avoid what officials called "a disorderly market."

However, they may have also had another motive.

"The Brazilian real at BRL2.00 to the dollar is not good for inflation," said Monaco.

Brazilian inflation is at a worrisome 6.6%, with the government pledging to pull it down to 4.5% by early 2013.

For the longer term, the Brazilian currency may find some sources of strength against the U.S. dollar.

Another trader, Olvidio Soares of Sao Paulo's Interbolsa brokerage, said, "The European crisis is very deep. It has been long in the making and it will take years to resolve. However, I believe Europe will soon be able to signal markets that it is at least on the path to solving its problems. At that point, markets will become less volatile."

According to Soares, the real could gain against the dollar later in 2012 on continued foreign interest in direct investment in Latin America's biggest economy. "Multinational companies know they have to be here," he said. "Also, investments will pour in ahead of the 2014 World Soccer Cup." The games will be hosted by a dozen Brazilian cities.

Soares said the real could strengthen to a range of BRL1.65 to BRL1.70 to the dollar by the end of 2012.

In the weekly market survey released by the Brazilian central bank, economists predicted a year-end 2012 value for the real of BRL1.75 to the dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real slides on trade lines; Mexico level
text:
* Expiring trade lines, credit crunch pressure Brazil real

* Mexico intervention concern pushes Brazil real selling

Updates prices, adds Mexico peso comment)

By Jeb Blount and Rachel Uranga

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY , Dec 14 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped to a three-week low against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as investors sought greenbacks to pay trade-finance credit lines unlikely to be renewed as Europe's debt crisis prompts banks to limit lending.

Brazil's real led a general slide in Latin American currencies, shedding 1.24 percent to 1.8727 to the dollar. Earlier it weakened as much as 1.36 percent to 1.8750, its weakest intraday level since Nov. 25. Mexico's peso weakened 0.40 percent to 13.9202.

The real's declines were likely amplified as some investors used the Brazilian currency as a way to reduce their exposure to Latin American risk without causing Mexico's peso, the most-traded regional currency, from falling enough to trigger an intervention by the country's central bank, said Diego Donadio, Latin America currency strategist with BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

"Not only do you have trade lines maturing with the prospect of higher rates and lower availability, you have the Mexican factor," he said.

Because of Mexico's Virgin of Guadalupe holiday on Monday, Mexico's official peso fixing rate showed only a 1.06 percent slide on Tuesday from Friday's fix, the previous business day's official rate.

That loss was short of the 2 percent loss required for Mexico's central bank to enter and buy $400 million of pesos, an act that could have caused losses for those betting against the Mexican currency, Donadio said.

Meanwhile, the spot rate slipped more than 2 percent when Monday's offshore, nonlocal trading was included.

"In a climate where risk aversion is high, it made more sense to sell the real than to sell the peso," Donadio said. "If people had sold the peso as heavily as the real it would have rapidly hit the intervention limit."

Donadio expects all the region's currencies to slide in coming days as investors continue to buy the dollar and dollar-denominated assets instead of Latin American currencies and local-currency assets, which are considered riskier than dollars.

In addition to the need for companies and investors to pay down year- and month-end credit lines, many want to hold dollars to protect against the risks related to a European debt crisis that threatens to push the world economy into recession.

The real, Donadio said, is likely to slide to 1.90 or 1.91 in the coming days and weeks, levels that will then likely spark a response from Brazil's central bank, concerned that a weaker real could stoke inflation or make it difficult for some Brazilian companies to pay dollar debts.

"The market is going to test the central bank at around 1.90 because it believes the central bank has made it clear that it won't tolerate bigger weakening," he said.

Mexico's peso will likely find resistance near 14.10 to the dollar based on Fibonacci retracement measures, he said.

Cesar Elizalde, a currency trader at Banorte-IXE, believes the peso could easily pass the 14 per dollar mark, thanks to European concerns and the failure of the U.S. Federal Reserve to take stronger action to prevent Europe's problems from hurting the United States.

On Wednesday, Italian 10-year debt yields, a proxy for government long-term borrowing costs, rose to a record 7.3 percent.

"There is no clear definition to the problem of the crisis in Europe and there is worry about the Federal Reserve, so this is the principal problem, the environment and a bit of liquidity," Elizalde said.

Intervention by Mexico's central bank is unlikely, he said, as investors appear to be increasing their bets on a stronger peso in the futures markets.

Elsewhere in Latin America, Chile's peso weakened 1.19 percent to 521.20 to the dollar, its weakest since Nov. 30. Colombia's peso weakened 0.42 percent to 1,937.60.
