title: Brazil Real Slightly Weaker On Renewed Europe Worries
text:
--Real weakens to BRL1.6850/dollar vs. BRL1.6795 Friday

--Investors worry about funding for Europe rescue plan

--Brazil government wary of any abrupt currency moves

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened slightly against the U.S. dollar in early trading Monday on renewed worries about the European debt crisis.

The real was trading at BRL1.6850 to the dollar early in the session, weaker than the Friday close of BRL1.6795, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

European leaders last week announced a broad rescue plan for debt-plagued governments and banks in the region. However, details on funding for the plan remained sketchy.

Worries were exacerbated over the weekend by comments from China's official news agency indicating reluctance by Chinese authorities to advance any financial aid to Europe.

"What investors are saying today to the Europeans is, 'Show me the money!'," said Guilherme Monoco, a trader at Sao Paulo's Hencorp Commcor brokerage.

Worries about funding for the European rescue plan led to losses for the euro against the U.S. dollar Monday. International metals and oil prices were down. Lower commodities prices tend to hurt the Brazilian real, since many Brazilian exporters depend on commodities prices for revenues.

Traders said the possibility of government intervention lurks in the background of Brazil's market.

"Intervention is unlikely Monday, because the real is weakening a bit," Monoco said. "However, any reversal could see a government move in the market. They don't want the real to strengthen too much."

Brazil's government intervened heavily in the market earlier this year when the real strengthened to BRL1.55 to the dollar. The strong real hurts exporters and manufacturers. Intervention came in the form of higher taxes on certain foreign investment inflows as well as frequent purchases of dollars from the market.

Such a view was reinforced in comments at a seminar Friday by a top central bank official. Central Bank Credit Operations Director Sidnei Marques said a new, highly automated foreign exchange system "gives the central bank the opportunity to view and identify any abrupt movements in foreign exchange that might do harm to the market." Marques said the central bank will act "with timely interventions" to maintain an orderly foreign exchange market.

Monday marks the expiry of monthly foreign exchange futures contracts. The expiry often leads to volatility on Brazil's foreign exchange market because the contracts are closed out based on the average foreign exchange quotation, or Ptax rate, on the last working day of the month.

However, traders said this month's expiry was likely to be calm. "Most of these contracts were rolled over Friday," Monoco said. "The volume of rollovers Monday will be low."

title: Brazil To Modernize Inter-Bank Market In 2012 - Central Bank
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank will kick off a broad technical and regulatory modernization of its inter-bank market in July of 2012, Central Bank Monetary Policy Director Aldo Mendes said Friday.

He said the modernization will be modeled after a similar effort that began on October 1 for Brazil's foreign-exchange market. The foreign-exchange modernization was based on technical upgrades of computer-driven trading and monitoring operations, Mendes said.

"The new foreign-exchange system creates greater transparency for all involved in the market, including the central bank itself," said Mendes at a seminar in Sao Paulo. "It has led to lower costs for all and we expect foreign-exchange agents to pass these savings on to their clients."

Geraldo Siqueira, director of the central bank's foreign-exchange regulatory bureau, said at the same event that "Costs for the central bank itself in monitoring and processing foreign-exchange transactions have fallen by 70% since October 1. We don't expect all of this saving to be passed on by agents to their clients, but certainly some of it will."

Mendes said the new foreign-exchange system introduced on October 1 reduces paperwork and regulations for virtually all foreign-exchange transactions. But at the same time it gives the central bank greater and faster access to information about foreign-exchange flows and transactions.

"We expect to be able to achieve the same gains in transparency and efficiency for the inter-bank market when a new modernization system is introduced in July 2012," he said.

Central Bank Credit Operations Director Sidnei Marques said the new foreign-exchange system "gives the central bank the opportunity to view and identify any abrupt movements in foreign exchange that might do harm to the market."

Brazil's central bank has consistently intervened in the foreign-exchange market in recent years, buying and selling dollars or holding auctions of dollar-linked futures contracts. The central bank held a swap auction of dollar-linked contracts earlier Friday, selling the equivalent of $791 million in swaps to the market.

Marques said the new foreign-exchange system will lead to "more timely and well targeted" market interventions.

Brazilian central-bank interventions in the foreign-exchange market are typically aimed at damping volatility, Marques noted. He also said the new foreign-exchange system will help the central bank to better identify possible money laundering or other illicit operations.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stable As  Intervention  Eases Volatility
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed virtually stable against the U.S. dollar Tuesday after the Central Bank sold exchange-rate swaps to ease some of the downward pressure on the currency caused by the turbulence in international markets.

The real exited trading at BRL1.8887 to the dollar, little changed from Monday's close at BRL1.8864, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Despite the stable close, trading was volatile amid nervousness after Greece's worsening debt problems hit global market sentiment and heightened risk aversion.

Global markets showed losses early in the day, after news that there would be a delay in new loan aid worth EUR8 billion to Greece due to the canceling of a European ministers' meeting that was expected to consider the issue on Oct. 13. Greek Finance Minister Evangelos Venizelos added to the panic by revealing that Greece has sufficient funds to honor its financial commitments only until mid-November.

Greece revealed Monday it's unlikely to meet its fiscal deficit targets for 2011 and 2012 unless revenue collection improves significantly.

Shares of European banks fell sharply amid the negative news that could spell significant problems for some financial institutions. Still in the euro zone, factory-gate product prices fell in August due to lower energy costs. Oil and metals fell significantly on international markets while the euro remained volatile.

The negative sentiment was aggravated by Goldman Sachs's downgrading of its global growth domestic product growth forecasts for 2012 to 3.5% from the previous 4.2%, mainly on Europe-related factors.

For Brazil, the merchant bank foresees 2011 GDP growth falling to 3.5% from the previously forecast 3.7%, with 2012 growth at 3.3% from the previously forecast 3.8%.

Reinforcing the lower expectations, Brazil's statistics bureau announced that industrial production in August fell 0.2% from July, while many economists expected an increase.

The central bank said it sold Tuesday 36.6% of the $4.5 billion on offer in four swap contracts, equivalent to just over $1.6 billion.

On Monday, Brazil's Central Bank also stepped into the fray, selling $1.7 billion in a foreign-exchange swap contracts auction to help shore up the real.

The auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange contracts indexed to domestic interest rates for paper linked to the U.S. dollar. The central bank holds such auctions when dollars are relatively scarce, causing the depreciation of the real.

"The Central Bank acted correctly," said Sidnei Nehme of NGO Corretora. "It reduced pressure in the derivatives markets. However, there's also demand in the spot market for a sale of dollars, as we now have a negative foreign-exchange inflow." Nehme said international companies are taking dollars out of Brazil to bolster cash reserves at their headquarters abroad.

Nehme said the central bank is likely to proceed with further swap auctions and possible cash market sales of dollars at auctions in line with market demand. "The market took up only a third of the swaps offered because the sales price was considered a little high," he said.

The real has depreciated sharply against the dollar in recent weeks. On Sept. 1, the real was at BRL1.61 to the dollar.

According to Tendencias Consultoria's Raphael Martello, Brazil's central bank successfully "neutralized" the impact of a worsening international scenario on the real, and will be forced to continue to intervene.

"It contained a bit of the real's fall. It's hard to foresee how much it will have to continue to intervene as this depends more on external factors than anything else," Martello said.

Brazil's central bank sold currency swap contracts with a nominal value of $1.71 billion on Monday, part of its effort to limit the real's decline against the U.S. dollar.

"This shows that the central bank is ready to act if they see a sharp movement in the currency," said Carlos Kawall, chief economist with Banco Safra in Sao Paulo. " This was more about the speed of today's movement than a specific level."

The real <BRBY> gained 0.56 percent to end at 1.8905 per dollar at the currency's 5 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) close. It earlier weakened as much as 1.88 percent to 1.9160.

Some investors have suggested that the central bank's auction showed it is ready to defend the real if it weakens beyond 1.90 per dollar.

Brazil plans to sell another $4.53 billion of swaps on Tuesday. [ID:nE5E7JI03W]

Only months ago, Brazil had been concerned about the real becoming too strong vis-a-vis the dollar. But now it is stepping in to halt the real's decline as concerns about potential European debt defaults and sluggish global growth prompt investors to sell assets in higher-risk emerging markets, such as Brazil.

The real, which had touched 12-year highs in late July, has reversed gains to fall nearly 12 percent against the greenback so far this year.

Much of the decline has come after Brazil's government in July imposed a 1 percent tax on investors who increase their bets the real will gain.

The real has also declined following a decision to cut the country's benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 12 percent on Aug. 31.

The real may be in for further declines after foreign investors cut their net bets the real will gain to their lowest level in 15 months. [ID:nN1E7920D3]

Without aid, Greece will likely default, an action that could saddle international banks with huge costs and crimp lending worldwide. At the same time, the U.S. and European economies, responsible for about half of world output, are already showing signs of a slowdown. [ID:nN1E7920VY]

If China, the world's second-largest economy also slows, demand for the oil, copper iron-ore and other commodities that are the backbone of Latin America's exports may fall.

"All emerging markets are very sensitive to every piece of news that is coming out about Europe's (debt) problem," said Enrique Trejo, head of currency trading at Banorte-Ixe in Mexico City. "There is fear of a recession in Europe and the United States. Investors are looking for less risk."

title: Brazil's  Central Bank  In Focus As Real Starts Another Bumpy Ride
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank was back in focus Friday morning as traders once again braced for a bumpy ride in the local currency market.

The real weakened early versus the dollar, but then reversed course, as markets remained jittery following Thursday's slump. While the underlying cause for much of the volatility is the financial uncertainty in Europe and the U.S. monetary policy, investors in Brazil are using the opportunity to reshape their portfolios.

Traders also have to deal with the prospect of a repeat of the massive intervention by the Brazilian central bank undertaken on Thursday. The bank offered $5.6 billion in swap contracts, effectively selling dollars, and sold about half.

"The central bank could come in again with swaps, promising to deliver dollars," said Luiz Carlos Baldan, a director at the Fourtrade brokerage in Sao Paulo.

At 1241 GMT the real was trading at BRL1.8885 per dollar, stronger than the BRL1.8971 at which it exited trading on Thursday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset. The currency had touched BRL1.9146 earlier in the session.

Foreigners aren't necessarily taking their money out of Brazil, but are changing around their investments, exiting the stock market, hedging their money and buying gold, Baldan said. Otherwise, trade flows are normal, though as expected there are some larger outflows into year-end as companies repatriate profits, he said.

RBS Securities said that there's likely to be more central bank action as it senses "a growing discomfort" among some groups, mainly Asian retail investors, with their exposure to the Brazilian real through packaged investment products.

The direct impact of these is on the offshore currency markets, but there is an indirect impact onshore, RBC said. The Brazilian central bank has less information about the offshore flows, but the warning signs in the moves in the relationship between the real and the yen are clear, it said.

"We expect intervention to remain concentrated in [Brazil's] futures market for now" as Japanese funds start to unwind positions, amid deteriorating onshore liquidity, it said.

Moreover, as the real weakens faster than commodities prices, inflation concerns are squarely back in view. The central bank had started cutting rates, but the inflation shock from imported inflation poses a dilemma.

"The implications for monetary policy are that unless we see a disruption in global credit markets and a sell-off in commodity prices...then stable interest rates would be the most appropriate policy path," RBS said. Given the uncertainty, the central bank is unlikely to change direction again so quickly, so there's likely to be more foreign exchange intervention against disorderly outflows, RBS said.

title: UPDATE 1- Brazil  says ready to  intervene  in  FX ; real firms
text:
* Real strengthens over 2 pct after cenbank comments

* Dollars not flowing out of the country, finmin says

* Cenbank monitoring FX impact on inflation

(Adds quotes, background, byline)

By Walter Brandimarte

WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank said on Friday it is ready to intervene in foreign exchange markets to curb volatility in its currency, one day after surprising markets with a move to stop the real from weakening.

Speaking to investors in Washington, the central bank president, Alexandre Tombini, said Brazilian policy makers want to see where the currency will stabilize "in the next days or weeks" to assess its impact on inflation, which he sees as declining overtime.

Meanwhile, the bank will work to avoid excessive volatility in the currency, providing liquidity to the market whenever necessary, Tombini said, helping the real strengthen more than 2 percent.

"We stand ready to intervene to make sure foreign exchange markets work properly," he said in an event organized by the Brazilian American Chamber of Commerce.

The real <BRBY> strengthened to 1.85 per dollar following his comments, after closing near 1.9 per greenback on the previous day.

The real had weakened to 1.95 during Thursday trading as investors became more averse to the risk of another global financial crisis, prompting Brazil's central bank to sell $2.75 billion in currency swaps to cushion its fall.

That move was designed to provide liquidity in the derivatives market, where investors were quickly turning more bearish on the real, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega told investors in the same event.

"The reason behind the weakening of the real is a sharp adjustment in the derivatives market, not dollar outflows," Mantega said.

He also promised the government will maintain its fiscal consolidation plans by cutting operating expenditures in order to make room for infrastructure investment and for further monetary policy easing, especially if the global financial crisis worsens.

The Brazilian economy had been resisting the global crisis so far, but the effects have started to become visible. Given global constraints, the central bank will likely revise down, by the end of the month, its 4 percent economic growth forecast for this year, Tombini said.

(Additional reporting by Pedro da Costa; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains after  FX  swap; Latam rebounds
text:
* Brazil c. bank swap sale checks real slide, sets 'limit'

* Mexico, Chile pesos rebound from sharp Thursday declines

* Peru intervenes in currency market; sol erases loss

(Updates prices, adds Brazil, Peru, Colombia comment)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real reversed losses to gain more than 3 percent against the dollar on Friday -- its biggest one-day gain in almost 16 months -- after the central bank's move to bolster the currency a day earlier raised expectations it will act again to limit sharp falls.

Thursday's sale of $2.75 billion of currency swaps effectively put a limit on how far the bank will allow the real to slide, said Mario Battistel, head of trading at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage. For more see [ID:nS1E78L0PK].

Currency swaps mimic the sale of dollars and provide investors with insurance against future declines in the real.

The real has lost more than 15 percent of its value since the central bank unexpectedly cut its benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point to 12 percent on Aug. 31. The move was based on the bank's expectation that a world economic slowdown would push down Brazil's 7 percent inflation rate. [ID:nE5E7IM05G] and [ID:nL3E7KN1BZ]

"The central bank swap intervention was a pleasant surprise," Battistel said in a telephone interview. "They're clearly worried about inflation and exporters and our other clients weren't about to start moving their large dollar holdings back into Brazil until they had some idea of when the real's plunge would stop."

Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 3.19 percent to 1.8360 to the U.S. dollar, its first gain in six sessions and its biggest one-day gain since May 27, 2010.

The currency had lost more than 1 percent in early trade and still ended the week down about 5.75 percent against the dollar.

The government is ready to intervene more in the currency market to curb wide swings, or volatility, in the market, Finance Minster Guido Mantega told investors in Washington. [ID:nS1E78M134]

Brazil's central bank targets inflation of 4.5 percent plus or minus 2 percentage points and has long said that inflation, now outside the target range, will come under control soon.

A strong real helps control inflation by cutting the cost of dollar-denominated commodities such as food and the cost of essential imports such as machine-tools for Brazil's industry.

Battistel said the central bank, which as recently as August was working to prevent the real from gaining against the dollar, is signaling that it will act any time the real weakens beyond 1.90 to the dollar or strengthens beyond 1.60.

Other traders said the bank is targeting the first dollar futures contract <DOLc1> on the Sao Paulo BM&FBovespa exchange, moving to weaken the real when it firms beyond 2.01 to the dollar and to strengthen the real when it weakens beyond 1.78.

The real-dollar spot exchange rate's close link to the futures market, where bets can be ramped up using loans or "leverage" is one of the reasons the real lost so much in recent weeks, the government said Wednesday.

In first futures trading, which measure expectations for late September, the real shed 2.16 percent to 1.8585.

Bets on a strong real were a key component in the real's nearly 8 percent rise through late July.

Since then the real has reversed all those gains and is now about 9 percent weaker than it was at the end of 2010.

Elsewhere in Latin America currencies rebounded from steep Thursday declines on expectation losses related to concern about a potential Greek default may be overdone.

Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> jumped 3.63 percent to 13.5584 to the dollar, reversing some of Thursday's losses that took the peso beyond 14 to the dollar for the first time since April 2009. For the week the peso trimmed losses to 3.89 percent.

"I think the market has pushed the currency too far too fast and we may see a bit of retracement in the peso's favor," said Francisco Diez, director of emerging-market trading at RBC Capital Markets in New York.

The next point the peso will test if it begins weakening again is 14.25 to the dollar Diez said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> gained 0.93 percent to 516.00 to the dollar after plunging more than 5 percent on Thursday.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> gained 0.58 percent to 1,904.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> trimmed early losses to trade little changed from Thursday at 2.7700 after the country's central bank sold $21 million dollars for pesos, driving up demand for the local currency and helping it firm.

(Additional reporting by Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Raymond Colitt and Kenneth Barry)

title: ANALYSIS-UPDATE 2-Brazil move to check  FX  slide unlikely soon
text:
* Real has shed 15 pct since 12-year high in July

* Cenbank last bolstered real after 35 pct two-month loss

* Brazil more stable, capital flow stronger than 2008-09

* Possible Greek default could change central bank outlook

* Cen bank not signaling intervention on swap roll -source

(Updates prices, adds comment on reverse-swap decision)

By Silvio Cascione and Jeb Blount

SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank is unlikely to act soon to limit a slide in the real that has sent the Brazilian currency <BRBY> to its weakest level in 13 months.

Capital flows in Brazil are strong, and the economy is more stable than it was when the central bank last intervened to prop up the real by selling dollars at auction, during the 2008-2009 U.S. banking crisis and world recession.

Central bank dollar sales remain unlikely despite the real's 13.6 percent decline this month, which has helped reverse one of the world's biggest currency gains into one of the biggest losses.

The currency has lost nearly 10 percent year-to-date against the dollar after erasing a nearly 8 percent gain from January though July 26, when the real hit a 12-year high of 1.5275 per dollar.

With the real now trading at about 1.85 per dollar, market players speculate the central bank will wait until the currency weakens much further before stepping in to buy the Brazilian currency in order to support it.

Some see the central bank comfortable with the real weakening to 1.90 reais per dollar or others to 2 reais per dollar since this would help manufacturers who have complained that a strong real has dented their competitive edge abroad.

"We don't see the possibility of intervention now," said Mario Battistel, head of currency trading at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage, when asked if the central bank would step in to curb the real's slide.

"When people say the central bank will sell dollars, they imagine that the real is very weak -- when the true consensus is that the real is strong," he said.

The last time the central bank began selling dollars to halt a plunge in the real was in Oct. 8, 2008, when the currency had lost more than a third of its value in two months and was trading as weak as 2.44 per dollar.

On Wednesday, the real weakened about 3.5 percent in afternoon trading to 1.8566 to the dollar.

From May 2009 until Sept. 13 this year -- with only short breaks of a day or two -- the central bank had been buying dollars as much as twice a day at auction to limit gains by the real. From its December 2009, post-U.S. crisis lows of 2.619, the real gained over 50 percent through September 2011.

The gains had raised the ire of Brazilian manufacturers who felt the strong currency was spurring a flood of imports and pricing their products out of foreign markets.

"The central bank intervene in the currency? Quite the contrary. Right now the central bank would be happy with the real at 2 to the dollar," said Andre Ferreira, partner and head of FX trading at brokerage Futura Corretora in Sao Paulo.

DOLLAR INFLOWS STILL STRONG

Current market conditions are also very different than they were in 2008 and 2009, said Arnaldo Puccinelli, head of currency trading at Banif Investment Bank in Sao Paulo.

Three years ago the world market was suffering with the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, a world-wide recession and the disappearance of interbank credit, which provoked capital flight from emerging markets such as Brazil.

A similar scenario is likely now only if a debt crisis in Europe results in a sovereign default. A default in Greece and other European countries could lead to massive banking losses and a restriction of credit that would threaten to choke off world growth. For details, see [ID:nL3E7KK0MS]

"If Greece defaults, all bets are off," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora, a local currency brokerage.

In the meantime, dollars continue to pour into Brazil. The central bank said on Wednesday that net dollar inflows were $8.52 billion in the first 15 days of September, boosting net flows in the year to more than $68 billion. [ID:nS1E78D0XW]

In the opinion of the head of treasury at one of Brazil's dealer banks, one of the 14 authorized to do business directly with the central bank, only a rapid change in the outlook for the country would lead to intervention before the real hits 1.90 to the dollar.

"The flows and exchange rate are still OK," he said on the condition of anonymity, citing company policy.

If it were to intervene selling dollars, the central bank has plenty of dollars to sell, as recent dollar buys have amassed a record $350 billion of foreign currency reserves.

Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini has mentioned the reserves as one of the main protections Brazil has against international financial crises.

A possible intermediate step toward direct dollar sales in the market would be to intervene in the futures market, the dealer bank treasurer said.

A principal source of foreign bets on a stronger real in recent months was in the futures market, although much of this long-real position has been undone.

About $2 billion of currency swaps come due this month, the treasurer said. The central bank could let them expire without selling new swaps.

As the sale of the reverse swaps mimics buying dollars, letting them expire, or buying back outstanding reverse swaps early, would help bolster the real without selling reserves.

The central bank said on Wednesday that it will not refinance, or "roll-over" the $1.98 billion of reverse swaps coming due Oct. 1.

The bank is not signaling plans to intervene in the spot market with the decision not to refinance the reverse swaps, a member of the Brazilian government's economic team told Reuters.

Currency flows to the country remain vigorous and the market is functioning well, the source said. [ID:nS1E78K1LE]

(Additional reporting by Isabel Versiani in Brasilia, Editing by Patricia Duarte, W Simon, Leslie Adler )

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Brazil
text:
BRASILIA, Sept 1 (Reuters) - President Dilma Rousseff's main challenge in coming months will be to maintain a course of austerity and clean government amid growing dissatisfaction as Latin America's largest economy slows.

She will have to face rebellious allies, who could stall her legislative agenda and approve costly bills that may undermine fiscal discipline. Other risks include resistance to long-term structural reforms, persistent inflationary pressures, and renewed intervention in currency markets.

SCANDALS

A series of scandals that have forced four of Rousseff's ministers to resign in less than 3 months has exposed her government's vulnerability to opposition and media scrutiny. It has also renewed tensions within Rousseff's ruling coalition, partly because she fired many officials before concluding an official inquiry.

Agriculture Minister Wagner Rossi resigned in August after intense media coverage alleging he peddled influence and used an agricultural firm's corporate jet. The wave of resignations began in June when Rousseff's chief of staff, Antonio Palocci, stepped down over an ethics scandal [ID:nN08245414].

If Rousseff, 63, continues her "clean-up" in other ministries and state agencies, as her aides say she intends to, the career civil servant risks losing support from some allies who expect to get "perks" from government contracts and posts.

Already her coalition had been plagued by in-fighting over key government posts and cuts in pork barrel spending that legislators traditionally use for public works projects in their constituencies. Her refusal to make political appointments to key jobs angered her main ally, the PMDB.

Rousseff's popularity is still high and tackling corruption and nepotism could boost her standing with middle-class voters. But her disapproval rating has doubled since March, hit by rising borrowing costs and slow progress in improving public services such as health and security.

POLICY SHIFTS, WORKS DELAYS

The resignations, which also included the removal of the top ranks of the transport ministry, are likely to delay a series of government projects as incoming ministers and senior officials take time to settle in.

There are growing signs that the construction of roads, ports and railways, which form part of Rousseff's flagship public works program, are already delayed. [ID:nN1E7651GA] This could hurt the economy, affecting grain exports at over-stretched ports or the construction of hydroelectric dams that rely on paved roads to bring in construction materials.

The latest accusations of kickback schemes could also slow other infrastructure projects, including preparations for the World Cup in 2014 and the 2016 Olympics, as government watchdogs step up scrutiny of contracts.

The departure of Rossi could also pave the way for more nationalist farming policies. Rossi was investor-friendly and tried to stem efforts within government to limit foreign investment in the farm sector by banning only speculative but not productive capital [ID:nN16140439].

LEGISLATIVE AGENDA

Budget cuts, the slowing economy and Rousseff's drive to cut political favors have upset many legislators. In a symbolic warning to Rousseff, several allied parties blocked voting in Congress for several days and could derail her bid to control spending and pass economic reforms. [ID:nN1E77F1GQ]

Rousseff has tried to govern without Congress as much as possible but will now have to engage congressional leaders more pro-actively to push through reforms. They include an overhaul of an unwieldy tax code, framework legislation for the mining sector and a bill regulating oil royalties, all aimed at easing legal uncertainty and attracting investment. [ID:nN1E75L0H2]

Other projects on hold include bills aimed at ensuring that Brazil builds stadiums, airports and other infrastructure needed not only for the World Cup and the 2016 Olympics but also to overcome bottlenecks holding back the entire economy.

With the sporting events drawing nearer and a slowing economy exposing glaring problems from unwieldy labor laws to heavy taxes, Rousseff may need to engage Congress to approve structural reforms and emergency bills to speed up government procurement. In doing so, she may have to ease some of the austerity adopted so far.

What to watch for:

- Signs that Rousseff will loosen spending controls or make appointments to please allies.

- New media revelations of scandal among top officials.

CURRENCY POLICY

The risk of government intervention in Brazil's currency market remains high, as even weeks of global financial turmoil did little to undermine the strength of the real <BRBY><BRL=>. By late August, the real was down only around 3 percent from its 12-year high in July of 1.54 per U.S. dollar. Then the government imposed a tax on currency derivatives, potentially the most aggressive measure so far designed to stem the currency rally [ID:nN1E76Q01I].

If the real tests new record highs, the government could hike the tax rate on currency derivatives from currently 1 percent to as much as 25 percent and adopt other measures as well, Finance Minister Guido Mantega has said.

Any fresh measures could hit fixed income and currency investors, while the stronger real can erode profit margins and the market share of exporters, particularly manufacturers.

FARMING AND MINING

A legislative proposal changing environmental regulations for farmers passed the lower house of Congress and could become law later this year. While the Forestry Code, which sets the percentage of native forest that farmers must preserve, reduces overall environmental liabilities for farmers, they would have to finance costs they have been putting off for years to reforest or invest in protected areas.

A mining bill Rousseff is expected to send to Congress this year would likely reduce the time companies have to develop mines to discourage speculation in mineral properties, and could hike royalties to promote mineral processing.

MONETARY POLICY

Consumer price pressure has remained surprisingly resilient and perhaps one of the biggest headaches for the Rousseff administration. Annual inflation in the 12 months through mid-August broke through the 7 percent level, well above the government's upper limit of 6.5 percent. [ID: nN1E77I06D].

Still, the central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 12 percent at the end of August, beginning an easing cycle after hiking rates five times this year by a combined 175 points.

The move prompted some concern among investors that the central bank may have moved prematurely and under pressure by the government to prevent an abrupt economic slowdown.

Two days before the interest rate cut, the government hiked its 2011 budget savings target, arguing tighter fiscal discipline would pave the way for monetary easing.

Inflation tends to hit hardest the poorer classes who form Rousseff's political base and sustained price rises could erode her approval rating. Inflation and rising interest rates have also weighed significantly on the stock market this year.

What to watch for:

- 12-month inflation rate failing to fall significantly.

- Signs of further rate cuts ahead.

ROUSSEFF'S HEALTH

Rousseff's hospitalization and her lengthy recovery from pneumonia in May renewed concerns over her health, which first surfaced in April 2009 when she announced she was being treated for lymphoma. [ID:nN01161483] [ID:nN12259498]

She has been given a clean bill of health by doctors but is reported to also suffer from diabetes, hypothyroidism, and high blood pressure. Rousseff's health is on investor radar screens. Were it to worsen, markets could slump due to uncertainty over economic policy under Vice President Michel Temer.

(Editing by Kieran Murray)

BRAZIL-RISKS/ (FACTBOX)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real, Mexican peso slides; Chile's gains
text:
* Germany gloom, Japan debt rating cloud world outlook

* U.S. data fails to lift Mexico peso as trade weakens

* Argentina's peso slides as trade surplus narrows.

(Updates prices, adds Argentine surplus, Mexican debt)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened or trimmed gains against the U.S. dollar in late trading on Wednesday as investors judged the prospects for world economic growth to be weak.

The declines came as business confidence in Germany, Europe's largest economy, dropped to its lowest level in 14 months and after Moody's Investors Service cut Japan's debt rating to Aa3 from Aa2.

The data from Germany does not bode well for investment in the world's second-largest exporter. The Japanese rating cut could boost borrowing costs in the world's third-largest economy, reducing the relative attractiveness of higher-yielding Latin American investments. For more see: [ID:nL5E7JO0XO] [ID:nL4E7JO0DF]

Japanese investors hunting higher returns than they can get at home have been a key source of speculative capital in Latin America, helping Brazil's real and other currencies rise.

"The market is very unstable and will likely remain so until we can get some clearer idea of the direction of world growth," said Mario Battistel, head of foreign exchange at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage.

"The short-term outlook is not good, investors are cautious, they see a minefield."

The outlook is so negative, Battistel added, that stronger-than-expected U.S. durable goods orders had little or no effect on Wednesday's regional declines. [ID:nN1E77N096]

"Frankly, people are waiting for Bernanke to talk on Friday," Battistel said referring to a scheduled address in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke that some expect to include new stimulus measures for the U.S. economy. [ID:nLDE77N0G1]

Increased orders for autos, aircraft, washing machines and other expensive, long-lasting manufactured products, under the umbrella term of durable goods, show the U.S. economy has more power to grow than previously thought.

Not even Mexico's peso pulled out of its dive in the wake of the U.S. durables data. Mexico gets about 80 percent of its export earnings from the United States, much of it from the sale of big-ticket durable goods.

The peso <MXN=D2>, Latin America's most-traded currency, weakened 1.24 percent to 12.4665 to the dollar.

Mexican local bonds <MX10YT=RR> also plunged, with the 10 year, peso-denominated "bono" falling 2.49 to 104.09 percent of face value, its biggest one-day drop since June 21. The yield rose to 6.12 percent.

The country posted a seasonally adjusted trade deficit <MXTBAL=ECI> of $364 million in July, 45 percent more than a year earlier and 18 percent more than in June, the government said on Wednesday. [ID:nEMS3ZP3JU]

The non-adjusted deficit was $1.179 billion in July compared with a surplus of $108 million in June.

Brazil's real <BRBY>, the region's second-most-traded currency, weakened 0.65 percent to 1.6097 to the dollar.

Argentina's peso <ARSB=> also dropped. The country's unofficial, or parallel, exchange rate slipped 0.51 percent to 4.385, a record low and its biggest one-day decline in two weeks.

The country's trade surplus shrank by nearly a quarter to $673 million in July compared with a year earlier as imports outpaced exports. [ID:nN1E77M1MY]. The median estimate in a survey of analysts by Thomson Reuters was for a surplus of $760 million.

Argentina's official, central-bank-controlled rate <ARS=RASL> was unchanged at 4.185 to the dollar.

The real and Argentina's peso may be in for more declines. In a note to investors on Wednesday, Flavia Cattan-Naslausky of RBS Capital in Greenwich, Connecticut, recommended selling the Brazilian real and Argentine peso, buying the Chilean and Colombian pesos and maintaining Mexican peso holdings.

Brazil's real will not strengthen much beyond 1.60 to the the dollar without prompting intervention by Brazil's central bank and finance ministry, Cattan-Naslausky said.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> was little changed from Tuesday at 2.7310 to the dollar.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> gave up some early gains to firm 0.11 percent to 467.70 to the dollar.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> firmed 0.17 percent to 1,786.01 after earlier strengthening as much as 0.25 percent.

(Editing by W Simon and Dan Grebler)

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Brazil
text:
BRASILIA, Aug 2 (Reuters) - High-profile scandals in President Dilma Rousseff's government have soured ties with her allies, stalling legislation in Congress and delaying key infrastructure projects before the 2014 World Cup.

Other risks include an apparent lack of interest in long-term structural reforms, pressure to heighten public spending, and renewed intervention in currency markets.

SCANDALS

A corruption scandal that forced the top ranks of the transport ministry to resign is delaying the construction of roads, ports and railways that form part of Rousseff's flagship public works program, PAC. [ID:nN1E7651GA].

This could have a broad impact in the real economy, affecting soy exporters facing shipping delays due to poor roads or IT manufacturers waiting for fiber optic cables to launch the assembly of new tablet plants.

The latest accusations of kickback schemes will likely also slow other infrastructure projects, including preparations for the World Cup in 2014 and the 2016 Olympics, as government watchdogs step up scrutiny of contracts.

"We're reviewing all the projects in the transport ministry -- with a strong magnifying glass," Transport Minister Paulo Passos said.

The shake-up also renewed tensions with Rousseff's allies, particularly because she decided to fire many officials before concluding an official inquiry.

If Rousseff continues her "cleanup" in other ministries and state agencies, as her aides say she intends to, the career civil servant may boost her popular approval ratings but risks losing support from some allies who expect to get extra "perks" from government contracts and posts.

Already her coalition had been plagued by infighting over key government posts and was recently hit by the resignation of her chief of staff, Antonio Palocci, over an ethics scandal [ID:nN08245414].

Her refusal to make political appointments to key jobs was one of the factors angering her main ally, the PMDB.

LEGISLATIVE AGENDA

In an effort to avoid potential blackmailing by allies seeking compensation for support, Rousseff has tried to govern without Congress as much as possible, her aides say.

Her agenda in Congress has been stalled for weeks.

Reforms to the tax code and the pension system, which investors say are necessary to keep the economy growing, may not be passed for months, if at all. [ID:nN1E75L0H2]

Other projects on hold include legislation related to new offshore oil fields, and bills aimed at ensuring that Brazil builds stadiums, airports and other infrastructure that is not only needed for the World Cup and the 2016 Olympics but also to overcome bottlenecks holding back the entire economy.

But with the sporting events drawing nearer and a slowing economy exposing glaring problems from unwieldy labor laws to heavy taxes, Rousseff may need to engage Congress to approve structural reforms and emergency bills to speed up government procurement. In doing so, she may have to ease some of the austerity adopted in the first six months of her term.

What to watch for:

- Signs that Rousseff will loosen spending controls or make appointments to please allies.

- A major financial crisis abroad, perhaps in Europe, that would require quick action from Brazil's Congress to prevent economic trouble at home.

- New media revelations of scandal among top officials. [20110802 145759 GMT]

GOVERNMENT MEDDLING

Rousseff's meddling in state and private companies has weighed on blue chips and helped push down the Bovespa <.BVSP> index by 15 percent this year.

Evidence that Rousseff helped oust the chief executive of heavyweight iron ore exporter Vale renewed concerns of meddling in strategic industries.

The move was intended to get Vale and the mining industry to invest more at home, buying Brazilian, not imported, ships and producing more steel and exporting less iron ore.

The government has also pressured state-controlled oil company Petrobras not to raise domestic gasoline prices, damaging its bottom line. Rousseff has also pushed Petrobras to cut natural gas prices in order to help lower costs for industries and keep domestic fuel prices at bay. [ID:nN1E75S0FM]

A mining bill Rousseff is expected to send to Congress this year would likely reduce the time companies have to develop mines to discourage speculation in mineral properties, and could hike royalties to promote mineral processing.

CURRENCY POLICY

The risk of government intervention in Brazil's currency market remains high, as a strengthening currency is undermining several exporters' international competitiveness.

When the real <BRBY><BRL=> hit a 12-year high in July at 1.54 per U.S. dollar, the government imposed a tax on currency derivatives, the latest and potentially most aggressive measure so far designed to stem the currency rally [ID:nN1E76Q01I].

If that measure proves ineffective, the government could hike the tax rate on currency derivatives from currently 1 percent to as much as 25 percent and adopt other measures as well, Finance Minister Guido Mantega has said.

With consumer price pressure slowly ebbing, the government will rely less on a strong currency to anchor inflation in coming months and may intervene more aggressively.

Any fresh measures could hit fixed income and currency investors, while the stronger real can erode profit margins and market share of exporters, particularly manufacturers.

AGRICULTURE

A legislative proposal changing environmental regulations for farmers passed the lower house of Congress and could become law later this year. While the Forestry Code, which sets the percentage of native forest farmers must preserve, reduces overall environmental liabilities for farmers, they would have to finance costs they have been putting off for years to reforest or invest in protected areas.

Apparent disagreement in the government over measures to restrict land purchases by foreigners has renewed concern among investors. The agriculture ministry would like to revise last year's measures to restrict foreign speculative capital but promote investments into production. [ID:nN16140439]

MONETARY POLICY

Annual inflation is starting to ease but remains very close to the government's upper limit of 6.5 percent. [ID:nN1E76O03S]

Rousseff has described rising prices as the biggest policy challenge for her government, aware that inflation tends to hit hardest the poorer classes who form her political base. A sustained rise in prices could result in a significant deterioration of her approval rating.

The central bank has extended its cycle of interest rate hikes, raising rates 175 basis points this year to 12.50 percent. The central bank has signaled it may soon end the tightening cycle but markets expect a further hike of 25 basis points.

That gives Brazil some of the world's highest rates, which in turn could brake consumer spending. Already there are signs of slowing demand. Sales of packaging material, a key indicator of consumer goods sales, fell 3.6 percent in June from May.

Inflation and rising interest rates have also weighed significantly on the stock market this year.

PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

After a spending boom ahead of the presidential election last October, the government has gradually improved its public finances. The primary budget surplus, which excludes interest payments on debt, jumped to 3.54 percent of GDP for the 12 months through June, up from about 2 percent in mid-2010.

But public accounts could worsen in the second half of the year. Much of the surplus has come from non-recurring tax revenue, and slower economic growth means lower tax revenue than expected. The economy grew 7.5 percent in 2010 and is now expected to slip to under 4 percent this year. [ID:nN1E76R0YM]

Also, Rousseff is facing rising pressure to increase pork barrel spending after more than 6 months of austerity.

What to watch for:

- Sliding tax revenue, rising expenditures.

- Growing political pressure to hike pork barrel spending.

ROUSSEFF'S HEALTH

Rousseff's hospitalization and her lengthy recovery from pneumonia in May renewed concerns over her health, which first surfaced in April 2009 when she announced she was being treated for lymphoma. [ID:nN01161483] [ID:nN12259498]

She has been given a clean bill of health by doctors, but fresh evidence shows that Rousseff suffers from several other ailments. The 63-year-old trained economist is reported to also suffer from diabetes, hypothyroidism, and occasionally high blood pressure. During her treatment for pneumonia she complained of stomach pains, showed signs of an over-worked liver and had a low white blood cell count.

Rousseff's health is on investor radar screens. Were it to worsen, markets could slump due to uncertainty over economic policy under Vice President Michel Temer.

title: Brazil  Currency  Market Weaker As Concerns About Growth Return
text:
--Brazil real weakens as investor concerns about global economic growth return

--Early session rally on U.S. debt deal fades on weak manufacturing data from China, Europe and U.S.

--Currency market has adapted to latest forex measures, with no lack of liquidity

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL1.5615 to the dollar


   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market ended weaker Monday as weak manufacturing data reignited concerns about global economic growth, cutting short an early session rally sparked by a deal to resolve the U.S. debt ceiling debate.

The real posted early session gains, tracking emerging-market currency advances abroad, after U.S. lawmakers reached a deal to raise the debt ceiling and reduce the deficit. The U.S. House and Senate are expected to vote on the measure later Monday. But the euphoria in global financial markets was short-lived.

A lower-than-expected reading in the Institute for Supply Management's July manufacturing index combined with weak output figures from Europe and China to once again showed that global economic growth is shaky, traders said. And despite a resolution on raising the U.S. debt ceiling, credit-rating companies could still decide to downgrade the U.S.

"The world is really passing through a deceleration," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at Sao Paulo trading house BGC Liquidez.

Concerns about the fiscal health of lesser European Union members also is returning, said Barbutti. The economist noted that spreads for sovereign bonds issued by Belgium, Italy and Spain were widening to historic highs. The movement shows that the situation in Europe is "deteriorating and could spread" to other countries in the single-currency bloc, Barbutti said.

The Brazilian real exited active trading at BRL1.5615, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset. That was weaker from Friday's close at BRL1.5504 to the dollar.

In Brazil, currency traders have already adjusted to last week's move to tax short currency-derivatives positions, said Reginaldo Siaca, foreign-exchange manager at the Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo. In the immediate aftermath of the measures, "the market was a mess," Siaca said. "Now, everyone has assimilated the changes. But if the government doesn't think the measures are working to its satisfaction, they'll raise the tax."

The financial-transactions tax is currently 1%, but it could be raised to as much as 25% by Brazil's National Monetary Council.

While the prospect of further intervention from the Brazilian Central Bank could weigh on the real in the short term, the broader trend for the currency remains tilted toward appreciation thanks to the dynamics of Latin America's largest economy, said the Brazilian unit of Spain's Banco Santander.

"Strong fiscal and external outlooks compared with the advanced world, massive interest-rate differentials and strong [foreign direct investment] inflows should help the [Brazilian real] remain around the BRL1.55 handle," Santander said in a research report.

Brazil's towering interest rates will likely be the source of most downward pressure on the currency, thanks to an inflation outlook that remains above the government's target. For a second-consecutive week, economists and analysts raised their 2012 outlook for inflation to 5.3% from 5.28% the previous week, according to the central bank's weekly market survey. For 2011, the year-end forecast was maintained at 6.31%. Both estimates are above the government's inflation target of 4.5%.

Economists also expect the central bank to boost the benchmark Selic base interest rate a sixth time in 2011 to 12.75%. Currently, the Selic stands at a towering 12.5%--by far the highest interest rate among the world's major economies. The Selic is expected to be 12.5% by year-end 2012, according to the survey.

title: WSJ:Vale CFO: Intervention  To Help Stabilize Strong  Brazil  Real
text:
Brazilian mining company Vale SA (VALE, VALE5.BR) expects government interventions to help stabilize the strong Brazilian real, said Guilherme Cavalcanti, the company's chief financial officer, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal on Friday.

"We think the exchange rate in Brazil will reach a bottom because the government is starting to bring measures to not let the real appreciate further," Mr. Cavalcanti said.

This week, Brazil imposed foreign-exchange measures aimed at curbing the strong real, including a 1% financial-transactions tax on short-dollar positions. The Central Bank of Brazil has also been purchasing dollars at spot market auctions to slow the gain of the real, as the local currency traded this week at its strongest levels against the dollar in 12 years.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Vale, the world's largest producer and exporter of iron ore, posted another round of strong quarterly profits Thursday on robust demand in Asia. But Mr. Cavalcanti said the real's appreciation is still having "a huge impact" on the company. That is because while Vale's revenue is in dollars, most of its costs for labor and other expenses at its Brazilian mines are in reais.

Mr. Cavalcanti said he tries to deal with this "currency mismatch" with hedging in the futures markets and by keeping a major part of the company's cash position in reais.

"My assets tend to be a hedge for my costs," he said. "I can't hedge everything because the amount is too big."

Brazil's rising currency, which appreciated 4.2% against the dollar in the second quarter, boosted Vale's costs in the period. At the same time, Vale made $360 million in the second quarter as a result of currency and interest rate swaps.

The strong real is generally a drag on Brazilian exporters, because it makes their products more expensive to foreign buyers. But in Vale's case, the booming market for iron ore has sent the company's profits soaring.

Vale reported Thursday that it had a profit of $6.45 billion in the second quarter, a 74% increase from a year earlier. That was down slightly from a record quarterly profit of $6.83 billion in the first quarter, and less than some analysts had forecast.

Mr. Cavalcanti said Vale expects to continue to benefit from strong demand from China and that iron ore prices will stabilize at current high levels.

China accounts for roughly 40% of Vale's shipments of iron ore and iron pellets. Vale said its average sales price for iron ore in the second quarter was $145.30 per metric ton, up 58% from the year-earlier period.

"We're not seeing any slowdown from China," Mr. Cavalcanti said, noting China's strong growth in GDP in the second quarter and solid increases in housing starts and sales. He added that Japan's rebuilding efforts following the earthquake earlier this year will provide another source of demand in the region.

"For Asia, we are very bullish, and prices will continue to stabilize," Mr. Cavalcanti said.

Mr. Cavalcanti said he is not worried about any potential fallout related to the debt discussions in Washington, in part because the U.S. is not a significant market for the company. In addition, he said he would expect that even if Western countries experienced economic repercussions, China would increase investment in infrastructure to keep its own economy strong.

"We think the Asian economy has this capacity to offset crises in the Western world," Mr. Cavalcanti said. [ 07-29-11 1400ET ]

title: *DJ Brazil's  Central Bank  Believes Real Weakening Too Fast - Source
text:
6 Dec 2012 14:27 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Central Bank Thinks Currency Movement Is 'Artificial' - Source

6 Dec 2012 14:27 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Central Bank: Exchange Rate Doesn't Reflect Fundamentals -Source

6 Dec 2012 14:27 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Central Bank Has No Floor or Ceiling for Real - Source

6 Dec 2012 14:42 EDT DJ  Brazil's Central Bank Thinks Real Weakening Too Fast - Source

--Brazil central bank believes market has made an incorrect assessment of government policy, a person familiar with the policy says

--That impression in the market led to an "artificial depreciation" of the real, according to the person

--Brazil central bank believes the real doesn't reflect economic fundamentals, the person says 


 
   By Luciana Magalhaes 
 

SAO PAULO--Brazil's central bank believes there has been "an artificial depreciation" of the Brazilian real as the market is working on an erroneous view of government policy, according to a person familiar with the central bank's thinking.

"The market is working based on conjectures, on a belief that the government wants a weaker real," said the person, who asked not to be identified. "But there's no band. There's no roof and no floor. The market determines the exchange rate."

Current exchange rate levels versus the dollar don't reflect the fundamentals of the Brazilian economy, which, in spite of the weak performance, is "growing more" than other economies, said the person.

While debate persists about the real's fair value--it's lost around 10% against the dollar so far this year, but many economists still see it as overvalued --there is also a general perception that it has shed weight too fast against the dollar in recent sessions.

There have been a series of press reports citing people close to the central bank that have helped strengthen the Brazilian real over the last two days. The real traded at BRL2.0782 on Thursday afternoon, stronger than Wednesday's close of BRL2.0978, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

The signals appear to have arrested a concerted effort by some in the market to test weaker levels for the Brazilian real. The real weakened to 2.1359 in intraday trading on Nov. 30.

Last week, as the currency touched BRL2.0978 per dollar during intraday trading, the central bank stepped in several times to strengthen the currency.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the central bank also relaxed some restrictions on capital inflows that had been introduced earlier this year to prevent an overappreciation of the currency. Although officially these were more aimed at specific issues in lending markets, market players saw the move as clearly directed at the currency market.

"We had a problem of dollar liquidity and the government acted to solve that", said Sidnei Nehme, executive director at Brazilian brokerage NGO. Next year could be challenging for the real, as the government intervention, combined with historic low interest rates, has made Brazil less attractive to overseas investors, Mr. Nehme said.

The efforts to avoid currency weakness come just as some in the rates market raised questions about monetary policy next year. There's a growing perception that the central won't raise rates in 2013 and may even start cutting them again to speed up the pace of recovery.

After timid 2.7% growth in 2011, the Brazilian economy is expected to grow just 1% or even less in 2012, despite a series of measures taken in an effort to spur growth. The government has often expressed concern that a strong currency hinders the competitiveness of Brazilian exporters.

But the central bank is also constrained from cutting interest rates by above-target inflation, which is running around 5.6%. That's more than a full point higher than its 4.5% target, though still within the 6.5% upper limit of its tolerance band.

Earlier Thursday, the central bank reaffirmed its commitment to the interest rate stability for a "sufficiently prolonged period," in the minutes of the central bank's monetary policy meeting from Nov. 27 and 28.

Meanwhile, the comments from the person familiar with the bank's consideration could once again raise tensions in Brasilia.

"The bigger question is whether this new 'strong BRL' policy signals, as some investors now believe, a change in the relative power between the Brazilian Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance over management of the currency," wrote Tony Volpon, a strategist at Nomura Securities in New York, suggesting the central bank may have recovered stewardship of the currency.

Still, there's no real contradiction between taking the real lower to help industry and the central bank's verbal intervention to moderate the recent sudden depreciation, Mr. Volpon said. The process has to be managed to minimize damage to companies from a stronger currency or inflation from a weaker real.

"But there is no doubt, given the dismal growth in Brazil, that a weaker real is what the government desires," he said. "We still believe that it will settle at a 2.08-2.12 level once the high levels of noise and uncertainty around the currency hopefully fade."

Write to Luciana Magalhaes at luciana.magalhaes@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Stronger After Measures Taken to Boost Liquidity
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real strengthened Thursday following the government's easing of capital controls, suggesting it wants to avoid further weakening of the local currency.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0772 to the dollar, after closing Wednesday at BRL2.0978, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSect.

"We had a problem of dollar liquidity and the government acted to solve that," said Sidnei Nehme, executive director at Brazilian brokerage NGO. "The market is quickly reacting to that," he added.

Earlier this week, Brazil's central bank extended the period of loans to qualify as export financing to five years from one. Those loans are exempt from the 6% financial-transactions tax, or IOF. The government also cut, from two years to one year, the maximum time limit of loans to which the IOF will apply.

"The government couldn't hold a spot auction, after complaining [earlier this year] that there was a tsunami of dollars coming into Brazil. So, they decided to ease the restrictions," said Mr. Nehme, who believes the easing of capital controls was adequate.

On Monday, the central bank intervened in the market to curtail the real's weakness after it approached BRL2.13 to the dollar.

With the recent measures, the currency is expected to go back to the trading range it kept for months, between BRL2.05 and BRL2.10 to the dollar, Mr. Nehme said. Still, he added, 2013 could again be a challenging year for the real, as the government's interventions, combined with historic low interest rates, have made Brazil less attractive to overseas investors.

Brazil's central bank has cut the benchmark interest rate Selic from 12.50% in August 2011 to an unprecedented low level of 7.25%. Many market players expect the central bank to maintain the Selic at the current rate until the end of 2013.

In the minutes of the central bank's monetary policy meeting on Nov. 27-28, released Thursday, the bank reaffirmed its commitment to keeping the interest rate stable for a "sufficiently prolonged period" to ensure inflation declines toward its 4.5% target.

Still, with growth weaker than expected in the third quarter, the market is sensing the possibility of more interest rate cuts next year. According to Citigroup strategist Dirk Willer, the term premium, as measured by the gap between market and economists' expectations, has turned negative, indicating the market is once again expecting more rate cuts than economists.

--Paulo Winterstein contributed to this report.

title: FX  GLOBAL CALL: Our Take on the Day's Big  FX  News
text:
The FX Global Call covers the main talking points from a news meeting involving DJ FX Trader editors in New York, London and Singapore, as well as other FX hot spots when warranted.


 
    By Brian Baskin 
 

1. It's official: Nothing can kill the Australian dollar. The Reserve Bank of Australia cut interest rates to 3%, the lowest since September 2009--and the Aussie rose. Traders say the gains came as the RBA's statement hinted there won't be any further cuts for a while, though the central bank wasn't scheduled to meet again until February anyway. And the bank was clear on a few points that should be negative for the Aussie, including that the "peak in resource investment is approaching." Still, foreign investors, central banks and sovereign wealth funds continue to flock to triple-A rated, relatively high-yielding Australian bonds. The currency trades at $1.0444, from $1.0421 before the announcement.

2. The Swiss franc weakened to an 11-week low of 1.2145 against the euro, extending a slide that began Monday after Credit Suisse imposed negative interest rates on deposits in the currency. Tuesday's drop followed rumors that the bank's measures would be more punitive than expected, or that other major banks were about to announce similar plans, neither of which bore out. But those were just the trigger--fact is, with virtually every euro-zone stress indicator nearing precrisis lows, investors don't feel as great a need to hold safe havens like the franc. Tellingly, the other recent time the franc's backed off the 1.20 floor enforced by the Swiss National Bank was in early September, when the European Central Bank outlined its bond-buying plan.

3. Speaking of those stress indicators: Italian 10-year bond yields fell to a two-year low, trading at about 4.43%. The euro itself hit a six-week high of $1.3077. In both cases, gains were slim.

4. Brazil's central bank is expected to intervene to support the real for a third consecutive trading day, as the currency remains above 2.10 to the dollar. While the central bank's made a show of support, it hasn't quieted the debate in the market over whether policy makers' true intent is to gradually guide the currency to a slightly weaker level to help Brazil's struggling economy.

5. South Korea and China tweaked a $59 billion bilateral currency swap arrangement to make it more attractive to businesses, which so far have yet to use it. Both countries want their currencies to be more easily used outside their borders.

6. The U.K. construction purchasing managers index showed the sector going back into contraction in November with a reading of 49.3. Sterling was largely unaffected, as markets wait for Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne's autumn statement on the economy.

7. Hong Kong sold HK$3.875 billion ($500 million) to keep the Hong Kong dollar in its target range against the dollar. The HK dollar is in demand and has traded on the high end of its band for nearly two months.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Stronger on  Central Bank Intervention
text:
--Brazil Central Bankintervenes three times in local currency market

--Market receives clear signal that central bank will defend BRL2.10

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.1175 to the U.S. dollar


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed sharply stronger against the U.S. dollar Monday as the central bank responded to an early session test from currency traders by intervening three times in the local market, driving the real back toward the ceiling of its recent trading range.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.1175 to the dollar, stronger from Friday's close at BRL2.1240, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. The real had started the session trading weaker from Friday's close, hovering around the BRL2.13 mark. Shortly after the bank's second of two swap auctions, the real briefly strengthened to BRL2.0969.

The Brazilian Central Bank returned to the currency market in force during Monday's session after sitting on the sidelines last week, when the real broke through the ceiling of its recent BRL2.00-to-BRL2.10 trading range. The bank allowed long- and short-position holders to engage in their month-end tug-of-war to set the Ptax, the average daily foreign-exchange rate used to settle futures contracts, without unnecessary interference, traders said.

But the party ended Monday, traders said.

"I think it's become perfectly clear that the central bank is going to defend BRL2.10," said Bruno Lavieri, an economist who tracks the foreign-exchange market for Sao Paulo consultants group Tendencias. While the largest part of the real's depreciation against the dollar was testing by traders, the central bank also could have been responding to a higher-than-normal demand for the greenback given the amount of interest in the three auctions held, Mr. Lavieri said.

The bank ended Monday's session by announcing that it would sell up to $5 billion in dollars into the spot market. The bank did not immediately reveal the volume of dollars sold. The dollars were to be sold at Monday's Ptax rate of 2.1121, with repurchase by the central bank set for Jan. 4 and Feb. 4, the bank said in the announcement.

The spot auction followed two separate swap auctions Monday. The bank effectively injected more than $3 billion in dollar liquidity into Brazil's futures market. The bank sold $1.09 billion and $997 million in dollar-swap contracts maturing Jan. 2. While $3.14 billion in reverse-swaps mature Monday, the bank had anticipated $1.62 billion Nov. 23 with a sale of swaps contracts.

"Today [the central bank] is not going to roll over the reverse-swap contracts and are making a complementary offer of swaps," said Sidnei Nehme, director at Sao Paul trading house NGO. "That's going to cause the real to correct its position. I think [the real] is going to strengthen further toward the comfort zone below BRL2.10."

The BRL2.00-to-BRL2.10 range is seen as comfortable by the government because the currency is weak enough to support local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation, traders said. But there has been increased market chatter since early November that the sluggish performance of Brazil's industrial sector could have the government thinking about letting the real weaken further to give manufacturers a boost.

In that case, Monday's action could be a move to smooth the path for a weaker real in the first quarter of 2013, traders said.

"Yes, the government could be opening the door for the real to weaken past the BRL2.10 ceiling. Not necessarily right now, but in the coming months," said Tendencias' Mr. Lavieri. Should inflation end 2012 at current rates around 5.5%, planned cuts in electricity rates and accounting maneuvers would give the government enough space to allow the real to trade at BRL2.30 per dollar without fear of missing its inflation target for year-end 2013, the economist said.

title: UPDATE 2- Brazil intervenes  heavily on  FX  market, real gains
text:
* Central bank calls 2 swap auctions in the morning

* Later, bank calls 2 auctions to sell dollars on spot market

* Real closes 0.5 pct stronger at 2.119 per dollar

(Adds quote from analysts, background)

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank on Monday intervened heavily in the foreign exchange market to halt a sharp currency depreciation and boost dollar liquidity at the end of the year, when greenbacks are traditionally scarce in the country.

The series of interventions, which included two currency swap auctions in the morning and two dollar auctions on the spot market in the afternoon, caused the real to close only 0.5 percent stronger at 2.1190 per U.S. dollar.

Despite the magnitude of the actions, investors believe the central bank is only trying to smooth out an expected weakening of the real, which lost 4.7 percent in November, half of that in the last week of the month.

Bets on a weaker real greatly increased on Friday after data showed the Brazilian economy grew in the third quarter at half the rate expected by economists, but investors still wonder how much the central bank will allow the real to slide.

"We still don't know how much weaker the government wants the currency to be," said Joao Medeiros, a currency director at Pioneer brokerage.

The real dropped to 2.1382 per dollar right after the market opened, its weakest level in more than 3-1/2 years, before the central bank called two consecutive auctions to sell traditional currency swaps - derivative contracts that support the real by emulating the sale of dollars in the futures market.

The real erased its losses and jumped as much as 1.6 percent after that initial move, which suggested the central bank was not comfortable with the currency's fast depreciation pace. But gains slowly faded in the afternoon as investors followed bank recommendations to reduce exposure to the real.

The central bank then announced two separate auctions to sell as much as $5 billion on the spot market with the agreement to repurchase the amounts sold in 30 and 61 days, respectively.

"Investors are becoming long dollars, I believe that is because they need to hedge their positions. Even after two swap auctions, the market wanted more," said Reginaldo Galhardo, head of currency trading at Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo.

It was the first time the central bank sold dollars with repurchase agreements since April 2009 - a strategy it normally uses to provide temporary liquidity to the foreign exchange market.

The central bank did not say how much it sold in the afternoon auctions, but it signaled there was demand for both. In a statement, the bank said it was setting cutoff prices of 2.12245 reais and 2.1324 reais for each of the auctions, with repurchase dates on January 4 and February 4, respectively.

Less than two weeks ago, central bank president Alexandre Tombini warned the bank was ready to protect the currency from speculative bouts and provide temporary liquidity to the exchange market at year-end.

(Additional reporting by Danielle Fonseca in Sao Paulo; Editing by Nick Zieminski and Steve Orlofsky)

title: 3Q Notwithstanding, Brazil's Economy Still Poised to Rebound - Goldman's O'Neill
text:
--Brazil will likely grow 1.7% in 2012 - O'Neill

--Brazil can grow 4% or more in 2013 - O'Neill

--Brazil's real still overvalued - O'Neill


 
   By Luciana Magalhaes 
 

SAO PAULO--Despite Brazil's disappointing economic performance in the third quarter, Latin America's biggest economy should still rebound with growth of 4% or more in 2013, said Jim O'Neill, the chairman of Goldman Sachs Asset Management.

"It was just one quarter," said Mr. O'Neill, who coined the famous acronym "BRIC," grouping the world's heavyweight emerging markets Brazil, Russia, India and China.

Mr. O'Neill's growth forecast for next year is above market consensus. He bases it on the hefty monetary and fiscal stimulus that Brazil's government has pumped into the economy this year.

Moreover, the country's currency, the real, is still overvalued, he said. Even though the real has lost 11% of its value against the dollar so far this year, Mr. O'Neill added that it could weaken further. That, in turn, would boost the competitiveness of the country's exports.

Brazil's gross domestic product expanded 0.9% in the third quarter compared with the third quarter of 2011, according to official data out Friday, far less than the expected 2.3%. On a quarterly basis, total economic output in July-through-September rose just 0.6%, making for an annualized 2.4% rate of growth.

In an email, Mr. O'Neill said the weakness was very specific to the financial sector, suggesting it was temporary.

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said much the same thing following the data release. The banking industry was hurt by a combination of lower lending and lower interest rates, Mr. Mantega told reporters. But lower interest rates should start to feed into higher lending, which will help banks recover, Mr. Mantega added.

Mr. O'Neill estimates the Brazilian economy will expand around 1.7% in 2012, and 4% or more next year. His forecasts are above market consensus of 1.5% growth this year and 3.94% in 2013. But the current consensus was polled before the data came out, so it could soon be revised even lower.

Mr. O'Neill suggested the market isn't taking into account just how much the monetary easing and some fiscal initiatives will likely catapult growth next year.

Brazil's central bank has cut the Selic base rate continuously since August 2011, when it stood at 12.50%, to a historic low of 7.25%. It has also cut taxes on consumer goods, aiming to fuel economic activity. "These are leading indicators of future growth."

On the real currency, Mr. O'Neill said that, despite its slide this year, an even lower exchange rate would be to the country's benefit. "Something closer to BRL2.30 or BRL2.35 to the dollar would be good for Brazil," he said.

Currency market intervention by the Brazilian central bank and fiscal measures taken by the government to protect local exporters have kept the real trading in a limited range between BRL2.00 to around BRL2.10 in recent months.

It broke through the weaker end of that range Friday in the wake of the data, exiting active trading at BRL2.1240 to the dollar, losing significant ground from Thursday's close at BRL2.0955.

Mr. O'Neill said if interest rates remain at their current level or go even lower in face of the weak growth, the "real will likely weaken further."

The central bank Wednesday left its key rate unchanged at 7.25%, and suggested in its statement that it would remain at that level for an extended period of time.

The latest GDP data, Mr. O'Neill said, doesn't change his views on Brazil or reduce the country's position in the global economy. "It is one of top 10 economies by size in the world, probably still sixth or seventh," he added.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management has $716.1 billion in assets under management, according to the company's website.
