title: EMERGING MARKETS-Argentine debt rallies; Brazil real slumps
text:
* Optimism on U.S. budget deal aids most Latam currencies

* Dollar-long players seek weaker month-end Brazil real rate

* Real weakens 0.33 pct, Mexican peso gains 0.24 pct

(Updates with Argentine bond rally, previous SAO PAULO)

By Jorge Otaola

BUENOS AIRES, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Argentine bonds rallied on Thursday after the country won a reprieve from a U.S. appeals court that eased investors' fears of a new default as early as next month.

Argentine debt prices had tumbled since a U.S. court ruled last week that the country must pay $1.33 billion by Dec. 15 to "holdout" investors who rejected a previous restructuring of its defaulted debt.

The South American nation had rejected paying the investors, who had filed the lawsuit, raising the risk of a technical default on about $24 billion worth of debt since Argentina was going to be barred from trying to only pay investors who had taken part in two debt exchanges in 2005 and 2010.

But an appeals court on Wednesday gave Argentina more time to fight last week's ruling by U.S. District Judge Thomas Griesa.

"For a few days at least, happiness is back," said Sabrina Corujo and analyst at consultancy Portfolio Personal.

After slumping nearly 30 percent since late October, the price on Argentina's June 2017 global bond jumped almost 14 percent on Thursday.

In currency trading, the Brazilian real extended its losses for a second day on Thursday, under pressure by dollar-heavy investors who wanted to weaken the currency as the central bank on Friday set a monthly exchange reference rate.

The real bid down 0.33 percent to 2.0963 per dollar, recovering from a drop of around 1 percent.

"The only thing that justifies this currency move is the fight over the Ptax," said Mario Battistel, manager of the currency trading desk at Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The Ptax is a benchmark exchange rate for a broad range of contracts, including foreign loans, trade, and derivatives. Dollar-laden speculators may have tried to keep the real weak through the Ptax fix, traders said. A higher Ptax means it costs more reais to buy dollars.

The real pared steeper losses as investors feared that Brazil's central bank could intervene again if the currency continued to slide.

Last Friday, as the real traded at a 3-1/2 year low of around 2.11 per dollar, the central bank called an auction of traditional currency swaps, derivative contracts that emulate the sale of dollars in the futures market.

Brazilian policymakers have used both verbal and market intervention to keep the real largely within a range of 2 per dollar to 2.05 since July.

But other analysts said authorities may be leaning toward allowing for a weaker currency to support exporters, and they may allow the real to drift lower, as long as the drop does not happen with too much velocity.

Elsewhere in Latin America, currencies gained along with emerging market stocks. Boosting investors' appetite for risk was optimism that U.S. leaders could reach a deal to avert steep spending cuts and tax hikes that could plunge the world's largest economy in recession next year.

"In the United States, they say there are growing chances of an agreement to avoid the fiscal cliff and that is bring optimism to the market," said Gloria Soto, a currency trader at FXCM Chile.

The Mexican peso firmed 0.24 percent and the Chilean peso gained 0.33 percent.

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger, Investors Wary Of  Central Bank
text:
--Brazil real opens at BRL2.0721/dlr vs. BRL2.0818/dlr Friday

--Investors "adjusting" positions after Friday central bank move

--Exporters sell dollars, help support real against greenback

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real opened stronger against the U.S. dollar on Monday as exporters sold dollars to the market and investors kept a wary eye on the central bank.

In early trading, the real was changing hands at BRL2.0721 to the dollar, stronger against the Friday close of BRL2.0818, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Friday was a roller-coaster ride for the Brazilian foreign exchange market, with the real weakening to nearly BRL2.12 to the dollar in early trading. But the swift weakening of the real brought central bank intervention in the form of an auction of foreign-exchange swap contracts. The real strengthened in the wake of the auction, which effectively added dollar-linked paper to the pool of contracts available in the futures market.

"Today [Monday], investors are adjusting their positions in the wake of the central bank intervention," said Reginaldo Siaca, manager of Sao Paulo's Advanced brokerage. "Of course, there is no formal trading band established by the central bank, but the market is beginning to perceive an informal band around BRL2.02 to BRL2.12. It was evident Friday that the central bank did not at all like the idea of having the real trade weaker than BRL2.12."

Traders said volatility was likely to be muted Monday, with any abrupt movement in the market meeting with central bank intervention.

Trading could turn move volatile later in the week in the runup to expiry of monthly foreign exchange futures contracts. The contracts will be closed out based on Friday's average foreign exchange rate, or Ptax rate.

"The Ptax close-out could bring some jockeying between holders of long-dollar positions and short positions," said Mr. Siaca.

Traders said overseas factors could have more impact than domestic news in the next few days.

"Europe will continue to be a focus," said Mr. Siaca.

European finance ministers are due to meet Monday to discuss the next phase of a bailout for debt-strapped Greece. Failure to aid Greece could bring a new round of pessimism about Europe's ability to confront deep debt and growth problems.

In Brazil, the central bank will hold its last monetary policy meeting of the year on Wednesday. However, analysts are virtually unanimous in saying the bank will hold its Selic base interest rate steady at 7.25%. Brazil's government is due to release third-quarter economic growth figures on Friday. Analysts expect a robust rebound from the sluggish growth registered in the first half of the year.

December could see more volatility in the foreign-exchange market. Traders noted that multinational companies typically increase their profit and dividend remittances toward the end of the year as they square their books with parent companies. Imports also increase ahead of the Christmas season, another factor that could increase the demand for dollars.

Heavy demand for the American currency could bring more central bank intervention in December in the event Brazil's central bank decides to hold the line against any depreciation beyond the BRL2.12 level.

Swap auctions are likely to be the preferred method for intervention. The auctions effectively dump dollar-linked paper into the futures market. Friday's auction added the equivalent of $1.62 billion. That was enough to offset more than half of the $3.14 billion in so-called reverse-swap contracts that will expire Dec. 3. Traders said it was possible the central bank will use another swap auction before Dec. 3 to offset the rest of the reverse swaps coming due.

 The Chilean peso lost 0.6 percent while the Mexican peso  fell 0.32 percent on the Greek uncertainty.

 But U.S. President Barack Obama's rejection on Monday of a Republican suggestion for avoiding the "fiscal cliff" has some analysts far from sanguine on the peso's near-term prospects.

 "We remain pretty neutral on the (Mexican) peso ... but we still think there is room for disappointment in terms of peso volatility," said Delia Paredes, a strategist at Banorte-IXE in Mexico, citing "signs of disagreement in the U.S." 

 She expects the Mexican peso to trade between 12.87 and 13.10 per dollar this week.

 The White House on Monday threw cold water on a Republican proposal for solving the so-called "fiscal cliff" by limiting tax deductions and loopholes, instead of allowing taxes to rise for the highest earners in the United States.

 The Brazilian real closed nearly flat, weakening only 0.03 percent to 2.0818 per greenback as investors digested conflicting signs from policymakers about the future of the country's foreign exchange policy.

 The real on Friday posted its largest single-day gain in nearly three months after the central bank stepped into the market to halt losses that were partly fueled by comments from Finance Minister Guido Mantega.

 The apparent tug of war between the central bank and Mantega left investors wondering whether policymakers still uphold an informal trading band of 2.0-2.1 per dollar, where the real has been stuck since early July.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real jumps as  central bank  eclipses Mantega
text:
(Adds quotes, other Latam currencies; updates prices)

* Real weakens to 2.11/dollar as Mantega says FX rate 'reasonable'

* Central bank calls swap auction, props real back to 2.08/dlr

* Hopes of Greece deal support Mexican peso, which gains 0.6 pct

By Walter Brandimarte and Natalia Cacioli

RIO DE JANEIRO, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real

on Friday posted its largest single-day gain in nearly three months after the central bank acted to halt losses that had taken the currency beyond the limits of an informal trading band.

The Mexican peso also posted gains, buoyed by hopes that Greece's lenders were nearing an agreement to release funds to Athens, but the Chilean peso dropped after hitting a one-month high in the previous session.

Brazil's intervention in the currency market came as the real quickly slid on comments by Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who told a crowd of business leaders in Sao Paulo that the exchange rate is at a "reasonable though not totally satisfactory level" to support industry.

The apparent tug of war between Mantega and the central bank left investors wondering whether policymakers still uphold an informal trading band of 2.0-2.1 per dollar where the real has been stuck since early July.

"The government is worried about industry, as we can tell by comments from several officials, but then comes the central bank worried about inflation and you have this tug of war," said a trader with a Brazilian bank.

"We can't say, however, that the central bank is defending the level of 2.1 per dollar. It only intervened today because the real was weakening too sharply," he added.

The real gained 0.8 percent to 2.0812 per dollar after the central bank sold about half of the 62,800 traditional swaps it offered in an auction.

Those contracts, which emulate the sale of dollars in the futures market, were apparently auctioned in an attempt to cancel some reverse currency swaps -- which mimic the purchase of dollars -- expiring in the beginning of December.

"The central bank announced the swap auction almost at the same time as Mantega said the exchange rate isn't totally satisfactory," said Alvaro Bandeira, chief economist with Orama in Rio de Janeiro. "The market is chaotic but so is the government."

The central bank announced the intervention shortly after the real slid more than 0.8 percent to an intraday low of 2.1168 per dollar -- its weakest in 3-1/2 years.

Hinting that some type of intervention was possible, central bank chief Alexandre Tombini had already said on Thursday that the bank was ready to provide liquidity to the foreign exchange market at year-end, when dollars are traditionally more scarce in Brazil.

"Today's (early) losses in the real were out of control and did not reflect the fundamentals," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist at BES Investimento in Sao Paulo. "The central bank wants to avoid market excess."

NEW TRADING RANGE?

The real had been trading weaker than 2.1 per dollar since the beginning of the session as small dollar outflows weighed on a market with thin trading volumes after the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States.

The 2.0-2.1 reais per dollar range, informally imposed by policymakers through a series of market interventions in the past several months, was considered at the same time favorable to Brazilian exporters and not too bad for inflation.

But signs that the government would favor a weaker currency to prop up the economy started to emerge early this week, when President Dilma Rousseff said in an interview that the government is "looking for an exchange rate that is not this one, with a devalued dollar and an over-valued real."

A weaker real could help Brazil's manufacturers, which have struggled with an over-valued currency and high input costs. The real has lost 10 percent this year, but remains more than 20 percent stronger than it was at the end of 2008.

Mantega, who coined the expression "currency war" in 2010 to complain about the strength of emerging market currencies, indicated that the real is approaching the levels desired by the government, although he made clear the currency still has some room to weaken.

title: Brazil 's Real Closes Stronger After  Central Bank Intervenes
text:
--The real strengthened to BRL2.0818 to the dollar, from BRL2.0957 Thursday

--It had weakened to BRL2.1172 in the late morning

--The central bank held a swap auction to halt the slide


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
 

BRASILIA--Brazil's real closed stronger against the dollar Friday after the country's central bank intervened to reverse a rapid weakening of the Brazilian currency.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0818 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset, after briefly weakening to BRL2.1172 in late morning trading, just before the central bank announced a swap auction that halted the slide.

Foreign exchange traders had already been on the lookout for an intervention Friday after the real closed Thursday near the BRL2.10 level the bank has defended on other occasions. The real quickly moved past that level in early trading Friday.

The central bank has been defending a trading band of BRL2.00 to BRL2.10 for months, while at the same time denying that it's doing any such thing.

Just Thursday the central bank's president, Alexandre Tombini, told Brazil's congress that "we don't have any formal or informal band for the currency."

Foreign exchange markets have received what might be conflicting signals from Brazilian officials recently. President Dilma Rousseff suggested in an interview published Tuesday in Valor newspaper that the real was still overvalued at current levels, while earlier Friday Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the real is in a "reasonable position," while adding the real's level is "still not totally satisfactory."

Friday's intervention could indicate the central bank might not be on board with a weaker real, and has left some traders with doubts about the country's foreign exchange policy.

"It looks like they're not all on the same page at the moment," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at the Pioneer Corretora brokerage in Sao Paulo. "That's making things a bit more complex for us."

The bank might really be moving its unofficial range for the real to BRL2.05-BRL2.15, said analysts Tony Volpon and George Lei at Nomura Securities in New York, because Brazilian authorities are relying on the weaker currency to boost economic growth despite the potential negative effect on inflation.

title: UPDATE 1-ANALYSIS-Brazil likely to let real slip, but not much
text:
* Rousseff likely to let real weaken beyond 2.10/dlr

* Central bank may still intervene to prevent volatility

* Inflation fears mean 2.12 or 2.15/dlr could be new floor

(Updates with Mantega, market movement, analyst comment)

By Brian Winter

SAO PAULO, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff is likely to loosen the informal trading band for the country's currency and let the real gradually weaken beyond 2.10 per dollar, but such an adjustment will be minor because of concerns over inflation.

The real was about 0.7 percent weaker in late trading on Wednesday at 2.095 per dollar, following rising aversion to riskier assets in global markets.

Traders were eager to see whether Brazil's central bank would intervene in the market, as it has done in recent months when the real threatened to break out of its de facto trading band of 2 to 2.10 per dollar.

Rousseff's recent statements on the real, plus comments from other senior officials, suggest the government will tolerate a slightly weaker currency in coming weeks if the market continues to push it in that direction.

A weaker real could help Brazil's manufacturers, which have struggled with an overvalued currency and high input costs. The real is 12 percent weaker this year, but is still 19 percent stronger than it was in 2008.

However, the central bank might still intervene to prevent an excessively quick depreciation that could destabilize the broader economy. It will likely tolerate only a small shift in the trading band, to 2.12 or 2.15 at most in the near term, because of concerns a weaker real could complicate the bank's inflation target in 2013 as economic activity picks up.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega told reporters on Wednesday that the real was "fluctuating normally" and that the government was intervening as little as possible in foreign exchange markets - comments that indicated a lack of concern as the real crept closer to 2.10.

In some of her most explicit comments about foreign exchange rates in recent months, Rousseff told Valor Economico newspaper this week that "we're looking for an exchange rate that is not this one, with a devalued dollar and an overvalued real."

Those comments helped push the real lower on Wednesday. The session was also unusually volatile because many traders were on holiday on Monday and Tuesday, and because of the coming Thanksgiving holiday in the United States.

WORRIES OVER INFLATION

Influential Valor columnist Cristiano Romero wrote on Wednesday that the government may be seeking a significantly weaker real in the medium term, at 2.20 to 2.25 per dollar.

However, some in the market thought that view was a misinterpretation of Rousseff's comments.

"We do not agree with this reading and believe that the ceiling is closer to 2.10 than it is to 2.15," Barclays said in a note to clients on Wednesday.

"With economic activity gaining momentum, another round of (real) depreciation could have a larger effect on inflation, which is an event we do not believe the (central bank) is looking for," Barclays said.

Financial markets expect that consumer inflation could hit 5.39 percent next year - above the mid-point of the government's inflation target of 4.5 percent, with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points in each direction.

Some analysts expressed concern that the apparent policy shift could signal a softer government stance on inflation - something officials rigorously deny.

"It seems to me that there is a coordinated policy effort ... which signals that they can live with a weaker real," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, an analyst with RBS Securities.

"But I don't see them having that much conviction on the inflation side. They seen to be ready to (let the real weaken) and that raises the question if they are also letting inflation go. This is negative for Brazil."

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso firmed on Tuesday, helped by optimism over U.S. fiscal negotiations, while Brazil's real teetered near a 3-1/2-year low, awaiting signs of central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso, one of the most freely traded emerging market currencies, has whipsawed in tandem with U.S. stocks over worries whether U.S. lawmakers will be able to stave off impending tax hikes and spending cuts that could hobble the economy.

The Mexican peso firmed 0.29 percent to 13.0175 per dollar, its fourth session of gains.

The peso has rallied 2 percent back from a 10-week low last week, on hopes the U.S. would avoid the "fiscal cliff," a combination of spending cuts and tax rises due to be implemented under existing law in early 2013 that may cut the federal budget deficit but also tip the economy back into recession.

Following U.S. President Barack Obama's re-election, the peso slumped and its technical outlook deteriorated sharply, suggesting deeper losses ahead.

But the currency's rally during the past four sessions drove the cost of dollars in pesos below its 200-day and 100 day moving averages.

After its recent rally, Nomura strategist Benito Berber reckons the peso is currently pricing in about a 10 percent to 15 percent chance of failure by U.S. lawmakers, down from about a 20 to 25 percent chance last week.

"There is at least a more amicable tone in the talks, but this is very short term," Berber said, adding the peso could slump back toward 13.50 per dollar if the market starts to bet on failure in Washington.

As the peso weakened, total bets on the Chicago exchange for

a stronger peso fell to $3.7 billion last week from a record high of $5.5 billion in late September.

That still leaves a lot of investors betting on a strong peso, investors who could face stop loss levels above the peso's low last week of 13.29 per dollar.

title: Weaker Brazilian Real Likely Here to Stay - Stuhlberger
text:
Current weaker levels for the Brazilian real are likely here to stay, given the reduction of short-term interest rates in Brazil, Luis Stuhlberger, co-founder and chief investment officer of one of Brazil's largest asset managers, Credit Suisse Hedging-Griffo, said Tuesday.

The Brazilian real has been trading in a range of BRL2 to BRL2.10 per dollar in recent months, kept in line by the threat of periodic central-bank interventions and comments by Brazil's finance minister.

But the Brazilian currency likely can depreciate without the help of the government, Mr. Stuhlberger said, while speaking at a New York event organized by the Brazilian-American Chamber of Commerce.

The dollar likely won't fall below BRL2 again "in our lifetime," he said.

In fact, the Brazilian government actually could reduce or remove the current 6% financial operations tax intended to prevent excessive real strength, as a way to test the markets, he said.

The main reason that the real is likely to see future weakness is the shift lower in real interest rates, he said. Brazil's central bank has slashed its benchmark Selic rate to a historic low of 7.25%, from as high at 12.50 in mid-2011.

He largely disagrees with market analysts who say the real could return to trading at BRL1.90 per dollar.

--Investors take "protective" dollar positions in spot, futures markets

--Investors worried about U.S., Europe fiscal problems, Mideast violence

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened against the U.S. dollar Friday as investors took "protective" dollar positions ahead of the weekend.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0747 to the dollar, weaker against the Wednesday close of BRL2.0659, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. Thursday was a national holiday in Brazil, with all financial markets closed.

"The global situation has turned even more delicate than usual," said Luiz Carlos Baldan, director of the Fourtrade brokerage in Sao Paulo. "Investors here in Brazil want to be holding dollars, not reais, ahead of the weekend. There could be news on any of several fronts over the weekend--Europe, the Middle East or the United States."

Europe is struggling with continued worries over the Greek debt crisis while the U.S. is riveted on political negotiations over crucial tax and spending issues that must be resolved by the end of the year. The Middle East this week erupted in violence between Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and Israel, sending global oil prices higher.

The real was also weaker in futures trading Friday, a key factor in the Brazilian market because of high trading volumes in the futures market. On the BM&FBovespa exchange, in late-afternoon trading the December foreign exchange futures contract saw the real weaken to BRL2.083 to the dollar while the January contract weakened to BRL2.098 to the dollar.

The real briefly weakened to BRL2.08 to the dollar in the spot market Friday, its weakest level since June.

In recent days, many traders had offered the view that Brazil's central bank might intervene in the market at the BRL2.08 to-the-dollar level in an effort to prevent a disorderly depreciation of the currency. A weaker real could bring inflationary pressures, especially as imports of consumer goods and even some perishables tend to rise ahead of the Christmas season.

However, the central bank was sidelined Friday. Traders noted that the real quickly backed away from the BRL2.08 to-the-dollar level as exporters sold dollars to the market.

Mr. Baldan added, "The market was a little more volatile than usual Friday because of thin volume. One or two transactions can send the exchange rate flying in one direction or the other."

Volume was thin after Thursday's national holiday, Brazil's Day of the Republic.

Volume is likely to be thin again Monday ahead of a Tuesday holiday in Brazil, Black Consciousness Day.

"I think we'll see the real gain a little strength when trading resumes at normal volumes next Wednesday," said Mr. Baldan. "I don't think we're heading to BRL2.10 to the dollar."

title: Brazil Real Weakens as U.S., Europe Fiscal Issues Weigh
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0385 to the dollar vs. BRL2.0325 Wednesday

--U.S., European fiscal problems continue to weigh on global investors

--Volume on Brazilian foreign-exchange market grows heading into year-end

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened against the U.S. dollar for the second straight day Thursday as U.S. and European debt problems once again took center stage.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0385 to the dollar, weaker against the Wednesday close of BRL2.0325, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

In a statement Thursday, the International Monetary Fund said looming U.S. political negotiations over tax and spending policies were already creating "uncertainties" in global financial markets. Newly re-elected President Barack Obama must reach agreement with a Republican-controlled House of Representatives on fiscal policies for 2013 by the end of the year or face the risk of a new recession.

Meanwhile, the IMF offered little solace on global growth prospects, saying recent projections for 2013 growth by the Group of 20 finance ministers may have been overly optimistic.

European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, in a news conference, also struck a pessimistic note when commenting on regional growth prospects. He praised Greece's parliament for passing fiscal austerity legislation Wednesday night but said Europe's battle for fiscal equilibrium was far from over.

The gloomy statements from the IMF and from Europe's top central banker led to weakness for the euro against the U.S. dollar, with the Brazilian real following suit.

Meanwhile, trading volume began to creep up in the Brazilian foreign-exchange market Thursday. Volume typically rises in the last weeks of the year as importers step up purchases of consumer goods ahead of the Christmas season and multinational companies increase profit remittances.

According to traders, demand for dollars has been met so far by heavy inflows of the U.S. currency from Brazilian companies placing overseas bonds.

"Brazilian companies are taking advantage of robust demand [for bond issues] from investors across the globe," said Leandro Miranda, head of fixed-income investments at Brazil's Banco Bradesco. Heavy demand has kept interest yields low, whetting the appetite of Brazilian companies for more issues, Mr. Miranda added.

Later in the year, demand for dollars from importers and multinational companies could outstrip inflows from bond issues. But, in that case, Brazil's central bank would be likely to intervene in the market as a seller of dollars, traders said. The central bank controls foreign reserves in excess of $370 billion.

title: Brazil Real Stronger Early as Market Tracks Inflation, Inflows
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real strengthened slightly in early trading Wednesday as investors gauged prospects for dollar inflows amid signs of continued firm inflation locally.

As of 6:50 a.m. EST, the real traded at BRL2.0304 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0318 to the dollar Tuesday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted fresh inflation data was grabbing the focus in early market action Wednesday.

Brazil's IBGE statistics institute reported the IPCA consumer price index accelerated 0.59% in October after a 0.57% advance in September. The October figure was the highest since April, and brought 12-month inflation to 5.45% from 5.28% through September.

The latest result helped bring expectations of more inflows alongside the view the country's central bank should stabilize interest rates as it pursues an annual inflation target of 4.5%. The bank has cut its benchmark Selic rate by more than 5 percentage points over the past year to a current 7.25%.

Traders said events abroad also reinforced as the re-election of U.S. President Barack Obama signaled the possible extension of monetary easing in the U.S.

That, and continued tough conditions in Europe are seen possibly encouraging more inflows to emerging markets such as Brazil.

"There's already a clearer vision for 2013 with perspectives for a slow recovery from the international crisis, and risks of deterioration before improvements come," said analysts Sidnei Nehme at the NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Local officials, meanwhile, appear determined to curb heavy inflows with a "dirty float" of the local currency that should involve further intervention from the government and central bank if Brazil's real moves far outside a narrow band maintained over recent months just above BRL2.00 to the dollar.

title: Brazil Real Slightly Stronger on Firm Global Markets
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0318/dlr vs BRL2.0336 Monday

--Stronger euro, stocks, commodities prices helped support real

--Central bank, foreign investors sidelined ahead of U.S. elections


 
  By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real strengthened slightly against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, tracking gains for the euro and higher global stocks and commodities prices.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0318 to the dollar, slightly stronger against the Monday close of BRL2.0336, according to Tullet Prebon via FactSet.

In Europe, stocks and the euro strengthened on improved corporate earnings. A stronger euro helped propel gains for international commodities prices. Higher commodities prices favor Brazilian export revenues.

An overall improved tone in global trading Tuesday came as U.S. voters lined up to choose a president and members of congress. Investors are increasingly hopeful the outcome of the U.S. presidential election will become clear within a few hours of the polls closing. If so, the result will also help clarify U.S. fiscal and monetary policies for the next four years.

But traders in Brazil also noted that while volatility was low Tuesday, so was volume.

"Trading is sideways," said Mauricianao Cavalcanti, a trader at Sao Paulo's Ouro Mina brokerage. "All eyes are on the U.S. election." He noted that international investors and the Brazilian Central Bank were essentially sidelined Tuesday.

In the longer term, however, pressure for the Brazilian real to appreciate against the U.S. dollar will grow.

One reason is an expected global weakening of the U.S. dollar because of continued loose monetary policy by the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, according to a study by economists at Goldman Sachs.

"Intervention to stem BRL appreciation this August and September has been as strong as in August and September 2010," the Goldman Sachs economists noted. "We see the scale of intervention recently as supporting our case for BRL appreciation in the medium term."

Another reason to expect pressure for an appreciation of the Brazilian real is inflows from corporate bond issues. A number of companies, including banking giants Itau (ITUB, ITUB4.BR) and government-run mortgage bank Caixa Economica Federal, are planning bond issues. Those dollars will pour into the Brazilian foreign exchange market in the coming weeks, forcing either an appreciation of the currency or additional heavy government intervention, according to traders.

Brazil's government has signaled its strong intention to fight back against any significant appreciation, however. In a recent interview, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said a strong real would hurt exporters and manufacturers.

title: Latest Wave of Overseas Issues Could Pressure Brazil Real
text:
--Brazil companies tapping debt market because of low interest rates

--But inflows could lead to unwanted appreciation of Brazilian real

--Central bank may act to contain appreciation pressure on currency


 
   By Rogerio Jelmayer 
 

SAO PAULO--A heavy inflow of U.S. dollars from overseas bond issues by Brazilian companies could bring an unwanted appreciation of the Brazilian real against the greenback, triggering a new round of central bank intervention in the market.

On Monday, a number of Brazilian companies set the tone, with nearly simultaneous news of overseas debt operations.

Banking giant Itau Unibanco Holding SA (ITUB) is planning to issue overseas bonds due in 2023. Others include oil and gas company Queiroz Galvao and Cielo SA (CIOXY, CIEL3.BR), Brazil's largest credit-card company. Meatpacker Marfrig (MRRTY, MRFG3.BR) is expected to announce a bond issue, and accompanying international road show, in the next few days.

The Brazilian companies are taking advantage of rock bottom international interest rates and low risk premiums for Brazil. The combination has brought record low yields on recent Brazilian debt issues.

"In the next few days, we could see a huge inflow of cash from these overseas bond issues," said Miriam Tavares, foreign exchange director at Sao Paulo's AGK brokerage. "The central bank will be very alert to this. I believe the central bank will use all of its instruments to defend the current trading range of BRL2.00 to BRL2.05 to-the-dollar."

The Brazilian real has been trading in that narrow range since July. Much of the reason is because that is how Brazil's government wants it.

Officials, including Finance Minister Guido Mantega, have argued that any abrupt appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar hurts exporters and manufacturers. In a recent interview, Mr. Mantega even admitted that Brazil's policy of frequent market interventions constitutes "a dirty float" of the nation's currency against the American dollar.

Interventions often come at the rate of one or more per week.

"The central bank is likely to absorb these new inflows via reverse swap auctions, similar to those used in recent sessions," said Ms. Tavares.

Reverse swap auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange dollar-linked contracts due at future dates for paper indexed to domestic interest rates. The auctions typically serve to strengthen the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real by reducing the availability of dollar-hedging contracts in the market. By using them, the central bank avoids direct buying and selling of dollars.

At the end of October, when state-run bank Caixa Economica Federal raised $1.5 billion via a bond issue, the central bank sold a total of around $3 billion in reverse swap contracts at two auctions, actions that helped keep the real within the tight trading band despite the heavy inflows.

More Brazilian debt issues are likely, according to analysts.

With interest rates across the globe at historically low levels and Europe in crisis, global investors are showing an increased appetite for assets previously considered high in risk.

"Currently, there is investor appetite even for small players, including Brazilian companies that are not rated investment grade but that can provide high yields for investors," said Rodrigo Fittipaldi, debt market director at BNP Paribas bank in Sao Paulo.

From January through September, the most recent figures available, overseas bonds issues totaled $37.5 billion, almost the same value as for the entire year of 2011, some $38.5 billion, according to the Brazilian Financial and Capital Markets Association, or Anbima.

title: Barron's(11/5) Brazil Round Table: Brazil Investors Take A Long View
text:
(From BARRON'S) 
   By Reshma Kapadia 

It has been an eventful year in Brazil, though perhaps not in the way investors would have liked. The country's growth has stalled to an expected 1.5% this year -- a figure not exactly befitting an emerging market, especially one that not so long ago had been growing at four times that rate.

That helped send the Brazilian real down 8% against the dollar this year, making it the year's second-worst currency performer. The MSCI Brazil stock market index is down 5% in dollar terms. Other battered economies, like India and China, have seen double-digit stock-market gains over the same period.

Brazil's central bank countered by slashing interest rates 5.25 percentage points in 15 months, to a record low of 7.25%. The government has also done its part, with stimulus aimed at reducing the cost of doing business by investing in much-needed infrastructure and by reducing taxes, including some on electricity that had accounted for almost half the average electric bill. But the government has also forced oil giant Petrobras, in which it has a 54% stake, to lower the gas prices it charges, and is pushing electric utilities whose contracts are up for renewal to lower the rates they charge. More recently, state-owned banks have been cutting fees and the rates they charge customers -- indirectly pushing private banks to follow suit. These steps may be good news for inflation, which ranked as one of the bigger threats facing Brazil last year. Now, however, investors are worried about increased government intervention and the impact that may have on the profits of the companies they own.

That said, some money managers are turning optimistic, encouraged by recent economic data that suggest a recovery is taking hold -- perhaps not to the 6% or 7% growth of the recent past, but a "new normal" of 3% to 4%. But unlike in 2010, when a robust economy fostered a stock market that seemed to do nothing but rise, success going forward will depend on more selectively picking individual stocks and bonds.

For help in navigating the latest developments -- and what the year ahead may offer -- we sat down with four fund managers with hefty Brazilian exposure and long experience investing in the world's sixth-largest economy.

Mark Jason is co-manager of the $3 billion Invesco Developing Markets fund (ticker: GTDDX) and has covered Brazil for 11 years. Jason doesn't care much about staying close to the benchmark, and his fund has 15% of its assets in Brazil, slightly more than the benchmark, making the country its biggest weighting. The reason: the large number of high-quality companies.

Nick Robinson heads Brazilian equities for Aberdeen and is a senior investment manager on the $8 billion Aberdeen Emerging Markets fund (GEGAX), which has almost 17% of assets in Brazil. Robinson is the only one of our participants who lives in Sao Paolo, giving him a first-hand view of the country's recent changes. He has been tactically adding to some of the cyclical companies that have suffered recently, but admits that government intervention may make investing more challenging.

David Robbins, co-manager of the $5.5 billion TCW Emerging Markets Income fund (TGEIX), invests in local and dollar-denominated sovereign and corporate debt. The fund has 14% of its assets in Brazil, its second-largest country weighting. With the run in dollar-denominated sovereign debt, Robbins is more interested recently in sovereign bonds denominated in Brazil's local currency, and corporate bonds.

Brazilian-born Will Landers manages the $568 million BlackRock Latin America fund (MDLTX) and oversees the firm's Latin American active equity investments. The calls-it-as-he-sees-it manager holds the market's biggest names, but favors mid-sized businesses that will benefit from increasing domestic demand.

Barron's: There's been no shortage of economic or market developments in the past year. What's been the most notable?

David Robbins: From a fixed-income perspective, the most interesting thing is how aggressive Brazil has been in reducing rates. When you reduce short-term rates by 5.25 percentage points, it takes a while to kick in. But you're going to get an impact by boosting economic growth.

Nick Robinson: The increasing willingness of the government to be more involved in the companies that are listed. The government has been tougher with Petroleo Brasileiro (PBR), better known as Petrobras, in terms of limiting the price at which it can sell gasoline to distributors. More recently, the government stepped into the banking sector, trying to lower fees and reduce the spreads between what they borrow and lend at. It has also stepped into the utility sector, trying to reduce the price of energy. It is quite tough to invest in that type of environment, in sectors the government can touch.

Will Landers: Most of the large-cap stocks in Brazil are under pressure right now. That's why you have global investors saying, "Well, this market isn't going anywhere and hasn't for two years." It may not go anywhere for a while. Brazil is not a China story, but Vale (VALE), the world's largest iron-ore miner, is. Petrobras, banks, utilities, telecoms, and retailers that depend on credit all have their issues with weak global demand or government intervention.

Barron's: In other words, the stock market faces challenges since its biggest components are under pressure, but you're still optimistic.

Landers: If you want to be negative, you can be negative. If you want to be positive, the government is moving to reduce the cost of doing business.

Barron's: All of you own Petrobras, the government-controlled oil giant. Given the risk of the government limiting its profitability, why own it?

Robinson: Clearly, that company is having a tougher time of it of late. But we think there is a chance that at some stage there will be some independent representation on the board, and perhaps that would be a step in the right direction toward getting minority shareholders treated a bit more fairly.

Landers: Petrobras is 10% of the MSCI Brazil index, so we will most likely always own some. But it is the biggest underweight in our portfolio. Over the past two years, that stock has been a huge underperformer. It has had a major impact on the performance of the market, and the perception investors have about Brazil overall, because the biggest stock in the country isn't necessarily treating all investors the same.

Robbins: It is one of the largest issuers in the investment-grade bond market, with debt outstanding equivalent to something like Comcast's. It is similarly rated and comes with a 1.2 percentage point higher yield. It is an issue that investment-grade investors have in their portfolios more and more frequently. Petrobras is going to pay its debts over the longer term; it has got a lot of asset value.

Barron's: Is political intervention less of an issue for bond investors?

Robbins: It's an issue. The question is: How is Petrobras going to invest its money?

Landers: In the short term, it is not exactly good for shareholders, because their return on invested capital continues to be much lower than it has been in the past. It could be a great company in 2020 from an equity perspective when they are producing four million barrels a day -- if they get there. It's producing about half that right now. To get there, they are going to have to spend $40 billion a year, which is hard for any company to do right -- let alone a government-owned company.

Barron's: Some of this intervention is aimed at reviving the economy. Is it working?

Mark Jason: We are seeing steps in the right direction. Brazil really lacks infrastructure, and the stimulus efforts on that end should improve efficiencies. Over the long term, all these factors should benefit Brazil.

Robinson: It is a fine line the government needs to tread. On one hand, it is trying to reduce the cost of doing business by cutting taxes and improving infrastructure. But by continuing to interfere in the companies, they are potentially threatening the health of the capital markets. With Petrobras, it feels like they have gone too far. With the banks, it is becoming more of a problem.

Barron's: There is some concern that Brazil's days of strong growth are behind it. Is sub-2% growth the "new normal?"

Robbins: Growth in the first half was a lot slower than anyone thought it was going to be, and that's why they had to reduce rates dramatically. Now that you are at the bottom of the interest-rate cycle, you should probably get pretty decent growth going forward. We expect 4% next year. Brazil, and Latin America in general, is the only part of the world that has a V-shaped recovery when you look at 2013.

Jason: There's a dichotomy in the market right now. We have groups like banks and utilities under government pressure, and commodity companies under pressure because of slowing global demand. But then you have other companies that are still seeing growth and trading at much higher valuations.

Barron's: It seems like consumer stocks could fit that description. But how is the consumer story different in a slower-growing Brazil?

Jason: We are at a transition point in the domestic-demand story. Interest rates are being lowered and longer-maturity-debt instruments like mortgages are becoming more common. The consumer should see some sort of relief. But we are at a point where that needs to happen right now because of the pressure on consumers and growth.

Robbins: It is happening. What consumers really care about is their monthly payment. So that monthly payment is starting to go down. Consumer debt had been rising, but pressure on the consumer is coming down as rates fall.

3 Nov 2012 00:05 EDT  Barron's(11/5) Brazil Round Table: Brazil -2-

Robinson: It's probably fair to say, though, that we are not going to have the powerful consumer demand over the next five years that we had over the past five, because household debt has increased markedly in the past four years. Maybe consumer demand just continues, but it is potentially a little bit weaker.

Barron's: Is the market pricing that in?

Landers: Consumer demand isn't going to be 25% to 30% growth, but it's still healthy growth. If you look at the growth of the middle class over the past five to 10 years, about 40 million people have become consumers. Over the next five years, it'll be more like 25 million, but that's 12.5% of today's population. The debt burden went up just as rates did, so as rates come down, it'll come down with it.

Barron's: So consumers will have more money in their pockets?

Robbins: Yes, plus the government's measures, like cutting the utility rates and other taxes, are helping the consumer.

Landers: On top of that, unemployment remains at a record-low level. Wages are going up, and banking unions are negotiating somewhere between 7% and 8% salary increases.

Barron's: What are ways to invest in the consumer?

Landers: We still like some of the mid-cap stocks like Lojas Renner (LREN3.Brazil), which is the country's largest department-store operator -- kind of like a Macy's -- or Companhia Hering (HGTX3.Brazil).

Barron's: What is Hering?

Landers: Hering is kind of like the Gap (GAP). It has a combination of owned stores and franchises, and is looking to extend the brand into areas like kids. If you look at the performance of the malls, these types of smaller stores are the ones that have been doing better. Valuations have come down in some of them because of the concerns around consumers' debt levels rising and worries about consumption if there is less credit available. But these concerns decline as interest rates fall. We are taking more of a medium- to long-term outlook and look to take advantage of some of these dips.

Barron's: What other stocks will do well as consumer spending resumes?

Jason: We are buying a derivative that feeds into housing demand. Duratex (DTEX3.Brazil) has a leading market share in wood-board and metal fittings used in toilets and faucets. They are seeing stronger earnings growth, but are also increasing their supply in the second half of next year. That should lead to further increases in earnings going forward. It trades at 17 times 2013 earnings, but it drops to 14 times 2014.

Robinson: We've got Renner and Hering as well, which we like. I would add Arezzo (ARZZ3.Brazil), which designs women's shoes.

Barron's: What are some nonretailing ways to play consumer demand?

Landers: It isn't the cheapest stock in the world, but Natura Cosmeticos (NATU3.Brazil) is like the Avon of Brazil and has been gaining share. You also have a company like Localiza Rent-A-Car (RENT3.Brazil) on the car-rental side that has been doing well despite the impact from the government lowering taxes on new car purchases.

Jason: We still like DASA (DASA3.Brazil), which is the largest medical-diagnostics company but only has 14% market share. It is a secular growth story. More prevention, more private insurance, an aging population, and increasing wages -- all these trends are good for DASA. We anticipate 12%-to-15% revenue growth for the sector, maybe through 2014. DASA is in the midst of a restructuring right now. With a new management, we feel they are going to turn this business around and improve profitability and efficiency. Not everybody believes that story.

Robinson: We like the shopping-mall companies like Multiplan (MULT3.Brazil) and Iguatemi (IGTA3.Brazil). They are just great companies. Once you've got the Multiplan malls in the right location and constructed, it's quite hard to make a mess of those businesses. Iguatemi has some very attractive high-end malls in Sao Paulo.

Barron's: What about the bond side?

Robbins: The best way to play the consumer is really through the banks. Margins are being squeezed, but they still trade at very attractive levels relative to sovereign debt. On the dollar-denominated side, we avoid the sovereign debt. It trades at 90 basis points [0.9 percentage point] over U.S. Treasuries. I don't think there's much upside. You can buy quality banks -- the largest, like Banco Bradesco (BBD) and Itau Unibanco Holding (ITUB) -- in the 10-year market somewhere around 200 basis points over the comparable sovereign bond. That's pretty attractive.

Barron's: The Brazilian real is second only to the Argentine peso in declines this year. What happens from here?

Robbins: The central bank wants to keep the currency in a range between 2 and 2.05 to the dollar. I think it will be successful. As you see growth pick up, there will be more pressure for it to appreciate. For the near-term, I see it staying stable. I think local currency debt is very attractive, with 9.5% yields with the currency stable or going to appreciate. You can't find those yields anywhere in investment grade.

Barron's: Many of you own the bank stocks. Given the potential risk with government intervention, how does it affect your view?

Jason: The long-term story for banking seems brighter because of this growth in the middle class. Brazil has 74 million people who don't have a bank account. Bradesco, Brazil's second-largest private-sector bank, gets 25% to 30% of its net income from insurance and pensions and almost another 25% from fees, so we have about 50% of the business that's fairly resilient. We may be under pressure right now in terms of margins and fees, but over the long term we think the future is still looking very strong.

Landers: These are well-capitalized banks. Reserve requirements are among the highest in the world. Bradesco and Itau, Latin America's largest bank, aren't going to do anything crazy. If they have to give up share, they will. But they are learning how to be banks in a lower-interest-rate world, rather than just loan money to the government at double-digits and be done with it. They are adjusting.

Barron's: Brazil's stock market yields 3% to 4%. What is the outlook for dividends?

Robinson: There is a rule in Brazil that companies need to pay out about 25% of net income as dividends, so naturally investors get a quite a good dividend.

Landers: Unless the government comes in and knocks out your net income, like they did with utilities.

Jason: There is a risk that dividends will come down.

Robinson: Vale has been paying huge dividends over the past few years. The special dividends aren't likely to be coming as quickly as they were.

Barron's: Is there still opportunity in smaller companies, or are the valuations too high, making a case for large-caps?

Landers: It's hard to really shift to the large-caps. We put some money back into the banks, and we are getting burned a little bit -- or a lot -- with this round of government interference. The risk of Petrobras is that they wake up tomorrow and raise gasoline and diesel prices. You want to be underweight large companies, but by how much? You have to be careful with that. With Vale, the new government is looking to make the company more efficient, but it's not going to be an overnight fix. In the meantime, its cash flow is going to go down.

Barron's: Are mid-size companies less burdened?

Landers: The mid-caps are still more interesting because it's cleaner in terms of consumer-growth story. You are going to have to pay a little bit more, but there are plenty of stocks that still offer pretty good upside.

Jason: About 60% of the market is made up of these sectors that are cheap for a reason. The small-caps tend to be the ones that are overlooked more because they are just not accessible to a lot of investors, and they tend to have lower valuation.

Robinson: Over the long term, the domestic-demand sectors will very much be the place to be. But over the short term, there is perhaps a tactical opportunity emerging in some of these larger-cap commodity companies like Petrobras and Vale and also the banks. They are very cheap.

We've just been kind of nudging things a little bit recently, adding a little bit more cyclicality.

Barron's: One piece of good news is that inflation has fallen a bit this year. But aren't risks rising again with food inflation and stimulus?

Landers: No central bank has control over food inflation. If it doesn't rain, if you don't get corn, if you don't get soybeans, prices will go up. It's a short-term phenomenon.

Barron's: What about liquidity?

Landers: Reserve requirements remain very high. I think they are committed to keeping rates at a single digit -- if they can, maybe forever.

Jason: We are at 5.2% inflation -- that is at an elevated level. The issue is that you have very little unemployment. There's not a lot of room to maneuver. Hopefully, they will be able to, but it is touchy ground at this point.

Robbins: Inflation probably becomes a bigger issue in 2013. They are cutting taxes, and that's going to help short-term. But when you have a tight labor market, potential food inflation, and some of the wage agreements, there is going to be inflationary pressure.

Barron's: Does that mean you are increasing your exposure to inflation-linked bonds, David?

Robbins: We have a fair amount of exposure. We are probably a little bit early, but we think the risks are that potentially inflation resurfaces, particularly along with our view that we are going to see much stronger growth in 2013.

Barron's: The 2016 Olympics and 2014 World Cup are often noted as drivers for the market, but no one has mentioned either so far. Why?

Landers: Petrobras' annual capital expenditure is more than the World Cup is going to cost. Brazil is a big country. And it's a theme you can't invest in through equities really, because the big construction and engineering companies are all privately held.

Robbins: You can buy them on the debt side. Odebrecht is one of our top picks in the corporate space. It's an investment-grade company that benefits from the long-term infrastructure investment. We also like Braskem, a chemicals firm owned by Petrobras. In general, we are avoiding dollar-based sovereign debt. We don't think there is much upside. Ten-year corporates make a lot of sense.

Barron's: Any infrastructure stock plays?

Robinson: We have Wilson Sons (WSON11. Brazil), which is a company that operates a couple of ports based in Brazil and also has a ship builder. So they are a big supplier for Petrobras, and they tow Petrobras' rigs. They stand to benefit from Petrobras' huge capex spend.

Barron's: David, you mentioned infrastructure bonds.

Robbins: Over the next five years [Brazil] has something like $125 billion in terms of infrastructure plans. They are creating a new security in the local-currency market called infrastructure bonds. Right now, the only way you can participate in local currency is through a fund that already has exposure, because otherwise you have to pay a 6% tax. You wouldn't have to pay that tax, so these bonds can be pretty compelling if you can believe in the project.

Barron's: What's the biggest risk for your investments beyond political intervention?

Robbins: The biggest risk for Brazil is really global. You've got to think about what's going on in Europe and potentially what's going on in China. Those will have the biggest impact on risk perception, and that's what will impact Brazil.

Barron's: There seems to be no small amount of risks looming, yet you seem relatively upbeat. Why?

Jason: We are already seeing positive signs, like business confidence improving and retail sales improving.

Landers: If rates are going to stay in the 7%-to-8% range, then pension funds that are very underweight equities are going have to invest into the equity market. It's going to make a big difference. Because they know the market, they will be more likely to go into small- and mid-cap stocks as well.

Robbins: Plus, fundamentals are strong from a balance-sheet perspective. And in this world, 3.5% to 4% economic growth is a high-class problem.

title: DJ Brazil Real Opens Stronger on China Data, Shrugs Off Greece Concerns
text:
--Brazil's real opens stronger vs. U.S. dollar as China manufacturing data improve

--Local markets are cautious ahead of Friday's U.S. jobs data, next week's election

--Brazilian real opens at BRL2.0294, stronger from Wednesday's close at BRL2.0301 


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real traded stronger against the U.S. dollar at the open Thursday as data from key trading partner China that showed improvement in the Asian country's manufacturing sector offset ongoing concerns about Europe.

The real shrugged off a slide by the euro, a key barometer for the local currency, amid renewed concerns about Greece's ability to implement austerity measures needed for its rescue package. The real opened trading at BRL2.0294 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger than Wednesday's close at BRL2.0301.

The local currency received a boost after manufacturing data in China showed signs of improvement in October, a sign that the country's industrial sector could be rebounding. China's official Purchasing Managers Index rose to 50.2 in October from 49.8 in September.

China is Brazil's largest trading partner, importing huge amounts of commodities such as iron ore and soy from Latin America's largest country. A dramatic slowdown in the Asian country would have a big impact on local commodities exporters.

The outlook for manufacturing was much gloomier in Brazil, where industrial production fell a larger-than-expected 1.0% in September from August. Economists had expected a 0.5% decline. Brazil's manufacturing sector has struggled for more than a year, despite massive reductions in local interest rates and central-bank intervention in currency markets that has caused the real to weaken.

Local markets will likely take further direction from overseas data releases, although players are expected to remain cautious ahead of a Brazilian holiday that will close financial markets on Friday.

Data out of the U.S. should give a better picture of the health of the world's largest economy heading into next week's presidential election. Employment figures and the Institute for Supply Management's activity index will be released later Thursday.

While changes to the methodology of the employment report make it less important, Kit Juckes of Societe Generale said that "a bounce in the ISM index would support a view that the U.S. economy, like China's, is turning a corner." Mr. Juckes said that the risk of the U.S. sliding back into recession appears to be receding, "which keeps the market focus, for now, firmly on hunting for yield."

The hunt for yield, however, is unlikely to hit Brazil with the central bank continuing to intervene in currency markets and tough government rhetoric keeping the real locked in its recent trading range. The real continues to trade between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 to the U.S. dollar, a level that the government considers comfortable, traders said. According to traders, the real is seen as weak enough to support local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation.

A recent upswing in capital outflows could test the government's willingness to let the real depreciate further against the dollar, risking inflationary pressures. Brazil registered net capital outflows of $748 million in the first four weeks of October, the central bank said Wednesday. While a rise in imports was behind the outflows, there are concerns that negative investment flows could emerge through the end of the year if foreign investors bail out of local stocks or multinational companies start to repatriate capital.

text:
* Hurricane Sandy shuts Wall St, cuts volumes in Latam

* Mexico peso weakens 0.67 pct, Brazil real off 0.31 pct

(Adds comments, changes dateline)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso slumped to a seven-week low on Monday as uncertainty over a much-awaited bailout request by Spain weighed on demand for riskier assets such as Latin American currencies.

Trading volumes were low as U.S. markets were closed due to the approach of Hurricane Sandy, which was expected to hit the U.S. East Coast later in the day.

Fears that Madrid would take too long to request a sovereign bailout increased after a European Central Bank policymaker, Ewald Nowotny, said over the weekend that Spain should try to refinance itself before requesting aid.

Investors consider a Spanish bailout crucial to stopping the spreading of the euro zone debt crisis.

"The effect of the hurricane and considerations that the situation remains delicate in Europe, particularly Spain, all added up to feed more demand for safe-haven assets," said Eduardo Avila, an analyst at brokerage Monex in Mexico City.

The Mexican peso led losses in Latin America's foreign exchange markets, dropping 0.67 percent to 13.0820 per dollar. The peso pared losses slightly after it hit its weakest intraday level since early September at 13.1095.

The peso posted slight gains on Friday after the central bank warned it could raise interest rates if inflation pressures persist. Higher interest rates in Mexico would boost the attraction of its debt to yield-hungry investors.

But analysts on Monday said the central bank was unlikely to raise borrowing costs with looming risks of slowing growth and some analysts recommended taking advantage of a recent rise in Mexican yields to snap up cheaper bonds.

When a bond's yield rises, its price falls.

The annual inflation rate in Latin America's second-largest economy eased from a 2-1/2 year high of 4.77 percent in September to 4.64 percent in the first half of October and many economist think inflation could fall further in the coming months.

"These inflation pressures will pass, but it will take time," Avila said.

The yield on Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond

bid up 5 basis points to 5.55 percent.

In Brazil, the real weakened 0.31 percent to 2.0320 per dollar.

Expectations of continued government intervention have drastically reduced volumes and volatility in the foreign exchange market, leaving the real in a narrow trading range of 2.02-2.05 per dollar.

Investors expect the Brazilian central bank may sell reverse currency swaps at any moment to keep the currency at current levels, which government officials consider beneficial to exporters.

Brazil intervened twice last week with the sale of those swaps, or derivatives contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market.

text:
* Brazil's central bankintervenes to stem currency gains

* Mexico peso, Brazil real little changed

(Repeats to additional subscribers; Adds details on Mexican peso)

By Natalia Cacioli and Moises Avila

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Chile's peso gained on Thursday on hopes Chinese factory output will accelerate at the end of the year and boost demand for South America's exports, but an intervention by Brazil's central bank capped gains in the real.

Mexico's peso gave up slight gains to weaken in late trading after weak quarterly earnings from Apple Inc, the most valuable public company in the United States, hit U.S. stock futures and investor appetite for riskier assets.

Chile's peso firmed 0.31 percent after a top Chinese official said the country's industrial output growth may be faster in the final three months of 2012 than in the third quarter.

China is the main consumer of Latin America's commodities exports and the positive outlook for the its economy boosted investors' appetite for risk in general.

The Chilean peso led gains among Latin American currencies, rising half a percentage point to 478.40 per dollar as the comments by the Chinese official boosted prices of copper, Chile's main export product.

"With copper and the euro rising, and stocks in positive territory, the (Chilean) peso could strengthen toward 478 units (per dollar)," said Jose Manuel Briceno, an analyst with GKFX in Santiago.

Chile's peso has appreciated around 8.5 percent so far this year, giving it a ranking as one of the top three performers among the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Chile Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said late on Wednesday in New York that the government is seeking ways to weaken the currency without resorting to capital controls.

Mexico's peso slipped 0.15 percent to 13.01 per dollar and was set to close at its weakest in more than six weeks.

The Mexican currency, the most freely traded in Latin America, usually tracks other liquid risky assets such as U.S. stocks and the euro. The peso weakened in tandem with a drop in U.S. stock futures once Apple reported its results after the U.S. stock market close.

Mexico's peso has been one of the top-performing emerging market currencies this year. But gains have flagged in recent weeks as investors cashed in on the rally.

Alfredo Puig, a trader at brokerage Vector in Monterrey, said the cost of dollars in pesos could weaken past its 200-day simple moving average to 13.20 per dollar if global market jitters persist.

The number of futures contracts betting on a stronger peso on the Chicago exchange hit a record high in late September. That position has fallen a bit, but the peso is still vulnerable to a stampede of investors who may try to get out of bullish bets at the same time.

"People think that the dollar shorts in Chicago are going to cover themselves due to the risk aversion we are seeing," Puig said.

In Brazil, a much stronger government hand has been curbing currency gains and keeping the real at a tight trading range of 2.02-2.05 per dollar for the past several sessions.

The Brazilian central bank reinforced the floor for the real early o n T hursday by intervening in the foreign exchange market for the second time this week.

The real traded nearly unchanged at 2.0240 per dollar after the central bank sold nearly all the 30,000 reverse currency swaps it offered in an auction, completing the early rollover of swaps that expire on Nov. 1.

Reverse swaps, or derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market, became the central bank's favorite instrument to intervene in the currency.

Combined with threats of additional government measures to curb inflows of speculative capital, those interventions have drastically reduced liquidity and volatility in Brazil's foreign exchange market.

"The market is completely stuck. The government has already admitted we have a dirty-floating regime with strong intervention," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist at BES Investimento in Sao Paulo.

"The economic fundamentals point to a stronger real, but this is a market with very low liquidity due to government intervention," he added.

By Walter Brandimarte and Lorena Segura

SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Chile's peso bounced back from a two-month low o n Wednesday after data pointed to a stronger economic performance in China, the region's top trading partner, and a top buyer of Chilean copper.

After slipping for four straight sessions to trade at its weakest since August, C hile's peso strengthene d 0 .3 5 p ercent a fter data showed Chinese manufacturers' output reached a three-month high in October, while order books were at their highest level since April.

"The peso is supported by China's strong manufacturing data, which boosted copper prices and European stocks," said Jose Manuel Briceno, an analyst with GKFX in Santiago.

Copper, Chile's main export product, traded slightly higher on the London Metal Exchange.

The Mexican peso dipped 0. 1 2 percent, however, as investors remained worried about the global economy after business surveys suggested Germany is being sucked into the euro zone crisis.

The peso slumped to a nearly six-week intraday low on Wednesday, breaking past 13 per dollar before bouncing back to trade at 12.99.

Data on Wednesday showed Mexican annual inflation eased in the first half of October from a 2-1/2 year high, bolstering expectations that the central bank will keep borrowing costs steady into 2014. [nL 3E8LO5LY].

The U.S. Federal Reserve said it would stick to its stimulus plan until the job market improves, in line with expectations.

The Fed's asset buying scheme is expected to help support demand for higher-yielding, riskier assets in coming months. A nalysts said that demand for Mexican assets could keep the peso from breaking past 13 per dollar. [ID :nL1E8LNFFD]

"We still have the idea that the exchange rate can return to levels around 12.80 plus or minus 10 centavos, " said Rafael Camarena, a n economist at Santander.

DIRTY FLOAT

In Brazil, the real edged up 0.1 percent to 2.0250 per greenback.

T raders were unwilling to push it much stronger amid e xpecta tions that the central bank could intervene in the foreign exchange market again to stop the currency from strengthening.

The bank intervened on Monday after a two-week hiatus with an auction of reverse currency swaps - derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market.

With the sale, the central bank rolled over about half of the contracts that expire on Nov. 1, leaving traders speculating that it could offer more swaps in the next few days to complete the rollover, or even increase the stock of reverse swaps if dollar inflows pick up.

In the latest sign of the government commitment to a weaker currency, Finance Minister Guido Mantega acknowledged in an interview that the real is now subject to a "dirty-floating" regime in which policymakers intervene to keep an exchange rate favorable to the local industry.

The constant threat of intervention has sapped volumes and liquidity of the Brazilian foreign exchange market, keeping the real in an increasingly tight trading range.

"We still work with a trading band of 2.0-2.1 reais per dollar, but the truth is that this range has been tightening. The central bank now intervenes whenever the real nears the level of 2.02 per dollar," said Mauricio Nakahodo, an economic research consultant with Tokyo-Mitsubishi bank in Sao Paulo.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Little Changed Against Dollar
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real chalked up a very slight gain against the dollar in steady trading Wednesday, as major stock indexes stopped bleeding after the steep declines of previous sessions.

The real exited active trading in Sao Paulo at BRL2.0250 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, barely stronger than Tuesday's close of BRL2.0255.

The currency's steadiness reflected a relative calm day in world financial markets. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, after sinking more than 1.8% on Tuesday, was slightly lower in afternoon trading.

Brazil's real historically tracks other currencies and key stock indexes but has hardly moved in recent months. Local authorities, seeking to prop up a flagging industrial sector, have used taxes, rhetoric and intervention in the exchange market this year to wrestle Brazil's once-volatile currency into a range of about BRL2.0 to BRL2.05 to the dollar.

"The exchange rate as I see it is frozen," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Sao Paulo's Pioneer Corretora. "We haven't ever had such a rigid freeze, as the one we have today in Brazil."

Brazil adopted a floating currency regime in 1999, after maintaining an official peg to the dollar when it launched the real in 1994. Local authorities, for their part, haven't disclosed any official change in the currency policy.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega, in an interview published Wednesday by financial daily Valor Economico, highlighted that the exchange rate "is not fixed."

"Our currency system is a dirty float, same as everybody," Mr. Mantega said. Brazilian officials consider the loose monetary policies that have lingered for years in the U.S. and other developed countries to be a form of currency manipulation.

But with annual inflation running more than a full percentage point above the central bank's 4.5% target, some economists say authorities may have to loosen the reins on the real, assuming they want to keep interest rates at record low levels.

"Were inflationary pressures to intensify and drive inflation above 5.50% at some point during 2013, then the authorities may choose to soften the current hard intervention stance," Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos said this week in a note. That would allow the real's range "to restrike at a moderately lower level in order to temporarily anchor the inflation dynamics and delay and/or moderate the use of rates to anchor inflation."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  falls on Spain,  Brazil intervenes
text:
* Moody's cuts 5 Spanish regions, sparking risk aversion

* Mexican peso drops nearly 1 pct; Brazil real down 0.1 pct

* Chilean peso loses 1.18 pct

* Brazil central bankintervenes with sale of FX swaps

(Adds detail, background, quotes)

By Walter Brandimarte and Alexandra Alper

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean currencies slumped on Tuesday as a credit downgrade of five Spanish regions and weak earnings at U.S. companies reinforced fears of anemic global growth and a deepening euro-zone crisis.

Spain's borrowing costs spiked after the Moody's ratings downgrade, which included the economically important but deeply indebted Catalonia region.

"Markets are negative on the unsettling European news," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

Investors are waiting for signs that Spain will request a sovereign bailout, something seen as a crucial step to stop the spreading of the euro zone debt crisis.

The Mexican peso dropped 0.92 percent to 12.97 per dollar. The currency briefly broke past the psychological 13 per dollar level to a nearly six-week low.

The Chilean peso fell to a two-month low in its biggest one-day percentage loss in four months. The peso lost 1.18 percent to close at 482.70 per greenback.

A drop in the price of copper, Chile's main export product, further pressured the currency.

The Brazilian central bankintervened in the market for the first time in more than two weeks to weaken the real currency.

The real slipped 0.1 percent to 2.0265 to the dollar.

The intervention came after a series of small gains led the real to close on Monday at 2.0244 per dollar, its strongest level since Oct. 4 and close to the 2 per dollar level that the central bank has been seen defending.

The central bank intervened by selling currency swaps, derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market. The central bank said the sale was merely intended to roll over similar contracts that expire on Nov. 1.

Traders speculated that the bank could act again because it sold only a little more than half of the 60,000 contracts it offered in an auction -- not enough to roll over all the 59,800 reverse swaps that expire next week.

The central bank sold 17,000 swaps maturing on Dec. 3, 2012, and 16,000 contracts maturing Jan. 2, 2013, it said in a statement.

The Mexican peso weakened to 13.01 per dollar, its weakest since Sept. 13, but recovered to close out the session in stronger territory. Market watchers said they did not expect the weakening trend to continue.

"I think the market is expecting a better close to the year in the U.S. economy....That will have a positive impact on the exchange rate," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico City.

Gordillo said he expects the currency to strengthen on Thursday or Friday back past the 12.90 level on the release of key U.S. data, which has been stronger in September and October.

The U.S. government will release data on durable good orders for September on Thursday and third-quarter gross domestic product numbers on Friday.
