title: Brazil  Real Weakens Slightly on  Intervention , Europe Worries
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0255/dollar versus BRL2.0235 Monday

--Central bank intervenes early in trading, selling forex swap contracts

--Central bank sells enough swap contracts to cover Nov. 1 expiry

--European worries, weak euro and lower commodities prices also weigh

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened slightly against the U.S. dollar Tuesday after the central bank intervened in the market through a foreign exchange swap auction.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0255 to the dollar, weaker against the Monday close of BRL2.0235, according to Tullet Prebon via FactSet.

The Brazilian Central Bankintervened in the market in the first minutes of trading with a so-called reverse swap auction.

The reverse swap auction allows investors to exchange dollar-linked foreign exchange contracts for paper indexed to domestic interest rates. Typically, the reverse swap auction supports the dollar against the real by removing dollar-hedged contracts from the market.

The central bank has used reverse swap auctions frequently in recent months to help avoid any significant appreciation of the real against the dollar. Brazilian officials have said a strong real hurts exporters and manufacturers.

Traders said the central bank held a reverse swap auction Tuesday for two reasons.

The first reason was to cover an upcoming Nov. 1 expiry of dollar-linked contracts. The expiry involves some $3 billion equivalent in contracts. At Tuesday's reverse swap auction, the central bank sold the equivalent of $1.648 billion in contracts. That, plus an early October reverse swap auction worth nearly $1.3 billion, will be enough to negate effects of the Nov. 1 expiry, traders said.

The second reason was to help counter effects of recent U.S. dollar inflows, including overseas corporate bond issues.

"The central bank is mopping up U.S. dollar liquidity and maintaining equilibrium in the foreign exchange rate," said Sidnei Nehme, director of Sao Paulo's NGO brokerage.

Mr. Nehme noted that government figures released Tuesday showed steady net inflows of dollars during the first three weeks of October. The central bank figures showed net inflows of $1.59 billion, up sharply from $647 million in the first three weeks of September.

Traders added, however, that the Brazilian government will have little difficulty avoiding any significant appreciation of the real.

"There is virtually no chance the Brazilian real will be able to free itself from the current narrow trading range," said Mario Battistel, foreign exchange manager at Sao Paulo's Fair brokerage.

The central bank's fire power includes both swap auctions and snap auctions at which it buys and sells large volumes of dollars on the spot market. The finance ministry, meanwhile, has used other tools in recent years to combat the unwanted appreciation of the currency. These have included high taxes on short-term investment positions.

In any case, according to Mr. Nehme, heavy new inflows of dollars aren't likely in the coming months. He noted that Tuesday's government data also showed a persistent current account deficit, during September some $2.6 billion.

The Brazilian real was also pressured Tuesday by a gloomy international outlook. Continued worries about the European debt crisis led to a weakening of the euro against the dollar and a decline in commodities prices. Stocks also lost ground, including in Brazil.

Lower commodities prices hit the Brazilian real directly because they translate into declining export revenue.

title: Brazil  Real Opens Weaker On  Intervention , European Worries
text:
--Brazil real opens weaker from Monday at BRL2.0272/dlr

--Central bank holds reverse-swap auction, weakening real

--Euro, commodities weaken on renewed worries about Spain


 
   By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday following disclosure of a reverse-swap auction by the Brazilian Central Bank.

The real opened at BRL2.0272 to the dollar, weaker against the Monday close of BRL2.0235, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

At the start of trading, the central bank called a reverse-swap auction, offering to exchange contracts worth up to the equivalent of $3 billion. In the auction, the central bank actually exchange the equivalent of $1.648 billion in contracts.

Reverse-swap auctions allow investors to exchange contracts linked to the U.S. dollar for paper indexed to domestic interest rates. Reverse-swap auctions tend to support the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real because they remove dollar-hedged contracts from the market.

The reverse-swap auctions are part of a government campaign to avoid any significant appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar. Officials have said a strong real hurts exporters and manufacturers.

In recent weeks, the real has at times signaled a strengthening against the dollar because of foreign-investment inflows. The most-recent inflows have been coming from a spate of overseas bonds issued by Brazilian companies.

"We're going to see this narrow band, just above BRL2.00 to the dollar, for quite some time," said Mario Battistel, foreign-exchange manager at Sao Paulo's Fair brokerage. "It could continue this way well into 2013."

The real was also weakening Tuesday because of renewed worries about the European debt crisis. A report by Spain's central bank said that country was facing a deeper recession than previously expected. Spain's declining economy could cause it to miss crucial fiscal-performance targets, according to analysts.

The European worries led to a weakening of the euro against the U.S. dollar as well as declining commodities prices.

Lower commodities prices hurt Brazilian exports and tend to weaken the real.

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil current account gap wider on weaker trade surplus
text:
* Brazil posts larger-than-expected $2.6 bln c/a deficit

* Foreign direct investment falls to $4.4 bln in Sept

* Cbank sees FDI rebounding to $6 bln in October

(Adds analyst comments and central bank estimates)

By Alonso Soto and Tiago Pariz

BRASILIA, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's current account deficit widened in September from a year ago as a weakening global economy drags down exports from the South American nation, central bank data showed on Tuesday.

Brazil had a current account deficit of $2.596 billion in September, stable from the gap posted in August, but above the $2.45 billion median forecast of analysts surveyed by Reuters.

Brazil's current account deficit, a broad measure of a country's foreign transactions including trade in goods and services but also profit remittances and interest payments, in September of last year was $2.234 billion.

"The current account remains well anchored: the erosion in the trade balance in the year to date has been more than offset by the decline in net remittances of profits and dividends," Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist for Goldman Sachs, said in a research note.

The repatriation of profits abroad was only $1.1 billion in September, down from $1.9 billion in September of last year and $2.5 billion in August. The fall in remittances reflects the drop in profits by foreign companies operating in Brazil as both the local and global economy struggle to recover.

A strong flow of foreign investment in Brazil despite the weak global economy has so far helped cover the country's current account gap this year.

Foreign direct investment in Latin America's largest economy was $4.393 billion in September, down from $5.03 billion in August and more than the expected $4 billion.

The bank's head of economic research Tulio Maciel said he expects FDI to rise again to $6 billion in October based on preliminary data.

President Dilma Rousseff's government efforts to open up public infrastructure concessions to private investors and major sporting events like the 2014 Soccer World Cup are expected to attract investors in coming years.

Signs of a recovery in local economic activity is also expected to bring in more foreign capital.

PORTFOLIO INVESTMENT SEEN UP

Portfolio inflows, which along with FDI is part of the capital account, fell sharply to $983 million from $2.141 billion in August mostly due the sale of local shares. Brazil's benchmark Bovespa stock index has fallen about 16 percent since hitting the year's high in early March.

Goldman Sachs' Ramos said the weak capital account numbers mirror the shift in foreign investors' sentiment as well as interventionist measures by the local government.

Brazil has slapped taxes on some capital inflows as a way to keep the local currency, the real, from gaining too much.

In the first nine months of the year, foreign investment in local shares tumbled to $2.89 billion from $5.95 billion in the same period last year. Foreign investment in local debt has remained mostly stable in that same period.

Still, the bank's Maciel said preliminary data shows a strong recovery in foreign investment in local shares. Foreign investment in shares was up to $1.2 billion as of Oct. 19.

Last month the central bank cut its 2012 current account deficit estimate to $53 billion from $56 billion.

Earlier this month, the trade ministry reported that Brazil's trade surplus narrowed for the sixth straight month to $ 2.557 billion in September, as a slowing global economy undermined prices of the commodity powerhouse's key exports.

The current account deficit in the 12 months through September was equal to 2.15 percent of the country's gross domestic product, the central bank said, up from a previously reported 2.12 percent in August.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia peso slumps on  intervention
text:
* Colombia central bank dollar purchases hit peso

* Brazil traders eye renewed intervention

* Mexican peso gains 0.34 pct, Brazil real firms 0.14 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Danielle Fonseca

BOGOTA/SAO PAULO, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso fell on Monday as the country's central bank bought dollars to stem recent gains while Brazil's real edged back toward a level that could trigger intervention by its central bank.

Colombia's peso weakened by the most in more than two months, shedding 0.53 percent against the dollar, after the central bank bought $30.6 million in the local market.

"The Colombian peso was the currency in the region with the biggest losses, due to these strong interventions since last week by the central bank," said Diana Guiza, an analyst at brokerage Corredores Asociados.

Last week, Colombia's central bank stepped up dollar purchases to an average of $35 million per day compared to a previous plan to buy $20 million a day.

Colombia, Brazil and Peru are trying to contain gains in their currencies as easy money policies in the United States, Europe and Japan push investors to seek out gains in higher-yielding emerging market assets.

Stronger local currencies hurt domestic manufacturers as they suffer from competition with cheaper imports while making less profit on their exports.

In Brazil, the real was up 0.14 percent at 2.0244 per dollar.

Investors expected the Brazilian central bank to soon roll over some $3 billion in reverse currency swaps that expire on Nov. 1.

The contracts, which mimic the purchase of dollars in the futures market, were sold by the central bank in early September to stop the real from strengthening past 2 per dollar - a level the bank has been defending since early July to support Brazilian exporters.

Traders expect the country's central bank or its government to take further measures if the real rises much more.

"We think that the dollar will remain around this level and within a narrow range," Joao Medeiros, head of currency trading at brokerage Pioneer.

The Mexican peso rose on renewed hopes that Spain would request financial aid.

Mexican policymakers are not expected to step up intervention efforts anytime soon. Gains in the peso are helping curb a spike in inflation by cheapening imports.

The Mexican currency gained 0.34 percent after the outcome of Spain's regional elections was seen as a boost to Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy's austerity drive.

The results rekindled hopes Madrid would soon request a sovereign bailout, seen by investors as crucial to mitigate the region's debt crisis.

Mexico's peso has been supported by signs of faster growth in its top trading partner, the United States, and data on Monday showed Mexican retail sales in August were stronger than expected.

Mexico's peso has been one of the top performing emerging market currencies this year, but gains have flagged in recent weeks as investors cashed in on the strong run-up in the currency. The peso has gained nearly 9 percent against the dollar this year.

Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission showed on Friday that the number of investors betting on a stronger peso dipped in the latest week of data, but still hovered near a record high.

Chile's peso slipped 0.5 percent as prices for copper, the country's top export, hit a more than one-month low.

title: Brazil Real Weaker Early As Market Mulls Inflation, Mood Abroad
text:
BRASILIA -- Brazil's real weakened slightly in early trading Monday as investors weighed prospects for dollar inflows amid signs of continued strong inflation locally and renewed risk aversion in markets abroad.

As of 7:40 EDT, the real traded at BRL2.0270 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0262 to the dollar Friday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

In a Brazilian central bank weekly market survey released early Monday, expectations for IPCA consumer price inflation inched up slightly after 12-month inflation posted late last week for mid-October rose to 5.56% from 5.31% the previous month under the influence of high food prices. Brazil has set a year-end inflation target of 4.5%.

The still-strong inflation has served as a factor to limit forecasts of possible continued interest rate cuts locally following 5.25 percentage points of rate reductions made over the past 12 months.

Meanwhile, factors abroad continued to offset expectations of growing inflows as markets showed heightened investor uncertainties late last week over prospects for a recovery of the global economy.

With strong selloffs overseas Friday, prices of key commodities sold by Brazil and other emerging markets fell early Monday, weighing against the likelihood of strong trade inflows in the near term.

Further, investors have continued to look toward the resolution of a nagging debt crisis in Europe and signals the U.S. can overcome sluggish growth, before resuming heavier investments in Brazil.

And with current moderate local demand, analysts expect Brazil's government may continue to carry out efforts to support local industry through stimulus measures and forex intervention.

Brazil's central bank has refrained from intervention in recent weeks, through reverse currency swaps, though some market players feel the monetary authority could try to encourage further weakening of the local currency from a current "band" seen between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 to the dollar.

In the meantime, the latest central bank market survey released Monday shows the Brazilian currency ending 2012 at around BRL2.01 to the dollar and remaining around that level through the end of 2013.

title: Brazil  Real Ends Firmer as Market Waits for More  Intervention
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real reversed early Monday, weakening to drift stronger through the end of the session as investors positioned for more possible central bank intervention in coming sessions.

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.0235 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0262 to the dollar Friday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the currency began the session weaker as factors abroad weighed in against key commodities prices and dollar inflows locally. The currency floated back later in the session alongside a strengthening euro and recovery in some key asset prices.

But analysts noted that investors remained positioned for possible further moves by the central bank amid recent affirmations by the government that it would continue to defend a weakened local currency.

"On the FX front, the authorities remain committed through heavy open-ended intervention and unambiguous rhetoric to keeping, at least for the time being, the BRL/USD trading pegged above the implicit 2.00 threshold," said Goldman Sachs analyst Alberto Ramos.

On the horizon for the local market is the possible rollover of some $3 billion in forex swaps at the beginning of next month aimed at maintaining the currency within a stable range.

The government, in the meantime, appears to be in a difficult position, weighing the positive impact of local currency appreciation on accelerated local inflation with the need to maintain a weaker real to stimulate Brazilian economic activity in a sluggish global environment.

But given recent hints that the central bank has been biased toward offering stimulus for the economy, market players Monday speculated the monetary authority may soon take action to push the Brazilian currency to weaken further to a band between BRL2.05 to BRL2.10 to the dollar before allowing it to strengthen again at a later date.

According to the latest central bank market survey released Monday, the Brazilian currency is seen ending 2012 at around BRL2.01 to the dollar and remaining around that level through the end of 2013.

title: Moody's downgrades Banco BVA's deposits and debt to Ca; continues review for downgrade
text:
Moody's Investors Service has today lowered the baseline credit assessment of Banco BVA S.A. (BVA) to ca from caa1, that maps from an E bank financial strength rating (BFSR) assigned to the bank. Concurrently, Moody's downgraded the bank's long-term global local and foreign currency deposit ratings to Ca from Caa1 as well as its foreign currency debt rating to Ca from Caa1. The long-term Brazilian national scale deposit rating was also downgraded to Ca.br from Caa1.br.

Moody's also maintained the review for possible downgrade on all deposits and debt ratings. Today's action follows the announcement that the Central Bank of Brazil has declared intervention on BVA.

RATING RATIONALE

The rating downgrades followed the announcement by Brazil's regulatory authorities on October 19, 2012 that a direct intervention was declared on BVA because of its weak financial position and inability to comply with Central Bank regulations. The intervention process entails the interruption of all of BVA's operations while the Central Bank conducts a thorough examination of the bank's financial condition and capacity to repay all of its obligations.

The Central Bank assigned one of its executives to oversee the intervention process. BVA's former executives are no longer allowed to manage the bank. The properties, possessions and financial resources of both former executives and BVA's controllers were blocked by force of law.

Moody's notes that the downgrade and continuing review for further downgrade of BVA's global local currency deposit rating reflects the bank's highly speculative standalone financial strength and the uncertainties regarding the resolution of the intervention process, with a high likelihood of liquidation and default on uninsured obligations. Moody's Ca global scale rating implies a 55% loss.

title: Brazil Real Weakens Slightly in Early Trading Following Report
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real weakened slightly in early trading Thursday after the minutes of the central bank's latest interest-rate meeting signaled a slow process of recovery ahead.

As of 0840 ET, the real traded at BRL2.0291 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0288 to the dollar Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders noted the market was closely following signs from the central bank on whether the institution could alter the path of interest rates as part of its efforts to stimulate growth and control inflation.

In the minutes of its latest meeting, the bank said it expected to leave the country's benchmark Selic interest rate at a historic low of 7.25% for a "sufficiently prolonged" period of time to allow for a recovery of the local economy.

At the rate meeting last week, the bank's rate committee voted by a margin of 5-to-3 to cut the rate by a quarter percentage point, noting local inflation would continue to converge toward its 4.5% annual target in a "non-linear" manner.

Investors were also closely monitoring factors abroad, including a meeting of European authorities to discuss bailout mechanisms for regional governments seeking recovery from an ongoing fiscal crisis.

Also affecting the real Thursday were trends in China, where recent stable growth figures signaled good prospects for continued firm sales of Brazilian commodities in that region.

Investors, meanwhile, remained on the lookout for signs of intervention in local markets by Brazil's government, as local authorities in recent sessions continued to pledge an active stance to prevent the country's currency from strengthening beyond a level of BRL2.00 to the dollar.

title: Brazil Real Ends Stronger as Market Sees More Dollar Inflows
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real climbed slightly to end stronger Thursday as investors continued to bet on incoming investment dollars ahead following the release of details from the country's latest interest rate meeting.

The real exited regular trading at BRL2.0270 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0288 to the dollar Wednesday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the currency began the session on a weakening trend amid concerns the latest central bank rate decision was the harbinger of a continued slow local recovery.

In the minutes of its latest rate meeting, the bank said it expected to leave the country's benchmark Selic interest rate at a historic low of 7.25% for a "sufficiently prolonged" period to allow for a recovery in activity.

At the meeting last week, the bank's rate committee voted 5 to 3 to cut the rate by a quarter percentage point.

Overseas factors, however, were also influencing the market. Among those were U.S. jobless claims, which surpassed expectations by rising 46,000 in the second week of October. The latest weak data in the U.S., helped convince investors that loose monetary conditions abroad should continue to favor returns and incoming foreign investment in Brazil, where rates still remain well above those elsewhere.

With Brazil's latest rate meeting minutes, analysts said the bank signaled it could eventually return to a tightening cycle by the end of next year.

"The balance of risks for growth and inflation would likely justify a moderate normalization of monetary conditions by at least 100bp-150bp sometime in 2H2013," said Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos in a note.

Brazil's central bank, meanwhile, refrained from intervening in the forex market Thursday, despite some strengthening of the local currency.

Analysts, however, said they believe the bank may still jump back into the market with an auction of reverse currency swaps if the local currency threatens to strengthen beyond BRL2.00 to the dollar.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Slightly Stronger After Rate Cut
text:
--The real traded at BRL2.0349 from BRL2.0384 at Wednesday's close

--Real still range-bound as markets expect central bank intervention

--Spain ratings cut, Brazil interest rate cut not enough to break out of range

By Jeffrey T. Lewis

BRASILIA--The Brazilian real opened slightly stronger against the dollar, keeping within the range of recent months amid expectations the central bank would intervene to keep it from strengthening.

The real traded at BRL2.0349 early in the session, after closing at BRL2.0384 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real has traded within a range of about BRL2.01 to BRL2.04 to the dollar in recent months because the Brazilian central bank has directly entered the market to protect the level of BRL2.0 to the dollar, and Finance Minister Guido Mantega has repeatedly said the government has other tools to maintain the real at current levels.

News that Standard & Poor's Ratings Services cut its rating on Spain and an interest rate cut by Brazil's central bank weren't enough to break the real out of its range.

"The central bank intervenes aggressively, and Mantega shoots his mouth off regularly," said Reginaldo Galhardo, forex manager at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "It would take bigger news than (Spain and the rate cut) to move the real."

S&P cut its rating on Spain to BBB-minus from BBB-plus and maintained a negative outlook Wednesday, citing the mounting pressures from the country's deepening economic recession. S&P said the country's ability to repay its debt could deteriorate as it struggles to shrink its budget deficit, and that Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy might have to ask the European Union for a bailout.

In Brazil, the central bank decided Wednesday night to reduce interest rates for the 10th straight time to spark local growth amid concerns about a prolonged global slump.

The bank cut its benchmark Selic interest rate a quarter-percentage point to a record low 7.25% and signaled the end to a cycle of cuts that started in August 2011.

The central bank's rate-setting committee was divided, with five directors in favor of the cut and three directors voting to hold interest rates steady.

With the latest cut, the bank has reduced the benchmark Selic by 5.25 percentage points over the past 13 months.

Brazilian retail sales volume rose a seasonally adjusted 0.2% in August compared with July, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, or IBGE, said Thursday.

The increase was greater than the median forecast of analysts polled by the local Estado news agency, which projected sales volume to decrease 0.1% in August versus July. The forecasts fell within a range of a 0.9% decline and 1.0% growth.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil yields fall on bets of interest rate cut
text:
* Mexico peso hits 6-month high on US data then sags

* Brazil intervenes to fight real's appreciation

* Mexico peso slips 0.35 pct, Brazil real drops 0.61 pct

(Adds comments)

By Danielle Fonseca and Jean Arce

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazil's interest rate futures fell sharply on Friday after comments from a central bank official pushed investors to bet that policymakers will cut interest rates next week.

In currency trading, Brazil's real fell after the central bank intervened to fight recent gains while Mexico's peso whipsawed, surging to a six-month high on a drop in the U.S. unemployment rate, before ending weaker.

Bets on a benchmark interest rate cut in Brazil were already on the rise this week, but they increased on Friday after a central bank director suggested additional monetary easing might be needed to stimulate the economy.

The yield on the interest-rate contract maturing January 2013 <0#2DIJ:>, the most traded at the Sao Paulo exchange, fell 9 basis points to 7.092 percent.

Luiz Awazu Pereira, a voting member of the central bank's monetary policy committee, said after markets closed on Thursday that a prolonged period of weak global growth would make it crucial for the central bank to "calibrate" its monetary policy in order to accelerate growth.

"Markets bought into what Awazu said yesterday," said Paulo Nepomucemo, a fixed-income strategist at Coinvalores brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The view that the current monetary easing cycle is still not over gained traction."

Brazil has slashed its benchmark rate by 500 bps since last August to 7.50 percent in a bid to fight a slowdown in Latin America's biggest economy.

Disappointing Brazilian industrial production data for August this week began to stoke bets of more monetary stimulus.

Driving early gains in the Mexican peso, the U.S. Labor Department said the U.S. jobless rate fell to 7.8 percent in September, its lowest in nearly four years.

The data initially backed hopes that U.S. demand for Mexican exports would hold up despite a global economic slowdown, but investors soon turned their focus to next week and concerns that earnings from U.S. companies could look weak.

A meeting of euro zone finance ministers next week could also bring concerns about Europe's debt crisis back into focus for the market, analysts said.

"People took advantage of the morning's gains to take profits and prepare for what is coming next week," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico City.

Mexico's peso rallied early in the session pushing the cost of dollars in pesos through support at the 12.70 level to touch its strongest intraday level since late March.

But the currency reversed direction to lose 0.35 percent to 12.79 per dollar.

"The focus will be Europe again next week, and so it will be difficult to get to levels stronger that 12.70," Gordillo said.

In Brazil the real lost 0.61 percent to 2.0298 per dollar after the central bank intervened with the sale of reverse currency swaps, derivative contracts designed to weaken the currency.

It was the first swap sale since Sept. 17, when the central bank intervened in the market to offset the impact of the U.S. Federal Reserve's stimulus policies.

Brazilian policy makers have pledged to use all the instruments available to keep the currency at a level that benefits exporters.

"The central bank intervened because the real gained past that level of 2.02, triggering the alarm. The central bank has made it clear that it will not allow the currency to strengthen past 2 per dollar," said Jaime Ferreira, head of foreign exchange at Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Weaker Following Reverse-Swap Auction
text:
--Brazil's real ends weaker after sale of reverse-swap contracts

--Central bank intervention was not a surprise, says trader

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0293 to the U.S. dollar

By Luciana Magalhaes

SAO PAULO-- The Brazilian real closed weaker to the dollar Friday after the country's central bank sold reverse-swap contracts to deter the currency appreciation.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0293 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, after Thursday closing price at BRL2.0167.

The Brazilian central bank sold the equivalent to $1.29 billion in reverse swap contracts Friday. Such auctions give the investors a chance to exchange dollar-linked bonds for paper indexed to domestic interest rates. They tend to support the dollar against the real by removing dollar-hedged contracts from the market.

The real lost strength immediately following the auction. Before the announcement of the auction, the real was trading at BRL2.0199 to the dollar. After the auction, the real was trading at BRL2.0229 to the dollar. In the morning, the currency traded as strong as BRL2.0154 to the dollar.

"When I saw the real trading at around BRL2.016, I expected the central bank would intervene," said Mauro Araujo, currency director at Brazilian brokerage Vision Corretora. "The Brazilian authorities clearly don't want to see the real stronger than something around BRL2.020 to the dollar."

Intervention by Brazil's central bank and declarations from government officials aiming to protect local exporters have kept the real in a tight trading range between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 in recent months.

Earlier Friday, the currency had weakened to around BRL2.0190 but recovered the loss after the U.S. Labor Department reported the unemployment rate fell to 7.8% in September from 8.1% in the previous month, the lowest level since January 2009. The U.S. economy added 114,000 jobs last month, according to the government's monthly survey of employers.

"Next week, the Brazilian currency market will be paying attention to the monetary-policy meeting," said Mr. Araujo. "We believe, given the inflation concerns, that the central bank will be conservative."

As Mr. Araujo does, many economists expect the central bank to keep its baseline Selic rate at the current 7.5%, a record low that followed a yearlong easing cycle that brought rates down from 12.5% in August 2011.

Brazil's consumer price index rose at a quicker pace in September as drought in Brazil and the U.S. caused food prices to jump, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, or IBGE, said Friday.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  firms on US data, upside seen limited
text:
* Positive U.S. data raises hopes ahead of payrolls report

* Intervention, global growth worries to limit gains -poll

* Brazil's real firms 0.24 pct; Mexico peso up 0.57 pct

(Add comments, poll results)

By Jean Arce and Patricia Duarte

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Thursday after U.S. labor market data helped ease concerns about slowing growth in one of the region's top trading partners, but a Reuters poll showed further gains are likely to be limited.

Mexico's peso jumped to a two-week high after data showed fewer Americans than expected filed for new unemployment benefits last week, leading to hopes that Friday's closely watched non-farm payrolls report would show improvement.

Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States, which is a major trading partner across Latin America.

"People seem to be anticipating a good jobs report tomorrow," said Rafael Camarena, an economist at Santander in Mexico City. "A good employment number would push off the fears of a deeper slowdown."

The Mexican peso strengthened 0.57 percent to trade at 12.7525 per U.S. dollar.

Also supporting Latin American currencies were renewed hopes for a much-awaited Spanish bailout. Expectations grew after European Central Bank President Mario Draghi confirmed the bank is ready to buy bonds of debt-ridden euro zone countries.

Concerns about Europe's debt troubles have repeatedly hammered riskier assets around the world this year, but concerns that Europe could trigger a global financial crisis have faded since Draghi promised to support euro zone bond markets in late July.

But Latin American currencies have limited room for gains in the year ahead as governments fight the massive dollar inflows expected after the latest round of stimulus from the U.S. Federal Reserve, a Reuters poll found on Thursday.

The Mexican peso's gains are expected to be limited in the coming year, the poll showed, on concerns about high local asset prices and a weak global economy. Mexican peso-denominated bonds and stocks are trading near record high prices.

REAL GAINS

The Brazilian real firmed 0.24 percent to 2.0175 per dollar at the local close, edging closer to the 2 per dollar level that the central bank is seen defending.

Since early July, the real's volatility has been constrained by intervention from the central bank. The Brazilian government has battled against the real's strength in recent years in an attempt to protect the competitiveness of exports.

Economists now expect the real to remain stable around the 2 per dollar level for at the least six months, the Reuters survey found.

"If the dollar falls, we know the central bank will act," said Mario Battistel, head of FX trading at brokerage Fair.

Chile's peso gained about 0.19 percent to trade at 472.50 per dollar as prices of copper, the country's main export, rose.

Analysts are speculating that Chile could soon join Brazil, Colombia and Peru in fighting currency gains if the peso firms much past 470 per dollar. Mexico is not expected to step up intervention efforts.

title: RPT-POLL-Brazil real seen stable at 2/dollar for months
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers with no change to text)

* For poll data see

* Real seen gaining a mere 2.5 percent in a year

* Gov't intervention, China, euro zone seen weighing on FX

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's interventions in the foreign exchange market have helped convince economists that the real will remain stable around 2 per dollar for at least the next six months, a Reuters survey found on Thursday.

Expectations that U.S. monetary stimulus would drive strong dollar inflows to Brazil have also given way to growing concerns about China and the euro zone, adding to bets on a stable currency.

Economists now expect the real to trade at 1.97 per dollar in one year, only 2.5 percent stronger than its current level, according to the median forecast of 32 financial institutions in Brazil and abroad.

The real currently hovers around 2.02 per greenback, more than 16 percent weaker from late February. Only a couple of months ago, economists had forecast it would recover to 1.96 by February of 2013 and to 1.92 by August.

"The world has changed, commodity prices have changed, China has changed, and we also see the central bank intervening more actively," said Dalton Gardiman, chief economist with Bradesco BBI, the investment banking arm of Banco Bradesco.

"Altogether, those factors totally justify a weaker real in the next few months," he added.

Worries about the magnitude of China's economic slowdown, which is likely to extend to a seventh consecutive quarter, have been tempering investors' bets on higher commodities prices, and on Brazil's trade performance as a result.

Adding to the cloudy global scenario is a persistent euro-zone debt crisis that is likely to trigger regular bouts of capital flight to dollar-denominated assets.

Dollar outflows from Brazil could also grow as local companies honor debt payments on a large number of bonds they issued in international capital markets, noted Marjorie Hernandez, Latin American strategist at HSBC in New York.

"All of a sudden the picture is a lot more neutral (for the real). We see slight dollar outflows," she said.

Even if all those factors turn out to be not as bad as feared, investors would still need to surmount a "wall" of interventionist measures that the Brazilian government has pledged to put in place if needed.

"Even if the international scenario improves next year, which I don't think is likely, it's still difficult to see the real strengthening too much because the government has been using administrative measures to curb currency gains," said Darwin Dib, chief economist at CM Capital Markets, a brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Government sources have recently told Reuters that the first line of defense against undesirable currency gains would be currency swap auctions and dollar purchases by the central bank. If that is not enough, the Finance Ministry would join the fight with targeted tax hikes on capital inflows.

The measures should ensure the real remains weaker than 2 per dollar, a level considered beneficial to exporters.

The plan is part of President Dilma Rousseff's campaign against what she has called a "monetary tsunami" caused by the expansionary monetary policies in the United States and Europe, which can potentially hurt Brazilian exporters by driving up the value of the real.

But many economists now believe markets have already priced in the impact of the latest rounds of monetary stimulus in the developed world, removing a key driver for currency gains in Latin America.

In Brazil, that leaves inflation as one of the main arguments for a stronger currency.

Brazil's 12-month inflation currently runs nearly 1 percentage point higher than the center of the government's 4.5 percent target. If price indexes continue to go up in the next few months, policymakers could choose to let the real strengthen in order to make imports cheaper.

That might be a more palatable alternative than raising interest rates, which Rousseff's government has lowered to an all-time low of 7.5 percent.

Still, many economists say there are other options to put a lid on inflation.

"That is going to be their last option before raising interest rates. Their priority will be (sales) tax cuts," said Dib from CM Capital Markets.

title: Brazil Real Closes Essentially Steady Versus Dollar
text:
--Brazilian currency doesn't react to uncertainties on Spain

--President Dilma Rousseff speaks in favor of market intervention

--Real trades in a tight range in market of low liquidity


 
   By Diana Kinch 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real closed virtually stable against the dollar Tuesday, after the Brazilian government signaled a continued determination to keep its currency within a tight trading band, which reduces the impact of market moves world-wide.

The real exited at BRL2.0246 to the dollar, marginally stronger than its Monday close of BRL2.0249, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

The real all day hovered midway in what is viewed as the government's chosen range, remaining impervious to new uncertainties over the Spanish economy that weighed on markets world-wide, economists said. The stability came after Brazil's President Dilma Rousseff spoke in favor of government intervention in the currency market to aid Brazilian exporters' competitiveness.

President Rousseff admitted at an event in Sao Paulo late Monday that the government is continuing to adopt measures to keep the real from strengthening because this improves Brazil's competitiveness on international markets.

"The Brazilian real's increasingly set in a plaster cast," said Flavio Serrano, economist with Espirito Santo Investment Bank BES. "It shifted just a half-centavo all day."

The government wants to avoid a significant weakening of the real, because that would be bad for inflation, and any significant strengthening, as that would be bad for industry and exporters, Mr. Serrano said.

Bruno Lavieri of Tendencias Consultoria said that Brazil's currency regime no longer can be considered floating.

"The currency is stuck within the BRL2 to BRL2.10 band," Mr. Lavieri said. With its continued speeches on the possibility of market intervention "the government's threatening not to let the real appreciate, and threatening to keep out the speculative capital from abroad."

"However, not only speculative capital, but also productive capital is being kept away by the new taxes, or threats of taxes," Mr. Lavieri said.

This is leading to reduced liquidity in the market, the economists said.

The real remained stable despite a "critical patch" in Europe, said Mr. Serrano.

Markets world-wide fell late Tuesday after Spain's prime minister, Mariano Rajoy, said the country won't imminently seek a new aid package from the European Union, despite its economic crisis, growing unemployment levels and movements toward regional separatism. The possibility that negotiations soon could start on a potential bailout package for Spain had buoyed markets earlier in the day. Such a package could allow the European Central Bank to buy Spanish sovereign-debt papers to reduce its costs of financing Spain, according to market reports.

"Spain really will need this help, but it's now uncertain when this will come and how much will be needed," Mr. Lavieri said. "Markets are in wait-and-see mode on Europe."

title: DJ Brazil Real Ends Slightly Stronger as Market Monitors Dollar Flows

Analysts noted the Brazilian currency has been showing only subdued reaction to such good news as traders look for strong intervention against forex volatility from the Brazilian government and central bank.

"The price of the dollar should continue being administered by the Central Bank of Brazil in an interval between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05," said Sidnei Nehme, trader at the NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Traders in the meantime are looking to see if a possible "flood" of incoming dollars from the U.S. Federal Reserve's third round of quantitative easing, announced last month, will work to strengthen Brazil's currency during the month of October.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  firm on US factory data
text:
* US manufacturing sector expands for 1st time since May

* Central bank intervention fears curb FX gains in Brazil

* Mexican peso up 0.2 pct, Brazilian real nearly flat

(Adds comments, changes dateline)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies gained on Monday after a surprise expansion in the U.S. manufacturing sector eased concerns about a global slowdown.

The Mexican peso firmed 0.2 percent to 12.84 per U.S. dollar after data showed the manufacturing sector of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner, expanded in September for the first time since May.

"This scenario is positive for manufacturing activity, which obviously has an impact in the local market," said Mario Copca, an analyst at brokerage CI in Mexico City.

Mexican factories tend to closely track activity in the United States. An index of manufacturing activity in Mexico slowed for a third month in a row in September, but still pointed to further expansion ahead.

Investors have been revising their estimates for stronger Latin American currencies as more dollars are expected to flow into emerging markets as a result of government and central bank efforts to stimulate growth.

Analysts now expect the peso to finish 2012 at 12.88 per dollar, stronger than the level of 13.01 forecast a month ago, a survey by the Mexican central bank with private analysts showed.

Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on Monday defended the U.S. central bank's controversial bond-buying stimulus plan.

Brazilian policymakers have complained that easy monetary policies in the United States are pushing speculators to buy up emerging market assets, strengthening local currencies and undermining the competitiveness of domestic manufacturers.

The Brazilian real bid a slight 0.05 percent firmer at 2.0254 per dollar on the local market close. Investors have been avoiding making strong bets on a stronger real currency for fear of central bank intervention.

Brazilian policymakers have managed to keep the real weaker than 2 per dollar -- a level they consider beneficial to exporters -- since early July.

"Here the concern is that the central bank will step into the market if the dollar weakens too much. For now, nobody is willing to fight the central bank," said Mario Battistel, head of the currency desk at Fair Corretora, a brokerage in Sao Paulo.

In Chile, the peso gained 0.4 percent, recovering part of the losses seen on Friday, when threats of government intervention caused the currency to slump the most in seven weeks.

Fears of intervention in Chile have grown after central bank chief Rodrigo Vergara said policymakers may intervene during "exceptional periods" in which the exchange rate is significantly out of line with fundamentals.

The move by Chile pushed it closer to the stance of policymakers in Brazil, Colombia and Peru who have been intervening in markets to fight dollar inflows.

title: Brazil Real Closes Stronger, But Tough Talk Limits Gains
text:
--Local currency's gains not tracking bigger movements overseas, traders say

--Real remains rangebound between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 on intervention concerns

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL2.0297 to the greenback


 
   By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Thursday, but failed to track bigger overseas gains versus the greenback as intervention concerns kept the currency locked into its recent trading range.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0297 to the U.S. dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Wednesday's closing price fix at BRL2.0320 to the dollar.

"Nothing has changed, foreign exchange in Brazil is at a standstill," said Silvio Campos Neto, an economist at the Tendencias consultants group in Sao Paulo. "The foreign-exchange rate here has been very stable at current levels."

Brazilian Central Bankintervention and recent government rhetoric have kept the real trading between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 in recent months. While officials have continued to cite the need to ward off volatility for various interventions and other measures, Brazil has made it clear that the government is comfortable with the currency at current levels because the real is weak enough to support local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation, traders said.

The Brazilian Central Bank's economic policy director, Carlos Hamilton Araujo, reaffirmed the government's intent Thursday. "We've intervened in the market recently and certainly we'll continue to do so," Mr. Araujo said. Recent central bank action has been focused on swap auctions, but Mr. Araujo didn't discount the use of spot-market auctions in the future.

"As market conditions allow us to continue reinforcing our reserves, we'll do so," Mr. Araujo said. Brazil's foreign reserves currently stand at $378.5 billion.

The local currency market shrugged off news from overseas that actually had other currencies performing better against the buck, traders noted. China, Brazil's largest trading partner, injected a record amount of liquidity into its financial system this week, adding nearly $58 billion this week--including $8 billion overnight. While the move was directed at softening seasonal tightness in China's banking system, it could have a positive impact on Brazilian exports to the country.

Europe, meanwhile, moved closer to a firmer resolution of its ongoing debt troubles. Greece's three-party coalition agreed on most of the austerity measures required to receive the next tranche of bailout funds, while Spain unveiled a 2013 budget that included spending cuts and other tough measures aimed at reducing the country's deficit.

"Around the world, the U.S. dollar depreciated because the moves alleviated risk concerns," Mr. Campos said. "But here, the movement [versus the dollar] was very small. [The real] is not tracking what the dollar is doing overseas."

Complicating Thursday's session was the month-end battle to set the average daily foreign-exchange rate used to settle futures contracts, known as the Ptax. Long- and short-position holders typically engage in a tug-of-war to influence the reference rate, adding a measure of volatility to trading at the end of each month.

While the Brazilian Central Bank could be tempted to intervene in currency markets should the real more closely approach the BRL2.02 mark, Durval Correa of Sao Paulo's Multi-Money brokerage said that he expected the bank to remain on the sidelines through the end of the week.

The real will likely continue trading in its recent range between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 to the dollar, Mr. Correa said. "Apparently everyone is happy" with the real at current levels, Mr. Correa said.

"I don't feel like we're going to see any big changes in the foreign-exchange rate," Mr. Correa said. "The real is going to stay where it is and the central bank is going to administer the currency. If the real strengthens, it will sell dollars. If the real weakens, it will buy dollars."

The local market is currently in equilibrium, Mr. Correa said. Local banks are shorting the dollar, while funds are holding long positions, he added. That caused just a few sharp movements in the foreign-exchange market that are largely related to light trading volume.

--Gerald Jeffris in Brasilia contributed to this article.

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger Ahead of Spain Budget, Ptax Fight
text:
--Brazil's real shrugs off concerns about European outlook weighing on euro

--Month-end battle to set real's reference rate likely to spark volatility

--Brazilian real opens at BRL2.0294, stronger from Wednesday's close at BRL2.0320


 
    By Jeff Fick 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real traded stronger against the U.S. dollar at the open Thursday despite ongoing concerns about Europe's crisis and expected volatility as a month-end battle between local currency traders heated up.

The real shrugged off declines by the euro, a key barometer for the local currency, ahead of the release of Spain's 2013 budget. Protests against austerity measures in Greece and Spain had rattled markets Wednesday. The real opened trading at BRL2.0294 to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was stronger from Wednesday's close at BRL2.0320.

Spain is at the forefront of concerns in Europe, with the government set to approve its 2013 budget, which contains cutbacks aimed at easing the country's debt troubles. Austerity measures in Greece and Spain have sparked protests in each country and unnerved investors. The market will be watching closely for signs that Spain will request international financial aid, which it has so far resisted. Italy, meanwhile, carried out a successful bond sale, avoiding any spillover from the recent problems in its troubled euro-zone partners.

News that Spain was delaying the release of the 2013 budget until later Thursday briefly rattled local currency markets, causing the real to weaken to BRL2.0321 to the dollar. The currency quickly recovered to again trade at BRL2.0294.

The currency market also reacted to positive news out of China, where the country's central bank injected nearly $58 billion into the financial system this week--including $8 billion overnight. While the move was directed at softening seasonal tightness in China's banking system, it could have a positive impact on Brazilian firms that export to the country. China is Brazil's largest trading partner.

In Brazil, traders were also digesting the latest quarterly inflation report. The Brazilian central bank boosted its outlook for 2012 inflation to 5.2% from the previous forecast of 4.7% on higher global commodity prices. Inflation, however, is expected to ease slightly next year as reductions on local energy rates take effect. In 2013, the central bank expects inflation to end the year at 4.9% versus the previous forecast of 5%.

The outlook for Brazil's stumbling economy was also reduced. Latin America's largest economy has slowed dramatically since mid-2011, with the manufacturing sector stagnating under the weight of an overvalued real that made local goods less competitive and resulted in a flood of cheap imports. The central bank expects Brazil to register gross domestic product growth of 1.6% in 2012, down from the previous forecast of 2.5% growth. In the second quarter, Brazil's economy expanded at an annual rate of 1.6%.

While local currency traders will closely watch developments abroad, the scene in Brazil will likely be dominated by the month-end battle to set the average daily foreign-exchange rate used to settle futures contracts, known as the Ptax. Long- and short-position holders typically engage in a tug-of-war to influence the reference rate, adding a measure of volatility to trading at the end of each month.

Despite movements overseas, Brazil's recent actions to intervene in local currency markets mean the real is expected to remain locked into the current trading range between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 to the dollar. The government and central bank have made it clear to the market that they are comfortable with the currency at that level, with the real weak enough to support local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation.

Protests against austerity measures erupted in Madrid, making it more difficult for Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy to request international financial aid -- a condition for Spain to receive support from the European Central Bank.

The cost of dollars in local currencies could keep rising, but it would likely hit resistance around 474 Chilean pesos per dollar, while losses in the Mexican currency were seen limited to 13.05 or 13.10 per dollar, traders said.

title: Mexico's Calderon Critiques Fed But Sees No Need for  Forex Intervention
text:
--Mexico's outgoing president warns against resumption of forex intervention

--Mr. Calderon, however, sympathizes with Brazil's complaints that loose U.S. monetary policy creates unwanted currency appreciation

--He expresses doubt that QE works effectively


   By Michael J. Casey 

Outgoing Mexican President Felipe Calderon expressed sympathy Wednesday for other emerging-market leaders' complaints about how the U.S. Federal Reserve's loose monetary policy leads to the unwanted appreciation of their currencies.

But Mr. Calderon, whose six-year term ends when President-elect Enrique Pena Nieto assumes power on Dec. 1, also mounted a solid defense of his government's noninterventionist approach to currency markets and recommended that his successor stick with it. He was speaking in an interview with editors and reporters from The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones Newswires.

In a thinly veiled criticism of the Fed's "quantitative-easing" bond-buying program, Mr. Calderon said serious discussion about its effectiveness was warranted.

"How much of these efforts are going to boost local demand and how much is going to appreciate the real in Brazil?" he asked. "How much is going to the peso in Mexico?"

Mr. Calderon said the Fed's strategy, by which it purchases bonds with freshly printed dollars, might well be counterproductive because it drives up commodity prices, which squeezes household demand in the U.S.

His comments followed Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff's speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, where she said that "expansionary monetary policy" from developed-world central banks "aggravates the global recession." She said "emerging countries lose market share because of the artificial appreciation of their currencies, which aggravates the global recession."

In the same remarks, Ms. Rousseff defended Brazil's response to this effect over the past two years, during which its central bank bought dollars in the open market and it implemented taxes on fund inflows to limit their appreciative impact on the exchange rate. Since the Fed announced its third round of quantitative easing, or QE3, two weeks ago, Brazil has intervened on a number of occasions to weaken the real. Peru and other countries in Latin America have either done similarly or warned that they might do so.

But Mr. Calderon said he would never counsel his successor to abandon the hands-off approach Mexico has maintained during his tenure, even though the peso has risen more than other currencies because of that policy.

"I would not resume any intervention in the markets," Mr. Calderon said, arguing instead that the country needed to instead boost its competitiveness by continuing to invest in infrastructure and education. Highlighting extensive programs that have added 20,000 kilometers of new highways over the past year, for example, and allowed Mexico to graduate 113,000 new engineers ever year, the outgoing president credited this approach with Mexico's rapid export growth and advances in value-added production.

Although Mexico has done nothing to prevent loose U.S. monetary policy from driving up the peso and undermining competitiveness, Mexican exports now account for 60% of all Latin American exports, Mr. Calderon said.

title: Brazil's Meirelles Sees Less Impact from QE3 on Brazil  Currency
text:
SAO PAULO--The former president of the Brazilian Central Bank, Henrique Meirelles, said Tuesday that he sees less of an impact on emerging-market countries such as Brazil from the U.S. Federal Reserve's latest round of monetary stimulus than in the past.

"In my estimation, it's possible that the marginal impact of this will be a bit less than previously," Mr. Meirelles told Dow Jones on the sidelines of an event, referring to the effect on Brazil.

The Fed earlier this month announced a third round of asset purchases known as quantitative easing. Previous such measures have been blamed by Brazilian authorities for appreciation in the local currency against the dollar, putting local businesses at a disadvantage to their international competitors.

In the wake of the latest round of quantitative easing, Brazil's central bank has intervened in the exchange market to weaken the real while Finance Minister Guido Mantega and other officials have warned that they'll "defend" the Brazilian real from appreciation.

Mr. Meirelles said that "each stimulus measure in each country generates collateral effects."

But he added that there's "a less accentuated contrast" between economic growth in emerging markets and developed countries than when the first and second rounds of quantitative easing were launched.

"The U.S. economy is a bit better, the actions of the European Central Bank have also reduced the level of uncertainty," Mr. Meirelles said. "There's an environment that's a little more balanced."

title: Brazil Current Account View Improves Amid Slow Economy
text:
--Brazil central bank cuts projection for 2012 current account gap by $3 billion

--Overseas profit remittances slowing on tepid activity, forex

--Investment inflows remain firm despite recent slowdown

By Gerald Jeffris

BRASILIA--Brazil's current account deficit should be fully financed by incoming investment for a fifth consecutive year in 2012 as slow local and overseas activity weighs in against significant dollar outflows.

The country's central bank said Tuesday it would cut its projection for the current account deficit by $3 billion as reduced overseas remittances help rein in net dollar flows from the economy.

At the same time, however, local officials believe the economy will stand to benefit from growing inflows of foreign direct investment as the country moves toward a recovery.

"The country has consolidated itself as a net receiver of foreign direct investment," said Brazilian central bank Economics Department Coordinator Tulio Maciel. "This reflects solid macroeconomic fundamentals and good prospects for growth."

The central bank said Tuesday that it raised its projection for FDI this year to $60 billion from $50 billion previously, in response to better-than-expected investment inflows seen in recent months. At the same time, it lowered its projection for the current account deficit to $53 billion from $56 billion.

Over 12 months through August, FDI in Brazil reached $65.8 billion, or the equivalent to 2.8% of gross domestic product. At the same time, the country's 12-month current account deficit in August came in at only to $49.7 billion, or 2.1% of gross domestic product.

Mr. Maciel said the main driver behind a narrowing current account deficit should be lower overseas profit and dividend remittances by foreign companies with local operations.

"We've seen moderate flows of profit and dividend remittances throughout the year," he said. "Economic activity has been slower, and the second factor is the stronger dollar--it's been more expensive to send remittances this year."

Brazil's real has weakened by more than 10% against the dollar since earlier this year under the impact of risk aversion in international markets.

But while the current account remains fully covered by foreign investment for now, analysts still caution that the country shouldn't become overly confident the trend will continue.

"The capital account remains vulnerable to shifts in external sentiment and the unpredictable nature of the domestic policy mix," said Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Goldman in a note Tuesday. Measures adopted by the government earlier this year to control capital inflows have "eroded sentiment toward Brazil," he added.

Brazilian officials have actively intervened in local markets over recent months with currency swap auctions in an effort to limit strengthening of Brazil's real, and keep the currency within a narrow range between BRL2.00 and BRL2.10 to the dollar.

But despite the measures, investors for the present appear to remain interested in sending cash to the South American country. Brazil's central bank Tuesday reported net dollar inflows into the economy so far in September, bringing dollar inflows for the year to date to $23.66 billion.

title: Brazil Real Weakens on President's Tough Line on  Currency  Appreciation
text:
--Brazil real exits active trading at BRL2.0290/dlr versus BRL2.0245 Monday

--At U.N., President Rousseff says tough line against currency appreciation "legitimate"

--Continued worries about European debt crisis also weigh on Brazilian market

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real weakened against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as the country's president took a tough line against an unwanted appreciation of the currency.

The real exited active trading against the dollar at BRL2.0290, weaker than Monday's close of BRL2.0245, according to Tullet Prebon via FactSet.

In a speech at the United Nations, Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff said actions by her government to prevent the unwanted appreciation of the currency were "legitimate." She told the General Assembly, "We cannot accept that legitimate initiatives of commercial defense by developing countries can be classified as protectionism... Protectionism and all the forms of commercial manipulation must be fought."

The president said central banks in industrially developed countries have taken "exaggerated steps" in combating a global slowdown, including a policy of flooding capital markets with currency. Much of that money, she said, finds its way to countries such as Brazil, where it leads to an unwanted appreciation of local currencies.

President Rousseff echoed the argument often made by Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who warned as recently as last week that any significant strengthening of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar would hurt exporters and manufacturers.

The message seems to be getting through to Brazilian investors.

"The government is virtually dictating the exchange rate these days," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at southern Brazil's Onnix brokerage. "The central bank sometimes intervenes even before there is any sign of volatility."

The constant possibility of government intervention has effectively kept the Brazilian real weaker than BRL2.00 against the dollar since late May.

According to most analysts, the narrow band between BRL2.00 and BRL2.05 is likely to remain in place for the foreseeable future.

"There is little reason to believe in any significant movement, one way or the other, for the Brazilian real in the near future," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist for Latin America at BNP Paribas bank.

Frequent interventions have come mainly in the form of so-called reverse swap auctions at which the central bank buys up dollar-linked futures contracts. The effect is to reduce the availability of dollar-hedged paper in the market, thus making the dollar slightly more valuable against the real than before the auction.

The central bank also has other tools it can use, including direct purchases of dollars from the market.

In comments to reporters last week, Finance Minister Mantega said the government was also prepared to use more powerful tools, such as higher taxes on short-term investment inflows. The government has used tax increases in the past to stem unwanted inflows.

Traders said the Brazilian market on Tuesday was also jittery because of renewed worries about the European debt crisis, including reports that Greece is increasingly unable to meet austere budget goals and that Spain may soon be in need of a debt bailout.

title: Brazil Real Opens Stronger as Exporters Sell Dollars
text:
--Brazil real opens stronger at BRL2.0240 to the dollar

By Tom Murphy

SAO PAULO--The Brazilian real opened stronger against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as exporters sold dollars to the market.

The real opened at BRL2.0240 to the dollar, stronger against the Monday close of BRL2.0245, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Traders said volume was thin.

"There is little or no investment capital entering the market," said Wanderlei Muniz, a trader at the Onnix brokerage in southern Brazil. "Investors know that any significant inflow of speculative capital will result in government action."

In recent weeks, the Central Bank of Brazil has intervened several times in the market via auctions of so-called reverse swap contracts. The auctions tend to support the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real by reducing the availability in the market of dollar-hedging contracts.

"The auctions are not the only tool the government has," said Muniz. "The government has ample tools to avoid market volatility."

In recent interviews, Finance Minister Guido Mantega raised the possibility of additional taxes on short-term investment inflows in the event of a significant appreciation of the Brazilian currency against the dollar. In recent years, Brazil's government has raised taxes on various types of investment in efforts to control what officials regard as "speculative" inflows.

Mantega and other officials have said any major appreciation of the real against the dollar would hurt exporters and manufacturers.

Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff is expected to reinforce the message in a speech later Tuesday at the United Nations in New York. She is widely expected to criticize efforts by the U.S. Federal Reserve and other central banks to increase financial market liquidity as a way to stimulate economic growth. According to Brazilian officials, much of the enhanced liquidity flows to emerging market countries such as Brazil, leading to an unwanted appreciation of the currency.

With thin volume and cautious trading, traders foresee little volatility in the market Tuesday.

"In fact, there is little prospect of volatility, going forward," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist for Latin America at BNP Paribas bank in Sao Paulo. "The Brazilian central bank seems to have effectively set a narrow trading band for the currency anchored around the current value."

* Brazil real, Mexican peso trade flat

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Moises Avila and Walter Brandimarte

SANTIAGO/SAO PAULO, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Chile's peso weakened sharply on Friday on concerns that authorities could intervene to st em c urrency gains that may hurt exporters while Brazil's real traded flat after a top official threatened to impl ement cap ital controls.

Investors are increasingly concerned that governments will intervene in the market to offset capital inflows resulting from U.S. and European stimulus measures.

Brazil, Colombia and Peru are already intervening to dampen currency gains, and some think Chile could be the next to act.

Chile's peso lost 0.6 percent to 473.20 per dollar after it failed to break the psychological barrier of 470 per greenback.

"Traders are hesitant to add long positions below 470 on fear of intervention," said Katia Diaz, an economist with 4CAST in New York.

With gains of more than 10 percent so far in the year, the Chilean peso has currencies that strengthened the most in 2012 an d it hit a one-year high this week.

Other traders said the peso slipped as investors took profits on the surge in the currency after the European Central Bank unveiled a bond-buying program to support indebted countries and the Fed launched its own asset-purchase stimulus to boost growth in the United States.

The Chilean central bank is increasingly expected to voice its concern about an over-valued currency before intervening in the market, analysts said. A trigger for central bank action could be a peso at 460 per dollar, they added.

"Close to 460, there will need to intervene in the exchange market. At that level the export sector will be less competitive and that will be reflected in the trade balance," said Carlos Rumie, trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

The Brazilian real held steady for the fourth consecutive session, to bid at 2.0225 per dollar.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega threatened to make use of short-term capital controls to curb any currency gains that could hurt exporters.

"Selling the dollar and buying the real is a global trend. But local investors are not following that, they are mindful of the intervention threats from the Brazilian authorities," said Alfredo Barbutti, chief economist at BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazilian policymakers intervened heavily in the foreign exchange market last week and on Monday to offset the appreciation trend. The bank has refrained from intervening since then, but it is widely expected to act again if the real firms significantly.

So far, the Brazilian central bank has been able to keep the real weaker than 2 per dollar since early July with the sale of reverse currency swaps -- derivatives contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market.

If dollar inflows pick up, however, it may resume outright dollar purchases in the spot market. If that fails, investors can probably count on the Finance Ministry to raise financial taxes on short-term capital flows.

The Mexican peso, one of the few currencies in the region that investors consider free of intervention risk, traded flat.

Traders said the Mexican currency's could advance back toward a more than five-month high next week if Spain requests financial aid to help ease the country's debt crisis.

title: UPDATE 3-Brazil may fire up tax artillery in ' currency  war'
text:
* Finance Minister says ready to act to keep lid on real currency

* Mantega says may ramp up short-term capital controls

* Tensions resurface over new U.S. monetary stimulus

* Brazil has taxed some foreign inflows since 2009

(Adds rising economic discord between U.S. and Brazil)

By Ana Nicolaci da Costa and Sujata Rao

LONDON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Brazil threatened on Friday a further clampdown on speculative foreign capital, firing a warning shot in a "currency war" its finance minister blamed on money-printing by Western central banks.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Brazil would not allow its currency, the real, to strengthen as a result of aggressive monetary stimulus by the United States and other developed nations.

"If necessary ... we have (the option) of short-term capital taxes," he told reporters on the sidelines of an Economist conference in London.

Mantega's comments reflect growing tension between the South American nation and the United States over its lax monetary policy, which Brazilian officials blame for an avalanche of cheap imports crippling local producers.

Since 2009, the Brazilian government has introduced a number of measures intended to curb excess inflows of foreign investors' dollars but recently reduced their scope after the real weakened.

Brazil shocked investors in October of that year by taxing some categories of foreign capital flowing into stocks and bonds. It said at the time that some of the flows constituted hot money and were harming the economy.

Brazil has also raised duties on dozens of foreign-made goods to help a local industry struggling with a stronger real as well as some of the world's highest input costs.

U.S. Trade Representative Ron Kirk's calls for Brazil to reconsider plans for more tariff increases prompted a stinging response from Brasilia on Thursday. In a letter, the Brazilian government said the hike was a legitimate tool unlike the "illegal subsidization of farm products by the United States, which impact Brazil and other developing countries." ID:nL1E8KK9QE]

Mantega has become one of the fiercest critics of the asset buying programmes that Western central banks have been using to shore up their economies, accusing them of in effect devaluing their currencies to boost competitiveness.

The real held steady around 2.0245 per dollar for the fourth consecutive session on Friday following Mantega's threats to ramp up capital controls. His remarks added to the perception that the central bank will keep intervening if the real nears the level of 2 per dollar.

Some of the extra funds generated by quantitative easing (QE) have in the past found their way into emerging markets, lured by higher interest rates and yields, driving gains in currencies including the real and Indonesia's rupiah.

Mantega said the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision this month to embark on a third round of bond-buying, followed by a similar move by Japan, would revive global "currency wars" by forcing other countries to act to protect their own economies.

"(The United States and Japan) will be stimulating the currency wars as (they) will lead all countries also to pursue these wars," Mantega said. "It's natural other countries will defend themselves."

BRAZIL CENTRAL BANKINTERVENTIONS

Brazil's central bank has also intervened heavily in currency markets to hold the real near the 2-per-dollar level via billions of dollars in reverse swaps. It has also cut interest rates to a record low of 7.5 percent.

Mantega told the conference there would be no let up in this process.

"The central bank will buy more reserves, we already have a very high level of reserves and we will purchase more if there is a strong offer of dollars in the Brazilian economy," he said.

"We will do more reverse-swapping ... we won't allow our economy to become uncompetitive."

The Brazilian economy - the world's sixth largest according to International Monetary Fund data - has been virtually flat since expanding 7.5 percent in 2010.

Economists expect the economy to grow only 1.5 percent this year, despite a series of rate cuts and tax breaks, and below the government's 2 percent forecast.

Mantega predicted growth would pick up again to around 4 percent to 4.5 percent on an annualized basis in 2013 in response to the lowered borrowing costs and stimulus measures the government has put in place.

Analysts are split over whether the central bank will hold or cut rates next time it meets on Oct. 10, with the latest data showing a rise in inflation on higher food prices.

Mantega said the central bank has room for further rate cuts.
