title: Real Weakens Vs Dollar as  Brazil  Government Says Ready to  Intervene
text:
--Brazil real weakens against the dollar after Brazil's finance minister speaks in London

--Real is set to stay within a narrow trading band

--Brazil government indicates it could seek further interest-rate cut


 
   By Diana Kinch 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--Brazil's real weakened against the dollar in late trading Friday, after Finance Minister Guido Mantega made it plain the government is ready for market intervention if the currency appreciates beyond a desired level.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0225, marginally weaker than its Thursday close of BRL2.0211, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet.

Economists said comments made by Mr. Mantega in London neutralized the impact on the real of rising risk appetite in markets world-wide after The Financial Times published news of a debt-alleviation package for Spain.

The dollar had lost ground against the euro and other currencies early Friday after the FT revealed that Spain's government is in negotiations with European Union authorities on a possible new rescue package to be announced Sept. 27. This would involve the purchase of Spanish bonds by the European Central Bank and the implementation of structural reforms to meet the demands of international creditors, the newspaper said.

However, Mr. Mantega's explicit declarations at The Economist's High-Growth Markets Summit kept the Brazilian currency stable and even reduced trading volumes as traders remained aware of the possibility of intervention.

This intervention could be via reverse swap auctions, equivalent to the purchase of dollars on the futures market, or by other measures that could include taxes on the entry of funds into Brazil, the minister said.

"Mantega reinforced what he had already said. They're putting a price tag on the real, at between BRL2 to BRL2.05," said Jankiel Santos, economist with Espirito Santo Investment Bank, or BES.

This trading range already has been virtually enforced by the government for the past two to three months, according to Silvio Campos Neto, economist with Tendencias Consultoria.

"The government's controlling (the market), they're getting more explicit," Mr. Campos Neto said. "The tone (of the statements) is stronger. They're not going to allow the currency to free float."

At the event in London, Mr. Mantega slammed the U.S. Federal Reserve's recent decision to launch a third-round of quantitative easing, saying it stimulates currency wars and stressed that whatever action is necessary to prevent speculative flows from flooding into his country as a result of a weaker dollar will be taken.

"Quantitative easing, in my view, does not have very much effect in terms of recovering the economy because it is done in isolation and not done in combination with fiscal policy," said Mr. Mantega at the summit, adding that all it does in the end is devalue the dollar, which in turn stimulates currency wars.

Mr. Mantega added that Brazil's government will continue to use monetary policy to stimulate growth. He said there is still space for a further reduction of the Selic base interest rate, which currently stands at an all-time low of 7.5%. Economists in Brazil criticized the minister's comments, which indicate that the government is seeking to apply pressure on the central bank, which is supposed to act as an autonomous and independent body.

"It's clear there's great government pressure to cut the interest rates further," Mr. Campos Neto said. "The government wants a further 0.25% interest rate cut."

The central bank monetary-policy council is due to meet Oct. 10 to decide on its forthcoming interest-rate policy.

title: As Fed Readies QE3, Foreign Governments Brace for  Currency  Onslaught
text:
--As with QE2, a weaker dollar is predicted for QE3

--Emerging market central banks might retaliate by weakening their currencies, but that could stoke inflation

--The risk is that this descends into an-out race to the bottom with tit-for-tat currency depreciations

The Federal Reserve's plan to embark on an open-ended round of asset purchases to bolster the U.S. economy has put financial authorities in other countries on high alert.

Looking back to the last time the Fed printed dollars to finance bond buying, which sent the U.S. currency on a year-long decline against most of its counterparts, officials are bracing for an unwanted flood of speculative money into their markets and a possible cycle of tit-for-tat retaliatory measures. The biggest fear is that it triggers a self-reinforcing and self-destructive race to the bottom in which monetary policy and direct interventions are used to prevent other countries from gaining a competitive advantage through weaker exchange rates.

The Bank of Japan provided fodder for such concerns Wednesday. Just six days after the Fed said it would purchase an additional $40 billion in mortgage bonds a month for an indefinite period, Japan's central bank announced it would add another 10 trillion yen ($127 billion) to its asset-buying program and extend it out to the end of 2013. Although the BOJ didn't explicitly cite the yen's strength as a motivating factor, Japan's currency immediately fell to a one-month low versus the dollar. Last Friday, following the Fed's announcement a day earlier, Finance Minister Jun Azumi forcefully complained that the strong yen was hurting the Japanese economy and hinted at direct intervention by vowing to "take decisive steps when it is deemed necessary."

Some emerging market governments have also taken matters into their own hands this past week. Brazil has conducted so-called "reverse dollar swaps" to prevent its currency, the real, from appreciating; Peru adjusted its intervention strategy toward weakening the Peruvian sol; and Turkey cut interest rates by more than expected.

Others have been notably more muted in their response. Officials in South Korea, Thailand, Singapore and the Philippines took a cautiously sanguine view of the uptick in their currencies, though they all asserted a readiness to smooth out market movement if capital inflows become excessive.

The moves from the Fed and BOJ come after the European Central Bank announced its own plan to buy bonds, in its case those of struggling governments in the periphery of the euro zone, in a bid to contain the region's debt crisis. Unlike the Fed and BOJ's actions, which will result in a net addition of fresh currency into global financial markets and are widely described as "quantitative easing," or QE, the ECB will "sterilize" its transactions by selling certificates that mop up the additional euros. Nonetheless, the moves are seen boosting the willingness of investors to take on risky investments generally, which typically results in large-scale transfers of funds out of dollars and into other currencies.

"All of this cash generated by the Federal Reserve is going to be entering foreign shores," said Komal Sri-Kumar, chief global strategist at TCW. "Emerging markets are going to be tempted to cut interest rates...to offset their currencies appreciating too much."

Emerging market currencies are in the crosshairs of speculators during such times because their interest rates tend to be higher than those in the U.S., European countries and Japan, allowing investors to book a profit on the difference between the two. But such countries often depend heavily on exports, which become more expensive when exchange rates rise. The dilemma for their central banks at times when global liquidity is rising is that they also face inflationary pressures from rising commodity prices and inflows into their real estate and other markets. If they were to combat those rising prices with higher rates, it would only further increase the appeal of their currencies.

In the previous round of Fed quantitative easing, which was dubbed "QE2," the dollar weakened significantly. In the 13 months from June 2010, when expectations of more Fed stimulus first began to rise, until the $600 billion bond-buying program wound up the following summer, the Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, a measure of the dollar's value against a basket of major currencies, lost 18% of its value. It dropped 20% against the Brazilian real over the same period and 18% versus the Korean won.

The dollar followed a similar, but slower path leading up to the QE3 announcement last week. The WSJ Dollar Index hit a 22-month high in July and then started to slide gradually before dropping sharply once Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke signaled the central bank's plans at his speech in Jackson Hole, Wyo, on Aug. 31. The index is now nearly 6% off its July high.

The fallout during QE2 in 2010 and 2011 prompted an especially bellicose response from a few foreign officials, with Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega famously declaring that the world had entered a "currency war," an allusion to the highly damaging competitive-depreciation policies that undermined world trade during the Great Depression. This time around, Mr. Mantega has been less bellicose, though he remains critical of Fed policy. Speaking in Paris on Tuesday, he said, "I don't believe that the new monetary easing will resolve many problems for the U.S., but it could cause several problems for emerging market countries."

The Fed declined to comment Wednesday. In the past, Fed officials have defended their actions by saying that efforts to strengthen the U.S. recovery help the global economy. Mr. Bernanke said in 2010 that different monetary policies may be appropriate for different groups of countries, drawing a distinction between advanced economies and countries with emerging markets that may see more inflation pressure. But he also noted that disparities between exchange rate policies had led to global spending imbalances as "those countries that have allowed their exchange rates to be determined primarily by market forces have seen their competitiveness erode relative to countries that have intervened more aggressively."

In general, the latest response from other emerging market governments has been muted. That may be because those countries' currencies are already well down from their 2011 highs, a function in part of the interventionist actions many undertook in the wake of QE2, with Brazil in particular resorting both to dollar purchases and taxes on short-term foreign investment.

Yet this hands-off response could merely embolden foreign investors. Paresh Upadhyaya, director of currencies at Pioneer Investments with $200 billion under management, said his firm has increased bets on the Korean won, Indian rupee, and Turkish lira over the past week, on expectations they'll benefit from monetary easing in the U.S, Japan, U.K. and euro zone. He says he doesn't expect as much of a backlash from emerging markets as there was during QE2.

The stakes may even be higher this time around. A much slower global growth environment and weakening international trade will make export-driven emerging market countries more protective of market share. And unlike the time limits that were placed on previous such programs, the Fed's new QE plan is open-ended, allowing the central bank to effectively print money until the employment picture in the U.S. meaningfully improves.

Meanwhile, other major central banks beyond the Fed, ECB and BOJ have programs in place that tend to steer money away from their currencies. The Swiss National Bank has been regularly entering the market to buy euros and sell francs since September 2011, setting a floor on the pair. And the Bank of England has conducted Fed-style "unsterilized" bond-buying that pumps extra pounds into financial markets.

Faced with such barriers, investors will tend to go for higher-yielding currencies that are allowed to float more freely.

"Within the EM universe there clearly are going to be relative value trades," said Jonathon Griggs, global chief investment officer of the currency group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. In choosing currencies from "laissez-faire" countries over those that are more interventionist, Mr. Griggs said one interesting trade is the Mexican peso against the Korean won. Other investors cite the Polish zloty, Norwegian krone and Canadian dollar.

The problem for policy makers in such countries, however, is that with so many other currencies off limits, theirs could end up bearing an even bigger burden from exchange rate appreciation.

And if China, the world's biggest goods exporter, gets into the currency devaluation game--either through direct moves to weaken the yuan or through a more aggressive round of monetary easing--the temptation for other countries to retaliate with their own actions could become even more intense.

"Three of the four major central banks have now acted and the last shoe to drop will be China," said James Rickards, partner at JAC Capital and author of the 2011 book "Currency Wars: The Making of the Next Global Crisis."

--Matthew Walter and Kristina Peterson contributed to this article.

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 18 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso weakened o n T uesday as concerns about Spain's willingness to ask for an aid package curbed investor appetite for emerging market assets, offsetting any strengthening effect from the latest round of U.S. monetary stimulus.

The Brazilian real ended slightly stronger, however, and even though the central bank did not intervene as it did on Monday, Finance Minister Guido Mantega made it clear policymakers would not hesitate to prevent the currency from appreciating. [ID: nL5E8KICU6]

Mexico's peso, Latin America's most traded currency, slipped 0.22 percent to 12.7950 per dollar as investors worried that the European debt crisis could get worse again if Spain delays a request for international aid they deem as inevitable.

It was the second straight day of minor setbacks for the peso after it had surged to more than a five-month high on Friday on bets that the U.S. Federal Reserve's third round of bond-buying would push a flood of cash into the region.

But the effects of the Fed's aggressive move so far seem milder than in the previous two rounds of money printing, said Enrique Alvarez, senior economist at IDEAglobal, though it is still too early to say for certain.

"The initial impact at this point is being attenuated by the usual jitters on the side of Europe," he said.

"As long as that occurs, it takes away from the positives that were set in the market by the Fed's latest plan to go ahead and buy mortgages."

The lack of volume and of key economic data left the market more vulnerable to swings in investor sentiment, analysts said.

In Brazil, the real bid 0.35 percent stronger at 2.0225 per dollar at the local market close as the central bank refrained from intervening in the market for the first session in three. Still, the currency remained within the narrow range of 2.0-2.1 per greenback it has been trading in since early July.

"The central bankinterventions left the real decoupled from overseas markets," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist at BES Investimentos in Sao Paulo. "As much as investors want to sell dollars, the central bank has intervened much more than expected and that has kept the real at weaker levels."

Brazil's central bank has been intervening more aggressively in the foreign exchange market to offset possible dollar inflows stemming from the stimulus measures announced by the U.S. Federal Reserve last week.

In less than one week, the Brazilian bank has sold about $5.7 billion worth of reverse currency swaps in four separate auctions, whenever the real strengthened toward the level of 2 per dollar. Those swaps emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market, weakening the real as a result.

In a sign that the government could make use of yet other measures to keep a lid on the real, Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Tu esday repeated that Brazil will continue to take measures to offset the impact of the Fed's monetary stimulus.

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Weaker as  Central Bank Intervenes
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's real opened weaker Monday, as equities in Europe and stock-market futures in the U.S. traded lower and the local central bank intervened in the exchange market to discourage appreciation in the currency.

Around 8:55 a.m. EDT, the real was quoted at 2.0244 reais to the dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL2.0105 at Friday's close.

The currency extended its losses against the dollar when the Brazilian Central Bank announced, shortly after 8:30 a.m. EDT, that it would sell up to $3.5 billion in reverse-swap contracts Monday.

Reverse-swap auctions typically strengthen the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real by offering investors the opportunity to exchange dollar-linked contracts for paper indexed to domestic interest rates.

But even before the auction was called, stock markets overseas suggested global investors were becoming cautious after a week full of encouraging headlines out of the U.S. and Europe.

The U.S. Federal Reserve said last week it will launch a third round of so-called quantitative easing and buy $40 billion of mortgage-backed securities every month until the labor market improves. The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, also said it plans to keep its federal-funds rate near zero through at least mid-2015.

The Fed's bond purchases and low-interest rates have tended to flood financial markets with liquidity, pressuring assets like the Brazilian real to strengthen.

Brazilian authorities are loath to let that happen, and the central bank last week intervened several times with reverse-swap auctions to arrest the real's appreciation.

In addition, market participants are starting to question how much further the markets can gain before a correction comes.

"We are in an overshoot, we all know that we are in an overshoot, but the machine continues to roll on," Sebastien Galy, senior currency strategist at Societe Generale in New York, said in a note.

"The impression I have is that advanced countries won't get out of this crisis very soon. They will continue with low growth for several years," Mr. Mantega said.

The minister said that Brazil's consumer demand will continue to grow in the next few years. The country has full employment, and is expected to create 1.6 million formal jobs this year, he said.

"Those that said the model of expanding the consumer market is exhausted are wrong," he said.

Nonetheless, "despite what many say, investment in Brazil has grown more than consumption," Mr. Mantega said.

Brazil will continue with its current policy of intervening in the currency market, he said.

"We have a currency policy which doesn't allow the appreciation of the real," Mr. Mantega said. The currency today at around BRL2.00 per dollar "improves the competitiveness of Brazilian companies," he said.

The Brazilian real is supposed to be a free-floating currency, but the government has in effect introduced a "dirty float" with some intervention and targeted capital controls to prevent what it considers to have been an over-appreciation of the currency in recent years. The real had strengthened as far as BRL1.55 per dollar in mid-2011.

"We will continue with an active currency policy until all the economies actually adopt a floating exchange rate," Mr. Mantega said.

The official said that, even with the tax cuts and spending increases to help growth, the government will reduce its nominal deficit next year, to 1% of GDP.

Inflation is "under control," despite the recent increase in global grains prices, he said. Recent tax cuts haven't yet taken effect, and will have a "positive" effect on inflation next year.

The country is "close to self-sufficiency" in oil, even before the country has begun to exploit massive fields discovered in recent years off the country's south-east coast.

The bond market was prevented from growing because the central bank's key overnight rate, the Selic, was very high, Mr. Mantega said. As the central bank has slashed the rate to a record low of 7.5% -- from 12.5% a year ago -- real interest rates in Brazil have fallen below 2%.

Government borrowing becomes less significant at these levels and companies will now be better able to finance themselves through the use of debentures, he said.

By 2020, Brazil will be the largest exporter of food in the world, according to the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organization, Mr. Mantega said.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Stronger, Extends Gains on Fed QE3 Announcement
text:
--Real strengthened to BRL2.0105 from BRL2.0192 Thursday

--Fed QE3 announcement caused flow of dollars to emerging markets

--Central bank auctions slowed appreciation

By Jeffrey T. Lewis

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real strengthened against the dollar Friday for the second day after the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank announced a program to buy assets to boost the U.S. economy.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0105 to the dollar, from Thursday's close of BRL2.0192. The currency strengthened even after two reverse swap auctions held by the central bank to stop the real from gaining too much against the dollar.

"We're seeing an arm-wrestling match between the market and the central bank," said Luiz Antonio Abdo, forex director at the Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The market is betting that the Fed measures will cause a flow of dollars into emerging markets, but I don't think the central bank will let it get below BRL2.00. They have plenty of tools they can use" to keep in the range they want.

The Fed said Thursday it would buy $40 billion of mortgage-backed securities every month until the labor market improves. The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, also said it plans to keep its federal-funds rate near zero though at least mid-2015.

The announcement cheered equity markets and weakened the dollar against many world currencies.

Brazil's central bank will remain ready to intervene to prevent the real from strengthening too far or too fast against the dollar should the Brazilian currency strengthen closer to the 2.01 level, said Luiz Carlos Baldan, director of the Fourtrade brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"They want the real between BRL2.0 and BRL2.05 to the dollar, so the central bank will step in" if necessary, he said.

title: WRAPUP 1-Fed's QE3 stirs LatAm differences over  currency
text:
* Brazil restarts currency intervention after Fed

 * Speculation that Chile, Colombia could follow

 * Mexico's QE3 enthusiasm stands out from crowd 

 By Krista Hughes and Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve's latest round of stimulus spotlights  a gulf between Mexico and its Latin American neighbors as the region girds itself for a likely revival of the "currency war."

 While Mexico embraced the Fed's decision to start a third round of bond-buying, Brazil vowed to unleash an arsenal of new measures to combat what it fears could be a sharp appreciation in its currency. 

 A stronger real could not come at a worse time for Brazil, which is battling slowing growth with a raft of measures to boost the domestic economy. This contrasts with Mexico, which is growing roughly twice as quickly as its rival and has been fretting about a weak peso pushing up prices. Close links to the United States give it a big stake in stronger U.S. growth.

 "Mexico is clearly one of the few countries in Latin America where you don't have any resistance to peso strength, and you are unlikely to do so, because the central bank prefers a hands-off attitude," said Clyde Wardle, a strategist at HSBC in New York. "That does set Mexico apart."

 Latin American currencies surged to new highs after the Fed's news, with Chile's peso hitting a one-year high against the U.S. dollar and Mexico's rising to a five-month peak on bets that yield-seeking investors will flood to the region, driving asset prices higher.

 During the Fed's second round of bond buying in late 2010 and the first half of 2011, a rush of capital pushed the Brazilian real up 12 percent against the dollar while the Mexican and Chilean pesos both gained 8 percent.

 Economists said a fresh round of currency intervention was in the cards, with Brazil kicking off o n F riday with two central bank interventions in two hours. Speculation is mounting about increased efforts in Chile and Colombia as well.

 South American officials, worried that a rise in their currencies will price their exports out of the market and drag on growth, have a history of intervening to limit currency gains.

 But in Mexico, policymakers face a different dynamic as the peso - one of the most liquid emerging market currencies and often used as a hedge for emerging market risk - has weakened about 30 percent since before the financial crisis.

 Mexican central bank Governor Agustin Carstens told Reuters the Fed's new bond buying program, dubbed QE3, would help the economy, giving no sign policymakers would try to stem the peso's rise. 

 In fact, Carstens said the stronger peso would help limit inflation by making imported goods cheaper - a much-needed break for the Banco de Mexico, which is confronting a spike in inflation to its highest level in more than two years due to fresh food prices. 

 MEXICO AT ODDS

 Mexico's laissez-faire stance will put it in a different class from Latin American counterparts that intervene to cap currency gains, like Brazil, which also fears competition from Asian powerhouse China and its yuan.

 Countries that keep their currencies cheap will face higher prices for imported goods at the same time a flush of cheap money probably drives commodity prices higher, economists said.

 Although price pressures are subdued in Chile, Colombia and Peru - meaning their central banks may not worry too much about the downside of intervention - inflation accelerated to 5.24 percent in Brazil last month.

 "QE3 will end up having two different kinds of effects on inflation," said BNP Paribas economist Nader Nazmi. 

 "In countries that fight against appreciation... the price of commodities will increase. This could lead to higher inflation in countries that do not allow their exchange rate to appreciate."

 Reacting to higher inflation by raising interest rates would make currencies even more expensive, a policy Catch-22 that the region faced during the Fed's previous stimulus, when Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega coined the term "currency war."

 The phrase has been adopted by officials in Colombia, whose peso has been the fourth-biggest gainer worldwide this year, firming 7 percent since January despite back-to-back interest rate cuts. The peso rose 0.4 percent on Friday.  

 "This shows that we should not remain silent in Colombia and that we will have to respond to these kinds of decisions from the United States," Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said.

 Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain had said even before the Fed's Thursday announcement that the country was worried about another round of stimulus, and the peso is approaching levels that have sparked intervention in the past. 

 "These levels for the peso are a concern for authorities. Although we don't expect imminent action, such as an outright intervention, we do expect to see in the short-term, over the next 30 days, verbal interventions or announcements that try to contain the currency's appreciation," said Ruben Catalan, senior analyst at Bci in Santiago.     

(Additional reporting by Anthony Esposito in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: FACTBOX-Brazil tackles weak economy with flurry of stimulus
text:
Sept 13 (Reuters) - Brazil has rolled out more than a dozen stimulus measures since a sharp slowdown in late 2011, trying to bolster a sluggish recovery in the world's sixth-largest economy.

In the latest move, President Dilma Rousseff's government extended targeted tax breaks on Thursday to reduce payroll taxes for 25 industries including pulp producers, meatpackers and freight transportation.

The following are other government initiatives aimed at rekindling domestic demand and reviving struggling industries:

LOWER INTEREST RATES

Brazil's central bank has slashed borrowing costs by 5 percentage points in 12 months, bringing its benchmark interest rate to a record low 7.5 percent in August.

FOREX INTERVENTIONS

The central bank's rate cuts and direct interventions in the foreign exchange market have helped to weaken Brazil's currency, the real. A weaker real helps make Brazilian goods more competitive on global markets and gives local producers an edge against imports.

TAX BREAKS FOR MANUFACTURED GOODS

The government has also offered temporary tax relief to spur consumption of manufactured goods including: cars, home appliances and building materials.

STRONG-ARMING BANKS

Government-controlled banks and political speeches have pressed private-sector lenders to reduce interest rates charged to consumers, passing on record low borrowing costs to encourage household consumption.

PROTECTIONISM

Brazil plans to raise tariffs on 100 foreign products to protect local manufacturers from a flood of imports. The increased barriers follow protections of the domestic auto industry, including a steep tax hike on foreign-made cars and a quota on Mexican auto imports.

GOVERNMENT PURCHASES

The government is expanding its purchases of military, educational and medical equipment, giving preference to Brazilian-made products.

SUBSIDIZED CREDIT FOR INVESTMENT

State development bank BNDES cut rates on its subsidized loans and offered new credit lines for machinery and other capital goods. Cheap loans to states and incentives for public-private partnerships were also aimed at lifting Brazil's slipping investment rate.

PRIVATIZING AIRPORTS, HIGHWAYS AND RAILROADS

Rousseff, whose leftist Workers' Party once railed against privatizations, has opened major airports, highways and railroads to private investment in order to reduce transport costs and improve industrial competitiveness.

LOWER ENERGY BILLS

The government plans to cut electricity taxes and renegotiate utility concessions in a bid to lower energy costs for industries and households, which are currently among the world's highest.

title: UPDATE:  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker Amid  Intervention  Concerns
text:
--Concerns about currency intervention limit real's reaction to overseas moves

--German court ruling clears way for bond purchases by European Central Bank

--Currency market also awaits news of fresh stimulus by U.S. Federal Reserve

--Brazilian real opens at BRL2.0177, weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL2.0168

(Updates with additional details, comment from trader)

By Jeff Fick

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real traded weaker against the U.S. dollar at the open Wednesday as concerns about local currency intervention offset positive news on Europe's ongoing debt crisis and expectations for fresh stimulus in the U.S.

The real failed to track gains by the euro, a key barometer for the local currency, and other global currencies against the U.S. dollar to open trading at BRL2.0177 to the greenback, according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet. That was weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL2.0168. The real later extended losses to trade at BRL2.0180 to the dollar as of 1300 GMT.

While global markets were enthused after Germany's highest court declined to block the country's ratification of the European Stability Mechanism, local traders were focused on possible intervention in currency markets by the Brazilian central bank. With the real churning steadily toward the BRL2.00 to the dollar mark, the central bank fired a warning shot across trading desks during Tuesday's session. The central bank informally polled market participations about interest in a reverse-swap auction, one trader confirmed.

"The central bank polled the market for interest, but didn't release the results," the Sao Paulo-based trader said. "It's not clear yet whether the bank will intervene or not. We're all waiting to find out."

The recent approach of the real toward the BRL2.00 to the dollar mark has in the past generated intervention by the central bank. Central bankers and government officials have kept the real trading in an informal band between BRL2.00 and BRL2.10 to the greenback in recent months via interventions and tough talk from key government officials. The government appears comfortable with the real in this range because the currency is weak enough to support local manufacturers and exporters without affecting inflation.

The auctions allow investors to swap foreign-exchange positions for government paper linked to interest rates. The interest rate paper is considered safer and less volatile. Typically, the auctions cause the dollar to strengthen against the Brazilian real by removing real exposure from the market. The central bank has actively used the reverse-swaps in recent months to avoid a swift weakening in the Brazilian currency that could hurt local businesses as the European crisis deepened.

On the flip side, the bank has also declined to roll over the swaps as overseas tensions eased in July and August. As the real strengthens toward the BRL2.00 mark ahead of the expiration of the swaps, the lack of a rollover then forces holders of the contracts to seek dollars in the spot market that causes the real to weaken back toward the middle of the informal BRL2.00-to-BRL2.10 trading band. The bank declined to roll over $4.1 billion in dollar-swap contracts that matured Sept. 3. An additional $1.8 billion will mature on Oct. 1, according to data on the central bank's Web site.

The currency market now expects the central bank to likely act as overseas moves give investors a green light to seek higher returns. The German court ruling paves the way for the creation of a permanent bailout mechanism that will provide large-scale financial assistance for debt-saddled countries in the single-currency bloc.

The move sent the euro to near a four-month high against the buck. In addition, yields on bonds issued by financially troubled euro-zone countries Italy and Spain tumbled. Now, European Central Bank President Mario Draghi will also be able to move forward with plans to buy sovereign debt of such countries on the secondary market.

Currency traders also expect global markets to get a fresh injection of liquidity this week from the U.S. Federal Reserve's meeting. The expectation is that a third round of asset purchases known as quantitative easing will be unveiled. Previous such measures by the Fed have caused the Brazilian real to strengthen against the dollar as investors seek higher rates of return.

The overseas news will likely add fuel to the risk-on sentiment, CitiFX said in a morning note. The firm expects the Brazilian central bank to intervene, "holding [the Brazilian real] at 2.01."

title: Brazil stocks a buy as risk aversion fades-Santander
text:
* Domestic-oriented stocks expected to take lead

* Investors may be making wrong assumptions about growth

* Foreign investors seen returning as recovery picks up

* Bovespa index could climb to 70,000 by year-end

By Guillermo Parra-Bernal and Asher Levine

SAO PAULO, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks are a buy because growth in Latin America's largest economy is recovering from a yearlong slowdown and the effect of excessive risk aversion on its economy is easing, strategists at Santander Global Banking & Markets said on Tuesday.

With an industry slowdown on the verge of turning and credit markets recovering as interest rates fall to record lows, shares in financial, real estate, transportation, retail and capital goods companies, known as domestic cyclicals, should gain, said Marcelo Audi, Santander GB&M's equity strategist for Brazil.

The benchmark Bovespa stock index, which is now trading at about 59,200 points, could reach levels somewhere between 65,000 and 70,000 by year-end as foreign investors ease concerns over growth and return to the region's biggest equity market, Audi said.

"Risk perception among investors for a while leaned towards pessimism, for the wrong reasons," Audi said at a presentation at the bank's headquarters in São Paulo. "Now we say: it's time to buy Brazilian stocks."

Audi's call comes as Santander prepares to host more than 180 key clients at a summit in the Brazilian beach resort of Guarujá this week - in which the bank will advise them to add exposure to Brazil's equity markets after two disappointing years for the Bovespa.

The Bovespa, which is up about 4 percent this year, was almost flat in 2010 before tumbling 18 percent last year.

Audi and his team are telling investors to raise allocations in Brazilian domestic cyclicals by a double-digit pace for the first time since mid-2009. Companies in that group include clearinghouse Cetip, capital goods maker Randon Participações, clothing maker Hering and Grupo Pão de Açúcar, the nation's largest retailer.

Analysts disagree over the outlook for corporate earnings in the third and fourth quarters following a slate of disappointing results in the second quarter of the year. Many companies reported weak earnings because of slowing domestic demand and the effects of a declining currency on existing debt, though Audi said that stronger readings of economic data are likely to more than offset the final stage of the "downgrading phase" in earnings estimates.

Domestic cyclicals will gain more weight on the Bovespa index in the coming years, chiefly at the expense of commodity-oriented shares - which right now account for nearly half the index.

Audi dismissed the idea that Brazil is losing its appeal among foreign investors as it becomes more difficult and costlier to do business in the country. Investors will return to the local equity market lured by the nation's growth potential.

Foreign investors flush with cheap capital provided by the European Central Bank early this year helped drive the Bovespa to a nearly 14 percent gain in the first quarter. However, deepening worries over the euro zone debt crisis and concern over heavy government intervention in Brazil's economy caused those gains to reverse in the second quarter. Since June, foreign investors have cautiously returned to Brazilian stocks in search of inexpensive shares and high returns.

Santander's chief economist, Mauricio Molan, expects gross domestic product to expand above 1.5 percent in the third quarter on a sequential basis, later speeding to a 4.2 percent growth rate next year, though below 4 percent for the next decade.

While Molan sees inflation under control at 5.4 percent this year, he expects recent stimulus measures enacted by Brazil's government to contribute to a 6 percent inflation rate in 2013.

title: Brazil's Real Stronger Early Following Industrial Production
text:
BRASILIA--Brazil's real strengthened slightly in early trading Tuesday amid signs from industrial production data that the country's economy may be warming.

As of 1240 GMT, the real traded at BRL2.0282 to the dollar after ending at BRL2.0302 to the dollar Monday, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Traders noted the real inched stronger at the open after the country's IBGE statistics institute reported that industrial output rose by 0.3% in July from the previous month. Though the figure was lower than July last year, it beat analyst forecasts of a 0.2% gain.

The latest data helped reinforce expectations that the local central bank's ongoing rate easing cycle could soon be brought to an end, pointing to stable or possible higher interest rates down the road.

The figures also brought some hopes that flows of investment into the country would resume after a slowdown of the economy seen in the first half of the year.

Also boosting the real Tuesday were rising commodities prices abroad amid expectations key central banks abroad could introduce measures to spur increased growth. In particular, investors are looking to actions by the European Central Bank at a policy meeting Thursday to ease monetary policy or increase purchase of sovereign debt from troubled countries in the region. The wait also continues on the other side of the Atlantic, amid continued speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve could soon announce another round of quantitative easing.

Investors also continued to be on the lookout for intervention actions by Brazil's own central bank to maintain the local currency at a competitive rate.

The bank this week allowed some $4 billion in currency swaps to expire in an effort to hold the local currency at recent levels.

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega last week, meanwhile, guaranteed that the government would maintain an "active" stance in the market in reaction to signs that the real might strengthen too far and compromise the competitiveness of local industries.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Weaker After Rate Cut; Eyes on Swaps, Fed, ECB
text:
SAO PAULO--Brazil's currency weakened slightly Thursday following a widely expected rate cut by the central bank, as investors turn to month-end swaps exipries and the possibility of more intervention by central banks in Europe and the U.S.

Brazil's central bank late Wednesday cut the country's key rate to 7.5%, from 8%, as expected, and gave a strong hint that the year-long easing cycle may come to an end, unless there's a turn for the worse in the domestic economy.

Any further moves would need to be conducted with "maximum parsimony," the bank said in a statement; furthermore, it dropped all mention of concerns about the deterioration in the global economy, which had been present in previous statements.

In the rates market, investors scaled back their bets on more interest rate cuts this year, and started putting more money on interest rate hikes in 2013.

The news has less direct impact on the Brazilian real given the targeted capital controls introduced by the government over the last year to prevent massive capital inflows.

Traders said the market was more focused on the month-end battle over the Ptax rate, which is used to settle monthly futures contracts. Some $4.1 billion in dollar-swap contracts sold in late June will mature Sept. 3, with the expiration of an additional $1.8 billion on Oct. 1, according to data on the central bank's website.

The real weakened to BRL2.0532 per dollar, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset, from BRL2.0472 late Wednesday.

The currency market is also wary of activity in the U.S., with Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke set to speak Friday at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City's annual economic symposium. The market is looking for hints from Mr. Bernanke that the Fed may launch a new round of quantitative easing.

In Europe, authorities are caught up in a row over the role of the ECB, and its ability to undertake massive intervention in European sovereign bond markets. The market has been hoping that government debt purchases by the ECB, as indicated by its president, Mario Draghi, would bring down Spanish and Italian debt yields to sustainable levels, but German officials have rebutted such a possibility.

According to Sidney Yoshiro at Citibank, the Brazilian central bank may opt to wait until there are clearer signs from the U.S. and Europe before making a move. The real is currently in the mid-point of the range of BRL2.00 to BRL2.10 which the market perceives as comfortable for the central bank.

"I think [the Brazilian central bank] will not roll the swaps, not only because of the level...but also because of potential easing coming out of the Fed and ECB. Instead of acting before Bernanke and Draghi, BCB could intervene at higher levels if necessary," Mr. Yoshiro said in a note.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso up on Fed minutes, Brazil real down
text:
* Investors eye central bank meetings next week

* Brazil's real down 0.07 pct, Mexico's peso gains 0.52

By Anna Irrera

RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso gained on Wednesday after minutes of the Federal Reserve's last policy meeting bolstered bets for another round of monetary stimulus, while Brazil's currency lost slightly.

Prompted by concerns about slow economic growth in the world's largest economy, the Fed's meeting minutes from August suggested that central bank was likely to provide another round of stimulus "fairly soon" unless conditions improve.

Monetary stimulus in the United States tends to drive down yields on Treasuries, boosting the appeal of higher-yielding emerging market assets.

Still, some analysts were not completely confident the Federal Reserve would deliver further monetary policy stimulus.

Since the meeting, there's been a spate of upbeat U.S. economic news that could counter the bank's willingness to open up a third round of bond-buying, known as quantitative easing or QE3.

"I don't think the minutes are decisive indication that the Fed will intervene," said Vassili Serebriakov, currency strategist at Wells Fargo in New York. "I'm not sure that this alone will provide sustained positive momentum (of the Mexican peso). Markets are still very much focused on whether European tensions are going to ease in the coming weeks."

Mexico's peso strengthened 0.52 percent to 13.0888 per dollar.

Brazil's real bid down -0.07 to 2.0186 per dollar at the local market close. The real traded in a narrow range as investors remained concerned that the country's central bank would intervene.

Brazil's central bank, which had not waded into the market for several weeks, on Tuesday sold $350.2 million of reverse currency swap contracts, which mimic the purchase of U.S. dollars in futures markets.

The central bank was seen again signaling to markets that it wanted to keep the real from reaching a point where it would hurt local industries competing against cheaper imports.

The real has been mostly trading between 2 per dollar and 2.05 per dollar since the end of June on the threat of central bankintervention.

In addition to acting to protect local exporters, Brazil's policymakers have acted to strengthen the currency if it weakens so much that it could raise import prices and stoke inflation.

Investors have been worried about slowing global growth as the euro zone crisis drags on.

To ease the crisis and spur growth, market players are looking for stimulus relief in the form of bond-buying programs. Both the Federal Reserve and ECB hold policy meetings next month that could decide which, if any, monetary measures they will take to address these problems.

GROWTH EXPECTATIONS IN CHILE

In Chile, the peso advanced 0.19 percent to 481.7000 further boosted by the expectation the economy will grow strongly and interest rates will remain steady.

That would boost revenue for companies while maintaining returns for investors. Interest rates in the United States, Europe and Japan are at or near zero and rates are falling in much of Latin America.

A central bank poll of traders said the bank is likely to hold its benchmark rate at 5.0 percent for three months.

A the same time, Chile's economy is expanding at a rate of about 5.0 percent, a trend that is likely to continue for the near term if economic conditions remain stable, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Tuesday. The estimate is part of planning for the country's 2013 budget.

"The country is passing through a good moment despite the difficulties abroad, and in our region," he said.

Larrain added that the government raised its long-term price estimate for copper to 3.06 a pound from 3.02 a pound. Copper is responsible for more than half the country's exports.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil 's real slips on cenbank  intervention
text:
* Investors bet on likelihood of ECB bond-buying plan

* Chile's peso up 0.4 pct, Mexican peso off 0.3 pct

By Rachel Uranga

MEXICO CITY, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Tuesday after the central bank moved to curb its rise against the dollar, while Chile's peso firmed on hopes the European Central Bank will soon begin buying Spanish and Italian bonds.

Brazil's central bank, which had not waded into the market for several weeks, sold $350.2 million of reverse currency swap contracts, which mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets.

The central bank was seen again signaling to markets that it wanted to keep the real from reaching a point where it would hurt local industries competing against cheaper imports.

"The market is being told 'don't move,'" said Pedro Tuesta, a Latin American currency strategist with Washington-based 4Cast. "The central bank has a lot of money. You don't defy a $350 billion central bank and one that is very willing to use its power," he said referring to the bank's reserves.

The real weakened 0.05 percent to 2.0166 per dollar. The real has been mostly trading between 2 per dollar and 2.05 per dollar since the end of June on the threat of central bank intervention.

In addition to acting to protect local exporters, Brazil's policymakers have acted to strengthen the currency if it weakens so much that it could raise import prices and stoke inflation.

The move to weaken the real comes after a spate of upbeat data showing that Brazil's economic doldrums may be hitting bottom. Last week the country reported the economy in June grew at its fastest pace in 15 months and retail sales clocked a surprising leap.

STIMULUS EXPECTATIONS WEIGH

Chile's peso gained 0.44 percent to 482.6000 as the price of copper, its top export, rose sharply on hopes for stimulus to the global economy from major central banks.

Copper for delivery in three months gained 1.72 percent in London, buoyed by both the outlook for Europe and expectations the United States and China may also provide more stimulus.

European central bankers on Monday sought to quash speculation that it will buy bonds of Spain and Italy to push down borrowing costs, but investors and traders contined to see hopes that the debt crisis is closer to resolution.

In Mexico, the optimism had a different affect on the peso with some traders selling off Latin America's most liquid currency to buy up European assets, Tuesta added.

title: Brazil Textiles Would Benefit From Weaker Real -Coteminas CEO
text:
--Brazilian real not weak enough to boost textile exports

--Currency imbalances should be discussed at the WTO

--Lower interest rates helping stabilize Brazil's exchange rate


 
   By Luciana Magalhaes 
 

SAO PAULO--Exchange-rate misalignments are still at the heart of the competitiveness problem faced by Brazil's industrial sector, according to Josue Gomes da Silva, chief executive officer of textile giant Coteminas.

While government intervention in the market and the systematic reduction of Brazil's base interest rate have helped to weaken the real in relation to the dollar, the textile industry could benefit from an even weaker real, the executive said in an interview.

Mr. da Silva said the current exchange rate of about BRL2.00 to the dollar eliminates the threat of heavy textile imports into Brazil that existed earlier this year, when the real traded around BRL1.70 against the greenback. "But I don't believe it creates the possibility of a significant rate of textile exports by the Brazilian industry," he said.

Coteminas is directly affected by currency trends. The company was able to multiply its exports more than six-fold from 2001 through 2007 because of a comparatively weak real. But a stronger Brazilian currency over the last five years has erased those gains. "Our exports in 2011 were similar to those of 2001," said Mr. da Silva.

The company, Brazil's largest textile conglomerate, was founded by Mr. Da Silva's father, former Brazilian Vice President Jose Alencar Gomes da Silva.

Mr. Da Silva said Coteminas was increasingly focused on the domestic market. He added that even if the exchange rate were to turn more favorable, he would still be cautious about boosting exports. "Exchange-rate trends can change," he noted. "And the countries we compete with have undervalued currencies."

Mr. da Silva declined to speculate on what would be an "equilibrium rate" for the Brazilian real today, saying that was up to economists, who possess "the right methodologies to calculate such misalignments."

However, he warned that a comparatively strong real was generally undermining Brazilian industry in a process economists have dubbed "de-industrialization."

Still, the executive said, currency asymmetries aren't a problem solely for Brazil. Currency imbalances should be part of a global trade discussion to be addressed at the World Trade Organization. "Currency is so crucial that it needs to be discussed by the WTO, and I think they are recognizing that," Mr. da Silva said. He participated earlier this year in debates promoted by the WTO to discuss the relationship between exchange rates and international trade.

In the specific case of Brazil, Mr. da Silva said an important change towards a more neutral exchange rate has been the Brazilian central bank's drive to reduce the country's sky-high interest rates. Brazil's Selic base rate has been cut from the 2011 peak of 12.5% to 8%. "Maybe a good by-product of the international crisis, if there is one, is that Brazil was able to break a long-lasting policy of high interest rates," he said. "As [former Brazilian Finance Minister] Mario Henrique Simonsen used to say, 'interest rates handicap, but currency kills.'"

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso up on rising inflation, Brazil real gains
text:
* Brazilian real seen testing 2-per-dollar level

* Colombia finmin "prays" for stronger intervention

* Brazil real gains 0.28 pct, Mexico peso up 0.53 pct

(Repeats to additional subscribers; Recasts, adds comments)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso gained on T hursday as high inflation boded steady interest rates ahead while Brazil's real got a lift after weak factory data in China backed hopes of more stimulus in Brazil's top trading partner.

Mexico's annual inflation accelerated to its highest rate in more than two years in July on a surge in egg and fresh produce prices, reinforcing bets that policymakers will hold interest rates steady at 4.50 percent in the coming months.

Mexico has held interest rates steady this year even as Brazil slashed borrowing costs to support growth. Rock-bottom interest rates in the United States and Europe have boosted the appeal of higher-yielding Latin American currencies.

Mexican annual inflation rose to 4.42 percent last month, above the central bank's 4 percent comfort zone. Even though there are signs Mexican growth may be slowing, high inflation should keep policymakers from cutting interest rates.

Lower benchmark rates would curb the gains investors can make from borrowing in dollars or euros to invest in Mexican fixed-income assets.

"With expectations that inflation could stay above 4 percent in the coming months, we think that the central bank of Mexico cannot cut interest rates," said Rafael Camarena, an economist at Santander in Mexico City. "In the short term, this helps the peso."

The Mexican peso strengthened 0.53 percent to 13.0860 per dollar, also boosted by data showing claims for unemployment benefits unexpectedly fell in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

Meanwhile, expectations for additional Chinese stimulus rose after data showed growth in the country's factory output slowed to the weakest pace in three years.

China is the largest consumer of Latin American commodities, and prices of raw materials have great sway over currencies in the region.

The Brazilian real gained 0.28 percent to 2.0160 per dollar, leading some analysts to forecast the market could soon test the central bank's willingness to defend the level of 2 reais per dollar, considered by investors an informal floor for the currency.

"The real is nearing the level of 2 per dollar and, with a possible decline in risk aversion, markets may test this level today," said Andre Perfeito, chief economist at Gradual Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

Government officials have repeatedly said that a real stronger than 2 per dollar could hurt Brazilian exporters, leading investors to believe the central bank would step into the market to defend that level.

The tide of yield-hungry global investors has been strengthening currencies around Latin America and pressuring exporters.

Colombian Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry called on industrialists to "pray" that the central bank boosts dollar purchases to ease gains in the currency after noting foreign direct investment in Colombia could reach $17 billion this year and boost the peso.

Echeverry said the monetary authority, which is independent from the government, should step up dollar purchases to $40 million a day to strengthen its arsenal to fight the gaining peso. The bank currently buys at least $20 million a day on the spot market.

text:
3 Aug 2012 11:06 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank  Director: Drought-Related Food Price Increase Is Temporary

3 Aug 2012 11:06 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank  Director: Can't Say How Long Drought Effect Will Last

3 Aug 2012 11:22 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank  Director: No Set Rules On When To Intervene In Forex Market

3 Aug 2012 11:22 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank  Director: Government Actions Should Improve Industry Competitiveness

3 Aug 2012 11:23 EDT *DJ  Brazil Central Bank  Director: Outlook Is For Slow World Economic Growth In Coming Years

3 Aug 2012 11:59 EDT DJ  Brazil CB Director: No Set Rules on When to Intervene in Forex Market


 
   By Jeffrey T. Lewis 
 

SALVADOR, Brazil--Brazil's central bank doesn't have a set of rules its directors apply to decide when to intervene in the foreign exchange market, bank director Carlos Hamilton Araujo said Friday.

"There's no level that determines if the central bank will intervene or not," he said at a press conference following a presentation on the regional economy. "We evaluate market conditions, and we make a decision to act or not."

The central bank has been stepping into the market in recent months, mostly to keep the dollar from weakening too much against the real, but it has also acted to slow the dollar's strengthening.

Earlier this week, the bank declined to roll over dollar swaps because market conditions didn't require it, Mr. Araujo said.

The Brazilian government has been concerned the real had strengthened too much and was hurting the country's exporters. Since the beginning of the year, the government has been taking measures to reduce costs for manufacturers.

Those measures, which include tax cuts and reducing red tape, will be the best way over the long run to improve the competitiveness of Brazilian industry, Mr. Araujo said.

"I don't think there's much doubt that some segments of the Brazilian economy suffer more than others from competition from the rest of the world," he explained. "Actions being taken by the government will improve efficiency in the medium- and long-term."

The government has also been acting to spur consumer demand to help boost domestic growth, as sluggish world economies have reduced demand abroad for Brazilian products.

The outlook is for global economic growth to remain slow in coming years, Mr. Araujo said.

Slower economic growth has led to slower but still steady new job creation, and there are currently no signs of weakness in Brazil's job market, he added.

The central bank expects the world economic situation to help bring the country's inflation rate close to the bank's annual target of 4.5% this year. The bank has a cushion of 2 percentage points in either direction, giving it a target range of 2.5% to 6.5%

The annual rate in 2011 was 6.5%, and it had been declining since then until a recent inflation report showed a spike in food prices. The spike, which was caused by a drought affecting the southern part of the country, will be temporary because the drought will end, Mr. Araujo said.

By Rachel Uranga and Natalia Cacioli

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, July 25 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies gained on Wednesday, halting a three-day slide, as investors speculate that the U.S. Federal Reserve may soon deploy additional monetary stimulus and hopes rose Europe could stem the region's debt crisis.

The Brazilian real firmed by 0.34 percent and the Mexican peso strengthened 0.78 percent. Meanwhile, the Chilean peso was 0.65 percent higher.

A European Central Bank policymaker said on Wednesday he was open to the idea of giving Europe's new permanent rescue fund a banking license, which would enable it to borrow unlimited central bank money and boost its capacity to fight the crisis.

"Anything that increases the ability to purchase sovereign debt and extend the timeframe to which some euro zone countries may need to lower their debt levels and boost growth is seen as a positive development," said Clyde Wardle, a Latin American currency strategist at HSBC in New York. "But all of this is all based on comments rather than firm decisions."

The currencies of Brazil, Mexico and Chile all posted losses in the past three sessions as concerns were heightened that Spain could need a full-fledged bailout.

In the days ahead, Wardle said a jump in yields in Spain and Italy could weaken the Mexican peso, one of the most widely traded currencies and highly sensitive to global economic sentiment.

Meanwhile, signs of a gloomy global economy limited gains in higher-risk assets. Weak readings on Britain's gross domestic product, falling U.S. new home sales and a German business sentiment survey all added to worries about the global economic outlook.

In Brazil, market players remained concerned the government would meddle in currency markets if the real moves outside of the central bank's comfort zone in the range between 2.00 and 2.10 per dollar.

Central bank governor Alexandre Tombini on Tuesday reiterated the bank is ready to intervene into local currency markets when they are "not working properly."

Riskier assets, including emerging market currencies, got a lift from a report in The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday saying the Federal Reserve may be moving closer to more stimulus that would aid the economy.

The Fed's past bond buying programs have driven down yields on U.S. Treasury debt and pushed investors to seek out higher yields in riskier assets.

"Expectations that the Fed may move up its third round of stimulus to August encouraged investors," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

title: Brazilian Real Weakens as Spain, Greece Struggle
text:
--Brazil real weakens as European crisis intensifies

--Brazil central bank will need to intervene, traders say

--Real exits active trading at BRL2.0465 to the dollar


 
   By Brian Asher 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO--The Brazilian real weakened against the dollar Tuesday, with investors seeking the safety of the U.S. currency as the euro-zone economic situation continued to deteriorate.

The real exited active trading at BRL2.0465 to the dollar according to Tullett Prebon via FactSet, weaker than Monday's close at BRL2.0395 to the dollar.

The real tracked the euro's losses against the dollar as Spain's public finances appeared increasingly fragile and Greece seemed ever more likely to leave the euro zone.

Yields on 10-year Spanish government bonds remained above 7.5% in Tuesday trading, a level that proved unsustainable for other euro-zone periphery economies such as Portugal and Greece. Yields shot up Monday on rumors that several of Spain's regional governments would seek central government financial assistance, adding to the chaos of an already-failing Spanish banking industry.

French government officials called Tuesday for greater support to the Spanish government in the form of a larger bailout fund or a European Central Bank bond-buying program to lower Spanish borrowing costs, but a solution to the European crisis remained elusive.

According to traders, the ongoing crisis will continue to pressure the real to weaken.

"The instability generated by the crisis in Spain is leaving investors with a lot of risk aversion," said Reginaldo Galhardo, forex manager at Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "Investors are looking for dollars not because of the fundamentals of the American economy but because there is a sense that the dollar is the only safe currency right now."

With no end to the European crisis in sight, some traders are expecting Brazil's central bank to begin playing a more active role in the forex market.

"The central bank has already announced new dollar-swap auctions for $4.570 billion on Aug. 1 and $6.250 billion on Sept. 2," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer brokerage in Sao Paulo, "but those auctions will only allow investors to roll over their existing positions, so I think the central bank will announce more aggressive actions very soon."

Mr. Medeiros added with net capital outflows, a shrinking trade surplus, and a deteriorating external situation, the real will continue to depreciate without central-bank intervention.

"I expect the central bank will begin selling dollars on the spot market," Mr. Medeiros said.

Net dollar outflows from Brazil were $1.95 billion in the first 20 days of July.

Meanwhile, Brazil's year-to-date trade surplus through July 15 was $7.782 billion, just a little more than half the surplus of $14.830 billion for the same period of 2011.

The real opened at BRL1.731 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.723 to the dollar in the previous session Friday on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange.

Brazil last month raised its financial operation tax, known as the IOF, on fixed-income securities to 6% from 2% as a method to slow heavy portfolio investment, but local authorities said the govenrment was prepared to introduce further measures if the real continued to strengthen.

In the meantime, however, renewed fiscal difficulties in European economies such as Greece, Portugal, and Ireland appeared to reduce the need for additional control measures as investor risk aversion slowed the flows of capital movements.

Further, the specter of monetary tightening in China withdrew some steam from investor intentions to continue pumping funds into Brazil.

But locally, investors Tuesday were also focused on interest rate trends as expectations for Brazilian inflation continued to rise.

China, Brazil's top trading partner, ordered its banks to put more money in reserve in an effort to put the brakes on its economy, which China worries may be overheating. For more see [ID:nSGE6A9091].

Weak Chinese import data added to fears that the Asian giant is not buying as many of Latin America's exports, such as soybeans and iron ore, as it has in previous months.

Fresh concerns about euro zone debt also came back to haunt the market, prompting investors to ditch higher-risk assets. [ID:nLDE6A924J]

The Brazilian real <BRBY> dropped 0.71 percent to 1.709 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, closing at its weakest level in about two weeks.

Investors were also cautious ahead of this week's Group of 20 rich and developing nations summit in South Korea, which is to tackle growing tensions over currency imbalances.

"We're in a very difficult situation. If there is no coordination this time, there is a risk that everyone will go their own way, taking their own measures," said Raphael Martello, an economist at Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

That could mean more intervention measures in Brazil, which has been struggling to contain a rise in the real.

Further tax increases on foreign purchases of local bonds or a reinstatement of income tax for foreigners on those bonds are the most likely options, said Martello.

MEXICAN PESO OUTPERFORMS

The Mexican currency <MXN=> gained 0.52 percent to 12.2365 per dollar after a U.S. government report showed jobless claims fell more than expected in the latest week.

Mexico is less reliant on the commodity trade with China, exporting mainly to the United States.

text:

   By Gerald Jeffris 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Foreign currency continued to pour into Brazil in October, further stoking concerns that the Brazilian currency will continue to gain ground against the dollar, and raising speculation about more government intervention.

A net $6.92 billion flowed into the country in October, well above the average $1.9 billion seen in the first nine months of the year, as investors dumped the damaged dollar and sought out Brazil's real, lured by strong economic growth and high local interest rates. A total of $24 billion has flowed in so far this year, up from $22.86 billion in a similar period in 2009.

"The supply of dollars locally remains much greater than demand, so pressure for strengthening of the real is likely to continue unless the government takes further actions," said Mario Paiva, trader at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Rio de Janeiro. More measures could be forthcoming if the real approaches BRL1.65 per dollar, he said.

The monetary authority also reported that the banks in Brazil increased their bets against the dollar in the futures market to $12.85 billion in October, from $12.43 billion in September. Higher short dollar positions usually mean investors expect the dollar to weaken down the line.

On Thursday, the real ended trading on the local BM&FBovespa exchange at BRL1.6773 per dollar, nearly 1.4% stronger on the day. The real has gained about 3% against the dollar since the beginning of the year, and is 12% stronger than its weakest point this year, in May.

Last month, the government raised the financial operations tax, known as the IOF, on foreign investments in some local financial assets to 6% from 2%, in an effort to slow heavy foreign portfolio investment. Other measures that the government is believed to be considering include the use of reverse swap options, which would reduce pressure on the real in the futures market, and additional tax increases.

Investment into Brazil totaled $5.14 billion in October, well above an average of $2.39 billion seen over the first nine months of this year, while trade inflows totaled $1.78 billion.

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the steps the government has already taken had prevented the strong inflows from taking too much effect on the currency, but said Wednesday's decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve to inject another $600 billion into the U.S. economy through bond purchases would have a detrimental effect for Brazil.

"We're not seeing a strengthening of the real, because of measures that we have taken," said Mantega. "But it's a problem that could be aggravated as long as the U.S. persists in its policies."

Mantega is scheduled to travel with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to the meeting of the Group of 20 heads of state in Seoul next week to discuss a resolution to what the minister has called global "currency wars."

The appreciation of the currency has caused concerns among Brazilian industry leaders and exporters, who argue the strong local currency is encouraging imports and undermining the competitiveness of Brazilian goods abroad.

Currency traders such as Paiva, meanwhile, point out that investors will likely remain attracted to Brazilian markets as long as the country maintains elevated interest rates. Brazil's central bank has set the country's reference Selic interest rate at 10.75% as part of its policy to combat accelerating inflation.

"The U.S. Treasury continues to issue dollars and banks take the money and come here seeking higher returns," he said.

Meanwhile, the central bank reported it bought $7.6 billion on the spot currency market in October, pushing the country's foreign currency reserves up to a record $285.2 billion.

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency surged on Wednesday while Mexico's peso hit a 6-month high ahead of a likely announcement on monetary stimulus measures in the United States.

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to announce after 2:15 p.m. EDT (1815 GMT) asset purchases of at least $500 billion via quantitative easing -- in effect printing money to buy bonds and lower borrowing costs. For more, see: [ID:nLDE6A2062]

That should keep yields on U.S. Treasuries close to record lows, encouraging investors to buy Latin America's higher-yielding bonds.

Brazil is a prime target because the country's benchmark interest rate of 10.75 percent is one of the highest in the world.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> surged as much as 1.1 percent in early trading on Wednesday and was later up 0.70 percent at 1.694 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

The real was also pricing in the region's gains on Tuesday, when Brazil's markets were closed for a public holiday.

"The market was shut yesterday, so there was a movement in other currencies that the real wasn't able to follow. But to a great extent, (the real is stronger) in anticipation of the results of the Fed meeting," said Marianna Costa, an economist with Link Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

"Anything close to $500 billion is already priced into the market. If it was something closer to $1 trillion, there could be some more space for appreciation. If it is less (than $500 billion), the market, like everywhere else in the world, is not going to take it well."

The Mexican currency <MXN=> edged up to its strongest level since May 3, later trading 0.10 percent stronger at 12.2927 per dollar.

"I believe the Fed will move to purchase the expected $500 billion in bonds and the peso won't see a huge move after the announcement," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at Vector brokerage in Monterrey, Mexico.

But if the amount is less than expected, the currency could rapidly weaken to 12.38, he added.

Some economists say the peso could outperform the region's other currencies in the months ahead because of the country's hands-off approach to its currency market. [ID:nN0147422]

WAITING TO STRIKE

Other governments across the region have taken a series of intervention measures, such as dollar purchases and capital controls, to slow rallies in their local currencies.

A stronger currency makes exports more expensive abroad and can cause long-term damage to a country's economy.

For example, data this week is expected to show that Brazil's industrial output slowed again last month because of the strong real.

Fears of new measures hit the Chilean peso <CLP=> on Wednesday. It weakened 0.33 percent to 488.6 per dollar. [ID:nN30113748]

"There are rumors in the market that after the Fed's decision, some new measures will be taken here to curb the peso," said one trader in Santiago.

The peso has strengthened 12 percent since the end of June as the country has recovered rapidly from a devastating earthquake in February.

President Sebastian Pinera said last week his government is working to open capital accounts and relax limits on investments abroad to battle the peso's appreciation.

Analysts say the central bank may also go back to buying dollars in the market or find others ways to encourage capital outflows. [ID:nN20242719] (Additional reporting by Caroline Stauffer and Noe Torres in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)
