title: WRAPUP 2-Brazil sees benign prices; Meirelles warns on  forex
text:
* Policy-makers see benign inflation scenario

* Meirelles warns on forex measures to protect economy

* Despite pressures, inflation seen converging to target

* Yields on rate futures firm after minutes (Adds Mantega comment on creation of IMF index in 8th paragraph)

By Elzio Barreto

SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank signaled Thursday that it is unlikely to raise interest rates in coming months, though concerns over food prices and an overvalued currency continue to hover over an otherwise robust economy.

In minutes from last week's monetary policy meeting, at which the bank left rates unchanged, policymakers said they saw inflation falling closer to the central bank's target range of 4.5 percent, plus or minus 2 percentage points.

The outlook underscored the bank's belief that Brazil's economy remains in a charmed pattern of high growth and relatively low inflation, despite some pressure from rising food prices and robust consumer demand.

"The assumption is that this (recent) hump in inflation will be temporary, despite the heated economy," said Zeina Latif, senior Latin America economist at RBS in Sao Paulo. "There are risks, of course, but I see no problem in keeping rates stable and waiting for more signs."

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on the Selic rate: http://link.reuters.com/pup68k

Graphic on forex intervention: http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p("http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p")

Analysis on Brazil's forex reform: [ID:nN26120199]

Factbox on political risks in Brazil: [ID:nRISKBR]

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Instead, Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles focused on what seems to be the biggest risk to Brazil's economy at the moment -- the real, which like the currencies of many other emerging markets is strengthening against a weak U.S. dollar.

Meirelles urged that the world's largest economies agree on coordinated efforts to prevent currency volatility at next month's meeting of G20 leaders in South Korea. However, he suggested Brazil could go its own way until a deal is reached.

"Obviously, while we don't get there, each country will have to take measures to protect their own currency," Meirelles told reporters in Sao Paulo. "We are taking action to protect the Brazilian economy."

In an interview with daily O Globo on Thursday, Finance Minister Guido Mantega echoed the call for action, suggesting the International Monetary Fund should create an index to measure currency manipulation by different countries. [ID:nN28110123]

NO RATE MOVE

This year Brazil's economy, the largest in Latin America, is set to grow more than 7 percent -- its fastest pace in more than two decades, boosted by public works projects and a surge in credit.

The rapid expansion pressured consumer prices as more and more Brazilians line up to buy new cars, homes and appliances, prompting the central bank to raise borrowing costs by 2 percentage points between April and September before pausing.

The benchmark Selic rate, at 10.75 percent, is among the highest in the world and is attracting a flood of U.S. dollars from overseas investors that has sparked a 5 percent rally in the Brazilian real <BRBY><BRL=> since the end of June.

Recent data point to an improved balance of risks for government administered prices, the central bank's economic policy committee, known as Copom, said in the minutes. Still, the bank said is ready to change monetary policy quickly if pressures on consumer prices increase.

Analysts in a weekly central bank survey expect the Selic to stay at 10.75 percent through the end of 2010, leaving it for central bank officials in Brazil's next administration to decide whether to hike rates to keep prices in check.

All polls released recently forecast Brazilian ruling party candidate Dilma Rousseff winning a runoff vote on Sunday by a wide margin. One of her biggest challenges will be to control government spending in a bid to slow the economy and ease pressures on inflation.

"In the minutes, they're basically saying they will not move, period. But unless there is a real fiscal consolidation, I mean real consolidation, by the second quarter of 2011 reality will sink in," said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington.

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures contracts <0#DIJ:> were little changed after the central bank minutes. The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2> dipped to 11.35 percent from 11.36 percent on late Wednesday.

Food prices that have surged in recent weeks are pressuring inflation more than in the recent past, but the central bank has taken those risks into consideration, the minutes said.

"Despite that, at this moment it remains our understanding that the convergence of inflation to the center of the target will likely happen," policymakers said in the minutes. title: Brazil ready to use swaps to curb real - report
text:
* No legal obstacles to measure, ready to be used

* Reverse currency swaps last used regularly in Sept. 2008

SAO PAULO, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank is ready to use reverse currency swaps in an effort to curb a recent rally in the real, the Valor Economico newspaper reported in its online edition.

"Reverse swaps is a mechanism that the central bank can use at any moment," said Aldo Mendes, the bank's director of monetary policy, according to Valor. "The legal conditions for its use are in place," he added.

Reverse currency swaps are a form of derivative, which would effectively allow Brazil's central bank to buy U.S. dollars in the futures market.

Investors have mulled use of the swaps since the central bank tested the market's demand on July 23, but they have gone off radar screens as the focus turned to other measures.

Brazil recently stepped up its dollar purchases in the spot market in an effort to slow a recent rally in the real <BRBY>, which is hurting exporters and worsening the current account deficit.

The government also this month tripled its tax on foreign bond purchases to 6 percent and raised a tax on the collateral investors must put down to trade in the futures market.

Under the reverse currency swap agreement, the central bank agrees to pay investors Brazil's local interbank rate in exchange for a rate in U.S. dollars for the duration of the contract.

The central bank began offering reverse currency swaps in February 2005, used them regularly until September 2008, and then once more on May 5, 2009. (Reporting by Samantha Pearson; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil's Meirelles: Too soon for new inflows actions
text:
(Adds comment, market prices)

 NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazil Central Bank Governor Henrique Meirelles said on Tuesday that all the necessary actions are being taken to prevent a bubble from occurring due to capital flows into the country.

 Meirelles, asked about possible new measures to slow inflows that have caused Brazil's currency to strengthen, said authorities needed to see the effect of measures already taken.

 "The market is volatile, precisely because of these measures. The market is reacting to news based on anonymous sources. So we have to wait for a while to see the effect of these measures to wait for the market to stabilize," Meirelles said on the sidelines of the Buttonwood Gathering, sponsored by The Economist magazine.

 Brazil adopted a policy of sterilizing investment inflows into the economy  -- issuing local notes that the central bank uses to pay investors from whom it buys dollars -- to try to keep its currency, the real, from appreciating too far or too fast while also adopting rules to stop investors from taking excessive risk in the credit markets.

 "The most dangerous part of the equation is when you have a bubble which is basically generated by credit expansion," Meirelles said.

 While Brazil's financial system has "solid conditions," inflows -- the result of a healthy pace of economic growth and "high level of liquidity in the U.S. and some other economies" -- are creating a challenging environment because of the surge of portfolio and fixed investments, he said.

 "The question again is to keep the equilibrium, to keep the balance in the economy, not to allow for that excess liquidity to create the kind of imbalances which are showing now to be so negative and creating so many losses for so many countries," Meirelles said.

 On Tuesday, the real traded down 0.47 percent at 1.7070 per U.S. dollar <BRBY>. The yield on the 10 percent, real-denominated bond due in January 2013, the most widely traded among the so-called NTN-F notes <BR3YT=RR>, fell for the first day in six, shedding 5 basis points to 11.96 percent. The yield was 12.01 percent on Monday.

 In the past month, Brazil has tripled a tax on foreign investment in local bonds and tightened potential loopholes to make the tax more effective.

 Those measures, along with fears of further intervention, have had some impact on the currency, but Brazil's real is still up about 6 percent against the U.S. dollar since late June.

 Speculation has mounted that the government is planning fresh measures to curb inflows to fixed-income markets. However, Brasilia on Monday ruled out new capital gains taxes on foreign holdings of local bonds to curb the real's rally.

 "At the end of the day, I would call the overall measures taken in general as prudential rules," Meirelles added.  (Additional reporting by William Schomberg in New York and Daniela Machado and Guillermo Parra Bernal in Sao Paulo; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: ANALYSIS-Brazil's  currency  battle endangers  forex  reform
text:
* Convertibility would attract even more FX speculation

* Global "currency war" to leave permanent scars

* Offshore NDF trading boosted by intervention measures

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's battle to slow a recent rally in its currency is jeopardizing plans to open the real to international trading.

With a view to one day becoming a major financial hub with as much clout as Hong Kong or New York, Brazil has been working to transform the real into a so-called convertible currency. That means putting behind it a past of painful currency crises and lifting heavy restrictions on the real <BRBY>.

But in recent months the government has taken a step backward, introducing even more regulation to the market in an effort to curb a currency rally that is hurting exporters and undermining the competitiveness of the Brazilian economy.

"It makes policymakers more reluctant to pursue full convertibility under these circumstances," said Mike Moran, a senior currency strategist at Standard Chartered in New York.

"They will continue to say this is their long term goal, but in the immediate future, the prospect for full convertibility for the likes of Brazil is very weak."

Currently, the central bank permits only a few big banks to trade in the local market, making foreign exchange transactions more costly and time-consuming for everybody else.

But if these restrictions were lifted, Brazil's currency problems would be even worse, some analysts say.

Foreign investors have flocked to Brazil partly due to its high-yielding bonds. The deluge of cash has boosted the real, making it one of the world's most overvalued currencies.

"Convertibility? Forget about it," says Carlos Gandolfo, a partner at Sao Paulo's Pioneer brokerage. A freely tradable real would attract even more hot money, or "motel money" as it is known locally -- thrill-seeking investors who are in and out of the country in hours.

That is exactly the type of investor Brazil has been fending off with recent intervention measures, such as tax rises on foreign purchases of bonds. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on intervention: http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p ("http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Convertibility could also bring more volatility to the market, as has been the case in Mexico, one of the few countries in Latin America to have a convertible currency.

BATTLE SCARS

In March this year, Brazil's trading institutions got together to launch 'Brain' -- the latest project to transform the country into a financial superpower, with one of its goals being to free up the local currency market.

The project has been on hold for the past three to four months because of Brazil's ongoing presidential election, said Alan Gandelman, chief executive officer of the Brazil division of ICAP, the world's biggest interdealer broker.

"The government wouldn't want (convertibility) now with the real at these levels, but maybe four or five years down the road it could be achieved," he said.

However, it could take even longer if the global battle over currency intervention, which dominated a G20 meeting last week, proves to be part of a long-term structural shift.

"There has been a mistrust of what you used to call the Washington Consensus of freely open capital markets, freely convertible, freely floating currencies," said Win Thin, a currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

But convertibility is not just up to the government: the market also has to want it.

If intervention were done "in a way to lead investors to believe that the risk of that currency had risen because of the force of government intervention, I think it could have an effect," said Gustavo Loyola, a former central bank president.

In contrast, Chile has taken softer measures to deal with its rallying currency, partly for fear that intervention will delay plans to make the peso convertible.

Despite its small size, Chile also dreams of becoming Latin America's financial hub.

Judging by the non-deliverable forward market, investors are souring on trading the real.

NDFs are derivatives that simulate trading in restricted currencies such as the real. The contracts are mostly traded in New York and settled in dollars.

Trading in Brazilian NDFs is facing long-term decline and should eventually die out when the real becomes convertible, as has happened in other developing countries such as Russia.

But after the government's tax rise last week on futures contracts, ICAP saw volumes in Brazilian NDFs soar about 20-30 percent, said Anna Didier, head of NDFs for the broker.

Other investors are weighing costs and contemplating coming back to the market, she said, because even though NDFs are expensive, the rules of the game are more transparent.

"Everyone is going back to the drawing board." (Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Ana Nicolaci da Costa in Brasilia, and Caroline Stauffer in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: UPDATE 2-INTERVIEW- Brazil  sees no limit to  forex intervention
text:
* Govt will do what is needed to contain real - Augustin

* Treasury seeking to expand real debt market abroad

* To do 2-3 more issuances of real debt this year (Adds details)

By Ana Nicolaci da Costa and Isabel Versiani

BRASILIA, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazil will spare no efforts to arrest excessive gains in its currency and is looking at expanding its real-denominated debt market abroad, Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said in an interview on Monday.

Brazil's government has increased efforts to contain a rally in the local currency in recent weeks.

Last Wednesday it sold real-denominated debt in global markets for the first time since June 2007 in an effort to reduce capital inflows.

Foreign investors have been flocking to Latin America's largest economy as Brazil's 10.75 percent lending rate offers an attractive alternative to ultra-low interest rates in advanced economies. Those inflows helped take Brazil's real <BRBY> to two-year highs earlier this month. For more, see http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p("http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p")].

"The government is placing no limits on its currency intervention, we will do whatever is necessary," Augustin told Reuters in an interview.

In the past month, Brazil's government has tripled a tax on foreign investment in local bonds and tightened potential loopholes to make the tax more effective. The central bank has also continued to buy dollars in the spot market.

Those measures, along with fears of further intervention, have had some impact on the currency, but Brazil's real is still up about 6 percent since late June.

For the Treasury, one option is to build a stronger real-denominated debt market abroad to arrest the flows of capital into Brazil.

"This means having a bigger volume, much bigger than we have today," Augustin said.

The government plans to issue global bonds denominated in reais at least another two or three times this year, he said. Brazil last week sold $597 million of real-denominated bonds due 2028, but Augustin said the next issuance would likely be in a shorter, 10-year maturity.

Brazil has the conditions to launch a 100-year bond, Augustin added, after Mexico launched Latin America's first century bond earlier this month. [ID:nN05194972].

"It's a possibility," he said. "Brazil today has very solid fundamentals and this allows us to have debt in the maturity we deem adequate."

Augustin did not rule out further increases in a tax on foreign investment in local bonds or the possibility of once again extending the settlement period for currency contracts, as authorities did earlier in October, to allow the Treasury to buy more dollars in the local market. [ID:nN06284208].

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latin American  currencies  firm after G20
text:
* Traders resume dollar selling after G20 meeting

* Brazil's real adds 0.5 pct, Mexican peso gains 0.3 pct

* Mexican peso hits highest level since early May

* Chilean peso adds 0.5 pct as copper price soars

(Adds data on Brazil's current account, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed early on Monday as the dollar suffered broad losses following an agreement over the weekend from a Group of 20 nations meeting in South Korea.

Finance ministers of the G20 group of rich and emerging nations vowed to shun competitive currency devaluations, agreeing that exchange rates should be determined by the market.

Investors took this as a green light to resume the status quo in currency markets, which has been to sell the dollar on expectations the Federal Reserve will soon unveil a second round of quantitative easing. [ID:nTOE69M004]

"As is often the case with such meetings, the communique that followed the G20 meeting has been deemed to be vague," said Jane Foley, senior currency strategist at Rabobank in London.

Latin American currencies have enjoyed a multi-week rally because of speculation over U.S. stimulus measures, which are likely to keep yields on U.S. Treasuries close to record lows and so encourage more investors to buy higher-yielding debt in countries such as Brazil.

But fears of government intervention have helped to keep a lid on Brazil's real <BRBY>, which bid 0.47 percent stronger to 1.699 percent on the local market.

This is not far from a two-year high against the dollar, which the real hit earlier this month, and just stronger than the 1.70-per dollar level, which is deemed unofficially to be the government's comfort level.

Brazil has taken aggressive action to curb the recent rally in the real, which is making exporters' goods more expensive abroad and worsening the current account deficit.

Data on Monday showed that the country's current account deficit widened by more than expected in September to $3.9 billion from a gap of $2.45 billion in the same month last year. [ID:nN25261248]

Investors were still trying to understand the full implications of recent measures, such as this month's tax increase on foreign bond purchases, said one head trader in New York.

"I continue to have a more tactical stance on the real, trading the extremes as the noise continues to be high," he said.

Brazil may also consider forcing foreign investors to pay income tax on any capital gains made from government securities as one possible way to curb inflows, local newspaper O Estado de S. Paulo newspaper reported on Monday. [ID:nN25275398]

MEXICAN PESO NEAR 6-MONTH HIGH

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.28 percent to 12.2969 per dollar, hitting its strongest level since the beginning of May.

As fears of a double-dip recession in the United States have faded, the peso has quickly recovered. As a more freely-traded currency, the peso also does not present any intervention risk for investors.

The Chilean peso <CLP=>, which has been under pressure because of fears of government intervention, firmed 0.45 percent to 484.80 per dollar. It was lifted by a rally in the price of copper, the country's main export.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said on Monday that the sharp appreciation of Chile's peso is comparable to that of other currencies in nominal terms. He did not signal any immediate intervention. [ID:nN25259357]

title: DJ AT A GLANCE: Exchange Rates Dominate G-20 Finance Officials' Meeting
text:
THE EVENT: Finance ministers and central bank governors from the Group of 20 leading industrialized and emerging nations are gathering in Gyeongju, southeastern Korea, for meetings Friday and Saturday. Dow Jones Newswires' coverage of the event can be found by searching the code N/G20.

THE SITUATION: While the meeting is for the ministers and governors to prepare for the G-20 summit in Seoul next month, the issue of exchange rates will likely dominate discussions amid the U.S. dollar's continued weakness, the Chinese yuan's relative strength and interventions by emerging economies to damp their currencies' rise.

An early draft communique being circulated shows the group aims to work toward a "more market-determined exchange-rate system" and promises to "refrain from competitive undervaluation" of their currencies.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Thursday he plans to use the meetings to advance efforts to "rebalance" the world economy so it is less reliant on U.S. consumers, to move toward establishing "norms" on exchange-rate policy, and to persuade others the U.S. doesn't aim to devalue its way to prosperity.

IN THE BACKGROUND: The U.S. has been pressuring China to speed up the appreciation of the yuan, saying it is being kept artificially low to support its exporters, resulting in the U.S. posting a massive trade deficit with the Asian giant. China has maintained, however, that the problem lies with U.S. and its easy money policies, which have weighed on the dollar.

In the meantime, other emerging nations, notably G-20 members Brazil and South Korea have had to repeatedly intervene in markets to slow the rise in their currencies and the tide of capital inflows as money from low-yielding developed markets seek higher returns in the less developed world.

There is concern that the currency tensions could escalate into an all-out "currency war" that leaves no winners.

Australian Treasury Secretary Ken Henry Thursday called on major world economies not to retreat to protectionist policies, warning that current weak conditions globally are a likely breeding ground for bad economic policy making.

MARKET ACTION: Foreign exchange majors are trading in a tight range as investors adopt a cautious approach. The dollar, which rose against its major rivals on Thursday, is steady as traders appear reluctant to push the greenback much higher before the G-20 outcome is known.

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Brazil
text:
BRASILIA, Oct 20 (Reuters) - An unexpectedly close battle in Brazil's presidential Oct. 31 runoff election has heightened investor unease and threatens to fuel financial market volatility in Latin America's largest economy.

The ruling Workers' Party candidate Dilma Rousseff, a pragmatic leftist, nearly won an outright majority in an Oct. 3 first-round ballot and is still the favorite to become the country's next president.

But markets have begun to price in the possibility that centrist Brazilian Social Democracy Party candidate Jose Serra could pull off a surprise victory win, spurred by some polls showing Rousseff's lead narrowing.

Rousseff, a former chief of staff to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has benefited from a booming economy and the president's popularity, but she has watched her lead over Serra narrow substantially ahead of the runoff..

With some opinion polls suggesting Serra, a former Sao Paulo state governor favored by some business leaders for his managerial experience, was within striking distance of an upset, bonds rallied and interest rate futures dipped on expectations he would cut government expenditures.

Expansive government spending, growing intervention in natural resource industries, such as oil and minerals, and volatile political support for the next president are among the risks to watch in Brazil over the next year.

ECONOMIC POLICY

Both candidates are expected to keep most of the market-friendly policies of Lula's center-left government.

Rousseff, however, is likely to continue heightening the role of state enterprises -- as Lula has done -- in strategic industries such as energy, oil and telecommunications, and steer clear of sweeping labor or fiscal reforms that some investors say would improve Brazil's business climate.

Serra has suggested a more interventionist role in monetary and currency policies and could scrap plans to increase state control over massive new oil reserves. He has called for lower interest rates, says the real currency is overvalued and wants the central bank to follow the government's economic policy.

Rousseff has praised the central bank and said it should keep focusing on controlling inflation before considering economic and job growth when setting monetary policy.

There are doubts about how firmly the candidates would push for a second generation of structural reforms to ensure Brazil's international competitiveness.

Both agree on the need to overhaul complicated tax system to encourage investment, but they have provided few details. Serra wants to reform the pension system by cutting benefits for some civil servants, while Rousseff plays down the need for far-reaching reforms soon.

Neither proposes nationalizing private companies, but Rousseff's proposal to strengthen state firms could weaken private sector participation in banking, oil and utilities.

Rousseff has said the growth of state banks would not infringe on private banks, which she said were necessary to drive economic expansion and spur competition.

Plans to use state-owned telephone company Telebras to expand broadband Internet access are moving ahead faster than expected, which could affect the share performance of private telecoms competing for the same market.

Rousseff also has adopted Lula's proposal to strengthen state-owned power company Eletrobras, though the intent may be to expand mostly abroad.

Serra is widely believed to be tougher than Rousseff on fiscal policy, even though he has made a series of electoral proposals, including a rise in the minimum wage and pension benefits, which would increase government spending by an estimated 1 percent of gross domestic product.

Cutting administrative expenditures, as he did in the Sao Paulo state and city governments, could offset such cost increases, but public accounts would likely improve more gradually and interest rates fall more slowly than some investors had initially assumed in a Serra administration.

Rousseff has pledged an ambitious primary budget surplus target of 3.3 percent of GDP but, wary of risking her poll lead, has been noncommittal on unpopular budget cuts.

What to watch:

-- Serra rising further in the polls

-- Details of Rousseff proposals for state enterprises.

-- Signs that Rousseff is preparing austerity measures to meet her budget target early in office.

GOVERNMENT SPENDING

Brazil's government is maintaining a high level of spending before the election, potentially fueling inflation and forcing the incoming president to adopt austerity measures.

Public spending rose sharply in 2009, cutting the primary budget surplus to an eight-year low of 2 percent of GDP. Finance Minister Guido Mantega has vowed to raise the surplus to 3.3 percent of GDP in 2010 -- in the 12 months to August it was 2.01 percent.

What to watch:

-- Continued weak monthly primary surplus figures would indicate worsening fiscal discipline and could push up interest rate futures.

-- Signs that Lula could tighten spending after the election to spare Rousseff from implementing unpopular austerity measures.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real sinks on tax rise, China move
text:
* China's surprise interest rate hike boosts U.S. dollar

* Brazil's real down 1.5 pct, Mexican peso loses 0.7 pct

* Analysts doubt long-term success of Brazil FX measures

* Chile's peso sinks 1.1 pct as copper prices fall (Adds comments by Brazil's finance minister, context, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real dropped sharply on Tuesday after an interest rate hike in China lent Brazil's government a hand in its fight to curb a currency rally.

The Brazilian government late Monday raised the tax it charges foreigners to buy local bonds and also increased the levy on any derivatives trading they do, hoping to scare away foreign investors the government blames for driving up the real.

The real <BRBY> was headed for its biggest one-day loss in about four months on Tuesday, sinking 1.48 percent to 1.689 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

But with gains of about 100 percent since 2003, the real is still the world's most overvalued major currency, according to Goldman Sachs.

Analysts said the currency's sharp losses against the dollar on Tuesday had just as much to do with China's decision to raise interest rates, adding that the increase to Brazil's so-called IOF tax would not keep foreigners away for long. For details, see [ID:nN18280200]

"The currency market is reflecting what's going on abroad just as much as the IOF," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo. "China's interest rate hike is making the dollar strengthen, which is also causing the real to depreciate."

The dollar's sharp gains caused weakness across the range of Latin America's currencies on Tuesday.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> dropped 0.74 percent to 12.5016 per dollar as investors saw China's announcement as an excuse to take profits following gains of roughly 6 percent since the beginning of September.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> lost 1.1 percent to 486.10 per dollar as the strong greenback also pushed down the price of copper, the country's main export. A Chilean central bank official told reporters on Tuesday that the bank was not currently discussing currency intervention. [ID:nDEP003370]

CALL FOR HELP

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, later Tuesday praised China's decision to raise interest rates, saying the hike was "in the right direction." [ID:nN19130365]

In the lead-up to this week's G20 finance ministers meeting in South Korea, Mantega has urged countries such as the United States to help ease the problems of emerging economies, saying Brazil could not fight the global "currency war" alone.

A weak U.S. dollar and low interest rates across much of the developed world have attracted a flood of money into emerging economies, forcing countries from Colombia to Thailand to intervene in their currency markets.

A strong currency makes exports more expensive and can cause long-term damage to a country's economy.

Speculation has mounted that the U.S. Fed will decide soon to pump more money into its struggling economy. Such a measure could keep the dollar weak and yields on U.S. Treasuries close to record lows, encouraging even more foreign investors to seek higher-yielding bonds in countries such as Brazil.

After hiking the IOF tax on bonds only two weeks earlier, Brazil's government raised its tax on foreign bond purchases to 6 percent from 4 percent.

The government also announced on Monday it will increase the tax on the collateral that foreign investors have to put up when they want to trade Brazilian derivatives -- to 6 percent from 0.38 percent.

But analysts doubted the effectiveness of the moves. The tax on bond purchases would need to be much higher to push investors away from Brazil's high yields and attractive economy, they said. Also, the government needs a constant stream of so-called "hot money" to plug it's growing current account deficit.

"Fundamentals are solid for Brazil and we will be ready to resume recommending buying the real as soon as the dust settles," analysts at BNP Paribas said in a note to clients Tuesday.

The reaction in the bond and interest rate futures market was limited. The yield on the 10-year fixed-rate, real-denominated note, known as NTN-F <BR10YT=RR>, rose slightly as investors moved out of the market.

The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily traded contracts early in the session, rose to 11.29 percent from 11.28 percent. (Additional reporting by Caroline Stauffer in Mexico City, editing by Todd Benson and Jeffrey Benkoe)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currency  rally falters after Fed
text:
* Dollar recovers worldwide, curbing regional rally

* Brazil's real seesaws, Chilean peso flat

* Colombia's peso falls after intervention rule change

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 15 (Reuters) - A recent rally in Latin America's foreign exchange markets ground to a halt on Friday as a stronger dollar and worries over regional currency interventions gave traders a good excuse to take profits.

Brazil's real and Chile's peso have hit their highest levels in two years against the dollar this week on the prospect of U.S. stimulus measures, which could bring a deluge of cash into the region.

U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on Friday said high unemployment and low inflation point to a need for a further easing of U.S. monetary policy. [ID:nN15187998]

Easing measures could keep yields on U.S. Treasuries close to record lows and weaken the dollar, encouraging investors to borrow cheaply and pour their money into higher-yielding debt in countries such as Brazil via the so-called 'carry trade'.

But after sinking to multi-month lows against a basket of currencies earlier in the session, the dollar recovered.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened as a result, but later recovered as traders also digested comments from the country's finance minister.

Guido Mantega told reporters on Friday the government was waiting for currency markets to stabilize before taking fresh measures to curb the real's rise. [ID:nN15201659]

The currency has also recently come under pressure as uncertainty has developed over the outcome of the country's presidential election. [ID:nN14103392]

Investors had previously dismissed Brazil's election as a "non-event" because ruling party candidate Dilma Rousseff looked set to sail to an easy victory, bringing few changes to current policy.

But opposition candidate Jose Serra has gradually gained in recent polls, prompting a last-minute scramble on trading floors. Serra is expected to take a tougher stance on Brazil's rallying currency.

"The way things are going, no one can now doubt that victory is apparently up for grabs, thus making the question as to how his tenure could differ from Dilma's even more relevant," said Mauricio Rosal, Latin American economist at Raymond James in Sao Paulo in a research note.

The threat of more aggressive intervention in Colombia prompted the country's peso to weaken 0.37 percent to 1808 per dollar on Friday.

The central bank modified its foreign exchange intervention rules, indicating it might be about to increase its dollar purchases in the market. [ID:nN15189451]

CHILEAN INTERVENTION SEEN UNLIKELY

The Chilean peso <CLP=> was flat at 479 per dollar, the day after the country's central bank raised the country's benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent.

The bank has slowed the pace at which it raises rates for fear that higher rates would fuel an even bigger rally in the peso, which is trading around a 29-month high.

"The main reasons for the slower tightening pace, compared with the 50 basis point rise last time, are weak growth in developed economies posing some risks to emerging market growth", along with less concern about inflation, said Nick Chamie of RBC Capital Markets.

"The central bank does not make as much reference to CLP strength as we would have expected suggesting that intervention risks are still not imminent," he said.

But the threats kept coming. Chile's peso appreciation is worrying and could soon have an adverse effect on economic activity and inflation, Central Bank board member Enrique Marshall said in a presentation posted on the bank's website on Friday. [ID:nN15190638]

Meanwhile, U.S. stimulus measures are likely to have mixed effects on Mexico. The country sends about 80 percent of its exports to the United States, and any perceived weakness in the U.S. economy suggests reduced demand for those goods.

The central bank kept its interest rate unchanged at 4.5 percent at a meeting on Friday, in an effort to boost growth.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> dropped 0.2 percent to 12.439 per dollar.

title: =DJ  FOREX  VIEW: Mexico Likely To Stay Neutral In  Currency  Battles
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Latin American countries fighting what some governments see as a currency war aren't likely to find an ally in Mexico.

Amid global tensions over exchange rates, Brazil has raised a tax on certain financial operations in an effort to discourage the heavy foreign capital inflows that are boosting its real, while Thailand this week removed a tax break on foreign investment in its government bonds in an attempt to slow the baht's rise, and the U.S. Federal Reserve appears poised for another round of quantitative easing that could weaken the dollar.

The Mexican peso still has room to recover from the beating it took in 2008 and 2009, despite its own recent appreciation. The peso is trading around MXN12.40 to the dollar, up 6.5% year-to-date and 26% from its all-time low in March 2009, but still nearly 20% weaker from before the 2008 crisis. Brazil's real, meanwhile, is up 5% year-to-date but 41% stronger from the end of 2008.

Mexican policy makers appear loathe to intervene to weaken the peso and give Mexican exports a competitive advantage.

During a weekend visit to Washington, Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero said his country "believes and trusts" in a free-floating currency, which has allowed Mexico to absorb external shocks in the past. Cordero said countries need to be careful when implementing "easy fixes" such as capital controls, noting that the Brazilian real continues to appreciate despite such measures. Exchange policy shouldn't be a trade policy tool, he added.

Cordero described Mexico's currency circumstance as "fortunately different" than that of some other Latin American countries, alluding to recent export gains in the U.S. market. Mexican products now represent 13% of U.S. imports compared with 10% just three years ago, Cordero said, attributing the advance to structural advantages that Mexico boasts over other countries--its geographical location, border trade infrastructure, and improving labor productivity--rather than relying on foreign exchange advantages.

"It's evident that Mexico is a stand-alone case compared with South American countries because of its greater exposure to the U.S. trade balance. We have seen that when the risk premium rises due to uncertainty about the U.S. recovery, the peso is the currency that most suffers," said Moises Junca, chief Latin America foreign exchange strategist with BBVA Securities.

Yet some see Mexico's export gains as a crutch.

"The Mexican peso has been a laggard among the region's appreciating currencies for a reason: whereas other countries can rely on some degree of domestic demand strength to cushion their economies against currency strength, the Mexican recovery remains externally driven," Luis Arcentales, an economist with Morgan Stanley, wrote in a Monday research note. "And with export-oriented industry already decelerating, Mexico seems to be the economy that can least afford significant currency strength."

Gross domestic product expanded 5.9% in the first half of the year and is expected to slow in the second half for full-year growth between 4% and 5%. Below-capacity output and low inflation have allowed the central bank to hold its benchmark overnight lending rate at 4.5% since July 2009, with no signs that it's contemplating a rate increase before the second half of 2011. Brazil's benchmark selic rate is 10.75% and expected to rise early next year.

The rebound in exports after a trade slump in 2009, rising crude prices, and remittances from Mexicans living in the U.S. are all sources of peso strength. Also this year, Mexico's Oct. 1 inclusion in Citibank's World Government Bond Index is seen attracting as much as $16 billion in fresh foreign investment, much of which has presumably already arrived.

While policy makers in countries like Brazil, Colombia and Peru are intervening to limit currency appreciation, Mexico has adhered to a comparatively subtle mechanism of selling $600 million in dollar put options each month. The Bank of Mexico uses the options to build foreign reserves when the peso is appreciating; commercial banks can exercise the options when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average.

Recent peso gains have led to some discussion on whether the central bank might opt to raise the dollar amount of the options it sells each month. RBC Capital Markets thinks that's a possibility, but adds that "the MXN is one of the least vulnerable emerging market currencies to foreign exchange intervention."

(Amy Guthrie first began covering emerging markets in 1999. Currently she writes about Mexican financial markets from Mexico City, and is a former managing editor of the LatinFinance magazine. She can be reached at amy.guthrie@dowjones.com)

title: Brazil  has ammunition to  intervene  in  FX  - finance minister
text:
* Brazil monitoring impact of tax on foreign investment

* May impose other measures if tax fails to curb FX gains (Recasts with quotes from finance minister, adds byline)

By Walter Brandimarte

NEW YORK, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Brazil has "a lot of ammunition" to intervene in its foreign exchange market if a recent increase in taxes on foreign investment fails to curb the strength of its currency, the real, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Tuesday.

Mantega considered it too early to gauge the currency impact of the government's decision to double to 4 percent the IOF tax on foreign investment in domestic sovereign bonds.

"At this moment we're waiting to see if the currency will stabilize. It's possible that it happens," he told reporters at the Council of the Americas. Earlier, in a presentation to investors, he said the tax had been successful in curbing currency gains when it was introduced last year.

"If it doesn't work this time, we will be thinking about other measures," Mantega said.

He said Brazil's sovereign wealth fund is "ready to buy dollars" but hasn't done so yet because, for now, the central bank has been acquiring enough dollars from the market.

Mantega, who attended the semi-annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Washington over the weekend, repeated his call for coordinated international action to rebalance the global economy and stop an ongoing "currency war (from turning) into a trade war."

He urged strong, developed economies to resort to more fiscal stimulus rather than monetary policy to boost domestic consumption and criticized the U.S. Federal Reserve for "considering more quantitative easing" to boost the economy.

"I don't think it will reactivate the economy, but it will weaken the dollar," he said. (Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: =DJ AT A GLANCE: Officials Warn  Currency  Fight Can Undermine Global Economy
text:
THE NEWS: A number of high-ranking officials spoke out Thursday on the currency battles that have spurred tensions around the globe, with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn warning that such conflict can undermine the world economy.

A day after U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner essentially accused China of sparking a global currency war, Strauss-Kahn said the IMF needs to launch a "systemic stability initiative" to build international consensus on global currency policies.

Also Thursday, European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet stressed that currency levels should reflect economic fundamentals, while World Bank head Robert Zoellick said multilateral bodies have a role to play in resolving currency tensions but that, ultimately, countries must tackle the issue by rebalancing their economies.

The comments come as the IMF and World Bank hold meetings in Washington this week.

COUNTRIES ON CURRENCY: China is committed to moving toward a flexible exchange rate regime, but the pace currency reform has to be gradual, a People's Bank of China official said. The official added that there are signs of a currency war, but China "is working hard against it."

India's central bank may move to cap gains in the rupee if it rises to 43-42 against the U.S. dollar, though intervention is unlikely at current levels, a senior finance ministry official said after the local currency hit a 25-month high against the greenback.

Meanwhile, Brazilian central bank President Henrique de Campos Meirelles said a combination of U.S. policies, European economics and China's fixed exchange rate has led to major distortions in currency markets.

THE MARKETS: The dollar recovered from a broad slump against most of its rivals Thursday as investors pared bets on riskier assets ahead of the closely watched reading of monthly U.S. employment figures due Friday.

The dollar early Thursday dropped to a 15-year low against the yen, a record low against the Swiss franc and its lowest level since 1983 against the Australian dollar.

Late Thursday, the euro was at $1.3912 from $1.3929 late Wednesday, according to EBS via CQG. The common currency rose as high as $1.4030. The dollar was at Y82.40 from Y82.96, after falling as low as Y82.11. The The dollar was at CHF0.9669 from CHF0.9618.

The ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, was at 77.464 from 77.435, rebounding from a dip below 77, its lowest level since January.

WHAT THEY'RE SAYING: "Many do consider their currency as a weapon, and that's certainly not for the good of the global economy," the IMF's Strauss-Kahn said.

"The current policies of the developed countries is leading to very significant capital flows into some of the emerging countries. This is putting upward pressure on exchange rates," said South African Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan, who heads the Group of 24 emerging and developing countries.

"More than ever, I think that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals," the ECB's Trichet said. "Excess volatility ... [has] adverse implications for economic and financial stability."

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso suffered its biggest one-day loss in over a month on Thursday as concerns about upcoming U.S. jobs data prompted investors to take profits.

The mood of caution across global markets boosted the dollar, while the rest of Latin America's major currencies gave up early gains.

Data on Friday is expected to show that U.S. nonfarm payrolls were broadly unchanged last month, suggesting the world's biggest economy continues to stagnate. For details, see [ID:nN05187700]

The peso <MXN=> plunged 0.73 percent to 12.5688, its biggest one-day loss since Sept. 7.

"Tomorrow's data is expected to be bad -- no one wants to go to sleep with an open position," said Ramon Cordova, a trader at brokerage BASE in Monterrey, Mexico.

Mexico's markets are often hit by weak U.S. economic data due to the country's close trade links with the United States. A lower-than-expected reading of Mexico's consumer prices also piled on the pressure.

"Inflation expectations were down and this caused the peso to depreciate a bit, but (Friday's U.S.) payrolls report is the most relevant factor," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at brokerage Vector in Mexico City.

Traders were also looking for any excuse to take profits with the peso having rallied more than 5 percent since the beginning of September, outperforming many of the region's currencies.

THE GOOD, THE BAD AND THE UGLY

But a weak U.S. payrolls report also has an upside for the region's currencies. Speculation has mounted that the U.S. central bank is about to inject more money into its struggling economy, prompting the dollar to weaken. [ID:nN06278713]

A worse-than-expected jobs number on Friday could further fuel that speculation, weakening the dollar and so boosting Latin America's currencies.

"If it comes out weak, that raises the chance that the Fed will take measures at its next meeting, at the beginning of November," said Luciano Rostagno, the chief strategist for CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo. But if it's strong, the dollar may briefly strengthen, he said.

However, if the number is particularly bad, causing a mass exodus from higher-risk assets, the real is also likely to weaken given its emerging-market status.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.679 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market in early afternoon trading, as traders evaluated these various options.

Concerns over intervention also weighed after the government this week doubled its tax on foreign purchases of bonds in an effort to curb inflows.

The stronger dollar also caused the price of copper, Chile's main export, to plunge in afternoon trading. This prompted the Chilean peso <CLP=> to reverse its gains and trade 0.19 percent weaker at 483.1 per dollar.

As in the case of Mexico, traders were also looking for opportunities to take profits on the peso which is trading at around a two year-high.

title: UPDATE: Geithner: China Yuan Policy Triggering  Currency  War
text:
(Adds Secretary comments and background.)


 
    By Ian Talley 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--China's undervalued currency is triggering an international currency war that risks undermining the global economic recovery, U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Wednesday.

"When large economies with undervalued exchange rates act to keep the currency from appreciating, that encourages other countries to do the same, and this sets off a dangerous dynamic," Geithner said.

Geithner addressed two issues--exchange rates and the fiscal strategies--expected to take center stage in ministerial meetings around the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting this week and ahead of the Group of 20 nations summits in coming weeks.

Over time, more and more countries face stronger pressure to lean against the market forces pushing up the value of their currencies and the collective impact causes inflation and asset bubbles in emerging economies or else depressed consumption growth, the secretary said.

Japan, South Korea and Brazil have each intervened in their currencies to counter rate strength. In the U.S., the House of Representatives has passed legislation that would slap tariffs on Chinese imports, and in Europe, the head of the European Central Bank warned that the strong euro was threatening already anemic growth there.

Without more domestic demand in surplus countries and more exchange rate flexibility, "We'll know with confidence that overall growth will be lower," the secretary said.

He said the IMF needed to play a more active role in convincing countries to float their currencies. Geithner explicitly linked progress on governance reform--giving emerging countries a greater voice and vote at the international financial institution--to currency reform.

"That's the basic deal on offer," the secretary said.

But, he warned, don't look for a quick fix.

"It's not something that we're going to solve in the next three months, definitively. It's going to take a sustained set of changes over time," he said.

Reiterating a call for a measured pace out of government-led growth into tough budget-cutting periods, Geithner said most advanced economies still had room to stimulate growth.

While different countries face varying challenges, "concern about the near-term limits to more growth-oriented economic policies are greatly exaggerated," the Treasury Secretary said in prepared remarks.

"Most of us still have the capacity to take additional actions that would improve both short-run and long-run growth prospects," and the biggest risk to the global recovery is that advanced nations underachieve on growth, Geithner said.

Although he didn't directly mention China, the secretary targeted Beijing's policy of an undervalued yuan and warned of the threat of a subsequent currency war.

Geithner said surplus emerging-market countries with undervalued exchange rates need to also accelerate domestic demand growth.

-By Ian Talley, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9285; ian.talley@dowjones.com [ 10-06-10 1118ET ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  mixed on  intervention  fears
text:
* Brazil's real drops 0.42 pct, Mexican peso down 0.03

* Colombia's peso closes at highest since August 2008

* Chile's central bank president warns of intervention

(Updates prices, adds details on Colombia, Chile)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Brazil's real weakened sharply Wednesday after the government authorized its treasury to increase its dollar purchases on the local market as the country steps up efforts to halt appreciation.

The real was bid 0.42 percent weaker at 1.680 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The government is going to make an effort to adopt more measures to get control of the currency in this currency war that is going on worldwide," said Luiz Eduardo Portella, a fixed-income and currency trader at Brazil's Banco Modal.

Brazil's central bank announced Wednesday it had extended to 1,500 days its maximum period for contracts to be settled in the currency market.

That would allow the treasury to buy more dollars. But confusion over the move prompted speculation that a much bigger measure was in the works, causing the real to plunge.

Brazil has stepped up its efforts to contain the currency's appreciation recently, Tuesday raising a tax on bond purchases by foreigners. The tax did little to tame the real's recent rally.

"To me the Brazilians have signaled another step up the ladder," said Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. "I think they may adjust the tax again."

Chile's peso strengthened 0.11 percent to 482.25 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, extended its rally. The peso has rallied nearly 13 percent since the end of July.

Chile's Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said Wednesday the bank could intervene to halt a sharp appreciation of the peso.

Colombia's peso also gained 0.69 percent to close at 1789.05, its highest level in more than two years.

In mid-September, the central bank started purchasing what it said would be at least $20 million daily for at least four months to help ease the peso's rise and investors fear additional measures will be taken.

"There's some investor caution because these are the levels that make the central bank uncomfortable," said Gustavo Sorzano, an analyst at Helm Bank in Bogota.

EYEING THE FED

Markets have been factoring in the prospect of the U.S. Federal Reserve announcing new asset purchase plans since the Bank of Japan eased monetary policy on Tuesday. A broadly weaker dollar has boosted emerging market currencies.

An unexpected fall in U.S. private sector employment on Wednesday led analysts to believe U.S. non-farm payroll reports due Friday could disappoint, which would further pressure the U.S. central bank to try to stimulate the economy.

Mexico's peso edged down 0.028 percent to 12.477 per dollar in volatile trading.

"The prospect of Fed easing is generally good for riskier assets, but if the Fed is considering quantitative easing, it shows they are really worried about economic recovery - that's the other side of the coin for Mexico," said Brown Brothers Harriman's Thin.

title: UPDATE: US To Press  Currency  Issues At IMF--Treasury Official
text:
(Adds additional official comment, details and background, in the third through ninth, 12th and 13th paragraphs.)


 
   By Ian Talley and Michael R. Crittenden 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--U.S. officials plan to press their foreign counterparts to avoid interfering in global currency markets at this weekend's International Monetary Fund meetings, warning of the potential effect on the global rebalancing efforts.

A senior Treasury Department official, speaking to reporters at a briefing, said U.S. officials will stress the need for countries to allow for "market-oriented exchange rates" as part of a broader rebalancing of the world economy.

Besides China's undervalued yuan, intervention by South Korea, Brazil and Tokyo in their currencies have raised foreign-exchange tensions, propelling the sensitive issue to the forefront of international talks.

The chorus of complaints internationally has grown louder for China to appreciate its undervalued yuan, particularly as Beijing's policy is exacerbating the global imbalance of trade and investment. Turbulence in the foreign-exchange markets was taken to a new level after Brazil warned of a currency war.

Earlier Tuesday, European Economic and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Olli Rehn warned that the euro area's economic recovery may suffer if the euro appreciates against the yuan and other world currencies. Officials in Brussels met with Chinese Prime Minister Wen Jiabao.

Asked about Japan's recent intervention on behalf of the yen, the Treasury official implicitly criticized Tokyo for the action as contrary to its commitments to the Group of 20 nations.

The official said Japan and others in the G-20 are focused on cultivating a more robust recovery, and that countries with trade surpluses, including Japan and China, have committed to encouraging domestic demand as a bigger engine of growth and so becoming less reliant on exports over time.

"Explicitly in those agreements are structural policies as well as ensuring that exchange rates represent market forces," the senior official said.

The official said those commitments would be "central to our conversations" at the upcoming IMF meetings.

The U.S. believes the IMF should play a more aggressive role in ensuring countries live up to their commitments on exchange-rate policy, the official said, stressing the fund's "very important surveillance mandate."

"The IMF has to have an ability to speak forcefully," the official said.

While the IMF has labeled the yuan as "substantially undervalued," the IMF has yet to call the currency "manipulated," which would ostensibly ratchet up pressure on Beijing to act.

Fueling tensions, the U.S. House of Representatives last month approved legislation targeting the yuan that would slap punitive tariffs on imports from countries such as China that have undervalued currencies.

The official said the Obama administration shared the underlying concerns addressed by the bill, but was reluctant to say whether the Treasury supported the legislation. Previously, officials have raised concerns about World Trade Organization obligations and the potential political and trade backlash such legislation may engender.

The issue of currencies is one of a range of topics finance ministers and central-bank officials are expected to discuss at a series of multi- and bilateral discussions in Washington over the weekend.

-By Michael R. Crittenden, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9273; michael.crittenden@dowjones.com

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Brazil
text:
BRASILIA, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Ruling party candidate Dilma Rousseff is favored to win Brazil's presidential election in a Oct. 31 runoff against opposition candidate Jose Serra.

Rousseff would likely keep most economic policies in place from President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's center-left government, but may strengthen the state's role in specific industries.

Heavy government spending, policies to develop vast oil reserves and the new balance of power in Congress after the presidential election are among the risks to watch in Brazil over the next year.

PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION

Rousseff, a pragmatic leftist from the ruling Workers' Party, is expected to win the runoff after falling just short of an outright victory in the first round on Sunday.

Her opponent is former Sao Paulo state governor Jose Serra, of the centrist Brazilian Social Democracy Party.

Rousseff is Lula's former chief of staff and has benefited from a booming economy and the president's huge popularity.

Unlike previous presidential races in Brazil, there is no clear market favorite as both contenders are expected to maintain most market-friendly policies that have been in place for the past decade.

Still, Rousseff and Serra both favor strong government and could extend the state's role in some parts of the economy.

Eager to win over centrist voters and avoid unsettling investors, Rousseff has emphasized policy continuity.

But she would likely heighten the role of state enterprises in strategic industries such as energy and telecommunications, a move that might pose risks for equities investors. She will probably also steer clear of sweeping reforms to labor laws or fiscal policy that some investors say would improve Brazil's business climate.

Serra, meanwhile, has suggested a more interventionist role in monetary and currency policies, raising concern in financial markets. He has called for lower interest rates, says the currency is overvalued and wants the central bank to follow the government's economic policy.

Rousseff, a former Marxist guerrilla, has praised the central bank and said the bank should keep focusing on controlling inflation in coming years before considering economic and job growth when setting monetary policy.

There is also some doubt about how firmly the candidates would push for a second generation of structural reforms to ensure Brazil's international competitiveness.

Both agree on the need to overhaul Brazil's complicated tax system to encourage investment but they have provided few details. Serra wants to reform the pension system by cutting benefits for some civil servants, while Rousseff plays down the need for far-reaching reforms any time soon.

Neither proposes nationalizing private companies but Rousseff's proposal to strengthen state firms could weaken private sector participation in banking, oil and utilities.

Rousseff has said the growth of state banks would not infringe on private banks, which she said were necessary to drive economic expansion and spur competition.

Government plans to use state-owned telephone company Telebras to expand broadband Internet access have moved its shares and could also affect share performance of private telecoms depending on their participation in deals.

Rousseff has adopted Lula's proposal to strengthen state-owned power company Eletrobras, though the intent may be to expand mostly abroad.

Serra is widely believed to be the tougher than Rousseff on fiscal discipline.

Rousseff has pledged an ambitious primary budget surplus target of 3.3 percent of GDP but, wary of risking her large poll lead, has been noncommittal on unpopular budget cuts.

What to watch:


 -- Details of Rousseff proposals for state enterprises.
 -- Signs Rousseff is preparing austerity measures to meet


her budget target early in office.

GOVERNMENT SPENDING

The government is maintaining a high level of spending before the election, potentially fueling inflation and forcing the incoming president to adopt austerity measures.

Public spending rose sharply in 2009, eroding the primary budget surplus to an eight-year low of 2 percent of gross domestic product. Finance Minister Guido Mantega has pledged to pursue a surplus of 3.3 percent of GDP in 2010 but in the 12 months to August it was only 2.01 percent.

What to watch:

-- Continued weak monthly primary surplus figures would indicate worsening fiscal discipline and could push up interest rate futures.

-- Signs that Lula could tighten spending after the election to spare Rousseff from implementing unpopular austerity measures.

CORRUPTION

During the next month of campaigning, more mud-slinging and corruption scandals may surface. They can not only influence swing voters but can paralyze Congress and spiral into wider scandals engulfing parties and coalitions. Lula himself came close to facing impeachment proceedings in 2005 when his party was involved in an illegal campaign-financing scandal.

OIL AND GAS

Brazil's government has increased its share in state-owned oil company Petrobras through a massive capitalization that drew more investor appetite than expected. But there are some risks associated with the deal.

Petrobras may use part of the $70 billion it raised to invest in projects such as refineries that further economic development but have a lower return, thereby harming minority shareholder interests. Also, the government boosted its stake in the company to 48 percent of total outstanding shares, up from 40 percent previously.

A legislative framework that has been held up in the Senate but is expected to be approved after the election would further heighten state control over some of the world's biggest recent oil finds. The bill would also ensure their proceeds help bankroll state investments in areas like infrastructure, education and poverty-reduction programs.

If approved, the measures will likely reduce competition in the sector while boosting the role of state energy giant Petrobras, offering fewer but still attractive opportunities for foreign investors.

Critics say the laws threaten the efficiency of Brazil's successful oil sector by stifling investment and increasing the dangers of political interference and corruption.

What to watch:

-- Signs that Congress can agree on how to distribute oil revenue between the federal government and states, paving the way for approval of the oil bills after the election.

MINING

The government plans to send to Congress this year framework legislation designed to stimulate exploration and production. It would improve regulatory oversight and reduce the life span of mining concessions in a bid to discourage speculation in mineral properties.

Industry leaders have warned that excessive restrictions could act as a disincentive to fresh investments.

Mining authorities say that once the new legislation is in place, the government could discuss a possible hike in royalties for the mining sector, including iron ore. This could hit the bottom line of Vale, the world's largest iron ore exporter, as well as other mining and steel companies. The Rousseff camp has denied she has any plans to hike royalties.

What to watch:

-- Presentation of the new mining bill to Congress with possible changes.

-- Leaks on discussions over royalties.

CONGRESSIONAL SUPPORT

Rousseff's coalition won a clear majority in the Senate, which will make it easier to advance her legislative agenda if she wins the runoff. The ruling coalition also appears to have made important gains in the lower house, according to partial results from Sunday's election. But progress in Congress would depend on how well the inexperienced Rousseff can deal with often unruly allies, a challenge that even stumped the savvy Lula at times.

If Serra were to win the Oct. 31 runoff, he might struggle to build a clear majority in Congress, even though legislators typically "migrate" to the governing coalition after elections. The process could create a hung parliament with little chance of approving major bills before Lula leaves office on Jan. 1.

FOREIGN POLICY

If elected, Serra is likely to cool ties with some of Lula's left-wing allies in Latin America. That could affect energy investments in Bolivia and Venezuela, where Lula had prodded Petrobras to invest to foster regional integration.

Serra accused the Bolivian government of turning a blind eye to cross-border drug trafficking. He has also criticized Venezuela for allegedly harboring Colombian rebels. Some analysts think Serra could take a harder line in trade disputes with Argentina and the South American trade block Mercosur.

Rousseff, by contrast, has pledged to continue current foreign policy and could maintain current Foreign Minister Celso Amorim in office or name his deputy, Antonio Patriota.

But given her priority on domestic issues and her relative lower international profile, she is unlikely to be as influential in diplomacy as Lula. (Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Kieran Murray)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real barely budges after tax hike
text:
* Brazil real flat in world market, holds key level

* Strong US dollar hits region, Mexican peso falls 0.6 pct

* Chile's peso slumps 1.1 pct after intervention threats

(Recasts to include increase to Brazil's tax on bonds)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's real showed a muted reaction on Monday to the government's decision to double its tax on foreign investment in the country's bonds.

Analysts were largely sceptical about the effectiveness of the measure, which the government hopes will slow the currency's recent rally by discouraging short-term investment.

Although the real dipped after the announcement, it still held above the key 1.70 threshold, which analysts believe is the authorities' unofficial comfort level.

And after two hours, the real had pared its losses and was flat at 1.6975, according to the international reference rate. But the local market <BRBY>, where most of the action takes place due to the country's currency controls, had already closed before the announcement.

The government said it would raise the so-called IOF tax on Brazilian bonds to 4.0 percent but leave the existing tax on foreign purchases of Brazilian stocks at 2.0 percent. [ID:nN04132890]

The move is designed to discourage investors from borrowing cheaply abroad and making the most of Brazil's high interest rates, via the so-called carry trade.

"The impact of this measure is going to be short-lived and won't be significant. The government is trying to stop a tsunami," said Ricardo Amorim, president of Ricam Consultoria, a Sao Paulo-based consulting firm.

Analysts had been divided over whether the government would take action following Sunday's presidential election, with some predicting that new measures were unlikely until after a runoff on Oct. 31.

ELECTION: WHAT ELECTION?

But aside from the debate over the inflows tax, the reaction to Brazil's election has been relatively muted. Neither of the top two candidates are expected to drastically alter current policies, making the election a "non-event" on trading floors.

The Brazilian dollar-denominated bond due in 2040 <BRAGLB40=RR> lingered around its previous closing level for most of the day.

The yield on the interest-rate futures contract due in Jan. 2012 <DIJF2> fell one basis points to 11.44 percent.

Elsewhere across Latin America, concerns about the stability of the euro zone on Monday made the dollar's safe-haven status more attractive, causing it to strengthen against the region's other major currencies.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> weakened 0.56 percent to 12.61.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL>, which was also under pressure from further intervention threats, plunged 1.13 percent to 486.30.

Chilean President Sebastian Pinera said that the central bank should do more to tame the currency's recent rally. The peso has strengthened more than 12 percent since July due to the country's rapid recovery from a devastating earthquake in February.

Asked if the bank should do more to control the currency Pinera said: "It can always do more." [ID:nN04108417] (Additional reporting by Isabel Versiani)

title: Chile's Stocks Close Higher, Following Gains In U.S. Markets
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's blue-chip Ipsa index ended higher Friday, with retailers leading the way, as it tracked rising U.S. markets.

The Ipsa ended 0.2% higher at 4802.93, while market volume slipped to 82.4 billion Chilean pesos ($171.2 million) compared with CLP112.4 billion the prior session.

As several of the Ipsa's heavier-weighted shares also trade in New York, the Ipsa often tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The DJIA grew 0.4% to 10830 although a key manufacturing report yielded conflicting signals.

Among dually listed shares, flagship carrier LAN Airlines (LFL, LAN.SN), which is in the process of merging with Brazilian airline TAM (TAM, TAMM4.BR), gained 0.5% to CLP14,360.00, while the nation's largest power generator Endesa (EOC, ENDESA.SN) increased 0.9% to CLP882.85.

Also, Chile's second biggest bank in terms of loans, Banco de Chile (BCH, CHILE.SN) expanded 1.5% to CLP72.59 after it posted a 10.9% year-on-year jump in its loans business in August, slightly above growth seen in July.

Retailers, which have consistently been among the Ipsa's biggest winners as Chile quickly rebounds from last year's recession and February's devastating earthquake on strong domestic demand, again led gains.

Retail holding giant Cencosud (CENCOSUD.SN) grew 1.7% to CLP3,320.00 after local investment bank Celfin Capital increased its end-2011 target price to CLP3,800 per share and gave it a buy recommendation. Department store Falabella (FALABELLA.SN) also rose as Celfin Capital upped its year-end 2011 target price to CLP5,622 per share and gave it a buy recommendation. Falabella ended 1.1% higher at CLP4,790.00.

Despite the Ipsa's rise, specialty chemical and fertilizer producer SQM (SQM) fell as the company's more liquid B-series shares (SQM-B.SN) continued to slip following Credit Suisse's recent downgrade of its stock from neutral to underperform.

"There are still a lot of investors, especially foreign investors, selling SQM after the Credit Suisse downgrade. However, the company's medium and long term perspectives look very auspicious," said analyst Raul Barros, with local brokerage BBVA Research.

Also slipping, information technology company Sonda (SONDA.SN) lost 3.2% to CLP1,054.90 as investors booked profits after its shares rose over 22% in September.

In other market news, the peso ended at a 28-month high against the dollar, as international copper prices surged and the euro posted strong gains against the greenback.

The peso finished at CLP481.00 to the dollar, compared to CLP483.50 the prior session, while trading in a range of CLP480.00 to CLP482.30.

With Chile producing more than one-third of the world's copper, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices. Copper futures in New York vaulted to two-year highs on positive economic data from China and a weaker dollar.

Also, as Europe is one of Chile's main trade partners, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar. The euro hit a six-month peak against the dollar, after the Federal Reserve said it is almost certain to have to offer fresh support to ensure that already tepid U.S. economic growth does not continue to falter.

Additionally, local market participants digested the Brazilian real's gains to 1.6780 to the dollar despite the Brazilian central bank's action to halt the currency's strengthening. Because Brazil and Mexico are the two largest economies in Latin America, the Chilean currency often takes cues from the real's and Mexican peso's movements against the dollar.

As the strength of the Chilean peso cuts into the competitiveness of the nation's exports and because the local economy is highly dependent on those products, exporters have been clamoring for market intervention.

The monetary authority, however, isn't expected to signal that it will intervene unless the peso gains to at least a range of CLP460 to CLP470 because in real terms the peso is still trading above levels that would merit an intervention, traders say.

That Brazil has intervened in its local currency market and the real is still strengthening against the dollar provides an argument for not intervening in Chile.

"Despite Brazil's interventions in the currency market, the real has continued to strengthen because there is broad dollar weakness at the international level. The way markets are reading this is that market intervention will only provide a short term solution, but it won't be too effective over the medium or long term considering the dollar's overall weakness," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with local currency trader Forex Chile.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower as the peso's strength fueled expectations that the monetary authority's future interest rate hikes will be less aggressive, traders said.

Chile's central bank raised interest rates by 50 basis points for a fourth consecutive month last month as the country quickly recovers from its first recession in a decade last year and a devastating February earthquake.

The monetary authority has said, though, that the peso's strength relieves some pressure from continuing rate hikes.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.72%, from 2.73% Thursday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.99%, from 3.08% the previous session.
