title: WRAPUP 1-Brazil public accounts struggle, inflation jumps
text:
* Brazil's primary budget surplus below expectations

* Overall budget deficit widens in August from year ago

* Broad measure of inflation jumps in September

By Ana Nicolaci da Costa and Isabel Versiani

BRASILIA, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Growth in Brazil's economy stoked inflation in September but the jump in activity wasn't enough to prevent a deterioration in public accounts, data showed on Wednesday.

Brazil posted a lower-than-expected primary budget surplus in August. The surplus remained far below the government's target as a percentage of gross domestic product, despite record tax collection.

While growth of around 9 percent annually in Brazil has generated robust tax receipts, this has not been enough to offset the surge in government spending ahead of Oct. 3 national elections.

The government still expects to achieve its primary budget target of 3.3 percent of GDP in 2010, by possibly excluding spending for its flagship infrastructure program from the primary budget tally.

A massive capitalization of oil giant Petrobras should also help inflate primary surplus numbers in September, Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said on Tuesday.

But analysts say the primary surplus may become less relevant to track the government's ability to meet debt payments as the overall budget shows a bulging nominal deficit and signs of deteriorating public accounts.

"The government is managing to do a lot of maneuvering in the public accounts to try to achieve the primary surplus (target)," Luiz Eduardo Portella, partner at Banco Modal in Sao Paulo said.

Runaway government spending worries investors partly because it can be inflationary by stimulating an economy that is already growing briskly. It also can push up borrowing costs in an economy that already suffers from some of the world's highest interest rates.

The consolidated primary budget surplus <BRPSPS=ECI>, which excludes interest payments, edged higher to 5.2 billion reais ($3.1 billion) in August from 5.04 billion reais a year earlier. It was below the 6 billion reais expected in the median forecast of 11 analysts surveyed by Reuters.

The surplus in the 12 months to August dipped to 2.01 percent of GDP from 2.02 percent in the year to July and stayed far below the government's 3.3 percent target for all of 2010.

The primary surplus "is no longer a good thermometer. (Brazil's) gross debt does not stop rising while the net debt is stable, but every one looks at the gross debt," Portella added.

RISING DEBT

Brazil's net public debt to GDP <BRDGDP=ECI> stood stable from July at 41.4 percent, while the gross debt eased slightly to 59.4 percent of GDP in August from 59.6 percent of GDP in July. The central bank expected it to rise to 60.4 percent of GDP in September, Altamir Lopes, head of the central bank's economic research department told reporters in Brasilia.

Analysts also fear that the country's debt burden could increase if Brazil's finance ministry decides to use the sovereign wealth fund to intervene in the foreign exchange market.

Brazil's Treasury has issued some 18 billion reais of bonds to capitalize the sovereign fund and could sell more debt as Finance Minister Guido Mantega has said there is no limit to size of the fund's potential intervention in currency markets.

The country's overall budget deficit <BRBUD=ECI> widened to 10.5 billion reais from 8.2 billion reais in August last year.

Growth in the labor and credit markets are some of the signs that economic activity is regaining momentum and filtering into inflation numbers.

Brazil's broadest inflation measure surged 1.15 percent in September, from 0.77 percent in August, data from the Fundacao Getulio Vargas on Wednesday showed. See [ID:nN29240232].

The IGP-M is closely monitored by analysts and investors because it provides a broad look at wholesale and consumer prices in Latin America's largest economy.

The numbers, along with rising inflation expectations and data last week showing consumer prices rose more than expected in the month to mid-September, help reinforce expectations the central bank may have to resume monetary tightening in 2011.

"We will have more pressure on inflation this semester, there is no way around it," Andre Perfeito, an economist at Gradual Investimentos in Sao Paulo said.

($1=1.704 reais)

(Additional reporting by Luciana Lopez in Sao Paulo; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

title: WSJ: Nations Race To Weaken  Currencies , Sparking Trade War Fears
text:
Tensions are growing in the global currency markets as political rhetoric heats up and countries battle to protect their exporters, raising concerns about potentially damaging trade wars.

At least half a dozen countries are actively trying to push down the value of their currencies, the most high-profile of which is Japan, which is attempting to halt the rise of the yen after a 14% rise since May. In the U.S., Congress is considering a law that targets China for keeping its currency artificially low, and in Brazil, the head of the central bank said the country to impose a tax on foreign investment, which has contributed to a big rise in the real.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal Web site, WSJ.com.)

Businesses always want to be more competitive and politicians often talk a big game. But in the current environment, as many economies are still struggling to recover from the global financial crisis, worries are growing that policy makers could be more aggressive in protecting their nation's business interests.

Rising protectionism is "a very big risk," says Erin Browne, a macro stock market strategist at Citigroup. "And it's something that could move more into the spotlight after the [U.S.] election.

Currency-market strains could also be a topic of discussion at next week's IMF/World Bank meeting in Washington, where central bank and government finance officials will be gathering.

The Japanese government earlier this month stepped into the currency markets for the first time in years. To counter the yen's rise, Japan sold some $20 billion worth of its currency, which traders said was its biggest-ever effort in a single day.

Japan joined many other Asian emerging-market countries that have fighting rising currencies on a near daily basis, such as Taiwan, South Korea and Thailand. In Latin America, Brazil, Colombia and Peru have also intervened to tamp down their currencies.

In the U.S., protectionist efforts have been on the rise, especially when it comes to China, which is widely seen as keeping its currency, the yuan, at artificially low levels in order to boost its exports and make it more expensive for the Chinese to purchase goods produced abroad.

The House of Representatives is expected to pass legislation on Thursday that would let U.S. companies argue that Chinese currency policy represents an unfair subsidy. Democratic Senator Charles Schumer plans to push similar legislation to punish China for currency manipulation in the lame-duck session following the election. But it is considered unlikely the bill will pass.

Even so, the administration could use the threat of congressional action to press Beijing to make further adjustments in its currency, particularly as a summit of the Group-of-20 leaders in mid November draws closer.

IMF Managing Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn said he wouldn't rule out a currency war and that officials at both the fund and the Group of 20 nations were actively working to prevent such a battle of competitive depreciations.

However, in a press briefing in Washington, Mr. Strauss-Kahn said he didn't believe there was a big risk of such a war.

"There is no good to expect from intervention," he said. "History has shown that the effect of this kind of intervention doesn't last for very long."

Part of the challenge is that the moves in the currency markets that are raising the ire of central banks and politicians are being driven by longer-term investors.

Stronger economies in the emerging markets are attracting capital from the developed world, pumping up demand for local currencies. Talk of additional quantitative easing in the U.S. signals to investors that interest rates there will remain close to zero for a long time.

Meanwhile, inflation is building in Asia, forcing interest rates higher. Investors see that mismatch and are shuttling money from west to east, attracted to the higher yields.

"The flows that we're seeing are soundly based," says Richard Yetsenga, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at HSBC.

Some countries intervene more forcefully than others. Technology exporter Taiwan sees little fluctuation in its currency, thanks partly to heavy government intervention. Its currency is up less than 2% against the dollar this year. Malaysia, on the other hand, has allowed a stronger ringgit for the independence a free-floating currency gives its monetary policy makers, and the spur it gives to its exporters to become more efficient.

Government officials outside China for the most part step gingerly when it comes to the region's largest economy and its approach to currency reform, if they say anything at all. Singapore Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said last week in an interview with The Wall Street Journal regarding China's appreciation: "I can understand their caution, but on balance they need not go so slow."

The rhetoric was much hotter this week out of Brazil, where its currency has risen more than 30% against the dollar this year as investors flock to its relatively high interest rates.

On Monday, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega lashed out at the U.S., Japan and other rich nations he says are letting their currencies weaken to spur growth--growth that comes at the expense of other exporters like Brazil.

"We're in the midst of an international currency war," Mr. Mantega said during an event in Sao Paulo. "This threatens us because it takes away our competitiveness."

The head of Brazil's central bank, which has been intervening in the currency markets to slow the real's rise, was more circumspect on Tuesday.

"There is a very serious currency problem which should be addressed," Henrique de Campos Meirelles said. Mr. Meirelles said that raising taxes on flows into Brazil was a possibility.

Officials say Brazil's 10.75% benchmark interest rate is necessary to squelch inflation and keep the Latin America's biggest economy from overheating. But it attracts a flood of investment from speculators who borrow in the U.S. or Japan where money is cheap, and deposit it in Brazil. The inflows of cash propel the real even higher.

With Brazil's presidential elections scheduled for Sunday, dealing with a strong currency is shaping up as the first major economic issue to face Brazil's next president. Dilma Rousseff, the former Energy Minister and handpicked successor to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva leading the polls, is an advocate of Brazil's 11-year-old floating exchange rate. But she is likely to face pressure from economists within her left-wing party, including Mr. Mantega, to intervene more heavily.

(Ian Talley, Bob Davis and Alex Frangos contributed to this article.)

Write to Tom Lauricella at tom.lauricella@wsj.com and John Lyons at john.lyons@wsj.com [ 09-28-10 1833ET ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real edges higher as peso rallies
text:
* Brazil real adds 0.1 pct, hurt by threat of inflows tax

* Mexico peso hits 14-week high after U.S. data

* Chile peso clings to 2-year high as c.bank concerns fade (Adds comments about Brazil's real, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Brazil's real edged higher on Tuesday, trailing the Mexican peso's sharp gains, as investors grew concerned about government attempts to manipulate the exchange rate.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.12 percent stronger at 1.706 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, climbing higher after early losses. Meanwhile, the Mexican peso hit its strongest in over three months thanks to the weak dollar and some strong U.S. housing data.

"There is some profit-taking in global currency markets. But it (the real's depreciation) is more to do with local factors, fears about measures which the government could take," said Roberto Padovani, chief Brazil economist with WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's real has rallied over 5.0 percent since the end of June, partly due to massive investment in last week's record share offering by national oil company Petrobras. That rally has put a huge pressure on exporters, whose goods are now more expensive and so harder to sell abroad.

The country's authorities have responded by buying even more dollars in the spot market and threatening a range of other measures, including intervening in the futures market via so-called 'reverse swaps'.

Imposing further taxes on capital inflows to restrain the rise of the currency also remains an "open possibility" for Brazil, the country's central bank governor said on Tuesday. [ID:nLDE68R0AT]

Brazil's government has also been blaming the real's rally on efforts by the United States to keep their currency weak, at the expense of developing countries such as Brazil. [ID:nN27256208]

And on Monday, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega sparked debate across the world when he said various government's attempts to manipulate their currencies equated to an "international currency war". While economists have been making this point for weeks, it was the strongest comments to date by a senior government official.

"Currency is a country's stock price," said Wolfgang Koester, chief executive of FIREapps, a provider of FX hedging software in Scottsdale, Arizona. "And there is massive unpredictability when so many companies are fighting to drive that share price down, rather than support it."

FLIP SIDE OF THE COIN

The U.S. dollar <.DXY> fell to its weakest level since February against a basket of the world's major currencies on Tuesday.

Those losses gave support to Latin America's other currencies, initially boosting the Chilean peso <CLP=> to a fresh 27-month high.

But profit-taking caused the peso to later trade flat at 485.30, but still at its highest level since June 2008.

Traders said they had been bidding up the currency because they were less worried about intervention.

"The dollar has kept depreciating against leading currencies and the local authorities have made clear that it's still not the moment to intervene in the market. So the path is cleared for the peso to keep appreciating," said one trader in Santiago.

While Brazil's authorities have intervened aggressively in the country's currency markets, Chile has been reluctant to interfere with the exchange rate.

Instead, Chile has raised interest rates at a slower pace than it otherwise might have done, in an effort to tame the peso's appreciation. [ID:nN24245807]

Goldman Sachs analyst Alberto Ramos now expects the Chilean central bank to slow its rate hikes at some point this year from 50 basis points to 25 basis points, possibly as early as October's meeting.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> strengthened 0.7 percent to 12.5000 per dollar, hitting its strongest level since June 21.

Due to Mexico's close trade ties with the United States, the peso has also benefited from improving U.S. economic data.

Tuesday's data on single-family home prices in the United States was better than expected, prompting the peso to extend its early gains. The report restored some confidence about the pace of the economic recovery in the United States and its future demand for Mexican exports. [ID:nN28171424]

The peso has also been boosted by expectations of investment ahead of the country's inclusion in October in a major global bond index, the WGBI, run by Citigroup.

(Additional reporting by Brad Haynes in Santiago)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains despite threats; peso firms
text:
* Brazil's real gains despite intervention warnings

* Mexico peso firms 0.2 percent on Fed hopes

* Chile's peso strengthens for fourth straight session

(Adds comments about Brazil's real, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/BRAZIL, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's real strengthened on Monday despite fresh efforts by the government to talk down the currency and protect the country's struggling exporters.

Brazil's finance minister said the country still has an arsenal of measures to stop the real strengthening during an "international currency war" in which governments are manipulating currencies to boost export competitiveness. See[ID:nN27256208]

But traders have gradually become used to hearing such threats, which have yet to be followed up by concrete action.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.708 reais on the local spot market after the warnings.

A record-breaking stock sale from state oil company Petrobras has prompted investors to pour money into Brazil over the past few weeks.

Since buyers must hand over their cash for the shares on Wednesday this week, Monday is the last day when foreign investors will bring their dollars into the country because it takes about 48 hours to make a currency transaction in Brazil.

It's possible Mantega's comments were just "a conditional threat he hopes not to have to act upon," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging market research for the Americas at Nomura Securities.

Even if the government does take further measures, it is likely they are "waiting for both the Petrobras transaction to close and next Sunday's presidential election to pass before acting," he said.

Mexico's peso extended gains on Monday, also boosted by the weaker dollar which sent investors looking for higher-yielding assets in Latin America.

The peso <MXN=><MEX01> strengthened 0.19 percent to 12.526 per dollar. The currency is poised to record its largest gains in the month of September in 28 years according to Mexican bank Banamex.

EYES ON FED

Investors are betting the U.S. central bank will boost money supply to aid economic recovery in the United States, Mexico's most important trading partner.

Investors expect the Fed will keep interest rates near zero through 2011 and could even increase its purchases of U.S. bonds, which would also help keep yields down on Treasuries.

The expectation of lower yields on U.S. Treasuries has prompted a rally in higher-yielding Latin American assets.

Still, traders said the peso's rapid acceleration could slow later in the session as U.S. stock markets edged lower.

"Last week's gains were helped by a strong performance in the stock markets, but the peso's acceleration is going to pause a bit as markets are a bit sluggish on renewed concerns about the health of European banks," said Ramon Cordova, a trader at brokerage BASE in Monterrey, Mexico. .

The euro earlier dipped after ratings firm Moody's cut Anglo Irish Bank's lower-grade debt and kept it on review for a downgrade, a move that highlighted concerns over the euro zone banking sector. [ID:nN27338134]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed for the fourth straight session, gaining 0.25 percent to 485.3 per dollar and closing at its strongest level since June 2008. A weaker dollar, booming growth, and strong demand for Chile's copper exports have boosted the currency over recent months.

Lower yields in the United States have also prompted investors to venture into some of the most inhospitable parts of Latin America's capital markets, such as Venezuelan debt.

Prices for Venezuela's benchmark bonds due in 2027 <VENGLB27=RR> were boosted further on Monday as investors bet that opposition gains in Sunday's parliamentary elections might temper the behavior of President Hugo Chavez. [ID:nN27245671]

title: UPDATE 3-World in a " currency  war," Brazil finmin says
text:
* Strength of Brazil's real hurting exporters

* Mantega blames United States, Europe and Japan

* Brazil central bank stepping up forex interventions (Adds comments)

By Samantha Pearson and Aluisio Alves

SAO PAULO, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The world is in an "international currency war" as governments manipulate their currencies to improve their export competitiveness, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Monday.

Mantega's speech to Brazilian industrial leaders included some of the strongest comments to date by any senior government official on the recent bout of currency intervention by countries, including Japan and China.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, is now the world's most overvalued major currency, according to Goldman Sachs.

Near a 10-month high against the dollar, the real continued to rise after Mantega's comment as traders bet the government may be waiting for the outcome of Sunday's presidential election before taking action.

"We're in the midst of an international currency war," Mantega said. "This threatens us because it takes away our competitiveness."

With some economies still reeling from the global financial crisis, countries have sought to weaken their currencies to boost exports and improve trade balances.

Currency intervention is likely to be a hotly disputed topic at the next meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Washington, D.C., Oct. 8-10.

Japan, Colombia, Thailand and other countries have been seeking to weaken their currencies to help accelerate their economic recovery. For details, see [ID:nTOE68F05F].

Low interest rates across much of the developed world have also prompted investors to pour cash into higher-yielding assets in countries such as Brazil, causing further outcry.

"The advanced countries are seeking to devalue their currencies," Mantega said, mentioning the United States, Europe and Japan in the context of what he portrayed as an intensifying trade competition.

Mantega has repeatedly tried to talk down the real. The government last week threatened to use the sovereign wealth fund to buy dollars.

But the government has been reluctant to follow through with concrete measures, and traders bid up the currency near the 1.70 per dollar level, which some see as the threshold for new, stronger action by the government.

Last week's share offering by state-oil company Petrobras contributed to a large inflow of dollars to Brazil, which is attractive to foreign investors because of high interest rates and its booming economy.

Mantega said the country still has an arsenal of tools available to weaken the real, although he did not offer details. Mantega said the government was not considering additional taxes on foreign investments but noted that the government has imposed such controls to hold back the real in the past.

MORE MEASURES COMING?

The remarks could be a sign that Brazil's government will beef up efforts to weaken its currency, said Raphael Martello, an analyst with Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

"He could be preparing the way for a stronger intervention. Since Japan intervened in the currency market, it gave other countries a justification to do the same thing," Martello said.

Tony Volpon, head of emerging market research for the Americas at Nomura Securities, added that Mantega's could also simply be "a conditional threat he hopes not to have to act upon."

Japanese authorities intervened to sell yen on Sept. 15, the first such intervention since March 2004. [ID:nTOE68E02W]

And the United States has vowed to rally global heavyweights on China's currency, the yuan, which many economists say is undervalued. (Editing by Brian Winter and Kenneth Barry)

title: News Highlights: Top Economic Stories Of The Day
text:
TOP STORIES 
 
US DURABLE GOODS ORDERS DROP 1.3% 
 

Demand for U.S. manufactured durable goods tumble more than expected in August, to an adjusted $191.17 billion, held back by steep drops in airplanes and cars. It was the biggest drop since August 2009. Economists were looking for a smaller decline of 1.0%.


 
US AUGUST NEW-HOME SALES FALL SHORT OF EXPECTATIONS 
 

U.S. new home sales come in unchanged from July at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 288,000, below economists' expectations of 295,000, as consumers lacking a government tax incentive are cautious in the face of high unemployment.


 
US STOCKS RALLY FOLLOWING ECONOMIC DATA 
 

U.S. stocks climb broadly, putting the market on pace for its fourth-straight weekly gain as investors are encouraged by readings on housing and capital spending by businesses that point toward a stabilizing economy. DJIA gains more than 150 points.


 
NORWAY'S CENTRAL BANK SUES CITIGROUP 
 

Norway's central bank sues Citigroup over alleged misstatements about the company's financial condition, which it claims caused it to buy Citi shares at inflated prices.


 
EU REGULATOR TO REVIEW ROCHE'S AVASTIN 
 

An advisory panel of the European Medicines Agency launches a review of Roche's cancer drug Avastin for the treatment of metastatic breast cancer, raising concerns about the medicine's risk-benefit profile.


 
BRAZIL SEES POSSIBLE CREDIT RISK IN DOLLAR FLOWS 
 

Brazilian Central Bank chief Henrique Meirelles says heavy dollar inflows could pose credit risk for the country's banking system. That is why Brazil has taken intervention measures in the forex market, he says.


 
HOUSE PANEL OKS CHINA CURRENCY LEGISLATION 
 

Legislation that targets imports from China and other countries with currencies similarly perceived to be undervalued sails through U.S. House Ways and Means Committee, preparing way for vote in full chamber perhaps as soon as next week.


 
MOTOROLA PLANS VOTE ON REVERSE STOCK SPLIT 
 

Shareholders will vote on the reverse stock split on Nov. 29. The split will range between 1-for-3 and 1-for-7 and is intended to raise the company's stock price before a planned split of the company.


 
PORTUGAL HIT BY OPPOSITION AUSTERITY BUDGET STANCE 
 

Portugal's standing in credit markets weakens further as the country's main opposition party continues to deny support for the minority government's 2011 austerity budget, the key to shoring up Portugal's public finances.


 
CERBERUS PLANS REVIVAL OF CHRYSLER FINANCIAL 
 

Cerberus Capital Management is plotting a revival of Chrysler Financial, the auto lender whose core business was effectively dissolved by the U.S. Treasury, sources say.


 
 
 
 
   ======== DOW JONES NEWSWIRES ANALYSIS AND COMMENTARY ======== 
 
The Wall Street Journal 
WHY THE FSA CAN'T SHOOT THE MESSENGER 
 

Before we journalists mount our collective high horse about the FSA's anti-leak measures, we should ask ourselves a question. Does anybody seriously think that the authorities have a hope in hell of stopping leaks? asks Joe Ortiz.


 
Heard on the Street 
THREE KEY ISSUES IRELAND MUST ADDRESS 
 

Irish 10-year bond yields have soared to 6.6%, 4.3 percentage points more than on German debt, generating fears that it may have to follow Greece in asking for a bailout. How does Ireland get out of this hole? Questions, Richard Barley.


 
Practice Management 
NOT LEAVING AN HEIR TOO MUCH, TOO SOON 
 

Preparing for the worst is never easy, but it can be even more complicated when a loved one is still a teenager. Wayne Copelin came up with a plan to not only protect the estates holdings, but the heir from herself, writes Peter McDougall.


 
Analysis 
THE ECONOMY CAN'T GROW FOREVER 
 

People may not want to admit it, but there are limits to the growth developed countries have experienced over the past few decades, and the reality is we may have to learn to live new personal, and economic, lives, writes Rex Nutting.


 
 
  ============ MARKETS ACTION ============ 
 
US STOCKS CLIMB BROADLY FOLLOWING HOUSING, DURABLE-GOODS DATA 
 

US stocks surge as fears over European economic growth ease.

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso strengthened sharply to a five-week high on Wednesday as markets braced for more monetary easing from the U.S. Federal Reserve.

The Fed suggested on Tuesday it could pump more money into the American economy, where investors remain concerned about the possibility of a second recession.

That resolve to keep the U.S. economy buoyant eased investors' nerves, making relatively risky Latin American assets more attractive, said Raphael Martello, an analyst with Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.57 percent to 12.6372 per dollar, hitting its strongest intraday level since Aug. 19. Chile's currencies also strengthened, which bolstered the price of its top export, copper.

"When you know the world is not going to end, investors start moving toward this carry trade and they buy (Latin American currencies)," Martello said.

Some analysts suggested Mexico's currency appealed to investors because the peso is more fairly priced than its Latin American counterparts.

"Currencies across Latin America have been on a tear lately and, with the notable exception of the Mexican peso, most are now trading above what might reasonably deemed to be fair value," Capital Economics said in a report.

INTERVENTION PLANS

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened 0.17 percent to 1.719 reais per dollar as traders grew cautious about more aggressive moves by the country's authorities to tame the currency's recent rally.

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Wednesday the central bank will carry out any dollar purchases made by the country's sovereign wealth fund in the spot foreign exchange market.

Even though no concrete measures were announced, the comments were enough to scare some investors into selling reais.

The central bank has also stepped up its dollar purchases in the spot market. Data released on Wednesday showed the bank has recently been buying as much as $1 billion a day. [ID:nN22239158]

Expectations of huge foreign investment in an upcoming share offering by state-controlled oil company Petrobras have caused the real to strengthen more than 5 percent since the end of June.

title: UPDATE: Brazil 's Real Weakens Slightly As Market Debates  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real switched course and weakened slightly against the dollar Tuesday as a debate raged in the markets over whether or not the government will step up measures to try to rein in the currency's strong appreciation.

Dollars have been flowing into Brazil attracted by strong growth, high domestic interest rates and plenty of investment opportunities, including an upcoming mammoth share issuance by the government-run oil company, Petroleo Brasileiro SA (PBR), or Petrobras.

The government has become ever more concerned about the impact of a strong currency on the rest of the economy, with exporters in particular feeling much of the pain, and officials have talked about taking steps to dent demand for the real.

In the latest announcement, late on Monday, the government said it has allowed Brazil's sovereign wealth fund to buy up foreign currency directly in the market. The government said there's no limit on how much the fund can use of its reserves, which are estimated at around BRL18 billion.

In addition, there is speculation that the central bank may start holding three auctions to buy dollars per day, instead of two, and that it might resort to reverse-swap auctions, in which investors exchange foreign-exchange positions for government debt linked to interest rates, to dampen demand for reals.

Tuesday morning, the real was trading at BRL1.7300 per dollar on the B&MFBovespa exchange in Sao Paulo, slightly weaker than Monday's close of BRL1.7292.

Analysts are divided over whether, or when, the government will actually take any steps. Some believe they won't be able to combat the longer-term appreciation trend; others believe the government may wait for an appropriate moment to intervene.

RBS Securites in a note said the government may choose to hold back some of its firepower until after the Petrobras share issuance is out of the way later this month. Petrobras is looking to raise some $20-25 billion from capital markets, and a large share of that is expected to come from overseas investors buying up locally-issued shares, which has driven up demand for the Brazilian currency in recent days.

Banco Santander is skeptical that the Brazilian government will take any drastic action, and sees the currency testing the BRL1.7 mark in the short term.

"Although the technical positioning seems less favorable for the currency and intervention seems to have reached another level, we still believe that strong dollar inflows and the lure of the carry and growth trades will prove formidable obstacles against real depreciation in the short term," Santander said in a note.

Meanwhile, the cost to the Brazilian government of buying dollars is rising, given the widening gap between interest rates in the U.S. and Brazil, said Brown Brothers Harriman in a note. Brazil issues bonds to finance its foreign exchange purchases; this is contributing to its growing budget deficit, which reached an eight-month high in July, BBH said. At the same time, growth differentials and strong currency contribute to the yawning current account deficit, which is approaching record levels, it said.

By Samantha Pearson and Noe Torres

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - The Mexican peso hovered around a four-week high against the dollar Monday as investors grew optimistic about Tuesday's U.S. Federal Reserve meeting.

Policymakers in the United States are unlikely to announce new monetary policy moves, but some analysts expect them to give a slightly more optimistic outlook for the economic growth.

That would be good news for Mexico. While Brazil sells vast amounts of its exports to China, Mexico relies almost entirely on trade with its northern neighbor.

Fears earlier this year of a double-dip recession in the United States hit the peso hard. But as those concerns have faded, the peso has begun to outperform the region.

The peso strengthened 0.28 percent to 12.7695 per dollar Monday, just shy of its strongest level since Aug. 23.

"It's possible that tomorrow, with more data indicating a deceleration instead of a recession, the Fed will show it's a bit more optimistic in general," said IXE economist Luis Flores in Mexico City.

The Brazilian real was bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.716 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, not far from its strongest level this year.

Flores said there was also a cautious mood across trading floors due to the prospect of more aggressive intervention in Brazil's local currency market by the central bank.

Foreign interest in the country's debt and optimism over high growth rates have helped the currency to double in value against the U.S. dollar since 2003.

"What is making the real gain strength against the dollar is not what is usually referred to as speculation, it's more of a fundamental shift," said Andre Perfeito, an economist at Gradual Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

PESO OPTIMISM SPREADING

The upcoming inclusion in October of Mexican debt in a major global bond index (WGBI) run by Citigroup is also supporting the currency, analysts said.

"The Mexican peso continues to recover well, likely aided by inflows associated with the imminent inclusion into the WGBI," said Clyde Wardle, an emerging markets analyst at HSBC, in a research note.

BNP Paribas, which has expressed some of the most optimistic views about the Mexican currency recently among international banks, advised clients to bet that the peso could strengthen to as much as 12.55 against the dollar.

RBC analysts also look set to join the bullish camp. "Risk reversals suggest that positioning in the Mexican peso has increased sharply in recent weeks and it may soon be worth expressing a bullish Mexican peso view as a relative value trade," they wrote in a report.

Markets were closed in Chile for Independence Day celebrations. (Additional reporting by Caroline Stauffer in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Brazil 's Real Gains Ground But  Intervention  Fears Linger
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real strengthened slightly against the dollar on Friday, wrapping up a week in which the fear of greater government intervention stalled the currency's strong gains.

The Brazilian government had been unable to do much to prevent the real from gaining ground on Monday and Tuesday, despite increasingly strong comments from Finance Minister Guido Mantega and the central bank's decision to hold twice-daily auctions to buy dollars.

But an unusual move on Wednesday by the Japanese government to weaken the yen changed the dynamic in global markets, and the real slipped sharply. Since then, the real recovered some poise but didn't get return to test what traders see as the next barrier of BRL1.70.

The real ended at BRL1.7165 Friday on the BM&FBovespa exchange, slightly stronger from Thursday's close. The real gained about 0.7% against the dollar this week, and is about 2.3% stronger against the dollar since the beginning of the month.

The real has been driven by the booming economy and strong appetite for investments in Brazil, but that has been compounded in recent weeks as companies issue bonds overseas and repatriate the proceeds. Investors have also been jockeying for position as state-owned oil company Petroleo Brasileiro SA (PBR), or Petrobras, embarks on a mammoth share issuance which is expected to wrap up later this month.

Many overseas investors are expected to participate in the share issuance, in which the Brazilian company is looking to raise roughly $25 billion from the private-sector capital markets.

Meanwhile, there was more evidence on Friday of the government's desire to capitalize on the doubts that have crept into investors' minds in recent sessions. Estado reported Friday that the order at the central bank was to "buy, buy, buy" dollars, to absorb the strong inflows and prevent an excessive appreciation.

Every day this week, the central bank held two auctions to buy dollars, ostensibly to build its foreign currency reserves, but markets are also keenly aware that the monetary authority wants to influence the market's perceptions. The central bank's reserves rose by $4.8 billion between Monday and Thursday, evidence of the stepped-up intervention, with the total amount rising to $267.2 billion as of Thursday.

Beyond the central bank, the government this week again promised to do what it can to absorb the dollars flowing into the economy.

"We're going to soak up any excess dollars that might come in with the Petrobrasoperation," Mantega said. "I'm giving advance warning; we're going to buy it all."

The strong appreciation hurt exports, reducing Brazil's trade surplus and feeding a rising current account deficit. The country's year-to-date trade surplus totaled $11.981 billion through mid-September, compared with $20.678 billion in the same period of 2009.

There's also some speculation that the government may use so-called reverse-swap auctions, which it has used in the past to influence the currency market. In a reverse currency-swap, investors exchange foreign-exchange positions for government paper linked to interest rates. The auctions typically help support the U.S. dollar against the real by removing real exposure from the futures market.

-By Matthew Cowley, Dow Jones Newswires; +55 11 3544 7082; matthew.cowley@dowjones.com [ 17-09-10 2016GMT ]

By Ana Nicolaci da Costa

BRASILIA, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Brazil's Finance Ministry will not for now use a tax on capital inflows to control the amount of foreign currency flooding the country and swelling the real, a government source told Reuters on Thursday.

The comments accompany moves by the government to step up intervention to keep the real <BRBY>, ranked the world's most overvalued currency by Goldman Sachs, from rallying further.

"The IOF tax would be the last resort," the source said on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue. "What would facilitate the work and maybe (would reduce) the need to use the sovereign wealth fund is if the central bank entered the market at both ends."

The Finance Ministry declined to comment on the issue when contacted by Reuters.

The central bank has been calling two auctions a day rather than just one since last Wednesday to buy dollars on the spot market. There is increasing speculation it could also offer reverse currency swaps -- a form of derivative which would have the same effect as buying dollars in the futures market.

Brazil is gearing up for massive inflows of U.S. dollars from an imminent stock offering for the capitalization of oil giant Petrobras . It is also struggling with a widening current account deficit.

This has helped push the real 4.8 percent higher since the end of June, even though it is only up 1.3 percent on the year.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega is also worried about the level of the currency, which makes the country less competitive by reducing the price of imports and making exports more expensive. See [ID:nN15168058]

He has said the ministry would take the necessary steps to prevent an excessive appreciation, increasing speculation it could soon use Brazil's sovereign wealth fund to buy dollars and do its bit to tame the currency.

Indeed, Mantega said on Wednesday one option would be to use the fund to soak up extra dollars from a massive share offering planned by Petrobras that could reach $65 billion.

Last year, the government introduced a tax on capital inflows to curb a 34 percent rally in the real, but the source did not expect this any time soon.

"(They) are not thinking of using the IOF at the moment," the source said. "The government is trying to manage expectations to avoid a surprise."

The source would not comment on the timing of any possible move, adding that "the sovereign fund will go in without the market knowing."

By Nelson Bocanegra and Caroline Stauffer

BOGOTA/MEXICO CITY, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso fell sharply on Wednesday after authorities said they would buy dollars to curb the currency's rally while Brazil's real weakened after worse-than-expected U.S. manufacturing data.

The Colombian currency lost 0.95 percent after the country's central bank said it would start purchasing at least $20 million daily for the next four months.

"Those who were short dollars yesterday had to exit to buy at whatever price," said Camilo Perez, chief economist at Banco de Bogota in the country's capital.

Investment in Colombia's booming oil and mining sectors has led the Colombian peso to strengthen more than 10 percent this year, putting pressure on the country's exporters.

Across the rest of the region, currencies mostly sagged after a surprise drop in manufacturing activity in New York state during September. [ID:nN15143494]

Brazil's real <BRBY> shed 0.4 percent to 1.716 on the local spot market after the U.S. data, while Chile's peso <CLP=> weakened 0.18 percent to 494.60 per dollar.

Latin America, a major producer of commodities and manufactured goods, would suffer should the global economy take a turn for the worse.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.37 percent to 12.7759 per dollar ahead of a two-day holiday that begins on Thursday. The peso has been supported in recent weeks by Mexico's scheduled entry into Citigroup's WGBI World Bond Index on October 1, which could boost flows into Latin America's second largest economy.

Regarding Colombia's intervention in its exchange market, analysts at Barclays Capital expect the central bank's measures will knock up to 2 percent off the peso in the near-term.

At the same time, some analysts said the bank could not hold the currency back indefinitely.

"These types of actions can't change a currency's long-term tendency," Correval economist Daniel Velandia wrote in a report.

JAPANESE INTERVENTION

Meanwhile, Japan's decision on Wednesday to sell yen in currency markets for the first time in six years fueled debate about how the measure might affect Brazil's real.

One head currency trader at an international bank in New York said the move could prompt Japanese retail investors, who already have some of the biggest bets on the real's appreciation, to sink more money into the real.

"Retail (investors) will look at this spike as a good opportunity to add," he said.

That might put pressure on Brazil's central bank to step up its intervention efforts in the market to protect exporters.

But other market players were less convinced.

"I don't think they will add much more to the position," said Pedro Tuesta, an economist at 4Cast in Washington.

Foreigners already hold near-record bets on the future appreciation of the real, so Japan's move is unlikely to prompt a huge shift into Brazil's currency, he said. [ID:nTOE68E02W] (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: UPDATE 3-Brazil defends exporters in global  currency  battle
text:
* Brazil's finance minister says will fight appreciation

* Real slumps 1.1 percent on intervention threats

* Brazil could use sovereign wealth fund to curb rally (Adds details, link to currency graphic, updates price)

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Brazil vowed on Wednesday to defend its exporters as governments worldwide moved to weaken their currencies as a way of speeding up an economic recovery.

Brazil's central bank is fighting to curb appreciation of the country's hard-charging currency, the real <BRL=>, now ranked the world's most overvalued major currency, according to Goldman Sachs. A strong real has made exports more expensive and could cause long-term damage to Brazil's industry.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega sought to talk down the real for the second time in two weeks, saying he would not sit on the sidelines "watching the game" while other countries weakened their currencies at the expense of Brazil.

"We're going to take appropriate measures to stop the real from appreciating," he said at an event in Rio de Janeiro.

One option, he said, would be to use Brazil's sovereign wealth fund to soak up extra dollars from a massive share offering planned by state-owned oil company Petrobras .

"We're watching every market, every part, for inflows," Mantega said. "If inflows come we'll buy it all. We're not going to leave any excess of dollars in the market."

Mantega said other countries are relying on exports to lift their struggling economies.

"The United States and Europe are also trying to escape the economic crisis by selling exports. They make their monetary policy weak to devalue their currencies and export more," he added. "We're aware of this and we won't let it happen."

Japan intervened in currency markets on Wednesday for the first time in six years while Colombia announced fresh measures to weaken its peso and protect its exporters. For details, see [ID:nN15191735] and [ID:nN15145483]

FIGHTING A LOSING BATTLE?

Despite the Brazilian government's best efforts so far, the real is still trading near its strongest level against the dollar this year.

Huge foreign investment in Brazil and growing demand for its higher-yielding debt have made the real double in value since President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva took office in 2003. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 


  Graphic on Brazil's real: http://link.reuters.com/xuv52p("http://link.reuters.com/xuv52p")
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>


U.S. dollar inflows <BRCAPF=ECI> to the country totaled $2.114 billion in the month through Sept. 10, the central bank said on Wednesday. That is almost half the total amount of dollars that has entered Brazil during the whole year.

One of the most talked-about measures recently on Sao Paulo's trading floors is the possibility of an auction of reverse swaps, a form of derivative which would have the same effect as buying dollars in the futures market.

That speculation also caused the real to weaken 1.1 percent to 1.725 per U.S. dollar <BRBY> on Wednesday.

"I don't know where it came from that the central bank was going to start offering swaps. But just with this, just with the threat, the (real) took a dive," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora, one of Brazil's biggest currency brokerages. "The market is tense."

Some analysts, however, believe the central bank is fighting a losing battle. For more see [ID:nN10251620]

The bank said earlier on Wednesday it had bought a staggering $815 million in dollars on the spot market in the month through Sept. 10. Last Thursday alone, the bank bought more than it did during the whole of February.

Since last Wednesday the bank has been calling two auctions daily, rather than just one, to buy dollars.

But these auctions are costly, since the bank gets next to nothing in interest for all the dollars that have piled up in its reserves. The same problem would arise if the government used its sovereign wealth fund to buy dollars.

Even reverse currency swaps did not stop a near 70 percent rally in the real when they were last used on a regular basis between 2005 and 2008. (Reporting by Rodrigo Viga Gaier in Rio de Janeiro and Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo; Writing by Samantha Pearson; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: Brazil  Real Weakens Against Dollar After Japan Govt  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real reversed course on Wednesday, weakening against the U.S. dollar after the Japanese government rattled global markets earlier in the day as it sought to weaken the yen.

"The Japanese move has given pause to everyone in the market here in Brazil," said a Sao Paulo-based currency trader. "The strength of the U.S. dollar against the yen and the euro Wednesday has helped prevent a strengthening of the real beyond the BRL1.70 barrier."

Japan sold yen in the market on Wednesday for the first time in six years and promised more to come in a bid to stop the currency's relentless rise from hurting exporters and threatening a fragile economic recovery.

At 1530 GMT, the real was trading at BRL1.7233 per dollar, weaker against Tuesday's close of BRL1.7055.

The Brazilian real gained against the dollar for six straight sessions through Tuesday, but stalled just as it was approaching the key BRL1.70 test. The Brazilian central bank added a further note of caution to the market on Wednesday, as it held an auction to buy dollars at BRL1.713.

"The Brazilian Central Bank has been making a determined effort to hold the line at BRL1.70," said Paulo Fujisaki, a currency trader at Sao Paulo's Socopa brokerage. "But there is no guarantee the BRL1.70 line will hold forever."

Since early September, the central bank has been purchasing dollars at twice-daily snap auctions in order to avoid a sharp rise in the real. Previously, the central bank tended to hold only a single daily auction.

Analysts said the central bank was interested in holding the line against a sharp appreciation of the real since a strong real hurts exports.

Socopa's Fujisaki said the real has been gaining strength in recent days because of heavy inflows of dollars from overseas bond placements. Meanwhile, investors have been bringing in dollars ahead of a massive offer of shares later this month by state-controlled oil company Petrobras (PBR, PETR4.BR).

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real tests cenbank, region firms
text:
* U.S. retail data raises hopes about global recovery

* Chile and Mexican pesos gain 0.2 pct

* Brazilian real pulls back from 2010 high (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real hit a fresh 2010 high on Tuesday as investors bet on massive future investment in Latin America's biggest economy.

Strong U.S. retail data also helped to boost the region's currencies, allowing the Mexican peso to shrug off early losses. [ID:nN14247794]

The Brazilian real <BRL=> edged up 0.018 percent from the previous day's close to bid 1.7092 reais per U.S. dollar, according to the international reference rate. Earlier in the session it closed at 1.703 on the local spot market <BRBY> -- its strongest level since Dec. 4, 2009.

Brazil's central bank has stepped up its intervention efforts to weaken the currency -- in a bid to protect exporters -- but it has so far failed to halt the real's rally

"The market is testing the government's willingness and they will continue to take the currency lower," said one head currency trader in New York.

Brazil announced on Tuesday plans to sell $500 million more of its 2041 global bond, underscoring a growing foreign interest in the country's markets.

Investors are also optimistic about huge foreign investment in an upcoming fund-raising deal by state-owned oil company Petrobras and a wave of other local corporate deals.

But if the real breaks the closely-watched 1.70 per dollar level, the central bank could be forced to take more aggressive action in the market, analysts said.

Authorities have already been increasing their dollar purchases in the spot market, calling multiple auctions each day, but some believe they may also start intervening in the futures market via derivatives called 'reverse swaps'.

PESO HOSTAGE TO U.S.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> gained 0.21 percent to 12.8277 per dollar, hitting a three-week high, after the strong U.S. data raised hopes about the global economic recovery.

Mexico's fragile recovery from a deep recession is especially dependent on U.S. growth because Mexico sends about 80 percent of its exports over its northern border.

"Mexico's peso in particular among Latin American currencies will remain hostage to what happens in the United States," Roberto Melzi, a Latin American currency strategist at Barclays Capital in New York said.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> gained 0.24 percent to 493.3 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, recouped early losses.

"In Chile, the lack of intervention in a scenario of rising risk appetite and rates normalization will continue to push the Chilean peso higher," said analysts at BNP Paribas in a note to clients.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Brazil may be outgunned in fight to weaken  currency
text:
* Government may be unable to stop appreciation of real

* Recent intervention efforts carry heavy fiscal cost

* Markets betting that currency will remain overvalued (Repeats Friday story for additional subscribers)

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Brazil is locked in a bitter struggle with investors over the value of its currency -- a battle it is unlikely to win without major casualties.

The government is increasingly desperate to halt the appreciation of the real <BRL=>, which has more than doubled in value against the dollar since President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva took office in 2003 and is now, by one measure, the world's most overvalued major currency.

The currency's rise is in part a reflection of Lula's success in transforming Brazil into a darling of foreign investors. Yet what was once seen as a blessing has become a curse, and Finance Minister Guido Mantega warned Thursday that the government will take whatever measures are necessary to keep the real from further damaging exporters. [ID:nN09214757]

Meanwhile, the central bank has resorted to unusual, multiple interventions in the market this week to try to keep the real at or above its current level of 1.72 per dollar, near its strongest level this year. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on Brazil's real: http://link.reuters.com/xuv52p ("http://link.reuters.com/xuv52p")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Yet Brazil's government and monetary authority may very well be outgunned in the near-term by a host of economic fundamentals and one-off events, namely the $65 billion share offering planned by state oil company Petrobras later this month. Analysts say that could unleash further deals and yet another wave of foreign investment inflows.

Continuing to fight the real's appreciation also carries potential fiscal costs that may prove too much to bear at a time when the government is already ramping up spending ahead of presidential elections on Oct. 3.

In fact, markets are increasingly betting that the government will blink. Wagers by foreign investors on a stronger real reached $14.1 billion as of Sep. 3, according to Brazil's Banco Safra -- not far below an all-time high.

"While most central banks carry a certain clout, markets have a tendency to become a groundswell of opinion backed by real positions, with real risk on the line," says Andrew Wilkinson at Interactive Brokers.

BRAZIL: A VICTIM OF ITS OWN SUCCESS

Brazil's combination of robust 7 percent annual economic growth and some of the world's highest interest rates -- the benchmark rate is at 10.75 percent -- has made it an irresistible target for foreign investors at a time when most of the world is dominated by low yields and weak growth.

The global growth hunt has also pushed Peru's currency <PEN=PE> close to an all-time high and boosted the Chilean peso <CLP=> to its strongest level in eight months.

But the real is the most overvalued of all the world's major 33 currencies, according to Goldman Sachs. Against the U.S. dollar, the real is overvalued by a whopping 53 percent, it says.

Even the threat of a double-dip recession in the United States seems to have had little effect on the real in recent weeks, says Michael Woolfolk, senior currency strategist at BNY Mellon in New York.

"The Brazilian real is hanging in there -- it's very tough, very strong. It seems to be trading off its own fundamentals rather than international investor risk appetite or the performance of the U.S. economy," he says.

While the central bank insists that it is not trying to fix Brazil's currency at a particular level, economists point to 1.70 real-per-dollar as the government's breaking point.

The central bank doubled its dollar purchases on the spot market last month, buying $3.04 billion, its biggest monthly purchase so far this year. On Wednesday, the bank took the unusual step of calling two, rather than one, auctions -- the first time that had happened since May.

The bank did the same thing on Thursday.

Yet, in a potentially foreboding sign, investors have barely flinched. The real closed stronger on the local spot market on both Wednesday and Thursday.

The interventions also carry a heavy cost, adding to Brazil's growing debt burden. Most of the dollars the bank buys are held in reserve in U.S. Treasuries, which are currently yielding next to nothing. Meanwhile, the bank still has to pay out much higher interest rates in reais.

MIXED RECORD OF INTERVENTION

Brazil doesn't have to look too far into its own past to see that currency interventions often don't work out.

Lula's predecessor as president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, spent billions of dollars trying to maintain the real's value when it was loosely pegged to the dollar in the late 1990s. The peg ultimately buckled, causing a traumatic devaluation.

Other countries such as China have got intervention down to a fine art, keeping the currency exactly where they want it.

If the real continues to appreciate, Brazilian authorities could resort to weapons of mass destruction such as raising a 2 percent tax on foreign purchases of bonds and stocks that was imposed last October during another bout of currency strength.

That would help to reduce foreign capital inflows. But it could also scare away the same investment that is helping to plug the country's gaping current account deficit, which reached a monthly record in July and is a source of growing concern. [ID:nN23194162]

Another option would be for the central bank to employ so-called "reverse swaps", a form of derivative that would have the same effect as buying dollars in the futures market. However, a previous period of swaps between 2005 and 2008 failed to stem a significant appreciation of the real.

The mere threat of such measures has been enough to make some investors wary.

PETROBRAS IMPACT

Diego Donadio, an analyst at BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo, says the possibility of greater intervention is the main reason that he is now advising his clients to buy other currencies instead of the real, such as the Mexican peso.

"There are so many deals in the pipeline, whether they be bonds or acquisitions and the capitalization of Petrobras. But on the other hand the risk from intervention is very high," he says.

Although many questions remain unanswered about the mechanics of the Petrobras capitalization, traders expect the deal to lure between $15 billion and $25 billion of foreign investment to Brazil.

Since other local companies have been afraid to come to market in recent months, for fear of being upstaged by the oil giant, a deluge of smaller deals could also follow.

Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities is among those who believe the central bank may choose to surrender somewhat to the currency's rally during this period.

Recent comments from Mantega show "some resignation to short-term appreciation around these large corporate deals," she says.

(Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo. Editing by Brian Winter and W Simon )

text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Strong U.S. data on jobless claims boosts region

* Brazil's real adds 0.1 pct, Mexican peso gains 0.5 pct

* Yields on Brazil rates fall on inflation slowdown (Updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Jean Luis Arce

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed on Thursday, defying attempts by the country's central bank to weaken the currency and protect local exporters.

Euphoria over booming foreign investment in Latin America's biggest economy has recently boosted the real, lifting it last week to its strongest level against the U.S. dollar this year.

After seesawing on Thursday, the real <BRBY> closed 0.12 percent stronger at 1.721 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market. It was boosted by a rally among the region's currencies following stronger U.S. jobs data that increased appetite for riskier assets.

Investors boosted the real despite the decision by Brazil's central bank to step up its intervention in the market on both Wednesday and Thursday by calling more than one auction to buy U.S. dollars. For details, see [ID:nN08128231]

Traders expect a massive share offering by state-owned oil company Petrobras, planned for later this month, to lure $15 billion to $25 billion of foreign investment.

The capitalization plan will not be the only deal to boost the real, Marjorie Hernandez, a currency strategist at HSBC in New York, said in a note to clients.

"The fulfillment of Petrobras' capitalization will also unclog the domestic capital markets pipeline, opening the door for other M&A deals in the latter part of the year," she said.

The bank changed its forecast for the Brazilian real to 1.70 in the third quarter and 1.74 in the fourth quarter, from a previous forecast of 1.84 for both quarters.

Elsewhere in the region, the Mexican peso <MXN=> strengthened 0.48 percent to 12.9900 per dollar after new U.S. claims for unemployment benefits fell more than expected last week to their lowest level in two months. [ID:nN09174403]

Mexico's fragile growth is dependent on the economic recovery of the United States since the country sends about 80 percent of its exports over its northern border.

"This good data got rid of the bad sentiment which has been accumulating in the last month and this is supporting the peso," said Ramon Cordova, a trader at brokerage BASE in Monterrey, Mexico.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.1 percent to 496.2 per dollar. The country's central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 2.5 percent at its Sept. 16 monetary policy meeting.

SLOWER BRAZIL INFLATION SURPRISES AGAIN

Yields fell on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> following data showing slower-than-expected inflation for August. [ID:nSPG003039]

Investors bet the data would put less pressure on the country's central bank to raise the cost of borrowing over coming months.

At the beginning of this month, Brazil's central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 10.75 percent, ending a monetary tightening cycle that helped cool a red-hot economy.

The central bank also released the minutes from that meeting on Thursday, showing it is not currently concerned about a possible sharp rise in the cost of consumer goods.

However, some economists believe that rising food prices next year will force the bank to revise its view and increase borrowing costs again.

The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily traded contracts of the early session, fell to 11.27 percent from 11.36 percent. (Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil says will not let real overvalue
text:
* Brazil will take measures to avoid real appreciating

 * Latest sign govt ramping up intervention in FX market  (Adds debentures comment last paragraph)

 RECIFE, Brazil, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's government on Thursday said it would take necessary steps to stop excessive appreciation of the country's currency, marking the latest sign it is ramping up intervention in foreign exchange markets.

Brazil is gearing up for what markets expect to be large inflows attracted by a massive stock offering from oil giant Petrobras , Finance Minister Guido Mantega said.

 "We will take the necessary measures to prevent that there be an excessive appreciation (of the real)," Mantega said in a speech at an event in the northeastern city of Recife.

 He made the comments after the central bank called its second auction on Thursday to buy U.S. dollars on the spot market.

 The bank has stepped up intervention in foreign exchange markets after the real firmed 4.7 percent against the dollar since the end of June, putting pressure on the country's exporters.

 Brazil's economy has been among the best performers in the world this year. Mantega said he expected the economy to continue to grow at a sustainable pace.

 He saw average annual growth of 5.8 percent in coming years, after expansion of more than 7 percent in 2010.

 A challenge for the next government following Oct. 3 elections will be to keep the current account balanced and keep investment compatible with the country's needs, he added.

 The government was studying tax breaks to help stimulate growth of the domestic debentures market, Mantega said without giving further detail.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currency  rally challenges cenbanks
text:
* Mexican peso jumps 1 pct after strong U.S. data

* Brazil's real pares gains ahead of public holidays

* Yields on Brazil rates rise after national GDP data (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Jean Luis Arce

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's and Chile's currencies hit multi-month highs on Friday, putting pressure on the countries' central banks to take more aggressive action to protect exporters.

The recent rallies could reduce demand for exports as strengthening currencies make them more expensive abroad, potentially weakening the countries' current accounts -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services.

Latin American currencies got a boost after U.S. monthly employment data came in much stronger than expected, raising investors' confidence in the global economic recovery. [ID:nN02227856]

But caution ahead of a public holiday in the United States on Monday and in Brazil on Tuesday caused the Brazilian real to pare gains in late trading.

The real <BRBY> hit its strongest level since Dec. 4, 2009 against the U.S. dollar in early trading. But it eventually closed only 0.1 percent stronger at 1.729 reais on the local spot market.

It still recorded a weekly gain of 1.27 pct -- its biggest weekly rise in 12 weeks.

Separate data showing Brazil's economy grew more than expected in the second quarter also boosted the currency. [ID:nN03239813]

The real is likely to trade around the 1.73-1.74 range next week against the dollar if there are no big changes to the outlook for global growth, said Raphael Martello, an analyst with Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

"It depends a lot on the external scenario. Because the agenda is pretty light in the United States next week compared to this week, it should remain around the current level."

If the real breaks below 1.70, the central bank could be forced to intervene more aggressively in the market, he said.

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Friday the government was determined not to allow the real to appreciate as a fund-raising plan by state oil company Petrobras, the world's largest offering, moves forward.

The Petrobras deal is expected to lure huge amounts of investment to the country. [ID:nN02239445]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> hit its strongest level in more than seven months, later paring gains to trade 0.30 percent stronger at 495.70 per dollar. Over the week, the currency was up 0.77 percent.

Analysts see the central bank intervening to stem the peso's rise if the currency firms to a range of 480 to 465 per dollar.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 1 percent to 12.9415 per dollar after the U.S. data -- its highest in more than a week. But over the week, it has gained only 0.6 percent.

Mexico has gradually limped out of a deep recession thanks to demand for its exports from the United States.

"The fear that the United States will fall back into recession is fading every day and because of this we could see a good rally in the peso next week," said Ramses Villela, head of currency trading at Bulltick Capital Markets in Mexico City.

YIELDS RISE AFTER GDP DATA

Yields rose on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> as investors bet Brazil's strong growth data would put more pressure on the country's central bank to combat inflation by raising the cost of borrowing.

The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily traded contracts of the early session, rose to 11.37 percent from 11.31 percent.

"Everything suggests that there is very strong domestic demand here, which could push interest rates higher," said Gradual Investimentos' Perfeito.

Brazil's central bank on Wednesday held its benchmark interest rate at 10.75 percent, ending a monetary tightening cycle that helped cool a red-hot economy as the country gears up for a presidential election in October.

"The central bank missed a golden opportunity at its last meeting (by not raising rates) to make a smooth transition between this and the next administration. I think this is where they went wrong," said Perfeito. (Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

text:
* U.S. jobs, housing and manufacturing data boosts region

* Brazil's real firms 0.7 pct, Mexican peso adds 0.1 pct

* Chilean peso 0.1 pct weaker as banks buy cheap dollars (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real extended its rally on Thursday after the government confirmed a long-awaited oil fundraising plan which should lure a huge amount of money to Brazil.

The gains put more pressure on the central bank to step up its intervention in the currency market to protect exporters, whose goods have become increasingly expensive abroad as a result of the real's rally.

Optimism over the U.S. economic recovery after a rush of strong employment, manufacturing and housing data over the past two days, also boosted the rest of Latin America's currencies.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.74 percent stronger at 1.732 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market -- the third straight day of gains, taking the real to a fresh four-month high.

After weeks of speculation, Brazil's government finally set the price it will charge state-owned oil company Petrobras for crude reserves to be used in a $43 billion oil-for-shares swap. [ID:nN01187399]

The announcement put an end to recent uncertainty and boosted the currency.

"For the currency, the biggest effect really is the confirmation of the capitalization. This is what is giving most support to the real, even though it's now under this support level of 1.75 (reais per dollar)," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for the CM Capital Markets brokerage in Sao Paulo.

INTERVENTION THREAT

If Brazil's currency remains stronger than 1.75 reais against the dollar for an extended period, the central bank could try to intervene in the market, analysts had said.

But now some believe the central bank could only take new measures once the 1.70 real-per-dollar level is broken.

Verbal warnings, bigger or multiple U.S. dollar purchases and intervention in the futures market via so-called reverse swaps are the most likely options. [ID:nN23213114]

"It is a near-term risk; either that they buy dollars more aggressively or possibly resume those FX reverse swap auctions as we approach 1.70," said Paul Biszko, a strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

But he said the central bank was unlikely to act before the key U.S. monthly payrolls report on Friday, which could have a big impact on the currency.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> edged 0.1 percent higher to 13.0560 per dollar following the strong U.S. data which raised hopes about the recovery of Mexico's top trading partner.

However, investors were cautious ahead of the payrolls report.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 0.1 percent to 497 per dollar after hitting its strongest level in more than seven months, as the price of copper, the country's main export, rose. [ID:nLDE6810SN]

Traders in Santiago said banks took advantage of the early rally to buy dollars at a relatively cheap level.

YIELDS FALL AFTER BRAZIL RATE HELD

Yields fell on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> after the country's central bank held the benchmark interest rate at 10.75 percent late on Wednesday.

Although the decision had been widely expected, the bank also signaled that there was little chance of further rate hikes in the months ahead. [ID:nN01111893]

"We retain our view of protracted pause of the monetary policy as long as commodities prices remain well behaved," said analysts at RBS Securities.

However, they said yields were also falling after sharp gains on Wednesday following strong manufacturing data from China and the United States.

The interest rate futures market in Brazil tends to react just as much to the changing outlook for global growth as it does to national interest rate expectations, they noted.

The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily traded contracts of the early session, fell to 11.29 percent from 11.37 percent.
