title: SCENARIOS-Brazil weighs options to halt real's rise
text:
By Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Compared to the rest of Latin America, Brazil is an old pro at currency intervention.

Haunted by memories of rampant inflation in the 1980s and 90s, Brazil's authorities have continued to play an active role in the currency market, primarily through U.S. dollar purchases.

But the real soared 34 percent against the greenback last year, putting a huge pressure on the country's exporters. Investors flocked to Brazil in the aftermath of the financial crisis since it was one of the few places offering high interest rates and returns, and thus big profits.

While the currency has weakened so far this year, fund-raising plans by local companies and renewed interest in Brazilian bonds has caused the real to firm 2 percent since June, prompting the government to consider getting tougher.

Following are measures which Brazil's authorities have used before and could use again to curb the real's appreciation:

* VERBAL WARNINGS

Brazil's central bank is adamant that it is not trying to secure the real at a specific level.

But that has not stopped economists and traders from fixating on 1.75 as the maximum value the real could be allowed to strengthen against the U.S. dollar before the government takes more aggressive action.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, has frequently issued cautionary comments about the currency's appreciation. Further warnings should be expected whenever this level is broken for more than a few days, analysts say.

* BIGGER OR MULTIPLE DOLLAR AUCTIONS

The central bank has already been increasing its dollar purchases in the spot market via daily auctions, which it resumed on a regular basis in May 2009.

But despite almost doubling its purchases so far this month, the currency has continued to test the 1.75 level.

Analysts argue that the auctions are also creating a guaranteed market for dollars in Brazil which could actually cause the real to strengthen in the long-term.

One temporary option would be to call more than one auction on the same day, as the central bank last did in May this year.

By changing their routine, the central bank would "wrong-foot" the market, sending a stronger signal to traders without necessarily buying more dollars, said Mike Moran, senior currency strategist at Standard Chartered in New York.

* SOVEREIGN WEALTH FUND PURCHASES

Brazil's Treasury has also been buying more dollars, making the most of cheap greenbacks to pay off foreign debt, but the effect on the currency has been minimal.

Brazil's sovereign wealth fund, which was authorized last December to buy dollars but has yet to do so, could also be used to slow the currency's rise.

However, after the initial shock to the market, this strategy faces the same pitfalls as the central bank's daily auctions, analysts say.

* REVERSE CURRENCY SWAP AUCTIONS

"Below 1.70 they would probably pull out the big guns, such as reverse swaps," says Kathryn Rooney Vera, an emerging markets strategist at Bulltick Capital Markets.

Reverse currency swaps are derivatives which, when auctioned to the market, would have the same effect as buying U.S. dollars in the futures market.

The central bank used them regularly between February 2005 and September 2008, and has recently considered reintroducing them, ringing up dealers last month to gauge demand.

While the auctions represent a warning to the market about the currency's strength, they do not actually weaken the real on a technical level. Under the swap contract, the central bank pays out the interbank lending rate on a set amount of reais in exchange for a fixed rate in dollars.

Their use did not stop the real strengthening to 1.56 in July 2008 from 2.60 reais in February.

JPMorgan analysts argue that the government is also reluctant to use derivatives because, unlike dollar purchases which are ostensibly made to accumulate reserves or pay off debts, swaps would be seen as a direct attempt to manipulate the market.

* CAPITAL INFLOWS TAX INCREASE

The currency's surge last year prompted the government in October to slap a 2 percent tax on foreign purchases of stocks and bonds to curb inflows and contain the real's appreciation.

This tax could be increased if the real decisively breaks below the 1.70 level, say analysts at RBC Capital Markets.

But such a policy change could be more tricky in the next few months given the country's upcoming presidential elections.

Aggressive intervention may be even more unlikely if Brazil's ruling party candidate and election favorite, Dilma Rousseff, wins, says Miriam Tavares, a currency director at the AGK brokerage in Sao Paulo. She believes opposition candidate Jose Serra would make more of an effort to curb the real's rise in an effort to boost exports.

However, the scope and scale of these various measures will ultimately depend on events abroad, says Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman.

"If we continue to get weak numbers of out of the United States and continue to see emerging markets weaken, then these policymakers are off the hook." (Editing by Kenneth Barry)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile, Brazil  currencies  break key levels
text:
* Bond flows support region's currencies

* Brazil's real firms 0.3 pct, Mexican peso flat

* Chilean peso pares gains after new government warning (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Chile's peso and the Brazilian real broke through key levels on Wednesday, putting pressure on the countries' central banks to follow through on threats to intervene in the market.

Chile's currency <CLP=CL><CLP=> broke through the 500 peso-per-dollar level for the first time since January.

The region's currencies were boosted by strong demand for a German government bond auction, increasing demand for some higher-risk assets.

Concerns over U.S. economic growth, which are expected to keep returns on U.S. Treasuries near record lows, have also prompted investors to pour money into Latin America's higher-yielding debt, lifting the region's currencies.

But the sharp rise in Chile's peso prompted the government to issue another warning to the market Wednesday, saying it is closely monitoring the peso's appreciation and wants a competitive exchange rate.

After firming to 498.20 per dollar, the peso pared gains but still traded 0.1 percent stronger at 501.60 per dollar.

"The market has already factored in strong growth for the country, and is foreseeing further interest rate hikes, which in turn strengthens the peso," one trader in Santiago said.

Chile's GDP expanded 4.3 percent in the second quarter compared with the first quarter, data Wednesday showed, the fastest pace since at least the mid-1990s. For details, see [ID:nN18182427]

Chile's economy has recovered much faster than expected from the effects of a devastating earthquake in February, boosting the currency to seven-month highs.

The government might decide to slow its repatriation of dollars from copper revenues as a way to curb the currency's rise, analysts said. [ID:nN17124678]

BRAZIL'S REAL BACKS OFF

Brazil's real <BRBY> also firmed past the psychologically important level of 1.75 real-per-dollar but struggled to remain there.

The currency toyed with the level throughout the session, and traded 0.28 percent stronger at 1.748 against the U.S. dollar.

"The economy is growing and rates are high, so inflows are inevitable," said Doug Smith, head of Latin American research at Standard Chartered.

"Brazil has allowed the currency to absorb a great deal of appreciation pressure, unlike the Chinese, and so have a legitimate argument that Brazil has carried much of the global appreciation pressure in the region."

If the real remains stronger than the 1.75 level for an extended period, analysts expect the central bank to act via verbal warnings, bigger or multiple dollar purchases in the spot market or intervention in the futures market.

But analysts at Brazil's Prosper brokerage said the currency could strengthen to 1.70 per dollar because of huge inflows, partly due to the upcoming capital-raising plan by state-run oil company Petrobras .

"Besides this, we expect additional foreign inflows (excluding investment in Petrobras) via bonds and/or shares of $5-6 billion in the short term."

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> closely tracked the performance of the U.S. stock market throughout the day, trading flat at 12.5990 in the afternoon session. U.S. stocks were slightly higher in afternoon trade.

The performance of U.S. assets is closely watched by investors in Mexico due to the countries' strong trade links.

Juan Carlos Lopez, head of trading at brokerage Intercam in Mexico City, said the peso would be stuck between 12.58 and 12.63 per dollar during the session due to the lack of important economic data in Mexico or the United States. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  dip on Fed, China worries
text:
* Slowdown in Chinese demand adds pressure to region

* Mexican peso weakens 0.7 pct, Brazil's real dips 0.5 pct

* Investors eye Brazil's central bank as real nears 1.75 (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Tuesday as cautious investors ditched higher-risk assets worldwide ahead of the outcome of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting later in the day.

If the Fed does not announce any further measures to boost the U.S. economy, as many expect it to do, the region's currencies and other riskier investments could suffer, analysts said.

The Fed's statement is expected to be released at around 1815 GMT.

Concerns over slowing demand from China, which buys the majority of Brazilian exports, also weighed on the region.

The Chinese government's self-induced slowdown caused imports to grow less than expected in July, according to data released on Tuesday. For details, see [ID:nTOE67904G].

"Several subtle data points emerged overnight confirming a recent cooling in overall economic activity and had the effect of washing out those who had feasted on a growing risk appetite during recent sessions," said Andrew Wilkinson, senior analyst at Interactive Brokers in Greenwich, Connecticut.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.46 percent weaker at 1.758 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market in mid-session trading.

If the negative mood in global markets persists, the real is likely to trade between 1.76 and 1.77 per dollar on Tuesday, Miriam Tavares, currency director at brokerage AGK Corretora in Sao Paulo, said in a note.

But if investors' appetite returns following the Fed statement, any local currency gains could be limited by the threat of intervention by Brazil's central bank (BCB), she added.

The central bank called currency dealers last month to gauge their demand for a possible offering of so-called reverse swaps -- a form of derivative which would allow the bank to effectively buy U.S. dollars in the futures market.

"Fresh inflows and the return of foreign capital to the stock market in the past few days, as well as the improving trade balance, is reinforcing expectations of a stronger real," she said.

Analysts at Brown Brothers Harriman noted on Tuesday that investors in Brazil are increasingly shifting from bond purchases to stocks. [ID:nN10139757]

"The central bank would have to adopt a more aggressive approach, whether it be via the auction purchases in the spot market or bringing up the issue of reverse currency swaps again, if it wants to secure the currency around the 1.75 per-dollar level," AGK's Tavares said.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.65 percent to 12.7010 per dollar. The Mexican economy is heavily dependent on U.S. growth since the country sends about 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

Data on Tuesday showing an unexpected drop in U.S. non-farm productivity in the second quarter, the first decline since late 2008, made investors even more cautious.

A sharp slowdown in U.S. activity would also reduce the amount of money Mexican workers in the United States send to their families back home.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 0.16 percent to 512.30 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, fell ahead of the Fed statement. ( Editing by W Simon )

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso leads region's losses on US data
text:
* Brazil's real dips 0.4 pct, Mexican peso loses 1.4 pct

* Chile outperforms region over week on growth optimism

* Investors eye intervention by Brazil's central bank

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso headed for its biggest daily loss in more than two months on Friday, leading the region's losses, after data showed twice as many U.S. jobs were lost last month than economists had forecast.

The report added to concerns that the United States is facing a sharp slowdown, which would reduce demand for Latin American exports and make jittery investors less likely to buy the region's higher-risk assets.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> lost 1.44 percent to 12.7409 per dollar, hitting its weakest level for a week and was set to record its steepest daily percentage decline since June 4.

"The peso's weakness is due to the perception of a slowdown in the United States and the impact this could have on economic activity in Mexico," said Salvador Orozco, a debt and currency strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

Mexico's fragile economic recovery from the financial crisis is particularly dependent on U.S. growth, since the country sends most of its exports across its northern border.

Slowing U.S. activity would also reduce the amount of money that Mexican workers in the United States send to their families back home.

The Mexican peso was also set to record the region's deepest weekly loss of 0.75 percent.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened 0.4 percent to 1.759 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market on Friday, and was heading for a weekly loss of 0.28 percent.

Implicit warnings from Brazilian officials that they will prevent the real from strengthening much past its current value have kept investors cautious around the 1.75 real-per dollar level.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said on Friday that the government was "concerned" about the real's strength. "The central bank and the Finance Ministry don't want (the real) to strengthen further," he said.

ANDEAN REGION STORMS AHEAD

While the Chilean peso was flat at 514.50 on Friday, the currency was set to gain 1.26 percent over the week.

The South American country's economy is recovering much faster than expected from the effects of a devastating earthquake earlier this year, recent data has shown.

Booming growth could also put more pressure on its central bank to sharply raise the cost of borrowing.

Analysts have widely been expecting the central bank to opt for a third straight monthly rate increase of 50 basis points when it meets on August 12, but interest rate futures show market expectations for the year-end are rising.

Higher interest rates would help boost the Chilean peso by attracting more yield-hungry foreign investors.

"What we have is an economy that's growing in an important way, and at the same time, we don't have any significant inflationary pressures," said Francisco Hazbun, a trader with the Tanner brokerage in Santiago.

The Colombian peso <COP=STFX> settled at its strongest closing level in two years on Friday, as investors continued to bet on inflows into the country's mining and energy sectors.

Peru's currency <PEN=PE>hit a fresh two-year intraday low on Friday.

The Peruvian economy grew more than 9 percent in the second quarter, central bank officials said on Friday, a day after raising interest rates by more than expected to avert inflationary pressures. [ID:nN06260729]

(Additional reporting by Molly Rosbach in Santiago; Editing by Paul Simao)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Peru's  currency  at 2-yr high, region struggles
text:
* Brazil's real loses 0.5 pct, Mexican peso dips 0.1 pct

* World Cup fever partly to blame for Brazil June slowdown

* Chilean peso firms as investors price in rate hike

(Recasts; adds comments)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Peru's currency climbed to its strongest level in two years on Tuesday, after a Brazilian industrial conglomerate became the latest company to take its share of one of the world's fastest growing economies.

Brazil's Votorantim announced that it had finally gained control of Peruvian miner Milpo on Tuesday. The Peruvian sol <PEN=PE> firmed 0.4 pct to 2.8050 as the Brazilian company moved to snap up the currency to complete the purchase of its latest stake, said traders in Peru's capital Lima.

The deal helped Peruvian markets shrug off a further battering of weak U.S. data which prompted losses among the continent's major currencies.

Peru's currency has surged about 16 percent since its low in March 2009 as the country's economy has bounced back from the financial crisis thanks to a huge construction boom.

Economic growth is expected to hit 6.6 percent in 2010, the government said in June, ranking Peru alongside Brazil as the fastest growing countries in the region and the world.

"Market players are expecting a greater appreciation of the nuevo sol, due to the strong fundamentals of Peru's economy and more dollars coming in thanks to higher exports and private investment," said Jose Razuri, analyst at the Maximixe consultancy in Lima.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> also firmed on Tuesday, gaining 0.3 percent to 516.50 per dollar to hit a fresh three-month intraday high against the U.S. dollar.

After a devastating earthquake in February, Chile's economy has sprung back faster than most economists were expecting. And strong growth has prompted investors to bet the country's central bank will have to raise interest rates by more than expected over the coming months in an effort to contain inflation.

BRAZIL AND MEXICO LOSE OUT

But the currencies of Brazil and Mexico, the dual powerhouse of Latin American growth, suffered losses on Tuesday due to concerns that the U.S. recovery is faltering.

Data showed U.S. factory orders fell steeply in June while an index of pending home sales plunged to a record low in the same month.

U.S. growth is vital for Latin America's own economic health since the region exports huge amounts of agricultural and mineral goods to the United States.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> dipped 0.1 percent to 12.5830 per dollar.

Brazil's real was under further pressure from a combination of local concerns, weakening 0.5 percent to 1.758.

A drop in industrial production in Brazil during June added to recent signs that growth in Latin America's biggest economy is slowing. For details, see [ID:nN03274323]

"The weak industrial performance in the second quarter confirms the expectation of a sharp slowdown of the economy during that period," said Luciano Rostagno, the chief strategist for CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo, in a note to clients. However, the recent World Cup soccer tournament may have affected production, since many fans in Brazil took days off work to watch the games, he said.

Investors were also cautious after the Brazilian real broke through the key 1.75 level in the previous session, prompting further speculation that Brazil's central bank may step up its intervention in the market.

(Additional reporting by Ursula Scollo in Lima and Alonso Soto in Santiago; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real slips as IP drop feeds rate view
text:
* Brazil's real slips as investors curb rate hike bets

* Third month of falling IP shows Brazil is cooling

* Petrobras delay speculation also weighs on real

* Mexico's peso slips, Chile's peso gains on China news (Recasts; adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's real led Latin American currencies' losses on Tuesday after a drop in industrial production fed expectations that the country's central bank may not hike interest rates as much as expected.

Pressuring Latin American currencies across the board, weak U.S. data highlighted the slackening pace of growth in the United States, one of the region's top trading partners.

Brazil's real saw the biggest losses after data showed industrial production dropped 1 percent in June from May, marking the third straight month of declines as Latin America's largest economy cools from booming growth earlier in the year. For details, see [ID:nN03274323]

A spate of weaker data in Brazil has pushed investors to pare back expectations for interest rate hikes.

"That is putting a little bit of a headwind into the appreciation of the real, along with the increased talk of intervention by the central bank," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, managing director of emerging markets at TD Securities in Toronto.

The real had gained more than 2 percent from a mid-July low before Tuesday's losses.

Analysts expect Brazil's central bank may step up its currency intervention if the real strengthens much past the 1.75 per dollar level. On Tuesday, the real <BRBY> bid 0.46 percent weaker at 1.757 per U.S. dollar.

WEAK U.S. DATA

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> seesawed after the industrial production data left investors unsure about whether Brazil's central bank would continue to raise rates at its next meeting.

Yields first dipped, before rising as market players who have bet on less-steep hikes took profits on recent gains, analysts said.

Bets on further rate hikes in Brazil have fallen sharply in the last month.

The market is currently pricing in only a 50 percent chance of a 25 basis point hike at the central bank's next policy decision, due September 1, said Tony Volpon, head of Americas emerging market research at Nomura Securities in New York.

The market has also been cutting back expectations of further hikes next year.

"A lot of people are backtracking furiously, and that is not good for the currency," Volpon said.

Also weighing on the real was market chatter about a further delay of an up to $25 billion share offering by Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company. Petrobras reaffirmed on Monday a previously reported September deadline, but doubts lingered about that timeframe. [ID:nN02111873]

"It is not clear what is going to happen but any postponement or noise can affect the foreign exchange market that is already positioned to absorb part of this deal," a New York-based trader said.

Weighing on sentiment across the region, data showed U.S. factory orders fell steeply in June while an index of pending home sales plunged to a record low in the same month. Data on U.S. personal income and spending in June was unexpectedly flat.

U.S. growth, which is largely driven by consumer spending, is vital for Latin America's own economic health since the region exports huge amounts of agricultural and mineral goods to the United States.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.13 percent to 12.5905 per dollar.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.27 percent stronger to 516.50 per dollar after Chile's state miner Codelco , the world's top copper producer, said China's plan to bring electricity to rural areas would demand one million tonnes of copper in the next two and a half years.

title: Brazil Real Closes Weaker On Possible Action By  Central Bank
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, facing resistance after hitting its strongest level in months Monday, on expectations of more aggressive market intervention by Brazil's central bank.

The real closed at BRL1.7587 to the dollar, weaker than Monday's close at BRL1.7500.

Traders said the real weakened on market ideas that any strengthening beyond the psychological barrier of BRL1.75 to the dollar could prompt more aggressive Brazilian central-bank intervention to support the U.S. currency.

On Monday, the real briefly traded between BRL1.74 and BRL1.75, closing at BRL1.7500 on possible central-bank intervention.

In recent weeks, Brazil's central bank has given signals that it could resume what are known as reverse swap auctions to prop up the U.S. dollar. Traders said these rumors have a greater effect in the currency market as the real strengthens toward BRL1.75 to the dollar.

The reverse swap auction is a form of intervention in the foreign-exchange futures market. At the auction, the central bank swaps contracts indexed to interest rates for futures contracts linked to foreign-exchange positions.

Such auctions are a way to relieve pressure against the dollar by eliminating short-dollar positions. Traders said Brazilian banks and funds have accumulated sizeable short-dollar positions.

Central-bank interest in supporting the dollar is based on the fact that Brazilian exporters lose revenue and market share when the real is strong.

In Brazil, the dollar bucked the prevalent global trend. In international trading, the dollar closed lower against the euro and Japanese yen on a string of weak U.S. economic figures and indications from the U.S. Federal Reserve that it could engage in another round of monetary easing to aid the sluggish U.S. economy.

Meanwhile, global metals prices were mostly lower on the uptick in global risk aversion, but oil prices closed higher. Prices in the commodities are important supports for the Brazilian currency, determining export revenue for Brazilian commodities producers.

On Brazilian credit markets, short-term interest-rate futures contracts were mostly higher Tuesday, as investors expected industrial production to pick up speed in July and August after data released Tuesday showed a decline in June.

The most actively traded interest-rate futures contract on the Brazilian Financial Exchange, that of January 2012, rose to 11.58% after closing Monday at 11.51%.

text:
* Brazil's real breaks 1.75 level, eyes on intervention

* European bank earnings, US factory survey data support

* Colombia peso hits 9-1/2 month high against dollar

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Brazil's real hit a three-month high on Monday despite the threat of more central bank intervention and other Latin American currencies also jumped on solid European bank earnings and U.S. factory data.

Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> hit a nine-month high while Mexico's peso <MXN=> traded at its strongest in six weeks.

Strong financial results from Europe's banking sector and data showing the U.S. manufacturing sector grew in July for the 12th straight month gave investors greater confidence in the strength of global economic recovery. [ID:nN02183874]

Brazil's real has gained around 3 percent from a mid-July low. Mexico's peso has risen close to 5 percent from its weakest level seen early last month.

Analysts said thin, summer trading was exaggerating recent gains.

"We have come a long way on these currencies without much volume. I would be cautious that people would be willing to take profits on these moves rather quickly," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> broke through the closely-watched level of 1.75 per dollar to bid 0.46 percent firmer at 1.746 per dollar in the local spot market.

Speculation has mounted that piercing the 1.75 level could push the country's central bank to start intervening in the futures market to tame the real's gains.

"The market is testing the central bank's resolve," said Cattan-Naslausky.

LOW-VOLUME GAINS

Foreign investors enamored with Brazil's growth prospects have gobbled up local assets and driven the currency to double in value against the dollar since President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva took office in 2003.

The flow of dollars into Brazil has strengthened the currency enough to put significant pressure on exporters' profit margins.

Local authorities are already using a capital inflows tax and daily dollar purchases in the spot market to break the tide. The central bank is expected to wade into the derivatives market soon, where most foreign market players are making their big bets.

Cattan-Naslausky doubted the central bank would step up its intervention efforts amid a low volume move of the real.

"The flows are not there, so coming in with this strategy to absorb flows doesn't make much sense, it would only sharpen volatility," she added.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.49 percent to 12.5745 per U.S. dollar as the U.S. manufacturing survey boded well for further recovery in Mexico's closely-linked factories.

The Chilean peso <> firmed 0.66 percent to 517.70 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, traded at three-month highs. [ID:nLDE6710PA]

Oil prices and higher commodity prices support Latin American currencies in general, given the region's big output in goods like Mexican oil and Brazil's iron ore and soy.

Colombia's currency gained 0.67 percent to 1,832 per dollar, pulling back slightly after hitting its strongest since mid-October 2009.

Yield spreads between emerging market bonds and U.S. Treasuries, a key gauge of risk aversion, narrowed 17 basis points to 270 basis points, according to the JPMorgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ>.

Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> bid down to a fresh all-time low early in the session, but pared back to bid down 1 basis point at 6.52 percent.

Mexican bonds have rallied this year as Europe's debt crisis put a shine on Mexico's relatively trim fiscal deficit and market players also bet on big flows later this year when Citigroup will include peso debt in a major index.

text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Thursday, tracking the euro and global commodities prices and ahead of dollar inflows expected in the near term.

Short-term interest rate futures contracts were lower and longer-term contracts higher Thursday, reflecting market adjustment to indications of a slower monetary tightening in the near term followed by renewed inflationary pressures in 2012 or 2013.

text:
* Unexpected drop in U.S. durable goods hits region

* Brazil's real under pressure over reverse swaps

* Chile's peso loses 0.7 pct on industrial slowdown (Adds details about Brazil inflows, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, July 28 (Reuters) - Brazil's real outperformed Latin American currencies for most of the session on Wednesday on data showing strong inflows, a day after the government sold bonds at a record-low yield.

But the effect was short-lived and the currency weakened in late trading, following the region's currencies downward, under pressure from weaker-than-expected U.S. data.

Brazil on Tuesday priced $750 million of its reopened 2021 global bond at a 4.547 percent yield, and it sold $75 million more in Asian markets on Wednesday, the Treasury said.

The bond sale is set to encourage local banks and companies to also raise money in the debt markets, bringing more dollars to Brazil.

Strong inflows related to existing deals in the market helped boost the currency temporarily on Wednesday, traders in Sao Paulo said. About $1.2 billion entered the market at the beginning of the session due to the actions of two large exporters, they said.

"Everything is indicating there was a big inflow today," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora in Sao Paulo. "Volume spiked a lot."

Currency volumes on the Brazilian exchange surged to more than $4 billion on Wednesday, above this year's daily average of $2.6 billion.

Brazil offers some of the highest yields among emerging market assets in its local currency bonds, which are a magnet for investors seeking high short-term returns.

But the real <BRBY> closed 0.1 percent weaker at 1.769 per dollar on the local spot market, under pressure from worries about a slowdown in the United States and intervention in the market.

Recent chatter regarding intervention in the futures market via derivatives by Brazil's central bank is also "increasing the likelihood of a sharp downward correction looking forward," Diego Donadio, an analyst at BNP Paribas, wrote in a note to clients.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, on Tuesday also voiced his support for central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets. For details, see [ID:nN2798713]

The real's sharp gains since the beginning of last year have put huge pressure on exporters, prompting the government last October to curb the currency's rise by imposing a tax on foreign purchases of stocks and bonds.

The central bank has also been holding daily dollar auctions to capture excess greenbacks.

Brazilian Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin said on Wednesday Brazil will return to international debt markets before the end of the year.

The issue would probably be for longer-term paper than the 2021 global bond that was reopened on Tuesday, he said, adding that he would not rule out a foreign issue denominated in local currency before the end of the year.

MEXICO, CHILE CURRENCIES SLIP

Mexico and Chile's currencies slipped on Wednesday after U.S. data showing an unexpected drop in new orders for long-lasting manufactured goods in June renewed concerns the U.S. economic recovery is slowing down.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> <MEX01> lost 0.4 percent to 12.720. Mexico, Latin America's second-biggest economy, depends on sustained demand in the United States, which buys around 80 percent of local exports.

Chile's peso was under further pressure after data showed industrial output was slowing in Chile. The country's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.7 percent weaker at 523.30 per dollar in afternoon trading.

Chile's industrial production <CLIP=ECI> rose a seasonally adjusted 0.8 percent in June from May, falling short of market expectations of a 2.25 percent increase.

"The slower growth in industrial output is prompting the expectation that the central bank could decide to put the brakes on its benchmark rate increases, which the peso is now reflecting," one trader in Santiago said.

The market has been betting on the central bank raising its key rate by another 50 basis points to 2 percent at its next monetary policy meeting. A bank poll of financial players released on Wednesday showed that economists expect the rate to be at around 3.63 percent within six months.

title: *DJ Brazil Finance Min Sees $45-$48B Current Account Deficit
text:
27 Jul 2010 12:58 EDT *DJ  Brazil Finance Minister: Imports Impacting Deficit

27 Jul 2010 13:00 EDT *DJ  Brazil Finance Min: Current Account Deficit Not A Threat

27 Jul 2010 13:02 EDT *DJ  Brazil Finance Min Favors Central Bank Action On Forex

27 Jul 2010 13:17 EDT =DJ  Brazil Finance Minister Sees $45B-$48B Current Account Deficit

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil faces a sharp rise in its current account deficit in 2010, but the increase doesn't spell a threat to Brazil's overseas accounts or its booming economy, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Tuesday.

Mantega predicted a current account deficit in 2010 that will be between $45 billion and $48 billion. The current account deficit in 2009 was $24.3 billion.

Mantega made the comments to reporters and was quoted by the local Estado news agency.

"The deficit does not represent any kind of threat," said Mantega. "It does not threaten economic growth. On the contrary, it is the result of economic growth."

Mantega said growth in the deficit was coming mainly from an increase in imports due to Brazil's booming economy. The economy is likely to expand some 7% this year, according to most economists.

Burgeoning imports have pulled down Brazil's trade surplus so far this year. Through July 25, Brazil posted a trade surplus of $9.36 billion, down from $16.71 billion for the same period in 2009.

Mantega also commented on Brazil's foreign exchange market, saying he favors central bank "monitoring" of the market to guard against excessive volatility.

He added, "I favor central bank action, when opportune." He said such action could include central bank intervention in the foreign exchange futures market.

Brazil's central bank, in past years, has conducted swap auctions involving foreign exchange and interest rate futures contracts as a way to reduce volatility in the foreign exchange market. The central bank also acts in the market as a buyer and seller of U.S. dollars.

title: Brazil Real Closes Weaker As Government Mulls Reverse Swaps
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as Brazil's government mulled possible intervention in the foreign exchange futures market through so-called reverse swap auctions.

The real closed at BRL1.7702 to the dollar, weaker against Monday's close of BRL1.7663.

Last week, the Brazilian Central Bank opened informal consultations with brokerages on the possibility of resuming so-called reverse swap auctions.

Such auctions were used in 2006 and 2007 to help support the U.S. dollar against the Brazilian real at a time when the real was appreciating rapidly against the American currency. A strong real hurts Brazilian exports.

The reverse swap auction is a form of intervention in the foreign exchange futures market. At the auction, the central bank swaps contracts indexed to interest rates for futures contracts linked to foreign exchange positions.

In comments to reporters Tuesday afternoon, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said he favored use of the reverse swap mechanism, raising speculation the central bank may call such an auction in the next few days.

The Brazilian currency also weakened Tuesday because of a weak euro and declining commodities prices. Commodities prices are a support for Brazilian export revenues.

In credit markets Tuesday, interest rate futures contracts declined on expectations for a continued benign inflation scenario. On the Brazilian Financial Exchange, interest rate futures contracts closed lower across the board. The contracts reflect investor expectations for annualized interest rates at future dates.

Among actively traded interest rate futures contracts Tuesday, that of January 2012 closed at 11.54%, down from 11.62% Monday.

text:
* Brazil Finance Minister tips possible intervention

* Brazil real loses 0.41 pct, Mexico peso slides 0.15 pct

* Chiles peso knocked off three-month high

(New throughout, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, July 27 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies slipped on Tuesday, hurt by a drop in U.S. consumer confidence, and Brazil's real lost ground after the country's finance minister backed further central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso hit its highest level in over a month early in the session and Chile's peso traded at a three-month high before lackluster stock markets pushed investors to cash in on recent gains in the region's currencies.

Confidence among American consumers dropped in July to the lowest level since February on worries about the job market, the Conference Board reported on Tuesday.

"There are a lot of mixed signals out there, such as talk of deflationary pressures but then you see good earnings reports," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, managing director of emerging markets at TD Securities in Toronto.

"We have seen a good rally in the last few days, so it is a bit of a technical rebound as people take some profits," Perez-Duarte said.

Mexico's peso has advanced 3 percent from a low on July 2, while the real has gained more than 2 percent since June 29.

Concerns have eased about a financial crisis in Europe following stress tests of banks, while solid revenue outlooks from some bellwether companies like FedEx have offset fears the U.S. economy is slowing.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> slipped 0.15 percent to 12.6895 per U.S. dollar while the Brazilian real <BRL=> bid 0.41 percent weaker in international trade to 1.7688 per dollar. Chile's peso <CLP=CL> shed 0.19 percent to 519.70 per dollar.

BRAZIL JAWBONING

Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega on Tuesday voiced his support for central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets. [ID:nN2798713]

Speculation is mounting that the central bank could step up measures to contain the real's strength, which is hurting exporters. The bank itself informally sounded out demand for reverse currency swaps last week.

But analysts were skeptical that new measures would have much more success than a capital inflow tax and daily dollar purchases.

"I do not think verbal intervention will be enough, because even actual intervention has not been enough," Perez-Duarte said.

Investors will continue to demand Brazilian assets due to the country's prospects for growth and some of the highest yields among investment-grade emerging markets, analysts said.

Brazil launched $750 million worth of reopened 2021 global bonds on Tuesday, more than the $500 million initially offered, as the deal found strong demand among investors, Thomson Reuters' IFR reported. [ID:nN27184714]

Yield spreads between emerging market bonds and U.S. Treasuries, a key gauge of risk aversion, narrowed 10 basis points to 273 basis points on Tuesday, according to the JPMorgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ>.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm  currencies  firm after U.S. data
text:
* Brazil's real under pressure on central bank plans

* Strong U.S. new home sales data boosts region

* Mexican peso firms 0.2 pct, Brazil's market split (Updates prices, adds comments)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, July 26 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Monday after data showed U.S. sales of new homes surged in June, restoring some confidence in the recovery of the world's biggest economy.

But Brazil's currency markets were mixed due to expectations that the country's central bank may shift its involvement in the market.

Fears over a fresh slowdown in U.S. growth have hit Mexico particularly badly since the country sells about 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

But data on Monday showing that sales of new, single-family homes rebounded in June sent Mexico's peso to its strongest level in more than a week. For details, see [ID:nN26203473]

The Mexican currency <MXN=> firmed 0.24 percent to 12.700 per dollar.

"The sales data came in above what was expected and by a lot, so this is giving a little more certainty to the outlook," said Omar Martin del Campo, a trader at Banco Ve Por Mas in Mexico City.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> edged 0.17 percent stronger to 519.10 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, touched a 10-week high. [ID:nLDE66P0SW]

But traders were cautious after the Chilean peso clocked its biggest weekly gain since May on Friday, due to the expectation of greater dollar inflows as the state moves to cash in its copper revenues.

According to the international reference rate, the Brazilian real <BRL=> was 0.34 percent stronger at 1.7675, buoyed by the strong U.S. economic data.

REVERSE SWAPS DIVIDE BRAZIL'S MARKET

But on the local spot market, the real <BRBY> was 0.57 percent weaker at 1.768 compared to Friday's closing level.

Traders attributed the difference to chatter about a possible shift in the way Brazil's central bank intervenes in the country's currency markets.

"Late last Friday the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) 'checked' with FX dealer desks the demand for 'reverse swaps'," said Tony Volpon, Latin America strategist with Nomura Securities.

Reverse swaps are a form of derivative that would allow the central bank to take a long position in the U.S. dollar futures market in exchange for a short position in the interest rate markets.

Selling reverse swaps would be a way to reduce the arbitrage opportunities in the market, which have arisen due to the huge reserves the central bank has amassed through daily U.S. dollar auctions.

Brazil's central bank informally consulted the market around 1740 local time on Friday, according to one trader, causing the international reference rate to weaken sharply in late trading.

But by that point, the local spot market in Sao Paulo had already closed for the day. As such, Friday's closing level on the local spot market was much stronger than the international reference rate, meaning that Monday's currency moves were compared against widely different bases.

The last time the central bank offered reverse swaps was in September 2008.

"In fact it is a bit of a mystery why the BCB is not doing this already if its implicit goal is to depreciate or dampen the Brazilian real," Nomura's Volpon said.

However, Brazil's central bank has been reluctant to use derivatives as a tool for currency intervention because of their lack of transparency, wrote analysts at J.P.Morgan in a note earlier this month.

The real also pared gains after Brazil's current account deficit for June came in far worse than expected compared to the year-ago period. Imports jumped faster than exports and companies sent more money abroad. [ID:nN26154475]

"But the current account deterioration has been going on for some time now," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities. The expectation that the central bank will resume reverse swaps was exerting a bigger pressure on the currency, she said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  slip on US data, Fed
text:
* Brazil's real loses 0.8 pct ahead of China data

* Gloomier Fed outlook dents sentiment

* Mexican peso hurt by drop in U.S. retail sales

* Chile's peso firms on rate hike bets

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, July 14 (Reuters) - Brazil and Mexico's currencies dipped on Wednesday as weak U.S. retail sales and concerns about upcoming Chinese economic growth data threatened to derail a recent rally on bets of solid U.S. corporate earnings.

Brazil's real slipped after hitting a two-month high on Tuesday, while the Mexican peso retreated from its strongest in two weeks. Chile's peso firmed ahead of a widely expected interest rate hike on Thursday by the country's central bank.

Also weighing on sentiment was a gloomier outlook on the U.S. economy from the Federal Reserve. Members of its interest-rate setting board said they had "slightly" revised down their outlook for economic growth. [ID:nWALEIE6D2]

"If the U.S. economy is not going to grow as much as expected, then Mexico as well will not grow as much, and that will hurt exports and the peso," said Alejandro Martinez, a currency and debt strategist at HSBC in Mexico City.

U.S. data showed retail sales fell in June for the second straight month, which offset better-than-expected results from technology bellwether Intel Corp.

"There is a tug of war. People are worried about growth in the second half, but then you have these stellar earnings," said Win Thin, an emerging markets currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

Riskier assets like emerging market currencies got a boost this month on bets that U.S. corporate earnings could compensate for a string of recent weak data in the United States.

Trading on Latin American stock exchanges was choppy on Wednesday. [ID:nN14143185]

Investors cut risky positions ahead of economic growth data due early Thursday from China, Brazil's top trading partner. Economists expect China's year-on-year growth rate slowed in the second quarter. [ID:nSGE6660AR]

"China could either throw gasoline on the fire and people will start worrying about the global slowdown again. But I think that the Chinese economy remains pretty strong, so hopefully it will underpin sentiment," Thin said.

CHILE RATE BETS

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.8 percent weaker at 1.765 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

Analysts also pointed to concerns of intervention by Brazil's central bank that could have pushed some to pare back on bets backing the real. Traders say policy makers are uncomfortable seeing the real stronger than 1.75 to the dollar.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> lost 0.31 percent to 12.7224 after hitting its strongest since June 28 early in the session.

The slack U.S. retail sales data for June put pressure on the peso.

The Mexican currency is closely tied to the health of the U.S. economy given that the United States buys about 80 percent of Mexico's exports.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.5 percent to 532.35 per dollar, helped by speculation that the country's central bank could raise interest rates more than a widely-expected 50 basis-point hike to 1.5 percent on Thursday.

Both Brazil and Chile are raising interest rates, which should keep up demand from yield-hungry investors for local debt.

Chile's economy has made a quick recovery from the effects of a massive earthquake in February, giving the central bank more reason to tighten monetary policy.

Chile's peso is seen firming to 521.63 per U.S. dollar by the end of the year, as rising rates attract greater foreign investment, a poll by the country's central bank showed on Wednesday. [ID:nN14122954] (Additional reporting by Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: Brazil justifies  forex  action on 'flash-crash' Thursday
text:
NEW YORK, May 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank bought U.S. dollars on May 6, the day the U.S. stockmarket briefly plunged, in order to absorb excess greenback inflows and to avoid alarming investors in a day of heightened market anxiety, the bank's president said on Tuesday.

U.S. stocks suddenly crashed on Thursday May 6, with the Dow Jones <.DJI> recording its largest-ever intraday point drop in a span of about 20 minutes, when the Brazilian central bank announced its usual auction to purchase dollars in the domestic currency market.

That decision was "absolutely" in accordance to the government policy of mopping up excess dollar liquidity, regardless of the foreign exchange level, central bank president Henrique Meirelles said.

"If you look at that period you'll observe that (dollar) flows were positive. They were actually extremely positive that day," Meirelles told Reuters in an interview.

Central bank data show a net inflow of $2.24 billion into Brazil's foreign exchange market on May 6, more than twice the level of the previous day, as exporters took advantage of a weakening currency to bring their dollars into the country.

Meirelles claimed that the central bank auction didn't add volatility to the market either, as the real trimmed losses of about 5.0 percent later in the day to close about 3 percent weaker.

The central bank action also aimed at transmitting a sense of normalcy to investors, he said.

"If the central bank had unnecessarily suspended the auction in a day of highly positive dollar inflows, that could have caused volatility in the market," Meirelles said.

"Investors would wonder what is that the central bank can see see and they can not."

The Brazilian central bank has been buying dollars in the domestic foreign exchange market on a daily basis, expect during holidays, since early May 2009, when it revived its strategy to boost foreign reserves.

It had halted those auctions after the collapse of Lehman Brothers in 2008, when global aversion to risk soared and dollars started flowing out of the country.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Weaker As  Central Bank Intervenes
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Friday as the central bank intervened twice in currency markets for the second-consecutive session.

The real ended at BRL1.7370 to the dollar on Brazil's BM&FBovespa exchange, weaker from Thursday's close at BRL1.7302.

The local currency traded stronger throughout the session as expectations for heavy foreign-investment inflows increased in the wake of Wednesday's decision by the Brazilian Central Bank to raise interest rates.

The central bank hiked the benchmark Selic base interest rate by 75 basis points to 9.5%. The bank is also expected to front-load a series of rate hikes aimed at controlling inflationary pressures and avoiding an overheated economy, according to economists.

Higher interest rates in Brazil typically attract heavy foreign inflows from investors seeking better rates of return. Brazil has been a favored destination for carry trade players, who borrow cheap cash overseas and invest in Brazil.

Currency markets also appeared to dismiss threats made by Treasury Secretary Arno Augustin, who said Thursday that the treasury was prepared to start buying dollars to counter any steep appreciation in the real. Traders said that until the treasury actually started buying dollars, the threat lacked credibility.

The central bank, however, was more than willing to back up the threat. For the second-consecutive session, the bank held two spot-market dollar purchase auctions. The bank bought an undisclosed volume of dollars at BRL1.7312 and BRL1.7342 to the dollar.

The auctions followed a similar move during Thursday's session, when the central bank was estimated to have purchased nearly $1.5 billion on the spot market, traders said.

The timing of the central bank's heavy hand was significant because the real was also getting a boost from market players holding short-dollar positions ahead of Friday's Ptax, traders said. The Ptax is the average daily foreign exchange rate used to settle futures contracts, and will be used to settle futures contracts Monday.

The typical month-end tug-of-war between short- and long-position holders adds a dose of volatility to trading each month. The timing of two-consecutive double auctions during the heat of the Ptax battle was significant--and shows the bank is serious about undercutting the real, traders said.

The bank has held a single daily purchase auction since May 2009. Before this month, the last double auction was held in 2007--with the more aggressive intervention starting on April 15, when the bank held its first double auction.

Local interest rate futures contracts also reflected the central bank's rate hike and expectations for future hikes.

The most actively traded contract, January 2011, rose to 11.12% after closing Thursday at 11.01%. The contracts reflect investor expectations for average annual interest rates at future dates.

Brazil's overnight interbank lending rate, known as the CDI, was even with Thursday's close at 9.36%.

Meanwhile, Brazil's benchmark Global 40 bond was flat at a bid of 133 7/8.

title: LATIN AMERICAN MARKETS: Brazil's Bovespa Falls As Net Servicos Slumps

Brazil's key equity index fell Thursday, with telecommunications stocks and cable operator Net Servicos struggling with losses after a broker downgrade of the Latin American telecom and media sector.

Goldman said it will focus on "pure mobile operators" Vivo Participacoes (VIV) and TIM Brasil (TSU), as they are fully exposed to "still-growing wireless demand in Brazil and should capture (and drive) mobile-data growth."

As part of its sector assessment, the broker downgraded NII Holdings (NIHD) to neutral from buy. Investors in the Brazilian equity market on Thursday appeared to have set aside data showing that China's economy expanded 11.9% in the first quarter from the year-earlier period, exceeding analyst expectations. China became Brazil's biggest trading partner last year.

In Brasilia Thursday, Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and China President Hu Jintao signed a four-year bilateral action plan as well as a number of separate agreements aimed in part at strengthening their trade ties.

Intervention

title: ANALYSIS- Brazil  cenbank brakes  currency  strength, not for long
text:
* Double intervention lays floor for the dollar

* Purchases haven't halted real's appreciation in the past

* Positive inflows to continue in the short term

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, April 16 (Reuters) - Stepped-up intervention by Brazil's central bank in currency markets should brake the real's appreciation as traders mull what other government actions could be on tap.

But analysts say strong dollar inflows over the next few weeks will eventually cause the real <BRBY> to strengthen anew.

Brazil's central bank on Thursday held two auctions to buy dollars on the spot market -- the first time it did so since July 13, 2007.

The back-to-back intervention came as the real had firmed 4.63 percent over the previous 12 sessions. Inflows into Brazil, a darling of foreign investors, as well as higher investor appetite for risk amid waning fears of a Greek default were seen factoring into the currency's climb.

That kind of appreciation is worrying to Brazil, Latin America's largest economy and a recent magnet for inflows.

"We're going to have a more aggressive foreign exchange policy, trying to brake things a bit," Ilan Goldfajn, a former central bank director and current chief economist for Itau Unibanco, said on Thursday, hours before the central bank surprised the markets.

"If there's more exchange rate pressure, we'll see action from the sovereign wealth fund to try to hold the line," he added.

While the central bank has occasionally even sold dollars, it has steadily been a buyer of dollars since last May as Brazil's swift rebound from the global economic crisis saw the currency begin its steady advance.

In 2009, the real surged 34 percent against the dollar, despite the central bank purchases.

The government slapped taxes on inflows into local stocks and bonds in October, and on American Depositary Receipts in November, in an effort to hold the currency's gains as Brazil's exporters wrung their hands over the sudden relative increase in expense for their products.

But the central bank says it has no exchange rate target, and that the dollar purchases are geared to boosting Brazil's international reserves, already above $245 billion.

"Perhaps in the next days or hours, investors will have some wariness about being long on the real," said Cristiano Oliveira, chief economist with Banco Safra de Investimento.

Tony Volpon, a strategist with Nomura Securities in New York, also saw a cause for the effect in the market.

"A second auction on the same day is a clear signal (the central bank) is not happy with current levels. Market is right to react," he wrote in a note to clients.

But the bank could also be preempting heavier inflows coming soon, said Nathan Blanche, a partner at Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo, especially in light of the 10-year bond launched by Brazil on Thursday.

The central bank's actions give the market a new reference point, Blanche said.

"Some traders could see this as a floor signaled by the central bank, but they're mistaken. It's an uphill battle for any government to try to establish an exchange rate ... they would have to change policy," he said.

EFFECT BACKFIRING

If the central bank is trying to weaken the real, Safra's Oliveira said the effect will not last long.

"All the central bank has to do is buy dollars -- or speed up the pace of buying -- and the real, days later, gains even more. We've seen this before," he said, referring to 2008.

Among the transactions likely to bring in dollars soon are a share offering from Banco do Brasil , Latin America's largest bank by assets, which hopes to sell another 286 million shares. At Thursday's close of 30.90 reais, that would bring in around 8.8 billion reais.

Later, the capitalization of state-controlled oil giant Petrobras , which could range from $20 billion to $50 billion.

Sidnei Nehme, executive director of the NGO brokerage, has argued that central bank dollar purchases could backfire.

title: Brazil plans no  forex  changes on inflation-report
text:
SAO PAULO, Feb 10 (Reuters) - Brazil plans no interventions in the foreign exchange market to prevent a weakening currency from stoking inflation, Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles said in an interview with the O Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper published on Wednesday.

Brazil's real <BRBY> surged 34 percent in 2009, making it among the best performing currencies against the dollar last year, but it has tumbled 5.6 percent so far in 2010, raising concerns that rising import prices may pressure consumer prices.

Meirelles said the exchange rate is only one of several components that may affect inflation and that the central bank's rate setting committee, known as Copom, considers all of the factors when deciding on borrowing costs.

"We have a target for inflation, not for the exchange rate," Meirelles said in the Estado interview. "We don't make a decision on the currency because of inflation."

Dollar inflows to Brazil have dropped in February after "substantial" volumes in January, but Meirelles said that decline was normal and the central bank would continue to purchase greenbacks on the spot market.

Meirelles told Estado he would have no qualms in hiking the benchmark Selic interest rate this year despite national elections in October, adding that the central bank bases its decisions on macroeconomic models and projections.

title: ANALYSIS-Controls prompting gradual rethink on emrg markets
text:
LONDON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - A wave of capital controls being imposed by emerging economies to prevent hot money flooding their markets may well prompt global investors to think twice before extending already stretched bets on the developing world.

The official concern is that near-zero Western interest rates and a falling U.S. dollar are herding short-term speculators to high-growth economies and high-yielding markets.

And this is destabilising because its volatility complicates economic management; it risks driving local currencies to uncompetitive levels for exporters; and, in the case of fixed exchange rates, it fuels inflation via currency intervention.

What is more, they fear that the bigger these "bubbles" blow the greater the threat of destructive reversal once the world economic recovery triggers an exit from ultra-easy U.S. and European monetary policy and the dollar stabilises.

Over the past six weeks, governments from Brasilia to Moscow to Jakarta are moving beyond central bank intervention to curb these speculative flows.

Brazil announced on Wednesday its second such measure in a month by introducing a 1.5 percent tax on certain trades involving American Depositary Receipts issued by local firms. It imposed a two percent tax on new foreign purchases of local equities and bonds in October.

"It is a risk. Zero interest rates and quantitative easing, that money is creating bubbles in many asset categories. Those regarded as riskier assets have seen the biggest rebound," said Rob Hepworth, senior fund manager at insurer Ecclesiastical.

"It is cause for concern. I would look to keep pretty cautious investment strategies."

Illustrating the sheer scale of investor stampede into emerging economies, net inflows into emerging market equities this year are already at all-time highs, attracting around $60 billion, according to global fund tracker EPFR.

This more than reverses 2008 outflows of $49.5 billion and surpasses the previous record of $54.3 billion posted in 2007.

The record flows come even as emerging economies as a whole are expected by the International Monetary Fund to grow just 1.7 percent this year, compared with 6.0 percent and 8.3 percent in 2008 and 2007 respectively.

While this year's expected expansion far outstrips a forecast contraction of some 3.4 percent in developed economies, next year's likely growth rebound to about 5 percent still leaves it well below 2007 peak.

LEVERAGE ROLLERCOASTER

Investors have been lured partly to diversify their portfolios by adding assets that are supposed to be "uncorrelated" or decoupled from traditional markets. However, as the credit crisis showed, emerging markets may outperform or underperform but they remain hugely correlated with core markets and display far more volatility.

According to an article in Thursday's Financial Times by fund manager Richard Bernstein, total returns data over the past five years show some 75 percent correlation between MSCI's BRIC index (Brazil, Russia, India, China) and the S&P 500 -- with moves in the former 1.6 times that of the Wall St bellwether.

Emerging market stocks, measured by MSCI, rose 71 percent this year, after falling 54.5 percent in 2008. MSCI world equity index has risen just over 30 percent, after a 43.5 percent fall last year.

And this long-running leveraged rollercoaster is the essence of the problem many governments are trying to address -- especially now that many economies, such as Brazil, do not need the international capital in a way they did ten years ago.

"The problem emerging markets face is capital flows are never even. They experience either feast or famine and nothing in between," said Avinash Persuad, chairman of Intelligence Capital and an adviser to many governments on financial risk.

"This has proven over many years as unsustainable and has sown the seeds for what we have seen," he added. "As long as the new stance is just about smoothing capital flows, I don't think it's a retrograde step. But it is risky -- and the risk is they will turn capital away when they need it as the competition among governments for capital increases in the years ahead."

For now investors are happy to exploit correlations that have this year dominated all investment strategies from commodities to equities to currencies and alternatives.

"The bottom line is if you look at the world economy there is a limited amount of countries and geographies that are growing," said Veronica Pechlaner, asset manager at Ashburton.

"Until currency appreciation is allowed to happen it will attract even more flows. You have to make decision that whether returns are enough to offset the barrier that is put on you. It doesn't seem to be a huge deterrent yet."

Authorities are spending tens of billions of dollars to prevent local currencies from appreciating to keep export competitiveness. Kazakhstan bought over $2 billion to stop the tenge from appreciating, while Russia has bought nearly $25 billion since September to dampen rouble strength.

But this does risk stoking domestic inflation as central banks flood the domestic banking system with local currency in their attempts to prevent the exchange rate rising.

"Restricting inflows is perceived as one way of continuing to target currencies with incurring the inflation cost," Phil Poole, head of emerging markets research at HSBC said in a note.

"Expect more ad hoc measures from emerging governments and central banks both to restrict inflows and to limit their consequences."

(Additional reporting by Mike Dolan, Sebastian Tong and Carolyn Cohn; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: COLUMN-The Brazilian example: Christopher Swann
text:
-- Christopher Swann is a Reuters columnist. The views expressed are his own --

By Christopher Swann

NEW YORK, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's decision to impose capital controls has caused investors to howl. But a tax on foreign investment makes a good deal of sense for emerging nations seeking to stem inflows of hot money and slow a rising currency.

In the case of Brazil, action was needed. The nation has become a darling of international investors attracted by a combination of rising commodity prices, strong domestic consumption and sound macro policies. Overzealous traders were clearly becoming a liability.

The real is up by a third against the dollar so far this year -- making it the strongest major currency in the world. Overseas interest has also helped catapult the stock market up about 75 percent. Aside from the obvious danger to Brazil's exporters, enthusiasm from foreign investors is raising the risk of asset price bubbles.

On its own, the modest 2 percent tax on local bonds and stocks will not do much to calm the ardor of investors. A similar tax was in place in 2008 and did not prevent the real from reaching its highest level against the dollar of the decade.

Even so, the tax is a useful addition to the tool kit.

As a method for tempering currency appreciation, a tax on foreign investment has several advantages over buying dollars. Foreign exchange intervention can be costly for countries like Brazil. To avoid stoking inflation, intervention has to be offset by issuing domestic bonds.

For nations with high interest rates, this is a terrible deal. From its U.S. Treasuries, Brazil gets a tiny yield, with the three-month bill offering just 0.08 percent. Yet it has to issue bonds that pay out nearly 9 percent. A tax on foreign investments, by contrast, actually raises revenue.

For the same reason, such a tax may make sense for countries like India and South Korea that are paying dearly for their accumulation of dollar reserves. With foreign exchange reserves rising beyond a quarter of a trillion dollars each, the countries need to issue more bonds, and their costs quickly mount.

India has three-month securities that pay out 4.4 percent, while South Korea pays out 2.8 percent. A Brazil-style tax could at least help defray part of the expense.

For the United States, such taxes are the worst possible outcome. Foreign exchange intervention may hurt American exporters, but at least central bank purchases of U.S. Treasuries put downward pressure on their borrowing costs. By contrast an investment tax could end up damaging U.S. exporters and investors without helping U.S. Treasuries.

But assuming U.S. annoyance can be held in check, Brazil's strategy is extremely sensible and worthy of emulation. -- For previous columns, Reuters customers can click on [SWANN/] (Editing by Martin Langfield)

title: =DJ Brazil Sovereign Wealth Fund Little More Than Pipe Dream
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Despite the enormous influx of capital going into Brazil, a sovereign wealth fund in the near term is little more than a pipe dream.

Brazil needs all the money it can get to pay for its deficit and debt. Second, much of the capital flows are private and do not go into the government's pocket.

Moreover, if Brazil takes anything away from the historic financial crisis the world is just beginning to get over, it is that the country needs to build and preserve domestic reserves to shield it from another bubble. Given the growth in Brazilian assets over the last year, a bubble may not be far off. Brazilian stocks hit a 16-month high Thursday and the real has gained 37% against the U.S. dollar this year.

A sovereign wealth fund is a higher-risk investment portfolio, wielded by monetary authorities or central banks to diversify surplus reserves outside of the economy and potentially make a profit.

According to recent reports, Brazil's government is planning to set up a new sovereign wealth fund to invest dollars that the central bank buys on the spot market to limit the appreciation of the real.

Brazil's reserves have swelled in recent months, up to $231 billion, on the central bank's actions - a testament to recovering risk appetite and Brazil's appeal as a growing and relatively stable economy.

But, economists say this is deceiving.

"There is nothing about wealth in that fund because Brazil does not have a fiscal surplus to capitalize on," said Alberto M. Ramos, a senior Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs in New York.

Brazil is spending well beyond its means. The country's 12-month public sector primary budget surplus declined in August to 1.59% of gross domestic product, well below the year-end target of 2.5%. Primary figures don't include service costs on debt. With such costs included, Brazil posted an August nominal deficit equal to 3.53% of GDP.

"The only way to capitalize is to issue more debt. Then it would be a sovereign debt fund rather than wealth, because there is no wealth being created," said Ramos.

Brazil is a net borrower.

Foreign debt rose in August to $204.1 billion from $195.9 billion in July. Dividend and profit remittances by multinationals increased to $1.9 billion from July's $1.75 billion. Meanwhile, the central bank predicted a rising current account deficit in 2010 to $29 billion from an estimated $18 billion this year.

Noted Latin American country risk specialist Armen Kouyoumdjian asked: "How can you say I am putting money aside when you are not even covering your expenses?" He added that Brazil has the largest stimulus program in Latin America, which will increase its debt even more.

Brazil's government may be floating the idea of a wealth fund for the prestige it carries. This may also be the government's way to tell the central bank to intervene more, according to Affonso Pastore, former Brazil Central Bank President and adviser for GlobalSource Partners. But, analysts say the country must reinvest in itself to fund development, rather than try to turn profits with money abroad.

Brazil already tried to launch an outside-looking sovereign wealth fund last year, but had to change plans when the financial crisis struck. Monetary authorities realized they needed to use those dollar reserves for their originally intended purpose, selling dollars in order to stabilize the market.

"The downturn has led to a reconsideration of what really represents too much reserves from a pure currency standpoint," said Alan Ruskin, head of global strategy at RBS.

He said Brazil's central bank will probably want to build reserves even more before investing them.

The central bank is the other hurdle in the government's supposed plans. It is in the market daily trying to prevent further appreciation of the real, and another authority affecting the foreign exchange market could be counterproductive.

-By Riva Froymovich, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2217; riva.froymovich@dowjones.com

title: Brazil Central Bk Acts On Real Rally But Draws No Line In Sand
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank has intervened to slow the upward march of the Brazilian real over the last week, but it was unwilling to draw a line in the sand.

Last Tuesday, Brazil offered to swap $3.4 billion in long positions in the Brazilian real for interest rate-linked paper to take pressure off the U.S. currency on the futures market. It then repeated the dose in spot trading, buying dollars on Friday and Monday. But the volumes are seen as too timid to reverse the real's rally.

"The central bank is not buying dollars in quantities that would revert the trend. It doesn't want to set bands," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging-markets research at RBC Capital Markets.

In recent weeks, investors have shed concerns that the global recession will deepen and flocked back to the emerging-market destinations abandoned during the financial meltdown in the third quarter of last year.

Those investment flows have been backed up by dollars from exports, which have proven more resilient to the global downturn than many expected.

As a result, the real has gone on a massive tear, rising 14% against the dollar since the start of April to trade at about BRL2.05 as investors unwind safe-haven dollar positions and Brazil regains its status as the darling of the equities investment world.

Identifying a strong tail wind, local banks piled into long positions in reals on the futures market, accentuating the gains.

That was the trigger for the central bank to intervene, traders said.

Officially, the central bank said it is buying dollars to replenish reserves, although few believe that.

However, its tentative dollar purchases on the spot market indicate that it is offering a reference, rather than trying to set a band, traders said.

"It is providing a signal that it isn't comfortable with the dollar below BRL2.00 at a time when exports are just starting to recover. It wouldn't be foolish enough to try and defend that, though," said Joao Medeiros, partner at Pioneer brokerage, Brazil's biggest interbank currency broker.

In the first dollar auction in eight months Friday, the central bank bought between $250 million and $300 million.

In similar auctions held on a near-daily basis on occasions between October 2006 and September 2008, the central bank bought an average of around $500 million, but market volume were much greater then.

According to Ilan Goldfajn, chief economist at Itau Unibanco, Brazil's largest bank, the central bank can easily afford to accumulate another $5 billion to $10 billion in reserves. But any more than that would start to create inflationary pressure, said the former central-bank director.

If the current appetite for Brazilian assets persists, the real could march well past BRL2.00 per dollar, although it probably wouldn't reach the eight-year high of BRL1.56 to the dollar registered in August of 2008.

However, Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles last week went as far as to warn investors about excessive optimism about Brazil's prospects for recovery and counseled them that they could be setting themselves up for disappointment.

-By Alastair Stewart, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-2847-4520; alastair.stewart@dowjones.com
