title: WRAPUP 1-Fiscal discipline to help Brazil through crisis-govt
text:
BRASILIA, March 5 (Reuters) - Brazil will brave the financial crisis by sticking to austere fiscal policies, a strategy that should help it grow above the global average, the country's top two economic officials said on Thursday.

Slowing growth and falling tax revenues fanned fears Brazil would abandon the kind of fiscal discipline that helped the country revamp its public accounts, earned it an investment grade and made it a favorite among investors in recent years.

While many countries around the world are spending billions of dollars to counteract a global recession, Brazil's government has sought to strike a delicate balance between targeted spending on investments and fiscal restraint so as to keep its debt burden manageable.

"We will continue with a serious fiscal policy, balanced, so that we will have to cut current expenditures to be able to adjust to the drop in tax receipts that is actually taking place because of the crisis," Finance Minister Guido Mantega said in a speech at an economic conference in Brasilia.

On Wednesday, Mantega said the government would decide by March 20 if it will lower its primary budget surplus target this year from 3.8 percent of gross domestic product currently to free up cash for stimulus spending.

Brazil's 12-month primary budget surplus -- which excludes interest payments and is closely watched by investors as a gauge of a country's ability to service its debt -- already fell below that target in January to 3.58 percent, its lowest level in five years.

But officials reinforced they would stick to planned investments, especially in the Program to Accelerate Growth, which aims to improve the country's aging infrastructure, including roads, railways and houses.

"We will maintain all of the investment programs," Mantega added.

BRAZIL GROWTH

Balanced fiscal policies and anti-crisis measures of the past months would put Brazil in a good place to brave the global financial crisis, officials said.

"Brazil will grow less this year than in previous ones, it's a very difficult situation but will grow more than the global average, will be among the first countries to come out of the crisis and will be stronger after the crisis," Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles said at the same event.

The government has taken a series of measures ranging from selling dollars on the spot market to meet growing demand for the U.S. currency to giving tax breaks to hard-hit industries to try to alleviate the impact of the crisis on the economy.

Meirelles said Brazil has spent $14.5 billion in intervention in the spot foreign exchange market since early October, some $9.7 billion in dollar repurchase agreements and another $9.6 billion in foreign trade lines through March 2.

Brazil's government is also considering extending the temporary reduction of taxes on industrial goods that have helped sales in the automobile sector for a longer period of time, Trade and Industry Minister Miguel Jorge told reporters on the sidelines of the same event.

Despite all the efforts, analysts expect economic growth to slow to 1.5 percent in 2009 from above 5 percent growth last year, with some economists already forecasting zero growth or a contraction.

Mantega also acknowledged that credit problems continue as it remains scarce and costly despite government efforts to facilitate lending.

"There is a lack of credit in the economy," he said.

title: Brazil's Real Ends 3.0% Weaker At BRL2.442 Per Dollar

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real dropped sharply to end 3% weaker against the dollar Monday as concerns over the health of major global financial sector players and a continuing decline in key commodities prices prompted investors to dump the local currency.

The real ended at BRL2.442 per dollar in spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange after ending at BRL2.3695 per dollar Friday.

Traders noted the currency suffered from the outset of the session under the weight of global risk aversion raised by weak fourth-quarter results from major international financial sector players.

Top among those was insurer American International Group Inc. (AIG), which posted a record loss of $61.66 billion in the fourth quarter. The result prompted the U.S. government to offer additional assistance to the company of near $30 billion.

Adding to the signs of trouble was HSBC Holdings PLC's (HBC) report of a 70% decline in profits in 2008 to $5.7 billion. That result forced the bank to cut dividend estimates and close a number of consumer lending operations in North America.

Compounding the effect of that news was further disappointing economic data abroad. Early in the session, the Euro Zone and the U.K. both reported record lows in their February manufacturing indices and both Italy and Canada reported sharp economic contractions in the fourth quarter.

Alongside those factors were a steep decline in commodities prices, including oil and metals. Those price declines, analysts note, could have an adverse impact on Brazil's trade balance, which has already been negatively affected this year by diminished global demand.

Brazil's central bank, meanwhile, refrained from intervening in the currency market with a dollar sale auction, strengthening market perceptions that the monetary authority is willing to let the currency seek a natural equilibrium point as the global economy continues to adjust to an ongoing slowdown.

Despite the recent weakening of the real, market participants continued to show some belief the currency could stage a recovery through the end of the year. According to a central bank weekly market survey released Monday, the real is seen strengthening to around BRL2.30 per dollar by the end of 2009. According to the same survey, the country's reference Selic interest rate is seen falling through the end of the year to 10.25% annually from a current 12.75%.

title: ANALYSIS-Fundamentals favor stronger Brazil  currency
text:
BRASILIA, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency has fallen nearly 40 percent since August but looks poised to rebound next year thanks to ample foreign exchange reserves, a relatively lively economy and the potential for tougher central bank intervention.

A weaker currency is a double-edged sword for Brazil, making exports more competitive but also potentially fueling inflation just when the central bank is under pressure to cut interest rates and boost growth.

After hitting a nine-year high in August, Brazil's real <BRBY> has shed nearly 37 percent as investors have jostled for a dwindling supply of dollar-denominated credit, pulled funds from Brazil to cover losses abroad and sought refuge in U.S. assets.

The real has also suffered from the bruising drop in the prices of commodities, which make up much of Brazil's exports. Hefty losses by Brazilian companies in the derivatives markets, also increased currency volatility. The real traded at 2.458 against the dollar on Wednesday, weakening from around 1.560 in August.

"Up to 2.50 is the fair value for the currency in these poor conditions of liquidity, credit and international demand," said Alexandre Lintz, chief strategist in Brazil for BNP Paribas.

Like many emerging market currencies, the real is vulnerable in the near term, with few investors willing to risk capital in the midst of the worst economic uncertainty in a generation.

Already, a deepening global recession is draining the available pool of dollars for investment in Brazil.

Net U.S. dollars outflows from Brazil totaled $7.16 billion in November, its highest outflow since 1999, according to the central bank.

Foreign direct investment is expected to fall to $24 billion in 2009 from $34.7 billion through October this year, economists have said.

"The risk is for a lot of pressure unless we really see a more active central bank policy. That could at least contain some of the volatility," said Zeina Latif, economist at ING.

MORE ACTION

However, longer-term fundamentals favor a stronger currency.

The central bank has taken a series of measures in recent months to keep liquidity flowing, selling dollars on the spot market and carrying out foreign exchange swap auctions. Unlike other commodity exporters such as Russia, which have run down reserves as their currencies have weakened, Brazil has spent only $6.7 billion of its reserves to stem the currency.

Reserves of around $207.2 billion are now actually slightly higher than in September when the crisis worsened with the collapse of Lehman Brothers. Analysts say that is because they are mostly held in U.S. Treasuries which gained sharply in recent months.

With such ample reserves, analysts say the central bank could intervene more aggressively.

"The central bank should sell a bigger percentage of the reserves than it has done," said Alexandre Ferreira, vice president of treasury at WestLB, who said the real at 2.50 already seemed cheap.

"It is letting the real weaken a bit more than it should," Ferreira said.

Economists say Brazil's resilient economic growth as well as solid public accounts will eventually allow the real to bounce back to around 2.00 or 2.30 per dollar next year.

The economy remains a standout in a world clouded by recession, and growth will top 5 percent this year. Depending on the extent of the global crisis and the impact of domestic stimulus measures, it could grow around 3 percent next year.

"There is a gap between the implementation of policies of fiscal and monetary stimulus and their impact on the economy," Lintz said.

"We see room for a good appreciation (of the real) in the second half of (2009)," Lintz added. (Editing by Raymond Colitt and Tom Hals)

title: Brazil unveils more steps to contain credit crisis

BRASILIA, Brazil, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Brazil will grant companies more time to pay taxes and will provide 10 billion reais ($4.6 bln) in loans for working capital, the country's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Thursday, in the latest step to help the economy brave a global credit crisis.

Companies will get an extension to pay wholesale taxes on industrial products as well as on social welfare contributions.

The national development bank, BNDES, is to offer the 10 billion reais line of credit.

"It's another 10 billion reais, on top of the 90 billion reais which the (BNDES) already has to irrigate the market directly," Mantega told reporters at an event in Brasilia.

Mantega also said the government had instructed state-run bank, Banco do Brasil , to make available a total of 4 billion reais to automakers' financing units to increase car loans and help spur sales.

"With these resources, we're ensuring that there will be enough financing available for the automobile industry to maintain sales in November and December," Mantega said.

New automobile sales in Brazil slumped 11 percent in October from September, the national automakers' association Anfavea said earlier.

$40 BLN SPENT

Brazil's government has taken a series of measures in recent weeks aimed at easing the global liquidity crunch, such as reducing banks' mandatory reserve requirements, offering foreign-exchange swap auctions, and allowing bigger banks to take over loan portfolios of distressed smaller banks.

The country's economy has been growing above 5.0 percent annually.

Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles, speaking at the same event, said Brazil had spent $40 billion in foreign exchange interventions in a bid to meet surging demand for U.S. dollars in the currency market.

Despite the massive interventions, Brazil's international reserves have only been reduced by $5.1 billion, he said. Foreign exchange swaps it used do not eat into the reserves.

The central bank held such swap auctions daily and regularly sold dollars in the spot market in recent weeks to boost liquidity as the real plunged nearly 12 percent against the dollar in October.

The government also offered bridge loans to exporters and farmers seeing demand slump.

Mantega said the worst of the financial crisis had passed and that Brazil had a solid fiscal situation and robust domestic demand.

"Our outlook is that we can continue growing around 4 percent in 2009," Mantega said.

The solution to the Aracruz derivatives problem was welcomed by currency traders because the company had been the subject of daily commentaries - and blamed by some for market volatility in recent weeks.

Aracruz hit the headlines in early October when it said that it held negative positions of BRL1.95 billion ($928 million) in derivatives markets as of Sept. 30, following the sharp depreciation of the real against the dollar.

The Brazilian real also benefitted from the good humor of the local stock market, which traded increasingly higher through most of Tuesday. The Ibovespa stock index traded above the psychologically important 40,000-point barrier in late afternoon trading.

Investors were showing a reduced aversion to risk with banking stocks doing particularly well, after the announced planned merger of Banco Itau (ITA) and Unibanco (UBB). The merger will create Brazil's largest private bank and increase confidence in the solidity of Brazil's banking system.

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market debt came under intense pressure again Thursday, while developing country stocks traded in the U.S. closed flat following a highly volatile session.

The intervention of the governments of Brazil and Mexico to prop up the value of their falling currencies, and news that the International Monetary Fund is in discussions with a number of countries about possible loan packages, helped to pare the losses.

Both the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso, which have been pounded of late, benefited from central bank interventions. The peso closed in Mexico City at MXN13.3940, compared with Wednesday's close of MXN13.8550, while the real ended at BRL2.3050 to the dollar, markedly stronger than Wednesday's close at BRL2.3795.

With 10 minutes to go before the closing bell, ADRs pared losses from a session that featured several momentum reversals, as investors went into a buying frenzy.

The Bank of New York Emerging Markets American Depositary Receipt index closed up 0.02% at 174 points after hitting a low of 159 points earlier in the day. The Latin American ADR index climbed 0.93% and the Asian ADR index gained 0.23%.

The reversal tracked the U.S. market where the Dow Jones Industrial Average, in another roller-coaster session, closed up 2%, led by a big bounce in energy companies.

The exodus from emerging markets external debt, however, found no relief, as a combination of fear and deleveraging drove spreads sharply upward.

The spread on JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Global Diversified increased by 31 basis pointsto 850 basis points over Treasurys, its widest this year.

"Equities underperformed external debt and credit default swaps earlier this year (following U.S. equities), so now it's somewhat of a catch-up," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research for RBC Dominion Securities in Toronto.

"This global credit crisis is having a significant impact on global banking systems and capital flows, so this is much more than about equity valuations. It's about unwinding of a massive credit bubble that eventually raises the overall level of risk," he added.

In Central and Eastern Europe, where worries are mounting about current account deficits and large external debts in several countries, credit spreads were at all-time highs. Five-year credit-default swaps on Hungary were trading around 650 basis points, up more than 100 basis points on the day and 202 basis points on the week.

Pakistan, Ukraine, Belarus and Hungary are among the countries with which the IMF has said it's discussing potential loan packages.

The cost of insuring sovereign debt against default for five years rose across the board Thursday, regardless of the credit quality of the sovereign.

Brazil, the emerging markets' credit heavyweight, saw the cost of insuring its debt against default for five years jump 66 basis points to 610 basis points over Treasurys.

Even China, which sits on the world's largest foreign reserves cushion and is believed to be better shielded than other developing economies from the global financial crisis, saw its five-year CDS spread climb 23 basis points to 255 basis points over Treasurys, according to Markit.

"Right now fundamentals are put on the sidelines," said Roberto Sanchez-Dahl, who manages $600 million in emerging markets debt with Federated Investors. "It's all about technicals and the large liquidity needs that put pressure on prices. People are selling whatever they can, anticipating redemption and lower prices... it's like a vicious cycle."

title: Argentina To Expand Trade Barriers To Protect Local Industry
text:
BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--Faced with expectations of a widespread economic slowdown owing to the international financial crisis, Argentina is poised to step up protective barriers to shield local industry from cheap imports from China and Brazil.

On Thursday, Customs Director Silvina Tirabassi announced that 120 additional products would be added to a list of goods carrying a reference price fixed by the government. These prices are used by the government to designate goods that will suffer sanctions when they enter the country at a cheaper price than the reference price. When this occurs, the government alleges dumping on the part of the exporting country.

The list is mostly made up of textiles, shoes, domestic appliances, farm machinery and linens.

"In the past months we've detected fraud totaling $15 million, particularly in textiles and motorcycles," Tirabassi said, according to local daily Clarin.

While the measures aren't officially targeted at imports from any country in particular, local industrialists are worried about competition from Argentina's largest trading partner, Brazil.

Brazil has seen its currency plunge this month in relation to the dollar, while Argentina's peso has remained relatively stable owing to central-bank intervention. This has made goods coming from Brazil much cheaper than those produced domestically.

Brazil and Argentina are members of regional trading block Mercosur, which also includes Paraguay and Uruguay with Venezuela in the process of becoming a full member.

title: Emerging Market Central Banks Turn Focus To Economic Growth
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--As the global financial crisis engulfs the developing world from Moscow to Rio, central banks are starting to shift their monetary policy focus to slowing economic growth from the fight against inflation.

In the last few days a slew of central banks have either slowed their pace of tightening, paused it or have started to cut rates.

"Inflation-fighting credibility takes a back seat to preventing economic recession in the current environment," said Paul Biszko, an emerging markets strategist with RBC Dominion Securities in Toronto.

But the transition into easing monetary policy won't be easy, swift or painless.

Developing world central bankers have it tougher than their developed world brethren, whose chief focus is to reignite the engines of their stagnating economies.

Despite some slowing, the developing world continues to grow at a solid pace thanks to resilient domestic demand. Nevertheless, recession in the developed world is taking a toll on emerging market economies. Morgan Stanley on Monday cut its 2009 gross domestic product growth forecast for developing economies to 5.5% from 6.2%.

Controlling inflation has been the top priority for emerging market central banks in 2008. Just this summer rising inflation was a global news story with the soaring cost of food and energy becoming politically volatile issues for the developing world. It also upset developed nations as inflation ate into disposable income and depressed consumer and business confidence.

But, while in the West such concerns have subsided amid a decline in commodity prices, slowing growth and plunging stock markets, in emerging markets such events have had an undesired effect on local currencies.

The strong resurgence of the U.S. dollar in recent weeks sent domestic currencies plunging sharply across emerging markets, raising fears that imported inflation will add to existing inflation already above central bank targets.

Brazil's annual inflation was hovering at 6.25% in September, above the government's target of 4.5%. Chile's stood at 9.2%, or roughly three times the central bank's 3% plus-or-minus one percentage point target.

As the credit crisis washes onto emerging market shores, central banks are caught between a rock and a hard place. They can tighten monetary policy to prevent higher inflation becoming entrenched, or they can cut interest rates to cushion financial weakness.

With companies throughout the developing world finding it difficult to raise money and dollar-denominated bond deals not getting sold, banks are being forced to shift their priorities.

"Liquidity is broken. This is a severe situation that has gone global in scope," said Biszko. "We are going to see a broad shift across central banks prioritizing growth over inflation."

On Thursday, Chile's central bank held rates steady at 8.5% despite wide expectations of another 25-basis-point hike. Peru's central bank also kept its rate unchanged at 6.5% Thursday evening after increasing the reference rate six times this year.

Echoing Wednesday's coordinated rate cut in many of the largest economies in the world, other central banks are expected to follow suit.

Brazil's central bank, which has been hiking interest rates throughout 2008, mindful of its history of hyper-inflation, could hold the Selic steady at its next rate-setting committee meeting on Oct. 29, according to some analysts.

"I would say at this moment that (Brazil's) central bank is looking at external factors," said Alex Agostini, an economist at Sao Paulo-based Austin Rating Servicos Financeiros. "The coordinated action by central banks (Wednesday) lends support to the possibility that (our) central bank will maintain interest rates unchanged at the next meeting."

But the pace and size of any monetary policy easing will be done with a view to the strength or weakness of domestic currencies.

Mexico's and Russia's central banks dipped into their large foreign reserves this week to shore up their respective tumbling currencies.

Brazil's central bank, which has also been intervening in the foreign exchange markets to boost dollar liquidity, cut reserve requirements on cash and term deposits to aid the banking system facing thinning short-term credit lines for export and business operating capital.

After a decade of solid growth on the back of a boom in commodities prices, emerging market central banks are well aware that if they don't keep inflation in check this year, it will return perhaps with greater vengeance in the future.

"The worst of the rate hikes is over," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin American markets at ABN Amro. "The markets are easing, but the timing and the amount is uncertain given their own respective domestic cycles and the passthrough to higher inflation expectations."

-By Giada Cardoletti, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4290; giada.cardoletti@dowjones.com [ 10-10-08 2207GMT ]

title: Brazil's real sinks to 2-year low, stocks tumble
text:

SAO PAULO, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency sank to its weakest level in more than two years on Friday even as the central bank flooded the foreign exchange market with dollars, while stocks dropped for a seventh session as investors fled emerging market securities.

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo stock exchange sank rapidly from the start of trade to rack up losses of 10 percent, triggering an automatic 30-minute halt to trading.

After resuming trade, the index clawed back in a volatile session to end 3.97 percent lower at 35,609.54 points, its lowest close since September 2006.

The real <BRBY> plunged 5.3 percent to 2.326 per U.S. dollar, its weakest close since May 2006, despite three central bank auctions in the spot currency market. It was the third time the bank intervened in the spot foreign exchange market this week to help prop up the real.

The bank also sold $589 million in currency swaps, which work like the sale of dollars in the futures market.

With Friday's losses, the real has now shed more than a third of its value since Aug. 1, when it hit a nine-year high.

"The market is looking very bad," said Luis Piason, head of currency trading at the Concordia brokerage. "The central bank intervened, but it didn't have much of an impact."

Brazil's central bank also sought to reassure investors on Friday, saying it has no limit as a lender of last resort to the local banking system and that its main objective was for local markets to function properly.

Over just the last four months, the Bovespa has given up all its gains made in a long rally since the start of 2006 that took it to a high of 73,920 at the end of May.

Traders said Friday's fall was on concerns that plummeting global markets will cut capital flows to developing countries and on fears that the worst may not be over for U.S. stocks.

Energy giant Petrobras , the top-weighted stock in the index, dropped 7.26 percent to 24.00 reais, as oil prices fell below $80 a barrel for the first time in a year.

It sold an unspecified amount of dollars in three separate auctions. Late in the session, the bank also sold $1.3 billion in dollar swap contracts, helping to nudge the real into positive territory.

Despite Wednesday's gains, the real has still shed a third of its value since Aug. 1, when it hit a nine-year high. A weaker real threatens to stoke inflation in Brazil, meaning the central bank is unlikely to join other countries in cutting rates in the coming months.

BRASILIA, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency posted its biggest loss in more than nine years and stocks plummeted by as much as 15 percent on Monday, forcing the stock exchange to halt trading twice as a deepening financial crisis battered markets around the globe.

The latest scare came over the weekend when moves by European governments to rescue large banks and protect ordinary depositors triggered widespread concerns about the fate of the world economy.

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange plunged near a two-year low but pared losses late in the session to end 5.43 percent lower at 42,100.79 points. The index has now fallen a whopping 43 percent from its all-time high of 73,920 reached on May 29.

"There's no way to explain this. ... All parameters have been lost," said Joao Medeiros, head of foreign exchange at Pioneer, a Sao Paulo brokerage. "Panic is the word for this."

As shares nosedived early in the session, the stock exchange was forced to halt trading twice. The last time it suspended trading more than once on the same day was in January 1999, when a financial crisis forced Brazil to allow its currency to float freely against the dollar.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, also took a pounding on Monday, clocking its biggest one-day loss since it was allowed to float nine years ago. The real slumped 7 percent to a two-year low of 2.20 per dollar.

With Monday's losses, the real has weakened 19.2 percent so far this year, nearly wiping out a 20 percent surge in 2007.

Brazil's central bank intervened during the session in a bid to quench surging demand for greenbacks, offering dollar swaps for the first time in more than two years. It sold $1.47 billion in swaps of $2.1 billion on offer in an auction.

"I think what is happening to the real in particular is the end of an era," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief Brazil economist at Morgan Stanley.

"The last five years were extremely favorable for emerging countries such as Brazil; this world has ended, the global environment is one of significant slowdown."

The market turmoil also sent interest-rate futures <0#DIJ:> sharply higher on the BM&F commodities and futures exchange.

At the stock exchange, commodity stocks were among the hardest hit on fears a global financial crisis will hurt demand for metals and oil. Crude prices fell to eight-month lows below $90 a barrel while copper prices fell more than 6 percent.

State-run oil giant Petrobras fell 3.23 percent to 30.00 reais and mining company Vale dropped 6.8 percent to 26.99 reais. Steelmaker Usiminas plunged 11 percent to 30.50 reais.

Banks also took a thumping, with Banco Bradesco falling 6.58 percent to 25.55 reais, Banco Itau tumbling 4.74 percent to 26.55 reais and Unibanco slipping 2.63 percent to 15.89 reais.

The losses tracked those on major stock markets, with U.S. equities plunging and the key pan-European share index suffering its worst one-day percentage fall on record. (Additional reporting by Jenifer Correa in Sao Paulo, Writing by Todd Benson; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: Investors Bail From Brazil Assets On US Crisis Fears
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Investors bailed out of Brazilian assets with a passion Wednesday amid fears that the U.S. financial crisis may not be over yet.

Dollars flew out of the country as investors sought to cover liabilities and reserve requirements abroad and put money in safe-haven investments such as U.S. Treasury bonds.

"We are seeing funds and banks repositioning in safe assets amid the turmoil. Brazilian assets don't fit into that profile," said Roberto Padovani, chief strategist at WestLb bank.

The Brazilian real slumped more than 3% to trade at BRL1.885 to the U.S. dollar by early afternoon, taking the losses for the month to stunning 15%. Meanwhile, the benchmark Ibovespa index was 5.9% lower at 46,325 points. The index has shed 17% this month.

The U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to bail out insurer American International Group Inc. (AIG) did little to calm global markets as investors began speculating on who would be the next casualty of the current crisis.

"Investors continue to repatriate funds to cover losses suffered abroad and to reposition in rock-solid positions ahead of further revelations. It's a fire-sale scenario," said Miriam Tavares, forex trader at the AGK brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Traders said investors were also repositioning after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, imposed a firm close-out requirement on short sellers and their brokers.

There is also a lot of money moving into derivatives on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, or BM&F, as local investors seek hedges. That movement is weighing on the local currency, said AGK's Tavares.

While local officials insist that the Brazilian financial system isn't suceptible to contagion from abroad, investors are becoming increasingly concerned about the impact of the crisis on the wider economy.

The decline of commodities prices will hit Brazil's larger companies and the trade balance, while the tightness of credit on the international market may limit the expansion plans of local companies.

Earlier Wednesday, Finance Minister Guido Mantega promised the government would intervene if corporate credit remained tight.

The idea that Brazil can decouple from the crisis has long gone out of the window. Now, investors are simply attempting to gauge the extent of the damage.

For example, the accentuated decline of the real could lead to increased local inflation pressure at a time when the economy shows signs of slowing, leaving the central bank with a difficult conundrum to solve.

Official 12-month inflation stands at a perilous 6.2%, while the Selic base interest rate is currently at 13.75%.

Faced with a multitude of uncertainties, liquidity is the priority and cash is increasingly the position of choice, noted Padovani.

-By Alastair Stewart; Dow Jones Newswires; 5511 2847-4520; alastair.stewart@dowjones.com

(Rogerio Jelmayer contributed to this report.) [ 17-09-08 1708GMT ]

title: Brazil Real Weaker Early On Commodities Decline, Dollar Climb
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened in early trading Tuesday as investors reacted cautiously to continued declines in key commodities prices and the climb of the dollar against major currencies amid international uncertainties.

As of 1350 GMT, the real was trading at BRL1.6545 per dollar after ending at BRL1.6460 on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange Monday.

Traders said the real continued to slide as investors unwound defensive positions in oil, metals and grains markets with Hurricane Gustav, now a tropical depression, passing through the Gulf of Mexico causing less damage than had been feared.

Investors, meanwhile, were closely monitoring the dollar's continued climb against the euro, after adverse economic data in recent sessions cast doubts over the trajectory of the Euro zone economy.

The market Tuesday was also closely watching Asia, where a political crisis in Thailand prompted at least five banks in the region to intervene in currency markets.

Locally, meanwhile, Brazil's IBGE statistics institute reported that industrial production continued at a strong pace in July, rising by 1% from the previous month and by 8.5% compared with the same month a year earlier. The figures came in at the high end of market estimates, and according to analysts, could prompt the central bank to maintain its current tight monetary policy stance at upcoming interest rate meetings. The bank has raised the country's reference Selic rate by 1.75 percentage points so far this year to 13% annually in an effort to curb inflation pressure.

The central bank, meanwhile, is seen maintaining some pressure on the real later in the session Tuesday with a customary daily dollar auction.

The bank has purchased dollars in daily auctions since late 2005 in an effort to boost foreign currency reserves.

As of the latest available figures Monday, reserves stand at $205.12 billion.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Stronger On Recovering Commodities
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real rebounded Tuesday as commodities prices recovered overseas.   

The local currency ended trading at BRL1.731 per dollar per dollar spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, or BM&F, stronger than Monday's close of BRL1.746.   

The recovery of commodities prices overseas brought money back into Brazil's raw material heavy assets.   

Meanwhile, short-term investment inflows were boosted Tuesday by rising expectations of a hike in local interest rates amid concerns over creeping inflation. According to a market survey released by the central bank Monday, expectations for IPCA consumer price inflation over the coming 12 months rose to 4.33% from 4.29% seen previously.   

The threat that Brazil's monetary authority could be forced to raise the country's reference Selic interest rate from its current level of 11.25% annually has heightened investor interest in local government securities.   

The real was undermined by the news that Sao Paulo state canceled the privatization auction of electric utility  Companhia Energetica de Sao Paulo SA (CESP5.BR), or Cesp, due to take place Wednesday, because of a lack of interest from potential bidders.   

Investors had expected heavy inflows following the sale of the asset, which was priced in excess of BRL6.6 billion.   

Brazil's central bank chose to intervene in the foreign exchange market Tuesday, after staying on the sidelines Monday.   

The bank has purchased dollars in daily auctions since late 2005 in an effort to boost foreign reserves.   

Meanwhile, in local rate futures trading, rates rose amid strengthening ideas that an interest rate hike is around the corner.   

The rate on the most heavily traded contract, January 2010, ended at 13.23%, up from 13.20% on Monday. Brazil's interbank overnight rate was flat at 11.10%.

title: Brazil Real Closes Weaker On Failed Tax Vote, Credit Mkts
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Thursday after the government failed to get a key tax measure passed and amid renewed concerns about global credit markets.   

The real closed at BRL1.7810 in trading on the Brazilian Mercantile & Futures Exchange, or BM&F, weaker from Wednesday's close at BRL1.7720.   

Traders said the government's failure to win an extension of the CPMF financial transactions tax, which expires Dec. 31, overhung the market Thursday. The tax generated about 40 billion Brazilian reals ($22.6 billion) in revenue for the government.   

The measure's defeat could generate serious budget difficulties in 2008, as well as cause the government to revise its fiscal targets, analysts said.   

Brazil's government has pledged to post a public sector primary budget surplus this year and next equivalent to 3.8% of gross domestic product, or more than BRL90 billion annually. The surplus funding is aimed at paying down the public sector debt, which as of October stood at BRL1.13 trillion, or the equivalent of about 43.7% of GDP.   

Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the government would maintain its commitment to meeting fiscal targets. In the meantime, the government will suspend all budget spending and planned exemptions until it announces measures to cover the CPMF tax loss next week, Mantega said.   

Global credit concerns also weighed on financial markets, analysts said. Wednesday's injection of liquidity into credit markets, while well met, also raised apprehension about future negative surprises from financial institutions exposed to the troubled U.S. subprime mortgage sector.   

The real had traded stronger throughout the session after weakening early, but intervention by the Central Bank of Brazil late in the session sapped the currency's momentum.   

The bank bought U.S. dollars at the snap auction Thursday for BRL1.7800 per dollar, the bank said. The bank did not reveal the volume of dollars purchased. The bank said it is purchasing dollars to build up foreign reserves.   

Meanwhile, the risk to investing in Brazil as measured by the  JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus, or EMBI+, tightened to a spread of 207 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. Brazil's benchmark Global 40 bond traded 1/2 lower at a bid of 133 3/4 as of 1809 GMT.

title: Brazil stocks rise on joint bank moves, real dips
text:
(Updates to close)   

SAO PAULO, Dec 12 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock market ended higher on Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve joined with other central banks to ease tight conditions in global credit markets, but the local currency weakened in volatile trading.   

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange finished 0.36 percent higher at 64,741.69 points after rising more than 1 percent earlier in the session, snapping three days of losses that pushed the index down nearly 2 percent.   

The Brazilian real <BRBY> initially rose in tandem with the stock market, but reversed course late in the session and finished almost 1 percent weaker at 1.774 per U.S. dollar. Brazil's central bank intervened to buy dollars late in the day, helping to push the real lower.   

The Fed said on Wednesday it would launch a temporary short-term lending facility that banks can use at its discount window, a move that was coordinated with similar moves by the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and other major central banks.   

The initiative revived some of the appetite for riskier emerging market assets, which has sagged recently. It also came after the Fed's decision on Tuesday to cut its benchmark lending rate by 25 basis points, which disappointed some investors.   

"This move by the central banks will help calm down the markets. It is as if with this announcement to add liquidity, they're saying they're not going to let anyone go broke," said Hamilton Moreira, a senior investment analyst at BB Investimentos.   

Interest-rate futures <0#DIJ:> on the Brazilian commodities and futures bourse BM&F were mixed even after the Fed move helped improve investor sentiment.   

At the stock market, shares of state-controlled oil company  Petrobras , the heaviest-weighted stock in the Bovespa index, jumped 5.06 percent to 84.99 reais as oil prices soared in New York and London.   

Petrobras also said it had cranked up a huge 180,000-barrel-per-day rig after many delays, finally meeting this year's capacity growth target.   

Retailer CBD rose 3.53 percent to 35.20 reais after the company late on Tuesday named named Claudio Galeazzi, an executive known for turning around struggling companies, as its new chief executive. CBD on Monday fired Cassio Casseb, who was CEO for nearly two years. (Reporting by Rodolfo Barbosa and Todd Benson; editing by Gary Crosse)

title: Brazil Fin Min: New Fund Will Counter Real's Appreciation -FT
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said the nation will create a sovereign wealth fund with the primary aim of intervening in foreign exchange markets to counter the appreciation of Brazil's currency, The Financial Times reported Sunday on its Web site.   

Since the fund was announced by Mantega in October, funding plans and objectives have undergone several revisions, the FT reported.   

According to the FT, a central bank official said, "The big victory for the central bank is that the fund will have nothing to do with Brazil's foreign reserves and nothing to do with the central bank."   

But in an interview with the FT in Brasilia, Mantega said the fund would indeed affect the accumulation of reserves and would share the central bank's source of funding at the national treasury. Under current rules, intervention in currency markets is the sole prerogative of Brazil's central bank.   

"It will have the function of reducing the offer of dollars in the market and helping the real to appreciate less," Mantega told the FT.   

Under Mantega's original plan, the sovereign wealth fund would have drawn on Brazil's foreign reserves, which have risen quickly this year to about $180 billion. That plan sparked a behind-the-scenes row between the Finance Ministry and the central bank, the FT said.

title: Brazil real eases, stocks cut losses with Wall St.
text:
(Updates to close)   

SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock market cut losses to end nearly flat on Wednesday after following international markets down sharply early, while the currency closed weaker due to market volatility.   

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange scrambled late in the day to close down 0.12 percent at 62,624 points after earlier falling to a low of 61,447.   

The index has hit a slew of record highs in recent weeks and is up about 40 percent this year.   

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened in tandem with the Bovespa earlier in the day but closed down 0.61 percent at 1.809 per U.S. dollar. The real has rallied more than 18 percent this year, buoyed by a steady flow of dollars into Latin America's largest economy.   

Interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> on the BM&F commodities and futures exchange drifted lower, indicating optimism among investors.   

Brazilian markets followed U.S. markets down sharply most of the session after  Merrill Lynch & Co Inc posted steep quarterly losses and executives warned the worst of the credit crisis may not be over.   

But speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve may cut the discount rate imminently triggered a late-hour rally in New York that reversed most of the day's losses.   

Brazil's central bank intervened again in the foreign exchange market to buy dollars. The bank has been purchasing dollars on a daily basis since Oct. 8, helping to mop up excess dollars in the market and to lift Brazil's foreign reserves to an all-time high of more than $164 billion.   

Bovespa's top heavyweight, state oil company  Petrobras , gained momentum late in the day to close up 4.2 percent at 67.20 reais, far outperforming most of the Brazilian market.   

Mining giant CVRD , which will post quarterly earnings on Thursday, fell 2.62 percent to 49.42 reais, however. Analysts on average expect CVRD profit to rise 47 percent from a year ago, according to a Reuters poll. CVRD is the second most heavily weighted stock in the index. (Reporting by Reese Ewing)

title: Brazil Real Weakens Slightly From 7-Yr High In Light Trade
text:
Gerald Jeffris   

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real was slightly weaker against the dollar in early trading Monday, falling away from a seven-year high amid reduced foreign currency inflows brought about by the closure of some U.S. markets for the Columbus Day holiday.   

As of 1340 GMT, the real was trading at BRL1.807 per dollar after ending at BRL1.803 per dollar Friday in spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange.   

Traders noted participants would likely take profits while waiting for further data due out during the week on the strength of the international economy.   

"The real will likely depreciate a bit today as market players tend to be cautious in relation to indicators due out this week," said trader at a Sao Paulo-based brokerage.   

In particular, analysts said the market would be looking to the minutes of the U.S. Federal Reserve's September monetary policy meeting for hints about whether that monetary authority would continue to cut interest rates at upcoming rate meetings.   

Locally, meanwhile, economic forecasts remained mostly tame, with projections for IPCA consumer price inflation holding practically unchanged in a weekly central bank market survey.   

According to the survey, the forecast for the year-end 2007 ICPA moved up a tick to 4.01% from 4.00% seen the previous week. The projection for 2008 IPCA inflation held steady at 4.10%.   

Brazil's government has set year-end inflation targets of 4.5% for both years.   

Investors remained in doubt meanwhile about whether Brazil's central bank would resume intervention in the local currency market through daily dollar purchase auctions.   

The bank suspended auctions in August after having purchased more than $75 billion in the first seven months of the year to build foreign reserves.   

Some analysts, however, have warned that the bank may resume auctions if the real rises firmly above the BRL1.80 per dollar market.   

Meanwhile, according to the bank's latest market survey, the real is seen ending October at BRL1.85 per dollar and also finishing 2007 at the same level.

title: Brazil  stocks,  currency  slip as c.bank  intervenes
text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock market slipped early on Monday from a record high, and the local currency weakened after the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in nearly two months.   

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange was down 0.19 percent at 62,202.8 points by noon, with shares of mining giant CVRD helping to push the market lower. The index, which has gained about 40 percent this year, surged to an all-time high of 62,337.9 on Friday.   

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, was off 0.44 percent at 1.812 per U.S. dollar, extending losses after the central bank called an auction to buy dollars on the spot foreign exchange market for the first time since Aug. 13.   

The bank intervened after the real closed on Friday at its strongest level since August 2000. The real has rallied almost 20 percent so far this year, buoyed by strong dollar inflows to Latin America's largest economy.   

"This is one more sign that the central bank believes that the worst of the crisis afflicting global markets has passed," said Vladimir Caramaschi, chief economist at Fator Corretora, a Sao Paulo brokerage.   

"But I don't think the bank is going to be able to prevent the real from strengthening further," he added. "The dollar inflows into the country are too strong."   

The central bank called the auction on an unusually quiet day in the market due to the Columbus Day holiday in the United States, which reduced trading volumes significantly.   

Interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> on the BM&F commodities and futures exchange in Sao Paulo rose slightly, mirroring the downturn in the stock and currency markets.   

At the Bovespa, CVRD -- the second-heaviest-weighted stock in the index -- dragged the market lower. CVRD shares tumbled 1.06 percent to 50.64 reais after  UBS Pactual cut its recommendation on the stock to "neutral" from "buy."   

JP Morgan took a similar step last week, lowering its recommendation on CVRD shares to "neutral" from "overweight."   

State-run oil giant  Petrobras , the heaviest weighted stock in the Bovespa index, was among the few shares posting gains.  Petrobras shares were up 0.18 percent at 61.26 reais, preventing the Bovespa from falling further.   

Another actively traded stock posting gains was aircraft manufacturer Embraer , whose shares rose 2.34 percent to 22.26 reais. On Friday, Embraer said it delivered 47 jets in the third quarter, up from just 30 in the year-earlier period.

title: Brazil stocks surge to record, real up on Fed hope
text:
(Updates to close)   

SAO PAULO, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock market rose to a record high on Wednesday and the national currency gained on growing expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve would cut interest rates in October, raising the appeal of emerging market securities.   

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange jumped 1.39 percent to 59,676.4 points, closing at a record high for a third straight session. The index surged about 34 percent so far in 2007.   

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, strengthened 0.75 percent to 1.847 per U.S. dollar rising for the second session.   

The currency closed near its strongest level since 2000, taking cues from strong gains in the Bovespa index and equity markets in the United States and Europe.   

Expectations the Fed may cut interest rates again next month sent Brazilian assets higher as lower U.S. rates generally fuel the appetite for high-yield, riskier emerging market securities.   

Brazil's central bank hasn't intervened in the currency markets in more than a month and isn't likely to step in even as investment inflows surge, traders said.   

"The central bank will have to register a very strong flow to resume buying dollars," said Jorge Knauer, a foreign exchange manager at Banco Proper in Rio de Janeiro.   

Interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> on the BM&F futures exchange in Sao Paulo were mostly down, reflecting the positive investor sentiment and gains in the currency and stock markets.   

On the stock market, shares of iron ore miner CVRD , the second-heaviest stock in the index, was up 1.76 percent to 50.8 reais even as nickel and copper prices eased in international markets.   

State-controlled oil company  Petrobras , the top-weighted stock in the index, gained 1.25 percent to 59.85 reais. title: Brazil Mantega: Local Bks Not Highly Exposed To Risk -Estado
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's financial system is very solid and has the capacity to weather ongoing turbulence in world markets without severe losses, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Thursday, according to the Estado news agency.   

The minister attributed steep declines in Brazilian asset prices over recent sessions to investor panic over weakness in U.S. credit markets and subsequent stop-loss trading. But he said that local banks and other institutions so far haven't suffered great damage from the market shift.   

"There is a market exaggeration but then things return to normal," the minister said in an interview with Estado. "Until now, I haven't seen one financial institution here in Brazil show problems." [ 16-08-07 1713GMT ]   

Mantega's comments came as Brazil's Bovespa stock index declined for a sixth consecutive session, dropping by more than 8% in Thursday's session to near 45,150 points. The index has racked up losses of more than 22% since July 19, when it closed at a record high of 58,125 points.   

Brazil's currency, the real, meanwhile, declined by more than 4% Thursday to BRL2.12 against the dollar, while the country's sovereign debt spread, as measured by the  JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus, widened by 39 basis points to 239 points over U.S. Treasurys.   

The real has weakened by more than 12% against the dollar in the past month amid investor nervousness.   

Despite the negative impact of the currency's depreciation, Mantega said it was too early to ascertain whether the real would remain at its current level, and he sees no need for the central bank to intervene to support the currency.   

Brazil's central bank had been moving in a contrary direction over the past 21 months, buying dollars on the spot market at daily auctions in an effort to build foreign reserves. As of Wednesday, reserves stood at $159.66 billion. [ 16-08-07 1748GMT ]   

The minister also said the volatile conditions reinforced the government's recent decision to maintain its target for IPCA consumer price inflation at a conservative level of 4.5% annually. According to recent market surveys by the central bank, IPCA inflation is seen well below that level for the end of 2007, at around 3.8%.   

Mantega said that Brazil's low inflation, fiscal stability, and growth potential put it in an advantageous position to receive foreign investment and that this would help steer the country through the current turbulence.   

"I don't see how this financial turbulence, even though it has become more serious, can damage Brazil's performance," he said. "Following the turbulence, some countries, as is Brazil's case, will benefit because they have solid fundamentals, offer security, guarantees, and the potential for profits." [ 16-08-07 1821GMT ]   

Because of this, the finance minister said Brazil remained in a good position to see an elevation in its sovereign debt ratings to investment grade status.   

Fitch Ratings and  Standard & Poor's maintain Brazil's sovereign credit rating at BB+, one notch short of investment grade.   

Moody's Investor Services rates Brazil Ba2, two notches away from investment grade.  Moody's officials have said they may meet to review the rating this month, however.   

Mantega, meanwhile, lauded recent moves by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank to reduce turbulence by providing heavy injections of liquidity to the financial system. "They are guaranteeing necessary liquidity at this moment," he said. "The Fed declared that it will provide all the liquidity necessary, and that's a very important stance."   

Mantega, however, said he believed that the Fed would have to take additional measures, such as easing interest rates should the situation worsen.   

"If there's a worsening of the crisis, the Fed will have to lower rates to counteract high rates in the market, which have occurred because of scarce credit," he said.   

-By Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; (5561) 4501-7143; gerald.jeffris@dowjones.com [ 16-08-07 1903GMT ]

title: DJ Brazil Real Ends Stronger On Inflows Despite Ctrl Bk Moves
text:
Jun 11, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

Gerald Jeffris   

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real ended stronger against the dollar Monday as foreign currency continued to flow into the country despite central bank policy changes and a late session effort to intervene in the market.   

The real ended at BRL1.9405 per dollar after ending BRL1.960 in spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange Friday.

title: DJ Brazil's Meirelles: Pace Of Interest Rate Easing Adequate
text:
BRASILIA, May 24, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

The pace of interest rate easing in Brazil has been adequate and shouldn't be altered solely in reaction to recent exchange rate appreciation, Brazilian Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles said Thursday.   

"The fact is that interest rates are falling," he said. "Some people might believe that the trajectory of their decline is timid and others might even believe that it is too fast, but we believe that it is adequate to maintain inflation within targets and country risk in decline."   

Brazil's central bank has cut the country's reference Selic interest rate by 7.25 percentage points since September 2005 to a current 12.5% annually.   

Speaking at a joint hearing before six congressional committees on central bank activities, Meirelles denied that the real's appreciation was prompted by speculative foreign investment in high Brazilian interest rates and said it was mostly influenced by robust foreign trade surpluses and a weakening of the U.S. dollar internationally.   

Brazil's real has strengthened about 9% against the dollar since the beginning of the year.   

Some analysts have suggested that Brazil should accelerate interest rate cuts to diminish strong flows of foreign currency into the country.   

According to data presented by Meirelles, despite the real's appreciation against the dollar it has remained mostly stable against a group of at least 15 other world currencies examined by the central bank.   

Meirelles Thursday reiterated past declarations that the central bank had no intention to set a target for the exchange rate.   

"Brazil has already used a target for the exchange rate, but that had to be abandoned during a crisis in 1998," he said.   

Despite Meirelles' declarations, Brazil's central bank has intervened in the currency market with dollar purchase auctions almost daily since 2005. The central bank says it intervenes to diminish market volatility and build the country's foreign reserves.   

Meirelles, meanwhile, said he believed the country's interest rates would continue to decline amid low inflation expectations.   

According to recent market surveys, Brazil's IPCA consumer price inflation is seen ending 2007 and 2008 at below the country's official target of 4.5%.   

Meirelles noted that Brazil's real interest rate is currently around 7.5% annually, a level well below highs of around 22% seen in the previous 10 years.

title: Brazil stocks hit record high,  currency  slips
text:
(Updates to close)   

SAO PAULO, May 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock index surged to another all-time high on Friday, while the nation's currency weakened on concerns China's decision to raise interest rates and let the yuan trade more freely may hurt investment flows into Latin American markets.   

The Bovespa <.BVSP> index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange broke through 52,000 points for the first time ever, finishing up 0.86 percent at an all-time high of 52,077.6 points. That topped the previous record, set on Thursday.   

Wall Street gains also boosted Brazilian stocks, as well as an upgrade of Brazil's credit rating this week by  Standard & Poor's.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, weakened 0.46 percent to finish at 1.961 per U.S dollar, after closing the previous day at its strongest level since Jan. 16, 2001.   

Brazil's central bank intervened once again during the session to build up foreign reserves and curb the real's gains.   

Exporters complain the Brazilian real is too strong and is hurting their sales. Economists say the most effective way to weaken it would be by cutting the benchmark interest rate faster from 12.5 percent.   

"We think that with the real at 1.95 (per dollar), it will permit the central bank to be more aggressive in terms of monetary loosening," said Alexandre Lintz, chief strategist at  BNP Paribas. "So that would limit the space the real has to gain."   

The central bank has been cutting rates 25 basis points at a time and many think a 50-basis-point cut will be made at its next monetary policy meeting in June.   

Among overseas factors that hit the real, the People's Bank of China raised interest rates and bank reserve requirements while saying it would increase the trading band for the yuan to 0.5 percent from 0.3 percent.   

Interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> rose at the BM&F futures exchange in Sao Paulo on bets China's policy changes and potential interest rate rises by other central banks around the world might crimp inflows to Brazil a bit.   

At the stock exchange, iron ore miner CVRD , the second-heaviest stock in the Bovespa index, rose 0.67 percent to 73.69 reais.   

State-controlled oil company Petrobras , the heaviest-weighted stock in the index, rose 0.98 percent to 46.50 reais. The company signed a deal on Friday with Portuguese oil firms Galp and Partex to search for oil off the coast of Peniche, a fishing village north of Lisbon.

title: Brazil's  FX  reserves help lower risk premium-c.bank
text:
LONDON, May 9 (Reuters) - The lower risk now attached to holding Brazilian assets cushions the cost from the central bank's recent dollar-buying intervention to steady its currency, the head of Brazil's central bank said on Wednesday.   

The central bank has recently aggressively bought lower-yielding dollars to weaken the real <BRL=>, which is hovering at 6 1/2 year highs.   

"There is no doubt there is a cost of carrying the reserves or carrying a long position in hard currency," Henrique Meirelles, the central bank president told a news conference in London.   

"But that basically also generates a saving, which is the lower perceived risk for the country. The risk for the balance of payments decreases and that is reflected in the decrease of the risk premium on Brazilian paper."   

The spread between Brazilian debt and U.S. Treasuries on the  JP Morgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ> is currently around 155 basis points near a recent record tight level of 146 basis points.   

Brazil's international reserves have been rising rapidly and Meirelles said they were currently around $120 billion, the bulk of which is held in U.S.-denominated assets.   

He was upbeat on Brazil's economic fundamentals and asked whether he was worried inflation was reaching too low a level he said: "We are well within the target zone. The inflation targeting regime is working properly."   

He said the target zone for Brazilian inflation was between 2.5 and 6.5 percent with a mid point at 4.5 percent.   

With annual inflation running at about 3 percent, the bank has come under pressure from some business leaders and politicians to relax monetary policy and cut interest rates faster to give the economy a boost.   

But Meirelles said over the weekend the central bank will not ease up in the battle against inflation, even though consumer prices are rising at the slowest pace in years.   

He declined to comment on monetary policy.

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk Nominee Defends  Forex  Mrkt  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian Central Bank should continue its pattern of direct intervention in the foreign exchange market in order to reduce market volatility and build foreign reserves, central bank governor-nominee Mario Gomes Toros said Tuesday.   

"The central bank should intervene in the foreign exchange market whenever there is excessive volatility or lack of liquidity," Toros said. However, he said the main objective of central bank policy should continue to be control over inflation.   

Toros also defended the need for continued buildup of foreign reserves. He said, "Brazil has a clear policy of accumulating foreign reserves. Reserves help to redress problems of volatility."   

Brazilian foreign reserves as of Monday were $118.5 billion.   

Toros made the comments in televised testimony before a Senate committee. The committee will likely vote later Tuesday on Toros' nomination to be the Brazilian Central Bank governor in charge of monetary policy. The post is considered the second most important in the central bank, below that of Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles. The committee is widely expected to approve Toros' nomination. [ 24-04-07 1506GMT ]   

Questioned about eventual costs associated with maintenance of a high level of foreign reserves, Toros said, "Any costs are more than compensated by the protection a cushion of reserves gives Brazil in times of crisis."   

The Brazilian Central Bank has been buying U.S. dollars on the foreign exchange market nearly every day for the last several months, partly to build foreign reserves and partly to slow down the swift appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar.   

Typically, the central bank seeks to "sterilize" the Brazilian reals it emits for such purchases by selling more government bonds on the domestic bond market. Critics have complained that the practice unnecessarily boosts the size of the domestic debt.   

The real has gained more than 5% against the U.S. dollar so far in 2007 after gaining 8.8% in 2006. The strength of the real has led to complaints from Brazilian manufacturers that they are losing domestic market share to cheap imports. Exporters have also complained about losing their competitive edge in foreign markets because of the strong real.   

Toros said, "We are living through a period of a strong domestic currency, especially in the last two years. This strength is a reflection of our positive economic fundamentals, chiefly our strong foreign trade surplus and strong current account performance."   

Brazil rolled up a foreign trade surplus of $46.07 billion in 2006. Earlier Tuesday, the central bank released current account figures showing a 12-month current account surplus through March of $13.396 billion.   

Toros noted, however, that "while, on the one hand, the strong real hurts some domestic industries, it also helps control inflation and boost domestic consumption."   

He avoided direct comments on monetary policy. Brazil's central bank has been criticized by many business leaders and economists for maintenance of high interest rates. The Selic base rate is currently a towering 12.5%.   

Toros limited his comments to saying, "The biggest contribution that monetary policy can make is to price stability."   

Brazil's official IPCA inflation rate is currently running at a 12-month rate of 2.96%, its lowest in eight years.   

Toros added, "Price stability is a necessary condition for sustainable growth. It is not the only condition, but it is one of the necessary conditions."   

-By Tom Murphy and Rogerio Jelmayer, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3145-1478; brazil@dowjones.com [ 24-04-07 1525GMT ]

title: Brazil to add reserves while liquidity high-cenbank
text:
NEW YORK, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Brazil's policy of building foreign reserves should continue as long as global imbalances support a steady flow of dollars into the country, central bank director Paulo Vieira da Cunha said on Friday.  

"I don't think we will be building up reserves for 10 years ... but we are comfortable with our policy right now," Vieira da Cunha, who heads the international affairs department at the central bank, told analysts in New York.  

He explained that Brazil, like many other countries, keeps intervening in the foreign exchange market to counteract the effect of "global imbalances" caused by a mismatch in world interest rates.  

Low interest rates in the United States, Japan and Europe create carry trade opportunities, allowing investors to borrow in low-yielding currencies to invest in emerging countries like Brazil.  

As a result, Brazilian foreign reserves hit an all-time high of $95.9 billion on Wednesday. They are expected to keep growing as the central bank continues to buy dollars on the foreign exchange market to dry up excess liquidity and, indirectly, prevent the currency from appreciating further.  

Despite the central bank's efforts, the Brazilian real <BRBY> has been trading close to nine-month highs, raising complaints from the industrial sector.  

The interventions are costly because the central bank has to offset them by selling bonds in the local market, in order to drain the excess of reais resulting from the buying of dollars.  

But Vieira da Cunha said that "rather than looking at domestic issues," the central bank focuses on global liquidity conditions to decide whether to stop the currency interventions.  

He acknowledged that one of the costs of the foreign exchange interventions is a delay in a planned reduction of the stock of Brazil's local floating-rate debt, or LFTs.  

The Brazilian Treasury intends to cut as much as possible the share of public debt indexed to the country's base Selic rate. But the paper is the most efficient instrument the central bank has to offset the currency interventions, Vieira da Cunha said.  

"The Treasury would have reduced its stock of LFT much faster if it did not agree with our policy of sterilized interventions, because it knows we need this kind of paper," he said.

The currency strengthened even as the central bank intervened to buy dollars on the spot foreign exchange market, as it has done almost daily for months. With a steady flow of foreign capital pouring into the country from booming exports, some analysts said the real would strengthen even more if the central bank stopped holding daily dollar auctions.  

"The only reason the real isn't closer to the 2.0-per-dollar mark is because the central bank keeps intervening," said Tarcisio Rodrigues, heading of currency trading at Banco Paulista in Sao Paulo.  

The real has also been propped up by bets among investors that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hold off from raising interest rates for some time. High rates in the United States tend to lure cash out of emerging markets like Brazil.  

After the currency market closed, Fitch Ratings revised the outlook on Brazil's long-term foreign and local currency bonds to positive from stable, citing an improvement in the country's public finances.  

It also reaffirmed Brazil's rating at 'BB,' two notches below investment grade, and said the country could be upgraded within the next two years. A higher credit rating would make it easier for Brazil to borrow money abroad and attract a wider pool of investors to the country's capital markets.  

Fitch also said on Monday that it had assigned steelmaker Usiminas a 'BBB-' rating, giving it investment grade. That helped drive the company's shares 5.26 percent higher in Sao Paulo to 90.00 reais.

title: Fitch Affirms Banco Rural S.A.; Outlook Negative
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil & SAO PAULO, Brazil - (BUSINESS WIRE) - Today, Fitch Ratings has affirmed Banco Rural S.A.'s ('Rural') National ratings at Long-term 'BB-(BB minus)(bra)' with a Negative Outlook and Short-term 'B(bra)'. In addition, Fitch has affirmed the Support rating at '5'.  

The National ratings reflect the effects of Rural's tarnished image on its funding, liquidity, activities, risk profile and earnings as a result of its name being linked to the political crisis in June 2005. Funding and liquidity at Rural, alongside most small and medium-sized banks, had already experienced severe pressure from investor withdrawals following the Central Bank of Brazil intervention of Banco Santos S.A. in November 2004.  

From November 2004 to early 2006, Rural experienced deterioration in its asset quality and saw a sharp reduction in its assets, funding and equity. It also experienced an increase in intangible assets in its capital base and faced low liquidity. Although Fitch has seen an improvement in Rural's liquidity and funding ratios since mid-2006, it is still not sufficient to reverse the trend of the bank's ratings.  

The Negative Outlook reflects Fitch's opinion that Rural remains vulnerable to volatile operational performance and that the bank faces an arduous task in maintaining its profitability. Rural is looking at alternative funding sources, which Fitch views as being fundamental to the bank's earnings sustainability and long-term viability. The agency will continue to monitor closely the implementation of these new funding methods.  

Founded in 1948, Rural is a multiple bank controlled by five members of the Rabello family - 84.7% of the common shares - with a tradition in lending to small and medium-sized companies. Headquartered in Minas Gerais, it had 39 service posts (29 branches) in Brazil at June 2006 (126 in December 2004) and two overseas subsidiaries.  

Fitch's national ratings provide a relative measure of creditworthiness for rated entities in countries where the sovereign's foreign and local currency ratings are below 'AAA'. National ratings are not internationally comparable since the best relative risk within a country is rated 'AAA' and other credits are rated only relative to this risk. They are signified by the addition of an identifier, for the country concerned, such as 'AAA (bra)' for national ratings in Brazil.  

Fitch's rating definitions and the terms of use of such ratings are available on the agency's public site,  www.fitchratings.com ("http://www.fitchratings.com"). Published ratings, criteria and methodologies are available from this site, at all times. Fitch's code of conduct, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, affiliate firewall, compliance and other relevant policies and procedures are also available from the 'Code of Conduct' section of this site.

title: Brazil's Real Opens Stronger At New 12-Year High Vs Dollar
text:
--Brazil's real gives up some ground after breaking BRL1.53 in early trades.

--Debt-related risks in developed markets have been supporting emerging-market currencies.

--Brazilian central bank set intervene in exchange market.

By Paul Kiernan

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real continued its recent offensive against the dollar Tuesday, opening at the strongest level since 1999 as emerging-market currencies proved resilient to the debt-related risks that have been punishing assets in Europe and the U.S.

The real was quoted in Sao Paulo trading at BRL1.5319 to the dollar, according to Tullet Prebon via FactSet, compared with BRL1.5299 in earlier trades and BRL1.5408 at Monday's close.

Helping to fuel the currency's rally, some market participants say, is the ongoing stalemate among U.S. politicians in talks to raise the country's borrowing limit. As the U.S. grinds closer to an unprecedented default on its sovereign debt -- something that could happen as soon as Aug. 2 -- one view is that emerging-market countries with comparatively strong fiscal and macroeconomic fundamentals are being treated as safe havens.

But few, if any, investors know what would ultimately happen if the U.S. failed to make good on its financial obligations, with a powerful shock to the global financial system among the possibilities not to be discarded.

Win Thin, a currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York, characterized the recent appreciation of the real and other emerging-market currencies as "surprising."

"Maybe the market is being too complacent, but the general feeling is that, even if it comes down to an eleventh-hour thing, the U.S. is not going to default," Thin said.

He said Brazilian authorities can be expected to roll out new "roadblocks" to the real's gains, as currency strength is reducing the competitiveness of local manufacturers and exporters. At some point, the appreciation can be expected to slow.

"But every time the real weakens, it's seen as a buying opportunity," Thin said, adding that foreign investment money appears set to continue flowing into Brazil and supporting the currency.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Monday said local authorities reserve their right to implement further measures to limit the real's gains.

The Central Bank of Brazil on Tuesday was preparing a round of interventions in the exchange market. The bank held an auction Tuesday morning to buy dollars for forward delivery on Aug. 2, the deadline set by the U.S. government for raising its debt ceiling. According to the results of the auction, the bank purchased dollars at BRL1.5340.

Brazil's central bank also said it will poll market participants to gauge interest in a possible so-called reverse swap to be held Wednesday. Reverse swap auctions allow investors to exchange volatile foreign-exchange-linked contracts for paper indexed to domestic rates, and have been used by the central bank to reduce the volume of dollar-linked paper in the local market.
