title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real hits 12-yr high, minister jawbones
text:
* Investors test Brazil's resolve to limit gains

* Finance minister threatens more intervention

* Brazil real firms 0.7 pct, Mexico peso off 0.1 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, July 25 (Reuters) - Brazil's real hit a more than 12-year high on Monday as investors tested the resolve of Brazilian authorities worried by its gains, while fears about the U.S. debt stalemate held back other Latin American currencies.

Brazil's real broke past the 1.55 level to trade at its strongest since the currency was freely floated in early 1999.

Local authorities have tried to undermine bets on the real with a range of intervention measures, from dollar purchases to taxes. The currency's strength is hurting local industries by cutting into export profits and making rival imports cheaper.

But the market is betting that authorities may allow further gains in the real to help keep import prices down and cool inflation, analysts said. Inflation expectations for 2012 crept up in a poll released on Monday. [ID:nN1E76O03S]

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Monday scoffed at the idea that the country uses its currency to fight inflation and said the government stood ready to take further intervention measures. [ID:nN1E76O18G]

But analysts doubt authorities are willing to turn to more draconian measures, such as higher taxes on stock market investments, that could spur sharp losses in the real and end up further fanning price pressures.

"There is very little the government can do unless they turn to less market-friendly measures," said Marianna Costa, chief economist with Link Investimentos, a Sao Paulo brokerage.

The real <BRBY> bid 0.71 percent stronger to close at 1.5427 per dollar. Some analysts expect the real to hit 1.50 per dollar this year.

RATE ALLURE

Costa said the central bank could step up its dollar purchases in the spot and futures markets, but that would do little more than slow a further appreciation of the real.

Last week, Brazil tightened borrowing costs for the fifth time this year to raise its benchmark rate to 12.50 percent, the highest of any major economy <0#PRIME=>.

The allure of Brazilian interest rates has spurred a tide of money flows into Latin America's top economy. Signs that slowing global growth will keep the United States, Europe and Japan rates down for the foreseeable future will fuel further demand for Brazilian assets, analysts said.

"With those rate hikes postponed, this only insures that the flows to Brazil could continue at the same pace," Costa said.

Moreover, continued concerns that the U.S. debt rating could be downgraded should weigh on the dollar, thereby supporting commodity prices and currencies linked to raw materials exports, such as the real.

A divided U.S. Congress on Monday pursued rival budget plans that appeared unlikely to win broad support, pushing the country closer to a debt default. Even if the debt limit is raised, the country may face a ratings downgrade if lawmakers cannot find a way to cut the deficit. [ID:nN1E76M0B0]

The currencies of Mexico and Colombia, the two Latin American economies with the closest trade ties to the United States, saw volatile trading. But their pesos pared losses as the market held to bets that politicians would manage to avert a U.S. default.

"I think everyone still has this hope that they will do something. They are playing politics as politicians do, but in the end, it will get done," said Ramses Villela, head of currency trading at Bulltick Capital Markets in Mexico City.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.11 to 11.6430 per dollar, but the currency erased steep losses that had pushed the cost of dollars in pesos up to just below its 50-day moving average at 11.7250.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> bid 0.44 percent weaker at 1,763.50 per dollar, but it recovered from an earlier 1.5 percent loss.

In a recent poll of analysts, all but one of the 25 analysts surveyed expected that Colombia's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 4.5 percent at its Friday meeting, marking the sixth straight rate increase since February. [ID:nN1E76O172]

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.24 percent weaker at 462.40 per dollar.

The currencies of Chile and Colombia remain near three-year highs and further strength could push their authorities to try further intervention measures, analysts said.

title: Brazil  Real Weakens On Government  Intervention , Inflation Bets
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real opened weaker on Monday as investors see government intervention in the market holding down potential gains and as inflation bets stabilize, signaling less need for significantly higher interest rates.

The real opened at 1.5795 to the dollar, according to Telekurs via FactSet. That's weaker than Friday's close of BRL1.5745.

Economists expect Brazilian inflation to end this year at 6.31%, and next year at 5.2%, according to a weekly survey conducted by the country's central bank. Both estimates are unchanged from the previous survey as economists begin to see the effect of already high interest rates.

Economists also maintained expectations that the benchmark Selic rate will rise to 12.75% at the end of this year, from 12.25% currently. The central bank meets this week and investors are expecting a quarter-point rate increase.

One of the highest interest rates in the world has attracted massive investment to Latin America's biggest economy, pushing up the value of the real. The looming rate, together with a hot domestic consumer market and high prices for the country's mineral and agricultural commodity exports, has fed into demand for the currency. Foreign investment in the country has picked up this month, with daily inflows reaching an average of $254 million in July, according to Banco Santander.

But a steady stream of government intervention, from higher taxes to rising bank reserve requirements, has mitigated gains. The latest move was to restrict banks' net short position on the U.S. dollar, announced July 8.

"We continue to see the BRL testing the 1.55 record low, but we now believe that the potential beyond that is more modest on the back of more elevated intervention risks," Banco Santander economist Alejandro Estevez-Breton wrote in a note Monday.

The rate broke past 1.55 earlier this month, surpassing a 2008 record to trade at the strongest level since the country instituted a free-floating currency in 1999.

title: Brazil  Currency  Market Strengthens, Casts Wary Eye Abroad
text:
--Brazil real strengthens, but Europe's debt troubles remain on the radar

--U.S. dollar loses ground against global currencies after Federal Reserve releases minutes from June meeting

--Federal Reserve discusses exit from easy-money policies, but end unlikely in near future

--Brazilian real exits active trading at BRL1.5795 to the dollar


   By Jeff Fick 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market strengthened Tuesday, rebounding from early session losses related to debt troubles abroad amid signs that the end to easy-money policies in the U.S. may not be near.

The trading session kicked off with renewed concerns about the fiscal health of Europe, where several of the European Union's lesser members are struggling with heavy debt loads and sluggish growth. The latest victim is Italy, which was forced to pay higher-than-expected interest rates in a successful bond sale. Yields on Spanish bonds also soared due to fears of contagion after Greece last month narrowly avoided the single-currency zone's first debt default.

"The market in general remained tense because of the situation in Europe," said Alberto Orsovay, a trader at Sao Paulo-based brokerage house Hencorp Commcor. "It looks like the hole is getting deeper and it's going to be awhile before Europe's troubles are resolved."

The European debt troubles undermined the euro, which fell to an all-time low against the Swiss franc and its lowest level in four months against the greenback. The single currency tumbled further after Moody's Investors Service downgraded the sovereign debt of Ireland to Ba1, with a negative outlook.

But global currencies received a boost late in the session, when the U.S. Federal Reserve released minutes from its June meeting. Fed officials took a wait-and-see approach at the meeting as the world's largest economy continued to struggle. The Fed discussed how to unwind its asset-purchase program designed to stimulate the economy, but the minutes emphasized that the discussion "did not imply that a move toward such normalization would necessarily begin sometime soon."

The Fed minutes "sent the dollar a little lower," noted Hencorp Commcor's Orsovay.

The Brazilian real shrugged off the latest market uncertainty to exit active trading at BRL1.5795, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset. That was slightly stronger from Monday's closing quote at BRL1.5801 to the dollar.

The real's surprising strength came despite last Friday's measures to crimp bank's short-dollar positions, with banks having five days to comply. Brazilian banks will now have to deposit 60% of the value of their short-dollar positions above $1 billion without remuneration, which will boost local demand for dollars.

The measure had an immediate impact on the cost of borrowing dollars in Brazil, known as the foreign-exchange coupon, with interest rates on dollar loans jumping. The central bank move is aimed at stemming so-called "hot money" short-term inflows into Brazil and at curtailing the real's recent strength.

Despite the market's quick adjustment to the move, volatility could be heightened this week "as some banks are likely to unwind their net short-dollar positions via buying foreign currency in the spot and selling foreign currency in the futures and forwards curves," said Banco Santander.

Currency market intervention in Brazil also indicates that central bankers have drawn a "line in the sand" at BRL1.55 to the dollar, BofA Merrill Lynch said. The central bank implemented the latest reserve requirement and held its first reverse-swap auction since March on Friday, far from a "coincidence" after the currency had broken through a key technical barrier at BRL1.5519 to the dollar--the currency's strongest level since August 2008, the firm said.

Further intervention measures can be expected if the real keeps getting stronger, with moves likely to be unpredictable because "there is a big toolbox that could be used," BofA Merrill Lynch said.

But government officials face a difficult task in reining in the currency, with sky-high local interest rates attracting heavy foreign investor interest. Brazil's benchmark Selic base interest rate stands at 12.25%, one of the highest benchmark rates in the world. Brazil's central bank is expected to raise the Selic once again later this month in an effort to tamp down domestic demand and contain rising prices.

"I think the market has already priced in [an interest rate rise], but it could increase inflows," said Hencorp Commcor's Orsovay. For this week, however, the real is likely to remain rangebound between BRL1.57 and BRL1.60 to the dollar unless there is a resolution or further bad news out of Europe, the trader added.

title: UPDATE: Brazil  Central Bank  Seeks To Reduce Banks'  Forex  Short Positions
text:
(Update with Barclays Capital's comments in the 6th and 7th paragraphs)

By Rogerio Jelmayer

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank sought to reduce dollar short positions in the foreign exchange market to slow currency flows into Brazil, at least in the short-term.

Banks will now have to deposit 60% of the value of their positions above $1 billion without any remuneration, and have just five days to adjust respective positions, the central bank said over the weekend.

In January, the central bank announced a similar measure. Then, however, banks had more time to adjust. At the time, banks had to deposit 60% of the value of their positions above $3 billion without any remuneration, and had 90 days to adjust their positions.

Brazilian banks had a net $14.7 billion in bets against the dollar at the end of June, said the central bank.

The bets against the dollar are a constant source of upward pressure on the Brazilian real, which worries the government because of the impact of a stronger real on exporters, particularly manufacturers. With a stronger real, Brazilian goods become more expensive in terms of other currencies.

"Clearly, the recent bout of BRL appreciation has generated some discomfort in the government. We believe the measures should force banks that are not in compliance with the new limits to increase demand for spot USD (US Dollar) and also increase the supply of short USD in the futures markets, hence affecting the on-off short basis as well," Barclays Capital said in a research report for its clients.

"The BCB's (Brazil's Central Bank) first move on spot short USD positions was last January (announcing the $3 billion threshold) and by tightening the limits again, this means that authorities know some institutions will have to move to the market to square their positions. Even though we do not have individual information, the system carries $14.7 billion in short spot USD positions. And we believe the BCB is aiming to drive this stock to closer to $10 billion," Barclays added.

On Friday, the Brazilian real finished active trading at BRL1.5627 to the dollar, weaker against Thursday's close of BRL1.5556, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset.

Brazil's central bank on Friday stepped up its market intervention, in an apparent attempt to "take advantage" of risk aversion to roll back some of the real's recent gains.

Brazilian officials have been keen to stall, or even reverse, the real's appreciation against the dollar. The real has gained 20% against the dollar over the past two years.

The central bank intervened in the market three times Friday, twice with snap auctions to buy dollars and once with a reverse swap auction.

title: Brazil Real Weaker On Europe Woes, US Jobs Data
text:
--Brazil government steps up market intervention

--Global risk aversion could persist next week

--Brazil real seen weaker next week on Europe woes


 
   By Tom Murphy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real was weaker against the U.S. dollar at the end of regular trading Friday as global risk aversion rose in the face of renewed European debt worries and disappointing U.S. jobs data.

The real finished active trading at BRL1.5627 to the dollar, weaker against Thursday's close of BRL1.5556, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset.

The euro dropped against the dollar Friday on reports that Italian Finance Minister Giulio Tremonti might resign over disagreements on how to handle the country's debt problems. The reports come at an especially bad time for Europe, with Greece already teetering on the brink of default and severe debt problems plaguing Spain, Ireland and Portugal.

Meanwhile, the U.S. reported creation of only 18,000 jobs in June. Analysts had expected more than 100,000 new jobs.

One Brazilian traders said, "At first, we thought they had left off a zero when releasing the figure."

The combination of European debt woes and a sluggish U.S. economic recovery led to rising risk aversion among investors everywhere.

"Risk aversion is likely to continue next week," said Marcos Morais, a trader at Sao Paulo's Intercam brokerage. "We're forecasting some slight additional weakening for the real against the dollar."

Brazil's central bank on Friday stepped up its market intervention, in an apparent attempt to "take advantage" of risk aversion to roll back some of the currency's recent gains, said Morais.

Brazilian officials have been keen to stall, or even reverse, the real's appreciation against the dollar. The strong real hurts exporters and manufacturers. The real has gained 20% against the dollar over the past two years.

The central bank intervened in the market three times Friday, twice with snap auctions to buy dollars and once with a reverse swap auction.

Reverse swap auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange dollar-linked bonds for paper indexed to domestic interest rates. The auctions tend to support the dollar by removing future dollar inflows that overhang the market. At Friday's auction, the government sold reverse swaps equal to $483 million.

Lower international commodities prices Friday also contributed to a weakening of the real. Lower commodities prices mean reduced export revenues.

On credit markets Friday, investors showed renewed worries about inflation pressure and possible central-bank interest-rate hikes to come. Analysts at RBC bank in a research note forecast a quarter-point rate hike in the central bank's base rate in July and another quarter-point hike in August. The base rate is already a towering 12.25%.

On the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, interest rate futures contracts closed mostly higher Friday. The contracts reflect investor expectations for annualized interest rates at future dates.

Among actively traded contracts, that of January 2012 closed at 12.50%, up from 12.49% Thursday.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  slide on weak US jobs data
text:
* U.S. jobs data worst in 9 months; hits growth outlook

* Mexico, Chile pesos, Brazil real weaken vs dollar

* Brazil buys dollars, sells swaps to check real's gains

* Foreign bets on stronger real reach record Thursday

(Updates prices, adds second Brazil dollar auction)

By Jeb Blount and Jean Luis Arce

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened against the dollar Friday, led by Mexico's peso and Brazil's real, as weak U.S. job creation dimmed expectations for growth in the world's largest economy.

Job growth in the United States almost came to a halt in June with nonfarm employers hiring 18,000 workers, the weakest reading since September. The unemployment rate rose to 9.2 percent, a six-month high, the U.S. Labor Department said.

The data comes after a separate report Thursday signaled robust private-sector job growth and helped Latin American currencies surge to or near to record highs.

"These numbers were clearly disappointing and break the momentum of gains in recent weeks," said Alejandro Padilla, a foreign exchange strategist at Banorte-IXE in Mexico City. "Yesterday's gains have helped increase the size of today's falls."

Mexico's peso weakened 0.7 percent to 11.6202 to the U.S. dollar, putting the Mexican currency on track for its biggest one-day slide since June 16 and its first weekly loss -- 0.2 percent -- in a month.

The peso's declines were the largest of the region's currencies. Mexico's close relationship with its larger northern neighbor -- it gets 80 percent of its export earnings from the United States -- makes it more dependent on U.S. trends than other major Latin American economies.

"This was a very bad day for the world economy and for the prospects of global recovery because the data shows that the United States is suffering in its recovery and that it is very weak," said Benito Berber, currency analyst with Nomura Securities in New York. "This obviously has clear consequences for Mexican growth expectations."

The slowing U.S. economy makes it likely that the peso will slip to the 11.70 to 11.80 range, he added.

Brazil's real also weakened, shedding 0.5 percent to 1.563 to the dollar. The declines come as Brazil's central bank steps up intervention in the markets. The real shed 0.2 percent this week.

"I've been concerned about U.S. growth for some time, but the jobs number today was even worse than most expected," said Carlos Kawall, chief economist with Banco Safra SA in Sao Paulo. "This does not bode well for world growth."

Despite the real's decline, Brazil's central bank moved to help the real weaken even further.

During morning trading Friday, the bank bought dollars and sold reverse-swap contracts at auction to drive up demand for the U.S. currency while putting pressure on the real to weaken. It held a second dollar auction in the afternoon.

The auctions come days after comments from Finance Minister Guido Mantega suggesting the government might act to halt the currency's 7 percent gain this year. Mantega's comments, though, have gone largely unheeded by foreign investors.

Friday's declines in the real came a day after foreign bets the real will gain further reached a record high Wednesday on Sao Paulo's BM&F exchange.

Foreign "net real longs" rose 5.6 percent to a notional value of $24.6 billion on Thursday -- the most recent day for which data is available -- from $23.3 billion on Wednesday, according to the BM&F and Reuters.

The net real longs represent bets that the real will gain minus the bets the real will weaken made by nonresident individuals and companies using two BM&F contracts -- the dollar future and cupom cambial DDI future.

Chile's peso slipped 0.3 percent to 462.45 to the dollar, easing back from its strongest in three months. It closed the week 0.6 percent stronger than last Friday.

Colombia's peso was little changed, gaining 45 centavos to 1,760.45 to the dollar and extending Thursday's eight-year high. Gains for the week were 0.5 percent.

The day after Peru's central bank held the country's benchmark lending rate at 4.25 percent, the country's currency, the sol, was little changed at 2.7420 for a weekly gain of 0.3 percent.

(Writing by Jeb Blount; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: Brazil  May  Intervene  More If  Currency  Crosses 2008 Peaks
text:
-Some more gains seen possible for the Brazilian real

-BRL1.55 per dollar seen as a key level for currency


 
   By Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real has rallied for two weeks and investment flows may push the currency a little further, although policymakers are expected to intervene more forcefully if the currency strengthens past the highs it reached in 2008.

The real was recently at BRL1.5755 per dollar, according to CQG, its strongest level since its August 2008 peak of about BRL1.56 per dollar. The previous peak was reached just before the global economic crisis exploded.

Enrique Alvarez, an analyst at IDEAGlobal says that after the recent lengthy rally the market will try and test the 2008 peak and BRL1.55 is the next key level to watch.

"That's where I think the market wants to trend and test. That's where the authorities will feel obliged to take another stand," he said. Allowing an unfettered appreciation of the real would cause problems for domestic exporters as well as create an overflow of Chinese imports, he said.

The real has strengthened past several key levels in recent weeks, although Brazilian authorities have tried to stem the appreciation by building dollar reserves and by extending an existing 6% tax on short-term foreign loans to loans of up to two years. Still, those measures weren't viewed as very stringent.

As the real has strengthened investors have grown more hopeful that Brazil, which has aggressively fought currency appreciation in the past, is becoming more willing to permit a stronger real. Brazil, like much of the emerging world, faces rising inflation and a stronger real would help the country fight inflationary pressures.

Government figures released Thursday showed a rise in the 12-month inflation rate to 6.3% as of March from 6.01% as of February.

RBS strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky feels that it is "very doable" for the real to appreciate to BRL1.55 per dollar. The risk of the government introducing draconian capital controls has abated, she said. "The government doesn't want to risk any disorderly selloff in the real triggered by draconian measures. Now the big game changer is inflation."

Brazil's government on Thursday adopted a new 1.5% financial operations tax on virtually all forms of consumer credit in a bid to help reduce galloping inflation.

Policymakers could intervene more as the currency appreciates past further key levels, Cattan-Naslausky said. But she expects such intervention to remain fairly orthodox and to be done through measures such as the central bank building dollar reserves or a fine-tuning of existing taxes and measures.

On Friday, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Brazil will enact future measures to contain its strengthening currency in order to avoid asset bubbles that could harm its economy should the steady inflow of foreign investment reverse.

Since March 28, the dollar has declined about 5% against the real. Still, investors aren't sure just how much Brazilian authorities will be able to do over the long term to control appreciation and heavy investment flows. At a towering 11.75%, Brazil's benchmark interest rate is among the world's highest, making the country an attractive investment destination.

"As much as they want to limit the appreciation of the currency, there is certainly a very large need for foreign financing...foreign direct investment," said Roberto Sanchez-Dahl, an emerging-market portfolio manager with Federated Investors, who manages about $1.1 billion in assets out of Pittsburgh.

Foreigners aren't the only ones to blame for the currency appreciating as local investors are also making speculative bets on the real, he said. His team has positions in real-denominated debt in Brazil, but they aren't making too many changes to their positions because taxes announced last year on foreign fixed income investments make it costlier to buy and sell such assets.

-By Anjali Cordeiro, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com

title: Traders Eye  Brazil Forex Intervention  As Real Starts Week Quietly
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--After last week's tumultous trading, the Brazilian foreign exchange market began the week on a quiet note, and with little in terms of data to drive the market on Monday, all eyes will be on government intervention efforts.

The Brazilian real gained nearly 3.4% last week against the dollar, as money flooded into Brazil and pushed the currency right past the BRL1.65 level which had been seen as an unofficial barrier. Banks piled on the pressure in what traders attempted as a battle of wills with the monetary authority.

On Monday, the real opened slightly weaker, trading at BRL1.6190 according to Tullett Prebon via Factset, slightly weaker from the level BRL1.6156 at which it exited active trading on Friday.

As long as the currency is steady, it seems unlikely the government will come out with any forceful capital control measures, although there is plenty of speculation, said Alberto Orsovay, of the Hencorp Commcor brokerage. In the meantime, the central bank is expected to turn to its regular auctions to buy dollars, or offer reverse swap contracts, he said.

Brazil's foreign-currency reserves increased $9.6 billion in March from the previous month on continued dollar purchases in the foreign-exchange market by the monetary authority, according to figures published on the central bank's website Monday.

Foreign reserves totaled $317.1 billion as of March 31, up from $307.5 billion at the end of February.

In the first three months of this year, reserves grew by $28.6 billion. Reserves began growing sharply when the central bank started purchasing dollars from the spot market in October 2005. They totaled $53.779 billion at the end of 2005.

They declined beginning in October 2008 as the central bank loaned dollars to Brazilian businesses in the face of the global credit crunch. The central bank also sold dollars from the reserves to the foreign-exchange market via spot auctions.

In mid-2009, however, the government reversed course, buying dollars from the market at spot auctions since then.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real, Mexico peso mark 2008 highs
text:
* Brazil resigned to more currency gains - for now

* U.S. jobs data supports bids for region's currencies

* Brazil real firms 1.16 pct, Mexico peso up 0.41 pct

By Michael O'Boyle and Jean Luis Arce

MEXICO CITY, April 1 (Reuters) - Brazil's real and Mexico's peso hit their strongest levels in more than 2 years on Friday, but further gains ahead may be limited by increased intervention in Brazil and heavy positioning in the peso.

Investors were expecting tough new measures from Brazil this week, but a tax on foreign debt held by locals fell far short of expectations, and investors bet policymakers had lost their nerve to impose severe capital controls.

The real surged this week by nearly 3 percent in its biggest weekly gain in a year week as investors tested the resolve of authorities to contain currency strength that is hurting local manufacturers.

Brazilian officials confirmed to Reuters they were unwilling to impose -- at least for now -- more severe capital controls to weaken one of the world's most overvalued currencies. [ID:nN01172691]

After trying a range of measures to contain gains in the real, policymakers are left with drastic capital control options that could spur sharp losses - and further inflame inflation by making imports more expensive.

"The government's increased concerns about inflation and its effects on the population's real income are probably driving this increased tolerance for currency strength," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging market research at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

The real <BRBY> bid 1.16 percent firmer at 1.61 per dollar on the local spot market, its strongest levels since August 2008.

The currency blew past the 1.65 per dollar level that was considered authorities unofficial limit, and now the market expects the next line in the sand to be drawn around 1.60 per dollar level.

Brazilian authorities have been trying to block unwanted flows attracted to the country's double-digit interest rates, but investors continue to find ways around each new barrier.

The central bank did its best to contain the real's gains, holding three auctions in the spot market, in a marked increase in of its efforts. Increased intervention by the central bank would likely contain further gains next week, analysts said.

Supporting demand for riskier emerging market assets, U.S. employment recorded a second straight month of solid gains in March. [ID:nNOAT00477]

The gains were seen as solid enough to keep up confidence in the U.S. recovery, but not strong enough to discourage the Federal Reserve from its ultra-easy monetary policies that has boosted the appeal of higher yielding Latin American debt.

"This is helping risk appetite, and should carry emerging market currencies stronger as economic prospects improve," Chamie said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> gained 0.41 percent to 11.84 per dollar. The currency touched its strongest level since October 2008 and gained around 1 percent this week.

The currency has benefited from signs of an improving economic recovery in the United States, its top trading partner, as well as expectations that Mexican authorities will not increase their current pace of building dollar reserves.

However, so many people are betting on a stronger peso, that the lack of important U.S. economic data next week to back up optimism could leave the currency open to profit taking.

Data showed a net $3.7 billion in speculative futures contracts betting on a stronger peso, the highest number of speculative contracts of the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. [ID:nN01141556]

"If we get a negative shock, (the peso) will turn around in a second," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital.

Chile's peso hit a three-week high, boosted by market expectations of another 50 basis-point interest rate increase in April following publication of central bank minutes from the March rate-setting meeting. [ID:nN01110945]

The peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.42 percent stronger at 475.5 per dollar, for an around 0.7 percent advance for the week.

title: Brazil Says No Offers Accepted In Reverse Auction

title: Brazil  Central Bank  Fights On All Fronts, But Real Still Shines
text:
-Brazil's central bank faces a credibility problem as inflation expectations deteriorate

-The real has outperformed despite new intervention measures

-Carry trades remain attractive as some intervention moves have removed currency volatility


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian central bank's ongoing efforts to curb its currency's appreciation have removed volatility from the Brazilian real, but that could mean that's backfiring.

Less volatility, some investors say, only makes the Brazilian real more attractive for carry trades. In such trades, investors borrow money in a low-yielding currency such as the dollar and reinvest the proceeds in short-term securities in a high-yielding currency such as the real. Such trades can be highly profitable but risky because sharp, unexpected turns can impose big losses on leveraged positions.

That leaves the central bank in a tight bind and is raising concern it is falling behind the inflation curve. Prices continue to rise in Brazil, despite its towering interest rates. Yet, its currency interventions haven't spooked international investors away from the currency, with the real breaking through the bank's unofficial line in the sand this week. That makes Brazilian exports less competitive and leaves the country's financial system vulnerable if at some time in the future the inflows in yield-seeking "hot money" turn into rapid outflows.

Indeed, the real stayed significantly stronger than BRL1.65 to the dollar on Thursday, just days after the bank announced its newest intervention efforts, a 6% tax on foreign bond issuance to help stem repatriation flows that drive real-buying.

The bank's methods, which include such macroprudential measures as taxes on certain types of investments, have slowed the pace of inflows and the real's appreciation, analysts say. The bank also regularly buys dollars in the spot, forward and futures markets.

But these moves have actually taken volatility out of the currency, which only further entices carry-trade investors into Brazilian money markets, where interest rates are among the highest in the world. The central bank's Selic base rate is at 11.75%.

"We like [the] Brazilian real even with the macroprudential tools that have been put in place," said Michael Mata, who manages the ING Global Bond Fund. "We don't think it's going to appreciate dramatically from here, but it doesn't need to with a 12% carry."

The bank's moves have also reduced "speculative elements," helping to further diminish volatility, said Adnan Akant, head of foreign exchange and managing director at money manager Fischer Francis Trees & Watts, a New York unit of BNP Paribas.

What's more, with Brazil being such a costly market to enter, and with such a stable currency making carry-trades a relatively safe bet, few investors are willing to leave the real, even in intervention's wake. "It's one of those buy-and-hold currencies," Akant said.

Such views are giving the central bank a headache.

The real's relentless popularity is evident in the central bank's most recent published weekly figures for money flows. Although they showed some money slipped away from Brazil over the last week, net dollar receipts still stood at $10.52 billion in March through last Friday, up from only $462 million in the same period of last year.

Corporate flows have been a primary source of the real's strength, while hot money flows represent only a portion, said RBS strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky. In addition, excess global liquidity has driven investors to emerging-market currencies like the real.

The flipside of this, however, is that the combination of macroprudential and more orthodox intervention measures have created a growing credibility problem for the bank, as inflation expectations continue to deteriorate.

The central bank, in its quarterly report out Wednesday, raised its 2011 inflation forecast to 5.6% from 5.0%.

Meanwhile, its intervention efforts up-to-date have been deemed ineffective.

"We don't really think any of this is really going to have an impact [on the real]," said Tony Volpon, head of Americas emerging-market research at Nomura.

Still, by allowing the real to go stronger than BRL1.65, the bank may be signaling a small shift in its line in the sand, though it will likely defend new levels, analysts said.

In coming weeks, the bank could focus on more orthodox measures in the spot and futures markets, Cattan-Naslausky said. It may allow more volatility through sporadic intervention, ending the real's predictability, which could squeeze out some of the stale positions in dollar-Brazil and help it weaken, she added.

The next few days will be crucial in telling where the bank plans to head, as markets wait to see how far the bank will let the real go, analysts said. In the mean time, investors will likely stay in the real unless more volatility surfaces or if global events damp risk sentiment.

"As long as you have confidence that at some future date everything is going to be okay in Brazil, then you're okay," Akant said.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

title: Brazil Real Weakens In Late Trade After  Central Bank  Acts
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened marginally in late trading Thursday, after heavy intervention by Brazil's Central Bank limited the U.S. dollar's fall amid continued speculative trading in the run-up to the setting of the end-of-month Ptax foreign-exchange rate used to settle futures contracts.

The real traded at BRL1.6305 at 2000 GMT, weaker than its Wednesday close of BRL1.6275, according to Tullett Prebon via Factset.

Investors, including Brazilian banks, were reported to have driven down the dollar rate against the real for the fourth consecutive day in a move to gain on futures and reverse swap maturities. Traders noted that Brazil's Central Bank is likely to wait until these "technical" market movements subside before resuming its strategy to curb the real's trend to appreciation.

However, economists said new measures could now be adopted anytime as more market stability should be seen following the settling of the Ptax rate later Thursday.

"We believe that the market may return to normal levels [Friday], with a higher, more civilized rate for the dollar, maybe of around BRL1.65 to BRL1.66," said Luiz Antonio Abdo of Corretora Souza Barros. "The downwards movement we've been seeing on the dollar since the start of the week is because of the tug of war between banks and the Central Bank on the Ptax rate."

A new increased tax on foreign loans announced earlier this week was seen to be having little immediate impact on market exchange rates. Traders said large quantities of foreign currency continue to enter Brazil as Brazilian companies including banks continue to seek financing in foreign currencies.

The spot dollar, which lost 1.39% against the real amid Wednesday's speculative movements, opened trading Thursday at its lowest level since August 27, 2008, at the start of the subprime crisis. However, massive intervention by the Central Bank, which bought up dollars at three spot auctions and organized two reverse-swap auctions, propped up the dollar to the extent that it showed small gains towards the end of the trading day.

"The true face of the exchange market will, however, be apparent only next week," said Raphael Martello of Tendencias Consultoria.

The Central Bank's first reverse-swap auction, at which 30,000 contracts were offered at auction, found no takers, demonstrating Brazilian banks' unwillingness to participate in this kind of trade, which doesn't bring them any specific benefit, Martello said. "The banks think they won't make any gain from this instrument, as they believe the real's going to appreciate further," the economist observed. "The banks prefer not to take the risk."

The Central Bank's second reverse-swap auction in early afternoon sold just 22% of the lots on offer.

Reverse-swap contracts offer investors the opportunity to exchange dollar-linked futures contracts for paper linked to interest rates.

The government has been using reverse-swap auctions, along with other mechanisms, in recent months in order to arrest the appreciation of the real. The strong real hurts Brazilian exporters and manufacturers.

The real has gained 45% against the dollar over the past two years.

-By Diana Kinch, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-21-2586-6086; diana.kinch@dowjones.com [ 31-03-11 2046GMT ]

title: MARKET TALK: Oil Prices 'Sideways' Since UN No-Fly Zone Began
text:
11:51 (Dow Jones) Oil prices have moved "sideways" since the UN authorized a no-fly zone in Libya earlier this month, Barclays oil analysts point out. "At some point on each of the past 11 trading days, front-month Brent futures have reached $115.50/bbl," they write. "Perhaps surprisingly, the involvement of external forces in Libya under the UN resolution has so far been associated with a reduction in volatility." But they add that the $115/bbl equilibrium may be unstable. A sudden decline in geopolitical tensions would send Brent to $90, they say. Brent crude up $1.64 at $116.77. Nymex crude up $1.59 at $105.86. (dan.strumpf@dowjones.com)

11:48 (Dow Jones) Fourth-quarter net profits at Brazilian meatpacker Marfrig Alimentos (MRFG3.BR), the world's fourth-largest, show the company is making progress as it integrates recently acquired rivals Seara and Keystone Foods, says Link Investimentos. Better capacity utilization in Brazil and higher exports to Europe offset increased prices for livestock and feed, firm says. "The fourth-quarter numbers present an improvement from the previous quarter, and the market should react positively," firm says. Shares up 0.5% at BRL14.10 in Sao Paulo. (jeff.fick@dowjones.com)

11:46 (Dow Jones) Rated defaults of municipal bonds are likely to rise in 2011, reaching two to three times the number seen in 2008, says Bob Kurtter, managing director for US public finance at Moody's. That would mean 12 to 15 rated defaults. "All of this depends on what we're seeing state and local government officials doing across the country, which is making the tough decisions that need to be made to address their problems," Kurtter says at a Federal Reserve conference in Charlotte. (jeffrey.sparshott@dowjones.com)

11:45 (Dow Jones) The British press is buzzing about builder Taylor Wimpey (TW.LN) selling its North American operations - which include a large private builder that has operations in Arizona and Texas - for about $955M to investors including TPG Capital. But on this side of the pond, the deal isn't generating much chatter because nothing really changes. "It doesn't appear to change the competitive landscape at all," says competitor Meritage Homes' (MTH) Brent Anderson. (dawn.wotapka@dowjones.com)

11:40 (Dow Jones) Grain traders fear season-end US corn supplies could reach a record low near 500M bushels unless high prices slow demand. The US next week is expected to cut its current forecast of 675M, a 15-year low, after reporting Thursday that March 1 inventories were tighter than expected. MaxYield Cooperative in Iowa reports talk of season-end supplies dropping to 490M, while an exchange-traded fund manager says he hears forecasts for 500M. "That is terrifyingly low," says Sal Gilbertie, lead portfolio manager of The Teucrium Corn Fund. CBOT May corn futures remain up the daily 30c limit at $6.93 1/4 a bushel. (tom.polansek@dowjones.com)

11:37 (Dow Jones) Bond prices stay marginally lower. Investors are digesting the release, which says the banks there face EUR24B capital shortfall. The Irish government has tapped EU bailout fund to rescue the struggling banking system. The benchmark US 10-year note is 1/32 lower, yielding 3.45%. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

11:36 (Dow Jones) Pratt & Whitney now two-for-two over GE in the battle to provide new engines for the Airbus A320neo. The big order from IndiGo for the United Technologies (UTX) unit will see the contest move on to Deutsche Lufthansa (DLA.XE), an industry bellwether whose choice could give the Pratt GTF engine even more momentum, or allow GE's Leap-X joint venture to regain some ground. ILFC, the leasing company, has already chosen the GTF for 60 of the 100 A320neos it has on order. Virgin America has also yet to decide on its engine choice. (doug.cameron@dowjones.com)

11:33 (Dow Jones) Right before it failed in 2008, Washington Mutual was a heavy Fed borrower at the discount window, new data reveal, confirming at least the historical norm that desperate borrowers go there at last resort. The first time it appears that September in 2008 was Thursday, Sept. 18, a week before it went down, taking $2B to carry the weekend. Starting Monday, when that first loan was due, it turned to taking $2B overnight each night. It even took $2B on Thursday. Sept. 25, as JPMorgan (JPM) took it over late that day in the biggest bank failure in history. Last resort wasn't enough for WaMu. (david.benoit@dowjones.com)

11:14 (Dow Jones) Middleburg Financial (MBRG) shares on a tear today as investors digest David Sokol's comments that he'd be interested in starting his own investment company modeled on Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA, BRKB). Sokol, who said he did nothing wrong in buying shares of Lubrizol (LZ) before Berkshire's purchase, is the largest shareholder in Middleburg with about a 20% stake. Sandler O'Neill analyst Casey Orr says shares up 9.3% to $16.45 on nearly twice average daily volume as traders "speculating what's going to happen next." MBRG wasn't immediately available for comment. (corrie.driebusch@dowjones.com)

11:09 (Dow Jones) Stockpiles of natural gas in traditional gas-producing states hit the highest level ever recorded in March in the EIA's weekly storage report, a bearish data point amid the widely held view that supply will overwhelm demand during the first half of this year. Gas in storage in the region rises to 740B cubic feet last week, 25% above 2010 levels. Last year, when a similar supply imbalance pressured the market, inventories didn't reach that level until the end of April. Nymex May gas recently down 2.2% at $4.259/MMBtu. EIA has tracked regional inventories since 1994. (matt.day@dowjones.com)

11:04 (Dow Jones) The USDA's lower-than-expected estimate for corn inventories as of March 1 fuels fears that season-end supplies will drop to a record low. Government could slash 50M-75M bushels from the latest season-end supply estimate of 675M in a crop report next week, says Rich Nelson at Allendale. Season-end supplies are already at a 15-year low, representing 18 days worth of corn, he notes. CBOT May corn trades up the daily 30c limit to $6.93 1/4 a bushel. (tom.polansek@dowjones.com)

11:03 (Dow Jones) After tepid, routine intervention earlier in the week, Brazil's central bank turns aggressive in the currency market. In morning trading, the central bank buys dollars at a snap auction and then calls an auction of reverse swap contracts that could sweep up as much as $1.5B in future dollar deliveries. More intervention could follow in the afternoon. The bank is sweating to arrest further unwanted appreciation of the Brazilian real, which gained sharply against the American currency Wednesday. In late morning trading, the real is again stronger against the dollar at BRL1.6244 versus BRL1.6275 at the close Wednesday. (tom.murphy@dowjones.com)

title: MARKET TALK:  Central Bank  Aggressive In  Brazil  Real Trade
text:
11:03 (Dow Jones) After tepid, routine intervention earlier in the week, Brazil's central bank turns aggressive in the currency market. In morning trading, the central bank buys dollars at a snap auction and then calls an auction of reverse swap contracts that could sweep up as much as $1.5B in future dollar deliveries. In late morning trading, the real is again stronger against the dollar at BRL1.6244 versus BRL1.6275 at the close Wednesday. (tom.murphy@dowjones.com)

11:01 (Dow Jones) While Entergy (ETR) says it completed negotiations on a 20-year power-purchase agreement with Vermont's third-largest utility, the Vermont Electric Cooperative's board is "struggling" and divided about approving the contract, VEC CEO David Hallquist says in an interview. "Entergy has a very bad track record in Vermont" about leaks of toxic materials and other safety issues, and those concerns have risen with the Japan nuclear crisis, he notes. VEC's 12-member board opts to take another month to gauge constituent sentiment before voting. If the contract is dropped, that could strengthen state lawmakers' hand in shutting down the Vermont Yankee plant. Federal regulators have said it is safe extend operations to 2022. ETR down 1% at $67.34. (naureen.malik@dowjones.com)

11:00 (Dow Jones) US inflation will rise enough this year to make Federal Reserve officials "squirm," Bank of America Chief Economist Mickey Levy says. "I think core inflation will be above 1.5% by mid-year and 2% by year end. I think the big concern here is a spike in inflationary expectations," Levy says at a Fed conference in Charlotte. (jeffrey.sparshott@dowjones.com)

10:57 (Dow Jones) Brazil's government appears to be hearing the calls from the central bank for greater restraint on spending, says Gradual Investimetos. The central bank has made it clear that reining in spending is "sine qua non condition for a less aggressive monetary policy," it says. Government accounts published Thursday show the primary surplus is edging closer to its target for year end. "From what we can see, the homework is being done." (matthew.cowley@dowjones.com)

10:48 (Dow Jones) Some block trades occur in bond futures and the selling spills over into the cash market. Thin trading exaggerates the move as many investors await Friday's payrolls data. The benchmark 10-year note is now 7/32 lower, yield 3.470%. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

10:41 (Dow Jones) Goldman Sachs was a major Treasurys bull until late last year. Now the top bond dealer says the growth/inflation mix has become less "bond friendly" of late and its rate strategists see higher 5-year yields, betting they will rise to 2.5% in coming months, compared to the 2.3% previously called. Correspondingly, the benchmark 10-year yield, recently at 3.45%, should trade in a 3.50-3.75% range in 2Q, they say in their monthly bond-market research report. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

10:32 (Dow Jones) Jeff Matthews, the founder of hedge fund Ram Partners and author of "Pilgrimage to Warren Buffett's Omaha" isn't a Buffett apologist, but he isn't often a harsh critic of the company either. Consider that as you digest his take on David Sokol's purchase of Lubrizol (LZ) shares before recommending Buffett buy the company outright. "If you've been on Wall Street for even six months, you know you don't do this," Matthews said. "It's front running. Maybe it's not illegal, but it's definitely ethically dubious." BRKB off 1.5% at $84.18. (erik.holm@dowjones.com)

10:26 (Dow Jones) Canadian-based energy company Pacific Rubiales (PEGFF) has acquired a 50% interest in the Colombian assets of French company Maurel & Prom. Rubiales would be oh-so-pleased if investors view the move as a sign the company's focus has returned to exploring and drilling for oil following a dreadful month on the PR front that saw its share price plunge 25%. Rubiales' problems started with unexpectedly low 2010 production and reserves data and got worse when it surprised investors by "announcing" a years-old, but hardly-known, clause to its key Quifa contract that could pinch future earnings. (dan.molinski@dowjones.com)

10:21 (Dow Jones) Barclays Capital says resignation of David Sokol from Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA BRKB) "again highlights the key-man risk involved in investing in BRK shares." Warren Buffett, the firm warns, "may be the only one who can manage the company with as much success as in the past." Sokol had been presumed to be the most likely candidate to replace Buffett as CEO. His departure moves other managers of BRKB subsidiaries higher on the list of candidates, including Burlington Northern CEO Matt Rose and MidAmerican CEO Greg Abel, Barclays says. BRKB off 1.5% at $84.18. (erik.holm@dowjones.com)

10:08 (Dow Jones) Brazil's central bank is losing the credibility battle on inflation, according to banking consultant Paulo Faria-Tavares of PTX Lending. "Interest rate futures are rising, which indicates inflation will keep accelerating," Faria-Tavares says. In recent statements, the central bank has downplayed long-term inflation worries. "The central bank is being tested by the market and it is losing credibility," he said. "They are forgetting the most important thing. They have to convince the market, ordinary people and economic agents, and they are failing." (tom.murphy@dowjones.com)

10:06 (Dow Jones) Bombardier (BBD.B.T) up 11% after FY4Q results blow past consensus. JPMorgan says company's results were strong, particularly its margins and cash. Aerospace is seeing clear signs of resurgent business jet demand, while transportation looks poised for growth on continued order strength, firm says. Scotia Capital agrees, noting aerospace was the major reason for the beat, with better-than-expected margins. In Toronto, BBD class B shares up 69 Canadian cents to C$6.99. (caroline.vanhasselt@dowjones.com)

10:02 (Dow Jones) Bullish USDA corn report is unable to lift Mosaic (MOS) shares after mixed F3Q earnings report. While prices soared for the fertilizer producer, volumes were weaker than expected. Earnings conference call at 10:00am EDT. USDA report today showed lower-than-expected supplies as of March 1, which has corn futures poised for a sharp rally. That normally boosts fertilizer, but MOS flat at $80.44. Rival CF Industries, meanwhile, up 4% to $137.88. (ian.berry@dowjones.com)

text:
1:42 (Dow Jones) Brazil's central bank's move to call a snap reverse auction is an attempt to weaken the real, says Brown Brothers Harriman strategist Win Thin. Still, he says he is surprised policymakers "haven't been more forceful. It's nothing new in their arsenal, which people were waiting for." Real sharply stronger against dollar today with USD/BRL down 1% to 1.6320. (anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com)

Jun 10-year Tsy note futures pull back a bit from 119-07 session high. Recently 9+/32 higher at 119-02. Quarterly 2012 Eurodollar futures recently as much as 5.5 BP higher, having been up as much as 7.5 BP at the pre-auction high. (howard.packowitz@dowjones.com)

1535 GMT [Dow Jones] Portugal's five-year sovereign CDS are at 566 bps, which would represent its highest ever closing level, although it is possible that higher intraday prices were seen in January, Markit says. 5-year protection prices appear to have been volatile, rising to 555 bps early before dropping down to 548 bps mid-morning, 2 bps tighter from Tuesday. Fitch says Wednesday that Portugal needs financial support and a "timely and credible" economic program from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund to avoid a likely downgrade. (mark.brown@dowjones.com)

1511 GMT [Dow Jones] HSBC says to sell the zloty ahead of Poland's revised 4Q current account release due Thursday. The bank warns the imports data may be substantially upwardly revised and this could be very negative for the currency. "A possible revision of the huge 'errors & omissions' constitutes a threat to the PLN, particularly in a context of high fiscal deficit," HSBC says, adds the emergence of a 'twin deficit' would have a lasting negative impact on the PLN. "In our view only a more aggressive central bank action would offer PLN protection," HSBC says.(malgorzata.halaba@dowjones.com)

1506 GMT [Dow Jones] June gilts are ending Wednesday off their lows, but are still down 0.40 at 117.31 on the day, after what one strategist calls an "uneventful" day with moves "mostly flow driven." Adds that the market has been inclined to sell off as the relative stability in peripheral euro-zone sovereign bonds Wednesday means there is no flight-to-safety bid. Thursday brings Nationwide and Hometrack UK housing data. 10-year gilts yield 3.67%, up from 3.62% Tuesday. (mark.brown@dowjones.com)

1448 GMT [Dow Jones] Hungarian government bonds strengthen mainly in the long end of the curve by around 15bp due to high interest in the series 2019/A bond at Wednesday morning's exchange auction. The 3-year benchmark bond yield is 6.72%-6.62%, 5-year is 6.98%-6.88%, 10-year is 7.22%-7.12%. Bonds could weaken over the coming days, as signaled by low trading volumes and a decreasing number of buyers on the scene, one trader says. Yields could weaken by around 15-20bp from current levels until the end of this week. (veronika.gulyas@dowjones.com)

10:29 (Dow Jones) Brazil's central bank indicated rate hikes are likely coming to an end in its quarterly inflation report out today, says BES Investimentos. Central bank's inflation forecasts point to lower inflation in 2011 and 2012, despite the current upward trend, so "we believe the tightening cycle is getting close to an end," it says. "Therefore, we stick to our call the Brazilian Central Bank will increase benchmark rates by 50bps in April, which should be the last movement on basic interest rates." (matthew.cowley@dowjones.com)

Visit the Market Talk blog at www.djnmarkettalk.com.

1415 GMT [Dow Jones] Export-driven Hungary is expected to have generated a current account surplus of EUR180 million in 4Q 2010 due to its steadily strong trade surplus, 7 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires say. The 3Q surplus was EUR476.7 million. Forecasts came in a wide range: between a deficit of EUR800 million and a surplus of EUR255 million, reflecting uncertainties surrounding profit repatriations by foreign companies operating in Hungary. 2010 current account surplus is forecast at EUR1.8 billion, a swing from a 2009 deficit of EUR119.8 million. Hungary hasn't generated an annual surplus for the past 15 years, or for as long as data go back on the central bank's website. Figures are due at 0630 GMT Thursday. (margit.feher@dowjones.com)

1351 GMT [Dow Jones] Polish bonds are almost flat ahead of rate decision next week, traders say. Also, the market awaits details of debt supply for April to be issued Thursday or Friday. Average yields on 2 and 5-year bonds are unchanged from late Tuesday, at 5.01% and 5.78%, respectively. Average yield on 10-year paper is at 6.28% from 6.29%. (malgorzata.halaba@dowjones.com)

1348 GMT [Dow Jones] A lackluster, risk-neutral day in the bund market, with low volumes and a very narrow trading range. The June contract, currently down 0.18 at 121.32, has been stuck in a 121.16-121.40 band with investors now looking ahead to the outcome of Thursday's Irish bank stress tests and Friday's U.S. non-farm payrolls reading. In the cash space, the 2s/5s/10s yield 1.758%/2.652%/3.343% with cross-currency spreads against gilts widening by 1-3 bps and remaining unchanged against US Treasurys. In the core markets, Italy's successful EUR9B multi-tranche auction caused bund/BTP spreads to tighten by 1.5-3.5 bps over the 2/10-year curve. (nick.cawley@dowjones.com)

title: Ocean Wilsons Holdings Ld Final Results
text:
TIDMOCN

RNS Number : 7121D

Ocean Wilsons Holdings Ld

28 March 2011

OCEAN WILSONS HOLDINGS LIMITED

Preliminary announcement

CHAIRMAN'S STATEMENT

Overview

Ocean Wilsons Holdings Limited ("Ocean Wilsons or the Company") is a Bermuda based investment Company and through its subsidiary operates as a maritime services company in Brazil. The Company is listed on both the Bermuda Stock exchange and the London Stock Exchange. It has two principal subsidiaries: Wilson Sons Limited and Ocean Wilsons Investments Limited.

Wilson Sons Limited ("Wilson Sons") is an autonomous Bermuda company listed on the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange (BOVESPA) and Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Ocean Wilsons holds a 58.25% interest in Wilson Sons, which is fully consolidated in its accounts with a 41.75% non-controlling interest. Wilson Sons is one of the largest providers of maritime services in Brazil. Wilson Sons activities include harbour and ocean towage, container terminal operation, offshore support services, logistics, small vessel construction and ship agency.

Ocean Wilsons Investments Limited is a wholly owned Bermuda investment company. The company holds a portfolio of international investments.

Introduction

I am pleased to report another good year of trading for Ocean Wilsons Holdings Limited. Our maritime services business continued to experience strong demand across all business segments and the investment portfolio generated significant returns in the period. During the year we continued to invest heavily in our core businesses and the Group remains well positioned to meet our customers evolving needs and benefit from the strong growth in Brazil.

Group Results

Revenue for the Group grew by 20% to US$575.6 million (2009: US$477.9 million) principally due to increases in port terminal and logistics revenue. Operating profit margins for the Group were 5 % lower at 12% (2009: 17%) reflecting the change in sales mix, the adverse impact of a stronger Brazilian Real against our reporting currency the US Dollar, higher employee expenses and increased depreciation.

Profit before tax decreased by US$22.6 million from US$139.8 million to US$117.2million principally due to the decrease in operating profit US$67.9 million (2009: US$79.3 million) lower gains from the investment portfolio of US$22.5 million (2009: US$34.3 million) and exchange gains on cash balances of US$4.0 million.(2009: US$23.7 million). These were partially offset by the profit realised on formation of the joint venture of US$20.4 million.

Earnings per share based on ordinary activities after taxation and non-controlling interests were 160.8 cents (2009: 198.5 cents).

Offshore Joint Venture

In June 2010 we were pleased to announce the formation of our offshore joint venture between Wilson Sons Limited, through two of its subsidiaries in Brazil, and Remolcadores Ultratug Ltda., a company owned by the Chilean maritime group, Ultratug.

The joint venture vehicle named Wilson, Sons Ultratug Participacoes S.A. ("Wilson Sons Ultratug") is a 50/50 company set up between Wilson Sons and the Ultratug groups that owns and operates offshore vessels to support oil and gas exploration and production activities in Brazil.

Both Wilson Sons and Ultratug transferred their existing Brazilian offshore businesses into the new joint venture. The principal objective of the joint venture is to take advantage of the growing opportunities in Brazil's oil and gas industry and expand both groups' operations in the offshore segment.

Tecon Salvador

In September 2010 Tecon Salvador signed an amendment to the terminal lease agreement with the Companhia das Docas do Estado da Bahia (CODEBA). The amendment granted the company the area adjacent to Tecon Salvador known as Ponta Norte for an initial payment of US$14.5 million and amendments to the rental and container handling fee agreements. This additional area will allow Tecon Salvador to extend the quay and back area while deepening the draft to accommodate the larger container vessels operating in Brazil.

Brasco

In June 2010 we acquired the remaining 25% non-controlling interest in our onshore base manager and logistics business, Brasco Logistica Offshore Ltda for US$9.0 million. The acquisition of the non-controlling interest increases our exposure to the growing offshore oil and gas industry.

Investment Portfolio

Investment managers

The Group's investment portfolio is held by Ocean Wilson Investments Limited ("OWIL") a wholly owned subsidiary registered in Bermuda. OWIL appointed Hanseatic Asset Management LBG a Guernsey registered and regulated investment group as its Investment Manager in November 2000.

Investment strategy

The Board of OWIL determines investment guidelines and restrictions in conjunction with the investment manager, these together with the investment managers reports are reviewed at the OWIL board meetings.

The investment strategy agreed with the Company's investment managers is to maximise the total return on assets, by investing in a portfolio of diversified assets including global equities, fixed income and alternative assets with a particular emphasis on emerging markets. Investments are intended to add value over the medium to longer-term through a non-market correlated, conviction based investment style.

Investment portfolio performance

Following the fall in equity markets in the second quarter, share prices rose across the board in the second half of the year generating satisfactory returns for the period. The trading investment portfolio and cash under management increased US$18.2million (after capital redemptions of US$5million), from US$245.2 million at 31 December 2009 to $263.4million at year end.

Approximately 50% of the investment portfolio is invested in global equities, 31% in alternative assets, 9% in bonds and the balance in cash and liquidity funds. The investment managers continued to deploy the portfolio's cash and liquidity funds in new investments and at year end the investment portfolio held US$24.7 million in cash and liquidity funds, down from US$67 million in 2009. Details of the individual investment holdings at 31 December 2010, new investments made during the period and performance, are contained within the Investment Managers report.

Wilson Sons Limited
