MARKET BACKGROUND

Global equity markets recovered from a second quarter slump and rallied strongly in the second half of 2010. Many indices ended the year at or above their levels at the time of the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy in September 2008. The MSCI World Index of Developed Markets gained 11.8% over the period and the MSCI Emerging Markets Index gained 18.9%.

In the first half of the year, investors became anxious as China introduced tightening measures to combat rising inflation and intensified concerns over Greece led to a significant Greek rescue package and the introduction of a EUR750bn regional bailout facility. Market jitters heightened in May when the Dow Jones plunged 700 points in eight minutes following a system failure and BP's oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico wiped off GBP60bn from the company's market capitalisation. In the second half of the year, a significant rally in risk assets commenced ahead of the US Federal Reserve's announcement of an additional $600bn round of quantitative easing in November. The US economy developed some positive momentum in the fourth quarter as corporations continued to beat earnings estimates and manufacturing activity remained strong.

With the exception of some European indices, Developed Markets rallied strongly in the second half of the year to finish 2010 at post crisis highs. The S&P 500 Index in the US rose 15.1%, the FTSE 100 Index in the UK rose 9.2% and the DAX Index in Germany was a standout performer amongst continental European markets gaining 8.5% whilst the CAC Index in France fell by 6.0%. The Topix Index in Japan posted a significant gain of 15.9%; nevertheless performance was flat on a local currency basis.

Amongst Emerging Markets, the strongest performances came from the RTS Index of Russia which gained 22.6% and the Bombay Sensex Index of India which rose 22.2%. The Bovespa Index of Brazil, which had posted the largest gains of the BRIC countries in 2009, saw a comparatively modest rise of 6.1% in 2010, most of which was attributable to currency appreciation. The MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan Index rose 16.9%, driven by South-East Asian economies including Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, whilst the Chinese market was a notable laggard as the domestic A-share CSI 300 Index lost 8.4% over the year.

Commodity prices rallied during the year, driven by continued strength of demand from Emerging Markets and supply constraints resulting from extreme global weather events and continued political instability in certain supplier countries. Precious Metals and Agriculture posted the largest gains. Gold rose 29.5%, ending the year at $1,420 per ounce on the back of continued concerns about the increasing supply of paper money and agricultural commodities rebounded with Corn prices increasing by 30.7%, Soybeans 34.9% and Wheat 21.2%. The price of West Texas Intermediate crude oil gained 8.5%, ending the year at $92 per barrel. Industrial metals rallied on the back of further quantitative easing as Copper prices increased by 29.7%.

In currency markets, the US Dollar reversed some of its 2009 losses, appreciating 3.4% against Sterling and 7.1% against the Euro. However it depreciated against the Yen by 12.9% and weakened against commodity currencies, losing 12.2% against the Australian Dollar, 4.6% against the Canadian Dollar and 4.8% against the Brazilian Real. The notion of competitive currency devaluations amongst nations to improve their growth prospects gained impetus during the year as significant currency interventions were seen from the central banks of Brazil and Japan. In June the People's Bank of China announced that it would manage the Renminbi exchange rate more flexibly, allowing the currency to appreciate or depreciate by up to 0.5% against the US Dollar in a single day. This move saw a slight appreciation of the Renminbi by approximately 3% versus the US Dollar. China's refusal to let its currency appreciate more significantly remains at the centre of global imbalances.

In fixed income markets, positive performance continued across all sectors, however at a declining pace after significant spread contraction in the prior year. The broad global indices of Sovereign Debt, Investment Grade Corporate Debt, High Yield Corporate Debt and Emerging Markets Debt all posted gains over the period. Additional quantitative easing in the US led treasury yields on a continued downwards trajectory. US ten year treasury yields fell to 3.3% from 3.9%, albeit having posted a significant rebound from a low of 2.4% in October, UK ten year gilt yields fell to 3.4% from 4.0% and the European Central Bank ten year yield fell to 3.0% from 3.4%. Elsewhere, yields on Japanese 10 year government bonds continued to tighten, moving to 1.13% from 1.30%, despite snowballing government debt approaching 200% of GDP.

MARKET OUTLOOK

Economists are anticipating a two tier economy in 2011. The International Monetary Fund is forecasting economic growth of 2.2% in the developed economies and 6.4% in the developing world with world GDP expanding at 4.2% overall. It is an environment where the developing world is doing the bulk of the 'heavy lifting'. For example, car sales and oil imports in these economies have exceeded the developed world for the first time.

Although there have been some muted signs of growth in the US, it has tended to be focused on technology and productivity improvement and has not necessarily been beneficial for job creation. The ongoing deleveraging cycle in the West is a huge headwind for growth. US total debt as a percentage of GDP peaked during the first quarter of 2009 at 373% (its previous peak being 300% in 1933). This exponential rise in total outstanding debt in the US economy is clearly unsustainable and correcting it will be a serious constraint on their economic growth prospects. The other central issue undermining growth in the West is the collapse in the velocity of money. Despite the scale of the increase in the monetary base, banks have been guilty of 'monetary constipation', sitting on an improved reserve position with no benefit to the real economy. As a result of the two tier nature of the world economy, governments and central banks are pursuing differing agendas with the West keen to avoid slumping into Japanese style deflation while policy makers in the developing world are confronted by either rising inflationary pressures or unwanted strength in their currencies, which threatens to undermine their competitiveness.

Following the recovery in the capital markets from the 2008 crisis, there remains significant unease amongst investors about the lasting legacy of the policy response to the crisis and the deep rooted structural challenges many economies are facing. 'Quantitative Easing' has succeeded in supporting asset prices but it defies investor logic to assume the creation of excess liquidity will bring structural benefit to problems created by an excess of liquidity. The unintended consequences and distortions caused by current policy settings will become clearer over time but there can be little doubt that they will occur.

Much of the developed world has to confront a poor demographic profile and deteriorating dependency ratios as fewer people in work support increasing numbers of people who are not. In terms of investment strategy, the 'big picture' still favours the Emerging Markets which have superior growth prospects and a lower debt burden at both public and private levels. However, the case for their capital markets outperforming those of the developed world is not as clear cut in 2011 as it has been through much of the last decade. [ 28-03-11 0722GMT ]

For one thing, inflation is increasingly a concern for many Emerging Markets as a consequence of rapid GDP growth, strong capital inflows and higher food and raw material prices. In India, for instance, core inflation is running at 8.5% and food price inflation at close to 17%. The Food and Agriculture Organisation price index is at an all-time high following a very strong increase in a range of agricultural commodities resulting from weather related crop losses, rising demand and high input costs such as fertiliser. In China, inflationary pressures are also returning, exacerbated by an artificially low level for the currency and wage settlements are rising. Ultimately, it is hard to see how the Chinese and other Asian economies with US Dollar pegs can avoid allowing their undervalued currencies to float freely. Any tightening of monetary policy has historically been negative for Emerging Markets. Emerging Market equities tend to be much more closely correlated with their fixed income markets and therefore a rise in bond yields is likely to be more threatening than it would be in stock markets in more mature economies where a rise in bond yields would signal improved economic vitality.

Emerging Markets are much more fashionable with investors than they were a decade ago and capital flows from both institutional and retail investors have grown markedly. This greater weight of investor exposure also makes them more vulnerable to any potential setbacks. By contrast, the US stock market has recently experienced the worst decade in its history with the annualised real rate of return in the ten years to March 2010 being -6%. In this context, US fund flows have seen high inflows into bond funds and Emerging Market equity funds, largely at the expense of neglected domestic equities. Despite the softness of the US economy and a consumer undermined by poor job prospects and a weak housing market, Corporate America is in strong shape. Profit margins for the S&P 500 Index exceeded 8% for the first time in over 30 years. Balance sheets are strong and many US corporations enjoy dominant global franchises.

For much of 2010, capital markets were focused on the significant strains evident within the Euro project and the peripheral European countries in particular stumbled under the weight of their debt burden. These concerns are still likely to be high on the list of investor unease in 2011. What is apparent, however, is a divergence within Europe. Germany for instance, is experiencing significant strength in its industrial sector buoyed by capital good sales to the Emerging Markets. Unemployment is now at its lowest level since re-unification and consumer sentiment has recovered. The German IFO business survey, which reflects general business confidence, is at its highest level since it was started in 2000. Elsewhere in Europe the picture is not as bright as policy makers seem reluctant to grapple with serious structural negatives such as deteriorating dependency ratios and an 'entitlement culture' that seems to be on a collision course with reality.

Notwithstanding the complexity of the current investment landscape and conflicting policy agendas, there is still a strong central case to be made for a diversified portfolio of international equities. With effectively zero available on cash deposits and extremely low nominal bond yields (close to negative in real terms), the balance of risk / reward favours shares. Analyst forecasts for the MSCI (Developed) World Index suggest a forward price earnings multiple of 12x and a price to book ratio of less than two. These are amongst the lowest valuations seen in the last 20 years. Furthermore, with dividends in many cases exceeding bond yields, shares are a competitive asset as a source of income as well as having long term appreciation prospects. Interest rates at either the short or long end would have to spike upwards much more than seems likely in the current scenario to undermine this fundamental valuation support for equities.

At the time of writing, recent headlines have been dominated by events in the Middle East. Unrest against the long-term undemocratic regimes originated from widespread concerns including food price inflation, unemployment and corruption, with the people of Tunisia and Egypt and subsequently Bahrain, Yemen and Libya attempting to enact political change to differing degrees. These popular uprisings could represent the vanguard of democracy in a volatile region long starved of political freedoms. Alternatively, it remains to be seen to what extent power vacuums will be filled by religious extremists. The impact on risk assets has not been inconsiderable, with oil prices spiking to two year highs and equities, especially Emerging Markets, generally retrenching. Given the portfolio's relatively low geographic exposure to the region, and far greater exposure to oil related entities, the direct impact on portfolio performance should be relatively muted. However, the Investment Manager is conscious that further geopolitical tensions have the potential to cause oil prices to rise further and, should they approach the highs of 2008, could be capable of destabilising a fragile global economic recovery.

ANALYSIS OF INVESTMENT SILOS

There are four main 'silos' in the OWIL portfolio: (i) Global Equities, (ii) Alternative Assets, (iii) Bonds and (iv) Cash.

'Global Equities' (50.2% of NAV as at 31 December 2010) is comprised of holdings that are sensitive to stock market movements and may take the form of investments in open-ended funds, closed-ended list funds (such as Investment Trusts), UCITS funds, long / short directional hedge funds as well as direct quoted equities. Global Equities achieved performance of +16.2% in 2010.

'Alternative Assets' (31.2% of NAV) is comprised of three constituents: (i) Private Assets, (ii) Market Neutral Funds and (iii) Liquid Real Assets.

Private Assets (10.1% of NAV) contains fixed life investments typically with lives of approximately ten years and often structured through commitments to Limited Partnership vehicles that make investments in private equity, private real assets (such as property and natural resources) and private debt (such as distressed debt and mezzanine financing). These investments offer access to longer cycle plays, typically with less volatility than and lower correlation to public security markets. Phased drawdown of capital reduces market timing risk. The first commitment to Private Assets was made in 2007. A total of 14 commitments (totalling $61.6m) have been made as at 31 December 2010. $31.0m has been drawn down to date, indicating that this silo is at an immature stage of value realisation. Private Assets achieved performance of +3.5% in 2010.

Market Neutral Funds (18.5% of NAV) contains 'all-weather' holdings in funds which exhibit low correlation to public security markets and have the ability to generate positive absolute returns regardless of the prevailing market environment. Several of the underlying holdings are hedge funds which engage in shorter term trading across asset classes. Market Neutral Funds achieved performance of +11.5% in 2010.

Marketable Real Assets (2.6% of NAV) contains real asset investments (such as property and natural resources) which are quoted on a stock market. Liquid Real Assets achieved performance of +24.9% in 2010.

'Bonds' (9.2% of NAV) is comprised of two constituents: (i) High Yield Bonds and (ii) Corporate Bonds. Returns may be generated from an increased capital value, coupons as well as currency exposure.

High Yield Bonds (9.2% of NAV) contains investments in Emerging Market (both sovereign and corporate debt) and other high yield corporate debt. High Yield Bonds achieved performance of +12.9% in 2010.

Investment Grade Bonds (0% of NAV) contains investments in sovereign (government) bonds as well as corporate bonds with high credit ratings (typically at least 'BBB' as defined by Standard & Poor's). Investment Grade Bonds achieved performance of +1.8% in 2010.

'Cash' (9.4% of NAV) is comprised of cash and cash equivalents including money market / liquidity funds. Cash may be held in currencies other than the US Dollar. Cash achieved performance of +1.8% in 2010.

WILSON SONS LIMITED OPERATING REVIEW

We have summarised the following highlights from the Wilson Sons 2010 Earnings Report released on 25 March 2011. Wilson Sons represents one segment for IFRS 8 segmental reporting purposes in the Ocean Wilsons Holdings Limited accounts. The full report is available on the Wilson Sons Limited website: www.wilsonsons.com("http://www.wilsonsons.com"):

Cezar Baiao CEO of Operations in Brazil said:

"We are pleased to deliver another strong year to our shareholders. Wilson, Sons' record investment of US$190.3 million in 2010 demonstrates our commitment to developing port, maritime, and logistics infrastructure for the service of our clients. The Company is experiencing outstanding demand in the areas of international trade, oil and gas, and the Brazilian domestic economy.

In 2011, we are expanding our container terminal in Salvador and doubling our shipbuilding capacity in Guaruja, together with the on-going fleet expansion in Offshore and Towage. As such, we have unprecedented confidence that Wilson, Sons' investments will set the stage for a successful future."

Net Revenues

Port Terminal revenue for the year is up 30% due to higher volumes, the strong Brazilian Real stimulating higher-yielding imports which, in turn, favoured warehousing revenues and increased activity at Brasco. Towage revenue grew 7%, with strong demand for special operations which accounted for 16% of towage revenue in the year. Offshore revenue is down 27% as a result of the formation of WSUT joint venture in May 2010 and the migration of 4 vessels from spot market operations to long-term contracts.

Capital Expenditure

The Group invested record capital expenditure in the year. The capital expenditure is a result of the Company's fleet expansion in offshore and towage, new equipment for Tecon Rio Grande, the expansions of both Tecon Salvador and the shipyard in Guaruja. Equipment for port terminals included 2 new ship-to-shore cranes (portainers) and 4 rubber-tyre gantry cranes (transtainers) at Tecon Rio Grande, and the aforementioned expansion of Tecon Salvador. Equipment was also purchased for logistics to attend new client in-house operations.

Port Terminals

Wilson Sons port terminals operates two container terminals, located in Rio Grande, Rio Grande do Sul and Salvador in Bahia, Brazil (Tecon Rio Grande and Tecon Salvador). Both terminals, offer assistance in port operations for loading and unloading of vessels, storage, and auxiliary services. Wilson Sons also operates Brasco, located in Rio de Janeiro, which provides support services to the oil and gas industry

Total port terminal revenue grew 30% from US$175.4 million to US$228.0 million due to increased container volumes and revenue from Brasco. Revenue also benefitted from an improved container sales mix and increased warehousing revenues. Brasco had a particularly strong year with revenue growing 84% to US$49.2 million (2009: US$26.7 million). Revenue growth reflects the higher demand for auxiliary services, such as warehousing, transportation, waste management, container rental, and utilisation of manpower and equipment. The Company experienced strong demand at all our facilities in Rio de Janeiro, Niteroi, and Vitoria.

Container terminal volumes for the year were 5% higher at 928,700 TEUs (Twenty foot equivalent units) benefitting from the strong domestic economy and growth in cabotage volumes. Deep sea volumes in the period were lower due to the negative effect of the strong Brazilian Real on our predominantly export-driven ports although this was mainly reflected in a fall in low value empty container movements. Imports of parts and machinery, chemicals, and plastics at Tecon Rio Grande partially offset the fall in export volumes at this terminal. The Full-to-Empty container mix improved with full containers up 15.1% for the year. Warehousing revenues benefitted from greater import volumes.

Volumes at Tecon Salvador were up 13% at 262,500 TEUs with increases in transhipment, inland navigation and cabotage volumes. Chemicals, ores, grains, pulps, and rubber were particularly strong.

The increase in revenue was reflected in increased EBITDA which improved 31% to US$76.3 million from US$58.3 million. Within this Brasco EBITDA improved 63% to US$14.9million (2009: US$9.1 million).

Towage

Wilson Sons offers harbour towage, ocean towage, salvage support and maritime support to the offshore oil and gas industry.

Towage revenues increased 7% to US$156.0 million from US$145.7million helped by better volumes in both harbour towage and special operations. The Company continues to focus on developing our higher margin special operations business which accounted for 16% of towage revenue in the year (2009: 14%). Special operations are mainly support to offshore oil & gas platforms and FPSO (Floating, Production, Storage and Offloading vessels) construction. Special Operations accounted for 35% of Towage EBITDA in the year (2009: 25%).

We continue to invest in renewing and expanding our fleet with the addition of 5 tugboats during the year. (Lyra, Regulus, Sculptur, Carina, and Vela) Currently, the company has 3 tugboats in different stages of construction at our shipyard in Guaruja.

Offshore

Through our 50/50 joint venture Wilson, Sons Ultratug (WSUT),Wilson Sons operates platform supply vessels (PSVs), to transport equipment and supplies to and from offshore oil and gas installations.

The Wilson, Sons Ultratug joint venture results are proportionally consolidated since the formation of the joint venture in May 2010. Prior to this the Group reported 100% of our subsidiary results.

Offshore revenue at US$28 million decreased 27% compared to prior year (2009 US$38.1 million) due to the formation of the joint venture and the migration of four PSVs operating in the high value spot market to long-term contracts with Petrobras during the year.

Operating profit is down 53% for the year to US$6.5 million (2009: US$13.7 million) because of the joint venture formation, lower spot market rates, the migration of four vessels from spot contracts to 8-year, long-term contracts with Petrobras (long-term contracts bring guaranteed revenue but carry lower daily rates than riskier spot market rates). Operating costs were adversely impacted by higher depreciation due to the expansion of our fleet and higher personnel costs driven by collective labour agreements and increased headcount. [ 28-03-11 0722GMT ]

The Groups shipyard delivered two new PSVs during the year (Fulmar and Talha-Mar). At the end of 2010 the joint venture operated 10 PSVs of which 9 were on long-term contract to Petrobras. The PSV Torda was delivered in March 2011 and the company has a further 3 PSVs in different stages of construction at the Wilson, Sons Guaruja Shipyard.

Shipyards

Shipyard revenues were up 58% in the year as a result of faster build programs and completion of higher specification vessels during 2010. EBITDA at US$ 6.0million was US$3.8 million lower than 2009 (US$9.8 million) principally due to higher start-up costs associated with the new shipyards in Guaruja and Rio Grande.

Following the formation of the WSUT joint venture, 50% of shipyard construction for WSUT is treated as third-party revenues in the Wilson Sons Limited accounts with the remaining 50% treated as fixed asset investment. Any profits generated by the shipyard relating to the 50% treated as fixed asset investment is considered intercompany and therefore eliminated on consolidation.

All tugboats constructed for Wilson, Sons towage business are considered intercompany and recorded at cost in the consolidated balance sheet.

Ship Agency

Wilson Sons acts as the ship owners' representative as well providing the following services to ship owners: commercial representation, cargo documentation, container control and vessel support.

Ship Agency revenues increased 16% to US$17.6 million compared to 2009 (US$15.2 million) as a result of strong volumes. The number of vessel calls attended increased 11% to 7,258 with increases also in the number of bill of ladings issued and containers controlled. Volumes benefitted from both higher domestic and international shipping demand.

EBITDA margins decreased as a result of higher personnel costs and the strength of the Brazilian Real against the US Dollar. A stronger Brazilian Real erodes ship agency margins as the 100% of costs are Real-denominated and the majority of revenues are USD-denominated.

Logistics

Wilson Sons develops and provides differentiated logistics solutions for the management of the supply chain of our clients and the distribution of products, including a number of logistics services, such as, storage, customs storage, distribution, highway transportation, multimodal transportation and NVOCC - Non Vessel Operating Common Carrier.

Revenue from our logistics business increased 35% to US$102.4 million from US$75.8million principally due to new operations in the steel, mining and pulp and paper industries.

Logistics EBITDA improved 86% to US$13.1 million (2009: US$7.1 million) due to the ramp up in new operation volumes and improved performances across the in-house logistics operations. The Company's bonded-warehouse operations in Santo Andre (SP) performed particularly strong benefitting from robust import volumes driven by the strong Brazilian Real.

title: Brazil Currency  Market Stronger On Low Volume,  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market trended stronger Monday, marked by a wave of intervention actions by the Brazilian Central Bank that had little effect on trading because of unusually low volume.

"Volume was super weak today, well below normal," said a Sao Paulo-based trader who asked not to be named. "There was a very small variation in the market, which is especially unusual for a week when futures contracts will expire."

Trading sessions at the end of each month are typically marked by high volume and increased volatility as long- and short-position holders battle to influence the Ptax, or the average daily foreign-exchange rate used to settle futures contracts. The central bank also usually sits on the sidelines to not unfairly influence trading during the key month-end tug-of-war.

But the central bank was much more than a wallflower during Monday's session, engaging in no less than four separate interventions. The bank kicked off the day with a morning auction to buy dollars from the spot market, then in quick succession held an auction to buy forward-dollar contracts and reverse swaps. Late in the session, the bank held a second spot-market auction. The forward-dollar contract and reverse-swap auction were designed to roll over previous contracts coming due April 1, traders said.

"The volume of interventions was heavy," said Jankiel Santos, an economist at investment bank BES Investimentos. "The central bank must have identified some foreign-exchange movement expected in coming days."

Foreign-exchange inflows have been heavy in the first three months of 2011, topping the net dollar inflows from all of 2010. According to the latest data available, net dollar inflows through March 18 totaled $34.66 billion, outpacing the $24.35 billion that flowed into Brazil for all of last year.

The central bank may have tried to head off inflows related to recent overseas bond issues, which include a $500 million debt sale last week by a unit of closely held industrial conglomerate Odebrecht.

Despite the central bank's heavy hand, the real still was slightly stronger than Friday's close at BRL1.6605 to the dollar. The real traded at BRL1.6599 to the dollar as of 1825 GMT, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset. Many traders expect the real to remain rangebound between BRL1.65 and BRL1.70 to the dollar, the unofficial target range that the central bank appears willing to accept before issuing the market a stern response.

"The market has no real motive to push the dollar stronger," said the Sao Paulo-based trader. "Forex flows continue strong. And the interventions are practically daily, so the market has already priced them in."

While trading volume was light Monday, it should pick up Tuesday and Wednesday as currency players take part in the Ptax battle and prepare to roll over positions, the trader said. That could add a measure of volatility ahead of the week's key indicator: the release of the Brazilian Central Bank's quarterly inflation report on Wednesday.

The central bank's inflation report will shed some light on how the bank plans to fight growing inflationary pressures in Latin America's largest economy, economists at the local unit of Spain's Banco Santander said. Bank President Alexandre Tombini took a more hawkish tone last week, but continued to indicate the bank will look toward measures other than interest-rate increases to contain prices.

Banco Santander called the report a key piece of information, predicting that the central bank "might change its main inflation and growth forecasts in line with market expectations." That could give the bank, currently seen as behind the curve in the fight against inflation, more credibility with the market.

title: Brazil Currency  Market Stronger As  Intervention  Fears Fade
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market traded stronger Monday as concerns about more government measures to contain the real's appreciation faded and dollar inflows remained strong.

While events in Japan, the Middle East and North Africa continued to attract attention from investors, the focus has shifted somewhat to the recurrent theme of strong foreign investment inflows into Brazil's resilient economy. Not even the first signs that U.S. interest rates could be heading higher were enough to undercut the real at the start of Monday's session.

Charles Plosser, president of the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank in Philadelphia, said Friday that interest rates in the world's largest economy would need to rise "in the not-too-distant future." Those comments were echoed by colleague James Bullard of the St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank, who suggested that it would be a "good idea" to discuss the end of the Fed's asset purchase program, dubbed quantitative easing II, at the monetary authority's April meeting.

The Fed's $600 billion plan to purchase U.S. Treasurys has created excess liquidity in the market that has undercut the value of the U.S. dollar, causing emerging-market currencies around the world to appreciate in response. Higher U.S. interest rates, however, typically cause emerging-market currencies such as the real to weaken as investors opt for the safety of Treasurys.

In Brazil, the market now expects the government to hold off implementing additional measures to contain the real to assess the impact of recent shocks to the global economy. The nuclear crisis in Japan in the wake of the massive 8.9 magnitude earthquake and tsunami continued Monday, with climbing radiation levels at a stricken reactor reigniting worries about how quickly the world's third-largest economy can recover from the disaster. Libyan rebels, meanwhile, continue to make gains against embattled dictator Moammar Gadhafi in the wake of the NATO-imposed no-fly zone over the country.

Brazil's real traded stronger shortly after the open Monday at BRL1.6590 to the dollar, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset. That was stronger from Friday's close at BRL1.6605 to the dollar.

The real remains rangebound between BRL1.65 and BRL1.70 to the dollar as the Brazilian Central Bank continues to buy dollars on the spot market and banks trim short-dollar positions to meet reserve requirements implemented earlier this year.

This week, the real will likely trade between BRL1.65 to BRL1.68 to the dollar this week, "corresponding to the external scenario and depending on whether the global appetite for risk is more or less favorable," said Miriam Tavares, foreign-exchange director at Sao Paulo-based AGK Corretora.

The market will gain further direction Wednesday, when the central bank releases its next quarterly inflation report. The report should give investors a better sense of the direction of future interest rates. Although recent comments by bank President Alexandre Tombini were more hawkish on inflation, many traders expect the bank to pursue alternative measures to fight inflation rather than relying solely on traditional interest rate hikes.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  firms; Peru sol hit by political risk
text:
* Latam currencies seen poised for further gains

* Mexico peso firms 0.16 pct, Brazil real 0.06 pct

* Peru sol slides to 2-month low on election jitters

By Michael O'Boyle and Silvio Cascione

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, March 25 (Reuters) - Peru's sol hit a two-month low on Friday on worries about a resurgent leftist presidential hopeful, while Latin America's key currencies seemed poised to extend this week's rally.

Investors were concerned that major polls due on Sunday may confirm the second-place position of Peru's nationalist presidential candidate Ollanta Humala ahead of an April 10 vote.

"People are worried (Humala) could go after mining interests," said Dirk Willer, head of Latin America local markets strategy at Citigroup in New York.

Humala's surge to second place in a poll last Sunday spurred a sharp drop in the sol and a spike in the cost of insuring the country's bonds.

The sol <PEN=PEN> bid 0.18 percent weaker at 2.7880 and hit its weakest level against the dollar since January.

Meanwhile, Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.16 percent to 11.9355 after clearing the psychological level of 11.95 per dollar in the prior session.

Traders have set their sights on testing the peso's nearly 2-1/2-year high hit earlier this month at 11.8585 per dollar.

Mexico's peso was on track to post a near 0.85 percent gain for the week, outpacing the rebound by Brazil's real -- where intervention fears are weighing -- and Chile's peso.

Worries appeared to be fading that global growth could suffer a big setback from the ongoing unrest in the oil-producing Middle East and North African region, fears that Portugal will need a bailout and concerns about Japan's nuclear crisis.

Expectations are that monthly jobs data in the United States due next week could reinforce perceptions of a recovery there, which may back further gains for the region.

But if the data is much better than expected, some fear it will raise bets the United States may soon increase interest rates. Weak jobs data might hit expectations about U.S. demand for the region's exports.

"We should have a positive bias for the early part of next week and then if non-farm payrolls are not too strong and not too weak and along the lines of consensus, then the rally can continue," Willer said.

Latin America's currencies are broadly supported by high prices for the region's commodities, such as Chile's copper, Brazil's iron and soy and Mexico's oil. High interest rates as policymakers target inflation worries are also tempting yield-hungry global investors.

Mexico, which some market players see hiking interest rates as soon as this summer, is backed by the recovery of its manufacturing exports to the United States.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.655 per dollar as it traded around a three-week high.

The currency is inching back toward a 2-1/2-year high hit earlier this month that stirred concerns of fresh moves by authorities to tame the real's strength, which is hurting local manufacturers.

"The market is back to a level where it begins to have memories of a possible measure of the central bank," said Jose Carlos Amado, a trader at the Renaissance brokerage.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.08 percent firmer at 479.30 per dollar, supported by a recovery in prices for copper, Chile's biggest export.

The peso hit a two-week high, but the cost of pesos in dollars bounced off a key support level at 478 per dollar that locals say is attracting firm bids for greenbacks.

title: Brazil Currency  Market Weaker On Possible  Intervention , Portugal
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market traded weaker Wednesday amid renewed expectations for government intervention and concerns about Europe's debt troubles.

Skittish investors were once again searching for safety as fiscal and debt woes in Europe jumped into the headlines. The government of Portuguese Prime Minister Jose Socrates faces a key vote on a fiscal austerity package that had been expected to keep the country from asking for a European Union bailout. The package is not expected to pass, and Socrates has pledged to resign if the proposal is rejected. That could force Portugal to seek a rescue package.

In Brazil, the focus is on the possibility of additional "macroprudential" measures aimed at containing the strength of the real currency and reining in expanding credit. The market had expected a new package of measures shortly after the Carnival holiday earlier this month, but the earthquake and tsunami in Japan created uncertainty that caused the real to weaken.

Traders and analysts expect additional measures such as an increase to the IOF financial transactions tax, higher bank reserve requirements or the start of dollar purchases by Brazil's Sovereign Wealth Fund.

"Besides following movements abroad, currency market players will receive and react to weekly foreign-exchange flows and expectations for government forex measures," said Miriam Tavares, foreign-exchange director at Sao Paulo-based AGK Corretora de Cambio. "That should keep trading in the recent range."

The Brazilian real traded weaker at BRL1.6610 to the dollar shortly after the open, according to Tullet Prebon via Factset. The real closed Tuesday at BRL1.6585 to the dollar.

The market did find some support despite the gloomy outlook in Europe. In Japan, officials said that the troubled nuclear reactors had been reconnected to the power grid and control-room operations were being restarted. That should allow workers to start cooling operations and reduce the risk of a further meltdown of the nuclear fuel at the Fukushima Daiichi plant.

Inflation in Brazil, meanwhile, showed signs of easing in the period through mid-March. The mid-month inflation index rose 0.60% through mid-March compared with a 0.97% increase through mid-February. The widely watched rolling 12-month rate, however, was at 6.13%. That remained well above the government's 4.5% year-end target.

Low unemployment, higher disposable income and greater access to credit have sparked a surge in domestic demand that has pushed Brazil's inflation rate to just over 6%. The Brazilian Central Bank has boosted local interest rates to 11.75%, by far the highest of any major economy, in an effort to contain prices.

The towering interest rates, however, have also caused a surge in foreign investment inflows as investors seeking higher rates of return flood into Brazil. In Senate testimony Tuesday, Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini said that the surge in foreign-investment inflows had created unsustainable credit growth in Latin America's largest economy.

title: Brazil  Real Strengthens After Government Fails To  Intervene
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real opened stronger on Friday, recovering from a slide in the previous session after strong rumors of central bank intervention proved to be unfounded, and after the announcement of a cease-fire in Libya calmed markets.

The real opened at BRL1.6717 to the dollar, according to SIX Telekurs via Factset. That's weaker than Thursday's close of BRL1.6783.

The Brazilian currency slumped Thursday on speculation the Brazilian government would announce measures to contain appreciation of the real. The currency also declined on concern that Japanese investors would withdraw money from Brazil to rebuild their country after a massive earthquake and tsunami destroyed several cities.

Investors are wary of moves by the government to curb the real's gain, with traders saying Thursday they were expecting an increase in IOF taxes on foreign financial investments to be announced soon. The government raised the IOF to 6% from 2% last year in an effort to weaken the Brazilian currency, whose jump of more than 35% since 2009 has harmed Brazilian exports' competitiveness.

"Yesterday we saw the currency tumble on strong rumors of new measures, but since nothing came of it, the market is giving back those declines," said Roberto Kropp, director of fixed-income trading at Daycoval Asset Management in Sao Paulo.

The improving global environment also helped the currency. In addition to a stabilizing situation in Japan, Libya ordered an immediate ceasefire in the wake of a United Nations resolution passed Thursday. Libyan Foreign Minister Musa Kusa said Friday that the country would "respond positively" to the resolution and halt all military operations against rebel forces.

Efforts by the Group of Seven to halt the yen's gain also may be helping the real, Kropp said. The Group of Seven moved overnight to stem "excess volatility and disorderly movements" in the currency markets

"The Fed will intervene to sell the yen, and that could calm markets as well as strengthen riskier currencies" like the real, he said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso, Brazil real slump to 3-wk lows
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Chile hits 7-week low on Japan nuclear crisis

* JPMorgan cuts exposure to emerging FX by 10 pct

* Brazil government delays intervention measures

* Mexican peso sheds 1.4 pct, Brazil real 0.42 pct

By Michael O'Boyle and Walter Brandimarte

MEXICO CITY/NEW YORK, March 16 (Reuters) - Brazil and Mexico's currencies hit three-week lows on Wednesday while Chile's peso fell to its weakest since January as concerns about Japan's nuclear crisis drove investors into safer-haven assets.

Mexico's peso, the most-liquid and easily settled currency in the region, slumped the most in one day since last May.

Adding pressure to Latin American foreign exchange markets was a JPMorgan report recommending investors to cut exposure to emerging market currencies by 10 percent. [ID:nN16187257]

Selling of Latin American currencies accelerated as global officials sounded increasingly concerned over the situation

at the quake-stricken nuclear plant in Fukushima. [ID:nL3E7EF450] "This is panic and everything will depend on the developments out of Japan," said Alonso Madero, a fund manager at financial group Actinver in Mexico City. "Markets are overreacting and I think this will be transitory," he added.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> shed 1.84 percent to 12.21 per U.S. dollar.

Fears that the global economic recovery may be choked off have been increasing due to Japan's disaster and growing violence in oil-producing countries.

On Monday, Mexico's peso notched a nearly 2-1/2 year high, backed by an improving outlook for the U.S. economy. But some banks, like JPMorgan, have begun to revise down their U.S. growth forecasts. If the U.S. outlook worsens, the peso could lose support.

"Foreign investors were getting out of Mexico today," Rebeca Lizarraga, an analyst at Scotia Capital. "Risk aversion is getting really strong, because we were not seeing this before."

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> fell 0.51 percent to 486 per dollar. The peso has shed 3.7 percent from a high in late February amid concerns that unrest in the Middle East and North Africa will push oil prices higher. Chile imports almost all of its oil, unlike exporter Mexico and self-sufficient Brazil.

Expectations that Chilean policymakers will keep raising interest rates could help the currency snap back if global jitters calm down.

The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent on Thursday.

Chile's central bank said on Wednesday its short-term inflation outlook has deteriorated because of global turmoil in the past month, which may back some market player bets on a 50 basis point hike this week.

The Brazilian real <BRBY><BRL=> bid 0.42 percent weaker at 1.672 per dollar.

Losses in the Brazilian real were cushioned, however, after a Finance Ministry source said the government would delay measures to curb the currency's recent appreciation trend while Japan's crisis unfolds. For details, see [ID:nN15275186].

A Finance Ministry source told Reuters late on Tuesday that the government discarded for now the announcement of new measures to tame the currency appreciation because of global economic uncertainties stemming from Japan's crisis.

The new measures were expected to be unveiled as early as this week, after the real spiked to 2-1/2-year highs earlier this month. The real has shed 1.7 percent from that level, amid fears of intervention and the crisis in Japan.

(Additional reporting by Jose de Castro in Sao Paulo; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: ANALYSIS-No quick fix for Brazil's strong real
text:
* Gov't measures, global portfolio shift stabilize real

* Further intervention unlikely to weaken real much

* Deep fiscal reforms key to long-term strategy

By Alonso Soto

BRASILIA, March 15 (Reuters) - Brazil must learn to live with a strong currency as foreigners keep their appetite for local assets and the government faces diminishing options for braking the real's rise without hurting the economy.

Finance Minister Guido Mantega may announce as early as this week new steps that could include time limits on investments and taxes on international loans after the real rose to 2-1/2 year highs on March 4.

Those potential changes have helped the real stabilize in recent weeks after it firmed nearly 39 percent in the last two years to become one of the world's most overvalued currencies.

A barrage of government measures, along with some renewed appetite for assets in a recovering United States and Europe, have helped contain the real <BRBY> above the 1.65 per dollar mark -- considered the authorities' unofficial floor.

Still, analysts say there is little the government can do over the medium term to counteract upward pressure on the real stemming from Brazil's high interest rates and rapid recent growth.

<^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^


 Latin American currencies:    http://r.reuters.com/sux38r ("http://r.reuters.com/sux38r")
 FACTBOX Brazil latest interventions      [ID:nN15240336]
 SCENARIOS Brazil currency measures       [ID:nN14145427]


^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Brazil's economy grew 7.5 percent in 2010, its fastest pace in 24 years, spurring inflationary pressure that is expected to keep interest rates high and investors' dollars flowing in despite a recent lull in equities. [ID:nN14253010]

"It is practically impossible to weaken the real given the size of the international market and the tools available for the government," said Armando Castelar Pinheiro, senior economics researcher at the Getulio Vargas Foundation, a think tank.

"A strong real is here to stay for some time -- Brazilians will have to get used to it."

DIMINISHING OPTIONS

Despite signs the economy will slow sharply this year as higher interest rates and budget cuts bite, dollar inflows reached $23 billion in the first two months of 2011, nearly matching the $24.35 billion that arrived in all of 2010.

Brazilian consumers are reaping the benefits of a stronger real, traveling abroad like never before and flooding into home appliance stores to buy foreign-made electronics.

But the currency's strength is hurting the country's manufacturers as they struggle to cope with a wave of cheaper Chinese imports. Industrial output dropped 0.3 percent in the fourth quarter of last year from the third quarter as household consumption jumped 2.5 percent.

New President Dilma Rousseff faces a delicate balance between relieving exporters' pain and keeping Brazil attractive for foreign direct investment, funds that could be deterred by any new currency measures.

Brazil has already tripled, to 6 percent, the tax it charges foreigners when they buy local bonds, boosted dollar purchases and set limits on banks' short positions on the dollar.

More and deeper controls could start to hit investor sentiment in the energy and mining powerhouse.

"You see an intervention strategy that has quite frankly expired in terms of anything beyond marginal impact on the currency. It just buys the government time," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, currency strategist with RBS in New York.

Intervention is increasing Brazil's financing costs as heavily taxed investors see less incentive to buy longer term debt. The central bank's dollar purchases -- over $8 billion in the spot market in February alone -- may also hit the bank's balance sheet on rising carry costs.

"They are destroying some market sentiment," said Alberto Ramos, a senior economist with Goldman Sachs. "The government can anchor the real, but the question is, 'At what cost?'"

Many analysts see the real staying between 1.65 and 1.70 per dollar in most of 2011, although shocks in international markets resulting from the aftermath of Japan's earthquake and Middle East unrest could add some volatility.

Over the longer term, analysts say the only way Brazil can weaken the real is through deeper reforms, such as reducing the large state role in the economy and raising its relatively low savings rate. Lower state spending would ease pressure on interest rates and reduce incentives for investors seeking to profit from the rate differential.

Rousseff, who took office in January, has slashed some spending in this year's budget, but so far kept away from deeper reforms in her legislative agenda. [ID:nN02222605]

(Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Padraic Cassidy and Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso, Brazil real up; Chile peso slumps
text:
* Japan disaster keeps investors cautious

* Chile rate hikes seen backstopping peso losses

* Brazil seen preparing more intervention measures

* Brazil real firms 0.24 percent, Mexico peso 0.11 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 14 (Reuters) - Mexico peso and Brazil's real firmed on Monday as investors bet neither Japan's disaster nor oil prices will have a big enough impact on global growth to deter demand for Latin America's high-yielding debt.

Mexico's peso shook off losses to firm past 11.90 per dollar. The currency traded at its strongest level since October 2008 during the session.

The Mexican currency tracked a recovery from session lows in U.S. stocks markets as investors bet the broad impact on equities from Japan's disaster may be short-lived.

"People seem to be thinking the reaction to the Japan disaster was overdone," said Dirk Willer, head of Latin American local markets strategy at Citigroup in New York.

A catastrophe at one of Japan's nuclear power plants that was damaged in the earthquake could spur more losses, Willer said. "But if they get the reactors under control, the flooding and the earthquake itself will lead to a reconstruction boom, and that might, if anything, be seen as positive for global growth," he added.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.11 percent to 11.8950 per dollar while Brazil's real <BRBY> firmed 0.24 percent to 1.660 per dollar.

Brazil is offering some of the highest interest rates in the world, bolstering demand for its currency.

The market awaited news of more intervention measures from Brazilian authorities, who want to keep in check the real's gains that are hurting local manufacturers by cheapening imports.[ID:nN14145427]

However, any new measures may not be able to spur more than short-term losses in the currency, which has advanced more than 40 percent since 2009. Increasing intervention has slowed the currency's gains, but has not reversed its advance.

Unrest in North Africa and the Middle East has put pressure on oil prices, but analysts said that the cost of crude would have to rise much higher for a sustained period to take a major toll on global growth and derail the stability of the region's currencies.

Mexico's peso is seen getting further support from signs of an improving local economy that is tracking the recovery in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

Data showed Mexican industrial production rose at its fastest pace in 15 months as manufacturing output jumped and the construction sector posted a big increase. [ID:nN14143186].

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> lost 0.52 percent to 481 per dollar. Chile's local spot market closed before U.S. stocks pared losses.

Analysts said expectations of further interest rate hikes could limit losses in the Chilean peso this week.

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent this Thursday.

"Chile is still hiking and could hike more than what is priced in; you would have to have a very negative shock on the global growth outlook for this to change," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  sink on menace of Saudi unrest
text:
* Mexico peso bounces off key 12/dlr level

* Investors eye possible new intervention in Brazil

* Brazil real sheds 0.5 pct, Mexico peso 0.4 pct

* Chile peso slumps to weakest since early February

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 10 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened sharply on Thursday as reports of unrest in Saudi Arabia and sinking stock markets raised risks that the region's strong currencies could be hit by rising global uncertainty.

Brazil's real, already under pressure from concerns of more intervention, sank in international trade, while Mexico's peso managed to bounce off a key level, which may bode for a quick recovery if global tensions ease.

Reports of protest in Saudi Arabia, the top OPEC producer, revived concerns of further disruptions in oil supplies.

A sustained push higher in crude prices could weigh on global growth and push investors to dump riskier assets like emerging market currencies and retreat into safe-haven assets like U.S. Treasuries.

"The situation in the Middle East is far from being resolved and it will be the main driver. The question is if there will be a sustained pickup in risk aversion or not," said David Beker, head of Latin American debt and currency strategy at Bank of America-Merrill Lynch.

Fears drove the Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> down nearly 2 percent in its worst slump in seven months. [ID:nN10178483]

Brazil's real <BRL=> shed 0.51 percent to 1.6618 per dollar in international trade. Losses seemed more contained on the local spot market <BRBY>, with the real off 0.24 percent at 1.659 per dollar.

Investors remained leery of fresh intervention measures to keep the real's gains in check. Last week, the real closed at a 2-1/2 year high, stronger than what many see as the Finance Ministry's unofficial limit around 1.65 per dollar.

Brazil has steadily escalated its intervention in currency markets since 2009. But it has only slowed the ascent of the real, which has been buoyed by a tide of global investment that is drawn to its double-digit interest rates.

The real has firmed more than 40 percent since 2009.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> sank 0.8 percent to 481.50 per dollar, its weakest level since early February.

Chile's local spot market closed before news of the protest in Saudi Arabia, but the currency was hammered by falling prices for copper, Chile's main export, after a drop in Chinese import data cast doubt on demand from the world's top consumer of the metal.

Chile's central bank said on Thursday it would allow more foreigners to issue bonds in pesos in the domestic market. [ID:nN10144530]

A trader said the policy would not likely have a major impact on the currency, since local pension funds already buy foreign debt abroad.

Risk appetite had also been hurt during the session by renewed fears about Europe's debt after a rating agency downgrade of Spain.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> lost 0.38 percent to 11.9760 per dollar, paring steeper losses after bouncing off the key 12 per dollar level.

On Wednesday, Mexico's peso hit its strongest since October 2008, breaking past the 11.95 level that had marked a range since January. With that support for the dollar knocked out, traders said the currency could set out a new range between 11.80 and 12 per dollar.

As long as oil prices do not spike further and stay high, hitting U.S. demand, the peso should benefit from the economic recovery in the United States.

Moreover, the peso has lagged gains in other emerging market currencies, and policymakers have not threatened to fight the further gains, unlike Brazil and Chile.

"The peso will still trend stronger. You do not find any other country in the region where the central bank has given a green light to further FX appreciation," Beker said.

(Additional reporting by Jose de Castro in Sao Paulo; Editing by Dan Grebler)

* Euro bounce supports bids for emerging market currencies

* Market awaits possible intervention measures in Brazil

* Mexico peso up 0.23 pct, Chile peso firms 0.11 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean pesos firmed on Wednesday as a stronger euro backed bids for riskier assets, but further gains could be limited by uncertainty related to Europe's debt troubles and rising oil prices.

Meanwhile, investors awaited possible news of fresh government measures to tame gains in the Brazilian real when local markets reopen this afternoon following Carnival holidays.

The euro recovered from lows on Wednesday after Portugal successfully sold bonds, easing some concerns about European countries struggling with high debt burdens. [ID:nN09244748]

The euro is often a proxy for investor appetite for riskier assets such as emerging market currencies and the Mexican peso tracked the euro's bounce.

"We have seen a rebound in the euro, which has set a better tone for risky assets, so emerging markets are benefiting from that," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, a managing director at TD Securities in Toronto.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.23 percent to 11.9775 per dollar. The currency has struggled to definitively break past the 12 per dollar level since a rally stalled in late January.

"The peso does not have much more room to go, the outlook on Europe really is mixed," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones in Mexico City.

The cost of dollars in pesos would have to fall below a 2-1/2 year low hit in January at 11.9439 to open up the field for a significant break lower, Perez-Duarte said.

Worries about high oil prices could also begin to weigh on markets again and unravel peso gains, traders said.

Chile's currency <CLP=CL> firmed 0.11 percent to 474.50 per dollar on rising prices for copper, the country's main export.

However, higher oil prices could keep investors worried that inflationary pressures may hit economic growth and demand for copper.

Global markets are expected to remain jittery among concerns that political unrest in Egypt and Libya could spread to other oil states such as top producer Saudi Arabia.

PARTY'S OVER

With the end of Brazil's Carnival holiday, local authorities may move soon to try and sober up investors who pushed the real to a 2-1/2 year high last Friday, beyond what many see as the finance ministry's unofficial limit.

Brazil's financial markets reopen at 1 p.m. local time (1600 GMT). A Finance Ministry source told Reuters the government may announce a new round of measures this week. [ID:nN04241800]

The real closed at 1.645 per dollar on Friday in the local spot market, below the 1.65 per dollar level that has been seen as a trigger to intervention measures in the past.

Testing government resolve, the real bid stronger at 1.6443 in international trade <BRL=> on Wednesday.

Brazil has steadily escalated its intervention in currency markets since 2009 as a tide of global investment was drawn to its double-digit interest rates. The flows pumped up the real by more than 40 percent since the beginning of 2009.

The stronger real is hurting local manufacturers who have to compete with cheapening imports.

So far, Brazil's efforts to weaken the currency have slowed, but not deterred its advance.

Last October, the government tripled to 6 percent a tax on foreigners buying local bonds and trading in currency derivatives. The central bank, meanwhile, is buying dollars in the spot market as well as acting in the forward and swap markets.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso at highest since Oct 08, real sinks
text:
* Dollar flows help Mexican peso break past key level

* Intervention fears hit Brazil real

* Brazil real falls 0.73 pct, Mexico peso up 0.63 pct

* Chile peso loses 0.57 pct on copper slump

(Recasts; adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso blew past a key technical level on Wednesday to notch a nearly 2-1/2 year high, suggesting the currency may be able to make a further push higher after struggling in a range since January.

Traders said flows from long-term investors, including a big bet by a hedge fund, caught the market by surprise when many expected the currency's gains during the session to be less sharp. A resulting scramble to buy pesos and cover losses exacerbated the break.

Demand for Mexico's exports is expected to be lifted by the recovery in the U.S. economy, and the peso may be on track to hit levels close to 11.80 per dollar that some analysts have been signaling.

"Long-term investors are entering Mexico," said Francisco Diez, director of emerging markets trading at RBC Capital Markets in New York. "It looks like a lot of dollars went into Mexico today."

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.63 percent to 11.93 per dollar, its strongest since Oct. 2008. The currency punched through its previous high at 11.9439 set in January that many thought would hold during the session.

Mexico's currency has lagged the gains in other emerging market economies. But some investors think it could try and catch up this year as the U.S. economy gains steam.

Local banks exercised $367 million in dollar put options with the central bank on Wednesday, leaving $200 million of the $600 million the central bank is selling every month to build up its currency reserves.

The options give banks the right to sell dollars to the central bank at a better peso rate than the spot market.

"The fact that $200 million were not exercised suggests the holders of those options think the peso could get even stronger," said Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura Securities.

REAL SLUMPS

Brazil's real recoiled on fresh fears authorities could take new measures to stem the currency's gains, while Chile's peso slumped on falling copper prices.

As Brazil's local markets reopened after the Carnival holiday, the real <BRBY> bid at 1.655 per dollar, 0.73 percent weaker from its close last Friday at a 2-1/2-year high.

The real had then closed beyond what many see as the Finance Ministry's unofficial limit around 1.65 per dollar.

A ministry source told Reuters the government may announce a new round of measures this week aimed at curtailing the strong real.[ID:nN04241800]

Some analysts think Brazilian authorities could take more aggressive action than in the past. Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, an analyst at RBS Securities, said one option could be to raise a tax on foreign investments in equities.

"The risk is that they do something that is not very market-friendly," she said.

Last October the government tripled to 6 percent a tax on foreigners buying local bonds and trading in currency derivatives. The tax on equity investments held at 2 percent.

Brazil has steadily escalated its intervention in currency markets since 2009 as a tide of global investment was drawn to its double-digit interest rates. The flows pumped up the real by more than 40 percent since the beginning of 2009.

The stronger real is hurting local manufacturers who have to compete with cheapening imports. So far, Brazil's efforts to weaken the currency have slowed, but not deterred its advance.

title: Brazil  Markets Face Possible  Foreign Exchange Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazilian financial markets will wake up from the annual Carnival holiday on Wednesday afternoon with a hangover, composed of one-part European fiscal worry and two parts domestic foreign exchange uncertainty.

Trading in stocks, foreign exchange, and futures and options contracts will resume at 1600 GMT for the first time since the Friday close.

"There will be plenty of work for everyone," said Paulo Faria-Tavares, managing director of Sao Paulo's PTX Lending consultants. "A lot has happened this week -- Greece heavily downgraded, oil about to reach $120 a barrel, Libya fighting and new Brazilian foreign exchange measures, possibly Wednesday or Thursday."

The latter possibility is probably the most worrisome for investors, at least in the short term.

The Brazilian real closed Friday at BRL1.6424 to the dollar, slightly stronger against the Thursday close and breaking the key BRL1.65 barrier for the first time in 2011.

Over the last two years, the real has gained more than 35% against the dollar, leading to worries about declining exports and increasing competition from cheap imports of manufactured products.

Brazil's government has intervened directly in the market a number of times in recent months to contain the appreciation of the real, most notably in October when it raised taxes on short-term inflows destined for the fixed-income market.

"We would not at all be surprised to see new measures unveiled this week," according to Brown Brothers Harriman strategist Win Thin, in a research note.

Local news reports indicate new measures could include higher taxes on a broader range of inflows, aggressive new government purchases of dollars from the market or even a quarantine on some forms of foreign investment inflows.

"Implications for the BRL [Brazilian real] are negative on expectations of outflows and regulatory risk similar to that following the revisions in the IOF [financial transactions tax] in October," said analysts at RBS Securities in a research note.

Thin agreed that, in the short term, the trend for the Brazilian real might be negative, even including a rollback to BRL1.70 to the dollar. But he noted that the medium-term trend is still toward appreciation of the Brazilian currency because of high interest rates.

Brazil's Selic base interest rate is a towering 11.75%. Rates at this level have proven highly attractive to foreign investors at a time when U.S. and European interest rates are near zero.

In a research note, economists at Goldman Sachs noted Brazil's central bank "will have to continue to push rates higher in order to get a grip on deteriorating inflation dynamics."

Brazil's inflation rate is currently 6.0%, well above the government's 2011 target of 4.5%.

Meanwhile, Brazilian stocks will have to contend with increasing worries about the European fiscal crisis. Moody's Investors Service earlier this week downgraded Greece's sovereign rating for the second time in a year, this time to B1 with a "negative outlook."

Fiscal worries also continue to dog Portugal.

Volatile international oil prices in the face of a virtual civil war in Libya will likely increase risk aversion among foreign investors, according to analysts.

title: Brazil  Real Weaker On Possible Government  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real weakened against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, drifting back across the BRL1.65 barrier as investors mulled the possibility of enhanced government intervention in the market.

The real exited from active trading at BRL1.6542 to the dollar, weaker against Friday's close of BRL1.6424, according to SIX Telekurs via Factset.

Brazil's financial markets were closed Monday and Tuesday for the annual Carnival celebration.

Brazilian officials have been explicit in recent months about their desire to arrest further appreciation of the real. The currency has posted gains of about 45% against the dollar over the past two years, hurting Brazilian exports and undermining manufacturers with a flood of cheap imported products.

Press reports over the past week pointed to possible government measures to inhibit further appreciation. Measures might include higher taxes on some investment inflows, stepped up purchases of dollars by the government and even a quarantine on certain forms of foreign investment.

Currency trader Mario Araujo, of Sao Paulo's Vision brokerage, said the mere threat of such enhanced intervention was enough to ward off a currency appreciation Wednesday.

"The government will try traditional methods of intervention first," said Araujo, imposing restrictive new rules only if the traditional methods fail to stem the rise of the real.

Traditional methods include government purchases of dollars as well as so-called reverse swap auctions at which investors are given the chance to exchange dollar-linked contracts for paper tied to interest rates.

In Wednesday's session, the government managed to provoke a slight depreciation of the real with only a single intervention, buying dollars from the market at a snap auction late in trading.

Traders noted that Wednesday's session came against a background of thin trading because of the long holiday weekend.

They said market attention will shift Thursday to the Brazilian Central Bank, which will release minutes from its March 2 interest-rate meeting. At the meeting, the bank raised its Selic base rate by a half percentage point, to 11.75%.

Investors will scrutinize the minutes for signs of more monetary tightening in the next few months. Higher interest rates will tend to make Brazil more attractive for short-term investment inflows.

Trading on Brazilian credit markets Wednesday reflected expectations for comparatively dovish central bank comments when the March meeting minutes are released. On the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, interest-rate futures contracts closed mostly lower. The contracts reflect investor expectations for annualized interest rates at future dates.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real hits 2-1/2 yr high, oil hits pesos
text:
* Brazil breaks past key level, more intervention eyed

* Oil price rise weighs on Mexican and Chilean pesos

* Brazil real gains 0.42 percent, Mexico peso flat

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's real surged to its strongest in 2-1/2 years on Friday, pushing the government to contemplate new measures to curb the currency's gains next week.

Brazil's government may announce a new round of measures, possibly from the middle of next week, to tame the recent appreciation of the real, a finance ministry source told Reuters.

The comments came after the real jumped during Friday's session despite a series of dollar auctions meant to slow its gains.

U.S. February jobs data improved on Friday, but not at a fast enough pace to disturb bets that the United States keep interest rates low, insuring cheap funding for market players who borrow dollars to invest in Brazilian assets. [ID:nN04228803]

Meanwhile, Brazil's annual inflation rate ticked up to upper limit of the government's target range, backing expectations that policy-makers will further tighten borrowing costs. [ID:nN04261260]

"We did not have particularly strong U.S. (job) numbers, even though the underlying picture is improving, you could continue to see flows attracted into markets such as Brazil," said David Mann, head of Americas research at Standard Chartered in New York.

Brazil raised its benchmark rate to 11.75 percent late Wednesday. With some of the highest yields in the world, a tide of yield-hungry global investors are pushing up the real, which notched a more than 1.1 percent gain this week and a 44 percent gain since 2009.

The real <BRBY> bid 0.42 percent stronger on Friday to 1.643 per dollar, its strongest since August 2008.

The strong real is hurting local manufacturers and authorities are using a tool box of dollar auctions and taxes to try and ward off the flows. On Friday, the central bank deployed dollar auctions in both the forward and spot market.

When the real was trading around current levels last October, the finance ministry hiked taxes on foreign inflows.

"This is a key test right now and it remains to be seen if we will see more aggressive interventions or if there is a retreat and a new line in the sand is yet to be drawn," Mann added.

Credit Suisse told clients to bet of further gains in the real in the non-deliverable forwards market, where a position against the dollar could nab significant gains even if authorities manage to keep the real around current levels.

Meanwhile, renewed concerns about rising oil prices weighed on Mexico and Chile's pesos.

U.S. crude oil prices jumped amid clashes in Libya near a major oil terminal, reviving concerns that higher oil prices could weigh down global growth.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> traded flat at 12.0050 per dollar, paring early gains that had taken it to a more than three week high.

While Mexico exports oil, it has been hurt by concerns that higher oil prices will weigh down consumer demand in the United States, which buys around 80 percent of local exports.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> lost 0.15 percent to 473.70 per dollar. Any slowdown in global growth will hurt demand for copper, the country's top export.

Chile also imports most of its oil, unlike exporter Mexico and self-sufficient Brazil.

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 2 (Reuters) - Brazilian yields rose on Wednesday and the real firmed as surprisingly strong industrial data marginally backed bets for an aggressive interest rate hike, while Mexico's peso gained.

Brazil's central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by at least 50 basis point later on Wednesday to 11.75 percent. Higher rates should bolster the real, but central bank intervention is containing gains. [ID:nN01145534]

Data showed Brazil's industrial production rose 0.2 percent in January, pushing up yields in the interest rate futures market <0#DIJ:> as investors bet policymakers could deliver a three-quarter-percentage point hike. [ID:nN02140898]

"The bets are a bit higher, but in absolute terms the probability of a 75 basis point hike is very small," said Diego Donadio, an analyst at BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

Inflation expectations have worsened since the central bank's last 50-basis-point hike in January. But most economists think spending cuts by the new government and higher bank reserve requirements have eased pressure for a bigger hike.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> firmed 0.18 percent to 1.659 per dollar even after the central bank held a dollar forward auction.

The currency is expected to firm despite intervention and global jitters about higher oil prices as investors pile into the country's debt, which is offering among the highest interest rates in the world.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.26 percent to 12.0890 per dollar as the greenback was pressured by expectations that interest rates in the euro zone will rise earlier than those in the United States.

"There is a general sentiment of dollar weakness since the U.S. seems more worried about the recovery than inflation, and other central banks could raise interest rates first," said Alejandro Martinez, a debt and currency strategist at HSBC in Mexico City.

The Mexican peso gained about 5 percent from November to January on the back of an improving outlook for the U.S. economy, but concerns about the economic impact of higher oil prices have stalled the peso's rally.

"It will be difficult to see stronger gains, because risk appetite is really weak due to the situation in the Middle East. If oil prices remain high for a prolonged period, the United States economy could slow down, and that would hurt the peso," Martinez added.

Martinez said the currency would likely trade between 12.08 per dollar and 12.15 per dollar in the coming sessions.

Chile also imports most of its oil, making it susceptible to a sustained spike in oil prices.

title: Heavy  Central Bank  Action Holds Brazil Real To Small Gain
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--As in past sessions, heavy central bank action Wednesday helped hold the Brazilian real to only a small gain against the U.S. dollar as investors weighed possible effects of an expected interest rate hike.

The real exited from active trading at BRL1.6585 to the dollar, representing a small gain against Tuesday's close of BRL1.6620, according to SIX Telekurs via FactSet.

Wednesday night, the Brazilian central bank is due to review its Selic base rate, currently a towering 11.25%. Most analysts expect a half-point hike to 11.75% as part of a government drive to pull down inflation. Brazil's inflation rate is currently 6.1%.

"It's inevitable that this [rate hike] will attract more investment inflows into Brazil," said Luiz Henrique Didier, partner of the Didier-Levy brokerage in Sao Paulo. "This is especially true given that interest rates in many traditional investment venues are near zero."

Central bank figures released Wednesday underscored continued investor interest. The figures showed net inflows of U.S. dollars for the period Feb. 1 through Feb. 25 of $6.3 billion. During the same period a year ago, Brazil faced net outflows of $399 million.

But just as Brazilian government officials have been adamant about controlling inflation, they have also stated explicitly their distaste for any further appreciation of the Brazilian real.

"This is a delicate problem," said Demosthenes Madureira Pinho, director of asset management at Itau, Brazil's biggest private bank. "The central bank intervenes in the market, affecting the foreign exchange rate. But the intervention has to be just right. Too much currency appreciation hurts Brazilian exports; too much depreciation sparks inflation."

Intervention by the central bank Wednesday was entirely in the direction of attempting to prevent further appreciation of the currency. The central bank bought dollars from the spot market in two separate auctions. It also bought forward delivery contracts for dollars at an additional pair of auctions.

In addition to an expected interest rate hike, the real was also favored Wednesday by continued weakening of the U.S. dollar in world markets. The dollar lost out to the euro and other currencies on continued Middle East tensions, increasing global oil prices and rising risk aversion.

Trading on Brazilian credit markets Wednesday reflected market expectations for a half-point central bank interest rate hike. On the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, interest rate futures contracts closed mostly higher. The contracts reflect investor expectations for annualized interest rates at future dates. Among actively traded interest rate futures contracts, January 2012 closed at 12.53%, up from 12.50% Tuesday.
