title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  stuck in ranges as oil weighs
text:
* Brazil intervention pulls real back from 2-month high

* Chile peso slips as concerns of high oil prices weigh

* Mexico peso firms 0.19 pct, Brazil real 0.06 pct (New throughout, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, (Reuters) - Latin American currencies were trapped in narrow ranges Monday as investors remained cautious about the impact of higher oil prices on global growth and the region's importers, such as Chile.

Concerns that a spike in oil prices could hurt global growth have weighed on the region's currencies in recent weeks, softening a trend of steady appreciation as investors are drawn to Latin America's relatively high interest rates.

Brent crude oil prices rose above $112 a barrel, but the market calmed from last week's jumps as investors weighed a pledge of more supply from Saudi Arabia against the prospect of prolonged disruption to Libya's output.

The currencies of oil producers Mexico and Brazil managed to firm while the peso of Chile, an importer of crude, dipped.

"Mexico's peso has been strengthening since the peak of oil prices last week, so this is just unwinding these extreme scenarios on Middle East oil risk," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American fixed-income strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

"If we have a permanent increase in oil just because of lingering uncertainty in the Middle East, then it becomes actually favorable for oil exporters such as Mexico and less favorable for importers, countries like Chile," he added.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.19 percent to 12.1025 per dollar. Brazil's real bid 0.06 percent stronger on the local spot market to 1.661 per dollar.

Brazil's central bank knocked the currency back from a nearly two-month high hit early in the session by intervening with two auctions to buy dollars in the spot market, a reverse currency swap auction and two dollar forward auctions.

Chile's peso slipped 0.25 percent to 475.70 per dollar.

"Oil prices are more stable ... but the price is still near $112, which is very high for a country like ours that imports almost all of its petroleum," a Chilean trader said.

Investors pushed down yields on Brazilian interest rate futures on bets that government spending cuts may cool the need for an aggressive interest rate hike this week.

Brazil's government said Monday it will slash spending on defense and low-income housing as part of $30 billion in cuts to this year's budget.

Brazilian central bank policymakers meet Wednesday to decide on a possible hike in the country's interest rate.

While some market players were betting last week that they could raise rates by 75 basis points, the market began late last week to unwind those bets.

Yields on Mexican interest rate swaps edged up after the head of the country's central bank expressed worry about crop failures from bad weather and said policymakers may have to raise interest rates if they poison inflation expectations.

Mexico, whose economic recovery has been slower than that of Brazil or Chile, has widely been expected not to raise interest rates until early in 2012.

"Mexico has been spared a significant pick-up in food inflation, but that could change purely because of local conditions," Credit Suisse's Arsenin said. (Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo and Froilan Romero in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Brazil Central Bank  Flexes  Intervention  Muscle In  Currency  Market
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market appeared ready to shrug off ongoing violence in North Africa and the Middle East on Tuesday, but a surprise reverse-swap auction by the central bank and a message of defiance from Libya was enough to undercut foreign-investment inflows.

The latest hostilities in an ongoing wave of pro-democracy protests shocked the international community, as reports of Libyan Air Force pilots bombing their countrymen and indiscriminate shooting of protesters sent cautious investors scurrying for safety. Concerns about supply interruptions sent international oil prices skyrocketing, with crude oil for April delivery jumping 4.5%, to $96.45 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

But fears of a broader international impact were subdued in Brazil, where local currency traders confirmed a correction in early weakness for the real currency. The real strengthened throughout the session on expectations for increased foreign-investment inflows, including net inflows of about $460 million into Brazil's main stock exchange through Feb. 18.

The Brazilian Central Bank, however, reminded the market of its might via a surprise reverse-swap auction, traders said. The bank sold the equivalent of $848.2 million in reverse swap contracts on offer at three different maturities. It was the eighth reverse swap auction held by the central bank so far this year. At a reverse swap auction on Feb. 18, the central bank sold 86% of the contracts offered, worth $1.48 billion.

"The bank typically announces reverse-swap auctions when the market is closed," said Alberto Orsovay, a dealer at Sao Paulo-based brokerage Hencorp Commcor. "You could say that the market was expecting a reverse-swap auction, but not during trading hours."

Reverse swap auctions offer investors the opportunity to exchange futures positions in U.S. dollars for positions tied to domestic interest rates. Typically, a reverse swap auction supports the dollar against the Brazilian real by removing future dollar deliveries from the market. The government revived reverse swap auctions earlier this year in an effort to arrest the continued appreciation of the Brazilian real against the dollar.

The central bank then followed up the reverse-swap auction with a snap auction to buy dollars from the spot market. The bank purchased an undisclosed volume of dollars from the spot market at BRL1.6706 to the dollar.

Also undermining the currency market at about the same time was embattled Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi's pledge to go down fighting. In a speech broadcast on Libyan state TV, Gadhafi vowed to keep his hold on power and defied protesters to end his rule. The country also shut its ports.

Libya's descent into violence has had a greater impact than conflicts elsewhere because of the country's position as a member of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Libya produces about 1.8 million barrels of crude a day and has 41 billion barrels of proven reserves, about 3% of global supply.

The double-dip intervention and Gadhafi's speech combined to undercut the real currency, which traded weaker at BRL1.6695 to the dollar as of 1848 GMT, according to Telekurs via Factset. The real closed Monday at BRL1.6675 to the dollar.

The real likely would have ended even weaker if not for support from the latest inflation figures, which showed that consumer prices continued to grow through mid-February. The mid-month inflation rate was 0.97% through mid-February, versus a 0.76% advance through mid-January. The rolling 12 month inflation rate climbed to 6.08%, well above the government's official target of 4.5%. That will likely mean higher near-term interest rates in Brazil.

"The market is pricing in higher interest rates," said Hencorp Commcor's Orsovay. "The trend is still for the real to strengthen on investment inflows."

-By Jeff Fick, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-21-2586-6085, Jeff.Fick@dowjones.com [ 22-02-11 2012GMT ]

title: Brazilian Real, Chilean Peso Near Key Pre- Intervention  Levels
text:
-Brazil's central bank more likely to ramp up currency intervention than Chile's

-Central bank interventions could provide trade entry point--money manager


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Despite ongoing efforts by Brazil's and Chile's central banks to curb currency appreciation, the Brazilian real and Chilean peso are defiantly approaching pre-intervention levels, raising the question of whether these countries will make further efforts to curb them.

If central banks stand back, that could pave the way for more gains, but some strategists warn about the risks of more intense interventions.

Both central banks have argued that their currencies would be significantly stronger had they not intervened at all. But now rising inflation concerns have led both countries to raise interest rates recently, with more hikes expected this year, which only will encourage stronger currencies in the future.

With both currencies nearing major psychological and technical breakthroughs, investors who are already long on either currency should stay in those positions for now, since there is room for further strength, said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, currency strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland.

Though both currencies saw some losses on Tuesday from general risk aversion on Middle East worries, robust copper prices in Chile, the world's largest producer of the red metal, and strong capital inflows in Brazil have been key drivers of the peso's and real's strength in recent months.

For the real, reaching BRL1.65 to the dollar is a key psychological level that it could hit at "any time," while investors should watch for the peso to hit CLP466.70 to the dollar, Cattan-Naslausky said. If the real and peso do surpass those levels, investors could take profits before the currencies are able to stabilize, she added.

John Peta, who manages an emerging-market, local-currency bond fund at Acadian Asset Management, said they remain overweight on the Brazilian real and Chilean peso.

"We're long both currencies because we think the fundamentals are quite positive," he said, adding that the high carry on the Brazilian real still makes it an attractive position. Already-high interest rates in Brazil and expected interest-rate increases in Chile should drive appreciation pressures, he added.

Still, analysts say it's not a good time to enter into these trades, given their already-high valuations and further intervention risks.

Of the two, the real is riskier to buy right now, given Brazil's central bank's ongoing intervention efforts. It regularly intervenes in the spot, forward and futures markets. Most notably, in October, Brazil's central bank stepped up intervention by twice raising its financial operations tax on foreign purchases of local assets, in an effort to curb hot money inflows from abroad. Before that second tax hike, the real was near the BRL1.65 mark, which it is now approaching.

The threat of further measures in Brazil is a serious one, said Alberto Ramos, economist at Goldman Sachs. The Brazilian monetary authority could intensify its current measures or it could also employ more unorthodox capital controls, he said.

The Chilean peso, meanwhile, is more likely to be given some room to appreciate. In Chile, the central bank announced a $12 billion dollar purchasing program for the year in early January, after the peso gained more than 7% in 2010.

But further action from Chile's traditionally conservative central bank is less likely, even though it could increase the amount of its daily dollar purchases.

"They are not ready to go to places that the Brazilians are ready to go," Ramos said.

The Andean nation's hawkish monetary authority has hinted at a shift in priorities, from curbing the peso to focusing on the inflation battle, given its 25-basis-point rate hike last week--making it more likely that the peso will strengthen.

But if the two banks ultimately do intervene, it could provide a buying opportunity for these two currencies, said Adnan Akant, head of foreign exchange and managing director at money manager Fischer Francis Trees & Watts, a New York unit of BNP Paribas.

"Intervention is just a way of cheapening them up for those who really want to be involved in them," he said.

Currently the money manager is not exposed to the Chilean peso or the Brazilian real, after pulling out of a long-real position last year on intervention worries.

Given the recent bout of risk aversion on Middle East concerns, it's "wait-and-see" whether global markets stabilize, but if any new central bank interventions weaken the two currencies, it could provide an advantageous entry point, he said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed; Chile peso hits 6-week high
text:
* Chile peso hits 6-week high after rate hike

* Brazil real contained by intervention

* Bets on Mexican peso hit highest since April 2010 (Rewrites throughout)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Chile's peso jumped to a six-week high on Friday as the market bet on more interest rate hikes and doubted authorities would step up intervention efforts, while Mexico and Brazil's currencies lost steam.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.26 percent stronger to 468.50 per dollar after the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent, adding to the appeal of the currency. For details, see [ID:nN17302923]

A string of comments from Chilean officials also eased concerns that authorities will expand their efforts to contain the peso's gains after introducing a $50-million-a-day dollar purchase program at the beginning of January.

"There is a clear commitment to continue to fight inflation and we have heard from central bank board members that they will pay more attention to the inflation target than the exchange rate," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist at Roubini Global Economics in New York.

The Chilean peso racked up a 0.79 percent gain for the week, despite a sharp drop in the price of copper -- the country's main export -- which hurt the currency early in the week.

The currency would likely firm toward a nearly three-year high around 450 per dollar, "as long as nothing happens to the price of copper," Delgado said.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, slipped 0.06 percent to 1.662 per dollar as central bank intervention kept the currency within a narrow range.

Brazil's central bank held a forward auction and a reverse swap auction, both of which can weigh on the currency. Policymakers were apparently reacting to a jump in the previous session, when the real posted sharp gains.

The lower house of Brazil's Congress shook off pressure from labor unions and approved the new administration's proposal for a small increase in the minimum wage late Wednesday, boosting confidence in the new government's clout.

The real has been trading in increasingly narrow ranges in recent weeks, slowed by the central bank's intervention, but still steadily firming as investors are drawn to Brazil's interest rates, among the highest in the world.

The real gained 0.18 percent in the last week.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.12 percent on Friday to close at 12.023 per dollar, notching 0.08 percent gain for the week.

The peso ran into a brick wall at the psychologically key 12-per dollar after sharp gains on Thursday. Local companies have been heavy buyers of dollars around the 12 level.

Many local companies fixed their budgets for the year with expectations of a peso at 12.50 per dollar during 2011, making the 12-per-dollar level hard to resist.

The Mexican peso has been a favorite bet since last November, gaining more than 4 percent on an improving outlook for the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

Delgado said the peso would need surprisingly strong data in the United States to break below 12 per dollar in the short term, but he said the peso would eventually firm toward 11.50.

Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in Chicago showed on Friday that the net amount of bets in favor of the Mexican peso rose to their highest level since April 2010, according to Win Thin, a currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

"Everyone is really long and that makes me nervous," Thin said, noting the peso could be hit by any increase in global jitters related to political unrest in the Middle East or Europe's debt troubles. A spike in worries about Europe hammered the peso down from a high in May 2010.

The Mexican peso has the most bets in its favor of the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. [ID:nN18104672]

While that backs up the fundamental backdrop boding for futher gains, it also makes it vulnerable to any global shocks that could send speculators running for the door.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real firms, Chile peso trades flat

SAO PAULO, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency firmed slightly in early trading on Thursday while Chile's peso traded nearly flat ahead of a possible rise in the country's interest rates.

The country has been a prime target for investors that borrow money cheaply in a country with lower interest rates to chase higher yields elsewhere. Brazil's interest rates are among the world's highest.

Congressional approval on Wednesday of a small increase in the minimum wage had a slight market impact as it came as expected, brokers said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> was flat, bidding 473.80 against the U.S. dollar ahead of the country's decision on interest rates. In early trading it fell slightly, following a decline in prices of the country's top export, copper.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso firms to over 1-mo high,  Brazil  dips
text:
* Chile bets backed by rate view, lower intervention risks

* Real slumps from more than one-month high

* Mexican finance minister rules out intervention

* Brazil real slumps 0.6 pct, Mexico peso flat

By Michael O'Boyle and Ana Nicolaci da Costa

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO (Reuters) - Chile's peso hit its strongest level in more than a month Thursday after a poll backed bets of higher interest rates and intervention risks were seen receding, while Brazil's currency slumped.

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.50 percent next week, according to a poll.

Chilean policymakers held borrowing costs steady last month to try to discourage yield-hungry investors from pouring into its assets. The pause complemented a currency intervention program introduced at the beginning of the year.

But the move spooked bond investors, who fear the central bank is not doing enough to tame rising inflation. Now policymakers appear to be changing course.

The central bank held back from expanding the intervention program this week despite solid gains in the peso.

"People feel more comfortable that they will tolerate a stronger peso, because they need to worry about inflation," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American debt strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

Seven straight rate hikes last year drove the Chilean peso to a nearly three-year high, pushing the central bank to buy $50 million a day to help protect local exporters.

Chile's peso bid 0.57 percent stronger to 473.50 per dollar, its strongest since early January. The peso has clawed back more than 5 percent from a 7 percent loss spurred by news of the intervention in early January.

Brazil's real shed 0.6 percent to 1.669 per dollar, pulling back sharply after the currency hit a more than one-month high in the previous session.

A broadly stronger dollar and a slump in the euro, a key proxy for gauging demand for riskier assets like emerging market currencies, weighed on the real and Mexico's peso.

NO MEXICAN MEDDLING

Brazil's government unveiled budget cuts of about $30 billion Wednesday in a bid to regain credibility among investors worried that overspending is driving inflation higher and beyond the control of the central bank.

"Yesterday we had a positive economic context here, especially with the announcement of the budget cuts, it makes Brazil seem more trustworthy ... so the day after it is normal that you have an adjustment," said Andre Sacconato, economist at Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

Brazil has been waging an even more intense battle than Chile to contain the strength of the real, which is considered one of the most overvalued currencies in the world.

Brazil offers among the highest interest rates available, and a relentless flow of funds from global investors continues to bode further strength despite heavy intervention.

The central bank held a reserve currency swap auction Thursday, though the real did not react noticeably to the news.

The Mexican peso reversed steep early losses to trade flat at 12.0765 per dollar after Mexico's finance minister said the country will not intervene in foreign exchange markets, brushing off complaints from exporters who want a weaker peso.

Mexico's peso has lagged the gains in other emerging markets currencies, giving policymakers more room to stay on the sidelines.

But some had begun to bet Mexico could follow suit with greater intervention after the peso gained around 4 percent since November to hit a nearly 2-1/2 year high last month. (Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: =DJ UPDATE: Brazil Dollar Inflows Surge In Jan To $15.5B
text:
(Updates with analyst comments) 


 
   By Gerald Jeffris 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil continued to register voluminous dollar flows into its economy in January, revealing the limited effect of recent government efforts to curb strong incoming investment and a strengthened local currency.

According to data released Wednesday by the country's central bank, net dollar receipts in the month rose to $15.51 billion from only $1.08 billion in the same month last year, reaching their highest monthly level since June 2007.

Analysts, meanwhile, noted the result was a good sign abundant global liquidity would help Brazil finance its growing current account deficit, even as it struggled to limit appreciation of the currency with market intervention.

"This strong inflow in forex spot markets attests that despite growing governmental intervention, Brazil continues to attract massive capital inflows," said Goldman Sachs economist Luis Cezario.

Dollar inflows began the month strong and surged still more late in the period as investors appeared to call the bluff on the government's recent moves to discourage heavy portfolio investment inflows amid prospects of rising domestic interest rates.

The central bank reported incoming investment in the month totaled $14.44 billion, while net inflows from foreign trade totaled $1.08 billion.

In the same period last year, Brazil saw investment dollar inflows of $1.22 billion and net trade outflows of $140 million.

Brazil's government so far this year has gone to extra efforts to discourage an influx of foreign currency into the economy, introducing forward dollar purchase auctions to help delay entrance of dollars and "reverse" currency swaps that allow investors to exchange dollar-indexed bonds for paper linked to domestic interest rates.

In a sign of some market reaction, however, the trend for strong incoming dollar flows appeared to slow slightly in the first four days of February. The central bank reported dollar inflows in that period totaled only $39 million, compared to $1.86 billion in the same period last year. Early February result was based on net disinvestment of $118 million and incoming trade flows of $157 million.

Goldman Sach's Cezario said given the heavy dollar inflows this year to date, the government could be forced to introduce still more currency control measures to avoid further strengthening of the real.

"In all, we believe that the government will allow the Brazilian real to remain around BRL1.65 per U.S. dollar for a while, perhaps tolerating a slow appreciation toward BRL1.60 while inflation continues to be a concern," he said. "However, as the real continues to appreciate, we believe that the government may implement additional measures to curb capital inflows and arrest its appreciation, such as increases in IOF taxation on foreign investment and the introduction of more capital and reserve requirements on forex transactions."

With the heavy incoming dollar flows in January, Brazil's central bank Wednesday reported it purchased $7.99 billion in spot market currency auctions to build its foreign reserves. In the first four days of February, the bank purchased $2.84 billion.

Meanwhile, the central bank reported local banks reduced their short dollar positions to $11.02 billion in January from $16.78 billion the previous month. The reduction came after the central bank increased bank's reserve requirements on short positions.

Net foreign currency flowing into Brazil ended 2010 at $24.35 billion in 2010, down from $28.73 billion in 2009.

Still, heavy incoming portfolio investment inflows have continued to limit the government's success in protecting local industries from accelerating imports and a difficult outlook for exports brought by a strong local currency.

Brazil's currency, the real, has gained more than 30% against the dollar over the past 24 months, ending Wednesday's trading at BRL1.6599 to the dollar.

Yields on longer-term interest rate futures dropped <0#DIJ:> amid market chatter that the new government could deliver cuts close to 50 billion reais ($83.3 billion) later this week, analysts said.

By clamping down hard on government stimulus, the country's central bank may not have to raise interest rates as much as the market was expecting in order to contain fears that inflation could spiral out of policymakers' control.

Francisco Carvalho, head of currency trading at Sao Paulo-based Liquidez Corretora, Brazil's biggest currency futures broker, "intervention could be heavier" if the real gains further.

title: Brazil Currency  Market Wilts Under Weight Of Bank  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Central Bank of Brazil flexed its muscles Monday in a series of moves that weighed heavily on the currency market, taking a more aggressive tack in an effort to contain the real's appreciation against the U.S. dollar.

During Monday's session, the bank held two auctions to buy dollars on the spot market as well as the sale of forward dollar purchase contracts. The moves appeared to build on heavy dollar purchases by the central bank last week, traders said.

"The bank is certainly showing greater aggressiveness," said Alberto Orsovay, a dealer at Sao Paulo-based brokerage Hencorp Commcor.

Brazil has started 2011 with a concerted effort to contain the real's strength against the U.S. dollar, implementing heavy dollar purchases and other measures designed to stifle the wave of foreign investment flooding into Latin America's largest economy.

Investors seeking high rates of return have flocked to Brazil, lured by the country's towering interest rates and solid economic fundamentals. That has sent the real to gains of more than 30% against the greenback since the start of 2009.

The interventions undercut the real Monday, with the currency weakening to BRL1.6755 to the dollar as of 1857 GMT, according to Telekurs via Factset. The real closed Friday at BRL1.6725 to the dollar.

Despite the real's weakness in the wake of the central bank's latest moves, the broader trend remained tilted toward further appreciation of the currency, according to traders.

"It's complicated," Orsovay said. "Foreigners want to put money into Brazil, and the central bank is trying to hold the line on the foreign-exchange rate to facilitate exports."

The primary culprit is Brazil's benchmark Selic base interest rate, which currently stands at 11.25%. Alexandre Tombini, the new central bank president, faces a tough task balancing new President Dilma Rousseff's pledge to lower interest rates with the bank's promise to fight inflation.

For now, inflation is dictating the fight. Inflation ended 2010 at 5.91%--the highest since 2004--and is expected to continue climbing in January. The Brazilian Census Bureau, or IBGE, will release January's IPCA consumer price index Tuesday, with economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires expecting a climb of 0.79%.

Many economists believe the central bank is already behind the curve in its fight against inflation and will need to raise interest rates further. That will attract even more attention from foreign investors and place additional pressure on the foreign-exchange rate, economists said.

The central bank, meanwhile, is likely betting that aggressive action will bear fruit similar to what happened in January. Brazil registered dollar inflows of more than $12 billion in the first month of 2011, but the central bank sopped up more than $7 billion worth of greenbacks that helped stop the real from posting any appreciable gains for the month.

January's relative success means that Brazil's currency market will likely see a steady dose of the same measures--spot-market auctions, reverse swaps and forward-dollar contract sales--to keep the real stable in the face of steady inflows, Hencorp Commcor's Orsovay said.

title: Emerging Mkts Spend Big On  Forex Intervention  Amid Dubious Success
text:
-Emerging-Market Currencies Rising Despite Interventions

-Effectiveness of Interventions Seen As Mixed

-Interventions Bring Costs Of Soaking Up Excess Liquidity


 
   By Erin McCarthy and Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market countries have been undertaking costly interventions to hold down the value of their currencies, but how effective these efforts have been in containing investment inflows is debatable.

Countries from Brazil to South Korea have raised their reserves, taxed outside investments or instituted other types of capital controls to prevent foreign inflows from driving up their currencies. Yet the success in halting currency appreciation remains hard to gauge, with the focus more on slowing the rate of increase rather than on reversing it. At the same time, the interventions have imposed a battery of hidden costs on these countries' central banks and capital markets.

In Brazil, where taxes have been placed on various types of foreign flows and where the central bank has been buying up U.S. dollars on a nearly daily basis, the real has generally stayed on an upward path. It was at BRL1.6722 recently, according to CQG, putting it up roughly 1.7% since increased taxes were announced on outside investments in October.

Still, HSBC strategist Maya Hernandez estimated that the real might have strengthened to as much as BRL1.50 to the dollar, without the policy moves.

"There is a limit to how much [countries] can intervene," she said. "So, going forward, the best intervention can hope for is stability [in the currency] or a slowdown in the pace of appreciation," she said.

In South Korea, policymakers have implemented a cap on banks' foreign-exchange forward positions and imposed a levy against banks' balance of nondeposit foreign-currency debt. Still, the won has been strengthening lately, recently reaching about KRW1115 to the dollar, compared with KRW1165 in mid-December.

"Korea has tried it and it's [apparently] not working but who knows where we'd be without [the policy moves]," said Brown Brothers Harriman strategist Win Thin.

Some argue that these policies can backfire even with regards to the currency's valuation. For instance, Nomura Securities strategist Tony Volpon argued that Brazil's interventions have reduced volatility in its foreign-exchange market and so have made its super high-yielding currency, the real, even more attractive to outside investors.

"This is actually making the currency a better bet and is generating inflows that I don't think would have been there if there had been more actual volatility," he said.

What is more, intervening directly in foreign-exchange markets can be expensive for central banks, which must issue interest-bearing bonds to soak up the excess local currency liquidity that is created in the process.

As Brazil's central bank continues to purchase a mix of euros and dollars, which pay rates of around 1.5% to 2%, it has to offset the added market liquidity by issuing debt at an average local cost of 11%. That 9% shortfall on its reserves amounts to "a very big negative carry," said Nomura's Volpon. "They're really stretching the edge of the envelope by this kind of intervention." He estimated that the costs of sterilization for Brazil may have reached up to 40 billion Brazilian reais in 2010.

Chile in January launched a $12 billion currency-market intervention program. That foreign-exchange intervention has been more successful because it had a "combined coordinated policy response," Volpon said. Chile initiated a large dollar-purchasing program and at the same time held interest rates steady in January. According to CQG, the Chilean peso has weakened to CLP479.05 to the dollar, compared to a close of CLP466.65 on Jan. 3.

As with Chile, Colombia has also made several moves to weaken its currency, including making daily dollar purchases of at least $20 million and placing restrictions on public-sector flows.

Beyond building their reserves, emerging markets in Asia and Latin America have taken other steps. Taiwan last year tightened restrictions on foreign investments in certain short-term local-currency products. In October, Thailand imposed a tax on income that foreign investors could earn on Thai bonds.

While capital controls can be cheaper to implement, they can also have far-reaching effects on investor sentiment. While the jitters that they create among investors might help in keeping speculators away in the short term, the longer-term impact on sentiment is hard to gauge.

"Investors are getting spooked," said Brown Brothers Harriman's Thin. "What if [the restrictions] get out of control? If you prick investor confidence, it's hard to get it back."

Meanwhile, inflation pressure is becoming more of a headache for emerging markets everywhere, a development that will make it even more complicated for policymakers looking to fight price pressures and keep their currencies from rising too much. By raising rates to battle inflation, policymakers risk pushing up their currencies even more.

-By Erin McCarthy and Anjali Cordeiro; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com [ 04-02-11 1625GMT ]

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil industry shrinks in Dec as  currency  weighs
text:
* Industrial output contracts 0.7 pct in December from Nov

* Production up 10.5 pct in 2010, biggest gain since 1986

* Yields on interest rate futures fall on industry data (Recasts, adds analyst comments, interest rate futures)

By Elzio Barreto

SAO PAULO, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Industrial production in Brazil unexpectedly fell in December from the previous month, ending the year on a sour note as manufacturers struggle with a strong real and a flood of cheap imports.

The surprise contraction could signal a slowdown in Latin America's largest economy and help ease pressure on the central bank to increase interest rates to cool growth and inflation. Yields on interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> fell after the data were released.

Industrial output fell 0.7 percent in December from November <BRIO=ECI>, while November figures were revised lower to a 0.2 percent decline from a drop of 0.1 percent, statistics agency IBGE said on Wednesday.

The weak figures could spark calls for the central bank to intervene more aggressively in the foreign exchange market to prevent Brazil's real <BRBY> from gaining further. A strong real is making local products expensive compared to imports and making it harder for Brazilian exporters to sell goods abroad.

The real firmed 4.6 percent in 2010, on top of a 34 percent rally the previous year, spurring a jump in imports and prompting analysts at Goldman Sachs to call it the world's most overvalued major currency.

Despite an otherwise strong economy -- surging retail sales, record-low unemployment and rising wages -- the industry data suggest that foreign manufacturers are increasingly reaping the benefits of Brazil's consumption boom.

"The very weak performance at the end of the year justifies the concerns by the government and manufacturers about the very strong currency," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at brokerage CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

"Amid strong consumption in the country, production is just not responding."

Despite the decline in December, industrial output climbed 10.5 percent for the whole of 2010, the biggest annual gain since 1986, the IBGE said. In 2009, when Brazil was recovering from a brief recession, production slumped 7.4 percent.

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures fell across the board on Wednesday as investors reduced bets for an increase in borrowing costs in the months ahead. With Brazil's rates already among the world's highest, an increase in borrowing costs could lure more capital into the country and increase pressure on the national currency.

The yield on the contract due July 2011 <DIJN1>, one of the most heavily-traded contracts of the session, dipped to 11.90 percent from 11.91 percent late on Tuesday. The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2> fell to 12.34 percent from 12.38 percent.

INDUSTRIAL SECTORS

Production had been expected to rise 0.85 percent in December from November, according to the median estimate of 12 analysts in a Reuters survey. Forecasts for the increase ranged from of 0.4 percent to 1.5 percent.

Among industrial sectors surveyed, 11 posted a decline in production, led by a 13.3 percent slump in electronic materials and communications equipment. Fifteen sectors increased output, including office material and computers and chemical products.

In broader industrial categories, output of capital goods fell 0.5 percent in December from November. Production of consumer goods dropped 0.9 percent month on month, while durable consumer goods output slipped 0.6 percent.

Industrial production climbed 2.7 percent in December compared with the same month in 2009 <BRIOY=ECI>, far less than the 5.3 percent median forecast in the Reuters survey. Estimates ranged from 4.5 percent to 6.9 percent.

title: Brazil Real Slightly Weaker On Egypt, Euro Zone Inflation
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real was trading slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar early Wednesday on Euro Zone inflation worries and continued uncertainties surrounding the Egyptian political crisis.

Early in the session, the real was trading at BRL1.6648 to the dollar, according to Telekurs via Factset. The real ended Tuesday's session at BRL1.6625.

The Egyptian political crisis has led to wobbly currency and commodities markets worldwide. For Brazil, the crisis has meant an increase in risk aversion by global investors.

"The Brazilian currency market is basically in wait-and-see mode," said a Sao Paulo trader who wished not to be named. "We're waiting to see how the Egyptian crisis plays out."

Meanwhile, the Euro Zone's producer price index, released earlier Wednesday, showed a 0.8% rise in December over November, the biggest jump in two years. The 12-month figure was 5.3%, fueling ideas that the European Central Bank will have to hike interest rates.

Higher European interest rates would tend to divert global investors from emerging markets like Brazil toward Europe.

The Brazilian market is also overshadowed by the possibility of fresh government intervention. Brazil's government has intervened frequently in the market in recent months in a frank attempt to stem the appreciation of the Brazilian currency. The strong real hurts Brazilian exports.

"At any moment, the government can call an auction to soak up dollar liquidity," said the Sao Paulo trader.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Chile  currencies  hit 1-mo highs
text:
* Brazil real, Chilean pesos hit nearly 1-month highs

* Mexican peso firms 1 pct, below 12/dlr level

* Strong U.S. manufacturing data boosts growth hopes

* Brazil real firms 0.6 pct (Recasts; adds comment, updates closing prices)

By Jean Luis Arce and Elzio Barreto

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO(Reuters) - Brazil's and Chile's currencies hit nearly one-month highs Tuesday and Mexico's peso broke the 12 per dollar level after surveys showed global factories were gaining steam in January.

Bets that Brazil and Chile will raise interest rates to cool strong growth and rising inflation have boosted the allure of their currencies despite major intervention programs.

A survey released Tuesday showed the U.S. manufacturing sector expanded at its fastest pace in almost seven years in January, following similar surveys showing growth in Europe's and China's factories.

Mexico's peso, which closely tracks the outlook for the U.S. economy, led gains with a more than 1 percent surge to strengthen past the psychological 12-per-dollar level.

"There was good data in Europe and good data in the United States that are helping the whole risk trade," said Ramses Villela, head of currency trading at Bulltick Capital Markets in Mexico City, referring to bets on assets like stocks, emerging market currencies and commodities.

Chile's peso bid 0.69 percent firmer at 479.70 per U.S. dollar, driven by a record price for copper, the country's main export.

The Chilean peso has gained around 4 percent against the dollar in since mid-January, cutting back into the 7 percent loss it suffered after the central bank launched a $12 billion currency intervention early last month.

BACK BELOW 12

Mexico's peso firmed 1.04 percent to 11.99 per dollar, nearing an almost 2-1/2-year high hit last month.

The Mexican peso has gained more than 4 percent from a November intraday low as improving U.S. economic data promises to support solid demand for Mexico's exports.

A monthly poll showed that analysts following Mexico's economy raised their expectations for both growth and inflation this year. But some analysts said the stronger peso will curb the need for an interest rate hike in Mexico.

"We believe the currency appreciation will absorb the inflation pressures from higher food prices and therefore allow (Mexico's central bank) to leave the policy rate unchanged throughout the year," wrote Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura in New York, in a note to clients.

Mexico placed 25 billion pesos ($2.08 billion) of a new 10-year bond Tuesday with a yield of 7.44 percent.

Brazil's real gained in spite of heavy intervention in the previous session by the central bank, which held three dollar-forward auctions and two spot-dollar auctions in a bid to undermine the real's strength.

"The combination of lower risk aversion and expectations of higher rates in Brazil beats anything they put there," said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington. "Money is still pouring in."

Brazil's economy is posting solid growth and the central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rates from 11.25 percent to 12.50 percent by year-end, boosting the appeal of local assets to yield-hungry investors.

The Brazilian real was bid 0.6 percent stronger at 1.662 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market. (Additional reporting and writing by Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Mexico  currencies  hit 2-wk low on Egypt
text:
* Brazil calls first-ever currency forwards auction

* Mexico peso, Brazil real hit around 2-week lows

* Mexico peso loses 1.3 pct, Brazil's real 0.36 pct

* Chile's peso up 1.8 pct in week on rate hike bets (Recasts to reflect reversal in region's markets)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Global jitters over political unrest in Egypt drove Mexico's peso and Brazil's real on Friday to their weakest levels in about two weeks as investors dumped riskier assets across the board.

Egypt's president imposed curfews in the country as anti-government protests turned violent, sparking fears about similar unrest across the Middle East, which could lead to higher oil prices that could hurt global growth. For details, see [ID:nLDE70Q2OZ]

"Above all there were rumors that they could close the Suez Canal, that would hit trade and the region and get passed on around the world," said Mario Copca, an analyst at brokerage Vanguardia in Mexico City. "If they manage to calm down the social unrest over the weekend, we will surely see a big bounce back in markets," he added.

Analysts said months of solid gains in riskier assets like emerging market currencies and stocks had set markets up to be quick to take profits on any surprisingly negative news. Before Friday's losses, the Mexican peso was up about 4 percent against the dollar from an intraday low in November.

"The market was ripe for a correction," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, a managing director for emerging markets at TD Securities in Toronto. "Hopefully this will not turn out to be anything bigger than a healthy correction."

The real <BRBY> gave up early gains to trade 0.36 percent weaker at 1.683 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, its weakest level since Jan. 14.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> fell 1.31 percent to 12.1950 per dollar to trade at its weakest since January 11. It was the worst one-day loss for the peso since late November, when it began to rally on an improving outlook for the economy in the United States, its top trading partner.

However, the Chilean peso <CLP=>, which closed trading before the worst of Friday's global losses, gained 0.17 pct to 484.20. The peso gained 1.8 percent during the week to trade at its strongest since a $12 billion central bank intervention program at the beginning of January.

The peso has been backed by bets that the central bank will resume hiking interest rates next month after pausing in January to complement the intervention program. [ID:nN13283103]

BRAZIL'S REAL PROBLEMS

The events in Egypt had a more significant impact on Brazil's real than earlier attempts by the central bank to curb the currency's appreciation.

The country's central bank on Friday said it will buy dollar forwards via three separate auctions on Monday, the latest in a series of technical measures to curb the currency's recent rise. [ID:nN28245256]

The real barely budged after the announcement.

"If you just think about the number of IPOs (initial public offerings) in the works, the amount of cash which came into Brazil during the last few days, the last month ... there is not much you can do," said Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora, one of Brazil's biggest currency brokerages.

Other analysts were skeptical about the nature of the auctions. The central bank said it would auction contracts for the following settlement dates: Feb. 9, 16 and 23.

"I have strong doubts about the forward auctions because they are all being called on Wednesdays and the inflows won't necessarily happen on those days," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

If the market gets used to them every Wednesday, investors will also find a way around them, he said. (Additional reporting by Noe Torres in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil 's real up on minutes,  intervention  eyed
text:
* Brazil's real adds 0.2 pct after central bank minutes

* Bank seen stepping up intervention via swaps, forwards

* Chilean peso up 0.4 pct, Mexican peso flat

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency, the real, pushed higher on Thursday after minutes from the country's latest central bank meeting indicated further interest rate hikes in the months ahead.

Rising prices are likely to force Brazil to keep increasing its benchmark interest rate, which would attract more foreign investment and boost the already overvalued local currency.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.24 percent stronger at 1.665 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market in early trading, getting closer to the 1.65-per-dollar level which could prompt more aggressive intervention in the market.

Meanwhile, higher copper prices pushed up the Chilean peso but Mexico's currency struggled to break free of the key 12-per-dollar level.

"The minutes (from Brazil's central bank meeting) showed even more interest rate hikes. The long end of the interest rate futures curve is continuing to rise, which shows the market is beginning to prepare for a longer tightening cycle," said Andre Ferreira, director of the Futura Corretora brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"That will end up bringing more dollars to the market," he added.

In the minutes from last week's rate-setting meeting, Brazil's central bank said it would require "prompt corrections" to bring inflation back on target. [ID:nN27240799]

At that meeting, policy-makers raised Brazil's benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent and indicated further hikes were to come.

But the real's gains could force the authorities to take even more aggressive action in the market to curb the currency's appreciation and protect local manufacturers.

"We'll see two auctions today for sure," said Futura's Ferreira, referring to the central bank's daily purchases of dollars in the spot market.

The central bank may also later announce another reverse swap auction, which has the same effect as buying dollars in the futures market, or even call its first forwards auction. [ID:nN25294325]

COPPER RISE BOOSTS PESO

The Chilean peso <CLP=>, which has also become a source of concern for the country's authorities, firmed 0.43 percent to 486.7 per dollar.

The currency was boosted as the price of copper, the country's main export and economic lifeline, rose on supply worries. [ID:nLDE70Q1B6]

Earlier this month, Chile announced a record $12 billion in dollar purchases during 2011. The government has said it will also invest its military copper funds abroad and look to increase local financing of foreign businesses in an effort to ease pressure on the peso. [ID:nN26126403]

The Mexican currency <MXN=> was flat at 11.99 per dollar in early trading, struggling to definitively break the 12-per-dollar level.

Mexico's non-interventionist stance has made the peso a relatively attractive bet in the region but the 12-per-dollar level has proved to be a strong barrier of resistance. ( Editing by W Simon )

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real flat; Fed pledge supports region
text:
* Brazil real flat after latest intervention move

* Mexico peso firms 0.79 pct, Chile peso adds 0.8 pct (Adds comments, updates prices; changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Samantha Pearson and Walter Brandimarte

SAO PAULO/NEW YORK, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real shook off the latest intervention measures deployed by local authorities to end unchanged on Wednesday, while Mexico's and Chile's peso currencies were supported by solid U.S. housing data.

Latin American currencies received further support from a pledge by the U.S. Federal Reserve that it would keep up its bond-buying program, which has boosted higher-risk assets around the world. For details, see [ID:nN25283937]

By underpinning demand for the U.S. bond market to keep yields down, the Fed is pushing investors to seek higher returns in other assets.

"We will continue to have a very large overhang of liquidity," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York. "That continues to point to currency appreciation in Latin America."

The pledge from the Fed after its first meeting of the year was largely anticipated by markets.

Low interest rates in the United States and across the industrialized world have boosted demand for Latin American assets, driving currencies to multiyear highs. Regional policymakers have waded into foreign exchange markets to weaken their respective currencies in an effort to protect the competitiveness of local manufacturers.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid unchanged at 1.669 per dollar on the local spot market, although it firmed in international trade <BRL=> after the Fed's statement.

Brazil's central bank said late on Tuesday that it could for the first time ever offer currency forwards at auction, adding to its growing toolbox of market mechanisms aimed at cooling the real's gains. [ID:nN25294325]

CLOSING LOOPHOLES

The lack of market reaction to the announcement was blamed on uncertainty about the frequency of such auctions as well as their aim, since the forwards market is tiny compared to Brazil's spot and futures markets.

Analysts said this latest measure is likely an attempt to keep speculators from trying to get around previous measures.

"The decision looks like an effort to close a loophole to capture all sides of the market," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York, in a research note.

Brazil has the highest yields in the region as it hikes interest rates to keep its strong economy from overheating.

The real is expected to keep strengthening until authorities introduce more drastic measures such as widespread quarantines or capital controls, analysts said.

"The next instrument (to be announced) could be some type of restriction on a specific inflow, something like the quarantine," said Jorge Lima, a consultant at Previbank DTVM in Sao Paulo. "But Brazil can't shut itself off from long-term investment, so it would have to be a very specific restriction on speculative transactions."

The Mexican and Chilean pesos both firmed on Wednesday, helped by data showing U.S. single-family home sales in December rose to their highest in eight months.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.79 percent to 12.0025 per dollar.

"The outlook for the U.S. housing sector could be improving, and that is a good sign for the economy. (The United States) is our biggest trading partner and so this is having a good influence on the peso," said Mario Copca, an analyst at the Vanguardia brokerage in Mexico City.

In Chile, the peso <CLP=CL> firmed 0.8 percent to 489.90 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, was supported by the U.S. economic data.

The Chilean peso closed at its strongest close since the country's central bank announced a $12 billion currency intervention Jan. 3 aimed at keeping the currency in check.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil 's real up despite  intervention  move
text:
* Brazil's central bank says could buy dollar forwards

* Brazil's real adds 0.1 pct, Mexican peso up 0.4 pct

* Chile's peso gains 0.6 pct as copper price surges (Adds comments from Chile, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Nathalia Ferreira

SAO PAULO, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed on Wednesday despite the central bank's latest effort to curb the currency's appreciation and protect local manufacturers.

The bank said late on Tuesday that for the first time ever it could offer currency forwards at auction. The auctions would be similar to those currently conducted in the spot market but the contracts would be settled at a date in the future. [ID:nN25294325]

But the Brazilian real <BRBY> barely reacted, bidding 0.12 percent stronger at 1.667 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

The Mexican and Chilean pesos were also firmer on Wednesday as the dollar weakened broadly following U.S. President Barack Obama's promise of spending cuts. [ID:nLDE70P0HM]

Data showing U.S. single-family home sales in December rose to their highest in eight months also helped to boost the peso.

Economists and traders said one reason for the real's muted reaction to the central bank's assault was that it was not clear exactly how often these auctions would be called and the reason behind them.

"If there is some specific deal, if there is going to be an inflow from 'company X' on Wednesday next week for example, the central bank already knows about it and it could use this measure," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"But the intention behind this measure is still not clear...if the point is to control the exchange rate then it would be better to just use reverse swaps as they have a more direct effect."

Also, the forwards market is tiny compared to Brazil's spot and futures market. As such, they said, this latest measure is more likely to be an attempt to close off a loophole and make the central bank's current intervention policy more efficient.

"Judging how the liquidity is concentrated between the spot market (average US$2bln daily) and the futures market (as much as 7 times that) with the forward market much smaller...the measure should not have much of an impact," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York, in a research note.

"The decision looks like an effort to close a loophole to capture all sides of the market," she added.

Thirdly, Brazil still remains an attractive place to invest and the real will continue to appreciate until the authorities introduce drastic measures such as widespread quarantines or capital controls, they said.

"The next instrument (to be announced) could be some type of restriction on a specific inflow, something like the quarantine," said Jorge Lima, a consultant at Previbank DTVM in Sao Paulo. "But Brazil can't shut itself off from long-term investment, so it would have to be a very specific restriction on speculative transactions."

WEAK DOLLAR BOOSTS REGION

Elsewhere, the Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.43 percent to 12.045 per dollar in early trading, as the greenback weakened broadly.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.57 percent to 489.90 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, surged due to the weaker dollar.

"The peso is strengthening because of a better performance by European stocks, copper has also recovered and the euro is maintaining an upward tendency," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

" With the markets so positive, the tendency is for the peso to keep firming" he added.

The greenback was suffering after a promise of spending cuts from U.S. President Barack Obama late on Tuesday cemented expectations the Fed will retain faith in its ultra-loose policy.

title: UPDATE 1- Brazil  steps up  forex intervention  with forwards
text:
* Brazil cenbank to offer currency forwards for first time

* Forward auctions add to moves to curb real's rally (Adds analyst comments, more details on cenbank measure)

By Elzio Barreto

SAO PAULO (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank said Tuesday it could offer currency forwards in market auctions for the first time ever, adding to several moves in recent weeks to help curb a rally in the national currency.

The bank said only financial firms already registered as dealers in its electronic system may participate in the auctions.

Just like its regular currency auctions in the spot foreign exchange market, the bank will call the forward auctions and will unveil terms of the transactions, with the key difference that contracts are settled at a future date.

Brazil's currency, the real, firmed 4.6 percent last year against the dollar, following gains of 34 percent in 2009, raising concerns among executives and government officials about the effects on local exporters and a flood of cheap imports into the country. The surge has prompted Goldman Sachs recently to dub the real the world's most overvalued major currency.

The central bank began selling reverse currency swaps on Jan. 14 for the first time since May 2009. The swaps, a currency derivative that effectively allows the bank to buy U.S. dollars on the futures market, came on top of an increase in reserve requirements on banks' short U.S. dollar positions and its daily spot market auctions.

"They've announce so many tools, it's looking like a patchwork of measures," said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington. "It seems they feel they are losing the battle, that's why they keep adding more tools."

"It looks like they are finding holes and putting their fingers in the dam, but then another hole comes up and they have to put another finger," he added.

Like several emerging economies, Brazil has had to tackle a flood of cheap capital from abroad as rates in the United States, Japan and other developed nations hover close to zero. Countries including South Korea, Taiwan, Peru and Turkey have taken several measures to stop speculative capital inflows that are aiming for higher yields in emerging markets.

The currency headache will likely last for a while, with private money flowing into emerging markets seen reaching more than $1 trillion by 2012, the Institute of International Finance global bank group said on Monday. The IIF warned it may become harder for countries to reduce the effects of the flood of capital.

title: ANALYSIS-Latin America  FX intervention  may be here to stay
text:
* Commodity prices, Chinese demand to pressure currencies

* Brazil real would be 10 pct firmer without intervention

* Measures more acceptable because of Chile, China

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO (Reuters) - Intervention to tame Latin America's currencies could be here to stay as strong Chinese demand for commodities and rising inflation make governments reluctant to cede control over their markets.

Brazil, Peru, Colombia and even Chile's conservative authorities have aggressively intervened over recent months, surprising nerve-racked investors with an arsenal of measures.

Politicians such as Brazil's finance minister have blamed the rallies on the developed world, slamming the United States for keeping interest rates low and the dollar weak through its quantitative easing policy.

But rising Chinese demand for many of Latin America's key exports is likely to support commodity prices even as the dollar recovers, pushing the region's currencies to new highs and maintaining the need for intervention.

"There's a long-term case for Chinese demand as a fundamental element underpinning Latin American currencies," says Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin American research at IDEAglobal in New York.

"This has become one of the major driving forces for Latin American economies, especially those that export traditional commodity-based materials such as Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia -- just about the entire gamut of Latin American countries."

China's trade with Latin America grew ten-fold between 2000 and 2007, according to the U.S. Congressional Research Service, and in 2009 the Asian giant overtook the United States to become Brazil's top trading partner.

Higher inflation, partly as a result of a global surge in commodity prices and food costs, is also likely to force policymakers to raise interest rates across the region, boosting currencies further.

Brazil's central bank is expected to hike its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent later Wednesday to curb inflation, currently at a six-year high.

Chile is also set to raise lending costs in coming months.

"As the central bank keeps raising its benchmark rate and attracting foreign investment, it's likely that we'll see additional (currency) measures," said Alejandro Puente, an economist with BBVA Chile in Santiago.

INTERVENTION: THE NEW NORM?

Although countries such as Brazil are working on long-term solutions to bring down interest rates and relieve pressure on their currencies, intervention is likely to remain a popular and necessary option in the meantime.

Without such measures, the Brazilian real and the Chilean peso would now be trading around 10 percent stronger at 1.50 and 450 per dollar respectively, analysts say.

"Lock-up" periods on foreign capital could be imposed in Brazil while countries such as Colombia may choose to extend dollar purchases.

"Oh intervention does work! It may not change the theoretical value of where the currency should be but in the short-term it absolutely does have an impact on markets," says Michael Woolfolk, senior currency strategist at BNY Mellon in New York.

The difficulty of exiting intervention policies is amplified by their beggar-thy-neighbor nature.

Many currency speculators make money via regional cross trades (buying one Latin American currency against another), which means whichever country ditches intervention first risks luring the wave of cash washing around the continent.

Before Chile's central bank shocked investors earlier this month with a $12 billion dollar-buying plan, many banks were advising buying the peso against the Brazilian real. Those same banks then advised clients to buy the Mexican peso against Chile's currency, driving Mexico's peso to a two-year high this week. Now speculation is rising Mexico may also have to intervene to match its neighbors' aggressive efforts.

The proliferation of such policies has also made them more acceptable among investors, giving countries little incentive to ditch them prematurely.

"Chile gave intervention more respectability because its central bank has long held the view that intervention is not successful in the medium term and that the (19)90s capital controls had limited impact at best," says Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at 4Cast Inc in Washington.

China's growing economic clout, achieved despite its fixed-rate foreign exchange policy, could also be changing the rules of the game globally, says Paul Biszko, senior strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

"There is the view that: China is doing it, the United States is doing it indirectly, why can't we do it?!" (Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real firms, helped by rate hike bets
text:
* Mexican peso retreats after break below 12/dlr

* Easing euro zone worries support region's currencies

* Brazil's real up 0.3 pct, Chile's peso up 0.2 pct (Updates to afternoon)

By Samantha Pearson and Sean Mattson

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed on Tuesday ahead of an expected interest rate hike, while Mexico's peso retreated after breaking the psychological 12 per dollar barrier for the first time since late 2008.

Expectations that Brazil's central bank will have to raise interest rates on Wednesday helped the real to outperform the region. For more, see: [ID:nSPG003198]

Brazil has been reluctant to raise its already high borrowing costs for fear of attracting even more short-term, speculative money. The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.3 percent stronger at 1.676 per dollar on the local spot market.

Rising inflation has made an interest rate hike seem inevitable. While the consensus among economists and market participants is for a 50-basis-point rise, the market has also partially priced in a 75-basis-point increase.

"(A) recent surge in food commodity prices ... could aggravate the situation further and could further deteriorate inflation expectations," Zeina Latif, chief Brazil economist at RBS in Sao Paulo, said in a research note.

Rising investor sentiment in Germany and signs that policymakers will eventually firm up plans to ease the euro zone's debt crisis helped support riskier assets worldwide and weakened the dollar. [ID:nLDE70H0UU] [ID:nLDE70H0DQ]

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> also firmed 0.2 percent to 490.20 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, rose because of the weak dollar. [ID:nLDE70H0DP]

PESO PULLBACK

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.51 percent to 12.0325 per dollar as investors took profits after the peso broke below the key 12-per-dollar level on Monday for the first time since a steep devaluation in October 2008.

The Mexican peso, which has lagged the gains in other emerging market currencies, strengthened more than 5 percent from a November intraday low to Tuesday's session high boosted by an improving outlook for U.S. and Mexican growth.

"It looks like a good opportunity to lock in some of the gains," said Marjorie Hernandez, an analyst at HSBC in New York, who expected the peso to firm back toward 11.80 per dollar.

"The underlying story hasn't changed. It's still a great macro call for the year, people believe the U.S. is going to recover, it's still cheap, and they still aren't intervening," she added.

The Mexican currency has also been supported by flows from investors looking for a haven from intervention tactics of other central banks.

Mexico's peso is barely clawing back toward its pre-crisis levels, but analysts say Mexico's central bank could move to increase a program under which it is selling $600 million of dollar put options every month to local banks.

Luis Flores, an analyst at brokerage IXE in Mexico City, said a bigger options program would still be seen "as a more patient and subtle" reaction compared with intervention mechanisms in Chile, Brazil and Turkey. The shock of the announcement could derail peso gains, but "only for a matter of days," he said.

"Fundamentally it will not remove the favorable tendency for the peso," Flores said.

The options allow local banks to sell dollars to the central bank at a slightly preferential rate when the peso has been on a winning streak and is below a 20-day moving average. By sucking up dollars directly from banks, policymakers can keep some dollar off the open market.

Gabriel Casillas, an analyst at JP Morgan in Mexico City, said the central bank could take a bolder move to begin daily dollar purchases if further peso gains take the currency quickly and significantly below 12 per dollar.

"This would still be a market-friendly mechanism -- relative to capital control measures that other countries have recently adopted -- and could reduce the speed of appreciation of the peso," Casillas wrote in a report. (Writing by Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Brazil Currency  Market Eyes  Intervention ,  Central Bank  Move
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's currency market joined in the ebullient mood coming out of Europe on Tuesday, but cast a wary eye at the central bank's heavy hand ahead of monetary authority's first meeting of 2011.

Global markets got a boost earlier in the session from a series of successful bond sales by European Union member countries, including Belgium, Greece, Hungary and Spain, traders said. Brazil's real joined the euro and other currencies to post solid gains against the greenback.

Tensions surrounding the debt and fiscal crisis in Europe appear to be waning, placing investor focus back on fundamentals. Thanks to sky-high interest rates and a booming economy, Brazil has enjoyed a select position among investors seeking high returns.

The real has reflected the return to normal in recent sessions, continuing a relentless appreciation that has seen the currency strengthen more than 30% against the dollar since the start of 2009. As of 1850 GMT, the real traded at BRL1.6745, stronger from Monday's close at BRL1.6800, according to Telekurs via Factset.

The real's strength has drawn the attention from new President Dilma Rousseff's administration, including new central bank chief Alexandre Tombini. As the real approached the BRL1.67 to the dollar mark Tuesday, the central bank quickly acted by holding two spot-market auctions to snap up dollars.

The bank purchased an undisclosed volume of dollars at BRL1.6727 and BRL1.6758 to the dollar.

The return of daily double dollar auctions followed last week's reverse-swap auction, the first held by the bank since May 2009. The reverse-swap auctions allow investors to swap foreign-exchange positions in futures markets for government paper linked to interest rates.

Quick action has so far been the calling card of Brazil's government under Rousseff. In two swift moves under her leadership, Brazil has forced banks to make compulsory reserve deposits on foreign-exchange futures contracts and allowed the country's Sovereign Wealth Fund to operate in the foreign exchange derivatives market. The measures were designed to stem further appreciation of the real against the greenback.

Brazil's booming economy, however, is undercutting the administration's ability to use capital measures to stem the currency's appreciation. The central bank will likely raise interest rates Wednesday because of increasing inflationary pressures.

The country ended 2010 with an inflation rate of 5.9%, well above the government's year-end target of 4.5%. The government maintained the 4.5% target for 2011, but analysts and economists expect prices to once again top that figure.

While a rate hike is seen as necessary to contain rising prices, it will also prove a powerful lure for foreign investors seeking higher rates of return. Economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires expect the bank's Copom rate-setting panel to raise the benchmark Selic base interest rate by a half-percentage point to 11.25%.

title: *DJ Brazil Finance Minister: Budget Cuts Still Under Study
text:
14 Jan 2011 07:52 EDT *DJ  Brazil Finance Minister To Announce Budget Cuts Early Feb

14 Jan 2011 07:54 EDT *DJ  Brazil Fin Min: Foreign Exchange Intervention A Necessity

14 Jan 2011 08:18 EDT =DJ  Brazil Finance Minister: Budget Cuts Still Under Study

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's government is still studying 2011 budget cuts, with no specific target figure in mind, and will announce the size and shape of the cuts in early February, Finance Minister Guido Mantega told reporters Friday.

"There is no specific figure," he said, in a tape-recorded interview circulated by the ministry. "I can't tell you that it's 30 billion or 40 billion or 50 billion...We will announce the cuts in early February."

Press reports earlier Friday indicated the government was focused on cuts totaling some 50 billion Brazilian reais ($30 billion).

"We will aim for the maximum possible savings in the area of government operations," he said. "Social programs, health and education will be preserved."

Many economists have called for budget cuts as a way to counter rising Brazilian inflation. Inflation ended 2010 at 5.9%, well above the government's target for the year of 4.5%.

Mantega also commented on rising concerns over the appreciation of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar. The real has gained more than 30% against the dollar since 2009. The strong real hurts Brazilian exports.

"This is the time for greater intervention in the futures market," Mantega said, defending the government's decision Thursday to hold so-called reverse swap auctions. "The reverse swap auction is a classic device for reducing pressure on the dollar."

The Brazilian Central Bank will hold a reverse swap auction later Friday. The auction permits investors to exchange dollar positions in the futures market for positions tied to interest rates. The reduction in dollar positions reduces speculation and volatility in the foreign exchange market.

title: *DJ Brazil Fin Min: High Commodity Prices Driving Inflation
text:
14 Jan 2011 16:11 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Mantega: Recent Floods Will Have Impact On Food Prices

14 Jan 2011 16:12 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Mantega: Foreign-Exchange Intervention Was Necessary

14 Jan 2011 16:12 EDT *DJ  Brazil's Mantega: Dollar Would Be At BRL1.45-1.50 Without Action

14 Jan 2011 16:36 EDT =DJ  Brazil Finance Minister: High Commodity Prices Driving Inflation

RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)-Rising commodity prices were the driving force behind inflationary pressures in Brazil, which will also be affected by recent floods, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said late Friday.

"In 2010 and the start of 2011, we had inflation in food prices that hit practically all of the countries in Latin America," Mantega said. Inflation, however, wasn't based on supply--Brazil had its largest harvest ever in 2010--but on global demand for commodities, the minister said.

New President Dilma Rousseff and her cabinet have pledged to fight rising prices in Brazil, where consumer prices surged 5.9% in 2010--well above the government's official target of 4.5%. The central bank meets Wednesday, when it is expected to raise interest rates to cool price pressures.

Unfortunately, the recent natural disaster in the mountains northwest of the beachfront city of Rio de Janeiro will likely also have an impact on food prices in the near term, Mantega said. More than 500 people were killed in the flooding and landslides.

"I imagine that, in the areas where there was flooding, they are going to have elevated [food] prices," the minister said.

The rise in global commodity prices was also hitting export countries, where currencies are appreciating rapidly, according to Mantega. Brazil's government has recently implemented measures aimed at stopping speculative inflows and supporting the local currency, called the real.

"The measures are working," Mantega said. "We've been able to stabilize the currency at its current level."

The real, which closed trading Friday at BRL1.6825 to the dollar, would likely be trading between BRL1.45 and BRL1.50 to the dollar without intervention by Brazil's government, Mantega said.

Mantega was part of a cabinet meeting with Rousseff earlier Thursday, where he presented the Finance Ministry's five-year economic outlook for Brazil.

According to Mantega, the new president didn't discuss a raise in the minimum salary, which would stay at BRL545.
