title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile's peso up on rate move, Mexican peso dips
text:
* Brazil's real and Chilean peso both gain 0.5 pct

* Mexican peso dips 0.2 pct after U.S. jobs data

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Chile's currency firmed on Thursday, helped by bets the central bank would hike interest rates, drawing in yield-hungry investors even as policymakers intervene to weaken the currency.

Chile and Brazil's currencies were also supported by successful bond auctions in Spain and Italy that helped to ease euro zone fiscal concerns, while Mexico's peso dipped on a rise in U.S. jobless claims.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.47 percent to 488.20 per dollar as some investors in a divided market bet that Chile's central bank will hike its benchmark interest rate for the eighth consecutive time later on Thursday. [ID:nN13261867c]

"There should be an increase of 25 points," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago. "And we should keep seeing increases from here onward, especially because of the inflation pressures," he added.

Others think policymakers will leave borrowing costs steady so as not to lure even more hot money to the country and undermine the $12 billion intervention plan launched last week that knocked the peso off a nearly three year high.

Broadly supporting bids for riskier assets, Spain sold 3 billion euros of five-year bonds, raising the maximum amount targeted. Italy's auction of 5- and 15-year government bonds also went well. [ID:nLDE70C0IA].

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.48 percent stronger at 1.667 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The worries over Europe are diminishing a little... I'm not seeing any real difference to yesterday, we're continuing on the same track," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

However, investors were reluctant to push the currency much higher in case it triggered more aggressive government intervention in the market, he said.

MEXICAN PESO RETREATS FROM 2-YR HIGH

The Mexican currency <MXN=> slipped 0.21 percent to 12.0965 per dollar after jobless claims in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner, jumped to their highest level since October. [ID:nN13271305]

The news helped weaken the peso after the currency hit its strongest level since Oct. 2008 in the previous session. But overall, U.S. data was mixed, with higher producer prices and a jump in U.S. exports.

"The fact that there was inflation in the United States tells you the economy is recovering and it is not all bad," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones.

The peso has won favor among investors since it is one of the few currencies in the region which is not at risk from intervention.

However, Mexico's free-market orthodoxy has not been challenged too much with the peso barely clawing back from pre-crisis levels.

If the peso reaches 11.50 per dollar, the Mexican central bank could take measures similar to Chile's dollar-buying plan, said Benito Berber, an economist at Nomura in New York.

title: UPDATE 3- Brazil  cenbank sets  intervention  move as real firms
text:
* Brazil central bank to hold reverse swap auction

* Auction could be worth up to $1 billion

* Strength of currency is worry for government (Recasts with bank decision, details)

SAO PAULO, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank said it will launch a new currency measure on Friday, which could help curb the surging real and protect exports as developed and emerging economies lock horns over imbalances in trade and growth.

The central bank on Thursday said it would sell up to $1 billion of reverse currency swaps, a derivative that effectively allows the bank to buy U.S. dollars on the futures market, which could in turn help weaken the real <BRBY>.

The central bank has not deployed the derivatives since May 2009, and economists saw the move as squarely aimed at curbing gains in the real, which firmed 4.6 percent against the dollar last year after gaining 34 percent in 2009.

"They're adopting erratic measures, with intervention rules that are hardly clear," said Roberto Padovani, chief Brazil economist at WestLB. "The policy goal is to increase the uncertainty for those who trade in the Brazilian market."

Emerging markets around the world have seen their currencies surge, as their economic growth outpaces that of a number of still-struggling developed nations. Low interest rates in developed countries designed to spur economic growth -- most notably the United States and the 17-member euro zone -- have spurred huge inflows of capitals to countries like Brazil.

The trend has led to a wave of interventions around the world. Chile's central bank, for example, this month said it would buy $12 billion to try to tame the peso.

In Brazil the measures have ranged from daily auctions to buy dollars on the spot market to a reserve requirement, announced last week, on banks' short U.S. dollar positions.

The reverse currency swap to be launched in Brazil on Friday will be sold over as many as 20,000 contracts. They will include expirations in April and July 2011 and January 2012.

The auction will run from 12 p.m. to 12:30 p.m. local time (1400 to 1430 GMT), with the results announced after 12:45 p.m. (1445 GMT). For a factbox, see [ID:nN13101362].

But analysts say few government measures, if any, have had a long-term effect in Brazil.

The country's continued strong economy -- coupled with some of the world's highest interest rates -- has drawn money borrowed at near zero-rates abroad into Brazilian assets.

And the central bank, confronted with a consumer inflation rate that jumped to 5.91 percent in 2010, is expected to raise its benchmark lending rate to 11.25 percent from 10.75 percent at a meeting next Wednesday, which would likely put even more upward pressure on the real. [ID:nSPG003198]

"While more measures cannot be ruled out going ahead, one concern is that more dramatic steps ahead might lead observers to start wondering whether the currency regime can still be described as a truly floating exchange rate regime," BNP Paribas economist Marcelo Carvalho wrote to clients.

Brazil's finance minister has termed the global tensions an "international currency war," with countries such as the United States and China facing pressure to allow their currencies to strengthen further.

When used regularly for an extended period, reverse currency swaps are considered a tool of currency intervention. In the current context, they would be used to prevent the real from strengthening too much.

Under the agreement, the central bank agrees to pay investors Brazil's local interbank rate in exchange for a rate in U.S. dollars for the duration of the contract.

The difference between the two rates is calculated and paid out on a daily basis for the duration of the contract.

The central bank first started offering reverse currency swaps in February 2005, used them regularly until September 2008, and then once more on May 5, 2009.

Reverse currency swaps have been used on a one-off basis by the central bank to smooth out distortions in Brazil's currency markets, closing off arbitrage opportunities.

title: UPDATE:OppenheimerFunds Cuts Brazil, Mexico Sovereign-Debt Exposure
text:
(Updates with firm's complete name in first paragraph.)


 
   By Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--OppenheimerFunds's emerging-market bond funds have sold all their Mexican and Brazilian sovereign-debt holdings, and are paring exposure to currencies of countries intervening in foreign-exchange markets, a senior portfolio manager for the firm said in an interview.

Sara Zervos--who oversees about $11 billion in emerging-market debt for OppenheimerFunds and is among the biggest emerging-market portfolio managers in the U.S.--said her funds have reduced their exposure to Chile's peso and Brazil's real as central bankers in these countries take steps to prevent their currencies from appreciating.

The funds she manages cut their exposure to Brazil and Mexico sovereign bonds at the end of last year because they see little room for substantial returns on these assets, whose spreads with Treasurys are already narrow. In search of higher returns in emerging markets, her emerging-market teams are moving more money to higher yielding emerging-market corporate debt. For exposure to Brazil and Mexico, her funds now own only corporate debt from those countries.

Zervos's funds can also invest in local currency bonds to get exposure to a country's currency and benefit from any potential appreciation. Her funds are increasing their exposure to the South African rand, partly because it stands to benefit from increased demand for commodities.

Zervos's comments highlight the changing landscape that emerging-market fund managers are facing as money rushes into these fast-growing regions. As more money has moved to the developing world, spreads between emerging-market sovereign bonds and Treasurys have tightened significantly, making it harder to project big returns on such investments. Meanwhile, the surge in capital flows to developing countries has driven up their currencies, pushing local policymakers in countries from Brazil to Chile to intervene in foreign-exchange markets. That is making emerging-market investing more challenging.

"Last year was a pure rebound year, extending from 2009. We got through the double-dip fear and then it was all ships ahead," she said. "But this year we are worried about intervention, we are worried about central banks being behind the curve and it makes the outlook much trickier."

Earlier in January, Chile's central bank announced that it would intervene in the local currency market with plans to increase its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion in 2011 in an effort to hold down the peso and assuage the worries of Chile's exporters.

Zervos, who is based in New York, said her funds had a small exposure to Chile's peso, which she completely erased right after the intervention was announced, even though she has a strong fundamental outlook for the Chilean peso. Along similar lines she has cut back exposure her funds have to the Brazilian real via local currency bonds, bringing down that allocation to marketweight from overweight.

Brazil's central bank recently moved to reduce the size of banks' bets in the foreign-exchange market to protect the financial system and investors have grown more concerned that the government will be more aggressive in halting the currency's gain.

"There might be every macro reason in the world to love the Brazilian currency, but the randomness of policy to try and stop appreciation makes us want to have a smaller position," Zervos said.

Zervos, an emerging-markets veteran, is portfolio manager of the Oppenheimer International Bond Fund, Oppenheimer Emerging Markets Debt Fund, and Oppenheimer Global Strategic Income Fund. Her comments underscore how countries risk pushing even longer term investors away when they intervene in foreign-exchange markets.

"I tend to be more overweight stories with good fundamentals plus lack of intervention," she said. She is bullish on the Mexican peso on expectations that the U.S. economy will keep recovering and pull Mexico with it. Also, Mexican authorities don't interfere with the currency.

Zervos says despite her more cautious tone on Brazilian sovereign bonds, she is bullish on corporate debt from the country. "That's where the best bang for the buck is," she said, referring to high yield emerging-market corporate bonds.

-By Anjali Cordeiro, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com [ 12-01-11 1852GMT ]

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso hits 8-month high, Brazil lags
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Mexican peso gains 0.6 pct, Chilean peso up 0.6 pct

* Brazil's real dips 0.06 pct as intervention fears weigh (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso jumped to an 8-month high on Tuesday, helped by surprisingly strong local industrial output data.

Chile's currency firmed after rising copper prices helped reverse some of the recent losses from a central bank intervention launched last week, while Brazil's currency was held back by concerns of further meddling in markets.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.6 percent to 12.1400 per dollar, hitting its strongest level since April of last year, helped by data that showed local factories were gaining momentum at the end of 2010 as U.S. demand picked up. [ID:nN11130858]

"It seems that industrial production continues to do well and domestic consumption is picking up," said Benito Berber, an economist at Nomura in New York.

The Mexican currency was poised to post an over two-year high if it firms a bit past 12.13 per dollar.

Berber said the peso could have some trouble breaking past option barriers around 12.10 per dollar. However, if the currency pierces that level, the peso could quickly firm past 12 per dollar.

"The forecasts that are calling for the peso to trade below 12 per dollar are likely to be reached in the first quarter," Berber said.

In the short term, other analysts said that too many investors may have piled into the Mexican peso trade, too quickly, leaving the currency open to profit-taking in the short term.

"The Mexican trade is pretty crowded," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York. "We need to take a breather here before we take another move."

INTERVENTION LOOMS

Brazil's real underperformed Latin American currencies on Tuesday as the threat of more aggressive intervention in the Brazilian market weighed on the real <BRBY>, which bid only 0.06 percent stronger at 1.685 per dollar.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said Monday he was sure the country's currency would not strengthen further, adding that intervention via so-called reverse swaps in the futures market would carry little financial risk. [ID:nN10282474]

If reverse swaps are used, the real could weaken to 1.75-1.77 per dollar, according to one New York-based head currency trader.

The government has taken a number of measures to try to put the brakes on the real's recent gains, including a new reserve requirement on banks' short U.S. dollar positions.

"Mantega's threats went largely ignored by the market, though he is making it quite clear that policymakers will fight very hard against any further BRL appreciation," said Nick Chamie of RBC in a research note.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.6 percent to 496.50 per dollar, helped by higher prices for copper, the country's main export.

"The peso's performance here is mainly following what is going on abroad," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

"We have copper going up, so we should see the market here trying to test new levels. We could see corrections between 15 and 18 pesos in the next few days, which would be half of how much the peso fell following intervention," he added.

Chile's peso slumped last week after the central bank announced a massive dollar-buying plan to curb its strength. For more, see: [ID:nN1124735]. (Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

* Chile's peso falls to 4-month low against dollar

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Monday as fears over euro zone debt resurfaced, prompting an exodus from riskier assets worldwide.

The European Central Bank threw Portugal a temporary lifeline on Monday by buying up its bonds, traders said, as market and peer pressure mounted for Lisbon to seek an international bailout. [ID:nLDE7090U2]

Brazil's real also suffered from concerns that the government could make further efforts to control the currency's recent appreciation.

The authorization of the country's sovereign wealth fund to operate in the foreign exchange market was finally completed on Monday while speculation about action in the futures market intensified.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.47 percent weaker at 1.692 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market in early trading.

"The expectation that the central bank could act in (the) derivatives (futures market) is reinforcing the global move, it's a mix of global moves and local noise," said Roberto Padovani, chief Brazil economist with WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened to a four-month low, falling 0.54 percent to 500.2 per dollar.

A major financial crisis in Europe would not only deter investment in emerging markets, but also the global economy, reducing demand for Latin American exports.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> slipped 0.29 percent to 12.2700 per dollar in dawn trading in Mexico City.

title: Brazil 's Real Weaker As Government  Intervention  Weighs On Market
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened against the dollar on Monday, as investors are shy about taking a position with the constant threat of government intervention hanging over their heads.

On Monday, the government authorized its wealth fund to buy dollars, coming on the back of last week's move by the central bank to rein in the size of Brazilian banks' bets against the U.S. dollar.

"On the back of the steps announced last week, the tendency is for the real to weaken today and probably for the whole week, and it could test BRL1.70 soon," said Marcos Trabold, head of operations at the BT Associados Corretora de Cambio brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The government managed to cut part of the bank's speculative position."

The government's wealth fund can now buy or sell dollars in the foreign exchange spot and futures markets along with the central bank and the treasury, according to the authorization published in the federal register. The measure formalized the government's intention, expressed at the end of 2010, to allow the wealth fund to act in the foreign exchange market.

It's the latest in a series of measures which the government has taken to prevent the Brazilian currency from gaining too much ground against the dollar.

Markets are also likely to spend much of the week debating the outcome of next week's monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank is expected to raise interest rates. Higher rates are part of the reason why Brazil has been so attractive to foreign portfolio investment, especially given the low rates in the U.S. and Europe.

On Monday, expectations for IPCA consumer inflation in 2011 again nudged higher, to 5.34%, up from 5.32% a week earlier and up from 5.21% four weeks ago. The outlook for 2012 was stable at 4.50%, in line with the government's target. Last year, inflation reached 5.91%, the highest level since 2004.

The U.S. dollar was firmer against most major currencies amid concerns over European sovereign financing. At 1253 GMT the real was trading at BRL1.6916 per dollar, weaker than the previous close of BRL1.6825, according to Telekurs via Factset.

Meanwhile, the real was slightly stronger against the Chinese yuan, according to Telekurs, trading at CNY3.91 per real, from the previous close of CNY3.93. China is Brazil's largest trading partner.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  flat after jobs,  intervention
text:
* Brazil's real flat, Mexican peso weakens 0.1 pct

* U.S. jobs data offer no direction to region's markets

* Chile's peso gets temporary lift from copper export data

(Adds comments, reaction to U.S. data, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies traded little changed on Friday after a mixed U.S. employment report left investors unclear about the pace of the economic recovery.

Investors were also reluctant to push the Brazilian real or the Chilean peso higher after both countries moved aggressively this week to curb the recent rise in their currencies.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> lingered around its previous close, trading flat at 1.686 per dollar on the local market.

In the latest attempt to curb the real's gains, the central bank said on Thursday it will impose an unremunerated reserve requirement of 60 percent on U.S. dollar short positions when certain limits are exceeded.

"Brazil seems to be moving in the direction of countries such as Colombia, where banks cannot carry short (dollar) positions in the spot market," said analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note.

"Regardless of whether the latest measures prove effective or not, one thing is clear: regulatory uncertainty is rising, and investors are asking, 'What next'? " according to the note.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.09 percent to 12.2425 per dollar. Mexico's markets follow U.S. data closely because of the countries' strong trading links.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> seesawed in early trading and was later down 0.44 percent at 497.50 per dollar. The currency had weakened in early trading but managed to pare losses after data showed the country's copper export revenue rose 43 percent in 2010. [ID:nSGO002116]

"At the beginning of the day, the peso was around 497 per dollar, and then the export data helped to bring the peso to the 495 level," said one trader in Santiago.

But the U.S. payrolls data sent the peso down to the levels it dipped to in early trading. [ID:nN06134458]

Investors were also looking to Chile's interest rate decision next week, which could affect the short-term performance of the currency.

Chilean analysts are evenly divided on whether the central bank will hold its benchmark interest rate or raise it by 25 basis points, according to a Reuters poll conducted on Friday. [ID:nSAG002684]

"Some analysts are calling for a pause in the rate tightening cycle this month, but we still expect the central bank to continue raising rates, quite possibly for a few more months yet," said Clyde Wardle, an analyst with HSBC in New York, in a research note.

SAO PAULO, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Brazil's real sank on Thursday after officials said they would make it more expensive for banks to continue to bet on the fast-rising currency, while Chile's peso stabilized after this week's government intervention.

Brazil's central bank imposed a reserve requirement on banks' short positions on the U.S. dollar, turning up the heat on speculators authorities blame for overvaluing the real. For details, see [ID:nLDE7050Z6] and [ID:nN06102054].

"It is not the most powerful measure, but it is one more, and the threat is there that they could do even more," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclay's Capital in New York.

The country has been buying dollars in daily auctions and also raised taxes on foreign investments.

Like many emerging Latin and Asian economies, Brazil has struggled with currency appreciation that has made its exports more difficult to sell abroad and flooded the country with cheap imports.

Banks have 90 days to get ready for the new rules, meaning there was not a mad rush to reduce positions.

"It won't necessarily change the trend -- it could hold the market back a little," said Jose Carlos Amado, a currency trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The real <BRBY> was bid 0.78 percent weaker at 1.686 per dollar, extending losses as investors broadly bet in favor of the greenback ahead of Friday's U.S. monthly payrolls data for December.

The jobs report could support the view that the U.S. economy is growing faster than expected.

Expectations of better U.S. growth have pushed up U.S. bond yields, making dollar investments more attractive compared to higher-yielding, but riskier, emerging market assets.

The currency has lost 6 percent of its value against the dollar and suffered its worst one-day plunge in a quarter century since Chile unveiled its plan to intervene in the currency late Tuesday. "The market has calmed, and we're not seeing the exuberance of the first days," said one trader in Santiago.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> hit an eight-month high early in the session but then fell as the dollar broadly gained. The peso weakened 0.4 percent to 12.2340 per dollar.

Analysts at some banks see the Mexican peso soon firming to a more than two-year high and then breaking past the 12-per dollar per level.

Even with such gains, the peso remains below the levels it traded at before the 2008 financial crisis, easing concerns that officials could intervene any time soon. (Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City and Frolin Romero and Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: FACTBOX-Steps Latin America is taking to counter hot money
text:
Jan 6 (Reuters) - Brazil made its boldest intervention yet on Thursday to contain a surging currency, imposing reserve requirements on banks' short dollar positions in the latest in a series of similar moves by Latin American countries.

Foreign investors have poured money into the region's high-yielding economies, shunning markets in developed countries still struggling to recover from the global financial crisis.

Below are the main measures Latin American countries have adopted to curb the strength of their currencies:

BRAZIL SEEKS TO CUT BANKS' FOREIGN EXCHANGE POSITIONS, BUYS DOLLARS, FIGHTS INFLOWS

* Central bank creates a 60 percent reserve requirement on banks' foreign exchange positions, aimed at curbing speculation on a stronger real and volatility in the currency market.

* Central bank resumed daily dollar purchases soon after the financial crisis, recently buying as much as $1 billion a day in two daily auctions.

* Sovereign wealth fund authorized to buy dollars on spot market but has yet to act.

* A tripling of the tax on foreign purchases of bonds to 6 percent to curb capital inflows into fixed income market.

* Higher taxes on derivatives margins to dissuade short-term investors.

* Raises bank reserve requirements to cool a credit boom and ease the currency situation by paving the way for lower interest rates.

* Aggressive measures including targeted tariff increases and tax breaks in the works to address effects of strong real .

-- Story links:

CHILE ANNOUNCES LONG-AWAITED FOREX INTERVENTION

* Central bank announces record $12 billion in dollar purchases during 2011. It stresses that intervention is exceptional, warns against "addiction" to it.

* Peso plunges from near three-year high after central bank announcement.

* Chilean President Sebastian Pinera says no plans for capital controls.

* Central bank lifts limits on pension funds' overseas investment.

* Bank slows pace of interest rate hikes, citing peso.

-- Story links:

COLOMBIA BUYS DOLLARS, INTRODUCES STRUCTURAL REFORMS

* Government kept $1.5 billion abroad last year, which included $1.4 billion in government dividends from state oil firm Ecopetrol.

* Plans to possibly hedge up to $3.7 billion in external debt service payments in 2011.

* Will only use external financing this year to meet outside obligations to ease pressure on peso.

* Eliminated tax exemption on foreign loan interest

* Central bank buying at least $20 million daily until at least March 15.

-- Story links:

PERU BUYS DOLLARS, ENCOURAGES INVESTMENT ABROAD

* Government trims average tariff to 3.4 percent from 5 percent, targeting increased imports and less appreciation pressure on the sol.

* Central bank buys about $9 billion dollars on the spot market in 2010, equivalent to around 6 percent of GDP. The treasury also bought around $500 million.

* Banking regulator SBS drawing up rule to curb use of non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) -- a short-term derivative -- to ease pressure on the sol.

* Central bank raises deposit requirements on bank accounts, especially those tied to foreign loans, in a bid to limit speculation on the sol.

* Regulators allow pension funds to invest more abroad.

-- Story links:

MEXICO ESCHEWS INTERVENTION, PESO SET TO OUTPERFORM

* Central bank buying $600 million per month by selling dollar put options as a means to build up its reserves.

* Mexico has said capital controls do not work.

* Mexican peso has lagged gains in other currencies; yet to firm back to pre-crisis levels.

* Strategists see intervention measures across Latin America boosting attraction of free-floating Mexican peso.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile's peso tumbles; Mexican peso gains on US
text:
* Chile's peso falls 1.2 pct on first day of intervention

* Brazil's real dips 0.1 pct, Mexican peso gains 0.1 pct

* Mexico's currency outperforms region after U.S. data (Adds reaction to U.S. employment data, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Chile's peso and Brazil's real weakened on Wednesday as commodity prices fell and investors fretted over meddling in the countries' markets.

But Mexico's currency, which is not seen to be at risk from intervention, managed to edge back into positive territory after encouraging U.S. employment data.

Chile's market was still reeling from Monday's news that the central bank will buy $50 million daily to curb the peso's rise -- a program that kicks off on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, investors in the Brazilian market were cautious after the government issued fresh warnings on Tuesday that it was ready to take tougher action if the real firms further.

The lower price of commodities, a key export and economic lifeline for the continent, also hit the region's currencies. [ID:nL3E7C50FQ]

After suffering its biggest one-day loss in more than 25 years in the previous session, the Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 1.2 percent to a two-month low of 493.3 per dollar.

The effect of the central bank's intervention could be magnified as the price of Chile's main export copper slips from record highs, but analysts are not expecting another drop as dramatic as Tuesday's plunge.

"Yesterday we saw the announcement effect, but starting today we'll be seeing the impact of real purchases by the central bank," said analyst Osvaldo Cruz with BCI in Santiago.

"With the dollar auction included, we see the exchange rate between 487 and 493 pesos per dollar today."

MANTEGA'S MANTRA

The Brazilian real <BRBY> seesawed in early trading, later bid 0.12 percent weaker at 1.664 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

If the currency continues to weaken it is likely to find strong technical support at 1.70 per dollar -- a psychologically important level in itself. At that point, the real will bump against its 50-day simple moving average (1.699), its 100-day simple moving average (1.7052) and then the 23.6 percent Fibonacci retracement level from the May-to-October rally (1.7072).

"Finance Minister Mantega keeps repeating his mantra that the government has tools to prevent excessive appreciation, including further measures to restrain capital flows," said Zeina Latif, chief Brazil economist at RBS in Sao Paulo, in a research note. "But the point is that there might be few options remaining without crossing over to more heterodox measures."

"We should expect more verbal intervention with (the real) below 1.65, but not meaningful currency measures," she added.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> also weakened in early trading but reversed after better-than-expected data on private sector employment in the United States, the country's top trading partner. [ID:nN05266445]

The peso firmed 0.17 percent to 12.205 per dollar. (Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre in Santiago; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

title: Brazil  Real Slips Early On  Intervention  Threat, Factors Abroad
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened in early trading Wednesday as investors reacted cautiously to threats of local market intervention by the government and uncertainties abroad.

As of 1200 GMT, the real traded at BRL1.667 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.662 to the dollar Tuesday according to Telekurs via Factset.

Traders noted the market was closely monitoring local government moves after Finance Minister Guido Mantega renewed threats Tuesday to take measures to curb the strength of the real.

"The government always has a group of measures prepared for the forex area," Mantega said. "If there's a greater deterioration, we'll take additional measures."

Mantega said recent exchange rate levels have been harmful to the country's exports and trade balance and pledged to maintain Brazil 2011 trade surplus above the $20 billion posted in 2010.

Brazil's government in October raised the country's IOF Financial Operations Tax on foreign investment in fixed-income and certain derivatives in an effort to discourage incoming investment and currency appreciation.

Alongside possible local actions, the currency was also influenced Wednesday by market declines abroad and falling commodities prices.

Also on the horizon for investors is the possibility of interest rate tightening in other emerging markets such as China. Rate hikes abroad, analysts note, could siphon off some of the heavy foreign invesment that has pushed Brazil's currency to recent highs.

Brazil itself, however, could see the beginning of its own cycle of rate hikes at a central bank monetary policy committee meeting later this month as 12-month local inflation continues to remain above the government's official 4.5% inflation target.

In the meantime, Brazil's central bank is seen maintaining a presence in the local currency market Wednesday with its daily dollar purchase auctions to build foreign reserves.

Brazil's reserves as of Tuesday stood at $289.1 billion.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso slumps on  intervention ;real recovers
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Chile's peso closes down 4.5 pct at 9-week low

* Brazilian real pares losses after press conference

* Finance Minister Guido Mantega announces no new measures

* Mexico eschews intervention, benefiting peso (Adds comments from Mexico, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Chile's peso suffered its biggest daily drop in more than 25 years on Tuesday on tough new intervention plans while the Brazilian real recovered after Brasilia stopped short of introducing further measures.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> slumped as much as 4.9 percent to 489.60 per dollar. It later closed 4.5 percent down at a 9-week low of 487.60 -- its biggest daily loss since February 1985, according to daily central bank data.

Brazil's real <BRBY> also weakened sharply after the government announced it would hold a news conference in the afternoon to tackle foreign exchange issues, prompting speculation fresh measures could be announced.

But Finance Minister Guido Mantega said very little and only reiterated that the government was ready to act, causing the real immediately to pare losses.

Chile has taken one of the most hands-off approaches in Latin America to its foreign exchange market. But it surprised investors late on Monday with a massive dollar-buying plan.

The central bank announced it will buy $12 billion to tame the peso, which has appreciated more than 17 percent against the greenback since the end of June. For details, see [ID:nN03137860].

Like many attractive emerging economies across Latin America and Asia, Chile has struggled with currency appreciation that has made its exports more difficult to sell abroad and flooded the country with cheap imports. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Chile's surprise move added to existing concerns about intervention across the region as it could give countries such as Brazil an excuse to implement more currency measures.

"If the pretty conservative Chilean central bank intervenes, what can you expect of the Brazilian central bank!" said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington.

However, others played down a possible regional impact.

"Chile is just the last domino to fall into intervention. I don't think it changes others' attitudes as they are already intervening," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging markets research for the Americas at Nomura in New York.

BRAZIL: KING OF INTERVENTION

The Brazilian real pared its losses to close 0.79 percent weaker at 1.662 per dollar on the local spot market, after closing at its strongest level since Sept. 1 2008 in the previous session.

Brazil's trade and industry minister said on Monday the country would not remain "passive" while the real continues to strengthen.

Latin America's biggest economy has already taken the lead in the region when it comes to intervention, buying vast amounts of dollars on a daily basis and raising taxes on inflows. But investors worry the government could increase those levies even further and take other measures, such as intervening in the futures market. For possible measures, see [ID:nN01117570].

Mexico is now the only major Latin American country that is not heavily intervening in its currency market, partly because the peso is fully convertible and thus more widely traded and harder to control.

The country has also suffered more from the financial crisis, which means it has not seen the flood of currency-boosting investment experienced by Chile and Brazil.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> gained 0.14 percent to 12.2318 per dollar, even as U.S. stocks were mixed.

"If you believe that intervention in Mexico is pretty moderate and subtle, then the peso become more attractive in the eyes of investors," said Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE in Mexico City. (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Venezuela devalues; Chile's peso gains
text:
* Chile's peso top gains for 2010 in Latam FX

 * Brazil's real jumps on month-end positioning

 * Mexican, Colombian pesos also set to beat real in 2010  (Recasts, adds comment; dateline previously SANTIAGO/SAO PAOLO)

 By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

 MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Dec 30 (Reuters) - Venezuela devalued its currency on Thursday in a move that will help government finances and could help support the country's volatile debt in 2011, while Chile's peso rose to a 31-month high.

 Venezuela's benchmark 2027 global bond <VENGLB27=RR> has rallied more than a percentage point this month, helped by higher oil prices and advances in President Hugo Chavez's bid to raise taxes next year. Analysts said the devaluation help spur could further gains early next year.

 "The tax increases and the devaluation will help the government position in the year ahead ... and should benefit Venezuelan assets, " said Alejandro Arreaza, an analyst at Barclays Capital in New York

 The devaluation was the second such move in the last 12 months and it will push down local costs for the state run-oil company, improving its financial flexibility and the government's fiscal position.  For details, see [ID:nN30116504]

 Venezuela may not issue any new dollar debt in the first half of 2011, and scarcity of the country's high-yielding debt should further underpin the market for its bonds, Arreaza said.

 In currency trading, Chile's peso highlighted its position as the top gainer among major Latin American peers, after the surging price of copper pushed it to a 31-month high on Thursday.

 Chile is the world's top copper producer and has been flooded with dollars as investors bet commodity prices will keep rising in 2011.

 High copper prices have kept local authorities from matching intervention efforts seen in Brazil and Colombia to tame currency gains that are hurting local exporters. [ID:nN30111514]

 Demand for Latin American debt and currencies has been fueled by low interest rates in major economies that are trying to spur growth and underpin a recovery from the 2008 financial crisis. Strong currency gains have raised concerns that asset bubbles could be forming in the region.

 The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.24 percent to 467.70 per dollar on Thursday, closing the trading year 8.4 percent stronger.

 "The peso could approach 465 in the first few days of 2011, but the market sees this as a critical level and after that it could start to reverse and test 470," said one currency trader in Santiago.

 The Brazilian real <BRBY> surged 0.83 percent against the dollar in the local spot market on month-end positioning to trade at 1.664. Brazil, Latin America's biggest economy, continues to post strong economic growth and draw investors.

 The Brazilian real is heading toward a more than two-year high despite efforts by authorities to curb the currency's strength.

 The real gained 4.6 percent in 2010, underperforming its peers due to dollar buying by the central bank as well as uncertainty about a presidential election and the world's biggest share offering by state-run oil firm Petrobras.

 Colombia's peso <COP=> gained 0.63 percent to 1,924.90 to the dollar on the last day of local trading, closing the year with a 5.8 percent gain.

 The Colombian peso often outperformed its peers this year, but was battered down from a more than two-year high hit in October as local authorities took measures to weaken the currency.

 The peso plunged early this week as a scarcity of dollars was overwhelmed by demand for greenbacks on end-of-year corporate demand.

 Meanwhile, the Mexican currency <MXN=> edged up 0.04 percent to 12.3925 per dollar on Thursday, heading for a 5.7 percent gain for the year on the back of growth in the United States, which buys most of the exports from Latin America's second biggest economy.  (Additional reporting by Froilan Romero in Santiago; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: ANALYSIS-Mexico builds buffers against investment swings
text:
* Mexico sits still as Brazil frets over flows

* IMF cheaply insures against investor flight

* With weak growth, Mexico draws fewer investor eyes

By Jean Luis Arce and Patrick Rucker

MEXICO CITY, Dec 17 (Reuters) - As Mexico's regional peers noisily guard against the day when foreign investors will pack up and go home, policymakers here are taking a wait-and-see approach.

Suppressing the urge to cool white-hot markets with capital controls, Mexico is quietly putting buffers in place against the swings and roundabouts of investor sentiment by modestly soaking up dollars and tapping global reserves without the clamor and howl heard from its neighbors.

Mexico was rewarded for its forbearance this week when the International Monetary Fund topped up its safety-net credit line to about $73 billion and extended its life for two years.

"We can only keep this (program) for our platinum members who are really having the right policy," IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn said. "Mexico is among them."

Combined with central bank reserves, the credit line gives Mexico access to roughly $185 billion to defend its currency from potential shocks, still short of the $280-plus billion that Brazil has socked away. Mexico's reserves are worth about 10 percent of overall economic output, compared to about 15 percent in Brazil.

The lower level of international reserves means Mexico is not burdened by having to offset extra liquidity created by dollar purchases the same way Brazil is.

Analysts applauded the credit line as a cheap insurance policy against investor flight.

"(This is) a low-cost precautionary move that will provide a cushion in the event that re-normalization of U.S. interest rates triggers a disruptive... capital flight shock," RBC Capital Markets' Eduardo Suarez wrote in a client note.

While Brazil tries to stifle inflows with high costs and other Latin American peers step up currency controls, Mexico's patient blend of soft talk and slow action should serve the country in the long-term.

The Mexican peso was battered during the financial crisis in part because the central bank did not have enough foreign currency ballast, but now hard-cash reserves and the IMF lifeline should shield the currency from a punishing loss in value if another crisis hits, said Roberto Melzi, economist with Barclays Capital.

"The market penalized Mexico more than Brazil during the crisis," he said. "One could argue that in the event of another shock, Mexico would not be so severely penalized."

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

For a graphic on capital flows to Latam:

http://r.reuters.com/qeg94q ("http://r.reuters.com/qeg94q")

right-click on <aMXFCRES>

<aBRFCRES> ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

CASH BONANZA

Along with other emerging markets, Latin America has been flooded with foreign cash from investors looking for returns that can outpace yields in developed economies.

The cash bonanza will likely sour when Europe and the United States get back on their feet and begin to raise interest rates, attracting funds back to the developed world.

In the meantime, emerging markets are trying to get the most out of the attention by locking in cheap funding and keeping a lid on currency gains that could damage exports, while limiting the potential damage from a sharp reverse of flows.

Local economies are each balancing those tensions in their fashion: Chile's central bank is warning of intervention to weaken its peso, while Brazil has ramped up the tax on outsiders buying local bonds. For factbox, see [ID:nSGE69503F]

Mexico, by comparison, has been squirreling away dollars in a passive auction process since March and pushed reserves to record highs, a position now bolstered by the IMF credit line which was first extended in 2009, although never used.

IMF officials congratulated Mexico this week as they topped up the fund and said the credit line could be a model for pre-crisis financial help that discourages nations with strong finances from building a bloated dollar war-chest.

In late September, Brazil's finance minister rapped nations for spurring a damaging currency war - driving down the value of their home currency in order to give exports a lift.

But IMF Western Hemisphere chief Nicolas Eyzaguirre has also warned of the dangers of a global 'reserve war' where healthy nations spur a race to build out-sized reserves, sapping energy from the rest of the economy and fanning global imbalances.

The IMF would prefer to act as the liquidity provider of last resort in case of capital flight, Eyzaguirre has said. (Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico and Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo, Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  dip on Spanish debt threat
text:
* Brazil's real and Chilean peso weaken 0.2 pct

* Mexican peso weakens less than 0.1 pct after U.S. data

* Flows dwindle as 2010 draws to a close (Recasts after U.S. data, adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Wednesday after ratings agency Moody's threatened to downgrade Spanish debt, renewing euro zone fears and prompting investors to sell higher-risk assets.

A major financial fallout in Europe would not only deter investment in emerging markets but also hit global growth, reducing demand for Latin American exports. For details, see [ID:nLDE6BE0BP].

Strong U.S. economic data offered some support later on Wednesday but failed to reverse the currencies' earlier losses.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 0.21 percent to 473.7 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, fell.

"The peso is depreciating slightly because the external backdrop is pretty bad. Most stock markets are down and the U.S. dollar is also recovering against the euro," said one trader in Santiago.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.18 percent weaker at 1.696 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, but trading just stronger than the closely watched 1.70 level.

Over recent months, Brazil's authorities have stepped up their intervention efforts in the market when the currency has strengthened past 1.70 and threatened to break the 1.65 per-dollar level.

SPORADIC HOLIDAY FLOWS

But as investors do their last few trades of the year, the central bank may feel less need to intervene aggressively, said Tony Volpon, head of emerging markets research for the Americas at Nomura in New York.

"They're reacting more sporadically because the flows are more sporadic," he said. "They have a good idea of what's going in and out because a lot of people call the central bank and tell them beforehand."

The central bank, which has a tight grip over the country's foreign exchange market, called two auctions to buy U.S. dollars almost every day between Sept. 8 and Nov. 10 but has ditched the second auction in recent weeks.

"They'll schedule their auctions to meet the flows," added Nomura's Volpon. "And this time of year, the flows are more balanced because there is profit remittance and a lot of people here in New York are spending money so they're buying a lot of dollars."

The Mexican currency <MXN=> was only 0.03 percent weaker at 12.395 per dollar, supported by some strong economic data from the United States.

U.S. manufacturing activity in New York rebounded in December and the country's industrial output posted its biggest gain since July, separate data showed on Wednesday. [ID:nN15122981]

The Mexican peso is more responsive to changes in the U.S. economic outlook due to the countries' strong trading links.

"The market didn't take the (U.S.) positive numbers well enough to build positions...you have two forces here, the dollar is gaining strength, so that puts a little bit of pressure on dollar bears," said Italo Lombardi, a Latin American economist and strategist with BNP Paribas in New York. * Chile invokes intervention as peso hits 30-mo high

* Brazil's real firms 0.35 pct, Mexico peso adds 0.13 pct (Adds comments, changes byline, updates prices)

By Jose de Castro and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures fell on Tuesday after weaker than expected retail sales prompted bets the central bank will be under less pressure to raise borrowing costs.

Brazilian retail sales rose only 0.4 percent in October from the prior month, which pushed market players to rethink widely-held expectations that Brazil's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate - called the Selic - early next year to cool inflation pressures. For details, see [ID:nN14196422]

"Now there is some doubt over if, in fact, the Selic will go up and, if it goes up, by how much." said Jason Vieira, an analyst at the Cruzeiro do Sul brokerage.

The yield on the interest rate contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily-traded of the session, fell 5 basis points to 11.85 percent.

A head trader at a bank in New York noted that the drop in rates on Tuesday showed the market is now pricing in a rate hike of only about 30 basis points at the central bank's next meeting in January. Last week, the market had been betting on a 50-basis-point increase.

Currencies across Latin America firmed after surprisingly strong November U.S. retail sales boosted optimism about consumer spending in one of the region's top trading partners.

Brazil's currency <BRBY> bid 0.35 percent stronger at 1.693 per dollar. Traders were buying up the currency after the real pierced the key 1.70 level without without prompting additional intervention measures, traders said.

CHILE JAWBONES

Chile's peso surged to a 30-month high on the back of record prices for the country's main export, copper, and despite warnings from officials that they could intervene in the market.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.44 percent to 472.70 per dollar even after the country's central bank chief said policymakers were continuing to evaluate the possibility of intervening to slow the peso's gains. [ID:nN14274122]

Mexico's peso initially firmed the U.S. retail sales data, which boosted the outlook for Mexican exports to its top trading partner.

But the Mexican currency gave up gains late in the session after the U.S. Federal Reserve showed no signs of curtailing its economic stimulus measures, raising the prospect of accelerating U.S. economic growth and also inflation.

The Fed's statement sparked steep losses in the price of U.S. bonds, driving up yields.

That pushed investors to dump riskier Mexican debt in favor of the rising yields on safer U.S. bonds, undermining the peso currency as investors bought dollars to sink into U.S. government debt.

The yield on the government's 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> jumped 13 basis points to bid at 7.17 percent.

"People are expecting a possible boom now in the U.S. economy, and with that pushing up returns on U.S. bonds, it is more attractive to be in Treasuries," said an analyst at a foreign bank in Mexico who does not have permission to speak to media. title: Brazil Real Ends Stronger On Lift From Commodities, Market Trends
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real gained back some recently lost ground to end stronger against the dollar Monday as elevated commodities prices and trends in markets around the globe brought fresh inflows of funds locally.

The real ended at BRL1.697 to the dollar on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange after ending at BRL1.7195 to the dollar Friday.

Traders noted the real began the session strengthening as investors took encouragement from China's resolve to keep interest rates steady over the weekend after a tightening of bank reserve requirements late last week.

Expectations of a still-strong Chinese economy also helped give lift to prices of metals and other major commodities, of which Brazil is a key exporter.

The global and local rate outlook, meanwhile, continues to be an important focus for the local currency markets. Analysts note the U.S. Federal Reserve's open market committee isn't expected to unveil any surprises this week, with interest rates likely to remain low for an "extended period" and the bond-buying program likely to stay in place. That trend should help maintain investor appetite for Brazilian assets, which have provided an attractive alternative to investments elsewhere.

Locally, analysts are mulling whether or when Brazil's central bank will start to raise interest rates.

Brazil's general price index, known as the IGP-M, rose 0.83% in the Nov. 21-30 period compared with an increase of 0.79% during the Oct. 21-31 period, the private Getulio Vargas Foundation said Monday. The latest figure was in line with analysts' expectations, and pushed the 12-month figure up to 11.48%.

The IGP-M index is used to adjust a number of contracts in Brazil, including rental agreements and utilities rates.

Brazilian financial market analysts and economists once again raised their 2010 and 2011 year-end average inflation forecasts, according to the Central Bank of Brazil's market survey published Monday.

They see the IPCA consumer price inflation rate at 5.85% by year's end, up from 5.78% a week earlier and above the central bank's inflation target of 4.5% for the year. In addition, economists increased their average estimate for 2011 inflation to 5.21% from 5.20%.

The survey, however, showed that the economists still expect the central bank's key interest rate, the Selic, to end 2011 at 12.25%, suggesting 1.50 percentage points of rate hikes from the current 10.75%.

With a likelihood of rising rates locally, investors have remained eager to pump foreign currency into the market.

The government, meanwhile, has managed to maintain the real at or near the BRL1.70 mark with recent threats of stepped up intervention.

Earlier this year Brazil raised the IOF tax on foreign investment in fixed-income securities to 6% from 2% and also raised the tax for guarantees on derivatives investments. Late last week, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega reiterated a pledge to step in against the real should it strengthen significantly.

Brazil's central bank, meanwhile, did its part Monday also to help curb the strengthening real with a customary dollar purchase auction to build foreign reserves. The bank bought an undisclosed amount of dollars in a late session auction at a rate of BRL1.7001.

As of Friday, Brazil's reserves stood at $285.9 billion.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real slips, Mexico peso firms slightly
text:
* Brazil's real hurt by intervention expectations

* Higher copper price helps support Chilean peso

* China rate hike fears, EU debt woes may weigh next week

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Friday, hurt by expectations of intervention by the local authorities to curb the currencies gains, while the Mexican peso edged up, helped by stronger than expected U.S. data.

The real closed 0.35 percent weaker at 1.713 on the local spot market <BRBY>, recording a 1.64 percent loss for the week.

Traders pointed to comments from Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Thursday that authorities could step up efforts to contain the real's gains, which are hurting exporters.

"After Mantega spoke yesterday, people became even more alert to the possibility that the government could act with more force in the currency market," said Jose Carlos Amado, a currency trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's central bank (BCB) has recently started calling two auctions a day, instead of just one, to buy U.S. dollars.

"With the USDBRL now close to 1.71, the BCB resumed intervening once during the day, reinforcing our thesis that BCB becomes more aggressive below 1.70," wrote analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed to a fresh 30-month high in early trading but was later flat at 475.80 per dollar. The price of copper, the country's main export, pared early gains.

Chinese imports, including copper, soared in November while bank lending topped forecasts, suggesting the booming Chinese economy will continue to gobble up Latin American commodities such as Chilean copper and Brazilian soybeans.

Chile's currency gained 0.86 percent during the week.

CHINA, EUROPE LOOM

The Mexican currency <MXN=> firmed 0.21 percent to 12.4505 per dollar after U.S. data consumer confidence to its highest level in six months and trade data showed that imports from Mexico rose to a record high in October. [ID:nN10163525]

Mexico sends around 80 percent of its exports to the United States and Latin America's No. 2 economy is counting on a firm recovery north of the border to support its own rebound from a deep recession.

The Mexican peso was on track to post a weekly loss of around 1 percent.

Analysts said Latin American currencies could be hurt by signs that China could soon move to hike interest rates. Chinese data on Saturday that is expected to show another pick-up in inflation.

"The intensity of the depreciation will depend on the comments that are made in China and the measures they take to keep the economy from overheating," said Mario Copca, an analyst at brokerage Vanguardia in Mexico City.

Further signs of trouble in Europe's debt crisis could also weigh next week.

EU heads of state and government meet on Dec. 16-17 to discuss the region's spreading debt crisis. Expectations of meaningful progress are low after Germany and France on Friday rejected calls for an increase in the bloc's rescue fund and joint sovereign bonds. [ID:nLDE6B90K3]

"There is going to be more noise from Europe ... the big risk is that Italy gets downgraded," Copca said. (Additional reporting by Jose de Castro in Sao Paulo and Lorena Segura in Mexico City; Editing by Andrew Hay)

text:
* U.S. data boosts dollar, hitting region's FX

* Brazil's real sinks 0.7 pct on outflows, intervention

* Higher copper price helps support Chilean peso

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies surrendered most of their early gains on Friday after the U.S. trade deficit narrowed much more than expected in October, boosting the dollar worldwide. [ID:nN10198692]

The region's currencies had all firmed earlier in the session following a rush of strong data from China, one of the region's top trading partners.

Chinese imports and exports soared in November while bank lending topped forecasts, suggesting the booming Chinese economy will continue to gobble up Latin American commodities such as Chilean copper and Brazilian soybeans.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed to a fresh 30-month high in early trading but was later flat at 476 per dollar. The price of copper, the country's main export, pared gains as the greenback strengthened but remained in positive territory, helping the peso to outperform.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> also gave up most of its early gains to trade 0.13 percent stronger at 12.4600 per dollar.

BRAZIL'S REAL SUFFERS MOST

But the Brazilian real <BRBY> reversed early gains to bid 0.70 percent weaker at 1.719 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market, heading for a weekly decline of 2 percent.

Traders said companies were moving money out of the country as the year comes to a close.

"At the end of the year there are a lot of remittances abroad, they're very localized deals," said Andre Ferreira, director of the Futura brokerage in Sao Paulo.

At these levels, investors are also particularly wary of attempts by the authorities to curb the real's recent rally.

Brazil's central bank (BCB) has recently started calling two auctions a day, instead of just one, to buy U.S. dollars. Finance Minister Guido Mantega this week also threatened to take further action to contain the currency's rise as exporters continue to struggle to sell their produce abroad.

"With the USDBRL now close to 1.71, the BCB resumed intervening once during the day, reinforcing our thesis that BCB becomes more aggressive below 1.70," wrote analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note. "We do not like BRL in the near-term."

title: Brazil Real Strengthens Early On Solid Growth Data

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real strengthened in early trading Thursday despite continued uncertainties abroad as investors showed an enthusiastic response to upbeat local third-quarter growth data.

The real opened at BRL1.688 to the dollar after ending at BRL1.693 to the dollar Wednesday on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange.

Brazil's IBGE statistics institute Thursday reported the country posted 6.7% growth in the third quarter from the same period last year. The figure matched market expectations and maintained the economy on pace to post growth of more than 7% this year.

Meanwhile, not even Brazil's central bank decision late Wednesday to hold the country's reference Selic rate unchanged was enough to discourage buying in Brazilian assets as investors seek out attractive returns in local markets.

Brazil's elevated local interest rates have served as a catalyst for incoming investment over recent months as local authorities struggle to put a ceiling on a continuously strengthening real.

The local currency has gained more than 30% against the dollar since early 2009, causing headaches for the country's exporters and a weakening of its trade balance.

Brazil's central bank, meanwhile, is expected to maintain its intervention in the currency market Thursday with customary dollar purchases.

The bank in recent months had stepped up its dollar purchase auctions to two daily as part of an effort to contain the strengthening of the real and build the country's foreign reserves.

As of Wednesday, Brazil's reserves stood at $286.6 billion.

title: Brazil Soy - Limited old-crop sales as CW planting starts
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's soybean producers are selling small lots of the remaining old-crop stocks as planting for the 2005/06 (Oct/Sept) season starts slowly in the center-west, traders and analysts said.  

"There was some light business this week through Thursday but things are getting off to a slow start on Friday," soy trader Steve Cachia at Cerealpar said. "No sign of new-crop sales yet but with planting under way, forward sales should start soon."  

Cachia said 60-kg bags of beans sold at 32 reais on Thursday in Paranagua.  

Spot export premiums at the main grain port of Paranagua fell sharply this week to 55/65 cents (buy/sell) over front month Chicago Board of Trade futures, compared with 60/80 cents over a week ago.  

March new-crop premiums fell only slightly to 22/28 cents over from 25/30 cents above Chicago last week. April-May premiums fell to 5/10 cents from 11/15 cents last week.  

Jaquelini Maria Alves at analyst Multisafras Consultoria in Mato Grosso, Brazil's No. 1 soybean state, said early planting was under way and progressing well, overall, but some regions were still waiting for better rains.  

"Sorriso hasn't had sufficient rains yet to begin widespread planting but this isn't unusual. Rains in Mato Grosso pick up in the middle of October and wide-scale planting follows in this period, too," she said.  

Multisafras estimated about 8 percent of Mato Grosso's soy crop had been planted but said that the state's total planted area to the oilseed would fall this year from last by at least 8 percent due to the lack of producer resources.  

"There are still about 500,000 to 700,000 tonnes of old-crop beans in stocks around the state yet to be sold," Alves said. "Business is very quiet right now. Producers are focusing on planting."  

A bag of beans was selling at 24.5 reais in Rondonopolis, Mato Grosso this week and at 22 reais in Lucas do Rio Verde. "Prices just aren't attractive enough to move producers to sell right now," she said.  

Somar meteorologist Nadja Marinho said Mato Grosso has been receiving irregular showers over the past few days, principally in the southwest, with drier conditions in the east and some regions in the north of the state.  

"There will continue to be isolated rains next week. More generalized rains typically start about this time in the soy regions of the state, so we are a bit behind schedule -- nothing out of the norm though," Marinho said.  

In a foreign reserve building effort, Brazil's central bank has intervened several times since early last week to buy the U.S. currency and the real has weakened slightly against the dollar.  

But the real was still trading at around 2.261 to the dollar on Friday, firmer than the 2.269 reais on Oct. 5 and around 2.90 reais a year ago.

title: Brazil markets end mixed after volatile trading
text:
(Updates with markets close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Strong dollar inflows helped Brazil's currency strengthen on Friday despite another intervention by the central bank, but stocks weakened as investors mulled a batch of mixed U.S. economic data.  

The Bovespa index <.BVSP> of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange slipped 0.37 percent to 29,770 points, losing the 30,000 points level it had reached on Monday.  

But the Brazilian real <BRBY> strengthened 0.58 percent to 2.245 reais, supported by dollar inflows from exports, traders said, even as the central bank bought dollars for the eighth time this month to boost the country's foreign reserves.  

Trading in both markets was hectic and asset prices seesawed between positive and negative territories with investors prone to speculation.  

Early in the morning, news that the September U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) excluding food and energy came in below market expectations boosted Brazilian markets, leading the Bovespa index to rise more than 1 percent.  

The core CPI rose 0.1 percent against forecasts of a 0.2 percent increase, raising some hopes U.S. interest rates may stop going up sooner than expected, what could boost the lure of riskier assets in emerging markets like Brazil.  

On the other hand, the full CPI jumped 1.2 percent, much higher than the 0.9 percent expected by economists, and U.S. consumer confidence unexpectedly dropped in the first reading of October, putting some pressure on the market.  

News that U.S. commodities brokerage Refco Inc. began shutting down its main business amid a scandal involving its former chief executive also rattled investors. Fearing the collapse of the company may lead to a call of margins and a liquidity squeeze, some investors decided to sell riskier emerging markets assets to make cash, traders said.  

"We had the CPI and markets reacted positively, but then we had all that confusion with Refco and markets fell again," said Alvaro Bandeira, director at Agora Senior brokerage in Rio de Janeiro, adding that the stock market is lacking a clear trend at the moment.  

Ademir Carvalho, a trader with Finabank brokerage in Sao Paulo, said stock investors are still pocketing recent gains.  

"The exchange is going through a period of profit-taking, but there is room for a rebound later.  

Shares for state-owned oil firm Petrobras fell 0.7 percent to 31.18 reais with the exchange's highest trading volume while miner Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) gained 1 percent to 79.70 reais with the market's second highest turnover.  

Speculation that the departure of influential Mohamed El-Erian from Pacific Investment Management Company (PIMCO) could trigger a portfolio reshuffle at the fund manager, which holds about $28 billion in emerging markets, also pressured emerging bonds during the session, traders said.  

As bond prices fell and yields rose, risk spreads over comparable U.S. Treasury notes widened to more than 400 points for the first time since early September. At the end of the day, however, spreads retreated to end 3 basis points tighter at 388 points.  

El-Erian was appointed new investment chief at Harvard University, replacing Jack Meyer, who had run the university's $26 billion endowment for 15 years.

title: Brazil Real Stronger On US CPI Data, Ctrl Bk Dlr Auction
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed stronger Friday, after softer-than-expected core inflation data were released in the U.S., and after Brazil's central bank entered the market for a fourth time this week, purchasing dollars.  

The real closed at 2.246 per dollar, stronger than Thursday's close at BRL2.257 to the dollar.  

The Brazilian currency Friday reacted to both external and domestic news Friday, traders said.  

While headline consumer price inflation in the U.S. was up 1.2% in September, the core number - stripped of energy and food prices - was up 0.1%, while economists had expected a rise of 0.2%.  

A positive reaction by markets abroad to the U.S. CPI figure helped Brazil's real, traders said. A more benign U.S. inflation reading diminishes the need for further interest rate increases in the U.S. that would diminish the spread between U.S. rates and Brazilian rates, luring out funds from Brazil to the U.S.  

The dollar also lost ground against major world currencies Friday, such as the euro and the yen, helping the real to strengthen further.  

An intervention by Brazil's Central Bank to buy U.S. dollars at an auction early Friday afternoon for BRL2.254 to the dollar, may also have boosted the Brazilian currency.  

The Brazilian real was trading at BRL2.2541 to the dollar before the bank called the auction at 1507 GMT. The real traded slightly stronger, at BRL2.252 to the dollar, shortly after the auction.  

It was the fourth time this week that the central bank has bought dollars from the market, continuing a string of purchases aimed at beefing up the country's foreign reserves.  

The bank also bought dollars on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday. Brazil's financial markets were closed Wednesday for a holiday.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Weaker After Ctrl Bank  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Thursday in the wake of the central bank's third auction this week to purchase dollars from the market.  

The real closed at BRL2.257 to the dollar, down from Tuesday's close of BRL2.234. Brazilian financial markets were closed Wednesday for a holiday.  

At 1535 GMT, the central bank called an auction to purchase dollars from the market, following similar moves on Monday and Tuesday. The bank bought dollars at BRL2.260. The real traded slightly weaker at BRL2.261 shortly after the auction, but reversed course and strengthened toward the close.  

The central bank's purchase Thursday followed a series dollar buying by the bank that began last week. The bank had said it would begin to enter the currency markets in an effort to beef up Brazil's foreign reserves.  

The real also was pressured by continued expectations of interest rate hikes in the U.S., analysts said.  

The release Tuesday of minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserve's recent meeting and comments Wednesday by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan signaled that the U.S. monetary body would likely continue its recent monetary tightening cycle. The rate hikes are aimed at warding off inflationary pressures.  

The Federal Open Market Committee, the U.S. Federal Reserve's rate-setting body, next meets Nov. 1.  

In addition, the real suffered with the discovery of foot-and-mouth disease on a farm in Mato Grosso do Sul state, the heart of Brazil's beef-producing region, analysts said. Discovery of the outbreak caused the European Union and Russia to ban some imports of Brazilian beef.  

Because the state produces up to 50% of Brazil's world-leading beef exports, current shipments of up to $3 billion per year could be slashed significantly in the fourth quarter of 2005 and, perhaps, all of 2006.  

Strong Brazilian exports have been a primary factor in the currency's strength in 2005. The real has gained 18% against the U.S. dollar so far this year.  

The country's risk spread against U.S. Treasurys also widened Thursday.  

At 1943 GMT, the spread as measured by the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus widened 8 basis points to 388 basis points over U.S. Treasurys. Brazil's benchmark 2040 bond was down 0.550 at 117.900.  

-By Jeff Fick, Dow Jones Newswires; (55 11) 3145-1481; jeff.fick@dowjones.com [ 13-10-05 1946GMT ]

title: Brazil Soy - Market seen recovering from 8-mth low
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Brazilian soybean prices are expected to recover from an eight-month low if Chicago consolidates strong gains this week and the dollar strengthens against the real, traders said on Thursday.  

Benchmark Chicago futures jumped to a one-month high on Wednesday on the back of a smaller-than-expected monthly government U.S. crop estimate.  

In a bid to weaken the real which is at multiyear highs against the dollar, Brazil's central bank has intervened seven times since early last week to buy the U.S. currency.  

Despite the bank's purchases, the dollar was lower on Thursday than a week ago, settling at around 2.258 reais, vs. 2.269 reais on Oct. 5 and around 2.90 reais a year ago.  

"Domestic soy prices have been falling due to the firm real and weak world prices," said analyst Fernando Muraro at Agencia Rural, adding, "There's a lot of soy and little local demand."  

Muraro estimated that about 20 percent of the 2005 crop was unsold and that demand had been reduced by the recent closures of soybean crushing plants by Archer Daniels Midland in Paranagau and by Bunge in Cuiaba.  

On Monday, a 60-kg bag of soybeans was quoted at 23.50 reais in Rondonopolis, Mato Grosso state, the lowest level since Feb. 8, 2005. Prices at the main grains export port of Paranagua were near the year's low at 29 reais per bag.  

Premiums for new crop deliveries next year, however, have risen. March premiums rose to 25/30 cents over Chicago compared with 20/25 cents last week. April-May premiums were higher at 11/15 cents over compared with 7/12 over last week.  

"The (Brazilian) market should react (to Chicago) but it doesn't mean a new trend," said Steve Cachia, analyst at Cerealpar in Curitiba, Parana state.  

He added that Brazilian prices had taken an unusual fall during the inter-harvest period, due mainly to the weakness of the dollar against the real.  

Agencia Rural's Muraro said that the United States was harvesting for the second successive year a huge crop of more than 80 million tonnes.  

South America is starting to sow its new soybean crop which is expected to total 105 million tonnes, Muraro said, estimating Brazilian output at 57 million tonnes, Argentine at 41 million and Paraguay, Bolivia and Uruguay a combined 7 million tonnes.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil real firm as  central bank  offers to buy dlrs
text:
(Adds details, background)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank on Monday offered to buy dollars on the local foreign exchange market at 2.238 as part of a program to build up hard currency reserves.  

After the announcement, the real <BRBY> trimmed its gains to 2.241 a dollar, 0.36 percent stronger than Friday's close. Traders said the central bank bought dollars from many dealers.  

The central bank last week resumed buying dollars on the forex market after a six-month hiatus.  

The real is trading near a four-year high thanks to heavy dollar inflows from trade and overseas corporate bond sales. Foreign investors have also boosted the real as they seek high returns from local bonds that offer yields greater than the benchmark interest rate of 19.5 percent.  

Exporters favor the interventions as they would help fuel foreign sales.
