title: ADR Report-ADRs buoyed by oil and Brazilian shares
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Overseas shares traded in the United States rose on Friday, as a rebound in oil prices lifted oil companies' American Depositary Receipts and U.S.-listed stocks of Brazilian companies rose sharply as inflation appeared to be getting under control there.  

However, better-than-expected U.S. job data kept the market in check as investors believe that meant another interest-rate hike would be almost certain.  

The Bank of New York's index of leading ADRs <.BKADR> was up 0.4 percent at a time when the 30-share Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> was up 0.2 percent at 10,304.64.  

The U.S.-listed shares of Brazilian companies soared on Friday as Brazil's central bank intervened in the foreign- exchange market by buying dollars for the fourth time this week.  

The interventions could be a boon to Brazil's exporters as its central bank's dollar purchases help control inflation and the Brazilian real has been near four-year-highs. Controlling inflation could help exporters keep foreign sales from slowing.  

Shares of Brazilian oil producer Petrobras climbed 5.5 percent to $64.76, while shares of Brazilian bank Unibanco advanced 4.6 percent to $50.82.  

The Bank of New York's index of leading Latin American ADRs <.BKLA> rose 3.3 percent to 186.39.  

Shares of Chilean power company Enersis jumped 4.7 percent to $12.06 after it said it would merge Chilectra, Chile's top power distributor, with its Elesur unit in a deal that could help it save $187 million in coming years. Enersis holds a majority stake in Chilectra.  

Oil companies' shares also gained some ground as U.S. crude oil futures prices stayed above $61 a barrel on Friday. Royal Dutch Shell shares rose 0.3 percent to $62.90.  

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for November delivery rose as high as $61.90 a barrel, up from Thursday's close, and up sharply from a two-month low of $60.70 hit on Thursday. By Friday afternoon, though, NYMEX November crude was down 6 cents at $61.30.  

But shares of European and Asian companies made mostly muted gains in U.S. trading on Friday, as investors fretted over hawkish comments this week from officials of the European Central Bank and the U.S. Federal Reserve. Comments from officials this week suggested that further monetary tightening would be necessary to contain inflationary pressures.  

The Bank of New York's index of leading European ADRs <.BKEUR> was up 0.1 percent at 131.16, while its index of leading Asian ADRs <.BKAS> was up 1.1 percent at 120.84.

title: Brazil  Palocci: Govt Won't  Intervene  In Exch Rate-Report
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's Finance Minister Antonio Palocci Thursday said the government won't intervene to stop a rally in the country's currency, the real, the Agencia Estado newswires reported.  

Interventions in the exchange market are "not a good policy and never work," Palocci is quoted as saying.  

Auctions Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at which the Central Bank bought an undisclosed amount of U.S. dollars were only aimed at increasing Brazil's foreign currency reserves, he said.  

"The accumulation of reserves is necessary for Brazil to back up the stability of our economy," Palocci said.  

The real weakened to BRL2.282 per dollar at 1405 GMT Thursday, down from Wednesday's close of BRL2.268. The Brazilian currency, however, this year has gained more than 16% against the dollar. [ 06-10-05 1414GMT ]  

Palocci also rejected any change in Brazil's current exchange rate policy.  

"We won't discuss our exchange rate policy again," Palocci is quoted as saying. "We think that the floating exchange rate (in place) since 1999 has served the Brazilian economy well."  

The recent strength of the real was caused by improving salaries, he added, while exports continue to develop well.  

Exporting companies have criticized government inactivity to stem the rise in the real, saying they are losing competitiveness.  

Exports, however, continue to boom. Brazil's foreign trade surplus in the year through September reached $32.67 billion, nearing 2004's full-year surplus of $34 billion. Analysts estimate the country will attain a trade surplus of $41 billion this year.  

Brazilian motor vehicle exports, however, fell 4.1 in September from the previous month. Carmakers have long complained that the current strength of the real renders their exports unprofitable.  

-By Bernd Radowitz, Dow Jones Newswires; (55 21) 3288 5004; bernd.radowitz@dowjones.com [ 06-10-05 1437GMT ]

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Closes Weaker After Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 05, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Wednesday after the central bank entered the market for a third day, buying the U.S. currency.  

The real closed at BRL2.268 to the dollar, 0.3% weaker than Tuesday's close of BRL2.261.  

Late Wednesday morning the central bank bought U.S. dollars from the market at a rate of BRL2.272 per dollar, the bank said. The dollars were acquired at an auction, but the bank didn't disclose the volume of its purchases.  

The real was trading at BRL2.276 shortly after the auction, weaker than the BRL2.274 at which it traded shortly before the auction was announced. However, the real strengthened from that level to its close.  

The bank already had intervened in the market both on Monday and Tuesday. According to market participants, the bank bought small lots of dollars from institutions Monday, while making larger purchases on Tuesday.  

Before the current round of interventions, the central bank last entered the spot currency market on March 16.  

The central bank doesn't try to impose a ceiling for the real through its interventions, former central bank Director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo was quoted as saying on the Agencia Estado newswire. Instead, he said, it was trying to prop up Brazil's foreign reserves - an explanation also given by Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles during interventions earlier this year.  

However, said Figueiredo, without the bank's interventions, the real would already trade stronger than BRL2.00 per dollar. Figueiredo now works at the brokerage Maua Investimentos.  

The Brazilian real has gained 17% against the U.S. currency this year amid strong dollar inflows from exporting businesses and positive market sentiment toward Brazil's macroeconomic fundamentals.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker As Ctrl Bk  Intervention  Expected
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 05, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Wednesday amid expectations the central bank may enter the market again to buy the U.S. currency.  

The real opened at BRL2.278, weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL2.261 per dollar. The real then, however, strengthened to BRL2.273 in early morning trading until 1309 GMT.  

The central bank had intervened in the market both on Monday and Tuesday, supposedly to buy dollars to increase Brazil's foreign reserves, but most traders think the bank is trying to prop up the real, and impede it from strengthening further.  

The Brazilian currency this year through early Wednesday has gained almost 17% against the greenback.  

After the central bank early Tuesday bought dollars at BRL2.240 per dollar, the real fell steadily through the afternoon.  

It was unclear, however, how many dollars the bank bought. Tuesday marked the second day in a row of central bank purchases of the U.S. currency through an auction system.  

This week's auctions were the first at which the central bank bought dollars since March.  

If the central bank abstains from intervening in the market, the real could rebound Wednesday amid continued strong inflows of exporter dollars.

title: Brazil  stocks plunge; real falls on  intervention
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks tumbled on Wednesday after setting a record high the previous session while the country's currency slipped as the central bank intervened to buy dollars for a third consecutive day.  

The Bovespa <.BVSP> index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange fell 3.58 percent to close at 30,163. It broke through 32,000 for the first time on Tuesday before investors started booking profits after heady gains that surpassed 12 percent in September alone.  

Most stocks slipped, with oil giant Petrobras off 5.35 percent to 32.75 reais on falling global oil prices.  

The broader selling was prompted in part by worries about potential U.S. interest rate hikes, which could lure capital away from emerging markets.  

"People are taking gains after several strong weeks and at the same time there are more worries about inflation in the U.S.," said Andre Querne of Maxima Asset Management in Rio de Janeiro. Faster inflation may prompt more aggressive rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.  

In foreign exchange trading, the real <BRBY> weakened 0.40 percent to end at 2.269 against the dollar as the government bought dollars as part of a broader program to rebuild foreign reserves and try to attain investment grade status.  

The intervention pleases exporters who are worried that their foreign sales may slow if the currency remains near the four-year highs it has reached recently.  

Traders say the intervention may prevent the real, which has gained on heavy dollar inflows, from gaining beyond 2.20.  

"The real won't stay as strong as we had thought (because of the intervention), which was stronger than 2.20," said Tarcisio Rodrigues, director of currencies at the Paulista brokerage.  

The central bank resumed buying dollars after a six-month hiatus on Monday and is expected to intervene further in the days ahead as inflation, which normally accelerates when the real weakens, is firmly under control.  

Some say the intervention would need to be aggressive to absorb heavy dollar inflows from exports, overseas bond sales and yield-hungry foreign investors who are snapping up Brazilian assets to buy exposure to the country's lofty benchmark interest rate of 19.5 percent.  

Brazilian assets have rallied in recent months on sound economic fundamentals that have resisted a bribes scandal that weakened President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's administration. (Additional reporting by Nathalia Ferreira and Juliana Siqueira)

title: Brazil  Real Closes Weaker After Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Wednesday after the central bank entered the market for a third day, buying the U.S. currency.  

The real closed at BRL2.268 to the dollar, 0.3% weaker than Tuesday's close of BRL2.261.  

Late Wednesday morning the central bank bought U.S. dollars from the market at a rate of BRL2.272 per dollar, the bank said. The dollars were acquired at an auction, but the bank didn't disclose the volume of its purchases.  

The real was trading at BRL2.276 shortly after the auction, weaker than the BRL2.274 at which it traded shortly before the auction was announced. However, the real strengthened from that level to its close.  

The bank already had intervened in the market both on Monday and Tuesday. According to market participants, the bank bought small lots of dollars from institutions Monday, while making larger purchases on Tuesday.  

Before the current round of interventions, the central bank last entered the spot currency market on March 16.  

The central bank doesn't try to impose a ceiling for the real through its interventions, former central bank Director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo was quoted as saying on the Agencia Estado newswire. Instead, he said, it was trying to prop up Brazil's foreign reserves - an explanation also given by Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles during interventions earlier this year.  

However, said Figueiredo, without the bank's interventions, the real would already trade stronger than BRL2.00 per dollar. Figueiredo now works at the brokerage Maua Investimentos.  

The Brazilian real has gained 17% against the U.S. currency this year amid strong dollar inflows from exporting businesses and positive market sentiment toward Brazil's macroeconomic fundamentals.  

-By Bernd Radowitz, Dow Jones Newswires; 5521-3288-5004; bernd.radowitz@dowjones.com [ 05-10-05 1957GMT ]

title: Brazil  Real Opens Weaker As Ctrl Bk  Intervention  Expected
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Wednesday amid expectations the central bank may enter the market again to buy the U.S. currency.  

The real opened at BRL2.278, weaker from Tuesday's close at BRL2.261 per dollar. The real then, however, strengthened to BRL2.273 in early morning trading until 1309 GMT.  

The central bank had intervened in the market both on Monday and Tuesday, supposedly to buy dollars to increase Brazil's foreign reserves, but most traders think the bank is trying to prop up the real, and impede it from strengthening further.  

The Brazilian currency this year through early Wednesday has gained almost 17% against the greenback.  

After the central bank early Tuesday bought dollars at BRL2.240 per dollar, the real fell steadily through the afternoon.  

It was unclear, however, how many dollars the bank bought. Tuesday marked the second day in a row of central bank purchases of the U.S. currency through an auction system.  

This week's auctions were the first at which the central bank bought dollars since March.  

If the central bank abstains from intervening in the market, the real could rebound Wednesday amid continued strong inflows of exporter dollars.

SAO PAULO, Oct 04, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday after the central bank entered the market to buy the U.S. currency.  

The real closed at BRL2.261 per dollar, down from the Monday close of BRL2.230.  

The central bank intervened early in trading. The bank bought dollars at BRL2.240 per dollar, and the real fell steadily through the afternoon.  

Traders said the bank bought modest volumes of dollars. However, Tuesday marked the second day in a row of central bank purchases of the U.S. currency through an auction system.  

This week's auctions were the first at which the central bank bought dollars since March.  

Analysts said the emerging pattern of central bank intervention could mean the government is ready to establish a ceiling for the real, which has gained more than 18% against the dollar so far this year. A policy of supporting the dollar against the real would help to assure continued robust exports in 2006, according to analysts.  

Another reason for central bank purchases of dollars would be to beef up foreign reserves. As of Thursday, foreign reserves stood at $57.04 billion, less than one year's imports of about $75 billion.  

Traders said the real could rebound Wednesday on exporter and investor inflows. Brazil posted a September foreign trade surplus of $4.329 billion. Meanwhile, Votorantim Bank and Gerdau Steel later this week will bring in some $400 million in proceeds from bond issues.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker Amid  Intervention  Expectations
text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 04, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday amid expectations of a possible central bank intervention in the market as a buyer of the U.S. currency.  

The real opened at BRL2.239 per dollar, versus the Monday close of BRL2.230.  

The central bank intervened in the market Monday, buying small lots of dollars from two or three banks, traders said. Monday marked the first purchases of dollars by the central bank since March.  

Traders said the central bank was expected to step up its purchases partly as a way to brake the appreciation of the real, which has risen nearly 20% against the dollar so far in 2005. Putting a floor under the dollar would be a way to assure continued heavy exports in 2006, according to analysts.  

Another reason for central bank purchases of dollars would be to beef up foreign reserves. As of Thursday, foreign reserves stood at $57.04 billion, less than one year's imports of about $75 billion.  

Another factor that could support the dollar going forward is the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates, with many analysts predicting another hike in Fed rates in November. Higher U.S. interest rates typically cause a reduction in investment flows to risky emerging markets such as Brazil.  

Brazilian interest rates, on the other hand, are expected to decline, another factor tending to reduce investment inflows. The central bank is due to meet again to review interest rates on Oct 19. Many analysts are predicting a cut of 50 basis points in the benchmark Selic rate, currently 19.5%.

title: Brazil  stocks end down;  intervention  weakens real
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's real weakened sharply on Tuesday after the central bank intervened to buy dollars for the second straight day, while stocks fell after breaking 32,000 for the first time early in the session.  

The central bank intervened to rebuild scant foreign reserves and, indirectly, weaken the real <BRBY> from a four-year high to help exporters.  

The real lost 1.35 percent to end at 2.26 a U.S. dollar.  

After a six-month hiatus, the central bank is expected to make more interventions in the days ahead as inflation, which normally accelerates when the real weakens, is firmly under control.  

"The central bank will likely be doing this often from now on. So long as dollar inflows are positive it will step in to soak them up," a currency trader at a Brazilian brokerage in Rio de Janeiro said.  

Some said the interventions, part of a broader government program to boost hard reserves and attain investment grade status, would need to be aggressive to absorb heavy dollar inflows.  

"Overseas corporate bond sales this year are 40 percent higher than last year and exports are very strong," the director of currencies at a Brazilian national bank said.  

Meanwhile, Brazil's Bovespa <.BVSP> lost ground after breaking the latest in a string of records and traders said it could slip even more after gaining some 12 percent last month.  

The stock index finished 1.8 percent down at 31,283. Most stocks fell and blue chip Petrobras slumped 3.89 percent to 34.60 reais on tumbling world oil prices.  

Tuesday's sell-offs were the sharpest in several weeks and cut into months of gains.  

Brazilian assets prices have rallied during the past several months on sound economic fundamentals that have resisted a bribes scandal that has weakened President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's administration.  

Investors fleeing low yields in the United States and Europe have also bought Brazilian bonds to gain exposure to the central bank's benchmark interest rate of 19.5 percent.  

(Additional reporting by Nathalia Ferreira and Juliana Siqueira)

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil  central bank  resumes dollar buying
text:
(Adds quotes)  

BRASILIA, Brazil, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Just two trading sessions after warning investors it could intervene "at any moment," Brazil's central bank held an auction to buy dollars on the local foreign exchange market after a six-month hiatus.  

But the intervention did little to weaken the real from a four-year high that has curbed inflationary pressures yet worried exporters.  

The buying price was fixed at 2.231 reais per U.S. dollar in the 10-minute auction which began at 11:18 a.m. (1418 GMT), the bank said in a statement. The bank took three offers, according to traders. It normally doesn't say how much it might have bought.  

After the central bank said it had returned to the dollar market, the real <BRBY> weakened 0.45 percent to 2.24 to the dollar.  

"On Thursday the central bank said it could intervene in the next hour, or next month. It was signaled," said Alexandre Vasarhelyi, head of currencies at ING in Sao Paulo.  

The real later recovered slightly and was trading near where it opened the session, at 2.237, or 0.31 percent weaker on the day.  

The central bank halted the purchases back in March and since then the real reached four-year highs.  

Even though exports this year are forecast to hit a record, exporters have clamored for interventions by the central bank to make their even products more competitive on global markets.  

Under the central bank's intervention policy, it can wade into the market to correct liquidity imbalances and use the dollars it buys to rebuild scant foreign reserves, which credit rating agencies say need to rise if Brazil is to attain investment grade status.

title: Brazil currency  gains despite  intervention  threat
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency strengthened to a fresh four-year high on Thursday as heavy dollar inflows offset comments from the central bank that it could intervene "at any time" to stop the rally.  

At the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, the benchmark Bovespa <.BVSP> index dipped 0.35 percent to end at 31,208.8 points after closing at a record high on Wednesday, the latest set during the past week.  

The real <BRBY> rose 0.98 percent to end at 2.213 per dollar, its strongest finish since May 2001.  

It weakened briefly after Central Bank Economic Policy Director Afonso Bevilaqua reiterated the bank could resume dollar purchases halted in March under a program to rebuild foreign reserves and make Brazil more resistant to financial shocks.  

But he did not promise the central bank would return to the market or say when it might resume buying dollars. As a result, the real recovered quickly.  

Bevilaqua said that under the program the government has no preferred price for the currency and would only intervene to correct imbalances in a market awash with dollars.  

Inflows are heavy as exporters repatriate sales dollars, companies bring back proceeds from bonds sold overseas and high domestic interest rates lure foreign investors fleeing low yield in the United States and Europe.  

"With these high interest rates, everyone is buying the real," said a currency trader at a Brazilian bank.  

Exporters want the government to buy dollars to weaken the real and boost the global competitiveness of their products.  

But the central bank has frequently indicated it wants to avoid intervening to let the real strengthen and cut inflationary pressure even further.  

Tame inflation allowed the central bank to make its first interest rate cut in 17 months this month. More reductions from the current 19.5 percent base rate are expected to boost economic growth.  

Stock market bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes closed off 0.71 percent at 36.40 reais.  

Sound economic fundamentals have allowed Brazilian stocks and the real to gain markedly despite a bribery scandal that has plagued President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's government since June. (Additional reporting by Nathalia Ferreira and Juliana Siqueira)

title: DJ Brazil Real Closes Slightly Weaker On Profit-Taking
text:
SAO PAULO, Sep 22, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar Thursday as profit-taking and importer purchases of dollars helped offset continued strong foreign-capital inflows, analysts said.  

The real closed at BRL2.276 per dollar, slightly weaker from Wednesday's close of BRL2.275.  

Importers took advantage of the real's strength in early trading to purchase dollars at an attractive price, analysts said. Furthermore, investors locked in profits after the real's recent surge pushed the currency on Wednesday to its highest level since April 10, 2002.  

Later Thursday, foreign-capital inflows helped offset the real's early weakness. Traders expect proceeds from several overseas debt issues to arrive in Brazil shortly. Several Brazilian companies, as well as the Brazilian government, have made large overseas debt offerings in the past two weeks, driven by demand from foreign investors for high-yield issues.  

The combination of importers' appetite for dollars and profit-taking in the Brazilian currency by foreign investors helped stem the dollar's fall and keep the central bank from intervening in the currency market, traders said.  

Brazil's bright economic picture, which includes tame inflation, falling interest rates and a growing economy, have made investing in the country and its companies more attractive and less risky in the eyes of investors.  

Brazil's risk rating as measured by the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus was one basis point wider at 364 basis points over U.S. Treasurys as of 1940 GMT. That's one basis point off the tightest the rating has been since 1997. Brazil's benchmark 2040 bond was down 0.100 at 121.200.  

-By Jeff Fick, Dow Jones Newswires; (55 11) 3145-1481; brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil stocks end at record close;  currency  flat
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Sept 16 (Reuters) - The Bovespa <.BVSP> stock index set historic closing and intraday highs on Friday, with Brazil's risk premium trading at an eight-year low and domestic interest rate cuts spurring hopes of faster growth in South America's largest economy.  

The rally meant Brazil joined Mexico and Argentina, where stock market records were broken this week as tame U.S. inflation staves off worries that aggressive U.S. rate rises that could lure money away from emerging markets.  

The benchmark index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange gained 1.53 percent to finish at 29,815.8 points. It also set a historic intraday peak at 29,863.42, topping record highs set in March.  

"Scenarios for the domestic and international economies are positive ... and U.S. rate hikes should continue to be very gradual," said Andre Querne, a fund manager at Maxima Asset Management in Rio de Janeiro.  

As the U.S. Federal Reserve hikes rates slowly, on Wednesday Brazil's central bank trimmed its benchmark rate to 19.5 percent a year. It was the first cut in 17 months and tame inflation makes it likely more will follow.  

"Now that the easing cycle has started, the consensus is that we're going to get successive rate cuts, which is a good sign," said Ademir Carvalho, an equities trader at Finabank.  

Demand for Brazilian assets is strong, despite a government bribes scandal that has hobbled President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's administration since June.  

J.P. Morgan's country risk premium, which measures the interest rate penalty Brazil must pay to sell bonds globally, fell slightly to 3.63 percentage points. Changes in the premium often drive the direction of stocks.  

CVRD , the world's leading producer and exporter of iron ore. led stocks higher for a second straight day after it offered to buy Canadian mining group Canico Resource Corp. for $669 million. CVRD shares rose 4.8 percent to 79.96 reais.  

In the foreign exchange market, the Brazilian real <BRBY> currency dipped 0.09 percent to end at 2.299 to the U.S. dollar.  

On Thursday, the real rallied nearly 1.4 percent, boosted by heavy inflows of greenbacks from exports and corporate bond sales as well as news the Treasury is planning to launch its first-ever global bond denominated in reais.  

But with the real trading close to a 40-month high, currency traders warned that the likelihood the central bank could intervene in the market was growing, limiting potential gains.

title: UPDATE: Argentina Peso, Bonds Stronger As Mood Improves
text:
(Updates with information from central bank on its intervention activity) 
   

BUENOS AIRES (Dow Jones)--The Argentine peso strengthened modestly Thursday, and it took significant official intervention to prevent it from rising further as concerns over Brazil's political crisis waned.  

Meanwhile, Argentine bonds also benefited from the improved mood, rising across the board after a series of declines in preceding trading sessions. This time, the local fixed-income market moved in tandem with the stock market, where the large-cap Merval index was approaching a record Thursday afternoon.  

The peso closed at ARS2.9050 to the dollar, slightly stronger than its close of ARS2.9075 Wednesday. This follows a gain of the same magnitude Wednesday after the peso had reached it weakest point in four months on Tuesday when concerns were growing over the regional market fallout from a widening corruption scandal in Brazil.  

Daniel Bou Kahir, a trader at Banco de la Pampa, said the real's positive reaction following testimony against Brazilian Finance Minister Antonio Palocci on Thursday by a former aide, meant market participants "no longer saw a reason to hold dollars" against the peso.  

Although municipal aide Rogerio Buratti reiterated his accusations that Palocci received kickbacks from private contractors when he was mayor of the southern city of Riberirao Preto in the 1990s, investors were heartened by the absence of documentary proof. At 1850 GMT, the real was at BRL2.4085, considerably stronger than its Wednesday close of BRL2.4525.  

Bou Kahir said demand for the peso, which fell in sympathy with the real last week and earlier this week, was evident in some strong volumes of around $180 million traded in the local electronic market. The fact that the exchange rate hardly moved offered strong evidence, he said, of dollar buying by either the central bank or state-owned commercial bank Banco de la Nacion.  

Later in the day, the central bank said it purchased $53 million in the open market, following two days in which it participation in the market was below $6 million.  

Bou Kahir added that this intervention suggested that authorities have set ARS2.90 to the dollar as the new level to protect. By contrast, he said, there had been little intervention in the preceding days, when the currency was trading weaker.  

Gains in the bond market were led by the discount bond in pesos. As of late afternoon it was up 2.47% at ARS118.4.  

The peso-denominated Bogar 2018, a bond issued as part of the restructuring of provincial debts, was up 1.16% at ARS139.1. Given the apparent preference for longer-dated paper, traders said this longer duration bond may have gone higher if it weren't for news that the government will issue ARS1.8 billion in Bogar 2020 bonds as part of the continued provincial debt refinancing program.  

Meanwhile, the dollar-denominated Boden 2012 was up 0.47% at a dollar equivalent ARS255.20 and the New York law dollar-based discount bond was unchanged at a dollar equivalent ARS94.3.  

Adrian Salvucci, an analyst at Silver Cloud Advisors, said the gain in the fixed-income market suggested an end to the profit-taking that was seen through much of August, as investors shifted into rebounding Argentine stocks.  

With both stocks and bonds rising Thursday, "it looks as if valuations have now become attractive," Salvucci said.  

-By Michael Casey, Dow Jones Newswires; michael.j.casey@dowjones; 54-11-4313 1918 [ 25-08-05 2133GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Fitch cuts Brazil bank tied to bribery scandal
text:
(Adds comments from Banco Rural, Moody's negative outlook)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, July 11 (Reuters) - Fitch Ratings on Monday cut the credit rating of medium-sized Brazilian bank Banco Rural after it was tied to an alleged bribes-for-votes scheme involving the ruling Workers' Party and five of its executives were indicted in a separate case.  

Fitch said it cut the bank's long-term, national scale ratings to "BBB-" from "BBB" and signaled another downgrade is possible by revising its outlook to negative.  

The ratings agency said the indictment of five executives last week amid a federal investigation into illegal offshore money transfers "may have a relevant impact on the bank's funding, liquidity and ongoing business development."  

Federal public prosecutors filed lawsuits against the executives last week.  

In a statement, Fitch said: "these rating actions reflect the continued negative impact on the bank's image due to coverage in the press following allegations brought forward against members of Congress that were allegedly receiving improper payments through a scheme operated using current accounts held with Rural."  

"The impact on Rural's image was further aggravated by the indictment presented in the Fourth Federal Court in Belo Horizonte against five bank executives last week," Fitch said.  

Later on Monday, Moody's Investors Service changed to negative from stable the outlook for Banco Rural's "D-" financial strength rating and "Ba3" rating for long-term local currency deposits in global scale.  

"Moody's action reflected the view that the bank may face pressure on its funding base in the wake of recent legal actions involving Rural's operations and its management team", the agency said in a statement.  

Banco Rural said in a statement that Fitch's decision was not based on the quality of its credit portfolio, adding that the bank has "net assets of excellent quality."  

The bank also noted an analysis from local ratings agency Austin Rating, saying it had recorded in recent weeks "normal and predictable withdrawals which had not even scratched the bank's financial health."  

Banco Rural, according to testimony in Congressional investigations, was the bank from which lawmakers withdrew cash offered by the Workers' Party in exchange for political support.  

The bank also loaned 3 million reais ($1.3 million) to the Workers' Party. The party has acknowledged the loan was made but said the money was used for legitimate purposes.  

The loan, the party said, was co-signed by Marcos Valerio, the owner of an advertising agency with lucrative government contracts who has been accused of operating the alleged bribery scheme.  

The bank has been under stress since the end of last year when Brazil's central bank intervened to prop up Banco Santos, sparking concerns about the financial health of other small financial institutions.  

Banco Rural, which is headquartered in Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais, has 75 branches in Brazil and net assets of 678 million reais ($288.5 million). ($1=2.35 Brazilian reais)

title: Brazil  Real Ends Lower On Ctrl Bk Hints Of  Intervention
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--After reaching a three-year high Monday, the Brazilian real weakened against the dollar Tuesday following hints from a central bank director that the monetary authority could resume intervention in the country's currency market in the near future to boost foreign reserves.   

The real ended at BRL2.409 per dollar, compared with BRL2.371 at Monday's close.   

Traders said the local currency slid early in the session after comments by Central Bank Monetary Policy Director Rodrigo Azevedo suggesting the bank would extend a program begun last year to bolster reserves.   

"Certainly we will return to buying dollars if this doesn't generate volatility," Azevedo said in an address to investment fund managers in Sao Paulo. "Purchases in 2004 and in the beginning of 2005 resulted in an important improvement in the position of foreign reserves. However, this doesn't give a considerable level of comfort."   

The real dropped more than 1.0% shortly following the remarks and stayed lower for the remainder of the session.   

Azevedo said the central bank has purchased about $10.2 billion so far this year, but noted that net foreign currency inflows through the end year were projected at $12.3 billion, which would leave a gap of more than $2 billion for possible further purchases to boost reserves.   

Brazil's foreign reserves under the international liquidity concept stand at $61.1 billion. Excluding IMF loan funding, however, reserves stand at only around $39.0 billion.   

The hints at the possibility of further dollar purchases come as the real has rolled up appreciation of about 10% against the dollar so far this year.   

The strong local currency has caused increasing discomfort for Brazilian exporters, who despite record-breaking overseas sales have said the appreciation of the real will likely cause negative effects on the trade balance and investment.   

Speaking to investors in Europe Tuesday, Brazilian Trade Minister Luiz Fernando Furlan said an ideal level for the real according to local industries would be around BRL2.70 per dollar.   

Meanwhile, according to the latest central bank market survey released this week, the real is seen ending June at around BRL2.50 per dollar and dropping to BRL2.70 per dollar by the end of the year.

title: DJ Brazil Real Opens Down On Higher Inflation Expectations
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, May 09, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar on Monday as traders believe that a rise in inflation expectations, contained in a survey published Monday, will keep Brazil's central bank from intervening in the currency market.  

The real opened at BRL2.464 per dollar, down from BRL2.462 per dollar from Friday's close, which was the strongest close of the Brazilian currency since May 8, 2002.  

Expectations for the IPCA inflation index the central bank uses to guide its monetary policy went up to 6.3% for the end of April from 6.28% a week earlier, according to a survey of more than 100 economists and market analysts polled by the central bank.

Traders said the central bank was likely to continue to abstain from currency market interventions as a stronger real helps to fight inflation.

title: Strong Brazilian Real Leaves Execs Sleepless In Sao Paulo
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The appreciation of the Brazilian real is keeping some local executives awake at night.  

With the local currency at a three-year high against the dollar, the head of the Brazilian unit of General Motors Corp. (GM), Ray Young, said this week in an interview with Sao Paulo daily Valor Futuro that he's in a state of "panic" and can't sleep because of the currency movement.  

GM, like many other companies here, is worried that the surprising continued strengthening of the real will cut into export growth. Though the country's trade accounts don't appear to be suffering yet, the government is keenly aware of concerns raised by big business and is considering steps to ensure that competitiveness is maintained.  

"Profit margins of all companies working with exports are falling," says Jose Augusto de Castro, vice president of the Brazilian Exporters Association, or AEB. "And it's getting worse."  

Indeed, the real was strengthening again Wednesday. At about BRL2.51 per dollar, the local currency is at its strongest point since May 2002 and a far cry from the now-unthinkable level of BRL3.21 registered last May.  

In practical terms, what it means is that exporters are taking in about 20% less in revenues than they did a year ago while simultaneously dealing with the production-cost increases implicit in Brazil's 7.6% annual inflation rate. Eventually, according to Castro, the cost-price squeeze is going to drive some companies out of exports and others out of business.  

Fearful of the negative impact the real's strength is having, Trade and Development Minister Luiz Fernando Furlan earlier this week said the government is studying ways to "compensate" exporters. Without providing details, Furlan said that the government will take steps to reduce red tape and improve transportation logistics.  

Furlan, former chief executive of food company Sadia SA, itself a major exporter, has been at odds with others in the administration on the issue of the real's appreciation.  

In November, when the real began strengthening in earnest, Furlan admitted that the trend was "a worry" and would likely hurt exports. He was immediately castigated by leaders of the governing Workers' Party for a lack of "team spirit." Asked about the strong real at a news conference in January, Furlan rolled his eyes, saying, "I guess we have to learn to live with it."  


 
    Exports Growth Continues, But Data Spark Concerns 
   

Furlan's warning about weaker exports hasn't come to pass. First quarter exports of $24.451 billion were up 28% from the same period the previous year.  

Indeed, booming exports are the main reason that the real has appreciated far beyond levels that had been expected by market participants.  

"The export dollars keep pouring in," said Raquel Fleury, a foreign exchange market analyst at the Tendencias Consulting Group. "Demand is robust among Brazil's trading partners. Meanwhile, Brazilian exporters have shown skill in winning market share."  

The exporter association's Castro, however, says that first quarter trade number indicated a subtle threat. Imports of $16.13 billion showed a slower rise, about 23%, than did exports during the first quarter of the year, he noted.  

"It should be the other way around," said Castro. "With a stronger real, imports should be rising faster than exports."  

What the lag in imports shows is that Brazilian consumers are not biting the lure represented by cheaper foreign products.  

"The rise in imports is temporary and comes from an increase in easy terms for consumer credit," said Castro. "It's all non-durable goods and foodstuffs. People are not buying big-ticket imports. The rise in imports will not endure."  

The danger, said Castro, is that Brazilian consumers will stop buying domestic big-ticket items. At that point, Brazilian manufacturers will be losing money on exports but without the safety net represented by a robust domestic market.  

Said Castro, "Right now, exporters are shipping mainly in order to honor contracts and maintain market share."  

That's exactly what Ray Young told Valor Economico. Exports accounted for a third of GM's Brazilian revenue in 2004. But exports are producing per-unit losses so far in 2005. "We may have to lose export contracts and reduce volume (if the real remains strong)," Young said.  

In some areas, Brazil is only retaining its edge because of the weakness of others.  

"The biggest problem for Argentina at present is a lack of competitiveness," said Cristiano Souza, an economist at the MCM Consulting Group in Sao Paulo, "Much of the Argentine industrial platform is outdated. Brazil has won an edge because of this."  

Meantime, the debate continues over how much further strengthening could be in store for the real, which has also benefited from sky-high interest rates - the central bank's key rate is at 19.5% per year - that have lured portfolio investments by overseas investors.  

Market participants say there's room for further appreciation, but say that the central bank won't stay on the sidelines for long.  

"The central bank will set an effective ceiling on the appreciation," said a trader at a large Sao Paulo brokerage. "It could be BRL2.50 or it could be BRL2.40 or it could be something else, but there will be a limit."  

As recently as last month, the central bank bought dollars on the foreign exchange market daily, ostensibly to bolster foreign currency reserves. However, analysts said that the bank may have also been testing the market reaction to its interventions.

title: DJ Brazil Real Opens Slightly Weaker As Importers Buy Dlrs
text:
SAO PAULO, Apr 26, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened just a tad weaker against the U.S. dollar on Monday as importers snapped up "cheap" U.S. dollars.  

The real opened at BRL2.524 per dollar, compared with   BRL2.523 at Monday's close.
  

Monday's close represented the strongest value for the Brazilian currency against the U.S. dollar since May of 2002.  

A "cheap" dollar led importers to buy the U.S. currency at the open on Tuesday, traders said. They said some banks and investment funds also were in a mood to buy dollars. The reason is the possibility of intervention in the foreign exchange market by the Brazilian Central Bank.  

The central bank made heavy purchases of dollars in February and early March. The stated purpose of the effort was to build foreign reserves. But an effect of the purchases was to raise the dollar to BRL2.76 by mid-March. But the absence of the central bank since mid-March has led to a steady appreciation of the Brazilian currency.  

Analysts said the central bank may be ready to reenter the market in order to prevent the real from strengthening beyond the psychologically important barrier of BRL2.50 per dollar.  

Pressure for intervention has been growing in recent days, with exporters saying the strong real could hurt Brazil's trade balance.  

Trade and Development Minister Luis Fernando Furlan on Monday responded indirectly to the concerns by saying the government was studying ways to "compensate" exporters for eventual losses caused by the strong real. Furlan declined to spell out what measures the government might adopt. Nor did he directly advocate central bank intervention.

title: Latin America  Currencies  Diverge Vs Dollar In January
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Latin America's major currencies turned in a mixed performance in the first month of 2005, marked especially by a divergence in the movements of Brazil's real and Mexico's peso.  

While Brazil's currency has been flying, Mexico's continues to sag. Elsewhere, currencies in Argentina and Peru gained ground, and those in Colombia and especially Chile lost it.  

Brazil's real jumped 1.4% Monday to a two-a-year-high of BRL2.611. That brought the monthly advance to 1.6% and built upon a 9.4% gain in 2004. The real has strengthened despite routine central bank intervention aimed at propping up the falling U.S. dollar in Brazil's local market.  

But Brazil's COPOM monetary authority also wants to throttle inflation expectations, and has been aggressively driving up interest rates.  

"A more hawkish tone from the central bank and inconsequential intervention has led USD-BRL to fall over 3% in the past 10 days," HSBC said in a report Monday. "While many - including ourselves - had thought the last interest rate hike would be the end of the tightening cycle, the Copom's latest minutes made clear this is not necessarily the case, and certainly any monetary loosening will be some time coming."  

Brazil's central bank will continue to intervene, "although this shouldn't prevent further BRL gains," HSBC said in a separate note.  

UBS Investment Research revised its projections for Brazil's economic growth, benchmark Selic interest rate and foreign exchange rate in a Monday report, raising its 2005 growth forecast to 5.3% from 4.3% and year-end Selic rate to 17.75% from 15%.  

It now sees the real at BRL2.80 by the end of December, rather than BRL3.00 thanks to the "consistent improvement in the external accounts and our current view regarding a much healthier balance of payments based on a strong capital account." Despite a recovery in domestic demand, Brazil keeps posting very large surpluses and the external accounts "continue to show an extraordinary adjustment," UBS noted.  

Although Mexico's peso has also been bolstered by monetary policy - the tenth tightening in a year came last Friday - it still weakened 0.3% against the dollar last month. In 2004, it lagged most other currencies from the region, strengthening just 0.7% versus the greenback.  

On Monday, Standard & Poor's upgraded the country's sovereign debt one notch to "BBB," which contributed to the peso's advance to MXN11.1823 against the dollar. "While the upgrade and Friday's corto hike have helped lift the peso, a sustained MSN rally seems unlikely given an expected deterioration in the trade balance, reduced interest differentials with the U.S. and ongoing political concerns" ahead of 2006 elections, HSBC said in a Tuesday report.  

Guillermo Estebanez, foreign-exchange analyst at Banc of America Securities, said Mexico can't afford a strengthening in its currency due to a "competitiveness problem: export growth in Mexico hasn't been as solid as in about any other exporting market."  

He also expects continued monetary tightening in Mexico, but thinks it will lag the U.S. Federal Reserve's rate rises. "So I don't think it (the peso) can strengthen that much," Estebanez added.  

Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz seemed to hint Monday the tightening would top out at some point sooner than later, saying he expects core inflation will run around 3.8% for several months before starting to decline "more significantly" in the second half. The consumer price index should end the year within the targeted 2%-to-4% range, he said.  

Following Ortiz's comments, ABN Amro revised its year-end peso forecast to MXN11.80 from MXN12.00 a dollar, citing a report that the Bank of Mexico has set a floor for overnight interest rates, among "a number of other reasons."  

Ortiz also said that while oil prices may remain relatively high this year, he expects other commodities prices to fall.  

High commodities prices have been a boon to resource-rich Andean countries and Argentina.  

Argentina's peso ($1=ARS2.9225) climbed 1.8% against the dollar last month. Thanks to heavy central bank intervention, it was mostly stable against the dollar last year. Although authorities in Colombia and Peru also have tried to keep their currencies from gaining on the dollar, both countries' currencies advanced strongly in 2004, though Colombia's peso ($1=COP2363) shed 0.6% last month while Peru's sol ($1=PEN3.266) strengthened 0.4%.  

Chile's peso ($1=CLP580.20), though, has been captured by an interesting dynamic. After it climbed 6% against the dollar last year, it plummeted 4.1% against the greenback in January, including a 1.4% jump Monday.  

In a Friday report, Goldman Sachs said it expects Chile's peso to trade in a CLP570-to-CLP590 range for the remainder of the year in "an enduring tussle between supportive fundamentals and low-to-negative carry."  

Banc Of America's Estebanez said speculators have taken to borrowing pesos to go long Brazil's real given the huge differential between Chile's low and Brazil's sky-high interest rates. "It's shooting fish in a barrel," he said.  

"I'm sure the Chileans don't mind because it (the peso) was probably too strong anyway," Estebanez noted. He added that the peso-real carry trade helps Chile maintain its currency's export competitiveness while it enjoys both low inflation and solid economic growth.

title: Brazil Real Slips Early As Mkt Awaits Rate Hike, Eyes USD
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real traded just a shade weaker early Thursday, as local traders looked to overseas foreign exchange markets for direction and awaited an expected domestic interest rate hike next week.  

The currency opened at BRL2.703 to the dollar, compared with Wednesday's BRL2.701 close, and continued to hold near that level as the session got under way.  

The real has been trading at 2 1/2-year highs near the BRL2.7 level for almost two months as the U.S. dollar plunges against major world currencies and strong exports bring in a steady flow of dollars to the local market.  

Adding to the real's strength Thursday was the fact that a fifth straight monthly interest rate hike is widely expected from Brazil's central bank next week. The rate hike, if it comes, will lift Brazil's base rate to a lucrative 18% per year or higher.  

Meanwhile, Moody's upgrade Wednesday of Brazil's credit rating outlook to positive added to perceptions that more dollars might continue flowing in. If the positive outlook turns to an actual credit upgrade, corporate and government borrowers might float more bonds and debt servicing costs would fall.  

But market participants mostly looked to the U.S. Thursday morning, where the release of fresh data on retail sales and unemployment claims could affect the dollar's trajectory.  

Traders were also on guard for further interventions by Brazil's central bank, which has entered the market with offers to buy dollars almost daily since the start of December. The dollar purchases have helped the bank build up reserves and also have discouraged bets that the real will continue to gain.  

-By Andrea Welsh, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1481; andrea.welsh@dowjones.com [ 13-01-05 1340GMT ]

title: Brazil  Real Opens Little Changed After Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real opened little changed Wednesday, after the Central Bank intervened in the market again on Tuesday and revealed that the amount of U.S. dollars it acquired in December so far was higher than most market estimates.  

The real opened down at 2.693 to the dollar, but then strengthened to Tuesday's close of BRL2.690 again during early morning trading.

Investors typically battle on the last working days of each month to influence the so-called Ptax, or average foreign exchange rate, for the past calendar month.

title: Brazil  real gains early, but  intervention  possible.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency strengthened early on Monday with traders saying a potential central bank intervention may not be enough to weaken the real.    


The real  gained 0.30 percent in early trade to 2.703 per U.S. dollar.
The Bovespa         index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange fell 0.33
percent to 25,573 points as it hovered around a record closing high set
last week.
   

The central bank has been buying dollars on the spot market for the last two weeks to rebuild foreign reserves, but last week its purchases were too small to weaken the real, which exporters fears is losing its competitiveness.   

Booming exports in the last two years have allowed Brazil to post current account surpluses and close its external financing gap but, the government on Monday said it posted a $242 million current account deficit in November.

Analysts say the government would be wise to keep the real weak, at around 3 per dollar.   

"The central bank has its hands tied. It can't say it's acting for exporters because that would be a subsidy," Hideaki Iha, a currency analyst at the Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo, said.   

"But it needs to do something more proactive because the interventions aren't working," he added.   

Stocks, meanwhile, stood to gain as Brazil's country risk rating, a measure of the interest rate penalty Brazil must pay to borrow abroad, was at its lowest levels since 1997.

Traders believe inflation is now in check, permitting the country's benchmark rate to stay unchanged at 17.75 percent a year at the central bank's next monetary policy meeting in January.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Strengthens Despite  Central Bank Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 15, 2004 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

The Brazilian real strengthened Wednesday although the country's central bank for a fifth time this month intervened to buy dollars in the market. The real closed at 2.725 to the dollar, up from BRL2.765 per dollar at Tuesday's close. The central bank bought an estimated $100 million in the market at a rate of BRL2.754, traders said. But that wasn't enough to revert a strengthening trend of the real that rose after Brazil's lower house of Congress in a final vote late Tuesday approved an overhaul of the country's bankruptcy code. The government believes the measure could have a significant effect in reducing the country's high credit costs and increasing lending volume. Brazil's central bank's interventions in the currency market this month came in an effort to avoid a too rapid valuation of the Brazilian currency that may hurt exporters. The real's strengthening came ahead of a decision by the central bank on its base interest rates later Wednesday. Most analysts expected the bank to raise the rate 50 basis points to 17.75%. Many investors hope that after a new hike Wednesday, the central bank may have ended its cycle of interest rate increases as inflation moves toward a government-set target. A weekly survey conducted by the central bank among more than 100 economists and analysts, predicted Brazil's IPCA consumer price index will rise 7.38% in 2004, and 5.78% in 2005. The government's inflation target for 2004 is 5.5% with a 2.5-percentage-point tolerance, while for 2005 it is 4.5%, also with a 2.5-percentage-point tolerance. -By Bernd Radowitz, Dow Jones Newswires; (55 21) 3288 5004; bernd.radowitz@dowjones.com

title: Brazil 's real gains early,  intervention  unlikely.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Brazil's real strengthened early on Tuesday as traders bet Banco do Brasil would soon repatriate 200 million reais in global bonds sold on Monday and that the central bank would refrain from buying dollars.  

The local currency, the real , gained 0.33 percent to 2.757 per dollar. The Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange rose 0.54 percent to 25,357 points.

title: Brazil  real gains despite  intervention , stocks up.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency strengthened on Monday despite an intervention by the central bank to buy U.S. dollars, while stocks also scaled higher toward a historic high reached last week.   

Boosted by an expected interest rate hike on Wednesday by the central bank and the dollar's slide against the euro, the local currency, the real , gained 0.36 percent to close at 2.766 per dollar. The Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange rose 1.17 percent to 25,225 points.   

The real gained even though the central bank held its fourth auction to buy dollars since last Monday, when the monetary authority said it would start buying greenbacks to rebuild scant foreign reserves. Economists have said the plan will also help weaken a currency that some exporters believe is overvalued. The real lost about 3 percent last week.   

The central bank bought dollars at 2.768 on Monday, traders said. The central bank normally does not disclose the price and amount of dollars it purchases.   

Traders said Monday's purchase appeared to be small and left them guessing about how much the central bank wants to weaken the currency. Many exporters want the real to weaken to 3 per dollar.   

"I don't know if the market is testing the central bank, but I think the central bank didn't buy a lot of dollars," Francisco Carvalho, a currency trader at the Liquidez brokerage said. "The market is selling dollars heavily and as soon as the auction was over, the selling resumed."   

Traders said that the real may rally on Tuesday after state-run Banco do Brasil sold 200 million reais in global bonds on Monday that are denominated in the local currency.   

Stocks posted moderate gains and finished within several hundred points of its record high close of 25,632.50 posted last Monday.   

Though they have been buoyed by a positive outlook for growth and stability in Latin America's largest country, stocks are expected to come under pressure this week as the central bank prepares for a likely interest rate hike on Wednesday.   

Still, some traders are betting falling inflation expectations may allow the central bank to refrain from hiking rates in January.   

Bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes (TNLP4.SA), which comprises about 12 percent of the index, rose 1.23 percent to 42.01 reais.   

Banco Bradesco (BBDC4.SA) gained 3.2 percent after closing a financing agreement with a small bank and Banco Itau (ITAU4.SA) climbed 1.79 percent to 397 reais after buying a small car loan company. title: Brazil  currency , stocks gain after slipping early.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency and stocks recovered from early losses to end higher on Friday, as President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said two years of strict policies have produced the fastest growth in a decade.   

The benchmark Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange rose 1.66 percent to finish at 24,933.3 points, nearly erasing losses from the previous session.   

The local currency, the real, finished 0.18 percent stronger at 2.776 reais per U.S. dollar to close higher for the first time since Monday.   

It briefly weakened beyond 2.8 per dollar for the first time in a month as the dollar rallied for a third straight day against the euro and threats of interventions by Brazil's central bank limited gains.   

Despite a gain for the real, bets the local currency will gradually weaken encouraged buying of companies that are big exporters. The index is still trying to return to historic highs reached on Monday.   

"The real gained today only because the central bank didn't intervene," Miriam Tavares, head of currencies at the AGK brokerage in Sao Paulo, said.   

The central bank on Monday said it would start buying dollars to rebuild scant foreign reserves. At the same time, the purchases weaken a currency that exporters fear is overvalued.   

The central bank announced auctions to buy dollars on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday. It accepted bids in the first two auctions but rejected them in the third.   

Still, the threat of interventions, whether they materialize or not, is limiting would-be gains in a currency that gained nearly 5 percent in November on strong dollar inflows from exports and overseas bond sales. Interventions and rallies by the dollar this week weakened the real nearly 3 percent.   

Shares of companies that gain the bulk of their revenues from exports were among the strong gainers as the real looks like it will continue to weaken in the short-term.   

Miner CVRD rose 2.41 percent to 57.05 reais, steelmaker Gerdau gained 1.32 percent to 45.19 and jetmaker Embraer finished 3.26 higher at 20.30 reais.   

Bovespa bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes, which makes up about 12 percent of the index, dipped 0.22 percent to 41.50 reais.   

At a ministerial meeting on Friday, Lula took credit for the strong markets and economy.   

"The catastrophe predicted by some never happened," he said.   

He said fears his government would adopt inflationary populist policies were misplaced and that the last two years of tight monetary and fiscal policies are producing stable growth.   

"GDP grew more than hoped and this isn't an unstable bubble," he said.   

Brazil's gross domestic product is expected to surpass 4.6 percent this year, the fastest rate of growth in a decade, and cool next year to 3.5 percent.

title: DJ Brazil's Real Steady Early As Mkt Eyes Econ Data, Ctrl Bk
text:
SAO PAULO, Dec 09, 2004 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

Brazil's real held steady in early trade Thursday as investors eyed industrial output data and wondered whether the central bank might intervene to weaken the real as it did twice earlier this week. The real opened a shade weaker at 2.762 to the dollar, compared with Wednesday's BRL2.759 close, but then reversed course and firmed to BRL2.758 to the dollar as the session got underway. Foreign exchange market participants took in stride a Thursday morning report showing Brazil's industrial output slowed slightly in October from September even as it climbed 2.7% from October last year. The central bank started raising interest rates in September, but most economists don't expect the rate hikes to fully affect the economy before next year. Meanwhile, traders were on guard for further interventions by Brazil's central bank after the institution stepped into the market to stock up on dollar reserves Monday after the real hit two-and-a-half year highs better than BRL2.70. The bank bought even more dollars Tuesday, leading foreign exchange traders to conclude the purchases were meant to prop up the real. Caution hung over the market Thursday, even though the real has softened almost 2% since the start of this week and the bank stayed on the sidelines Wednesday. Trade Minister Luis Furlan has said lately he's worried the stronger real will slow an export boom that has revived Brazil's economy and lifted the trade surplus above $30 billion so far this year. Traders were also keenly attuned to a modest strengthening of the U.S. dollar against the euro Thursday morning. Most of Brazil's major exports are dollar-linked commodities, although Furlan has encouraged exporters to try to sell for euros if they can. Dollars are continuing to flow into the market, as Brazil exports keep bringing about $400 million per working day. Also supporting the real are expectations that banks will bring in more dollars by selling real-denominated debt to overseas investors eager to bet on emerging market currencies. Such sales have brought in more than $200 million in the past few weeks, and talk is circulating that the government will launch its own real-linked debt issue in coming months. Government-controlled retail bank Banco do Brasil (BBAS3.BR) became the latest bank to announce a real-denominated overseas bond issue Tuesday.

title: Brazil  real falls on  intervention , stocks stumble.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency, the real, weakened on Thursday as the central bank bought dollars for the third time this week, widening the real's losses to nearly 3 percent since Monday. Stocks also lost ground.   

The real fell 0.8 percent to 2.781 per U.S. dollar after the intervention. The Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange stumbled 1.77 percent to 24,526 points as it also eased back from historic highs reached on Monday.

"Any gains are limited because the market is always expecting the central bank to enter the market," Jorge Kattar, a derivatives trader at Rabobank, said.   

The real also slipped as the troubled dollar strengthened for a second straight day against the euro.   

Nearly all stocks declined.   

"It's healthy to fall a bit after these record highs. The gains should return in the second half of December," said Ademir Carvalho, an equities trader at Finabank.   

Bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes fell 1.68 percent to 41.59 reais and Banco Itau rose 0.23 percent to 377 reais after saying it entered a 1.5 billion reais credit accord with Minas Gerais state bank BMG.   

Steelmaker Gerdau fell 3.25 percent to 44.60 reais after selling a block of shares equal to 10 percent of its float as part of a strategy to boost liquidity in its stock.

The real closed at 2.759 to the dollar, compared with BRL2.748 Tuesday. title: Brazil stocks and  currency  end down, paring losses.
text:

title: FOREX  VIEW:Weak Dlr Sparks Global  Central Bank  Headaches
text:
By Laurence Norman 
   A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN 
   

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--As European and Japanese officials grab headlines with their statements of concern, pleas for help and angry foot-stamping about the dollar's declines, attention to the conundrums the currency's weakness is sparking for other central banks has been somewhat sidelined.  

That may have changed somewhat Tuesday, when the Bank of Canada cited local dollar strength as a potential drag on its economy and therefore a central reason for keeping its benchmark overnight rate at 2.50%.  

And Canada isn't alone. From South America to the Far East, the dollar's long bout of decline is adding an extra dimension to the always delicate balancing act that central banks face: keeping economies growing and inflation in-check, while steering clear of currency manipulation.  

In explaining its decision to hold rates steady - a move that came to be widely expected in recent days - the Bank of Canada said that while inflation was on track, there was some downside risk to growth because of a strong Canadian dollar.  

"The U.S. dollar has depreciated further against major floating currencies, including the Canadian dollar," the central bank said in a statement. "If exchange rates were to persist at current levels, and if all other economic and financial factors were to remain unchanged, there would be a dampening effect on aggregate demand for Canadian goods and services."  

The dollar had lost around 8.4% year-to-date until Tuesday morning against the Canadian dollar, making the latter one of the year's best performers. By comparison, the euro has gained just 6.3% this year, despite now trading at all-time lows.  

Loose monetary policy in the U.S. is seen as at least partly responsible for the dollar's fall. By keeping the currency printing presses on, the Federal Reserve has placed cheap dollars in the hands of U.S. consumers, who can spend them on imports and in the hands of businesses and speculators, who can invest them abroad.  

Many analysts continue to believe the Bank of Canada will raise rates in the medium-term, as authorities keep the inflationary effects of a growing economy that may be close to capacity in check. But the rate-tightening cycle may be tougher going now. "Judging by the comments on the exchange rate, it almost sounds like rates need to be at stimulative levels to offset the impact of the currency, so this is pretty close to neutral," said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc.  

A few thousand miles south, the Colombian central bank is facing a similar dilemma. The peso had gained around 11% by the end of November in the spot market, despite the bank saying in September it would buy $1 billion by year's end. That's hurting exporters, something President Alvaro Uribe acknowledged in September when he said the country needed a competitive foreign exchange rate," adding "I dislike the appreciation."  

Cutting rates would be an ideal solution and the central bank did that in March, reducing them to 6.75%, but with inflation at the upper end of where the bank wants it, Clyde Wardle, head of emerging market FX strategy at HSBC, says that will be tough.  

"I think in Colombia there is obviously concern about the strength of the Colombian peso ... They may be interested in cutting rates, but inflation is above where they might want it to be," he said.  

Intervention Qualms 
   

Dollar weakness presents a different problem for some Asian countries - more a political complication than an outright economic one. South Korea, for instance, has not only cut interest rates but has once again gone down the controversial currency intervention road as it attempts to weaken the won, which is trading close to seven-year highs.  

That's politically sensitive at a time when the rest of the world is calling on Asian countries to stop trying to manipulate their currencies and insulate them from the effects of the weakening dollar. Even Japan, the most ardent practitioner of currency market intervention in the industrialized world, hasn't intervened in the markets since the first quarter.  

Yet dollar weakness need not always be a central bank headache. HSBC's Wardle said Brazil's decision to openly intervene in the currency markets to buy dollars and stem the real's appreciation this week doesn't mean it's losing out from the dollar's slide. The central bank says it's doing so to build reserves not to target an exchange rate. The government has some $10-$11 billion of interest and principal payments on its foreign debt due next year. Part of that is expected to come from exchange reserves.  

Wardle points out that a weaker dollar reduces the country's debt load and helps it deal with high international oil prices. As a deflationary factor, the stronger real may be pushing Brazil toward a time when it can stop raising its reference Selic rate, which now stands at 17.25%.  

And while he admits that some sectors of the economy and the government may fret about the headline exchange rate of the real to the dollar, the Brazilian currency is actually "really unchanged" year-to-date against the currencies of its largest trading partners, noting that Brazil exports more to Europe than it does to the U.S. The result: Brazil can lift its reserves and quieten political complaints via occasional interventions, while it enjoys the beneficial side-effects of a weaker dollar.  

"Politicians can have a somewhat distorted viewpoint of the real impact of the currency," Wardle said. "But there really isn't any justification" for worrying about the strength of the Brazilian real right now.  

(Laurence Norman covers foreign exchange for Dow Jones Newswires in New York. He has previously covered the Argentine economy for Dow Jones in Buenos Aires.)  

-Laurence Norman, Dow Jones Newswires, 1-201-938-2096; laurence.norman@dowjones.com  

(Don Curren in Toronto contributed to this report.) [ 12-07-04 1608ET ]

title: Brazil  real drops as cenbank  intervenes , stocks ebb.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank bought dollars for a second day in a row on the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, sending the local currency 1 percent lower, and stocks took a blow from low prices at a giant energy auction.  

The Brazilian currency, the real, fell just over 1 percent to 2.747 per U.S. dollar after the central bank bought dollars at 2.722 to rebuild foreign reserves.  

The real, which hit a 2-1/2-year closing peak against the dollar on Friday, reversed course on Monday sliding 0.37 percent after the central bank announced it was intervening in the market for the first time since February.  

"They are not buying big lots, but their presence inhibits dollar sales. If the central bank maintains its stance, the dollar easing trend should be inverted," said Marco Antonio Azevedo, head of forex at Brascan bank.  

Some government ministers say the real is too strong and could hurt export competitiveness in coming months.  

Meanwhile, the main Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange fell 2.5 percent to 24,988 points after failing to hang onto historic highs reached in the previous session as power utilities crumbled.  

Analysts said lower-than-expected prices for electricity at a groundbreaking power auction caused the power utilities index to drop 4.2 percent as hopes for higher revenues in the sector faded away. The price for 2005 delivery fell to 62 reais by Bovespa's close while the market had expected 70 reais.  

Stocks in federal power holding Eletrobras, one of the main sellers at the auction, fell 9.2 percent to 42.02 reais. Even shares in power distributors who bought cheap electricity at the auction fell as analysts saw the prices there as bad for investment in the sector.  

Sao Paulo's distributor Eletropaulo fell 3.7 percent to 69 reais.  

Elsewhere, shares in telecommunications firm Embratel Participacoes SA slid 12.6 percent to 5.55 reais after the company said it plans to issue up to 1.9 billion reais ($703 million) in new shares.  

Analysts fear Embratel's parent company, Telefonos de Mexico, could use Embratel as a vehicle to finance its pending acquisition of Brazil's Net Servicos de Comunicacao, the debt-laden struggling cable television company, or AT&T Latin America, which Telmex bought in February.  

Net's shares ended flat 0.6 reais.
