title: Brazil Central Bank Intervenes  On  Forex  Mkt, Weakens Real
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Amid growing concern that the strength of the local currency could hamper the country's export competitiveness, Brazil's Central Bank intervened on the foreign exchange market Monday for the first time since February.  

Brazilian officials have come under increased pressure the last two weeks to halt the steady rise of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar as a way to stimulate exports and assure a continued surplus in overseas accounts.  

Though the monetary authority denied that it aims to weaken the real - saying instead that Monday's move was part of a strategy to build up foreign currency reserves - some market participants said it was an indication that officials are uncomfortable with the current trend.  

"There has been a perception in the market over the last two or three sessions that the Central Bank doesn't want the real to strengthen beyond BRL2.70," said a currency trader. "Today (Monday) they brought out one of their weapons."  

Early in the session, the Central Bank bought what traders characterized as a a modest volume of U.S. dollars. The intervention came at a critical moment in trading, as the Brazilian real strengthened beyond the BRL2.70-per-dollar barrier. The monetary authority bought dollars at BRL2.697. The real had opened Monday's session at BRL2.701 per dollar.  

If the government's intention was to establish BRL2.70 as a ceiling for the real, then its first effort to do so was a success, traders admitted. The real hovered around the BRL2.72 mark during the rest of Monday's trading session.  

Over the long run, however, it is unlikely the Central Bank will be able to enforce the BRL2.70 level, if that is what the bank seeks to accomplish.  

"The Central Bank does not have the firepower to enforce a floor or a ceiling for the currency," said Darwin Dib, macroeconomic analyst for Unibanco, Brazil's third largest private bank.  

Said Ana Paula Rocha, an economist at ABN-Amro Bank in Sao Paulo, "The U.S. dollar is weakening all over the world. It's not the Brazilian Central Bank that is going to be able to go against the tide."  

"It looks to me like the Central Bank has been looking for a good moment to buy dollars in order to build up foreign reserves," said Rocha. "The Central Bank has been talking about doing this all year and they found a good opportunity to do it."  

Reserves stood at $50.4 billion as of Friday.  


 
     Exporters Worried About Strength Of Real 
   

But worries about exports and their relation to the foreign exchange rate have surfaced in recent weeks as the real consistently gained ground against the dollar. The real opened the year at BRL2.90 per dollar.  

Trade and Development Minister Luis Fernando Furlan gave voice to concerns about exports in remarks made only minutes before the actual Central Bank intervention Monday, saying, "the current level of the real scares exporters because they have had to absorb rising domestic costs this year in areas such as raw materials, public utilities rates and taxes, all of which cause their costs to rise."  

Indeed, even at Monday's close of BRL2.719 per dollar, the Brazilian real has gained more than 6% against the American currency so far in 2004, while annual inflation has hovered at around 7%. The combination is enough to put some exporters into the red, said Furlan.  

Such worries are well founded, according to the weekly survey of financial market analysts published every Monday by the Central Bank. In this week's survey, the analysts forecast a 2005 foreign trade surplus of only $27 billion, down from this year's expected surplus of $33 billion.  

But does that matter?  

Not really, according to former central bank president Affonso Celso Pastore. "Brazil's macroeconomic numbers today would seem to support a rise in the value of the real," Pastore said, during a presentation at a Rio de Janeiro seminar. "Maybe exporters will suffer a little bit but the rest of society is doing quite well at the current exchange rate."  

Pastore argued that a $27 billion 2005 trade surplus was more than enough to assure another current account surplus for Brazil. Meanwhile, "a strong real will encourage investments in capital goods imports needed to boost Brazil's plant and equipment."  

A strong real also helps counter domestic inflation by holding down the prices of imported goods, he said. In addition, it reduces the cost of paying off the dollar-indexed debts held by many Brazilian companies, especially in the public utilities area.  

Brazilian Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles himself attempted to dispel the idea that Monday's intervention was aimed at setting some kind of currency band.  

Meirelles told the same Rio de Janeiro seminar, "We don't have any foreign exchange rate target. There is neither a ceiling nor a floor (for the real against the dollar)."  

Said a trader, "Meirelles was a little vague, as he always is, but maybe this time he was telling it straight."

title: Latin American news in brief at 2 p.m. EST.
text:
NEW YORK, Dec 6 (Reuters) - The following are top Latin American news briefs compiled from full-length stories that have run separately:   

Brazil currency falls on central bank intervention

SAO PAULO, Brazil - Brazil's real fell abruptly against the dollar Monday after the central bank announced its first intervention to purchase dollars since February. The currency fell as much as 0.7 percent against the dollar after the central bank real strengthened in the morning to hit a 2-1/2-year peak of 2.699 to the dollar. The bank denied it sought to weaken the real at a time when exporters complain the strengthening currency was eroding their competitiveness. The bank said it acted to rebuild foreign reserves. The real trimmed its losses, trading down 0.37 percent at 2.719.   

-   

Brazil auto production jumps in 2004, strong 2005 seen   

SAO PAULO, Brazil - Brazil's auto manufacturers should boost their production by 5.4 percent to 2.3 million vehicles next year following a jump in output this year fueled by an economic rebound and strong exports, the sector's main trade group said Monday. Production in the first 11 months of this year was 2.02 million vehicles, 20.8 percent higher than a year earlier, with 1.4 million cars being sold domestically. Exports of motor vehicles rose 50 percent to $7.52 billion.   

-   

Peru workers strike to back U.S. smelter company demands   

LIMA, Peru - About 4,000 smelter workers launched a two-day stoppage Monday to support their employer, U.S.-owned Doe Run Peru, in a push to roll back a year-end government environmental deadline. Farmers in Peru's central Andes, where Doe Run's metals smelter is located, also blocked roads to pressure the government to agree to a five-year extension for the company to comply with toxic waste standards. Doe Run, an engine of the local economy, last month said it pull out of Peru if the government failed to give it more time to meet the ordered cut in toxic emissions. The company expects to export $510 million of refined minerals in 2004.   

-

HAVANA - The Cuban government freed an independent journalist Monday, the 14th member of a group of 75 jailed dissidents released on medical grounds as Havana seeks to repair relations with the European Union. title: Brazil real eases as gov't steps up dollar purchases.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Brazil intensified its dollar purchases on Monday, weakening its real currency in the process while taking advantage of extraordinary foreign exchange inflows to rebuild cash reserves.   

Less than two weeks after the Treasury made a similar announcement, Brazil's central bank said it would also intervene in the market. The unexpected announcement occurred after the local currency strengthened past 2.70 per dollar to 2.699 earlier on Monday.   

After the intervention, the first by the central bank since February, the real weakened 0.70 percent to 2.728.   

Under the rules of the central bank's floating-rate currency regime, the monetary authority cannot target a value for the real and can only intervene if one of the two currencies in the spot market lacks liquidity.   

Nonetheless, the purchases on Monday occurred against a backdrop of worries among industrialists that the real, currently at 2-1/2-year highs, is too strong and will hurt the country's record trade surplus in coming months.   

"There could be a new floor or a trading band, but we would need to have another strong rally to test this and see at what price the central bank intervenes," said Jose Roberto Carreira, head currency trader at the Novacao brokerge in Sao Paulo.   

Later on Monday, the central bank will likely disclose the exchange rate at which it purchased dollars, but not the amount bought. Traders said the rate was around 2.715.   

Brazil Trade Minister Luiz Fernando Furlan and Agriculture Minister Roberto Rodrigues have sided with industrialists, who are pushing for a weaker real at about three per dollar.   

Despite the calls for a weaker currency, some economists say the central bank should let the real strengthen in the short term to better contain inflation that is being pressured by high global oil prices.   

Central bank and Treasury officials maintain they have no desired value for the real. The Treasury said less than two weeks ago it earmarked $3.0 billion for spot market purchases through June to pay down foreign debt.   

Afonso Bevilaqua, the central bank's economic policy director, said Monday's purchases will help rebuild scant foreign reserves.   

The central bank in January said it would buy dollars this year via spot market interventions. The purchases were curtailed after only one month but are now starting again.   

"This continues the plan we announced January 6. We want to rebuild reserves over the medium term without any specific worry about the exchange rate," Bevilaqua said.   

According to the latest central bank data, Brazil's net foreign reserves are estimated at $24 billion, well below the $70 billion it had before trying unsuccessfully to defend the then fixed-rate real from speculation starting in late 1998.   

Including IMF funds, Brazil has $50 billion in reserves, but economists say the country needs to rebuild reserves if it hopes to go it alone without aid from the IMF when its current accord with the lender expires early in 2005.   

"This is an atypical period for emerging markets, with huge dollar inflows, so the government has an opportunity to accelerate its dollar purchases," said Mauro Schneider, economist at ING in Sao Paulo.   

"This is the correct strategy. I think the Treasury could buy more and do this without implying a desired level for the real," he said.   

In the past, the Treasury has bought more than expected. In 2003, it said it would buy around $6 billion on the spot market to fund external debt payments but bought $11.2 billion.   

The real is currently trading at its strongest levels since June 2002. It rallied last week on strong economic data, heavy dollar inflows from exports and overseas corporate bond sales, and a dollar that is sliding to record lows against the euro.   

Analysts say more central bank purchases may be in store as the only external factor seen causing the real to weaken in the near term would be an intervention by the European Central Bank to stop the euro's rally against the dollar. (Additional reporting by Rodrigo Gaier).

The Brazilian currency slid 0.44 percent to 2.721 to the dollar after the intervention, reversing an earlier gain of 0.37 percent to 2.699. Meanwhile, the Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange was treading water and virtually unchanged 25,492 points after finishing at a record high on Friday.   

The central bank denied it was deliberately trying to weaken the real at a time when some investors fear exports could slow.   

"This is an effort to rebuild foreign reserves in the context of a floating rate currency regime and inflation targeting," Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles said on Monday on nationwide television.   

"There was no liquidity in the real before the intervention. The central bank bought up all dollars offered at 2.715 but we don't know how much the market offered," Jose Roberto Carreira, head currency trader at the Novacao brokerage in Sao Paulo, said.   

The central bank will likely disclose the exchange rate at which it purchased dollars, but not the amount bought, later on Monday. Traders said the rate will likely be around 2.715.   

Under the central bank's rules, it can only intervene if one of the two currencies in the spot market lacks liquidity.   

The intervention follows a government plan announced less than two weeks ago to buy $3 billion on the spot market through June via the Treasury. That plan, the government says, is aimed at paying down foreign debt and rebuilding foreign reserves.   

Economists, however, say both strategies amount to an attempt to weaken the real or stem its appreciation.   

The real is trading at its strongest levels in two-and-a-half years. It rallied last week on strong economic data and heavy dollar inflows from exports and overseas corporate bond sales.   

But its strength has worried some industrialists who say the real needs to weaken to around three per dollar to keep exports competitive. Some economists, however, say the central bank could better contain inflation expectations if it lets the real strengthen to limit the impact of high global oil prices.   

Among individual stocks, Unibanco was up 0.56 percent at 16.02 reais after Commerzbank said it would sell its stake of about 5 percent in the Brazilian bank through a secondary share offering.

title: Brazil Real Closes At 2 1/2-Year High On Bond Sales
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed stronger Friday, hitting a two-and-a-half-year high, on news of fresh overseas bond placements.  

The real closed at BRL2.709 per dollar, up from the Thursday close of BRL2.733.  

Three different Brazilian banks announced overseas bond sales through the trading day Friday. The bond placements will total $225 million.  

Meanwhile, the Brazilian government announced plans to raise an additional $500 million by reopening an existing dollar-denominated global bond that was originally issued in July and which matures in 2014.  

The fresh inflows will add to Brazil's existing flood of export dollars coming into the market. Brazil has averaged about $600 million per week in its foreign trade surplus so far this year.  

News of the bond issues led to a strong rise in the real in mid-afternoon trading, with the Brazilian currency briefly trading at better than BRL2.70. The real traded as high as BRL2.695 per dollar.  

Dollar purchases by banks and importers pulled the real back across the BRL2.70 barrier by the close, however.  

The market was also reacting to comments late Thursday by Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles, who said, "Neither Brazil, nor any country in the world is in a condition to control international (currency) flows and control the dollar."  

Market players took the comment as one more piece of evidence that Brazil's government won't intervene in the market to sustain the value of the U.S. dollar even though exporters have complained that a strong real hurts exports.

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Up As Ctrl Bank Rejects  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real opened stronger Friday after comments by Brazil's central bank president indicating that Brazil isn't going to intervene against a strengthening of its currency and amid expectations of a possible real-dominated bond issue outside the country by Brazil's government.  

The real opened at BRL2.731 to the dollar, up from BRL2.733 at Thursday's close, and then quickly rose to BRL2.725 in early morning trading.  

"Neither Brazil nor any country in the world is in a condition to control international (currency) flows and control the dollar," Central Bank President Henrique Mereilles said.  

Brazil's real has surged from a low of BRL3.212 against the greenback on May 20 to its current level of between BRL2.7 to BRL2.75 amid improving macroeconomic data and rising exports.  

Also, expectations the government could take advantage of the current strong levels of the Brazilian currency to issue a global bond or Eurobond denominated in reals, made investors hesitant to bet against the real.  

The government may wait for U.S. payroll data to be released later Friday before placing the real-denominated foreign bond in the market, traders said.  

Exporting companies flush with dollars in recent days had flooded the market, contributing to the rally of the dollar.  

On Wednesday, the government said Brazil reached a $2.08 billion trade surplus in November. While that was less than the average surplus of about $3 billion of recent months, it still pushed the year-to-date surplus to a record $30.2 billion, indicating that export dollars are likely to keep driving the real up.  

Falling international petroleum prices were good news for exporters as pressures on freight costs are likely to diminish.

title: Brazil's  currency  eases early, stocks gain.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency eased in early trade on Thursday after hitting its strongest level of the year in the previous session, while stocks added to historic gains as global oil prices slipped.   

The local currency, the real , weakened 0.37 percent early to 2.721 reais per U.S. dollar after finishing the previous session at its best level since June 19, 2002.   

"There is a little bit of pressure on the real because people think the European Central Bank will say something to limit the euro's gains against the dollar," Davi Azevedo, a currency trader at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo, said.   

ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet is speaking on Thursday. Traders in Brazil are waiting for signs of a potential intervention scheme.   

The main Bovespa index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange rose 0.15 percent to 25,273 points, extending gains that put it at its highest level ever on Wednesday.   

Bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes (TNLP4.SA) was 0.36 percent higher at 42.10 reais.   

Oil prices retreated to their lowest levels since September, alleviating fears high petroleum costs would crimp global growth.   

The currency and stocks rose in the previous session as Brazil's country risk rating, defined as the difference between yields on the country's sovereign bonds and U.S. Treasuries, fell to its lowest level since October 1997, when the Asia crisis rattled global markets.   

Falling country risk suggests foreign investors are increasingly betting on Brazil, along with other emerging markets, as the U.S. dollar tests new lows.   

Though traders warned that profit taking could start to take effect, markets have a very positive tone. Good news, like a rash of overseas bond sales, an improving current account surplus and a strong outlook for economic growth are undergirding buying.   

So far, markets have chosen to ignore bad news. On Wednesday, the monthly trade result for November showed imports hit an all-time high of $6.08 billion as a stronger real makes foreign made goods more affordable. If this trend continues, Brazil could see its trade surplus shrink.   

Some key government officials, like Trade Minister Luiz Furlan, have said the real should be weakened to around three per dollar to keep exports competitive.   

The central bank last week said the Treasury would gradually make $3 billion in purchases on the spot market through June, but traders said the effort will only stem pronounced appreciation of the real.   

"So far the central bank isn't acting heavily to buy dollars, they are going to wait until January. By then, inflation will be more under control, thanks in part to a strong real," Azevedo said.

title: UPDATE 4-Brazil to buy $3 bln in  forex  market to pay debt.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank on Wednesday said the country would buy $3 billion on the currency market to pay down its foreign debt, a move seen by some as an attempt to halt the appreciation of its currency.   

The move eroded a rally in Brazil's real , which hit its strongest level of the year against the dollar shortly before the announcement.   

The currency closed 0.55 percent weaker at 2.755 per dollar on the news, although economists were unsure whether the announced purchases were big enough to weaken the real.   

Fueled by Brazil's widening trade and current account surpluses, the real has strengthened for much of the last two years.   

But a pronounced rally in the real in recent weeks, sparked by surging dollar inflows and a deeper weakening of the greenback, has worried economists as Brazilian exports become more expensive and less competitive.   

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has also said the currency was too strong.   

If left unchecked, some analysts fear a rally in the real could eventually cut the country's current account surplus. Brazil posted a surplus last year for the first time in a decade, helping cut its historically worrisome external financing gap.   

As of September, Brazil's public sector debt was pegged at an estimated $340 billion.   

NO INTERVENTION

Alfonso Bevilaqua, head of the central bank's economic policy department, said at a news conference that $646 million of the $3 billion will be used to pay down debt maturing this year with the rest used in the first half of 2005.   

Denying the decision amounted to an intervention, Bevilaqua stressed that Brazil has a floating currency and that the government has no set target for the exchange rate.   

"The fact of this measure being announced implies a commitment with transparency but also that the economic policymakers were uncomfortable with the pace of appreciation of the real," said Mario Mesquita, chief economist at ABN Amro in Sao Paulo.   

"This does not imply the definition of a floor (for the currency), but discomfort with the speed of the dollar's decline," he added.   

The Brazilian Treasury will carry out the purchases over a period of time though traders said $500 million has already been purchased.   

Jorge Knauer, head of foreign exchange at Banco Prosper in Sao Paulo, said the Treasury had already been buying dollars in the market and traders had been aware of that.   

"This is not huge news for the market, but it is a way to act on the market's expectation," Knauer said. "When the dollar gets very low, analysts and political scientists begin to complain that the country can loose competitiveness abroad."   

In 2003, the Treasury bought more than $11 billion to pay down debt and rebuild the country's foreign reserves. Some of the purchases continued into early 2004.   

Brazil's currency was floated early in 1999 after it was kept in a crawling peg against the dollar since 1994.   

Since its float in 1999, it slowly weakened to an all-time low of about four-per-dollar in 2002 on concerns that Lula, then a presidential candidate, would mismanage the economy.   

However, since Lula took office in January 2003 and impressed markets with budget cuts and a tough anti-inflation stance, the currency has been on a gradual upward trend.   

Brazil is headed for a record trade surplus in 2004 with exports seen totaling $94 billion for a surplus of $32.5 billion. But the trade surplus is expected to narrow next year, partly as a result of the relatively strong real.   

The central bank on Wednesday raised its 2004 current account surplus estimate to $9.2 billion.

title: FOREX  VIEW: Brazil's Real Shows Life After Fed Hike
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--So far for Brazil, the U.S. Federal Reserve's bark has proven worse than its bite.  

Two months ago, with the Fed poised to tighten monetary policy for the first time in four years, the real tumbled to its weakest level in 13 months as investors backed away from South America's most-liquid currency.  

Since the Fed hiked its benchmark lending rate a quarter percentage point to 1.25% at the end of June, though, the real has strengthened around 3% and was hovering at about three to the dollar on Monday - roughly where it was trading before Fed fears kicked in.  

"You're kind of back to where you were before the scare," said Guillermo Estebanez, a Latin American currency strategist with Bank of America in San Francisco.  

Brazil is a heavily indebted country and much of its debt is linked to the dollar or floating interest rates, making it particularly sensitive to monetary policy signals from Washington.  

But investors are finding a comfort zone again after the Fed signaled at its June 30 meeting that it plans to raise interest rates at a "measured" pace - and have grown even more comfortable in the wake of subsequent U.S. data showing a fall-off in job creation and benign inflation.  

That's helped bring back the so-called carry trade, whereby investors sell their dollars in order to invest in a country that offers higher bond yields.  

Brazil's debt was trading Monday at a spread of just under 590 basis points over U.S. Treasurys - narrower than 650 basis points at the end of June, but still providing plenty of room to make money. Brazilian bondholders had booked a 5.1% return in July as of Friday's close, according to J.P. Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus.  

"In our view, Brazil is the most improved story over the past month," Credit Suisse First Boston's emerging markets research group wrote in a strategy note Friday, adding that two recent debt sales by the government had brought financing needs "to very manageable levels."  

While the Fed's go-slow approach has given the Brazilian real a lift, some local indicators - including an accelerating economy - are lending a further boost.  

Government officials are now predicting that gross domestic product will expand on the order of 4% this year, up from earlier talk of a 3.5% expansion and a healthy turnaround from last year's 0.2% contraction.  

"In our view, Brazil is one of the last remaining cyclical stories to be played out," Morgan Stanley's Latin American equities research group, which has an overweight recommendation on the country, wrote in a strategy note Monday.  

Much of this year's growth is being fueled by surging exports from the commodities-rich country. The last time the Fed began a tightening cycle, back in 1999, Brazil exported $48 billion. Local exporters expect that number to hit $90 billion this year.  

Economists are forecasting the country will book a $6 billion current account surplus this year - generated in large part by a $29 billion trade surplus, up from last year's record $24.83 billion windfall, according to a central bank survey published Monday.  

Recent data, meanwhile, show inflation is receding as Brazil's central bank interrupts its rate-cut cycle. Monetary authorities in Brasilia haven't cut their benchmark lending rate, currently at 16%, since April and market participants don't expect to see a change when the monthly policy meeting ends on Wednesday.  

Reflecting the improved sentiment, traders in New York and Sao Paulo swapped rumors last week of a possible credit ratings upgrade for the junk-rated country even as credit agencies suggested no quick move was in the cards.  

Most currency analysts say the real could log some more advances in the coming days and weeks - but probably just baby steps, given that Brazil's central bank is likely to intervene if the rally picks up too much steam.  

"The government's not going to let the currency appreciate much more from here, because they really need the weak real to lock in the trade surplus," said Lara Rhame, a foreign exchange strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.  

The government and central bank bought greenbacks and stopped rolling over dollar-denominated debt in 2003 and earlier this year, when the currency threatened to strengthen to less than BRL2.80 to the dollar.  

Momentum also could be capped by some residual concern that rising wholesale prices could feed into consumer prices, added Rhame, who reckons the real could strengthen to BRL2.95 to the dollar in the near term but will have a hard time reaching BRL2.90.  

The central bank is seen as eager to boost its international reserves, particularly after Finance Minister Antonio Palocci said last month the government doesn't plan to renew a $14 billion loan program with the International Monetary Fund that expires at the end of the year.  

"Basically, we see the real as range-bound," said Marcelo Mesquita, ABN Amro's chief economist in Sao Paulo.  

Mesquita said he expects Brazil's currency to end the year at BRL3.05, even though he plans to raise his economic growth forecast for 2004, currently at 3.7%, later this week on the heels of better-than-expected manufacturing data.  

But investors also will keep a wary eye on the Fed to make sure it doesn't bare its fangs any time soon.  

If the Fed discards its talk of "measured" rate hikes, analysts say, the real could quickly retreat back above BRL3.20, a level it reached in intraday trade on May 21, when market nervousness peaked.  


   (Mike Esterl, a former Mexico bureau chief and Latin America editor for Dow Jones Newswires, is a special writer in the emerging markets group.)

title: Brazil's Real Ends Weaker As Investors Eye Overseas Rates
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real ended slightly weaker against the dollar Tuesday as investors moved assets away from emerging markets amid the lure of rising rates on U.S. Treasurys.   

The real ended at BRL2.917 per dollar, compared with BRL2.911 at Monday's close.   

Traders said the prospect of an interest rate hike in the U.S. over the coming months has had investors reevaluating the allocation of portfolios in the local market.   

The shift in sentiment continued to show up Tuesday in Brazil's rising risk premium. The country's debt spreads rose as measured by the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus rose to 631 points above U.S. Treasurys from 618 points at the open.   

Investors, meanwhile, also had their eyes trained to the government's market intervention strategies.   

Commenting on balance of payments data released Tuesday, Central Bank Economics Department Coordinator Altamir Lopes noted the government had used about $6.4 billion of $6.6 billion in foreign currency purchased in the market through January, and would soon be forced to dip into foreign reserves to steady market volatility.   

Analysts said the comments had local players pondering whether the currency could move lower over coming weeks.   

Meanwhile, the weakening of the local currency was moderated by continued strong export activity that has brought foreign currency inflows to the country.   

The country posted an $817 million current account surplus in March with help of a $2.6 billion trade surplus during the month.   

Given strategic government intervention, Brazil's real has held steady for most of the first quarter. However, according to recent market surveys by the central bank, the currency is expected to weaken to BRL3.05 per dollar by the year's end.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Flat At BRL2.876/Dollar
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real closed unchanged Tuesday in a light trading session ahead of the Easter holiday, which begins Friday.  

The real closed at BRL2.876 to the dollar, the same level as Monday.  

There is little in the way of market-moving news expected this week, say traders, who are marking time in a holiday-shortened week. Markets will be closed on Good Friday.  

However, some traders are on guard for possible intervention by Brazil's central bank as part of a policy of buying dollars to build up its international reserves. The bank hasn't purchased dollars since February, but some analysts believe that the current dollar exchange rate of under BRL2.9, may tempt the bank to enter the market over the next week or two.  

If the central bank opts to buy dollars, the currency is likely to be weakened as more reals will be put into circulation.  

The market had been watching for comments from the central bank's head of international affairs, Alexandre Schwartsman, who met with analysts in New York Tuesday.  

Traders wanted to know if the central bank would sell international bonds in April. Last Tuesday, Brazilian Treasury Secretary Joaquim Levy said that the government was considering a sovereign bond offering in overseas markets during April, according to a report that day by the Agencia Estado news agency of Sao Paulo.  

However Schwartsman stuck to a review of Brazil's economy during his meeting Tuesday with analysts and didn't mention bond sales, said one analyst who heard Schwartsman speak.  

Whatever the case, news about booming exports continues to underpin the real. A growing number of economists and analysts believe that Brazil's trade surplus this year will break last year's $24.8 billion record.  

Economic consultancy IDEAglobal said in report Tuesday that it had increased its forecast of the trade surplus to $26 billion from $22.9 billion.

title: Brazil Central Bank intervention  seen on hold.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, March 11 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank will probably refrain from buying dollars on the foreign exchange market any time soon unless there is a sharp spike in the value of the country's currency, analysts say.   

After buying $2.6 billion from the market through 26 dollar auctions in January, the monetary authority carried out only one such operation in February and has done none since then.   

The bank said this year it would intervene regularly to boost foreign exchange reserves, which were seriously depleted in the 1990s when they were used to prop up the real.   

But analysts say a political scandal putting pressure on the real and fears that dollar buying could fuel inflation by increasing the amount of reais in circulation are keeping the bank out of the market for now.   

The real has depreciated 0.8 percent since mid-February when an aide to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's chief of staff was caught on videotape peddling political favors when he was head of the Rio de Janeiro state lottery.   

The scandal has kept markets on edge as the government tries to head off a congressional probe.   

It would also be counterproductive for the bank to buy dollars now given a raft of upcoming maturities for its domestically traded debt, some of which is tied to the greenback, analysts said.   

"It would be odd for the Central Bank to buy (dollars) at a time when it is buying back dollar-denominated debt maturities, which could pressure the currency and make those buybacks more expensive," said Eduardo Castro, head of the fixed income department at ABN AMRO Asset Management in Sao Paulo.   

Some $4.1 billion in government and private sector debt comes due in March. The government intends to buy back all $2.4 billion of the debt that matures in the month.   

"I think the Central Bank changed its strategy and I'm not sure what the new one will be, but I think it will only intervene again if there are strongly positive flows (in favor of the real)," said Alexandre Vasarhelyi, head of foreign exchange at ING Bank in Sao Paulo.   

The Central Bank declined to comment on intervention.   

Carlos Cintra, a fixed income manager at Banco Prosper, said he believed the Central Bank would continue buying dollars on the market, but would wait for the political scandal to blow over first so as not to pressure the real too much.   

Other specialists said the Central Bank could wade back into the market if the real strengthened too much.   

The real was trading at 2.92 per dollar on Thursday, or about 0.6 percent weaker than where it began the year and 4 percent lower than its strongest close so far this year, at 2.791 on Jan. 12.   

"If it hit 2.7 (reais per dollar), it would intervene again because that (exchange rate) would be bad. It would not be good for the trade balance," said Christiani Rinaldim, head analyst at Consultoria Global Invest.

title: Brazil says bought $2.6 bln on  forex  market in Jan.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank said on Wednesday it bought $2.6 billion on the foreign exchange market in January to bolster international reserves.   

In early January, the bank changed its intervention policy and began snapping up dollars on the currency market on a regular basis.   

But when the monetary authority intervenes it only provides the exchange rate at which it buys greenbacks, declining to confirm the amount of each purchase.   

Previously, state-run Banco do Brasil (BBAS3.SA) would buy dollars on the Treasury's behalf but rarely confirmed its presence in the market.   

The Treasury bought $11.2 billion on the spot market in 2003, $6.3 billion of which came in the fourth quarter alone. In addition to bolstering reserves, the Treasury uses that money to make debt payments abroad.   

So far in February, the Central Bank has only intervened once in the currency market to buy dollars.   

Brazil has been struggling to beef up its international reserves after a series of financial crises in the late 1990s, when the Central Bank sold billions of dollars as it sought to prop up the local currency, the real .   

The country finished last year with net international reserves of just $17.37 billion, which excludes loan money from the International Monetary Fund. That's a far cry from the mid-1990s, when Brazil's net reserves surpassed $60 billion.   

Most economists expect the country to finish 2004 with net reserves of around $30 billion, which should help make Latin America's largest economy less vulnerable to external shocks.   

In addition to buying dollars on the spot market, Brazil is also expected to raise extra cash by issuing sovereign bonds abroad. In January, Brazil sold $1.5 billion in global bonds.

title: Brazil's Real Strengthens Following US CPI Data
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real was stronger in early trade Wednesday following the release of benign U.S. inflation data.  

At 1345 GMT, the real stood at BRL2.138 to the U.S. dollar, strengthening from Tuesday's close of BRL2.140.  

Earlier in the morning, the U.S. government announced the consumer price index rose by 0.4% in July, while core prices only rose by 0.2%, which was a relief after four straight 0.3% increases. The consumer inflation outlook is restrained, indicating that the U.S. Federal Reserve may extend the current pause in its monetary tightening policy.  

That's good news for the real as rising U.S. interest rates tend to attract investment away from emerging markets such as Brazil.  

The U.S. decision canceled out the effect of news that Brazil's central bank appears to be upping its intervention on the local market following large gains by the real on Tuesday.  

The central bank announced Wednesday that it will sound out market demand with a view to holding a foreign exchange reverse swap auction.  

The auctions allow investors to swap paper linked to forex variation for government paper linked to interest rates. The swap allows foreign investors to enjoy Brazil's high interest rates without forex exposure.  

If the monetary authority detects interest in this kind of operation during its survey later Wednesday, the bank will hold an auction on Thursday.  

The central bank will also likely hold another snap auction to buy dollars on the spot market Wednesday.  

The real actually opened weaker against the dollar at BRL2.145, minutes before the U.S. data were issued.

title: Brazil 's stocks fall; real slips on  intervention
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, July 20 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks fell on Thursday on profit-taking after a rally the previous day and the currency weakened as the central bank intervened in the market by buying dollars and selling debt instruments.  

The Brazilian real <BRBY> finished 0.73 percent weaker at 2.193 per dollar after giving up all of Wednesday's gains. The real is still near its strongest level in five years.  

The central bank sold $1.35 billion worth of so-called reverse currency swaps, rolling over a similar batch of paper maturing in August, in the first such auction since April.  

Joao Medeiros, head of foreign exchange at Pioneer brokerage, said the swap "works as if the central bank was effectively buying dollars," and attributed the fall to the auction.  

The swaps, which allow investors to buy exposure to Brazil's lofty domestic interest rate without having to purchase the local currency, were originally sold to prevent the real from strengthening too much.  

Although the central bank trimmed the key Selic interest rate by 0.5 percentage point to 20-year lows on Wednesday, as the market had been expecting, the rate of 14.75 percent is still high even for emerging markets.  

The bank also bought dollars on the spot foreign exchange market for the 13th time in 14 sessions. Exporters have complained that the real's strength may hurt foreign sales.  

Wednesday's rally was triggered by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's suggestion that U.S. inflation is under control and U.S. interest rates may not rise as much as previously expected. That eased concerns that higher U.S. rates would reduce the attractiveness of Brazilian securities.  

The benchmark Bovespa index at the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange <.BVSP> dropped 2.55 percent to 35,847 points after soaring 4.71 percent the previous day.  

Still, Alvaro Bandera, director of Agora Senior brokerage, said the market's general mood was positive after Bernanke's speech and Thursday's fall was mere profit-taking.  

"If there is a truce between Israel and Lebanon, things can get better a little more. We're still going to have volatility, but I'm working with a positive scenario," he said.  

Meanwhile, state oil company Petrobras -- the index's top heavyweight -- fell nearly 3 percent to 42.35 reais after its president, Jose Sergio Gabrielli, once again ruled out a fuel price hike while there is strong volatility on the world oil market. Petrobras last raised it gasoline and diesel prices in in September 2005.  

Shares in troubled airline Varig , which was sold for $24 million in an auction on Thursday, slumped 32.7 percent to 2.55 reais. Varig shares are not included in the Bovespa index but they traded actively on the eve of the auction, which was aimed to avoid the airline's bankruptcy.  

Shares of Perdigao , a food processing company, soared 4.4 percent to 28.6 reais on bets that rival Sadia would sweeten its recent takeover bid, rejected by Perdigao. Sadia shares ended practically flat at 6.1 reais. [20060720 153238 GMT]

title: DJ Brazil's Real Closes Slightly Stronger In Volatile Trade
text:
SAO PAULO, Jun 23, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed slightly higher Friday after a day of volatile trade as export dollar inflows counterbalanced earlier concerns that Federal Reserve could extend their tightening monetary policy at a meeting next week.  

The real ended at BRL2.230 to the dollar in spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, or BMF, up from Thursday's close of BRL2.233.  

According to analysts, the real was pressured as investors awaited further direction on U.S. interest rates. The Federal Reserve's policy-setting committee, which next meets June 28-29, is expected to raise the target federal-funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.25%.  

Rising interest rates in the U.S. and other developed nations typically draw investments away from emerging markets such as Brazil.  

The local currency drifted in the morning on concerns that the U.S. monetary tightening cycle would be extended before rallying in mid afternoon due to an influx of export dollars, traders said.  

Worries about U.S. rate hikes had caused the Turkish lira to slide sharply in the morning before Central Bank intervention. But Brazil's fundamentals are much stronger than those of many other emerging markets and the real weathered the storm well, traders said.  

Local markets largely shrugged off a mixed report on U.S. durable good demand.  

May durable-goods orders fell by 0.3% to a seasonally adjusted $208.67 billion, slightly less than the 0.5% decline expected, as orders for commercial aircraft declined. However, orders for nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft rose 1%, reversing a 1.9% decline the previous month.  

The health of nondefense orders indicates underlying U.S. economic strength.  

Meanwhile, benign Brazilian inflation data will give the Central Bank more incentive to extend the loosening cycle on monetary policy.  

The Brazilian Census Bureau announced that Brazil's benchmark IPCA inflation index fell 0.15% in the month-long period through mid-June compared with a 0.27% rise in the same period to mid-May.  

The decline was greater than the 0.07% forecast by market platers.  

The Brazilian Central Bank has lowered the benchmark Selic interest rate eight times in a row since September. The rate currently stands at 15.25% per year.  

Local interest rate contracts fell Friday amid the quiet inflation outlook.  

The day's most actively traded contract, the January 2007 contract, fell to 14.80% from 14.81% on Thursday.  

The contract's project probable annualized interest charges for the overnight interbank rate at future dates.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, firmed 0.61 percent to 2.106 to the dollar. It opened weaker but reversed direction after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the U.S. central bank may take no action at one or more future meetings on official interest rates after a long series of increases.

A pause in U.S. rate hikes would give the real room to gain further on high domestic interest rates -- currently at 15.75 percent -- and record exports that have flooded the domestic currency market with dollars.  

Brazil's central bank has intervened to prevent excessive real strength, but instead has only slowed the pace of appreciation. It bought dollars on the spot market on Thursday as part of an effort to build up foreign reserves. Exporters favor a weaker real.  

After closing above 40,000 for the first time on Wednesday, the the Bovespa <.BVSP> index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange slipped 1.44 percent to a preliminary close of 39,830 points.

The bank has been aggressively buying dollars on the market in recent months as it seeks to build up international reserves and, indirectly, weaken the national currency.  

Despite the interventions, the real <BRBY> continues to trade near a five-year high, irking exporters who say their products are becoming less competitive on global markets.  

As of Wednesday, Brazil had $59.84 billion in foreign reserves, up from $52.9 billion just over a year ago.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker On Palocci,  Intervention  Ideas
text:
SAO PAULO, Mar 21, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as investors prepared for the possibility that Finance Minister Antonio Palocci may be forced to resign over allegations of corruption, and the possibility that the Brazilian Central Bank will impose a tax on short-term foreign capital inflows.  

The real opened at BRL2.158 to the dollar in spot contract trading on the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange, weaker from Monday's close of BRL2.149 to the dollar.  

Last week, a new witness linked Palocci, a market favorite, to an alleged kickback scheme run by the ruling Workers' Party, or PT.  

Palocci has repeatedly denied involvement in any corruption, but political opposition leaders are ramping up pressure to force the finance minister out.  

Analysts said that economic policy likely wouldn't change significantly if Palocci departs but he is a key figure in the government and his resignation would weaken President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.  

Traders also talked of rumors that the central bank may introduce restrictions on foreign short-term capital inflows in order to weaken the local currency.  

The bank is considering raising taxes on short term inflows that aren't destined for stocks or Treasury note issues, according to the local business daily Valor Economico.  

Until recently, the central bank had been using foreign exchange debt swaps to contain the rise of the real. Under the scheme, the institution took dollar-denominated debt and offered paper linked to local interest rates in return. This allowed foreign investors to take advantage of Brazil's towering local interest rates without bringing dollars into Brazil. However, the institution ceased these operations two weeks days ago as, according to analysts, the bank had canceled out all its dollar-denominated debt and was uncomfortable about taking an active futures position in the greenback.  

Traders said there was little new in the comments of Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke after the market close Monday. His speech to the Economic Club of New York indicated U.S. fed funds would continue to rise but this would not greatly affect the liquidity in emerging markets, said one analyst.  

The market will be waiting for the release of February current account data later in the morning. Investors are divided over what figure will be announced, with estimates ranging from a deficit of $1 million to a surplus of $700 million according to a survey of analysts conducted by the local Estado news agency.  

Any figure at the lower end of this range would lead the real to weaken, traders said.  

Investors are also waiting for the release of the U.S. producer price index later in the day. The index is expected to have declined in February due to lower energy costs.  

-By Alastair Stewart, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-3145-1479; brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil candidate Alckmin wants new economic policy
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil, March 16 (Reuters) - Brazilian presidential hopeful Geraldo Alckmin said on Thursday that if elected in October he would change economic policies that have been favored by Wall Street but which he blames for causing sluggish growth.  

"The economic model is wrong," said Alckmin, who is supported by many Brazilian industrialists and other corporate chieftains, said in a broadcast by CBN radio.  

"Monetary policy is too conservative, there is no reason to have real interest rates of 12 percent," said the governor of Brazil's most populous state of Sao Paulo and the leading opposition contender for the presidency.  

He was chosen Tuesday as the candidate of the centrist Brazilian Social Democracy Party and trails President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in opinion polls by wide margins.  

Brazil's real interest rate, or the nominal rate of 16.5 percent less inflation of about 4.5 percent, is about 12 percent.  

Banks have posted record profits during the administration of Lula, a former union leader who adopted economic policies favored by investors after winning in a 2002 landslide.  

The central bank says high interest rates are needed to control inflation, but many manufacturing companies disagree.  

Corporate chiefs supporting Alckmin complain that economic growth under Lula has averaged less than 3 percent a year.  

"The exchange rate is overvalued," he said of Brazil's real <BRBY>, which is near a five-year high against the dollar. Exporters fear their sales will retreat this year, hurting the agricultural, clothing and shoe sectors.  

"I wouldn't disregard a dirty float," he said. "You can do interventions," he said. Brazil's central bank has heavily bought dollars on the foreign exchange market since November to build up foreign reserves, but the purchases have done little to dampen the real's gains.  

FISCAL POLICY  

"Fiscal policy is bad and we need to improve the quality of spending," Alckmin said.  

Brazil has a tax burden like a Western European country, but inefficient public services, regressive tax rules, and inflexible spending requirements.  

Most of the budget is eaten up by debt payments, salaries for civil servants and deficit-ridden pension and social security funds. Money for capital investments is scant.  

"The government ... didn't control superfluous costs," he said.  

Even though he has made efforts to close budget deficits, Lula has allowed spending growth to outpace economic growth, frustrating economists who say the added outlays have contributed to inflation.

title: Brazil's Foreign Tax Breaks Add Fuel To Real's March
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian government's decision to offer tax breaks to foreign investors in government bonds added further fuel to the ramping local currency Thursday.  

While Brazilian officials gave investors a signal two weeks ago that the rules will change, the psychological impact of the formal announcement acted as a trigger for more overseas money to flow in.  

"The market knew this was coming, but investors are looking for motives to pour money into Brazil and this announcement is seen as another green light," said Andre Deluca of Sao Paulo-based brokerage Intra.  

The Brazilian real opened 0.8% higher at 2.12 to the dollar on Thursday, its strongest level since March 2001.  

A presidential decree published Thursday exempts overseas investors from a 15% capital gains tax and a 0.38% financial transaction tax on buying government bonds. The step is an attempt to switch Brazil's public debt profile to a more home-based one.  

The long-term impact of the move on the exchange rate won't not be great, but it definitely contributes to the positive feeling investors have about Brazil, said Adauto Lima, an economist at investment bank WestLB in Sao Paulo.  

The Brazilian real has strengthened 22% against the dollar over the past 12 months, fueled by heavy export inflows and foreign investment in Brazilian stocks. Now, the local currency threatens to test the two-to-one barrier in the next few weeks, traders and analysts said.  

"The pressure of export dollars on the futures market is extreme," said Mauro Giorgi at local brokerage Geracao Futuro.  

Brazil continues to register record trade surpluses despite the rise of the real against the dollar.  

Exporters have been warning of an imminent drop in shipments for the last two years, but that just hasn't happened. Between Jan. 1 and Feb. 12, 2006, Brazil's trade surplus totaled $3.87 billion, up 19% on year.  

In part, this is because the cost of financing Brazilian exports has dropped sharply over the past year along with an improvement in Brazil's credit risk rating, offsetting the impact of the strengthening real, said Geracao Futuro's Giorgi.  

Meanwhile, a large portion of Brazil's exports are denominated not in dollars, but in euros and yen, which has allowed the country's shipments to retain their price edge, according to Ricardo Amorim, head of Latin America research at WestLB.  

In addition, other major commodity exporters, like Brazil, have also seen their currencies rise.  

But perhaps most importantly, astronomical gains in global prices of commodities - a key part of Brazil's trade balance - have more than offset any losses incurred because of the stronger real.  

The seemingly insatiable appetite of foreign investors for emerging market assets amid abundant global liquidity is also driving up the exchange rate.  

"The outlook for Brazilian stocks looks extremely positive. It seems foreign investors have their eyes firmly fixed on the stocks here and if the international situation continues to be benign, it will stay that way," said Intra's Deluca.  

Meanwhile, the improvement in Brazil's risk rating only serves to reinforce the 'virtuous cycle' of investments and brings the prospect of an upgrade to the speculative grade double-B-minus rating on Brazil's sovereign debt ever closer.  

Brazil's central bank has been intervening in the foreign exchange spot and futures market since October - moves that most analysts view as an attempt to limit the rise of the real.  

However, since January, the bank has chosen to pare back the level of forex swaps it offers after it canceled out virtually all its dollar-denominated debt. The swaps are used to shift the government's liability away from dollar-denominated debt to local currency debt.  

The central bank is trying to construct "a wall in the middle of the sea to contain a tidal wave," said WestLB's Amorim. "It's an impossible task."  

In the last quarter of 2005, the central bank was buying up to $500 million a day on the spot market, but it has now reduced those purchases to between around $80 million to $140 million in an apparent admission that it can't contain the currency.  

Given these factors, most analysts now believe the real will inevitably hit the 2.00 level against the dollar. But few are willing to believe it will fall below that level.  

If the dollar hits two, the outcry from Brazil's industry will be enormous and the government may be forced to take "administrative" steps to reverse the situation, according to some analysts.  

Those steps could include an end to the rule requiring exporters to repatriate dollars. Currently, exporters must bring dollars into the country within 210 days of completing a transaction and can't use these funds to pay offshore costs or for imports.  

"If we hit two-to-one, the market believes the government will be forced to do something more dynamic," said Geracao Futuro's Giorgi.  

But a sharp reduction in interest rates, which analysts said would be the most effective measure, is unlikely to happen as this government appears firmly focused on controlling inflation, analysts and traders added.  

Brazil's central bank has been easing its monetary policy since September but the Selic base interest rate still stands at a towering 17.25%.  

-By Alastair Stewart, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3145 1479; alastair Stewart@dowjones.com [ 16-02-06 1705GMT ]

If the dollar hits two, the outcry from Brazil's industry will be enormous and the government may be forced to take "administrative" steps to reverse the situation, according to some analysts.  

Those steps could include an end to the rule requiring exporters to repatriate dollars. Currently, exporters must bring dollars into the country within 210 days of completing a transaction and can't use these funds to pay offshore costs or for imports.  

"If we hit two-to-one, the market believes the government will be forced to do something more dynamic," said Geracao Futuro's Giorgi.  

But a sharp reduction in interest rates, which analysts said would be the most effective measure, is unlikely to happen as this government appears firmly focused on controlling inflation, analysts and traders added.  

Brazil's central bank has been easing its monetary policy since September but the Selic base interest rate still stands at a towering 17.25%.

title: If  intervention  stops,  Brazil  real may gain 10 pct
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Jan 31 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real, which outperformed most of the world's currencies in 2005, could rally as much as 10 percent in the first quarter of this year if the central bank stops entering the market, economists say.  

Demand for the real <BRBY> and dollar inflows are heavy as Brazilian companies repatriate record exports and proceeds from overseas bond sales. At the same time, a likely end to U.S. interest rate hikes has made foreign investors even hungrier for high returns in Latin America's largest country, where the benchmark rate is 17.25 percent.  

What is more, most economists think the central bank, which has acted to weaken the real twice a day since November, will change tactics sometime in March. It could do that by no longer purchasing dollars, stopping the sale of currency swaps, or both.  

If the central bank were to stop intervening, the real's rally might be very swift. In January the real managed to gain about 4 percent even though the central bank regularly waded into the market.  

Ricardo Amorim, head of Latin American Research at WestLB, said he expects the real to strengthen to 2 per U.S. dollar in the next several months.  

Others also see a rally from its current level of 2.21.  

"It's not unreasonable that the real would go to 2 by the end of the first quarter," said Douglas Smith, chief economist for the Americas at Standard Chartered Bank in New York.  

"2.20 is our official line but it could go lower for sure. Some of our traders think it will easily go to 2.1."  

Since November, the central bank has heavily sold currency swaps that allow investors to get exposure to Brazil's high interest rates, currently at 17.25 percent, without buying reais.  

The swaps also convert dollar-denominated debt into real-based debt.  

To accompany its swap sales, the central bank has bought dollars heavily on the foreign exchange market since October to boost international reserves, now at about $53.8 billion.  

The combined efforts have cut Brazil's net foreign debt to around $10 billion when reserves are discounted.  

At its current pace of entering the market, the central bank will have canceled the exchange-rate risk of its net foreign debt within two months.  

"By selling swaps they are actually increasing floating-rate debt, which is contrary to their stated goal. So I think they are going to stop," said John Welch, senior vice president for sovereign strategy at Lehman Brothers in New York.  

"It would also make sense for them to stop buying dollars" because of negative carry.  

When the bank holds dollars, it must invest them abroad at low interest rates -- of, say, 5 percent -- whereas when it invests reais locally it can earn at double-digit rates.  

Some economists say making money is not one of the central bank's priorities and that dollar buying could continue.  

"Central banks aren't big on making profits on their reserves. And nearly all have the problem of negative carry when buying dollars," said Smith of Standard Chartered. "They key thing for them is liquidity instead of returns."  

RATE CUTS MAY STEM RALLY  

Brazilian companies have complained the strong real is hurting the competitiveness of exports, even though the trade surplus was a record $44.76 billion in 2005.  

But a stronger real would cut inflationary pressures and allow the central bank, which has lowered interest rates five times since September, to loosen monetary policy more aggressively.  

Lower interest rates would also help the government further cut the burden of servicing its debt since about half of it floats on short-term interest rates.  

If the central bank does cut rates more aggressively, as is widely expected, it could also help stem the real's gains.  

"There's a way they can keep it from going to 2, which is to cut rates and increase the money supply," Welch said.

title: UPDATE 3-Brazil cuts all domestic dlr-linked debt exposure
text:
(Adds comment from central bank president)  

BRASILIA, Brazil, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's government eliminated all of its exposure to domestic dollar-linked debt in January, the central bank said on Monday, as officials work to cut the riskiness of the public debt load.  

The central bank also said it may continue selling interest rate-linked currency swaps that have been used to cancel out dollar-linked liabilities, which were originally sold to prevent the local currency from weakening.  

On Monday the bank sold $201.5 million in swaps, suggesting it will start using the swaps to cancel out exposure to foreign debt denominated in dollars.  

Credit rating agencies have frowned on the use of dollar-linked liabilities, which in 2002 comprised as much as 40 percent of domestic debt.  

The swaps have also been sold to pull back the local currency, the real <BRBY>, from some of its highest levels in 4-1/2 years.  

The currency swaps, which have been sold 41 times since November, allow investors to get exposure to Brazil's high interest rates, currently at 17.25 percent, without having to buy reais.  

The central bank has bought dollars 74 times since October to blunt the real and boost international reserves, which have tripled in the past few years to $53.8 billion.  

But some economists say the central bank is running out of room to intervene. Brazil has about $62 billion in external sovereign debt, or only about $8 billion in net foreign debt when reserves are discounted.  

At the current pace of intervening, Brazil will have canceled the exchange-rate risk of its net foreign debt within two months.  

At that point, some economists say, the central bank might have a more difficult time justifying interventions. When the bank holds dollars, it must invest them abroad at low interest rates -- of, say, 5 percent -- whereas when it invests reais locally it can earn at double-digit rates.  

"The central bank's ability to continue intervening is getting smaller and smaller. And there will be a deep structural adjustment that happens very fast when the central bank stops intervening," said Ricardo Amorim, chief economist at WestLB in New York.  

"If international liquidity keeps up, we will see the real stronger than 2 per dollar in the first part of the year."  

That means the real could rally 13 percent from its current level of about 2.26.  

Asked if there are any plans to stop selling the currency swaps or purchasing dollars on the spot market, Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles told Reuters: "Unfortunately we don't comment about this subject."  

TOTAL DEBT LOAD GROWS  

Brazilian companies and Trade Minister Luiz Furlan have complained the strong real is hurting the competitiveness of exports.  

But economists say Brazil, which had a record $44.76 billion trade surplus in 2005, could afford to see its trade surplus shrink.  

A stronger real would cut inflationary pressures and allow the central bank, which has cut interest rates five times since September, to loosen monetary policy more aggressively. Lower interest rates would also help the government further cut the burden of servicing its debt.  

Even as dollar-linked debt fell, Brazil's federal domestic debt at the end of 2005 was larger than ever.  

It also remained risky because the average length of debt is short, at about 27 months, and half of the debt floats on short-term interest rates.  

The total domestic debt at the end of December was 979.7 billion reais ($433.5 billion), up from 810.3 billion reais debt at the end of 2004.  

The share of debt linked to the overnight Selic interest rate rose marginally to 53.3 percent in December from 52.41 percent a year before.  

The share of fixed-rate domestic debt rose to 27.86 percent from 20.09 a year before. Much of the rest of the domestic debt load is tied to inflation indexes.

title: Brazil 's  Central Bank  Eases  Forex  Market  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--A Brazilian Central Bank decision to reduce the sales volume of so-called reverse swap contracts at daily auctions could be a signal that the bank wishes to intervene less in the foreign exchange market.  

The decision will almost certainly lead to a strengthening of the Brazilian real against the U.S. dollar, at least in the short term, analysts added.  

Thursday night, the central bank announced that it would offer the equivalent of only $200 million in the reverse swap contracts at Friday's auction. The bank had been offering the equivalent of $400 million per day in recent weeks.  

"The trend is toward a reduction of central bank intervention in the market," said Joao Nunes, chief economist at Agora Senior, Brazil's largest stock brokerage. "This could even be the beginning of the end for intervention."  

The central bank took a similar tack once before. From mid-November until early December, the bank was offering the equivalent of $600 million per day in the swap contracts. In early December, the bank suddenly downshifted to $400 million, causing initial losses to the dollar against the real but with quotations subsequently stabilizing.  

The reverse swap contracts offer investors the opportunity to exchange dollar-linked paper for bonds indexed to the Selic base rate. The attraction for investors is the high Selic rate of 17.25%. The auctions tend to support the dollar against the real by removing dollar-hedging instruments from the market.  

The central bank began the auctions two months ago after the real hit a four-year high against the dollar of BRL2.169. The interventions helped strengthen the dollar, with the real closing out 2005 at BRL2.325.  

The intervention was welcome news to exporters, who complained that the appreciation of the real hurts their ability to remain competitive in overseas markets.  

Even with central bank's year-end intervention, the real appreciated 14.2% against the dollar in 2005. A record 2005 foreign trade surplus of $44.76 billion strongly supported the real.  

Exporters say the full effect of the real's appreciation will only be felt in 2006. Indeed, the latest central bank survey of market opinion, released Monday, shows a 2006 foreign trade surplus forecast of $38 billion.  

As for the real's near-term outlook, ABN-Amro Bank chief economist for Brazil Jakiel Santos said the central bank's announcement means "the bank is searching for a point of equilibrium for its interventions." He said the bank will try to find the right volume of daily swap contract sales to assure a trading range of about BRL2.25 to BRL2.30. In fact, that was the market range in trading Friday, although not without a significant dose of volatility. The real opened at BRL2.268 per dollar, up sharply from the Thursday close of BRL2.328. As of 1730 GMT, the real was trading at BRL2.280, after hitting a high of BRL2.267 and a low of BRL2.281. But Agora's Nunes said the real could drift higher next week if the central bank maintains the $200 million level for the daily swap auctions. He said the real could reach about BRL2.20 per dollar before stabilizing. "This kind of intervention has a limit and could be close to ending now," said Jose Carlos de Faria, chief economist for Brazil at Deutsche Bank.  

The drumbeat of daily swap contract sales, supplemented by nearly daily cash dollar purchases at snap auctions, also goes against the central bank's own 1999 decision to end its tight control of the local currency, and allow for a floating exchange rate.

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk  Intervention  To Ease As Trade Surplus Ebbs
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian Central Bank may deny it, but to the rest of the market it clearly appears that the aim of the monetary authority's daily interventions in the foreign exchange market is to counter the local currency's strength against the U.S. dollar.  

The bank's heavy hand will only withdraw when net trade dollar inflows recede, analysts reckon.  

"The central bank is trying to kid everyone, but nobody is buying it. They are waiting for the first sign that exports will slip and, more significantly, that imports will grow," said Thiago Davino, economist at local GRC Visao brokerage.  

Brazil's monetary guardians began intervening heavily after the real strengthened by as much as 25% in the first eleven months of 2005. By buying dollars on the spot market and then offering so-called reverse swaps, which exchange dollar exposure for local interest rate returns, the bank has halted the real's march.  

As of Thursday, the local currency was trading at around BRL2.32 to the dollar after reaching a four-year high of BRL2.16 in November. The real's appreciation during the calendar year of 2005 was held down to 14.2%.  

"Without this intervention, the real could have hit 2-to-1," said Pedro Silveira, an economist at Sao Paulo-based GlobalInvest Asset Management.  

So when will the intervention recede?  

The central bank officially said it was offering the swap contacts to offset government dollar-indexed debt in the market. But after buying $16.7 billion in dollar-linked debt since mid-November, the central bank has now wiped out its exposure to this type of risk, according to investment bank estimates.  

The sale of swap contracts has continued, however, and is as popular with foreign investors as ever, offering them the opportunity to enjoy Brazil's towering interest rates without assuming currency risk. And by stemming the flow of dollars into Brazil for the length of the contracts, the central bank is easing pressure on the exchange rate.  

A central bank spokesman said the monetary authority would maintain its current intervention policy, though he didn't say for how long.  

Global Invest's Silveira said the central bank seems "fully committed to intervention at present."  

But rather than trying to control the currency, or set targets, the central bank's objective appears to be to contain overshooting, as it has done in the past, said Gustavo Loyola, ex-central bank president, in a recent report. Loyola is a partner at the Tendencias Consulting Group in Sao Paulo.  

Back in 2002, it offered dollar-linked debt to stem an outflow of dollars.  

Two factors caused the steep appreciation of the Brazilian real last year: the extraordinary growth in the trade surplus and the arrival of speculative capital attracted by Brazil's towering interest rates. At 17.25%, Brazil's base Selic rate is one of the highest of any emerging market.  

One of these factors will have to change for the strength of the Brazilian real to ease, but it is unlikely that the central bank will lower interest rates sufficiently to cause investors to search for better returns elsewhere, analysts said.  

It has been incrementally reducing the base rate since September, but the rate remains high and analysts say the monetary loosening policy will falter later this year as the central bank eyes inflation nervously.  

"The central bank only has one objective, and that's to control inflation. It does it obsessively," said Silveira.  

The base rate has not dipped below 15% in the last 15 years and a central bank survey of analysts, released Monday, put the rate at a stubbornly high 15% by the end of 2006.  

That leaves the trade balance. Luckily for the central bank, clear signs are emerging that export orders are declining for the first half of the year while imports are expected to rise as local companies lose competitiveness because of the strong real.  

"The trade balance could dip as soon as February, which will allow the central bank to reduce the amount of dollar debt swaps offered," said Davino.  

The trade surplus is expected to slip to $37 billion to $38 billion in 2006 from a record $44.76 billion in 2005, according to the central bank's most recent survey of economists. As a result, the current account surplus is seen falling to $8 billion in 2006 from $14.2 billion in 2005.  

The level of central bank intervention has been elevated over the past two months.  

On top of offering between $400 million and $600 million in swaps per day, the monetary body bought up as much as $800 million per day on the spot market during the height of the intervention in December, according to traders. Currently it is buying around $500 million in spot purchases per day.  

The spot dollar purchases are likely to continue as it takes advantage of the strong real to build foreign reserves, thus reducing the country's exposure to the whims of international markets. Currently, central bank foreign reserves stand at $56.9 billion.  

In the near term, the central bank will continue to pull in opposing directions by, on the one hand, buying dollars but, on the other hand, spurring dollar inflows by maintaining interest rates at elevated levels.  

"In truth, Meirelles is just easing the pressure a little, the only real way to weaken the real is to lower interest rates," said Davino.  

But reducing rates prematurely could undermine the bank's so far successful efforts against inflation, which moderated to 5.7% last year from 7.6% in 2004.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Weaker On  Central Bank Interventions
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Thursday as two interventions in the currency market by the central bank weighed down the real in light trading.  

The real closed at BRL2.328 per dollar, weaker from Wednesday's close of BRL2.323 per dollar.  

According to traders, weak volume and some profit-taking gave more strength to the Brazilian Central Bank's double-dip in the currency market.  

The bank held another in its continuing series of "reverse-swap" auctions, which allow investors to exchange foreign-exchange linked debt for paper indexed to local interest rates. The auctions help remove an excess of dollar-linked paper from the futures market.  

The bank said it sold 8,500 of the 8,800 contracts on offer for $401.41 million. The swaps offered four maturities between October 2006 and July 2008.  

The central bank also purchased dollars from the market in a snap auction late Thursday afternoon at BRL2.3345 per dollar.  

The Brazilian real was trading at BRL2.335 per dollar before the bank called the auction at 1735 GMT. The real traded stable at BRL2.335 per dollar shortly after results of the auction were announced.  

The central bank began purchasing dollars at near-daily snap auctions in October as a way to build foreign reserves. It then restarted the "reverse-swap" auctions in November, after previously halting the practice in March.  

The real was also undermined by an inflation report that showed price pressures picking up.  

Earlier Thursday, the private Getulio Vargas Foundation, or FGV, said Brazil's General Price index, known as the IGP-M, rose 0.82% in the 10 days through Jan. 20, compared with a fall of 0.06% for the same period of December, FGV said. The results were in line with market expectations, which had forecast a figure ranging from inflation of 0.6% to 1.1%.  

The report followed on fresh language in the central bank's rate-setting statement released late Wednesday. While the bank reduced the Selic base interest rate by 75 basis points to 17.25% per year, it said that it was still on the lookout for signs of inflationary pressures.  

In the statement, the bank said it will "attentively follow the evolution of the inflation outlook until its next meeting to then define the next steps in the monetary policy strategy that has been implemented since September 2005."  

Inflation as measured by the official IPCA index closed 2005 at 5.69%, the lowest rate since 1998's 1.65%. While the central bank's 2005 calendar-year target for IPCA inflation was 5.1%, a tolerance band allowed for a maximum inflation rate of 7%. It was the second consecutive year that inflation came in within the government's established tolerance band.  

Central bankers next meet March 7-8.  

Meanwhile, Brazil's risk spread as measured by the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus tightened slightly during the day to a spread of 288 basis points over U.S. Treasurys as of 1844 GMT. Brazil's benchmark 2040 bond was up 0.650 at 130.750.
