title: Brazil stocks, real weaken before likely rate cut
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Jan 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's stocks retreated on Wednesday for a second straight day after setting a record, while its currency lost ground on expectations of a sharper than usual interest rate cut and central bank dollar purchases.  

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, closed 0.5 percent weaker at 2.324 to the dollar in cautious trade on turnover of about $700 million, sharply lower than Tuesday's $2 billion, traders said.  

"The dollar has been rising since yesterday on talk about the rate (cut) ... The push came mainly from futures due to price adjustments over Copom expectations," said the head of foreign exchange with a big local brokerage.  

The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) will announce its rate decision later on Wednesday. It hopes to spur economic growth, which suffered last year, with an interest rate cut which would be its fifth since September.  

In a Reuters poll on Friday, 15 of 20 economists predicted a cut in the benchmark lending rate of 0.75 percentage point to 17.25 percent. Five said a half-point cut, as seen last month, was more likely.  

Lower domestic interest rates may diminish demand for reais among foreign investors. Some traders say rate cuts would blunt the real's gains more effectively than official intervention.  

The central bank bought dollars for the 71st time since early October at a cut-off price of 2.232 reais per dollar and sold some $400 million in currency swap contracts linked to short-term interest rates for the 38th time since November.  

The swaps cut demand for reais from foreign investors who seek exposure to Brazil's lofty benchmark rate.  

Exporters favor both types of intervention because they have helped knock the real off a 4-1/2-year high, making Brazilian goods cheaper abroad. The central bank says it buys dollars to boost currency reserves.  

The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa index <.BVSP> fell 0.9 percent to 35,805, dropping below the recently-conquered 36,000 mark.  

The market's bellwether, state oil company Petrobras , dropped about 1 percent to 42.4 reais. Power company Light rose 2.4 percent to 15.65 reais per share after a newspaper report said its owner, Electricite de France, had hired Citibank to step up efforts to sell Light.  

Morgan Stanley on Tuesday recommended a defensive stance on Latin American stocks, suggesting prices may have neared a peak. Higher oil prices <CLc1> were also hurting local markets and driving up global risk, traders said.

title: Brazil  Real Closes Weaker On US Data,  Interventions
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real closed weaker against the U.S. dollar Friday after the central bank intervened twice in the spot currency market and disappointing economic data in the U.S. raised expectations of continued interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.  

The real closed at BRL2.276 per dollar, weaker from Thursday's close of BRL2.265 per dollar.  

According to traders, Friday saw some profit-taking and caution by investors as data from the U.S. raised expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve would continue to raise interest rates in an effort to ward off inflation pressures. Rising interest rates in the U.S. tend to attract investment away from emerging markets such as Brazil.  

Earlier Friday, the U.S. Labor Department reported that its Producer Price Index, which measures price pressures before they reach the consumer, rose 0.9% in December. The increase was the most since a 1.7% jump in September. Higher gasoline prices were behind the advance.  

For the year, wholesale prices climbed 5.4%, the most since a 5.7% rise in 1990.  

Currency markets were also affected by news of Banco do Brasil's (BBAS3.BR) pricing of a $500 million overseas perpetual bond issue, analysts said. State-owned Banco do Brasil, the country's largest bank, priced the issue at par to yield 7.95%. Banco do Brasil raised the issue from its original forecast of $300 million after demand reached $4.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the deal.  

Brazilian debt issues have seen heated demand from overseas investors hungry for high-yield paper.  

Furthermore, the Brazilian Central Bank continued its purchase activities in the spot market Friday, with reverse-swap and snap auctions.  

The bank said it sold $406.5 million of foreign-exchange linked debt swaps in a reverse-swap auction, selling 8,600 of the 8,800 contracts on offer. The swaps offered four maturities between October 2006 and July 2008.  

The auctions allow investors to swap dollar-linked bonds for paper indexed to local interest rates. The auctions help remove an excess of dollar-linked paper from the futures market.  

In the first 13 days of 2005, the bank has sold $4.05 billion in foreign-exchange swaps.  

In addition, the bank bought dollars at BRL2.268 per dollar in a snap auction called at 1736 GMT.

title: Brazil  currency  ends 5-day gainer, stocks slip too
text:
(Adds closing figures, writes through)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency ended weaker against the dollar on Tuesday, the first time in six sessions after lackluster industrial data, while stocks fell for the second day after hitting a record high on Friday.  

The real <BRBY> closed trade 0.53 percent weaker at 2.262 against the dollar on Tuesday after the government's IBGE statistic's agency said industrial activity rose an anemic 0.6 percent in November from the month earlier.  

The weak economic data raised expectations among economists that the central bank would next Wednesday cut the benchmark interest rate, now at 18 percent, by a more aggressive 0.75 points to revive the flagging economy.  

"The indicator on industrial production early in the morning reversed the expectation of a fall (in the dollar)," Daniel Szikszay, the manager of the currency desk at Schahin bank, said.  

Brazil's domestic interest rate, one of the world's highest, has attracted foreign investors seeking better returns and is a reason the real has rallied to its strongest in 4-1/2 years in recent months.  

The industrial output data overshadowed news that would normally help strengthen the real. Brazil's Treasury offered on Tuesday $1 billion in global bonds maturing in 2037 at 295 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasury notes, the lead managers Deutsche Bank and UBS said.  

The Treasury confirmed the yield at 7.557 percent with a coupon of 7.125 percent. The sale marks Brazil's first sovereign issue in 2006. The last time the government tapped global capital markets was on Nov. 29, when it sold $500 million in bonds due 2034.  

The central bank continued its intervention on the currency markets to keep Brazil's exports competitive.  

The central bank offered to buy dollars on the country's foreign exchange market for the 65th time since early October. The bank also sold 8,800 currency swap contracts linked to short-term interest rates, canceling out about $416.5 million in debt instruments indexed to the dollar.  

The auction marked the 32nd time since November that the bank has offered such swaps, which have helped weaken the Brazilian currency.  

The swaps allow investors to buy exposure to Brazil's benchmark interest rate of 18 percent without having to purchase reais. They also cancel out dollar-linked debt notes that were originally sold to prevent the real from weakening.  

The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa <.BVSP> index dropped 0.81 percent to 35.049 points as investors took profits for the second day after last week's rally. Wall Street was also down as the Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> was off 0.19 percent in late trade.  

Bovespa turnover of 2.2 billion reais was above last year's daily average of 1.6 billion.  

The Bovespa hit three record highs last week after the U.S. Federal Reserve signaled that interest rate increases are nearly over, boosting investor appetite for high-yielding emerging markets like Brazil.  

The new market bellwether, state-run oil company Petrobras , finished up 0.17 percent at 40.91 reais.  

But telecommunications stock Telemar and steel company Usiminas were among the blue chips that posted expressive losses. Telemar fell 1.22 percent to 40.65 reais and Usiminas fell 1.87 percent to 52.60 reais.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker On Continued  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO, Jan 03, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday as the central bank looks set to continue its policy of buying dollars and dollar-linked debt.  

The real opened at BRL2.347 to the dollar, down from the Monday's close of BRL2.340.  

A change in central bank rules allowing banks to buy unlimited quantities of dollars on the spot market also will start to weigh on the market Tuesday.  

Late Friday, the Brazilian Central Bank ordered a rules change, abolishing previous limits on purchases of dollars on the spot market by banks. Previously, banks were limited to purchases of up to $6 million per day. As of Monday, banks faced no daily limits.  

The impact of the move was limited on Monday during light trade because of holidays in major financial centers such as New York and London, but the influence would increase Tuesday, they said.  

However, should the central bank reduce the level of intervention, the local currency is likely to strengthen as investors continue to be attracted by Brazil's high domestic interest rates. Brazil's Selic base interest rate is a towering 18% per month.  

Market players see little indication that the central bank will institute a sharp reduction in the base rate during 2006, despite political pressure to do so in this electoral year. A central bank survey of analysts, released Monday, indicated a base rate of 15.94% for the end of the year, up slightly from the 15.92% forecast in last week's report.  

The central bank announced it will auction approximately $400 million in reverse swap contracts Tuesday, the latest in a series of daily auctions. The auction offers investors the opportunity to swap dollar-indexed paper for bonds linked to domestic interest rates.  

Typically, the auctions favor the U.S. currency because they remove a hedging mechanism from the market.  

On Monday, the bank sold swaps worth $412.5 million.

title: Brazil  real slips on  central bank interventions
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Jan 2 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Monday as the central bank intervened in the market and after it scrapped a rule that discouraged brokerages from holding more than $6 million in their foreign exchange accounts.  

The decision to change the rule, made on Friday, seemed consistent with actions the central bank has taken since October to pull the real back from some of its strongest levels in 4 1/2 years in order to keep exports competitive.  

On Monday the central bank bought dollars on the spot market to build up foreign reserves for the 59th time since October and sold currency swaps that cut demand for reais for the 26th time since November. Another sale of $440 million in swaps is slated for Tuesday.  

The real <BRBY> ended off 0.65 percent at 2.34 to the U.S. dollar.  

"In principal, the market is thinking that the central bank wants to see the real at a weaker level," said Miriam Tavares, head of currencies at the AGK brokerage in Sao Paulo.  

Starting on Monday, brokerages were able to boost their holdings of dollars without penalty. Previously, brokerages were required to deposit dollar holdings in excess of $6 million at the central bank and were not allowed to receive interest on them. The rule dated from a time when there was less faith in the local currency.  

The real gained as much as 20 percent against the U.S. dollar in 2005, thanks to inflows of dollars from record exports, better economic fundamentals and foreign investors who were anxious to buy exposure to Brazil's lofty benchmark interest rate of 18 percent.  

The real ended the year about 14 percent stronger after central bank interventions weakened it.  

At the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, the Bovespa <.BVSP> index gained 0.15 percent to 33,507 in thin volume.  

The index's new bellwether, state-run oil giant Petrobras , rose 3.76 percent to 38.09 reais. Weightings in the index are changed several times a year according to trailing trading volumes.

title: Emerging  FX -Trading flat in holiday lull, outlook for 2006 solid
text:
LONDON, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies were firm on Thursday in lacklustre trade given the holiday period, but the outlook for a strong start to 2006 is set, say analysts.  

 Price changes were driven by what few commercial transactions came through the market, as position taking was nil given books have closed on the year.  

 "I think January is going to be a good month for emerging markets. Gradually during the autumn, it seems to have become more of a consensus view that the balance of risks and opportunities for emerging markets continues to be pretty good," said Mats Olausson, chief strategist for emerging markets at SEB Merchant Banking in Stockholm.  

 Highlighting the tighter monetary policies from the U.S. Federal Reserve and of late the European Central Bank, Olausson said the global growth outlook is still likely going to provide opportunities from which emerging market economies can benefit.  

 Thinly traded markets might show outsized reaction to U.S. economic data due later on Thursday, including weekly employment data at 1330 GMT, manufacturing data at 1500 GMT and existing home sales, also at 1500 GMT.  

 "Politically of course all the elections in South America will have the potential to change some trends. Mexico, there is quite a high likelihood of a hung parliament and not much will actually change. Whereas the risks in Brazil are perhaps larger," he added.  

 The major Latin American emerging market currencies were little changed however Brazil's real traded slightly weaker on the interbank market at 2.343 per dollar <BRBY>. title: DJ Brazil Real Closes Stronger In Light Holiday Trading
text:
SAO PAULO, Dec 23, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed stronger against the U.S. dollar on Friday in light trading before the Christmas holiday weekend, and despite two auctions by the Brazilian Central Bank to purchase dollars from the market.  

The real closed at BRL2.318 per dollar, stronger from Thursday's close of BRL2.330 per dollar.  

The currency was bolstered by comments from Finance Minister Antonio Palocci, who predicted a strong performance for the Brazilian economy in 2006.  

Palocci said falling interest rates and an improved investment environment will help the economy repeat in 2006 its performance of 2004, when the economy grew 4.9%.  

"The conditions for strong growth are there," Palocci said. "I believe the scenario for that is being created for 2006 is very close to that seen in 2003 and 2004."  

Palocci also cited improving sovereign debt risk, a growing foreign trade surplus and rising consumer incomes, as well as growing domestic credit and sales as strong indicators that the country is heading for a rebound over the next 12 months.  

The government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has been lauded by its austere economic policies, which culminated in the early payment of debt obligations with the International Monetary Fund.  

On Friday, the government was expected to pay the IMF remaining credits worth $13.4 billion, after a $2.04 billion payment Thursday. The $15.44 billion in payments cover debts that would have been due in 2006 and 2007. The government also said that will pay off its remaining $2.6 billion in debt to the Paris Club of international creditors in January.  

The payments have dented Brazil's foreign reserves, which stood at $67 billion before the IMF payments. Traders expect the central bank to continue its recent efforts to build reserves through market purchases into 2006.  

Palocci's positive forecast for Brazil's economy in 2006 helped offset two interventions in the currency market carried out by the central bank.  

Early Friday afternoon, the central bank said it sold $277 million of foreign-exchange linked debt swaps on offer at an auction, selling 5,800 of the 8,400 contracts on offer. The swaps offered maturities between September 2006 and July 2008.  

The auctions allow investors to swap dollar-linked bonds for paper indexed to local interest rates. The auctions help remove an excess of dollar-linked paper from the futures market.  

Later in the day, the bank bought dollars at a snap auction for BRL2.308 per dollar.  

The Brazilian real was trading at BRL2.312 per dollar shortly before the bank called the auction at 1729 GMT. The real traded slightly weaker at BRL2.319 per dollar shortly after the auction.  

Meanwhile, Brazil's risk spread as measured by the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus stood at a spread of 303 basis points over U.S. Treasurys as of 1843 GMT. Brazil's benchmark 2040 bond was up 0.400 at 129.250.

title: Brazil  real tumbles on  intervention , stocks flat
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency fell on Thursday after two days of gains as the central bank intervened to weaken the real, while stocks finished little changed after flirting with a record high earlier in the session.  

The real <BRBY> finished at 2.331 to the dollar, weakening 1 percent in thin trade, while the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa <.BVSP> index ended 0.01 percent lower at 33,512.  

The currency had strengthened the previous two days, rebounding slightly from nine straight sessions of losses. But it backtracked again on Thursday after the central bank sold $399.5 million in currency swaps linked to short-term interest rates and bought dollars on the foreign exchange market.  

"On a day like today, with little volume, the interventions end up having more of an impact," forcing the real lower, said one currency trader at Brazilian bank.  

The bank has been aggressively selling currency swaps and buying greenbacks in recent weeks, helping to knock the real off a 4-1/2-year high while also placating exporters who have complained that a strong local currency is making their products less competitive on world markets.  

The so-called reverse swaps allow investors to buy exposure to Brazil's lofty benchmark interest rate of 18 percent without having to purchase reais. They also cancel out old dollar-linked debt sold to prevent the real from weakening.  

On Friday the bank will offer about $420 million in swaps. The bank has now sold swaps 20 times since November and bought dollars on the spot market 54 times since early October.  

In the stock market, bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes, or Telemar , fell 1.37 percent to 42.41 reais, weighing on the Bovespa index.  

On the upside, state-run oil giant Petrobras rose 0.24 percent to 36.90 reais after it said it would pay about $140 million to buy gas stations from Royal Dutch Shell in Uruguay, Paraguay and Colombia.

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil to pay off all $15.5 bln in IMF debt early
text:
(Adds comments, details)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's Finance Ministry on Tuesday said it will pay back $15.5 billion to the International Monetary Fund by year-end, marking the end of a long history of financial turbulence in Latin America's largest country.  

The ministry said the decision, which would retire all liabilities owed to the multilateral lender ahead of schedule, is the "result of stronger external accounts and macroeconomic fundamentals."  

Brazil was slated to repay $7.03 billion in principal to the IMF in 2006 and $8.43 billion in 2007, the ministry said.  

Brazil is expected to post record trade and current account surpluses this year. The central bank has also aggressively intervened on the local foreign exchange market to build up low foreign reserves.  

The combined factors have allowed the government to repay the debt early. Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles, in a statement, called it "a historic moment for the country," which at times was the IMF's biggest borrower.  

Brazil obtained a series of IMF loans around the time that it devalued its currency in 1999 amid a balance of payments crisis. The country later renewed agreements with the IMF several times, but let its last one lapse earlier this year.  

According to central bank data, the prepayments would retire all debt Brazil has with the IMF.  

"This makes perfectly good sense from a couple of perspectives," said Michael Hood, strategist with Barclays Capital in New York. "It symbolically represents an exit from the financial turmoil of the '90s and 2002 and it also makes some cashflow sense because the carrying costs of holding reserves are quite high."  

Brazil's government earns low interest rates in the United States and Europe on its hard currency reserves and cannot reap the benefits of the country's high benchmark interest rate of 18.5 percent. Additionally, Finance Minister Antonio Palocci said, the prepayments would save Brazil some $900 million in interest costs.  

"I don't think this will change the central bank's actions in the forex market because the actions there seem to have less to do with reserves and more about the forex valuation," Hood said.  

Brazil's net reserves have tripled over the last few years to about $50 billion, thanks in part to central bank interventions.  

Credit rating agencies have said Brazil needs to build up foreign reserves to attain investment grade status.  

The interventions were resumed in October to pull the local currency, the real <BRBY>, back from some of its strongest levels in 4-1/2 years and keep exports competitive.

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Closes Weaker On Continued Govt  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO, Dec 12, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real closed stronger Monday amid speculation that the central bank will increase intervention in the market.  

The real closed at BRL2.260 to the dollar, up from Friday's close of BRL2.253.  

The central bank has been buying dollars and dollar-debt nearly every day in recent months, but local banks are now speculating that the bank will resort to other measures to weaken the currency amid loud complaints from politicians and exporters that a real near four-and-a-half-year highs is hurting the economy.  

"There comes a point when intervening becomes a matter of honor," said Jose Julio Senna, director of the Sao Paulo-based MCM consultancy.  

Among the banks options are to allow exporters to delay the repatriation of dollars or to impose restrictions on real futures trading.  

The central bank intervened Monday, mopping up dollars on the spot market in the afternoon at BRL2.264 to the dollar and offering swaps of dollar-linked debt for interest rate-linked paper. The bank sold 7,600 contracts of the 12,500 contracts offered, or about $365 million worth of swaps, between 1400 GMT and 1500 GMT.  

Investors are on standby awaiting some key meetings this week. All eyes will be on the U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday amid speculation that the policy statement after the Federal Open Market Committee meeting may indicate an end to the series of interest rate hikes.  

Then on Wednesday, Brazilian central bank will decide whether to adjust local interest rates, which are some of the world's highest.  

Domestic banks say the central bank may take a more aggressive stance on interest rate cuts when it meets Wednesday. The base Selic interest rate currently stands at current 18.5% per year.  

Market expectations are for a cut of 50 basis points, but one trader said that some banks had already priced in a 75-basis-point cut, resulting in some volatility in the market as domestic banks started buying January futures contracts and putting pressure on the spot market.  

News that local inflation appears to have cooled off in December fueled that speculation.  

Sao Paulo's Fipe research institute said its consumer price index rose 0.18% in the four week period to December 7 compared with an increase of 0.29% in November. The result came in below market forecasts, which pegged the rate between 0.23% and 0.36%.  

Meanwhile, Brazil's General Price Index, or IGP-M, was 0.06% higher in the first 10 days of December, a lower rate of acceleration than the 0.16% rise seen in the first 10 days of November. The result was in line with market expectations, which posted forecasts ranging from a drop of 0.03% to an increase of 0.21% for the period.  

Early indications that the Brazilian economy is bouncing back after a disappointing third quarter are offering support for the local currency. A number of firms have announced the cancellation of collective holidays over the Christmas period after seeing stocks fall over the last month.  

-By Alastair Stewart, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-3145-1479; brazil@dowjones.com

title: DJ  Brazil  Real Opens Weaker On  Intervention  Ideas
text:
SAO PAULO, Dec 12, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar Monday amid speculation that the central bank would increase its intervention in the foreign currency market.  

The real opened at BRL2.268 per dollar, down from Friday's close of BRL2.253 per dollar.  

Recently, Brazil's central bank has been very active on the foreign currency market buying dollars on the spot market and foreign-exchange linked debt through swap auctions.  

The auctions will continue Monday when the central bank expects to swap approximately $600 million dollar-linked debt for interest-linked paper. The results will be released at around 1630 GMT.  

But local banks are now speculating that the bank will resort to other measures to weaken the currency amid loud complaints from politicians and exporters that a real near four-and-a-half-year highs is hurting the economy.  

The central banks could allow exporters to delay the repatriation of dollars or it could restrict banks' ability to build short positions in the real, analysts said.  

Faced with this possibility, last week Brazilian banks were unwinding short positions, which reached a high for the year in November at $3.421 billion.  

Domestic banks are also wary that the central bank will now take a more aggressive stance on interest rate cuts when it meets Wednesday.  

Market expectations are for a cut of 50 basis points, but one trader said that some banks had already priced in a 75-basis-point cut, resulting in some volatility in the market as domestic banks started buying January futures contracts and putting pressure on the spot market.  

News that Sao Paulo inflation came in lower than expected for the four-week period to Dec. 7 fueled that speculation.  

Sao Paulo's Fipe research institute said its consumer price index rose 0.18% in the four week period compared with an increase of 0.29% in November. The institute is associated with the University of Sao Paulo. The result came in below market forecasts, which pegged the rate between 0.23% and 0.36%.  

Meanwhile, Brazil's General Price Index, or IGP-M, was 0.06% higher in the first 10 days of December, a lower rate of acceleration than the 0.16% rise seen in the first 10 days of November. The result was in line with market expectations, which posted forecasts ranging from a drop of 0.03% to an increase of 0.21% for the period.  

The base Selic interest rate currently stands at 18.5% per year.  

The Brazilian real rose against the dollar for the last three sessions. However, this is only because of central bank intervention and the market trend is still for the real to weaken, traders said.  

With real interest rates at around 13% per year, Brazil continues to attract foreign short-term investment capital.

title: Brazil  real stumbles on  intervention , stocks fall
text:
(Updates to close)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Dec 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency fell for the second straight day on Thursday after the central bank acted to weaken the real, while stocks slipped further from a record high set on Tuesday.  

The real <BRBY> lost 1.32 percent to end at 2.224 to the dollar.  

The central bank has sought to pull the real back from some of its strongest levels in 4-1/2 years by intervening regularly in the market over the last two months, selling currency swaps linked to short-term interest rates and buying dollars on the spot foreign exchange market as it did on Thursday.  

The currency has rallied about 20 percent this year, lifted by a steady flow of dollars into the market from booming exports and corporate bond sales overseas.  

It has also benefited from high domestic interest rates, which attract foreign investors seeking higher returns than those available in Europe and the United States. Brazil's benchmark lending rate stands at a lofty 18.5 percent.  

But the rally has worried exporters who fear their products could lose market share abroad.  

"The central bank has made it clear that it wants the dollar to rise (versus the real) and that's what the market is reacting to," said Alexandre Vasarhelyi, head of currency trading at ING Bank in Sao Paulo.  

The central bank sold $519.7 million in currency swaps, which allow investors to buy exposure to Brazil's base interest rate without having to purchase reais.  

The auction marked the 10th time since November that the bank has offered such swaps, which also cancel out old dollar-linked debt that was originally sold to prevent the real from weakening. On Friday it will offer an additional $625 million in swaps.  

The central bank also bought dollars on the spot market for the 44th time since October.  

On the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, the benchmark Bovespa <.BVSP> index fell 0.84 percent to end at 32,480, according to preliminary closing figures. Bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes fell 1.43 percent to 41.45 reais.  

Still the index is near a record high hit this week. Low inflation and heavy demand among yield-hungry foreign investors have helped raise the Bovespa to records this year. On Tuesday it closed above the 33,000 points for the first time.  

The stock market has also gained of late on expectations the central bank will cut interest rates further to boost growth and revive the economy, which contracted in the third quarter from the second for the first time in two years.

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil seen resuming growth in Q4-FinMin
text:
(Updates with more Palocci quotes, adds WTO comments)  

LONDON, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Brazilian Finance Minister Antonio Palocci said on Friday his nation's economic growth this year was likely to undershoot previous forecasts but would end 2005 on a positive note after a dip in the third quarter.  

Palocci said that growth this year could be below the government's forecast of 3.4 percent.  

Brazil's economy contracted 1.2 percent in the third quarter compared with the second quarter, marking its first fall in two years and leaving the government vulnerable to attack as 2006 elections loom.  

"If we take a look ahead, if we were to take the data from this quarter (it) indicates a positive outlook in spite of the drop in GDP which was detected for the third quarter," Palocci told journalists through a translator.  

When asked whether growth would be below 3.4 percent this year, he said: "probably below 3.4".  

When asked whether it would be below 3.00 percent he said: "I have to wait for new data."  

TRADE WRANGLE  

Palocci was speaking on the sidelines of a meeting of finance ministers from the Group of Seven industrialised nations.  

Both London and Washington hope the London meeting of the G7 will inject fresh life into faltering talks on trade liberalisation in the run-up to a Hong Kong meeting of 148 World Trade Organization countries in less than two weeks' time.  

Britain's Gordon Brown, who chairs the G7 this year, put much of the blame on other European nations and called for an end to subsidies for farmers in rich countries, which the OECD says total about $280 billion a year.  

Palocci said there was no guarantee that the Hong Kong talks would be an outright success but that he was optimistic.  

"Our focus tomorrow is to make an appeal to the countries that are present at the G7 and the guests, so that we can take one step forward on the question of Hong Kong," he said.  

"The proposition of the Americans and English is that we take a step forward. What I told them is that Brazil has the disposition to advance positons, but this won't be done if there isn't a more daring position on the part of the EU."  

CRIMP IN GROWTH  

Brazilian growth was hurt by high interest rates aimed at curbing inflation and a steep drop in the agricultural sector.  

Inflation has steadily declined from 12.5 percent in 2002. Next year's target is 4.5 percent.  

Despite the drop in third quarter growth, Palocci said there is no need for a change in Brazil's monetary policy.  

"The intensity of the policy is a legitimate debate... but I would not say that the reduction of the GDP in one quarter would be an indicator that the policy should change," Palocci said.  

The central bank began to cut its base Selic lending rate in September for the first time in nearly a year-and-a-half after it reached a high of 19.75 percent. The Selic rate remains one of the highest in the world after discounting inflation.  

On Nov. 23 the Selic rate was cut by half of a percentage point to 18.50 percent.  

Palocci said the appreciation of the real, Brazil's currency, should not be taken as a negative factor for the economy.  

He said the effect of exchange rate developments would not be the same for everyone, "but overall there has been a positive outlook."  

He said the main pressure seen on the exchange rate was from trade and foreign investments.  

"So if you take the sum of these two with all the money coming into the country, there is an appreciation of the real," Palocci added.  

"So I think the appreciation of the real cannot be seen as a negative effect, which is an effect of the trade openness...but it should be interpreted in the fact that the country's income is also increasing."  

While Palocci was meeting in London, Brazil's central bank intervened in the market for the 40th time since October, offering to buy dollars to build up foreign reserves.

title: DJ Brazil Real Opens Stronger On Possible Interest Rate Cut
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 23, 2005 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

The Brazilian real opened stronger against the U.S. dollar Wednesday as the currency continued the momentum that it gained late in the previous session, with investors expecting the central bank to announce additional interest rate cuts after markets close.  

The real opened at BRL2.232 per dollar, stronger from Tuesday's close of BRL2.247 per dollar.  

The markets are expected to be more upbeat in Wednesday's trading session, according to analysts.  

Market watchers expect the Brazilian Central Bank to cut the benchmark Selic interest rate by 50 basis points to 18.5% per year. The bank cut the Selic rate at its meetings in September and October.  

Analysts expect markets to react positively to minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserves meeting Nov. 1, which were released late Tuesday.  

In the minutes, the Fed's rate-setting panel expressed concern about raising interest rates too high. The minutes could signal an end to the Fed's recent monetary tightening cycle, creating a more favorable climate for emerging market investments, analysts said.  

Rising interest rates in the U.S. typically drain investments from emerging markets such as Brazil.  

However, additional intervention in the currency market by Brazil's central bankers could put pressure on the real, according to analysts.  

Traders expect the central bank to make an exchange-linked debt offering Friday or Monday.  

The bank sold out similar "reverse swap" offerings in auctions last Friday and this past Tuesday, with demand strong for the paper.  

On Tuesday, the bank sold 10,500 contracts valued at $501.5 million, while last Friday's auction netted $404 million for 8,400 contracts.  

The bank began holding the swap auctions last week for the first time since March to allow investors to exchange dollar-indexed bonds for more popular paper linked to domestic interest rates.  

Investors' fears that Finance Minister Antonio Palocci, the architect of the government's market friendly economic policies, would soon leave the government appeared to have faded, analysts said.  

Palocci, who denied published reports he had offered his resignation last week, soothed markets with testimony before a congressional committee on Tuesday.  

However, Palocci still faces a congressional inquiry into corruption allegations leveled against him by a former aide. His appearance before that panel is expected to take place by Dec. 10.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil cenbank sells  currency  swaps, real weakens
text:
(Adds details, exchange rate, background)  

SAO PAULO, Brazil, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank on Friday sold 8,400 currency swap contracts linked to short-term interest rates to replace $404 million in outstanding debt instruments indexed to the dollar.  

The auction marked the first time since March that the central bank offered currency swaps, which are designed to help prevent Brazil's hard-charging real <BRBY> from strengthening further against the dollar.  

The real, which opened sharply lower on Friday after the central bank announced the auction, weakened further once the results were made public. In late afternoon trading, the real was 1.74 percent weaker than Thursday's close at 2.228 to the greenback, leaving it 20 percent stronger than where it started the year.  

The bank sold all contracts on offer at the auction, suggesting that demand for the swaps is strong. The swaps carried maturities between March 2006 and January 2008.  

The new swaps enable investors to buy exposure to Brazil's lofty benchmark interest rate without having to purchase reais and help diminish the impact of dollar-linked debt notes that were originally sold to prevent the real from weakening.  

The government heavily sold the dollar-linked debt in 2002 to prevent the real from weakening, later refinancing the bonds with foreign exchange swaps as they matured. Brokerage houses bought the paper to hedge against a potential depreciation of the local currency.  

These debt and foreign exchange swaps are denominated in reais but pay investors at the current real-dollar exchange rate when they mature.  

The new swaps linked to short-term rates should help cut the riskiness of Brazil's big debt load by getting rid of dollar-linked debt at a faster pace, and allow foreign investment to keep pouring into the country without strengthening the local currency too much.  

The real's rally has become a hot political issue of late, sparking an outcry from exporters who fear their products will become less competitive on world markets.  

The central bank has also tried to beat back the real's surge by buying dollars on the local foreign exchange market, though it says the interventions are aimed at building up hard currency reserves.

title: FOREX  VIEW: Despite Headwinds, Real Seen Staying Strong
text:
By Laurence Norman 
   A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN 
   

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--It's become a commonplace of currency markets.  

Alongside periodic panics about U.S. deficits and the regular ripples stirred by Europe's political problems, the market works up a sweat every few months over whether Brazil's real is due for a fall.  

The latest round of real-fretting has come this week. Continued political problems for President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and dollar buying from the central bank have a few analysts warning the real could be hitting some headwinds.  

That may be, but most market-watchers agree it would be foolhardy to predict the real will come far off its current levels as 2005 ends and the new year begins.  

After a big drop in 2003, the dollar tumbled 8.7% last year against the real and another 17.7% so far this year. The real's 2005 climb has been all the more remarkable since it comes when the dollar has gained sharply versus most major currencies. The dollar ended last week at a 55-month low of BRL2.169 before lifting to BRL2.204 in local markets Wednesday.  

The real's modest drop of recent days came alongside the latest bout of worries about the future of Finance Minister Antonio Palocci and his market-friendly economic policies.  

Palocci has come under increasing scrutiny after a former aide alleged the minister's former municipal administration in the city of Ribeirao Preto ran a kickback operation aimed at financing political campaigns for the governing Workers' Party. Over the weekend, there were reports that he may resign.  

Those worries sent Brazilian markets lower Monday and the real dropped 2% in a day. However, the currency eked out modest gains Wednesday after Palocci, in testimony before a senate committee, denied any wrongdoing and staunchly defended the government's economic policies.  


 
   Slowdown Concerns 
   

Still, Monday's market jitters had some banks wondering about the real's next step. In a research note Tuesday, Nick Benenbroek, currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman, said that "whether the real's fall ... develops into something more significant will depend on whether political jitters are reinforced by economic fundamentals."  

Bennenbroek noted a recent slowdown in industrial production growth, with September's 0.2% annual rise the lowest in more than two years. He also said Thursday's retail sales data could show a slowing from August's pace. Overall, with the domestic economy shouldering the burden of 19% nominal interest-rates, Bennenbroek said "recent data suggest that Q3 (third quarter) GDP growth will slow from its surprisingly strong Q2 (second quarter) pace."  

Monday's price movements, Bennenbroek said, opened up the possibility of the dollar enjoying a "significant correction" and testing BRL2.3050 by year end.  

Meanwhile, after months of standing on the sidelines, Brazil's central bank has intervened regularly since early October, buying dollars via public auctions, though the bank has not said how much it has bought. Authorities say the dollar buying aims to build reserves to make future debt payments. However, some analysts believe the recent spurt of intervention is also aimed at stemming dollar gains.  

Clyde Wardle, currency strategist at HSBC in New York, said all these factors mean investors may have become "a little over-extended" on the real in recent weeks. HSBC sees the dollar rising to BRL2.25 per dollar at year end.  


 
   Stay Calm: Real Has Tailwinds Too 
   

Yet none of these factors offers convincing reasons for investors to turn seriously bearish on the real as the market heads into a new year. Lawrence Goodman, Head of Global Emerging Markets Foreign Exchange strategy at Bank of America in New York, said many fundamental factors remain real-friendly.  

With commodity prices lending a hand, Brazil has run a $38.2 billion trade surplus so far this year, with a central bank survey Monday forecasting a record $42 billion surplus by year end. Meanwhile, with the local stock market hitting record highs, the economy set to grow over 3% in 2005 and interest-rates among the highest of any major economy, capital inflows - from foreign direct investment to hot money flows - remain copious. Brazil's current account surplus in the year-to-September equaled 1.78% of GDP.  

Some worry that, in 2006, the carry trade - borrowing in low yield currencies and buying assets of high yielding ones like Brazil - may start turning against Brazil. That's because Brazil is likely to continue cutting rates while the Fed - and possibly the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan - tighten their monetary stances. Just as the real has benefited from high levels of global liquidity and rising rates, it could suffer as the tide turns, they warn.  

Yet not only are Brazil's nominal rates still very high, so are the country's real interest-rates - currently around 12%. Moreover, Goodman said, any reduction in the currency's carry trade advantage could be outweighed by the positive impact of falling interest-rates on Brazilian growth.  

And while it's likely that global liquidity will gradually be squeezed next year, the world economy is still growing at a strong tick, meaning prices of the commodities that Brazil exports should remain firm.  

Goodman said the real may indeed face some choppiness in the days ahead but there remains "greater scope for the currency to appreciate." The bank sees the real setting a new high at BRL2.15 per dollar in coming weeks. Nor is HSBC's Wardle too bearish on the real. The bank sees the dollar staying at BRL2.25 at the end of the first quarter.  

If that's right, prepare to ride out for a few more round of real-fretting in the months ahead. . (Laurence Norman covers foreign exchange for Dow Jones Newswires in New York. He has previously covered the Argentine economy for Dow Jones in Buenos Aires.)

title: Brazil  currency  extends rally, stocks drift lower
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency edged firmer on Friday in its 10th straight session of gains, buoyed by an inflow of dollars, while stocks slipped as investors pocketed gains from a recent run-up.  

The Brazilian real <BRBY> gained 0.28 percent in thin turnover ahead of Monday's holiday in the United States to a fresh 4-1/2-year high of 2.163 to the dollar, leaving it over 22 percent stronger since the start of the year.  

"Not even politics gets to influence the market ... The (dollar) flow is very positive and nothing can beat the flows," said Tarcisio Rodrigues, head of forex at Paulista bank.  

He said there were some political concerns about the opposition's victory in Congress earlier in the day, when it managed to extend an investigation into alleged corruption in the government's Postal Service until April.  

Another currency trader in Sao Paulo added: "The market only has one direction -- everyone selling dollars."  

The real continued to benefit from a heavy inflow of dollars from exports and corporate bond sales overseas. It has also been propped up by foreign investors, who have been buying exposure to Brazil's lofty 19 percent benchmark interest rate rather than the low yields available in Europe and the United States.  

The real has rallied even as the central bank has intervened regularly to buy dollars on the spot market. The intervention aims to build up Brazil's foreign reserves and, indirectly, weaken the real, whose surge is irking exporters.  

The central bank on Friday said it would from now on make decisions on whether to hold "reverse exchange swap auctions" based on market conditions rather than on a weekly timetable.  

The swap auctions allow investors to enter contracts that rise or fall based on the rate of the U.S. dollar and domestic interest rates. The idea of the swaps is to reduce the country's exposure to a falling dollar.  

On the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, the benchmark Bovespa <.BVSP> index fell 0.7 percent to 30,511 as investors took profits on the heels of a recent rally.  

Shares in state-run oil giant Petrobras weighed on the broader market, dropping almost 3 percent to 30.85 reais. The losses came after Petrobras reported a third-quarter net profit that came up short of the market consensus. Still, most analysts said the results were solid and could not justify the big drop, which some attributed to easing oil prices.  

Stocks in Companhia Vale do Rio Doce eased 0.3 percent to 82.2 reais after Canada's Canico Resource Corp. agreed to be taken over by CVRD which had sweetened its offer to as much as C$940 million ($790 million). (Additional reporting by Daniela Machado)

title: POLL-Brazilian real seen weakening as rate cuts continue
text:
LONDON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real is set to weaken in coming months as the central bank continues to buy dollars, interest rates fall and markets start to price in a risk premium before elections in 2006, a Reuters poll shows.  

The median forecast in the Oct. 24-27 survey of 15 emerging market strategists showed the real <BRL=> <BRBY> softening to 2.31 per dollar in three months, 2.39 in six and 2.46 a year from now, compared with Friday's levels of around 2.28.  

"(There will be) a narrower interest rate differential as there is monetary easing in Brazil and monetary tightening in the U.S., a narrower current account surplus (and) some residual intervention by the Brazilian authorities," said Mario Mesquita at ABN AMRO in Sao Paulo.  

"Finally we are going to have elections here next year and expect some nervousness in the market derived from that."  

A long corruption scandal in Brazil has undermined President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's standing for the run up to a presidential election in October 2006.  

Strategists said markets could start pricing in a risk premium related to the elections from the first quarter.  

Brazil's central bank resumed interventions in the foreign exchange market on Oct. 3 after a six-month break. Strategists estimate it has bought at least $2.5 billion in October, pushing the real off a pre-intervention 4-year high of 2.213 per dollar.  

Nine of the strategists expect the central bank to continue regular interventions in the foreign exchange market in early 2006 or even for the whole of next year.  

However, opinion was split on where the real would be now if the central bank had not started buying up dollars, with estimates ranging from 1.85 per dollar to current levels.  

"(Without intervention) appreciation would have continued on the back of robust U.S. dollar inflows from the trade surplus and new debt issuance," said Suhas Ketkar at Royal Bank of Scotland in New York.  

But others said the intervention was having less impact on the market than monetary policy and the real would still be at around current levels without it.  

MORE RATE CUTS  

Falling inflation enabled the Brazilian central bank to cut rates for the first time in 17 months in September. This month it lowered the key Selic rate by more than expected, to 19 percent from 19.5.  

The poll showed the central bank cutting rates by 50 basis points in both November and December -- a view supported by the tone of the October minutes published on Thursday -- with the pace of easing then slowing in spring next year.  

The median showed rates at 18 percent at the end of 2005 and 16.75 percent at the end of March.  

By then, official U.S. interest rates are widely expected to rise to 4.5 percent from the current 3.75. This would reduce the rates differential between Brazil and the United States to 1225 basis points from 1525.  

"The cost of going long dollars in Brazil will be much lower than it is now," said John Welch at Lehman Brothers in New York.  

But whilst a weaker currency may boost exports and thus help the economy, it could also spark inflationary pressures.  

The benchmark IPCA consumer price inflation is expected to come in broadly in line with the central bank's 5.1 percent target for the end of this year, slowing from 7.6 percent in 2004, 9.3 in 2003 and 12.5 in 2002. For 2006, the inflation target is 4.5 percent.  

"It will require tight monetary policy to ensure they meet the CPI targets," said Alexandre Lintz at BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo. He sees the pace of rate cuts slowing to 50 basis points each quarter during 2006.  

The median showed a pause in rate cuts later next year, with the Selic seen at 16 percent at both end-June and end-September and at 15.5 percent at the end of 2006. End-2006 rates forecasts ranged from 14.50 to 16.50 percent.  

On the foreign exchange front, all 14 strategists who gave a view expected the real to be weaker than current levels in 12 months, with end-October 2006 forecasts ranging from 2.33 to 2.70 real per dollar.

title: Brazil's Real Opens At BRR2.690/Dlr Vs BRR2.671 End Fri
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real opened under pressure Monday, reflecting continuing worries about the global economic outlook and reduced foreign investment flows into emerging markets. 

 The local currency opened 1.9 centavo weaker at BRR2.690 to the dollar, as investors fret over possible imminent U.S. military reprisal against terrorist networks. The real closed slightly stronger at BRR2.671 Friday, following a central bank intervention. 

 "The outlook is very uncertain and demand for forex hedge remains strong," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 In addition to reduced foreign capital inflows, one key factor sending the real weaker in recent weeks has been large corporate demand for dollars to protect their balance sheets from forex losses. 

 Even though the market regulator has allowed companies to defer forex losses over the next four years, traders said many firms continue to sell reals and buy dollars to avoid running any forex risks going forward. 

 The real has lost nearly 30% of its value this year to date, despite massive central bank intervention to contain the depreciation. 

Brazil on Friday said it was drawing down a $4.7 billion aid tranche by the International Monetary Fund as part of a recently-inked $15.5 billion package. The move aims to boost the country's hard-currency reserves and try to calm investors at a time when the real is under added pressure.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Tad Stronger, Aided By Ctrl Bk Auction
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- On a Friday of expiring dollar futures, local banks opened fire against Brazil's embattled real after a one-day truce Thursday, forcing the central bank to intervene and contain the sell-off. 

Brazil's real closed slightly stronger at BRR2.671 to the dollar, following a central bank move to call an emergency sale of BRR500 million in May 2002 dollar-indexed notes. The auction was announced as the currency hit its weakest point of the day at BRR2.690 in late trading. 

 The dollar-linked notes sold for an average rate of 6.36% 

 "Today it was pure speculation because of the expiring futures contracts," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 He noted the late-afternoon weakening wasn't caused by corporate demand for hedge against forex depreciation, as was the case in recent days. 

 The real strengthened 6.3 centavos Thursday to BRR2.675 to the dollar, reacting to a series of central bank measures to tighten liquidity and a market regulator ruling allowing companies to dilute forex losses over the next four years. 

 The rally kept the central bank from intervening to prop up the currency for the first time since last Friday. 

 Brazil's real came under added strain after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. raised fear that foreign capital flows into emerging economies will fall significantly. 

 The real, which was already weak amid a host of regional and homegrown worries, lost 4% of its value since the U.S tragedy despite a central bank move to flood the market with $5.74 billion in short-term dollar-indexed notes in the period. 

 The year-to-date depreciation is 27%. 

 The central bank said earlier Friday Brazil would draw down a $4.7 billion aid tranche from the International Monetary Fund to boost its international reserves, but the news didn't move the real. 

 The tranche is part of a recently-inked $15.5 billion loan program set to expire in December. 

 Brazil's international reserves were at $35.291 billion Thursday, down from $35.395 billion Wednesday. The central bank said the $4.7 billion IMF tranche will add to reserves today.

title: Brazil In Spotlight As Volatile Week Ends In Latin Mkts
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- A turbulent week for Latin American financial markets drew to a close with the spotlight on Brazil, where repeated central bank interventions failed to keep the country's currency from weakening to an all-time low. 

 The real fell 2.6% to BRR2.835 per dollar Friday, despite five impromptu central bank auctions - in which more than BRR2 billion in dollar-linked debt was sold - aimed at stabilizing a market fearful of the economic fallout from last week's terrorist attacks in the U.S. A sixth auction was called after the close, a move which could ease pressure on the real early Monday. 

 The real weakened almost 6% during the week and has lost nearly a third of its value year-to-date. Traders pointed to heavy corporate demand for hedge. 

 "With Brazil, it's definitely a question of `who-would-have-thunk it?," said Daniel Tillotson, head emerging markets strategist at Prudential Securities in New York, noting that the market is being driven by psychological rather than fundamental considerations. 

 FleetBoston said Friday in a report that it had thought BRR2.75 per dollar was the "absolute top" for the currency, even if economically-troubled Argentina were forced to devalue. 

 "We think anything above 2.60 is overdone, but we also think 3.00 could trade next week based on the fear in the market that comes from reaching a new reference along with the fear from the external environment," the report added. 

 The anxiety was evident in New York-based debt trading Friday. Yield spreads widened 50 points to 1150 over comparable U.S. Treasurys, or about 400 points wider than at the end of 2000. 


          Mexican Peso Holds Ground



Brazilian equities faired relatively better, taking their cue from the
see-saw performance of U.S. stocks throughout the day.



The main Sao Paulo IBovespa index shed 1.2% Friday to 10,419, but
still managed to gain 3.8% for the week. The Sao Paulo bourse suffered
most of its losses last week, while U.S. markets were closed in the wake
of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.



In New York, Brazilian blue chips were mixed, with aircraft
manufacturer Embraer (EMJ) gaining 2.9% to $12.30 - after having lost
half of its value the previous four sessions -  and wireless phone
service provider Telesp Celular (TCP) sliding 4.8% to $4.95, pushing its
cumulative loss for the week to 33%.



Trading activity elsewhere in the region Friday was more subdued,
though strategists say volatility is bound to continue as the markets
await details of U.S. plans for retaliation against the attacks and more
information on the extent to which the global economy will suffer.



In Mexico, the peso weakened slightly to MXN9.465 per dollar from
MXN9.462, after plunging to around MXN9.53 early in the session on the
heels of a sharp downturn on Wall Street. The peso gained nearly seven
centavos during the week, recovering from a 20 centavo weakening the
previous week.



Mexico's main IPC stock index, for its part, inched up 0.1% Friday to

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk To Continue  Forex  Mkt  Intervention  - Paper
text:
PARIS -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian central bank will continue intervening on the foreign exchange market at least until the end of this year, selling $50 million a day, in order to guarantee liquidity on the market, Luiz Fernando Figueiredo, head of the bank's monetary policy, said Tuesday in an interview with French newspaper Agefi. 

 "We have decided to sell $50 million a day, whatever the market conditions are. This strategy has to be continued until the end of the year and will be extended if necessary," Figueiredo said. 

 But he said the central bank has no target for the real's exchange rate. 

 Despite repeated interventions in the forex market since June, the real has lost about 30% of its value this year and is currently trading just above its historic lows. 

 Monday, the real hit a historic intraday low of BRR2.610 to the dollar, before settling at BRR2.606. 

 In order to maintain its inflation target of 4% in 2001, over the summer the central bank raised interest rates to 19%. 

 Figueiredo said this level could still change. 

 "This valuation is subject to information concerning the economic health of the country and could be modified in case of improvement or degradation of the situation," Figueiredo said. 

 He said the real's depreciation limited the fall in external demand, and said direct foreign investment could increase to $25 billion in 2002, from a projected $20 billion in 2001. 

 Figueiredo said financing of external debt "isn't a problem" for Brazil. 

 He said the country meets International Monetary Fund requirements and expressed optimism about the budget surplus target of 3.4% of gross domestic product this year and 3.5% in 2002. 

 "The energy rationing will weigh on GDP but will have only an indirect and limited impact on the public finances and won't stop the government reaching its budget targets," Figueiredo said.

title: Brazil Govt Sees 2001 Fiscal Deficit At 6% GDP
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian government forecasts that the country's fiscal deficit will grow to 6% of gross domestic product this year from 4.5% in 2000, as regional turmoil sent interest rates soaring and weakened the local currency sharply in recent months. 

 Addressing investors in a conference call Wednesday, Finance Ministry Executive Secretary Amaury Bier also said next year's fiscal deficit is expected to fall to 4.05% of GDP. 

 He said the forecast, which is included in the recently inked $15 billion loan program with the International Monetary Fund, is based on a set of interest-rate and exchange-rate assumptions that wasn't disclosed. 

 Under the new IMF agreement, the details of which were unveiled Tuesday, Brazil raised its primary budget surplus target - which excludes debt servicing costs - to 3.35% of GDP this year and 3.5% in 2002, from 3% previously. The surplus aims to keep Brazil's public debt burden from growing. 

 Bier said the federal government will be responsible for the bulk of the 2002 primary budget surplus target, contributing 2.8% of GDP to the 3.5% target. 

 Regional governments and the companies they control are expected to contribute the remaining 0.7% of GDP. 

 With the surplus, the government expects Brazil's net public debt to rise to 53.95% of GDP at the end of 2001, from 49.5% at the end of last year. 

 By the end of 2002, the net debt burden is seen at 53.22% of GDP and headed toward a "very clear downward trend," said Bier during the conference sponsored by Salomon Smith Barney. 

 He said the estimate takes into account a plan to recognize hidden public-sector liabilities totaling 0.8% of GDP between this year and next and is net of any privatization revenues. 

 Bier declined to say which state-owned assets are listed for sale. 

 He said the new tax on fuels, which is being debated by lawmakers for approval, is expected to generate revenue of some BRR4 billion annually. The new tax will replace the so-called oil account as of 2002, which is an indirect tax on fuel. 

 Even though the IMF has revised Brazil's end-2001 inflation target to 5.8% from 4%, central bank director for economic research Ilan Goldfajn stressed that the monetary authority will continue to pursue the government-set 4% goal. 

 As a result, the new IMF target won't affect the handling of monetary policy, Goldfajn said. He added that the new IMF target was just a "more realistic" forecast for inflation this year, since the Brazilian economy went through many shocks, such as the energy crisis and a weak currency. Goldfajn noted that the IMF and government's inflation targets converge to 3.5% at the end of 2002. 

 Market consensus is that inflation will be 6.2% 

 Goldfajn said the central bank expects to see the country's net international reserves at $28 billion at the end of the year. 

 This means that Brazil can spend up to $8 billion on interventions in the forex market to prop up the currency, if needed. 

 He also said the $28-billion figure doesn't take into account new possible loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and World Bank that Brazil is currently negotiating. 

 -By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11 3145-1481; adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: IMF To Give  Brazil  More Room To  Intervene  On  FX  -Source
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The International Monetary Fund has agreed to give Brazil more freedom to use its hard-currency reserves to defend its sagging currency if needed, a top Brazilian government official told Dow Jones Newswires Monday. 

 The official, who is directly involved in Brazil's talks with the IMF and spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed talk that South America's biggest economy will be allowed to use up to an extra $5 billion of its international reserves to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the central bank feels it's necessary. 

 The IMF said late Friday it's preparing a fresh $15 billion loan program for Brazil in a bid to halt contagion from cash-strapped neighbor Argentina, whose financial woes have sent Brazilian markets reeling in recent months. Contagion fears are largely blamed for the real's 20%-plus depreciation since the start of the year. 

 Brazil currently has about $35.5 billion in hard-currency reserves, including $3.8 billion in IMF funds. Under an existing $41.5 billion IMF aid program that will be replaced in September, the country is committed to keeping reserves above $25 billion. 

 That reserve floor will be lowered to some $20 billion, the official said. 

 The Finance Ministry said it's set to unveil the details of the new aid package Tuesday at 1730 GMT. 

 The central bank earlier said it will sell $6 billion in dollars on the foreign exchange market by the end of the year, by means of daily sales worth about $50 million. The move aims to bridge a lack of foreign currency on the market amid regional turbulence. 

Brazil is hoping that the extra $5 billion freed for intervention purposes will help ward off speculative pressure on the real. 

 A strategy in late June to intervene heavily on the market failed, though. The central bank pumped $1.3 billion in dollars into the market during a two-week period, but the real's recovery was very short-lived. 

 The government official also confirmed that the IMF demanded that Brazil raise its primary budget surplus target - which excludes debt servicing costs - this year and next in order to keep Brazil's net public debt burden of some 50% of GDP from growing further. 

 This year's surplus target will be raised to 3.4% of gross domestic product and next year's to around 3.5%, the source said. The goals had been set at 3%. 

 The official said no more budget cuts will be needed this year to meet the new 2001 target after the government last month unveiled spending cuts totaling 1 billion reals ($1=BRR2.46). 

 Some of next year's investments will likely have to be sacrificed, though. 

 "We're going to work on the budget, and the 2002 budget proposal that we're presenting to Congress on August 30 will show how we'll manage to meet the target," said the official. 

 He said new tax hikes, which made up the bulk of the government's austerity measures in recent years, won't be necessary this time around. 

 An energy crisis and Argentine turmoil led economists to downgrade their forecasts for Brazil's growth this year to 2% to 3%, down from earlier projections of a 4% to 4.5% expansion. 

 -By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11 3145-1481 adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  Real Ends Stronger On New IMF Deal,  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended stronger Monday on a new agreement with the International Monetary Fund for $15 billion and central bank intervention to prop up the battered currency. 

 Gains, however, were muted as the market continued to fret about a possible debt default in Argentina, where the IMF said Friday it would accelerate a $1.2 billion disbursement needed to help keep the country solvent. 

 Doubts remain about whether Brazil's IMF deal would be enough to fend off the likely heavy contagion that a potential rupture in Argentina would bring, traders said. 

 A central bank intervention also added to the real's gains. "They (the central bank) intervened today, but it's getting harder to see how much effect they are having because they are doing it more quietly," said a trader in Rio de Janeiro. 

 Since late June, the central bank has been selling about $50 million daily after earmarking $6 billion for the rest of the year to intervene on the spot market and contain the weakening of the real, which has slipped by over 20% this year. 

 Signs indicate interventions may continue. Reports have said the IMF has agreed to give Brazil added room to intervene to prop up the real, by reducing the country's foreign currency reserve floor to about $20 billion from $25 billion. Reserves currently sit at about $35 billion. 

 The real ended at BRR2.460 to the dollar on a spread of BRR2.459-BRR2.461 spread. On Friday, the real closed at BRR2.505 to the dollar.

title: Brazil Real Ends Stronger On Ctrl Bk Dlr Sale, Argentina
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real finished stronger Monday, thanks to central bank intervention and the Argentine government winning approval for a plan to cut spending by $1.5 billion in the second half of this year. 

 The real finished a midrate of BRR2.415 to the dollar on a spread of BRR2.414 to BRR2.416. The real closed Friday at BRR2.460 to the dollar. 

 Traders said the market was encouraged by the opposition-led Senate approving the Argentine government's bill but added it continued to remain skeptical about the country being able to emerge from its three-year recession. 

 This doubt crept into the real's price during midsession after the initial lift in the currency in early trading, but the central bankintervened and sold dollars to prop up the real. 

 The latest Argentine update comes as press reports circulated in the local market that Brazil has asked the International Monetary Fund to allow it to have the flexibility to lower the minimum amount it has to hold in its reserves. 

 According to daily newspaper Folha de S. Paulo, the Brazilian government would like to have more firepower to prop up the beleaguered real, which has depreciated about 19% so far this year. 

 The current agreement allows Brazil to lower its reserve levels to a minimum of $25 billion. Reserves are currently worth about $35.7 billion. 

 The request comes during talks with the IMF about the possibility of setting up a new accord. According to the latest press speculation, a new accord could be worth between $10 billion and $20 billion. Talks between Brazil and the IMF began in Washington last week. If put together, a new accord would succeed an existing $41.5 billion IMF-led bailout package that was brokered in late 1998. 

 Economists say Brazil needs a lifeline from the IMF because recent regional economic shocks threaten to produce a vicious cycle in which rising interest rates, a weakening currency and slowing economic growth aggravate the country's already heavy debt burden. 

 Also, Brazil's commercial and retail users have to cut electricity use by an average 20% a month between June and December to preserve depleted water-reservoir levels in a country that is largely dependent on hydroelectric power. 

 Economists believe the power crunch could shave one to two percentage points off of this year's initially forecast 4.0% to 4.5% economic growth rate. 

 -By Anthony Dovkants, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3145-1478; anthony.dovkants@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  Real Ends Stronger;  Central Bank Intervenes  Again
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real finished stronger Thursday after the central bank sold dollars to prop up its beleaguered currency. 

 The real closed at a midrate of BRR2.480 to the dollar on a spread of BRR2.479 to BRR2.481. Wednesday, the real finished at a midrate of BRR2.487, weaker compared with Tuesday, despite central bankintervention. 

 Thursday's improved finish comes despite growing concern about the Argentine government's bid to try and get its so-called zero-deficit plan approved by the Senate. 

 Traders said they continued to worry over news that Argentine lawmakers had postponed a vote on a key plan to cut government spending. In addition, the market was concerned about whether the opposition party wants to introduce changes to the bill in a move that would require the bill to return to the lower house. 

 The market is concerned because the new austerity plan, which seeks to cut government spending by $1.5 billion, plays a key role in Argentina's effort to alleviate pressures on its troubled economy. Markets are largely worried that Argentina could end up defaulting on its debt.

title: Brazil  Real Ends Weaker Despite Ctrl Bk  Intervening
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real finished weaker Wednesday even though the central bank intervened again. 

 The real closed at a midrate of BRR2.487 to the dollar on a spread of BRR2.486 to BRR2.488, pulled down by worry over troubled Argentina. Tuesday, the real finished at a midrate of BRR2.470 to the dollar, despite the local currency being boosted by $545.7 million in receipts from a Petrobras share offering last week and central bank intervention. 

 Wednesday, traders said comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill fueled market worry about Argentina after he voiced support for Brazil's new funding accord with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Traders interpreted the comment as a sign that Brazil needs to shore up its defenses against possible fallout from Argentine contagion. 

 The market was partly reassured, however, by Brazil's announcement that this year it will cut BRR1 billion from its budget, which will now total BRR51.2 billion. Traders said the market was also encouraged by the start of talks between the IMF and Brazil Wednesday morning. 

 According to latest press speculation, Brazil will ask for a six-month "standby" fund from the IMF and a loan of between $15 billion and $20 billion. The accord is expected to be in place once the current $41.5 billion IMF-led bailout package ends in December. 

 Economists say Brazil needs a lifeline from the IMF because recent regional economic shocks threaten to produce a vicious cycle in which rising interest rates, a weakening currency and slowing economic growth aggravate Brazil's already heavy debt burden. Argentina's fiscal crisis, marked by its recession and a $130 billion public-sector debt of its own, has also hurt Brazil. 

 What's more, Brazil's trade deficit is growing, and foreign investment, needed to finance this gap, is sharply down. Also, Brazil's commercial and retail electricity customers are having to cut usage by an average 20% a month between June to December to preserve depleted water reservoir levels in a country that's largely dependent on hydroelectric power. 

 Economists believe the power crunch could shave one to two percentage points off this year's initially forecast 4% to 4.5% economic growth rate. 

 -By Anthony Dovkants, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3145-1478; anthony.dovkants@dowjones.com

title: Brazil Real Ends Weaker On Argentina Deficit Bill Worry
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Despite central bank intervention, Brazil's real closed weaker Tuesday on renewed concern about troubled Argentina. 

 The real finished at a midrate of BRR2.470 to the dollar on a spread of BRR2.469 to BRR2.471. Monday, the real closed at BRR2.415 to the dollar. 

 Initially, the local currency was boosted by trickles of $545.7 million in receipts from a Petrobras share offering last week. Also, the central bank helped prop up the real by selling dollars. 

 However, market concerns over Argentina started to push the real lower by early afternoon. 

 Traders said the market was worried about possible delays or a clash between the Argentine government and the opposition-controlled Senate over approval of a so-called zero-deficit plan geared toward cutting $1.5 billion in spending by the end of the year. 

 While the government said it would be able to fast track the bill through the Senate, market concerns have mounted over whether the opposition will delay the move in protest of the budget-cutting plan. 

 The program is part of Argentine President Fernando de la Rua's latest effort to try to revive an economy that is mired in three years of recession.

title: Brazil Real Ends Weaker, Despite Ctrl Bk Moves,Rate Hike
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Despite central bank intervention and an interest-rate hike, Brazil's real succumbed to gravity yet again and finished weaker Thursday. 

 The real closed at a midrate of BRR2.508 on a spread of BRR2.507 to BRR2.509 a day after the central bank raised interest rates by 75 basis points to 19%. 

 This compares with the real's finish of BRR2.500 Wednesday when it also weakened, despite central bank efforts to rescue it by selling dollars in the market. 

 The currency is losing value after fears of an economic meltdown in Argentina resurfaced. The real posted gains Tuesday when the Argentine government late Monday announced it had clinched political backing for a deficit-cutting plan. 

 However, investors now fear that such measures won't be enough to avert a default in debt, traders said. 

 At the start Thursday, the real weakened to as much as BRR2.535, prompting the central bank to sell dollars - a move that was confirmed by the monetary authority at the end of the session. 

 Traders said the early decline partly stemmed from concerns that the central bank didn't move in favor of a bigger rate hike. The market was expecting the central bank to raise interest rates by 50 to 175 basis points to boost the currency, help stave off possible contagion from Argentina and curb inflation. A Dow Jones Newswires survey of 14 financial institutions this week generated a consensus forecast of a 150-basis point increase.
