title: Brazil  currency  rallies on Argentina debt progress.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, July 17 (Reuters) - Brazil's battered real currency rallied 3.3 percent against the dollar on Tuesday after the Argentine government won key political support for an austerity plan that could help avert a debt default, traders said. 

 Taking advantage of the optimistic mood and to secure a significant rebound in the flagging real, Brazil's Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market. Traders said the bank sold dollars, giving the currency the stamina to extend its gains. 

 The real firmed for a second straight day to close at 2.50 reais per dollar from 2.582 reais at Monday's close. The real on Monday gained for the first time in five days after it hit consecutive record lows last week. 

 The Brazilian currency gained even after ratings agency Fitch changed its outlook on Brazil's ratings to negative from stable, the first negative rating move on Brazil since January 1999. 

 "Our neighbors declared a truce and market players here gave us some respite," said Joao Marcos Cicarelli, a consultant at Agente brokerage in Sao Paulo. "It was the inverse domino effect of past days." 

 The respite came after the Argentine government gained the backing of powerful opposition Peronist governors for a program of spending cuts aimed at reducing the public deficit to zero. 

 The program is the government's latest attempt to assuage chronic investor anxiety of an Argentine default on its $128 billion in debt, and is seen as a prerequisite to dragging Latin America's No. 3 economy out of three-years of recession. 

 Argentine default fears have sparked capital flight from emerging market assets from Turkey to Russia and particularly from neighboring Brazil in what some have taken to calling the "Tango effect." 

 The real market has felt the Argentine crisis more acutely than other assets as it added to concerns about the impact of a U.S. economic slowdown and emergency energy rationing at home. 

 The real is 22 percent lower against the dollar than at the start of the year. 

 But Brazil's Central Bank has been determined to shore up the currency. Central Bank interventions have become a regular event in Brazil after the bank said on July 5 that it would spend $6 billion in the market in regular doses this year to help support the real. 

 The bank has intervened almost daily with $50 million cash injections. 

 Market players said they were also bracing themselves ahead of the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Meeting (Copom), which started on Tuesday and is expected to announce a fifth consecutive interest rate hike on Wednesday. 

 Seventeen of 22 economists polled by Reuters in the last two trading days said they expected a hike in the current 18.25 percent benchmark Selic rate, but forecasts ranged from 50 basis points to 200 basis points. The other five respondents expected the bank to hold rates steady.

title: Brazil real  currency  firms on Argentina pact.
text:
SAO PAULO, July 17 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency strengthened in Tuesday afternoon trading as Central Bank dollar sales added to optimism that recession-hit Argentina was reducing the risk of debt default, traders said. 

 The real strengthened to 2.508 per dollar from Monday's close of 2.582 or about 22 percent weaker than where it began the year. Monday was the first time in five days the currency firmed after hitting consecutive record lows on fears of fallout from Argentina's economic woes. 

 Argentina's powerful opposition Peronist governors agreed late Monday to back the government's "zero deficit" plan, which would restrict the provincial governments to spend only what they receive in tax revenues. 

 Emerging market players across the world read the deal as a sign Latin America's No. 3 economy was making progress in reducing the risk of a dreaded debt default. 

 The fear Argentina may not make its debt payments has punished Latin American markets in recent months and has weighed on emerging markets from Turkey to Russia, in what some have taken to calling the "Tango effect." 

 The real market has felt the Argentine crisis more acutely than other assets as it added to concerns about the impact of a U.S. economic slowdown and emergency energy rationing at home. 

 "Apart from an interruption of the 'Tango effect,' at least for now, the Central Bank helped the dollar slip," one trader said. Other dealers said they too had seen the bank intervening in the market. 

Central Bank interventions have become a regular event in Brazil after the bank's said on July 5 that it would spend $6 billion in the market in regular doses this year to help support the real. It has intervened almost daily with $50 million cash injections.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Stronger For First Time In 5 Sessions
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Thanks to central bank intervention, Brazil's real Monday finished on a stronger note for the first time in five sessions despite continuing concern about troubled Argentina. 

 Brazil's real closed at a midrate of BRR2.581 on a spread of BRR2.580 to BRR2.582. Friday, the real ended at BRR2.590 to the dollar - its weakest closing point since the currency was first introduced in 1994 to stamp out hyperinflation. 

 The stronger finish Monday, however, comes after the central bank was forced to rescue the currency after it breached the psychologically important level of BRR2.600 to the dollar for the first time ever. 

 At its weakest point, the real depreciated to as much as BRR2.606, making it the fourth session in a row that the real has set a record intraday low. 

 Traders said there was concern Monday that Argentine President Fernando de la Rua may not find the political support necessary to carry out a proposal to cut government spending by $1.5 billion through the end of 2001. This plan still awaits support from the majority of Argentina's political heavyweights. 

 The market is worried that Argentina is close to defaulting, as a number of analysts don't believe that Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo and de la Rua will be able to revive an economy mired in three years of recession. 

 Troubled Argentina has also been bogged down by rumors over the last week that de la Rua could resign. This was also coupled with speculation that Cavallo was planning to quit because of de la Rua's rising frustration at the economy minister's failure to spark economic growth. 

 -By Anthony Dovkants, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3145-1478; anthony.dovkants@dowjones.com

title: Loser:IMF Is Confident Of Argentine Recovery- Estado
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- A top official of the International Monetary Fund reiterated that he's confident about President Fernando De la Rua and Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo's ability to lift Argentina out of a financial crisis, local news agency Agencia Estado reported Thursday. 

 Argentine securities have come under heavy selling in recent days amid fears that the government's lackluster revenues won't be enough to cover its debt obligations. 

 The government is now pushing through spending cuts in an attempt to stay solvent, while trying to end a three-year recession. 

 Speaking in Brasilia, Claudio Loser - the IMF's head for the Western Hemisphere - said he doesn't believe Argentina will declare a debt moratorium or devalue its peso, which is pegged 1-for-1 to the dollar, except for foreign trade transactions. 

 Loser added that the IMF isn't considering extending additional credit to Argentina. The two parties entered a loan agreement about six months ago. 

 Loser is in Brasilia to review Brazil's compliance with fiscal goals set by the IMF as part of a January 1999 bailout package. 

 The IMF put together a $41.5 billion loan to Brazil after a devaluation of the real, which had been pegged to the dollar for about five years. 

 So far, Loser has kept to the IMF's stance that the IMF is willing to talk about extending Brazil's existing IMF agreement in some form, but only if Brazil requested such assistance. 

 Loser said Brazil doesn't need additional IMF funds at this time to fend off contagion from Argentina. 

 In an interview earlier this week with a local newspaper, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso didn't rule out extending the IMF accord, but said he doesn't think an extension is necessary at the moment. 

 Analysts have said it might be wise for Brazil - which has already seen its currency weaken over 20% since January amid Argentine trouble and an energy crisis - to obtain a contingent credit line, or CCL, from the IMF to use as an insurance policy. 

 Also, Loser denied that the IMF was talking with Brazil's central bank about allowing the monetary authority to intervene in the futures market for the real, Estado reported. 

 The central bank has intervened frequently in the real's spot market in recent months to prop up the sagging currency, but entering the forex futures market is prohibited under the existing IMF accord, which expires in December. 

 If Brazil wanted to enter a new IMF agreement, it would have to wait until its existing program expires in December before closing such a deal, under normal IMF rules. 

 -Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil real hits new low on Argentine pandemonium.
text:
SAO PAULO, July 12 (Reuters) - Brazil's embattled currency ignored intervention to chalk up its third record low close in a row on Thursday as players took a dim view of Argentina's latest bid to pull itself out of recessionary quagmire. 

 The real weakened to the fresh all-time low close of 2.552 per dollar, below Wednesday's previous historic low finish of 2.500, leaving the currency nearly 31 percent below where it began the year. 

 The real also hit a new record intraday low of 2.58 along the way as fears Latin America's No.3 economy could default sent the world's emerging markets reeling for the second day in a row despite Argentina's attempts to calm the storm. 

 Traders were skeptical that Argentine President Fernando de la Rua would be able to muster enough political support to make good on his vow late Wednesday to eliminate the budget gap for the rest of the year by cutting spending and tax evasion. 

 "The (Brazilian) market is 100 percent looking at Argentina," said Banif-Primus head of forex Rodrigo Trotta. 

 As the real headed toward its record close President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and members of his cabinet gave upbeat speeches at an event to commemorate seven years of the real plan, the policy which gave birth to the currency. 

 "Our public debt is going to increase...our face is still ugly, " Cardoso said. "But we are going to improve. We are not afraid of anything." 

 THREE REAIS TO THE DOLLAR? 

 Pressured the past months by concern over the U.S. economic slowdown and the impact of an acute energy shortage, the real's latest slide has made front page news and led to regular updates of its daily trajectory on television news shows. 

 One local newspaper said the real could sink to 3.0 per dollar. Economists do not rule that out but add it would be a knee-jerk reaction to an Argentine collapse and would not last as it would not reflect Brazil's economic fundamentals. 

 "It's not impossible that it could reach 3.0...but that would not be sustained," said BES Investimento chief economist Sandra Utsumi. "As long as there's no definition (for Argentina), the trend is for the dollar to keep pressuring." 

 As traders expected, the Central Bank intervened in the market for the seventh time this month on Thursday. Its sale of $2.7 billion reais in NBC-E dollar-indexed notes to roll over debt due to expire on Monday also gave the real some support. 

 Traders say the monetary authority has placed a $50 million cushion into the market in each of the last six trading days in the hope of breaking the real's fall. 

 The bank, which has repeatedly voiced its well-worn mantra that it targets inflation and not the exchange rate, has said it will spend $6 billion in the local market this year. 

 But players fear that may not be enough and the bank may need to jack up interest rates to up to 30 percent if Argentina collapses, putting the brakes on economic growth which has already been slowed by energy rationing. 

 In a reflection of how worried investors have become, Brazil's risk rating, or the spread between its bond prices and safe-haven U.S. Treasuries, rose past 1,000 basis points, putting it near Turkey and beyond Russia. 

 BCP Latin American economist Walter Molano said Argentina had to bite the bullet and implement economically tough measures to put its economy back on track just as Mexico did after the so-called 1995 Tequila crisis. 

 "Otherwise Argentina will go into the abyss and we will all lose," he said in his daily report. "The contagion from an Argentine collapse will be real. The losses will be severe, and emerging markets will die as an asset class."

title: Emerging Debt-Sentiment sagging depsite technical bounce.
text:
NEW YORK, July 6 (Reuters) - Emerging market bonds on Friday rose for the first time in nine trading sessions in a technical bounce, but confidence was frail amid political strife in Argentina and concern that Brazil's efforts to prop up its flagging currency were failing. 

 "There is continued political noise in Argentina and uncertainties about the effectiveness of intervention efforts announced in Brazil," said Lacey Gallagher, director of Latin American research at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 The J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Index, which on Thursday lost 2.6 percent, widened three basis points to 809 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. 

 Technical analysts said Argentine FRBs and Brazil C bonds were "deeply oversold" on Thursday. On Friday, the FRB rose 3 percent to 77.750 points, and the C bond rose three-quarters of a point to 72.625 points. 

 "External debt markets are up purely on the back of shortcovering. Higher prices do not indicate a change in sentiment and people are squaring their books before they go home," a head emerging market trader said. 

 Meanwhile the Brazilian real ended firmer on Friday after a yo-yo session in which the Central Bank sold dollars to boost the currency after it plumbed record lows against the U.S. dollar. 

 The real, which is off 24.8 percent for the year, ended at 2.435 per dollar. 

 IMPASSE BROKEN 

 An impasse between the Argentine federal government and province leaders was broken on Thursday when the government agreed to hand over $600 million to the provinces in exchange for a series of spending cuts. 

 The Buenos Aires province will cut $500 million, the other 11 provinces will cut an additional $150 million, and the federal government itself will slash $150 million off its expenditure sheet. 

 "There's still not consensus across the political spectrum in terms of an economic policy approach so the agreement with the governors beginning with the Province of Buenos Aires - and we expect more - is positive but it's not the only political issue." 

 Michael Gavin, head of Latin American research at UBS Warburg, said the main risk in Argentina relates to whether the current market panic translates into a financial one leading to sharp declines in bank deposits. 

 "Deposits in the banking system have been relatively stable recently and ... there has been no indication of a deposit run amid (Thursday's) panic ... we think yesterday's price action was more a reflection of panic selling than a response to any specific news," Gavin said. 

 Argentina's four-day peso-denominated interbank lending rate hit 20 percent on Friday ahead of a long weekend - Argentina is closed on Monday for Independence Day - in another sign of growing discontent with the country's inability to turn around ten straight quarters of economic contraction. 

 And Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo in Rome announced changes to the $850 million Letes auction, cutting the maturity of the domestic bonds from one year to 90 days. 

 Meanwhile, emerging market star Mexico, with one foot in the full investment grade door, succumbed to the pessimism as its benchmark 2026 global bond fell 0.750 points to 124.375 - its lowest level since May 30.

 The Argentine concerns heightened this week as investors feared the country's government would lose cross-party support for measures to end three years of economic stagnation. CENTRAL BANK UNDER FIRE 

 Players said the weakness of the real and the Central Bank's efforts to support it were casting an ever darker cloud over the performance of Latin America's biggest economy.

 Some economists argue that the Central Bank's stance, especially Thursday's announcement of how much it would spend to support the currency, was tantamount to making itself a sitting duck for speculators.

Central Bank President Arminio Fraga defended himself from criticism in Friday's edition of the daily newspaper Estado de S. Paulo. "The rule is to be transparent and that's what we are doing," Fraga told Estado columnist Sonia Racy.

title: Brazil Central Bank  confirms Friday  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, July 6 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank on Friday said it had intervened in the foreign exchange market after traders said they noticed the monetary authority selling dollars to boost the local real BRBY) currency. 

 The real clawed its way back to 2.435 reais per dollar in afternoon trading, compared with Thursday's close of 2.470 reais per dollar. In early trading Friday, the real tanked more than 3 percent to 2.560 reais, a record low.

 Investor skittishness over Argentina's deepening financial and political crisis and over Brazil's energy shortage and local political unrest have pummeled the real currency in past months.

title: Brazilian real drop prompts rate hike consideration.
text:
NEW YORK, July 6 (Reuters) - As Brazil's currency tumbles and inflation gathers speed, Wall Street is mulling the possibility that the Brazilian central bank may be forced to raise interest rates to stem the tide of money flowing out of Latin America's biggest economy. 

 The Central Bank has been unable to prick the bubble in the real currency - on Friday it hit a fresh all-time low, sinking 31 percent this year - despite a 150 basis point hike in the benchmark Selic interest rate and numerous interventions in the foreign exchange market using a $6 billion war chest. 

 Moreover, inflation targets were last week raised a full percentage point to 5.8 percent, propelled higher by an energy crisis and the real's weakness while flaccid U.S. growth threatens Brazil's fiscal stability. 

 While repeated interventions merely line the pocket of speculators - in the ranks of which Central Bank President Arminio Fraga once belonged - economists say the bank's next move might be an interest rate hike, not a cut as indicated two weeks ago. 

 "It's fair to say the Central Bank's strategy hasn't worked as well as they would have liked," Graham Stock, Latin American sovereign debt strategist at J.P. Morgan, said of the bank's declaration of war to do what it takes to save the drowning real. 

 "They don't have too many tools, and if they are going to maintain their focus on the inflation target this year and next, then they will almost certainly need to raise rates at the next meeting or even call an extraordinary meeting before July 17." 

 The minutes of the June 20 meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) showed the bank jacked up rates to combat persistent inflationary pressures and to head off the potential effect of an unstable currency on consumer prices. 

 Indeed, interest rate futures markets have priced in higher Brazilian rates. On Thursday the 30-day interest rate future closed at 21.21 percent, up from 20.44 percent on Wednesday. 

 The Selic rate stands at 18.25 percent. 

 Yet raising interest rates two weeks after the Central Bank adopted an easing bias - meaning it was more inclined to lower borrowing costs - might damage the bank's credibility, some economists say. 

 "If Argentina has stabilized, then raising interest rates would somewhat tarnish the Central Bank's credibility," said Tulio Vera, emerging market strategist at Merrill Lynch. "But I don't think we're quite at the point where we can say raising interest rates is the most likely scenario ... I don't think the Central Bank will give up so easily." 

 ARGENTINE CONTAGION 

 What's most unfortunate for Brazil is that economic and political turmoil in Argentina has shot investors' confidence in much of Latin America, with trade partner Brazil taking the biggest hit. 

 On Thursday Brazil's benchmark sovereign bond, the C bond, touched 13-month lows as political cohesion in Argentina threatened to come undone, further complicating the government's efforts to end 10 straight quarters of economic contraction. 

 "If Argentina deteriorates and the Brazilian Central Bank views this as a near-term threat, then they certainly would raise interest rates," one New York based fund manager said, adding that Brazil could always request support from the International Monetary Fund or even the U.S. Treasury Department. 

 Yet if Brazil keeps raising rates, it risks choking off growth in the $450 billion economy that the government expects to grow 2.8 percent in 2001. 

 "Brazil should let the real find its natural level," one Miami-based fund manager said. "They could find themselves in a worse predicament if they keep raising interest rates. If the Central Bank overreacts, it gives the market another target to shoot at." 

 Santiago Millan, Latin American economist at HSBC, said Central Bank President Arminio Fraga has not run out of ammunition in the battle to save the currency before Copom meets on July 17-18. 

 While the Central Bank on Thursday announced it was ready to deploy $6 billion by year's end to lift the sagging currency, Brazil can still use $11 billion more from its foreign reserves before broaching the IMF's prescribed $25 billion target. 

 "But the idea here is not to use it up too quickly - if there is a real crisis, you want to be prepared and have all your bullets," Millan said.

title: Emerging Debt-Shortcovering bounce yet sentiment shaky.
text:
NEW YORK, July 6 (Reuters) - Benchmark emerging market bonds on Friday rose for the first time in nine trading sessions in a technical bounce, but confidence was frail in the absence of political consensus toward economic policy approach in Argentina and amid concern that Brazil's efforts to prop up its flagging currency were failing. 

 "There is continued political noise in Argentina and uncertainties about the effectiveness of intervention efforts announced in Brazil," said Lacey Gallagher, director of Latin American research at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 The J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Index, which on Thursday lost 2.6 percent, widened three basis points to 809 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. 

 Technical analysts say Argentine FRBs and Brazil C bonds were "deeply oversold" on Thursday. On Friday, the FRB rose a full point to bid around 76.500 and the C bond inched 0.625 points higher to bid around 72.500 points. 

 "External debt markets are up purely on the back of shortcovering. Higher prices do not indicate a change in sentiment and people are squaring their books before they go home," a head emerging market trader said. 

 Moreover, the Brazilian real fell to record lows early on Friday, trading at 2.560 per dollar. The slump came despite the Central Bank's announcement on Thursday that it would spend $6 billion in the foreign exchange market by the end of the year to support the currency that has so far this year lost 31 percent of its value. 

 IMPASSE BROKEN 

 An impasse between the Argentine federal government and province leaders was broken on Thursday when the government agreed to hand over $600 million to the provinces in exchange for a series of spending cuts. 

 The Buenos Aires province will cut $500 million, the other 11 provinces will cut an additional $150 million, and the federal government itself will slash $150 million off its expenditure sheet. 

 "There's still not consensus across the political spectrum in terms of an economic policy approach so the agreement with the governors beginning with the Province of Buenos Aires - and we expect more - is positive but it's not the only political issue." 

 Michael Gavin, head of Latin American research at UBS Warburg, said the main risk in Argentina relates to whether the current market panic translates into a financial one leading to sharp declines in bank deposits. 

 "Deposits in the banking system have been relatively stable recently and ... there has been no indication of a deposit run amid (Thursday's) panic ... we think yesterday's price action was more a reflection of panic selling than a response to any specific news," Gavin said. 

 UBS holds a neutral position on Argentine bonds - meaning the bank recommends investors should hold the same ratio of Argentine bonds as allocated in the EMBI-plus at 21 percent: "But we advise investors to position for a technically driven relief rally in the days ahead," Gavin said. 

 Even emerging market star Mexico, with one foot in the full investment grade door, succumbed to wave of selling in Latin America. The 2026 bond fell 0.875 points to bid around 124.250 points.

title: Brazil currency  slumps despite Cenbank  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, July 5 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency closed sharply weaker on Thursday despite intervention by the Central Bank to buttress the real from market worries about neighboring Argentina's economy. 

 The real slipped 2.1 percent to 2.47 reais per U.S. dollar from Wednesday's close of 2.42, bringing the currency back near its record low of 2.48 reached two weeks ago. 

 The bank confirmed it had intervened in the foreign exchange market, but as usual, did not give details as to how. However, the move went unnoticed by some traders, who have been testing the bank's resolve and are also worried about renewed political instability in neighboring Argentina. 

 The weakening for the fifth day running came despite renewed promises by the Central Bank on Thursday to prop up the currency through plans to inject $6 billion in the market through year's end. 

 The Central Bank's newest effort to bolster the real comes just two weeks after it unveiled an arsenal of measures to prop up the currency, including plans to build up a $10.8 billion war chest to build its foreign reserves and, if necessary, defend the real.

title: Man sees white sugar prices falling in medium term.
text:
LONDON, July 6 (Reuters) - Physical demand for white sugar is likely to slow in the future due to the high whites premium, but prices may subsequently slip as supply increases, British commodity house ED & F Man said Friday. 

 "We see white sugar values coming off in the medium term as fresh supplies from Brazil and possibly India and the EU come to the market," Man said. 

 In its latest monthly sugar report, Man said sugar supplies from EU producers continued to be priced at a premium to the terminal market. 

 "The upward move in the physical differential value indicates a break-out from the oversupply situation seen earlier in the year," the report stated. 

 The London daily sugar price (LDP) rose from $10 to $15 over the nearby August contract during the past month, reflecting nearby tightness in deliverable EU supplies. 

 But Man said other origins had not been able to follow the EU differential higher. 

 "Physical differentials for low-quality sugars from other origins have declined in reaction to a subdued demand situation," it said. 

 Brazilian 150 ICUMSA sugar fell from $12 under the term to a $25 discount to the August contract at the end of May for July shipment onward 

 Thai premiums fell to $5 over August, having remained at around $16 over for most of the year. 

 Raw sugar supplies from Brazil were seen continuing to be abundant in the near future, partly due to the real devaluation. 

 On Wednesday, the real suffered its worst one-day percentage loss in over two years and Brazil's Central Bank has been forced to intervene to prop up the country's sagging currency. 

 Brazilian shipments from the main Centre-South growing region during May were far in excess of last year's tonnage, Man said, with more than one million tonnes expected to be shipped up to the middle of June. 

 It said current expectations for the southern Brazil crop (May/April) were for an export availability of around 5.5 million tonnes, but may be subject to revision depending on alcohol consumption. 

 "A range of estimates for the current cane crop has so far been released, the crucial number seems to be the alcohol consumption figure," according to the report. 

 Man said it was maintaining its estimate of 12 billion litres of alcohol, but warned it may have to be lowered if the Brazilian economy was affected by the Argentine financial and economic turmoil.

title: Brazil 's real weakens despite CenBank  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, July 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency weakened on Tuesday despite attempts by the Central Bank to buttress its real as renewed worries over neighboring Argentina's political and economic problems rocked the market. 

Foreign exchange traders said the Central Bank sold greenbacks on Tuesday and the bank confirmed an intervention, although it did not specify what kind. But the helping hand was not enough to counteract the impact of new political jitters in Argentina. 

 The real still finished near its lowest point in the day at 2.353 reais per U.S. dollar, its third straight decline and a 0.90 percent depreciation from Monday's closing price. It is about 20 percent lower on the year. 

 Turnover was thin ahead of the U.S. Independence Day holiday on Wednesday, traders said. 

 "The market has an eye on Argentina," said a trader at a Sao Paulo bank. 

 Argentina's on-going failure to kick-start its economy out of a three-year recession has helped chip away at the real's worth all year as investors in Brazil worry its neighbors' woes may further roil its own economy. 

 The currency has recovered from its all-time low of 2.48 last month - a 27 percent slide in the year - after the Central Bank announced it would aggressively intervene in the market to prop up the currency. 

 Although Argentine officials denied rumors that President Fernando de la Rua would resign, the political climate remains tight as opposition Peronist Party governors adopt a belligerent stance against his government. 

 Traders said investors are still unsure of what level the real will steady at.

title: Emerging Debt-Down amid Argentine economy, Brazil real woes.
text:
NEW YORK, June 28 (Reuters) - Emerging market sovereign bond prices drifted slightly lower on Thursday as investors looked for positive news to counter recent signs of weakness in the Argentine economy and nagging worry about Brazil's currency. 

 "The market is a little weaker today because there are no positive developments and we do not see real money stepping in at these levels to support prices," said Owi Ruivivar, fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 Emerging market bond spreads widened by three basis points to 746 over U.S. Treasuries, according to J.P. Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus. Argentina's portion of the index widened seven basis points to 1,003 while Brazil spreads remained flat at 845. 

 Wider spreads reflect the perception of increased risk as measured against safe-haven U.S. Treasury bonds. 

 "The market is trading off of the negative developments that have accumulated over the last week, such as the inefficacy of the Central Bank intervention in Brazil and disappointing retail sales data from Argentina," Ruivivar said. 

 On Wednesday, Brazil's Central Bank intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market, carrying out four emergency operations to prop up the wilting real, which ended nearly one percent stronger. 

 Argentina supermarket sales fell 2 percent in May versus the same month in 2000 and May construction activity fell 1.1 percent year-on-year, Economy Ministry data shows. 

 Argentina's new global bond due 2008 fell a half point to bid 77.8, while the country's FRB paper shed 1/8 point to bid 83-3/4. 

 "Argentine FRB bonds are very vulnerable right now due to a deterioration in Argentine fundamentals, as will be the new 2008s and 2018s," Ruivivar said. 

 Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday cut U.S. interest rates a modest quarter-percentage point, slowing the pace of its aggressive rate-cutting campaign while signaling it remained ready to do more if needed. 

 "There might have been some people who were hoping for 50 basis points who took a bit of profit," emerging debt trader said. "If we would have seen a 50 basis point cut, our market might have taken a little relief from that and rallied." 

 VENEZUELA DIPS WITH OIL PRICES 

 Venezuelan DCB bonds dropped 3/8 to bid 83-3/8 while the country's spread widened four basis points to 842 on Thursday amid jitters in the oil market. The solvency of Venezuela, a major oil exporter, is seen by Wall Street as dependent on petroleum prices remaining high. 

 NYMEX crude oil futures extended losses early Thursday after plummeting Wednesday, amid growing worries that the weakening economy is cutting demand. 

 NYMEX August crude fell 39 cents to an early low of $25.22 a barrel, extending an overnight loss of 24 cents. On Wednesday, the contract plunged $1.37 and hit a 14-month low. 

 "We recommend a defensive position on Venezuela, Argentina and Brazil," Ruivivar said. "We continue to like Mexico." 

 Ratings agency Standard & Poor's has said it is considering raising Mexico to investment grade status thanks to the country's improving fundamentals. 

 Ruivivar said her favorite Mexican bond is the global due 2019. "This is Mexico's cheapest dollar-priced bond and should attract good crossover investor activity," she said.

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  By Selling Dlrs - Traders
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian central bank came to the real's rescue for the second time Wednesday, this time selling dollars directly to banks in an attempt to prop up the sagging currency. 

 The real reacted immediately, moving to BRR2.316 to the dollar from an intraday low of BRR2.338. A trader who bought dollars from the central bank told Dow Jones Newswires that the price was BRR2.315, the same as Monday, the last time the monetary authority had intervened. 

 At around 1820 GMT, the real was changing hands at BRR2.311, the strongest level of the day. Tuesday's close was BRR2.326 to the dollar. 

 The previous attempt to halt the real's decline earlier in the day by selling BRR1 billion worth of short-term dollar-indexed bonds failed, leading the monetary authority to a second intervention. 

 Investors bought the entire lot of dollar-indexed bills, but the real didn't bounce back. 

 This is the third direct intervention by selling dollars since the central bank unveiled a package of measures Thursday to boost the currency. 

 At around 1840 GMT, the real was at BRR2.32 to the dollar. 

 Brazil's real came under pressure Tuesday following a three-session rally after the central bank didn't intervene on the market despite a slight depreciation of the currency. 

 Investors got nervous and started to test the central bank's new policy of active interventions. 

 Even though the central bank's initiative helped the real bounce back from a historic low of BRR2.48 to the dollar June 19, analysts are skeptical that the move will help the currency get any stronger. 

 There is still concern that Brazil may have trouble financing its balance of payments this year and next as political jitters and an energy crisis threaten to knock down foreign direct investments in the country by half.

title: Brazil  real firms after multi CenBank  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, June 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's beleaguered real currency firmed on Wednesday after the Central Bank intervened four times in the foreign exchange market to shore up the real against the dollar, traders said. 

 The real clawed its way back to end at 2.305 reais per dollar, a strengthening of 0.95 percent from Tuesday's close of 2.327 reais. 

 The Central Bank confirmed that it carried out two emergency sales of dollar-linked notes worth a total of 4 billion reais ($1.7 billion). Traders also said the bank entered the market twice to sell dollars. 

 The emergency action forms part of a more aggressive Central Bank approach, announced last week, to protect the much suffering real from speculative attacks. 

 The real is off 18 percent against the dollar so far this year but it has strengthened since last week, when it was 27 percent weaker than at the start of January, prompting the Central Bank to raise rates and announce that it was building a $10.8 billion war chest of reserves to shore up the currency.

title: Brazil  Real Ends Stronger As Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  4 Times
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real finished 0.9% stronger Wednesday thanks to central bank intervention on four occasions. 

 The central bank salvaged the ailing real by twice selling dollars on the market and twice offering dollar-indexed debt. 

 The first double whammy combination of dollar and debt selling failed to help the real after it hit an intraday low of BRR2.338 to the dollar, forcing the central bank to wade in again as part of its new hands-on approach to keeping the real's decline in check. 

 Second time round, the central bank helped revive the real by selling debt and dollars again, and it closed at BRR2.305 - its strongest point of the session. This compares with Tuesday's finish of BRR2.326. 

 The monetary authority sold undisclosed sums of dollars into the market, while managing to sell all of its dollar-indexed debt on offer. First time round, the central bank sold a total BRR1 billion. On the second occasion, officials held an emergency auction and sold all BRR3 billion in dollar-indexed bills due August 2002. The maturity is one year shorter than the BRR1 billion worth of dollar-linked bonds that were sold earlier in the day. 

 It was the third session in which the monetary authority sold dollars on the spot market since Thursday's announcement of a package of measures to boost the currency, which has lost 15% of its value since the start of the year. 

 "It's too early to say whether the central bank has won or lost this battle," said Fabio Fukuda, analyst with Tendencias Consultoria Integrada in Sao Paulo. 

 "Right now the market is looking for equilibrium and trying to position in relation to the central bank's new hands-on policy." 

 "If the central bank sticks to its firm stance, as it did today, I see room for the real to get stronger than the BRR2.30 level. Of course, this will also depend on capital inflows and the external scenario," he added. 

 Traders noted that this week marks the end of the first half of the year, and Friday is the expiration day of dollar futures - two events that add volatility to trading and may mask the true impact of the central bank's new policy of active interventions. 

 The central bank is trying to fight investors' need for dollars as there is much concern about Brazil's fundamentals. 

 Even though the central bank increased interest rates by 150 basis points to 18.25% last week and unveiled a set of measures to boost international reserves and secure the payment of foreign liabilities, market participants said Brazil's widening current account deficit remains a source of concern. 

 Monday, the central bank said it forecast a widening in the current account deficit to $26.5 billion, or 4.97% of gross domestic product, compared with a previous prediction of $26.3 billion. 

 Also, the market continues to be worried about Brasilia's political outlook, a local power crunch and troubled Argentina.

title: Brazil  currency  slips as jitters sweep markets.
text:
SAO PAULO, June 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency slipped against the dollar in early trading on Tuesday as jittery markets on Wall Street and in Europe prompted investors to withdraw some capital from Brazilian assets, traders said. 

 The embattled real, which has been whipped to record lows in past weeks, weakened to 2.314 reais per dollar after strengthening on Monday for a fourth straight day to close at 2.30 reais. 

 "The market opened without definition. The predominant trend is the rough times we are seeing in foreign markets," said one foreign exchange trader. 

 Stock indices in Europe and the United States dropped amid jitters over corporate earnings in an environment of slower growth. That unnerved emerging market investors who often seek out safer havens for their assets at times of global volatility. 

 Brazil's benchmark Bovespa stock index was off 0.6 percent by mid-morning. 

 Traders said the renewed slide in Brazil's currency could prompt the Central Bank to intervene again in the foreign exchange market by selling dollars to banks. The Central Bank has intervened twice since Thursday of last week. 

Central Bank action last week helped pull the currency back from an all-time low when it was trading 27 percent weaker than at the start of the year. 

 The bank hiked interest rates by 150 basis points and said it was building a war chest of $10.8 billion to bolster its foreign reserves and buttress the currency when need be. 

 Brazil's currency has been rocked this year by nervousness over a financial crisis in neighboring Argentina and more recently, by Brazil's chronic energy shortage that is forecast to cut growth and nudge up inflation levels.

title: Emerging Markets Debt Up As Brazil's Real Strengthens
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Emerging markets debt prices were rising slightly in thin trading late Monday as Brazil's strengthened currency cheered participants. 

 Most investors were avoiding placing major bets before the U.S. Federal Reserve meets on Wednesday, according to traders. Still, in a sign that market sentiment is improving, spreads on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus, or EMBI+, were tightening around 9 basis points to 738 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasurys. 

 The Brazilian real opened 1.2% stronger against the dollar Monday, extending its rally into a third straight session and reversing declines that sent the currency to record lows earlier this month. The central bank hiked interest rates last Wednesday and has vowed to intervene as much as necessary to shore up the real, which in turn has shored up investor confidence. 

 Brazil's Capitalization bond was climbing around 1/2 a point to 76 1/8 bid, amid reports that the central bank had intervened again. 

 While Brazil was enjoying its positive thunder for the day, Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo on Monday had his own words about his country's currency, calling the present and future value of the peso "the best in the world" at a conferencein Buenos Aires. He predicted his country's currency will strengthen against the dollar and that lending rates in the local currency will fall below those on dollar- and euro-denominated credits. 

 While investors might not be as optimistic, they also seemed less worried than last week, when they dumped Argentine debt in the wake of a surprise devaluation of the peso for foreign trade transactions. Economists are estimating Argentina can place debt at its biweekly local Treasury bill auction Tuesday to yield around 9.0% - well below the 12% the government was forced to pay earlier in the year when fears grew it wouldn't be able to make its debt payments. 

 Near closing time Argentina's Floating Rate Bond was rising around 9/16 of a point to 85 1/8 bid. 

 Bigger bets will likely have to wait until after the Fed rules on interest rates Wednesday, though. Investors expect the Fed to cut rates 25 or 50 basis points - the more substantial the cut, the greater the anticipated lift for emerging markets. 

 Mexican debt prices improved slightly less than Brazilian and Argentine paper, tightening around 6 basis points on the day on the EMBI+. 

 Morgan Stanley raised its debt recommendation on Mexico to "outperform," citing the likelihood of an investment grade rating from Standard & Poor's before the year is out. 

 But investors might be in for a bit of a wait. 

 "People are saying the upgrade won't happen until late summer or early fall," a trader said. 


Moody's bestowed an investment grade rating on Mexico in March 2000.

text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazilian Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga said Monday the monetary authority hasn't ruled the possibility of intervening in the foreign exchange market by means of derivatives in the future, the local Estado news agency said. 

 Currently Brazil's central bank can't use derivatives such as futures contracts for interventions because of a restriction imposed by the International Monetary Fund as part of a $41.5 billion aid package. This IMF agreement expires at the end of this year. 

 "I don't discard the possibility of, in the long term, having adjustments (to the current rules), but we don't have any plans in the sense at the moment," he told reporters. 

 The bank has been relying on the sale of foreign currency or dollar-indexed bonds on the spot market whenever it feels it has to prop up the value of the real against the greenback. 

 Faced with the dramatic weakening of the currency in recent weeks, the central bank unveiled a package of measures Thursday aimed at containing the real's depreciation. Fraga said the central bank would boost reserves and intervene on the market whenever deemed necessary. 

 The measures follow a 150-basis-point hike in the country's basic interest rate to 18.25% late Wednesday.

title: Santander Suggests Move Out Of Venezuela Debt Into Brazil
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Santander Central Hispano Investment on Friday recommended that investors switch out of Venezuelan debt and into Brazil paper following the Brazilian central bank's recent announcement of measures to shore up the real and boost international reserves. 

 "Venezuela already looked toppish at current levels with little positive news to sustain asset prices' upward trend, aside from the potential for a push from the broader market," Santander said in a report, noting that Venezuela was the only Latin America credit to lose ground Thursday. 

 "Quite the contrary, Brazil could steal some of this momentum from Venezuela with new (Brazilian) Central Bank measures - for the time being at least," Santander added. 

 Brazil's monetary authority late Wednesday hiked interest rates 150 basis points to 18.25% to keep the real, which had lost more than 20% of its value year to date, from tumbling further. The central bank did, however, established an easing policy bias. 

 The currency weakness had sparked concerns about the outlook for inflation and fiscal stability. 

 On Thursday, the central bank announced measures to boost the country's international reserves by $6.2 billion by year's end, through the issue of an additional $1.4 billion in sovereign debt and the sale of certain state assets. Brazil also plans to draw down $2 billion in International Monetary Fund aid. 

 "Brazil's plans to increase international reserves should give Brazilian assets renewed vigor - at least as long as they appear affective in boosting the value of the real," Santander said. 

 Early Friday, the real strengthened to BRR2.337 per dollar compared to Thursday's closing mark of BRR2.381. The real had tested the BRR2.50 per dollar earlier in the week. 

 Until this week, the central bank had relied on a gradual cycle of monetary tightening and occasional interventions to address a deteriorating economic scenario. Brazil's prospects have sourced this year amid economic turmoil in neighboring Argentina, local political jitters and an energy crisis. 

 Santander said that the surprisingly large increase in Brazil's benchmark interest rate, coupled with the easing bias, "sends a front-loaded, credible signal of Central Bank intentions to stop the slide of the real and meet inflation targets." 

 "Minimizing uncertainty about the extent and duration of future monetary tightening should be especially positive at the short end (of the debt curve) where assets ...have experienced unusually high volatility relative to longer assets," the report said.

title: UPDATE 2-Brazil mounts offensive to prop up mauled  currency .
text:
(updates with closing prices, Cenbank intervention confirmed, inflation goals) 

 BRASILIA, Brazil, June 21 (Reuters) - Brazil unleashed an arsenal of measures on Thursday to shore up the country's foreign exchange reserves and the embattled local currency after neighboring Argentina's financial crisis this week pushed the real to all-time lows. 

 The morning after Brazil shocked markets with a bold 1.5 percentage point increase in the key Selic interest rate to 18.25 percent, Central Bank President Arminio Fraga surprised them again with news that Brazil would draw down $2 billion from an International Monetary Fund credit line next week. 

 The IMF money - to be drawn from a $41 billion package assembled for Brazil during the country's last currency crisis in late 1998 - will be part of a war chest of $10.8 billion announced by Fraga to bolster reserves and intervene in the exchange market. 

 The Central Bank also confirmed it intervened on the currency market on Thursday - the second time this week - by selling dollars for reais. The bank would not reveal how much it spent, but Fraga earlier told reporters that $445 million was employed in Monday's intervention. 

 The real soared on Fraga's strategy, recovering 3.5 percent to close at 2.381 reais per dollar from 2.47 on Wednesday, but is still 22 percent weaker so far this year. 

 "You can see the positive impact of the comments in the forex market today," said Mario Mesquita, chief economist at ABN Amro in Brazil. "The tendency over the next few weeks will be for the dollar to fall even more." 

 The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa stock index also gained ground on the measures, closing 1.7 percent higher. 

 Fraga stressed that the pressure on the real was temporary and the country was making no changes to its exchange regime, a free-floating system adopted in 1999 which paved the way for a sharp devaluation of the currency followed by a period of relative stability. 

 "Our destiny is not to live crisis after crisis after crisis," Fraga told reporters. " 

 HOW GREEN WAS BRAZIL'S VALLEY 

 Two years after the currency crisis, Latin America's largest country kicked off the year with a sound economy set to grow 4 percent for the second consecutive year while inflation was forecast at a low 4 percent. 

 The only dark cloud was in neighboring Argentina, the key Brazilian trading partner, that was struggling after nearly three years of recession and investor fears of a debt default. 

 But the lack of progress in reviving the Argentine economy has spilled over to Brazil and investors sold reais in favor of safe-haven U.S. dollars. 

 A string of corruption scandals in the highest levels of Congress and the surprise announcement of energy rationing a month ago further undermined investment and growth prospects for the year. 

 The real had lost more than 25 percent of its value against the dollar and hit an all-time low of 2.48 Tuesday after Argentina tinkered with its decade-old currency peg to spur exports, a move many saw as a hint of a devaluation in the works. 

 "There's no sense in crying over spilled milk," Fraga said. "The important thing is to react and that's what we're doing. 

 Of the total planned war chest of $10.8 billion, Fraga said $6.2 billion would be channeled into reserves while the remaining $4.6 billion could used to intervene in the exchange market. 

 In addition to the $2 billion to be drawn from the IMF, Brazil has decided to defer a $1.8 billion loan payment to the IMF it had planned to pay ahead of schedule this year. 

 Fraga said the changes do not mean Brazil will extend its three-year loan accord with the IMF, which expires at the end of the year. 

 He said Brazil would also secure $1.8 billion from international lending agencies and issue $1 billion more in international bonds than originally planned, bringing the total for the year to $7 billion. 

 The total also included a $400 million bond already issued by the BNDES, the National Development Bank. The remaining $3.8 billion will come from sales of stock in publicly-owned companies. 

 Fraga also said inflation goals of 4 percent for 2001 and 3.5 percent for 2002, plus or minus two percentage points, remained intact. 

 Brazil's inflation risks are relatively mild compared to the days of hyperinflation in the early 1990s, when prices spiraled up by 7,000 percent a year. But interest rates can only come down if Brazil meets its inflation goals, threatened by higher import prices as the currency weakens. 

 With higher rates and electricity rationing for the next six months, Brazil's economy is likely to grow by only 2 to 2.5 percent rather than 4 percent this year, economists say.

title: Brazil To Draw Down $2 Bln In IMF Funds - Fraga
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Faced with a dramatic weakening of the real in recent weeks, Brazil said Thursday it will drawn down $2 billion in aid funds from the International Monetary Fund while also holding on to an existing $1.8 billion loan. 

Central bank governor Arminio Fraga said the decision aims at reinforcing the Brazilian balance of payments, which is current under pressure amid an energy crisis, turmoil in neighboring Argentina and local political jitters. 

 The announcement comes less than 14 hours after the central bank's monetary policy committee decided to raise interest rates by 150 basis points to 18.25%, the biggest increase since March 1999. Economists were expecting a 50-basis-point hike. 

 Fraga said such problems are "transitory," and Brazil is just improving its safety margin to go through this "transition phase." 

 He said the government will unveil in coming days a set of measures to boost the energy supply and foster exports. 

 No new measures regarding interventions in the foreign-exchange market were announced, as many market players were expecting earlier Thursday. 

 Fraga said the central bank will continue to intervene on the market whenever it considers necessary. Brazil's real has lost more than 20% of its value since the start of the year. 

 Brazil received a $41.5 billion aid package from the IMF and other international lenders in late 1998, to help South America's biggest nation weather world financial turmoil. A year ago, Brazil said the crisis was over and decided to pay down nearly all the loans it had drawn down. 

 This IMF agreement expires in November, and government officials have said they don't intend to renew this accord. 

 Fraga also said Brazil will raise a total $7 billion on international capital markets this year, up from an initial forecast of $6 billion, to help finance the balance of payments. 

 Additionally, he said a total $3.8 billion in foreign capital will enter the country's foreign-exchange market. The funds come from the sale of state-owned assets and bond sales by the National Development Bank, or BNDES, and Petroleo Brasileiro SA (PBR). 

 He said these measures will help Brazil close the year with international reserves of some $37 billion, up from $36.3 billion this week. 

 Fraga's comments helped lift the real to as strong as BRR2.390 to the dollar - its best level since June 12. 

 Before Fraga started speaking the real was trading at around the BRR2.424 mark. Earlier Thursday, the real opened at BRR2.454 after closing Wednesday at BRR2.468 following a larger-than-expected 150 basis points hike in interest rates to 18.25%. 

 During the session so far, the real has gained as much as 3.3%. By 1452 GMT, the real was trading a little weaker compared to the intraday high at a midrate of BRR2.413 to the dollar. Over the year to date, the real has depreciated as much as 21%. 

 The comments also helped lift stocks which were largely trading flat at the start of the session. The main Sao Paulo index was up 1.1% at 14,730 points on volume of BRR177 million. 

 Fraga also said the Treasury will no longer buy dollars on the market to honor foreign debt payments. 

 Under a plan unveiled at the beginning of the year, the government would buy up to $1.2 billion in foreign currency on the market instead of using international reserves. The measure was among the first factors putting pressure on the real in early 2001. 

 At the same time, reserves will get a boost from the sale of some state assets. 

 Fraga said the government expects to net $900 million from the sale of a stake in Petrobras. A stake sale in CVRD - expected near the end of the year - will net the government about $1.2 billion, Fraga added. 

 This is part of the planned 2001 sale of about $4.9 billion of stock held by the BNDES in local companies. 

 Stock sales of about $3 billion in mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce SA (RIO) and $1 billion in shares of oil giant Petrobras were planned. 

 Participation in the $1 billion February sale of insurer Cia Nacional de Seguros Gerais, or Sasse, should give the government some $300 million, Fraga said. 

 Last week, the government and BNDES participated in a $750 million secondary stock offering by aircraft maker Empresa Brasileira de Aeronautica SA (ERJ), or Embraer. 

 On the forex intervention front, Fraga said the central bank spent $445 million from international reserves to prop up the sagging real on Monday. 

 Fraga also said the government will also move to lift the controversial PIS and Cofins taxes to make exports more competitive. 

 Unlike a value added tax, the two taxes apply to revenues from corporations at all stages of the production process, leading to double taxation. 

 The central bank governor also said the government is studying changes to the financial movements tax, or CPMF, for capital markets transactions. The CPMF, currently at 0.38%, applies to everything from checking account deposits to stock purchases. 

 The potential tax cuts - along with measures to boost energy supply and exports - are part of an attempt by the government to create a better "investment environment," for private companies, Fraga said. 

 In total, the central bank expects that the additional bond sales unveiled Thursday, plus the IMF loan and other credit lines from multilateral lenders, will reinforce reserves by $6.2 billion by year-end. 

 At the same time, the monetary authority expects to see a total inflow of $4.6 billion into the forex market by the end of 2001. 

 The BNDES is expected to raise $400 million on international capital markets - funds which will go to the forex market. The additional $1 billion in sovereign debt planned this year will go to reserves. 

 From multilateral lenders excluding the IMF, Brazil plans to get $800 million to boost reserves while another $1 billion loan would come through the forex market. 

 Of the $3.8 billion in sales of state assets, the central bank sees $600 million going to reserves. 

 The $2 billion IMF tranche will also reinforce the country's stock of hard currency. 

 Fraga said Wednesday's interest-rate hike, the set of "topical" measures unveiled Thursday, along with the "solid fundamentals of our economy" will help Brazil weather the current turbulence. 

 "Our response is firm and clear, and we believe there's room to reverse this (current) situation," he said. 

 The central bank will unveil a detailed forecast for the country's balance of payments financing needs next week, said Fraga. 

 Fraga later reiterated that the decision to draw down the additional $2 billion IMF tranche and not settle the outstanding $1.8 billion IMF loan ahead of schedule doesn't mean Brazil is seeking to renew the IMF agreement. 

 He said these loans are medium-term credit lines that expire in three to five years. 

 Fraga also said the government would unveil measures to tighten the books of federal banks over the next few days. 

 Such measures will look to improve corporate governance and transparency of banks such as Banco do Brasil SA (E.BDB) - the nation's biggest bank in terms of total assets. 

 The government is currently putting the final touches to a federal bank restructuring program to rescue capital-deficient banks. As a part of this, the program will also recapitalize the banks. 

 Fraga declined to elaborate on the plan. 

 Robert Lacoursiere, banking analyst at Lehman Brothers in New York, welcomed the move, saying it would "infuse more rationality in the manner that government-backed banks compete." 

 Lacoursiere, who recently talked to Banco do Brasil, said: "Management indicated that they have been pushing for compliance with government capital requirements and expect to do so by as early as the end of the second quarter, implying that an announcement by the end of next week for a solution for its capital deficit of approximately BRR2.7 billion may be forthcoming." 

 He said management wouldn't comment on the exact mechanism that would resolve the problem but added that a likely option could involve the issuance of subordinated debt combined with a swap of approximately BRR2.7 billion, or a portion of it, of 20-year, zero-coupon non-tradable government paper. 

 According to O Estado de S. Paulo Thursday, the government is looking at the possibility of issuing more than BRR80 billion worth of debt to rescue the federal banks. The government is studying ways of using special financial mechanisms to avoid putting pressure on the handling of state debt and not hurt surpluses that are expected to contribute to the consolidated public sector primary surplus going forward. 

 By the end of March, Banco do Brasil had BRR143.4 billion in total assets.

text:

 SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank has just intervened in the foreign exchange market by selling dollars to prop up the country's weak real, traders said.

 Argentina is adopting the new currency regime on the exports side to revive the nation's trade balance and help alleviate pressure on an economy mired in recession for some three years.

title: Brazil  real bounces off record low on  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, May 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's embattled real recovered from record lows Friday after the Central Bank intervened to counter the impact of jitters caused by stormy local politics and Argentina's economic woes, traders said. 

 The real firmed to 2.320 per dollar from the previous record low equaling close of 2.346 per dollar, after plumbing record intraday lows before the Central Bank stepped into the market. It stands 19 percent weaker than the start of he year. 

 The Central Bank boosted the real first with a sale of 2.0 billion reais in dollar-indexed notes to provide an alternative hedge to the dollar and then again later selling dollars to let the air out of the compressed market, traders said. 

 After the close, the Bank confirmed it intervened in the market but, as is its policy, gave no indication of how or by how much. 

 "We had the conditions for intervention from early on as the exchange rate was dropping and liquidity was tight even for a Friday," said Banco Schahin chief economist Cristiano Oliveira. 

 The Central bank has repeatedly said in the past it has no target level or range for the real, but will intervene if there is a liquidity crunch. 

 The currency had slumped to record intraday lows on fears former senate head Antonio Carlos Magalhaes would kick up a storm when he plans to resign Wednesday after being fingered for getting access to a secret senate vote list. 

 The fear is Magalhaes, a former presidential ally and kingmaker, has amassed a mountain of compromising material on several high-ranking politicians in his 50 years in politics. The other senator involved in the scandal quit Thursday. 

 Argentina was still on the market's radar as worries about fallout from the neighboring recession-hit economy despite the country releasing details of a confidence-building debt swap which would ease the country's risk of default.

title: Brazil Central Bank  confirms  FX intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, May 25 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank said on Friday it had intervened in the foreign exchange market following talk by traders that the bank had sold U.S. dollars to firm the nation's real currency, which has declined 20 percent since January. 

 As is its usual policy, the bank did not specify how it had intervened in the market in its statement, but traders said the bank sold greenbacks to bolster its own currency. 

 The real finished at 2.32 per dollar, clawing back from an intraday low of 2.375 and closing 1.1 percent stronger than its ending price on Thursday, a historic closing low of 2.346. 

 The real has lost about 20 percent of its worth since the start of the year as investors have pulled out of the currency amid worries about economic woes in neighboring Argentina, and an energy crisis and political scandals in Brazil.

title: Brazil 's Real Breaks 4-Day Losing Streak On  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real broke a four-session losing streak Friday after the central bank intervened on the market to prop up the sagging currency. 

 Traders said the monetary authority sold an undisclosed sum of dollars on the spot market as well as a BRR2 billion lot of dollar-indexed bonds to help boost the real, which has been persistently weak of late amid regional turmoil, local political jitters and a brimming energy crisis. 

 The central bank reiterated it has a no-comment policy on direct interventions. 

 Unlike Thursday's intervention, today's move to sell dollars on the spot market made the real appreciate significantly from the historic low of BRR2.375 to the dollar and the Brazilian currency finished at a midrate of BRR2.317 on a BRR2.315-BRR2.319 spread. That's stronger from Thursday's close of BRR2.348 to the dollar, its weakest point ever. 

 This marked the first time since mid-March that the central bank tried to prop up the currency by selling U.S. greenbacks to investors. 

 "Our preliminary reading is that the central bank is establishing a new intervention pattern, and maybe they'll have to pursue this strategy," said Octavio de Barros, chief economist with BBV Banco in Sao Paulo. 

 He noted, however, that there isn't much room for the real to appreciate in the near term amid the uncertainties that the energy crisis brings to Brazil's economic outlook. 

 Later, the central bank confirmed that it intervened in the market by directly selling dollars to investors but didn't disclose the amount. 

 Even though investors are growing confident that troubled neighbor Argentina's plan to swap short-term debt for long-term bonds will go forward, the Brazilian currency has been reacting to homegrown problems such as the energy crunch and political turbulence. 

 Economists have cut their growth forecast for Brazil to below 3% from 4% to 4.5% after the government unveiled a rationing plan that calls for a 20% reduction in electricity use during at least six months, beginning in June. 

 BBV Banco's Barros said it is still unclear how big will be the overall impact of the energy crisis on the country's balance of payments, noting nonetheless that foreign direct investment will certainly fall. 

 "Right now we have a $19 billion foreign direct investment forecast for 2001, but this is an optimistic scenario and we maybe have to revise it downward in the future," he said. His real estimate is BRR2.30 to the dollar by year end. 

 Brazil received $6.76 billion in foreign investment in production of goods and services locally between January and April, while the country's current account deficit was $8.33 billion in the period. 

 The central bank had a $24 billion forecast for FDI in 2001 but said it is currently revising its estimates. 

 The energy crisis is also widely expected to hit Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's popularity hard, reducing the chances that he will be able to elect a nominated successor in the 2002 presidential elections. 

 Meanwhile, the bank said Brazilian international reserves inched lower to $35.731 billion Thursday from $35.730 billion Wednesday. Daily reserve figures are available at the central bank's Internet site with a one-day lag. 

Central bank's Web site: www.bcb.gov.br("http://www.bcb.gov.br/").

title: Brazil Ctrl Bk Calls Emergency Dollar-Indexed Bond Sale
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank late Thursday intervened to help prop up the weakening local currency by holding an emergency sale of up to 1 billion reals ($1=BRR2.3600) in dollar-indexed debt. 

 The move to offer debt comes as the real depreciated to BRR2.368 to the dollar - its weakest-ever point in its seven-year history. The debt offer began at 1820 GMT and will finish at 1850 GMT. 

 By 1840 GMT, the real improved and was trading at BRR2.360. The previous all-time intraday low was BRR2.348 set on Wednesday. 

 Despite the auction, the currency still looks set to close at another all-time low. Wednesday, the local currency finished at a midrate of BRR2.345 to the dollar, its weakest point since the currency was first introduced in 1994 to stamp out inflation. 

 The central bank last offered dollar-indexed debt on April 20 but failed to sell all the bonds on offer. 

 The central bank then managed to sell just BRR1.06 billion, or 53%, of the BRR2 billion batch of 7-month dollar-pegged bonds on offer. The yield was 13.6%, up from 8.9% on 5-month bonds sold earlier the same week. 

 The real is declining primarily on Argentina's announcement on its much-awaited debt swap. 

 While the Argentine government Thursday said it would offer four new bonds - three dollar-denominated and one peso-denominated - and that the offer expires June 1, with the results being released June 4, the market here remained disappointed with the level of disclosure. 

 Traders blamed the decline on the real largely because the Argentine government didn't provide any estimate on how large the swap will be. While speculation pegs the size at around $20 billion, traders said the market was worried that there wouldn't be enough investor support for such a swap. 

 "The Argentine government's silence on this point has the market worried here, and it looks like we are going to have to wait a bit longer before the market gets the details it wants, possibly another week," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 Traders also pointed to Brazil's current energy crisis, saying that a government plan to introduce rationing at the start of June was doing much damage to the real as the market is uncertain as to how much such a move will hurt the local economy. 

 "The energy crisis has taken the real to new lows over the last week, it hasn't gone away and the worst is about to come," said a Rio de Janeiro-based trader. 

 The government energy rationing plan will finish in December. Brasilia has called on industry, commerce and consumers to cut consumption by 20% to try and conserve depleted water reservoir levels. More than 90% of electricity comes from hydroelectric plants. 

 -By Anthony Dovkants and Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11-3813-1988; brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Opens At BRR2.2965/Dlr Vs BRR2.266 End Tue
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real opened at an all-time intraday low Wednesday, dragged down by mounting concerns about neighboring Argentina and local political jitters. 

 The real opened at midrate of BRR2.2965 on a wide BRR2.294-BRR2.299 spread. At around 1300 GMT, the real had crossed the key psychological barrier of BRR2.30 to the dollar, being quoted at a midrate of BRR2.3015 on a BRR2.300-BRR2.3030 spread. 

 Tuesday the real finished at BRR2.266, a historic closing low. 

 The slide follows fears that Argentine President Fernando de la Rua will face problems in the widely-expected process to replace Argentina's central bank governor and concern over further noise on the local political front. 

 "There are rumors that (Argentine central bank governor Pedro) Pou will take legal action to stay in his position," said a Sao Paulo trader. 

 The trader added that on the Brazilian political front, the odds are growing that Brazilian legislators will start a congressional inquiry committee to look into allegations of high-level government corruption. 

 Expectations that de la Rua would fire Pou helped Brazilian and Argentine equity markets rebound Tuesday. Pou and Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo disagreed over certain measures to revive their nation's struggling economy. 

 At around 1330 GMT, the real was changing hands at a midrate of BRR2.3065 to the dollar, off an earlier intraday low of BRR2.31 to the dollar. 

 A trader with a major foreign bank said the central bank isn't expected to intervene on the market by selling dollar-indexed bonds as it did last week because the chances that its action will be effective are very little. 

 "Banks have dollars coming out of their ears so there's no demand for hedge" against foreign exchange fluctuations, said the trader. 

 "The central bank has to either enter the market directly selling dollars to investors or nothing will work," he said. 

Brazil has a floating exchange rate regime and usually avoids intervening directly on the market unless volatility is high amid thin liquidity, when market movements decouple from the currency's fundamentals.

title: Brazil 's Real -3: No Ctrl Bank  Intervention  Reported
text:
Despite the sharp weakening from Thursday's close of BRR2.154 to the dollar, traders said the central bank didn't make any attempts to intervene on the market. 

 The monetary authority sometimes calls the main banks' trading desks to show that it's worried about the currency. 

 "That would have been an attempt to try to fix the unfixable," said a trader, who criticized the central bank's move to sell longer-dated dollar-indexed bonds this week. 

 Earlier Monday, the central bank sold 55-month dollar-pegged bonds with a total face value of BRR750 million at an average yield of 11.20%. This is higher than the previous sale of the same bond maturity, which was at 10.87%. 

 The central bank is scheduled to sell another BRR1.55 billion batch of dollar-indexed bonds due April 2003 on Tuesday. The Monday and Tuesday sales should be enough to roll over all dollar-indexed coming due later this week. 

 The Argentine concerns built on an already nervous market, with a key decision on rates expected Wednesday and corruption allegations surfacing against the head of the Senate over the weekend. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank said Brazilian international reserves edged higher to $35.696 billion Thursday from $35.686 billion Wednesday. Daily reserve figures are available at the central bank's Internet site, www.bcb.gov.br("http://www.bcb.gov.br/") with a one-day lag. Friday was a national holiday. 

 -By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-3813-1988; adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: Brazil 's Real Ends -3:  Interventions  Unlikely - Traders
text:
The central bank isn't expected to intervene in the market by selling dollar-indexed bonds due to the limited efficacy that such moves had earlier this week. 

 "There's nothing they can do now but wait for things in Argentina to be resolved," said a trader. 

 Between Monday and Tuesday, the monetary authority injected some $1.5 billion in six-month, dollar-linked bonds in the market, to provide investors with hedge against further depreciation of the real. That followed a direct intervention where the central bank sold estimated $300 million in dollars last Thursday. 

 Economists are saying that Wednesday's rate hike may be the start of a cycle of monetary tightening in Brazil after two years of rate cuts, unless Argentina manages to turn things around quickly. 

 Concern is that inflation here could take an upturn following the currency depreciation, so more hikes may be needed. The real, which was already weaker due to concerns about a global slowdown, has lost as much as 6% of its value so far this month on Argentine worries. 

 Brazil uses an inflation-targeting program to guide its monetary policy. The inflation target this year is 4%, with a two-percentage-point leeway on either side. 

 -By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11 3813-1988; adriana.arai@dowjones.com
