title: Brazil Intervenes  In  Forex  To Fight Argentine Contagion
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil is scrambling to keep two years of hard-fought stability from going down the tubes amid growing fears of Argentine contagion. 

 For the second time in three sessions, the central bank on Monday intervened in the market after the currency threatened to finish at its weakest mark since it was introduced in 1994. 

 Investors are dumping reals on expectations that Brazil's neighbor to the south is on the brink of collapse. Many believe Argentine President Fernando de la Rua won't have enough political support to carry out Friday's announced plan to cut spending by $4.45 billion over the next two years, in the latest bid to reduce the fiscal deficit and regain investor confidence. 

 Ultimately, the fear is that Argentina may have to restructure its debt or devalue its currency, which is pegged at one to one to the dollar through a currency board. And that's largely why the Brazilian real has lost as much as 5.9% of its value since the start of March, say analysts. 

 "Investors are looking for protection in light of a possible contagion from a crisis in Argentina," said Fabio Akira, a senior economist at BBV Banco in Sao Paulo. "If there were an economic shock in Argentina, all emerging markets worldwide would suffer." 

 Argentine contagion fears build on a cluster of existing negative factors already hurting the real, including the U.S. economic slowdown, a widening trade deficit and bickering within President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's ruling coalition. 

 The real, which closed 2000 at BRR1.95 to the dollar, had already weakened to BRR2.047 by the end of February. But losses have mounted in the past week as Argentine sentiment turns south again, with the real sinking to a new 24-month low of BRR2.1760 in intraday activity Monday. 

 Analysts say the recent decline of the real has little to do with Brazil's domestic economic outlook, which remains largely healthy amid 4% to 5% growth forecasts. 

 But a persistently weakening currency can contaminate healthy fundamentals. Such a trend may compromise the government's 4% inflation target this year, increase the country's debt burden and force the central bank to raise interest rates for the first time since March 1999. 

 After burning through an undisclosed amount of dollars to prop up the currency last Thursday, the monetary authority opted to flood the market with short-term dollar indexed bonds Monday. 

 While direct intervention Thursday did little to arrest the real's decline, the two emergency bond sales late Monday injected the equivalent of some $500 million into the market, helping the real finish on a stronger note for the first time in six consecutive sessions. It ended Monday at BRR2.1190 to the dollar. 

Central Bank Seeks To Preserve Economy On Two Fronts



On the fiscal front, the currency's depreciation could make Brazilian
accounts look fragile again despite a two-year track record of austerity
efforts.



The immediate impact would be on the country's debt burden, as around
one-fifth of Brazil's BRR554-billion in domestic debt is linked to the
foreign exchange rate. There's also a smaller effect on Brazil's net
foreign debt of BRR102 billion, as the government only factors in the
currency depreciation on payments being made in the current month rather
than on the whole stock of debt.



A first sign of deterioration may be seen next week, when the central
bank releases public accounts for February.



"There's a big risk that the debt ratio (to gross domestic product)
rose in February, which would raise a red flag and questions about
Brazil's fiscal health," said Raul Velloso, an economist and former
government official based in Brasilia.



The other concern is inflation.



After successfully meeting its goal of reducing inflation to 6% in
2000, the Brazilian government is aiming to further quell the rate to 4%
by the end of 2001.



However, such a target could be complicated by a weakening real as
local companies - which are starting to face extra costs for imported
materials and equipment - become increasingly anxious to pass along
higher prices to costumers. While companies weren't able to do this over
the past couple of years, analysts say that this pattern may be changing
as consumer purchasing power grows amid wage hikes and more accessible
credit.



  Real Taking Cues From 1-Month Argentine Peso Forward



Over the last few sessions, Brazil's real has been tracking the
direction of the one-month forward contract on Argentina's peso,
according to currency analysts.



Premiums on peso forwards - which investors use to hedge against any
change in Argentina's currency policy when they buy peso-denominated
bonds - have risen about five-fold in the last week.



"The level of the one-month peso has shot up dramatically in the last
few sessions...and this has an immediate effect on the real," said Greg
Anderson, emerging markets foreign exchange strategist with FleetBoston
Financial.



The most recent round of Argentine worries is different from the last
one, which eased when the International Monetary Fund announced a $40
billion bailout package for Argentina in December.



At that time, Argentina's situation appeared less dire, and it was the
six-month peso forward that was spiking.



Argentine government officials managed to secure some breathing room
late last year, after the IMF also agreed to allow the country to
increase its 2001 fiscal deficit targets.



But officials have acknowledged in recent days that they'll overshoot
the revised first-quarter target by an ample margin.



-By Adriana Arai, Terry Wade and Anthony Dovkants, Dow Jones
Newswires; 55-11 3813-1988 brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  Central Bank  says decline in real  currency  overdone.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 19 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank on Monday said the decline in the beleaguered real currency, in response to concerns about the economy of neighboring Argentina, had been overdone. 

 "Clearly, we are in a situation of overshooting," Central Bank Monetary Policy Director Luis Fernando Figueiredo said. "Liquidity is not working and there is bad price formation." 

 The real slumped to 2.174 per dollar, its second-weakest level ever. The only time it has been weaker was on March 2, 1999, when it dipped to 2.220 per dollar a couple of months after it was devalued. 

 The currency has slid on worries that Argentina will not be able to muster the necessary political support for a $4.45 billion austerity package. 

 Separately, Brazil's finance minister said the Central Bank would not intervene to dictate trading levels for the real and added that the country's firm fundamentals meant the currency would appreciate in time. The Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the real last week, but without any noticeable impact.

title: Brazil 's Real Ends Stronger On Bond Auction  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Following two unscheduled sales of dollar-indexed bonds by the Brazilian central bank, the country's local currency managed to close slightly stronger Monday after threatening, at one point, to finish at an all-time low. 

 By the close, the real ended at a midrate of BRR2.119 per dollar on a spread of BRR2.118-BRR2.120, after weakening as much as BRR2.176 per dollar earlier in the session. The real closed Friday at a 24-month low of BRR2.129 to the dollar. 

 The real has been hurt by concern that Argentina's austerity program, unveiled Friday, won't have enough support in Congress to be carried through, and that it won't revive an economy that has been in recession for three years. 

 "The central bank's plan seems to have worked and has helped pull the real from the edge of a new historic low," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 "But I think it's only delaying the inevitable, because it hasn't removed the market's primary source of concern - Argentina," he added. 

 Traders said the real would probably have finished at an all-time low if the central bank hadn't decided to sell dollar-linked debt. By midsession, the real was threatening to finish at its weakest point since March 2, 1999, when it closed at BRR2.17 to the dollar. 

 Another trader, based in Rio de Janeiro, however, was more optimistic about the real's direction going forward. 

 "I think the real will strengthen further tomorrow because the central bank is offering market operators an opportunity to hedge their positions," he said. 

 The central bank plans to hold a third auction Tuesday, and the trader said he thought this would help the real regain the BRR2.100 level and maintain its position below the key psychological barrier until the end of the week. 

 The central bank tried to sell a total of BRR4 billion worth of six-month dollar-indexed bonds in two separate emergency auctions Monday. In the first, the central bank sold 47% of BRR2 billion worth of debt put on offer, and in the second the sales totaled just 1.5% of the BRR2 billion on offer. 

 The intervention comes as concern mounts in the market that the depreciating real will lead to inflation and this threatens to undermine the country's economic recovery the country following the currency's early 1999 devaluation. 

 Brazil uses an inflation-targeting program to guide its monetary policy. The government has a 4% target for the Broad Consumer Price Index, or IPCA, this year. It successfully met the 2000 IPCA goal of 6%. 

 -By Anthony Dovkants, Dow Jones Newswires;55-11-3813-1988; anthony.dovkants@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk To  Intervene  In Real Only On Volatility
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's Central Bank will only intervene in the currency market to support the real at moments of "high volatility or liquidity problems," a Central Bank official said Saturday on the sidelines of a Deutsche Bank conference. 

 Brazil's real ended Friday at a midrate of BRR2.129 to the dollar, the currency's lowest close in over two years. The currency has been on a weakening trend on concern that neighboring Argentina may not emerge from a three-year recession anytime soon. 

 Daso Maranhao Coimbra, who heads the Brazilian Central Bank's international reserves operations department, or DEPIN, also said the Bank is maintaining its 4% year-end inflation target for 2001 despite fears that inflation is climbing. 

 Meanwhile, the Bank's Director for International Affairs Daniel Gleizer said Saturday that the real's recent slump would have to continue for an extended period of time before the Central Bank implemented a mechanism to keep the real from slipping further. 

 Brazil, South America's largest economy, floated the real in 1999, causing fears other Latin American economies would have to devaluate their currencies as well.

title: Brazil  real at 2-year low after failed  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, March 16 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real reached new two year lows at the open on Friday after Central Bank intervention in the previous session failed to lift a weight of U.S. and Argentine jitters, traders said. 

 The real fell to 2.109 per dollar from Thursday's second lowest ever close of 2.097 per dollar. The only time the real closed lower than that since it was introduced in mid-1994 was when it ended at 2.17 per dollar on March 2, 1999. 

 The real's weakest intraday level is 2.220 per dollar on March 2, 1999, a couple of months after it was devalued amid an emerging market crisis. 

 "Some investors are looking for the (dollar) hedge and another part of the market is speculating," said Novacao head dealer Mario Battistel. "What's clear is that it's best to stay on the defensive." 

 Thursday's fall came despite Central bank buying dollars during the afternoon. The Bank said it had bought three lots of dollars because the real had decoupled from the reality of Brazil's economy and was taking on a life of its own. 

 Traders said the bank acted too little too late and had given confidence to players who wanted to test the Bank's resolve to support the currency. 

 On Thursday the real suffered concerns about the U.S. economic slowdown, worries ahead of a keenly-awaited Argentine economic announcement on Friday, and an explosion on Brazilian state oil giant Petrobras' biggest oil platform. 

 The market is anxiously waiting for Argentina's recently appointed economy minister Ricardo Lopez Murphy to announce new measures to revive the moribund neighbouring economy. 

 Traders will have their eyes peeled for any indications of legislator support or opposition to his keenly awaited plan. 

 Despite the market turbulence Brazil's Central Bank said on Friday that Brazil sold 80 billion yen ($650 million) of six-year Samurai bonds with a coupon rate of 4.75 percent. It last launched Samurais in late November with a 60 billion yen offering.

title: UPDATE 3- Brazil  real ends at 2-year low despite  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, March 15 (Reuters) - Brazil's real closed at its second-lowest-ever level on Thursday after Central Bank intervention failed to halt the currency's slide on the back of U.S. and Argentine economic jitters, traders said. 

 The real fell to 2.097 per dollar from 2.078 per dollar on Wednesday. The currency, which was born in mid-1994, has closed weaker just once before when it ended at 2.17 per dollar on March 2, 1999, a couple of months after its devaluation. 

 After the close, Central Bank Monetary Policy Director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said the Bank had sold three lots of dollars. He justified the intervention saying the real had stopped reflecting the economy, but denied the Bank was dictating to the market. 

 "We have no intention of defining the price, floor or ceiling, because it is a floating exchange rate," he said. "The market took on a life of its own, dislocating itself from the fundamentals of the Brazilian economy." 

 Figueiredo did say that the foreign markets were turbulent, but declined to give the size of the intervention or whether he thought the real was now under control. 

 "We shall have to see over the next few days," he said. 

 "INTERVENTION FAILED" 

 Traders reported the Central Bank bought dollars after the real spiked higher to 2.075 per dollar in the afternoon, but said the support was a case of too little too late. 

 "The Central Bank intervened and it didn't work," one trader said. "The market is testing the Central bank...There is no doubt that it's serious." 

 The bank last confirmed intervention in November when it bought U.S. dollars and sold reais to redress a surge in the real following the country's biggest ever bank privatization. 

 The Central Bank president Arminio Fraga has said he does not believe in intervention but that the bank will act in the case of a liquidity crunch. Traders criticized the bank's relaxed attitude to the real's slide. 

 "Their relaxed policy since January reached a critical point today which gives serious confidence to the players who were betting against the real to bet against it again," the trader said. "It's a classic intervention fight." 

 TRIPLE WHAMMY HITS REAL 

 Traders said the real was hit by concerns about the U.S. economic slowdown, worries ahead of a keenly-awaited Argentine economic announcement on Friday, and an explosion on Brazilian state oil giant Petrobras' biggest oil platform. 

 Fears about the extent of the downturn in the U.S. economy have been instrumental in wiping 7.4 percent off the value of the currency since the start of the year. 

 Worries Argentina's dire straights would take the shine off Brazilian assets came to a head this week as the market was made to wait anxiously for new economy minister Ricardo Lopez Murphy to announce a plan to revive the moribund economy. 

 Officially denied rumors that Lopez Murphy was ready to resign just two weeks into his term and fears that legislators would put up tough opposition to his plan also weighed. 

 Explosions on the Petrobras platform, the world's biggest, weakened the currency by raising fears the trade balance could suffer if Brazil had to buy more oil abroad. 

 "The trade balance is on sketchy ground as it is," said IDEAglobal market analyst Aryam Vasquez from New York. 

 The platform off the Rio de Janeiro coast was rocked by two explosions before daybreak, killing at least one person and threatening to sink the rig. The platform pumped 80,000 barrels of crude per day, five percent of Brazil's total.

text:
The central bank's decision to sell dollars on the market was welcome by traders and analysts, who said the real was weakening amid thin liquidity on speculation, rather than on concrete facts.

title: Brazil  Ctrl Bk  Intervenes  In  Forex  Mkt,Buys Dlrs -Trader
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market in midafternoon trading Thursday to prop up the real after the local currency crossed the key psychological barrier of BRR2.10 per dollar a couple of hours earlier. 

 The monetary authority sold millions of dollars, in a move that almost instantaneously strengthened the currency to BRR2.0800 per dollar from a midrate of BRR2.1025 earlier. 

 The central bank injected an estimated $400 million in the market, according to the local Estado news agency, based on information provided by various traders. 

 However, a Rio de Janeiro-based trader said it was impossible to tell at this point the amount of dollars sold by the central bank. 

 "The central bank can do this (intervention) through a number of dealers and any estimate that I make would be nothing more than a shot in the dark," said the trader. 

 The real, which ended at BRR2.076 Wednesday, had been weakening on broad concerns, including fears over the financial heath of neighboring Argentina and the U.S. economic slowdown. Earlier Thursday, the weakening was amplified by fears that Brazil will have to import more oil after two explosions halted production at the country's biggest oil rig. 

 Around 1840 GMT (1:40 p.m. EST), the real was changing hands at a midrate of BRR2.081 to the dollar, after hitting an intraday high of BRR2.074 shortly after the central bank intervention. 

 Despite the central bank's move, traders don't expect the real to strengthen much further in coming days unless there's a dramatic improvement in the situation in Argentina. 

 "Investors will stay long on dollars (betting that the real will weaken) until things change in Argentina," said a Rio de Janeiro trader. 

 Newly appointed Argentine Economy Minister Ricardo Lopez Murphy is expected to announce measures Friday to revive that country's economy from three years of recession. 

 "Looks like it may be difficult to muster enough support to pass some key reforms there, and we're worried about it," the trader said. 

 The central bank is expected to confirm the intervention after 2000 GMT (3:00 p.m. EST) when markets are closed. The bank usually says whether it sold or bought dollars, but often doesn't disclose the intervention amount. A spokeswoman said bank had no immediate comment on the matter.

title: Emerging Mkt Debt Slumps As Nervous Market Eyes Argentina
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Emerging market debt players likely could use some relaxation on a beach, but probably not one in Argentina. 

 Debt prices got hit Thursday by mounting nervousness about Argentina's economic woes. The weakening of the Brazilian currency and continued volatility in U.S. stocks hardly helped the situation. 

 Reflecting the loss in confidence, the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus, or EMBI+, cheapened around 14 basis points on the day to 754 basis points over U.S. Treasurys. 

 "People think it's better to be nervous and safe today than daring," a trader said. Price changes remained mainly dealer driven, due to the relative absence of investors in the marketplace as they wait for uncertain conditions to clear. 

 Argentina wound up as the most whipped for the day, cheapening around 42 basis points to 844 basis points over U.S. Treasurys. This wiped away many of the gains Argentina had won following the appointment of Ricardo Lopez Murphy as economy minister on March 5. 

 Jittery market players spread rumors Thursday that Lopez Murphy had already thrown in the towel on his challenging new job, even though the man in question had already denied such an accusation in Thursday's edition of La Nacion. 

 "The rumor about the resignation sounded weird to me," an investor said. Most New York-based market participants admitted that they didn't have enough information to make an educated guess about what was going on. 

 Market participants are eagerly awaiting the unveiling - expected to occur late Friday - of the economy minister's plan to cut government spending and improve tax collections in a bid to restore economic stability. 

 Argentina's woes didn't help neighboring Brazil, whose currency hit its lowest point in over two years, leading the country's central bank to intervene. The real's weakness was amplified by fears that Brazil's trade deficit will widen in coming months, after two explosions Thursday halted production indefinitely at a key oil rig off the coast of Rio de Janeiro. 

 Brazilian debt widened 16 basis points on the day. The Capitalization bond dropped to 79 bid from a closing price of around 80 bid on Wednesday, according to Maxemg.com. 

 In other market news Thursday, Mexico announced it would launch a new 2019 Global Bond of at least $1 billion to retire a portion of its outstanding Brady bond debt. The swap offer, which expires Mar. 22, is being managed by Credit Suisse First Boston and Salomon Smith Barney.

title: Brazil 's Real Ends Weaker Despite Ctrl Bank  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The downward slope for Brazil's real steepened Thursday on mounting worries of continuing recession in Argentina, leading the central bank to intervene in the market for the first time in as many times to stop the currency from weakening. 

 Concern that newly-appointed Argentine Economy Ministry Ricardo Lopez Murphy may not be able to pull that country out of a three-year recession drove the real to a new 24-month closing low of BRR2.096 to the dollar, despite the central bank intervention. 

 The weakening was amplified by fears that Brazil's trade deficit will widen in coming months after two explosions earlier today halted production at a key oil rig off the coast of Rio de Janeiro. Brazil may have to spend an additional $50 million monthly on oil imports until the rig resumes production. 

 The monetary authority entered the market selling dollars a couple of hours after the real crossed the key psychological barrier of BRR2.10/dollar for the first time since March 1999. The real strengthened to BRR2.074 almost instantaneously before losing ground again. 

 "The outlook hinges on the situation in Argentina," said a trader. "If things don't improve there, the real won't recover." 

 The real has lost 6.5% of its value since the start of the year amid concerns over the global economic slowdown and Argentina. The continued weakening is now raising concern that inflation may rise and upset the government's 4% target this year. 

 "If the real remains too weak, inflation may rise as companies will seek to pass on to consumers their increased costs," said Simone Passini, an economist with UBS Warburg in Rio de Janeiro.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil real ends at second weakest close ever.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 14 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency fell to its second weakest ever close on Wednesday after sharp losses on U.S. stock markets heightened worries about America's economic slowdown, traders said. 

 The real softened to 2.078 per dollar from Tuesday's close of 2.063 per dollar. The only time the real closed weaker since it was introduced in mid-1994 was when it sank to 2.17 per dollar on March 2, 1999 after the currency was devalued. 

 "The market is totally at the mercy of the United States and Argentina," said ING Barings trader Guilherme Abbud. 

 Argentina also weighed on the currency as players waited nervously for newly appointed economy minister Ricardo Lopez Murphy to announce measures to get the neighboring economy out of its two and a half years of stagnation. 

 The real was under pressure from the word go as a lack of dollar offers and heightened fears that U.S. stock markets were going to fall out of bed knocked the currency deep into two-year low territory. 

 The U.S. markets lived up to expectations. The Dow Jones Industrial average lost three percent and the technology-laden Nasdaq index dropped two percent. 

 The falls completely overshadowed a successful bond swap. 

 Brazil's Central Bank sold $2.15 billion in new 24-year global bonds allowing it to retire the same amount of Brady debt which both cuts the country's borrowing costs and frees up collateral that was tied to the old debt. 

 "The Brady swap didn't influence a thing," one trader said. 

 Players also began to voice worries that the weakness of the currency and Brazilians' hunger for imports could lead to imported inflation which might threaten future interest rate cuts. 

 Official data released during the morning showed Brazil's IPCA inflation index, a key government gauge for setting interest rates, slowed to 0.46 percent in February, compared to 0.57 percent in January. 

 The IPCA consumer price index accelerated a cumulative 1.03 percent in the first two months of the year and 6.27 percent in the past 12 months. 

 But despite the inflation fears, players said they did not expect the Central Bank to intervene in the market to prop up the ailing currency. Abbud said any intervention would be viewed as "exaggerated". 

Brazil's Central Bank president Arminio Fraga has said in the past that he does not believe in intervention but the bank will act in the case of a liquidity crunch. 

 The bank last intervened in the market in November buying U.S. dollars and selling reais to redress a surge in the Brazilian currency after a major bank privatization.

title: Brazil  Calls It Transparency, Mkt Dubs It  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- They said they did it in the name of transparency, but the market dubbed it a case of  good old intervention. 

 Top guns handling Brazil's finances Thursday unveiled a two-year plan to buy a total $2.4 billion in the local currency market, or about $100 million each month. They said the aim is to make central bank and treasury operations more transparent. And analysts say that they have indeed achieved that goal. 

 But the announcement, which also sought to remove speculation about possible future intervention after the central bank recently said it would randomly buy up to $3 billion this year, came the morning after the local currency sagged to its weakest point in 23 months. 

 The real strengthened on the back of the clarification and was standing at BRR1.997 against the dollar within 30 minutes of the start of trading, compared to Wednesday's close of BRR2.005. This came after senior officials paused their press conference to enable journalists to file the news ahead of the market's opening. 

 "Certainly, I think it was an attempt to pacify the market at the moment," said a Sao Paulo-based trader with an overseas investment bank. "But the fundamental problems still persist," he added. 

 Ultimately, it remains to be seen whether this morning's move will do any good for the real in the longer term this year. 

 Two traders said they wouldn't care to bet on just how long the real would bob just below the BRR2.00 level before weakening again as Brazil's foreign exchange and equity markets continue to be hurt by worry about an unstable political scenario in Brasilia, a widening trade deficit - brought on by a robust local economy and a slowing U.S. economy - and an escalating trade dispute with Canada. 


      Will Dollar-Buying Plan Keep Real Strong?



The central bank said the buying plan will amount to about $5 million
a day on the open market.



That would give the real some strength, but probably not enough to
beat the odds of further weakening.



But given an unusual confluence of factors, the real is probably going
to slip more.



While the country's rate of GDP growth is expected to hit 4.5% in 2001
and surpass the rate of inflation for the first time in decades, the
U.S. economy has slowed and oil prices remain high - two factors which
are causing the trade deficit for Latin America's biggest economy to
widen.



"From the point of view of macroeconomic variables, indeed, it looks
like the currency is more likely to weaken than to strengthen through
the end of the year," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist with JP
Morgan in Sao Paulo.



And there is no fast way out of this dilemma. As the local economy
heats up, Brazilians buy more imported luxury goods, creating further
pressure on the trade deficit.



"To narrow the trade deficit, Brazil could boost its exports and
reduce the so-called Brazil risk, which would bring in foreign
investment," said Carvalho.



Some of Brazil's efforts to reduce its risk, however, are being
delayed at the moment.



Legislation to beef up shareholder rights rules and push through
further fiscal reforms appear to be stalled in Congress as President
Fernando Henrique Cardoso scrambles for a solution after a key party in
his governing coalition walked away from him earlier this month.


Central Bank Takes Another Step To Solidify Credibility



Regardless of what happens to the real, no one doubts the central bank
Thursday went some way to further build its reputation, which has
gradually improved since the clumsy early-1999 devaluation of the real.



"I think it (the announcement) really does clarify a misunderstanding
that arose in the market last year about how much demand the treasury
has for dollars," said David Roberts, economist at Banc Of America
Securities in New York.



"This is one piece of a very long story of Brazilian monetary policy
that's being moved towards a more predictable, transparent and
consistent pattern," he added. "But you can't achieve such a goal all at
once. It's all about credibility. This is something that is built and
not just done in one announcement, but this is yet another step in that
right direction."



The person credited with being the key architect behind much of the
change is central bank president Arminio Fraga.



Since his arrival in March 1999, the former George Soros fund manager
has, among other steps, introduced minutes detailing the monthly
interest rate meeting, set up an investor relations department and
introduced a market report about demand for bonds.



Analysts credit Fraga with removing some of the mystery about
Brazilian monetary policy. By 1900 GMT, the real stood at BRR1.991.

title: Brazil  real drops on fear of more  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's real lost ground in early trade on Wednesday as players sold the currency for fear of a repeat of Tuesday's Central Bank intervention to knock it lower against the dollar, traders said. 

 By mid-morning the real had softened to 1.937 to the dollar from Tuesday's close of 1.920. 

 The Central Bank intervened in the market on Tuesday, buying dollars to weaken the real as it surged on the back of the sale of state bank Banespa to No.1 Spanish bank BSCH for 7.0 billion reais ($3.6 billion). 

 "The market is on the back foot and has pushed down the real so it does not get surprised again," one trader said. 

 The Central Bank said it had bought at 1.91 reais per dollar at an informal auction and had another $3.0 billion available for such operations in the future. 

 The real rose to a high of about 1.901 to the dollar in early trade on Tuesday before the Bank intervened. BSCH is scheduled to pay for Banespa on November 27.

title: Brazil  real falls as  Central Bank intervenes .
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency weakened against the dollar on Tuesday after the Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market, reversing the currency's earlier sharp gain, traders said. 

 The real weakened to 1.920 per dollar from 1.918 reais at Monday's close. 

 The Central Bank bought dollars and sold reais in the market ahead of an imminent influx of foreign funds. Spanish bank Banco Santander Central Hispano is set to pay 7.05 billion reais ($3.6 billion) for Brazil's Banespa bank in coming days. 

 "There was a relevant fact here - the sale of Banespa to a foreign bank...which has few days to bring in a very large volume of funds," said Luis Fernando Figueiredo, Central Bank monetary policy director. "This provoked volatility." 

 Figueiredo said the Central Bank bought dollars and sold reais at 1.91 reais per dollar during an informal auction Tuesday. 

 BSCH is scheduled to pay for the bank Nov 27.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil, Argentina to set common economic goals.
text:
(updates with Buenos Aires Declaration details paras 4, 9, 13 and 14) 

 BUENOS AIRES, April 28 (Reuters) - Brazil and Argentina agreed on Friday to set common debt, deficit and inflation targets next March with a view to integrating six regional economies into an EU-like common market, ministers said. 

 "Next March we will have convergence targets," Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan told reporters. "The idea is to keep inflation under control and ensure fiscal austerity." 

 Foreign, finance and defence ministers from South America's two largest nations met Thursday and Friday to forge closer trade, diplomatic and military ties to convert the Mercosur customs union into a European Union-style common market. 

 Among the 30 points of the so-called Buenos Aires Declaration is a resolution to eliminate intra-Mercosur nontariff barriers to trade by June 30, 2000. 

 Brazil and Argentina are members of the world's third largest trade bloc, which also includes Paraguay and Uruguay. Chile and Bolivia are associate members of the bloc that links 210 million people who produce $1 trillion in goods and services. 

 "We're seeking a common market with the free circulation of goods, services and people," said Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia. 

 Chile and Bolivia will be invited to talks aimed at setting common macroeconomic targets which would see the region's economies march at the same pace, said Argentine Economy Minister Jose Luis Machinea. 

 Brazil's more than 30 percent devaluation in January 1999 priced many Argentine exports out of the Brazilian market. The devaluation surprised Brazil's Mercosur partners and led to many trade disputes. 

 "We've also discussed the subject of setting up permanent (trade) tribunals," Argentine Foreign Minister Adalberto Rodriguez Giavarini said. Disputes have mostly been settled by political intervention by Brazil and Argentina's presidents. 

 The declaration proposes "scaling back investment incentives to limit distortions" in the regional market. Argentine provincial governors often complain some Brazilian states offer large tax breaks to attract manufacturers. 

 Common economic goals should help keep those dangers in check and assure the region's economies move in sync. 

 Brazil and Argentina agreed to begin sharing debt, deficit and inflation statistics in September. This would serve as an early warning mechanism for potential future economic shocks. 

 Sharing data is a "fundamental step" to setting common debt, deficit and inflation targets, Brazil's Malan said, adding convergence would be achieved in years, not decades. 

 A bilateral macroeconomic monitoring group consisting of central bank and finance ministry officials will oversee the sharing of data and future adherence to the targets. Officials from the four other nations will be invited to join the body. 

 A task force will also work to detect money laundering. 

 The future deal has been dubbed "little Maastricht" due to its similarities to the EU's 1997 macroeconomic Maastricht Treaty which led to last year's creation of the euro currency. 

 Mercosur monetary union, however, may be a long way off with Argentina keener than Brazil. 

 Argentina has a matching amount of U.S. dollars in central bank reserves for every peso in circulation to ensure its currency is valued at a par with the greenback while Brazil's real currency floats freely on foreign exchange markets. 

 Joint infrastructure, transport and energy projects to improve the flow of goods were discussed, Brazil's Malan said. 

 Argentine Industry Secretary Debora Giorgi said the partners agreed to study reducing Mercosur's common external tariff capital goods imports to improve regional productivity.

title: Brazil 's real ends weaker on Cenbank  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, March 24 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real	  ended trading Friday markedly weaker against the dollar after the Central Bank intervened on the foreign exchange market, buying dollars, traders said.



After opening trading notably stronger at around 1.714 per dollar, the real closed the session at 1.734, 0.7 percent weaker than its closing rate on Thursday.


 The real had been trading most of the week at its strongest against the dollar since May, boosted by capital inflows linked to foreign direct investment. It ended 0.3 percent stronger on the week 

 "The purchase of dollars made this morning by the Central Bank was sufficient to hold the price of the dollar higher the rest of the day," a trader at a local bank said. 

 The Central Bank confirmed after the market's close that it intervened on the local currency market, thought it did not specify whether it bought or sold dollars. 

 Excluding the Central Bank's operation on the market, analysts said there should be a strong net inflow of dollars by the end of the day. They added that traders are expecting a net inflow of $400 million. 

 "The deals were basically from direct foreign investments, especially in the telecommunication sector," a trader at a local bank said. 

 ((Sao Paulo newsroom 55 11 248 5417)).

title: Brazil 's Real Ends -2:  Central Bank Intervenes , Buys Dlrs
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real ended weaker against the dollar Friday after the central bank intervened in the market, buying dollars for the first time since tight controls on currency fluctuations were abandoned by the monetary authority 14 months ago. 

 After threatening to break the BRR1.70 per dollar barrier early in the session, the real ended at a midrate of BRR1.733 to the dollar on a spread of BRR1.732 to 1.734/dlr, compared with Thursday's close of BRR1.719/dlr on a similar spread of BRR1.718-BRR1.720. 

 The real had strengthened continually throughout the week, hitting a high of BRR1.708/dlr on Friday, compared with Monday's opening quote of BRR1.741/dlr. 

 Market participants were expecting the central bank to try to restrain the currency by cutting back on rolling over of dollar-linked papers, but not by entering the foreign exchange market directly. 

 "The intervention was a surprise, but we can't say it will affect the market's mood negatively," said a dealer with a large European bank in Sao Paulo. 

 Late Friday, the central bank confirmed it had intervened on the market but didn't provide any details. Estimates from traders on how much the central bank purchased ranged from as little as $5 million to $100 million. 

 More important than the exact amount, traders said, was the signal that the central bank was sending to the market. 

 According to some, the central bank's move Friday confirms suspicions that the government wants to keep the real floating within an informal band of BRR1.75-BRR1.85/dlr. 

 Within this band, they said, exports would remain competitive and the country would have a better chance of meeting its BRR5-billion trade surplus goal for 2000, thus recovering from a BRR1.19-billion trade deficit posted last year. 

 Volume of business Friday was reported as heavy, with favorable capital inflow that wasn't characterized as speculation. 

 "The inflow was really great today (Friday). There was a large volume of dollars being sold," said a dealer.

title: Brazil's Real Opens BRR1.7710/Dlr Vs BRR1.7735 End Mon
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real opened stronger against the dollar Tuesday, on expectations of further capital flows into Brazil and a better day for U.S. stocks, traders said. Volume is expected to be very low due to a local holiday in Brazil's industrial and financial powerhouse Sao Paulo. 

 The Brazilian real opened at a midrate of BRR1.7710 to the dollar on a spread of BRR1.7700 to BRR1.7720 per dollar, compared with a close of BRR1.7735 to the dollar Monday on a wider spread of BRR1.7720 to BRR1.7750 per dollar. 

 Traders said the auction of government-held shares in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo electrical utilities, Light and Eletropaulo Metropoitan, expected for Wednesday, is expected to bring a further influx of dollars into Brazil, as the buyers are expected to be the utilities' existing foreign shareholders. 

 As reported, the government controlled National Economic Development Bank (BNDES) plans to sell its 32.34% stake in the Rio de Janeiro based Light and its 59.13% stake in Sao Paulo based Eletropaulo. 

 The market is also expecting a better day for U.S. stocks. On Monday, the real closed slightly weaker following losses on U.S. stock exchanges, breaking the strengthening trend of the previous 2 weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed Monday down 243 points, at 11008. 

 Also seen as bullish for the real were comments made to the daily newspaper Estado de Sao Paulo by the central bank's director of monetary policy, Luis Fernando Figueiredo, that the bank doesn't consider BRR1.7500 to be an informal floor for the real. 

 Traders had been speculating that the government doesn't favor a real which is any stronger than BRR1.7500/dlr, as this will hurt Brazil's exports, and the government would intervene to stop the local currency from strengthening beyond this level. 

 On Monday, the central bank's daily average, known as Ptax, which forms the basis for all forward contracts, stood at BRR1.7648 per dollar.

title: Brazil's Real Opens -2: All Eyes On  Central Bank
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real opened stronger against the dollar Monday, on optimism over Brazil's economic recovery, leaving traders wondering how much further the government will allow the currency to strengthen, dealers said. 

 The Brazilian real opened at a midrate of BRR1.7675 to the dollar on a spread of BRR1.7660 to BRR1.7690 per dollar, compared with a close of BRR1.7725 to the dollar Friday on a tighter spread of BRR1.7720 to BRR1.7730 per dollar. 

 "People are wondering how long the central bank will allow this to go on," said a Rio de Janeiro based currency trader, referring to the rally in the real since November, which has brought the local currency to its strongest level in 6 months. 

 Traders are speculating that the government doesn't favor a real which is any stronger than BRR1.7500/dlr, as this will hurt Brazil's exports. 

 Some expect the central bank to directly intervene in the market by buying dollars if the real reaches this level, while others expect the bank to attempt to weaken the local currency by reducing the amount of dollar linked papers which it offers to the market to roll over existing positions, thus creating more liquidity in reals. 

 "On the other hand, it could be that the market itself takes profits when it reaches BRR1.7500, given that everyone expects the central bank to stop it from going beyond this level," said another Rio de Janeiro based currency trader. 

 On Friday, the central bank's daily average, known as Ptax, which forms the basis for all forward contracts, stood at BRR1.7780 per dollar.

title: Brazil 's Ctrl Bk Spent $170 Million In Dec  Forex Intervention
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil spent a net $3.5 billion in foreign exchange interventions in 1999 after the government decided to float the local currency in mid-January, according to central bank data obtained by Dow Jones Newswires Tuesday. 

 In December alone, the central bank carried out four interventions totaling $170 million, according to the data. 

 However, the data show that interventions dropped significantly in the final quarter of 1999, with the bulk of intervention funds concentrated in the first four months of the year. 

 Brazil's central bank kept the real within a narrow trading band for four-and-a-half years before the adoption of a dirty float, which allows the central bank to intervene on occasion.

title: Brazil's real ends firmer at 1.815 per dollar.
text:
SAO PAULO, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency, the real	 , ended stronger Monday as a favourable outlook for Latin America's largest economy overshadowed concerns over rising U.S. interest rates.



The real finished 0.7 percent firmer at 1.815 per dollar, boosted by dollars that flowed into the country on the back of a calmer market setting, traders said.


 "The dollar inflows that began in the morning continued throughout the day," one local trader said. 

 "Economic indicators are looking brighter this year," said another, underlining the capital inflows. Economists were pointing to more foreign direct investment, positive growth and stable inflation among other things this year. 

 The Brazilian currency had weakened last week, in line with a crumbling stock market, as investors watched Wall Street shares drop amid concerns over rising U.S. interest rates. 

Brazil's Central Bank was forced to intervene, selling dollars to calm investors and help the real turn around from a weak point of 1.850 per dollar reached on Tuesday. 

 While recovering from last week's losses, the real, at 1.815, was still 33 percent weaker compared to its pre-devaluation level one year ago.

title: Brazil  real firms at open after Cenbank  intervenes .
text:
SAO PAULO, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency	  firmed slightly at Wednesday's opening with traders leery that the Central Bank could intervene again as it did on Tuesday to sell dollars and support the local unit, traders said.



The real started trading at 1.848 per dollar, 0.11 percent stronger than its previous close of 1.850.


 "After the Central Bank was able to reduce the slide of the (local) currency on Tuesday, everyone is going to be careful today," one trader said. 

 The real had weakened 2.14 percent to 1.860 per dollar on Tuesday before the Central Bank stepped in. 

 The weakness came as speculators played on growing fears of a possible credit tightening in the United States, which could slow an expected influx of investment dollars into emerging markets, traders said. 

 "The slide yesterday was exaggerated and reflected the hysteria of the market in relation to the fears of a rise in rates in the U.S.," one trader said. 

 He downplayed the situation saying a U.S. hike should have been put in effect last month, but had been put off because of nervousness about problems from the millennium computer bug. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve meets on Feb. 1-2 to define its monetary policy with regards to the basic interest rate, which now stands at 5.5 percent.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRR1.8100/Dlr Vs BRR1.8280 Tuesday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real (BRR) closed stronger against the dollar Wednesday, in very thin volume, as capital inflows outweighed outflows, traders said. 

 "Today's (Wednesday) gains are not very significant as volume is so light it doesn't take much to influence the exchange rate," said a Rio de Janeiro-based currency trader. 

 The Brazilian real closed at a midrate of BRR1.8100 to the dollar on a spread of BRR1.8090-1.8110 per dollar, compared with an opening rate of BRR1.8260 on a similar spread. 

 Traders said volume is likely to be even thinner Thursday ahead of the New Year holiday period and that the central bank will be extra vigilant to prevent sharp movements in the exchange rate. 

 "With volume so low it is relatively easy for players to influence the exchange rate to their advantage," said the trader. 

 Traders said the central bank was absent from the market Wednesday, after having intervened Monday after the real dipped to BRR1.8320 against the dollar. This was the fourth intervention by the monetary authority so far in December. 

 Meanwhile, Brazil's foreign reserves stood at $38.174 billion Tuesday, slightly up from Monday's $38.142 billion level.

title: Brazil's Central Bk Comes Full Circle In Real's Defense
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank has come full circle over the past year and is once again intervening regularly to defend the local currency. 

 But unlike last December and early January, when the real was attacked by speculators and dollars fled the country in droves, this time around the central bank doesn't have its back up against the wall. 

 "These are basically technical operations to inject some liquidity when needed. Before the real was devalued, the central bank had no choice but to intervene" to keep the real within its trading band, said Carlos Augusto Levorim, director at Oryx Asset Management in Sao Paulo. 

 "The central bank is selling small amounts now, and only doing so when they know the operation will work," he added, praising the skills of central banker Arminio Fraga, who took the reigns at the monetary authority in March. 

 The central bank has intervened six times in the past five weeks, most recently on Monday. In the process, the real (BRR) has strengthened to BRR1.8615 per dollar, from BRR1.9420 at the start of November. 

 Many market participants expect the currency to strengthen further, to around BRR1.80/dollar by year-end. 

 "The central bank isn't trying to artificially strenghten (the real) with these interventions, but rather trying to minimize excessive volatility from compromising inflation goals and (fiscal) targets," said Carlos Geraldo Langoni, director of the Getulio Vargas Foundation's center for World Economics and a former central bank president. 

 When Brazil decided to float its currency in mid-January, the central bank said it would intervene as necessary to contain brusque movements in the exchange rate. 

 As the months passed, Brazil moved dangerously close to the floor for international reserves stipulated in an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, generating concerns the central bank was helpless to defend the real as it tested the BRR2.00/dollar barrier. 

 The more frequent interventions of late were made possible by a revised agreement with the IMF in late October, which lowered the floor of currency reserves, giving the central bank an extra $2 billion in ammunition to shore up the currency. 

 Observers agree that the spate of recent interventions, in which the central bank typically spends less than $100 million, doesn't imply the monetary authority has a specific exchange rate target, as some have charged. 

 "It appears that the psychological barrier of BRR2.00 was something the central bank wasn't comfortable with," said Dalton Gardimam, senior economist at CLSA in Sao Paulo. "But if (officials) had a formal or informal target in mind, they would be much more aggressive than they've been." 


Market Optimism About 2000 Makes Interventions Viable



What differentiates today's scenario from a year ago is that the
potential weakness of the real appears to be a temporary phenomenon,
with Brazilian debt obligations bunched up at the end of the year. The
country has around $3 billion in debt payments coming due this month.



Analysts said that even if the central bank wasn't intervening
regularly, there's no reason to believe the real would weaken
significantly because market optimism about the prospects for 2000 is
running high.



Brazil's trade accounts are expected to show a significant improvement
next year, which will help reduce a current account deficit that hovers
around 4% of gross domestic product.



According to the revised terms of the IMF deal announced last week,
Brazil should show a trade surplus of $5 billion in 2000, down from an
expected $1.5 billion deficit this year. It's also seen reducing its
current account deficit to $22.5 billion next year, from $26 billion in
1999.



"If the central bank is completely convinced outflows will be much
lower in the first half of 2000, the recent interventions are just
designed to smooth the process," said CLSA's Gardimam.



"If you believed the real would weaken significantly, you'd just be
throwing dollars away," he added. "We believe the improvement in the
scenario is coming, so (the interventions) are justified."



Added another former central bank director who now works at a leading
local investment bank: "The good thing now is that, with relatively few
resources, you can stabilize the market."



Given the expected improvement in the country's current accounts -
which continue being completely financed by huge foreign direct
investment - there's no reason to allow the currency to weaken
significantly and possibly threaten inflation targets, added former
central bank head Langoni.



Brazilian consumer prices are now expected to rise about 8.5% this
year, well below initial post-devaluation forecasts. And the government
projects the rate will fall to around 6% next year and 4% in 2001.



"With the improved trade performance, a better international scenario
and calmer political situation here, there's no reason to have such a
weak real," Langoni said.



He added that he expects the central bank will continue intervening
until Brazil starts showing monthly trade surpluses on a consistent
basis, which he predicted won't happen until the second quarter of 2000.



    Current Account Situation Remains Big Threat



Aside from the periodic interventions, the central bank has also
helped strengthen the real the past few days by auctioning dollars to
investors willing to sell them back in January, as part of a strategy to
increase liquidity in the transition to the year 2000.



Last Friday, the central bank sold $800 million. The bank announced
late Monday it will offer another $500 million this coming Friday.



"These are just necessary moves. No central bank in the world can
afford to do nothing about Y2K," CLSA's Gardimam said.



While there's consensus the central bank's actions on the exchange
market are the right moves in the short term, Brazil may not be out of
the woods entirely.



Some observers point out that the government isn't paying enough
attention to the potential hazards associated with the huge current
account deficit.



"We have an exchange rate that isn't sufficient to bring the current
account gap down to a level that is sustainable over time," said the
former central bank official who asked to remain anonymous.



He said the exchange rate would probably have to remain above
BRR2.00/dollar to effect a serious improvement of the current account.



"What makes me nervous about the forex situation is that the current
account deficit is still 4% of GDP, and we have a huge internal debt
stock that is dollar-linked," he added, pegging that debt at about $50
billion.



While the internal debt stock is lower now than it was at the start of
the year, the central bank has continuously sold dollar-linked debt this
year.



The former central bank official acknowledged, however, that the
monetary authority isn't in a position now to allow the currency to
weaken.



"The central bank has to keep the real within a range that doesn't
affect inflation and doesn't compromise the economic policy of the
government," he said. "In many ways, the exchange rate is a barometer of
economic policy."

title: Summers Leaves S America Having Spread Fiscal Gospel
text:
RIO DE JANEIRIO -(Dow Jones)- U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers completed a four-day swing through South America over the weekend, having imparted his doctrine of fiscal discipline and open markets while global trade talks in Seattle fell apart amid violent demonstrations and political infighting. 

 The contrast wasn't lost on the Secretary and his delegation as they caught glimpses of television footage of protesters clashing with police outside the ministerial meetings of the World Trade Organization in Washington state. 

 Confronted by recession across the region in the past year, South American governments have shifted their focus from their own unsteady efforts at trade liberalization to revamping their economic policies, mimicking many of the fiscal steps taken by the U.S. in early nineties. 

 Accordingly, the U.S. Treasury secretary - and his gospel of fiscal propriety - was greeted by an eager and appreciative fan club of presidents, finance ministers and central bankers as he made brief stops in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil before returning to Washington DC Sunday. 

 Despite the considerable cost of fiscal austerity programs - already experienced in Brazil and likely to soon become apparent in Argentina - there were no obvious dissenters as Summers preached his message of budgetary restraint to an already converted audience. 

 The affection and admiration is mutual. The Treasury secretary is known to respect the economic aptitude of his South American counterparts and their readiness to embrace economic policies favored among Washington's international financial elite. 

 Summers met with the economic team behind incoming Argentine President Fernando de la Rua Wednesday and left confident that the close economic rapport between Argentina and the U.S. will be preserved after Jose Luis Machinea takes up the reins at Argentina's finance ministry Dec. 10. 

 He also repeated his opinion that the new government will persevere with a currency board arrangement that oversees the peso's parity with the U.S. dollar. 

 "I think that the convertibility system has served Argentina extremely well. It has provided a framework and a backdrop both for the establishment of price stability and the establishment of a much more market-oriented economy, with a much sounder financial system," Summers said. 

 "Everyone I talked to...was committed to maintaining it. I found that a welcome and appropriate commitment in the context of the success that it has helped to produce in Argentina, and I certainly expect it to be an important part of the Argentine economic landscape going forward," he added. 

 De la Rua's new administration faces the twin challenges posed by a sizable budget deficit and large public debt that will almost certainly result in Machinea signing a new loan arrangement with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Summers discussed this issue with de la Rua and his economic team. 

 "There was no discussion of specific amounts, modalities or timetables with respect to IMF financing. into details such as the size or nature of the loan," Summers insisted. 

 Argentina has access to - but so far hasn't drawn upon - a $2.8 billion standby loan from the IMF. With the threat of financial crisis receding with the budding economic rebound in Argentina, Machinea will be anxious to replace the standby loan with a new facility that can be drawn down without creating unease among international investors. 

 From Argentina, Summers flew to Santa Cruz in Bolivia, to meet President Hugo Banzer and sign an agreement to forgive or reschedule $21.7 million in Bolivian debts to the U.S. 

 He expressed his admiration for Bolivia's emphasis on tackling the country's desperate poverty through targeted social programs while also adhering to sound fiscal practices that have nurtured a healthy growth rate in recent years. 

 The next stop for Summers and his entourage of Treasury officials was Sao Paulo in Brazil, where he delivered a speech to the local chapter of the American Chamber of Commerce. 

 Afterwards, he remarked that the Brazilian government, having wrested the economy from the bring of disaster at the beginning of the year, now faces a lengthy list of tasks to bring prosperity to a nation where millions live in abject poverty. 

 While Summers was mindful to show concern for Brazil's human miseries - using academically-tinted phrases such as "social capital" - he made clear President Fernando Henrique Cardoso must first rebuild confidence in financial markets. 

 "One has to be gratified by the sense of confidence returning much more rapidly than I think most people would have expected nine months ago," Summers said, "while at the same time recognizing that there are very large challenges." 

 "I think tax reform, pension reform, provincial fiscal relations are all issues that go the heart of the challenge...of reconciling the state's defined needs with the capacity to mobilize resources," he said. 

 Stressed Fundamentals Vs Intervention In Brazil

 Summers said that "there are important tactical questions" that must be answered by the Brazilian central bank, headed by bank president Arminio Fraga.

title: Summers Leaves S America Having Spread Fiscal Gospel
text:
RIO DE JANEIRIO -(Dow Jones)- U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers completed a four-day swing through South America over the weekend, having imparted his doctrine of fiscal discipline and open markets while global trade talks in Seattle fell apart amid violent demonstrations and political infighting. 

 The contrast wasn't lost on the Secretary and his delegation as they caught glimpses of television footage of protesters clashing with police outside the ministerial meetings of the World Trade Organization in Washington state. 

 Confronted by recession across the region in the past year, South American governments have shifted their focus from their own unsteady efforts at trade liberalization to revamping their economic policies, mimicking many of the fiscal steps taken by the U.S. in early nineties. 

 Accordingly, the U.S. Treasury secretary - and his gospel of fiscal propriety - was greeted by an eager and appreciative fan club of presidents, finance ministers and central bankers as he made brief stops in Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil before returning to Washington DC Sunday. 

 Despite the considerable cost of fiscal austerity programs - already experienced in Brazil and likely to soon become apparent in Argentina - there were no obvious dissenters as Summers preached his message of budgetary restraint to an already converted audience. 

 The affection and admiration is mutual. The Treasury secretary is known to respect the economic aptitude of his South American counterparts and their readiness to embrace economic policies favored among Washington's international financial elite. 

 Summers met with the economic team behind incoming Argentine President Fernando de la Rua Wednesday and left confident that the close economic rapport between Argentina and the U.S. will be preserved after Jose Luis Machinea takes up the reins at Argentina's finance ministry Dec. 10. 

 He also repeated his opinion that the new government will persevere with a currency board arrangement that oversees the peso's parity with the U.S. dollar. 

 "I think that the convertibility system has served Argentina extremely well. It has provided a framework and a backdrop both for the establishment of price stability and the establishment of a much more market-oriented economy, with a much sounder financial system," Summers said. 

 "Everyone I talked to...was committed to maintaining it. I found that a welcome and appropriate commitment in the context of the success that it has helped to produce in Argentina, and I certainly expect it to be an important part of the Argentine economic landscape going forward," he added. 

 De la Rua's new administration faces the twin challenges posed by a sizable budget deficit and large public debt that will almost certainly result in Machinea signing a new loan arrangement with the International Monetary Fund. 

 Summers discussed this issue with de la Rua and his economic team. 

 "There was no discussion of specific amounts, modalities or timetables with respect to IMF financing. into details such as the size or nature of the loan," Summers insisted. 

 Argentina has access to - but so far hasn't drawn upon - a $2.8 billion standby loan from the IMF. With the threat of financial crisis receding with the budding economic rebound in Argentina, Machinea will be anxious to replace the standby loan with a new facility that can be drawn down without creating unease among international investors. 

 From Argentina, Summers flew to Santa Cruz in Bolivia, to meet President Hugo Banzer and sign an agreement to forgive or reschedule $21.7 million in Bolivian debts to the U.S. 

 He expressed his admiration for Bolivia's emphasis on tackling the country's desperate poverty through targeted social programs while also adhering to sound fiscal practices that have nurtured a healthy growth rate in recent years. 

 The next stop for Summers and his entourage of Treasury officials was Sao Paulo in Brazil, where he delivered a speech to the local chapter of the American Chamber of Commerce. 

 Afterwards, he remarked that the Brazilian government, having wrested the economy from the bring of disaster at the beginning of the year, now faces a lengthy list of tasks to bring prosperity to a nation where millions live in abject poverty. 

 While Summers was mindful to show concern for Brazil's human miseries - using academically-tinted phrases such as "social capital" - he made clear President Fernando Henrique Cardoso must first rebuild confidence in financial markets. 

 "One has to be gratified by the sense of confidence returning much more rapidly than I think most people would have expected nine months ago," Summers said, "while at the same time recognizing that there are very large challenges." 

 "I think tax reform, pension reform, provincial fiscal relations are all issues that go the heart of the challenge...of reconciling the state's defined needs with the capacity to mobilize resources," he said.

title: Brazil To Amortize $5.14 Billion Of IMF-Led Aid Package In Dec
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil will amortize in December nearly one-third of emergency credit lines contracted with the International Monetary Fund, the Bank of International Settlements, and the Bank of Japan, central bank international affairs director Daniel Gleizer said Thursday. 

 Totaling $16.28 billion, the credit lines are part of an IMF-led $41.5 billion rescue package assembled one year ago. 

 Gleizer said Brazil on Dec. 14 will pay $1.97 billion back to the IMF; and on Dec. 20 another $3.06 billion to the BIS, and $288 million to the BOJ. Payments total $5.32 billion. 

 Of the $3.35 billion to be paid to the BIS and BOJ, $179 million correspond to interest payments. The amount paid to the IMF is amortization exclusively. 

 As reported, Gleizer also announced that Brazil decided to draw down $1.114 billion of $4.7 billion available through the rescue package. 

 As Brazil won't be able to use any IMF funds for foreign exchange market interventions, Gleizer explained that the withdrawal may be useful for future negotiations with the Fund. 

 "We have plenty of funds for intervention. But just in case they're not enough, we'll be in a more comfortable position to negotiate the use of these ($1.114 billion) funds" to defend the currency, Gleizer said at a news conference. 

 According to Gleizer, Brazil has "some $4 billion" to intervene in the market in December. 

 With the December repayments and withdrawal, Brazil will have drawn down $20.24 billion of the total $32.37 billion standby loan offered by the IMF, BIS, and BOJ. Of the $20.24 billion credit, Brazil has yet to pay back $12.25 billion. 


The World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank also
contributed $4.5 billion each to the $41.5 billion aid package. Brazil
has so far borrowed $1 billion from the World Bank and the total $4.5
billion from the IDB.

The local currency also firmed on capital inflows, they added. "Some $140 million flowed into the market in the afternoon, but nobody knows what it was for," traders said.

text:

 At a press conference, Central Bank President Pablo Better also outlined a series of other measures aimed at boosting the currency - including calling on domestic banks to renegotiate commercial credit lines with foreign banks. 

 Around 1930 GMT, the sucre was trading at a midrate of ECS19,000 to the dollar, on a spread of ECS18,800 to ECS19,200, after ending Monday at a midrate of ECS19,450 on a spread of ECS19,200 to ECS19,700.

 Rumors of central bank intervention helped Brazil's real (BRR) to a stronger finish, traders said.

 In Mexico City on 48-hour spot dollar markets, banking leader Banamex quoted the peso closing at a midrate of 9.3400 per dollar, weaker than its open of MXN9.3320 and weaker than its close Monday of MXN9.3250.

 "The central bank came in when the real weakened to BRR1.9340 per dollar," said a Rio de Janeiro based trader. 

 The real quickly strengthened to BRR1.9315 on the intervention. 

 On Wednesday the central bank intervened for the second time this month when the real slid to BRR1.9390, quickly pushing the local currency back to BRR1.9290.

of 7.27%. The Brazilian government has a target for inflation, as
measured by the IPCA, of less than 8% in 1999.

title: Brazil  Fin Min: Intervention  Best Way To Limit Inflation
text:

 "This (recent) inflation wasn't triggered by excess demand," he told Estado in an exclusive interview. "That's why hiking rates would be worthless," he was quoted as saying.

title: Brazil  central bank  seen cutting rates Wednesday.
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank could reap the benefits of a series of steps to bolster its real currency and cut interest rates Wednesday when its policy-setting Copom committee meets, economists said. 

 A Reuters poll of 20 economists this week found 14 respondents predicting a rate cut of at least 0.25 percentage point in the benchmark Selic reference rate, currently at 19 percent. 

 "I think there is a combination of factors favouring a rate reduction, like declining inflationary pressures and improvements in the real currency," said Carlos Kawall, an economist at Citibank. 

 He predicted half a percentage point cut. 

 At its last meeting October 6, the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) made no rate change, but adopted a bias to lower rates in the future. 

 At the time, Brazil's financial markets and the real were slumping as the government struggled to restore confidence after a court ruling slashed some 2.4 billion reais in expected revenues for 2000 from higher pension contributions. 

 But since then, the government has moved aggressively to change the law governing pensions and the Central Bank has worked hard to steady the real. 

 In the last two weeks, the Central Bank announced two important policy changes - an increase in the amount of currency reserves it can use to intervene in the forex market and steps to overhaul Brazil's huge domestic debt market. 

 The Central Bank's measures have been cheered by the markets and the real has strengthened. 

 The Central Bank officially only targets inflation in setting rates. But a weakening currency is seen as a harbinger of imported inflation, so the real's recovery has opened the door to lower rates. 

 Price rises have remained modest since Brazil devalued its currency in January. The Central Bank has an inflation target of 8 percent for this year, measured by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics' IPCA inflation index. From January to September, cumulative price rises came to only 6.01 percent. 

 Everything is working in the direction of a rate cut, said Dany Rappaport, chief economist at Banco Santander in Sao Paulo, who predicts a 25-basis-point cut in the Selic rate. "The fundamentals are ready, the foreign and fiscal accounts are improving." 

 The government's response to the court ruling has been to send a constitutional amendment to Congress. The bill is currently at the committee stage. 

 Specifically, the amendment aims to overturn the part of the constitution stipulating that retired civil servants cannot be required to make pension contributions even if their pensions are as high as their previous wages. The Supreme Court ruled that forcing retired pensioners to pay in was unconstitutional. 

 The results of the Reuters poll found seven economists predicting a 25-basis-point cut, and five forecasting a 50-basis-point cut. One economist expected a 100-basis-point cut, and another a 30-basis-point cut. The remaining six saw no change in rates Wednesday. 

 ((Brasilia Newsroom, +55-61-314-1193)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Brazil Sees Free Convertibility As Next  Forex  Policy Step
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's future foreign exchange policy plans include the free convertibility of reals into U.S. dollars and vice versa, central banker Arminio Fraga said Wednesday during a TV interview with GloboNews. 

 Fraga said the move would be "a next step to fine tune the concept" of a free floating currency policy, which Brazil adopted in January following a currency crisis. 

 He didn't provide any timeframe for the start of the free convertibility, which he defined as being "the right (for capital) to freely enter and leave Brazil." 

 "In practice, we're working on a project which seeks to provide the citizen who respects the law and pays taxes with more freedom, and make life more difficult for those living out of the law," he said. 

 "We're seeking to give more freedom to send capital abroad," he added. 

 Fraga said the only capital control Brazil's foreign exchange regime will "likely" have in the future is the "possibility of temporarily controlling the inflow of foreign capital," specially short-term investments. 

 He rejected restrictions to capital outflow. 

 "Trying to control outflows isn't viable and is dangerous," Fraga said. "Because then there's no inflow." 

 Fraga also pictured a rosy scenario for Brazil and its currency, the real, from the start of 2000. 

 He said the increased funds for intervention which Brazil has just negotiated with the International Monetary Fund as part of a $41.5 billion rescue package "are more than enough to resolve" the currency's problems. 

 Next year "the millennium bug concerns are over and we'll have an important decline in amortizations," he said, adding that "improved trade balance figures are also very likely." 

 The Brazilian real (BRR) gradually weakened for almost five months in a row until the end of last week, when the central bank announced it would have more than $4 billion to defend the currency in November under the new terms of an agreement closed with the IMF. 

 Wednesday, the currency closed at BRR1.941/per dollar, compared with BRR1.21 before the devaluation and BRR1.73 in early June. 


Fraga also said "it won't be a surprise" if Brazil grows more than the
4% forecast for 2000, "with inflation being equal or inferior to the
target" of 6% for consumer prices.

title: Brazil 's  Central Bank  Has Additional $2 Billion For  Forex Intervention
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- A revised agreement between Brazil and the International Monetary Fund gives the central bank an extra $2 billion in ammunition to intervene in the foreign exchange market defending the real, central bank President Arminio Fraga said Thursday. 

 The extra funds derive from a lower floor for net international reserves that the Brazilian government managed to negotiate with the IMF during a two-week visit of Fund economists that ended earlier this week. This was the fourth time the two sides reworked the terms of a $41.5 billion aid package assembled in November 1998. 

 The new floor for net international reserves - which excludes money received from the IMF - at the end of November is $20.99 billion. With this new floor, the central bank will have $4.18 billion to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 Fraga said the figure is net of Treasury foreign commitments and possible new bond issues, which would raise this limit.

title: Brazil  Real Opens -2: Caution After Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real opened slightly stronger against the dollar Thursday with the market cautious after the central bank intervened to support the local currency late Wednesday, traders said. 

 The Brazilian real opened at a midrate of BRR1.9830 per dollar on a wide spread of BRR1.9810 to BRR1.9850, compared with Wednesday's close of BRR1.9880 per dollar on a spread of BRR1.9870 to BRR1.9890 per dollar. 

 "Nobody really knows what the new rules are," said a Rio de Janeiro trader, referring to a new accord with the International Monetary Fund. 

 "Does the new agreement with the IMF give the bank freedom to intervene for a defined period or at a defined level, and how much is it permitted to run down reserves?", he added. 

 A Finance Ministry official said Wednesday the IMF and Brazil had reached an agreement that would change existing rules for the floor of Brazil's international reserves, allowing the central bank more flexibility to intervene in the foreign exchange market. The agreement has yet to be formalized, and details will be released late next week. 

 The central bank said it intervened in the foreign exchange market Wednesday, selling dollars to several financial institutions, as the local currency weakened to below the 2.00 reals per dollar psychological barrier. 

 As part of a $41.5 billion IMF-led international aid package introduced last November, the Brazilian government agreed not to allow foreign reserves to slip below $22 billion, excluding more than $18 billion in aid received. 

 Brazil's foreign reserves were $39.934 billion Tuesday, compared with $39.921 billion the previous day. 

 "All that we know is that the central bank will intervene to stop the currency from going beyond BRR2.0 (per dollar)," said another Rio trader. "We don't know how solid a base there is behind this policy." 

 The central bank will offer BRR3 billion in fixed rate LTN papers later Thursday and BRR1.5 billion in floating rate LFT's. 

 Wednesday, the central bank's daily average rate - known as the Ptax - was BRR1.9950 per dollar. 

 Beginning Wednesday, the central bank began to publish its official foreign exchange rate every half hour during trading hours, instead of simply publishing the Ptax at the end of the day.
