title: Brazil's real firms on slew of cenbank measures.
text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency	  closed 0.75 percent firmer on Thursday at 1.974 per dollar, helped by a slew of Central Bank measures, including a possible strengthening of the bank's dollar intervention pool, traders said.



"The dollar fell here because of an inflow of dollars caused by a bunch of good news," said one trader.


Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said Thursday Brazil was discussing with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cut the floor for the country's foreign currency reserves by $2 billion, which would give Brazil more flexibility to intervene in the volatile forex market. 

 Fraga said pressure on the real currency in recent weeks have been motivated by a large amount of foreign debt payments coming due and "a wrong perception that we don't have flexibility," in the foreign exchange market. 

 The Central Bank intervened in the market on Wednesday, helping the real spring back from under the psychological two-reais-per-dollar mark. 

 The Central Bank also said Thursday it was scrapping limits on banks' short foreign exchange market positions in a move to free up liquidity in the market and allowing banks to sell more dollars. 

 Further, the market warmed to Brazil's successful sovereign bond issue of 500 million euros. The government had initially placed 300 million euros, but increased the size in just a few hours on the back of good market reception. 

 The real has now firmed two days in a row, but was still 38.7 percent weaker compared to its pre-devaluation level in January.

title: Brazil set to cut floor of foreign reserve levels.
text:
BRASILIA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazil is negotiating with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cut the projected floor for the country's foreign currency reserves by $2 billion, Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said Thursday. 

 The new levels will give Brazil more flexibility to intervene in the volatile foreign exchange market and will create a new floor for projected foreign reserves in December of $20.3 billion. 

 Government officials said earlier this week the government was renegotiating the foreign reserves requirements agreed with the IMF under the terms of a $41.5 billion international loan deal. 

 Under the deal, foreign reserves levels are projected for every month, with an allowed deviance level of $3 billion, and a year-end target for reserves of $26.3 billion. The new agreement announced Thursday will simply lower those levels. 

Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said the projected level for foreign currency reserves at the end of the year will now be $23.532 billion, while the allowed floor will be $20.3 billion. 

 At the end of November, reserve levels are projected to stand at $25.173 billion, and there will be a minimum allowed floor of $20.99 billion. 

 The reserve levels targeted with the IMF exclude disbursements from the loan deal. 

 Fraga said pressure on the real currency in recent weeks have been motivated by a large amount of foreign debt payments coming due and "a wrong perception that we don't have flexibility," in the foreign exchange market. 

 The Central Bank intervened in the market on Wednesday, helping the real firm up a bit.

title: Brazil stocks up with Wall St, helped by local news.
text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks rose in tandem with Wall Street on Thursday, boosted by the successful launch of a 7-year euro bond and by a Central Bank promise to set aside more money to back the real currency. 

 Traders only singled out Telesp telecommunications company, whose preferred stock rose 5.5 percent following an announcement the firm had set up a telephony services unit. 

 "Telesp has been undervalued for a while compared to other companies in the sector," said Felipe Padua, portfolio manager with Banco Opportunity in Rio de Janeiro. 

 "All other stocks rose almost indiscriminately on a general market upturn," said Marcelo Porto of Concordia brokerage. 

 Sao Paulo's blue chip Bovespa index closed 1.47 percent stronger at 11,700 points, bringing the market's gains this month to 5.4 percent. It is up 2 percent so far this week. Volume was a moderate 467 million reais ($233 million). 

 The Dow Jones industrial average rose over 2.2 percent, finishing at 10,622 points. 

 "The market had every reason to perform well today with U.S. shares rising and good local news," said Padua. 

 "Brazil made clear it could sell additional reserves to calm down the forex market at least until December. Money from the newly-launched bonds will also boost reserves. Turbulence in the forex market has been a big concern recently." 

 Added Concordia's Porto: "The day was very active. Sellers didn't have a chance. If it weren't for technical problems at the bourse, which sidelined foreigners a bit, we could have registered a bigger rise." 

 The bourse's data feed failed to update for a couple of hours in the morning. 

 Phone operator Embratel rose 3 percent on growing optimism that the government was likely to negotiate the company's back taxes. 

 Among other blue chips, benchmark stock Telebras rose 2.78 percent to 151.8 reais. Petrobras preferred edged up 0.06 percent to 314.10 reais. Eletrobras preferred shares were among the few day's losers, slipping 0.31 percent to 35.41 reais. 

Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said Thursday Brazil planned to cut the floor for the country's foreign currency reserves by $2 billion, which would give Brazil more flexibility to intervene in the volatile forex market. 

 The market also warmed to Brazil's successful sovereign bond issue of 500 million euros. The government had initially placed 300 million euros, but increased the size in just a few hours on the back of good market reception. 

 The real has firmed for two days in a row and now stands at 1.974 per dollar.

title: Latin America  Forex  Roundup:  Brazil 's Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real once again broke the BRR2.00 level Wednesday, prompting the country's central bank to intervene and sell dollars to support its currency. 

Brazil's central bank confirmed that it had intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time since Aug. 18. It didn't specify the size and level of intervention. 

 At 3:00 p.m. EDT, the Brazilian real recouped earlier losses, trading at BRR1.988, sliding from Tuesday's close of BRR1.9960. 

 Traders said the Brazilian real had moved lower as a result of general bearishness over emerging markets, rather than any one particular piece of news. 

 One New York-based trader noted the expected inflow of dollars from the privatization auction of a power generator failed to boost the currency. 

 As reported earlier, U.S. energy concern, AES Corp. Wednesday acquired a controlling stake in Brazil's power generator Companhia de Geracao de Energia Electrica Tiete, known as Cesp Tiete, for BRR938.1 million. The deal was seen as a vote of confidence from foreign investors but failed to curb the real's slide. 

 The drop marks the second time the real dipped below the BRR2.00-level since Oct. 19, when it hit a seven-month low due to concerns over the country's fiscal reforms and U.S. rate hike fears that could stall the U.S. stock market's phenomenal rise. 

 Separately, the central bank plans to have dollar-linked note auctions Friday and Nov. 4 of BRR1 billion and BRR1.5 billion, respectively. These auctions had given some support to the falling currency in the past, but have recently been less effective. 

 Meanwhile, the Mexican peso weakened against the dollar in very quiet trading on a dearth of major market-moving news, according to New York-based traders. 

 In Mexico City on 48-hour spot dollar markets, banking leader Banamex quoted the Mexican peso at MXN9.653 Wednesday, compared with MXN9.640 at Tuesday's close. 

 "No one wants to take big positions," said one trader, adding that the market is "dead." 

 The trader said market participants are looking for an excuse to trade, and closely watching for U.S. economic data due out early Thursday. The data include third-quarter gross domestic product growth and the employment cost index, which is considered one of many measures to gauge inflationary pressures. 

 Meanwhile, smaller Latin American currencies were a mixed bag. 

 The Chilean peso hit a historical low against the dollar Wednesday at CLP546.70 as foreign banks engaged in vigorous selling in the peso, said a currency dealer with a local bank. 

 The dealer said he wasn't aware of any particular event that could have instigated selling in the peso, which, in turn, stimulated activity to sharply above normal. 

 The fact that local banks and companies were reluctant to satiate foreigners' appetite for dollars also helped keep the peso weak, the trader said. "It's clear that no one wants to get rid of their dollars," he added.

title: Brazil's Real Closes Weaker At BRL2.932 To Dollar Thu
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened slightly Thursday as sovereign bond prices fell overseas, driving up interest rates.  

The weakness occurred even though the central bank didn't buy dollars under its new intervention policy designed to rebuild scant foreign reserves.  

The real ended at BRL2.932 to the dollar, compared with BRL2.919 at Wednesday's close.  

The real has been in a weakening cycle for more than a week, as fears about interest-rate hikes abroad and inflation at home pressure Brazilian assets.  

Also, the real is also being pinched by periodic dollar purchases by the central bank under its new policy aimed at rebuilding reserves.  

The monetary authority is frequently buying dollars to help reduce potential volatility and weaken the local currency to help make it more competitive for exporters to sell their goods.  

Ultimately, the central bank's intervention strategy is aimed at helping Brazil close its external financing gap in 2004 after the nation last year recorded its first current account surplus in about a decade.  

Wednesday, the central bank decided to not roll over $1.13 billion in dollar-linked debt and, instead, pay it off. Since mid-2003, the monetary authority has reduced the amount of dollar-linked paper in the market to help reduce potential volatility and currency weakness if there were any economic shocks in the future.

title: Brazil's Foreign Reserves May Rise By About $2.7B In Jan
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's foreign reserves likely rose sharply in January as the central bank aggressively bought dollars to insulate against future economic shocks.  

Credit Suisse First Boston and the Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo on Thursday estimated January purchases, respectively, at $2.6 billion and $2.7 billion.  

The central bank won't detail its purchases for the month until Feb. 20, but its release Wednesday of flows in the foreign exchange market for January allowed economists to deduce the amount of interventions for the month.  

Some $3.3 billion entered Brazil in January. And despite central bank dollar purchases, the local currency, the real, strengthened 1.3% in January until fears of potential interest rate hikes in the U.S. weakened the currency last week. The real's strength for most of the month occurred as commercial banks sold about $700 million more on the local spot market than the central bank bought.  

The interventions, combined with a $1.5 billion sovereign bond issued in January, should boost net foreign reserves to $24.5 billion from $20.5 billion in December, CSFB said in a Thursday note.  

If the country continues to post strong trade surpluses and international liquidity remains heavy, CSFB said reserves could end the year between $30 billion and $35 billion.  

Still, Brazil's net foreign reserves, excluding some $30 billion in cash from the International Monetary Fund, would remain remarkably low and leave the real vulnerable to external and internal economic shocks.  

Net reserves fell sharply in 1998 as the country tried to defend its currency from a balance of payments crisis before floating the real in early 1999. During the turmoil, the central bank burned through much of the country's net $70 billion in reserves.  

Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles has said Brazil wants to go it alone in the world economy and leave the IMF when its current accord expires late this year.  

To do that, reserves need to rise sharply. Compared with its emerging market peers, Brazil's reserves are woefully inadequate. China has $450 billion in reserves and Taiwan $100 million. Mexico also has substantial foreign reserves, a key factor that allowed it to reach investment grade status, unlike Brazil.

"The central bank has denied it has set a floor and a ceiling for the real but it looks like it isn't prepared to let the real strengthen beyond the BRL2.900 to the dollar level," said a Sao Paulo-based trader.  

Meantime, the central bank said it wouldn't roll over $1.13 billion in dollar-linked debt and that it would buy the debt back. Monday's rally brought the real back to where it was in late 2002 before the election of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a one-time fiery leftist who has since become a favorite on Wall Street by proving his mettle as a fiscal conservative.

title: Brazil Targets  Forex  Reserves, Debt Buyback, IMF Freedom
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazilian monetary authorities have adopted an ambitious strategy to replenish foreign reserves that could lead to a large debt buyback in April and eventually free the country from reliance on the International Monetary Fund.  

Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles said late Tuesday the bank will start purchasing dollars on the spot market and directly deposit them into international reserves. Meirelles said no target exists for the amount of purchases, but big buys are likely if dollar inflows remain strong.  

The Treasury, for example, bought $11.2 billion on the spot market in 2003, much more than expected, to meet overseas debt payments extending into June of 2004. Unlike those of the Treasury, the central bank's purchases will be transparent, with announcements of auctions and their results.  

Though some acknowledged the new intervention policy might imply Brazil's exchange-rate regime is a "dirty" instead of "clean" float, or that fewer interest rate cuts are likely as a weaker real will add to inflation, analysts reacted positively overall to the change.  

"The new policy of the central bank is wise because it'll use real strength to rebuild foreign reserves and reduce reliance on the IMF," said Roger Scher, Latin American sovereign ratings director with Fitch in New York. "Ultimately, Brazil would like to leave the IMF program."  

In December, Brazil signed a $14 billion, one-year IMF deal when the government, after considerable internal debate, decided potential economic shocks were still too threatening to operate without a security blanket from the multilateral lender. Excluding some $30 billion in IMF funds, Brazil's net foreign reserves are only about $17 billion. The country had $70 billion in reserves in 1998 before it unsuccesfully tried to defend the real, then pegged to the dollar, from speculative attack.  

Octavio de Barros, chief economist for Banco Bradesco in Sao Paulo, thinks the central bank's increased emphasis on foreign reserves will direct debt issuance plans.  

"The central bank, in my view, is giving a signal about the possibility of a debt buyback," he said. "Getting rid of Brady bonds would really help improve Brazil's image, because these bonds were sold as the country was coming out of a moratorium."  

Barros said Brazil might issue new bonds in the first quarter to refinance a host of Brady bonds. A buyback would eliminate millions of dollars in interest costs and reduce pressure on foreign reserves.  

Brazil has about $6.5 billion in outstanding Brady bonds, with an option to buy them back at face value on April 15, the next interest payment date. Making a buyback more likely, Brazil's closely-watched C-bond is trading nearly at par, at 99.563 bid. Brazil's central bank declined to comment.  

Besides debt policy, analysts agree a slightly weaker real in the near term will create conditions for a stronger local currency in the long term by improving Brazil's external accounts. Strong external accounts will attract foreign investment levels and reduce borrowing costs.  

"If there is any goal here it is to run a trade surplus of more than $20 billion and keep the balance of payments healthy," while hitting the central bank's 5.5% inflation target for this year, said Barros.  

Brazil posted a record $25 billion trade surplus in 2003 and a current account surplus for the first time in a decade. Exporters say an exchange rate of BRL3.00 to the dollar will allow continued growth in foreign sales. Bradesco forecasts an average real price of BRL3.03 this year.  

The first day after the policy change, Brazil's real strengthened 0.3% to close at BRL2.858 per dollar Wednesday, with little sign the central bank purchases had undermined a currency that gained 22% in 2003.  

"I'd have expected weakness today. But the central bank wants to let this sink in," said Yianos Kontopoulos, chief global foreign exchange strategist with Merrill Lynch in New York. "We'll probably have to wait a few more days to see the full impacts."  


   -By Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-3145-1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  Tsy Secy Denies Broader  Forex Intervention  Policy
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazilian Treasury Secretary Joaquim Levy on Monday denied the government has adopted a broader foreign exchange intervention strategy to impact the value of the local currency.  

The government has bought $7.8 billion on the local spot market so far this year, considerably more than the guidance of $5.7 billion provided in October.  

Among other items, the extra purchases of more than $2.0 billion were made to pay back multilateral loans, buy drugs for the health ministry and obtain supplies for the army, according to a central bank official.  

Originally, the Treasury indicated the purchases would be made solely to service sovereign bonds.  

Explaining the larger than expected purchases, Levy said: "Sometimes there's a concentration of debt payments like we just had."  

He added that purchasing dollars for the army and health ministry doesn't indicate a shift in policy.  

"This is normal. Sometimes you have demands from specific sectors (of the government)," he said after speaking at a capital markets seminar here.  

He reiterated that "in a floating exchange-rate environment, everybody has the obligation to go to the market and buy and sell. This is true for both the Treasury and the private sector."  

Despite Levy's comments, the higher than expected purchases follow a November central bank decision that extended the settlement period for the Treasury's dollar purchases on the spot market to six months from about three. That substantially boosted the ability of the government to intervene in the foreign-exchange market.  

Still, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's administration claims it has no targeted forex rate, as adopting one would contradict the central bank's inflation-targeting program, which was put in place just after the real was allowed to float freely in early 1999.  

Officials also refuse to accept the word intervention when discussing the dollar purchases. Yet the real, currently at about three per dollar, only changed 1.4% in value between June 1 and Dec. 1, suggesting to many the government has a preferred foreign exchange rate.  

Besides collecting funds for debt payments abroad, the dollar purchases effectively meet other objectives.  

The government wants a relatively cheap real to maintain Brazil's export boom and deepen import substitution. Those trends created a surging trade surplus in recent quarters that may close the country's current account gap this year for the first time in a decade.  

At the same time, the aggressive dollar purchases diminish pressure on the country's scant net foreign reserves. They are woefully low and need to rise before the country can convince all investors it can function without the security blanket of an accord with the International Monetary Fund.  

Brazil's net reserves, excluding some $30 billion in IMF funds, total only about $18 billion. This compares with some $70 billion in reserves just before the central bank started burning through dollars to fend off a balance of payments crisis in 1998, and $35 billion just after the real floated.  

Regarding dollar purchases in the future, Levy didn't explicitly back comments made in October that the Treasury would purchase $5.0 billion next year to make good on overseas debt payments.  

"Our purchases will be proportional to our obligations," he said.  

On other matters, Levy said market conditions are "favorable" for Brazil to issue sovereign debt but declined to provide specifics on when the government would start selling bonds to fund its $4.0 billion borrowing program for 2004.  

He also said the country's economic recovery remains solid and that the economy should expand by at least 3.0% to 3.5% next year. Levy said official data released Monday that showed industrial output fell 0.5% in October was expected after September's stellar result.  

-Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com

title: Brazil  real falls on  intervention  talk, stocks dip.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency tumbled more than 1 percent on Thursday, notching its biggest loss in three months amid heavy speculation that the Treasury was snapping up dollars to bolster reserves.  

The Treasury denied any responsibility for the fall.  

The real BRBY) weakened 1.25 percent to 2.94 to the greenback, its largest single-day drop since Aug. 1. That left the currency 20.6 percent stronger year to date.  

The losses, traders said, came after federal bank Banco do Brasil swept into the spot market and bought dollars on behalf of the Treasury, which has been actively seeking to boost the country's scant international reserves lately.  

"Everyone knew the government was going to intervene (in the market) at some point and today they didn't even try to hide it," said Hideaki Iha, a senior currency trader at Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo.  

"Banco do Brasil showed its face early on, letting everyone know that they were there."  

A spokeswoman for Banco do Brasil declined to comment and the Treasury denied being behind the tumble.  

"Today's movement is not related to Treasury operations," Jose Antonio Gragnani, head of the Treasury's public debt department, told Reuters. "The Treasury tries to act in the most discreet way possible."  

But just last week the Central Bank made it easier for the Treasury to intervene in the currency market, extending the settlement period for its dollar purchases on the spot market to six months from 90 days.  

STOCKS HIT NEW HIGH  

Brazil's stock market also fell on Thursday, slipping 0.21 percent to 18,754.5 points as investors locked in gains after hitting a new record high in early trading.  

The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa index .BVSP) jumped 1.71 percent to 19,115.2 soon after the opening bell, surpassing its previous all-time high of 19,046, set on March 27, 2000.  

The early surge came on the back of news that MCI, the beleaguered U.S. phone giant formerly known as WorldCom Inc., had put its controlling stake in Brazilian long-distance carrier Embratel Participacoes up for sale.  

Embratel's ordinary shares, which have voting rights, soared 39.24 percent to 11.00 reais on the news, briefly lifting the broader market. Its preferred, or minority shares, rose 3.24 percent to 10.20 reais.  

MCI said Wednesday it had not yet identified a buyer for its 19.26 percent economic interest and 51.79 percent voting stake in Embratel, which it bought in 1998 for $2.3 billion as part of the privatization of Brazil's telecom sector.  

"The good news is that the lack of definition about whether Embratel would be sold is finally over," said Marcelo Mesquita, Brazil strategist at UBS investment bank in Rio de Janeiro.  

"Now the race is on to find out who the buyer is, and the talk is that it could be the Mexicans," he added, referring to Telefonos de Mexico, the fixed-line giant owned by telecom tycoon Carlos Slim.  

Other analysts, however, said local players like Tele Norte Leste Participacoes, or Telemar, and Brasil Telecom Participacoes were better positioned to snatch up Embratel.  

Still, both companies' shares fell on Thursday, with Telemar sliding 0.22 percent to 40.01 reais and Brasil Telecom falling 1.64 percent to 20.95 reais. (Additional reporting by Rodrigo Menderico).

title: Brazil 's Real Opens Softer; Govt Boosts  Intervention  Pwr

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank late Monday extended the settlement period for the Treasury's dollar purchases on the spot market to six months from about three, a change that should substantially boost the ability of the government to intervene in the foreign-exchange market.

The Treasury has said it bought more than $5.0 billion on the spot market this year, and plans to buy another $5.0 billion next year.

title: Once A Dirty Word In  Brazil ,  Intervention  Becomes Vogue
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Long the dirtiest word in Brazilian economics, intervention has made a startling comeback in the foreign exchange market.  

In investment circles, it's now as acceptable as President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a once-feared left-wing rabble-rouser who has become a market-friendly darling since taking office in January.  

It's in vogue even though Brazilians still vilify the man responsible for the country's biggest-ever intervention: Gustavo Franco, the central banker who spent $40 billion in foreign reserves in late 1998 and 1999 unsuccessfully trying to defend the Brazilian currency - which at the time was pegged to the dollar - from speculative attack.  

So far this year, the Treasury has bought nearly $5.0 billion on the local foreign exchange market to prevent the local currency, the real, from strengthening too much amid strong dollar inflows. Some $700 million in purchases are slated through December, along with another $5.0 billion next year.  

Though the government refuses to call them interventions, critics of the purchases are hard to find.  

"What the government has been doing is extremely prudent," said Carlos Thadeu de Freitas, a professor at the Ibmec business school in Rio de Janeiro and former central bank director.  

Lula's administration claims it has no targeted forex rate, as adopting one would contradict - and impede - the central bank's inflation-targeting program, which was put in place just after the real was allowed to float freely in early 1999.  

But other priorities are in play. The government wants a relatively cheap real to maintain Brazil's export boom and deepen import substitution. Those trends created a surging trade surplus in recent quarters that may close the country's current account gap this year for the first time in a decade.  

At the same time, the aggressive dollar purchases diminish pressure on the country's scant net foreign reserves. They are woefully low and need to rise before the country can convince all investors it can function without the security blanket of an accord with the International Monetary Fund. The government will decide this month if it will renegotiate an IMF package slated to expire later this year.  

Brazil's net reserves, excluding some $30 billion in IMF funds, total only about $18 billion. This compares with some $70 billion in reserves just before the central bank started burning through dollars to fend off a balance of payments crisis in 1998, and $35 billion just after the real floated. The Treasury hopes to boost net reserves next year to about $20 billion.  

Treasury Secretary Joaquim Levy said Wednesday the recent dollar purchases don't amount to intervention. "It's not our intent (to intervene), that's why we're buying dollars in the most homogenous way possible. The Treasury doesn't play the market: it goes up and down," he said Wednesday in Brasilia.  

A closer look, however, shows traders are correct when they say BRL2.90 per dollar is the level the government is targeting. It has barely moved from that rate for the last four months.  

Between June 1 and Oct. 1, the real stayed in an unusually tight trading range and moved just 1.5% - an extremely rare feat for one of the world's most volatile currencies. Wednesday it closed at BRL2.905.  

Though he disavowed intervention, Levy suggested the government's currency practices are changing and no longer restricted by the official policy of the last four years: that interventions will only occur when liquidity problems arise. Levy has yet to detail the size and frequency of the "homogenous" purchases, but more data are expected this week.  

"Increasingly, in a floating exchange-rate environment, everyone has their own obligation to go to the market and buy and sell. This is true for the private sector and the Treasury," he said.  

Treasury officials weren't available to further comment on Levy's statements, which didn't impact a real that's pricing in $5.0 billion in interventions next year.  

-By Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-8147-0853; terry.wade@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE:Brazil Meirelles:Curr Acct May Be Positive In '03
text:
(Adds analysis, analyst comments and background)  


 
   By Terry Wade 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
   

SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Central Bank Governor Henrique Meirelles Monday said Brazil may post a current account surplus in 2003, a result that would prove the country made the right decision in 1999 to float its currency to escape from a suffocating external financing gap.  

"With all the adjustments we've been making, our current account deficit has been on a downward trend," Meirelles said at a conference in Rio de Janeiro.  

"Our estimate of a $1.2 billion deficit (for 2003) is conservative. There's a strong possibility that we'll have a positive result in 2003," he added.  

A swelling trade surplus, expected to hit about $20 billion this year, is helping to produce current account surpluses on a monthly basis. August's surplus was $1.2 billion.  

If the current account for the year ends up positive, it would mark the first time since 1993, just before the country essentially pegged its currency to the dollar and a balance of payments shortfall began to worry investors. In 1998, just before Brazil floated its currency, the current account deficit was $33.5 billion.  

With a cheap currency deepening Brazil's external orientation by encouraging exports and import substitution, the trade surplus has grown sharply in recent quarters - and at just the right time - to plug up the current account gap.  

Brazil relied heavily on foreign direct investment and privatization proceeds to fund its current account gap after floating its currency. Rising trade surpluses are now compensating for falling foreign direct investment, which is expected to total about $9.0 billion this year, down from more than $30 billion only three years ago.  

When combined with international credit lines that have been restored since being cut in 2002 on the eve of presidential elections, monthly current account surpluses have helped boost the currency 22% this year.  

And this historic turnaround in Brazil's external accounts would have had a more pronounced effect on the real if the Treasury weren't indirectly intervening in the market.  

"The appreciation in the exchange rate in recent months as a result of the good external flows would have been much bigger without the intervention of the Treasury," Octavio de Barros, chief economist at Banco Bradesco, said Monday in a research note.  

Brazil's government has been pursuing an aggressive two-pronged strategy to preserve foreign reserves and prevent the local currency from strengthening too much.  

The central bank Friday said the Treasury has bought $4.95 billion on the local foreign exchange market since January. The money is being used to pay off the government's external debts. Another $700 million in purchases will be made through December. And next year, some $5.0 billion in purchases are planned.  

Though the government says its dollar purchases don't amount to an intervention strategy, traders disagree, as Brazil's exporters say the country's rising trade balance would be hurt by a real stronger than BRL2.90 to the dollar. The real was quoted at BRL2.9350 to the dollar midafternoon Monday.  

The purchases, funded by reals, diminish pressure on the country's scant net foreign reserves, which are expected to total about $16.9 billion at year-end. Including International Monetary Fund money, Brazil will end the year with about $46.2 billion in foreign reserves. In 2004, net foreign reserves are expected to climb to $20 billion and gross reserves to ease to $43.7 billion.  

-Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com  

(Adriana Brasileiro in Rio de Janeiro contributed to this report)

title: Brazil's Real Ends Unchanged At BRL2.903/Dlr
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real ended unchanged Monday in mostly quiet trading, with dollar inflows offsetting worries about a potential intervention to weaken the currency and a small rollover of dollar-linked debt later this week.  

After trading in a tight range, the real closed at BRL2.903 to the dollar, even with Friday's finish.  

Traders continued to think the government doesn't want to see the real stronger than BRL2.90 for a prolonged period of time and may indirectly intervene to weaken it. Otherwise, a rising trade surplus and a narrowing current account deficit could deteriorate.  

State-run Banco do Brasil has been active buying dollars for the Treasury, in recent weeks purchasing upwards of $700 million.  

Some think more interventions are coming after Brazil's monetary authority late last week raised to 90 days from 60 days the time period in which the Treasury must settle dollar futures contracts. For other players, the 60-day rule remains in effect.  

The central bank didn't explain its decision, but market players believe the move will make it easier for the Treasury to buy dollars in local forex markets.  

In other news hitting the market, on Wednesday, the central bank will start rolling over a still unknown portion of about $2.35 billion in forex swaps maturing on Oct. 1.  

The central bank has been trying to reduce its exposure to the securities, a tactic that in recent weeks has caused slight short-term weakening of the real.  

But helping to support the real, traders say, are inflows from corporate bond sales overseas. The market is waiting for inflows from a $500 million bond drinks giant Ambev has placed overseas.  

-By Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Ends Stronger At BRL2.902 To The Dollar
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real ended stronger Thursday, as heavy dollar inflows prevented the real from slipping on an interest-rate cut made late Wednesday by the central bank.  

The currency ended at BRL2.902 to the dollar, compared with Wednesday's BRL2.911 finish.  

The inflows supported the real after a 2.0 percentage point interest-rate cut to 20% a year for the benchmark rate. Traders said the cut was largely priced in.  

The lower base rate should help revive a stalled economy in the coming months and that's helping attract dollar inflows for Brazilian assets like stocks.  

But the bulk of inflows are coming from corporate recent debt sales overseas. Among the larger deals, drinks giant AmBev sold $500 million overseas last week, while oil giant Petrobras placed $250 million.  

Traders continue to doubt the real can hold onto levels stronger than BRL2.90, a point where dollar-buying by government entities has occurred in recent weeks. State-run Banco do Brasil has routinely been buying dollars for the Treasury to make payments on external debts.  

Traders interpret this as a way of indirectly intervening in the forex market to keep Brazil's real cheap enough to ensure continued strong exports.

title: Brazil 's Real Ends Weaker On Ctrl Bank  Intervention  Talk
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended weaker Thursday as state-run Banco do Brasil bought dollars for the Treasury and the central bank offered to snap up greenbacks below the BRL2.90 level, traders said. 

 Though it strengthened early to as far as BRL2.874 on expectations of a sovereign bond sale and a big debt offering by drinks giant Ambev, the real weakened during the session to end at BRL2.915 a dollar, compared with BRL2.890 per dollar at Wednesday's close. 

 "The government is behaving the right way. The market thinks a real stronger than BRL2.90 would hurt exports and external accounts. This creates intervention expectations," said Rodrigo Boulous, head trader at Banco Santos in Sao Paulo. 

 Traders put purchases by Banco do Brasil at at least $80 million. The official explanation for these purchases is that they will allow the Treasury to honor foreign debt. But traders consider the buys intervention as the government has foreign reserves. 

 The central bank, for its part, has no official forex target and only operates in the market via primary dealers when liquidity problems arise. Its offers to buy dollars didn't result in purchases Thursday, traders said. The central bank wasn't immediately available for comment. 

 There were some liquidity problems and few dollar buyers Thursday as good news hit the market. 

 The central bank placed its third foreign bond sale this year and Ambev said it increased the size of an overseas bond to $500 million from $300 million. 

 Wednesday, the real was helped by a central bank sale of $482 million in forex swaps to roll over more than 32% of some $1.5 billion in securities expiring Sept. 17. 

 Inflows from rising exports and overseas debt placements have helped lift the real about 22% since the start of the year.

title: Brazil stocks slump on phone spat,  currency  firms.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, June 27 (Reuters) - Brazilian stocks tumbled on Friday as the government butted heads with telephone companies over rate hikes, but the country's currency firmed amid a heavy inflow of dollars. 

 Tracking Wall Street's sharp decline, the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's benchmark Bovespa index fell 0.67 percent to 13,024.1 points, marking a 0.8 percent drop for the week. 

 Brazil's new left-leaning government said it was studying ways to block an increase in phone rates authorized late on Thursday by the National Telecommunications Agency, the sector regulator known as Anatel. 

 The new tariff guidelines allow fixed-line operators to raise residential rates by between 24.5 percent and 25 percent, while authorizing a 41.7 percent hike on business lines, public phones and installation fees. 

 Though the new fees are expected to significantly boost revenues for phone companies, investors were worried about the brewing spat between the government and Anatel. 

 "The situation caused a lot of unease in the market," said Helio Ozaki, a financial analyst at Finambras brokerage in Sao Paulo. "It just highlights the fragility of the regulatory system in Brazil and how vulnerable these agencies are to government intervention." 

 The dispute sent telecommunications shares tumbling, led by Brasil Telecom and market bellwether Tele Norte Leste Participacoes, both of which were allowed to raise rates by 25 percent. 

 Stock in Brasil Telecom skidded 2.5 percent to 21.45 reais, while Telemar shares - which account for 14 percent of the Bovespa index - slipped 0.6 percent to 33.10 reais. 

 Shares in the Brazilian unit of Spain's Telefonica, which can hike rates by 24.5 percent, fell 0.27 percent to 33.80 reais. 

 The currency market, however, largely ignored the row. The Brazilian real firmed 0.7 percent to 2.88 per dollar, finishing the week a half-percentage point stronger. 

 The real, which has rallied 23 percent against the greenback so far this year, crept higher as fresh cash flowed into the market following a slew of recent bond issues by Brazilian companies abroad, traders said. 

 "With all the cash companies are raising abroad right now, it's hard to bet against the real," said Hideaki Iha, senior currency trader at Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo. 

 "Not even the debt auction was enough to stress out the market," Iha added, referring to the Central Bank's attempt to roll over $700 million in dollar-linked debt. It ended up only selling $335.7 million.

title: Brazil  Lacks Interest In Argentine  FX Intervention  Idea
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Argentina wants to adopt a joint currency targeting system with its northern neighbor at a time when Brazilian officials indicate that intervention is a dirty word. 

 That means a plan Argentine Vice Foreign Minister Martin Redrado presented Monday in Brasilia that would aim to keep Brazil's real and Argentina's peso around three per dollar may be rejected unless it's revised. 

 Though the blueprint would mark the strongest effort yet to integrate the currencies since the Common Market of the South, or Mercosur, trade bloc adopted it as a medium-term goal in the late 1990s, it likely won't be put into practice for a long time. Mercosur includes Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. 

 "There's no timeframe for implementation," Redrado said in Brasilia. He suggested attaining near parity between the peso and real by adopting trading bands or increasing the use of reciprocal credits. "This would be a transitional system to a common currency." 

 Brazilian Central Bank Governor Henrique Meirelles and Finance Minister Antonio Palocci, the top economic policy-makers in President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's center-left administration, have said repeatedly in the last month that they won't intervene in the foreign exchange market or adopt currency targets. 

 Monday, Meirelles and Palocci tried to distance themselves from Redrado's approach. 

 Meirelles said he was unaware of any debate on currency bands. Palocci met Redrado and said they didn't discuss foreign exchange bands but agreed to study "macroeconomic policy convergence" between the two countries. 

 There are a host of stumbling blocks to Redrado's plans. Mercosur leaders have never said how the central bank for an integrated currency would be composed, and heavyweight Brazil would prefer to create currency integration without using interventions. 

 Redrado's scheme also assumes a win of Argentina's presidential election May 18 by government-backed candidate Nestor Kirchner over former President Carlos Menem, who opposes Mercosur currency integration and strongly favors closer ties with the U.S. 

 Redrado said the creation of a band for the peso and real would give more certainty to exporters, importers and investors. On the trade front, Redrado indicated Brazil will offer increased export financing to Argentina. 

 Though currency weakness rattled their economies for much of 2002, worries of excessive currency strength have recently jumped to the forefront of economic policy debates in Argentina and Brazil. 

 Since January, the peso and real have each gained about 20% against the dollar - prompting fears that surging exports and increased import substitution may slow to the  detriment of the countries' best performing sectors. 

 The peso hit its highest levels in more than a year last week and Monday closed at ARS2.80 a dollar, while the real finished at BRL3.04 and is hovering around its strongest levels since August. 

 Top aides of Lula, who is still trying to cultivate a pro-market image after decades of advocating policies that frighten investors, say intervening in the currency markets is a tricky game that's not worthwhile. 

 But Lula's planning and trade ministers have advocated interventions to ensure exports keep growing and the current account gap continues narrowing. 

 Lula himself last week suggested too much real strength was bad. But that surprised investors and he quickly backtracked. 

 "The real will continue to fluctuate and the government won't interfere with it," he said Friday. 

 -Terry Wade and Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.9117.0969; brazil@dowjones.com 

 (Michael Casey in Buenos Aires contributed to this report)

title: Brazil's Real Opens At BRL2.900/Dlr Vs BRL2.912 End Wed
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real opened slightly stronger against the dollar Friday as investors are optimistic the success of the country's $1 billion sovereign bond last week will lead local corporate borrowers to tap capital markets in the short term. 

 The real opened at BRL2.900 per dollar compared with Wednesday's closing mark of BRL2.912 to the dollar. Local markets were closed Thursday for Labor Day. 

 By 1320 GMT, the real was trading at BRL2.904 to the dollar, but traders cautioned that volume was lower-than-average and that the currency would likely remain stable. 

 Traders said investors overlooked comments by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva that the government doesn't want the real to rally too much because it may hurt exports. 

 Brazilian media reported Friday the president made the comments during Labor Day celebrations in Sao Paulo, Brazil's financial center. 

 "The real didn't really react to Lula's comments, but liquidity is very thin today, so it's hard to judge," said a trader in Sao Paulo. "Once the market digests his comments and its possible implications, the real may move lower," he added. 

 Some market watchers believe the central bank may take steps to rein in the real's rally to ensure export growth. But the central bank and finance ministry have repeatedly denied the possibility of intervention and lauded Brazil's free currency regime. 

 Still, export growth is key for Brazil's trade surplus, which is seen hitting $16 billion this year, and for a smaller current account deficit. 

 On the other hand, a stronger real spells easing inflation, which is seen topping 12% in 2003.

title: Brazil 's Palocci rules out  forex intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, April 4 (Reuters) - Brazil's Finance Minister Antonio Palocci said on Friday the government will not intervene to keep the exchange rate at a more favorable rate for exporters. 

 "The dollar will find its own value. We cannot interfere with the exchange rate. It's inappropriate, it's an unsound macroeconomic policy ...," Palocci told reporters after visiting the Sao Paulo stock exchange. 

 Palocci's comment came after the real firmed against the dollar for the sixth straight session to its best close since Sept.16. It ended at 3.22 per dollar, marking a 4.4 percent gain for the week and a 10 percent advance so far in 2003. 

 Palocci said that Brazil's floating exchange rate policy, adopted in January 1999, was as important as inflation targets. 

Central Bank President Henrique Meirelles also denied on Friday any plans to intervene to maintain the exchange rate at a favorable level for exports, saying the bank would only act if there were liquidity problems. 

 On Thursday, Planning Minister Guido Mantega said that 3.20 reais per dollar would ease inflationary pressure while keeping Brazilian exports competitive.

title: Brazil Real Opens At BRL3.515/Dlr V BRL3.530/Dlr End Thu
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real strengthened in early trading Friday amid capital inflows and growing investor optimism toward Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's new Workers' Party government. 

 By 1210 GMT (7:10 a.m. EST), the real was trading at BRL3.495 to the dollar after closing Thursday at BRL3.530. 

 The gains come despite news that Rio de Janeiro state defaulted on a BRL85 million debt payment - a move that raises concern about the financial health of many Brazilian states at the start of Lula's government this week. The state is asking for the government to find a solution to the problem and help it pay its workers their year-end bonus. 

 Usually such bad news weakens the local currency, but a Sao Paulo-based trader said capital inflows of some $400 million were helping lift the real amid thin liquidity during the holiday season. 

 He added the market was also warming to a series of Workers' Party second-tier appointments to its economic team. Among those named are left-leaning economists who are members of the Workers' Party, moderate and liberal economists with solid technical and academic background, and officials who will remain in their posts after serving four years under the former President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's administration. 

 Traders said the market continued to warm up to comments by Antonio Palocci at his inaugural speech as finance minister Thursday. 

 Seeking to reassure investors about a party that once advocated a debt moratorium but now says it will stick to sound economic policy, Palocci reiterated the government would work to keep inflation in check, maintain fiscal discipline to stabilize Brazil's debt to goss-domestic-product ratio. 

 While he didn't address the issue of full central bank independence directly, Palocci said the monetary authority would have the freedom to act in any way that it chose to ensure it met its inflationary goals. 

 Investors have been worried that the Workers' Party, which wants to revive Brazil's sluggish economy, would intervene and force the central bank to cut rates prematurely and allow inflation to get out of control.

He added this would be the best way to reduce interest rates, which were raised three percentage points to 25% last month. 

 While he didn't address the issue of full central bank independence directly, Palocci said the monetary authority would have the freedom to act in any way that it chose to ensure it met its inflationary goals.

title: Brazil Petrobras To Unveil Fuel Price Adjustment Fri
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's oil giant Petroleo Brasileiro (PBR), or Petrobras, Friday unveiled a 12.09% raise in gasoline prices at the refinery level effective Nov. 4. 

 Petrobras said in a statement it's also hiking diesel fuel prices by 20.5%, effective Nov. 4, and the price of liquefied petroleum gas, known as cooking gas, by 22.8%, effective Nov. 5. 

 This comes four months after Petrobras made the last adjustment to gasoline prices. 

 The company said in a statement it opted to wait for the  volatility of the last few months to ease before making a decision on fuel prices. 

 "Today, with most of the uncertainties out of the way, international oil prices and foreign exchange variations are  at higher levels than those registered by the company when local fuel prices were last adjusted," Petrobras said in the statement. 

 Petrobras said the impact of the wholesale price hikes at the pump will likely be 9% on average for gasoline, 17% for diesel fuel and 12% for cooking gas. 

 The state-owned company, which had its hands tied with government regulation for the past two months, was expected to hike fuel prices right after the Oct. 27 runoff election in which left-leaning Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a landslide victory against the government-backed candidate Jose Serra. 

 Market watchers said the government's intervention in Petrobras' free-market pricing policy - effective since January this year - was a politically motivated attempt to boost Serra's chances in the polls. 

 Analysts estimated it would be necessary for Petrobras to raise gasoline prices by around 20% to make up for higher oil prices abroad and the sharp depreciation of the real in past months. While predicting adjustments would come in installments to ease the impact  on inflation, many estimated a hike of around 10% by early November, with the rest to be administered by the next government, which takes office Jan. 1. 

 Economists fear gas price hikes will fuel Brazil's recent surge in inflation, which looks likely to close at  8% this year - well above the government's 1.5%-5.5% target band for this year and 4% goal for 2003. 

 On Wednesday, the central bank said gasoline prices for consumers would likely increase by 9% by the end of the year. The monetary authority also predicted a further 9% increase in gasoline prices in 2003. 

 Gasoline prices had been unchanged since June 30, when Petrobras announced a 6.75% hike. Petrobras hiked diesel prices by 9.5% on the same date. 

 Since then the Brazilian real ($1=BRL3.63) has lost about 22%, while international oil prices abroad have climbed on fears of conflict in the Middle East. 

 Local prices are heavily affected by foreign exchange variations  and international prices. Even though Petrobras exports oil, it must import about a quarter of the 1.8 million barrels that Brazil consumes daily as the country lacks refining capacity. Petrobras also imports about 40% of the natural gas used in the country. 

 In mid-August President Fernando Henrique Cardoso ordered Brazil's oil sector watchdog to intervene in fuel prices, effectively returning to a policy of regulation that was to have ended Jan. 1. 

 Prior to that date, Petrobras held a monopoly on oil product imports and prices were regulated by the government. 

 -By Adriana Brasileiro, Dow Jones Newswires; (5521) 3288-5004, adriana.brasileiro@dowjones.com

title: Chile peso rises after gains for Brazilian real.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Chile's peso continued to firm on Thursday, following gains in the Brazilian real as traders said calm was returning to Brazilian markets following the election of leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as president. 

 The currency closed at 726.50/727.00, an appreciation of 0.99 percent compared with 733.70/734.20 on Wednesday. 

 The real currency was 2.2 percent stronger at 3.635 per dollar at midday on Thursday as investor worries that the president-elect will mishandle the country's ailing economy gave way to cautious optimism about the nation's outlook. 

 "I think that what is happening in Brazil is similar to what happened in Chile (in 2000) when polls gave (current center-left President) Ricardo Lagos the lead in the elections. The peso began to slide but once he was elected it recovered," said Pedro Verdugo, trader with Viajes Mercury. 

 Ricardo lagos, the first Chilean President to call himself a socialist since Salvador Allende was ousted in a 1973 coup, was elected by a narrow margin in 2000. 

 "Of course Lagos did not have the pressure of negotiating a huge public debt, as is the case in Brazil, but in any case the performance of the markets indicates that confidence is returning to the country," Verdugo added. 

 The Brazilian real lost around 40 percent of its value in 2002 before the elections, dragging the peso to historic lows of 760.50/761.00 on Oct. 10. 

 The peso has strengthened since on the calmer outlook in Brazil and after the Central Bank said it would intervene directly and indirectly in the currency market when necessary. 

 Traders also speculated it was looking likely that Argentina would soon reach an agreement for financial aid with the International Monetary Fund to prop up its battered economy.

title: UPDATE 1-Brazil's president-elect hails democratic transfer.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Brazil's President-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva hailed the outgoing president on Tuesday for initiating an unprecedented transition of power which could prove key to the success of the country's first elected left-wing administration. 

 Kicking off the transition of power after his watershed victory in a presidential election runoff on Sunday, Lula met with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to ensure a smooth handover at a time of financial turmoil. 

 After the meeting, Lula, as he is known universally in Brazil, announced that his Workers' Party's government program coordinator Antonio Palocci would head a team to establish the new administration ahead of the January takeover. 

 "I think the moment we are living has to be unique in Latin America's political history," Lula said in his first statement from the presidential palace since winning the elections. 

 "And who knows if this lesson will not remain forever for those of us who have seen ministers and rulers leave by the back door in order not to receive the elected one," said the former union leader. 

 Lula's warm thanks to Cardoso for helping the transition underlined the significance of this transfer of power in a country whose turbulent political history is pot-marked with military interventions and unfinished presidencies. 

 Since Brazil's return to democracy in 1985 after two decades of dictatorship, only one president - Cardoso - has seen out his rule normally. One died, while another resigned when faced with possible impeachment amid a graft scandal. 

 This will be only the second time in the history of Latin America's largest country that one elected president hands over the presidential sash to another. 

 A smooth transition from Cardoso's eight-year rule is also crucial to ensure that Brazil's delicate economy returns to robust growth after months of turmoil in financial markets over the prospect of a left turn in the country. 

 Markets were eagerly expecting the announcement of more members of Lula's transition team, in the hope of learning more about his government's likely economic policies. 

 But stocks and the currency were higher after the Central Bank managed to sell $951.5 million in dollar-linked domestic debt just a week after the bank was unable to roll over debts. 

 Palocci said he would have his full transition team ready in two days, even though there was no guarantee that the members of the team would become ministers in Lula's cabinet. 

 "Palocci was always going to be part of Lula's command team," said Sandra Utsumi, chief economist at BES Investimentos in Sao Paulo. "There is a big expectation about potentials for the ministries and as there are no names, as they are delayed for two days, that creates a climate of apprehension." 

 GAPING SOCIAL DIVIDE 

 Lula has promised to calm financial jitters in the world's ninth largest economy by honoring debt commitments and keeping low inflation policies, in addition to pushing for swift changes to Brazil's cumbersome tax and public pension systems, which have long been desired by investors. 

 After Sunday's win he also pledged to quickly address the gaping social divide in one of the world's most unequal societies. He is planning to create a special secretariat to address the plight of Brazil's 50 million people who live below the poverty line. 

 But the rapid naming of the economic team was key. The head of the Cardoso government's transition task force to the new administration also urged Lula to name his team quickly. 

 "We believe the sooner they name the economic team the better it will be for markets and investors," Pedro Parente told Globo television on Tuesday. 

 Lula won 61 percent of the vote in Sunday's runoff election against candidate Jose Serra of Cardoso's centrist ruling coalition, realizing a 22-year dream for his Workers' Party which was created during the country's 1964-85 military rule. 

 The 52.8 million votes won by Lula on Sunday made him the most popular elected president in Brazil's history, giving him a strong mandate to rule this vast country, stretching from the Amazon in the north to massive industrial cities in the south.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.920/Dlr Vs BRL3.850 End Tue
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Despite a central bank intervention, Brazil's real ended weaker Wednesday as concerns about the country's fiscal future and debt-servicing ability intensify ahead of Oct. 27 presidential elections. 

 The real finished 1.8% down at BRL3.920 to the dollar, compared with BRL3.850 at Tuesday's close. 

 While investors continue to fret that likely presidential victor Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will struggle to reverse the country's deteriorating financial situation, much of the pressure Wednesday came from $3.6 billion in dollar-linked debt maturing Thursday. 

 In a bevy of attempts, the central bank has so far only refinanced about 60% of the paper. Now traders expect the debt to be paid off, increasing the country's monetary base at a time when the central bank is working to remove liquidity from the foreign-exchange market. 

 Though a rate hike Monday by the central bank to 21% from 18% and tightening of reserve requirements late last week helped stabilize the currency Tuesday, the real has again come under pressure in what traders say is an escalating struggle for the monetary authority. 

 And the real is expected to experience added pressure as many more dollar-linked bonds with short maturities fall due in the next several weeks. 

 Holders of the bonds have an incentive to bet against the real. The weaker the currency, the bigger the return for investors that own maturing dollar-linked paper.

title: Mexico's Peso Opens At 10.1470/Dlr Vs 10.0950 Wed End
text:
MEXICO CITY -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's peso opened weaker against the dollar Thursday, tracking the Brazilian currency as that country's presidential elections approach. 

 In Mexico City around 1435 GMT, on 48-hour spot dollar markets, banking leader Banamex quoted the peso trading at a mid rate of 10.1420 per dollar against 10.0950 per dollar at Wednesday's close. 

 Spreads were 10.1370/10.1470 pesos per dollar, compared with MXN10.0850/10.1050 at Wednesday's close.

 Brazil's first round of elections is Sunday. If front-runner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party wins a simple majority, then the race will not go into a run off. 

 However, investors would rather that left-leaning Lula didn't win. Brazil is shouldering about $240 billion in government debt, a third of which is owed to foreign creditors. And investors fear that Lula may bring about a debt default in one of Latin America's two largest economies. 

 The Brazilian real extended losses at Thursday's open as traders hoped for central bank intervention. 

 "We're watching very closely what Brazil does, and tomorrow should be the same," said one Mexico City-based peso trader.

title: Brazil Spent $1.2B On Spot Mkt To Boost Real In Sept
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil spent $1.2 billion on interventions in the currency market in September, the central bank said Tuesday. 

 The September dollar sales brought total spot market intervention since June to $4.1 billion. The central bank estimated last week that it would spend a total of about $9 billion with intervention this year to defend the currency. 

 The latest large intervention on the spot market came Monday when the central bank injected $350 million into the local market after the local currency bottomed out at 3.94 reals per dollar ahead of the expiration of about $1 billion  in dollar-linked debt. 

 Brazil's real has lost more than 35% against the dollar this year amid investor nervousness about the outcome of the  country's upcoming presidential elections scheduled for Sunday. 

 Meanwhile, according to central bank Monetary Policy Director Luis Fernando Figueiredo, the worst of market anxiety should pass this week. "My vision is that we have passed a climax of anxiety and that after election day we'll  see a calming that will facilitate the rollover of dollar-linked debt," Figueiredo said. 

 The central bank however, said it has two more large debt expirations coming due before a possible second round runoff election Oct. 27. 

 About $3.6 billion in debt is scheduled to come due Oct. 17 and another $1.9 billion will come due Oct. 23. 

 Some critics of central bank policy note that market players tend to bid up the dollar ahead of such expirations to guarantee higher returns. 

 Figueiredo said however the central bank has found no evidence that large institutional investors were manipulating the exchange rate unduly in their favor. 

 Meanwhile, he said the central bank would continue it efforts to try to "dilute" the effect of events such as debt  expirations on currency market volatility. 

 "We are trying to maintain a volume of intervention that  is responsible," he said. "We can't intervene at a level that will deplete our reserves for future use excessively. We have to guarantee the solvency of the country." 

 -By Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; 5561-9965-6883 gerald.effris@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.610/Dlr Vs BRL3.760 End Mon
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- A threat of big interventions by the central bank helped the Brazil's real rally for a second-straight day Tuesday, preventing losses for a currency that has been battered by worries about a win Sunday by left-wing presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

 After a 3.1% rally in the previous session on big dollar sales by the monetary authority, the real finished 4.1% stronger Tuesday at BRL3.610 per dollar, compared with BRL3.760 per dollar at Monday's close. 

 Traders said rumors throughout the day that the central bank would intervene at anytime pushed the real stronger. After the real's close, the central bank confirmed it intervened in the forex market. 

 "There were lots of rumors that the central bank would intervene, but there was no evidence of selling until late in the day," said one Sao Paulo trader. 

 The interventions came in addition to a sale of export credit lines and debt buybacks held to stabilize bond and currency prices. 

 According to central bank data, at least $162 million was spent on interventions Monday, though some analysts put the number at as much as $300 million. 

 Besides the interventions, there is also a sense here among some commentators that the real is grossly undervalued and that a Lula presidency would be less dangerous than some investors would believe. 

 Roberto Setubal, the head of banking giant Banco Itau SA (ITU), Monday said Lula would be a pragmatist as president, rather than a left-wing ideologue. He also said market jitters shouldn't be allowed to impact the presidential transition. 

 Later Tuesday, Central Bank Monetary Policy Director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo is slated to hold a press conference on plans for debt rollovers and forex interventions.

title: Chile's Massad Warns Of Downside Risk To GDP Forecasts
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Chilean Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad said Tuesday there is a downside risk to the country's economic growth forecasts, given the shaky environment globally and in its own backyard. 

 "We judge the bias to be downward," said Massad in a speech at the Council of Americas in New York. 

 The central bank has already revised downward its 2002 economic growth forecast to the 2.0% to 2.5% range, as much of the global economy sputters and financial shock waves emanate from Argentina and Brazil, its two larger South American neighbors. 

 Chile's economy is one of the most outward looking in the world, with exports of goods and services comprising an estimated 36% of gross domestic product. During the 1990s, it routinely booked 5%-plus GDP growth. 

 The central bank is forecasting tentatively that GDP will grow between 3.5% and 4.5% in 2003 and 5% in 2004, but Massad acknowledged he wasn't heartened by the mood at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund in Washington this past weekend. 

 "As the meetings went on, the question marks were bigger and bigger," he said in reference to the global economic outlook. 

 The IMF is projecting Latin American GDP will contract 0.6% this year, despite pockets of growth in a handful of countries, including Chile. 

 The slowdown in the world and regional economy has pushed prices for copper, Chile's single-largest export, down to around $0.67 a pound, "the lowest we've had since 1934" in real terms, according to the central banker. 

 Regional turmoil isn't helping matters. Massad estimated that the travails of Argentina, where the economy is expected to contract around 15% in the wake of last December's debt default, have probably had a negative impact of half a percentage point on Chile's GDP. 

 Market upheaval in Brazil this year ahead of presidential elections has probably had a negative impact of only around 0.2 or 0.3 percentage point of GDP, according to the central banker, who pointed out that Chilean corporate investments in Brazil are only about half as big as in Argentina. 

 But he admitted that his country is vulnerable to a continued market sell-off in Brazil, which has seen its currency weaken around 40% and bond spreads widen more than 1500 basis points this year amid growing fears that it too may be headed to default. 

 "The main risk," Massad warned, is that a Brazilian crisis might "weaken the capacity of the markets to discriminate the situations of different countries." 

 Chile is South America's last remaining investment-grade credit, after ratings agencies demoted Uruguay to junk status as contagion from Argentina and Brazil overwhelmed the tiny country. 

Forex Intervention Only In `Extraordinary' Case



Chile's markets have been feeling some heat in recent weeks, with the
peso weakening to CLP748.80 to the dollar Monday, a new record closing
low and down 8.3% from the end of June.



"We are looking closely at what's going on with the peso rate," said
Massad, adding that the bank's international reserves, at around $15
billion, are available to intervene in the foreign exchange market if
necessary.



But he also suggested that he wasn't overly concerned with the current
exchange rate, and that intervention would require more than the peso
weakening only against the greenback, given the country's diversified
export markets.



"For intervention to be justified, we have to consider that the
situation is extraordinary, that is, that the peso is not moving with
the rest of the currencies, but that it has taken a loss by itself,"
said Massad, adding that this hasn't been the case until now.



He also noted that a weaker peso helps the export sector, which, along
with construction, is the main driver of the Chilean economy.



And unlike Argentina and Brazil, which are saddled with heavy
dollar-linked debt obligations, a weakening local currency actually
eases fiscal pressures in Chile, given that the government only has $7
billion in foreign debt, Massad added.



Chile last intervened in the foreign exchange market last year, in the
wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. that sent financial
markets reeling.



Massad said he felt comfortable that Chile will be able to meet its 3%
inflation target this year. He pointed out that yields on domestic debt
indicate that the market also believes annual inflation will be around
3%, not just this year, but over the next five years.



-By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026;
mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Ends Stronger At BRL3.760/Dlr Vs BRL3.875
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Dashing expectations that the real would slip to BRL4.00 per dollar on worries that Workers' Party presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is moving closer to an Oct. 6 victory, Brazil's central bank intervened heavily Monday to help the currency finish 3.1% stronger. 

 The real ended at BRL3.760 per dollar, compared with BRL3.875 at Friday's close. The central bank said it sold dollars on the spot market, but didn't disclose the size of the interventions, as is customary. 

 Traders, however, said the monetary authority acted in larger volumes than usual. One forex consultancy put the size of the interventions at $300 million, about triple the amount of other recent interventions. 

 The central bank was active throughout the session, selling some $43.3 million in export credit lines and buying back BRL110 million in floating-rate bills to help stabilize currency and bond markets. 

 Traders had expected the real to fall on polls released over the weekend and early Monday that showed Lula's support base is rising, and on a view that the monetary authority would fail to roll over a large batch of dollar-linked debt set to mature Tuesday. Paying off the debt would boost the amount of reals in circulation in a forex market that already has too few dollars. 

 Traders said the central bank appeared to be acting to squeeze any speculators out of the market and offer liquidity to firms buying dollars to service external debts. 

 "This was a very crazy day," said one Sao Paulo trader, noting that the real opened 2.1% weaker at BRL3.96 per dollar Monday, its weakest-ever intraday level since being introduced in 1994 to stamp out hyperinflation. 

 While analysts expect extreme volatility to continue for the rest of this week, key members of Brazil's business and political community are saying positive things about Lula to help calm investors' nerves about a victory that looks increasingly likely. 

 Monday, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's wife Ruth said a Lula presidency "wouldn't be a disaster" and Roberto Setubal, the head of banking giant Banco Itau SA (ITU), called Lula a pragmatist, instead of a left-wing ideologue. 

 Speaking in Washington, Setubal said Lula "will be the next president for sure." He also said the recent selloff of the real amounts to an "overreaction" by the market and said Brazil's banking system is "well prepared" for a political transition. 

 The comments by the first lady and Setubal complemented a growing list of endorsements Lula has received in recent weeks from some members of Brazil's business community. 

 Monday Lula reiterated commitments to honoring all international contracts and primary budget surplus targets. 

 -By Terry Wade, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511.3145.1479; terry.wade@dowjones.com 

 Despite Monday's rally, the real lost 23% of its value against the dollar in the third quarter of 2002.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.126/Dlr Vs BRL3.105 Wednesday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real weakened Thursday, dragged lower by lingering concerns about the pace of recovery in the world's largest economy and how a slowdown there may delay a rebound in economic activity here. 

 The real shed 2.1 centavos to close at BRL3.126 to the dollar, following a downturn in U.S. equity markets following worse-than-expected jobless data. The Brazilian currency, down 26% so far this year, closed Wednesday at BRL3.105. 

 The Central Bank of Brazil intervened, selling $50 million in 77-day dollar repurchase agreements and $43.9 million in six-month export credit lines. 

 Yet traders said President George W. Bush's call on the United Nations to support the U.S. in taking action against Iraq fueled fears of war on a day when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan also warned of continued pressures on the U.S. federal budget outlook. 

 "Things look pretty ugly overseas and there's not much reason for optimism," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 On the local front, a presidential poll was less favorable than expected. The Vox Populi survey showed the government's candidate Jose Serra stuck at 19% in second, countering expectations of a steady rise in the run-up to the Oct. 6 first-round vote. Front-runner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party advanced three points to 39%. 

 There is still hope that Serra's strategy of late to attack Lula's lack of experience in television commercials may bear fruit in the coming weeks. However, a Middle East conflict could undo much of the improvement in sentiment, as Brazil is a net importer of oil and relies on foreign capital to finance much of its growth. 

 "Further improvements on the Serra front in the coming weeks should have positive impacts on Brazilian assets and the real, but a U.S. attack against Iraq, and its potential impacts on risk aversion and oil prices, will at least neutralize and possibly reverse those impacts," wrote Ricardo Amorim, head of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York. 

 By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11 3145-1481 adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: Brazil 's Real Ends Weaker Despite Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended weaker Tuesday, despite a central bank intervention on the spot market to stop the currency's slide. 

 The real ended at BRL3.137 per dollar, compared with BRL3.100 at Monday's close. The real lost as much as 1.8% Tuesday after rallying 1.9% in the previous session. 

 "Things are very volatile and there won't be clear trend in the real until the elections are over," said a Rio  de Janeiro-based trader. 

 He added that the dollar is still in relatively short supply on the local forex market, despite words of support from foreign banks that they will keep existing credit lines  open to Brazilian companies. 

 Finance Minister Pedro Malan and Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga are meeting with European officials this week to ask them to boost trade financing to local exporters. 

 On the politics front, traders say they are pleased that government-backed candidate Jose Serra consolidated his second-place spot at about 20% in two polls Tuesday. 

 But any gains in the real were held in check by frontrunner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hit 40% in the polls, leading some to speculate that he could win the presidency in a first-round vote Oct. 6 by gaining more than  50% of the vote on election day. The market hopes Serra will beat Lula in a second-round runoff Oct. 27. 

 The week dollar is keeping inflationary pressures relatively high, diminishing hopes that the central bank will take advantage of its negative bias on interest rates and cut the country's base rate of 18.0% in coming weeks. 

 Meanwhile, Brazil's futures exchange, the BM&F said it will hold a minute of silence Wednesday at 1300 GMT to remember Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S.
