title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.152/Dlr Vs BRL3.120 Wednesday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Growing fears of a U.S. invasion of Iraq ahead of the anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. sent the Brazilian real weaker for the fourth session running Thursday, and investors are losing hope that news on the domestic front may reverse the declining trend in the near term. 

 The real closed at BRL3.152 to the dollar, near the weak point of the day of BRL3.160, despite a central bank intervention on the spot market and a sale of $52.5 million in six-month export credits. Wednesday, the real finished at BRL3.120. 

 Traders said most of Thursday's weakening followed worries about the global and domestic economic outlooks as there was little pressure on the spot market, unlike the three previous sessions. 

 "We saw signs of a bear market setting in today," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 Going forward, traders expect volatility to continue in both directions, as war fears are likely to continue depressing global stock markets while the outlook for the Brazilian presidential elections coming up in October remains uncertain. 

 The real has shed 14.2 centavos since closing Friday at BRL3.010 to the dollar. So far this year, the currency has lost 27% of its value. 

 As concern grows about the near future, traders are once  again questioning the central bank's intervention firepower  to tame a possible bear market. 

 Under the $30 billion agreement with the International Monetary Fund, the central bank is allowed to sell dollars on the market - via spot sales or export credits - and buy back external debt up to $3 billion every moving 30-day period. 

 So far this month, market players estimate that the monetary authority has spent about $2.1 billion of the country's reserves in interventions and buybacks. Brazil's international reserves, net of IMF funds, currently stand at  about $23.5 billion. 

 "What the central bank has left to intervene is enough to tame markets under relatively normal conditions, but not a market that's growing pessimistic," said another Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 Meanwhile, not even a relatively successful sale of foreign-exchange swap contracts managed to lift investors' spirits. 

 The central bank sold $716 million in 2002 and 2003 currency swaps, securing the rollover of 36% of a $1.97 billion lot of dollar-linked debt coming due Sept. 11. The rates on the swaps were high - between 24.50% and 27.49% - but in line with market rates. 

 The monetary authority has another three sessions to try  to refinance the rest of the maturing debt, increasing the likelihood that it may be successful.

title: Brazil's Real Ends Weaker At BRL3.100 Vs BRL3.062 Monday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Rattled by slumping markets and heightened risk aversion overseas, Brazil's real ended weaker Tuesday despite an intervention and sale of export credits by the central bank. 

 The real closed at BRL3.100 per dollar, compared with BRL3.062 at Monday's close. 

 The central bank's sale of $50 million in export credits, which helped boost the supply of dollars on the local foreign exchange market, saw demand of about $120 million. 

 The size of the monetary authority's spot market intervention wasn't disclosed. 

 During the session, Brazil's Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga said that a tough external environment is limiting chances for an interest rate cut to the current base rate of 18.00%. 

 The real has lost about 2.9% of its value since Friday, when it was trading at BRL3.01 and analysts have said the central bank might cut rates if the currency held steady around the BRL3.00 level. 

 But Fraga noted that signs of renewed lending here by foreign banks are very encouraging. 

 Brazil's national development bank, or BNDES, received commitments for $300 million in trade financing from an Asian lender late Monday. 

 The currency also weakened despite a Vox Populi poll for the country's October presidential election showing government-backed candidate Jose Serra is technically tied for second place with arch rival Ciro Gomes, a former Ceara state governor. 

 Serra, who is viewed as market friendly, and Gomes are each hoping to make it past an Oct. 6 first round vote to face frontrunner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in an Oct. 27 runoff. 

 The market also shrugged off a poll by survey firm Ibope that showed Serra has now overtaken Gomes in the state of Sao Paulo, Brazil's biggest electorate.

title: Brazil Fraga: External Scenario Hampering Rate Cut
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga Tuesday said an adverse global environment was  hampering a further reduction in the short-term benchmark rate of 18.00%. 

 Talking on a conference call sponsored by local press agency Agencia Estado, Fraga also said markets should be more aware that Brazil "will be able to manage its fate well." 

 "The global backdrop has gotten in our way but we are closely watching" how the external scenario develops, he said, referring to the possibility of a reduction in interest rates. 

 The comments come as investors were starting to grow hopeful that the central bank would be able to deliver an intermeeting rate cut as soon as this week because of encouraging signs of currency appreciation and less volatility in the last week of August. 

 In August, the central bank kept the interest rates on hold but set a downward bias. 

 However, the real weakened Monday and Tuesday. Since Friday's close of BRL3.010 to the dollar, the currency has shed 2.9% of its value. It's a depreciation that Fraga attributed to a hostile global environment. 

 By 1355 GMT, the real was trading at BRL3.103 to the dollar after closing at BRL3.062. Meanwhile, the main Sao Paulo stocks index was trading 2.6% lower at 10,109 points. The markets were reacting to lower-than-expected U.S. manufacturing activity. 

 Fraga added the decision to set a downward bias for interest rates follows a central bank 2003 inflation forecast that was well below the government's 4% target for the year. 

 He wouldn't comment on the exact estimate. 

 Fraga said there are "preliminary signs" that foreign banks are resuming the supply of trade finance lines to Brazilian companies following his trip to New York last week. He wouldn't provide figures. 

 He added that it was an extremely positive sign to see low demand for trade credit lines being offered by the central bank. 

 "This means that supply (of trade lines) is improving and also that there's a rhythm for the market to absorb (the lines provided by the central bank," he said. 

 The central bank decided to offer trade lines to local banks to arrest a severe overseas credit crunch at a time when foreign banks are holding back amid worry about Brazil's debt outlook and presidential elections in October. So far, the monetary authority has placed nearly $500 million in trade credit lines. Officials said they could go beyond $2 billion in such offerings. 

 He also said Brazil could negotiate better terms with the International Monetary Fund for a $30 billion aid package and seek permission to dig deeper into the country's reserves to carry out interventions and buy back debt. Under the current terms, Brazil committed to keeping its international reserves higher than $10 billion. 

 ""It would be a lot easier to renegotiate the floor for international reserves than seek more aid funds," he said, adding that there's a precedent within the IMF for a negative reserve floor "if the circumstances demand it." 

 He said such measures could be necessary in the event that global environment "remains dry and hostile." 

 Fraga also said the government's recent forecast that the primary budget surplus for 2002 would reach 3.9% of gross domestic product - compared with an IMF target of 3.75% - was just "fine tuning."

title: Emerging debt-Brazil inches upward as default fears subside.
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Emerging market sovereign bonds inched upwards on Wednesday as profit-taking following Brazil's recently-announced $30 billion IMF package trailed off and investor fears of a near-term default on Brazilian debt appeared to subside. 

 Brazil's share of the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Plus rose 1.92 percent in terms of daily returns, while the broader market edged up 0.72 percent in thin trading. 

 Last week the International Monetary Fund delivered a $30 billion rescue package to Brazil, virtually guaranteeing the country's ability to meet its debt obligations at least through the remainder of 2002. 

 The IMF bailout gave temporary reprieve to Brazil's strapped bonds, which are down about 30 percent for the year on investor fears about the lead of leftist candidates in the October presidential elections, but the euphoria did not last long as nervous investors sparked a massive sell-off lasting well into this week. 

 "Prices as they are now, particularly in the debt market, are extremely low," said Ricardo Amorim, head of Latin American research at IDEAGlobal. "The risk of a default in Brazilian debt this year is virtually zero and I think that was why there was a small bounce." 

 Some analysts say Brazilian bond prices currently reflect a default probability of about 50 percent and were due for a rebound. 

 Knut Langholm, a senior vice-president at State Street Research, said he was not surprised to see an uptick in Brazil's bonds because the bout of profit-taking had largely run its course. 

 Many investors, however, preferred to sit on the sidelines, after Brazil's latest presidential polls showed market favorite Jose Serra's support stagnating at around 13 percent less than two months before the Oct. 6 election. 

 "It is just natural that since the polls are largely unchanged, volatility will decline," said Langholm. "The decline in volatility is consistent with slightly firmer prices." 

 A poll released Wednesday afternoon showed center-leftist Ciro Gomes closing the gap on front-runner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, while Serra remained wedged in a distant third with only 13.4 percent of the votes. A poll on Tuesday night showed similar results. 

 MARKET SHOULD STABILIZE 

 Brazil's benchmark C bonds were up 1.5 points at 53 and are expected to settle in the 50 to 55 range over the next few days, according to Langholm. 

 "I really don't see the polls changing that," he said. 

 Still, others are concerned the rally will be difficult to sustain. 

 "The markets still feel heavy and are trading without much conviction on the upside," Amorim said in a research report. 

 Serra's support in recent weeks has lagged that of the two leftist front-runners, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Ciro Gomes, by about 20 percentage points. 

 Investors are worried that Lula or Gomes, if elected, would undo critical economic policies and push the country toward a default on its $250 billion public debt-load. 

 Traders said the bonds were also propped up on talk Brazil's Central Bank is considering intervening in the market to improve credit conditions for local companies. 

 "The use of net international reserves should be announced in the next few days and should help the currency stabilize, at least on a temporary basis," Morgan Stanley said in a Tuesday research report. 

 The market also welcomed news that all the leading candidates in the presidential race said on Tuesday they would meet with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to discuss the country's economic state and lay the groundwork for a smooth transition of power in January. 

 "There have been a couple of local banks that are buying on speculation that the meetings will go well, and then you'll have some follow-on buying," said one trader.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.205/Dlr Vs BRL3.165 End Tue
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Though the central bank intervened on the spot market, Brazil's real ended weaker Wednesday as a lackluster sale of foreign exchange  swaps pressured the currency, along with worries about the outcome of October presidential elections and a lack of export financing for local companies. 

 The real finished at BRL3.205 per dollar, about 1.2% weaker than BRL3.165 at Tuesday's close. 

 During the session, the monetary authority sold about $24 million in Oct. 1 forex swaps at a linear rate of 28.5%. Though it rejected many bids, the central bank was hoping to sell as much as $800 million in forex swaps Wednesday to complete the rollover of a batch of $2.5 billion in dollar-linked debt set to mature Thursday. 

 Between Monday and Tuesday, the central bank sold about $1.5 billion in forex swaps. If the rollovers aren't completed, hedging instruments currently in the market will expire and likely force the real to weaken. 

 The central bank confirmed after the market closed that it intervened in the market Wednesday. As is customary, it didn't say how many dollars it sold. 

 Traders said the monetary authority intervened five times on the market Wednesday but were unable to estimate the volume of dollars sold to foreign exchange dealers. 

Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga discontinued daily interventions
last week, though he said he would act to affect the market's direction
or provide liquidity as necessary.

title: Emerging Debt-Brazil slides as political woes weigh.
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Brazilian sovereign bonds slipped almost 2 percent in a see-saw session on Tuesday as persistent concerns about the sizable lead of two left-leaning candidates in October's presidential candidates curdled the mood of investors. 

 Brazil's share of the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Plus turned lower in late afternoon trading, falling 1.73 percent in terms of daily returns in the thinly traded session. The nation's benchmark C bond shed 0.625 points to 51.375 bid. 

 The slide came as investors continue to fret about the chasm separating Wall Street's favorite candidate, government-backed Jose Serra, and leftish candidates Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Ciro Gomes. 

 "The relative dominance of political concerns over all else will probably continue to prevail, at least in the near term," said Mark Siegel, an emerging market fund manager with D.L. Babson & Co., a member of the MassMutual Financial Group. 

 Politics has been the overreaching theme in Brazilian markets for months and has returned to the spotlight in recent days, in spite of last week's $30 billion International Monetary Fund lifeline aimed at shoring up battered markets. 

 Investors are worried that Lula or Gomes, if elected, would mismanage the economy and push Brazil toward a default on its $250 billion debt load. Some analysts say Brazilian bond prices currently reflect a default probability of about 50 percent. 

 Brazil's bonds also swung on rumors that an election poll due out late on Tuesday would show Serra, now trailing his opponents in a distant third place by some 20 percentage points, making a bit of headway. 

 "There's a rumor that Serra will get 2 percent better in the next poll," said one emerging debt trader. "I don't think anyone's going to get too excited about that, but the volume is so thin it's tough to get a read for what's going on." 

 Traders in Sao Paulo said there was also speculation Brazil's central bank might be buying up bonds, but the central bank declined to comment. 

 In the midst of the election-linked turmoil, ratings agency Moody's Investors Service late on Monday cut its ceiling for foreign currency bonds one notch to B2, or five notches below investment grade. 

 Moody's said the downgrade came amid concerns the incoming government will face growing fiscal pressures that could translate into risks in the external sector, particularly if a further weakening of Brazil's real increases the burden on dollar borrowers. 

 Moody's now has Brazil rated below Bolivia and Bulgaria and on par with Honduras, Venezuela and Lebanon. 

 The move by Moody's weighed on the real earlier on Tuesday, but bond and currency investors had largely looked past the news by late in the day. Traders said bonds were already trading at levels below the new Moody's rating. 

 "It doesn't help, but I don't think it has a tremendous drive on taking prices lower right now," said another emerging debt trader. The volatile session came instead because "there are political concerns, there's poor liquidity in the market overall and there's uncertainty about central bank intervention." 

Brazil weighed on the broader market, sinking the EMBI-Plus 0.50 percent in terms of daily returns and pressuring the neighbors of Latin America's largest economy. 

 Colombian debt lost 1.48 percent in terms of daily returns, Venezuela shed 0.38 percent and Peru lost 2.09 percent. 

 Even Mexico, seen as a relative safe haven as its close trade ties with the United States help to insulate it from Latin American fallout, slid 0.41 percent on the day.

title: Brazil rejoices in record $30 bln IMF loan accord.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's government and markets rejoiced on Thursday over a record $30 billion IMF loan that boosted global optimism that the country can smoothly ride out turbulent presidential elections. 

 Markets from New York to Europe rallied after the International Monetary Fund came to the rescue of Latin America's largest economy, which has struggled for months to restore eroding investor confidence ahead of October elections which the leftist opposition has strong chances of winning. 

 Brazil's currency, the real, plunged to record lows late last month, stocks fell and bond spreads spiraled as investors feared the hard-won economic stability of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's government was under threat. 

 But with the IMF credit, which was much larger than expected, investors took the view that Brazil is now safe from turning into another Argentina, Brazil's southern neighbor which is in the grip of its worst economic crisis in memory. 

 "This is going to give markets what they need to recover and make a safe transition to a new government," said Roberto Dantas, an economist at Banco Schahin, a Sao Paulo brokerage. 

 The real closed 3.8 percent higher at 2.91 per dollar, after reaching 3.605 on July 31. Stocks ended 4.5 percent higher and Brazil's foreign bonds rose 5.5 percent. 

 "With this international aid, the next president will have a base, a support to consolidate his program and policies, and calm down investors, savers, citizens and society," Central Bank President Arminio Fraga told investors in a videoconference. "With this the economy will grow." 

 CARDOSO LEGACY AT STAKE? 

 Cardoso's low inflation policies, mass privatizations and controlled public spending helped make Brazil the second largest recipient of foreign direct investment in the emerging market universe in recent years. "This is not just a vote of confidence in the government but in the country, which has the ability to fulfill its commitments," Cardoso said. 

 Concerns that Cardoso's achievements could be undone by the incoming president have been a driving force behind investor worries and helped explain why many analysts were still reluctant to sound the all-clear on Brazil's economic health. 

 "There is uncertainty because these politicians don't have a track record and that is still a risk that continues," said Siobhan Manning, a Latin American debt strategist at the Italian investment bank Caboto. 

 Credit rating agency Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it retained a negative outlook on Brazil's ratings despite the IMF loan, saying doubts about the economy linger. 

 Still, the deal won supportive comments from rich nations. In a statement on behalf of the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations, Canada's Finance Minister John Manley said the G7 welcomed the agreement, adding it "should help restore market confidence." 

 Investors' central concern has been that the next president would be unable to handle Brazil's $250 billion public debt, the cost of which has soared as the currency has slumped. 

 But IMF first deputy managing director Anne Krueger said Brazil's debt is sustainable and there were big differences between Brazil and Argentina. Argentina's debt default led some investors to believe Brazil could go the same way. 

 "There are a number of issues in Argentina which simply are not there in Brazil," Krueger said in Geneva. 

 A major reason why markets have worried about the debt burden - which represents just under 60 percent of economic output - is that leading left-wing presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the past had espoused renegotiating the terms of Brazil's public debt and frowned on IMF policies. 

 CANDIDATES SUPPORT IMF DEAL 

 But in a sign that Lula has changed his stance, his running mate, businessman Jose Alencar, told foreign correspondents on Thursday that: "The responsibility of this deal with the IMF is the responsibility of Brazil, not just this government." 

 Eighty percent of the $30 billion in new funds from the IMF would be disbursed in 2003, the first year of the new administration, as long as the next president meets a 2003 primary budget surplus target of 3.75 percent of economic output. Progress toward that target will be revised quarterly. 

 The primary budget surplus excludes debt-servicing costs. 

 Government candidate Jose Serra, who is lagging far behind in polls, and center-left former finance minister Ciro Gomes, have also indicated they support a deal with the IMF. 

 "Support of the main candidates for this deal will not be missing," Finance Minister Pedro Malan said. 

 Fraga said that with the IMF agreement, his country will halt daily intervention in foreign exchange markets to prop up the real but stood ready to step in whenever necessary. 

 Under the accord, the permitted floor on Brazil's foreign exchange reserves was cut to $5 billion from $15 billion, giving the central bank a much larger intervention war chest. 

 Malan said Brazil is also talking with the Inter-American Development Bank and the World Bank, but gave no details. 

 (Additional reporting by Isabel Versiani, Claudia Pires, Katherine Baldwin).

title: Brazil 's Fraga says daily  forex intervention  over.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank will stop its daily intervention in the foreign exchange market as of now, with future intervention carried out as necessary to stabilize the nation's battered currency, the real, Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said on Thursday. 

 The end of daily intervention came after Latin America's largest economy won a $30 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund, sending the real, stocks and bonds sharply higher after weeks of slumps on investor nervousness ahead of October presidential elections. 

 Under the IMF accord, the allowed floor on Brazil's foreign exchange reserves was cut to $5 billion from $15 billion, giving the central bank a much larger war chest to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 Fraga said that under the IMF deal, if foreign exchange market intervention exceeds $3 billion in any 30-day period, Brazil will have to hold a "dialogue" with the IMF. 

 Through July, the Central Bank had been selling $50 million a day in the currency market in an effort to halt the slide of the real, which continued to fall to record lows at the end of last month.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL2.910/Dlr Vs BRL3.020 Wednesday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- A larger-than-expected $30 billion International Monetary Fund rescue package for Brazil boosted the local currency Thursday, though investors are still unsure about foreign banks' willingness to resume lending to local companies ahead of the October presidential election. 

 The real opened at BRL2.860 to the dollar and hit an intraday low of BRL2.930 before settling at BRL2.910 to the dollar, its strongest close since July 22. Wednesday, the real gained 9.5 centavos to BRL3.020. 

 Traders said the IMF package, the biggest of the Fund's history, restores confidence in a nation that saw its bonds and currency fall so fast in recent weeks to the point that, for a few days, a default was appeared imminent. 

 But Thursday's rally was interrupted by a number of transactions that had been put on hold ever since the real hit the unimaginable level of BRL3.610 during nervous intraday trading last Wednesday. 

 "The IMF package is large and important, but it's going to take a while before the local market returns to normal," said Alexandre Vasarhelyi, head of the forex desk at ING Barings in Sao Paulo. 

 "Some investors seeking to do (currency) hedging, importers, people seeking to send funds to offshore accounts, they were all waiting for a respite to do business," he added. 

 Market players were quick to say that the IMF's decision to allow the central bank to use an additional $10 billion from the country's international reserves to intervene on the market was by far the most important feature of the new IMF program. 

 The decision prompted Brazil's central bank to change its intervention strategy and introduce an element of surprise to it. 

Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga said the central bank would from now on intervene only when deemed necessary, halting a program that called for daily interventions of $50 million that had been in place since early July. He also suggested the central bank would intervene more aggressively going forward, saying that Brazil has the IMF's green light to do interventions of up to $3 billion in a moving 30-day period. 

 The first actions under the intervention policy took place as soon as Thursday. In addition to selling an undisclosed sum of dollars on the spot market, the central bank also sold $50 million worth of 85-day repos at a maximum exchange rate of BRL2.962554. 

 Yet, traders say the Brazilian economic outlook remains uncertain as two opposition candidates are leading in the polls for Brazil's presidency, raising concern that the country may shift toward unorthodox or market-unfriendly policies. 

 Also, one of the country's three main presidential candidates, Ciro Gomes of the center-left Labor Front, is yet to announce his formal support for the IMF agreement. Front-runner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the left-wing Workers' Party did so earlier Thursday. Government-backed Jose Serra also said he's in favor of the agreement. 

 The main indication of confidence would be a return of foreign financing and credit lines to the country, say traders, which isn't happening just yet. 

 But there one important positive sign Thursday. The September currency futures contract finished implying a rate that equaled the spot rate for the first time in nearly two months. Recently, the forward rate was trading below the spot rate, a market anomaly that only occurs when there's too much demand for physical dollars amid perceived conversion and counterparty risk.

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL3.020/Dlr Vs BRL3.115 Tuesday
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real rallied Wednesday, boosted by expectations that the International Monetary Fund will soon provide the nation with a fresh aid package that could extend into 2003. 

 The real added 9.5 centavos to end at BRL3.020 to the dollar, also supported by rumors that the upcoming presidential poll will show that the government-backed candidate still stands a chance of winning. 

 On Tuesday, the real gained 10.5 centavos to close at BRL3.115. 

 Talk is that the new IMF agreement, which investors expect to be announced as soon as late Wednesday, would allow the central bank to boost its intervention power. Also, Brazil would be allowed to use part of the IMF funds to help restore scarce commercial credit lines for Brazilian companies, according to market rumors. 

 "If the rumors are true, and I've no reason to believe they aren't, it becomes more difficult for people to bet against the real," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 President Fernando Henrique Cardoso had lunch with Finance Minister Pedro Malan, Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga, Planning Minister Guilherme Dias and Presidential Chief of Staff Pedro Parente Wednesday, suggesting that an official announcement about the IMF deal may come soon. 

 But the Finance Ministry said it had no news on the IMF agreement just yet and wouldn't comment on any rumors. 

 Market players said the new agreement would include $2 billion in new IMF aid funds, plus $2.5 billion in World Bank loans. 

 In addition, talk is that the $7 billion of IMF funds that Brazil has already drawn down from an existing $15.5 billion facility may be used to back commercial credit lines for local firms. 

 The Fund also would allow the central bank to use an extra $5 billion from the country's international reserves to intervene on the market. 

 On the October elections front, rumors started to circulate that an Ibope poll set for release Thursday evening would show opposition candidate Ciro Gomes - who is second in the polls - falling by as many as five percentage points. That would mark an interruption in Gomes's fast-rising trend, fueling hope that lagging government-backed candidate Jose Serra, now third, still stands a chance of making it to a runoff vote Oct. 27. 

 In the latest July 27-29 Ibope poll, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the left-wing Workers' Party rose to 34% from 33%, while challenger Gomes dropped to 25% from 26%. Support for Serra rose to 14% from 13%. Voting intentions for former Rio de Janeiro governor Anthony Garotinho remained at 11%. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank confirmed it intervened on the spot market as part of its daily intervention program. The institution said it would sell $50 million in foreign currency daily and roll over all dollar repos coming due this month in a total August program of at least $1.84 billion.

title: THE BOTTOM LINE: Spanish Blue Chips Suffer In Brazil
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 MADRID -(Dow Jones)- The decline of the Brazilian real is posing an increasing threat to the earnings and balance sheets of Spain's largest companies. 

 Investor concern about Brazil's ability to service its debt, combined with fears that the presidency could fall into the hands of a left-leaning candidate in October, pushed the Brazilian real down 19% against the dollar in July alone. That may now force Spain's blue chips into additional provisions, write downs, and asset sales, and explains much of the recent slump in the IBEX-35 index, down 16% over the last month. 

 The crisis is weighing heavily on the earnings and capital ratios of Spain's two largest banks, Santander Central Hispano SA (STD) and Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria SA (BBV). It's also weakening the key earnings to debt ratios of telecom giant Telefonica SA (TEF), and prompting ratings agencies to downgrade the companies' bonds. 

 "But it's wider concerns than just the technical ones on debt," said Goldman Sachs credit analyst Felix Kaiser. "The real worry is that Brazil gets a more interventionist government and the environment for Telefonica and other companies in Brazil worsens. Brazil has performed really well for Telefonica, but that could change." 

 Telefonica's shares have dropped 40% so far this year, while SCH and BBVA shares are both down 36%. 

 Given the importance of Brazil to their businesses, withdrawal from the country isn't an option for any of the companies, even in the nightmare scenario of a leftist election victory, debt default, and the imposition of capital controls. 

 There are, too, strong cultural ties with Latin America and Spanish companies have stuck it out through the even graver crisis in Argentina. 

 Of the two banks, SCH has a much larger exposure to Brazil with total investment of around EUR7.39 billion and 8.3% of total assets in the troubled country, compared with investment of EUR1.5 billion and 1.9% of assets for BBVA. 

 Last week, SCH posted a fall in profits as weaker Latin American currencies resulted in lower revenues, and a EUR190 million loss of Brazilian government debt resulted in a 43% decline in trading profits. 

 The bank may have to establish provisions to cover further losses of its $6.5 billion portfolio of Brazilian government debt. 

 And charges against reserves of around EUR1.2 billion to account for currency depreciation lowered the bank's core capital ratio (minus preferred shares) to 4.56% from 5.15% at the end of the first quarter. 

 Core capital includes a bank's equity capital - which includes ordinary and preferred shares - and retained earnings minus goodwill. It measures the amount freely available for a bank to absorb losses without having to stop trading. Preferred shares are normally excluded from the calculation because, as they require guaranteed dividend payments, they are considered lower quality capital. 

 The Bank of Spain recommends banks maintain a ratio of core capital minus preferred shares of 6%. 

 Even before it published its results, SCH was downgraded by Standard & Poor's Corp. Following the earnings, Moody's Investors Service Inc. placed the bank's ratings under review. 

 SCH is now under pressure to sell off some of the stakes it holds in Spanish companies and banks around the world, although the bank's management admits market conditions aren't encouraging and sales would reduce its cushion to cover further losses from Latin America. 

 The alternative, however, would be to hold a rights issue, diluting shareholder equity and reducing earnings per share. 

 Analysts expect SCH to realize capital gains before resorting to a rights issue.The bank said its investment portfolio held latent capital gains of EUR5 billion at the end of the first half including its 20% stake in Spanish oil company Compania Espanola de Petroleos SA (E.CES) and a 12% stake in utility Union Fenosa SA (E.FEN). 


   Telefonica Cashflows Under Threat



Telefonica has invested around EUR24 billion in Brazil since 1998, and
about a quarter of its total EBITDA and cashflow comes from there.



Friday, Moody's put Telefonica's A2 debt rating on downgrade review
"on concerns related to the uncertainties in Brazil, ahead of the
October general elections."



The market now anticipates negative action from Standard & Poor's.



While a Telefonica spokeswoman said 99.3% of its EUR1.5 billion debt
in Brazil is hedged, financial gains made from hedging aren't included
in the EBITDA line, so don't help offset the deterioration in the EBITDA
to debt ratio.



Felix Kaiser at Goldman Sachs said the fall of the real could require
Telefonica to write down the value of its Brazilian assets. After the
drop in the currency at the beginning of 1999, Telefonica made a EUR717
million write down of its assets there.



Key to the Moody's review will be Telefonica's decision to freeze its
expansion in European 3G, which will save it billions of euro in capital
expenditure and operating losses, potentially mitigating the effects of
Brazil.



However, some bears argue too much of the company's ability to pay
down debt and distribute dividends is still hinged on the repatriation
of cash from Latin America.



Lehman Brothers warned in a downgrade note last week: "The decision to
pay a dividend is laudable, but we note that 60% of deleveraging post
the dividend comes from Latin America."



The company's repatriation of cash will only add to the outflow of
capital that is contributing to the regional crisis and to the fall of
currencies like the real, and could prompt action from the Brazilian
central bank and government.



Moody's said: "The review process will mainly focus on the potential
impact on Telefonica's future free cash flow of the high volatility of
the real as well as the hypothetical measures which the central bank
might consider in the future to stabilise the local currency."



And observers warn that Telefonica's wireline business in Spain,
currently the source of the bulk of its cashflow, is under increasing
pressure.



Standard & Poor's said in its latest comment July 25: "The primary
ratings focus will continue to be the impact of the volatile financial
and political environment in Brazil...and regulatory pressures in
domestic fixed-line operations."



   BBVA Faces Indirect Risks



Although BBVA posted an 8.9% fall in first half net profit and gave a
full-year warning in line with SCH's, Brazil is seen having less of an
impact on the bank.



BBVA said it had charged about EUR950 million against reserves for
currency depreciation, which helped to lower its core capital ratio
(minus preferred shares) to 5.9%, which although lower than the 6%
recommended by the Bank of Spain, remains considerably better than
SCH's.



But Brazil could affect BBVA through an investment portfolio that
carries significant exposure there.



BBVA said a EUR209 million provision made to account for a EUR4.8
billion charge made by Telefonica, primarily to restructure European 3G
operations, is one of the main factors behind its expected decline in
2002 profits.



Continued meltdown in the Brazilian economy could also force BBVA to
provision against losses there.



"We caution that BBVA's exposure to Brazil is by no means immaterial,"
Bear Stearns warned in a research note.



Spain's second largest electricity company Iberdrola SA (E.IBR) has
also suffered from its exposure to Brazil, which accounts for 3.6% of
operating profit. Iberdrola charged EUR47 million against reserves in
the first half on account of the decline in the real.



Regardless of the extent of their Brazilian exposure, the real risk
for the Spanish companies is that a crisis which originally seemed
contained to Argentina could now extend from Tierra del Fuego in the
south all the way up to the Rio Grande.

title: U.S. Signals Its Support for Aid to Brazil
text:
Staff Reporters of The Wall Street Journal 

 The Bush administration signaled it would support a financial rescue package for embattled Brazil, beating a retreat from its anti-bailout policy. 

 Shortly after he irked Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso by suggesting new aid might be siphoned off to Swiss bank accounts, and just days before his first official visit to the trouble spots of South America, Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill indicated the U.S. would support an agreement now being negotiated between Brasilia and the International Monetary Fund. 

 "The economic team in Brazil has done a remarkable job of maintaining sound fiscal and monetary policies," Mr. O'Neill said Thursday. "I continue to favor support for Brazil and other nations that take appropriate policy steps to build sound, sustainable and growing economies." 

 The announcement came as the Brazilian currency, rocked for days by Mr. O'Neill's criticisms and investor worries about the country's political future and huge public debt, shot up almost 10% on news that talks between IMF and top Brazilian financial officials were going well. After a week that has witnessed panicked selling of Brazil's real, the currency closed Thursday at 3.16 to the dollar, up from Wednesday's close of 3.47. Boosted by Central Bank of Brazil intervention, the real posted its largest single-day percentage gain ever; Monday was the largest single-day loss. 

 "The main reason for the rise is the IMF," said Paulo Vieira da Cunha, senior vice president of Lehman Bros. in New York. "An agreement is likely to be achieved, but I don't think it will be imminent and it could yet disappoint the market." 

 U.S. officials stressed that their support for a Brazil rescue loan is contingent upon the Brazilian authorities' agreeing to continued sound spending and monetary policies. An IMF deal that extends into next year will also require reassurance from the main presidential candidates that they will honor the agreement reached by the current government. One of the factors distressing investors is the possibility that either of two left-wing candidates, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Ciro Gomes, will win in October's vote. 

 There was no word Thursday on how large the IMF loan package might be or how it would address the country's $264 billion public debt, which some economists say can be paid only if creditors accept a restructuring agreement. Mr. O'Neill avoided the question of whether a debt restructuring would be necessary to keep the country solvent. 

 Mr. O'Neill's willingness to back an IMF deal will likely make his trip to Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina, starting Sunday, more pleasant. The president is dispatching Mr. O'Neill to the region to demonstrate that his administration empathizes with its suffering, a claim that many Latin Americans had begun to doubt. Mr. O'Neill himself contributed to those doubts, hinting that corruption in the three nations was at the heart of their economic woes and casually suggesting to a reporter on a long elevator ride some weeks back that he opposed additional aid for Brazil. 

 The latest comment, about Swiss accounts, prompted the Jornal do Brasil newspaper to opine that Mr. O'Neill is as "polite and careful as a monkey in a china shop." 

 "What can we do?" said Rubens Barbosa, Brazil's ambassador in Washington. "The problem is, if the secretary of the treasury of Uganda said the same thing, nobody would pay attention. If the secretary of the Treasury here says it, it has an immediate effect." 

 Amid the slights, the administration has been trying to reassure Latin Americans that they are indeed the foreign-policy priority Mr. Bush claimed they were during his presidential campaign. Mr. O'Neill pointed to Thursday's Senate passage of a major trade bill as evidence that the U.S. is engaged with the region; the bill extends trade benefits to Andean nations and facilitates negotiations for a free-trade deal with Chile, as well as a hemisphere-wide trade zone. 

 And the Treasury conspicuously announced its enthusiastic support this week for a new or accelerated IMF loan for tiny, beleaguered Uruguay, whose banks have been sapped largely by Argentines desperate to get their money home. 

 The U.S. has been tougher on Argentina, which is in the throes of a complete economic meltdown and mired in difficult talks with the IMF to roll over some $10 billion in debt. Given past failures of Argentine economic plans, both IMF and U.S. officials take the government's promises of fiscal prudence with a grain or two of salt. 

 "The people of Argentina have suffered from the economic turmoil there," Mr. O'Neill said, "and we are eager to see that nation return to a position of strength and stability."

title: Argentine peso posts strong gains, shares dip.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Aug 1 (Reuters) - Argentina's peso firmed over 2 percent on Thursday due mostly to Central Bank intervention while shares fell amid investor fears over debt-laden Brazil and crisis-hit Uruguay. 

 Argentina's peso ended at 3.63/3.65 per dollar in large-scale transactions on the foreign exchange market , stronger than Wednesday's close of 3.71/3.73. 

 The peso is still down about 70 percent this year, though it gained 4.5 percent in July amid signs of economic stability after Argentina's chaotic four-year recession. 

 Traders said the peso's gains were due largely to very heavy selling of $70.6 million into the market by the Central Bank. 

 Argentina's leading MerVal share index closed down 0.42 percent at 357.79 on brisk volume of 42.7 million pesos. The index is now up about 10 percent since the beginning of the year, having clawed back from sharp losses in recent months. 

 "Regional uncertainty is entrenched and all the bourses are paying the consequences," said one local trader. 

 Uruguay's economy has been hammered by a run on banks, a dive in reserves and consumer spending, and the ripple effects of Argentina's own prolonged economic crisis. 

 Brazil, meanwhile, is being buffeted by fears that the regional giant could be pushed toward default on its $250 billion public debt if a leftist wins the October presidential election. 

 The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday that talks about a potential new loan for Argentina were going well, but it said more work remained before a new loan could be agreed. 

 Argentina has been in talks for months to restart aid from the IMF, and in recent weeks the pace of negotiations has quickened. The IMF cut off access to a $22 billion credit line in December after the government failed to control public spending. 

 The IMF also said it was in talks with Brazil to extend its current aid package through the end of 2003 but declined to comment on whether additional cash would be sent to the Latin American giant. 

 The IMF said it was approaching talks with Uruguay on how to deal with a banking crisis there with a sense of urgency but hinted that no deal was imminent. 

 Shares in Argentine energy group Perez Companc , the target of a $1.13 billion takeover bid by Brazil's Petrobras , gained slightly after its main unit announced a swap of nearly $1 billion in bonds had closed. 

 Perez shares are down roughly 18 percent since the deal, dependent on Perez restructuring its debt, was announced on July 22. Investors are worried about the buyout's effect on minority shareholders.

title: Brazil  cenbank seen beefing up  forex intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, July 30 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank is expected to beef up in coming days its policy of selling at least $50 million daily in the foreign exchange market, currency analysts said on Tuesday. 

 As Brazil's currency has slumped to consecutive record lows in recent days, players are closely watching what course the Central Bank will take when its current minimum level of intervention ends its month-long run on Wednesday. 

Currency analysts say the Central Bank must at least double its sales to at least $100 million daily to arrest the downward spiral of the real. 

 In July, the bank fed the market with an estimated $1.5 billion, selling at least $50 million a day to boost liquidity and help prop up the flagging real , battered in part by investor nervousness over Brazil's October presidential vote. 

 Despite the Central Bank's daily dollar injections, the real has shed about 9 percent of its value so far in July, plunging to six straight record low closes over the past week. Earlier Tuesday, the currency hit a new all-time intraday low of 3.305 reais per dollar. 

 While the market welcomed what it dubbed the "daily ration" of dollars, foreign exchange analysts say the Central Bank will have to at least double the amount to quench the market's thirst for greenbacks and ease pressure on the real. 

 "The market consensus is that the Central Bank needs to increase the amount to at least $100 million a day," said Bertrand Wanclik, a currency analyst at Itau Corretora, a brokerage in Sao Paulo. 

 Though the market expects the bank to announce a new foreign exchange policy in the coming days, no date has been set. 

 The bank's strategy may also depend on the outcome of talks between Brazilian officials and the International Monetary Fund starting Wednesday in Washington. 

 "Even more important than increasing the so-called daily ration of dollars is some sort of deal with the IMF," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at Bank of America in Sao Paulo. 

 "Without that, the Central Bank may not have enough ammunition to satisfy the market" in the near term, he added. 

 Under Brazil's current IMF agreement, which expires by December, the Central Bank is required to maintain a minimum of $15 billion in reserves, thereby limiting the amount of dollars it can inject into the market. 

 In a bid to soothe market jitters and shore up more cash, the government announced late Monday that it is sending a high-level team to Washington to further talks already underway with the Fund. Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said last week Brazil would seek a new IMF loan deal if market turbulence persists. 

 With the approach of Brazil's presidential elections, dollars have been in short supply in recent weeks as the market frets over opinion polls, which show the government candidate and market favorite trailing in a distant third behind two left-of-center candidates. 

 Investors fear that a left-wing president would be more likely to resort to populist economic measures in the event of a debt crunch next year. Brazil's public debt is $250 billion, about 58 percent of the country's gross domestic product.

title: ODJ  Brazil / Intervention  -2: Mkt Hoped For More Aggressiveness
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- The Central Bank of Brazil Tuesday said it will continue
with its $50 million daily intervention program in August even though the plan
failed to keep the local currency from hitting record low levels this month.
Local markets shrugged off the announcement, which frustrated expectations
that the monetary authority would intervene more aggressively as the Brazilian
real is losing ground fast. The real didn't react and was quoted at BRL3.300
to the dollar, a record intraday low, during late trading.



Monetary Policy Director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said the August
interventions will total $1.835 billion, split between spot market sales and
dollar repurchase agreements. He said the central bank will sell $1.1 billion
in U.S. dollars on the spot market, while the remaining $735 million may
involve spot sales and repos.
Figueiredo added that the monetary authority may increase interventions next
month beyond the $1.835 billion mark if liquidity dries up.
In July, the central banks said it would intervene to the tune of $1.5
billion, also split between repos and spot sales.
The real has lost as much as 30% of its value this year to date. Traders say
there is a lack of dollars on the local market as international credit markets
are shut for Brazilian corporate risk. There is fear that the dramatic
weakening of the real may infect the country's economic fundamentals and
compromise its ability to stay current on debt payments.

title: Roaring Equities Boost Dollar, While Brazilian Real Plunges
text:
Dow Jones Newswires 

 NEW YORK -- The dollar posted solid gains against both the euro and the yen Monday as U.S. equities surged on a storm of bargain hunting, but the greenback had to share the limelight with the Brazilian real, which sank amid a stampede of selling by domestic accounts. 

 Late Monday in New York, the dollar was at 119.74 yen, close to its intraday high and tantalizingly close to the key 120 yen mark, up from 118.94 yen late Friday. The dollar soared as high as 119.97 yen, but lacked momentum to make a decisive breakthrough. 

 Should it breach and remain above 120 yen, then stop-loss orders would likely be triggered giving the dollar momentum to quickly reach as high as 120.50 yen or even 121 yen. 

 The euro was at 98.00 U.S. cents, down from 98.74 cents Friday. Against the Swiss franc, the dollar was at 1.4876 Swiss franc, up from 1.4650 francs. Sterling was at $1.5617, down from $1.5645. 

 While the U.S. currency extended last week's rally, the real teetered on the verge of collapse. 

 "It's panic," said Gustavo Rangel, an emerging markets strategist with Barclays Capital in New York. He added Monday's fall of the Brazilian real to record lows, breaching 3.2 Brazilian reals to the dollar, was "mostly [driven by] demand for physical dollars by corporates in Brazil." 

 Previously, currency market participants had anticipated there would soon be some $10 billion of International Monetary Fund money flowing to Brazil, Latin America's biggest economy, but U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill over the weekend "said basically it would not be forthcoming in the near term," commented Marc Chandler, chief currency strategist with HSBC in New York. 

 "The pressure on Brazil is real. To shrug it off as just a speculative attack obscures the underlying problems," the country faces, he added. "Brazilians themselves are taking money out of the country." 

 The frantic foreign-exchange-market action in Brazil, including intervention by the Brazilian central bank, didn't cause widespread turmoil in emerging markets Monday, but it did help the dollar recapture something of its allure as a currency of refuge. 

 The U.S. currency rejoined the trajectory of equity markets and hitched a ride on soaring U.S. stocks to trade at three-week highs against the euro and the yen. This caused some wavering among currency market participants who have been betting the greenback is trapped in a decline. 

 "The jury is still out," on whether the dollar's short-term recovery may turn into something more enduring, said Grant Wilson, senior foreign-exchange trader with Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. 

 In the past week, the dollar has sprung back more than 3% against both the Japanese and the common European currency. That pares the dollar's losses for 2002 to about 9% against the yen and around 10% versus the euro. 

 Analysts called attention to the stronger performance of some of the so-called "commodity currencies" Monday. Earlier this month, the stumble of the Australian, Canadian and New Zealand dollars had heralded a brightening of dollar sentiment. Now, these currencies' recovery may indicate the U.S. dollar's short-lived rally may be about to play itself out, some said. 

 Late Monday, the Australian dollar was trading at 54.05 U.S. cents, up from 53.59 cents late in New York Friday. Against the Canadian dollar, the U.S. dollar was at $1.5721 Canadian, down from C$1.5868 late Friday in New York. 

 The Canadian dollar ended sharply higher, boosted by news that Standard & Poor's upgraded Canada's foreign-currency sovereign credit rating to AAA from AA plus, market watchers said. Stabilizing equity markets and reduced risk aversion also helped the currency recover from last week's plummet. 

 After New Zealand's elections over the weekend, in which the Labour party had increased its share of the vote and appeared in a strong enough position to form another minority coalition government, the New Zealand dollar was trading at 46.85 U.S. cents late Monday in New York, up from 46.25 cents in late New York trading Friday. 

 "If we see stabilization in those currencies, that would be evidence that the U.S. dollar recovery ... is approaching its end," said Sean Callow, currency strategist with IDEAGlobal in New York. 

 Nonetheless, some technical factors indicated that the until-recently gloomy U.S. dollar sentiment might have turned on its heel and have embarked on a more upbeat march for a while to come. 

 "From a technical perspective, the dollar is finding more support," while after four straight sessions of U.S. stock averages gaining, "the dollar market is settling," said James McCormick, foreign-exchange strategist with Lehman Brothers in New York. 

 He noted his firm's "Bull and Bear Model" currency-market sentiment index showed the dollar's bearish trend that started in April -- the longest-running since 1995 -- flipped into bullish mode on Friday for the first time in four months. 

 A key factor driving the dollar higher appears to be the crumbling of the yen, which started last week and helped ignite the greenback's ascent against other widely-traded rivals. 

 Newfound concerns about Japan's financial sector could enable the dollar to rise to between 120 yen and 122 yen in the very short term, wrote Robert Sinche, chief currency strategist with Citibank in New York in a research note Monday. Japan's banks are burdened with 150 trillion yen of bad and potentially non-performing loans and are also heavily exposed to the domestic stock market. 

 Longer-term dollar-negative factors including the burgeoning U.S. current account deficit and a cloud of doubt remaining about U.S. corporate accounting which may yet return to plague the dollar, some warned. 

 As the Aug. 14 deadline by which U.S. chief executives must certify their financial statements approaches, a sense of unease about whether more flaws in corporate accounts will surface in the coming weeks "is tilted in the direction of bad news," and it has the potential to defuse the dollar's current rebound, said HSBC's Mr. Chandler. 

 "The stock market has been moving up, but let's put this in perspective," he noted, adding U.S. stock averages are still much lower than a month ago. "The downside risks" to U.S. asset prices "are for real."

title: O'Neill Comments, Local Selling Thrash Brazilian Real
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real plunged to its lowest levels ever against the dollar Monday, as worries over a U.S. official's comments over the weekend were compounded by widespread selling of South America's largest currency. 

 Still, market professionals downplayed talk that currency speculators were jumping on board, furthering the pressure on the real. 

 "I hardly think this is speculative; that's not the key problem," said Marc Chandler, chief currency strategist with HSBC in New York. 

 "The pressure on Brazil is real: To shrug it off as just a speculative attack obscures the underlying problems," said Chandler. "Brazilians themselves are taking money out of the country," he said. 

 The currency weakened to as far as BRL3.29 per dollar in afternoon trade, before rallying to BRL3.185 in late activity after the central market intervened in the spot market, according to traders in Brazil. But that was still far weaker than Friday's close of BRL3.105. 

 The real's latest problems began with "(Treasury Secretary Paul) O'Neill's comments about not going to Argentina and Brazil with aid packages," the head of one New York currency desk said. 

 O'Neill, who will visit Argentina and Brazil in early August, said he won't offer either country a bailout at that time. "These are important friends and allies of the United States," he said on 'Fox News Sunday'. "Critically, they need to put in place policies that would ensure that as assistance money comes it does some good and it doesn't just go out of the country to Swiss bank accounts." 

 Previously, market participants had anticipated that there would be $10 billion of International Monetary Fund money coming to Brazil, but O'Neill over the weekend "basically said it would not be forthcoming in the near term," according to HSBC's Chandler. 

 Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan early Monday sought to soothe markets by announcing that a fresh IMF program is on its way. But his remarks fell on deaf ears, as electoral and financing concerns pushed Brazil's bond spreads into uncharted territory and sent the real plunging to new historic lows. 

 `It's panic," said Gustavo Rangel, a strategist with Barclays Capital in New York. The fall of the Brazilian real Monday was "mostly (driven by) demand for physical dollars by corporates in Brazil that need to pay their amortizations," he said. 

 The slide of the real to another historic low, beyond BRL3.20 to the dollar Monday, surprised strategists. Rangel has a forecast for the BRL3.40 by late September, but now wonders if that target will be reached sooner. 

 He was also skeptical about the chances of IMF funding anytime soon. Such funding would only be likely if all candidates in the October presidential elections agreed beforehand to sign an agreement on economic policy with the IMF, a scenario Rangel said was difficult to imagine. 

 Government-backed candidate Jose Serra, a market favorite, is trailing two left-leaning presidential hopefuls in opinion polls ahead of the Oct. 6 election. President Fernando Henrique Cardoso is ineligible to run for a third straight term. 

 Brazil's debt-servicing costs have skyrocketed in recent months. About 80% of Brazil's domestic debt is tied to the dollar or the central bank's benchmark Selic lending rate, which currently stands at 18%. 

 The real has lost more than 20% against the dollar so far this year. 

 -By Tyler Lifton and John Parry, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-2248, 201-938-2096; tyler.lifton@dowjones.com 

 (Joe Rebello in Washington D.C. and Angela Pruitt in New York contributed to this story)

title: Brazil's Real Ends At BRL2.995/Dollar; Worst Close Ever
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real plunged Thursday, breaching for the first time ever the psychologically-important barrier of BRL3.000 to the dollar during intraday trade amid mounting concerns about the country's ability to stay afloat and unstable U.S. equity markets. 

 The real hit an intraday low of BRL3.030 to the dollar before settling at BRL2.995 to the dollar - its weakest closing ever for the fourth session in a row. This is the eighth time in a month that the real has set a new record closing low. On Wednesday, the real finished at BRL2.946. 

 Market players said investors were increasingly nervous about the political platforms of presidential candidates ahead of elections in October. 

 "Not even an accord with the International Monetary Fund would help right now. That would only bring a temporary  relief to the market," said Solange Frour, senior economist at Mellon Global Investment in Rio de Janeiro. 

 Frour said there are candidates defending contradictory positions, such as keeping the fiscal budget in check while also raising the minimum wage. 

 "The social security system's deficit continues to grow, so it's absurd to even think of raising spending now," she added. 

 Earlier Thursday, the central bank said Brazil's net public debt hit a record high for the second month running, reaching 58.6% of gross domestic product at the end of June.  A bank official said the ratio is expected to increase a bit further in July due to "transitory factors," adding that the debt is sustainable. 

 These domestic worries are being compounded by weak U.S.  stock markets following a slew of corporate accounting scandals. 

 The real was also being pressured lower by rumors that an Ibope presidential poll slated to be unveiled Thursday evening could show Ciro Gomes, of the center-left Labor Front coalition, growing in popularity ahead of government-backed candidate Jose Serra, considered market-friendly. 

 Gomes has previously talked about a "voluntary lengthening" of Brazil's public debt, which has left some investors suspicious of him, traders said. 

 Market players were speculating the poll could show Gomes rising to 26-28%  from 20%, while Serra is seen dropping to 13% from 15% in a previous poll. 

 Opposition-candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva was expected to show a slight drop in popularity, to 32% from 33%, while voting intentions for former  Rio de Janeiro governor Anthony Garotinho probably remained stable at 10% to 11%. 

 Meanwhile, Brazil's central bank Thursday sold $220 million, three-month dollar repurchase agreements at a rate of BRL3.05 a dollar. The deal was just a renewal of expiring repos. 

 Separately, Brazil's central bank confirmed it intervened in the market with $50 million in foreign currency. This is part of a daily intervention program designed to contain the real's decline.

text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real ended at its lowest close ever Wednesday, largely reacting to a surprise interest rates cut to 18.00% from 18.50%. 

 The real ended at BRL2.897 to the dollar, slightly weaker than its worst previous close of BRL2.896 July 1. Tuesday, the currency closed at BRL2.872 to the dollar. 

 A Sao Paulo-based trader said the central bank's decision to cut rates was unexpected and investors were still trying to position themselves, increasing volatility in the real. 

 Also, traders said investors were still concerned about the political outlook ahead of presidential elections in October. 

 They added there was talk that government-backed candidate Jose Serra's campaign could lose running mate Rita Camata. The rumor was dismissed by Serra's Brazilian Social Democracy Party, or PSDB, and by a spokesperson for Camata. 

 If true, though, a Rita pullout would be bad news for Serra's already flagging campaign. Late Tuesday, he fell to third in the polls behind front-runner Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, of the Workers' Party, and leftist Ciro Gomes. 

 Camata is seen as key to helping dour Serra be more appealing to voters. Investors are rooting for Serra, who is considered to be market-friendly. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank sold $100 million in 60-day repurchase agreements at a rate of BRL2.920 per dollar. 

 Banks buying the contracts agreed to sell dollars back to the monetary authority Sept. 17. The sale of the contracts was held to roll over similar repos coming due. 

 The size of the offering is double the size of Brazil's current daily interventions in the forex market that come in the form of dollar spot sales, or repos. 

 The central bank also said it sold $50 million onto the market. 


The operations did little to help bolster the real during the session
amid investor unease.

title: Brazil's Fraga Describes IMF Meetings As 'Good'
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Brazilian Central Bank President Arminio Fraga, his country's financial markets in turmoil ahead of an October presidential election, said Thursday that he received strong signals of support during recent high-level meetings in Washington. 

 "I see Brazil being supported...by the IMF, by our fellow partners in the global economy in G7," Fraga told a group of investors in Manhattan after meeting Wednesday with officials from the International Monetary Fund and U.S. Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill. 

 Brazil recently drew down $10 billion from a $15.5 billion IMF credit line that expires in December. Fraga, who described the Washington meetings as "good," said more help could be on the way, if necessary. 

 "I do see many possibilities going forward," he said. Fraga was speaking during a presentation to investors hosted by Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 Fraga downplayed recent market speculation that a transitional IMF accord is in the works, which would involve Brazil's four leading presidential candidates agreeing to common macroeconomic targets. 

 "My expectation is that that is not the way we're going," he said. 

 Brazil's currency, bonds and stocks have been punished in past weeks amid opinion polls showing leftist candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with a commanding lead. 

 Fraga, however, insisted there are "no signs of big outflows" with many Brazilians shifting their funds to local certificates of deposit and into savings accounts. The biggest single monthly outflow had been around $100 million, he added. 

 "In a country our size, that is nothing," Fraga said. 

 He denied media reports that Brazil is seeking commitments from international banks on commercial credit lines, saying the government had made "no request of any kind." 

 "This isn't 1999," Fraga said. 

 U.S. banks, in a show of public support, agreed to maintain commercial credit lines in early 1999 after Brazil was forced to devalue its currency, plunging Latin American markets into turmoil. 

Brazil recently began intervening in the foreign-exchange market to break the fall of the real ($1=BRL2.794), a strategy that had begun to pay dividends. It has also maintained its benchmark interest rates at 18.50%, despite single-digit inflation. 

 Fraga said authorities are dedicated to tightening fiscal and monetary policy as much as is needed to calm jittery investors. 

 "We can go as far as I see necessary for this uncertainty to go away," Fraga said. 

 Fraga added that he believes the currency is undervalued "if you take a long-term view." 

 The central bank also has been buying back its bonds on the open market to soothe concerns about its heavy debt load. Fraga said the bank has repurchased about two-thirds of the planned $3 billion bond buyback. 

 The central banker said that whoever wins the presidential elections in October will inherit healthy economic fundamentals, including low inflation, solid banks and rising productivity. 

 "Whoever comes next will benefit from a lot of the work that has been done," Fraga said. 

 Fraga said he had briefed Aloysio Mercadante, the economic adviser to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, on his meetings in Washington. 

 Fraga promised to work with all the presidential candidates to ensure a smooth transition. 

 -By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newsiwires; 201-938-4026; Mike.Esterl@dowjones.com

title: CORRECTED -  Brazil  real firm on  intervention  plan, stocks drop.
text:
In SAO PAULO story headlined "Brazil real firm on 

intervention plan, stocks drop," please read in fifth paragraph 

  ... to cover in July after covering about $2.5 billion in June 

  ... instead of ... to cover in June after covering about $2.5 

  billion in July ..." (Correcting respective months) 

 A corrected version follows: 

 By Nicholas Winning 

 SAO PAULO, Brazil, July 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency strengthened from record low territory on Wednesday as players bet a Central Bankintervention plan could break its seemingly interminable slide on local election and debt fears, traders said. 

 But hard-hit stock prices weakened further after Tuesday's Brazil sovereign rating cut by Standard & Poor's (S&P) and Wall Street volatility reinforced fears of reduced overseas investment in emerging markets. 

 Brazil's real reversed early losses to close at 2.862 per dollar from Tuesday's close of 2.895, leaving it 19.1 percent below where it began 2002 after the Central Bank said it would intervene with a total of $1.5 billion in July. 

 "In the short term, it should give it (market) a good boost and the market should calm down," ING Barings director of foreign exchange Diniz Pignatari said of the plan. "I think it (real) could stabilize around 2.80 in the short term." 

 New election polls could unsettle markets, but pressure on the real from companies should ease as they only had some $1.1 billion in overseas debt commitments to cover in July after covering about $2.5 billion in June, he said. 

 Just one day after the currency closed at par with Monday's record low, the Central Bank said it would pump $100 million into the market every day this week and then daily injections of $50 million for the rest of the month either on the spot market or with repurchase agreements. 

 On Wednesday it sold all $100 million offered in an auction priced at 2.855 reais per dollar with a commitment to buy it back on Oct. 2 at 2.955 per dollar. 

 The resumption of daily interventions, which were used in the second half of 2001 to stave off the impact of neighboring Argentina's economic crisis, aim to dull the impact of concerns about October's elections and meet local corporate needs. 

 Meanwhile, the benchmark Bovespa stock index fell 1.9 percent to 10,635.5 points, or 21.7 percent weaker than where it began 2002. Losers outweighed gainers by 51 to six. 

 Telephone company Telemar , the market's heaviest-weighted stock with about 15 percent of the index, fell 1.2 percent drop to 26.41 reais. State oil giant Petrobras , the second-heaviest weighted stock, fell 1 percent to 46.81 reais. 

 Brazil's markets dove in June on Wall Street weakness and fears of mismanagement of the Brazil's economy and its $250 billion debt load should leftist presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva turn his big poll lead into a victory. 

 The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange said earlier that it had a $351 million net foreign investment outflow in June, its largest monthly record since December 1998. 

 Unlike the real, Brazilian stocks received no respite on Wednesday suffered in the wake of the S&P downgrade and ongoing Wall Street volatility and fears of new accounting scandals. 

 S&P cut Brazil's sovereign rating citing growing difficulties Latin America's biggest economy could manage its debt as fears of a Lula presidential election victory raised debt interest rates and servicing costs. 

 Traders said Thursday's Independence holiday in the United States would leave the Bovespa rudderless. 

 "Tomorrow will complicated as there won't be Bradys (bonds) so volume will be light and there won't be a reference point," said Concordia brokearge trader Tomi Taterka.

title: Chilean peso firms on  Brazil forex intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, July 3 (Reuters) - Chile's peso ended firmer on Wednesday, following gains in the Brazilian real after the Brazilian Central Bank announced it would intervene in the foreign exchange market to prop up the weakened currency, traders said. 

 At closing, the Chilean currency traded at 694.50/695.00 pesos per U.S. dollar, up 0.71 percent from Tuesday's close of 699.50/699.80 but still down about 5 percent since the start of the year. 

 Traders said the peso would remain volatile until turbulence in Brazilian markets subsided, probably after that country's presidential election in October. 

 "Even though the Central Bank injects liquidity to defend the real, there is still a lot of pressure in the market and that is affecting the peso," said Gabriela Clivio, analyst with Santiago brokerage. 

 Brazil's battered real currency rebounded on Wednesday after the Brazilian Central Bank announced it would inject $1.5 billion into the market in July to prop up the currency. The real firmed to 2.845 per dollar from Tuesday's close of 2.895. 

 Traders in Chile's peso, battered last year by the Argentine financial crisis, have now turned to Brazil's financial markets as a barometer of investor confidence in the region. 

 Chilean traders said they expected the real to continue losing ground despite the Central Bank move. 

 Brazil's financial markets have been whipped in recent weeks by fears economic problems could hinder its debt payments and by the lead in polls of a leftist presidential candidate.

title: Brazil stocks fall on S&P rating cut, Wall Street.
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil, July 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's hard-hit stock market fell up to 3 percent in afternoon trading on Wednesday, a day after Standard & Poor's lowered the country's rating due to election and debt fears, and also hit by new Wall Street declines. 

 The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's Bovespa index were off 2.45 percent to 10,580.2 points at 2:45 p.m. (1745 GMT). The index has lost about 22 percent since the start of the year. Top mobile phone firm Telesp Cel , which announced a giant stock offering earlier this week, weighed with a 3 percent fall to 3.8 reais. 

 Turnover was thin and liquidity low, traders said. The U.S. Dow Industrial Average was trading about 1.1 percent lower at the time while the tech-laden Nasdaq was down 0.5 percent. Still, traders said they were closely watching the real currency , which bounced on Wednesday as the Central Bank announced a supportive intervention plan. 

Brazil's markets are also suffering from underlying concerns of mismanagement of the economy and its $250 billion debt load should leftist presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva win the October elections.

title: Emerging debt-Downgrade hurts  Brazil , CenBank  intervention  helps.
text:
NEW YORK, July 3 (Reuters) - Brazilian sovereign bonds led the emerging debt market slightly lower Wednesday as investors tried to balance Tuesday's credit rating downgrade against news the government will intervene in the country's currency market. 

 "The Brazil downgrade scared a few people and bonds traded down," one emerging debt trader said. "Then the Central Bank said it would intervene, which gave the market a bit of a pop. These two things offset each other, but Brazil is going to end the day down." 

 Brazil slumped 2.7 percent in total returns at midday, while the market as a whole edged 0.8 percent lower, according to JP Morgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus. For the year, Brazil, which has been battered by political uncertainty ahead of the October presidential election, is down 21.6 percent, while the wider index is down 0.4 percent. 

 "I don't think the market is severely underweight Brazil and there's risk aversion out there, so there are still some sellers," said Jim Barrineau, a vice president in emerging markets research at Alliance Capital Management. "Trading is active for the day before July 4th." 

 The market was set to close early ahead of the U.S. Independence Day holiday. 

Brazil's Central Bank said Wednesday it will intervene in the foreign exchange market with a combination of dollar sale operations to the value of $1.5 billion in the month of July, to boost liquidity in the market after the currency sank to record lows. 

 The bank said it will intervene with $100 million per day through the rest of this week, after intervening Monday with $300 million. Through the rest of the month from Monday next week, the Central Bank said it would intervene with $50 million per day. 

 Standard & Poor's on Tuesday lowered Brazil's sovereign rating, citing growing difficulties in managing its public debt. 

 Brazilian debt prices have plunged in recent weeks, pushing interest rates to levels not seen in more than three years and raising the cost of servicing its estimated $250 billion debt profile on worries about a victory by left-leaning Workers Party candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

 S&P cut Brazil's long-term foreign currency rating to B-plus - four notches below investment grade - from BB-minus and its local currency debt rating to BB from BB-plus. 

 "Brazil is up and down," another debt trader said of Wednesday's market. "No one knows what the right level is for Brazil to trade at, considering the political side of the story and the economic side."

title: Brazil  real firm on  intervention  plan, stocks soft.
text:

 Hard-hit stock prices weakened, however, as Wall Street weakness and concerns of more U.S. accounting scandals dictated the mood on the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange (Bovespa) for fear of reduced overseas investment in emerging markets like Brazil.

title: Brazil  to  intervene  with $1.5 bln in  forex  market.
text:
BRASILIA, Brazil, July 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank said on Wednesday that it will intervene in the foreign exchange market with a combination of dollar sale operations to the value of $1.5 billion in the month of July, to boost liquidity in the market after the real currency sunk to record lows. 

 The bank said it will intervene with $100 million per day through the rest of this week, after intervening already on Monday with $300 million. Through the rest of the month from Monday next week, the Central Bank said it would intervene with $50 million per day. 

 Luiz Fernando Figueiredo, the bank's monetary policy director, said the move was designed to bolster liquidity in the foreign exchange market. "The objective is not to interfere in the exchange rate but to create the conditions for the market to operate normally. The market is suffering from exaggerated anxiety," he said. 

 The operations will either be straight dollar sales or a combination of spot and forward foreign exchange operations. The bank will decide daily which operation to choose. In addition, the bank plans to roll over $320 million coming due in July from previous combined spot and forward dollar sales.
