title: Brazil's Real Opens At BRL2.790 Vs BRL2.770 End Thurs
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real continued to weaken against the dollar at the open Friday, as the market awaited signs of more intervention from the Central Bank. 

 At 1250 GMT, the real was trading at BRL2.790 per dollar  compared with BRL2.770 per dollar at Thursday's close. 

 "If the Central Bank doesn't intervene, the real's going to sink into the BRL2.80 per dollar range," said a trader in Sao Paulo. 

Brazil's central bank has intervened in the currency market repeatedly this week to try to ease pressure on the real, but has so far seen limited success in calming investors' nerves. 

 The interventions came after a battery of other measures  adopted last week, including the announcement of a $10 billion drawdown on a loan from the International Monetary Fund, a hike in bank reserve requirements to 15% from 10%, swaps of domestic debt to shorten maturities, and buybacks of overseas debt. 

 Nonetheless, the country's risk rating as measured by the JP Morgan EMBI+ this week rose to more than 1,500 points, second only to Argentina. 

 Market participants, meanwhile, are waiting for the central bank to formally draw down on its available IMF loan  funding to determine to what extent it is willing to inject  foreign currency into the local market. 

 Brazil's real has lost more than 17% against the dollar this year amid market nervousness over the presidential succession to take place after the country's October 6 elections. 

 Despite the currency's slide, recent market surveys released by the central bank show the real is expected to end the year at around BRR2.50 per dollar.

title: Charting Trends: Getting Real About  Brazil Intervention
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Last week's chart of USD/BRL might  have been a roadmap for this week's currency operation. 

 This afternoon the Brazilian central bank performed two rounds of intervention in the spot forex markets, buying the  Brazilian real to the tune of $50 million. 

 USD/BRL is trading at 2.7110 late in the Tuesday New York session. If the intervention has done its job, USD/BRL will sink to 2.6444 or to 2.6316 before the month is out. 

 The point is that the fundamental influence of central bankintervention was in the charts last week just ahead of the past two operations by the central bank. 

 Last week, USD/BRL recorded a weekly high of 2.7945, the  high of a two-month uptrend. The high was recorded on June 12, just before central bank intervention on Friday, June 14. Last week's high practically represented a test of last October's high for the multi-year bull market, which was 2.8060 resistance. The market closed out last week in the middle of the week's high-low range. That was a technical signal of lost upside momentum and the possibility of a sell-off. 

 In other words, the time was right for a strengthening of the real against the dollar. 

 This isn't to say that central bank intervention necessarily had to happen. Certainly, it's not to say that the intervention will work in the sense of meaningfully strengthening the real against the dollar, although last week's USD/BRL hit on long-term resistance puts the odds in the central bank's favor. 

 In fact, the intervention won't have meaningfully strengthened the real unless USD/BRL falls below 2.6444 this  week. Late-day trading under 2.6444 on Friday implies an eventual move down to 2.6316 at least. And a move below 2.6316 would leave USD/BRL open to a serious technical breakdown. 

 A decisive move above 2.7210 means that the central bank  has been foiled, according to the charts. In that case, USD/BRL will soon move up to 2.7930.

title: Brazil Rally Fizzles As Market Seeks Actions, Not Words
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's financial markets gave back some gains that came as the government Thursday unveiled a host of policies to shore up the country's fiscal position, with investors daring the central bank to actively intervene in the market instead of just talking about it. 

 In late trading, Brazil's real was at BRR2.71 a dollar, weaker than its strongest point Thursday of BRR2.640, but better than BRR2.795 at Wednesday's close, a nine-month low. The country's main stocks index was down 0.5% at 12,064 points after being up about 1% shortly after the government announced its measures. 

 Strong follow-through from the government may help. But the current administration can do little to assuage investor concerns that the next president - set to take office in January - will continue to pursue this government's economic stability goals. Finance Minister Pedro Malan said Thursday voters will demand sound fiscal policies when they cast their ballots in October, but investors aren't so sure. 

 "The country's now much better equipped to fight fires and the next possible rounds of panic selling will likely be less intense and shorter," said Alexandre Mathias, chief economist at Unibanco Asset Management. "But that doesn't mean they've resolved the election worries." 

 Currently, left-wing Workers' Party candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has a commanding 20 percentage point lead over government-backed candidate Jose Serra. Though he vows to maintain stability, the former union leader's past anti-market talk and signs of internal party divisions on key economic policy issues unnerve some investors. 

 But some analysts say the central bank will soon catch the shorts leaning the wrong way as the government is pulling out stops on a variety of fronts to allay investor fears about the outcome of elections and the country's ability to manage its hefty debt burden. 

 Merrill Lynch's Yianos Kontopoulous put out a research note Thursday afternoon recommending that investors go long real, saying: "The Brazilian intervention arsenal (size and flexibility) is an order of difference stronger than it was in last year's intervention cycle (which was successful)." 

 He added: "Some in the market are saying they heard the general outline of the policy response but not the specifics, thus, maybe the authorities are bluffing. Well, they are most likely not." 

 The arsenal includes about $10 billion from existing IMF credit lines by next week, a raising of the government's primary surplus target to 3.75% of GDP from 3.5% in 2002, a $3 billion buyback program for global bonds and the freeing up of an added $5 billion in reserves for intervening on the spot market. 

 But in this jittery environment, traders are hoping to see these interventions occur as soon as possible and aren't happy about waiting around a few days for formal sign-offs from the IMF. 

 About half of the $10 billion Brazil hopes to draw from the IMF needs formal approval next week, along with a lowering of the country's international reserves floor to $15 billion from $20 billion to free up cash to defend its currency. Once approved, Brazil would have around $10 billion in cash for forex interventions, up from less than $4 billion. 

 Traders are also anxious to see the government start buying back about $3 billion of the $9 billion in dollar-denominated global bonds maturing in 2003 and 2004. Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga said the buybacks will provide a double dose of relief by cutting debt servicing costs and making it easier and cheaper for Brazilian companies to continue borrowing overseas. 

 -By Terry Wade and Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-3145-1479; brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil Malan: Ups Primary Surplus Target To 3.75% In '02
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Two months after paying back nearly a third of its $15 billion International Monetary Fund loan brokered last year, Finance Minister Pedro Malan confirmed Brazil would draw down $10 billion from the existing program. 

 As part of an effort to calm financial markets amid worries about Brazil's future debt obligations, Malan said the Brazilian government is further tightening its grip on fiscal accounts in this election year. 

 Speaking at a press conference in Brasilia, the finance minister said the government is raising this year's consolidated public primary budget surplus target to 3.75% of gross domestic product from 3.50%. 

 Also, Malan said Brazil would seek permission from the IMF for additional room to intervene in the foreign exchange market. Brazil is looking to lower the floor on its net international reserves to $15 billion from $20 billion. 

 Looking to alleviate market concern about Brazil's debt outlook, Central Bank Governor Arminio Fraga at the same press conference said Brazil would engage in an international debt buyback program. 

 The program will involve spending up to $3 billion to retire 2003 and 2004 debt. 

 Fraga also reiterated recent government comments that the central bank would intervene in the foreign exchange market when necessary, by making use of the usual tools at hand. 

 The central bank usually sells dollars on the spot currency market at times of high volatility or low liquidity. Seeking to reassure investors, Fraga added that June foreign capital outflows have so far been smaller than in May. 

 Ahead of the confirmation, market players said the central bank would be smart to draw down the country's pre-approved credit lines and boost its reserves as investors worry about Brazil's ability to meet future debt obligations. 

 Fraga spent this week in Washington, chairing an IMF seminar, while Brazil's currency weakened to levels not seen since the Sept. 11 attacks on the U.S. 

 The central bank is looking to boost its gross reserves which currently stand at about $33 billion. Net of IMF funds, reserves stand at a total $28 billion. 

 Fraga said the central bank would continue to swap medium- and long-term debt for short-term securities to help further calm the markets. The same applies for foreign exchange swap contracts. 

 The exchanges would continue to involve floating-rate LFT treasury bills and dollar-linked NTN-D notes. 

 Finance Deputy Minister Amaury Bier said the government wouldn't need to take additional fiscal measures to increase its primary budget surplus this year. 

 He said a May government decision to withhold as much as BRR5.3 billion in public spending plus continued fiscal  discipline on regional governments would ensure Brazil meets its new 3.75% goal. 

 "If additional (federal) effort were necessary, we will do it," Bier said. 

 Fraga said the current situation is manageable, "without having to pull the rabbit out of the hat." Fine-tuning would continue on the open market, he added. 

 Fraga also said the central bank would resume offering 60-day external lines of credit to banks, as was done during the transition from 2000 to 2001. This transaction, he said, means that the monetary authority will sell dollars and buy reals from banks for a period of 60 days. 

 He added that a senior-ranking IMF team will recommend that the Fund's board next week approve the country's request to dip deeper into international reserves to defend its currency, if necessary. 

 The IMF's board is expected to approve Brazil's latest performance review next week, which would allow the country to draw down on $5 billion in aid funds. 

 Fraga said the current turbulence in financial markets, which Wednesday sent the real close to record lows, is rooted in "anxiety in relation to the future" as the presidential election approaches. 

 Such jitters would go away once markets are confident that "the country's commitment to fiscal responsibility won't go straight out of the window," he said, in a veiled reference to the opposition Workers' Party's current lack of commitment to fiscal austerity. 

 Fraga said he expected the IMF to approve the change to the floor on net international reserves next week. 

 Talking about debt maturing in 2003 and 2004, Fraga said $3.5 billion would come due in 2003, and $5.5 billion in 2004. 

 Clarifying the government position on the primary budget surplus target change, Planning Minister Guilherme Dias said the decision to further tighten fiscal policy was the government's own move, and the higher target wouldn't be part of the IMF program. He added that the 3.75% primary budget surplus corresponds to about BRR48.7 billion ($1=BRR2.795). 

 Bier emphasized that the IMF-set 3.5% primary budget surplus target would remain in place until the end of September, when the current accord closes. But Brazil will then go into fiscal austerity overdrive for the remainder of the year to try and meet the full 2002 target of 3.75%. 

 Fraga said he would risk saying that "the real is now undervalued and should strengthen in nominal and real terms in the long run." 

 He said the external debt buyback program, in addition to being "a noble use for the country's reserves," will also help lower short-term spreads and pave the way for Brazilian companies to continue borrowing overseas. 

 Confirming expectations that the government wouldn't look to broker a 2003 accord with the IMF, Malan said it would be up to the next administration to decide on such a matter. 

 Brazil has a reputation for meeting IMF targets and has consistently fulfilled its goals since the end of 1998. 

 In April, Brazil smashed market expectations and posted a consolidated public sector primary budget surplus of BRR8.97 billion. 

 The government has agreed with the IMF to post an accumulated surplus of BRR25 billion by June and BRR34.1 billion by September's end, when the current accord between the government and the IMF closes. 

 The government marginally beat the IMF target of BRR11.4 billion, posting a first quarter surplus of BRR11.555 billion. 

 But the April consolidated primary budget surplus numbers will likely dispel last month's fears. The government has to post a BRR4.5 billion surplus a month to meet its second quarter goal. April's result effectively takes care of two months in one go. 

 Separately, Dias said the government expects the Brazilian economy to grow 2% to 2.5% this year, which is in line with world growth and better than any other country in South America.

title: Brazil 's Real Opens -2:Traders Defy Ctrl Bk To  Intervene
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Investors continued to dump Brazilian reals at the open Wednesday, testing the central bank's tolerance of a sinking currency amid growing worries that the government may fail to roll over a heavy load of dollar-linked debt maturing next next. 

 After ending Tuesday at its lowest close in seven and a half months at BRR2.712 to the dollar, the real opened at BRR2.732 and was extending losses. At around 1300 GMT, the currency was changing hands at BRR2.742. 

 Traders are growing concerned that Brazil may be en route to a debt crisis amid jitters ahead of the October presidential election and the collapse of its neighbor Argentina's economy, which is also making the life of another neighbor, Uruguay, extremely difficult these days. 

 "There's a complete mistrust in the country at the moment," said a Sao Paulo-based trader. "The market is now  defying the central bank to intervene." 

 The real has lost about 8% of its value so far this month, after the central bank unexpectedly introduced new accounting rules for mutual funds which ended up sparking debt worries. 

 Following the government's failed attempt Tuesday to sell fixed-rate treasury bills that mature before Brazil's Oct. 6 presidential election, the market is now growing worried that the central bank's bid to use December 2002 derivatives to roll over maturing dollar-linked may fall through. 

 Market players are saying they'll demand high premiums to buy the lot of 12,500 December 2002 forex swap contracts at an auction later Wednesday - which may lead the monetary authority to reject bids. 

 The currency swap offering, valued at $600 million, is designed to start the rollover process of an unusually-large  $2.4 billion maturity of dollar-linked debt due June 19. 

 "I don't what would be worse: the central bank rejecting bids or the central bank accepting to pay a high premium to place the swaps," said another Sao Paulo-based trader. 

 Such worries and the continued slide of the local currency are prompting companies and rich individuals to seek greenback protection as well as send some of their money overseas. Cemig, a Minas Gerais state power utility, for instance, said Tuesday its board approved the currency hedging for all its $600 million dollar-linked liabilities. 

 The government has said it can draw down from an existing $15 billion International Monetary Fund aid package  as well as sell dollars on the spot market. Brazil currently has about $8 billion in hard-currency reserves it could use for spot-market intervention. 

 Meanwhile, market players shrugged off benign May inflation data unveiled earlier Wednesday. The government said the May consumer price index was 0.21%, below market expectations of 0.25% to 0.50%. During normal times, such a benign inflation figure would push markets higher as it would pave the way for the central bank to cut interest rates. 

 The monetary authority had signaled last month it would resume cutting rates at the June 18-19 policy meeting, but analysts said a rate reduction is becoming an increasingly remote possibility in view of the recent market's downturn. Nominal interest rates have been above 18% for nearly a year  and are among the world's highest in real terms.

title: Brazil Real Ends Weaker At BRR2.712 As Mkt Tests Ctrl Bk
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Hit by worries over the government's ability to manage its hefty debt load, Brazil's real weakened sharply Tuesday as investors snapped up dollars in an attempt to avoid losses from a weakening local currency. 

 With political uncertainties ahead of the October presidential elections contributing to the volatility, traders said the market is now testing the central bank to intervene to prop up the currency. 

Brazil's real ended at BRR2.712 to a dollar, compared with BRR2.636 at Monday's close. Ten days ago, the real was at BRR2.510. 

 Among those looking for or planning to hedge are power company Cemig, which approved the use of hedging to protect up to 100% of the company's dollar-linked debt against forex fluctuations, a company official said Tuesday. 

 Expectations of a weakening real and hedging interest, traders say, will likely create a self-reinforing process that will force the local currency to weaken further in the near term. 

 Brazil's net debt load as a percentage of gross domestic product has increased over the last several years and currently runs at about 54.5%, a ratio that weighs on the real. And with October elections approaching, investors reluctant to hold paper maturing after October have forced the central bank to shorten the maturities it offers. 

 Left-wing presidential candidate Luis Inacio Lula da Silva is leading polls at about 40%, with government-backed candidate Jose Serra running around 20%. 

 As a result of investor concerns, the government has been busy swapping longer-term debt for short-term paper. Last week, the central bank swapped more than BRR20 billion of bills. 

 A third of Brazil's BRR600 billion-plus public debt will mature in the short term and analysts say investor worries could complicate debt rollover and management operations. Brazil has cash reserves of about BRR50 billion to ward-off debt jitters.

 With the sharp fall Tuesday, the real ended at its weakest level in about seven and a half months. On Oct. 30, the currency closed at BRR2.723 a dollar.

title: Brazil 's Malan:  Forex Intervention  Only For Extreme Cases
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's Finance Minister Pedro Malan on Monday said that intervention in the foreign-exchange market should be limited to extreme situations, as there is always a risk that the market will misinterpret the move as an attempt to target a "desired" exchange rate. 

 In a speech during a seminar on central bank independence here, Malan added that forex intervention "may be necessary at times when the market is taken by herd mentality...one way or the other, leading to an overshooting." 

 "I think there's a consensus that it (intervention) should be an exception rather than a rule... One must avoid the perception that there's an alternative (forex) regime...in which the government would secretly set a band within which the currency would move, a desired exchange rate around which the government would try to carry out interventions," said Malan. 

 His comments follow a turbulent week when the Brazilian real lost 13 centavos, or 5% of its value, to BRR2.64 to the dollar. The sudden depreciation was sparked by a central bank move to improve transparency in mutual funds ended up exacerbating jitters about a possible victory of a left-wing candidate in the October presidential election. 

 Now traders said the real has temporarily stabilized at around BRR2.640. Yet many market players said they expect some sort of central bank intervention if the currency weakens again. 

 Malan also urged all presidential candidates to clarify their positions about economic policy to help calm market jitters. 

 "Some parties are against the fiscal responsibility law, saying it's incompatible with social responsibility," he said, noting that "saying such things is irresponsible." 

 Members of the Workers' Party - its candidate leading the polls ahead of the presidential vote - have said that inflation targets have equal standing with social targets. 

 Investors fear that, if faced with large budget constraints, the left would seek debt renegotiation or cut interest rates very quickly to be able to boost public spending. 

 The central bank isn't independent in Brazil and the next president will have the authority to nominate a new central bank governor. 

 By Paula Lace and Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; 55-11 3145-1481; brazil@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Real Opens At BRR2.637/Dlr Vs BRR2.609 End Wed
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's real continued to lose  ground at the open Thursday, as the country's debt selloff of late keeps on amplifying pre-election jitters. 

 The real opened at BRR2.637 to the dollar and was changing hands at BRR2.643 around 1300 GMT. Wednesday's close, the lowest in seven months for the second day running, was BRR2.609 to the dollar. 

 Meanwhile, Brazil's Capitalization Bond was 2.94 lower  at 67.25, according to quotes provided by local financial  service Broadcast. 

 The recent downturn in domestic markets and growing worries that the government might have trouble rolling over its burdensome public debt are also paving the way for speculation, traders said. 

 Market players, unhappy about a recent central bank measure tightening accounting rules for fixed-income mutual funds, are taking the opportunity to test the monetary authority's tolerance for a sinking currency. 

 "There's people speculating against the currency to see if the central bank will intervene," a Sao Paulo-based trader said. 

 The real has shed more than 10 centavos - or 5% of its  value - since May 31, the day when the central bank enacted the new rules demanding funds to register debt price swings on a daily basis. 

 The new accounting rules for funds has dramatically weakened demand for treasury debt, as political jitters ahead of the October presidential election and an oversupply of bills have been adding unprecedented volatility to debt prices. 

 To calm markets, the central bank this week agreed to swap medium- and long-term government bills held by the market for shorter bonds that mature before President Fernando Henrique Cardoso leaves office at the end of the year. He can't seek a third mandate. 

 While the move initially helped ease tension, now analysts are worried about the country's ability to refund  domestic debt, one-third of which is maturing in the short run. 

 Yet investors selling reals and buying dollars at the current price level are betting on an extremely bearish scenario, traders said. Assuming an average interest rate of 17% this year, the real would have to weaken to about BRR2.90 to the dollar by the end of the year for them to make a profit, one bank director said. 

 The Central Bank of Brazil says it will only intervene  on the market, selling or buying dollars, if there's extreme volatility or low liquidity that could make the currency decouple from the country's economic fundamentals. It did so last year to ward pressure stemming from the fallout of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. and Argentine crisis contagion. 

 -By Adriana Arai, Dow Jones Newswires; (5511) 3145-1481; adriana.arai@dowjones.com

title: Brazil's Fraga Says Turbulence On Funds Temporary
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Market turbulence surrounding changes in fixed-income accounting rules for local investment funds is a temporary phenomenon, Brazil's Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said Tuesday. 

 "Over time, the market should return to normality," Fraga said, testifying before a congressional committee. 

 Brazil's investment-fund industry was thrown into momentary shock last week when the Central Bank advanced the deadline for funds to adjust the value of their fixed-income holdings to market rates on a daily basis. 

 According to some estimates, the market lost some 4 billion reals ($1=BRR2.59) overnight as funds reduced their asset values by about 1% on average. 

 The market havoc has coincided with a heavy schedule of dollar-linked debt coming due as a consequence of Brazil's market intervention last year during the unfolding of an Argentine economic crisis and uncertainties following the Sept. 11 attacks in New York. 

 Fraga, meanwhile, Tuesday also gave reassurances that the country's Treasury wouldn't increase its exchange risk exposure with recent foreign exchange debt-swap operations. He explained the bank decided to roll over only the principal of debt coming due and not the interest. 

 Some analysts have shown concern about Brazil's exchanged-linked debt load amid recent pressure on the country's exchange rate. Brazil's real currency has devalued more than 12% against the dollar since early April. 

 The country has offered the exchange swaps in tandem with LFT floating rate bills as a way to encourage investors to purchase more government debt. 

 Investors in Brazil, however, have been reluctant to take on new domestic debt ahead of the Oct. 6 presidential elections. The government on Tuesday sold just half of the BRR1.5 billion batch of January 2003 LTN fixed-rate treasury bills on offer at a rate of 19.45%. Last week, the government sold December 2002 bills at an average rate of 18.91%. 

 -By Gerald Jeffris, Dow Jones Newswires; (5561) 9965-6883; gerald.jeffris@dowjones.com

title: Eyeing  Brazil  Presidency, PT Vows More Govt  Intervention
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian Workers' Party, with its candidate leading in the polls ahead of the October presidential election, is advocating more state intervention and increased public spending to reactivate growth in Latin America's largest nation. 

 While party leader and presidential contender Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has toned down his anti-capitalism rhetoric and no longer talks about returning privatized companies to state control, Brazil's biggest left-wing group - better known by its Portuguese initials PT - says government subsidies are key to meet a wide range of goals, from boosting exports to fighting inflation. 

 It would be a break from nearly a decade of "excess liberalism and a certain dose of incompetence," says the PT's top economic adviser, Guido Mantega, who blames President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's free-market reform and stabilization policies for the low growth rates Brazil saw over the past seven and a half years. Since Cardoso took office in 1995, the annual growth rate has averaged 2.4%. 

 "When they floated the currency, they finally put economic policy on the right track. But the pace of improvement ever since hasn't been fast enough," Mantega told Dow Jones Newswires. "Three years later, the country has the same external vulnerability as before." 

 Since Cardoso abandoned currency controls in January 1999, fifteen days into his second term, exports have advanced 14% while imports declined 4%. A $6.6 billion trade deficit in 1998 turned into a surplus forecast at $4 billion this year, helping narrow Brazil's current account gap to $20 billion from $33 billion in the period. 

 But the PT's 53-year-old economist says Brazil must use intervention to boost its trade surplus more rapidly. His plan involves across-the-board export subsidies and tax breaks or trade protection for certain industries, to encourage import substitution. 

 With less pressure to borrow, Mantega says Brazil would be able to pay less interest on its debt, have a less volatile currency, and resume growth. A trade surplus of $10 billion would be "comfortable," he adds, noting that tourism promotion efforts could slash the external deficit by another $1.5 billion in coming years. 


    Desire To Loosen Fiscal Policy Worries Market



The essence of the PT's recipe to pull Brazil out of the low growth,
high interest trap is similar to a plan being proposed by Cardoso's
hand-picked successor, Jose Serra, who also thinks the current account
deficit is the country's main weaknesses.



If effective, the proposed measures would translate into a big fiscal
relief. Interest payments, currently running at above 7% of GDP
annually, would no longer eat into the government's primary budget
surplus of about 3.5% of GDP and, consequently, increase the public
debt.



Mantega says lower interest rates combined with an expected resumption
of economic growth would significantly improve Brazil's net debt-to-GDP
ratio, which currently stands at 54.5%.



So much so that Brazil would finally be ready to loosen fiscal policy
after four consecutive years of belt-tightening.



"If you create conditions for interest rates to fall, you could reduce
the primary budget surplus target, so long as the fiscal deficit is
under control," said Mantega. "This administration failed to find
instruments to reduce rates, so it shifted the focus to the primary
surplus from the nominal fiscal deficit, which is what really matters,"
he added.



How much lower could the primary surplus be? "It depends on the pace
of decline of interest rates, which is impossible to predict, as
interest rates are set by market dynamics and cannot be cut by decree,"
answers Mantega.



That's where the PT's policy intentions cause a few raised eyebrows in
the financial community.



Though few economists would disagree with Mantega's remarks that
Cardoso's tight-budget efforts have been largely undone by the high
level of interest rates, they say maintaining a primary surplus at 3.5%
of GDP in the next few years is imperative to keep Brazil's fiscal house
in order.



Cardoso, for example, did try to loosen fiscal targets when the
economy was booming in 2000. But the attempt failed. In August 2000, he
reduced the primary surplus goal to 3% for 2001 and 2.7% for 2002, from
3.35% and 3%, respectively. One year later, financial turmoil in the
region and at home forced the Brazilian president to reset the targets
at 3.35% in 2001 and 3.5% in 2002.



Still, Mantega thinks Brazil can get away with running a fiscal
deficit after interest payments of 4% to 4.5% of GDP, about where it
stands now, as long as the debt-to-GDP ratio is at a "reasonable level."



At 40% in opinion polls, PT's Lula says lowering rates and increasing
public spending would all be a gradual process, emphasizing that
"keeping fiscal responsibility and inflation under control are "a
commitment of honor the Workers' Party has with 170 million Brazilians."



But market analysts say the PT's emphasis on social projects and the
blatant desire to increase spending raise questions about whether Lula,
if in command, would have the guts to cut the budget in times of crisis.



Aware of the market's concerns about Brazil's fragile fiscal
situation, Serra, for his part, has said he would maintain the 3.5%
primary surplus target unchanged if elected.



In local and state governments, the PT has shown it can be even more
responsible when it comes to fiscal accounts than administrators from
parties allied with Cardoso.



Yet monetary policy is at stake this time around.



If elected, Lula said he would appoint a new central bank governor who
certainly won't be Arminio Fraga. Mantega, meanwhile, says the
inflation-targeting regime Fraga introduced in 1999 would stay, but
changes would be made and targets would be loosened. He says 5% sounds
like a more reasonable number for annual inflation here than Fraga's

title: Brazil 's Ctrl Bk  Intervenes ; Offering Dlr-Pegged Debt
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank offered dollar-pegged debt and other securities to primary forex dealers in an unscheduled midafternoon sale Monday, in a move that was initially interpreted by some traders as an intervention to prop up the sagging real. 

 The monetary authority's open-market trading desk couldn't promptly provide the terms of the debt auction, but an official there confirmed that dollar-linked securities were on offer. 

 Later, the head of the central bank's trading desk and a primary dealer said the offering wasn't an intervention and shouldn't have an impact on the currency. 

 The offering - involving a series of dollar-linked maturities and floating-rate LFT bills - has to do with an intraday discount operation that one institution failed to settle within the proper hours Friday, the central bank said. 

 Regardless of the reasons for the dollar-debt sale, the Brazilian real strengthened slightly to BRR2.431 to the dollar from BRR2.437 in wake of the debt sale news. 

 The real closed Friday at BRR2.409, its worst finish in about 10 weeks. Monday's weakness reflects political jitters ahead of the October presidential election. 

 Since that one institution failed to settle the intraday discount transaction Friday, the central bank ended up sitting on a number of public securities that the institution provided as guarantee for the discount credit line. The institution took the discount funds and gave the central bank the public securities, but it failed to pay back the money and get back the guarantee. 

 The central bank official said the offering Monday simply was aimed at giving these securities back to the market. 

 He added that some market players thought it was an intervention sale because the offering was unexpected, and the central bank had to call many dealers to explain what was going on. 

 The Brazilian real has come under pressure in the last several sessions amid an outlook of weakening economic indicators and jitters among some investors about left-wing presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's continued strength in polls for the October vote.

title: BARRON'S: The Real Thing: A Floating  Currency  And Fiscal Reforms Have Stabilized Brazil, Paving The Way For Investors
text:
-- In October, 180 million Brazilians will choose a new government for the first time since 1994. Whether they give the nod to Jose Serra, of the ruling Brazil Social Democrats, or leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, or a candidate somewhere between these political poles, the populace will be affirming the success of the fiscal reforms implemented eight years ago by current president Fernando Henrique Cardoso, who is precluded by law from running for a third term. Under Cardoso's Real Plan, named for the country's currency, the nation's political parties agreed to pursue fiscal restraint, a dramatic reversal from decades of political mismanagement and hyperinflation. As a result, gross domestic product is up; inflation, once an unthinkable 1,000%, has been cut to less than 6%, and Brazil has become the neighbor its neighbors envy. 

 Central to the Real Plan was an ill-fated currency peg that fixed the real to the dollar, following the example of Argentina. In 1999, however, the Cardoso government was forced to devalue the currency after a spike in the trade deficit, increases in unemployment and capital flight. The real today is worth 43 cents, compared with $1.17 at the start of '99 -- a 63% loss in value. 

 Yet, Cardoso's decision to float the real three years before Argentina broke its own link to the dollar in December seems brilliant in hindsight. Unlike Argentina, which has fallen into financial chaos and attendant social crisis, Brazil began 2002 with a solvent banking system and strong capital inflows, and the recovery now is in full swing. Despite recession in much of the region, growth in GDP reached 1.5% last year, and is expected to double in 2002, according to John Welch at Barclays Capital. The weaker real boosted Brazilian commerce, thereby transforming the nation's trade deficit into a $2.6 billion surplus, also likely to double, and then some, this year. 

 "Unlike Argentina, Brazil traditionally has been an exporter of manufactured goods,  and has always attracted foreign investment," says William Gruben, vice president for research at the Dallas Federal Reserve Bank. Gruben notes Brazil received $23 billion in direct investment during 2001, compared with Mexico's $13 billion (not including Citigroup's $12.5 billion purchase of Banamex). 

 Since Brazil accounts for one-quarter of Latin America's total equity-market value of $1.6 trillion, news of fiscal reform and responsible behavior from the main political parties spells big potential for investors. Last year the country's Bovespa stock index fell 25% in dollar terms, compared with Mexico's 18% gain and a loss of 29% in Argentina. 

 In this year's first quarter, the best for Latin American debt and equity since 1995, Mexico rallied another 17% and Argentina's Merval fell almost 50%. The Bovespa declined 3%, a loss that since has been cut to 1%. 

 Nothwithstanding some recent weakness, Argentina's continuing woes, Venezuela's currency devaluation and rising oil prices -- Brazil is a net importer -- a growing number of foreign investors are raising their holdings of Brazilian stocks and bonds. Some see an opportunity to play Brazil's election politics, but others plan to stick around to reap the benefits of improved fundamentals. Moody's, which rates Brazil's foreign debt B1, just upgraded its rating outlook to "positive" from "stable". Standard & Poor's rates Brazil debt B. 

 Credit for Brazil's return to prosperity rests as much with central bank chief Arminio Fraga Neto as it does with Cardoso. In March 1999, just after the real's devaluation, Fraga left his job as a fund manager in New York to become Governor of Banco Central do Brazil, or BCB. The Rio de Janiero native didn't know how long the job would last: The currency was under siege, the economy was weak and turnover among BCB governors was brisk. 

 But Fraga, 44, is now in his third year on the job, thanks in part to having followed the examples set by Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker in the early 1980s, and Mexico after 1994. Brazil's central bank used high interest rates to break the psychology of inflation and stabilize a floating currency. Then, in last year's fourth quarter, with the real bouncing off its low of 2.8 to the dollar, Fraga started easing. The BCB cut short-term interest rates in late February to "only" 18%, and with inflation low, some observers expect another rate-cut before the elections. 

 "We believe Brazilian debt offers good value," says Julian Eisner, head of quantitative strategy at Banco Santander in New York. Although yields fell more than one percentage point in the first-quarter, and price gains might be constrained in the near term, Eisner thinks Brazilian bonds, still yielding more than seven points over U.S. Treasuries, offer investors better risk-adjusted returns than Mexican paper, at two points over Treasuries, or Russian debt, at 3.75 points over Treasuries. Last month Brazil raised $1.25 billion via a six-year bond issue led by Goldman Sachs & Merrill Lynch, that priced at 7.30 percentage points over the Treasury yield curve. 

 Scott MacDonald, chief strategist at Aladdin Capital in Stamford, Conn., a $1.6 billion hedge fund, sees more upside in Brazil than in most markets globally, including those in Asia that already have rallied sharply. "There are not many choices for investors," says MacDonald, who argues that Mexico now has a de facto peso-dollar currency peg and is suffering the same deteriorating terms of trade seen in Brazil prior to 1999. 

 Like many analysts, he puzzles over the fact that Mexico's equity and debt markets continue to benefit from strong capital inflows, despite the country's deteriorating economic fundamentals and a currency that is by some counts 30% overvalued. A former analyst for the U.S. Treasury, MacDonald foresees no credit upgrade for Mexico in 2002, but expects a rating upgrade for Brazil. 

 As Brazil attracts new inflows of foreign investment, the shares of oil giant Petrobras, financial conglomerate Unibanco and Banco Bradesco, the nation's second-largest retail bank, all are catching an updraft. Renewed merger-and-acquisition activity in the telecom sector and elsewhere also is boosting shares. This year, ING Groep acquired 49% of insurer Sul America Seguros for $400 million, and Molson of Canada announced the $765 million purchase of Cervejarias Kaiser, Brazil's second-largest brewer. Nestle soon will boost its share of the country's chocolate market to more than 50%, with the announced purchase of local rival Garoto, Brazil's last independent chocolate brand. 

 Damian Fraser, chief Latin American strategist for UBS Warburg, considers Brazil's equity market cheap at seven times 2003 estimated earnings. Mexico, he notes, is selling for 11 times projected earnings, while the Standard & Poor's 500 fetches 18 times estimates for 2003. Fraser likes Telemar Norte Leste, a local telecom operated by Tele Norte Leste, which began trading as a separate listing on the Sao Paulo exchange last September. He's also recommending cyclicals such as Petrobras and Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, the world's largest iron-ore producer. After the final sale of government shares on March 21, CVRD's American depositary receipts began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol RIO. The ADRs have rallied 2, to 27.50. 

 Fraser thinks Brazil's market can defy expectations of a pre-summer retreat, and rally strongly into the fall election. With inflation around 5%, he also looks for the BCB to lower rates. That said, most analysts expect Brazil's interest rates to remain in the mid-teens for the balance of the year. 

 Investing in Brazilian stocks means owning the floating real, whose gyrations greatly affect the dollar value of Brazilian assets. If the BCB allows the nation's money supply to grow too fast, says Barclays' Welch, the markets push the real lower, forcing the central bank to raise rates. For example, the ratio of M2 to hard-currencyforeign-exchange reserves hit a peak of almost 5-to-1 in the third quarter of 2000, after which the real weakened and the BCB raised interest rates. 

 By last year's fourth quarter the money-supply/foreign-exchange-reserve ratio had retreated to 3-to-1. It's no coincidence that the real then rebounded, says Welch, who expects the Brazilian currency to finish 2002 above current levels. 

 The BCB can afford to let the real float freely because Brazilian banks for the most part have been weaned from currency speculation, and unlike Argentina's banks hold mostly domestic assets and liabilities. Fraga credits the BCB's tough regulation of banks, as well as the government's no-nonsense approach to tax collection, with enabling the Cardoso Administration to improve the Brazil's fiscal health in the midst of a recession. Disputing advocates of a dollar peg, Fraga says a "clean" float, free of central-bank intervention, is the best way for Brazil to maintain price stability and compete globally. 

 The markets may test the BCB's inflation-fighting resolve as the October elections approach, though most foreign analysts think the broad commitment to low inflation and job creation is shared across the political spectrum. Yet, investors also may wonder why Brazil's interest rates remain so high and its foreign debt so cheap compared to Mexico. 

 Says Fraga, "Investors remember the 1980s -- the failed policies and broken promises. The reforms led by Cardoso and others were the government's first test to earn credibility from our citizens and global investors. The October elections and the transition will be the second test for Brazil, to see if the commitment to reform is permanent and above politics. When we make a successful transition, the world will see that we are very serious about price stability and fiscal discipline. The cost of capital will decline internally and abroad, and Brazil will move to the next level in terms of economic growth." 

 Among Fraga's supporters is former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, who helped establish Brazil's central bank in 1965 and visits the country frequently. Volcker continues to worry about the effects of Argentina's default on global capital flows, but likes Brazil's prospects and says he expects his fellow Princeton alumnus to have a long tenure as governor of the BCB.

title: Brazil  To Handle  Currency  Exchange  Interventions  Online
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank will transfer interventionoperations in the currency exchange market to an online system, Central Bank Monetary Policy Directory Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said late Wednesday. 

 The changeover to the electronic system, known as Sisbex, will take place within 60 days. 

 Figueiredo said the new system would make central bank operations more transparent for the market. 

 Currently, currency interventions are handled with the central bank's 25 primary dealers over the phone. 

 The Sisbex system, which is administered in Rio de Janeiro, already handles approximately $250 million a day in foreign exchange transactions, or about 25% of the country's total volume.

title: ANALYSIS-Brazil's CenBank sells dollars for 100th time.
text:
SAO PAULO, Brazil, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank racked up on Tuesday its 100th intervention in the currency market since it began the controversial policy in July, but experts said the daily dollar sales may be rendered unnecessary. 

 In an attempt to inject more reais into Brazil's financial system and buoy what then appeared to be a sinking currency, the Central Bank announced on July 5 that it would spend up to $6 billion by year-end in the exchange market, selling about $50 million per day. 

 At 2.471 per dollar on Tuesday, the real is still 21 percent weaker than where it began 2001, but it is far off the 2.83 reais to which it plunged soon after the Sept. 11 attacks on the United States roiled markets worldwide. 

 While analysts say the daily sale of dollars has indeed helped steady the currency, many argue that it has also played only a supporting role in the real's recent stabilization. 

 "In my opinion, they don't need to continue now because the market has reached a point of maturity, but I think the Central Bank will continue nonetheless," said Emilio Garofalo, the bank's former chief for international reserve operations. 

 "This team has a certain style; they prefer clarity and following through with what they've announced." 

 When asked about the possibility of discontinuing the daily interventions, the bank's director of monetary policy Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said: "That will happen after an announcement that will be made one day. 

 "What we need to remember is that our policy is that the less we need to intervene, the better." 

 Many experts say the daily sales should at least continue until the bank finishes spending the $6 billion. Since July, it has spent about $5.12 billion. 

 PART OF LARGER ARSENAL 

 The real was hit repeatedly this year by tensions in Argentina, an electricity shortage and political corruption scandals that weakened investors' confidence in the country. 

 Worries of a global economic slowdown that would quash investment in Brazil was only exacerbated by the Sept. 11 attacks. 

 But Brazil's economy appears to have been more resilient than initially expected despite the global slowdown, and investors have largely stopped selling Brazilian assets solely because of the country's ties to troubled Argentina. 

 Analysts admit the daily dollar sales helped steady the real but add that the program was part of a larger arsenal of measures meant to keep investors from buying dollars. 

 Moreover, as the currency continued to depreciate through July, August and September, critics of the policy said the Central Bank was being too transparent and had lost its advantage of surprising the market with its interventions. 

 "The $50 million per day are part of the story. They were a group of measures, and it is difficult to say what role the interventions played alone," said Antonio Correa de Lacerda, the president of the Brazilian Society for the Study of Transnational Companies (Sobeet). 

 By the end of September, the bank had tightened liquidity by raising reserve requirements on banks and the cost of their exposure to foreign exchange. At the same time, it has sold dollar-linked notes that were sometimes more popular with investors than dollars themselves. 

 "The objective of the dollar sales was very clear. It wasn't to steady the dollar but to reduce volatility in the market, which would have caused problems for exporters and importers," said William Eid Junior, a professor at Sao Paulo's Fundacao Getulio Vargas. 

 PSYCHOLOGICAL EFFECT 

 Garofalo believes the Central Bank could even use reverse psychology on the market if it decided to suspend the daily sales before the $6 billion was spent. He said such a move could have the opposite effect to what happened when the Central Bank raised interest rates at the start of the year. 

 "At that point, the feeling in the market was that the Central Bank was lending credence to a pessimistic outlook," he said. 

 "Now, markets might say, 'The scenario is better and, if the Central Bank is suspending the daily sales, it's because it must be true.'".

title: Brazil 's Real Ends A Tad Stronger On Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazil's central bank came to the real's rescue Wednesday and its intervention helped the currency close slightly stronger, despite persistent concerns about the global economy. 

 The real closed one centavo stronger at BRR2.771 to the dollar after the monetary authority called an emergency auction of BRR1 billion in short-term dollar-linked T-bills as the real hit an intraday weak point of BRR2.791. Tuesday's close was BRR2.781, the second-worst ever. 

 "We saw a couple of (corporate) names shopping around for price quotes for forex hedging, and when that happens, the real weakens, even if the company doesn't close the deal in the end," said a Sao Paulo-based forex trader. 

 There has been large corporate demand for forex hedging in recent months, in particular after the Sept. 11 acts of terrorism, as market participants believe the real could weaken further amid so much uncertainty about the global economic outlook. Some investment banks forecast the real as weak as BRR3.00 to the dollar by year end. 

 Such worries became evident at the central bank auction of dollar-linked T-bills, which also serve as protection against further forex depreciation. 

 The central bank said the BRR1 billion lot of June 2002 dollar-indexed T-bills was more than twice oversubscribed, with demand reaching BRR2.18 billion. The paper sold for an average annualized rate of 8.04%. 

 Meanwhile, benign September inflation data helped bring money market rates slightly lower as it reinforced the view that the central bank won't likely have to raise interest rates to control prices. 

 Futures contracts finished projecting the interbank rates at 22% in early January, down from 22.35% Tuesday. 

 The September consumer price index was 0.28%, the lowest rate in 11 months, and in line with market expectations. 

 The 30% depreciation of the real this year is inflating public debt, fueling inflation and forcing the central bank to keep monetary policy tight. But it's also helping Latin America's biggest nation narrow its external financing needs by means of trade. 

 The central bank said the country's international reserves inched lower to $39.602 billion Tuesday from $39.662 billion Monday.

title: IMF hopes for deal on new Brazil funds this week.
text:
WASHINGTON, Feb 24 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund hopes to finish a deal with Brazil this week that will allow the resumption of payments under a $41.5 billion rescue deal, an IMF spokesman said on Wednesday. 

 "We still hope that a deal can be reached this week," the spokesman said. He said no details would be available until the arrangement was finished and declined to comment on the latest actions by the authorities, including central bank intervention to defend the fragile Brazilian currency, the real. 

Brazil, the world's eighth largest economy, turned to the IMF for help last year after crisis in Russia and other countries exposed its own financial weaknesses. 

 An international rescue package was approved in November and a first $5.3 billion payment handed over in December. 

 The IMF had initially expected to pay a second, $4.5 billion instalment of its loan to Brazil by the end of this month. But the plans were thrown into disarray after Brazil was forced to bow to market pressure and devalue the real. 

 The two sides have been negotiating terms for payments to restart for the last weeks. Growth and inflation forecasts will have to be revised and new foreign exchange guidelines set. 

 A Brazilian finance ministry official said demands from Brazilian states for debt relief should not affect the IMF talks, and the fund spokesman confirmed the IMF negotiated with the central government rather than with individual states. 

 Finance Ministry Executive Secretary Pedro Parente said the talks were making progress and only "two or three" technical questions remained unresolved. 

 He did not believe the IMF would wait for agreement to increase the CPMF financial transaction tax, expected to reach a final vote in March, before freeing the next tranche of aid.

title: Brazil  Intl Reserves -3: Drop Linked To  Forex Intervention
text:
Later Wednesday, a source at the central bank press office said that the $19 million drop in Tuesday's international reserves figure was a result of the monetary authority's intervention on the foreign exchange market Tuesday.

title: FOCUS- Brazil  cenbank  intervenes  in  forex  market.
text:
SAO PAULO, Feb 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank intervened selling dollars on Tuesday for the first time since the real was floated last month in a bid to keep the currency's downward tilt from spinning out of control, traders said. 

 The bank sold an unknown amount of dollars - estimated at up to $50 million by the market - to specific dealers in order to rein in the real after it sank 5 percent to 2.07 per dollar. 

 "We have the flexibility to, when we deem necessary, intervene in the forex market," the Central Bank press office quoted interim president Demosthenes Madureira de Pinho Neto as saying. 

 "That is the policy, occasional intervention when we deem it adequate," he said, though he warned that there will not be specific levels at which the bank will sell dollars. 

 Global financial turmoil sparked huge capital flight in Brazil in 1998, eventually forcing the Central Bank to let the currency float freely against the dollar last month. The real, once the foundation of Brazil's economic stabilisation plan, has slid 40 percent since Jan. 13. 

 Even after the intervention, the real closed 2 percent weaker at 2.01 per dollar on Tuesday on concern over dollar outflows, breaking the 2-to-1 psychological barrier for only the second time since the currency's devastating devaluation began. 

 "The market was very nervous, pushing the rate up too high," a forex trader at Banco Bozano, Simonsen said. "The bank surprised the market with a discreet intervention directly through the trading tables." 

 Dollars continue to flow out of the country to pay off the roughly $3.8 billion in corporate bonds maturing in February and March, while sorely-needed export income has failed so far to offset the capital flight, traders said. 

 The deepening devaluation has forced Brazil to raise interest rates to ward off inflation and has thrown the economy into an even deeper recession. 

 Traders said the Central Bank's intervention Tuesday does not necessarily reflect a new policy, however, even though the real is expected to come under further pressure this week. 

 "The bank wants to be unpredictable," a trader at a local brokerage said. "Tomorrow the real could go to 2.1 and the bank might not do anything." 

 With forex futures expiring at the end of the week and banks adjusting their dollar positions to comply with bank regulations by the end of the month, the real could continue its tumble. 

 The Central Bank is not expected to adopt a more formal forex policy until after Arminio Fraga, who was handpicked by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to head the institution, is approved by the Senate. 

 "I wasn't expecting them to do anything before Arminio was confirmed at the central bank," a trader at a local brokerage said. 

Currency pressures should subside if Fraga is confirmed and if the newly-installed Congress shows support for Cardoso's austerity plan, traders said. 

 Such moves would also pave the way for the next instalment of a $41.5 billion rescue loan put together by the International Monetary Fund, which would bolster reserves and investor confidence.

title: FOCUS-Brazil's Cardoso says IMF talks advancing.
text:
BRASILIA, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Fernando Cardoso met with International Monetary Fund negotiators on Wednesday and said crucial talks on how to stem a deep currency crisis in Latin America's giant economy were making progress. 

 "The situation in Brazil is developing the way we wanted ... with the return of confidence in the markets," Cardoso told reporters as the negotiations resumed. "We took strong necessary decisions. We are advancing in talks with (the IMF)." 

 Cardoso also said he would not allow the days of roaring inflation to return, a major concern after a near 35 percent devaluation of the real currency over the last three weeks. 

 The real ended a day of light trading at 1.79 per dollar, down 4 cents from Tuesday's closing price but 32 percent weaker since Brazil's worst crisis in years erupted on Jan. 13. 

 Traders said markets were still happy with Tuesday's surprise nomination of Arminio Fraga, an aide to billionaire market mogul George Soros, as the new president of Brazil's Central Bank. 

 The government hopes Fraga will bring a market-savvy edge to its attempts to regain credibility among foreign investors. Left-wing leader Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said the appointment was "submission to the interests of international bankers." 

 But all eyes were on the three-day-old talks which are key to Brazil's hopes of averting a Russia-style crash. 

 Brazil and the IMF are hammering out a new set of fiscal and monetary targets to help narrow Brazil's huge budget deficit and pave the way for a second $9 billion instalment of loans from a $41.5 billion rescue package assembled by the IMF in November. 

 Original targets are now impossible to meet after the devaluation and a subsequent hike in interest rates to nearly 40 percent a year added to the already huge cost of Brazil's 340-billion-reais debt mountain. 

 The talks were also likely to focus on new ways for Brazil to intervene in its newly floating foreign exchange regime. Cardoso ruled out the possibility of introducing a "virtual band" to peg the real against the dollar. 

 Last Friday, the real plunged to a low of 2.18 to the dollar as fears of drastic action by the government prompted some Brazilians to run to the banks to pull out their savings. 

 The IMF's number two, First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer, decided to stay in Brasilia an extra day until Thursday, but the talks were expected to continue after his departure. 

 Another top IMF official said on Wednesday that Brazil and the fund were on the same track and that, despite criticism, the country's high interest rate policy was the right one. 

 "Clearly the tightness in monetary policy will continue," said IMF Deputy Managing Director Alassane Ouattara. "Our experience in Asia has shown that it is important to see a firm monetary framework at the beginning of a crisis." 

 Some leading economists fear Brazil's interest rates, designed to keep a grip on inflation, will plunge the country into a major recession and add to the risk of a devastating debt default that could set economic development back by years. 

 With Brazil facing at best a fierce recession, officials and businessmen in other South American countries are increasingly concerned for their own economies. 

 A senior Argentine industry representative claimed on Wednesday that Brazilian exports to its southern neighbour doubled after the devaluation of the real. 

 So far, however, the Argentine government has resisted calls from business leaders to put up barriers to Brazilian exports. 

 Cardoso was due to discuss the crisis with his Argentine counterpart Carlos Menem on Feb. 12, and a summit with the presidents of the other countries in the Mercosur customs union - Paraguay and Uruguay - was under preparation, officials said. 

 "We are going to come out of all this turbulence with an even stronger feeling that we must reinforce the relationship within Mercosur," Cardoso said after meeting with Uruguayan president Julio Maria Sanguinetti on Wednesday in Brasilia. 

 Brazil's priority for now, however, is smothering any return of sky-high inflation. Only five years ago, prices were rising by 5,000 percent a year, requiring Brazilians to carry bundles of grubby bank notes just to pay for bus fares and newspapers. 

 After nearly zero inflation last year, prices could rise by as much as 80 percent in 1999 on the back of the devaluation, according to some private predictions. 

 Should they prove correct, the government will be virtually helpless to prevent the return of indexation, the practice of raising pay and prices to compensate for expected inflation. That would plunge Brazil back into economic chaos. 

 "The big worry of the government is to avoid the return of inflation," said a presidential spokesman after Cardoso urged food industry executives not to follow the lead of local carmakers and other manufacturers who have begun raising prices. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Brazil-IMF talks focus after bank drama.
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Feb 3 (Reuters) - World market attention should return Wednesday to protracted talks aiming to save Brazil from an Asian-style meltdown, the day after the nation stunned markets by suddenly naming a new Central Bank chief. 

 A team from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has been huddled with government officials since Sunday over how to rebuild Brazil's credibility after its surprise devaluation of its currency, the real, three weeks ago. 

 The two sides hope to hammer out new targets for Brazil's budget, interest rates and foreign exchange rules following the devaluation, which was outside the terms of the deal struck by the government with the IMF last November. 

 Brazil stunned markets again on Tuesday when it entrusted its huge crisis-torn economy to an aide of billionaire speculator George Soros, replacing its interim president Francisco Lopes. 

 Arminio Fraga, 42, a former Central Bank director who was most recently managing director of Soros's powerful investment fund in New York, is expected to bring priceless experience of working in volatile markets to the Brazilian government. 

 But as the dust settled after the surprise announcement of a second Central Bank president in three weeks, economists said while the replacement would give initial confidence to Brazil's economy, it could not mask its serious underlying problems. 

 "The real challenge now for the Central Bank, like the government as a whole, is to stop the devaluation from causing inflation to rise again," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Bank in Sao Paulo. "There's no escape, the main thrust has to be fiscal." 

 "I don't think replacing Lopes with Fraga at the Central Bank resolves the problems of the external financing and investor confidence. The same set of problems are still there," said economist Siobhan Manning at Paine Webber in New York. 

 One of Fraga's first tasks may be to hammer out an agreement with the IMF for it to speed up the release of a second $9 billion tranche of international loans to see Brazil through its crisis. 

 Brazil agreed last November to a series of fiscal and monetary targets in return for a $41.5 billion IMF-sponsored international rescue deal to prevent Latin America's giant from spiraling into an economic black hole. 

 In the meantime, the country is engaged in a desperate juggling act to keep a grip on the currency, cut its massive budget deficit and put a lid on inflation. 

 However, the higher cost of Brazil's huge debt mountain resulting from the devaluation has dashed any chance the government had of meeting the targets, now being revised. 

 The talks in Brasilia should also focus on new ways for Brazil to intervene in its foreign exchange markets to protect the real against the kind of wild fluctuations suffered last week, when it sank below two-per-dollar for the first time. 

 The real, introduced in 1994 as Brazil's inflation-busting currency and once stronger than the dollar, has lost some 35 percent of its value since the government eased its rigid foreign exchange policy last month and allowed a free-float. 

 IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer arrived in Brazil late on Monday to speed up the negotiations. 

 Economists said while the IMF team might be wary about Brazil's sudden move to replace its Central Bank chief in the midst of the crisis, it was likely to view it as a short-term confidence boost for the world's eighth-largest economy. 

 "Ultimately the IMF will be a little wary about the sudden replacement of governors because it shows that the Central Bank is not independent, but that's more of a medium-term concern," Paine Webber's Manning said. 

 "At this point anything to restore confidence is going to be well regarded and received by markets and the IMF...though it's probably a little early to expect any revision of targets. They only just got there and there's a lot to hash over." 

 Analysts say Brazil's economy already looks well on its way to a recession that could mean an economic contraction of five percent this year. 

 Brazil could then be left with no choice but to default on its rapidly expanding debt - a devastating worst-case scenario that would wreck the country's financial system and ruin its already rock-bottom ratings among investors.

title: Wall Street expects Brazil  FX  rules by Friday.
text:
NEW YORK, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Wall Street analysts said they expect Brazil to announce a new policy on foreign exchange intervention rules by this Friday. 

 The policy will likely stipulate the minimum percentage move in the real currency before the central bank can intervene in the markets, traders said. 

 The guidelines will also provide some detail on the mechanisms that the central bank would use to support the currency, such as use of currency options, traders said. 

 The International Monetary Fund and the U.S. Treasury do not in principal support currency market intervention, but would go along with a well-defined and limited programme, said analysts who have talked with Brazilian officials. 

 Brazilians have examined the currency intervention system now in place in Mexico but the Brazilian version will be different, traders said. 

 Mexico's current policy allows an infusion of dollars into the market through an auction process if the peso drops more than five percent in one day. 

 Brazil's central bank "could use some type of options to intervene in the markets ... or some other mechanism while holding to some inflation target," said John Welch, chief Latin American economist at Paribas. 

 Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Wednesday that any new exchange rate policy would steer clear of any type of "band" to contain the movement of the real. 

 The Cardoso government is in negotiations with the International Monetary Fund on resetting monetary and fiscal targets after Brazil allowed the real currency to float last month. 

 The shift in the exchange rate policy triggered a series of changes at the central bank. On Tuesday, Arminio Fraga, former aide to international financier George Soros, was appointed president of the central bank. He succeeds Francisco Lopes, who held the job for three weeks after Gustavo Franco, staunch proponent of a strong real, resigned as central bank chief. 

 ((-Apu Sikri; N.A. Treasury Desk; 212 859-1562 )).

title: FOCUS-Brazil turns to Soros aide amid crisis.
text:
BRASILIA, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Crisis-torn Brazil stunned markets again on Tuesday when it named its second Central Bank president in three weeks, entrusting its giant but ailing economy to an aide of billionaire speculator George Soros. 

 Arminio Fraga, a former Central Bank director and until now managing director of Soros' powerful investment fund, rushed from New York to the Finance Ministry in Brasilia, where the International Monetary Fund and local officials were searching for ways to avoid a Russia-style collapse in Brazil. 

 The battered real currency wobbled on the surprise appointment but staged a healthy recovery, closing at 1.75 to the dollar. That was its strongest level in more than a week, though it was still down 31 percent since Brazil's currency crisis erupted on Jan 13. 

 Also helping the real on Tuesday were new rules making it easier for banks to sell dollars, traders said. 

 Economists said Fraga, 42, was a brilliant thinker who would bring priceless experience of working in volatile markets to the government as it scrambled keep a grip on the real and a lid on inflation amid Brazil's worst financial crisis in decades. 

 "International investors are going to take this news very positively," said Walter Molano, head of research at BCP Securities in Greenwich, Conn. "Arminio Fraga is very well known, prominent and he has credibility among international economists." 

 Some Brazilians worried about Fraga's links to Soros, whose activities have been linked in the past to other countries' currency problems. 

 "The speculators were so successful in their attack on our currency that they not only devalued the real but they've taken over the Central Bank," said Workers Party lawmaker and left-wing economist Aloisio Mercadante. 

 But Mercadante conceded Fraga would probably manage to stabilise Brazil's newly floated real, an essential first step before the government can cut soaring interest rates to ease a looming recession and reduce the threat of a debt default. 

 Soros on Monday criticised Brazil's recent hike in rates to nearly 40 percent a year, calling it a "disastrous move" that increased the risk of a devastating debt default. 

 But people who know Fraga said he would have his own ideas on how the world's eighth-biggest economy should be run. 

 "You shouldn't confuse George Soros with Arminio Fraga," said Paulo Leme, director of emerging markets at Goldman Sachs in New York. "He has independent ideas that sometimes may coincide with those of Soros but at other times differ radically." 

 Fraga's name had been mentioned as a possible adviser to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, but his nomination to run the Central Bank caught the country by surprise. 

 Only last week the Senate confirmed Francisco Lopes as president of the Central Bank following the resignation of Gustavo Franco, a key economic policy-maker, on Jan. 13. That was when Brazil tried to stage a controlled devaluation, only to be forced by the markets to float the currency two days later. 

 Finance Minister Pedro Malan told reporters on Tuesday he had submitted his own resignation during the crisis but that the president had insisted he stay on. 

 "I will remain in the position as long as I have the benefit of the president's confidence," he said. 

 Both Malan and Cardoso have been criticised for going back on pledges not to devalue the real. The president - reelected with a huge majority in October - has seen his ratings plunge to new lows in recent opinion polls. 

 Analysts said the arrival of Fraga might help restore some of Brazil's battered credibility in international markets. 

 Lopes was considered a text-book economist but quickly lost face after the Central Bank refused to intervene in foreign exchange markets last week, allowing the real to plunge to 2.18 to the dollar on Friday, when many Brazilians rushed to the banks to pull out their savings. 

 The powerful president of the Senate - which has to approve the nomination - gave Fraga his all-important blessing shortly after the news broke. 

 "I have known Dr. Arminio Fraga for a long time and I can say that he is extremely competent," Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, a political ally of Cardoso, told reporters. 

 Before running the massive portfolio operations of the Soros Fund Management investment fund, Fraga was international affairs director at Brazil's Central Bank between 1991 and 1992 and was involved in negotiations with the IMF. 

 One of Fraga's first tasks may be to hammer out an agreement with the IMF over the release of a second $9 billion tranche of international loans to see Brazil through its crisis. 

 Brazil agreed in November to fiscal and monetary targets in return for a $41.5 billion loan package from the IMF, other international lenders and top industrial nations. 

 However, the higher cost of Brazil's massive debt mountain resulting from the devaluation has dashed any chance the government had of meeting the targets, which are now being revised. 

 The talks in Brasilia were also focused on new ways for Brazil to intervene in its foreign exchange markets to protect the real against the kind of wild fluctuations seen last week. 

 IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer arrived in Brazil late on Monday to speed up the negotiations.

title: IMF's Fischer Arrives In Brazil Around 1400 GMT Mon -Estado
text:
SAO PAULO (Dow Jones)--International Monetary Fund First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer will arrive in Brasilia Monday around 1400 GMT for meetings with Brazilian officials to review the terms of a $41.5 billion aid package finalized last year, the Estado news agency reported Monday. 

 An IMF delegation met Sunday with Brazilian officials to discuss macroeconomic issues. The two sides were meeting again early Monday, ahead of Fischer's arrival. 

 Finance Ministry executive secretary Pedro Parente said Sunday that Fischer's arrival should help expedite the release of a second tranche from international lenders. Brazil received a first allotment of $9.4 billion last December. 

 Fischer is expected to meet Tuesday and Wednesday with Finance Minister Pedro Malan. Last week, Malan said that Brazil would discuss rules for the government to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 The local currency, the real, has lost about 40% of its value against the dollar since the central bank loosed restrictions on exchange rate fluctuations on Jan. 13. 

 Speaking Sunday at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Fischer said that the real has depreciated far beyond where it should, but said the country still needs a credible monetary policy.

title: Brazil cenbank chief sees IMF targets maintained.
text:
BRASILIA, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Brazil Central Bank President Francisco Lopes said Friday he saw no need for the country to revise targets for its primary budget surplus and net public sector debt agreed with the International Monetary Fund last year. 

 Brazil is going through its deepest financial crisis in years after the Central Bank relaxed its stiff foreign exchange policy on Jan. 13. Since then, the real has lost about 40 percent of its value against the dollar. 

 Despite the devaluation, the Central Bank sees net public sector debt in 1999 remaining below 46.7 percent of gross domestic product, the level agreed with the IMF, Lopes said in an interview with foreign correspondents. 

 The Central Bank chief said Brazil had not intervened in the foreign exchange markets despite the real's plunge through a psychological barrier of two reais per dollar on Friday. 

 He said foreign reserves remained at $36 billion Friday and the Central Bank would begin daily reports on foreign currency reserve levels to show when the bank had intervened. 

 At the moment, forex traders judge by the levels of dollars flowing out of the country whether the Central Bank has started selling dollars to prop up the local currency. 

 "We are going to start reports on Monday, given this situation, this absurd thing that people are reading the outflow statistics in a totally incorrect way," he said. 

 "It's clear that any intervention on our part will be known the following day. For us to give confidence to the market, it's good to give transparency." 

 Market transparency is one of the topics that Brazil is covering with an International Monetary Fund (IMF) team that is arriving this weekend to review a $41.5 billion rescue package that had been hammered out before the currency devaluation. 

 The IMF agreed to provide the credit along with other international financing bodies to prevent Brazil's economy from collapsing completely as long as the government pushed through the reforms necessary to meet fiscal goals. 

 Lopes said Brazil should be able to meet the target on the primary budget, which excludes debt costs, to get a surplus of 2.6 percent of gross domestic product in 1999 and to hold net public sector debt at 42.5 percent of GDP. ((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom +55 21 507 4151)).
