title: Brazil Cenbank to stop releasing daily  forex  flows.
text:
BRASILIA, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank said on Friday it will stop releasing daily foreign exchange market flows and begin publishing reserves levels every day to avoid misinterpretations about the country's reserves. 

 "In the last few days, the outflows in the commercial and floating market based on information in the Sisbacen (Central Bank computerized information system), were wrongly interpreted as a loss in reserves," the Central Bank said in a statement. 

 The Central Bank said this interpretation is "obviously inadequate" in a free-float exchange regime, in which the only loss in reserves takes place when the Central Bank sends money abroad or sells dollars in the market. 

 "Except for this situation, all information about the demand and supply of currencies in the market is completely reflected in the exchange rate," the Central Bank statement said. 

 Brazil abandoned its crawling peg system on Jan. 13 by attempting a controlled 8 percent devaluation, but two days later, it was forced to float the currency and said it would only intervene occasionally. Under the old regime, it had to intervene frequently to defend the peg. 

Brazil has lost a net $8.385 billion through its foreign exchange markets so far this month, after a net $5.16 billion was pulled out in December. 

 ((Sao Paulo newsroom, 55 11 248 5537)).

title: Brazil Central Bank /Reserves -2: No Plans To  Intervene
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's foreign reserves are "steady," as a result of no intervention by the central bank on the foreign exchange market to defend the real, a top official said Thursday. 

 The central bank's foreign affairs director, Demosthenes Madureira de Pinho Neto, said the monetary authority has no plans to intervene and the real will continue to float freely against the dollar. The central bank officially adopted a policy allowing the local currency to float freely against the dollar on Jan. 18. 

 Pinho Neto also pointed out the difference between foreign exchange outflows, which have reached over $8.2 billion, and losses in reserves. 

 "The two are not the same and the impression sometimes created is that the recent outflows are in fact from the country's reserves," he said. "That's not the case, and reserves are absolutely steady." 

 Pinho Neto didn't say at what level reserves stood at Thursday, but earlier this week new central banker Francisco Lopes said at his senate confirmation hearing that Brazil's reserves amounted to $36 billion. 

 (END) Dow Jones Newswires 28-01-99

title: FOCUS-Brazil real drops despite interest rate hike.
text:
SAO PAULO, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency was edging toward a new low on Wednesday after an early morning interest rate hike by the Central Bank failed to appease nervous market players, traders said. 

 The sagging currency was offered at 1.90 to the dollar when traders broke for lunch - trading 3 percent weaker from its Tuesday close. It was down 36 percent since the government first relaxed its stiff foreign exchange policy on January 13. 

 The level was a new low for the real. The currency has been setting new troughs every day since the Central Bank floated the fortress-like currency on January 15, two days after a failed attempt at a controlled devaluation. 

 "Honestly, we don't have any sense of direction," said one forex analyst in Rio de Janeiro. "I'm not making new predictions after my stabilisation theory of 1.7 reais to the dollar became outdated quite some time ago." 

 The real's weakness on Wednesday came despite the Central Bank's initiative to set benchmark overnight market interest rates at 35.5 percent, up from Tuesday's 32.5 percent. 

 Market players said that by raising interest rates, the Bank was encouraging investors to keep money in the fixed-income market and prevent a further wave of dollar outflows. That would take pressure off the real. 

 Brazil lost a net $541 million through its currency markets on Tuesday, a bigger-than-expected dollar flight. More than $8 billion has been pulled out of foreign exchange markets in January alone. 

 An ongoing wave of hard currency outflows has eaten away at Brazil's international reserves, now estimated at around a net $28 billion, excluding the financial aid package Brazil has received from the International Monetary Fund and other rich lenders. 

 Traders and economists said Wednesday's Central Bank move did little to calm currency markets, and even raised more doubts about Brazil's ability to meet its huge debt obligations. 

 High interest rates will have a negative effect on Brazil's burgeoning fiscal deficit, as 60 percent of the debt is now linked to the overnight rate. 

 "We're in a vicious cycle," said the Rio analyst. "The government wants to contain capital flight with higher interest rates, but that just makes it tough for the government, especially when people are still worried whether Brazil can pay its debts." 

 Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank in Sao Paulo, said Brazil should be prepared to "lose its foreign reserves and intervene in the currency market", as a transition cost after it floated the real. 

 "The outflows are not stopping because exporters are not in the market, fearing the currency could devalue more," said Abate. Export revenues, had they entered, would offset dollar outflows. 

 Abate said that by intervening in currency markets, the Central Bank would indicate an appropriate real/dollar level at least for the short term. 

 ((Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248 5423, noriko.yamaguchi@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Bradys End Up On Alleged  Brazil Central Bank Intervention
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Brady bonds have stretched their early gains, ending sharply stronger Tuesday. 

 Market participants attributed the strength of today's rally to widespread intervention by the Brazilian government to support local markets.

text:

title: Brazil  debt up on stocks rise,  intervention  rumour.
text:
LONDON, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazilian dollar debt prices rallied on Tuesday, bolstered by a sharp rise in the country's share prices and suspicion among London traders that the Brazilian government may have been supporting the market. 

 The rise in Brazil's benchmark "C" Brady bond flew in the face of a fresh plunge in the real early in the session to within a whisker of two per dollar and also followed a cut in the country's foreign currency debt rating by Fitch IBCA. 

 One trader said market speculation that demand for the debt was coming from a buyer on behalf of the Brazilian government helped drive prices higher. 

 "I'm sure about it. They took all the bonds from the Street," said one Brady bond trader at a European bank. "There were a lot of Brazilian C bonds traded at 49-3/4 and then suddenly everything came back." 

 Others said technical features of the market resulting from local hedging practises squeezed prices higher. 

 "There is no upper limit to the futures market in Brazil today so that has given the market some liquidity to be able to hedge," said one Brady trader based at a U.S. bank in London. 

 "Our market is a function of the local markets in Brazil, especially with the Bovespa up pretty strong today," he added. 

 At 1500 GMT, Brazilian "C" bonds were up 2-1/8 at 51-7/8 bid compared with earlier levels below the critical 50 level. 


The Sao Paolo Bovespa share index	   was up 5.6 percent at 7.590 and the newly floating real snapped back to 1.89 to the dollar compared with earlier levels of 1.96 to the dollar.



Market analysts said comments from Brazil's interim Central Bank President Francisco Lopes to a Senate panel which is considering his nomination for bank president also helped prices.



Lopes said Brazil had a solid position with $36 billion in foreign exchange reserves and expected to end the year with reserves of around $50 billion.



The sharp rise in Brazilian debt also helped boost other Latin debt prices. Argentine FRBs		 were 1-1/4 better at 77 bid and the Mexican UMS global bonds due 2026 were 3/4 firmer at 103 bid.

title: CORRECTED - Brazil real plunges ahead of IMF meeting.
text:
In Sao Paulo story headlined "Brazil real plunges ahead of 

 IMF meeting" please read in 17th paragraph French Finance 

 Minister  Dominique Strauss-Kahn ... instead of ....French 

 Prime Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn (correcting title) 

 By John Miller 

 SAO PAULO, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's fragile currency plunged to a new low on Tuesday as officials prepared for talks with the International Monetary Fund amid growing global concern over Latin America's biggest economy. 

 IMF technical experts were scheduled to arrive in Brasilia on Tuesday to pave the way for talks on the future of the $41.5 billion IMF-sponsored international rescue package that Brazil received last year. 

 The money was intended to support Brazil's relentless, four-year drive to back the real currency, which officials were forced to float on Jan. 15 as panicked investors withdrew dollars from the country. 

 Investors got another jolt on Tuesday when London-based Fitch IBCA became the latest international rating agency to cut Brazil's credit ratings, an indication the world's eighth-largest economy was one step closer to defaulting on its massive debt. 

 The real opened on Tuesday at 1.83 to the dollar but quickly plunged to about 1.94 per dollar, approaching the psychological barrier of 2 reais per dollar. 

 "The devaluation just keeps going and people don't know when it's going to stop. It's stressing out all of the markets," said Roque Sut Ribeiro, a fund manager at Banco Marka in Rio de Janeiro. 

 Still, stocks on Brazil's key Bovespa index were up 2.8 percent at the open on Tuesday as investors hunted for bargains. 

 Since allowing the real to float earlier this month, Brazil's Central Bank has intervened only once to support it, preferring to let markets choose a new value for the once-strong currency. 

 The real's fall represents a 37.5 percent devaluation since the Central Bank first relaxed its rigid exchange policy on Jan. 13. 

 The currency's plummet was accompanied by more worrying signals from abroad about Brazil's ability to dig itself out of its worst financial crisis in years. 

 "The longer the exchange rate remains under pressure, the more likely it is that inflation rises, the higher interest rates will be," Fitch IBCA's Richard Fox told Reuters Television. "It just makes it all more difficult." 

 Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Service said on Monday that it saw a 1-in-3 risk that Brazil would default on its 300 billion reais local debt because of huge debt servicing costs related to years of sky-high interest rates. 

 Economists expected little news from this week's IMF visit, at which technical experts will swap facts ahead of talks involving higher-level officials, who will assess Brazil's adherence to an IMF-sponsored programme of economic reforms. 

 Instead, Brazilian officials hope markets will take some relief in the passage of a crucial pension reform bill, expected to go before the Senate on Tuesday evening. The bill, which is expected to be passed, would raise contributions paid by federal civil servants and make public-sector workers pay for their pensions for the first time. 

 On Monday, the Central Bank attempted to soothe investors by merging the two rates at which dollars are exchanged with the real. This sent a signal it did not intend to prevent investors from pulling cash out of the country - a measure Malaysia resorted to late last year during its financial crisis. 

 Brazil's efforts to contain the crisis have so far received nods of encouragement from world powers. 

 French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Tuesday that Brazil should survive its current economic crisis because it was following a proper course of adjustment. 

 But even U.S. officials were bracing for the effects of a prolonged recession in Latin America's leading economy. 

 "We're sort of in a little race against time here. We obviously would like to see Japan and Asia lift up while other countries in the world go through adjustments," said Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Richard Fisher on a visit to Japan. 

 "This makes us even more eager for Japan to resume economic growth and to begin to sort of carry the load in Asia as the economy in Brazil and perhaps some of their neighbours slows down." 

 In Brazil, newspapers spoke of growing restlessness over the government's ability to handle the crisis. 

 An editorial in the leading Sao Paulo newspaper Folha de S.Paulo praised the Central Bank's move on Monday for increasing market transparency, but said that in the current siege mentality, it was doubtful it would boost confidence. 

 "The scene at the moment is like the sinking of the Titanic. While the ship was going down, its musicians insisted on continuing to play pleasing sonnets. An edifying option, but with no practical results," the editorial said.

 One trader said market speculation that demand for the debt was coming from a buyer on behalf of the Brazilian government helped drive prices higher. 

 "I'm sure about it. They took all the bonds from the Street," said one Brady bond trader at a European bank. "There were a lot of Brazilian C bonds traded at 49-3/4 and then suddenly everything came back." 

 Others said technical features of the market resulting from local hedging practises squeezed prices higher. 

 "There is no upper limit to the futures market in Brazil today so that has given the market some liquidity to be able to hedge," said one Brady trader based at a U.S. bank in London. 

 "Our market is a function of the local markets in Brazil, especially with the Bovespa up pretty strong today," he added. 

 At 1500 GMT, Brazilian "C" bonds were up 2-1/8 at 51-7/8 bid compared with earlier levels below the critical 50 level. 


The Sao Paolo Bovespa share index	   was up 5.6 percent at 7.590 and the newly floating real snapped back to 1.89 to the dollar compared with earlier levels of 1.96 to the dollar.



Market analysts said comments from Brazil's interim Central Bank President Francisco Lopes to a Senate panel which is considering his nomination for bank president also helped prices.



Lopes said Brazil had a solid position with $36 billion in foreign exchange reserves and expected to end the year with reserves of around $50 billion.



The sharp rise in Brazilian debt also helped boost other Latin debt prices. Argentine FRBs		 were 1-1/4 better at 77 bid and the Mexican UMS global bonds due 2026 were 3/4 firmer at 103 bid.

title: CSCE coffee futures end weaker, in mid-range.
text:
NEW YORK, Jan 22 (Reuters) - CSCE arabica coffee futures ended slightly lower on Friday, with prices finally settling in mid-range, after speculators played both sides of the market, dealers said. 

 "The main players were specs," said one trader. "The specs sold it and the specs bought it back." 

 Benchmark March coffee fell 0.50 cent a lb, to settle at 105.50 cents, after ranging between 107.00 and 104.00 cents, its lowest level in 12 weeks. 

 Second-month May ended 0.70 cent weaker, at 107.60 cents, while the rest of the board closed down 0.60 to 1.00 cent. 

 The March/May contango finished at 2.10 cents, compared with 2.30 cents at the close on Thursday. 

 Traders said economic turmoil in Brazil continued to keep the coffee market on the defensive. 

Brazil's Central Bank on Friday intervened in local currency markets for the first time since it free-floated the real, defending the embattled currency from engaging in a freefall. 

 The Brazilian real has depreciated some 30 percent since January 13, when the government devalued the currency before allowing it to float freely two days later. 

 Some traders feared the world's largest producer of coffee would cash in on the higher local currency earnings from dollar-denominated exports and flood the market with coffee. 

 Since January 13, the March contract has lost 14.80 cents or more than 12 percent. 

 However, traders noted that March coffee has barely moved during the last three sessions, easing a little over a penny in heavy volumes. 

 "I think the selling has just been absorbed by roaster buying," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "But if roasters have done all this pricing and buying, what happens next? I don't think it bodes well for coffee." 

 Some traders said increased shipments of coffee from Mexico and Central America is also likely to keep prices under pressure. In addition, they expected cheaper differentials for their coffee will draw more coffee to the board. 

 "Differentials are down and people are buying coffee at differentials they can tender it, so you're going to see a lot of coffee come to the board," said one physical trader, adding, "I don't see roasters bending over backward to buy coffee from us." 

 Other traders, however, said the market was oversold and due for a correction. They reckoned the funds had substantially reduced their net long position from the 11,227 lots reported as of January 12. 

 In addition, prospects for a sharply reduced 1999-2000 crop from Brazil following this season's bumper crop of 35-36 million bags was likely to underpin the market, they said. 

 Technically, traders pegged March support at 104.00-103.00 cents, with key psychological support noted at 100.00 cents. Resistance was seen at 107.00 cents, then 108.50-109.00 cents, they said. 

 After Friday's close, CSCE reported certified coffee stocks fell by 250 bags as of January 21, to 96,961 60-kg bags. There were 5,502 bags pending grading, the exchange said. 

 CSCE also reported 7,000 bags of coffee were graded and 1,750 bags passed exchange approval.

title: Brazil  real ends steady 1.72/dlr post- intervention .

 The bank stepped in to sell dollars in foreign exchange markets through state-owned Banco do Brasil early Friday after it had tumbled 7.6 percent to an all-time low of 1.72 reais per dollar Thursday as dollar stocks started to get depleted.

title: FOCUS-Brazil's Cenbank defends real from freefall.
text:
SAO PAULO, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank on Friday intervened in local currency markets for the first time since it free-floated the real, defending the once long-stable currency from engaging in a freefall. 

 The Central Bank sold dollars in foreign exchange markets via state-owned Banco do Brasil shortly after the open, when the real plunged to as low as 1.77 per dollar - posting a depreciation of 31.5 percent since Jan. 13, when the goverment devalued the currency before allowing it to float freely two days later. 

 The real quickly firmed to 1.65 following the intervention but swung back to its opening level of 1.74 before finishing the morning session at 1.69 reais. 

 "The Central Bank is sending a message to the market, although not that powerful at this point, that it will not leave the real run out of control," said one trader at an international bank in Sao Paulo. 

 Markets predicted the Central Bank had spent more than $100 million in trying to defend the real by 1300 local/1500 gmt. 

Currency dealers said the market was testing the Central Bank at this point on what level it would come in to rescue the real and how it would step in, after the Bank said it would intervene "occasionally and in a limited fashion" at the time of the flotation last Friday. 

 "For a while 1.6 reais to the dollar seemed an appropriate rate. But consensus has shifted away from that due to dollar liquidity problems. Now, it's also a confidence problem. A lot of people out there are scared," said Constantin Jancso, an analyst at MCM Consultores. 

 The Central Bank has kept silent about traders' reports today that it was intervening. 

 But according to traders, the Bank used Banco do Brasil on Friday, like it has always done when it used to supply dollars to markets and maintain the real trading within a set band. "The Central Bank has to study how it does this from now, in a floating market, because the way it is now, everybody short of dollars will run to Banco do Brasil," said one economist who requested anonymity. 

 One way of intervening was to sell dollars randomly through a number of banks, without letting the market know, or the Central Bank could come in directly and sell dollars through auctions. 

 While the real appeared to settle at around 1.70 reais after the intervention Friday, it was too early to determine this was the level at which the Central Bank hoped to maintain the real, some forex traders added. 

 Traders predicted the Central Bank came in Friday more in an effort to supply dollars rather than set any level. 

 Friday's intervention came one day after the real had tumbled 7.6 percent to finish at an all-time low of 1.72 reais, due to a depletion of dollars in the market amid a tidal wave of hard currency outflows. 

 Local currency markets lost a net $411 million on Thursday, up from a daily $300 million outflows that had been fleeing since last Friday, and more were expected to escape. 

 About $700 million in private corporate eurobonds were still expected to come due this month, bringing the total amount of overseas debt due to $4.4 billion, including $1.2 billion in interest payments. 

 Another $2.8 billion was seen maturing in February. 

 "The Central Bank made it clear that with the new policy it could intervene to iron out market volatility. It's basically anybody's guess how and when that will work out." 

 "The problem is there are substantial amounts of debt coming due, combined with limited dollar liquidity. Banks are starting to hold on to their dollars," said MCM's Jancso. "By letting the currency float, the Central Bank opened a Pandora's box and things are flying out of it."

title: Brazil  c.bank says will not  intervene  in  forex  mkt.
text:

 The foreign exchange rate will be set by the market in function of dollar flows, Altamir Lopes, the head of the Central Bank's economic department, said.

title: Brazil 's Malan -3: No Specific  Intervention  Point For Real

Exiting the talks, Malan said he had "no comment on the appropriate level of the real," adding that the government hadn't set any specific point at which to intervene in defense of the currency. 

 He added that there has been no discussion of restructuring Brazil's mounting debt, saying "We are not going to have any domestic debt restructuring." 

 On the fiscal front, Malan said he expected congress to vote on and approve social security reform Wednesday, calling it a "very important vote." 

 International investors have been watching Brazil closely for signs that it will carry out the reforms required under its $41.5 billion rescue from the International Monetary Fund. That includes passage by congress of the necessary reforms to the pension system. 

 Finally, Malan said the bankers gathered Wednesday in New York didn't discuss any alternative to the new free-floating currency regime for the real.

title: FOCUS-Brazil will honor debts, finmin tells bankers.
text:
NEW YORK, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Brazil will honour all loan obligations and do its best to contain a domestic financial crisis that has threatened global financial stability, Finance Minister Pedro Malan told a dozen top bankers on Wednesday. 

 "We are not going to have any domestic debt restructuring," Malan told reporters after meeting with U.S. banking leaders at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. 

 Brazil owes international banks about $70 billion in short-term debt, according to bankers, and another $300 billion to domestic financial institutions. Economists have questioned the Latin American giant's ability to meet its obligations. 

 Malan on Wednesday assured bankers - including Goldman Sachs co-chairman Jon Corzine, Merrill Lynch chief executive David Komansky and financier George Soros - that Brazil will not intervene in the currency markets to defend its currency, the real. 

 Malan called the meeting "constructive." Brazil hopes to win back investor confidence after a decision last Friday to float the real - a move that will help the country preserve precious foreign exchange reserves. 

 "It is up to the markets to decide what is the appropriate exchange rate. We do not have intervention points, virtual bands, notional bands. And we do not have a hidden agenda," Malan told reporters after the meeting. 

 Brazil has also ruled out adoption of a currency board - which would link the value of the real to the dollar and take away most decision-making from the central bank, Malan said. 

 "We have decided on a floating exchange rate regime and this is the regime we are going to have," Malan said. "This is not a criticism of any country that adopts the currency board scheme." 

 Brazil's neighbour Argentina has implemented a currency board deemed successful by most economists. 

 The real has lost more than a quarter of its value against the dollar since last week's devaluation and subsequent abandoning of exchange rate bands. 

 Bankers have privately asserted that Brazil needs the support of private lenders to avoid a debt default of the sort that trapped Russia last year and set off panic in financial markets. 

 Official lenders led by the International Monetary Fund and the United States arranged $41.5 billion in loans to Brazil late last year to contain financial turmoil that threatened to infect Latin America and other regions. 

 Malan was accompanied by Secretary of Economic Policy Amaury Bier and International Affairs Secretary Marcos Caramuru.

title: =Brazil's Real Float Could Weaken U.S. Bonds, Boost Dollar
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Brazil's decision to float its currency against the dollar probably will lead to further liquidation of safe-haven Treasury bond positions when New York trading resumes Tuesday. 

 But foreign-exchange dealers, largely sidelined Monday for a U.S. public holiday, are expected to bid the dollar higher when they return to their desks Tuesday. 

 Monday, Brazil's central bank said the real will be allowed to float freely against the dollar. That decision came after last Friday's decision by Brazil not to intervene in foreign-exchange markets to support the real. 

 Both actions convinced a lot of observers that Brazil was taking the rights steps to prevent its problems from getting worse or spreading, in turn making it safe for investors to start buying stocks again. 

 Indeed, U.S. and Latin American stocks rallied Friday while the Treasury's 30-year bond lost a point. 

 Latin American stocks were higher again Monday, and analysts expected that bid to extend to New York shares Tuesday, when U.S. markets reopen. Stock and bond markets in the U.S. were closed Monday for Martin Luther King Day. The dollar should see support for the same reasons. 

 "The fact that (Latin American markets) are up right now bodes well for the dollar," said Robert Fullem, corporate trader at NatWest Global Financial Markets in New York. 

 Around midday in New York, the dollar was up slightly against the yen from where it closed last Friday. 

 The downside for Treasurys could be limited by the appearance of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who is scheduled to testify before the House Wednesday. Greenspan's expected to be quizzed extensively about Brazil's impact on the U.S. economy, and investors might want to hold off making substantial portfolio shifts before that event.

especially with Greenspan speaking Wednesday," said Danyelle Guyatt,

title: Brazil seeks IMF, U.S. backing in  currency  crisis.

WASHINGTON, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan will meet U.S. officials on Sunday seeking their endorsement of a shock decision to allow Brazil's currency, the real, to devalue. 

 Malan was due to meet Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Larry Summers on Sunday, after meeting with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus on Saturday. 

 An aide to Malan said they discussed Friday's decision to give in to market pressure and let Brazil's currency float freely and the impact the devaluation will have on the world's eighth-largest economy. 

 "Brazil came to explain and try to obtain support for the changes made this week," the aide told Reuters. 

 He said the talks also covered the impact a devalued real will have on Brazil's economic programme with the IMF. 

 That programme was agreed to in November as part of a $41.5 billion international rescue plan by rich industrial nations to save Brazil from following Russia into a financial maelstrom. 

 The plan had succeeded in bolstering confidence in the real until the governor of Brazil's third-largest state, Minas Gerais, spooked investors by declaring a 90-day moratorium on debt payments to the federal government. 

 Faced with a renewed run on the currency, Brazil tried a controlled devaluation on Wednesday and on Friday stopped intervening to prop up the real, the pillar of Brazil's economic stability since 1994. 

 The real fell as low as 1.55 to the dollar, but then stabilised at around 1.42 to the dollar, down some 15 percent in value in the week. 

 Dollar outflows from Brazil slowed on Friday and shares soared 33 percent on the Sao Paulo stock market as investors saw the currency would not tumble out of control. 

 "You saw what happened. There was no big run," Malan told reporters on arrival in Washington. "The market set the value and it was a stronger level than some people had expected." 

 "It was a positive step," he said. 

 Malan, who was accompanied by newly-appointed Central Bank president Francisco Lopes, said the bank will announce new currency exchange rules on Monday in Brasilia. 

 The alternatives range from a permanently floating rate to a currency board like the one Argentina adopted successfully in 1991 - a rigid regime that pegs the currency firmly one-to-one to the dollar. 

 A middle road is a new rate loosely pegged to the dollar like the one abandoned on Friday, but with wider ranges for the real to fluctuate in. 

 The decision to float the real essentially scrapped the cornerstone of the Real Plan, which based itself on a strong currency to successfully tame hyperinflation in Brazil. 

 Analysts said Brazil will have to move faster now to put its public accounts in order by passing fiscal reforms that were delayed in Congress. 

 They said Brazil does not need to ask for more funds from the IMF and the Group of Seven rich nations, because it has hardly used any of the $41.5 billion loan package. 

 But they stressed that Brazil must enact promised reforms to cut its huge fiscal deficit if it wants markets to maintain confidence in its currency. 

 Malan's aide said the Brazilian government may ask the IMF to speed up the second disbursement from the international rescue package, some $4.5 billion due at the end of February. 

 The IMF said in December it was prepared to pay out this money sooner if Brazil requested it.

title: Brazil Floats Real In Bid To Stem Capital Flight, Conserve Reserves
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Yielding to pressures from the international foreign-exchange market, Brazil on Friday set its embattled currency free to trade unhindered against other currencies. The move to float the real, which should allow Brazil to conserve currency reserves and reduce crippling interest rates, was viewed favorably by investors. 

 Meanwhile, a respected central-bank veteran rescinded the resignation he announced Thursday, helping to allay the fears about the nation's deteriorating fiscal picture that rocked world markets this week. And the country's finance minister will head to Washington for high-level talks about the financial crisis with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and other top U.S. and international monetary officials. 

 In allowing the real to float freely, Brazil's central bank revoked the new trading band set for the currency Wednesday. That move, which widened the band, resulting in an effective devaluation of about 8%, roiled world markets. Following Friday's announcement, the real fell by another 12% before stabilizing in afternoon dealings. 

 The central bank didn't say that it was abandoning the band altogether, only that it wouldn't intervene on the foreign-exchange market Friday to keep the real within the latest band, whose ceiling was 1.32 reals to the dollar. That was the level the real closed at Thursday after the central bank repeatedly sold dollars to defend its currency. The bank promised to issue a full communique regarding the country's exchange-rate policy on Monday. 

 Investors across the globe focused on the positives in the latest policy shift. By giving up its costly defense of the real, Brazil will have more room to reduce interest rates to boost its recessionary economy. A weaker real also makes the price of Brazilian exports more competitive, which could create jobs and help lead the economy out of recession. That, in turn, would go a long way in fending off any serious downdraft in Latin America as a whole, which is a significant U.S. trading partner. 

 "So the bottom line is that Brazil's economy could actually do better than we anticipated only yesterday," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Wells Fargo in Minneapolis. 

 The move to float the real, which had been widely anticipated, came after senior Clinton administration officials and the International Monetary Fund warned Brazil's president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, that his government wouldn't likely to be able to support the currency at artificial levels in the face of an exodus of foreign investors, the New York Times reported Friday. They told Cardoso Brazil might waste billions of dollars of its precious foreign-currency reserves attempting to do so, the paper said. 

 The government had also come under pressure to let the real float so it wouldn't have to maintain the high interest rates used to defend the currency at stronger valuations. The nation's steep rates, which were effective in stamping out hyperinflation earlier in the decade, have shackled the economy. Brazil's benchmark rate stands at a smothering 29%. 

 Cardoso said Friday that the decision to let the currency float was designed to protect the nation's reserves, adding that the move helped reduce the level of distrust in Brazil. 

 Finance Minister Pedro Malan, speaking to reporters after meeting with Cardoso, said, "After the exchange rate shot through the ceiling (of the trading band), we thought it better to let the market act freely to find its own balance." He addded that investors' reaction Friday was "an expression of confidence" in the decision not to intervene in foreign-exchange markets. 

 However, the float raises questions about the $41.5 billion, IMF-led bailout of Brazil announced last fall. Indeed, that likely will be one of the issues on the table when Malan visits Washington this weekend. Malan, who will be accompanied by Francisco Lopes, the new central bank president, said he and Lopes will meet with officials of the IMF, the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the U.S. Treasury. 

 The rescue package assembled for Brazil was designed to keep investor panic from flooding Latin America. In exchange, Cardoso agreed to slash the enormous federal budget deficit to persuade investors to keep their money in the country. The IMF agreement also envisioned Brazil maintaining its exchange-rate policy. But Cardoso was only able to persuade politicians to accept some of his budgetary proposals, resulting in investor flight and the devaluation of the real on Wednesday. 

 The latest developments have put the IMF in a tough spot. IMF and Brazilian officials may have to renegotiate the loan-aid terms, since the devaluation will increase the amount the government must pay to service its considerable debts and throw it off its IMF-endorsed deficit targets. 

 The IMF said Friday that Brazil's decision to pull back from further intervention in support of the real "appears to be a wise move" that will protect the country's foreign-exchange reserves. An IMF spokesperson said the Brazilian government contacted the fund before its latest move. 

 Asked whether Friday's events will lead to any changes in the aid package, Treasury Secretary Rubin replied: "To the best of my knowledge, no." 

 But if Cardoso can't follow through on his fiscal promises, the IMF and its backers at the Treasury might have to decide whether to cut off the rescue effort. And there is recent precedent for the global lending agency doing just that. Since Russia effectively devalued its currency and declared a moratorium on some domestic debt in August, the IMF has refused to provide new funding to Moscow, for fear of throwing good money after bad. The Russian moves sparked the run on Brazil last September. 

 The markets, which were buoyed across Europe and the Americas following Brazil's move to float the real, have now turned their attention to what permanent foreign-exchange system Brazil will adopt and where the real will finally settle. Most economists rule out the possibility of the central bank even attempting to return to the sort of rigid system that Brazil had clung to for the past four years. Rather, they say the bank will either stick to the free float or adopt an extremely wide band for the real. 

 Allowing the real to float to weaker levels will increase the price Brazilians pay for essential imported goods and could reignite the inflation the Cardoso government stamped out with its previous monetary policies. But the deep recession and high interest rates are seen mitigating the inflationary pressures. 

 At the close Friday, the real was trading at about 1.43 to the dollar, down 8.3% from Thursday's close of 1.32 to the dollar. Earlier, the real had slipped 12%, trading as low as 1.50 per dollar. 

 The main Bovespa stock index, which had plunged 25% since the start of the year through Thursday, rebounded 33% Friday, on hopes that the worst may behind Brazil - namely, that the weaker real will eventually allow the government to maintain reserves, trim rates and revitalize the economy. 

 But the country continues to face daunting challenges, especially as it tries to reach its goal of shaving $28 billion off its deficit in 1999. And fears likely will continue that the turmoil in the world's eighth-largest economy could spread across Latin America and lead to a round of currency devaluations in other emerging-market economies. 

 The crisis deepened Thursday as financial markets took another beating and the government struggled to support the real in the wake of Wednesday's devaluation. One factor undercutting confidence was the announced resignation of Claudio Mauch, the central bank's director responsible for supervising the country's banking system. However, on Friday Mauch rescinded his resignation following a request from Malan and Lopes. 

 Mauch's resignation announcement was poorly timed because it closely followed Wednesday's surprise resignation of Central Bank president Gustavo Franco. Although Mauch stressed that his planned departure was for personal reasons, the news raised worries that Brazil's top monetary officials might be abandoning a sinking ship. 

 Another main concern among investors has been the capital fleeing Brazil. A reported $1.79 billion flowed out of the country Thursday, up from the $1.09 billion in outflows Wednesday. Amid the renewed optimism Friday, Brazil's central bank reported just $160 million in net outflows from the foreign-exchange market. Significantly, there was no capital drawn from the nation's central-bank reserves, said spokeswoman Silvia Faria. 

 "For the Central Bank the most favorable results Friday were that - despite the monetary authority's absence - the market didn't appear to be left without liquidity ... and that the exchange rate didn't skyrocket," she said. 

 Brazil reportedly has about $44 billion in dollar reserves, a still-sizable amount, but down by almost half of what it held before the Russian crisis erupted in August. 

 The wave of capital flight intensified over the past week following the announcement by Minas Gerais - Brazil's third-wealthiest state - of a 90-day moratorium on debt payments to the federal government. The state's move sparked fears that the central government wouldn't have the revenue to meet its deficit-cutting goals. 

 Cardoso said Friday that "irresponsible" comments on further state debt moratoria "forced Brazilians as well as foreigners to withdraw their funds from Brazil," leading to the foreign-exchange policy shift Friday.

title: U.K., European Banks Rise As Brazil Allows  Currency  Float
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--European banks stocks are up Friday, following Brazil's decision to allow its currency to float. 

 Despite significant exposure to Brazil, bank shares were higher on the view that floating the currency had removed artificial supports. European bank stocks also got hammered earlier in the week, when Brazil effectively devalued its currency. 

 At 1515 GMT, The Dow Jones Stoxx banking index was up 1.1%, or 3.22 points, at 301.85 

 The U.K. retail bank sector was down 0.37%. The index lost 7.8%, since the start of the week. 

 Analysts said investors had overestimated the risk from Brazil earlier this week. Latin American markets account for 5% or less of most European banks' earnings. 

 Further, many banks have been cutting their exposure. U.K. banks, for example, have scaled back their already small exposure to riskier trading activities in emerging markets such as derivatives. And Latin America is not nearly as significant a component of U.K. banks' emerging market portfolios as Asia. 

Brazil's central bank said Friday it wouldn't intervene in the foreign exchange market, allowing its currency, the real, to float freely. That move follows an effective 8% devaluation of the real earlier this week. 

 Earlier this month the country's third-wealthiest state announced a 90-day moratorium on debt payments to the federal government. 

 Among continental European banks, which have greater exposure than U.K. banks, the Spanish and Germany banks have the most to lose from a collapse in Brazil. 

 But although many market-watchers, like Paribas European banking analyst Romain Burnand, are reserving judgment on whether the caution investors are displaying towards the sector in Continental Europe is warranted, they say that European banks in general had a less risky lending portfolio than in other emerging markets. 

 "Latin America is an environment which was always regarded as risky anyway," Burnand said. "This was not the case in Asia, which was regarded as a booming economy." Loans made in Asia were higher risk, he said, whereas those made in Latin America were "much more selected and protected." 

 Another analyst was more forthright, saying he regarded Continental European banking stocks as well as U.K. banking stocks as oversold. "The market for European banks in aggregate is getting better," he said, adding "investors have overreacted to the Brazilian crisis."

title: FOCUS-Argentine shares fly after six day doze.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Argentine shares roared back to life Friday after Brazil, the country's main trading partner, put an end to days of nail-biting by regional brokers and let its battered currency float free. 

 "The news is calming, at least," said Mario Zawadzki, a trader with Schweber brokerage. 

 The leading MerVal index of traded shares was over 10 percent higher in afternoon trade in encouraging turnover of 31.7 million pesos. 

 Led by an over 30 percent rise in Brazilian stocks, Argentina's surge followed a 23 percent drop since Jan. 6, when a rebellious Brazilian state sent markets reeling by postponing debt payments to the central government. 

 By Wednesday, speculative pressure on the real forced the Brazilian government to widen a thin band in which the currency traded, devaluing it by about 8 percent. 

 But the outflows failed to cease and Brazil's Central Bank said it would not intervene in the foreign exchange markets Friday morning, effectively allowing the currency to float. The real fell another 12 percent. 

 Argentine banking stocks, hit hard the days before, skyrocketed on expectations that the fall would mean lower interest rates and higher prices for their bond holdings. 

 Banco Frances de la Plata SA  was up nearly 16 percent after slipping almost 34 percent in the prior six days of trade. 

 Telecommunications stocks were also shooting higher, with Telecom Argentina  up 17.7 percent and Telefonica Argentina SA  15.7 percent stronger. 

 "If the scenario in Brazil turns out positive, the risk for Argentina will be limited a lack of economic activity, but we won't have solvency problems or troubles with our financial system," said Paula Premrou, head analyst at Lopez Leon brokerage. 

 Argentina, which sends about a third of its exports to Brazil, has already cut its growth expectations for 1999 on an expected slowdown in economic activity. The government's most recent forecast is a 3.0 percent rise in gross domestic product. 

 Premrou said many of the companies with strong trade links to Brazil had already seen their share prices dive last year. 

 "Steel and auto stocks have already been tremendously punished," she said.

title: IMF says Brazil devaluation could stem dollar flight.
text:
WASHINGTON, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund welcomed Brazil's decision to stop defending its currency on Friday, changing tack to describe it as a wise move which could stem the flood of dollars from the country. 

 A spokesman said the IMF, brains behind a $41.5 billion international rescue package for Brazil, had been informed in advance about Brazil's abrupt decision to stop intervening to support the once-proud real. "It appears to be a wise move to stop the loss of reserves," he said. 

 The announcement marked a none-too-subtle change of course for the IMF, which had so far steered clear of endorsing a floating exchange rate for Brazil, the world's eighth largest economy and Latin America's biggest economy by far. 

 IMF officials said when they announced the loan package last November that they expected Brazil to accelerate the pace of devaluation by widening the sloping corridor within which the real was allowed to trade against the dollar. 

 But they said Brazil planned to continue its exchange rate regime - a crawling peg with neither the flexibility of a floating rate nor the rigid rules adopted by neighbouring Argentina, where one peso is worth exactly one dollar. 

 Brazil's letter of intent to the IMF, a 35-point document outlining government proposals, said the government, which viewed the real as the cornerstone of its anti-inflation policy, was fully committed to a stable real. 

 "The priority goal is continued low inflation," said the letter, sent to the IMF on Nov. 13. "The current exchange rate regime is an essential means to this end." 

 Economists, who have long complained that the real was overvalued, broadly welcomed Brazil's change of plan, viewing the currency's new exchange rate of around 1.42 to the dollar as more sustainable than the one which went before. 

 "This may be the first emerging market devaluation that actually works, that boosts confidence rather than undermines it," said Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist for the Americas at ING-Barings in New York. 

 "For better or for worse, Brazil now has a more realistic exchange rate that reflects market pressures - but nothing has happened to change underlying market pressures." 

 Markets had punished Brazil after a regional governor's decision to default on some debts highlighted a rift between Brasilia and the provinces and cast doubts over the government's ability to cut spending as prescribed by the IMF. 

 Billions of dollars flooded out of Brazil and the central bank first widened the real's trading band against the dollar and then stopped defending the currency entirely. 

 The real dropped to 1.58 to the dollar before bouncing back to steady at around 1.41. Brazilian shares, under pressure for days, reversed course abruptly and soared 33 percent. 

 A weaker real means far heavier debt servicing costs for Brazil and changes many of the assumptions behind the rescue package. Brazilian officials will arrive in Washington on Saturday for talks with the IMF and the U.S. Treasury. 

 "This trip is to make amends, to break down the very frosty relationship that had developed in recent weeks," Porzecanski said. 

 The Brazilian rescue deal was the fifth multi-billion dollar bailout in 18 months after packages in Asia and Russia. Mexico won its own big bailout in 1995. 

 But analysts said Brazil was not as worrisome as the IMF's previous patients. Banks were better developed and the government was committed to change even if it was finding it hard to persuade Congress to approve painful spending cuts. 

 "Brazil is very different from both Mexico and Asia," said David Hale, of Zurich Kemper Investments. 

 "There will be some shocks and there will be risks, but I just don't think Brazil, because of its historical circumstances, has to have the kind of shocks we saw in Mexico a few years ago and in Asia over the last two years." 

 Most economists did not expect Brazil to need extra financing at this stage, although World Bank President James Wolfensohn said he was ready to consider accelerating loan payments to help Brazil out of its crisis. 

 "I would consider it. I may consider it positively, I may consider it negatively, but I will consider it," Wolfensohn told reporters. 

 The World Bank has promised to contribute $4.5 billion to the Brazilian package. It has approved payments totalling just over $1 billion, but has not yet handed over the money because Brazil's Congress has not yet approved the loan.

title: Brazil devaluation offers opportunity for Argentina.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Argentine economic growth may suffer from a devaluation in Brazil, but the move by its northern neighbour could offer Buenos Aires an opportunity to show off its stronger fundamentals, economists said on Friday. 

Brazil's Central Bank on Friday stopped intervening in the foreign exchange market, leaving its embattled currency, the real, to float. The move came two days after Latin America's largest economy devalued the currency by about 8 percent. 

 "This is a chance for Argentina to differentiate itself" from Brazil, said Ricardo Daud, a fund manager at Bansud. 

 Economists have long believed the biggest threat to Argentina's economy is its proximity to Brazil, its biggest trading partner. An economic blow-out in Brazil could have a ripple effect in Argentina, just as Mexico's devaluation did in December 1994. 

 During the "Tequila Crisis," investors hurried for the exit door and savers withdrew about 20 percent of the banking system's deposits on fears Argentina would drop its peso peg to the dollar. Argentina's economy contracted 4.6 percent in 1995. 

 Now, there are worries that Brazil's decision to float its currency will have the same effect. 

 But with the economy having changed drastically since 1995 - most notably by reforms of the banking sector - the government is betting things will be very different now. 

 Buenos Aires is counting on investors to remember that the country rode out the 1995 storm without any doubt about its maintaining the peso's one-to-one peg to the dollar. 

 "The 1995 experience helped us a lot," said Gustavo Canonero, head of research for Mercosur at Deutsche Bank Global Markets. "It really demonstrated that there is strong support across all elements of society (for government economic policies)." 

 The biggest change in the economy since 1995 has been a buying spree of Argentine banks by foreign ones, meaning huge multinational financial institutions now account for more than 40 percent of bank deposits, compared with half that in 1995. 

 Banks' cash reserves have been sharply bolstered by strict new minimum liquidity requirements and the government has a $6.1 billion standby liquidity credit facility for the banking system that it can draw on in case of an emergency. Bank deposits are currently at record highs. 

 This means that now, unlike in 1995, savers will leave their money in the banks. "People will not withdraw their deposits," Daud said. 

 Another measure of investor confidence, foreign currency reserves, is currently at record highs thanks to government efforts to return to Argentina some $7 billion in reserves held abroad by the central bank. 

 A lot of the confidence in Argentina comes from an Extended Fund Facility deal with the International Monetary Fund. This agreement offers $2.8 billion that can be drawn down when needed, and it builds confidence among investors because of the external monitoring of Argentina's fiscal accounts carried out by the IMF, economists said. 

 It includes economic targets, which is one of the reasons the government has worked hard to reduce the budget deficit to about 1 percent of gross domestic product, far from Brazil's 7.45 percent. 

 An IMF spokesman voiced support for Argentina on Friday, saying the IMF "would be willing to help if needed." 

 The big uncertainty, however, is how much growth will be stunted by the higher interest rates resulting from Brazil's devaluation. 

 Those higher rates have already prevented Argentina from raising money in international markets, and lack of credit for Argentina's small firms will cut deep into their pockets. 

 Some economists say there will be a recession in 1999, but the government stuck to its 3 percent growth estimate this week. 

 For interest rates to come down, allowing growth to bounce back up, the government will have to convince international investors that the risks of putting money into Argentina are not as great as they think. 

 To do that, the government has to be able to convince investors of its ability to meet its own financing needs. 

 As a result of careful planning at the end of last year, Buenos Aires already has secured the financing it needs for the first half of 1999 through a credit line from international lenders and bond issues to domestic investors. 

 If it drew on the IMF's $2.8 billion it could nearly fill all third-quarter financing needs as well. 

 "I hope we can differentiate (between the Argentine and Brazilian economies)," Canonero said. "That would really be the beginning of a new era for Argentina."

title: Latin America relieved Brazil bites bullet.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jan 15 (Reuters) - After the initial shock of a Brazilian devaluation earlier in the week, Latin Americans praised Brazil's decision on Friday to let its currency float and not waste billions of dollars trying to prop it up. 

Brazil's Central Bank on Friday stopped intervening in the foreign exchange market, allowing its embattled real currency to sink by 12 percent. The move came two days after the world's eighth-largest economy devalued the real by about 8 percent. 

 While tempered by the knowledge that letting the real float would likely drag Brazil further into recession, there was an overwhelming sense of relief by Latin American officials and economists that Brazil had finally thrown in the towel. 

 "The fact that one of the biggest countries in the world, in this case Brazil ..., has taken this decision, represents for all of us a very important and a very positive piece of news," said Mexico's Finance Minister Jose Angel Gurria, who predicted interest rates would fall now that the uncertainty was removed. 

 Ever since Russia's devaluation and debt default in August, Latin Americans had feared the worst would also come to pass with their region's largest economy. 

 When Brazil devalued by about 8 percent on Wednesday there were ominous reminders of Mexico's December 1994 devaluation when it also attempted a managed devaluation only to be followed by a free float a few days later. 

 "Just let it happen," many said, as foreign currency reserves bled at about $1 billion a day this week. 

 "There was no other alternative," said Ricardo Daud, a fund manager at Bansud in Buenos Aires. "Continuing to kick the ball forward made no sense." 

 Economists said the Brazilian government can now focus its efforts on getting its fiscal situation in order and meeting the targets it set itself last year in a massive expenditure-cutting programme. That programme formed the basis of a $41.5 billion International Monetary Fund-led rescue package Brazil agreed to at the end of last year. 

 "If Brazil passes its austerity measures, and interest rates fall, things are going to get better for the region," said Pablo Secada, an analyst at Santander in Peru. 

 Argentina's Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said he did not think the crisis would last for long because Brazil is pushing ahead with its measures. 

 "I don't think the crisis will be long-lived because many of the measures Brazil needs have already been approved, maybe not as fast as markets wanted but they have been passed," Fernandez said. 

 However, as markets headed skyward after Brazil's announcement, some remembered why a Brazilian devaluation was so feared in the first place - because it could unleash an Asian-style crisis of devaluing currency dominoes. 

 In Colombia, which itself devalued the trading bands of its peso last year, economist Javier Fernandez Riva said the Brazilian move was a "wake-up call." 

 He said the authorities would now likely have to hike interest rates yet further - damaging the slowing economy - or follow Brazil and float. 

 The Colombian peso fell to a historic low as Finance Minister Juan Camilo Restrapo called the Brazil news "disconcerting." 

 But he vowed "there will be no new devaluations in response to those that may occur in neighbouring countries." 

 Venezuela, which faced constant rumours of a devaluation last year, was still benefiting from the honeymoon markets have granted President-elect Hugo Chavez. 

 "The repercussions have not been felt so much here because we have our own fiscal and political problems," said Eduardo Franco of Caracas' Profimerca brokerage. 

 In Ecuador, which also devalued its currency band last year, Central Bank Chief Luis Jacome said his country would not follow Brazil's path despite strong pressures on the sucre this week. 

 "We will continue to defend the sucre; there is no reason to think about devaluation. The currency market is going to calm down," he said. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Brazil float "wise move" to halt dollar flight-IMF.
text:
WASHINGTON, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund backed Brazil's decision to float its currency, the real, on Friday, describing it as a wise move which could stem the flood of dollars from the country. 

 "It appears to be a wise move to stop the loss of reserves," an IMF spokesman said. 

 The spokesman said the IMF had been informed in advance about Brazil's decision to stop intervening in the foreign exchange market. 

 A previous statement, issued when the Brazilian central bank widened the real's trading band in what amounted to the first stage of the country's two-stage devaluation, said only that Brazil had informed the IMF of the change and analysts said the fund was annoyed at the lack of consultation. 

 The spokesman confirmed that Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan and central bank chief Francisco Lopes would visit Washington for talks with IMF management this weekend. 

 "The next set of contacts between Brazil and the IMF will be in Washington and, for the time being, there are no plans for our staff to travel to Brazil," he said.

title: LatAm markets roar after Brazil floats  currency .
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Latin American stocks and bonds shot higher Friday after Brazil's decision to float its currency eased concerns that the region's largest economy would unravel. 

 Some regional currencies were also stronger, although most had not fully recovered from an initial dive after Brazil's real quickly depreciated by about 12 percent after the government early Friday abandoned its attempt to keep it within a trading band. 

 By mid-afternoon, Brazil's Bovespa index had surged over 28 percent on news the Central Bank would allow the real to trade freely on the market. 

 Argentina's MerVal stock index was over 7.7 percent higher and Mexico's IPC was up more than 6.2 percent. 

 "They're buying for the medium and long term, because prices are rock bottom now," a Mexican desk trader said, echoing regional enthusiasm for severely-punished equities in the region. 


Shares in Chile were four percent higher, and Venezuela's IBC      index was up 1.5 percent.



Latin American stocks had been sorely battered in the latest round of Brazil's financial crisis, triggered by the Jan. 6 debt moratorium declaration by Minas Gerais state. The rebellious state said it would halt payments for 90 days on $13.4 billion owed to central government.



Spooked investors fled Latin American markets in droves and Brazil haemorrhaged several billion dollars to keep the real stable - a backbone of a five-year-old economic policy to crush inflation.



Friday's slide in the long-steady real came on top of an 8 percent devaluation Wednesday when the central bank widened a narrow foreign exchange trading band.



But the move failed to inspire investor confidence and $2.8 billion stampeded out of the country's foreign exchange markets by Thursday. The Sao Paulo stock exchange's blue-chip Bovespa index also fell by a cumulative 15 percent on Wednesday and Thursday.



On Friday morning Brazil's Central Bank said it would not intervene in the foreign exchange market, effectively allowing the currency to float.



Traders seemed relieved.



"This (the float) was the worst thing everyone was expecting and now it's over," an Argentine trader said.



Bond prices, also pummeled recently, surged at the news.



Brazilian's "C" bonds - considered the benchmark of Latin America's internationally traded bonds - rose 6.125 points Friday to a bid price of 55.125, Argentina's "FRBS" had gained 5.375 points to 78.625 and Mexico's "PAR" bonds were 2.375 points higher at 73.625.



Latin American currencies, initially jolted by the real's dive early Friday, were mixed by midday.



Mexico's peso was stronger at 10.3510/10.3800 after sliding to 10.73/10.83 in pre-opening bids.



Chile's peso had also calmed after the initial shock, trading at 478 per dollar back from 485 at its open. It has lost less than one percent of its value since Tuesday, the day before Brazil's first devaluation.

title: Argentina's  Central Bank  says banking system solid.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Argentina's banking system is virtually bullet proof to the crisis caused by Brazil's devaluation and the Argentine economy is well positioned to cope with Brazil's devaluation, the Central Bank said Friday. 

 "Today the banking system could lose 40 percent of deposits without credit being affected," said an internal Central Bank memo which Reuters obtained Friday from a Central Bank source. 

 During the worst moment of the 1995 Tequila crisis following Mexico's peso devaluation, some 18 percent of the banking system's deposits were withdrawn, the memo said. 

 Commenting on expectations in the government on the impact on Argentina's economy of Brazil's devaluation, the memo listed a number of points which should reduce the damaging impact. 

Brazil's Central Bank on Friday stopped intervening in the foreign exchange market, leaving its embattled currency, the real, to float. 

 "As an element in its favour, the (Economy Ministry) points out that Argentina's economy has already proven itself by overcoming the (1995) Tequila effect, the Asian crisis and more recently, Russia's default as well," the memo said. 

 The memo said the "Economy Ministry leadership" considers Brazil's devaluation will have an impact on economic activity "which will be most felt in certain determined sectors, but that in no way is the country's macro-economic balance or its fixed currency peg at risk." 

 Many economists have said Argentina's economy could be hit hard because a third of its exports go to Brazil but the memo pointed out that exports represent just 8 percent of Argentina's gross domestic product. 

 Anyway, most of the the exports are commodity products which could easily be sent to other markets, it said. 

 "In sum, the global impact of Brazil's devaluation will be slight in commercial terms and shouldn't affect more than 1 percent of Argentina's GDP," the memo said. 

 However, the memo warned of a "psychological phenomenon, whereby foreign investors tend to associate Argentina with what happens in Brazil." That impact should make it more difficult to raise foreign financing. 

 But near the end it said: "Without downplaying the importance of Brazil's crisis, the Economy Ministry leadership is confident a rebound in the economy can be relatively quick. They pointed out that recent history showed that during the Tequila the economy took a year to recover and after the Russian default it took just three months." 

 Lastly, it pointed to politics, saying that while in "Brazil there is a power dispute which creates uncertainty, in Argentina there is a president who does not hesitate to veto laws which challenge his economic model." ((Buenos Aires Newsroom, +541 318-0668, buenosaires.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Dollar ends easier in Asia, softer bias seen.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The dollar ended a quiet Asian session weaker amid continued worries over the financial situation in Brazil, traders and analysts said. 

 The dollar ended at 112.78/88 yen at 0730 GMT compared with its New York close of 113.75/85. The euro was trading at US$1.1720/30, firmer than its U.S. close of 1.1690/95. 

 Activity was light with Tokyo on holiday. 

 The dollar had a soft tone and would continue under pressure until Brazil's future became more clear, sources said. 

 Brazilian traders said about US$1 billion flooded out of foreign exchange markets for the third day in a row on Thursday, forcing the central bank to sell dollars from its falling reserves and keep the real within its new, lower band. 

 Brazil devalued its currency on Wednesday. 

 The situation put pressure on the dollar amid fears that the United States, which has major trade flows with Latin America, would be particularly hurt if the Brazilian crisis became a regional one. 

 "The dollar is still susceptible to downside risk against the majors, probably more so against the euro, the Swiss franc and sterling and less so against the yen," said a currency analyst at a Hong Kong bank. 

 "The lesser weakness against the yen is partly due to Bank of Japan intervention, but also to the idea that if Brazil goes there may be some contagion in Asia," he said. 

 The BOJ engaged in dollar-buying intervention earlier this week to stem the rise in the yen. 

 Dealers said the dollar was likely to come under further selling pressure in Europe and the U.S. because few traders would want to hold long dollar positions over a three-day weekend in the U.S. 

 U.S. markets will be closed Monday for a holiday. 

 "I think the euro will test around the 1.1750/80 level," said a trader at a local bank. 

 "But I think the euro is toppish overall and I would sell it at 1.1780," he said.

title: U.S. Tsys Dn Late; Reverse Flight-To-Quality Bid; 30Y -1 Pt
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--U.S. Treasurys were trading down, but off intraday lows, late Friday, capping a shortened session of intense volatility fueled by the unexpected, dramatic rally in Brazilian stocks which underpinned neighboring U.S. equity markets. 

 At 2:47 p.m. EST, the benchmark 30-year bond was down one point at 101 30/32 to yield 5.12%. At the Chicago Board of Trade, the March bond contract settled at 126-17, down 24/32. Bond markets observed an early close. 

 The Sao Paulo Bovespa stock index soared as high as 30% by afternoon New York trading, following the session's free float of the Brazilian real. Brazil's central bank said that it would not intervene in the forex markets Friday - two days after the government widened the real's trading band against the dollar that effectively devalued the currency by 8%. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average was trading about 157 points higher by 2:57 p.m. EST. 

 Analysts said that financial markets have known the value of the real would fall, but the uncertainty was when. The move by Brazil to let the real go this week was seen as removing some of that uncertainty. 

 Treasurys fell as the flight-to-quality bid reversed out of the market, but managed to find support near yields of 5.12% in the long bond. In the shift out of bonds and into stocks, traders said that market participants were also squaring up their positions going into the three-day weekend. U.S. financial markets will be closed Monday to observe Martin Luther King Day. 

 "Basically, investors realize that after they float the currency where people are comfortable, buying (Brazilian assets) can recommence," said Richard Gilhooly, bond market strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in New York. "Whether or not this is sustainable is another matter."

title: LatAm stocks hard hit by shock Brazil devaluation.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Latin American stocks fell hard in step with equities worldwide on Wednesday as investors' worst fears were confirmed by a devaluation of the currency of regional giant Brazil. 

 Stock markets from Mexico to Argentina all staggered under fallout from Brazil, although by the close they had partly recovered from early panic selling caused by Brazilian central bank Gov. Gustavo Franco's sudden resignation and the immediate widening of the intervention band used to control Brazil's real currency. 

 "I'm sitting here crying," said trader Oswaldo Vasquez at Gysin brokerage in Buenos Aires, echoing his counterparts from around the region. "Spirits are pretty low." 


Argentina was the worst performer in Latin America after next-door neighbour Brazil pummeled the MerVal index	   and pushed it down 10.2 percent to 356.16 points.



Analysts had expected a Brazilian devaluation at some stage due to hefty capital flight, which totalled an estimated $1.2 billion on Tuesday alone, but were surprised when they woke up to Wednesday's move.



"I would say the way they did it was worse than anybody expected," said Jorge Mariscal, Latin America investment strategist at Goldman Sachs in New York. "They've done it in a very disorganized, uncoordinated fashion, with no support from the International Monetary Fund, or the (U.S.) Treasury."



Brazilian shares plummeted by more than 10 percent and activated circuit breakers after 13 minutes of trade on expectations that a weaker currency would send interest rates soaring and shift the economy into a deep recession.



Mariscal estimated that Brazil's economy would shrink some 4 percent in 1999.



The benchmark Bovespa	   index of stocks traded in Brazil's financial capital Sao Paulo ended down 5.05 percent at 5617 points, off a session low of 5278.

text:
Although he said the move wasn't drastic, Lopes said that the new band will serve as a transition to a floating exchange rate policy. He didn't, however, provide a time frame for a shift to a new policy. 

 "With the changes in the foreign exchange policy, the central bank is in reality speeding up a process which had been occurring in a gradual manner," Lopes said. 

 The attempt to fiddle with policy in the middle of the storm didn't go over well with markets anywhere. 

 In Brazil, the real immediately popped past the new outer limit of the band. 

 The real moved as weak as BRR1.33 to the dollar by early afternoon, prompting the Central Bank to step in to intervene in the interbank market. The Central Bank declined to confirm the levels at which it held its dollar auction, although traders reported it was at the official ceiling of BRR1.3200. 

 By 1520 GMT, the real was trading at BRR1.3210. 

 Walter Stoeppelwerth, head of research at Flemings in Sao Paulo, noted that Lopes in the past has espoused having an even wider band during the transitional phase prior to the full float. Stoeppelwerth said he wouldn't be surprised to see a band of BRR1.30-BRR1.70 or BRR1.35-BRR1.70 in the near future. 

 "Our sense is that this is a baby step. They're effectively on the edge of the abyss," Stoeppelwerth said. "I think it's a not very effective attempt to buy some time." 

 The key to the longevity of the new policy is, of course, how quickly investors leave Brazil and how much the country is willing to spend to defend its currency. 

 As of Wednesday, the country had just over $31 billion of foreign exchange reserves - in addition to a $41.5-billion International Monetary Fund package. On Tuesday, Brazil suffered a massive $1.2 billion capital outflow.

title: Brazil Cenbank sells dollars in  forex  mkts-traders.
text:
SAO PAULO, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank was seen intervening in local foreign exchange markets on Monday, selling dollars to offset an outflow of the U.S. currency, traders said. 

 The Bank was selling dollars through federal bank Banco do Brasil to prevent the real from weakening amid a wave of dollar outflows, they said. 

 The real was quoted at 1.2065 per U.S. currency at 1120 local/1320 gmt, unchanged from Friday's close, but close enough to the current foreign exchange mini-band's limit to trigger an intervention. 

 The Central Bank also intervened on Friday, when the real nudged close to the mini-band limits, which are now set at 1.2070 and 1.1940 reais against the dollar. 

Forex dealers said dollar outflows have stepped up again this month due to maturing foreign bonds and loans. 

 A net $317 million exited forex markets on Friday after a net $311 million flew out on Thursday - both days posting substantially higher outflows when compared to a daily net outflow of about $100 million in November. 

Currency markets have already lost a net $2.639 billion so far this month, after a net $1.91 billion exited in November. 

 Dollar flight from Brazil's forex markets have been closely monitored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the world's rich nations which have promised Brazil an anti-crisis loan package of $41.5 billion in November. 

 The IMF had put together the massive credit, worried about Brazil's excessive capital flight and its impact on foreign currency reserves - the country's main weapon against speculative currency attacks. 

 A senior official at Brazil's Central Bank told Reuters on Friday that the country's reserves now stood at about $49 billion according to the international liquidity concept, which includes accounts receivable.

title: Brazil's real stable as  forex  mkts lose $500 mln.
text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency closed stable Thursday after the Central Bank intervened selling dollars to offset capital flight of about $500 million from foreign exchange markets, traders said. 

 Traders said the Central Bank, via federally owned Banco do Brasil, sold dollars, bolstering a weakening currency. The Central Bank declined to comment on the speculation. 

 The real closed unchanged at 1.19 to the dollar in the commercial forex market. 

 About $500 million fled the country's forex markets Thursday, according to traders' preliminary estimates. If the amount is confirmed, it will mark the biggest day of dollar flight in more than a week. 

 Some $30 billion fled Brazil in August and September. A sharp hike in interest rates slowed outflows and spurts of foreign direct investment in October enabled Brazil to register a net dollar inflow so far this month. 

 Still, more money could leave as foreign loans and bonds come due and as investors await confirmation of an international loan to Brazil. 

 As of 1700 local/1900 gmt a net $250 million were registered leaving Brazil through the commercial forex market, the Central Bank said, while another $79 million had left through the floating forex market, according to traders. 

 The currency closed unchanged at 1.1921 reais to the dollar in the floating market and stable at 1.285 to the dollar in the parallel market.
