title: Brazilian stocks tumble on Greenspan speech.
text:
SAO PAULO, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Brazilian equities markets tumbled Thursday, joining Wall Street and Asian bourses after hopes for coordinated rate cuts in the U.S. and other industrialised nations were dashed, market players said. 

 "Markets had been operating on the assumption of a rates cut, and now they're adjusting for the fact that there might not be any," said a fund manager at Banco Patrimonio. 

 Sao Paulo's key Bovespa index crumbled in the first hour of trading, plunging more than 10 percent and setting off the circuit-breaker to halt trade. Later in the session, it reduced its losses to around 7 percent. 

 The Bovespa tumbled along with bourses in Asia, Europe and the United States after Chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve Alan Greenspan quashed hopes Wednesday that a number of industrialised countries were in talks to lower interest rates. 

 "Greenspan's speech yesterday disappointed the market, which was pressing for an immediate, instant solution (to the global financial turbulence)," said one local trader. 

 Investors were also cautious as they awaited firmer news from international agencies on a support programme reportedly being coordinated by the International Monetary Fund and aimed at shielding Latin America from the global financial turmoil. 

 "There is a continuous dialogue which has been intensified in the last few weeks," a monetary source in Washington said on Thursday of contact between Brazil and the IMF. 

 "It's talks on talks," the source said, adding that Brazil has not asked the IMF for cash. 

Brazil's Central Bank was also forced to intervene in the foreign exchange market Thursday to keep the currency from weakening as more dollars continued to leave the country, traders said. 

 Two consecutive rate hikes in Brazil and expectations of an international support plan slowed the outflow of dollars on Tuesday and Wednesday, but no new details have surfaced since, and dollars continue to leave the country. 

 Traders expect another $400 million in dollars to wash out of Brazil on Thursday. While low compared to average daily outflows of $1.5 billion last week, the departure of hard currency has not stopped. 

 And without more concrete news, many market players worry that the government's recent efforts to fend off a crisis may not be sufficient. 

 Wednesday night, Brazil came up with more spending cuts and belt-tightening measures in a bid to narrow a gaping budget deficit that will be exacerbated by interest rates now jacked up to 50 percent. 

 The government announced five proposals which could reduce federal government spending by as much as 2.1 billion reais ($1.8 billion) between now and the end of the year, ensuring Brazil meets its target of a 5 billion real ($4.23 billion) surplus in its primary account in 1998. 

 That target, included in a decree, was announced last week along with 4 billion reais ($3.38 billion) of federal government spending cuts as Brazilian markets took a beating amid fallout from Russia's devaluation. 

 But the primary account does not include debt costs. The nominal deficit, which does, is nearing a precarious 8 percent of GDP, frightening already skittish investors. 

 The Central Bank also plans to sell its brand new NBC-F paper for the first time Thursday. The newly-created notes are pegged to the floating exchange rate and are aimed at stemming outflows. 

 Still, many traders said words of support from U.S. leaders were enough to ensure that Brazilian markets will not be headed back for the lows it hit last week. 

 "The worst has passed," Patrimonio's fund manager said. "The United States recognised that Brazil is more important than Russia, more important than Asia to its economy and that's a sign that there is support."

title: LatAm bourses battered despite economic measures.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Latin American financial markets were hammered on Thursday by investors blind to government efforts to bolster their economies against the financial earthquake rolling across the continents. 

 The Brazilian Bovespa index led the dive slipping 6.13 percent in the first 30 minutes of trade and ending 15.8 percent lower, its largest one-day drop in 11 years. 

 The plunge caught other regional markets in its tailwind, dragging bourses down from Mexico City to Buenos Aires. 

 "The order is get out of the market, regardless of price," said Fernando Romero Caranza, a Latin American analyst with ABN Amro in New York. "We're stuck in a perverse cycle of self-fulfilling prophesies. The market wants blood and it is getting it." 

 The Argentine exchange posted the second-harshest fall in the region, finishing down 13.32 percent, and Mexican shares tumbled 9.82 percent. 

 Chile closed down 7.38 percent, its largest one-day percentage drop since Oct. 6, 1998, and Venezuelan shares ended at a 30-month low, off 4.48 percent for the day. 

 Latin American currencies and bonds also reeled from the turmoil. Mexico's peso closed at a record low of 10.52/10.55 to the U.S. dollar even after the central bank intervened three times in efforts to shore it up. 

Brazil's benchmark "C" bonds finished down 3.625 at 52.125/52.5. Argentina's FRB bonds closed down 5.25 at 64.5/65.625. 

 Investors fear that a currency devaluation in Brazil, Latin America's biggest economy, could ripple across Latin America and devastate economies recovering from the 1994 "Tequila crisis" triggered by a devaluation in Mexico. 

 Those concerns pummeled the Brazilian bourse and led to almost $2 billion in net outflows from its foreign exchange markets on Thursday, Brazilian traders said. 

 That is in addition to about $8.77 billion lost in in the first nine days of September and $12 billion lost in August. 

 "The market doesn't know how long the government will be able to sustain this situation," one trader said. 

 U.S. President Bill Clinton's problems only worsened the already fragile situation by adding the prospect of impeachment to the world's list of worries, said traders. 

 The Dow Jones index closed down 3.17 percent. 

 "Clinton is basically affecting the market in the United States, and by affecting the United States, it is affecting us," said Argentine trader Julian Cohen. 

 Investors appear unconvinced by Latin American governments that have moved to shield their economies from the problems that devastated Asia and Russia. 

 On Tuesday, Brazil announced much-anticipated measures aimed at trimming the country's budget deficit, currently at a gaping 7 percent of gross domestic product. 

 In Mexico, Latin America's second largest economy, President Ernesto Zedillo promised to do all he can to end the recurring six-year cycle of economic breakdowns and warned Mexicans of more tough times due to the harsh economic environment in his State of the Union speech last week. 

 Zedillo also sent Congress a series of financial reforms designed to improve the country's banking system. 

 Argentine officials have already cut $2 billion from this year's planned spending and the government passed labour and tax reforms aimed at reducing the financial burden on employers. 

 President Carlos Menem also said he had frozen public spending for next year at 1998 levels. 

 Other countries have also enacted protective measures. 

 Venezuela announced last Friday fresh spending cuts of $540 million, combined with the sale of government assets and a fresh dividend from state oil company PDVSA, which together would total $2 billion. 

 But analysts said the reforms have failed to help, mostly because investors are not convinced by Brazil's attempts. 

 "For the size of Brazil's problems, the cuts were insufficient," said Cohen. "They didn't do anything." 

 "Brazil has a lack of credibility, and since it's an important market, that lack of credibility is flowing into other countries in the region," said ABN Amro's Romero Caranza.

title: Brazil Forex : Real Weakens On  Intervention , Outflows Wane
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real (BRL) weakened against the dollar Wednesday after the Central Bank intervened to adjust the crawling band in which the two currencies trade. 

 The trading session, however, was marked by a positive tone as the bleeding of dollars seemed to diminish considerably. 

 At 1950 GMT, preliminary Central Bank figures showed an outflow of $272 million via the commercial exchange market and $100 million via the floating-rate market. 

 Market participants told Dow Jones Newswires they estimated the two markets would post a total outflow of $700 million Wednesday.

 The bank was seen intervening through state-owned Banco do Brasil, selling the U.S. currency at around 1.1780 to the dollar, traders said.

Forex dealers said the commercial foreign exchange market was suffering a large net outflow of dollars amid an escalating crisis.

 Traders said they expect a dollar outflow of $1 billion to $1.5 billion Monday, with part of that figure related to the settlement of the September dollar futures on the Commodities & Futures Exchange (BM&F).

title: Brazil Well-Positioned -2: Govt's Ability To React Cited
text:
Analysts said that Brazil's markets have been particularly hard hit lately because they are highly liquid and fund managers that need to reduce positions worldwide find it easy to sell their Brazilian assets. 

 While analysts distinguish Brazil's financial situation from that of other emerging markets, they acknowledge that there's room for local markets to fall even further. 

 "The situation abroad is extremely complicated and I don't expect investor sentiment toward emerging markets to change soon," said Jose Carlos de Faria, senior economist at ING Barings in Sao Paulo. "Only when things calm down everywhere else will people take a look at Brazil again." 

 Confidence in the government's ability and willingness to intervene when necessary is a key reason for optimism that Brazil will emerge unscathed from the turmoil. 

 "The government has proven that it knows how to handle monetary crises," said Faria. "Currency stability is obviously a top priority for the government." 

 Late last October, the central bank nearly doubled interest rates to protect the real from speculative attack amid financial turbulence in Asia. The government followed that up 10 days later with a broad fiscal package. 

 Government involvement in the most recent crisis has been limited, but sufficient to guarantee that Brazilian authorities will be proactive, analysts said. 

 Over the past two weeks, forex dealers have detected state-run Banco do Brasil selling dollars on behalf of the central bank, though the monetary authority denies it. Also, stock traders said that the securities arm of the National Development Bank, known as BNDESPar, has snapped up shares at rock-bottom prices to support local exchanges.

title: CORRECTED - ANALYSIS - Brazil's real seen riding out mkt.
text:
In Sao Paulo item "ANALYSIS - Brazil's real seen riding out mkt storm", please read in eleventh paragraph, "Last Friday, Brazil saw a record one-day net dollar outflow for the year of $2.43 billion," instead of $2.89 billion. Corrects figure. 

 A corrected version follows. 

 By Noriko Yamaguchi 

 SAO PAULO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's strong local currency should survive the lashing global financial markets have dealt emerging economies recently thanks to high foreign reserves and the promise of ample dollar inflows, economists said Monday. 

 In fact, economists said Brazil was in a stronger position now to support its real against the dollar than it was last October, when speculators tested the government's resolve at the height of the Asian crisis. 

 "Brazil has clearly increased its capability to face a crisis because the level and quality of its foreign reserves have improved," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank in Brazil. "The country is seen surviving due to the continuous inflow of dollars," Abate said, noting much of the new money is going into long-term investment. 

 World markets keep a close eye on Brazil's real, which is widely seen overvalued by between 10 percent and 30 percent. Brazil is Latin America's largest economy and a sharp devaluation would likely trigger a regional economic slump comparable to the one that followed the 1994 Mexican peso crisis. 

 Russia's troubled economy has sent shockwaves through world markets, and traders on Monday were quick to draw parallels between Brazil and Russia - two giant emerging markets whose governments have failed to tame bloating budget deficits. 

 But Brazilian officials have spent the last two weeks trying to differentiate the two economies, mainly pointing to Brazil's vast $70 billion in reserves versus Russia's $17 billion. 

 Analysts say Brazil has a much more stable political outlook, with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso widely expected to be re-elected in October. And Brazil's banking sector has strengthened over the last four years on improved regulation, stiffer competition and a wave of mergers with foreign institutions. 

 "The banking system is in an infinitely better situation now than it was at the height of the Asian crisis," said Roberto Setubal, president of the Federation of Brazilian Banks. 

 Setubal, who is also the president of private retail bank Banco Itau , said Brazilian banks had significantly reduced their leverage and exposure to highly volatile dollar-denominated Brazilian foreign debt. 

 Still, market jitters have not been limited to stocks. The Central Bank has had to intervene in Brazil's currency market almost every day for the past two weeks to support the real, which trades within a tightly regulated band against the dollar. 

 Last Friday, Brazil saw a record one-day net dollar outflow for the year of $2.43 billion. (Corrects figure.) Some of the money fled from local stocks and another chunk went to repay foreign agricultural loans, which had been expected. 

 But economists say there are plenty more dollars coming in to cover the outflows. And they add that the new money is longer term and therefore less likely to flee during market panics. 

 For example, Brazil sold off Latin America's largest telephone operator Telebras in late July, raising $19 billion, of which $5.5 billion has already entered the country. The rest will come in over the next two years. 

 Also, an estimated $3.0 billion is expected to flow into Brazil over the next few weeks to pay for two local banks and a steelmaker, which were snatched up by European firms earlier this year. 

 And several of Brazil's state-owned power utilities remain to be sold, guaranteeing billions more dollars over the next two years. 

 The Central Bank says the inflows will keep reserves at about the $70 billion through the end of the year, a sum equal to 14 months worth of imports. 

 "The reserves underline the government's credibility when it says it will sustain the currency," said Cassio Schmitt, senior economist at retail bank Unibanco. 

 ((Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511-248-5423, noriko.yamaguchi@reuters.com))

BRASILIA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank confirmed it intervened in the foreign exchange market Wednesday, after the real currency fell through the 2-per-1 dollar level in early trade. 

 "The Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market today," a spokesman from the bank said. Traders said earlier Wednesday that the Central Bank had sold dollars, sparking a sharp strengthening of the real currency from its weakest levels of the session. 

 The real rose to 1.992 per dollar shortly after traders said the Central Bank intervened in the middle of the afternoon. Wednesday morning the real hit a session low of 2.004 per dollar. 

 The Central Bank last intervened in the foreign exchange market in August, but has more frequently used dollar-indexed domestic debt auctions to take pressure off the real. 

 The currency weakened early on market disappointment that much of the 938 million ($470 million) reais offered Wednesday by AES Corp.  in the privatisation of utility Tiete will be financed inside the country, meaning less foreign currency inflows. ((Brasilia Newsroom, +55-61-314-1193)).

title: Wall Street supports some  Brazil FX intervention .
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Wall Street analysts and international investors Wednesday voiced support for Brazil's limited intervention in currency markets, saying a stable real is key to containing inflationary expectations and holding down interest rates. 

 The Latin American country, operating in relatively illiquid markets, needs the flexibility to avoid any sharp declines in the real, analysts said. 

 "These can be fairly illiquid markets which can result in sharp moves in the currency," said Paulo Leme, managing director of emerging markets research at Goldman Sachs & Co. 

 "With a temporary deterioration in cash flows, having scope for intervention is the smart thing to do," Leme said, adding that he sees the Brazilian currency as undervalued by 25 percent on a trade-weighted basis. 

 Traders said Brazil's central bank sold dollars in currency markets Wednesday, driving the real to 1.992 to the dollar from the day's weak point of 2.004. The central bank later confirmed that it had intervened in the foreign exchange market. 

Brazil announced earlier this week it will seek to renegotiate minimum foreign exchange reserve requirements with the International Monetary Fund, to have more reserves at its disposal for intervention. 

Brazil "needs to stabilise the currency because a weaker real has an adverse impact on the budget though the debt structure and secondly, it restrains the central bank from reducing interest rates," said Mohamed El-Erian, portfolio manager at the Pacific Investment Management Co. (PIMCO). 

 "Even in a flexible currency regime, they just can't let the real go," said Jose Barrionuevo, head of sovereign bond research at Lehman Brothers. "It would have too much of an impact on interest rates and the fiscal side," he said. 

 A weaker real would ignite inflationary pressures and limit the central bank's ability to lower interest rates and trim the government's expenditure on interest payments. 

 Supporters of the central bank policy are quick to add that Brazil's monetary authority is likely to support the real only on the margins and abstain from any large-scale use of reserves. 

 "When a country needs to revert a big current account deficit like the $25 billion that Brazil has and there is no funding for it from external sources, then there is a school of thought that says that during the transition, you should support the currency," said a trader at a large European bank. 

 "It's worth intervening until exports pick up owing to the weak currency, but it is still a bet the central bank is taking," said the trader. 

 Investors pointed out that Brazil central bank President Arminio Fraga, who came to the bank from the hedge fund Soros Fund Management LP, strongly believes in free-floating currencies and has indicated he supports intervening only in limited measure to smooth out any sharp currency movement. 

 Brazil let the real float in January after spending billions defending a fixed foreign exchange regime at a time when many traders said the real was over-valued. 

 Fraga joined the central bank after the currency was floated and vowed to respect market forces. 

 The Latin country also finalised an agreement with the IMF for a $41.5 million instalment loan. The accord stipulates that Brazil hold foreign currency reserves at $23.3 billion net of loans from the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements. 

 With Brazil making payments on several external bond and loan obligations in the last few weeks, foreign reserves at year-end would be around $22.6 billion net of IMF and BIS loans, traders estimate, leaving the country slightly short of its agreed IMF target. 

 Brazil has been unable to attract additional foreign capital into the stock or debt markets or raise new cash in the international bond markets, forcing the government to buy dollars to meet payments on interest and maturing debt. 

 A $2 billion debt swap, exchanging Brady bonds for global bonds completed two weeks ago, was originally designed to include a cash component - that is sell bonds for cash. But the cash tranche had to be quashed as higher interest rates in the U.S. lowered investor appetite for emerging market assets, traders said. 

 IMF officials have declined to comment on Brazil's request for lower reserve limits.

title: Brazilian Real Seen Under Pressure Through Year-End
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- The Brazilian real sent shivers down investors' spines this week as it dropped to BRR2.00 per dollar, and likely will cause more goosebumps in the months ahead. 

 Financing requirements and uncertainties over domestic and international economic trends will hinder a recovery for the local currency, at least until the end of the year, economists and analysts said. 

 For the second day running, the real on Wednesday hovered above the BRR2.00 per dollar rate, levels that hadn't been tested since March, at the height of the Brazilian currency crisis. 

 "The pressure will continue. It is difficult to foresee any appreciation of the real in the short-term," said Carlos Geraldo Langoni, former central bank president and now director of the center for world economy at the Fundacao Getulio Vargas economics institute. 

 The real managed to close stronger Wednesday, at BRR1.9880 per dollar compared to BRR2.0020 Tuesday. The currency opened Thursday at BRR1.9910. 

 "The real will float between BRR1.90 and BRR2.00 (per dollar), depending on the central bank's disposition to intervene more or less," Langoni said. 

 But the central bank isn't offering any palliatives and has repeatedly stated it will remain out of the market. 

 Not that it has much of a choice, either. The monetary authority is hamstringed by a commitment with the International Monetary Fund to keep Brazil's international reserves at $22.2 billion in October, excluding the $17.8 billion already received as part of an aid package. On Tuesday, Brazilian reserves stood at $40.035 billion, the central bank said. 

 Private-sector financing requirements, which indicate the level of demand for the foreign currency, are estimated at $500 million in October. These exclude obligations from the government, which usually taps reserves to make payments. 

 But with tight reserves, the Treasury was reportedly a buyer on Tuesday to meet commitments of around $3.35 million due this month, bearing the brunt of the blame for the real's weakness. 

 The Treasury on Wednesday denied it had instructed federally-run Banco do Brasil to purchase dollars on behalf of the government, as had been reported by local media. 


      Financing, Politics, Economy A Drag On Currency


Until year-end, financing requirements will remain high, according to
analysts, at $300 million in November and $2 billion in December, not
including the government's needs.



"We know there will be pressure in these months and, as markets do, the
December pressure is likely to be brought forward," said Sergio Machado, head
of Banco Fator's treasury department.



"It (the financing requirement) sort of creates a disposition for a more
expensive currency," he added.



On top of the palpable pressure of financial obligations, the real is also
reflecting the market stress over the uncertainty on political and economic
developments both domestically and abroad.



While Brazil's political scenario is much calmer than in the last quarter,
the government's attempts to push ahead with key structural reforms have born
little fruit.



"Even with the excuse of the obligations due, the currency moves tend to
reflect the strength of the economy and the confidence in it," said Carlos
Augusto Levorim, director at Oryx Asset Management in Sao Paulo.



Doubts over whether Brazil will be able to achieve a sustainable fiscal
adjustment remain and the chances of getting the fiscal reform approved this
year are thinning, said Getulio Vargas' Langoni.



Economists also expressed concerns over the direction of the U.S. economy,
projecting that a rise in interest rates there would further discourage
investments in Brazil. At the same time, the rise could slow down the U.S.
economy and hamper prospects at one of Brazil's main export client.



"The domestic question mark relates to the management of the fiscal
adjustment, while from abroad, if the U.S. economy deteriorates, it will catch
Brazil at a fragile moment," Langoni added.



       Some Call For More Central Bank Intervention


For most of those interviewed, the central bank position of not intervening
in the market isn't wise.



"This academic stance of the central bank is extremely dangerous," said
Fator's Machado. In his opinion, the claim that the market should be left
alone to find its own exchange level doesn't bode well in a country such as
Brazil, where the flow is very volatile.



Echoing his opinion is Pedro Thomazoni, fixed-income director at Lloyds
Asset Management in Sao Paulo: "A floating exchange rate is a beautiful
concept but it doesn't much fit reality in Brazil which has to have some level
of intervention because the flow isn't a constant one."



Observers pointed out that the central bank's presence in the market would
function as a guiding hand, besides imposing a sense of discipline.



"This (non-intervention) stance is threatening to turn the dollar into an
asset-hedging tool which could then generate hysterical action" in the market,
said Fator's Machado.



"The central bank let the market get this stressed over legitimate currency
demand, but it has to remember that we no longer have a fixed currency to
control inflation," he added.



While concerns over the inflationary pressure of a weak real abound,
analysts agreed that, in the short-term, Brazil should be able to contain
inflation as interest rates remain high.



"The central bank's stance seems to be very cool because it is seeing
inflation within the target, but all this rationale will be affected if
inflation numbers change in the future," said Dalton Gardimam, chief economist
at Credit Lyonnais in Sao Paulo.



Brazil's benchmark lending rate stands at 19% per year, down from a peak 45%
in March.



After abandoning the exchange rate trading band in mid-January, Brazil
adopted an inflation targeting system to guide monetary policy. The target for
the current year is 8%, with a tolerance interval of two percentage points
either way.



Inflation indices released this week point to a growing pressure on consumer
prices, with prices in Brazil's largest city of Sao Paulo rising 1.13% in the
period Sep. 16-Oct. 15, the University of Sao Paulo's Economic Research
Institute said Wednesday. This compares with the latest Sao Paulo CPI figure
compares with inflation of 0.91% in September and 0.74% in August.
-By Mara Lemos; Dow Jones Newswires; 5511-813-1988; mara.lemos@dowjones.com

to reflect the strength of the economy and the confidence in it," said
Carlos Augusto Levorim, director at Oryx Asset Management in Sao Paulo.



Doubts over whether Brazil will be able to achieve a sustainable
fiscal adjustment remain and the chances of getting the fiscal reform
approved this year are thinning, said Getulio Vargas' Langoni.



Economists also expressed concerns over the direction of the U.S.
economy, projecting that a rise in interest rates there would further
discourage investments in Brazil. At the same time, the rise could slow
down the U.S. economy and hamper prospects at one of Brazil's main
export client.



"The domestic question mark relates to the management of the fiscal
adjustment, while from abroad, if the U.S. economy deteriorates, it will
catch Brazil at a fragile moment," Langoni added.



       Some Call For More Central Bank Intervention


For most of those interviewed, the central bank position of not
intervening in the market isn't wise.



"This academic stance of the central bank is extremely dangerous,"
said Fator's Machado. In his opinion, the claim that the market should
be left alone to find its own exchange level doesn't bode well in a
country such as Brazil, where the flow is very volatile.



Echoing his opinion is Pedro Thomazoni, fixed-income director at
Lloyds Asset Management in Sao Paulo: "A floating exchange rate is a
beautiful concept but it doesn't much fit reality in Brazil which has to
have some level of intervention because the flow isn't a constant one."



Observers pointed out that the central bank's presence in the market
would function as a guiding hand, besides imposing a sense of
discipline.



"This (non-intervention) stance is threatening to turn the dollar into
an asset-hedging tool which could then generate hysterical action" in
the market, said Fator's Machado.



"The central bank let the market get this stressed over legitimate
currency demand, but it has to remember that we no longer have a fixed
currency to control inflation," he added.



While concerns over the inflationary pressure of a weak real abound,
analysts agreed that, in the short-term, Brazil should be able to
contain inflation as interest rates remain high.



"The central bank's stance seems to be very cool because it is seeing
inflation within the target, but all this rationale will be affected if
inflation numbers change in the future," said Dalton Gardimam, chief
economist at Credit Lyonnais in Sao Paulo.



Brazil's benchmark lending rate stands at 19% per year, down from a
peak 45% in March.



After abandoning the exchange rate trading band in mid-January, Brazil
adopted an inflation targeting system to guide monetary policy. The
target for the current year is 8%, with a tolerance interval of two
percentage points either way.

consumer prices, with prices in Brazil's largest city of Sao Paulo
rising 1.13% in the period Sep. 16-Oct. 15, the University of Sao
Paulo's Economic Research Institute said Wednesday. This compares with
the latest Sao Paulo CPI figure compares with inflation of 0.91% in
September and 0.74% in August.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Profit-taking brakes Asia slide.
text:
LONDON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies took another beating on Friday before profit-taking brought respite in the London morning, analysts said. 

 In Latin America overnight Colombia's embattled peso crashed to the bottom of its trading band for the third day running despite frantic central bank intervention, while Brazil's real lurched back to the weak side of 1.90 to the dollar. 

 Central European currencies were steady to firmer, with the Czech and Slovak crowns both adding to recent gains. 

 Asian currencies tumbled again for most of the Asian trading day as a patchwork of domestic factors compounded a broader regional retreat, worsened by widespread stock market losses on the back of Thursday's 1.95 percent drop on Wall Street. 

 Profit-taking kicked in during the London morning, lifting currencies sharply off their lows, but analysts said the overall trend was still down. 

 "We could be seeing a little bit of a mini-crisis developing here," said Mitul Kotecha, emerging market economist at Standard Chartered in London. 

 "We've seen a bit of retracement over our (London) morning but in Asian time we saw a lot more weakness. Things still look very vulnerable in the region." 

 The Thai baht remained under pressure beyond 41 to the dollar while the Philippine peso, which has been hanging onto the baht's coat-tails, slithered through its own psychological barrier of 41 to the greenback before edging back. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chaun Leekpai provided more soothing comments, saying the country had no intention of pegging the baht to the dollar or imposing Malaysian-style capital controls, but he said rising oil prices were complicating efforts to stabilise the currency. 

 The Indonesian rupiah extended Thursday's slide to touch 8,900 to the dollar as student riots over a new security bill spooked the market. 

 The currency rebounded strongly after parliament issued hard-hitting recommendations to tackle the Bank Bali scandal, saying seven top officials including the central bank governor and finance minister should face swift legal action. 

 Analysts said the report itself was positive but it remained to be seen whether concrete action would be taken, while the implication of senior figures could aggravate popular anger and fuel unrest. 

 South Korea's forex market was closed for a local holiday, but the won followed the wider downtrend in offshore trade. 

 Colombia's central bank poured a further $142.4 million of foreign reserves into defending the peso's trading band on Thursday and analysts questioned how long the band, one of only three left in Latin America, could survive. 

 The currency again ended on the floor of the band, at 1,993.97 to the dollar. 

 Since September 10 the central bank has haemorrhaged an estimated $290 million from net foreign reserves of some $8.24 billion to shore up the peso. 

 Some analysts said it would hang on by its fingernails until what is expected to be an imminent new funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund. Others said the bank could be forced to scrap the band in a matter of days. 

 "We think that the exchange rate regime could be abandoned as early as next week, as soon as the IMF meetings are over," analysts at Chase Manhattan said in a note to investors, adding that the peso would weaken as a result. 

 Fears of another U.S. interest rate rise helped push Brazil's real back to the weak side of 1.90 to the dollar on Thursday, its lowest in just over two weeks. The currency was unmoved in the London morning but analysts saw further weakness when American markets opened. 

 The Polish zloty, often swayed by global factors, eased very slightly against its currency basket on general world stock market jitters. By 0845 GMT it was quoted around 0.5 percent above parity against 0.65 percent late on Thursday. 

 The Czech crown stayed on the strong side of the key barrier of 36 to the euro, breached on Thursday on optimism that the economy is improving. ((Gill Tudor, London Capital Markets +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, gill.tudor@reuters.com)).

title: Latin America  Forex  Roundup: Brazil Weak Despite Auction
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Brazilian real was slipping mid-Thursday after opening stronger, despite the central bank's continued auctioning off of dollar-linked notes that have supported the currency in the past few weeks. Bits of positive news on the domestic political front also failed to substantially boost the real. 

 Due to Hurricane Floyd, many New York offices are closing by 1 p.m. EDT. Fixed-income markets will be closed by 1 p.m. EDT, while the New York Stock Exchange will remain open. 

 At 12:15 p.m. EDT, the Brazilian real was trading at a mid-rate of BRR1.8800, compared with Wednesday's close of BRR1.8790. 

 The central bank, which had announced Friday it would steadily reduce the amount of dollar-notes it auctions, offered over double its daily average Thursday. 

 One New York-based trader said many market participants were simply rolling over their positions. Those snapping up new bonds are those whose notes matured today, he added. 

 The central bank has been offering dollars in the market by auctioning off dollar-linked notes, allowing market participants to hedge against currency swings. The central bank has been able to support the real through the auction, since the currency nearly hit a record-low of BRR2.00 on Aug. 20. The auction has allowed the central bank to defend its currency without directly intervening in foreign exchange markets. 

 Separately, Brazil's government scored a victory in Congress late Wednesday, after a debt relief proposal for farmers that would have drained the government's coffers by about BRR25 billion was shelved. 

 The move would have aggravated the country's growing fiscal deficit and hampered Brazil's economic recovery. 

 Markets in Mexico were closed Thursday for a holiday.

title: Brazil's Ctrl Bk Uses Dlr-Linked Bonds To Control  Forex
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Backed into a corner as its currency plunged Friday, Brazil's central bank eschewed direct intervention in favor of virtually the only other tool at hand to ease pressure: dollar-linked bonds. 

 And if the pace of much-needed fiscal reform doesn't pick up in the capital Brasilia, observers say the monetary authority could find itself increasingly reliant on this measure. 

 "The central bank was hit by the speed of the (real's) depreciation Friday, and so had to offer the bonds," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds in Sao Paulo. 

 Abate added that the central bank may have set the psychological barrier of BRR2.00 per dollar as an "informal target." 

 In a surprise move Friday, the central bank offered BRR3 billion-worth of 'NBC-E' bills when exchange rates hit BRR1.9950 per dollar, the real's weakest point in almost five months. 

 The central bank has repeatedly denied it has any floor or ceiling for exchange rates, stressing that it's concerned only with market volatility and liquidity. 

 The real rebounded to close Friday at BRR1.9250/dollar on the auction announcement Friday, however, and opened stronger again Monday at BRR1.8675/dollar. Market participants were unanmious in attributing the sharp rally to the NBC-E placements. 

 The central bank will offer BRR1.85 billion-worth of Friday's unsold bills later Monday, ahead of a scheduled BRR1 billion placement Wednesday. 

 Placing the bills gives the market a hedge against exchange rate fluctuations, with players buying them up instead of spot or future dollars. 

 The return to offering NBC-Es - the last placement before last week was Aug. 6 - is seen as not only welcome, but necessary. 

 "The advantage in offering the NBC-Es is that it creates a mechanism for preserving international reserves," said Jaime Valdivia, Brazil sovereign debt strategist at Morgan Stanley in New York. 


Brazil's international reserves stood at $42.069 billion Thursday.
     Minimizing Forex Volatility To Control Inflation



As important as the placement of NBC-Es was the term of the bills.



"The central bank cut the maturity of the papers, which is extremely
important, as the market doesn't want long-term credit risk," said
Leonardo Veras, a fund manager at Rio de Janeiro-based brokerage Graphus
Participacoes who welcomed the central bank's strategy.



The second lot of bills offered Friday had a maturity of just under
six months, as do the bills on offer Monday, compared with 12 months
previously.



Abate and Valdivia both noted the restrictions on the central bank's
freedom to intervene directly in foreign exchange markets.



Under the revised terms of the macroeconomic framework agreement with
the International Monetary Fund, the central bank can only spend up to
$3 billion in foreign exchange market intervention between July and the
end of the year. That's less than half the $8 billion it had available
for intervention in the March-June period.



"For the free-float (regime) to have any credibility, intervention
must be kept to a minimum," said Morgan Stanley's Valdivia.



He added that the high 21.50% yield paid Friday on the NBC-Es reflects
the central bank's willingness to trade off higher interest rates for
more stable foreign exchange markets.



Analysts said the central bank's foreign exchange policy is based on
staving off the threat of inflation, which they say will return if
exchange rates remain too high.



Brazil's IPCA consumer price index rose 1.09% in July from the
previous month, up sharply from the 0.19% increase in June over May. The
government has set an end-1999 IPCA target of 8%.



But the central bank can't be left to do it alone, they said. The
government must do its part too, amid what appears to be waning
popularity on the policy front.



"The government has to convince Brazilian society that it's in a
better situation now than it was six months ago," said Lloyds's Abate,
referring to the depths of Brazil's crisis following the mid-January
devaluation of the real.



Abate cited various factors that could weigh heavily on sentiment in
the short term, including the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision on
interest rates Tuesday and jitters over Ecuador's financial stability.



Ultimately, analysts said, the central bank's most effective weapon in
controlling volatility in foreign exchange markets is completely outside
its control.



"The market needs fundamentals, and if nothing is approved, then
there's no reason for any optimism," said a Rio trader, referring to
fiscal reforms up for debate in Congress.



Congress returned from recess earlier this month with a full slate of
fiscal measures on its agenda - including legislation that would limit
spending in all levels of government.



But many observers are skeptical the administration of President
Fernando Henrique Cardoso can push through the belt-tightening reforms.
Cardoso's popularity is languishing at all-time lows according to recent
polls, which may futher embolden a Congress that is already divided in
its support for the president.



Analysts have said the country's credibility in the eyes of the
international financial community rests on fiscal reforms being passed.

title: IMF urges tough Brazil budget, 1999 output to ease.
text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Monday praised Brazil's stronger than expected economic performance but urged the government not to ease up in its quest for a wider budget surplus next year. 

 An IMF report summarizing a July 28 review of the Brazilian economy said Brazil's 2000 federal budget should target a primary surplus, excluding debt servicing costs, of 3.25 percent of gross domestic product, up from 3.1 percent this year. 

 "Directors noted that the performance of the Brazilian economy...has been significantly better than projected," the IMF said. 

 "For the year as a whole, real GDP is expected to decline by 1 percent or less (compared with the decline of almost 4 percent projected in the revised March program) and consumer price inflation is expected to be contained at around 8 percent." 

 The Brazilian government is trying to persuade a reluctant Congress to approve its cost-cutting 2000 budget. 

 President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, his popularity under threat because of the austerity plans, said on Monday that the economy could grow by at least 4 percent in 2000 if Congress passed the measures. 

 "To lay the foundation for sustained recovery, the authorities' principle challenges are to build on the progress already achieved in implementing fiscal consolidation and to accelerate structural reforms," the IMF said. 

 The fund said some directors believed Brazil should aim for an even more ambitious 2000 primary budget surplus than the targeted 3.25 percent. The government needed to be ready to act if the targeted 1999 surplus of 3.1 percent was threatened. 

 The IMF gave no forecasts for Brazilian economic output in 2000, but it urged caution on interest rate reductions. 

 "Consideration of further interest rate reductions should be approached carefully and to ensure the credibility of the new framework, the authorities should stand ready to raise interest rates if expected inflation turns upwards," he said. 

 Brazil has set inflation targets of 8 percent for 1999, 6 percent for 2000 and 4 percent for 2001, with a margin of error of 2 percentage points, but the IMF said some of its directors believed that narrower target bands would be appropriate. 

 Meeting the targets was crucial to ensure the credibility of Brazilian monetary policy, the IMF said. 

 The IMF said Brazil's banking system had done well to withstand the devaluation of the currency, the real, earlier this year, and to cope with high interest rates of 1998-99. 

 It welcomed Brazil's flexible exchange rate and limited central bank intervention, but stressed that central bank action should be limited to "countering disorderly market conditions."

title: INTERVIEW- Brazil  won't  intervene  aggressively.
text:
BRASILIA, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank does not intend to intervene aggressively in the foreign exchange market despite the real currency falling to 5-month lows this week, prompting intervention, a senior Central Bank official said. 

 The Central Bank sold dollars for reais on Wednesday after the currency fell below 1.90 to the dollar in a move it said was motivated by a shortage of liquidity in the market. 

 The currency continued falling Friday on worries that Brazil will not pass further fiscal reforms and after Ecuador said it may defer a coupon payment on a Brady bond. 

 This week's slide in the real has been one of the most dramatic since Brazil floated its currency in January due to a loss of confidence by the market that the government would be able to maintain the currency within its crawling band system. 

 Luiz Fernando Figueiredo, director of monetary policy at the Central Bank, told Reuters in an interview Thursday that the bank would not intervene aggressively to control the currency. 

 "If the Central Bank calms the market, selling a lot of foreign currency, it would be having a big influence on the exchange rate...and not leaving players to feel the onus of taking a stance in situations like these," Figueiredo said. 

 He said that the market is learning how to deal with the floating currency system. 

 "The difference with the old system is that players did not lose money (hedging in anticipation of more loses for the real) and today they can lose," if the real strengthens, he said. "We are seeing that various players are beginning to think that the cost of hedging is very expensive and this is a sign that the system is working." 

 Figueiredo said the intervention on Wednesday was intended to smooth the functioning of the currency market. But he said that with the floating currency players can lose money, which is part of the way the system should work. 

 "The money that enters to speculate on currency movements is the kind of money that helps the system work," he said. 

 Hedging in anticipation of more loses by the real can turn out to be expensive. "That is what a floating currency is all about...all portfolio decisions carry risks, and these risks may become reality." 

 But the official sought to calm market worries that Brazil will not continue its efforts to control its huge budget deficit. 

 "We want to tell the foreign exchange market the following: Gentlemen, look at the fundamentals. We are in a completely sustainable situation, we are doing our duty on the fiscal front."

title: Brazil  Selic rate unchanged, no  intervention  seen.
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank refrained from adding or draining liquidity in the money markets on Friday, leaving the key Selic rate unchanged at 19.5 percent, traders said. 

 "The bank did not need to intervene because banks' positions are balanced," said one trader. 

 The central bank normally borrows or lends funds to keep the market Selic rate in line with its reference Selic rate, now at 19.5 percent, but this week it only intervened twice as the market has been quiet. 

 The bank cut the rate from 21 percent July 28 at its monthly policymakers' Copom (Monetary Policy Committee) meeting, where it also shifted its bias on rates to neutral from easing. 

 Depending on banks' demand for cash, the Central Bank can inch the market's Selic up or down in daily operations. The Selic is used as a benchmark in setting domestic government debt yields and consumer credit rates. 

 The bank has gradually lowered the Selic from a peak of 45 percent reached in early March as inflation remains under control following the country's steep currency devaluation in mid-January.

title: EMERGING DEBT-Steady despite Brazil worries.
text:
LONDON, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Emerging debt prices were little changed on Thursday despite worries that Brazil could slip on its tough fiscal stance, dealers said. 

Brazil's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday for the first time in three months to defend the real currency, which has hit a five-month low on concern that President Fernando Henrique Cardoso faces mounting opposition to austerity measures needed to balance the budget. 

 Brazil jitters helped pull emerging debt prices down on Wednesday, but by 1150 GMT on Thursday the spread over comparable U.S. Treasuries on the benchmark J.P. Morgan EMBI+ index had edged in four points to 1,176. 

 Brazil's spread on the EMBI+ was seven points tighter at 1,118 and dealers in London said the country's "C" bonds were well bid around current levels. 

 At 1150 GMT the "C" bond was quoted 1/8 up on late New York levels at 59-1/4 bid. 

 "Everybody's careful but (concern over Brazil) doesn't seem to have affected prices today," said one trader at a European bank in London. 

 "The market is basically trading at yesterday's close." 

 The latest blow to Cardoso came on Wednesday when the Brazilian Congress passed a measure to speed up voting on a proposal to pardon farmers' debts with the central government. 

 Cardoso, who holds a presidential veto, has said he will oppose any pardon if it is approved in a vote next week. But analysts said he would continue to come under pressure over unpopular measures aimed at meeting fiscal targets with the International Monetary Fund. 

 "If Congress backs the farmers on this issue, Cardoso's fiscal reform will be perceived by the market as in trouble," Mike Noone, Latin America economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank, said in a note to clients. 

 Seemingly undeterred by the uncertain climate, Brazilian national development bank BNDES was set to issue a three-year bond of around 200 million euros ($211 million), possibly on Thursday, through ABN AMRO. 

 Bankers said BNDES hoped to price the deal at a premium of 100 basis points over Brazil's 800 million euro 2002 bond, but had been forced to revise initial terms after the sovereign bond fell 0.75 percentage points in the secondary market. 

 Among other emerging debt issues, traders said there was buying interest in Mexico's PAR bonds and Russia's longer-dated globals.

title: FOCUS-Brazil cenbank moves to prop up sinking real.
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank sold dollars in the forex market on Wednesday and removed a tax on foreign investment in a bid to lure more of the precious greenbacks into the country and halt a slide in the national currency, which has hit a 5-month low. 

Brazil's Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in three months, selling dollars in an unsuccessful effort to prop up Brazil's embattled real. The currency ended down 1.4 percent at 1.906 per dollar, its weakest since March. 

 As mounting political fears roiled markets, Central Bank chief Arminio Fraga also announced that foreign investors will be exempted from paying a 0.5 percent financial transactions Tax (IOF) on fixed-income funds and foreign exchange deals. 

 "The market was illiquid, and therefore we thought it was time to intervene, something we haven't done for about three months," Fraga said after markets closed. 

 The real has lost 5.4 percent of its value so far this month amid concerns that President Fernando Henrique Cardoso could face growing opposition to crucial but unpopular austerity measures needed to balance the budget. 

 Cardoso saw his popularity sink to all-time lows in August, fuelling speculation his political alliance could be undermined. The latest blow to his authority came earlier Wednesday when Congress passed a measure to speed up voting on a proposal to relieve a chunk of farmers' debt with the federal government. 

 Cardoso responded with a televised message to lawmakers and the thousands of agricultural protesters camped out in Brasilia. 

 "The government cannot agree. I will not agree with the pardon for those who are big debtors, especially when they are stubbornly disobedient debtors," he said in a speech at the presidential palace. 

 The measure paves the way for voting on a farm lobby bill, which proposes an effective write-off of between 40 percent and 60 percent of the face value of farmers' $13 billion debts with the government. 

 The government has offered counter-proposals in a bid to prevent voting on the bill, which would threaten Brazil's budget balancing targets. 

 The bill will not come up for debate until next week, and it likely to face a presidential veto. Still, initial support for the proposal sent markets into a tailspin Wednesday. 

 "The political climate is leaving a lot of people nervous about the fiscal situation," said Francisco Carlos Laje, a forex trader at Banco Real. 

 "Brazil's fiscal targets with the IMF (International Monetary Fund) could be compromised," he added, referring to strict budget goals agreed to in exchange for a $41.5 billion rescue loan. 

 The Central Bank tried to prop the real up with dollar sales when it weakened beyond 1.9 per dollar for the first time in morning trade. 

 After markets closed, Fraga announced the tax changes and said the bank would extend to 360 days from 180 days the time period for exporters to received special cash advances against anticipated foreign currency income. 


Sao Paulo's benchmark Bovespa index	   also ended down 2.4 percent at 9689 points, its lowest close since March 12, dragging neighbouring Argentina's markets down with it.



((Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248 5408, shasta.darlington@reuters.com)).

title: Brazil  confirms  intervention  in  forex  market.
text:
BRASILIA, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank President Arminio Fraga confirmed the bank sold dollars for reais Wednesday due to a shortage of liquidity in the foreign exchange market. 

 Fraga told journalists the bank will also exempt foreign investors from paying a Financial Transactions Tax (IOF) on fixed-income investments and foreign exchange deals, in a move which could lure dollars to the country. The real currency fell to five-month lows against the dollar Wednesday. 

 "The market was completely illiquid, and therefore we thought it was time to intervene, something we haven't done for about three months," Fraga said. The official said the 0.5 percent IOF for foreigners could still be reinstated in the case of large capital inflows. 

 The Central Bank chief said the bank is also going to extend to 360 days from 180 days the time period for exporters to receive special cash advances against anticipated foreign currency income. 

 Fraga said he expects foreign direct investment to reach a total $25 billion in 1999, saying a total of around $19 billion has been invested in the country so far this year. 

 The Central Bank chief predicted that Brazil's trade surplus will reach $7 billion next year, compared with an estimate of $1.5 billion for 1999. 

 Foreign currency reserves according to the international liquidity concept, which includes accounts receivable, are seen reaching $45.2 billion at the end of next year, compared with $38.9 billion at the end of 1999. ((Brasilia Newsroom, +55-61-314-1193)).

title: Brazil 's Ctrl Bank To Announce  Forex  Market  Intervention
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank is to inform the market of every occasion it intervenes in local foreign exchange markets immediately after the session in question, a spokesman confirmed late Tuesday. 

 The spokesman said, however, that neither the amount used nor the point at which the monetary authority intervenes will be made public. Nor will the bank reveal if it has bought or sold dollars.

 "It intervened three times that month, twice buying (dollars), and once selling," he said.

the International Monetary Fund earlier this month, Brazil has up to $3

text:
SAO PAULO, July 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank said Tuesday it would inform markets if it intervenes in the local foreign exchange market, beginning Wednesday, in a new policy designed to foster better transparency. 

 "The Central Bank of Brazil...maintaining its stance to carry out transparent operations...announces that it will turn public when it buys or sells foreign currency in the market," the bank said in a statement. 

 The monetary authority said however it will not disclose the amount of the intervention or whether the operation was a buy or a sell of foreign currency. The bank will report whether there was an intervention or not after the market close, it added. 


The Central Bank has been discreetly intervening in the market, selling or buying dollars to avoid abrupt swings in the foreign exchange rate since the local currency real	  was free-floated in mid-January.

title: Brazil  sets  foreign exchange intervention  limits.
text:
BRASILIA, July 5 (Reuters) - Intervention in the foreign exchange market by Brazil's Central Bank cannot reduce the country's projected liquid foreign reserves by more than $3 billion each month in the second half of 1999, a top government official said Monday. 

 "The government can bring the reserves down by up to $3 billion from these projections for this whole period (the second half)," Finance Ministry Executive Secretary Amaury Bier said. The official projections look for liquid, or net foreign reserves of $23.8 billion in July and $26.3 billion in December. 

 The new guidelines form part of the government and the International Monetary Fund's latest revision of Brazil's economic performance under a $41.5 billion loan agreement. 

 Preliminary results for June show liquid reserves stood at $23.2 billion, Bier said. 

 Brazil's liquid reserves refer to its foreign currency reserves according to the international liquidity concept, which includes accounts receivable. It excludes loans from the International Monetary Fund, the Bank for International Settlements and the Bank of Japan. 

 Bier said the projections for net reserves are: $24.6 billion in August, $25 billion in September, $25.5 billion in October, $25.6 billion for November and $26.3 billion in December. 

 He said these projections could vary by $1 billion higher or lower, depending on disbursements from the Inter-American Bank of Development and the World Bank during the second half of the year. 

 The official said the rules on intervention in the second half would give the government "more space and liberty to act" in the foreign exchange market. 

 Under the agreement the country signed with the IMF in March following its devaluation in January, Brazil could only intervene with set amounts of money every month. 

 Bier said the intervention guidelines could be changed again when the loan agreement is next revised in September or October. 

 The government predicted a rate of 1.75 for the real to the dollar for December in the revision announced Monday. 

 ((Brasilia Newsroom, 55-61 314-1193)).

title: BRAZIL MARKETS WEEK-Real ready to stabilize.
text:
SAO PAULO, June 14 (Reuters) - Brazil's real currency	  is set to settle down in a new range after weakening steadily against the dollar in the first half of the month, foreign exchange experts said on Monday.



They said they expect the real to trade in a range of 1.73-1.80 for the rest of the month of June after holding to a 1.65-1.75 band between March 30 and June 9.


 At midday Monday, the real was trading at 1.78 to the dollar after closing at an 11-week low of 1.782 on Friday. 

 The real is now 32 percent weaker since Brazil abandoned its semi-rigid exchange regime for a free float in mid-January amid heavy capital flight. 

 The local currency has slipped 5 centavos thus far in June on maturing Eurobonds and high-yield domestic debt auctioned by government. Around half of the $3.5 billion in foreign obligations coming due in June is estimated to have already passed through the market. 

 "We already new June was going to be an unfavourable month," said Sergio Machado, head of foreign exchange at Banco Fator in Sao Paulo. "Not only in terms of debt maturities, but also for payments of interest, goods and services." 

 "But the dollar doesn't have to keep rising. At 1.80 reais you should have a strong resistance, while 1.70 becomes a solid support." 

 One development which could put pressure on the real this week is the reintroduction of the financial transactions tax, CPMF, this Thursday. 

 The 0.38 percent CPMF charge on transactions will make financial operations in Brazil more expensive and may spur an initial outflow of capital in search of more tax friendly investment. 

 "But we don't think we will see such a big movement there," said Machado. 

Foreign exchange desks will also be looking at the local stock market for a possible reentry of foreign capital after investment from abroad dropped off sharply in the last weeks. 

 "There could be some inflow of capital," said the head foreign exchange trader at a Rio de Janeiro bank. "But really it is hard to predict what the flows will be like." 


After a 65 percent gain since the beginning of the year, the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange's Bovespa Index	   has been flat so far in June as fears of a rate rise in the U.S. discourage investment in emerging markets, like Brazil.



But market players say investors seem to have already priced in a 25-50 basis point rise in U.S. rates at the Federal Open Market Committee's next meeting on June 29-30.



Prospects of a rate hike in the U.S. also have not damped expectations of a fresh rate cut in Brazil's benchmark rate, the Selic, next week.



After an encouraging cut in the Selic to 22 percent from 23.5 percent using the bias to ease rates, the market is betting that the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) will chop it to 20-21 percent at its June 23 meeting.



The foreign exchange market will also be watching out for any announcement from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission now in Brasilia on repealing a limit as to how much Brazil can spend on currency market intervention.



The limit was agreed in March as part of the agreement to secure a second tranche of the $41.5 billion rescue package.



But the improvement in the economy and the currency's stability might encourage the IMF to lift the curb, sending a new sign of confidence to the market.

title: Brazil 's Ctrl Bk Announces Norms For Market  Interventions
text:
BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--Brazil's central bank Thursday announced norms regulating the use of intermediaries to intervene in foreign exchange and money markets. 

 As of Friday, the central bank will be allowed to intervene in those markets only through agents previously accredited, said monetary policy director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo. 

 In practice that had been happening, he said, but the measure will provide the central bank's moves with more transparency. 

 When intervening, the central bank will also have to offer or bid in the market to five intermediaries simultaneously, which didn't occur before. 

 "We're seeking to prevent the central bank from skirting this criterion during abnormal situations," Figueiredo said, referring to a bailout package given to Banco Marka SA and Banco FonteCindam SA in wake of the devaluation. 

 As reported, the central bank sold dollars to these two institutions at below-market rates on a perceived risk of a systemic crisis following the liquidation of Marka.

title: Brazil's  Central-Bank  Head Cuts Benchmark Interest Rate To 32%
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Brazilian central bank President Arminio Fraga on Wednesday cut the benchmark Selic interest-rate target to 32% from 34%, citing low inflation and a successful global-bond issue. 

 Fraga said that he decided to trim rates "in light of the successful global-bond issue, perception that (capital) markets are opening for our companies, good rollover rates and excellent news on the inflation front." 

 It was the fourth time Brazil lowered interest rates since late March, after having raised the Selic as high as 45% at the start of March. 

 Fraga said that, in the last three weeks, interbank credit lines are being rolled over at a pace of 150%. He also said credit lines between foreign banks and Brazilian companies have exceeded levels reached at the end of February. 

 Fraga said the central bank in March used $1.5 billion of International Monetary Fund money to prop up the currency, the real, of the $3 billion earmarked for interventions in the foreign-exchange market that month. 

 The leftover funds boosted the amount destined for interventions in April to $2.5 billion from the $2 billion originally predicted. Fraga declined to reveal how much was spent to prevent the real from weakening so far in April, but said "there were funds left" for May. 

 Fraga did say, however, that May's original $1.5 billion will be boosted by $375 million, the maximum possible. This is because the agreement Brazil inked with the IMF says the country is allowed to carry intervention leftovers to the following month, equivalent to one-fourth of the total funds allotted for interventions that period. 

 The IMF lent Brazil a total $8 billion exclusively for interventions in the foreign-exchange market through June. 

 Fraga also said the $3 billion raised from the global-bond issue announced last week will enter Brazil Apr. 30. He added Brazil isn't planning another sovereign debt issue "at this moment."

Regarding the foreign exchange market, Fraga reiterated that the central bank doesn't seek to fix parameters for real/dollar quotes through its regular interventions.

 Malan said that a second disbursement, of about $9 billion, from the IMF-led credit line should be available to Brazil within the next few days. The IMF executive board is expected to approve the revised macroeconomic framework of the aid pact at a meeting Tuesday.

 He noted, however, that the responsibility for restoring investor confidence rests on Brazil's shoulders.

title: POLL - Outlook on Brazil's real  currency  improves.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 24 (Reuters) - The outlook on Brazil's weakened currency is improving considerably as investors feel a devaluation-sparked crisis in Latin America's largest economy probably has bottomed out, a Reuters poll of economists showed Wednesday. 

 The average forecast of the 26 economists polled predicted a real rate of 1.80 per dollar by the end of June, 10 cents stronger than the 1.91 projection in an earlier poll conducted a month ago. 

 The real, which is currently hovering around 1.85 to the dollar, should end the year at 1.71, in line with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast of 1.70, the poll showed. 

 The economists, polled on March 22 and 23, specialise in Latin America and hold posts in banks and brokerages in Brazil, the United States and Britain. 

 Economists said the real, which is now 35 percent weaker since the government first relaxed its rigid foreign exchange policy in mid-January, has already seen its worst level and was now on its way toward a gradual recovery. 

 "I think we saw the low for the real at 2.15. They've got the economic team in place, the policies look right, there's strong IMF support. There's a good chance the worst is over for the real," said Kevin Grice, economist at American Express in London. 

 Sentiment in the Brazilian foreign exchange market picked up earlier this month after the IMF and the government struck a new accord to free up the second tranche of a $41.5 billion financial bailout programme, which was assembled late last year. 

Currency traders also took heart from the change of presidency at the Central Bank to Arminio Fraga, who was former aide to billionaire George Soros. 

 Fraga, equipped with a fresh team full of market savvy directors, started aggressively intervening in the local currency market to support the real and limit volatility. 

 Economists polled by Reuters said however that persistent dollar outflows linked to a load of foreign debt maturity would likely keep a lid on the real's recently budding strength. 

 The real's recovery hinges on foreign capital inflows, a bulk of which major global investors guaranteed recently by vowing to restore precious credit lines to Brazil. 

 "It will be difficult to turn around the real's trend unless there is a lot of foreign investor inflow pumping into the market," said Felipe Garcia, economist at I.D.E.A. consultants in New York. 

 Garcia also cast doubt on the real's trend, once the Central Bank's ammunition of $8 billion to intervene in the currency market ran out. The IMF allowed Brazil to spend up to $8 billion from its reserves and IMF funds until June. 

 While the 1.71 per dollar projection for the end of December was a big improvement from 1.86 for the same period in the previous poll, economists saw the real weakening again to 1.81 by March 2000. 

 Once the real reaches a certain equilibrium, speculative funds may flow back into the country, fuelling volatility, said Alexandre Bittencourt, economist at Banco Primus in Rio de Janeiro. "The Central Bank will not leave the real alone, but it will probably start protecting foreign reserves and limit intervention," he added. 

Brazil's real could come under fresh pressure if the IMF's fiscal target of a primary budget surplus, excluding interest payments, of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product, is not met by the year's end, economists added. 

 "There is still scope for disappointment on the fiscal side. What they have to do is very politically contentious," said American Express' Grice. "It's crucial for (President Fernando Henrique) Cardoso and his administration to keep up the pressure on the Congress to keep up the reforms."

 Where do you see the real trading against the dollar:

 2) by September's end? average: 1.73/dlr, median: 1.75/dlr 

 3) by December's end? average: 1.71/dlr, median: 1.70/dlr

title: Brazil  cenbank to  intervene  rarely in  forex  mkts.
text:
BRASILIA, March 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank will intervene rarely in foreign exchange markets in the second half of 1999 after floating the domestic currency against the dollar, Central Bank President Arminio Fraga said Wednesday. 

 The Central Bank has stepped in several times to reduce market volatility since it relaxed its stiff foreign exchange controls in mid-January. The real currency hit a low of 2.22 per dollar before recovering to around 1.86 per dollar. 

 "The presence of the Central Bank in foreign exchange markets in the second half of the year will be quite rare," Fraga told a Senate economic commission. 

 The Central Bank chief said he expected Brazil's balance of payments situation to be comfortable in 1999 and there would be no need for short-term borrowing. 

 Officials were still working on inflation targets in the aftermath of the currency devaluation, he said, adding that the targets eventually chosen would be the most appropriate for Brazil's situation. 

 Fraga said he hoped the current account deficit in 1999 would be significantly lower than the gap registered in 1998, which was equivalent to 4.52 percent of gross domestic product.

title: BRAZIL  FOREX  WEEK-Maturing debt caps real strength.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 22 (Reuters) - A mountain of maturing foreign debt may cap budding strength in Brazil's real this week, but volatility may be limited as the Central Bank is seen jumping in if the currency spins out of control, experts said. 

 The real, which ended last week at its strongest closing level since February 5, or at 1.855 per dollar, started Monday a tad weaker at 1.87, pressured by corporate debt expiries of more than $1 billion scheduled until the end of March. 

 "The market will certainly be strained this week and next week due to the maturities," said Luis Cervenca, trader at Lloyds Bank in Sao Paulo. 

 Bonds worth $275 million issued by Sao Paulo's water-sewer utility Sabesp  will come due on March 29, while some major bank bonds, each worth more than $100 million, are coming due this week and next. 

 Traders expect the real/dollar rate to be stuck in the weaker end of a 1.80 to 1.95 per dollar range this week. 

 The real, which has lost 35 percent of its value since the government relaxed its rigid foreign exchange policy in mid-January, started firming last week as investors became more confident Latin America's biggest economy was emerging out of its worst crisis in recent decades. 

 Some traders predicted the real would hold steady despite the pressure this week, or at least volatility would be limited, if the Central Bank keeps its recent vigil over the exchange rate. 

 "The pressure on the real this week seems to be smaller than expected earlier," said Sergio Machado, director of treasury at Banco Fator. "Many firms should have already bought their dollars and prepared for their expiries by last week. And despite the maturities, we expect the Central Bank to have sufficient reserves to keep the market stable." 

 The Central Bank, under a fresh agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to free up a second tranche of last year's $41.5 billion financial bailout programme, has been allowed to spend up to $3 billion from its foreign reserves to intervene in the local currency market this month. 

Brazil's foreign reserves, which have been dwindling earlier this month as the Central Bank constantly intervened in the market supplying precious dollars, have actually grew late last week. 

 Reserves stood at $34.398 billion by Thursday, up from Wednesday's $34.386 billion. 

Currency traders suspected the Central Bank was buying dollars in the foreign exchange market, contrary to what it has been doing in recent weeks to support the real. 

 The monetary authority could be replenishing its reserves after it sold millions of dollars from the country's reserves earlier in March, they said. 

 Still, the reserves, which serve as the country's main weapon against speculative attacks on the currency, were down $930 million from the start of March and down $1.712 billion from the beginning of February, when the Central Bank started reporting daily reserve levels.

title: =Exotic  Currency  Focus: Horizon Brightens For Brazil's Real
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--Brazil's real is on the cusp of stability after undergoing the most turbulent two months of its nearly five-year history, local analysts maintain. 

 Revised terms of a $41.5 billion multilateral credit line, significant government strides in its three-year fiscal adjustment plan and confidence in new central bank chief Arminio Fraga have all helped lift dark clouds of recent market pessimism. 

 Local market sentiment is now betting the real will strengthen to around BRR1.75 per dollar by the end of June after a dramatic "overshoot" in the wake of January's forced devaluation, according to three Brazil-based analysts consulted by Dow Jones Newswires. 

 The real's recent performance is providing the best proof of the sudden optimism. At the height of market pessimism earlier this month, the real sank to a historic low of BRR2.22/dollar amid a perceived lack of definition on the policy front. It opened at a mid rate of BRR1.845 on Tuesday, building further on solid gains posted last week, when it closed at BRR1.91. 

 Rules governing Brazil's central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets under last week's reworked economic framework with the International Monetary Fund has particulary pleased market watchers. 

 "The central bank has dollars to sell, so there will be less speculation (against the real)," predicted Alexandre Azara, chief economist at Bank BBA Creditanstalt in Sao Paulo. 


     Market Reacts Positively To Intervention Rules



The monetary authority has vowed to contain volatility in forex
trading - and while it hasn't specified at what points it will do so, it
has declared the volume of intervention funds it has at its disposal
through June.



As reported, the central bank may use up to $3 billion of IMF-led aid
in March to maintain stability in the local forex market. Another $2
billion may be spent in April, with $1.5 billion limits in both May and
June.



"The central bank now has an impressive foreign exchange policy, and
the real will surely not return to over BRR2.00/dollar," predicted
Antonio Costa, head of fixed income Oryx Asset Management in Sao Paulo.



The IMF is widely tipped to disburse the second tranche of last year's
package in April, providing the market with a $9.2 billion liquidity
injection to offset still negative capital flows.



"This is a very credible policy," said Azara, who likens the IMF aid
to a bridge loan.



With the near-term funds in place, inflation fears are also easing.



A Dow Jones Newswires survey of nine U.S. investment houses in late
January pegged 1999 inflation at 28% - with Salomon Smith Barney and
Lehman Brothers providing the most bearish estimates, at 35% and a
whopping 80%, respectively.



President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's government has since set a
provisional target of 16.8% inflation for 1999 under the revised IMF
targets, and local analysts aren't scoffing.



"The inflationary peak has passed, and that peak was when the real was
at BRR2.20 to the dollar," said Leonardo Freire, associate director at
Warburg Dillon Read in Rio de Janeiro.



Freier, Costa and Azara all described 15% as a reasonable estimate for
inflation this year.



        Inflation Fears Already Easing



In February, Brazil's IGP-DI index, a broad measure of wholesale,
consumer and construction prices, rose 4.44% from a month earlier.

 In February, Brazil's IGP-DI index, a broad measure of wholesale, consumer and construction prices, rose 4.44% from a month earlier. Wholesale prices, which account for 60% of the index, jumped a higher-than-expected 6.99%. 

 But with real-dollar rates on the slide, retailers will be less likely to pass on recent increased production costs to consumers, according to Freire. 

 Costa thinks inflation won't be quite the problem initially feared because of an expected recession. 

 The government is predicting a 3.5% to 4% contraction in gross domestic product this year, after the economy grew a scant 0.15% in 1998.

Direct foreign investments this year - as much as $17 billion according to government estimates - are expected to finance Brazil's current account deficit, allowing companies to tap trade finance lines to kick-start exports.

 In another positive development, leading commercial bankers in Europe, the U.S. and Japan have pledged to maintain February's trade and interbank lines through August after Finance Minister Pedro Malan and the central bank's Fraga lobbied for such guarantees in a global roadshow that began last week. 

 Once harvest exports start rolling in May and an estimated $5.2 billion in foreign debt obligations over the next two months are met, analysts say real-dollar rates will begin to settle. That, in turn, should allow the country to tap international capital markets once again.
