title: Brazil says 4 Japan banks to maintain lines to Aug.
text:
TOKYO, March 15 (Reuters) - Four Japanese banks agreed on Monday to maintain their interbank and trade lines with Brazil until August 31 at the same levels as at the end of February, a senior Brazilian official said. 

 Marcos Caramuru, secretary for international affairs at the Finance Ministry, said the banks were Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi , Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank , Sanwa Bank  and Sumitomo Bank . 

 Sergio Werlang, director of economic policy at Brazil's central bank, said the real was "completely undervalued" but that Brazil would seek to boost the real's value through sound macroeconomic policies, not through intervention in the currency market. 

 "The real exchange rate in Brazil is way off - too devalued," he said. 

 But he said Brazil's agreement with the IMF called for the central bank to intervene only to control volatility, not to boost the rate of the real against the dollar. 

 "Yes, I think the market's expectations are overblown - pessimistic," Werlang said. 

 "We are going to convince them we're right," as the results of inflation and debt reduction programmes emerge. He added that January and February data looked favourable, but he did not provide specifics. ((Tokyo Newsroom +81-3 3432 8022 tokyo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Brazil 's New  Forex Intervention  Funds Seen Bridging Gap
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- The $8 billion the International Monetary Fund has granted Brazil to prop up its real from now through June should bridge the country's current account gap until foreign capital inflows return to normal, analysts said. 

 According to the revised terms of an IMF-led credit line, Brazil will have $3 billion available to inject in the foreign exchange market in March, another $2 billion in April, $1.5 billion in May, and $1.5 billion in June. 

 "The $8 billion are largely enough," said Octavio de Barros, chief economist with Banco Bilbao Vizcaya in Sao Paulo, adding that the funds are "very well distributed" over the four months. 

 The funds are seen as essential. 

 "This amount corresponds to the lack of liquidity for balance-of-payments financing until June," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist for BMC bank in Sao Paulo, referring to bonds and amortizations due in coming months. "Foreign banks won't allow these (debts) to be rolled over, as they're restraining their exposure to Brazil." 

Central bank monetary policy director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said Tuesday that the monetary authority may actually spend more than the $8 billion specified in the IMF pact, noting that it depends on whether Brazil is able to boost its international reserves, local daily O Estado de Sao Paulo reported Wednesday. 

 "New money that is added to reserves may be used in the interventions," Figueiredo was quoted as saying. 

 Tuesday, a day after the new IMF terms and forex intervention figures were announced, the real (BRR) strengthened to BRR1.88 per dollar from Monday's close of BRR1.98/dlr. The local currency opened trading Wednesday at BRR1.87/dlr. Before the free-float in mid-January, the real was quoted at BRR1.21. 

 Analysts also welcomed the disclosure Monday of the economic framework for the $41.5-billion aid package. The new agreement with the IMF made public all the macroeconomic variables used in the model and expected currency quotes against the dollar each month. 

 "We had zero idea of what the central bank's parameters for forexintervention were before," said Christian Stracke, economist at BT Alex Brown in New York. 

 For Barros, the government introduced a little "predictability" in the performance of international reserves and foreign exchange rates, essential for private-sector decision-making. 

 "And most importantly, the government didn't water down the free-float regime," Barros added. 

 The Finance Ministry's economic policy secretary Amaury Bier said Tuesday that there will be two types of intervention in the forex market. 

 One, with the IMF's $8 billion, aims to cover Brazil's current account deficit during four months of an expected sharp shortage of dollars. The other, Bier said, has no pre-set limits and is a type of intervention designed to control excess volatility, using what is left of Brazil's reserves - at $34.572 billion Monday. 

 According to calculations by BBV's Barros, Brazil's public- and private-sector foreign commitments tally up to $4.385 billion in March. That figure includes bonds coming due, amortizations, interest, repatriation of profits, and other loans. 

 "I don't think Brazil will have to use all the $3 billion this month," he said, estimating there will be around $1 billion a month in foreign direct investment and 10% to 20% of debt rollover. It's "too naive" to think that "dollar inflows have dried completely," he said. 

 "The margin is comfortable, and Brazil may save some of March's munition for April, when the pressure on the real will be bigger," he said, without revealing his calculations for next month. 

 To restore dollar inflows, the government is counting on the return of foreign credit lines to Brazilian companies and a sharp turnaround in its trade balance - to an $11 billion surplus in 1999 from a $8.4 billion deficit last year. 

 Most analysts think the $11 billion surplus goal is overly ambitious, but they agree exports will pick up fast, becoming the short-term supplier of dollars in the market aside from the central bank. 

 In February, Brazil posted its first real trade surplus, totaling $219 million, since May 1996 - real because in June 1998 technical factors generated a small surplus. 

 Barros estimated that the trade surplus will stand around $400 million in March, $700 million in April, and will surpass the $1 billion mark in May. 

 "Until the end of the year, exports should outpace imports by $7.9 billion," he said. 

 BMC's Allain is more optimistic about the second half of the year, when he believes the supply and demand for dollars will even out. 

 "There may be four, five months which may not be so positive, when foreign debt commitments must be met," he said. "But in the second half, an improving trade balance and lower debt burden will lead to a more balanced forex market." 


As a result of the improved trade balance figures, Brazil's current
account deficit is expected to shrink to 3%-3.3% of GDP in 1999,
according to analysts, from last year's 4.5%.

title: Brazil 's New  Forex Intervention  Funds Seen Bridging Gap

BRASILIA (Dow Jones)--The $8 billion the International Monetary Fund has granted Brazil to prop up its real from now through June should bridge the country's current account gap until foreign capital inflows return to normal, analysts said.

Central bank monetary policy director Luiz Fernando Figueiredo said Tuesday that the monetary authority may actually spend more than the $8 billion specified in the IMF pact, noting that it depends on whether Brazil is able to boost its international reserves, local daily O Estado de Sao Paulo reported Wednesday. 

 "New money that is added to reserves may be used in the interventions," Figueiredo was quoted as saying.

title: Emerging debt firms amid optimism over Brazil.
text:
NEW YORK, March 10 (Reuters) - Emerging market bond prices rose sharply on Wednesday amid a flurry of positive news on Brazil this week including the promise of fresh funds from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), traders and analysts said. 

 Optimism about the Brazilian central bank's new foreign exchange policy as well as approval on Wednesday of a key fiscal bill by the country's lower house that would raise the financial transactions tax also buoyed prices. 

 Market experts said they expected Brazil's new central bank chief Arminio Fraga to get a warm response from investors during his foreign tour which begins on Thursday in New York. 

 "The market is being driven higher by continued optimism over what Arminio has been able to put in place so far in Brazil," said one head trader at a U.S. investment bank in New York. 

 "I expect he will get a favourable response," the trader added. 


At 1300 EDT/1800 GMT, benchmark Brazil C bonds		  were one percentage point higher at 60-1/8 and its global bonds due 2008 were 1-1/2 stronger at 72-3/4.



Brazil's currency, the real, rose 1.1 percent by midday to 1.87 reais per dollar on talk the country's Central Bank was intervening earlier on Wednesday.



Earlier news that Brazil plans to return to the foreign debt markets after it receives a second instalment of $9.2 billion in loans from an IMF-led rescue package was viewed favourably but some analysts said Brazil still would have to pay a high price to reenter international capital markets.



"It would be great if they could do that but do they want to sell debt at the 15 percent level that I think the market would require?" said one emerging market debt strategist at a U.S. investment bank.



"There are a lot of people underweight Brazil that may be compelled to come back into the market because prices have done better so conceivably there would be some demand," the source said.



But the analyst said a lot would depend on the size and maturity of the issue and he noted that even a five-year issue would have to come in at around 13 percent to get the deal done.



One source said market rumours were that Brazil may try to come with up to $5.0 billion in the international capital markets after they receive the IMF funds.



Meanwhile, market sources said Panama is expected to price a $500 million global bond issue on Thursday through underwriter BankBoston, which declined to comment.



In the broader secondary Latin market, prices were also firmer on the positive news from Brazil. Argentine FRBs bonds		 were 1/2 higher at 84-5/8 bid and Mexican PAR bonds		 were 1/4 firmer at 77-1/8.



Elsewhere, Russian debt prices rose on renewed hopes of a breakthrough on talks between Russia and the IMF.

title: Brazil real ends firmer at 1.89 to dollar - traders.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency firmed 4.8 percent to 1.89 per dollar on Tuesday after the International Monetary Fund and the government reached a new accord that set rules on Central Bank intervention in the foreign exchange market, traders said. 

Brazil's national currency, the real, closed at its strongest against the dollar in a month, traders said. 

 Under the fresh accord with the IMF, the Central Bank may now use up to $8 billion from the country's foreign reserves and IMF funds to intervene in local currency markets until June, supplying dollars to help support the real. 

 The real, at 1.89, has lost 36 percent of its value against the U.S. currency since the government relaxed its tight foreign exchange policy on Jan. 13. 

 "Markets received the new measure well," said Marcelo Allain, economist at BMC Bank in Sao Paulo. "The measure will at least serve as a bridge for a market suffering from a huge demand for dollars." 

 Markets were recently parched of dollars as Brazilian companies sought U.S. currency to pay off their maturing foreign debt. Allain estimated that some $6.5 billion in Eurobonds were coming due between March and June. 

 Traders said the Central Bank did not intervene on Tuesday, though a foreign firm carried out a deal to bring about $100 million into the country, which helped the real to firm in late trading. 

 In the money market, the benchmark overnight Selic rate ended at 45 percent a year after the Central Bank signalled rates at that level in its morning auction Tuesday. 

 Interest rate futures traded on the BM&F Futures and Commodities Exchange ended mixed. title: ANALYSIS-New IMF deal gives Brazil real a reprieve.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 9 (Reuters) - The new IMF deal should buoy Brazil's embattled currency for the first half of 1999, but some overly confident forecasts on the rest of the year may leave the real struggling again, analysts said. 

 The currency got a boost after new terms set in the International Monetary Fund's rescue plan allowed the government to spend more dollars to defend the real. Brazil's Finance Ministry announced Monday that the new rescue plan authorises the Central Bank to spend up to $8 billion by June to intervene in currency markets. 

 Those precious dollars will come from Brazil's foreign reserves, currently at $34.8 billion, and the $9 billion second tranche of a $41.5 billion financial bailout package, expected to be freed up in April. 

 Markets parched of dollars welcomed the additional cash and analysts said that, in the short term at least, it would help ease pressure from foreign corporate bonds, with maturities concentrated in the first half of this year. 

 In a first sign of relief, the real jumped 3.7 percent to 1.91 reais per dollar by midday Tuesday. 

 "The measure will at least serve as a bridge for a market suffering from a huge demand for dollars," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC Bank in Sao Paulo. 

 Allain said about $6.5 billion in Eurobonds were expected to come due between March and June this year. 

 Brazil's Central Bank, under the terms laid out by the IMF, was allowed to spend $3 billion in March, $2 billion in April, $1.5 billion in May and another $1.5 billion in June to "water markets" in which the U.S. currency was seen drying up. 

 Analysts said the amount is sufficient to keep the real stable in the first half, as it just about covers the needs of Brazilian companies paying off debt - the main source of market turbulence at the moment. 

 But with no intervention levels set for the second half, Brazil's real will have to rely on fundamental progress in cutting its budget deficit and taming the high inflation expected this year. 

 The IMF was due to review Brazil's progress in the future but it was not clear whether new intervention targets would be set, analysts said. 

 Analysts said Brazil was likely to meet its new target of a primary budget surplus, excluding interest payments, of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product, up from an original 2.6 percent. 

 But the government still faces a big challenge in getting the rest of its fiscal austerity measures through Congress. 

 First on the political agenda was the government's battle to get a key financial transactions tax known as the CPMF through Congress. Voting was set to resume this week. 

 "President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has more to do on the fiscal front," Allain said. 

 Analysts in particular doubted the government would be able to control inflation, after the IMF forecast Brazil would end 1999 with an inflation of 16.8 percent. 

 "It's a 'show me' story. We have to see that inflation comes down, but there is absolutely no guarantee," said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging market strategist at Deutsche Bank in London. 

 Dennis noted that Brazil's benchmark inflation index Fipe, which measures consumer prices in industrial Sao Paulo, was already up 1.4 percent in February, translating into annualized inflation of 18 percent. 

 The Brazil-IMF accord also forecast the real at 1.7 per dollar by the end of the year. 

 But for the fragile currency to settle around that level without strong intervention, markets would have to receive an influx of export revenues, analysts said. 

 The 1999 trade surplus target in the IMF agreement is way too optimistic at $11 billion, analysts said. In 1998, Brazil posted a $6.4 billion trade deficit. 

 "The measure foresees the trade balance turning into a surplus in the second half, with fewer imports and more exports. But I think the surplus will only reach $6 billion..." Allain said. "It would be hard to get a surplus of $11 billion." 

 Both Allain and Dennis said Brazil had a long way to go to regain investor confidence and calm currency markets. 

 "Brazilians have given themselves the biggest possible chance yet of stabilising markets and moving towards key targets," said Deutsche Bank's Dennis. 

 In the meantime, Brazil's Central Bank President Arminio Fraga and Finance Minister Pedro Malan were due to travel separately to New York, London, Frankfurt, Paris and Tokyo this week for talks with private banks and authorities to help restore credit flows to Latin America's biggest economy.

title: Latin America  Forex  Roundup: Brazil Sparking New Optimism
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Most Latin American currencies were strengthening against the U.S. dollar late Tuesday, underpinned by renewed optimism after Monday's release of a new fiscal accord between the International Monetary Fund and Brazil, 

 Meanwhile, trading of the Ecuadorean sucre was still halted as the government extended a surprise banking holiday to a second day Tuesday. 

 At 1845 GMT, New York-based traders quoted the Brazilian real at BRR1.91 per dollar on a spread of BRR1.90-BRR1.92, stronger from Monday's close of BRR1.98/dollar.

 "It's definitely a good start, and the real will likely trade at these levels this week," a trader in New York said. "But it's now up to Congress to keep the good mood alive and make targets attainable." 

 Among the IMF-sponsored targets is a year-end exchange rate of BRR1.70/dlr, or a 29% depreciation from Jan. 13, when the central bank first widened the real's trading band. The real sank to an intraday low of BRR2.22/dlr at its weakest point last week. 

 Under the new foreign exchange regime, Brazil's central bank can intervene in the foreign exchange market with a maximum of $8 billion until the end of June, when these levels will be reviewed with the IMF once again. 

 "It's very positive news, because now the central bank has a cap and it won't just waste its reserves and the IMF money in defending the currency," a trader in New York said. 

 Meanwhile in Mexico, the peso has gained ground for its fifth straight session, despite coming off slightly from its opening levels. At 1845 GMT, the peso was changing hands at MXN9.7990 per dollar from Monday's close of 9.8050. 

 The Mexican currency has strengthened 8.3% since Jan. 14, the day before the Brazilian central bank allowed the real to float. 

 Mexico's relatively strong economy, links to the U.S. and high interest rates are providing the backdrop for the peso's strength. title: Brazil -IMF deal limits Cenbank  intervention  - gov't.
text:
BRASILIA, March 8 (Reuters) - A revised rescue deal put together by the International Monetary Fund for Brazil includes limits on Central Bank intervention to protect the real currency, according to a letter of intent between the two sides released by the Finance Ministry on Monday. 

 Under the agreement, the Central Bank may spend up to $3 billion in March1, $2 billion in April and $1.5 billion in May and again in June. The Central Bank is also limited to spending 30 percent of its monthly maximum in any one week, the document said. 

 Financial markets have been waiting for details on how Brazil will intervene in foreign exchange markets to defend the real which has slumped by nearly 40 percent since the country was forced to float the currency in mid-January. 

 Further intervention limits for the second half of 1999 would be set at a future review of Brazil's agreement with the IMF. 

 The letter of intent also spelled out macroeconomic forecasts for Brazil's economy with net public debt expected to rise sharply to 49.3 percent of GDP by the end of the year. In November, the ratio stood at 41.9 percent of GDP. 

 Brazil's economy was seen shrinking by between 3.5 and 4 percent this year, but would recover in 2000 to grow by between 3.5 percent and 4 percent and to between 4.5 and 5 percent in 2001. 

 Brazil's trade balance, which went $6.43 billion into the red in 1998, would post a huge surplus of $11 billion in 1999 and the current account deficit, 4.48 percent of GDP in 1998, would fall to about 3 percent this year, the document said. 

 The benchmark overnight Selic interest rate would also fall to an average 28.8 percent in 1999, down from 45 percent now, the real currency would end the year at a forecast 1.70 to the dollar and inflation for the year would be 16.8 percent.

title: Brazil  central bank  to "water"  forex  markets-Fraga.
text:
BRASILIA, March 8 (Reuters) - Brazil's Central Bank intends to use cash from a proposed new loan from the International Monetary Fund to "water" foreign exchange markets and ensure liquidity, the bank's new president Arminio Fraga said on Monday. 

 "It's not our intention to go back to a policy of fixing the exchange rate," Fraga told a news conference. "We have limits in mind, but it's not the moment (to disclose them)." 

 Under the terms of a letter of intent between Brazil and the IMF, the Central Bank may spend up to $3 billion in March on foreign exchange markets to prop up the real, $2 billion in April, $1.5 billion in May and another $1.5 billion in June. 

 The document forecast the real would end the year at 1.70 to the dollar, up from 1.98 now. 

 Fraga said the intervention rules would allow the Central Bank to carry over unspent cash from one month to another. The carry-over, however, could not exceed 25 percent of the new month's limit, he said. 

 Furthermore, any foreign borrowing by Brazil's government - excluding operations involving the National Development Bank (BNDES) and state companies - would be added to the amount of cash the Central Bank was allowed to spend. 

 The letter of intent also said Brazil's Central Bank would stop intervening in foreign exchange futures from March. 

 ((Brasilia newsroom 5561 314 1193; brasilia.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Brazil's Fraga sees similarities with Mexico.
text:
BRASILIA, March 4 (Reuters) - The new president of Brazil's Central Bank said on Thursday that Brazil's floating foreign exchange system and its plan to set inflation targets was similar to Mexico's strategy after the peso's devaluation in 1994. 

 "We are not adopting a regime identical to Mexico's, although some similarities exist given that Mexico also has inflation targets and a floating foreign exchange. The operational details will be different, but the general principle is not very different," Fraga told a news conference. 

 He was answering a question from a reporter about whether Brazil would adopt Mexico's system of automatic intervention in the foreign exchange market whenever the peso falls or rises by more than 2 percent against the dollar. 

 Fraga said earlier that the Brazilian Central Bank would intervene in foreign exchange markets when necessary and the interventions would "discrete and limited." 

 He also said Brazil would use overseas borrowing to help provide local foreign exchange markets with liquidity. 

 While private markets remain closed to Brazil as it scrambles to recover from a 40 percent-plus devaluation, a second instalment of loans from the International Monetary Fund, currently under discussion in Washington, would also be used partly to fund the country's balance of payments deficit, he said.

title: Brazil real ends up on dlr inflows, Fraga comments.

Currency dealers cheered the announcement, saying higher interest rates, at least for the time being, would support the real.

 Fraga, in a news conference given after the announcement of the interest rate hike, said Brazil may use part of the money extended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to "attend dollar needs" in the country. 

 "Players interpreted that comment as the Central Bank would use reserves to intervene in markets," said one trader at Banco Fator. 

Brazil's real, at 2.07 per dollar, has lost 41.5 percent of its value since the government relaxed its rigid foreign exchange policy on January 13.

title: ANALYSIS - Brazil's Fraga to clear final Senate vote.
text:
BRASILIA, March 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's Senate was expected to confirm economist Arminio Fraga as the new president of the Central Bank Wednesday, ending weeks of uncertainty which have seen the local currency spiral to a record low. 

 Economists said markets would heave a sigh of relief at the confirmation of Fraga and five new Central Bank directors, a team of former market operators handpicked to steer Brazil's currency through a turbulent post-devaluation period. 

 Fraga's first task will be to send markets a clear signal of how the Central Bank plans to keep a lid on inflation after the domestic currency, the real, skidded to a new closing low of 2.17 per dollar Tuesday, economists said. 

 "He's really competent in explaining his ideas to the market," said Felipe Garcia, economist at I.D.E.A. in New York. "Everyone wants him to take over as soon as possible, but it's taking these days and these days have been very volatile," 

 Investors have been nervously twiddling their thumbs since Fraga was named over a month ago, as Senate delayed his confirmation while lawmakers took off for Carnival holidays and then installed new committees following elections last year. 

 The U.S.-educated Fraga was working as a top aide to billionaire speculator George Soros when he was invited to become Brazil's third Central Bank chief this year. 

 A Senate economic panel Friday approved his nomination, due to be sealed in a full vote on the Senate floor Wednesday. 

 With this hurdle cleared, economists said they were anxious to see the inflation target Brazil was said to be discussing with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as part of talks aimed at securing the release of more international loans. 

 They also want a clear set of rules for Central Bank intervention in the foreign exchange market, after a recent round of interventions left investors speculating whether Brazil was defending a set currency exchange rate. 

 The Central Bank can either intervene sporadically to ease swings in currency markets, or adopt a system similar to Mexico's, where the Central Bank automatically steps in if the currency fluctuates by more than a set percentage level. 

 "I think it's going to be a clear rule of intervention," said Garcia, referring to the latter system. 

 The real has lost 44 percent of its value against the dollar since Brazil was forced to abandon its strict foreign exchange controls on Jan. 13. 

 The Central Bank moved Tuesday to tighten liquidity and ease pressure on the real, which has weakened as the market is short of dollars while companies still have to honour some $2 billion in corporate Eurobond payments due this month. 

 Fraga will have no time to settle into his office - on his first day on the job Thursday, he is due to preside a meeting of the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (Copom). 

 Some economists said the Central Bank should jack up interest rates, already towering at an annualized 41 percent, despite fears this would increase the chances of Brazil defaulting on its mountain of domestic debt. 

 "That would be a signal of a very tough and determined policy," said Neil Dougall, chief Latin America economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London. "Debt default is not triggered by a 3 or 4 percent rise in interest rates." 

 Dougall noted that Mexico and South Korea both saw a surge in inflation following devaluations, meaning real interest rates turned negative for a short while. 

 Economists calculate Brazil's effective benchmark overnight rate stood at 2.38 percent in February. This meant real rates of return were negative last month, with inflation hitting 3.61 percent, according to the private Fundacao Getulio Vargas. 

 Dougall said a rate hike, in the context of an expected agreement with the IMF and improving trade figures, would encourage risk-averse investors to keep their precious dollars in Brazil and prevent a further overshooting of the real. 

 "You've got in place the factors which will prevent this overshooting," said Dougall. "In the meantime, maybe it's worth sending a strong signal from the Central Bank that it's not going to accommodate inflation expectations."

title: FOCUS-Brazil tries to rein in record-low real.
text:
SAO PAULO, March 2 (Reuters) - Brazil intervened in foreign exchange markets again on Tuesday to prop up the real currency as it tumbled to a record low, threatening to throw Latin America's biggest economy deeper into crisis. 

 Traders said the Central Bank reverted to selling dollars on Tuesday after a day on the sidelines in order to rein in the currency which bottomed out at a record intraday low of 2.22 reais per dollar. By midday the real had inched up to a still-fragile 2.16 per dollar. 

 "We're playing with fire," Augusto Lopez-Claros, an economist at Lehman Bros. in London, told Reuters Television. 

 "If confidence doesn't return to Brazil following the approval of the IMF programme there will be serious implications for the economies of the region and the whole continent," he said. 

 The government is hammering out new fiscal targets with the International Monetary Fund in an attempt to prevent the devaluation, which has already topped 40 percent, from spinning out of control. 

 A further slide could spark flyaway inflation and another hike in already crippling interest rates. The government's National Statistics Institute said on Tuesday that unemployment hit a record high of 7.73 percent in January as Brazil heads in to what is likely to be its worst recession in decades. 

 The IMF said talks with Brazilian officials should result in some "good news" in coming days but full details of a new rescue deal were only expected by mid-March. 

 Reserves fell by a slim $102 million during the first two days of Central Bank intervention in forex markets last week. Massive dollar outflows forced Brazil to float its currency six weeks ago, undermining initial targets set last year and sending the government back to the negotiating table with the IMF. 

 Markets are hoping new targets will pave the way for more financing options - and therefore greater access to sorely-needed dollars - as well as the next instalment of the $41.5 billion rescue loan to bolster Brazil's currency reserves. 

 Pessimism reigned in the forex market, however. A fundamental lack of dollars combined with dwindling investor confidence in the government's ability to sidestep an economic crisis put further pressure on the currency. 

 "In the short term, with a lack of decision on forex policy and dollar flows, the real should continue to be under pressure," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Barings Bank in Sao Paulo. 

 Arminio Fraga, a former aide of billionaire financier George Soros, is expected to be confirmed this week by the Senate as the new president of the Central Bank, allowing him to get on with the formation of a concrete forex policy. 

 Some economists forecast Fraga will further raise interest rates at a meeting of the bank's Copom monetary policy committee on Thursday to help rein in the currency. 

 Dollar demand is strong as some $2 billion in corporate Eurobonds come due this month and as importers snap up greenbacks to pay for their goods. Exports, on the other hand, have been seriously hampered because foreigners are unwilling to lend Brazilians cash. 

 The Central Bank said export financing has shown signs of picking up and a glimmer of hope appeared Monday when Brazil announced a monthly trade surplus of $219 million in January - its first since June 1998. 

 But concern that support for the government's crisis drive could be waning also put pressure on the currency. The lower house of Congress is due to vote this month on a higher financial transactions tax that is a key part of the plan.

title: Brazilian Markets Await Fraga Confirmation, Details Of Pact With IMF
text:
SAO PAULO -(Dow Jones)- Brazilian markets finally got the dose of good news they were craving Friday, but an assortment of unknowns continued to quell investor confidence as yet another crucial week got underway Monday. 

 "There's just not any interest in our market, and I don't see it picking up from one day to the next," said a fund manager at one Sao Paulo investment bank. "We still have a number of issues that have the potential to hurt the market, but none that really could give it a boost this week." 

 Last Friday, central bank president nominee Arminio Fraga easily won approval from the Senate's economic affairs committee. Fraga and five new central-bank directors are expected to breeze through final confirmation in a vote Wednesday in the Senate plenum. 

 Also Friday, tensions between President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and several recalcitrant governors - embroiled in a spat over state debt obligations - eased after a meeting between the two sides. The federal government refused to restructure existing debt contracts but did agree to some concessions. 

 Both events were seen as positive steps in the process to heal crippled credibility, but Brazil faces several more tests this week, and markets remain volatile as a result. 

 Monday, the real closed at 2.13 to the dollar, compared to Friday's close of 2.035 to the dollar. Traders said a scarcity of exports, combined with importers rushing to close exchange contracts, pressured the local currency. 

 The benchmark index of the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, or Bovespa, finished up 3.2% to 9198 in paper-thin trading. 

 "There's no volume so this isn't the start of an upward trend," the fund manager said, noting that investors will remain on the sidelines until the foreign-exchange market calms. 

 Financial markets are hopeful that Fraga's final approval will pave the way for the central bank to clarify its plans for foreign-exchange and monetary policy. Analysts, however, aren't convinced such information will be forthcoming. 

 "A lot of people have been talking about having specific rules for intervention, but we're not expecting (the central bank) to announce any formal mechanism yet," said Constantin Jansco, an economist at MCM Consultores in Sao Paulo. 

 Last week, Fraga said that the foreign-exchange policies that work best are those that are closest to being pure. He declined to comment on whether the central bank would announce formal intervention rules. 

Brazil adopted a free-float exchange policy in mid-January, which has resulted in a weakening of the real of more than 40% against the dollar. Last week, the central bank sold dollars on the exchange market to bolster the real for the first time since the free-float. 

 "Perhaps (the central bank) will tinker with some regulations on capital movements, but the moment you announce specific intervention rules, the market will test them immediately," Jansco added, noting that the central bank doesn't have enough reserves to determine under what circumstances it will always intervene to protect the real. Brazil's international reserves stood at $35.6 billion last Friday, down from $44.6 billion at the end of 1998. 

 On the monetary-policy front, the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee, or Copom, is scheduled to meet late Wednesday to discuss interest rates. The group last met on Jan. 18, when it raised the ceiling rate at which the central bank may lend to banks, known as the Tban, to 41% from 36%. 

 Since then, the central bank has intervened daily on the interbank market to set overnight rates. The interbank rate, which stood at 29.80% before the last Copom meeting, has remained at 39% since Feb. 1. 

 "I don't think we'll see any rate changes coming out of the Copom meeting. The central bank has been pretty clear that they'll keep them steady," said Jansco. 

 Indeed, Fraga said during his Senate appearance that, while rates could fall in the medium term, the government must maintain a strict monetary policy to contain the effects of the devaluation. The new central banker said that the monetary authority's primary aim is to protect the local currency and prevent the return of hyper-inflation. 

 Markets also are anxiously awaiting an announcement from the Brazilian government and the International Monetary Fund on the revised terms of the $41.5 billion IMF-led aid deal inked last November. A team of Brazilian officials has been in Washington for the past two weeks hammering out the details of the agreement. IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said Monday a new agreement is likely in the next few days. 

 The revised accord should include new macroeconomic targets. Brazil is expected to respond by announcing a series of additional budget cuts, of up to seven billion reals, according to market estimates. Brazil, which already has received $9.4 billion in funding, hopes to draw down a second tranche of about the same amount before the end of this month. 

 Finally, while progress was made on the state debt talks, Minas Gerais Governor Itamar Franco - who set the battle in motion on Jan. 6 by declaring a 90-day moratorium on debt payments to the federal government - continues to be a thorn in Cardoso's side. Franco, the only one of Brazil's 27 governors who didn't participate in last Friday's meeting, hinted over the weekend that the state might extend the moratorium. 

 On Monday, the Minas Gerais governor was in Brasilia meeting with Senators from his party - the government-allied Democratic Movement Party - and opposition party members in the lower house, but has so far declined to meet with Cardoso.

title: Brazil  cenbank to  intervene  less in futures - Fraga.
text:
SAO PAULO, Feb 26 (Reuters) - The president-designate of Brazil's Central Bank on Friday said intervention in the foreign exchange futures market would diminish now that the government has allowed the currency, the real, to float freely. 

 "Regarding the issue of selling dollars in the (BM&F futures and commodities) market, I believe that with the floating currency regime, such operation by the Central Bank would certainly diminish," Arminio Fraga said during his confirmation hearing before a Senate committee. "The market will now determine the exchange rate." 

 Before the move to a free-floating currency in mid-January, the Central Bank, according to currency traders, would intervene in the dollar futures market, selling or buying contracts to maintain the real/dollar exchange rate within a set band, called the mini-band.

title: Brazil's Fraga Sees Free-Float As Best Option For Embattled Real
text:
BRASILIA -(Dow Jones)- Arminio Fraga, in line to head Brazil's central bank amid a firestorm of volatility in Latin America's largest economy, Friday said the free-float foreign exchange system is the nation's best option as it tries to emerge from a crippling recession. 

 Fraga, a former adviser to financier George Soros, spoke before the Senate's economics affairs committee endorsed his nomination for the central bank presidency, as expected. He said he will use monetary policy as his primary weapon to manage the exchange rate - which analysts said is likely to mean high rates until the central bank is comfortable with the inflation outlook and the level of its embattled currency, the real. 

 Fraga told lawmakers the central bank must focus almost exclusively on maintaining a stable currency and controlling inflation, and said he considered free-float foreign exchange systems "viable and sustainable." Although he said the government wants to allow for a "responsible" cut in Brazil's sky-high rates, he indicated a strict monetary policy will be crucial for Brazil to adapt to its new free-float regime. 

 The remarks amounted to his first public statements on monetary and foreign-exchange rate policy since being nominated Feb. 2 to replace Francisco Lopes. Lopes was sacked earlier this month following the decision to devalue and then float the real in the face of an investor exodus in January. 

 The real, which stabilized somewhat after it was freed to trade at market levels against the dollar, came under strain again this week amid renewed worries about Brazil's weak fiscal condition, even as the central bank has returned repeatedly to the foreign-exchange markets as a dollar seller to prop up the currency. The interventions were the first since Brazil abandonded the real's widened trading band and let the currency float freely on Jan. 15. 

 "The preservation of the buying power of the currency should be the most important task of the central bank," Fraga told lawmakers Friday. 

 In endorsing Brazil's move to a floating exchange rate, Fraga said international experience had shown that the free-float is most successful over the long run when it is closest to "pure" - that the central bank intervenes only in exceptional cases and the currency is supported by underlying policies. 

 The government is now trying to enact fiscal-policy reforms that it hopes will win back investors, but its deficit-cutting drive remains mired in Congress and complicated by new revenue expectations linked to the plunge in the real. The government has also been working with the International Monetary Fund to readjust its fiscal program in hopes of receiving continued aid under a $41 billion rescue package arranged last November. 

 Investors began heading for the exits in droves last month over worries about Brazil's ability to cut budget deficits and meet debt obligations. After a lull, the stampede picked up again this week. 

 After a third straight day of Central Bank intervention Thursday, the real closed at 2.04 reals to the dollar, unchanged from Wednesday. Friday, the currency strengthened to 2.0350 reals to the dollar, amid unconfirmed rumors that the central bank again intervened. After Thursday's intervention, traders said the central bank appeared to have spent little of its precious dollar war chest: The country's hard-currency reserves stood at nearly $36 billion yesterday, little changed from a month ago. 

 In all, Brazil's currency has lost 41% of its dollar value since the country's first move to devalue on Jan. 13. On Tuesday, the real was trading safely below two reals to the dollar before it suddenly weakened to 2.09 reals to the dollar, forcing the central bank to intervene. 

 Fraga, who still must be approved by the full Senate Wednesday, said he intends to maintain a strict monetary stance. But at the same time, he said Brazilian interest rates must come down to international levels and that he sees room for a short-term decline. The central bank benchmark rate currently stands at 39%, a level designed to attract foreign investors to the weakened real. But Brazil's high interest rates have aggravated the economy's slide into recession. 

 On inflation, Fraga said Brazil can't return to the days of hyperinflation, which was stamped out by the Cardoso government's tight monetray policies in the mid-1990s. The central bank nominee avoided offering an annual inflation rate estimate for 1999, but he forecast single-digit annual inflation in the year 2000, which should drop below 5% in 2001. 

 Fraga also said he hopes to stabilize the relationship between public deficit and gross domestic product. Brazil's public deficit was equivalent to about 8% of GDP in 1998. "The government has total awareness of the dangers of not controlling the public deficit," Fraga said. The fiscal plan the government is trying to push through Congress aims to save more than 28 billion reals in 1999. 

 Fraga noted that Brazil has lost international credibility over the last 18 months, and will face a difficult first half of 1999, but said he sees a recovery in the final half of the year. 

 Throughout the committee session, questions and accusations returned to Fraga's last job: a New York-based managing director, in charge of emerging markets portfolio management and strategies, for Soros Fund Management LLC. 

 In essence, some senators accused Fraga of being in cahoots with the international speculators who they blame for Brazil's current economic situation: a devastated currency, possible double-digit inflation, and a growing recession. 

 "I can say that I never did anything that could have harmed my country," he responded. "I am here to serve my country as a technocrat and as an economist." 

 Fraga declined comment on the type of foreign exchange intervention policy that might be adopted by the central bank to defend the real. Brazilian officials have said in recent weeks that the government is discussing possible intervention rules with the IMF as part of the review of the aid package. The IMF said Friday that the revised accord with Brazil will be unveiled next week, in which the Brazilian government will make new committments to a number of economic targets in return for continued funding under the IMF-organized loan package. 

 Negative sentiment in the currency market had been effectively neutralized during recent Carnival celebrations, but pessimism is on the rise as President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's administration struggles to find a solution to the continuing economic crisis, which many fear could eventually spread throughout Latin America, and in turn weaken the U.S. economy. 

 Cardoso met Friday with state governors, seven of whom are pushing for renegotiation of their debts to the central government, something Cardoso has ruled out. Following the meeting, the Estado news agency reported federal and state officials as saying the Brazilian government will make some concessions to states with financial difficulties but won't revise the terms of existing debt contracts. 

 Itamar Franco, the governor of Brazil's third-largest state, helped reignite the capital flight last month when he declared a 90-day moratorium on his state's federal debt payments. Franco, who boycotted Friday's meeting of governors, has grown more bellicose in his opposition to Cardoso - all of which have contributed to worries about the government's ability to put Brazil's fiscal house in order. 

 Separately, the finance ministry, hoping to avoid a default on debt owed it by Brazilian towns and cities, said it has agreed to refinance municipal debts of 17.4 billion reals, with the debts to be paid over a period of 30 years at 9% annual interest rates. The government had earlier discarded the possibility of such a restructuring, but National Treasury Secretary Eduardo Guimaraes said the new proposal makes the payment of municipal debts viable. "It's unrealistic to think that they (municipalities) would be able to pay these debts on their own," he said. 

 If the federal government hadn't proposed rolling over the debts, the city of Sao Paulo, Latin America's largest, would have defaulted on 410 million reals worth of municipal bonds due March 1, according to authorities. 

 "Under the current circumstances, a default by Sao Paulo would have been a market disaster," said consultant Raul Velloso, a former government advisor. 

 "It ends the threat of a second Itamar effect," said the head trader at a Sao Paulo bank, referring to Minas Gerais governor Franco's moratorium on federal debt payments.

title: FOCUS- Brazil  Cenbank  intervenes  again, real firms.
text:
SAO PAULO, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Brazil's fragile real currency inched up to 2.04 per dollar at midday Thursday after the Central Bank intervened in the local foreign exchange market, supplying dollars for the third straight day, traders said. 

 The Central Bank was seen selling dollars in markets through particular banks at 2.04, a tad firmer against Wednesday's close of 2.05, to prevent the real from weakening again, traders said. Wednesday's 2.05 was the real's second weakest closing ever. 

 Pressure had increased Thursday when one big bank was seen scrambling for about $200 million in the market to pay off its maturing foreign debt, traders noted. 

 "The intervention, after two straight days of it (until Wednesday), is no longer a novelty," said one currency trader in Sao Paulo. "But now markets know that the Central Bank would support the real if it threatens to go out of control." 

 The Central Bank began selling dollars quietly via dealers on Tuesday as the real ratcheted past the 2.00 psychological barrier. The real has now lost 40.7 percent of its value since the government was forced to devalue in mid-January. 

 The Bank finally decided to step into markets after more than a month of absence following the devaluation, because local currency markets were recently parched for dollars, with about $3.8 billion in foreign debt expiring in February and March. 

 The Central Bank, according to traders, was trying to avoid a repeat of a foreign exchange nightmare seen on Jan. 29, widely known as "Black Friday". 

 A massive wave of foreign loan expiries put enormous pressure on the real/dollar exchange rate then and the real tumbled to its worst level ever of 2.1 per dollar. 

 Market analysts estimated the Central Bank has now spent somewhere between $50 million and $100 million through Wednesday with the intervention. 

 Actual figures were expected to be reflected in the country's foreign currency reserves in the coming days. The Central Bank now reports on international reserves on a daily basis. 

 While the amount of the dollar sales was considered small, some economists sounded an alarm at Brazil's random intervention. 

 "It would have been wiser for the Central Bank to avoid an intervention at this point," said Charles Blitzer, chief international economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette in London. 

 Blitzer said any commitment by a Central Bank to defend a currency would slowly eat away at reserves and eventually raise doubt on whether the country would be able to withstand further speculative attacks in the markets. 

 Brazil's foreign reserves stood at $35.74 billion by Tuesday, down from $36.11 billion at the beginning of the month.

title: EMERGING MARKETS  FX  - E. Europe hit by econ fears.
text:
LONDON, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies were weaker in thin trade on Thursday as fears of an economic slowdown in the euro zone weighed on eastern Europe. 

Brazil was also a focus following two straight days of intervention in support of the real by Brazil's central bank. 

 By 1040 GMT, the Hungarian forint had sagged by nearly 1.0 percent and the Polish zloty was 0.70 percent weaker. 

 "Euroland growth is being revised downward and that is what is hurting the eastern European markets," said Mark Rall, emerging markets strategist at HypoVereinsbank Research in Munich. 

 "People are lowering expectations of export-driven growth out of eastern Europe." 

 Two German states reported disappointing consumer price data on Thursday and French business confidence figures fell. 

 This exacerbated fears over growing current account deficits in eastern Europe, analysts said. 

 Sentiment toward Hungary faces a test on Thursday at an auction of two-and five-year government bonds, Rall said. 

 Foreign investors are expected to remain sidelined and this could exacerbate falls in Hungarian debt. 

 Brazil's shaky real was at 2.02 against the dollar, unchanged from Wednesday's European close but up from its $2.05 Sao Paolo close. 

 Brazil reported rising consumer price inflation on Thursday, heightening concerns that capital will seek to exit the real. 

 The nomination of new Central Bank president Arminio Fraga is up for a confirmation vote by lawmakers on Friday, a test the market is keen to be past. 

 For the time being, investors are avoiding the real and seeking to anticipate the effects of any further falls on outlying currencies, according to Gerry Celaya of American Express Bank in London. 

 "Right now the peripheral markets are ignoring Brazil but if Brazil gets hit they will catch a sniffle," Celaya said. 

 The Mexican peso was up marginally from its Wednesday European close but the Venezeulan and Chilean currencies were unchanged. 

 Asian currencies were mixed, with falls in the Korean won and Singapore dollar but small gains in the Thai baht and Taiwan dollar. 

 Analysts said losses on Wall Street on Wednesday had set a bad tone for Asia. 

 Asian markers were sitting tight before a news confernece by Japanese Vice Finance Minister Eisuke Sakakibara scheduled for 1200 GMT, they said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Brazil forex interventions  risky.
text:
LONDON, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's second currency market intervention in two days could create a dangerous target level for speculators to attack, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 Brazil's central bank stepped in to sell dollars on Tuesday for the first time since the embattled real was floated just over a month ago, hauling the currency back to around 2.0 to the dollar after it slid to 2.07. 

 A second intervention on Wednesday held the real at a similar level after it slipped to 2.02, surprising some analysts who had seen the previous day's move as a one-off. 

 "I'm not very positive about it," said Jerome Booth, head of research at ANZ Investment Bank in London. "If there's any hint of big support it would be a red rag to a bull - you really will get people having a go at it." 

 Analysts say the real is not currently under serious assault after last month's tumble, but it is under consistent pressure as forex futures near their expiry date on Friday and Brazilian firms repay maturing foreign debts which cannot be rolled over. 

 The currency has slid around 40 percent against the dollar since mid-January, when Brazil adjusted and then abandoned a tight currency regime that had snuffed out hyperinflation. 

 The devaluation, which threatened to throw wider emerging markets into fresh turmoil, has revived inflation fears and forced up interest rates, deepening Brazil's recession. 

 Analysts said the intervention seemed to be aimed at ironing out sharp daily currency shifts in thin liquidity. 

 A central bank spokeswoman said on Wednesday the bank "may intervene when necessary and in a limited way to contain unruly movements in the foreign exchange rate." 

 Analysts said the central bank would want to avoid giving any sign that it was defending a set exchange rate, for fear of sparking the very speculative attack it sought to head off. 

 But the market could start reading an implicit defence level into the interventions, they added, raising the spectre of a renewed onslaught on the real. 

 "I still don't think they want to give the market the impression they're defending any particular level, although two interventions around this 2.0 level do seem to be trying to establish some sort of temporary psychological barrier," said Peter West, chief economist at BBV Securities in London. 

 "The danger of doing that is you set up a target for the markets to shoot down." 

 Analysts said the central bank was unlikely to mount a strong defence of the currency in such circumstances, as it would want to avoid haemorrhaging foreign reserves in an ultimately futile battle against the market. 

 Some analysts said Tuesday's move may already have sent the wrong signal. 

 "Unfortunately, the Central Bank seems to have drawn a line in the sand at around two to the dollar, which we think is quite dangerous," said Jake Moore, emerging markets strategist at Barclay's Capital in London. 

 But others said the intervention gamble could pay off provided some kind of good news came swiftly to soothe investors' nerves. 

 That could be in the shape of a revised agreement with the International Monetary Fund, or the confirmation of the central bank's president-in-waiting, Arminio Fraga. 

 The IMF said on Wednesday it hoped to finalise a post-devaluation deal this week that would allow payments to resume under a $41.5 billion rescue package drawn up last year. 

 The Senate's confirmation hearing for Fraga, a former aide to billionaire financier George Soros, has been set for Friday. ((London Newsroom +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, gill.tudor@reuters.com)).

title: "Smart money" restrictions possible in  Brazil .
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 9 (Reuter) - Brazil's central bank intervened in foreign exchange markets Wednesday to narrow opportunities for arbitrage that has drawn "smart money" and fueled rumors that measures may be adopted to restrict foreign capital inflows. 

 While central bank directors met Wednesday morning, the bank set three buy/sell tenders in the floating market to reduce the difference between the commercial and interbank floating rates. 

 In August, foreign inflows in foreign exchange contracts have so far totaled $2.7 billion, and in the last four days an estimated $800 million passed through Brazil's money markets in arbitrage operations, private Invest News agency reported. 

 Brazil's government voiced its concern over speculative capital during a state visit to Washington D.C. in April when Finance Minister Pedro Malan presented to President Clinton his ideas for an international safety net to cushion against financial shocks. 

 The smart money now gravitating to Brazil creates problems for maintaining equilibrium in the economy, analysts said. 

 A sudden surge in foreign capital inflows which began in July could cause officials to adopt restrictive measures and poses several challenges for the economy, analysts said. 

 These types of foreign capital inflows are commonly called smart money, and are typically volatile, responding to momentary speculative opportunities. 

 Foreign capital inflows boosted the balance of payments to a record surplus of $815.3 million on August 4, fueled by operations that allow investors to profit on the difference between the two central bank exchange rates. 

 "This influx of money increases the public debt of the government and creates a greater supply of credit in the national market," said Antonio Madeira, economic analyst at MCM consulting firm. 

 The government must issue debt paper to back up the hard currency that enters Brazil and is banked in the foreign reserves account, he said. 

 Smart money introduces instability into the reserves account, said Francisco Petros, executive director of Brasilpar. 

 "The reserves become very volatile because if you lower the interest rate you effectively lose reserves almost immediately," he said. 

 More broadly, smart money creates pressures that could disturb the trade balance and shake the Real Plan stabilization program, analysts said.  By expanding the supply of credit, the inflow of dollars "increases economic activity and could cause the trade deficit to grow," Madeira said. 

 "The inconsistency between interest rates (foreign and domestic) interferes with the logic of the Real Plan," Petros said. 

 Consequently, adopting measures for reducing the flow of smart money requires fine tuning.  Traders and economists speculated Wednesday about what measures might be adopted if the government decided to take action to restrict foreign capital inflows. 

 The measures most likely to be adopted are to lower interest rates, impose a capital gains-type tax and set a time limit on how long foreign capital must remain in the country, sources said. 

 Last October, when foreign reserves had swelled to $40.8 billion, the previous administration imposed a tax on foreign capital inflows, Eurobonds and fixed income instruments, said MCM's Madeira. 

 Any measure can create new problems, Petros said. A tax can drive speculative capital into other types of financial operations, and time limits on investments "must be accompanied by a change in the foreign exchange rate," he said.

title: Brazil exchange band move a devaluation - analysts.
text:
BRASILIA, June 23 (Reuter) - Brazil's surprise announcement it would alter its exchange rate band is a currency devaluation that came because of pressure from persistent trade deficits, financial analysts said. 

 The Central Bank announced late Thursday that it was lowering its exchange rate band to 0.91/0.99 reais to the dollar from the rate of 0.88/0.93 reais, in place since March 10. 

 As recently as Wednesday President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Brazil would not alter its exchange rate in the face of a trade deficit of $4.85 billion for last November to May. 

Central Bank External Affairs Director Gustavo Franco stressed the bank would not let the exchange rate change abruptly or reach the 0.99 ceiling soon. 

 "The rate will not be altered abruptly because the central bank will be intervening in the band system," he told reporters. 

Brazil has been haunted by the chance that deficits could lead to a Mexico-style financial collapse as deficits eat up reserves and lead foreign capital to flee the country, the analysts said. Loosening the rate bands means Brazil can make its currency less valuable and its exports less expensive, aiding its trade deficit. 

 "This is a victory for the people that have been advocating this since the Mexican crisis," said Richard Foster, editor of the Brazil Watch financial and political newsletter in Brasilia. 

 He said likely Central Bank attempts to portray the adjustment as a normal change due to inflation would not wash. 

 "The trade deficit has run out of control and it is not hard to connect the two things." 

 Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Federation of Coffee Exporters, called the announcement "a sensible move." 

 "I don't know if this was the amount we needed but it's a step in the right direction." 

 The analysts said the change would disappoint foreign investors looking for high returns from Brazilian securities. 

 "This does sort of remind you of what the Mexicans did right up until the bitter end, denying that they would devalue," said Denis Parisien, a Latin American specialist at the IDEA financial analysis firm in New York. 

 He said loosening the exchange rate was likely to fuel inflation. In part, the cheaper real would make imports more expensive, reducing competition against domestic producers and thus forcing prices higher. 

 "You don't want to do that (devalue) when inflation is rising because the high exchange rate is the main reason inflation is down."

title: Brazil Stocks Open Lower After Last Week's Turbulence
text:

There was more than $1.5 billion in capital flight last week after the government ordered a de facto devaluation of Brazil's currency, the real, on Monday. The Central Bank intervened in foreign exchange markets a record 32 times on Thursday, selling an estimated $3 billion to $4 billion, to support the real. 

 The rally came after the government issued a package of measures to stimulate foreign investment, brake the outflow of dollars and set a more realistic forex scheme. 

 Among those measures was mandating a limit of only $6 billion in dollars that banks can hold, or 10% of the previous level. That will force banks to sell off a lot of the dollars they bought last week at a loss. 

 A stock broker said that the requirement that the banks sell dollars will tighten liquidity this week, thus shrinking funds available for stock investments. 

 'The stock market remains extremely nervous,' the broker said. 'There are so many factors affecting the market that it's impossible to keep up with them all.' 

 He noted that high U.S. interest rates continue to attract investment capital that might otherwise flow into Brazil. As well, he added that uncertainty over the economy in Argentina keeps investors jittery. 

 'A lot of people got hurt last week,' he said. 'That keeps them nervous.'

title: Brazil 's real pares losses after bank  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, March 8 (Reuter) - Brazil's real bounced from the day's lows to close off 0.1 percent in the commercial foreign exchange market after the central bank sold dollars once to bolster the local currency, analysts said. 

 The real, which has dropped over 3.0 percent since Monday, ended at 0.887 real to dollar, remaining within the central bank's previously announced foreign exchange rate band of 0.86 and 0.90 real to greenback. 

 Analysts said, however, uncertainty over the government's new foreign exchange rate policy continued to send jitters to the market. 

 The uncertainty hinges on a central bank statement saying it could "periodically define" the band, which was interpreted by the market as an indication the band could change at any time. 

 "The market is missing an horizon," Antonio Madeira, an economics analyst at MCM consultants, told Reuters. "People are concerned about when the central bank will eventually change the current foreign exchange band." 

 Madeira said the only concrete indication for the real's value in the near future came from the forward dollar sale Tuesday, which will settle May 4 at 0.93 real to greenback. 

 The central bank reiterated that perception today by accepting bids for a new forward sale of dollars to be liquidated on May 5 at 0.93 real to greenback. The central bank, however, did not disclose the amount of dollars sold. 

 "The market is assuming that the real is expected to continue sliding to 0.93 real to dollar by early May. But the concern now is how the market will trade from today until then," Maderia said. "That's still not clear." 

 Market analysts also said they noticed export firms had slowed down their requests for cash advances against future exports, the so-called ACC operations. 

 They said exporters usually carry out that kind of operation to profit from Brazil's high domestic interest rates, which are currently at 35 percent a year. 

 "The problem now is that export firms are not sure on how the real/dollar rate will perform over the next few weeks. Without that information the risk of running ACC operations increases a lot," a foreign exchange trader said.

text:
BRASILIA (AP-DJ)--Finance Minister Pedro Malan, under pressure to allow Brazil's real to depreciate in line with inflation, said Thursday that he has no plans to change the country's foreign exchange policy. 

 Asked by legislators in the Senate Economic Affairs Committee why he is refusing to peg the real to inflation, Malan said 'that would signify failure of the real plan ... a return to the past.' 

 In spite of the Central Bank's frequent intervention to support the real in Brazil's foreign exchange markets, Malan insists that the government is not managing the currency. He emphasized again Thursday that 'the government won't administer foreign exchange markets.'

title: Brady Bonds End Dn But Off Intra-day Lows; EMBI Widens 2.03
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Mounting speculations that Venezuela is on the verge of devaluing its currency pushed Brady bonds sharply weaker Friday. 

 Market participants noted, however, that the emerging market debt recovered from their intra-day lows, lifted by rebounding U.S. stocks. 

 After falling more than 270 points, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 77 points weaker to 8533 points. 

 The 34% devaluation of the Russian ruble Monday triggered speculative attacks on the Venezuelan bolivar driving the market into a selling frenzy. 

 Venezuelan Pars fell 1/2 to 59 1/2 bid, and the DCBs lost 1 1/2 to 46 1/2 bid. 

 Venezuela's government official - although reiterating they had no intention of devaluing the bolivar - said Friday that they will allow more flexibility of the currency within the same band. The bolivar ended at VEB575.50 to the dollar from the VEB574.50 Thursday. 

 "It's been a tough week," a trader said. "And there's more to come," he added, referring to the disclosure of the terms of Russia's domestic debt restructuring plan expected Monday. 

 Russian Principals retreated 1/2 to 18 1/2 bid, while the Eurobonds due in 2007 lost 5 1/2 to 32 bid. 

 Russia's State Duma is scheduled to consider the government's package of austerity measures in an emergency session Tuesday. 

 Traders attributed the slump in emerging market debt also to speculations that Brazil's central bank intervened heavily throughout the day to prop the country's markets. 

 Brazil's C-bonds tumbled 5 7/8 to 55 1/8 bid, while Pars surrendered 5 points to 57 1/2 bid. Mexican Pars gave up 3 3/4 to 71 3/4 bid, and the UMSs 2026 lost 9 1/2 to 88 bid. 


The spread of the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index widened
about 203 basis points to 1280 basis points over U.S. Treasurys.

title: Brazil 's real ends flat amid reported  intervention .
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Brazil's real ended flat at 1.1740 to the dollar in the commercial foreign exchange market on Wednesday amid speculation a large state bank stepped in selling the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Dealers said Banco do Brasil intervened throughout the day on behalf of the Central Bank, selling dollars in a bid to prevent the real from weakening. 

Central Bank officials would not confirm the reports. Dealers have repeatedly spotted the intervention since last week amid Asia and Russia's economic troubles. 

 At 1700 local/2000 GMT, preliminary figures for commercial and financial forex contracts showed a $200 million deficit, indicating a net outflow of dollars. 

 On Tuesday, forex contracts showed a huge net dollar outflow of $963.83 million mainly because of repayment of maturing agricultural loans. 

 Tuesday's outflow was the largest daily outflow of the U.S. currency since Oct. 28, when the net dollar drain totalled $2.89 billion as Brazil was roiled by turmoil in Asian markets. 

 In the floating interbank rate market, the real dropped 0.04 to 1.1765 per dollar on Wednesday. In the parallel market, the real ended steady at 1.215 per dollar. 

 ((Carlos Sbarai, Sao Paulo newsroom, 55 11 248 5413)).

title: Brazil Forex :  Intervention  Weakens Real; Dealers See Outflow
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO (Dow Jones)--A Central Bank intervention weakened the Brazilian real (BRL) against the dollar Tuesday. 

 Traders estimated the session will post a net outflow of between $200 million and $300 million, but the dollar buying didn't affect prices much because Banco do Brasil was reportedly providing liquidity to banks that needed to buy the U.S. currency. Banco do Brasil denies playing that role. 

 Early in the day, the Central Bank intervened to adjust the mini-band in which the real and dollar trade. The new band values the dollar at BRL1.1670-1.1760, up 0.10 centavos from the previous BRL1.1660-1.1750. 

 In the spot market, the commercial dollar's buy rate also moved up 0.10 centavos from Monday's closing level. The dollar for 48-hour delivery closed with a buy rate of BRL1.1739 and a sell rate of BRL1.1740. 

 The real continues to be under pressure as loans made under Central Bank's Rule 63 mature. Analysts estimate that 35% to 40% of those loans, which peaked in March, are being rolled over in August. The redemption of the remaining bonds is putting pressure on the real. 

 As reported, Central Bank President Gustavo Franco said Tuesday that the country might see more redemptions than originally expected as investors redeem maturing loans to buy Brazilian Brady bonds. 

 Brazilian Bradys, which trade in sympathy with Russian Principals, have taken a whack in recent sessions because of Russia's acute economic crisis. 

 Late in New York, Brazil's C-bonds gained 1 3/4 to 267 1/4  bid, while EIs climbed 1 1/4 to 77 bid. 

 In Brazil's money market, the average interbank rate, or CDI, slipped to 2.08% from 2.09% Monday.

bills are indexed, was close to zero.

title: FOCUS - Brazil economy seen weathering Russian woes.
text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Brazil's emerging economy is likely to keep steaming along and suffer no more than a ripple of spillover from Russia's effective currency devaluation and partial debt moratorium, officials and economists said on Monday. 

 After Russia widened its rouble trading band and imposed a 90-day halt to some debt repayments early Monday, Brazil's equity and bond markets stumbled - though the setbacks were relatively mild - while its currency, the real, seemed to be holding its own. 

 To be sure, traders were a bit jumpy after the news from Moscow, but Brazilian officials rushed to reassure the local financial markets that Russia's crisis would have minimum impact on Latin America's largest economy. 

 Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said the moves that Russia took on Monday to strengthen its fragile financial system would not hurt his country. 

 "There is no reason for this to have any effect on Brazil," Malan said at a banking conference. 

 He went even further to suggest that Brazil could continue its policy of gradually reducing interest rates despite renewed concern about the health of emerging markets worldwide. 

 "I hope that this trajectory of declining (rates) continues," Malan said at the conference in Porto Alegre, capital of the southern Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul. 

 Brazil's Central Bank nearly doubled interest rates late last year, jacking them up to 43 percent to protect the real from speculative attack after the financial crisis in Asia escalated in October. Since then, it has brought them back down to an annual 19.75 percent. 

 Malan said the economy was in a better position now than last October to withstand global market pressures, noting that foreign direct investment would climb this year to $21 billion from $17 billion in 1997. 

 Economists were generally in agreement with this official line, saying Brazil's external accounts were in very good shape compared with Russia's. 

 "Brazil is in a completely different situation than Russia," Marcelo Serfaty, economist and head of the equity group at Brazilian bank Pactual, said. 

 "There are no big sell-offs or any crisis. There is a very limited volume of orders with everybody waiting to see what happens. Of course the level of risk in emerging markets has increased, but that's a question of price not of viability." 

 He said there was an adjustment in the currency market after the Russian news but saw no major pressure and no reason to raise interest rates. 

 Brazil's Bovespa index of leading shares dropped more than 2 percent Monday to 8546 points at 1630 GMT, but traders said the index ought to stabilise. 

 At the same time, Brazil's "C" bonds were down 4 points at 65.50 percent, and the real was holding steady near 1.1730 to the dollar, after rumours of indirect Central Bank intervention helped relieve some initial pressure. 

 Economists said Brazil would stay in line with other emerging markets because of the high liquidity of its assets, rather than any underlying flaw in the economy. 

 Brazil was also helped by a stable political situation in which President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, the father of a inflation-slashing plan that turned the economy around in recent years, was expected to have no difficulty winning re-election on Oct. 4. 

 An massive privatisation programme was another factor fuelling the economy, economists said. 

 "The money flowing out is offset by privatisation money," Serfaty said. "There is no major pressure in the short term, but there needs to be a cut in taxes on fixed-income investments to reduce interest rates further." 

 Malan said sharp declines in the prices of dollar-denominated Brazilian Brady and Eurobonds over the past two weeks in New York and London had not reflected a negative outlook on Brazil. Rather investors had sold off Brazilian fixed-income assets because they were the most easily traded emerging market securities, he said. 

 "It's obvious that since we live in a global era, there will be some effects in the debt market. But those who need liquidity will sell off their Brazilian debt because ours are the most liquid securities," Malan said. 

 "There is nothing to sustain the idea that this is a reflection on Brazil's economy." ((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom +55 21 507 4151, fax ext 2120, tracey.ober@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS - Brazil stocks hit 9-mo. low,  currency  steady.
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Brazilian markets were rocked on Tuesday after more unfavourable economic news from abroad, with stocks plunging to a nine-month low and the currency stumbling, then regaining its feet amid reports of intervention by the central bank. 

 The blue-chip Bovespa index tumbled 4.14 percent after more overnight market instability in Russia and Japan. The slide marked the Brazilian index's eighth consecutive day in negative territory and extended its losses for the year to more than 13 percent. 

 The Brazilian currency, the real, held up despite morning nervousness. Brokers speculated that the Central Bank intervened by indirectly selling dollars to offset any perception that Brazil was facing mounting pressure to devaluate its currency. 

 Brazil's real is closely watched in times of market upheaval, as the country shares some of the traits of the Southeast Asian countries that were forced to devalue last fall: huge fiscal deficits, a trade gap and a closely regimented currency. 

 A sharp devaluation could likely trigger a regional crisis that would dwarf the meltdown of the Mexican peso in 1994. 

 On Tuesday morning, the tightly controlled Brazilian real jerked lower against the dollar in spot and futures trade, but it bounced back before lunch. 

 Officials pointed to the currency's stability as a sign that pressure from abroad would be limited to the stock market. 

 "For the time being, this is an equities phenomenon. It has not had any affect on the currency, which is what is most important," a Finance Ministry spokesman said. 

 Still, dollar traders attributed the real's strong rebound to heavy dollar-selling by federally-owned Banco do Brasil on behalf of the Central Bank. 

 The real is widely regarded to be overvalued by between 10 percent and 30 percent. Economists say Brazil may not be able to resist devaluation should China take that option in response to an ever-weakening Japanese yen. 

 The Brazilian real opened 0.16 percent weaker at 1.1708 reais per dollar from 1.1689 at Monday's close. But it strengthened to 1.1688 reais by the market's close. 

 "The market opened very nervous, but it is a lot calmer now. There are rumours Banco do Brasil was selling dollars for the Central Bank, which they have done in the past," said a forex trader at an international bank. 

 The speculation was backed by the fact that there was a net outflow of dollars from Brazil on Tuesday, a phenomenon that usually weakens the real. 

 Traders said Banco do Brasil may have sold up to $300 million Tuesday to bolster the real. By comparison, the Central Bank sold between $8 billion and $10 billion to support the real during one week last October and November at the height of the Asian crisis. 

 Brazil, in contrast with many emerging nations, has a huge foreign reserve war chest of around $70 billion, and thus is better able to defend its currency. 

 The Central Bank would not comment on the Banco do Brasil selling rumours or the declining stock market. "If anyone says anything, it will be at the end of day," a Central Bank spokesman said in Brasilia. 

 ((Shasta Darlington, Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511-248-5408, shasta.darlington@reuters.com)).
