title: Brazil 's real ends up on  intervention  - dealers.
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Brazil's real closed up 0.01 percent Tuesday at 1.1688 per dollar in the commercial foreign exchange market, supported by reported heavy dollar selling by a federal bank, dealers said. 

 Brazilian forex markets came under intense pressure Tuesday from financial turmoil in Japan and Russia, but the local currency stabilised on what dealers attributed to dollar selling by Banco do Brasil on behalf of the Central Bank. 

 "The real held steady because Banco do Brasil was selling a lot of dollars for the Central Bank," said one dealer. 

 Neither bank would comment on reports of the intervention, which dealers said may have amounted to $300 million. 

 The real held up despite moderate dollar outflows. At 1700 local/2000 GMT, preliminary figures for commercial and financial forex contacts showed a $156 million deficit. 

 In the floating interbank rate market, the real ended steady at 1.1745 per dollar. In the parallel market, the real also closed flat at 1.220 per dollar.

title: France's BNP opens subsidiary in Brazil.
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 11 (Reuters) - France's Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) on Tuesday inaugurated a fully-owned Brazilian subsidiary in a move that completes its network in the Latin American region, the bank's Chairman said. 

 "By setting up this bank in Brazil, BNP will complete its presence in Latin America," Michel Pebereau told a news conference, noting that BNP is already present in Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Mexico, Panama, Costa Rica and the Cayman Islands. 

 Though officially inaugurated Tuesday, the BNP subsidiary has been operating since May 1997, less than six months after the French bank was authorized by the Brazilian authorities to start business in the country. 

 BNP, which has been present in Brazil for the last 40 years through a representative office, began its investments by absorbing private bank Banco Comercial de Sao Paulo which was under Central Bank intervention. 

 With initial capital of $60 million, the BNP Brazil unit aims to offer all types of services provided by commercial and investment banks, including trade financing, treasury and foreign exchange products, focusing on institutional and corporate clients, Pebereau said. 

 He also said that over the next few weeks the bank plans to begin offering asset management services, which will allow it to also include individual clients in its portfolio. 

 BNP currently manages over $50 billion in investment funds worldwide. 

 Despite current worries about the Brazilian economy, Pebereau said the bank is optimistic about investing in the country and praised the steps taken by the government to face the difficulties following recent global financial turmoil. 

 "The Brazilian response by accelerating the fiscal adjustment shows the country is adapting itself to face the market turbulence," he said. 

 On Monday, the government unveiled a package of 51 tough fiscal measures designed to guarantee its defenses against global financial instability. 

 "As long as the government is taking the necessary measures, I don't see reason why the turbulence should last longer," Pebereau added. 

 BNP has been given the right to open 10 branches in Brazil. Its second office - the bank is headquarted in Sao Paulo - was likely to be open in Rio de Janeiro in the beginning of next year.

title: Brazil 's real weak despite  interventions .
text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 7 (Reuters) - A series of Central Bank interventions Friday failed to take pressure off the Brazilian real amid strong dollar demand due to next week's U.S. holiday and worries over weak global stock markets, dealers said. 

 "The market is very nervous. Even after the auctions, there is still strong dollar demand," said one trader. 

 The Central Bank held three dollar sell auctions in the commercial and floating exchange rate markets before lunch to bring the real back into the real-dollar mini-band of 1.1035-1.1085 reais per dollar. 

 The real was trading at 1.1086 reais per dollar prior to the auctions, when the bank sold dollars at 1.1085 reais. 

 While the interventions pushed the real back into the mini-band, the local currency was still trading at the ceiling of the band, indicating weakness, traders said. 

 When the forex market closed for lunch at 1300 local time/1500 GMT/1000 EST, the real was trading at 1.1085 reais per dollar, off 0.09 percent over the open of 1.1075 reais. 

 Dealers said that amid the nervousness, Friday's scheduled auction of Central Bank dollar-indexed NBC-E bonds in the afternoon might not calm markets as much as it normally does. 

 Auctions of the NBC-E bonds usually soothe the market because they signal that the government is not worried about taking on more dollar-indexed debt, something it would not do if it were mulling devaluation. 

 Dollar demand grew Friday in the spot market ahead of the U.S. Veteran's Day holiday next Tuesday, which encouraged banks to buy dollars, dealers said. 

 The market was also nervous over falls on global stock exchanges, which shoved Brazil's stock market down around nine percent at the open. The bolsa later retreated from its worst levels to trade off around seven percent. 

 Last week, the Central Bank was forced to jack up interest rates to an annualized 43 percent from about 20 percent after a week of forex market interventions failed to prop up the real. 

 The rate hike gave solid support to the real this week through Thursday, when dollar outflows to pay Eurobond commitments pressured the local currency. 

 The Central Bank uses the real-dollar mini-band to allow the real to trade within a controlled range against the dollar. 

 Over the past two years, it has devalued the band slightly about five times a month to arrive at a nominal seven or eight percent depreciation of the real over the year.

title: REPEAT:WSJ: Leveraged Players Spark Brazil Markets
text:
From Friday's Wall Street Journal 

 By Thomas T. Vogel, Jr. 

 NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The unabated turmoil in Brazilian financial markets is a lesson in how Latin America's slickest financiers became victims of their own excess. 

 The Sao Paulo stock exchange plunged 9.8% Thursday while the central bank intervened in the currency market for the third time this week as big losses by some highly leveraged bond players sparked a chain reaction across the country's financial markets. 

 Thursday, Brazil's central bank intervened at least two times to support the value of the real, which has come under pressure in the wake of the Asian currency crisis. A plunge in Hong Kong's stock exchange last week and fears of a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar, once considered one of the globe's strongest currencies, sparked a world-wide markets sell-off which continues to plague Latin America. The pressure has been most acute on Brazil, the region's biggest economy. 

 Local Brazilian dealers say the government may have spent as much as $2 billion Thursday to keep the real from slipping out of its crawling devaluation band pegged at 0.6% a month. This comes after it had reportedly shelled out as much as $5 billion on Tuesday and hundreds of millions more on Monday to support the currency. At the end of September, Brazil's foreign reserves stood at $61 billion. 

 The central bank called an emergency meeting of its monetary policy committee late Thursday and decided to sharply raise key short-term interest rates. Brazil's monthly prime rate, for example, was raised to 3.05% from 1.58%. Higher rates could help ease pressure on the real by making investments in the currency more attractive and making it more expensive to speculate. But it could also increase strains on the banking system. 

 "They feel that the real is under serious attack and they're hiking interest rates very sharply. I still wouldn't call them desperate at this stage, but clearly these are drastic measures which, if left in place for long, would create serious concerns over the impact on the financial sector," said Jene Frieda, senior Latin America economist at think tank IDEA Inc. 

 The central bank also offered to buy back several hundred million in short-term Brazilian notes denominated in reals several months before their maturity dates, a move designed to support the real. 

 As with many central banks, Brazil's top bank doesn't give out information on its market interventions. But local dealers can estimate how much the bank spent through informal surveys of a group of 60 financial institutions the government uses to buy or sell foreign currency. 

 Fallout from the Asian crisis has been more acute in Brazil than in any other Latin nation partly because of what many considered an overvalued currency and partly because of the aggressiveness of Brazilian financial players. Brazil has long had a reputution for having the most agile markets in the world, a legacy of the past three decades when rampant inflation forced traders to move very quickly to stay one step ahead. 

 "Brazil is a much more sophisticated investment-banking market than anywhere else in Latin America," said Igor Cornelsen, a merchant banker in Sao Paulo. "There are a lot of sophisticated banks and as a consequence, a lot of leveraged funds," he explained. "So when the big crisis came and there were margin calls, some funds . . . lost 50 to 60%."

title: Merrill Lynch's Latin American Strategists Are Bullish On Brazil
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Merrill Lynch & Co.'s Latin American strategists Friday said the troubled Brazilian stock market is the investment bank's top pick for the next three months despite the recent sell-off. 

 Strategists Ed Cabrera, Renato Grandmont and Robert Berges in a report said the Brazilian central bank's recent decision to double interest rates is likely to attract foreign capital inflows and help unwind speculative dollar positions, which would further build foreign reserves. 

 "Given the sharp sell-off and the negative expectations for Brazil, we are encouraged by the proactive policy actions and the strong political will of the (President Fernando Henrique) Cardoso administration to protect the real," Brazil's currency, they said. 

 The central bank raised two key interest rates late Thursday to stem speculative attacks on the the real. Its Basic Rate (TBC), or prime rate, was raised to 3.05% from 1.58% and its Assistance Rate, at which money is lent to banks, was raised to 3.23%, from 1.76%. 

 Reaction among market watchers was divided. While some expected the rate increase to calm the fears of foreign investors, others focused on the possibility that the higher rates could lead to a recession. 

 Indeed, Merrill Lynch cautioned that certain risks remain in the Brazilian market, including the possibility that high interest rates won't reduce capital outflows or that they will lead to bankruptcies in the banking industry. 

 "However, expected government action should reduce the risks," they said. "We do not expect a devaluation to occur." 

 Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said in a radio interview Friday that the elevated interest rates would only be in place until the market turmoil subsides. 

 The Merrill Lynch analysts noted that Brazil's central bank has intervened heavily in the foreign-exchange market to protect the ceiling of the real's exchange-rate band and it's estimated that international reserves declined by nearly $5 billion, from $62 billion, Merrill Lynch said. 

 While high interest rates will encourage foreign flows into debt markets and away from equities, the strategists contend the equity market is "equally attractive." Brazilian stocks, they said, could rally 45% in several weeks if the risk of devaluation is removed. 

 Brazil's stock market rose 1.5% Friday after plunging 9.8% Thursday. The benchmark Bovespa index for the Sao Paulo exchange - South America's largest market - has fallen a total of 22% in the last week. 

 For Brazil, the strategists recommend badly depressed, highly liquid, public sector stocks undergoing privatizations such as Telecomunicacoes Brasileiras SA (TBR) and Cemig (CEMGY). These stocks, they said, are attractively priced. 

 Meanwhile, the Merrill analysts reduced their recommended exposure to the smaller and outperforming markets of Chile and Colombia, while adding weight to Mexico. 

 Mexico's stocks and the peso are likely to rally once the currency turmoil in Brazil stabilizes, the strategists said. Top stock picks in Mexico include consumer-related companies such as retail giant Grupo Cifra SA (CFRAY), Coca-Cola Femsa (KOF) and Telefonos de Mexico (TMX). 

 "Mexico remains a fundamentally solid story," they said. 

 Merrill Lynch also is "overweight" - temporarily exceeding its normal investment allocations - in Argentina. Its favored stocks there include Telefonica de Argentina (TAR) and YPF SA (YPF).

title: Brazil spent $4-$5 bln to defend real - gov't aide.
text:
BRASILIA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Brazil's central bank has spent between $4 billion and $5 billion of its foreign currency reserves defending the real currency amid market turmoil this week, presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral said Thursday. 

 "It has used between four and five billion dollars to withstand speculation against the real," Amaral told reporters during a daily briefing. "Reserves are there to be used when necessary." 

 "The president has total confidence in the measures that the economic team has taken to meet the speculation," the spokesman said. "What the central bank did was correct. The Central Bank is prepared to take whatever measures necessary." 

 Amaral also said Brazil's trade deficit in October, excluding Friday, the last day of the month, was $760 million and "less than expected." 

 A latest Reuters survey of analysts forecast a trade deficit of about $1.24 billion in October. 

 Concerns over Brazil's trade gap and its currrent account deficit have contributed to questions about the country's ability to maintain the strength of its currency. 

 Amaral said other indicators showed the Brazilian economy was "growing stronger by the day" and that the recent slump in local stocks was part of a wider, international problem. 

 The Bovespa index  .BVSP index of 51 leading shares fell 9.81 percent on Thursday, bringing its decline since last Friday to 23.3 percent. 

Brazil's central bank intervened four times in the foreign exchange markets Thursday to prop up the real. It also intervened seven times on Tuesday. 

 Before this week's pressure, Brazil's foreign currency reserves stood at about $62 billion.

title: Brazil Cardoso Praises Nat Bank, Econ Team For Calming Mkt
text:
BRASILIA (AP-Dow Jones)--Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Wednesday lauded the Central Bank and the government's economic team for taking the proper measures to tranquilize markets and stop a run on the currency, the real. 

 'Brazil has a very strong line of defense,' Cardoso told reporters outside the presidential palace in his first public comments on the market turmoil that hit stocks and the real Monday and Tuesday. 

 'We have succeeded with tranquility in overcoming the difficult moment we went through yesterday, not only Brazil but the entire world,' Cardoso added. 

 The Central Bank intervened eight times in the currency market Tuesday to keep the real within a pre-set band. Stock market regulators changed the trading hours to coincide with New York and introduced a circuit-breaker system. 

 Cardoso is the father of the 1994 economic stability program, the Real Plan, which has brought annual inflation down from 2700% in 1994 to an estimated 7% for 1997. 

 'The strength of our economy was proved once again yesterday (Tuesday),' said Cardoso.

SAO PAULO (AP-Dow Jones)--Brazil's real weakened slightly Friday, closing at 1.09655 to the dollar on a calm trading day with no Central Bank interventions, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the buy rate at close was 1.0965 reals per dollar and the sell rate was 1.0966 reals for a midpoint of 1.09655, a slight rise over Thursday's 1.0964 mark. 

 'It was a relatively quiet day, with the dollar quote reaching 1.0968 early and slowly falling until close,' said one Rio de Janeiro broker. 

Brazil's Central Bank last intervened Tuesday to weaken the real against the dollar by adjusting the mini-band in which the currency trades. 

 The new band values the dollar at 1.0960-1.1010 reals, up 0.05 of a centavo from the previous levels of 1.0955-1.1005 reals, set last Friday. The Central Bank now buys dollars at 1.0960 reals per dollar and sells dollars at 1.1010 reals. 

 The change was made by shifting the mini band at which the real and dollar trade within the 1.05-1.14 reals per dollar wide band. 

 On April 23, the Central Bank forecast the real would be devalued by a total of around 7% during 1997.

title: Latin America Stocks/Amplifier -2: Brazil Stand Praised
text:
'There hasn't been any substantial change in Brazil's macroeconomic situation,' said Sidney Chameh, head of research at Sao Paulo investment bank Banco Fator. 'We see no risk of an exchange devaluation.' 

 Around 2020 GMT, the real was steady, trading at 1.0806 to the dollar on a day with no Central Bank interventions, dealers said. 

 Despite talk that Brazil can resort to tighter monetary policy to defend the real, Chameh said he expects to see a slight fall in interest rates in the second half of the year to reflect 'a significant fall in inflation,' now at an annualized 9%. 

 Mauro Schneider, ING Barings' senior economist for Brazil, said the possibility of a speculative attack on the real is quite low, although the currency's present overvaluation makes it vulnerable to devaluation. 

 But he said that if the government decides to devalue the real, it would not do so before national elections in 1998. 

 Fabio Fukuda, analyst at Trend Analise Economica in Sao Paulo, said recent comments about changes in exchange policy, interest rates and current-account financing problems were used for speculative purposes. He praised the government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso for reacting firmly to the speculation. 

 'The monetary authorities acted in an agile manner Tuesday by warning that there wouldn't be alterations in the exchange policy,' Fukuda said. 'That calmed the market.' 

 Some Brazilian investors are shell-shocked by Tuesday's fall, analysts said, and are likely to remain skittish for the rest of the week. 

 'The domestic funds were very much scared by the fall in the market,' said Fator's Chameh. 

 Fukuda noted that the hefty profit-taking 'breaks the bubble of super-optimistic expectations and brings us back to more realistic levels.' 

 In Argentina, the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange spent Wednesday's session following the recovering Brazilian markets, analysts said. 

 'The movements (Tuesday) and today were just because of Brazil,' said economist Raul Buonuome of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Buenos Aires. 

 After diving 3.4% on Tuesday, the blue-chip Merval Index recovered to close at 826.37, up 2.2%, in heavy trading.

title: Brazil C.Bank may operate in dlr futures mkts - paper.
text:
SAO PAULO, Feb 26 (Reuter) - Brazil's Central Bank may operate in the dollar futures markets by offering options and futures contracts to its dealers, Gazeta Mercantil financial newspaper said. 

 The move would be aimed at minimizing the impact of speculative movements in the dollar futures markets on the day-to-day foreign exchange and monetary policies, the newspaper said. 

 Gazeta said the Central Bank's studies are based on the Mexican dollar options system. 

 Currently Brazil's Central Bank only intervenes in the commercial and floating foreign exchange markets by selling and buying dollars. When it aims to reduce volatility in the dollar futures markets, the bank usually offers dollar-indexed papers.

title: Unibanco sees Nacional branches integrated in Feb.
text:
SAO PAULO, Aug 13 (Reuter) - Brazilian private bank Unibanco expects to complete the process of fully integrating the 568 branch outlets belonging to failed Banco Nacional to its own network by February 1997, a top bank executive said. 

 "We have already fully integrated 60 branches and we plan to integrate 88 more in August, some 80 in September and finalize the process early February next year," Adalberto de Moraes Schettert, Unibanco's vice-president, told reporters on Tuesday. 

 In November 1995, Unibanco took over selected assets and liabilities of Banco Nacional, which was among Brazil's top 10 banks, after the central bank intervened the bank. 

 Schettert said so far Unibanco has unified the automatic teller machines system, bank cards, Treasury and foreign exchange operations. 

 He also said Unibanco had set aside some 160-165 million reais, of which 40 percent has already been spent, to cover expenses with the acquisition of the healthy portion of Nacional. 

 He expects the remaining 60 percent will be enough to complete the process of uniting the two banks' operations. 

 Unibanco, Brazil's third-largest private bank, announced late Monday a 126.9 million real net profit for the first six months of the year, an increase of 83.3 percent when compared with the same period of 1995. 

 The bank showed a 12.77 percent return on assets in the first half, with a net worth of 2.048 billion reais and total assets of 23.4 billion reais, Unibanco said in a statement. 

 Unibanco said the bank's dividends totalled 42.2 million reais, which is equivalent to 35 percent of its net profit.

title: Brazil's real tumbles 0.48 pct on Argentine rumor.
text:
SAO PAULO, July 31 (Reuter) - Brazil's real tumbled 0.48 percent, closing at 1.0150 per dollar in the commercial forex market, in nervous trade following a rumor that Argentina would end its peso/dollar parity, dealers said. 

 Traders here speculated the rumor was fueled by players hoping to profit by a market stir ahead of today's expiry of interest rate and dollar future contracts. 

 The foreign exchange market remained jittery even though newly named Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez denied he was considering altering the parity. 

 "A denial like this is worth nothing," a dealer said, noting that former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo was sacked last Friday just a few hours after Argentine officials had denied his resignation. 

Brazil's Central Bank moved to calm the market by intervening five times in the floating foreign exchange market, dealers said. 

 The real closed up 0.19 percent at 1.0120 to the dollar in the floating market. 

 Despite the Central Bank's interventions, traders expect nervousness to continue at Thursday's open. 

 "To calm down the (forex) market, the Central Bank should intervene in the commercial market," another dealer said. 

 The rumor led Brazil's futures foreign exchange market to trade 696,640 contracts, an increase of 76 percent over Tuesday's volume. 

 September dollar contracts closed at 1,025 points, up 0.67 percent, while October contracts rose 0.8 percent, ending at 1,0335 points. 

 In the illegal parallel market, the real closed steady at 1.034 per dollar.

title: Brazil February Foreign Reserves $55.5 Bln: Report
text:
BRASILIA (AP-Dow Jones)--Brazil's foreign reserves stood at a record $55.5 billion at the end of February, up 3.7% from $53.5 billion at the end of January, Gazeta Mercantil reported Wednesday. 

 AP-Dow Jones was unable to confirm the newspaper's report with the Central Bank, which hasn't yet released official figures for the month. 

Brazil's reserves are growing through the policy of intervention in currency markets. The Central Bank buys incoming dollars to regulate foreign exchange values.

text:

 'So the Central Bank called an auction. It showed that it wants the market to remain calm, that it doesn't want panic,' the trader added. 

 'Some banks thought that they could make the real reach 1-1 earlier than previously believed. But they were wrong,' the trader noted. 

 The Central Bank called three 'spread auctions,' which are used to establish the forex commercial rate, Wednesday morning. It also sold dollars on the commercial market for 98.3 centavos, the same as Tuesday's rate.

title: U.S. Dollar Flat At 97.2 Centavos On Brazil  Forex  Market
text:
SAO PAULO (AP-DJ)--The U.S. dollar was flat Thursday at 97.2 centavos on Brazil's commercial foreign exchange market, with one Central Bankintervention. 

 At closing, foreign exchange dealers were quoting the dollar at a buy rate of 97.21 centavos and a sell rate of 97.20 centavos at the commercial rate, virtually the same as on Wednesday. 

 The Central Bank sold dollars on the floating exchange to push the U.S. currency down on that market. The floating rate is used for personal remittances, while the commercial rate is for foreign trade and investment. The Central Bank usually intervenes to force down the floating rate whenever it surpasses the commercial rate. 

 On June 22, the Central Bank announced a new exchange rate band for the dollar of 91-99 centavos, from a previous range of 88-93 centavos. The move is seen as allowing the real to continue its gradual devaluation against the dollar. At the end of 1994, the dollar was trading at around 85 centavos on Brazil's commercial forex market. 

 Since then, several mini-devaluations of the real have nudged the dollar upward in small increments.
